## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared from the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; embellished with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each Father on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the texts of each individual book of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they did so.

An edition more accurate than all others and easily preferable to them, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price; above all, this collection is a single, methodical, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but brought together for the first time in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# In the Year of the Lord 600: Saint Eutropius, Abbot and Bishop

## [Col. 0009] Historical Notice on Eutropius

*(Antonio, Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus, vol. I, p. 283, no. 44.)*

Eutropius follows Licinianus and Severus, already praised, and was their contemporary. Isidore describes him as follows (chapter 32):

> Eutropius, bishop of the Church of Valencia, while he was still living in the Servitan monastery and was father of the monks, wrote to Bishop Licinianus, whom we mentioned above, a very useful letter in which he asked him why the anointing of baptized infants with chrism is administered. We have spoken of this letter under Licinianus.

Isidore adds:

> He also wrote to Peter, bishop of Irtabica [Ercavica should be read], a letter composed in a salutary style concerning the strict discipline of monks and extremely necessary for monks.

**[Note: [Col. 0009B–0010C]]** I had long known that among the codices of the Vatican Library, formerly belonging to the most serene Christina, Queen of Sweden, under number 140, there existed this letter of Eutropius to Peter of Ercavica. Like our editor, as its silence at this point indicates, I had considered it entirely unpublished. On that account I wrote to the most distinguished royal counsellor and, in the king’s name, general administrator of Spanish affairs in Rome, Don Nicolás Azara, whose benevolence I had experienced on several other occasions, asking him to arrange for a copy to be made for me, unless the letter should prove to be of extraordinary length.

That most humane man, and one most devoted to letters and to the honor of his country, immediately granted my request and laid it before the Most Eminent Lord, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church Francisco Xavier Zelada, librarian of the Apostolic See and formerly an outstanding patron of my studies. Without delay, he ordered a copy of the letter to be taken from the Vatican codex I have mentioned, collated with the original, and entrusted to Don Azara for speedy transmission to me, so that within two months I might be fully granted the fulfillment of my long-desired wish.

For so distinguished and never-to-be-forgotten a benefit, I have nothing with which to repay my thanks, unless it be to proclaim everywhere and dedicate to posterity the benevolent disposition of both men toward letters and their cultivators—a disposition worthy of men so highly distinguished both by the very great honors with which they are adorned and, above all, by their outstanding services to the Christian and Spanish commonwealth. This I gladly do.

Nevertheless, Lucas Holstenius had published it long ago, and well before our time, in *Codex regularum monasticarum*, Paris, 1633, in the appendix, p. 82.

John of Biclaro, in his *Chronicle* (in the third year of Maurice), says:

> Eutropius, abbot of the Servitan monastery and disciple of Saint Donatus, is held in high renown.

Likewise, when reporting the acts of the Third Council of Toledo under Reccared, king of the Goths, and the condemnation of Arian impiety there, he says:

> Yet the chief responsibility for the synodal business rested with Saint Leander, bishop of the Church of Seville, and the most blessed Eutropius, abbot of the Servitan monastery.

What could have been said more illustriously or more honorably of Eutropius? He must have enjoyed the highest authority among the entire people, and must have flourished by reason of learning and holiness, since, although he was merely the abbot of a certain monastery, he was regarded as equal, among all the bishops of Spain, to Leander, metropolitan of the Church of Seville, a man of the greatest learning and holiness and the king’s uncle. Eutropius governed the chief affairs with him as his counsellor and prescribed the method and plan for the complete expulsion of the most pestilential sect from the borders of Spain.

The title “most blessed,” like the title “saint,” is scarcely ever seen bestowed on the living except on bishops, and hardly on anyone else. At this Third Council, Reccared calls the bishops who took part in it “most blessed priests.” When the title is applied to Eutropius outside that group, at a time when Saint Leander is merely called “saint,” it clearly contains an exceptional mark of distinction.

## [Col. 0009] Letter of Saint Eutropius, Abbot and Bishop, to Pope Peter: On the Eight Vices

*(From the Library of the Fathers, vol. VIII.)* (C)

### [Col. 0009D]

There are eight principal vices that afflict the human race. The first is *gastrimargia*, which means gluttony of the belly; the second is fornication; the third is *philargyria*, that is, avarice or love of money; the fourth is anger; the fifth is sadness; the sixth is *acedia*, that is, anxiety or weariness of heart; the seventh is *cenodoxia*, that is, vainglory or empty praise; the eighth is pride.

Although these eight vices have different origins and difficult effects, the first six—gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, and acedia—are nevertheless linked by a certain kinship and, so to speak, chain of connection, so that the excess of one becomes the beginning of the next.

For from an abundance of gluttony fornication must spring; from fornication, avarice; from avarice, anger; from anger, sadness; and from sadness, acedia. Therefore we must fight against them in a similar manner and according to the same order, and we ought always to begin our struggle against the preceding vice in opposition to the following one.

Accordingly, in order to conquer acedia, sadness must be overcome; to drive away sadness, anger must be extinguished; to extinguish anger, avarice must be trampled down; to overthrow avarice, fornication must be restrained; and to destroy fornication, the vice of gluttony must be chastised.

The remaining two, cenodoxia and pride, are likewise joined to each other by the same principle that we have described concerning the preceding vices, so that the growth of the former produces the origin of the latter. Excessive vainglory gives birth to the fuel of pride. Once those six have been torn out, these two bear fruit more violently; and when the others have died, these grow and increase more vigorously. Thus we are attacked by these two in a different manner.

We fall into each of those six vices when we have been defeated by their predecessors. In the case of these two, however, we are endangered even after victory, after our triumphs.

Moreover, the eight vices we have mentioned are divided into four unions or pairings. Gluttony and fornication are joined in a particular partnership; in the same way, avarice is joined with anger. Sadness and acedia are likewise linked in the same union. Cenodoxia and pride are also intimately joined to each other. You have heard their pairings; now hear the kinds of vices.

There are three kinds of gluttony. The first is the impulse that urges a Christian to eat before the appointed hour. Jonathan, son of Saul, sinned in this way when he violated his father’s oath; consequently, the people did not deserve to gain victory over their enemies. The second arises from excess in any kind of food or drink. In this the people of Israel sinned when they made the golden calf, as it is written (Exodus 32): “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” The third is the desire for the most carefully prepared and exquisite foods. The sons of Eli sinned in this way: they refused to accept cooked meat from the people, but wanted it raw so that they might prepare it more carefully for themselves (1 Samuel 2).

From these three kinds, different and very evil diseases of the soul are produced. From the first arise anger against the one who ought to have prepared the food; from the second, the goads of luxury and lust; while the third knots the inextricable chains of avarice around the necks of captives.

There are three kinds of fornication. The first is thought, of which the Lord says in the Gospel (Matthew 5): “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her,” and so forth. The second is completed through the sexual union of the two sexes. The third occurs without touching a woman and is called “uncleanness” by the Apostle (Galatians 4). We must guard against all three with equal vigilance, lest any one of them deter us from and exclude us from the kingdom of Christ.

There are three kinds of avarice. The first does not allow a person to be stripped of surplus possessions; Ananias and Sapphira sinned in this way (Acts 5). The second persuades us, with greater greed, to reclaim what we have distributed to the needy; Judas fell into this guilt when he sold the Lord. The third compels us to desire or acquire, without restraint, things we did not previously possess. Gehazi sinned in this way.

There are three kinds of anger. One burns inwardly and, because of indignation, is unable to speak. Another bursts forth into speech, action, and deed. The third is stored up for days and periods of time.

### [Col. 0012B]

There are two kinds of sadness. One is produced when anger has ended, because of an injury inflicted or a desire obstructed. The other descends from a reasonable anxiety of mind or from despair.

There are two kinds of acedia. One drives those who are burning with zeal headlong toward the summit; the other makes a person take pleasure neither in doing nor in hearing anything good. This is what drives a monk from his cell.

Although cenodoxia is manifold and multiform and is divided into various species, it has two kinds. The first is exalted on account of bodily and visible things. The second inflames us with a desire for vain praise on account of spiritual and hidden things.

Pride has two kinds. The first is carnal; the second is spiritual, and is also more dangerous. It attacks most especially those whom it finds to have made progress in certain virtues. You have heard the kinds, the conjunction, and the chain of connection; now hear what daughters are born from them.

From gluttony are born feasting and drunkenness; from fornication, obscene speech, buffoonery, frivolous entertainments, and foolish talk; from avarice, lying, fraud, perjury, the pursuit of disgraceful gain, false testimony, violence, inhumanity, and rapacity; from anger, homicide, shouting, and indignation; from sadness, resentment, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair; from acedia, cruelty, drowsiness, importunity, restlessness, wandering, instability of mind and body, loquacity, and curiosity; from cenodoxia, quarrels, heresies, boasting, and presumptuous novelty; from pride, contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, grumbling, and detraction.

These, then, are the eight vices. Although they assail the human race, they do not attack everyone in the same way. In one person the spirit of fornication occupies the chief place; in another, fury reigns supreme; in another, cenodoxia asserts its tyranny; in another, pride holds the citadel. Although it is clear that everyone is attacked by all of them, each of us struggles in a different manner and order.

Therefore we must take up our battles against them in such a way that each person examines the vice by which he is most severely afflicted and undertakes his principal struggle against it.

That we ought to follow a single order of battles and not rely on our own strength, the Lawgiver himself teaches us (Deuteronomy 7) in these words:

> You shall not fear them, because the Lord your God is in your midst, a great and terrible God. He himself will consume these nations before you, little by little and by degrees. You will not be able to destroy them all at once, lest perhaps the beasts of the earth multiply against you. The Lord your God will deliver them before you until they are utterly destroyed.

But he likewise warns us that we ought not to become exalted by victory over them (Deuteronomy 8):

> After you have eaten and are satisfied, have built beautiful houses and lived in them, and have acquired herds of cattle and flocks of sheep, silver and gold, and an abundance of all things, do not let your heart be lifted up and do not forget the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery, and who was your guide in the great and terrible wilderness.

Solomon likewise says in Proverbs (Proverbs 24):

> If your enemy falls, do not rejoice; and when he is overthrown, do not become exalted. Otherwise the Lord may see it and turn his anger away from him.

That is: do not divide the elation of your heart; he will withdraw from attacking you, and you, abandoned by him, will begin once again to be afflicted by the passion that, through God’s grace, you had overcome.

Therefore, instructed both by the facts themselves and by countless testimonies of Scripture, we ought to be certain that we cannot overcome such enemies by our own strength unless we are supported by God’s help, and that we must daily refer the whole of our victory back to him.

Thus the Lord also admonishes us through Moses (Deuteronomy 9):

> Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has destroyed them before you: “The Lord brought me in to possess this land because of my righteousness,” since these nations were destroyed because of their wickedness. For you do not enter to possess their land because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart; rather, because they acted wickedly, they were destroyed as you entered.

I ask: what could have been said more clearly or more cautiously? How greatly must we exercise caution!

These are the seven nations whose lands the Lord promises to give to the children of Israel after they have come out of Egypt. According to the Apostle, we must understand all these things as having happened to them in figure and as having been written for our admonition (Deuteronomy 7).

For it is said:

> When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are entering to possess, and he destroys many nations before you—the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, and the Hivites—seven nations much more numerous than you and stronger than you, and the Lord delivers them to you, and you strike them down until they are utterly destroyed …

The reason they are said to be much more numerous is that there are more vices than virtues. For this reason, seven nations are enumerated in the catalogue, but in the account of their conquest they are mentioned without an assigned number. Thus it is said: “And he destroys many nations before you.”

The people of carnal passions, which proceeds from this sevenfold fuel and root of vices, is more numerous than Israel; and from the eighth—which is known to all, the queen, so to speak, and mother of all vices—there spring and are born these daughters: feasting, drunkenness, obscene speech, and so forth, as described above, whose enumeration would be very lengthy.

Although these things seem trivial to us, let us hear what the Apostle thought about them and what judgment he pronounced concerning them (2 Corinthians 10):

> Do not grumble, as some of them grumbled and perished by the destroyer.

And concerning temptation:

> Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents.

Concerning detraction:

> Do not love to slander, lest you be uprooted;

and many other similar statements.

Although these vices are much more numerous than the virtues, once those eight principal vices from whose nature they clearly flow have been conquered, all the others immediately become quiet and are destroyed together with them in perpetual annihilation.

For, as ancient tradition teaches, these same lands of the Canaanites into which the children of Israel were brought had once been allotted, at the division of the world, to Shem, the son of Noah. Afterwards the descendants of Ham seized them by force and power through the wickedness of persuasion; and in this the justice of God is most rightly confirmed. He expelled those people from foreign lands which they had wrongly occupied and restored to these others the ancient possession of their fathers, which had been assigned to their lineage at the division of the world.

It is recognized with the greatest certainty that this figure also applies to us. For the Lord’s will naturally assigned possession of our heart not to vices but to virtues. After Adam’s transgression, when vices—that is, the Canaanite peoples—grew insolent, the virtues were driven from their own region. When, through God’s grace and by our diligence and labor, they have been restored to it again, we must believe that they have not occupied foreign lands but have recovered their own.

Solomon also describes this sevenfold fuel of vices in Proverbs (Proverbs 26):

> If your enemy pleads with you in a loud voice, do not consent to him, for there are seven wickednesses in his soul.

That is: if gluttony persuades you to relax the body in a way you had resolved to restrain, do not dissolve its subjection, because immediately seven spirits of vice will come upon you, more fierce than the passion that had previously been overcome at its beginning; and they will quickly drag you toward worse kinds of vice.

Therefore the Lord must be entreated in all things, so that where our strength is insufficient, his mercy may come to our aid.

## [Col. 0015] Letter of Saint Eutropius, Abbot and Bishop, to Pope Peter, on the Strict Discipline of Monks and the Ruin of Monasteries, Sent to Rome

*(Codex of Rules of Marianus Brocchius.)* (C)

[Col. 0015A] The almighty Lord, in his mercy taking pity on human errors, provided us through Moses, that most holy man, with a very certain example, and clearly and commendably demonstrated that it is entirely appropriate to be angry with those who offend and sin, but, conversely, to be gentle and kind toward those who live well and holily. For, on account of the sin of the offending people, as Scripture properly says, he became exceedingly angry and broke at the foot of the mountain the tablets that he had received from the Lord; moreover, he avenged the crime of the offending people by the sword of the Levites. That he was gentle and kind in this matter is beyond doubt, because, by repeatedly entreating the Lord on their behalf, he turned away the anger of God that was coming upon them; and he did not cease to entreat the Lord for those by whom he could at one time have been stoned.

For the present, let this suffice concerning the many testimonies from the Old Testament. But the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 22). Observe how this is to be understood. The one held guilty by this statement is he who wishes to apply the goad of anger not to the vice—which is evil in a human being—but to human nature itself, which God certainly created good.

Therefore the Apostle also says to certain people who were behaving badly and whom he had rebuked more harshly: “You compelled me to be bad” (II Cor. XII). And concerning the cutting off and separation of those who refuse to repent he says: “Would that those who are troubling you would cut themselves off!” (Gal. V, 12). Of such people the Lord also says in the Gospel—in other words—“If, after being repeatedly admonished, your brother refuses to be corrected, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. XVIII, 17).

But if we must remain silent and—something that is even impious to say—must not rebuke the offender in proportion to his fault, why, I ask, does the Lord command us through Isaiah, saying: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Israel their sins” (Isa. LVIII, 1); and in the words of Ezekiel: “If you do not announce to the wicked man that he should turn from his iniquity, that wicked man will indeed die in his iniquity, which he has committed; but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. XXXV, 8)?

To this statement we add that saying of the distinguished teacher: “What does it profit not to be punished for his own sin, the one who must be punished for another’s sin?” Paul the Apostle speaks openly to Timothy, saying: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (II Tim. IV, 2)—but those who, after being admonished once and again, have recognized their crime through repentance and have wished to correct their life for the better.

As for those who choose to persevere in an evil purpose and, by repenting, refuse to return to the path of an upright life, he commands elsewhere: “Rebuke them sharply” (Tit. I, 15). And again: “With such a person do not even take food” (I Cor. V, 11). For this reason he also says: “I have become your enemy by telling you the truth” (Gal. IV, 16).

Hence the secular poet says: “Compliance produces friends, truth hatred”; for truth is bitter, and those who love it are filled with bitterness. Therefore Jeremiah too says: “I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness” (Jerem. XV, 17). And what is that bitterness except the bad and unrighteous conduct of certain people?

What are we to do now, most holy man? Shall we remain silent and consent to dissolution, so that we may acquire the name of gentle and mild? And what benefit will this bring us before God, when, on account of our silence, the soul of the one who is perishing is said to be required from our hand?

If, however, we wish, by exhorting and rebuking, to recall the flock entrusted to us by God from the snares of the devil and from perverse conduct, we shall be called harsh and severe by the mouths of many. But although this is often said by many who do not understand the office entrusted to us, discretion must nevertheless be maintained, as must the institution of the holy rule, so that what the fathers established their successors and sons may preserve and observe whole and unimpaired.

For if one may deviate in any respect from the institution and path of the holy Fathers, and no one is to be rebuked according to the quality of his fault and conduct, who, I ask, will heed the evils of those who should at least now be frightened by punishments—those who do whatever they wish and rush headlong into vices?

Therefore the order and ineffable disposition of divine power commands [Col. 0016C] that in the world a ruler should be set over it, in the Church a pastor and bishop, and in monasteries a father, so that he may oppose wicked work and criminal and impious actions, and with the sword of strictness and severity may avenge an offense committed against the customs of the human race.

Saint Augustine, the renowned doctor of the Church, as you know very well, says the following in the eighth book of *The City of God*. Pay attention:

“Thus, in our discipline, the question is not so much whether a pious mind becomes angry, nor whether it is sad, but why it is sad; nor whether it is afraid, but what it fears. To become angry with the offender so that he may be corrected, to grieve for the afflicted so that he may be freed, and to fear for one in danger lest he perish—I do not know whether anyone would dare to condemn these things with sound judgment.”

The resources of this world, which the Lord in his mercy has deigned to grant us for the necessities and support of this transitory life, and not for luxury and excess—even if they could be sufficient in every respect, which they are not—do not for that reason justify living lavishly and splendidly or serving the belly and the appetite, even if we abound in all these things.

For Scripture forbids this, saying: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. XVI, 11). The Apostle says: “Do not provide for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII, 14). And again: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, while preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (I Cor. IX, 27). For this reason he also frequently declares that he glories in hunger and thirst, nakedness, and fasts. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your hearts not be weighed down with feasting and drunkenness” (Luke XXI, 34).

If this is not so, then we read the lives of the holy Fathers every day without purpose. We say that we maintain their profession, yet refuse to live according to their institution. Why also does our Lord, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, command, saying: “Do not go by the way of the gentiles” (Matt. X, 5), unless it is so that those whose religion is separate may also have a separate way of life?

There will be no distinction between the profane and the holy, between the secular person and the monk, between the frugal and the sparing, if we wish indiscriminately to serve and gratify our will and desire. Or what benefit will it bring us before God to profess our religious vocation in name only, and not also in holy and good life and commendable conduct?

First before God, and then before human beings, if we wish to show this, in accordance with what is written concerning Samuel: “And he was pleasing both to God and to men” (I Reg. II, 29). The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

This is because whatever good is said to exist in us must be attributed not to the merit of our life but to the gift of God’s grace, which he freely bestows upon us. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “Providing what is good not only before the Lord but also before all human beings” (II Cor. VIII, 21). Elsewhere, avoiding human praise as vain glory, he says: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I, 10).

Blessed Peter, the head and prince of all the Apostles, likewise says: “Keep your conscience and conduct good among the gentiles, so that in the very matter in which they slander you as evildoers, those who defame your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame” (II Pet. II, 12).

We desire, and desire this with our whole heart, my Father—what you too desire—and I am prepared, so to speak, to receive with open hands those who come to the house of God, and to carry and cherish them in our bosom, provided they are such as please God and understand and preserve their profession. For we do not desire to have many, but to have the right kind, and to live chastely and holily with them, so that in the profession of the perfect we may please the Lord.

For the Lord takes delight not in the name and number of the dissolute and lukewarm, but in the holiness of the perfect. Therefore “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXII, 14). And “it is a little flock to which it has pleased your Father to give the kingdom” (Luke XII, 32).

It is far better to enter into life with a few holy people than to be separated from the company of the saints with very many who live lukewarmly and luxuriously. Through the narrow and confined way few walk and reign in the homeland of eternal life; through the broad and spacious way many enter and are hurled into the depths of Gehenna.

For us, just as the founders and Fathers of this monastery held and handed down to us, with the Lord’s help we have held and continue to hold; nor do we do anything more or less, remembering that Scripture says: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers have set” (Prov. XXII, 28). And: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Eccli. XIX).

Thus, in the judgment of God, we may have as our advocates, not our adversaries, those lords and Fathers of ours who, according to the ancient standard, established this rule under God’s inspiration.

For even if someone should say that we act too strictly, and therefore someone should say that he is leaving us—and we speak with your peace and with due regard for the privilege of your most dear and God-worthy honor—we say that whoever else says this seems to us neither to know the monastic rule at all nor to understand it; and by this he appears not to detract from us but to make his own ignorance public.

Let each person say whatever he wishes to himself; but we hold to what we have received and learned. All the holy brothers who are with us, in whose hearts divine love and affection for charity reign, preserve it with the full intention of their minds, and trust, with the Lord protecting and helping them, to persevere in this.

For in such a matter, especially one belonging to God, neither does anyone’s reproach break us, nor does praise—even if falsely spoken—elatedly raise us up. For we say what the Apostle said: “Through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, etc.” (II Cor. VI, 8).

The only thing that matters is that, with the Lord helping us through your holy prayers, we may do this for the salvation of the servants of God and for God’s sake, so that, with his help, it may result for us not in condemnation but in reward at the judgment of the just Judge.

For if we wish to fear human detraction, we shall not do what pleases God. Since, as is well known to your holiness, if someone reproves and rebukes a sinner, he is immediately hated, immediately slandered, and immediately subjected to plots.

But the Lord consoles us, saying: “Blessed are you when people curse you on account of me; rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. V, 11).

This alone we must strive to ensure: that we suffer insult for no other reason than Christ; that Christ be the cause of the detraction; and that, having endured curses for the sake of truth, we know not to curse those who, for the salvation of those entrusted to us by God, we proclaim it with complete confidence.

Nor should we readily grant access to the monastery to those who with deranged speech tear apart every assembly of the Church. For, as Holy Scripture says, not only the one who slanders but also the one who willingly listens to the slanderer is considered guilty of one and the same offense.

We write these things to you, most blessed Father, so that you may know that we do nothing without reason, but act according to the custom of this monastery, whose institutions have been established both holily and according to the rule.

Certainly, if someone cannot endure the custom of our rule, let him attribute it not to our strictness but to his own lukewarm will. For if someone cannot look upon and see the brightness of the sun with bleary eyes, the fault is not therefore to be attributed to the sun but rather to the defect of blearedness and blindness.

What God established well, holily, and perfectly through holy and perfect men in this, his cell, and has wished to be maintained until now, can in no way now be transgressed, changed, or abandoned on account of a few lukewarm, wandering, and false monks who daily go around the houses of various people and say joyfully with Epicurus: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. XXII, 13).

For, as the holy Apostle says: “God’s firm foundation stands” (II Tim. II, 19), even if someone stumbles and falls upon it through the fault of his own evil will; nor does what almighty God protects and strengthens with his right hand waver or totter in any respect. Amen.

**In the Year of Our Lord 600. Tarra, monk.**

[Col. 0019]

## Historical Notice on Tarra

(Antonii, *Bibl. Hisp. Vet.*, vol. I, p. 502, no. 115.)

[Col. 0019B] A certain monk named Tarra also lived under King Reccared. Ambrosius Morales, book XII, chapter 22, informed us that he had found a letter addressed by Tarra to that same king in two ancient manuscripts. We possess this letter transcribed from the Toledo manuscript, but it has been so disfigured—either through the carelessness of copyists or through the corruption of the centuries—and is so full of errors that scarcely any of its meaning can be extracted.

**Cardinal de Aguirre.**

[Note: [Col. 0019B] There is also a copy of this letter in the royal library at Madrid, from the Toledo collection of monuments of the distinguished Juan Bautista Pérez; it is no better preserved, so that I tried in vain to restore it in any satisfactory way. The monk Tarra seems to be clearing himself before King Reccared of a very grave crime that had been charged against him by the brothers of the monastery of Cauliana, near Emerita. He mentions that he had long lived at Emerita and in Lusitania, both as a layman and as a married man, yet always blameless; and that after his wife’s death he had put on the monastic hood. As far as I know, the letter was first published by the distinguished Flórez, *Hisp. Sacr.*, vol. XIII, p. 414.]

[Col. 0019]

## Letter of Tarra the Monk to King Reccared (C)

[Col. 0019C] To be brought to the attention of my most pious lord, King Reccared, gloriously triumphant and reigning in unconquered faith: your servant Tarra, unworthy.

Most merciful lord and illustrious prince, you have ordered a servant well buried in a tomb to be brought forth and exposed to the world. Although this clemency is royal, the servant who obeys the king will experience grief while he goes, at your command, where he does not wish to go. For that beloved John cries out: “Jesus did not wish to go into Judea, because the Jews wanted to kill him.” Yet although the events are understood to have been accomplished through mysteries, because his hour had not yet come, nevertheless, if life avoids death, I shall call myself death-bearing: one pierced by tongues, always under suspicion, and one whom I do not think forgetful of the illustrious memory of your high office, since, oppressed long ago by the priest of the temple, I was making my way where I did not wish to go, driven unwillingly from my homeland and cast out because of scandalous deeds.

But my pious protector, my lord, hid me in his tabernacle; on the day of evils he protected me, saying: “In silence and hope shall be your strength.” And behold, lord, by your command I am unwillingly brought forward from silence into clamor, and even from rest into labors.

Nevertheless, ordered to do so, I faithfully give warning, in accordance with obscene proverbs once heard: “As the unwary yielded, let him not exceed the measure lest he be punished”; for I shall rightly say what the prophet said: “I will not conceal your mercy from the great assembly.”

Therefore, under that pious guardian, who also truly commands, I am unwillingly subjected to this, so that in an ordered written account I may disclose to the ignorant the gifts of the Lord that have until now been hidden. Accordingly, lord, neither oppressed by infamy nor raised up by praise, it is not I who speak but the Spirit of the Father who speaks in us. Against the intercourse of shameful impurity, by which I have been defamed as polluted through an assembly of Caulian [read: Caulian or Caulinian] monks, and fraudulently charged with a very grave crime—as a miscarriage is cast out and left unburied, and the whole earth mourned over me—no one was found who recognized me [Note: [Col. 0020D] The words “and did” are missing from the copies.] [and did] well.

But let your most serene tranquility know their deceitful voice. For throughout all time, under no sky, among men of any rank, whether layman or monk, has anyone endured me committing any deed described as criminal; nor did I ever learn to carry upon myself that entire harlotry, brought against me by fraud, in the city of Emerita and throughout Lusitania.

The first and last wife of Lusitania, and the one who remained mine, was one wife only, taken away by death according to a fatal destiny. Nor is it fitting for anyone, especially a monk, to long again for a woman; nor have my lips touched a woman with a kiss. [Note: [Col. 0021A] In the manuscript of the Royal Library at Madrid: “nor does it exist.”]

And so that what has been heard may be believed more firmly, I produce a faithful witness, present, through whom I always labor and stand: by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; by his right hand with which he crowns the saints; and by the hinges of heaven and the structure of the world, which he himself founded by power and word; by what this present page contains and by everything that has been stated [perhaps: “everything stated”], and that has not been frustrated by fraud; testified through Christ Jesus our Lord.

But I raise up praises, though I am not worthy, to God, who gives good things, who reproaches no one, and who is himself entreated to release the bound and lead those whom he has preserved unharmed until now to that new homeland.

In your times, most glorious prince, may those oppressed by fraud rejoice when they emerge, and may those exalted through fraud be bridled and repressed, so that, helped by Christ’s laws, both may come to the abbot at the wedding feast of the Lamb. May this produce your golden trophy; afterward, far from your kingdom [Mss.: “to your kingdom”], may we serve our Lord effectively, in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

**In the Year of Our Lord 600. Dinothus, abbot.**

[Col. 0021]

## Historical Notice on Dinothus the Abbot

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis*.)

[Col. 0021B] Dinothus, abbot of Bangor, praised by Bede in *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book II, chapter 2—called by others Dionotus of Avon—is said, according to Leland, chapter 44, to have argued at length, seriously, and learnedly in the Synod of Claudiana, or of the Vectians, that the authority of Pope Gregory, or of the monk Augustine sent by him, should not be admitted. He also defended the authority of the bishop of Menevia in ecclesiastical matters. In short, he concluded that it was not in the interest of the Britons to admit either Roman arrogance or Saxon tyranny into their communion.

According to the same Leland, judging from Dionotus’s learning, he held correctly that it did not belong to the Romans, as an alien people—the Saxons—under the pretext of faith, to establish them in power over another people’s territory, namely Britain. For if they admitted this, there would be no lack of a pretext for expelling any rulers from their kingdoms.

Some actual words of Dinothus, transcribed from an Anglo-Saxon manuscript and published in English with a Latin translation by Henry Spelman, vol. I of the *Councils of England*, p. 108, were thought by Schelstraten [Note: [Col. 0021C] *Mémoires de Trévoux*, year 1709, p. 823.] and certain others to have been fabricated under Dinothus’s name. It is easy to conjecture why they seemed so, but impossible to see the basis for the conjecture.

The sense of the words is this:

“Let it be known, and without doubt, to you that we all, and every one of us, are obedient and subject to the Church of God and to the pope of Rome, and to every true and pious Christian, to love each person in his own rank with perfect charity, and to help each of them by word and deed, so as to be children of God. I know no other obedience than this to be due to him whom you call the pope, nor that he should claim or demand to be the Father of Fathers; and this obedience we are ready continually to give and render to him and to every Christian.

Moreover, we are under the governance of the bishop of Caerleon-on-Usk, who, under God, is set over us to supervise us and to make us keep the spiritual way.”

The other works that Bale, I, 70, and Pits, p. 104 and following, report Dinothus to have written—*Defense of the Jurisdiction of the See of Menevia*, *On Preserving the Rites of the Britons*, a book of *Disputations*, another of *Orations and Letters*, and commentaries on Sacred Scripture—were seen by no one. I am persuaded that, as these authors often did elsewhere, they were attributed to him on the basis of mere conjecture.

[Col. 0021]

## Of Dinothus

[Note: [Col. 0021C] I transcribed this response of the abbot of Bangor from two Cotton manuscripts; but let us hear what the distinguished Spelman says about his own copy.]

[Col. 0022C] “Many years ago I myself transcribed this from an old manuscript belonging to Peter Mostyn, a Welsh gentleman, which unquestionably imitated an older one” (these are Spelman’s words), “with such care and diligence that I did not depart from the exemplar by a single stroke. But since it was written only in the Welsh language, with an English interlinear translation rendered word for word, I followed the same practice and added Latin for the benefit of foreigners.

“However, neither did I ascertain from that manuscript when it had been produced or by what author, nor was I able to investigate the matter elsewhere with certainty; but I believe the manuscript to be held in the Cotton Library.

“The abbot of Bangor who gave this response to Augustine was, without any doubt, that celebrated Dinothus whom we mentioned above. It is also clear, both from this response of his and from those matters that Bede himself reports here earlier, that at this time the British Church recognized no subjection either to the Roman pontiff himself or to any foreign patriarch, nor did it maintain any communion with the Roman Church.

“It was subject, as from the age of Eleutherius, to its own metropolitan—as to the pope or patriarch of another world—the archbishop of Caerleon, who, as is suggested here, recognized no superior among the ranks of the Church, but, ‘yn oligwr Dan Duw,’ that is, ‘under God, without any other intermediary,’ governed the people and Church entrusted to him. They had also adopted Eastern and Asian rites rather than Roman ones.

“This was not, however, because of any schismatic perversity—which the authors of that age would surely have mentioned—nor against the institutions of the holy Fathers, which were confirmed by the authority of the Third Ecumenical Council held at Ephesus in the year of grace 431, session 7, when the Cypriots promoted a similar case against the patriarch and clergy of Antioch.

“It is not our purpose to discuss the matter; I merely touch upon what arises and pass over it, considering it a sacrilege not to acknowledge with every expression of gratitude the notable benefits that our ancestors once received from the ancient Roman Church and its bishops.

“Yet who would not judge that Augustine acted without the sweetness of charity toward these poor Britons, when he suddenly tried to abolish their ancient customs and suddenly attempted to impose new ones? Especially since his own holy teacher, Gregory the Great, had advised that this should be done more cautiously. Gregory tolerated different customs in different churches and did not wish Roman customs themselves to be imposed everywhere, but observed the custom suited to place, time, and the character of believers. ‘For,’ he says, ‘things are not to be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of good things.’ See his response to Augustine’s third question.

“Among these matters, I ask how it happened that the bishops of Caerleon—otherwise called bishops of Menevia—and their successors, who from the age of King Lucius until Augustine’s days—that is, for nearly four hundred years—had flourished with metropolitan privileges and been called archbishops, were thereafter deprived and stripped of their province and ancient jurisdiction without, as far as I know, being summoned before any synod or charged with any offense.

“It is enough if this was done by Augustine, for his supporters defend all his actions tenaciously. And this one deed, which he is said to have contrived against the British clergy, was a grievous destruction. They proclaim that it was sent by God to confirm their traditions and teaching, while others maintain that Augustine himself provided the occasion for the deed and stirred up King Ethelbert against them.

“But if the evidence of the matter—as most people tend to do—is established from the outcome, one must think very differently about this destruction from the way those men related it, and conclude that God himself abhorred this cruelty.

“For when the avenger of Augustine’s anger, Edilfrid, king of the Northumbrians, had slaughtered those innocent Bangor monks at Chester in such a great massacre, and, exulting, hastened with his weapons to destroy their remnants together with their noble monastery, three British leaders, avengers of God’s anger, met him. They struck down the king of Northumbria, drenched with the blood of the innocent, together with his entire army; they slaughtered ten thousand and sixty men; and they drove the wounded king, with very few others, into flight. Thus God himself seems to have entered the battle against these Augustinians on behalf of those innocent Bangor monks and to have undertaken vengeance for their blood. May that good God grant that I suggest nothing except the truth.

“To free my conscience, therefore, I beg you to allow me to place before your judgment what is written in the *Life of Augustine*, near the end of the book *On the Antiquity of the British Church*, printed at London in the year of Our Lord 1572, which came into my possession while the press was engaged with this very subject:

“‘Some also write that Augustine himself was not only aware of the war I mentioned but was also its instigator; that he met the kings prepared for it at Chester, although the papal party tries in every way to conceal this by inserting a fabricated parenthesis of their own making into Bede’s History, recently printed by their printers contrary to the testimony of all manuscript Saxon books—although Augustine himself had long before been taken up into the heavenly kingdom. There will later be occasion to refute this error, indeed this manifest falsehood, against the testimony of Bede himself, if they should wish to find anyone to defend it amid such an abundance of empty rhetoric.’

“These are the words found there. I have not examined the Saxon manuscripts. But hear how the Dominican friar Nicholas Trivet—a monk among monks—recounts this history in his French chronicle, written in manuscript three hundred years ago. See Wilkins, *Councils*, vol. I, p. 27.”]

## Response to the Monk Augustine, Requesting Submission to the Roman Church

(From Wilkins, *Councils of Great Britain*, vol. I, p. 26.) (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0021C] Let it be known, and without doubt, to you that we all, and every one of us, are obedient and subject [Col. 0022C] to the Church of God and to the pope of Rome, and to every true [and] pious Christian, [Col. 0023A] to love each person in his own rank with perfect charity, and to help each of them by word and deed, so as to be children of God; and I know no other obedience than this to be due to him whom you call the pope, nor that he should be the Father of Fathers, to claim and demand it; and this [Col. 0024A] obedience we are ready continually to give and render to him and to every Christian.

Moreover, we are under the governance of the bishop of Caerleon-on-Usk, who, under God, is set over us to supervise us and to make us keep the spiritual way.

**In the Year of Our Lord 601. Dynamius Patricius.**

[Col. 0023]

## Historical Notice on Dynamius

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis*.)

[Col. 0023D] Dynamius, or Dinamius, an illustrious man and Patrician of Gaul, in the years 593–596, is mentioned by Gregory the Great (book II, indiction XI, letter 33; book V, letter 6), whom Venantius Fortunatus calls Massiliensis in book VI, poem 11.

[Col. 0024D] The epitaph of the same Dinamius and his wife Eucheria is found in André Duchesne, vol. I of *History of the Franks*, p. 519. According to Sigebert, chapter 444, and Usuard, January 27, Dinamius wrote a *Life of Saint Marius*, abbot of Bobacum or Bodanum, around the year 500. It was published by Bollandus on January 27, vol. II, p. 774, and by Mabillon, first century of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, p. 105.

He then wrote a *Life of Saint Maximus*, first abbot of Lérins and afterward, in the year 433, bishop of Riez or Réjus, addressed to Urbicus, bishop of Riez in the year 584. It appears in Surius under November 27 and in Vincentius Barralis’s *Chronology of the Abbots and Monastery of Lérins*, and is discussed by Barthius, *Adversaria* LIX, 12. Gregory of Tours also wrote about this same Maximus in his work *On the Glory of the Confessors*.

[Col. 0025]

## Two Letters of Dynamius Patricius

(Duchesne, *Historians of the Franks*.) (C, S)

### Letter I. To a Friend

[Col. 0025A]

Just as a cold spring, while relieving the dryness, refreshes the desires of a thirsty man exhausted by the summer heat of the sun or shaken by the hardships of a long journey, so the expression of your letters, when it brought me signs of your safety, nourished an increase of joys.

For whenever, through frequent remembrance, I recall the sweet wishes of your affection, I do not cease to make the desires of my heart known through sighs. This is because the one who is deprived of bodily sight is not absent from the secret place of the heart.

Therefore, having fulfilled the duty of wishing you health with the fullest right of charity, I hope that whenever the varying difficulties of time provide an opportunity, the desired expression of your letters may always strengthen my littleness, until, with divine assistance and the devotion of our hearts supplying what is lacking, we may rejoice in seeing one another, though we are never separated in undivided affection.

### Letter II. To His Ever-Especial Lord, the Steward Pope

[Col. 0025C]

I fear that, because of the lateness of this little book, I may be held guilty before your authority. But if, in your customary judgment of piety, you consider the burden of my sorrows, you will immediately show indulgence to necessity.

Nevertheless, to the extent of my ability, I have tried to fulfill what you commanded. For you do not doubt, most blessed pontiff, that the dominion of a single charity has already made me subject to you through continual devotion. Yet I do not consider this remarkable, since I trust that you are similarly bound in the hearts of all.

For in you the general prerogative of distinction magnifies you with proud recompense and varied generosity of benefaction, so that whatever is precious wherever it shines is proved to be innate in you. [Col. 0026A] And although you are adorned with the noble dignity of your birth, your humility makes you more noble and gives your whole self to freedom.

Thus the splendor of charity, which shines forth within the secrets of your heart with the brightness of immense light, both now displays the serenity of your body and is a mirror of the heart: grace that gleams in your face.

For this reason the whole world eagerly desires to be reconciled to your affection, since a love known to all invites them. I rejoice all the more to offer in return the pledges of my service in words, until, having recovered my strength, I may deserve to respond in deeds.

Therefore, humbly offering the interest of my good health, I beg you to commend me continually in the divine oracles—where your gracious favor has received me—to your intercession, and, to all those whom you see to be necessary, through whom my case may also be brought to the king’s ears, assert my need or obtain a speedy return for me. Thus, by the patronage you have granted, support the one whom you cherish with devoted affection.

Concerning the gifts you have sent, I am suspended between two thoughts: whether I ought to return thanks or remain silent, since one who cannot adequately fulfill a proclamation of praise rightly avoids the attempt. Nevertheless, the greatness of your crown [That is, of your priesthood or episcopate] does not believe it sufficient that your immense generosity never ceases to minister to everyone in the city over which you preside, unless you also provide with your own resources for those who inhabit another’s walls.

Such is my case, whom your kindness pursues with a desired visitation; and because I was unable to escape it when compelled, I seem to have received it with devotion. Hence, although the dryness of my intellect remains, a continuation of assistance could nevertheless have been extended, except that the letter had a limit and the paper denied the space.

[Col. 0025]

## Life of Saint Marius by Dynamius Patricius

(From Bollandus, January, vol. II, for the 27th day.) (C)*

### Chapter I. The Death and Prophecies of Saint Marius

[Col. 0025C]

1. When our Lord Jesus Christ, at the beginning of our calling, had laid the foundations of faith in human hearts, and when the harvest of that same faith, through the sending of the Holy Spirit, had grown far and wide throughout the whole world, the Christian religion became accustomed to commend the memorable deeds of the saints to writing for two reasons: namely, so that the choir of the faithful, hearing those deeds recited at annual festivals, might rejoice, exult, and grow; and so that the less perfect, inflamed by the examples of those same deeds, might strive and labor to do good.

2. Thus Saint Marius, whose faithful deeds we are now beginning to narrate according to the measure of our capacity, was born of a family of moderate rank and was a citizen of Orléans. Having become a monk in the monastery that is there, this boy, instructed from early childhood in monastic teachings, and later made a young man, devoted himself to serving God through good works.

When he shone among the brothers in the aforementioned monastery, like a lily among the trees of the forest, in character and life, [Col. 0027B] with the consent of Gundobad, prince of the Burgundians, he was chosen by the brothers of the monastery of Bodanum, situated in the diocese of Sisteron, to be their father.

[Note: [Col. 0027D] Concerning Gundobad, see January 21 under the *Life of Saint Epiphanius*; he will also be discussed under the *Life of Saint Clotildis*, June 3, and elsewhere.]

His election was confirmed by the authority of John, who at that time presided over the Church of Sisteron.

[Note: [Col. 0027D] The list of the bishops of Sisteron is incomplete in the work of the distinguished Robert. The first listed there is Pologronius, who signed the Second Council of Valence in 584 and the Second Council of Mâcon in 585. This John was much earlier.]

Divine providence and mercy arranged and favored this, so that the man who had governed himself well might be placed over others who needed governance.

What more is there to say? He was brought to the monastery just mentioned, and by his bishop he was consecrated abbot with the common consent of the brothers.

### 3

Once consecrated, he embraced the duties of his office with such devotion that every day he begot spiritual sons by the example of his venerable life, and, wonderfully instructing them in heavenly teachings, brought them to maturity. For he afflicted his outer man with fasts and vigils, while continually refreshing his inner man with prayers; in both respects he was gentle and humble, and in both praiseworthy and perfect.

Once, while he had withdrawn to another region to attend to the affairs of his monastery, it happened that, in the territory of Alegarnum, he was received as a guest by a distinguished farmer. [Note: Was “Arvernensian” perhaps written?] At the request of this host, he baptized the man’s daughter, named Sisagria, who was almost dead; and after baptizing her, he restored her through his prayers to life and to her former health.

When he was returning to the monastery after completing the business for which he had gone there, a noble matron named Licinia received him into her house. Her son was so gravely ill that the woman and her friends had despaired of his recovery. At his mother’s request, the old man visited the sick boy, prayed over him, and anointed him with holy oil. O, the swiftness of God’s power when the confessor prays! While the sick man was being anointed, the desired health unexpectedly returned, and the illness fled, cast aside. Thus it happened that the host whom he had found sorrowful he left joyful with her son as he returned to the monastery.

### 4

Since, as is customary among religious men, during Lent this man of God was shut up in his cell and lived more sparingly than usual, Bishop Lucretius of Die came to visit him constantly—partly because he had been this man of God’s monk and foster-son, and revered and honored him as a father; partly because he always wished to be refreshed by his sweet conversation.

One day, then, when the bishop knocked at the door of his cell, he heard him say that he should leave and return on the third day, and that during that interval no one should provide him with food or access. The bishop departed; and when he returned after three days, he entered to see the man of God. The man of God said to him:

“I was carried away in spirit, and I saw the heavens opened and the majesty of God, whose splendor of glory my mortal eyes could scarcely endure. I saw the blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, with the angels prostrate at his feet, pleading for the peace of Italy.

“But divine mercy so tempered the answer that it did not offend the Mother who was making her petition; yet he replied that Italy and many other provinces deserved an unalterable destruction.

“These things were revealed to me by God, and I have resolved to reveal them to you, adjuring you in God’s name and mine not to presume to disclose what you have heard to anyone while I am alive.”

After the bishop mentioned above had buried the body of this man of God, we learned the outcome of the vision, since we have no doubt that the monastery of Bodanum was destroyed.

> **Note:** Italy suffered much in his time at the hands of the Heruli, Goths, and Burgundians, and afterward from the Franks, Greeks, and Lombards.

## Chapter II. Various Miracles. His Death

### 5

At another time, the man of God desired to visit the threshold of Saint Martin of Tours for the sake of prayer. While he was sleeping that very night of the vigils in the city of Tours, a thief secretly stole his saddle-horse. But divine power so beset the thief through the merits of the aforesaid man of God that throughout the whole night he searched the city streets, and no exit from the city lay open to him. At daybreak the man of God forestalled the thief and recovered the horse. Although the thief, having been caught, deserved corporal punishment, the saint, out of his innate gentleness, allowed him to depart free. By a similar miracle, on another occasion he recovered his riding animals in the city of Lyon.

### 6

Nor should this be omitted: at a certain time, Nemphidius, accompanying Senator Agricola and Saint Marius, was traveling to Paris for the sake of prayer, to visit the threshold of Saint Denis. During the journey, Nemphidius recognized the holiness of the man and, with an unshaken mind, trusted in it. He asked him to obtain through his prayers the blessing of having a son.

The saint refused, humbly asserting that he was not worthy of such merit that Nemphidius could obtain through him what he requested.

Although, as is the custom of the just, he plainly declared that he could not in any way favor so great a petition, nevertheless, after three days, he foretold to the aforesaid Nemphidius that a son would be born to him at a definite time. That the saint was a true prophet in this matter was shown when Evodius was born to Nemphidius at the promised time.

### 7

We also judged it worthy to add that, before he departed from that city, he began to fall seriously ill, to the great sorrow of his companions. On the following night, he placed his limbs, almost dead with weakness, upon the bed. But within that same night divine mercy came so powerfully to his aid that at earliest dawn he rose joyful and sound, and encouraged his companions to continue the journey.

When all who were present marveled at his sudden recovery, he said:

“Saint Denis came to me during that night, touched me, and by his presence restored me to my former health.”

### 8

When, therefore, as we have said, he returned to the monastery restored to health, a certain householder received him as a guest. At the proper time the man of God approached the table, sat down, and blessed the bread that had been brought, as was customary. When one of those seated at table threw some of the blessed bread to a dog whom he loved, as soon as the dog appeared to have swallowed the bread it received, it lost its life. For it was unworthy that a dog should eat the bread which the priest’s right hand had sanctified.

### 9

At another time, while he was going to visit certain spiritual sons of the Church, a female dog with puppies suddenly leaped up and tore his little satchel. When the servant of God briefly lowered his face because of this, two wolves, avengers of the injury done to him, seized the dog itself and, intending to make it their prey, carried it into the forest in the presence of the people.

If anyone does not believe that at times wild beasts, laying aside their ferocity, have known how to serve the interests of the righteous, let him hear that lions made the burial of Paul, the first hermit, and of Saint Mary of Egypt. Let him hear, and in all things praise the Lord, marvel, and believe.

> **Note:** We gave the Life of Saint Paul on 10 January.

> **Note:** We will give the Life of Saint Mary of Egypt on 2 April.

### 10

We thought that the following should also be added to the events mentioned above: whenever the servant of God spread out sheaves of grain to be threshed in unsettled weather, or sat at table in any journey beneath the open sky, he was never troubled or hindered by a deluge of rain.

Thus God restrained the assaults of the clouds wherever they came rushing down, through the merits and power of the holy confessor. While they indiscriminately drenched other travelers going and returning, and their labors, with their downpours, they passed over the man of God and his companions unharmed, and left his threshing-floors untouched.

Nor is it surprising that he could drive away the pouring rain from the clouds, since from the first flowering of his youth he had striven to weaken within himself the dark gloom of vices. Indeed, he possessed such power and holiness that through him the Lord restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and the sick to their former health. The Lord also liberated through him a woman held captive by the assault of an evil spirit, when he prayed for her.

### 11

The following memorable event must also be added to those already recounted: although absent in body and present in spirit, he learned of the passing of a certain servant of God, Donatus, and tearfully announced what he had learned to the brothers.

One of those who were present, wishing to test whether the man of God’s vision rested on truth, sent to the place where the aforesaid Donatus had served God. From the report of the messengers he found that matters were exactly as the man of God had foretold.

What you have heard, dearest brothers, we have excerpted from the miracles of the confessor so often named, omitting very many lest the length of our discourse produce weariness in those listening. Thus crowned with the glory of such great virtues, and shining far and wide with the renown of so many miracles, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February—that is, today—the aforesaid confessor of the Lord, Marius Felix, departed from the body to Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong kingdom and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## Chapter III. Miracles after His Death

### Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew

### 12

At that time Jesus said this parable to his disciples: “A certain man departing on a journey called his servants and entrusted his possessions to them”; and so forth.

### Homily of Saint Gregory, Pope

This man, dearest brothers, who departs on a journey is our Redeemer, who, passing from the world to the Father, entrusted five talents—that is, spiritual goods—to his faithful servants. Since Saint Marius proved to be a faithful servant, he is believed to have received from the same Redeemer, together with the faithful, the aforementioned trust.

Therefore, departing from the body, he approached the feet of that same Redeemer, who demanded spiritual interest, himself also destined to render an account of what had been entrusted to him. And because he had gained another five talents upon the five, he deserved to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, enter into the joy of your Lord.”

### 13

After his blessed passing, when many periods of years had flowed by, and when, through the cruelty of savage peoples, almost all Gaul was considered stripped of its inhabitants, and the monasteries of Christ had been turned into wildernesses to be mourned with perpetual grief, certain men, by God’s providence, transferred the body of the aforesaid man of God from the church of Bodanum to this town of Forcalquier.

> **Note:** It lies between Sisteron and Apt.

He rests in the church, granting perpetual rest through the same church to those who serve him. Many assert that in this church the Lord has performed many miracles through him. To commend the memory of so great a confessor, we have excerpted a few of these, which we learned through the truthful testimony of witnesses.

### 14

At a certain time, a rather unruly little boy was playing profane games and leaping beneath the sarcophagus of the aforesaid father. While he was insolently carrying on before it, he was struck down by divine vengeance and fell. Immediately his limbs began to fail and the five bodily senses to weaken. The punishment increased, and the suffering increased; and when he withdrew from that place, supported by the hands of others, he breathed out his spirit amid punishment and suffering.

This makes clear that God is the God of vengeance. Although he may appear to be far away, he is nevertheless believed to judge continually the injuries done to the saints.

### 15

Nor must we by any means omit the following: on one occasion, a devout man who was custodian of the basilica of the same man of God came to the church around midnight to replenish the lamp, but found it extinguished.

“Ah,” he said, “my father, give counsel to your servant. Black night possesses everything; everyone is asleep; I do not know where fire may be found; my foot does not know the path of the road. What, then, shall I do?”

While his soul was anxious and he did not know which way to turn, suddenly, to his ineffable joy, the candle he held in his hands appeared burning.

### 16

At another time, a certain peasant, contracted in all his limbs, was so completely deformed throughout his body and so gathered into a single mass contrary to the human form that he was thought not to be a man but some kind of monster.

He had been brought to many saints’ shrines. But because, as we believe, he had been reserved for our holy confessor, he confessed that he had received no help from any of them. Finally, with divine mercy aiding him, he was brought with great difficulty to the desired shrine of the holy confessor and carried into his church, where he was laid down.

The wretched man prayed with tears for the raising of his pitiable body, and those present, sympathizing with him, made the same petition.

O God’s goodness, worthy of all devotion! O merits of the saints, entirely worthy of veneration by mortals! Amid the tears of the unhappy man and the words of the many who prayed, the wretched man was raised. Many heard the cracking of his bones and the stretching of his sinews. The whole company of his companions rushed up, summoned by the tumult of their astonishment; the nobles rushed up; people of both sexes and every class rushed up. All cried out, some overtaking others with their shouts:

“Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory!”

Thus the wretched man who had come there returned home with joyful steps, restored to health through the merits of the aforesaid man of God.

### 17

We have also decided to add the following: one day an unmarried girl, led by frivolity of mind, threw a stone at the altar of the holy confessor and struck it. Before the stone she had thrown had fallen to the floor, the girl collapsed, drained of strength in her sinews and weakened in the power of her limbs.

What more need be said? She who had come shortly before in wanton playfulness was mourned as [foeta: “pregnant”?, the reading is uncertain] and wretched. She was taken to the threshold of the confessor Marius to keep a faithful vigil. She offered herself, her prayers, and her tears; and she promised the saint annual vigils if she returned home restored to health.

O wondrous help of divine mercy! While the woman wept and offered herself wholly upon the altar of her mind through devoted prayers, she was heard and completely restored to her former health. Once she had recovered, she was joined in marriage. But as time passed, and the woman mentioned above, clinging too eagerly to marital pleasures, delayed fulfilling the vows she had made to the saint, forgetfulness was overtaken by her former illness. She was again weakened in the support of her sinews and entirely deprived of the health of her limbs.

Once again, through her husband’s care, she was taken to the aforesaid threshold of the holy confessor; once again, through his merits, she was restored to the greatly desired health. Rejoicing in the health unexpectedly returned to her, the woman vowed perpetual service to the saint and resolved never again to return home.

But when her husband became exceedingly angry with his wife over this vow, the frightened woman, intimidated by her husband’s threats and softened by his blandishments, returned home with him. As soon as she had returned, the pitiable woman was again afflicted by the illness already mentioned; again she was taken to the saint’s threshold; again she was restored to the health she desired.

O unhappy condition of our human nature! O shameful forgetfulness in fulfilling vows! Once again the saint was forgotten; once again the shameless woman was weakened by her accustomed illness; once again she hastened to the frequently mentioned threshold. Through a renewed vow the saint was again honored, and the woman was again restored to the health she had sought. Restored, joyful, and sound, she returned home through the merits of the holy confessor, never to return again for similar reasons.

Let those who in this church have promised stability of conduct to God and Saint Marius hear; let them also reverence [lacuna] of the mind with diligent care. If everything concerning the vow is in order, let them rejoice that all has gone well for them. But if it is otherwise, let them know that they suffer in their soul what the aforesaid woman is said to have suffered in her body.

Therefore, when vows have been broken, let them seek help through penance; let them approach the feet of the holy confessor; let them offer tears and prayers, so that, with their conduct restored to stability, they may once again, through God’s mercy, deserve to possess the salvation they lost by their actions. Amen.

> **Note:** Saint Donatus is celebrated on 19 August, where Ado relates this somewhat differently: “When the day of his calling was approaching, Saint Abbot Marius arrived, to whom this had been revealed; and amid the words of prayer he passed over to Christ.” He was buried by that same father in his proper place.

# Life of Saint Maximus by Saint Dynamius, Illustrious Man and Patrician

*(Surius, Acts of the Saints, volume II.) (C)*

## Dedication Letter

> To the most blessed Lord Father, Pope Urbicus, Dynamius the Patrician sends greetings.

Since, Father, inflamed by the ardor of apostolic faith, you diligently investigate everything concerning the virtues of Saint Maximus that a faithful account of his deeds reveals, you do not cease to press my incompetence. You also strengthen me with paternal admonitions and the authority of your command to preach, affirming that I shall become guilty of no small offense unless I strive to add to his Life—which, as is known, I composed in rustic language several years ago—whatever you have now clearly discovered concerning his miracles.

For this reason I am confused by a double shame: I am granted neither the ability to speak nor the security of remaining silent. If I speak, my exposed rusticity displays my ignorance of meaning. Had it been permitted, I might at least have pleased by concise expression, since I cannot be assisted by any enlargement of doctrine.

Placed, therefore, between these two difficulties, I have resolved to obey your commands, intending to please by obedience rather than by learning. You have informed me that you had searched through ancient volumes of documents, in which your devoted diligence had collected something from the works of the blessed Bishop Faustus, your predecessor; from these, by meaning rather than by outward appearance, you could scarcely discern a few things. For the devouring force of rival antiquity had consumed very much that lay hidden.

You judged that, unless the little that survived from the many things were entrusted to eternal memory through the sequence of my writings, it would be a sufficiently impious omission. Therefore I consider that I have partly satisfied your wishes, since a reading extended into a long succession follows in multiplied form.

Whenever this length of reading causes the long-familiar material to weary its hearers, the fault may belong to you. If it brings the reward of merit, nothing of that will likewise belong to me, since, compelled by your commands, I have written more at length than I wished and abandoned the refuge of brevity.

I therefore beseech you, pastor, whom you most wisely strip of his silent veil and lay bare of the covering of silence, to fortify me, exposed before the whole assembled people, with the protection of your intercession. Whenever the length of the reading is brought forward, let the unpolished expression not displease, since the tenor of the account of holy things commends it.

For there is no doubt that, in proportion as you present the deeds of this holy bishop with complete devotion of heart, you meditate upon his works and strive to follow his footsteps with the whole eagerness of your mind, loving the adornments of his actions—provided that, by divine favor and through his patronage, you are granted the prolonged tranquility of temporal life and the desired capacity for holy work.

Lord, truly holy and most blessed pope.

# Here Begins the Life

### 1

Today the holy solemnity of the most blessed Maximus, bishop of the city of Riez, is celebrated; it is renewed each year through the returning courses of time. Pious devotion of mind admonishes us, and ancient custom compels us, to recount his deeds.

For unless what has been discovered through the trustworthy account of others—things clear and entirely beyond doubt—is committed to written records, events of ancient times are often reported in various ways by later authors. Since, therefore, nothing in the marks of his mystical activity should be ambiguous, and since popular enthusiasm should turn none of them into fables or make them suspect of vanity, the things done and confirmed by him must be narrated in truthful speech.

Nevertheless, lest excessive length weary the listener, we have passed over very many things and recorded only a few.

### 2

Blessed Maximus began his life in his native village, called Decomecum, born to Christian parents and immediately made a Christian. From the earliest beginnings of infancy, he continually grew in exalted humility and disciplined the tender years of his age with such maturity of conduct that, by the grace of holiness, he claimed for himself the meaning of his name.

When he had passed beyond boyhood, he subdued the allurements and blandishments of sensuality by the guidance and discipline of his mind, so that he might obtain the palm of promised virginity and incorrupt integrity, and triumph in the heavenly kingdoms after subjecting his flesh to the yoke.

Indeed, he was endowed with every adornment of goodness and deservedly must be extolled with praise and proclamation: venerable in appearance, gentle in expression, peaceful in speech, serene in spirit, strong in patience, distinguished by greatness of soul, a lover of peace, generous toward enemies, disdainful of passing things, burning with desire for heavenly things, comparing eternal things with temporal, and scorning and despising temporal things for the sake of eternal ones.

And so that inwardly he might know the precepts of divine law, he advanced so far in letters through the natural sharpness of his intellect that he sought nourishment for his soul in an eagerness to read and drew up nectar of eternal sweetness like the bees.

Although he trampled down every source of carnal vice and shone on every side with an excellent way of life, he nevertheless weakened the strength of his body through continual abstinence, pursuing and restraining the vices of the flesh before they had even arisen. Thus it seemed that for his martyrdom nothing was lacking except an executioner. For beyond doubt he made himself a martyr both by suffering and by merit.

### 3
