Moreover, abandoning all the abundance of his possessions, he sought the monastery of Lérins, where the righteous man might find everlasting riches. He followed the evangelical precepts, knowing that he could not become perfect unless he sold everything he possessed and made himself free from all wealth.

In that community he loved everyone with perfect charity, and likewise was loved by everyone. Such fervor arose in him that, even before he had embraced the monastic rule of life or the mystical institutions, he already appeared outstanding in his conduct. Later he succeeded in honor and equaled in merit his predecessor, Saint Honoratus, richly adorned with the highest virtues, who had been abbot there.

While he guarded the flock entrusted to him with pastoral care and walked through the monastery each night while the others were asleep, it happened unusually that a certain monk, still a boy, moved by curiosity or concern, followed him.

Behold, before the eyes of the most blessed man the devil, lying in wait, appeared in a huge and terrifying form. But when he could not frighten the man clothed in spiritual armor, he struck the unsuspecting monk with such terror that, returning immediately to his cell with trembling steps, he was soon seized by a raging fever.

### 4

Again that persistent deceiver, hoping to disturb the holy man by some means, showed himself to him in the form of a fiery dragon. But immediately terrified by the sign of the cross, he vanished. For the unconquered athlete no longer feared an enemy whom he had often overcome.

After he had traversed the whole circuit of the island of Lérins, he quickly approached the bed of the sick monk whom we mentioned as having fallen into fever. Secretly pouring out prayers to God within the hidden chamber of his heart, he effected the monk’s immediate restoration to his former health and left the deceived enemy cheated of his prey.

Thus a twofold virtue won an unconquered victory: it restored strength to the sick man and overthrew the adversary—the enemy lamenting the loss he had suffered, and the monk rejoicing in the health he had recovered.

### 5

Each night, then, as the excellent shepherd walked around the Lord’s sheepfold lest anything harmful occur, he once approached the shore of the sea called the Mole. Immediately that old deceiver dared, through his tricks, to present before his eyes what appeared to be a loaded ship, with sailors busily at work in their customary fashion and gathering the ship’s equipment.

Two of them approached the blessed man and said that they had come there for purposes of trade, since the outcome of the affair would reveal that it would bring enormous profit. They said that they knew this Maximus, no less by his holiness than by his name, and that he was so greatly desired by everyone in overseas lands that, if they could obtain him, they would value nothing more highly.

They would therefore make no greater profit than if they could place him aboard the ship and carry him off to Jerusalem, having found him, beyond expectation, through a prosperous outcome. This would undoubtedly bring him great honor and dignity, if he were brought by a fortunate voyage to the place where he was so eagerly awaited by everyone’s prayers.

But the man of God recognized the ambush and the enemy’s evil deceit, fortified himself with the sign of the holy cross, invoked heavenly aid, and then replied with spiritual authority:

“The wickedness of a deceitful impostor cannot deceive Christ’s soldiers, nor can the Evil One mock them by his frauds, when God grants them the ability to foresee adversities. The prayers of the most blessed Honoratus have fortified this island to such a degree—he expelled the dragon who inhabited it—that from then on no avenue for harming it is open to the devil.”

As he spoke these words, the imaginary ship vanished from the eyes of the man praying. He soon returned to the oratory and encouraged the brothers to rise for the vigils. Together with that holy community, he himself offered celebrated praises to him through whom he had carried off victory over the enemy.

### 6

When the fame of his remarkable virtues flew throughout the whole world, he was carried—not merely elected—to the episcopate of the city of Riez through the enthusiasm not only of the citizens but also of all the priests and bishops; and, although unwilling, he was immediately consecrated.

Although he already seemed to be Maximus both in fact and in name, with little in which he could grow further, nevertheless, so that nothing might be lacking from his name, just as he remained Maximus in his works and deeds, so also he excelled in honor.

Among the other adornments of his rightly performed deeds that shone in him, he was strong in patience, patient in benevolence, joyful in freedom, abundant in generosity, beneficent in greatness of soul, gentle in humanity, diligent in attentiveness, sweet in charity, generous to all, outstanding in learning, singular in justice, exalted in humility, a despiser of wealth, and rich and overflowing in dignity.

With as much devotion of mind as he could muster, he founded a temple in the castle of Riez in honor of blessed Albinus. The columns that can still be seen there were dragged to the site by teams of oxen, but in such a way that they felt no discomfort from so great a weight, because his holiness made this possible as long as he was present as an untiring laborer in the construction of the temple.

But whenever he happened to be absent, through the hidden machination of the most wicked demon all the oxen were so weighed down by the burden that no goads could compel them to move forward. Even when many others were added, they all remained motionless, however cruelly they were beaten and wounded.

When a swift messenger reported this to the most blessed bishop, he came immediately and confidently to the place, neither trembling with fear nor disturbed by grief. Then the most wicked enemy could not deceive his eyes or withdraw from the sight of one whom he could not be seen by the eyes of the whole people.

The holy man said to them:

“You torment animals devoid of reason in vain, since you cannot see the obstacles of the enemy. But I see a little Ethiopian placing himself before the oxen.”

Then he fell upon his knees and humbly prayed to God to turn aside the enemy’s ambush. Unable to endure his prayers, the Evil One quickly withdrew, not without a most foul stench. As soon as the oxen that had been added were removed, the columns were dragged to their appointed place without any difficulty.

### 7

Nor did we think that the following should be omitted, since it strengthened the courage of the people of Riez. When the most blessed bishop was bringing sacred relics with the highest honor and singing to the basilica he himself had built, as he reached the city gate the following verse unexpectedly met him in due order:

> “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.”

From this it can undoubtedly be inferred that the city had been so fortified by his prayers that, just as until then, by Christ’s favor, it had suffered no assaults from enemies over the long course of time, so thereafter also, with God’s help, it would suffer none.

For that outstanding shepherd, whose works testify that he lives, could easily obtain from God after his death that the city in which he had been bishop should be fortified for all time by his glorious merits, while the power of his body, shining in the most sacred temple he founded, manifested itself through the many benefits granted there to everyone.

### 8

Once, while the holy man was celebrating vigils in the same basilica with pastoral zeal, Ansanus, a deacon of Riez, had a nephew—the son of his brother—whom his parents had left behind when they died while he was still a child. Ansanus had taken responsibility for raising him and loved him more than if he had been his own son.

While the boy was playing with other children on the wall of that city, he fell from the wall, broke his neck, and died. Greatly shaken by the news, Ansanus hurried there, took up the boy’s body, covered it with clothing, and secretly carried it to the blessed bishop. Meanwhile he considered how he might publicly lay the body at the bishop’s feet and humbly beg him to restore the boy to life.

But because he knew that the proven soldier of Christ wholly avoided display, he preferred to carry the boy to the bishop’s chamber and, after laying him on the bed, cover him with the bishop’s blankets, entirely confident that the spiritual physician could awaken him through his prayers, since he was accustomed to bring health to the sick.

Then, not without great sorrow of spirit but nevertheless full of confidence, he approached the bishop, who was keeping vigil in the church and standing in his appointed place. When he saw him, the most merciful bishop ordered the singers to be silent so that he might explain what had happened. After completing the customary prayers with devotion, he sharply rebuked the deacon Ansanus for what he had done.

But Ansanus could not be driven away by fear; rather, more deeply moved in spirit, he threw himself at the bishop’s feet and cried out that he would not release them unless the bishop raised the dead boy. He said that the bishop could do this very easily, since, without anyone telling him, he had already learned what had happened to the child.

Compelled by this insistence and bound by the reason of the request, the bishop wished to go secretly with Ansanus to his bed. But he could not avoid the crowd of people who wanted to witness the miracle of so great an event.

When he reached the boy’s lifeless body, he began to implore divine aid with his whole body. Taking the boy’s hand with great confidence, he restored him to his former health.

All the people cried out:

“Glory to you, God!”

None of them allowed himself to be removed from the place until he saw the boy moving and heard him speaking. Because of the tumult of the people, the bishop could scarcely be brought back to the vigils by the efforts of his clergy. In this miracle both the great faith of the deacon and the power of the illustrious bishop shone forth.

### 9

It also happened that the only daughter of a certain widow, a young woman, died. When the miserable mother had prepared her according to custom to be carried out on a bier, she hurried anxiously to the blessed bishop and made the cause of her sorrow known to him more through tears than words, praying that he would pour out prayers over the lifeless body.

The holy bishop, moved by compassion, could neither refuse nor delay. He approached the corpse, raised his hands to heaven, prostrated himself, and implored God; and the dead woman was restored to life.

Immediately she awoke as if released from a heavy sleep, opened her burdened eyes, and rose when called. Her mother was overwhelmed with immense joy, and the whole people stood astonished. The bishop, who by the merits of his virtues had loosened the rights of death, withdrew at once, fleeing display.

But the people, praising God with loud voices, seized and tore away a large part of his garment in a kind of civic violence, intending to possess it as a relic. Thus, to proclaim his virtues, what had scarcely been left upon his shoulders has been preserved to the present day through the devotion of the faithful.

### 10

A certain young man was killed by the bite of a rabid dog, which choked him. The people saw it, went to the bishop, and begged him to come to the dead man.

But the bishop was suspended between conflicting thoughts: on the one hand, he could not disregard the tears of those who pleaded; on the other, he feared display. At last compassion overcame him. He did what they requested, came to the dead man, raised his hands to heaven, and, with his eyes likewise streaming, restored the dead man to life before the watching people.

The parents arrived, beat their breasts with their fists, and drenched their faces with such a flood of tears over their son that he could scarcely rise from the ground, even though he had returned to life. Extending one hand to his father and the other to his mother, he was lifted up as they supported his wavering limbs.

The people cried out, “Thanks be to God!” The man restored to life returned to his lodging, for whom a grave had already been prepared. His parents rejoiced with unbelievable joy; they could scarcely believe with their own eyes that the man who had been dead was alive.

Then that dog—which had torn this young man and many others with its hostile bites—came into the bishop’s presence. The bishop was moved, threw down his staff, raised his hands upward, and prayed to the Lord. Then he breathed upon the dog, and it was deprived of life.

It is certainly not astonishing that the blessed bishop, wishing to protect the flock entrusted to him, destroyed its enemy with a deadly stroke—not by a sword or an armed hand, but by the breath of his mouth.

Moreover, the wounds that the dog had inflicted with its teeth upon many among the people were healed by the blessed bishop through prayers and the sign of the cross, so completely that no traces of them appeared.

11. A wild ox had horribly mangled a man with its horn, his intestines spilling out. Some people soon brought him to the bishop. Although the bishop feared in every miracle lest he be overcome by spiritual pride, he nevertheless received the grievously wounded man with compassion. He treated his exposed entrails with warm applications, handling them with his own hands; he replaced them in their proper place through the wound inflicted by the ox, gently bound the wound with a sponge, and earnestly ordered that no one but himself dare remove the dressing. On the seventh day, when he took off the bandages, he found the man so completely healed [Col. 0038C] that scarcely any trace of the wound seemed to remain.

12. The most holy man disciplined the tender limbs of his body with the perpetual roughness of a hair shirt, which he used in place of an inner garment; he never removed it out of devotion to the cross, but even ordered that he be buried in it. He never wished to use baths, lest the steadfastness of spirit by which, having trampled underfoot the pleasures and enticements of the flesh, he endured martyrdom should grow soft.

A certain blind man, condemned to perpetual darkness for fifteen years, continually begged the most holy man to restore his sight through his prayers. But since the bishop delayed doing this in order to avoid ostentation, the blind man asked Rusticus, a subdeacon accustomed to serve him, to lead him at night to the entrance of the church which the bishop would be leaving after visiting the churches. The subdeacon did so, and as the blessed man was about to leave the church, he gently struck the blind man with his feet. The blind man humbly embraced his venerable footsteps and begged him to restore his sight. The bishop therefore confidently entreated the Lord, made the sign of the cross upon his eyes, and his lights, extinguished for so long, were immediately restored.

The bishop kissed the man and solemnly charged him to keep the matter secret. Yet the man could not do so because of the immense joy of his heart. Even if he had wished to conceal what had been done secretly, however, it could not remain hidden, since what had happened was plainly visible to everyone’s eyes.

13. The miracles of the most blessed bishop are innumerable, [Col. 0039A] and they cannot all be recounted, however lengthy an account may be woven. It was very easy for him to give sight to the blind, heal the lame, and raise the dead to life. In short, there was nothing he could not accomplish, since he possessed within himself the Holy Spirit who dwells there.

Meanwhile, while he shone with so many miracles and immense mysteries, he learned by divine revelation the day of his death. Then publicly, with the greatest humility, he earnestly asked everyone to permit him first to visit his native land and his relatives. Although this caused them great sorrow, he went to his own people and foretold that his death was already near. Thus, his arrival wonderfully delighted them, but this most sorrowful announcement greatly disturbed them.

And behold, while he placed himself upon his little bed as though about to fall asleep, he breathed his last during the singing of psalms [Col. 0039B] in the course of the divine office, and happily departed to heaven on the fifth day before the Kalends of December. At that time such an abundance of the sweetest fragrance filled the place as though all the flowers of springtime had been brought together there.

The fame of his death quickly filled not only the city but the whole world. From every direction crowds of the faithful came forward, eagerly wishing even to touch the covering of his bier, regarding such contact as a source of saving protection.

14. A certain young girl from a village called Decimae was being carried dead to the grave. Her corpse had already been arranged in a wooden coffin, but the coffin itself had not yet been covered. When those carrying her heard the voices of the people singing psalms and accompanying the sacred body [Col. 0039C] of the blessed bishop, they tearfully asked that the bier they were carrying be drawn over the girl’s body. Those others, inflamed by the ardor of faith and having no doubt about the outcome, thought that their holy prayers should by no means be rejected.

When what they had requested had been done, the men spoke among themselves of the blessed apostolic man Maximus, from whom divine grace had never been absent: although he had already paid nature’s debt, he nevertheless lived through his virtues and merits. Then they all prostrated themselves with the most steadfast devotion of heart, prayed at length, and afterward rose. When they had cried out “Kyrie eleison” seven times, they saw that the girl had returned to life.

Consequently, great fear seized them, and they were filled with a mixture of amazement and joy. The girl put aside her funeral garments, clothed herself in others, and, joining the throngs of the assembled people, publicly gave testimony to her restoration, in praise of the holy bishop, in these words:

“O most blessed merits of the priest! O blessed man, and blessed life of the bishop, who, in order to show that he would live eternally through divine reward, raised a dead woman after his death!”

15. At last the body of the most blessed bishop was brought into the town of Rhegium and buried with great solemnity in the church of blessed Peter, which he himself had founded. It was later called by his name because of his frequent patronage. There, whatever is confidently requested is obtained with Christ’s help.

Let faith therefore not be doubtful, since the power is infinite.

Not long afterward, when many things were being reported by many people in memory of the holy man, the subdeacon Cariatto, a man of most holy life, publicly gave this testimony:

“Let none of us doubt,” he said, “that the most blessed Maximus, of whose virtues so many things are reported at the prompting of truth, lived no less among angels than among human beings while he dwelt in a mortal body. The human condition kept him with us, but the dignity of his merits presented him as a constant companion to the blessed spirits.

“One night, as the very celebrated feast of blessed Andrew was approaching, I had been assigned the task of waking the others for the vigils. At the beginning of the night, a gentle sleep overcame me as I was anxiously attending to this duty, and I heard the sweet melodies of those singing psalms. Immediately awakened, I leapt from my bed in great agitation, thinking that I had neglected the proper time for waking them. Then I heard with my ears melodies of spiritual songs far sweeter than human effort could produce.

“I therefore went at once, with cautious steps, to the entrance of the same fortress. There I, a sinner, heard those most blessed apostles Peter and Andrew, in alternately honoring one another, completing a prayer with holy Maximus. At last, compelled by their continual offering, blessed Maximus could no longer delay them, and he concluded the office with these words:

“‘May the glory of God be blessed forever and unto ages of ages.’

“The others replied, ‘Amen.’

“But as I approached more closely out of curiosity, I could see no one there except the most sacred Maximus, prostrate face and body upon the floor of the church [Col. 0040C]. When he rose, he rebuked my curiosity, unworthy sinner that I was, in these words:

“‘It is difficult for human weakness to know the secrets of the saints, and presumptuous to wish to investigate them. Hear, therefore, what I, foreknowing it, am now about to tell you: take care that you do not disclose what you have seen and heard. For on whatever day you do so, you will depart from this life. Whether that is already destined to happen depends upon God’s will.’”

For my part, I leave to posterity the memory and testimony of his outstanding virtue, so that no mortal may be ignorant of how righteous people may enjoy the fellowship and companionship of the saints.

“This account gained abundant credibility from the fact that on that same day the subdeacon, as blessed Maximus had foretold to him, ceased to live among human beings; and because he could neither prolong the term of his life [Col. 0040D] nor wished to conceal the mystery.”

16. Let us therefore ask almighty God with complete devotion and the greatest zeal of heart that, relying upon the patronage of this most blessed bishop, he may grant us forgiveness of our sins and that he may always preserve our spirit pure from deadly vices—the one whose office we are celebrating in the present rite. In fulfilling this, may we present ourselves bodily in such a way that our minds may shine with the light of charity, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## In the Year of Our Lord 604. Saint Augustine, Apostle of the English.

[Col. 0041]

# Notice Concerning the Life of Saint Augustine

*(Bollandist, Acts of the Saints, May, vol. VI.)*

1. The memory of Saint Augustine is celebrated throughout all the martyrologies published after his death. The venerable Bede has this entry concerning him in the authentic Martyrology:

“Seven days before the Kalends of June, in Britain, the deposition of Saint Augustine, first bishop of the English.”

Rabanus has the same. Usuard writes as follows:

“In Britain, Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor, who, sent by blessed Pope Gregory, first preached the Gospel of Christ to the English people.”

Ado and Notker add that he rested in Christ there, glorious in virtues and miracles. Later writers generally follow them, together with the Roman Martyrology.

The venerable Bede illuminated his deeds in Book I, chapters 23 and following, and in Book II, chapters 2 and 3, of his Ecclesiastical History of the English People. From this you will find a collected Life in Surius. Capgrave published a shorter one in his Legend, adding at the end certain material concerning the translation of the body. We also possess several manuscript abridgements.

In general, all writers of English history, both earlier and more recent, have followed Bede. Among them Gocelinus stands out—so he himself writes his name, although others write Goscelinus or Gotzelinus. He brought forth innumerable Lives of the saints in polished style, or more elegantly corrected those that had been crudely edited. After Bede, he is second in recounting the praises of the saints of England, as we established from Book IV, chapter 1, of William of Malmesbury’s Deeds of the Kings of the English on 3 February, in the Life of Saint Werburga, virgin and daughter of the kings of Mercia. Gocelinus composed that Life. There we discussed at length this author, who flourished around the year 1080 and afterward; we shall discuss him again on 10 June, in the Life of Saint Ivo the Persian.

This author, formerly a monk of Ramsey and later a Canterbury monk at Saint Augustine’s, published the Life of Augustine in two separate works, a longer and a shorter one, as is indicated in the following prologue. We give the longer work together with the book of miracles, in which the things written by Bede about Saint Augustine are often repeated once or twice. We give it as it has been printed since 1668 among the Acts of the Benedictine Saints, edited in volume I by Jean Mabillon. Through the same man’s efforts we append the previously unpublished work of the aforesaid Gocelinus addressed to Anselm, venerable archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the translation of Saint Augustine, apostle of the English, and his companions. It was written in the seventh year after the translation itself, in the year of Christ 109.

That work is divided into two books. The first properly concerns Saint Augustine; the second concerns his companions—that is, the bishops, kings, and abbots buried in the same church, and those transferred before him into the new church in the year 1091, two years before Anselm became archbishop. To him the history is dedicated, and it will cast great light upon English affairs and saints, especially in the second book. Although that book chiefly concerns others, it nevertheless should not have been separated from the first.

The shorter work of the same Gocelinus on Saint Augustine, with the author’s name omitted, is found in the appendix to the works of blessed Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, edited by Luc d’Achery; it can be read there. We take note of certain matters from it in the annotations.

2. It is not sufficiently clear among the authors in what year Saint Augustine departed from this mortal life to Christ. Bede merely notes that he died seven days before the Kalends of June. The Worcester writer adds that it was on a Tuesday; these indications correspond to the leap year 608, with the dominical letters G and F. The Westminster writer and Sigebert likewise assigned his death to that year.

We have argued for this chronology at greater length from the timing of the successions of Laurence and Mellitus, in the Life of Saint Laurence on 2 February, no. 10.

In volume I of the English Monastic, p. 90, the foundation of the monastery of Ely in the territory of Cambridge is presented. From a history of the church of Ely preserved in the Cottonian Library, the following is written:

“In the primitive Church of nascent faith and Christianity, blessed Augustine built a church there in honor of Mary, ever-virgin, in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 607, the second year after his arrival in England; King Ethelbert was the first founder of this work.”

It is therefore clear that Saint Augustine was still alive in that year. Many writers have said many things about his monastic profession and that of the other first apostles of England, but it is not possible here to report and examine them all. A few points suffice: those which we set forth in favor of the Benedictines before the Life of Saint Gregory, no. 11, on the authority of Saints Aldhelm and Wilfrid. There is no need to repeat them here, since they contain no force of entirely clear demonstration. For that reason we refrain from expressing any particular rule in the title, as we often do with monks of the first seven centuries.

Nevertheless, we do not wish to prejudice the Benedictines, who count Augustine among their own with the greatest probability and almost demonstrative evidence. A new and remarkably relevant support has also been added from the most ancient English litanies, which Mabillon published in volume II of his Ancient Collections and proved to have been in use before the end of the seventh century, on the basis of the absence of saints from later centuries, although those saints were otherwise very famous among the English.

In those litanies, among confessors, no founder of monastic life is prescribed by name except Saint Benedict—and he is named twice. This privilege is granted there to no other person except Saint Stephen, who is ordered to be named three times, just as Saint Mary is named three times. This is almost decisive evidence that either Saint Augustine himself, or the monks established by him in England who compiled these litanies, recognized that one man alone as the founder of their monastic life.

Since the litanies have been mentioned, it may also be noted that by decree of the Council of Clovesho, celebrated in the year 747, it was enacted that the day of the deposition of Saint Augustine, archbishop, should be kept as a holiday by clergy and monasteries, and that his name should always be recited in the chanting of the litany after that of Saint Gregory, as the apostle of England.

4. William Thorn, a monk of Saint Augustine’s, in the Chronicle of his monastery, which he brought from Augustine’s arrival down to the year 1397, briefly summarizes in chapter VIII, §3, the matters concerning the translation of the Saint, without considering any others who had been translated earlier or at the same time:

“In the year of the Lord 1091, Wydo, governing this church with pastoral dignity, happily completed his church, which his predecessor Scotland, prevented by death, could not finish completely, and diligently worked to translate the saints.

“Therefore, in the year mentioned above, on the eighth day before the Ides of September, he translated the body of blessed Augustine from the place where it had lain for five hundred years. He placed all the larger bones of that saint and his head in a stone tomb, most carefully sealed with iron and lead, upon which this inscription was written:

> Illustrious bishop of the English, devout and lofty ornament,  
> Here holy Augustine rests in body.

“He then goes on to relate how, out of fear of the barbarians who frequently invaded the regions of Kent, the same abbot removed most of the bones of the sacred body from the tomb on the following night and hid them in a nearby place. They remained concealed there until the year 1221, when they were again discovered and translated, as he explains more fully in chapter II, §2.

Gocelinus was partly unaware of all these matters because they were kept secret, and partly could not have known them because they had not yet occurred. They will be set forth below as an appendix at the end of the first book.

Here, from chapter IX, §3, as pertaining to the feast of the translation, I note that King William II in 1092 granted the monastery a holiday for the translation of Saint Augustine, lasting five days: two days before the feast and two days after it. He also granted that the church of Saint Augustine should meanwhile enjoy all the customs which the king possessed throughout the city of Canterbury.

The monks kept this holiday until the time of Edward, son of King Henry. At that time they abandoned it entirely because of quarrels, disputes, and even fights that frequently took place in their cemetery.

5. Furthermore, in the year 1356, as the same William Thorn writes, Pope Innocent VI, among the other privileges granted to the monastery, instructed the archbishop—probably the archbishop of Canterbury—to cause the feast of Saint Augustine to be celebrated as a double feast, in these words:

“We consider it fitting and proper that the glorious confessor, blessed Augustine, who was once sent by the Apostolic See to the English peoples, who at that time had not yet been reborn through the water of baptism, and who summoned them from the darkness of unbelief into the light of the Catholic faith through the mystery of preaching, and who first established a church in England, should be specially honored in those regions. For through this the devotion of the peoples there will increase, and he who is glorified in the assembly of the saints will look graciously upon the prayers of his devotees.

“Therefore, so that the feast of that confessor may be honored and venerated more solemnly and devoutly in the aforesaid regions, where, as we have learned, it is scarcely, or less than it should be, solemnly celebrated in the kingdom of England, we commit and order through apostolic letters that, by our authority, you cause the feast of that confessor in all the exempt churches of the said kingdom to be solemnly celebrated under a double office for all future time.

“Moreover, on the said feast, you shall cause mechanical and other work to cease, as is customary, by the practice, custom, or observance of those churches, on double feasts.”

[Col. 0043]

# Life of Saint Augustine, by Gocelinus the Monk

*(From the Paris edition of Jean Mabillon.)*

## Prologue

[Col. 0043A]

To the dearest lords and sons of paternal affection, the Church of Saint Augustine, together with its revered abbot, from that most abject and unworthy-to-be-remembered man, yet sincere friend of all: greetings in the Lord.

I had resolved not to bring this history—like a most beautiful daughter of the divine bride and mother Church—forth from its bridal chamber [Alt.: “proceed”], until, adorned with its ornaments, ribbons, and necklaces, it could proceed without reproach. But your commanding affection, impatient of delay and pressing me more urgently, has at last compelled me to present it in a shamefaced appearance, since we have been unable to make it beautiful. For many disturbances in our affairs have taken away the elegance and swift progress we had intended.

How truly what we have written is confirmed is shown incontestably by the times, places, and persons—when, where, and among whom the events are known to have occurred—by your ancient and modern writings, and also by the eyes of those who are present.

As for the fact that we have made new things from old, or have extended recently accomplished events in a recent style, let no inhabitant of antiquity be indignant at novelty, lest he seem to be indignant with God, who is always creating new things. For the God of Abraham is the God of Augustine; and the one who worked the signs of ancient times works the same signs today in his modern and present-day saints. To him the prophet cries: “Renew the signs and change the wonders” (Ecclesiasticus 36:6). He creates new heavens, and, seated upon the throne, makes all things new.

If the ancient Fathers had not accepted what was then considered new, we would now have nothing ancient. But Jews and other unbelievers, enemies of holy novelty and truth, prefer to remain in the darkness of their antiquity and error rather than be enlightened by the light of new grace. Even under grace, those seem to imitate them who, weighed down by resentment of ancient practice, shrink from being renewed for the better by God’s new miracles.

Many people also refuse to believe what they despise; what they love, they eagerly seek, readily believing it. Yet no one should despise any herald of truth, however humble or insignificant. For just as a lie cannot become true through anyone’s authority, so truth possesses its own authority in every person.

The things commanded through visions or dreams are proved true by what follows from them. Thus, we read that the sick were ordered in dreams to come to the tombs of saints for the sake of healing, and that, when they obeyed, they recovered their health there.

Anyone who prefers to mock this evident truth as empty dreams rather than attend to it could also reject Joseph and Daniel and the other prophets, as well as Joseph himself in the Gospel and the foreigner Nebuchadnezzar, who saw divine mysteries, as dreamers.

There are also people who foolishly become indignant when the miracles of saints are recounted as having occurred among lowly persons, as though the names or memory of such people were disgraceful [or: as though such names or memories were disgraceful]. Yet nothing is said on their account; everything is narrated for the glory of God in them, who performs marvelous works in the least of people.

For the Lord of all does not disdain to mention the beggar Lazarus by name. Indeed, neither Herod, nor the traitor Judas, nor Caiaphas would be named in the Gospel except for the sake of the Lord or of those against whom they plotted.

Let kindly souls understand that we have said these things because of the disputes of various people, lest, by beginning to listen to detractors, they grow weary of what they love and believe less firmly what they have recognized as more true: “Bad company corrupts good character.”

We have composed two books on the same subject, a larger and a smaller one. The smaller may courteously satisfy tedious friends from outside; the larger may overflow more abundantly for eager members of the household. Nevertheless, some things are found in the larger and some in the smaller; neither book contains everything. One has one kind of seasoning, the other another. The same events are also related differently in one and in the other, so that each may need the help and favor of the other.

The poet says of eloquent Ulysses:

> He often used to relate the same thing in another way.

[Col. 0045B]

With this pious allusion and pious commendation to devoted friends, we ask both those present and those to come to remember our affection and devoted service, although we have been ungrateful.

Thus far the prologue. In it we have corrected two words conjecturally, and henceforth we shall exercise the same freedom in what follows. We shall nevertheless place within brackets the reading which we think requires correction. Likewise, when words are lacking, we sometimes add them to complete the sense, but we place them within parentheses. They are to remain there only until, after comparison with other manuscripts that we have not yet been able to see, the original text may be restored by someone willing to undertake this labor for the sake of the saint and of our work.

Mabillon transferred the author’s division to the margin and gathered the chapter titles at the beginning. The same arrangement is preserved here by means of numbers, with only a new division of chapters introduced, suitable to our purpose of maintaining uniformity. The same will be done in the first book concerning the translation.

## Division of the Chapters

**Chapter I.** While the Lord, conqueror of the world, distributes the kingdoms of the captive tyrant to his palm-bearing servants, Augustine, the divine Legate, receives by lot an inheritance in Oceanic Britain from the Roman See.

**II.** Here the world of Augustine is described as a kind of earthly paradise, fertile and gracious in its resources.

**III.** The Lord prepared this vast dwelling for his Augustine, just as he prepared the created world for created humanity from the beginning; and Augustine, leaving his homeland, became a great nation.

**IV.** Pope Gregory took him up and intended to send him to England on his behalf, so that he might make the English, a white people, an angelic people.

**V.** The man of virtues is sent with forty evangelical companions to convert England. They go armed for the fruitful endurance of glory.

**VI.** The saints, terrified by an evil report, are more courageously encouraged by Augustine to begin their journey of virtue through Gregory’s letter.

**VII.** Blessed Gregory’s letter to them, instructing them to obey Augustine perseveringly.

**VIII.** A letter from the same pope to Aetherius, archbishop of Arles, asking him to provide what Augustine and his companions require.

**IX.** When Augustine reports the apostolic commands to his companions, they hasten through adversity and prosperity toward true rewards, while heavenly grace also consoles them with miracles.

**X.** The pilgrims of God are driven out of Angers by women. Following Augustine’s staff as it flies from his hand for three stadia, they rest outdoors under the open sky at night, are illumined by heavenly radiance, and are satisfied by a spring divinely brought forth from the ground. There the leader wrote his name and the reason for his journey.

**XI.** The neighbors, terrified by the great brightness seen at night, run to the place in the morning. They mourn their guilt over the saints whom they had driven away, and recognize Augustine from the letters written upon the ground. There they establish a church in his honor, which permanently excludes every woman.

**XII.** A matron attempts to enter it with a candle but dies before the threshold, at the very forbidden boundary, her intestines bursting; and she frightens all the women of her sex even more severely.

**XIII.** The miracle is heard by the bishop of Angers himself, who dedicates the rebuilt church. At its dedication, the crops that had been trampled completely down and regarded as utterly hopeless prove more abundant at harvest than all the others.

**XIV.** After passing through various dangers in different lands, Augustine and his companions reach Britain, the perpetual dwelling ordained by divine providence.

**XV.** The island of Thanet is the first to receive Christ in his saints: a blessed land, made most fortunate by its fertility in receiving so many God-bearing strangers.

**XVI.** Ethelbert, third among the kings of the English but first as a worshiper of Christ, more merciful because of his Christian wife, receives from Augustine the best message of eternal salvation; yet he does not readily consent, so that the difficulty may increase the saints’ glory. He comes to Thanet to hear the strangers, standard-bearers and heralds of the Lord’s cross.

**XVII.** Augustine explains to the king the best message he has brought: namely, that the creator and redeemer of the world has opened the kingdom of heaven to the human race, made heavenly citizens from earthly people, and loved human beings so much that he wished to become human and, after countless miracles and manifestations of his divinity, to die the death of the cross for the (love) of humankind. He also kindled his legates with an inextinguishable fire, making them invincible to every torture, so that they might convert the nations. It was because they were urged on by such a flame of charity that they had come.

**XVIII.** King Ethelbert praises the promises of eternal blessedness and gathers the saints because of their goodwill, but he does not yet know how to cast off the darkness of his ancient error and put on the new light.

**XIX.** Through the king’s mercy—or rather through God’s providence—the holy strangers enter Dorobernia, their perpetual dwelling, carrying aloft the standard of the Lord’s cross and accompanied by melodious prayers. They live angelically as pilgrims of the world and citizens of heaven, and as fellow heirs of the kingdom of God that is growing among them.

**XX.** In the eastern church of Saint Martin at Dorobernia, formerly founded by Roman Christians, the faithful guardian of the queen, blessed Bishop Liudhard, performed the divine offices. The most sacred Augustine, with his choir, illumined them by apostolic life and teaching and by an abundance of signs, through which he converted many.

**XXI.** The king, overcome by the sweet allurements of eternal blessedness and the irrefutable examples of virtue, submits to Christ with devoted faith.

**XXII.** The king, made most humble from his high position and ecclesiastical from being a prince, is baptized in confession of and in the name of the supreme Trinity. He is filled with Christ’s white dove and becomes a new worshiper of Christ from an old idolater. At this Augustine sings to God, with the highest chorus, rejoicing that his prayers have prospered in this way.

**XXIII.** The king rejoices in his new brotherhood of commanders and peoples baptized together. He no longer considers his kingdom his own to administer, but strives to transfer and extend it, together with the kings and peoples subject to him, into the sweet dominion of Christ. He builds bishops’ sees, monasteries, and churches royally, as though they were strongholds of the Lord.

**XXIV.** Augustine, submitting himself to apostolic and ecclesiastical election—indeed, to the Lord’s appointment—is consecrated by the archbishop of Arles as the first patriarch of England and brings perpetual blessing back to Dorobernia.

**XXV.** Augustine sends word to blessed Gregory in Rome that the king and people of the English have embraced the worship of Christ, that he has become a bishop, and that workers are now lacking for the great harvest. The pope sends him the apostolic pallium and many learned assistants, together with answers to various questions.

**XXVI.** Blessed Pope Gregory’s letter concerning the pallium that was sent, the jurisdiction of the bishop of London, the metropolitan of York, and Augustine’s authority over all the priests of Britain.

**XXVII.** Another letter of the same pope, sent through Mellitus to Augustine, ordering that idols be destroyed and well-built shrines be cleansed for divine worship with blessed water. The faithful are not to sacrifice animals to the devil, but are to kill animals for their own food in praise of God and give thanks to the giver of all things.

**XXVIII.** The same pope, having heard of so many and such continual miracles of Augustine, exclaims joyfully in God’s glory, yet, fearing that human weakness might become insolent, tempers his praise by sending a letter to the man of virtues.

**XXIX.** The same blessed Gregory, rejoicing with King Ethelbert over the Christianity he has embraced, urges him in a gentle letter carefully to preserve this grace and quickly extend it to the peoples subject to him. He tells him to overthrow the shrines and to exhort, terrify, and correct his subjects; to build [churches] after the example of Constantine, the most devout emperor, who cast aside idols and converted Rome, together with the peoples of the nations, to Christ with his whole mind. At the same time he advises him to obey Augustine, so that God may more quickly hear Augustine praying for him.

**XXX.** The same most outstanding illuminator of the churches also praises the venerable Queen Bertha graciously in a letter, both for the king’s conversion and for her pious care of blessed Augustine and his companions; he urges her to increase these famous merits with greater attention.

[Col. 0048A]

**XXXI.** Blessed Augustine gathers these honeycombs of the sweetness of Gregory’s letters, ascending beyond all the steps of virtue to the starry ladder. The king and queen also, drinking them in according to their devotion and capacity, strive to obey the apostolic instructions, so that after their perishing kingdoms they might deserve to attain the heavenly ones.

**XXXII.** With the king’s assistance, Augustine summoned the Britons, remnants of those who had fought against the English and dissenters from ecclesiastical discipline. With all the persistence of paternal affection, he strove to bring them into legitimate concord with everyone; but it is exceedingly difficult to correct those who irrationally oppose reason.

**XXXIII.** The Lord’s advocate, bringing a blind man forward, said: “Here let the Lord of all show whose doctrine is true.” He proposed that the blind man be healed before the Britons. When they refused, Augustine gave sight to the blind man by the sign of the cross. The defeated Britons asked for a postponement while they consulted their own people and the synod was convened again.

**XXXIV.** The bishops of the Britons, after consultation, replied that when Augustine approached them they should rise to receive him as gentle and humble of heart, but that when he remained seated they should reject him as proud and fierce. They came and angrily spurned him because he remained seated and did not rise for them.

Still desiring to win them more gently, he proposed three things to be observed, allowing tolerance in other matters for the time being: that they celebrate Easter at the proper time, like all the churches; that they administer the sacraments of baptism according to ecclesiastical order; and that, by evangelizing together with the English, they acquire brothers and fellow citizens of the kingdom of God.

But when they rejected everything, he foretold that they would perish at the hands of those whom they were unwilling to have saved.

**XXXV.** King Ethelfrid of the English savagely fulfilled this prophecy of the Lord’s herald. He destroyed the Britons in war and killed twelve hundred of their monks, who were fighting against him with especially intense prayer.

**XXXVI.** After the foretold evils had come upon the uncorrectable Britons, Augustine, intent upon the salvation of all, went to the metropolitan city of York. On the journey he raised up a man deprived of movement by paralysis and of sight by blindness, and makes him a Christian [Alt.: “made him”].

**XXXVII.** On the day of the Lord’s Nativity he baptized more than ten thousand believers in the river Sioalira, apart from the countless number of children and women.

[Col. 0048D]

**XXXVIII.** There they crossed the impassable depths not only unharmed but with all the sick receiving health. A church was also founded there in memory of blessed Augustine, where many benefits are bestowed upon the faithful.

**XXXIX.** Concerning the letter sent by blessed Pope Gregory to Saint Eulogius, patriarch, in which he rejoices in the Lord over the conversion of the English accomplished through Augustine, and says that Augustine and those sent with him appear to imitate the virtues and signs of the apostles; also concerning the ten thousand or more baptized in a single day.

**XL.** Returning successfully from York, he encounters a sick man wasting away in the foul whiteness of leprosy, who murmurs a tearful complaint for his paternal mercy. With the Lord he hears, in clamorous compassion, [Col. 0049A] the clamorous desire of the silent murmur [the syntax is uncertain]; and, through the power of the one who says in the Gospel, “Be cleansed,” he makes this pallid man wholly clean by holy faith [Alt.: “deed” instead of “faith”].

**XLI.** Augustine, desirable to all who are good but hateful to the enemies of light, deforms the indomitable abusers of the saints with eternal disgrace in the spirit of Elijah. He continually restores suppliant sick people to health.

**XLII.** Another judgment is added to this punishment upon another nation of the incorrigible: namely, that, by a new and previously unknown disease, all, from the least to the greatest, should burn in a sulfurous fire throughout the world until, smelted free from the dross of impiety and refined into the precious mass of faith, they were purified. The unquenchable punishment would be extinguished only by the baptism of Christ, with Augustine’s aid, and this calamity would be removed from that land forever.

[Col. 0049B] **XLIII.** Augustine and his companions, having withdrawn from the aforementioned opponents, were burning with severe thirst; but the Lord comforted the leader himself by appearing and speaking to him, so that he might firmly believe that, whatever he faithfully requested, he would obtain.

**XLIV.** The Lord’s prophet fixed his staff in the place where the fountain of life appeared, and brought forth a plentiful spring, health-giving for those who thirsted and for sufferers from various diseases. He called the place Cernel, from “seeing God,” and there built a church for the Lord the Savior in memory of so great a revelation; there also stands a distinguished monastery constructed in honor of the chief of the Apostles, Peter.

**XLV.** Augustine appeared by night to the parish priest of Cernel, who was gasping in a mortal illness, and ordered him to go to the aforesaid fountain, made famous by his name, and there to sing Psalm 50 three times, with a triple washing of the body. The priest rose and recovered the strength to go; obeying the commands, he returned healthy and in the morning performed the priestly offices for the people.

**XLVI.** After traveling through part of Britain, Augustine returned to his perpetual dwelling at Canterbury, and was received with joy by all, as the return of their sun.

**XLVII.** The merciful guardian restored a young man condemned by the loss of walking, hearing, and speech; and when he had again abused his restored health through his customary way of life and had been struck again by infirmity, the Father’s kindness once more restored him through a threefold healing.

**XLVIII.** It is read that he was present when the blessed martyr Livinus was being baptized; that heavenly splendor shone upon the baptized man; and that the divine right hand blessed him three times with the sign of the cross. Then, by angelic command and guidance, Livinus came to Augustine across the waves of the broad sea on foot, as though across a flowery meadow, and received from him instruction in complete perfection. Augustine kept him with himself for five years, consecrated him a priest to the Lord, generously furnished him with priestly insignia, and sent him back from being a disciple as a teacher of his own people. [Col. 0049D]

**XLIX.** The testimony of Veturnosus, whose third generation, still living today, asserts that he saw the blessed Augustine and that a modest Christian rose from his baptistery, slippery and covered in mist [reading uncertain]; and that Augustine himself, surrounded by a continual crowd, performed innumerable signs. A survivor of the present age also reported that, as transmitted from ancient times, the holy Father’s form and appearance were patrician, as was his stature; and that, as he traversed his native lands barefoot, he drew calluses upon the soles of his feet. [Col. 0050A]

**L.** Now wholly wounded by eternal loves, now absorbed from earthly tumults into the Lord’s rest, he was making forceful assault upon heaven through repeated blows of prayers, sighs, and tears. At last, understanding from the response of the Holy Spirit that his desire had been heard, he appointed blessed Laurence—renowned for apostolic virtues and chief among his companions—as his successor, with the king and the assembled people rejoicing immensely and with every solemn joy. This was in imitation of the chief of the Apostles, Peter, who once appointed Clement, namely because of the need for the instruction of a newly established community.

**LI.** Having sweetly exhorted the king, the Church, and the people to persevere in faith and love of Christ, and leaving to all pledges of perpetual affection, in the presence of the king and of Bishop Laurence, amid the tearful throng of everyone, while a heavenly choir surrounded him, he passed to the Lord’s eternal solemnities. Let us, feeble praisers, accompany them not with funeral lamentations but with triumphal songs. [Col. 0050B]

**LII.** In the monastery he founded, dedicated by Saint Laurence, the most precious pearl of his body was laid to rest amid rejoicing.

**LIII.** How beautifully Rome, mother of the Churches, produced such pledges, who stand forth as fathers and founders of the whole British Ocean! With what fragrance of sweetness and splendor of glory one love and one dwelling bind them together, though distributed among the various nations of the world, each shining forth like a sun as patron to his own people. [Col. 0050C]

# CHAPTER ONE  
## Deeds up to the Entry: Miracles Performed in Gaul

**I.** The most powerful conqueror of the world’s tyrant, drawing everything to himself in the trial of the cross and bearing the insignia of the name prescribed long ago—“Quickly strip off the spoils; hasten to plunder”—distributed all the spoils of the captive plunderer among his victorious commanders. Peter seized Rome, the citadel of affairs; Paul subdued everything in the battle array. Achaia fell to Andrew, Asia to John, Ethiopia to Matthew, and the vast India of the sunrise to Thomas and Bartholomew. And, not to prolong the account by treating each one separately, at last Gregory, the supreme leader of the Lord’s wedding-song, embraced the whole world with apostolic wings. Augustine, however, for whom this crown is woven with heavenly gems, encircled another world of the British Ocean with his apostleship.

Happy Rome, which, after the first theoretical leaders of the faith, produced such eminent consuls of the Church! Once dominant under the imperial monarchy, it afterward remained almost submerged beneath the storms of war, so that it might give birth to these two great lights of the world: one to rule the day, the other to rule the night that was to be turned into day. Gregory shone among the children of light over the Christian world like the sun of day; Augustine illumined the dark world of paganism and the nocturnal chaos of the Ocean with the lamp of the moon, and, as dawn succeeded, transformed it into the solar midday of Christ.

Augustine attacked this obstinate zone of the world, ringed by the arms of nations and demons, more courageously than great-hearted Caleb once attacked Hebron, the hundred-city [or perhaps city of giants]. This is your portion in Christ; this is your inheritance; this is your homeland transferred to heaven. O star born of Rome, and our patriarch in this region! You acquired it for the Lord; you acquired it for the Lord, and you yourself possessed it. Whatever piety this land produces, whatever it makes blossom, whatever fruit it bears—you are its cultivator, its sower, its planter. Everything is yours in the Lord.

Whatever it has produced of saints, you are its founder, its first-ranking leader, its prince. Everything looks to you, follows you, and crowns you—everything for which you labored with the Lord: “You shall eat the labor of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you.” Kings, nobles, fathers, and the people follow you; they celebrate you as protector and first father. [Col. 0051A]

**2.** But with what praise shall I exalt this Augustinian world? It is an earthly paradise upon the earth; whatever wealth is possessed anywhere either arises here or is brought here by Amphitrite, encircling it with nations flowing in from every direction. You might believe that the greatest world found or stored up here all together its riches and delights, which it distributes piecemeal among its several regions.

It is an imperial kingdom, ruled with august authority by Roman Caesars, who boasted that they possessed here as well as at Rome the throne of the world. The land is abundant, fertile in every kind of sowing and planting, and produces luxuriantly not only the plants accustomed to its own country but also those of Greece and more remote regions [alternative: of a more remote region]. It opens out most widely in rich fields, verdant meadows, broad plains, fat pastures, milk-flowing flocks, and horses and warlike herds. Frequent springs pour forth their hundredfold waters, along with leaping streams, notable and famous rivers, and lakes and ponds continually supplied with fish and birds and with transport for ships, convenient to cities and peoples. [Col. 0051B]

Groves and forests flourish, both lowland and mountain, full of acorns and wild fruits and rich in various kinds of hunting. There are also chestnut woods, welcome at the banquets of the wealthy. Vineyards too—[alternative: vines] not only Gallic and Italian but also Alban, Argive, and Punic—answer with the richest fields [alternative: will answer]. There are here salt springs, as well as hot springs and warm rivers, furnished with hot baths.

What shall I say of the wealth of the sea, which fills and adorns this kingdom not only with merchandise for ships but also with innumerable kinds of fish? Among these, diverse and enormous creatures of the sea are caught everywhere: dolphins, sea-calves, and, in addition, mountainous whales. Shellfish glow red beyond Indian and Sidonian dyes; while other things all change or diminish with age, these preserve and intensify their beauty, harmed neither by sun nor rain. The shells contain treasures fit for adornment—namely, gemlike circles of pearls, splendid in their whiteness, and the many-colored beauties of pearls. [Col. 0051C]

Some are red, others green; these are clothed in purple, those in hyacinth-blue, others in leek-green; but the greater multitude of them shines white. With these, the skill of goldsmiths adorns the golden necklaces of the Church among splendid stones. Even the golden embroidery of English maidens equals or surpasses them: their royal and pontifical insignia, glowing with dipped purple and scarlet dyed twice, are studded with shining pearls and gems set in bordering gold, and precious emblems shine more brilliantly through the mingling of workmanship.

Only Hesperia, Britain, and Eastern India are sisters in pearls. This land also produces jet in prodigious abundance, all the more precious because rarer in other ages. It shines with a gemlike blackness; it is also found purple, wax-colored, whitish, and green. It burns when brought near fire; when rubbed and heated, it attracts light material as a diamond attracts iron; when set alight [alternative: when intensified], it drives away snakes.

Moreover, rich masses of metals are extracted from veins of copper, iron, lead, tin, silver, and gold. You may also marvel at the rocks and crags of bronze-colored stone, and at the temples and walls constructed everywhere from rocky mountains and adorned with a kind of native marble. [Col. 0052A]

**3.** The Lord’s lavish hand prepared this vast dwelling-place of so beautiful and wealthy a world for his beloved Augustine. Once, when he had created the world and completed all its adornment, he finally introduced the human being whom he had created as a friend and for whom he had prepared these things.

Blessed Augustine therefore left his sweet foster-child and august mother, Rome, embracing a distant and dangerous pilgrimage as his homeland, so that from the raging nations he might bear fruit in patience and acquire an everlasting inheritance for Christ. He went out from his senatorial ancestry with the patriarch Abraham and, coming into a land provided by God, became a great nation. He multiplied like the stars of heaven in the multitude of saints who followed him and in the faithful people of the nations.

He therefore grew nobly into so many children of love, having come to lay down his life for foreigners. Others conquered bravely; he conquered both bravely and successfully, bearing a bloodless martyrdom with a warrior’s spirit. Blessed too was he who left everything, obtained the kingdom of heaven, and received everything here a hundredfold. His angelic charity and most noble generosity—most lavish toward everyone and most sparing toward himself—made this exceedingly abundant kingdom, splendid for proud emperors, beneficial to all by trampling down desire.

Happy poverty, which enriched so many! Blessed abstinence, which always feeds an unfailing household! The more he constrained himself, the more we are enlarged; what he fasted from, we feast upon. Indeed, he himself possesses and is exalted in all things through his heirs.

But while we write these things, this maritime Elysium flourished as the world renewed itself, and, with the starry birthday of glorious Augustine approaching amid the Easter flowers, it smiled with every beauty. It is therefore pleasing to return to the sequence of his aforesaid arrival and finally to unfold some of his innumerable virtues.

**4.** The illustrious lawgiver of the Lord, Gregory, had seen boys for sale at Rome, attractive with reddish hair and exceptional beauty. Since his charity extended to all from the depths of his heart, he eagerly asked the names of their people, province, and king. He learned that they were Angles, that their province was Deira, and that their king was called Alle; but that they all obeyed paganism.

The kindly soul groaned that flowers so suited to God’s paradise were devoted to the grim altars of demons. But immediately, like a prophetic interpreter, rejoicing in the auspices of their names, he said: “Good—Angles, bright with an angelic face! Good also—Deirans, destined to be seen from the wrath of God! Good too that the king is called Alle, whose land shall sing ‘alleluia.’”

He therefore undertook the journey to convert the Angles. But because of the Roman people’s resistance—or rather because the Spirit of the Lord Jesus, directing everything wisely, provided otherwise—he was recalled, the Lord reserving this grace for another friend. When, however, he assumed the apostolate at Rome, which had more seriously hindered him from his purpose, he found a more powerful means of carrying out his plan: what he could not accomplish personally, he fulfilled through his splendid lamp and armed right hand, Augustine.

In Augustine he found a man after his own heart, the sole remedy in the Lord for his holy desire, a man of every virtue, prepared for the Lord’s battles and eager for the crown through arduous and courageous deeds. He was like the fortified tower of David, in which are the shield, spear, and every armor of the strong, and adorned for every purpose; an evangelical vessel of the knowledge of God, the Lord’s golden vessel of election. He marveled at his noble spirit, so attentive to his exhortation, that he seemed not so much willing to follow toward the palm as to run ahead. [Col. 0053B]

**5.** Having therefore gathered a company like an angelic household of learned heralds of Christ, who would serve as companions, helpers, and fellow workers with the leader Augustine, and having found them all ready and unanimous for the proposed work, he offered tireless thanks to the author of every good will.

Without delay, he carefully exhorted and armed them for the fruitful endurance of glory; having provided everything suitable for pilgrims in the world, he commended them to God and the angels of peace and sent them on the road of eternal salvation.

It would be lengthy to explain, but it is pious to recall, what darts of wounded charity the blessed souls of Gregory and Augustine and of the holy brothers felt when they were torn from the maternal womb of the monastic Church by bodily separation; what prayers for a blessed restoration, what sighs, and what tears they exchanged, since they did not hope to see beyond their beloved homeland—or rather, again to see one another—the faces of such beloved fathers and companions in this exile, and were migrating to so distant and foreign a barbarism and to such uncertain dangers of life.

Thus once the cows carrying the Lord’s ark, after their calves had been taken away, lowed, yet never turned aside from the straight line of the road. For the saints went on, going and weeping as they crossed toward the homeland of life, sowing the seeds of virtues in tears; but when they come, they shall come in resurrection with rejoicing, carrying sheaves of gladness from mourning and death.

It was then the six-hundredth year from the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: Rather, it was only the year 595 of the common era, and it was the fourteenth year of Maurice; of Pope Gregory, the fourth year and, below in the letter of Saint Gregory also cited, the fourteenth indiction. In Bede, book I, chapter 23, the year of Christ is omitted.], and the fourteenth year of Maurice’s reign; the intervening dating phrase is textually corrupt. It was approximately the one hundred and fiftieth year since the Angles had invaded Britain, and the fourth year of the ordination of blessed Pope Gregory, when he, the most illustrious gem of the Roman pontiffs, sent these starry lights to the Angles, with Augustine shining before them.

There were forty bearers of the Lord’s embassy, namely four times ten, imitating the four living creatures of the Law and the Gospel. Once the Lawgiver had sent the same number of scouts to inspect the promised land; but those were faithless except for two, whereas these were faithful. Those, being sons of strangers, lied to the Lord; these, sons by adoption, clung to the truth.

They proceeded like sheep to the sacrifice—a great spectacle, visible to the world [alternative: of the world], to angels and human beings, and terrifying to the powers of the air like an army drawn up in battle array. [Col. 0054A]

**6.** They had already gone some days’ journey from their kindred house, eager to run along the road of the Lord’s commandments. But the Truth says, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mark 26:41 [citation as printed], and John 15:5), and, “Without me you can do nothing.” They had to be taught, through human weakness, to act manfully—not presuming on themselves but hoping in God—and to conquer in him who conquered the world. “In God,” says the Psalmist, “we shall perform valorous deeds” (Psalm 59:14).

The athletes of God, forgetful of their own steadfastness, were carried away by the empty talk of men, while the deception of demons was scattered about. It was reported that the people whom they sought were more savage than beasts; that they preferred cruelty to feasting; that they thirsted for innocent blood; that they abhorred the Christian faith; and that they answered teachers of salvation only with tortures and slaughter. It was said that the saints could be punished without cause, while enemies of the truth could be moved neither by reason nor by signs.

Thus, despairing of the salvation of such people and of their own progress, they made their superior Augustine, who was unable to resist them, their envoy to blessed Gregory. Gregory had appointed him bishop for the Angles if they accepted Christ. They humbly begged through Augustine that Gregory release them from the expenditure of labors so dangerous and fruitless among unknown languages and consent peacefully to their return home.

For they were still weak: ready indeed for the Lord’s expedition, but untrained, like the Lord’s disciples once, who wished but were unable to follow him to his Passion and were meanwhile kept under shelter until they should be clothed with power from on high. But when they saw the glory of his resurrection and ascension, they were so encouraged and made capable of the Paraclete Spirit that they rejoiced more in sharing his sufferings than they feared following him to heaven.

The charity of the great-hearted Gregory could then have been disturbed, as though by a frustrated undertaking and by the mockery of the demons who were taunting him, had he not hoped in the name of the Lord, in which he believed that his undertaking would be successfully completed. Filled, therefore, with the spirit of courage, he sent through the leader Augustine this letter of paternal exhortation to the pilgrims of Christ, urging them to obey him and confidently complete, with God’s help, the road and work they had begun, all the way to the palm and crown of glory. [Col. 0054D]

[Col. 0055A] **7. Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the servants of our Lord.**

Since it would have been better not to begin a good work than to turn back in thought from what has been begun, beloved sons, you must apply the greatest care to completing the good work which, with the Lord’s help, you have begun.

Therefore let neither toil nor the tongues of slanderous men frighten you; but with all urgency and fervor carry out, with God as author, what you have begun, knowing that a great labor is followed by the greater glory of eternal reward.

When your superior Augustine returns—whom we have also appointed your abbot—obey him humbly in everything, knowing that whatever you complete at his admonition will benefit your souls in every way.

May Almighty God protect you by his grace and grant that I may see the fruit of your labor in my eternal homeland; so that, although I cannot labor with you, I may nevertheless share in the joy of the reward, since I wish to labor.

May God keep you safe, beloved sons.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most devout Augustus, was reigning, in his fourteenth year; after the consulship of that same lord of ours, in his thirteenth year; in the fourteenth indiction.

**8.** Gregory, watchful on behalf of all according to his name, also wrote to Aetherius, archbishop of Arles, so that he might provide the necessities of Augustine and his companions, envoys of Christ to Britain:

“To the most reverend and most holy brother Aetherius, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God” (*Book V, Letter 55*).

“Although religious men among priests who possess charity pleasing to God need no recommendation from anyone, nevertheless, since a suitable occasion for writing has presented itself, we have taken care to send our letter to your Fraternity, informing you that the bearer of this letter, Augustine, a servant of God whose zeal we know to be dependable, has been sent there by us, with other servants of God, for the benefit of souls, God assisting us.

“It is necessary that Your Holiness help him with priestly zeal and hasten to offer him your support. [Note: Saint Laurence was among the companions of this mission and later succeeded Saint Augustine in the bishopric of Canterbury. We have illustrated his life under 2 February, and have shown that in Gaul he visited the following bishops in this order: Saint Serenus of Marseille, Protasius of Aix, Virgilius of Arles, Saint Desiderius of Vienne, Aetherius of Lyon—wrongly assigned here to the see of Arles—and Saint Siagrius of Autun. The annotations there may be consulted concerning them.]

“In order that you may be more ready to provide assistance, we have enjoined him to explain the matter to you in detail, knowing that, once you understand it, you will devote yourselves wholly, for God’s sake, to offering aid, since the situation itself demands it.

“We also commend to your charity in every respect Candidus, a priest and our common son, whom we have sent to administer the patrimony of our Church.

“May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.”

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most devout Augustus, was reigning, in his fourteenth year; after the consulship of that same lord of ours, in his thirteenth year; in the fourteenth indiction.

**9.** When these apostolic instructions had been reported and impressed more deeply upon Augustine’s companions, they were so strengthened that they rejoiced to proceed fearlessly with what they had begun, more vigorously than before, and, like the best soldiers, to wrest victory more fiercely after their flight.

They therefore went with the heavenly creatures before their faces, and, as they advanced, they did not turn back. Their own great-hearted leader, Augustine, seemed already to say to them in Gregory’s voice: “You shall go out with gladness, and be led forth with joy; for the mountains, kings, and the hills, leaders, shall leap before you, awaiting you in order to receive you with joy.”

O immense joy, by which, even through bitter and harsh things, one travels to an interminable kingdom with an unfailing abundance of merits and the sweet fruit of children sought for God! Understanding these things, the saints hastened through adversity and prosperity, across level ground and thickets, toward true rewards; patient in everything, they became obedient even unto death. [Col. 0056A]

Amid so many merits of virtue, the lights of miracles always accompanied blessed Augustine. Among innumerable miracles, the most celebrated is the one he performed while then a pilgrim in Anjou, a rich province of Gaul. In his honor a church was consecrated there which never admits any women.

For this reason many highly honored men of Anjou, coming to Canterbury to Saint Augustine, were greatly astonished that here, where he rests bodily, all women might enter so lawfully and freely, whereas there not one could obtain the grace of such permission. When they expressed their wonder, the brothers answered that those women who had driven the saint away were rightly rejected from his church, while those who had willingly received him deserved to be received by him.

For long ago many noble and distinguished leaders of that people, together with revered fathers of ecclesiastical rank, frequently and steadfastly celebrated in England—and especially before their own [as they boast] patron Augustine—the events he had performed among them. Through their successors they all blessed England, and especially apostolic Canterbury, both through the prerogative of the supreme Augustine and through his bodily presence itself, as though through bodily life. His memory remained so indelible among them, and his miracles were so frequent, whether written or more evident than writing.

Let us therefore report, from public knowledge, the signs of his presence which he left there.

**10.** As he was carrying out the Lord’s embassy, as has been mentioned, he traveled from Rome through the province of Anjou to a bridge called Pont Sai [alternative: Pontus Sai], extending for a mile over the river Loire in stonework [Note: Pons-Say, commonly called le Pont de Cé, formerly Pons Caesaris; so Mabillon.]. He crossed it with that holy choir of companions.

When they attempted to enter the neighboring village of Sai, whose name was the same as the bridge, the inhabitants returned hostility for hospitality and repelled the many foreign travelers, humble in gait and dress, as though they were so many wolves and unknown monsters.

But the women, gathered together in a crowd, raged against the saints of God with such irreverence—or rather madness—in howling, contempt, mocking, and derision, that by comparison the men seemed almost harmless and gentle. It was not enough that they had expelled them: they pursued them farther, dragged them, shoved them, harassed them, and drove them away with insulting persistence.

Nearby stood a large, shady elm, suitable for weary travelers to rest beneath. The saints wished to rest there that night, but could not because of the women’s harassment, as though they had been a pack of dogs. One woman, more shamelessly than the others, pressed upon the saints’ footsteps. Augustine himself raised his staff and attempted to drive her away as though fighting a beast and a ravenous wolf. Suddenly, through a new sign of God’s grace, the staff flew from his hand like an arrow shot from a bow and came to rest fixed in the ground almost three stadia away.

Augustine then followed with the blessed company—for through the divine Spirit he perceived that at the Lord’s command he was being summoned there—and hastened up. He drew out the staff, or rather, with the staff he drew forth a spring. Immediately abundant water burst forth. By it the servants of God, giving immense thanks to their generous provider, were relieved from severe thirst and refreshed with delight; and that very night they rested there in the deepest devotion, praising God.

Then the mercy of the Most High, unwilling that the children of his light and day should suffer the injury of night on the ground and under the open air, suddenly poured upon them from the highest heaven a light surpassing the sun’s rays and covered them throughout the night with heavenly brilliance, as though the church abandoned under the open sky had prayed in prophetic words:

“Give me a sign for good, O Lord, that those who hate me may see and be put to shame” (Psalm 58:17), “for you, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.”
