All the neighboring people therefore saw so immense a ray directed from the summit of heaven down to the saints that, to their own confusion, they recognized how many citizens of heaven they had driven from their hospitality.

The most sacred leader himself then wrote these words in the earth beside that spring:

[Note: Mabillon reports that the whole history of this miracle, as well as the inscription, is still read every year in the church consecrated to Saint Augustine near Angers; but he judges it more plausible that the inscription was dictated by the inhabitants. In the register of the benefices of this diocese it is called the Parish Priory of Canons—namely, of the Canons of Saint Augustine—subject to the Abbey of All Saints at Angers. This church is commonly called Saint-Outin.]

“Here Augustine, servant of the servants of God, had lodging—the Augustine whom blessed Pope Gregory sent to convert the Angles.” [Col. 0057D]

**11.** As the dawn of light was now approaching, they hastened through the city of Angers toward the place appointed for them, panting with eagerness. By God’s evident zeal, they left their former despisers—now eager for them but deprived of their abundance—without the benefit of their life-giving presence.

In the morning, therefore, the neighbors hurried from every direction to the place where they had seen so great a miracle of light. With deep groaning and mourning they sought to recover those whom they had driven away. Then, observing the benefits of the new spring, they wasted away in still sharper grief over their guilt.

“Alas for us wretched people!” they said. “How have we lost, through our impious rejection, so great a good which we freely held in our hands, and not even deserved to be blessed by such angels!”

Learning from the inscription mentioned above the desired name of blessed Augustine and the purpose of his embassy, and inflamed by the frequency of his miracles, they quickly built a church beside the spring and had it consecrated in the name of blessed Augustine. Where the letters of the inscription were found, they established an altar.

There the perpetual miracle mentioned above still endures: no woman has ever been able to enter that church or draw water from the spring [Note: At the present time, Mabillon observes that women enjoy entry into the church and use of the still-existing spring; he adds, from a letter of his confrere Alexandre Fournereau, that the spring mentioned here is enclosed in the south wall of the church, and that the sick frequently visit it for the sake of healing.]. Thus the world may know how greatly this sex offended God in its injury of his servants. [Col. 0058A]

**12.** A certain distinguished matron attempted to enter there with a large candle, as though the saint were now flattering her power and generosity. When those present tried to deter her, she replied that she had not sinned against the saint but wished to honor him, and she pressed forward boldly in her purpose.

Scarcely had she touched the forbidden boundary and sacred threshold when suddenly her intestines burst and the secretions of her belly boiled out onto the ground. The wretched woman collapsed and died. Dragged outside as a corpse, she taught everyone with terrifying clarity to believe what she herself had not believed.

After such a repulse, all the women were so instructed that they dreaded touching the open doors more than the closed ones. Yet, lest women should seem entirely abandoned there by the grace of the holy Father, the inhabitants, moved by long-standing [alternative: divine] compassion, built an appropriate shelter for them outside the church doors. There they could gather, pray, fulfill their offerings and vows, and attend the sacred mysteries. [Col. 0058C]

**13.** While these things were being confirmed both by ancient report and by the recent testimony of the most distinguished men of Anjou, it happened that the most reverend and prudent bishop of Anjou [Note: Gocelinus is called Guiffridus in the lesser manuscript. There were two men of this name: the first presided from 1081 to 1093 and was called of Tours to distinguish him from his successor, likewise Guiffridus, called of the Meduana, who surrendered the see to Rainaldus, consecrated on 12 January 1102. We do not know which of them is meant. But why should the exclusion of the female sex not have ceased immediately after the dedication of the new church?] came to the most desired patron Augustine and, with great devotion, revisited him as so ancient a guest of his homeland.

He was attentive not only to hearing the miracles written above from the brothers but also to reporting them spontaneously. He explained them with fixed affirmation in exactly the manner in which they are written, as though from a reading. He also added a new miracle, as though it had occurred yesterday, declared in his own presence, with the following favor and grace of the Father:

“O you happy people,” he said, “to whom the eternal presence of blessed Augustine has been granted! Nor are we so unhappy, since his blessed memory has remained with us forever. Our homeland knew him before yours; and Anjou saw him, mighty in signs, before England did.

“But I confess that our ancestors rejected him while he was present. Terrified, however, by heavenly signs, we pursued him with repentance as he departed. When we no longer deserved to touch him either with hand or with sight, we began to retain him by establishing a church in his honor.

“Why should I delay your hearing with a lengthy account of the miracle manifested there? As the people’s devotion toward so great a father—who is always ready to hear his suppliants and always able to help them—increased, they began to restore his reconciling church more nobly and to bind his patronage more closely to themselves.

“Therefore, in the month of May, on the day of the deposition of so great a father, I dedicated this church, which had previously belonged to him, to his memory, amid the great vows of both sexes and with an innumerable multitude of people gathering.

“Thick fields of grain stood all around, already approaching harvest and already growing into ears and bearded heads. The people, rushing in from every direction like a river, paid no attention to the grain or to the harvest, whoever might own it. It was trampled and crushed; as on a threshing floor where the work of men and oxen is confused, the hope of the fields and crops was destroyed. Indeed, the fruitful stalk seemed now not so much threshed and crushed as swept away and stripped bare.

“What, then, did they do? They bade farewell to all the wealth of that year; and they also bade farewell to Augustine, hoping that other gains would come to them through his generosity, since they had lost those crops.

“But at last, when matters seemed hopeless, a more wonderful power appeared, and Augustine’s merits did not fail. For such an abundance of grain sprang up for harvest in that same month throughout all that devastated region that no land in that province could equal it either in the richness or in the height of its crops.

“Amazed by these miracles, the people rejoice to exalt blessed Augustine with such praises that they believe and proclaim that, whatever he wishes, he can obtain from the Lord anywhere among the nations, and that whatever is faithfully requested can be granted through him.”

By proclaiming these things with the testimony of the whole homeland, the aforesaid bishop gave his grateful hearers worthy certainty about how sacredly the ancient signs ought to be believed when confirmed by such recent demonstrations. [Col. 0059C]

**14.** After Latium, Italy, Gaul, so many mountains, plains, forests, rivers, and the dangers of lands and peoples, at last Augustine, the bearer of God, the bringer of peace, and the giver of salvation, arrived in Britain with his blessed company on a prosperous journey—namely, at the dwelling and perpetual rest divinely ordained for him.

The way of the righteous was made straight, the path of the saints prepared, and the Lord our God led them by a wondrous road to the appointed place.

# CHAPTER TWO  
## Entry into England; the Conversion of King Æthelred; the Joy of Saint Gregory the Great

[Col.

[0059D]

### 15.

The kingdom of Kent possesses the very large and famous island of Thanet, capable, in extent, of holding six hundred families. It opens a gateway and harbor to frequent overseas traffic; its soil is exceedingly fertile and prosperous, and it is well suited to the kingdom of Kent. The river Wantsum—[Note: Bede calls it Wantsum; it is now called the Stour.]—which is three stadia wide and separates the island from the mainland, made it an island: extending both its headlands into the sea, it can be crossed only at two fords.

Thus this island was the first in its holy people to receive Christ [Note: In William Thorne’s chronicle it is said that Saint Augustine, descending from the ship, left the imprint of his foot upon a rock as though in mud; the rock was honorably placed in a chapel founded there.]—a blessed land in its fertility, but even more blessed in the hospitality of so many god-bearing immigrants, indeed so many heavenly citizens! Here, for a time, the new father of England, together with his holy company, is refreshed from the salt of the sea.

### 16.

At that time Aethelbert was king of the English [Note: We have treated the acts of Saint Aethelbert the king under 24 February; some additions from Book II of the Translation of Saint Augustine, chapter 4, will be needed there to confirm his cult.], third among the kings of the English, but destined already to become the first worshiper of Christ. By the providence of heavenly election, he presided over the other kings more than his predecessors had done and extended his rule as far as the Humber, an immense river [Col. 0060B] which separates the southern and northern peoples of the English by its intervening waters.

While he was royally enthroned in the metropolitan city of Canterbury, the Lord’s legate Augustine, through ambassadors and interpreters whom he had taken from related peoples overseas at the urging of blessed Gregory, informed him that he had come from Rome out of love and goodwill toward him and his people, and that he was bringing him an excellent message, worthy of all acceptance: a message which, if received, promised those who accepted it everlasting and boundless joys, and the ages of the heavenly kingdom with the eternal God, with the firmest possible assurance of faith.

The king received these words calmly and ordered them to remain on the very island where they had been received, and to be supplied with whatever the necessities of life required, until he had considered how he should deal with them. For Christianity, already shining everywhere, had become known to him, especially because [Col. 0060C] his royal wife was a most Christian woman from the Frankish kings, named Berta [Note: Berta is called Aldiberga by Saint Gregory in Book IX, Letter 59. She was the daughter not of Chlothar I, as Mabillon says, but of Charibert, king of Paris, as we established from Gregory of Tours and others in the life of Saint Leudhard, which we published together with the Life of the aforesaid King Aethelbert on 24 February, since we did not know the day of his birth. Later, however, we learned from the Roman manuscript of the Duke of Altemps and another ancient manuscript of ours that the day of her birth and the day sacred to her cult is 7 May, as we stated under that date. Some of her miracles are recorded below in Book I of the Translation of Saint Augustine, chapter 5.]. He had obtained her from her parents on the condition that he would permit her to preserve the Christian religion, always inviolate, with her companions.

For the most holy bishop Leudhard had been assigned as the queen’s companion and most faithful guardian; through pious admonitions and examples, amid the destructive practices of paganism, he continually strengthened her in the worship of Christ. She therefore made the king—although he still obeyed the ancestral darkness—more merciful toward the worshipers of Christ; and, as though he himself already worshiped Christ with half of his body, he opened the way for Christ’s bearers, until he too should enter it.

Accordingly, the king came to the island on an appropriate day and, sitting in the open air with a company of nobles, summoned Augustine and his little community to his presence. For the king was still deceived by the error of augury, like nocturnal Nicodemus, fearing that, if they came into some building with him, they might use some enchantment or magic they knew to deceive him once he had been confined there. But such a fear was as far removed from the innocent and upright men as light is from darkness: rather, they raised the Lord’s banners, by which they would test the devices of demons.

They came, therefore, without shame, prominently carrying the silver cross of the world’s conqueror and an image of the Lord and Savior, beautifully and richly gilded on a panel. Together they sang litanies, by which the hostile walls of God’s Jericho might fall; with contrite hearts they prayed for their own perpetual salvation and for that of those whom they had come to win for God.

### 17.

When they had taken their seats at the king’s command, Augustine first sounded forth with an evangelical voice:

“For your perpetual peace, O king, and for that of this entire kingdom, we have entered here and bring you, as we previously announced, the excellent message of eternal joy: if you receive it, you will be eternally blessed here and in the eternal kingdom.

“For the creator of the world and likewise its Redeemer has opened the kingdom of heaven to the human race and has made heavenly citizens out of those who were earthly. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world, as the only-begotten Son himself bears witness (John 3:16), so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.

“With so boundless a love did this same Son of God love the human beings whom he made that he deigned not only to become human among humans, but also to suffer death—indeed, the death of the cross—for human beings. For this pleased his ineffable mercy: that he should strike down the devil, our captor, not in the majesty of his divinity but in the weakness of our flesh, and should snatch us, his rightful prey, from the jaws of the most wicked tyrant through the unowed punishment of the cross.

“His incarnate divinity shone forth through countless displays of power: every weakness was healed, every mighty deed accomplished. In heaven, among the stars, on earth, at sea, and in hell, he showed himself to be God and Lord of all. By his command he calmed the winds and the sea; he trod the waves of the sea as though they were solid ground. At last, having deigned to die as a human being for human beings, he rose from death on the third day as God, and illumined the sun—which had been darkened at the death of its creator—with a radiance brighter than its own.

“He rose, I say, to raise us up; he ascended into heaven to lead us there in triumph. From there he will come as judge of all ages, to place believers eternally in his kingdom and condemn unbelievers.

“Therefore, O most excellent ruler, do not judge us superstitious because we have labored to come from Rome into your territories for the salvation of you and your people, and to offer unfamiliar peoples benefits that might seem unwelcome. Know, most pious one, that we undertook this because the necessity of a great glory impelled us [Col. 0061D]. For above every desire for worldly things and glory, we long to have as many fellow citizens as possible in the kingdom of our God; and we strive with all our strength to ensure that whoever can advance into the company of the holy angels may not perish.

“This goodwill has been infused by the kindness of our Christ, from the immeasurable sweetness of his Spirit, into all heralds of his truth everywhere, so that, setting aside their own necessities, they may burn with zeal for the salvation of every nation; may regard all peoples as parents and children, as brothers and relatives; and may embrace them all with one love of God, striving to lead them into the endless ages of every joy and celebration.

“Such standard-bearers of the king, having become witnesses of God through countless miracles, subjected the world most invincibly to its Savior through swords, fires, beasts, and [Col. 0062A] every kind of torture and death. Long ago Rome, long ago Greece, the kings and princes of the earth, and the islands of the nations, drawn by prophetic invitations, rejoiced with the rest of the world to worship and serve forever the Lord of kings, through whom and with whom they might reign eternally.

“With the same affection, the father of all Christianity today, Gregory, thirsting most ardently for your salvation, would not have been prevented by fear of punishment or death from coming to you himself, if he could have abandoned—which he cannot—the care of so many souls entrusted to him. Therefore he sent us in his place, so that we might open to you the way of eternal light and the gate of the heavenly kingdom; and, if you do not refuse to enter through Christ after rejecting idols and demonic powers, you may reign forever in the surest faith.”

### 18.

While the life-giving Augustine was expounding these and similar matters, his assistants added many further points, as the Lord granted them. But the king, not easily disentangled from his long-established error, answered like a sick man who favors his physicians but is not yet willing to undergo treatment:

“Beautiful indeed are the invitations, words, and promises you have presented, leading toward a certain infinite glory. But since they are new and hitherto unknown, it is not fitting for me to submit my mind to them and abandon the customs of my ancestors, which have been observed throughout England until now.

“Nevertheless, we did not wish to show ourselves hostile or ungrateful toward your goodwill, by which, as I see, you have struggled to come to us from afar and to care for our salvation according to what you know more truly and better. Rather, we wish to support you with kindly hospitality and provide sufficient necessities for life. We also permit you to take into your faith and profession, through preaching and exhortation, as many people as you can.”

Thus the king, so merciful toward the worshipers of Christ while still a pagan—who could worthily recount how widely this mercy was extended, so that Augustine’s crown might grow through difficulty and a greater joy arise for the Church of God from an unexpected salvation?

### 19.

Accordingly, through the king’s goodwill—or rather, through God’s providence—the saints were granted a suitable place of residence in the metropolitan city of Dorobernia, together with the promised provisions for bodily sustenance and permission to preach as they desired.

Therefore, as the peace-bringing Augustine approached the city that he was to possess, together with the blessed choir of the saints, he raised in the customary manner the triumphal banner of the Lord’s silver cross, bearing the life-giving image of Jesus Christ, himself the eternal king. He humbly invoked over the city the Savior’s saving mercy. Then he sweetly intoned this antiphon of the litany, and the first nursing Church of the English received it and sang it with harmonious melody and devotion:

“We beseech you, Lord, in all your mercy, that your fury and your anger may be taken away from this city and from your holy house, because we have sinned.”

It was fitting that they should add, “because we have sinned,” for out of Christ’s love they had come to wash away the sins of others as though they were their own, by instruction, prayers, and tears.

From this point onward, having been established in peace, not so much through concern for strangers as through divine dispensation, they devoted themselves more attentively to the fruit of the kingdom of God. They lived not merely as exiles from the Ocean but altogether [Col. 0063A] [Note: This note is printed at the foot of column 63, but its callout letter, a, does not appear in the text. Bede has the same account, from which it is clear that the ancient cult of Saint Martin—who died in 397, only about sixty years before Hengist occupied Kent in 457, as Florence of Worcester and others report—was already established.] as pilgrims throughout the whole world. They desired so little that was earthly or worldly that one would have been astonished to find them earth-dwellers rather than heaven-dwellers.

They had completely cut away pleasures, luxuries, riches, honors, and everything that might obstruct those approaching heaven. They persisted in fasting, vigils, prayers, almsgiving, chastity, and every form of holiness. They practiced Christ’s weapons—peaceful for virtue, but warlike in the battle against wickedness—with the greatest strength, defeating every unbelief; against every injury they presented patience as a breastplate; for dangers, punishments, and even death itself they displayed unconquerable steadfastness; toward the needy, wounded [sic] compassion; toward all people, even their adversaries, heartfelt charity.

Free and unburdened by earthly weight, they flew toward heaven like winged creatures; or rather, as the Apostle says, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). Except that they still dwelt on earth out of love for the nations to be saved, they already lived in heaven in mind.

### 20.

Before the arrival of the English, the Romans had possessed Britain for approximately four hundred years, from the time of Gaius Caesar to the emperor Maximus, who, having seized the purple against the Augusti Gratian and Valentinian, and with wars advancing, drained the very Ocean of Roman garrisons.

The remaining church and the church of blessed Martin, once founded by those Roman Christians, then illumined Kent. It remains to this day dutifully served by continual ministers, situated about half a stadium east of the authentic Church of Christ.

In this church the blessed bishop Leudhard, like a precursor or doorkeeper of the apostolic legates, first served the Christian queen in divine offices and sacraments, together with his clerics, as a faithful bridegroom’s attendant. And just as a deer, after being assailed by the venom of serpents, thirsts for springs of water, so he, tormented by the poisonous pagan rites hostile to the faith, hastened with the queen, his charge, to that church as to the fountain of life, whenever the Roman teachers—shining there like gold before silver—performed the things of God.

For among these foreigners and solitary strangers, in these heavenly visitors, God’s grace visited these pilgrims of Christ; and through them it visited the people who would believe, so that the queen might not only worship Christ freely, but also, through such great teachers, save her unbelieving husband.

In this oratory, therefore, Augustine and his choir celebrated the Lord’s daily offices; and in psalms, hymns, prayers, and the voice of the trumpet—by which the devil’s camps might perish—they raised the Lord’s praises day and night.

Meanwhile, the splendid merits of the saints were commended by an immense grace of signs and commandments of God. They could neither conceal nor keep silent about Christ’s imperial proclamations: through songs, through the thunder of preaching, and through the flashing of signs, they proclaimed him more and more loudly.

They in turn cured all the weak and sick, whether brought to them or visited by them. So thoroughly, or so frequently, did the grace of healing prevail in Augustine’s flock that scarcely anyone, or only rarely anyone, was found who did not possess it. Thus they illumined the darkness of the pagans no less by miracles than by preaching.

These promises of everlasting joy soothed the dull minds of men; such great flashes struck the obdurate that what the Psalmist sings of the Lord was fulfilled: “Your flashes illumined the world; the earth was shaken and trembled” (Psalm 76:19).

The trembling peoples cried out: “The heavenly gods, descending from their seats, dwell among human beings.” Thus once the nations, marveling at God’s Apostles as they transcended earthly things, said: “These are the holy gods of the earth.” Nor did they lie according to their own error, as the Psalmist testifies: “The strong gods of the earth have been greatly exalted” (Psalm 46:10).

Thus the formerly unyielding necks lovingly submitted to the Lord’s gentle yoke; the fertile fields received the seeds of life for everlasting fruits; many believed and, reborn in Christ, became sons of God by adoption instead of foreigners.

### 21.

Augustine, the soldier of the supreme King, attentive to everything, directed the whole mechanism of salvation especially against the highest head of the kingdom, so that, once the fortress of profanity had been overturned, he might raise the starry fortress of holiness, and the world, subjected to its king, might bow before the Savior.

Through the queen’s entreaties, the warnings of ambassadors, timely approaches, the sweet allurements of eternal happiness, every example and manifestation of virtue, and the Church’s watchful prayers to God, he strove to win the king for his Redeemer. He strove, and in the Lord God he says that he succeeded.

The great elephant of the earth and the enormous whale of the sea was triumphantly caught in the apostolic net. Captured by eternal sweetness, instructed by irrefutable truth, illumined by the holy and wondrous splendor of divine teaching, he rejected his ancestral paganism together with the author of death, and willingly surrendered himself to the author of life.

“Let us go,” he said, “to the great prince of kings, the most generous giver of kingdoms—not only temporal but eternal kingdoms. Let us not be ashamed to have come last, when we ought rightly to be ashamed that, just as we were not first in the kingdom, so we were not first in faith. Let us at last follow those whom it was fitting for us to precede—especially since we seek a king who weighs not the dignity of a person or rank, but devotion of soul.”

### 22.

Having spoken these words, he wished, laying aside his royal majesty, to worship the servant of Christ, through whom he might merit rebirth into the service and adoption of Christ.

The minister of salvation received him with paternal affection and urged him to wash away his former errors through abstinence, forgiveness, almsgiving, and tears, and through other pious works to go before the face of him who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.

The king forgives everyone, so that he may be forgiven, and prepares himself by human beneficence for heavenly benefits. Prisons are opened, bonds loosened, captives freed, and the poor and condemned feast with the king’s friends.

It is impossible—and there is no need—to explain with what joy the soul of blessed Augustine exulted at the salvation of a nation that had until then gasped for breath, or with what offerings of thanksgiving it sacrificed to God.

Now he sees his desire prospering, his land giving its fruit, and all the labors, pains, and difficulties of his travail producing everlasting joy for him, since, in the conversion of that king, he embraced the entire Ocean under the Lord’s yoke.

Thus dawned a day most solemn for the English and the angels, on which the God-devoted king Aethelbert, having cast off the idols and ancestral gods, was born a Christian.

Not only the royal court of princes and all Kent but also the most populous parts of England gathered to see the most excellent lord of the kingdom lying at the feet of Christ’s visiting servants and serving their every command as though he were their lowest slave—so that kingdoms abroad, which feared armed forces, might be bound by the word of unarmed poor men.

The church was adorned, the baptisteries decorated, and the font of the Jordanian and paradisal river consecrated.

Asked by Augustine whether he believed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and in the other things required by Catholic truth, the faithful confessor of the Lord answered, “I believe,” with all his heart and mouth, to everything.

In this confession and name of the Trinity, therefore, the king of the English was baptized and reborn. From an old idolater he became a new worshiper of Christ; from the dark night of his world, a morning lamp.

Our Sylvester baptized our Constantine, together with a renowned throng of dukes and nobles and a great multitude of believers.

At the voice of God’s minister, the heavens were opened, and the Lord Jesus poured upon this adopted son his dove, which the Father once testified from heaven to be his Son in the Jordan. It descended in brilliant whiteness and rested upon the received [Al.: receiving] one in simple purity, like a newborn infant.

From that moment the new Church, after Christ the firstborn and only-begotten Son of the Lord [Col. 0065C], rejoiced to sing, embracing the newly born one: “A child is born to us; a son is given to us.”

Thus the spirit of the Lord was directed into our David from that day and forever; and the same Solomon, through God’s wisdom, illumined him for the light of his people.

In the former David alone ten thousand are counted, and in our single prince broad Britain is surrendered to Christ.

Since the Savior testifies that the angels rejoice over one sinner who repents, we reasonably believe that the heavenly hosts themselves, over this saved head, then proclaimed with harmonious jubilation: “Glory to the Lord of the world, because the kingdom of the English has also become the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

### 23.

From then on, this evangelical disciple of the saints and most vigorous assistant of his teacher Augustine no longer regarded as his own the kingdom he governed, but rather regarded it as belonging to him to whom he had surrendered himself and all his people.

He longed rather to subject it to him and enlarge it, since he most justly administers all the kingdoms of the world by his nod. He strove to transfer the kings and peoples subject to him, not by force but by goodwill, as he had learned from the holy teachers, into Christ’s sweet dominion.

There was also such charity in the holy and God-beloved king that he no longer regarded believers in the Redeemer as clients, but bound them, as brothers and perpetual fellow citizens of God’s kingdom, with great joy and affection.

Then, as though they were the Lord’s castles by which the Lord’s kingdom might be held, he liberally and royally began everywhere to establish bishoprics and monasteries.

In his metropolis he most generously determined that a basilica of the Savior should be built and possessed by his Augustine. In its suburb he raised up a royal and apostolic monastery to preserve the bodies of bishops and kings until the day of the life-giving resurrection.

He also founded the suffragan see of Rochester and the episcopal hierarchy of London, together with churches and monasteries in other suitable places.

[Note: These events occurred in the year 601, when Saint Justus was created bishop of Rochester and Saint Mellitus bishop of London. We published the Life of the latter on 24 April; Saint Justus is to be treated on 10 November.]

### 24.

Above all, he urgently requested that Augustine, already chosen by the supreme pope Gregory, be consecrated as his apostle together with the whole country.

But Augustine, who had sought the salvation of so many people at such great peril during his journey, for whom he would not flee death [the printed text reads “would not rise to meet death”], did not refuse to undertake the principal labor.

He crossed the sea to Aetherius, archbishop of Arles [Note: Rather, to Vigilius, as we said above, unless Aetherius of Lyons should be substituted.], to be ordained by him, obedient, of course, to the apostolic election and the Church’s request—or rather, to the Lord’s appointment.

Gregory’s letters had preceded him, always most watchful on behalf of Augustine and the beloved English. Thus this first patriarch of England was consecrated and, with apostolic insignia, returned to his inheritance for an everlasting blessing; he was enthroned in the prepared see of Dorobernia.

### 25.

Among all the concerns involved in teaching the nations, Augustine considered it a crime of negligence if he delayed informing the soul of blessed Gregory, suspended in holy desire, of such great joys resulting from the gain of the Lord.

Therefore the most sacred Laurence, then a priest and later the distinguished successor of blessed Augustine, was sent to Rome; and Peter [Col. 0066C], a monk worthy of monastic leadership, who later became the first abbot to shine over the monastery of Augustine [Note: We published the Acts of Saint Peter the abbot on 6 January.]. Thus this messenger of mutual congratulation might also grow greatly into many fruits.

Augustine, rejoicing in a rich harvest, anxiously complained of the scarcity of laborers; on this subject he consulted the divine teacher about various questions, asking how he might restore the tottering Church and the inexperienced people.

But when Gregory, the man of holy desires, learned that the king of Britain had been consecrated to Christ together with his realm; that the hands of those baptizing the crowds flocking together were growing weary; that cultivators and seeds alike were becoming scarce in the fertile fields; and that the public hunger for hearing the word of the Lord needed many teachers—who could worthily recount with what joy he blessed the Most High, and with what ardor of mind and voice he prayed that these [Col. 0066D] increases might be strengthened forever?

“Yourself, O Lord,” he said, “the author of the salvation of all; yourself, wondrous and glorious in your saints and in all your mercies—we magnify you in every way through our frail praise.

“For behold: through your humble legate Augustine, the Ocean, once swollen with pride, now prostrate, serves at the feet of the saints; and the barbarous tongue of Britain has begun to resound with Hebrew ‘Alleluia’ in your praises.

“Receive, sower of blessings, the fruits of eternal grace which you planted in his most fertile heart. Receive your stranger and orphan, together with his speaking brothers, with whom, leaving house, homeland, and family, denying himself and taking up the cross, he followed you.

“You are powerful enough to multiply him into a great nation, after your ancient hearer, the patriarch. It is always yours, O Lord, to temper all the difficulties and anxieties of your saints and transform them into an immeasurable gain of joys.”

While the most holy pope offered these feelings of paternal charity to God as a pleasing fragrance, he added a prayer to the Lord of the harvest, asking that he direct his counsel so that he might send suitable laborers into his harvest [Al.: send them].

Accordingly, with heavenly providence inspiring them, distinguished men of virtue were sent with the aforesaid legates Laurence and Peter: Mellitus, Justus, [Note: Saint Paulinus, later created archbishop of York, is commemorated on 10 October.] Paulinus, and Rufinianus—in other words, four heralds of the Gospel.

They were accompanied by no inexperienced crowd of evangelical ministers and assistants, who would tear apart the camps of the demons in a terrible battle-line.

Everything that seemed appropriate for the worship and ministry of the Church was supplied through Gregory’s watchfulness by distinguished lettered [sic] bearers: sacred vessels; altar furnishings; church ornaments; priestly vestments; precious relics of the holy apostles and martyrs; numerous books; and every kind of beautiful ecclesiastical object [Note: In the monastery of Aldinghof at Paderborn there is preserved a pair of portable altars, shaped like little chests. It is believed that both contain sacred objects from the collection that Saint Gregory sent to Augustine. Each has been adorned by pious posterity with silver plates and precious stones; various relics of saints are enclosed in each; and each has margins inscribed with Leonine verses. One bears this notable inscription:

“Among all altars, you are called Gregory’s altar;

“From him who consecrated you, the English people ask and receive you;

“After this, you are carried here and joined to the bones;

“With them, you are said to possess equal worth and merit.”]

He also sent lucidly explained answers to the questions and inquiries mentioned above; these, whether deferred or omitted here, may be found in full in Bede.

In addition to all this there was added the following letter of apostolic prerogative.

[Col. 0067C]

### 26. Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and most holy brother and fellow bishop Augustine (Book XII, Letter 15).

“Since it is certain that ineffable rewards of the eternal kingdom are reserved for those who labor for almighty God, it is nevertheless necessary for us to grant them the benefits of honors, so that, encouraged by the reward, they may wish [Al.: be able] to labor even more abundantly in the zeal of spiritual work.

“And because the new Church of the English has been brought to the grace of almighty God, through the same Lord’s generosity and through your labor, we grant you the use of the pallium in it solely for celebrating the solemnities of Mass, provided that you ordain twelve bishops in the several places who shall be subject to your authority.

“This is so that the bishop of the city of London [Note: It was then, as it still is, a very famous city, London, for which he designates the archiepiscopal see. But, won over by the diligence of Saint Aethelbert the king and the affection of the citizens, Saint Augustine chose Canterbury, and the archiepiscopal see remained there with the approval of the Apostolic See.] may thereafter always be consecrated by his own synod and receive the pallium of honor from this holy and apostolic see, which, by God’s authority, I serve.

“As for the city of York, we wish you to send there as bishop the man whom you yourself judge [Al.: indicate] should be ordained. This is provided that, if that city and the neighboring regions receive the word of God, he too may ordain twelve bishops and enjoy metropolitan honor; for, if his life continues, we also intend, with the Lord’s favor, to grant him the pallium. Nevertheless, we wish him to remain subject to the arrangements of your fraternity.

“After your death, however, he is to preside over the bishops whom he has ordained in such a way that he is in no respect subject to the authority of the bishop of London. There is to be this distinction of honor between the bishops of London and York hereafter: the one who was ordained first is to be considered senior.

“By common counsel and harmonious action, let them unanimously determine what must be done for the zeal of Christ; let them think rightly, and let them carry out what they have thought without disagreement among themselves.

“Your fraternity is to have subject to you, by the authority of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, not only those bishops whom you have ordained, nor only those who have been ordained by the bishop of York, but also all the priests of Britain, so that from the tongue and life of your holiness they may receive a model of right belief and good living; and, carrying out their office in faith and conduct, may reach the heavenly kingdoms when the Lord wills.

“May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

“Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, during the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, in the nineteenth year, in the eighteenth year after the consulship of the same lord, in the fourth indiction.” [Note: This is the year of Christ 601.]

### 27.

By now the Lord’s company had gone farther, laden with apostolic treasures, and Gregory’s spirit did not cease to accompany those who were traveling, because infinite charity does not know how to end its services (Book IX, Letter 71).

Again he renews his unique concern for his Augustine, again for his English; and for this reason he sends the following letter to the aforementioned venerable Mellitus.

“Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son Mellitus, abbot.

“Since the departure of our congregation which is with you, we have been left in great suspense, because we have not happened to hear anything concerning the success of your journey.

“Therefore, when almighty God has brought you to our most reverend brother Augustine, the bishop, tell him what I have long considered and discussed with myself concerning the affairs of the English: namely, that the pagan temples among that people should by no means be destroyed, but that the idols in them should be destroyed; that holy water should be sprinkled in those same temples; that altars should be built and relics placed there.

“For if those temples have been well constructed, it is necessary that they be changed from the worship of demons into the service of the true [Al.: man] God, so that, when the people themselves do not see their temples destroyed, they may put away error from their hearts; and, recognizing and worshiping the true God, may run with greater familiarity to the places they are accustomed to frequent.

“And because they are accustomed to kill many oxen in sacrifice to demons, some solemnity should also be changed for them in this matter: on the day of the dedication or on the birthdays of the holy martyrs whose relics are placed there, let them make tents for themselves from branches of trees around the churches that have been converted from the temples, and celebrate the solemnity with religious feasts.

“They should no longer sacrifice animals to the devil, but kill animals for food in praise of God and give thanks to the giver of all things for their nourishment, so that, while some outward joys are preserved for them, they may more easily consent to inward joys.

“For there is no doubt that it is impossible to cut away everything at once from hardened minds, since the person who strives to climb to the highest place is raised by steps or paces, not by leaps.

“Thus, in Egypt, the Lord indeed made himself known to the Israelite people; but he nevertheless preserved for them the practice of sacrifices which they had been accustomed to offer to the devil in their own worship, commanding them to sacrifice animals in his service. In this way, while changing their hearts, they would lose one element of sacrifice and retain another; and although the animals were the very ones they had been accustomed to offer, since they sacrificed them to the true God rather than to idols, the sacrifices themselves would no longer be sacrifices.

“Therefore, it is necessary for your affection to tell the aforesaid brother these things, so that, being present there, he may carefully consider how he ought to arrange everything.

“May God keep you safe, my most beloved son.

“Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [Al.: July], during the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, in the nineteenth year, in the eighteenth year after the consulship of the same lord, in the fourth indiction.”

## CHAPTER III. Miracles Performed. The Letters of Saint Gregory the Pope. Events Concerning the Christian Britons.

[Col. 0069C]

28. Then, having heard so many and such continual miracles of blessed Augustine, [Gregory], just as he exclaims joyfully in praise of God, so also tempers him with this letter, fearing human weakness lest it grow insolent (Book IX, Letter 58):

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will, because the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, died, so that it might not reign alone in heaven: by whose death we live, by whose weakness we are strengthened, by whose passion we are freed from suffering, by whose love we seek in Britain brothers whom we did not know, and by whose gift we have found those whom, unknowingly, we sought.

“But who could adequately tell how great a joy arose here [Col. 0069D] in the hearts of all the faithful, because the nation of the English, through the working of Almighty God’s grace and through the labor of your Fraternity, has had the darkness of error expelled and been flooded with the light of such great faith; because, with utterly sound understanding, it now tramples the idols to which it was formerly subject through mad fear; because it bows with a pure heart before Almighty God; because it is bound by the rule of holy preaching against the falls of evil conduct; because in spirit it is subject to the divine commandments and is raised up by understanding; because it humbles itself to the ground in prayer, lest in mind it lie upon the ground? Whose work is this, if not his who says: ‘My Father is working until now, and I am working’ (John III, 17)?

“He wished to show the world that he converts it not by human wisdom but by his own power; therefore he chose as his preachers, whom he sent into the world, men without literary learning. He is doing the same thing now, since he has deigned to work great deeds among the English through the weak.

“But in this heavenly gift, dearest brother, there is something that must be feared with the greatest joy [Note: Something appears to be missing. EDIT.]. For I know that Almighty God has displayed great miracles through your Fraternity among the people whom he wished to choose. Therefore it is necessary that, with regard to this same heavenly gift, you should rejoice while fearing, and fear while rejoicing: rejoice, certainly, because the souls of the English are being drawn through outward miracles toward inward grace; but fear lest, amid the signs that are performed, a weak spirit lift itself into presumption, and, by the very means through which it is raised outwardly to honor, fall inwardly through empty glory.

“We must remember that when the disciples returned joyfully from preaching and said to their heavenly Master, ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name,’ they immediately heard: ‘Do not rejoice over this, but rather rejoice because your names are written in heaven’ (Luke 10:17). Those who rejoiced over miracles had placed their minds in private and temporal joy; but they are recalled from private to common joy, and from temporal to eternal joy, when they are told: ‘Rejoice in this, because your names are written in heaven.’ Not all the elect perform miracles, but their names are nevertheless kept written in heaven. The disciples of Truth ought to have no joy except in that good which they possess in common with all, and in which their joy has no end.

“It remains, therefore, dearest brother, that amid those things which, with God working, you perform outwardly, you should always judge yourself inwardly with careful scrutiny and understand precisely both who you are and how great is the grace in that same people, for whose conversion you have received the gifts by which signs are to be performed. And whenever you remember that you have sinned against our Creator, whether by word or by deed, always recall these things, so that remembrance of your guilt may suppress the rising glory of your heart; and whatever you have received or do receive concerning the performance of signs, attribute it not to yourself but to those for whose salvation it has been granted to you.

“As I reflect on this, there comes to mind what happened to one servant of God, and that one an exceptionally chosen man. Certainly, when Moses was leading God’s people out of Egypt, he performed wondrous signs in Egypt [as your Fraternity knows]. On Mount Sinai, fasting forty days and nights, he received the tablets of the Law; amid flashing thunders [Al.: “and thunders”], while the whole people trembled, he alone entered the service of Almighty God and was joined to him even in familiar conversation. He opened the Red Sea; on the journey he had a pillar of cloud as his guide; he brought manna down from heaven for the hungry people; and for those desiring meat he miraculously provided it in the wilderness, even to excessive satiety. But when, at a time of thirst, they had already come to the rock, he doubted; he questioned whether he could draw water from it, although at the Lord’s command he opened it into abundant streams.

“But who could count or investigate how many things he did afterward during thirty-eight years in the wilderness? Whenever some doubtful matter struck his mind, he would withdraw to the tabernacle and secretly seek the Lord, and, when God immediately spoke, he was instructed about it. By the intervention of his prayer he appeased the Lord when angry with the people. Those who rose in pride and quarreled in discord were swallowed by the opening earth; he crushed enemies with victories and displayed signs to his people. But when they had already reached the promised land, he was called up onto the mountain and heard what fault he had committed thirty-eight years earlier, as I have said: he had doubted about bringing forth water. He learned that, on account of this, he could not enter the promised land.

“In this matter we must consider how fearsome is the judgment of Almighty God, who performed so many signs through that servant while preserving his fault in his memory for so long. If, then, we recognize that even he died because of his fault after performing signs, although we know that he had been especially chosen by the Almighty, how greatly ought we to tremble with fear, who do not yet know whether we have been chosen?

“But what should I say about the miracles of the reprobate, when your Fraternity knows well what Truth says in the Gospel: ‘Many will come on that day and say to me, “Lord, we prophesied in your name, and in your name we cast out demons, and in your name we performed many mighty works”; but I will say to them, “I do not know who you are; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity”’ (Matthew VII)?

“Therefore the mind must be greatly restrained amid signs and miracles, lest perhaps it seek its own glory in them and exult in the private joy of its own exaltation. Through signs, the gain of souls must be sought, as well as the glory of him by whose power those very signs are performed.

“But the Lord has shown us one sign by which we may both rejoice greatly and recognize in ourselves the glory of election, when he says: ‘By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another’ (John XIII, 5). The prophet was seeking this sign when he said: ‘Deal with me, Lord, according to goodness, so that those who hate me may see and be confounded’ (Psalm 85:17).

“I say these things because I wish to lay my hearer’s mind low in humility. But let your very humility have its confidence: for I, a sinner, hold with the firmest hope that, through the grace of our omnipotent Creator and Redeemer, God the Lord Jesus Christ, your sins have already been forgiven [Col. 0071D]. And for this reason you have been chosen, so that through you the sins of others may be forgiven; nor will you henceforth have mourning over any guilt, since you strive to make the conversion of many a joy in heaven.

“Our same Creator and Redeemer, speaking of a person’s repentance, said: ‘Truly I tell you, there will be greater joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance’ (Luke 15:7). And if great joy is made in heaven over one repentant person, what joy do we believe was made over so great a people converted from its error, who, coming to the faith, condemned by repentance the evil things it had done?

“Therefore, amid this joy of heaven and of the angels, let us repeat the very words of the angels that we spoke earlier. Let us all say, then—let us all say: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.’”

29. The same pope, rejoicing also in the wholesome faith of King Æthelberht, wrote to him in this manner, together with pious gifts:

“For this reason Almighty God brings good men to the government of peoples: so that through them he may bestow the gifts of his mercy upon all those over whom they have been placed. We know that this has happened among the English, over whom your Glory has therefore been set, so that through the good things granted to you, heavenly benefits might also be bestowed upon the people subject to you.

“Therefore, glorious son, guard with vigilant mind the grace you have received from God; hasten to extend the Christian faith among the peoples subject to you; increase your zeal for righteousness in their conversion; pursue the worship of idols; overthrow the buildings of pagan shrines [Col. 0072B]. Build up the character of your subjects in great purity of life by exhorting, frightening, encouraging, correcting, and showing examples of good works, so that you may find in heaven as your rewarder him whose name and knowledge you have spread on earth. For he himself will make your name more glorious even to posterity, since you seek and preserve his honor among the nations.

“Thus Constantine, once a most pious emperor, recalled the Roman state from the perverse worship of idols, subjected it with himself to Almighty God our Lord Jesus Christ, and turned himself with all the peoples subject to him wholly toward him. As a result, that man surpassed the name of the ancient rulers by his own praises, and outstripped his predecessors in reputation by as much as he surpassed them in good works.

“Now, therefore, let your Glory hasten to pour the knowledge of the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, into the kings and peoples subject to you, so that you may surpass the ancient kings of your nation in praise and merit; and, the more you have wiped away the sins of others among your subjects, the more secure you may become concerning your own sins before the terrible judgment of Almighty God.

“Moreover, gladly listen to our most reverend brother Augustine, instructed in the rule of the monastery, filled with knowledge of Sacred Scripture, and endowed, by God’s authorship, with good works. Devoutly carry out whatever he admonishes you to do, and diligently preserve it in memory. For if you listen to him in what he speaks on behalf of Almighty God, that same Almighty God will more quickly hear him praying on your behalf. But if—which God forbid—you disregard his words, how will Almighty God be able to hear him on your behalf, when you yourselves neglect to hear him on behalf of God?

“Therefore bind yourselves to him with your whole mind in the fervor of faith, and support his effort by the strength that Divinity has granted you, so that he himself may make you participants in his kingdom, whose faith you cause to be received and preserved in your kingdom.

“Furthermore, we wish your Glory to know that, as we recognize from the words of Almighty God in Sacred Scripture, the end of the present world is now near, and the kingdom of the saints is coming, which will never be brought to an end. As that end of the world approaches, many things are impending that did not previously exist: many changes in the air, terrors from heaven, storms contrary to the order of the seasons, wars, famines, pestilences, and earthquakes in various places [Col. 0073A]. Yet not all these things will occur in our days; they will follow after our days.

“Therefore, if you recognize any of these things occurring in your land, do not in any way let your mind be disturbed. For this reason these signs of the end of the age are sent beforehand: so that we should be concerned for our souls, fearful of the hour of death, and found prepared in good works for the coming Judge.

“I have now spoken these few words, glorious son, so that, when the Christian faith has grown in your kingdom, my own speech also may grow broader among you; and the more the joys over the perfect conversion of your people multiply in our mind, the more gladly may we speak.

“I have sent small gifts, which will not be small to you once they have been received from the blessing of blessed Peter the apostle [Col. 0073B]. May Almighty God bring to perfection in you the grace he has begun; may he extend your life here through the course of many years, and after a long time receive you into the assembly of the heavenly homeland. May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency unharmed, my lord and son.

“Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most devout Augustus, was reigning, in the nineteenth year; after the consulship of the same lord, in the eighteenth year; indiction 4.”

30. The same most eminent illuminator of the churches also graciously praises the venerable Queen Bertha in this celebrated letter, both for the king’s conversion and for the care she herself provided to blessed Augustine and his companions; and he urges her to increase these renowned merits still more attentively (Book I, Letter 59):

“Whoever desires to acquire the glory of the heavenly kingdom after earthly power ought to labor with the greatest zeal to make gain for his Creator, so that by the steps of his actions he may ascend to what he desires, just as we rejoice that you have done.

“On their return, our most beloved son Lawrence the priest and Peter the monk reported how your Glory had conducted yourself toward our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine, and how much comfort and what love you had shown him. We blessed Almighty God, who in his mercy deigned to reserve the conversion of the English nation as a reward for you.

“For just as through the memorable Helena, mother of the most devout Emperor Constantine, he kindled the hearts of the Romans toward the Christian faith, so also through the zeal of your Glory we trust that he is working his mercy among the English.

“Indeed, for a long time now you ought, by the benefit of your wisdom, as befits one truly Christian, to have inclined the mind of your glorious son, your husband, so that he might follow the faith you embrace, for the salvation of his kingdom and his soul; so that both from him and through him a worthy reward for you might arise in the heavenly joys from the conversion of the whole nation.

“For after, as we have said, your Glory was fortified by right faith and instructed by letters, this ought neither to have been late nor difficult for you. And since, by God’s will, the right time is now at hand, act so that, with divine grace cooperating, you may repair with increase what has been neglected.

“Therefore strengthen the mind of your glorious husband by constant exhortation toward love of the Christian faith; let your solicitude pour into him an increase of love for God; and so inflame his mind for the fullest conversion of the people subject to him that, through the zeal of your devotion, you may offer a great sacrifice to Almighty God, and that the things reported about you may both increase and in every respect be proved true.

“For your good works have now reached not only the Romans, who prayed more fervently for your life, but also various places, and even the most serene emperor at Constantinople. Therefore, just as joy over the consolations of your Christianity has arisen for us, so also may there be joy in heaven among the angels over your complete accomplishment.

“Present yourselves, then, devotedly and with all your strength in support of the aforesaid most reverend brother and fellow bishop of ours, and of the servants of God whom we sent there, for the conversion of your people. Thus may you reign happily here with our glorious son, your husband, and after many long years may you also receive the joys of the future life, which knows no end.

“We pray Almighty God to inflame the heart of your Glory for carrying out the things we have said, and to grant you the fruit of eternal reward for an action pleasing to him.”

31. How eagerly and devoutly Augustine’s ardent spirit drank in these honey-sweet combs of the flower-bearing Gregory, these nourishment-giving caresses of apostolic and Roman affection, my poor understanding is not sufficient either to grasp or to express.

In this divine armor of his father’s letters, the veteran champion of God (Dei) [Al.: God (Deum)] took delight; in this clearest mirror, before the eyes of his most elegant king, he contemplated his beauty and adornments; on this scale he weighed what in him inclined downward and what outweighed the value of his merits. Since a holy conscience answered all these praises of so many virtues, he stored everything for the benefit of grace in the bosom of the giver of good things. Nor did he fear being overwhelmed by his triumph, since he relied not upon himself but upon his author.

He did not fear defilement, for holy fear of the Lord possessed him. Founded upon the firm rock, he was moved neither by glory nor by disgrace; he stood not in himself but in the Lord. For unending glory he emulated Peter—unstable through presumption, yet made steadfast by faith—and Paul, who gloried in weaknesses because of Christ’s power.

Finally, what should he boast of, since he had crushed every appearance of boasting; since he sought poverty and lowliness as his glory; since the foundations of his architecture were sunk and solidified by so great a height of humility that, while its tower, built of pure gold and every precious stone, rose toward heaven, it laughed unmoved and unharmed at the blows of every storm?

King Æthelberht, too, responded so greatly to the apostolic exhortations of the supreme Gregory because, redeemed in Christ, he knew himself to be so deeply indebted for grace and to have been made a son of God by adoption instead of eternal perdition. Unless royal power had made him supremely necessary for the extension of Christ’s kingdom, we believe that he would have preferred to serve rather than rule under monastic discipline, and to place Peter’s crown before the crown of a kingdom. But what was then not permitted to be done is now shown to have been present in his mind.

Nor should the devotion of the most Christian Queen Bertha be placed second. So great a pope likewise judged her worthy of the favor and commendatory praise of the preceding letter. For she was a doorway open to the light, through which Augustine, the Lord’s radiant paranymphus (bridegroom’s friend), poured the true Sun, Christ, into the inner chambers of the royal mind.

32. Since, then, this friend of God was the most faithful key-bearer of the royal heart—that is, of the king whose heart is in the hand of the Lord—and, with love diffused and his mind enlarged, extended his affection toward the salvation of all, he persuaded that highly obedient ruler to summon the British bishops (pontifices) [Al.: “of the bishops,” pontificum], who had strayed from ecclesiastical discipline (exorbitantes) [Al.: “of those straying,” exorbitantium], to a conference with him.

For this land had been called Britain from ancient times after these Britons, before the English, and it had also been initiated into Christ long ago. In the one hundred fifty-sixth year after the incarnation of the Word, while Marcus Antonius Verus was reigning as Augustus for the fourteenth year together with his brother Aurelius Commodus, Lucius, king of these Britons [Note: Saint Lucius is commemorated on 3 December and Saint Eleutherius the pope on 26 May; these matters are set out more fully in the latter’s Life.], humbly petitioned Saint Eleutherius, then pope, by letter, and gratefully obtained from him that he send faithful teachers who would regenerate him and his people in Christ.

The Britons did not fall away from the integrity of the piety they had received until the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, during which many were crowned through martyrdom.

Afterward, too, they persevered in the Lord’s faith, to such an extent that they did not yield even to the Pelagian heresy; rather, through bishops summoned from Gaul, they convicted and drove away from themselves its perfidious adherents and enemies.

Nevertheless, at length corrupted by luxury and arrogance, while preferring to be subjected to vices rather than to the Lord’s yoke, they were destroyed by the sword of the gentiles and, with only a few survivors [Al.: with their few remnants], driven from almost the whole country and confined in wooded and barren places.

The apostolic legate of the Lord, Augustine, therefore wished to remedy their condition and to make the English and the Britons themselves one nation and one body in Christ. He summoned the more distinguished men of the nation and began to persist with every appeal of paternal gentleness and with all the inward affection of charity, so that, abandoning every dissension opposed to Christ, they might receive the God of peace and, together with him, gain sons of adoption for God and fellow heirs of the heavenly kingdom for themselves.

He also pressed them with earnest prayers and admonitions to celebrate the Lord’s Passover at its proper time, in the common practice and concord of the whole world, abandoning the error by which they observed this feast from the fourteenth moon up to the twentieth—a cycle reckoned as eighty-four years. They were also urged to repent of many other ways in which they deviated from ecclesiastical discipline [Note: Bede and others discuss this controversy in various places, as do we in various Acts—for example, those of Saint Columba, bishop of Lindisfarne, 18 February; Saint Wilfrid, archbishop of York, 24 April; and others.].

But the more mildly the Britons were entreated, the more fiercely they resisted; and although they vaunted their observances as superior to all others [Al.: grassentur, “raged” or “ran riot”], they were moved by no moderation of reason.

They defended their ceremonies as having been prescribed not only by Saint Eleutherius, their first institutor, almost from the infancy of the Church [Col. 0076A], but also as having been observed until then by their holy fathers, friends of God and followers of the apostles; they said that they ought not to change them because of new dogmatists.

Let the discerning mind, not the contentious one, gather what the highly learned Augustine’s prudence answered:

“Your holy fathers, if they had recognized that these apostolic decrees which we bring—already accepted by the whole world—were holier, would have obeyed willingly and corrected their ignorance and irregular observances. Otherwise they would appear not holy but rebellious against holiness.

“Certainly, at the beginning of the faith, the apostles of the Lord practiced this one work everywhere: teaching all nations to believe in the Savior of the world and to hope for eternal life in him. Thus, not with mortal weapons but with all patience and with manifestations of signs and holy works, they subjected the whole world to Christ’s footsteps.

“At that time they could not publicly establish lunar cycles, lest they obscure the heavenly promises with earthly concerns and run in vain, with Christ’s cross emptied of meaning. Few or rare people then disputed about Easter, especially while the fury of the whole world was punishing every soul that believed in Christ.

“But once the Church began to reign after kings and tyrants had been subjected to Christ, then, with councils held publicly, apostolic decrees about Easter and the other ecclesiastical sacraments were sought. Whatever had previously been neglected or practiced in different ways in different places—whatever was required for the integrity of one faith—was shaped upon the anvil of the one Church.

“Let everyone who does not wish to be cut off from Christ share in this regular unity of Christianity.”

The Britons struggled to resist all these things rather than yield. I scarcely believe that the herald of God Augustine was ever wearied by a pagan with a greater maze of words; so true is it that nothing is more savage than a domestic enemy or civil irrationality. For this is to fight against beasts, or to wage intestine wars.

33. But the Lord’s follower, taught after Christ and the apostles to conquer through patience, strove to try everything, so that those who resisted the Lord’s legation might at least yield to divine judgment.

“Let us ask,” he said, “to be taught by the God of peace and truth, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house, through the evidence of an unmistakable sign, whose opinion is holier and which course ought to be followed in this controversy.

“Seek the experience of truth in some sick or disabled person, who, admitted before us, may prove in the Lord’s name the assertion of his healer to be true.”

With everyone approving this proposal, even the rebels against their will, a certain man from among the English came forward, whose eyes had been deprived of the joys of light. I believe that, by God’s will, an Englishman was found, so that the Britons might not puff up their brows if the man had been one of their own.

The blind man was therefore first brought to their priests to be healed, so that, when they failed, the true witness of the truth and the true physician might become clear. Thus, all rashness confounded, Augustine humbly bent his knees. He prayed to his most certain hearer and most illustrious illuminator of the world [Col. 0077A] to restore the blind man’s sight, so that the hearts of many might be illumined in faith and spiritual grace.

Then, after imposing the sign of the cross upon the man, he said these words of faith: “By this sign may the Lord of all show whose teaching is true.” The blind man’s eyelids opened, and he was illumined; after a long night, a clear day was poured into him.

The whole people acclaimed praise to the Lord, and Augustine was celebrated as God’s faithful witness and the truthful defender of the true teaching. The Britons themselves, overwhelmed by so great a light, now gave their support and testified that his assertions, demonstrated by so great a sign, were true; but they said that they could not abandon the laws of their fathers without the counsel and consent of their elders.

For this reason a truce was requested and granted, while the synod was to be convened again and, with more people assembled, the matter of what ought to be followed was to be considered. These events are remembered as having taken place at the place which to this day is called in the language of the English Augustineac, that is, Augustine’s Oak, on the border of the Wiccians [Note: Since those districts of the Cornavii which belong to the province of Worcester were called Wicci, Alford therefore thinks that Augustineac was already called, in contracted form, Ausric, for Augustinsric—that is, Augustine’s jurisdiction—situated on the edge of Worcestershire toward Herefordshire.], where the largest province of the Britons adjoins it.

34. Therefore seven British bishops, together with many highly learned men, were going to the council from their most distinguished monastery, which in English is called Bancornhabarhe [Note: Bangor, or Banchor, was a famous and very large monastery on the River Dee or its estuary of the Irish Sea, in Flintshire on the borders of Cheshire; scarcely any ruins of it now remain. We discussed it on 29 January in the Life of Saint Gildas the Wise, §2. Bede calls it Banchornaburg, to distinguish it from the famous monastery of Ireland, also called Banchor or Beanchor, where three thousand monks are said to have lived under Saint Comgall. See our notes there, 13 March, in the Life of Saint Mochaemog or Pulcharius the abbot.], at that time presided over by an abbot named Dinoot.

They visited a certain holy and prudent man, distinguished among them for his anchoritic life, explained the matter, and asked his advice as to whether they should follow Augustine’s teaching and abandon the observances of their fathers.

He said to them: “If you have recognized him as a servant of God, follow him.”

“But how,” they replied, “shall we recognize him?”

“Listen,” he said, “and learn from the Lord’s command: ‘Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart’ (Matthew XI, 39). From meekness and humility of heart, therefore, it will be recognizable to you that Augustine bears the Lord’s yoke and accommodates himself to those who bear it. But if he displays fierceness or stubbornness, how will it be evident that he is a man of God or from God?”

When they asked him for an example by which to understand this, he said: “Allow him to enter the synod first. If, when you arrive, he rises before you, obey him reverently as a servant of God. But if, while you are more numerous, he refuses to receive you with equal honor by remaining seated, let him himself be contemptible to you.”

35. Armed with these weapons for their own destruction, they arrived in his presence and found Augustine seated in an episcopal chair, not rising before them at all.

Then anger, indignation, contempt, rejection, quarrels, and disputes broke out; nor could barbarous fury be softened by any paternal gentleness. They not only refused to listen to him but also tried to reject and refute everything he proclaimed.

The man of God, still striving by every means to win them, proposed three matters that they should observe, so that the other things in which they differed might be tolerated: namely, that they celebrate Easter at its proper time, as all the churches did; that they administer the sacrament of baptism according to ecclesiastical order; and that, by preaching the Gospel together with him to the English, they gain brothers and fellow citizens of the kingdom of God.

But the adversaries rejected everything. They asserted not only that they did not wish to obey his commands or entreaties, but also that they did not wish to have him as a bishop.

“For he,” they said, “who disdained to rise when we arrived—how much more will he oppress us if we are subjected to his authority?”

It is therefore clear how meekly and humbly that faithful and prudent vicar of the Lord bore Christ’s yoke, as he sat; and how stiff-necked and proud of heart those who stood revealed themselves to be in rebelling against the Lord’s yoke.

Yet a man of God is recognized not by sitting or rising but by gentleness and fraternal love, since one may be found most merciful while seated and most savage while standing. Moreover, it would have been improper according to ecclesiastical discipline for him to inflate such fierce and erring men by rising before them, when he ought rather to correct them by rebuking them.

At last the Lord’s soldier, brandishing the sword of the Lord against the incorrigible, pronounced this sentence with prophetic spirit and mouth:

“If you do not yield to the one who warns you, believe the one who threatens you. For those whom you reject as peaceful brothers, you will have as most savage enemies; and by those whose fellowship in the kingdom of God you begrudge, you will be driven from this life and kingdom as they wage war against you.”

Thus the rebels against truth finally experienced the truth-speaking prophet. [Note: The Anglo-Saxon chronicler assigns this battle to the year 607.]

At length, after Augustine had already been taken to the Lord, the warlike King Æthelfrith of the English, with a vast force, invaded the city of the Legions, which the English call Lega Cestra, but which the Britons more correctly call Carlegion [Note: Caerlegio in other sources; it was formerly the seat of an archbishop on the River Isca or Usk. That dignity was later transferred to Menevia under Saint David, as we have explained on 1 March, §1, in his Life.].

A great assembly of Britons, priests, and monks had gathered there to pray against the king’s attack. From the monastery of Bangor there was so large a number that, divided into seven companies, no section contained fewer than three hundred men; all of them lived by the work of their hands, and their total was reckoned at more than two thousand.

All these men served against the enemy with the weapons of prayer and a three-day fast. When the king saw them drawn up in a safer place and understood their purpose, he said:

“Behold! These men fight against us with an unarmed hand but an armed prayer, and they assault their God against us more fiercely than with any battle. Let the soldier first disperse this deadly battle line and destroy it utterly.”

Their defender was a man named Broithmailus. When the enemy attacked, he fled and exposed to the swords those unarmed men whom he ought to have defended.

Twelve hundred of the men praying are reported to have been killed, while only fifty escaped by flight. Then the remaining forces of the faithless army were destroyed by the righteous ferocity of the victor.

Thus, in their punishment, the perverse learned that Augustine, long after he had triumphantly reached the stars, had spoken truthfully, although while he was still in the body they had despised his prophecy: namely, that they would be defeated by the English enemies with whom they refused to have peace as brothers in Christ.

## CHAPTER IV. Preaching and conversion throughout the kingdom. Various miracles.

36. Therefore, after this prophet of truth had foretold these evils to the implacable Britons, he departed for the city of York, solicitous for all. Throughout his journey, at every stopping-place, he laboured only to prepare everywhere a straight way and a people made perfect for the Lord. He always went on foot, without conveyance, patient in hardships—[who], as a true follower of the holy apostles, had carried with him on this way of the world nothing born of worldly desire. Free and unencumbered, he ran by the paths of God’s commandments toward heavenly things, drawing bands of followers with him. Companies of holy brethren, as auxiliaries, encircled their heavenly leader, together with a throng of believers; and the farther he proceeded, the more numerous grew his following, as fire gains strength as it goes. For who would not eagerly hasten to companionships so holy, desiring nothing from the world except the salvation even of those who persecuted them, and offering promises so certain of heavenly joys? Their assurance was supplied by examples of holy conduct, by the divine grace of signs, and by unanimity ready to die for truth.

Accordingly, near the borders of York, beside the road along which the Lord’s sower of the word was making his way, there lay a man paralysed in his whole body, deprived also of the light of both eyes, and a beggar. Learning, by asking at the noise of the passing crowd, who was leading the way, he is reported to have cried repeatedly to the saint: “Holy Augustine, by the bounty of your renowned compassion, help this man, destitute of all things and of health.”

At this the most merciful father, mindful of the Lord’s healing of the blind man in the Gospel, approached the sufferer; and in the words of Peter, the Lord’s key-bearer, whom with all devotion he emulated as a patrimum (sic; the term is uncertain) teacher, he said: “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you: rise healed in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts III, 6). He had scarcely spoken when the sick man, who until then had been unable to move himself, sprang up, healed by the power of so great a word; and, as the eyelids of his eyes opened again, he at once received the bright day.
