Believing gratefully in the Saviour whom Augustine taught, with full bodily strength he received a yet happier salvation of soul.

37. Thus the Lord’s herald, both during the procession and in the city of York and wherever he went, confirmed by manifold flashes of miracles what he proclaimed in his teaching. Rejoicing in his success, like those who rejoice at harvest and like victorious men exulting over captured spoil, he everywhere won abundant peoples for Christ—so much so that, on that day of the Lord’s Nativity, celebrated with the harmonies of all heaven, more than ten thousand English, besides an immeasurable number of children and women, were reborn through the washing of holy baptism in the river called in English the Sirarios [Note: [Col. 0079D] The city of York is on the River Ure, commonly called the Ouse, into which another smaller river flows there, already mentioned as the Fossa; and this seems here to be called Suarios. In the shorter Life, Sualavi.]—as though in a single birth and womb of the Church.

At the command of the divine teacher, as though at the voice of an angel crying from heaven, all together, two by two, they entered the threatening depth of the river as if it were solid ground. There, in true faith and confession of the supreme Trinity, they were baptized one by one, while the water was blessed by the apostolic leader.

O what solemnity! What joy! What a delightful spectacle for the citizens of heaven and earth! The capacious basin of the river seemed unable to contain so great a multitude; and the birth of so many bands and companies seemed to pour forth, like a single offspring from the womb of one parent. So great a progeny was born into heaven from the depths of the waters!

With how many lights of the newly born did the day and glory of Christ’s Nativity then shine! With what joy all the angels of God—who rejoice over one repentant sinner—then exulted over so great a shoot of the divine harvest, singing of the newborn Savior: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

38. With all these—the citizens of heaven—blessed Pope Gregory rejoiced in the Holy Spirit so greatly that, concerning so illustrious a number of believers, he sent a letter to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, who would likewise rejoice as the friend of God. This joy is further magnified by a remarkable miracle: amid the pressure of so many rushing crowds, amid such diversity of sexes, ages, and infirmities, although all crossed that unfordable depth, absolutely no one perished, and no one complained of being crushed or injured. Rather, the Lord transferred them all, reborn in Christ and ascending from the washing like flocks of shorn sheep, to the farther bank, so that all might have a single nativity—Christ’s and their own—in Christ.

I have said too little in saying that none there was injured: all the sick laid down in the water the afflictions not only of their souls but also of their bodies. With the salvation of both aspects of humanity, they came forth like the people of Israel from the Red Sea or from the midst of the Jordan, as a whitened army amid heavenly rejoicing.

The church still stands in that same place, founded and dedicated in honor and under the name of this illustrious baptizer Augustine. By healing the frequent crowds who seek such salvation, it provides the most celebrated evidence of his power. But, for the sake of faith, we add here what follows from the aforesaid letter of Pope Gregory to Eulogius (Book VII, Letter 30).

39. “We give thanks to the almighty Lord, because we see fulfilled in you what is written: ‘Where there are very many crops, there is manifest strength of oxen.’ For if the strong ox had not drawn the plow of the tongue across the soil of the hearts of the hearers, such a harvest of believers would certainly not have arisen.

“Since I know that in the good works you perform you rejoice with others, I return the favor of your grace to you and announce things not unlike them. While the nation of the English, situated in a corner of the world, remained until now faithless in the worship of wood and stone, it pleased God—through the help of your prayers to me—that I should send to it, under God’s authority, Augustine, a monk of my monastery, religious and worthy of God, to preach.

“After I had given him permission, he was made a bishop by the bishops of Germania [Note: [Col. 0081D] Rather, of Gaul; but on account of the Franks, who originated from Germania. Gaul was contained within Germania.], and with their assistance he was brought to the aforesaid nation at the end of the world. And now reports concerning its salvation and his work have reached us: he himself and those who were sent with him shine among that people with such miracles that they seem to imitate the apostles’ powers in the signs they display.

“On the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, which has just passed in this first indiction, more than ten thousand English, as our brother and fellow bishop has reported, were baptized by him [Note: [Col. 0082D] That is, in the year 598. But these words seem rather to be understood of the conversion of the people of Canterbury.]. I have related this so that you may recognize what you accomplish by speaking among the Alexandrian people and what you accomplish by praying at the ends of the earth. For your prayers are present in the place where you are not, while your holy works are displayed in the place where you are.”

From what the same sweet-speaking pope wrote to the bishops of the Franks, we extract these few words:

“Just as fire grows greater when fanned by the breeze, so the zeal of a good mind advances through commendation. Therefore, with the grace of our Redeemer cooperating, so great a multitude of the English nation is being converted to the grace of the Christian faith that our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine declares that those who are with him cannot suffice to carry out this work in different places. We have therefore determined to send to him some monks, together with our most beloved and common sons Laurence the priest and Mellitus the abbot” (Book IX, Letter 52).

“And therefore let your fraternity show them the charity that is fitting.”

How sweet it would be to recount what he also commended in grateful letters to King Lothar of the Franks concerning the reception of the saints, and to Queen Brunhild concerning their universally known miracles—to gather with eager hand so many pearls and honeycombs! But we must obey the one who listens either sluggishly or wearily, since most of these matters are found in the register of that most blessed Pope Gregory.

40. Therefore, to return to the journey mentioned above, at last the evangelist of the Lord, Augustine, departing from York with his company of holy companions and continual miracles, encountered a certain leper, disfigured by ulcerous and purulent foulness. The wretched man called upon Augustine, the bearer of spontaneous healing, with pitiable laments.

What do I mean by “called”? The pestilential disease had deprived him of his voice; a hiss served him for speech, and a rattling sound for a cry. The kindly healer needed no interpreter, and the compassionate man required no lengthy appeal. He perceived the sick man’s distress in the very sight of him, and the charity of Christ urged him to bring relief to the afflicted.

Why delay with circumlocutions the swift generosity of his words? The diseased man approached as a suppliant, and the lavish bishop blessed him with a blessing. Strengthened by Christ’s presence, he said: “In the name of the Lord and Savior, be cleansed from all the filth of your leprosy.”

He spoke, and immediately the whole calamity of the foul fluid fled like a cloud. The skin became clean, and, the impurity entirely absorbed, covered the whole man. Naaman the Syrian, whom the healer Elisha had previously commanded to wash seven times in the Jordan, was not cleansed so quickly. But Augustine, by the word of him who said in the Gospel, “Be cleansed,” surpassed him in speed (Mark 1:41).

O blessed and rich poverty of the apostolic preacher in Christ, richer than all the treasures of the earth! O most abundant treasure, in which not gold is poured out for greedy mortals, but salvation, free and incomparable to gold, is poured out for souls and bodies. Could the countless riches of Croesus or Darius have purchased health for the sick?

The cry of the astonished people over so great a sign therefore rose to heaven, and people converged from every direction upon the life-giving baptism.

41. Thus the Lord’s merchant, carrying on his work along the road, turned westward from the northern region. He followed not so much the manner of a traveler as of a hunter or fowler—not so much hastening toward his own affairs as seeking the Lord’s profits, stretching his nets wherever the divine catch might result.

When he reached the province called Dorset, and was received everywhere like an angel of the Lord, while he both fed his hearers’ faith and was himself nourished by it, he came upon a certain village, as though upon Tartarus, the dwelling of Pluto. There the impious populace, blinded by its own darkness and hating the divine light, could not merely refuse to hear the life-giving teachings; it also raged against the saints of God with every storm of mockery and abuse, drove them far from all its property, and, it is believed, did not spare them even physical violence.

But the messenger of God, following the Lord’s command and the apostles’ example, shook even the dust from his feet against them and imposed upon them a sentence worthy of their merits—not by the wish of one who cursed, since he desired the salvation of all, but by divine judgment and in the pattern of Elijah—so that he might rebuke with due punishment both the despisers of the saints themselves and all their descendants, because they had rejected the commandments of life.

It is said that those who were to be struck by lightning hung the projecting tails of sea-fish upon the saints. This brought them everlasting glory, but turned perpetual disgrace back upon themselves, so that the shame might be attributed to their degenerate descendants, not to an innocent and noble homeland.

42. Here it seems appropriate to append, as a corresponding example of correction, what is reported to have been performed by Augustine, the bringer of salvation, among another unbelieving people at that time.

That people, joined to demons through long-standing profanity, hated the friends of light because of its love of darkness. In its unbelief it might have said to God: “Depart from us; we do not desire the knowledge of your ways. We have made a covenant with death” (Isaiah 28:15). They not only rejected the angelic teacher, who by angelic conduct and the thunderbolts of miracles proved the truth of his teaching; they also burned to cut down the bearers of life with swords or to burn them alive in fires.

Whatever the kindly preacher promised to believers, they spat upon; whatever he threatened in prophetic fashion, they mocked. What could that soul, beloved of God and bringing forth the salvation of all, do among people so desperate—she who would have wished to give herself even for such persons in everlasting charity? What could be impossible to such great faith, or invincible to so strong a love?

Therefore, taking refuge in the inexhaustible mercy of Christ, he prayed that Christ would crush with an iron rod, like a potter’s vessel, that cauldron of worldly insolence and demonic worship which the prophet saw boiling from the face of the North; or that he would refine that mass in his furnace into something better and redeem those worthy of destruction through correction (Jeremiah 1).

Immediately that whole conspiracy of the wicked was seized by an extraordinary punishment, so that affliction alone might give understanding to their hearing. They all burned with an invisible fire—not like those fevered by quartan fevers or other inflammations of disease, but, wondrous to say and marvelous to see, with their skin burned and their flesh raw, they displayed bloodied feet and thighs eaten away.

Throughout that frenzied populace, just as there was no one who repented, so there was no one who escaped. Every age and sex—old men and infants, parents and children—was punished by the same sentence. Everywhere cries, groans, and howls of torment were thrown forth.

Then at last the transgressors returned to their senses and understood what the prophetic Augustine had threatened against them for despising the promises of heaven. Gathered together, they ran to the man whom they had scorned; they fled to him whom they had driven away. Weeping, they fell at the feet of the man whose prayers and admonitions they had ridiculed. They earnestly begged for the saving bath which they had attacked; and, their punitive heat changed into the heat of faith, they all implored to be reborn in Christ.

This was the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. They could no longer be unbelievers when Augustine promised that through baptism they would be regenerated to the salvation of mind and body.

A great solemnity therefore came to pass for the heavenly and earthly hosts, when so many thousands of the reborn were joined to the citizens above. And so that this rejoicing might shine more brightly once the cloud of grief had been wiped away, that pestilential fire—which devoured their rotting flesh, which no water could extinguish and no human art could heal—was extinguished in all who were baptized there, solely through baptism and Augustine’s intervention.

From that day onward, this plague, which sometimes rages in other lands, was, through Augustine’s patronage, driven out of that entire country. Then those freedmen of God could rightly cry: “Unless the Lord had delivered us through Augustine, or Augustine through the Lord, we would have become like Sodom or Gomorrah, or rightly perished in Elijah’s fire together with the men of fifty.”

43. From this detour of similar madness and just correction, let us return to the former road. The most holy messengers of God, Augustine and his companions, having gone forth five miles from the injurious people mentioned above through lonely places, across a deserted and waterless land, grew exhausted beneath the open sky, overcome by severe thirst and heat. Their sole hope of life lay in God and in the merits of their Augustine.

He, burning not so much for himself as for his brothers, took refuge with all of them in prayer before his beneficent Lord, whose help he had always experienced in every petition. As Jesus the Lord heard him praying, he pitied his martyr. For the mind prepared for martyrdom makes a martyr even without suffering; and Augustine’s martyrdom consisted in enduring kindly conduct among his persecutors.

In ineffable mercy, the Lord deigned to show himself there and consoled him with this familiar address:

“Take courage, my good and faithful servant, and act manfully, because I, the Lord your God, am with you in all that you undertake. My ears are open to your prayers, so that you may always obtain whatever you ask for those on whose behalf you petition. For the door of eternal life stands open to you, where you will rejoice with me without end.”

Blessed Augustine drank in with all the ardor of his heart such gifts of the Lord’s vision and address. Forgetting bodily thirst, he thirsted ever more intensely for the sweetness he had tasted; and as that sweetness gratefully met his tears, he followed its departure with still more abundant weeping.

44. Worshiping there and perceiving that the heavenly benefits of the Lord overflowed in the place where his feet had stood, he recognized that the land in which the fountain of life had appeared could not remain arid. At once he fixed his staff for the journey into that spot.

Without delay, a crystal-clear spring leapt forth as though from a struck vein. It abundantly refreshed everyone and brought joy through both its miracle and its healing. From that time onward, its waters, diverted into rivers and streams, made these places habitable and densely populated.

The holy father himself, having been granted so blessed a vision, named the place Cernhel, in perpetual memory of so great a grace, after the sight of God. The name is composed from Latin and Hebrew—for just as the first syllable derives from *cernere*, “to see,” so the second, *hel*, signifies “God”—and it has become permanently established there.

A church was also built and consecrated there in the name of the Lord and Savior, who had deigned to reveal himself in that place. Subsequently, a monastery, long ago raised in honor of blessed Peter the apostle by its buildings and wealth, now flourishes with a distinguished community of monks [Note: [Col. 0083D] Concerning this monastery of Cernel, consult the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, page 253 and the following page. There is given there a foundation charter made in the year 987, when the little monastery consisted of three monks.].

That sacred fountain is celebrated under the name of Augustine its administrator. It supplies water not only for those who drink, but also, for those who believe, a remedy for various diseases. We therefore give here an account of a recent miracle, which is very widely celebrated there and throughout the province.

45. The most learned abbot of Cernel has a parish priest who is accustomed to perform the divine offices for the people in the monastery itself. When illness brought him to the point of death, it compelled him to request the monastic habit. The garment of sacred profession was placed upon his head—he had recourse to it only when death was imminent; that is, he seized the armor of God only when the enemy was attacking.

It was night, and sleep was overcoming the exhausted sick man. The kindly Augustine stood beside him in his fear, distinguished by the very habit and episcopal staff. He did not long deny such a remedy to one who perhaps still lived with a worldly mind. He invited him to receive the prize that he freely gives to grateful and ungrateful alike, who makes his sun rise upon them and often recalls the estranged by favor rather than punishment.

The pious comforter restored the anxious man with this address:

“Rise,” he said, “and go to the fountain of Saint Augustine. There sing Psalm 50 three times in succession, and, invoking the help of Augustine, wash your body three times in the same fountain. In this way you will obtain the life and health you desire. So that no uncertainty may hinder you, know that he himself is present with you and gives this counsel—the one through whom you are to recover.”

During these words the dying man rose, seized his staff, and, to everyone’s amazement, went out. His attendants thought that he was wandering under the omen of approaching death; nevertheless, they preferred to follow him and observe where he was going rather than restrain him.

When he came to the sacred fountain, he washed himself three times in its stream, and Psalm 50 was sung three times with Augustine’s aid invoked. Before the sacrifice of prayer had been completed, the sick man marveled to find himself suddenly recalled from death to health.

What the ancient healer had done for the leper through seven washings, our Elisha, the confessor of the supreme Trinity, performed for the dying man in the threefold form of baptism. He returned, no longer sick but completely healthy, to his bed and rested peacefully. At the first light of day he entered the monastery and, as usual, sang the morning office for the people.

Great astonishment and amazement seized the abbot, the brothers, and the people, together with joy and an outpouring of thanks: they had expected to receive his funeral rites, yet saw him lively and unharmed, performing his accustomed service. He also explained publicly to the people how he had been healed so quickly through Saint Augustine.

46. Thus the angelic legate of the Lord, Augustine—to bring his journey to an end—after traversing long stretches of land and most of Britain, and after innumerable salutary consolations of miracles and teachings, returned with that most blessed company of companions to his perpetual seat and dwelling, Canterbury [*Dorobernia*]. There he was received with universal favor and joy, as the father of all, as the bringer of light, and as the most desired return of their sun.

47. Among the crowds who frequented so powerful a healer of the weak, a young man arrived, moving on his knees in place of his feet, twisted by severe contraction of both legs. He was also deprived of hearing and speech. Only his eyes had a path open to them, but his deformed gait denied him a way forward; he could see what he wanted, but the tongue that might have enabled him to ask for it had failed. He made his distress known by silence; being deaf, he could not hear what might have helped him. Whether one should call him half-alive or half-dead, he was a pitiable example of one deprived of so many functions of life.

But the compassionate Augustine released him from this misery by devout prayer. Through the grace of the Trinity he drove away his threefold affliction by a threefold cure. His legs were straightened, his tongue was released, and his ears were opened; the threefold invalid rejoiced in threefold health.

He walked, ran, spoke, and heard without difficulty—plainly and clearly.

Yet the man was frivolous. He abused the health he had received with such vanity and insolence that Augustine seemed to have forced God to grant salvation to one so undisciplined. To pass over his other faults of levity and buffoonery, when he came to the church he afflicted the people with such garrulousness and wantonness that he scandalized everyone by his shamelessness. He showed no reverence for the holy place and yielded to no one’s reproof.

Thus divine correction bound him more severely in his former chains. The health that had become a means of destruction for the untamed man was taken away, and he was subdued by the repeated return of his afflictions, now with greater pain. The mouth of the fool, overflowing with folly, and the ears intent upon tales and every kind of wantonness, as well as the feet running toward destruction, were closed with a bronze key and turned back toward self-restraint.

He was therefore confined by harsher torments and brought by friends and relatives to the heavenly physician. Clinging to the saint’s feet, he lamented with dreadful sighs what he could not express in words because his speech was obstructed. Weeping and wailing, he sought pardon and, by presumptuous confidence in mercy, begged again for the health he had forfeited.

The father’s compassion was wounded more deeply by another’s misery, and mercy wrestled with the judge of mercy—the mercy by which merciful justice is accustomed to be overcome. A mediator and advocate stood between the guilty man and God: on one side he reproved him as deserving punishment; on the other he pleaded that he be saved.

The wicked man was confounded by his guilt and corrected through repentance, so that once corrected he might be clothed in righteousness and, justified, obtain the grace of the righteous Savior.

Thus Augustine’s intercession prevailed. He wrested a blessing from the Lord like Jacob, obtained pardon like Moses, and, victorious, brought back to the wretched man the health that he had again snatched from the Lord.

Restored completely in walking, speech, and hearing, the man no longer needed to be led by another’s help; he no longer spoke with his fingers; and those who had previously been taught to satisfy a deaf man through signs no longer needed to do so. Restored also to sounder judgment, he ceased his former vanity—which was more beneficial than bodily health—through the instruction, correction, prayer, and salvation bestowed by his father Augustine.

## CHAPTER V. Saint Livinus Baptized and Instructed. The Death and Burial of Saint Augustine

48. Amid so many distinguished miracles, who could worthily proclaim the praises of so great a teacher, through whom not only the fiercest peoples received Christ’s gentle yoke, but holy men endowed with signs, even through angelic instruction, came to him by a wondrous road to be taught?

This matter should not be compressed into a brief chapter; it should be explained in a clear and lucid account. We read in the life of the most blessed bishop and martyr Livinus, faithfully written down from the testimony of his holy companions, how the most faithful steward of the Lord’s affairs, Augustine, concerned for the salvation of all, came to Coloman, the religious king of Scotland [Note: [Col. 0087D] That is, of present-day Ireland, which was then called Scotland.], and baptized the blessed Livinus, then a boy, together with the bishop Saint Monalchius; and how the king, the queen, and the nobles of the kingdom received him from the font.

Then, before everyone, a column of solar splendor shone upon the baptized child. In the radiance, a golden right hand, brighter than the sun, appeared and blessed the boy three times with the sign of the cross. A heavenly voice then sounded these words: “Beloved by God and by human beings, whose memory is in blessing.”

At this Augustine glorified the Lord and gave everyone an example of glorifying him.

Meanwhile, as that boy grew through holy practices, he was so dear to the king and to everyone—his spiritual son in both age and merit—that they tried with extraordinary affection and prayers to retain him. While he feared the snares of the world and anxiously wavered over this matter, an angel of light appeared to him and, greeting him by name, said:

“Hail, brother Livinus. Stop grieving, and hear how you are to be consoled. Go from here to Augustine, bishop of the English, and receive from him instruction in every kind of holy discipline. Through him, with God’s help, you will attain the summit of virtue.”

The Lord’s confessor hastened to obey the angelic commands. Having sought the king’s permission and broken the bonds of his supporters like spiders’ webs, he went willingly to the sea with his three blessed disciples, Foilanus, Helyas, and Kylianus [who also became distinguished as thoroughly trustworthy authors in recording his deeds], so that he might cross over to Augustine, his most desired father.

But an angel of the Lord met him on the way, youthful in appearance, radiant in face, gracious in bearing, and sweet in speech:

“Take courage, brother,” he said, “because the Lord has sent me to you as an inseparable guide and guardian on your entire journey. Only follow me without hesitation, for, with the Lord’s favor, I will bring you by prosperous progress to the teacher of your advancement whom you seek.”

Wise Livinus recognized the Spirit of truth speaking these words to him. He therefore confidently followed, with the disciples mentioned above, the one who went before him, and together they crossed that great and spacious sea with dry feet.

Throughout the entire journey, as they walked on foot across the waves of the vast deep as though treading solid ground, it seemed to the most sacred Livinus and his blessed companions that they were passing through meadows or green open fields, blooming with roses and lilies and with every beautiful variety of herbs and flowers.

When the starry guide had safely and successfully brought his followers ashore, he returned to the heavens before their eyes with indescribable brightness and a broad flash of light, as though by that splendor he were saying: “Hasten to follow me here, sons of light, having rejected the darkness of the world.”

Who, then, would hesitate either to ascribe or to attribute to the merits of the glorious Augustine these flower-filled and shining miracles—that for those seeking Augustine the water might become green, the sea blossom, and the waves flower; and that the deep itself might offer itself as solid ground beneath the feet of those seeking the evangelist of peace?

Thus, with the three aforementioned confessors of the holy Trinity, desirous Livinus came to the desired father Augustine. Under angelic guidance he came, as it were, to another angel: from a flower-filled road to a flower-bearing paradise, from the way across the sea to a honey-sweet fountain, from perishable riches to the treasurer of incorruptible wealth, who might draw forth from the chamber of the true King the infinite abundance of his possessions and the unfading beauty of all his forms.

O what festive joy arose for so exalted a teacher of the saints when he received such a disciple divinely destined for him—one whom he had foreknown through the Holy Spirit and who was worthy to become a teacher of others! Yet Livinus’s noble nature preferred humbly to learn from one divinely inspired so that later he might teach with confidence.

He heard Augustine, who had set his mouth in heaven, discoursing with an angelic voice on the infinite multitude and glorious order of the heavenly powers; on the most exalted hierarchy of apostolic dignity; on the innumerable army and triumphal palm of the martyrs; and on the most radiant crown of confessors and virgins.

Augustine taught him that no suffering in the world was worthy to be compared with such rewards, that nothing could be measured or valued against that beauty, that dignity, that unfailing solemnity and joy, and that one must now run toward them through every kind of labor and every fragrance of virtue.

He led his most eager disciple toward the prize of everlasting blessedness through all the flower gardens of sacred Scripture. He opened for him the treasuries and storerooms of Christ and the Church, filled with the delights and pleasures of the Lord’s treasures and with the life-breathing fragrances of the saints’ eternal charity and glory.

With these and many other exhortations, the illustrious leader armed the strongest athlete of Christ for the camps of the Lord and kindled him to the highest ardor. In accordance with the promise of the guiding angel, he raised him to the perfection of apostolic conduct, so that he might also attain the martyr’s palm.

After keeping him with himself for five years and three months and advancing him in all holiness through the most sacred examples and instructions—young in age but advanced in religious maturity—he finally consecrated him a priest, most choice for Christ.

At the very ordination of his beloved disciple, the most generous *catigeta* [Note: [Col. 0088D] *Catigeta* is a teacher or rhetorician in Papias; in Greek, καθηγητής (*katēgētēs*). The printed text incorrectly has *catigera*.] also gave him a most sweet pledge and memorial of his perpetual love: a purple chasuble, foreshadowing glorious martyrdom, bordered with gold and gems in imitation of his merits. He added a stole and an orarium, likewise adorned with golden stars and precious gems.

After invoking every blessing upon him and exchanging the support of their prayers, and not without mutual tears, he sent him back to his king and people as their most desired teacher, together with his holy companions mentioned above.

Finally, just as bees seek a honey-filled flower and deer a spring of water, so people everywhere sought Augustine, who made heavenly things sweet as honey.

49. There was a certain old man who asserted that his grandfather had been baptized by Saint Augustine, and that his grandfather had reported the matter to his father, and his father to him, in the following way:

“When I was a young man,” he said, “and saw crowds of people running to Augustine, that new and unheard-of chief teacher of our salvation, as though to an angel, I—whose crown was vanity, whose joy was folly, and whose delight was mockery—ridiculed everything with astonishing dullness of mind, as though it were a phantasm. I thought it a great absurdity that everyone except me and my fellow wanderers should be in error.

“When I heard that he healed every kind of body afflicted by weakness or death, I laughed even more loudly in my unbelieving madness. At last I devised a trick in my wantonness. Like an inflated wineskin, I went to see him as though he were a fraud, or to hear him utter but half a word, intending to snatch some jest from his mouth or from one of his healings by which I could provoke laughter among people like myself.

“When I had thrust myself into the pressing crowd like a plotter and a thief, and had marked with my eyes his fatherly and reverent gaze, I immediately froze, confounded by great terror. It seemed that a certain divine judgment in him was indignant at my impurity.

“But he, filled with the Holy Spirit of God, as has already become clear, looked upon me as though he knew me well. He sent a servant and said, ‘Bring that young man to me.’ He ordered me to be brought to him from the midst of the crowd.

“Then, realizing more deeply that I had become known to him without an informant, I trembled with such astonishment as if I had seen a prosecutor and punisher of my crime with drawn sword. At once I fled to the mercy of so great a prophet and, having thrown myself down, clasped his sacred feet.

“There I released all the swelling of my vanity like air from a punctured bladder, vomited out all the filth of my frivolous levity, and surrendered myself entirely to the commands and teachings of so kindly a father.

“He gently embraced me, reproved and instructed, in his fatherly arms; baptized me as a believer in Christ; and blessed me with a long life extending to children’s children [Note: [Col. 0089D] In the shorter Life this is explained more precisely as follows: he stated that the same grandfather lived more than one hundred years, and that the blessing of such longevity descended to his father; in his own case, too, he greatly surpassed the centenarian years of his ancestors.].”

The aforesaid old man presented these and many further things to his listeners with the assurance of faith: things heard by his father from his grandfather and related by his father to himself, as though known from another age.

He also made known that his parents had conveyed to him the appearance and patrician bearing of the blessed Augustine: his tall and lofty stature, so high that he towered above the people from the shoulders upward and displayed the height, though not the ferocity, of Saul. His face was kindly and reverend; his brow, framed by his hair, projected between its two columns like a window.

As for the miracles and healings he continually performed among the crowds who gathered around him and among the sick, the old man asserted that no one could recount or number them. He remembered that Augustine had continually traversed the provinces on foot in apostolic devotion, often barefoot, and had drawn the calluses of the knees of the Lord’s brother James onto the soles of his feet. He also maintained that several of Augustine’s holy companions were accustomed either to imitate or to equal these same virtues.

Therefore, since charity believes all that is credible, and since we readily believe what we love, while we show by our disbelief that we hate or despise what we do not believe, let the children of love—and not strangers—consider that the deeds performed by the saints in life, transmitted either through writings, through long-lived elders, or through fame, which is the law of history, from generation to generation, could have come to the knowledge of the holy Scriptures through God’s disclosure. It is not wrong to believe such things, and things of such a kind.

Now, after the rivers and savage rejections, let us unfold the chief palm of the glorious Augustine.

### 50

Long ago, that heavenly inhabitant, struck by the wound of heavenly love—which is strong as death—shrank from all earthly pleasures as from the losses of life, and from worldly glory as from chains, prisons, and punishments, although for the Savior it would have been sweet to suffer all these things, even death itself. Bound to earth only in body—or rather bound only by the fatherly care of begetting and forming children for God—in every other respect he dwelt wholly in that eternal homeland; with all his mind and soul, in continual and vehement longing, he sought heavenly things. What ardent prayers, what laments of holy desires, what unspeakable sighs he sent toward heaven! “Who,” he says, “will give me wings like a dove’s? Then I shall fly away and rest.” And: “When shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” “My soul has desired and languished for the courts of the Lord.”

Thus, with restless cries, he anticipated the face of the Lord and did violence to heaven, repeatedly knocking and begging to be admitted, longing to be dissolved and to be with Christ. At last, understanding from the response of the Holy Spirit that his desire had been heard—that he would come to the one desired by all who are upright in heart—he began, with anxious parental feeling, to fear that the tender infancy of the Church, newly born or about to be born after his departure, deprived of its shepherd, might be ravaged by the attack of wolves.

Therefore, with clear judgment and heavenly inspiration, he turned his attention to having blessed Laurence, a man of apostolic holiness, distinguished by apostolic signs and foremost among his companions, ordained in his place, the Lord saying to him in spirit: “Anoint this man for me as the chosen priest.” He reports the matter to the clergy, the king, and the people: all approve, all support it, all bless and desire it together. Thus, while the king and the assembled people offer immense congratulations, he ordains Laurence as his successor with every solemn joy, just as the prince of the apostles Peter once ordained Clement, because of the necessity of providing the aforesaid new formation—though no one afterward ought to presume to imitate this example. No one properly did this after Peter; no one incompetently should do it after Augustine. For Christ is one, the Church is one, and the bishop is one; the one and the unity are not divided.

Having therefore consecrated him and appointed him ready for every task, he sent him, like Paul sent Timothy, to the work of the ministry and to the building up of the body of Christ: to travel about, hasten, persist in season and out of season; to reprove, beseech, and exhort with all patience and teaching.

He himself, however, as a contemplative theorist, as a fugitive from the oppressive world, as a solitary sparrow on the housetop, rejoiced exceedingly that, having broken the fetters of worldly affairs, he might fly away to the Lord on the wings of eternal love, rest in Mary’s better portion, devote himself to God alone, stand with unveiled face before the glory of the Lord, and be nourished by its perpetual sweetness. Only then, he believed, did he truly live and reign; only then had he begun to serve God.

Nevertheless, he never ceased to increase the Lord’s gains by gathering peoples together, and even kings, so that they might serve the Lord; nor was he ever absent when divine affairs required it. Now, like an eagle, he flew toward heavenly things; now, when the Lord required it, he revisited the lowly pastures.

### 51

Why does the prayer fear, after such long evasion, to bring the present light to its end? At last the most victorious athlete of the Lord, having completed the course of his life in all holiness and perfection of merits, reached the prize and the long-desired rewards of the eternal kingdom. When the Lord, knocking through illness, came, he opened to him with indescribable rejoicing and an aromatic sacrifice of thanksgiving.

Then, with the magnanimous affection of paternal love, he exhorted both the king and the princes, and the clergy and the people, to serve the Lord in fear; having cast aside the defiling filth of demonic sacrifices, to remain steadfast in the faith of Christ divinely entrusted to them; to cling continually, in faith and love, to the one living and true God; and diligently to observe his commandments through the anointed pontiff and the Lord’s ministers.

Thus came the end of worldly storms, and the dawn of eternal joys shone forth. Having blessed the king and confirmed in Christ the primitive Church of his spiritual offspring, and leaving to all pledges of perpetual love and lessons of blessed life, amid the tearful ranks of his holy companions and disciples, while blessed Laurence stood with the assembled people, he laid down the burden of the flesh and was taken up into heaven, amid the triumph and glory of the heavenly powers, amid the immeasurable meeting and reception of all, and amid everlasting joy.

O how solemnly all heaven is then adorned and crowned for the arrival of so distinguished a citizen! The heavenly hosts surround the victor bearing the palm; the apostles invite their apostolic companion to their seats; the purple camps of the martyrs surround the standard-bearer of martyrdom; the radiant ranks of confessors and the venerable company of priests embrace the distinguished hierarch; the shining choirs of virgins sing sweet hymns to their virginal leader.

To speak in the language of mortal custom concerning those ineffable harmonies of heaven: then that great Jerusalem, the city of the great King, saw at once its peoples and tribes, all singing praises and unwearied thanks to the Lord in Augustine’s triumph.

Let us, the least of all, although as unworthy as we are unequal to the task, follow them as we can—not with funeral laments, but with these songs of triumph:

> You reign, Augustine, exalted above the age of Augustus in name and dignity,  
> You who increased Christ’s commonwealth and added Britain to the Roman Church,  
> Better than Caesar Augustus added Alexandria to Roman power.  
> Kings, princes, and the senate of the English, and the multitude of nations, accompany you into heaven;  
> Angels and archangels lead you forth in triumph;  
> Thrones and dominions receive you;  
> The King of kings crowns you.

### 52

The most precious pearl of his body, in that apostolic and royal monastery which the most distinguished Laurence had founded by God’s direction, was placed in the northern portico of the same sacred hall, after a magnificent dedication attended by the most devout King Æthelberht and the peoples assembled from throughout England. There he treasured the deposit of the heavenly kingdom in everlasting memory.

### 53

But while we hasten to bring this pious history to an end, we are still held back obstinately by the gracious sweetness of this angelic place and by the infinite gift of the saints’ love, which satisfies those who are full and fills those who desire, and we delight to recall how that portico was filled with the heavenly mausoleums of so many of Britain’s foremost learned men—or rather, of so many angels of God.

Among these it is gratefully worth observing what noble pledges the universal mother, Rome, produced: fathers and instructors for the British Ocean. While one love joined them together in one chamber, several nations possessed individual patrons, each distinguished by his own radiance.

The foremost of these, Augustine, made Laurence, the dedicator of that church, his successor, as has been shown. He ordained Mellitus bishop of London and Justus bishop of the Rochester church. When Laurence was exiled for Christ, Mellitus succeeded as the third and Justus as the fourth.

**[Note: The following are venerated: Honorius, 30 September; Deusdedit, 30 June; Theodore, 19 September; Adrian, 9 January; Mildrith, 13 July.]**

Honorius, himself distinguished by the honor of Roman instruction, was added as the fifth. Deusdedit was sixth in succession, but the first flower of the English race to enter the register of the Roman fathers. From England, the Roman foundations of Canterbury received nothing more welcome than his first fruits.

The seventh, Theodore, an excellent successor to Roman eminence, was buried beside the gracious Augustine on his right, with only the wall of the monastic burial chamber intervening, since the portico, not yet enlarged, could not receive them all. After it was later expanded, Adrian was added to these holy companions, worthy to be loved by all ages. He was the most merciful abbot of that monastery, and, chosen by the apostolic see of Rome as archbishop of Canterbury, brought the blessed Theodore there in his place. Together with him he made the English teachable in the learning of both Greek and Latin.

Likewise, Mildrith, a most shining lily of the English, a royal virgin of Christ, greatly illumines by her whiteness the splendid ornaments of so many fathers.

The most blessed Pope Gregory, therefore, the author of them all, having the central altar like a patrician throne and preserving the portico dedicated to God, embraces it with eternal love—not so much the tombs of those buried there as the dining chambers of those feasting. Before all the others, he binds Augustine to himself, as the chief of his institution, the firstborn of his spiritual labor, and first both in life and in rank.

The other sons, who are the ecclesiastical forefathers of England, likewise recline like young olive trees around his table.

For the tomb of the most eminent Augustine, the following epitaph is written in the official record:

> Here rests the lord Augustine, first archbishop of Canterbury, who was once sent here by the blessed Gregory, pontiff of the city of Rome, and, supported by God through the working of miracles, led King Æthelberht and his people from the worship of idols to the faith of Christ. Having completed the days of his office in peace, he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, while the same king was reigning.

Of these seven first pillars of the English Church, hewn from the Tarpeian rock at Rome, the following verses are also placed:

> Seven chief men and forefathers are there for the English,  
> Seven rulers and seven constellations through the heavens;  
> Seven are the stars, and one chamber holds them;  
> Seven fountains of life and seven lamps;  
> Seven palms of the kingdom and seven crowns.  
>   
> Seven, too, are the eyes by which Christ beholds this world,  
> As the world runs its course through seven ages of days.

Their titles, written above them in their order, are these:

> Duke Augustine is first, foremost in rank;  
> Laurel-bearing and pure, Laurence is second in his seat.  
> The third is gracious Mellitus, honey-bearing;  
> The fourth is Justus, giving sweet tastes in his name.  
>   
> The fifth is Honorius, the strength and honor of the Church;  
> Deusdedit is sixth, to whom Christ gives his gifts.  
> Theodore, seventh, likewise brings blessed Sabbaths.  
>   
> By these seven leaders England flourishes, and by so many days.  
> Adrian, leader of the monks, is added as the eighth.  
> The English star Mildrith brings back her own honey.  
>   
> Eight fathers are from Rome; the rest, born among the English, accompany them in honor,  
> Joined to them in merit.  
> From this source the way of the Gospel flows in divided streams.  
>   
> These are Brithwoald, Tatwin, and you, Nothelm,

**[Note: They presided over the Church of Canterbury as archbishops: Brithwoald from the year 693 until the year 730; Tatwin succeeded him and died in the year 734, being entered in the English martyrology on 30 July. Nothelm succeeded him and lived until the year 739. He is also regarded as a saint on the panel of the old altar of Saint Augustine, and his mausoleum stands there among the other saints.]**

> And now Berta, imitating the first fathers and nobles,  
> So many together encircle the brow of the Church with piety.

Of the countless miracles which blessed Augustine performed, in this place of his repose or anywhere among peoples and places, for the faith of those who asked, the following little book will recount some that were proven before the eyes of the faithful, with God guiding us in his truth. He reigns through all ages and always shows himself wondrous in his saints.

*(This little book may be read in the Bollandists, volume V of May, page 862.)*

## A Very Few Surviving Monuments of Saint Augustine, Apostle of the English

### Letters

No one can doubt that Saint Augustine wrote many letters; but all of them have perished except one, partly inserted in a letter of blessed Gregory the Great commonly known under the title *Responses*. See it in volume LXXVII of Migne’s *Patrology*, the sixty-fourth letter of book XI of Gregory’s letters.

In the same volume, two other letters written to Saint Augustine by the same pontiff should also be consulted—namely, letters 28 and 65 of book XI—as well as several others in which the distinguished Father commends the apostle to bishops and clergy who met him on his journey: book V, letter 53; book VI, letters 7, 22, and 53–59; book VIII, letter 30; and book XI, letters 29, 54–62, 66, and 76.

## Foundation of the Abbey of Saint Augustine of Canterbury

*(From the* Monasticum Anglicanum*.)*

The true light that enlightens every person coming into this world, although by a new ray of his light he illumines the whole Church when he appointed blessed Gregory chief shepherd and pontiff of his Church, visited the English people in a special way, when he deigned to call them from darkness and the shadow of death to knowledge of the light of his faith.

For Gregory, having been ordained supreme pontiff on the fourth day before the Nones of September in the year of the Lord 592, and having been divinely prompted, arranged to fulfill through his disciple, the servant of God Augustine, the word of God which he himself had intended to preach personally to the English people.

Therefore, in the fifth year after his ordination—that is, in the year of the Lord 597—Gregory sent blessed Augustine and many other monks and ministers of the word of God, about forty in number, to preach the Catholic faith to the English people. I omit discussing how these ministers of God conducted themselves on the journey toward England, how, upon coming to England, they landed at Thanet, how they were received by King Æthelberht, and how they reached Canterbury, since all these matters are treated in the text of Augustine’s Life.

Augustine, having obtained a place with his companions in the city of Canterbury, began to imitate the apostolic life. Meanwhile King Æthelberht, delighted by the most pure life of the servants of God and by their most gracious promises, which he had recognized as true through the display of miracles, was strengthened in the Catholic faith and was baptized with his companions in arms on Pentecost in the year of the Lord 597.

After the king had been baptized and confirmed in the faith, Augustine proceeded to Arelate, a city of Gaul, and was ordained bishop by Etherius, bishop of that city, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December. Having been ordained, Augustine returned to England and was received by the king and people with glory and every fitting solemnity. After obtaining the episcopal seat in Canterbury, he immediately sent Laurence the priest and Peter the monk to Rome, so that they might report to the blessed pontiff Gregory that the king and his kingdom had received the faith of Christ, that Augustine had been ordained bishop for the English people, and that he sought Gregory’s advice concerning matters that appeared necessary.

Whoever wishes to know these matters more fully should read Bede’s history of the English; there he will find what he seeks.

Meanwhile, after Augustine had obtained the episcopal seat in Canterbury, as we have said, he recovered there, with royal assistance, a church which he had learned had been built there long ago through the work of Roman Christians. He consecrated it in the name of the holy Savior, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, and established his dwelling there. It is called to this day the Church of Christ in Canterbury, nurse and metropolis of all England, and the home of all his successors.

Not far from the city itself, to the east, approximately midway along the road to the church of Saint Martin and the city walls, there stood a shrine, or idol, in which King Æthelberht used to pray according to the rite of his people and, together with his people, sacrifice more to demons than to God.

As soon as Augustine, ordained bishop by Etherius of Arelate, had returned to England, he cleansed this shrine of the pollution and filth of the pagans. After breaking the image that was in it, he transformed the synagogue into a church and dedicated it in the name of the holy martyr Pancratius. This was the first church dedicated by Augustine.

An altar still exists in the southern portico of that church, at which Augustine used to celebrate and where the king’s image had previously stood.

After these events, Augustine obtained from the king the aforesaid church of Saint Pancratius together with the adjoining land. On this property, the aforesaid Æthelberht, at the urging of blessed Father Augustine, built from the foundations a church in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Establishing monks there to serve perpetually in the same church, he endowed and enriched it with various gifts and possessions. In that same church the aforesaid king chose burial for himself and for his successors, the kings of Canterbury.

In this church Augustine also decreed that he and his successors, the bishops of Canterbury, should be buried.

### Charter of King Edward

**Edward, by the grace of God king of England, etc., to the archbishop, etc., greetings.**

We have examined the charter of Æthelberht, of good memory, formerly king of England, in these words:

> In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Every person who lives according to God and hopes and desires to be rewarded by God ought gladly and sincerely to give consent to pious requests, since it is certain that he will obtain all the more easily what he himself has asked of God the more willingly he grants something to God.
>
> Therefore I, Æthelberht, king of Kent, with the consent of the venerable archbishop Augustine and of my princes, give and grant to God, in honor of Saint Peter, a portion of the land belonging to me which lies to the east of the city of Canterbury, on the sole condition that a monastery be built and that the property mentioned above be under the authority of the abbot who shall be appointed there.
>
> Therefore I adjure and command, in the name of the Lord God almighty, who is the just judge of all things, that the aforesaid land be perpetually confirmed by the donation subscribed below, so that neither I nor any of my successors, kings or princes, nor any person of whatever condition, dignity, or ecclesiastical rank, may lawfully defraud it of anything.

If anyone diminishes anything from this our donation or attempts to invalidate it, let him at present be separated from the holy communion of the body and blood of Christ, and on the day of judgment let him, because of the merit of his wickedness, be separated from the company of all the saints.

This land is enclosed by these boundaries: to the east, the church of Saint Martin; to the south, the road from Burgate; to the west and north, Drutingestrete.

Done in the city of Canterbury in the year from the incarnation of Christ 605, indiction 6.

**[÷] I, Æthelberht, king of Kent, in sound mind and with unimpaired judgment, have strengthened and confirmed my donation with the sign of the holy cross in my own hand. I, Augustine, archbishop by the grace of God, a consenting witness, have willingly subscribed.**

Edbaldus, Hanngisilus, Angemundus, the referendary, Hocta, Gracys, Tougyl, Penca, Geddi.

## Privilege Granted by Saint Augustine to the Abbey of Canterbury

*(From the* Monasticon Anglicanum*.)*  
*(C, G, S)*

Augustine, servant of the see of Canterbury, whom the most blessed Pope Gregory, moved by heavenly clemency, sent as legate and minister to acquire the English people for God, to all his successors who are bishops, to all the kings of England with their descendants, and to all the faithful of God: peace and salvation in faith and grace.

It is evident to all that the God-beloved King Æthelberht, the first of the English kings consecrated to the kingdom of Christ, at our insistence and through his lavish benevolence, among the other churches and bishoprics that he established, founded outside his metropolis of Canterbury a monastery in honor of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. He enriched and magnified it with royal resources and extensive possessions, fortified it with perpetual liberty and every royal right, together with all property and jurisdiction belonging to it inside and outside, and confirmed it against every injury by his royal privilege, by an imprecation of heavenly judgment, and by the apostolic excommunication pronounced by the holy Pope Gregory.

I too, as a supporter and protector of this same liberty, beseech by the Lord Jesus Christ and by the reverence due to his apostles all my successors who are archbishops, and every ecclesiastical or secular authority. By the apostolic prohibition of the aforesaid Father, I forbid anyone ever to presume to usurp any power, lordship, or authority over this lordly and apostolic monastery, or over its lands or churches. Nor may anyone disturb or oppress God’s ministers by imposing any condition of subjection, servitude, or tribute, whether great or small.

The abbot elected by his brothers in the same monastery shall be ordained not for his personal service but for the Lord’s ministry. He should persuade him to obey not himself but God. He should regard him not as his subject but as a brother, companion, colleague, and fellow minister in the Lord’s work.

He shall not celebrate Masses there as though at an altar under his own jurisdiction, nor perform ordinations or benedictions presumptuously without the request of the abbot or brothers. He shall demand no customary right from them, not even in the smallest matter, so that the concord of peace may make them one in dominion on both sides, and so that no one—God forbid—may fall under the judgment of the devil through a dispute over rule, since the devil fell from heaven through the tyranny of pride.

“The kings of the nations,” says the Lord, “lord it over them, but you must not be so.” And since taxes are received from strangers, not from sons, the Lord himself concludes: “Therefore the sons are free.”

With what irreverence, then, do the fathers of churches claim dominion over the sons of the kingdom of God for themselves—especially over this treasury of the saints, in whose maternal womb we hope that the bodies of so many bishops of Canterbury, kings, and princes will be lovingly restored to the repose of burial by apostolic authority, and from there raised again to eternal glory?

If anyone, not fearing to offend such friends of the supreme Judge, violates the provisions of this privilege, or, by imitating the violator, maintains his own force, let him know that he will be punished by the apostolic sword of blessed Peter through his vicar Gregory, unless he makes amends.

We therefore decree that all these provisions, exactly as they are written here, shall be observed with the approval and authority of our apostolic founder Gregory; and we confirm them with our own mouth in the presence of the glorious King Æthelberht and his son Ethelbal d, with all the royal nobles joining him in praise, and with our most reverend brothers, freely willing, who were sent here with me or to me from the holy Church of Rome for the Gospel of the Lord—namely Laurence, whom, God willing, we appoint as our successor; Mellitus, bishop of London; Justus, bishop of Rochester; and Peter, the venerable first abbot of this monastery of the princes of the apostles—together with my other helpers in the Lord, who earnestly requested these things and at the same time pronounced a blessing upon those who faithfully observe them, and, upon the impenitent—which we do not wish—transgressors, condemnation.

## In the Year of the Lord 607: Saint Boniface IV, Pope

### Biographical Notice on Saint Pope Boniface IV

*(From the* Liber Pontificalis*, edited by Blanchini, volume IV.)*

**[Note:]**

**1.** On 18 September of the year 607, after an interregnum of ten months and six days, Boniface, fourth of that name, was made pontiff during the reign of Phocas.

Concerning the emperor Phocas, Cedrenus and Nicephorus preserve the memorable statement that, when a monk asked, “Why have you imposed so impious an emperor upon the Christians?”, God replied: “No one more evil than he could be found, and this is what the crimes of the people of Constantinople deserved.” —Binius.

**2.** Regarding the interregnum between Boniface III and Boniface IV, all manuscripts and catalogues agree: ten months and six days. The same number is counted from the death of Boniface III on 20 October 607 to the ordination of Boniface IV on 25 August 608, counting both terminal days in the customary manner.

That 25 August was the actual day of Boniface’s ordination is demonstrated not only by the Sunday letter F, which recurs in that year, but also most clearly by the certain date of his burial and the certain duration of his pontificate, as will be explained below.

Now, so that everyone may easily understand that Pagius has uselessly inserted a stroke, increasing or decreasing the periods prescribed by him as he pleased, I think Anastasius’s and Pagius’s chronologies should be set before the eyes.

If to the total of four years, five months, and fourteen days there are added the four years, two months, and two days included in Gregory’s death-date, the year 608 and the date 25 August will result—the date which we have said was the actual ordination of Boniface IV, as Pagius himself admits.

According to Pagius’s chronology, however, the total is four years, five months, and ten days. Thus, apart from the difficulties demonstrated in their proper places, four days are missing to complete the periods. Hence it is clear that Anastasius, rather than Pagius—otherwise a most learned man—must be followed.

As for the pontificate of Boniface IV, everyone agrees not only that he occupied the see for six years, eight months, and thirteen days, but also—and this confirms the matter more strongly—that the inscription placed beneath his epitaph, which Baronius and later writers use from the collection of Manlius, reads as follows:

> HERE RESTS BONIFACE THE YOUNGER, WHO SAT SIX YEARS, EIGHT MONTHS, TWELVE DAYS. HE WAS BURIED ON THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY, WHILE THE LORD HERACLIUS WAS EMPEROR, IN HIS FIFTH YEAR.

This inscription excludes the day of burial; consequently it counts not thirteen days but twelve, so that Boniface IV died on 7 May and, according to Anastasius and others who give thirteen days, was buried on the eighth of the same month.

No more impressive argument can be devised to demonstrate that the burial—or interment—in the church of Saint Peter was a different event. For most manuscripts and catalogues report that Boniface was buried at Saint Peter’s on 25 May.

Although Antoninus Pagius suspects that this may concern some translation of the body, it is hardly credible that the body was moved after only seventeen days; nor, if a later translation among several were being mentioned, would a writer who was plainly contemporary with those events have used the word “buried” in the very text. Moreover, the translations carried out many years later are not unknown.

Therefore, although the burial ceremonies mentioned by Papebrochius must, with Pagius, be regarded as apocryphal, Pagius nevertheless came closer to the truth regarding the papal chronology.

Accordingly, in the year 615, Boniface died on 7 May and was buried on the eighth in the Lateran church; on the twenty-fifth he was carried to Saint Peter’s. —Cennus.

**3.** Fabroti’s chronology: Saint Boniface IV, in the year of Christ 607, the fifth year of the Emperor Phocas. —Blanch.

Boniface, by nation a Marsian, from the city of Valeria, on his father’s side descended from John the physician, occupied the see for six years, eight months, and thirteen days. During his pontificate there were very severe famines, pestilences, and floods.

**[Note:]**

**1.** “At the same time … of all the martyrs.” The Farnese manuscript reads: “At the same time he asked from the emperor Phocas for the temple called the Pantheon.” —Blanch.

**2.** This church was called Saint Mary at the Martyrs. Anastasius, in his Life of Paul, says: “When he recognized this, he fled into the church of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, which is called ‘at the Martyrs.’”

It was so called because the pontiff established a solemnity there on the Kalends of November for all the martyrs; this later became the solemnity of All Saints.

Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 609, says: “He obtained the Pantheon at Rome from the emperor Phocas and converted it into a church of Saint Mary and all the martyrs. Later, as Christian devotion increased, it was decreed that it should be dedicated in honor of all the saints.” Later writers called it the Rotunda.

Bertold of Constance, a priest, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1087, says: “But the heresiarch Guibert did not cease from his perversity begun earlier; rather, he fortified himself in Saint Mary at the Martyrs, which they call the Rotunda.” —Altaserra.

**3.** With excellent judgment, the most holy pontiff Boniface IV consecrated the temple, famous throughout the world and dedicated by pagan superstition to the worship of all the gods, in honor of the most blessed Virgin Mary and all the martyrs. In doing so, he followed an example either given—or perhaps even received—from earlier pontiffs, who converted profane temples into sacred ones while retaining some resemblance and something like kinship between the ancient and the new worship.

Thus it happened that temples sacred to Mars were assigned to blessed Martina, and temples sacred to the brothers Romulus and Remus were likewise assigned to the honor of the brothers Cosmas and Damian.

The Pantheon was called the temple of all the gods. Antiquarians also used the term to indicate an image engraved on the reverse side of certain ancient coins and filled with symbols of several gods.

On a large Egyptian bronze coin, which Petrus Seguinus displays among his choice coins, one side shows the laureate head of Antoninus Pius; on the other is a bearded head adorned with the attributes of the chief deities. Among these, the modius placed on the head indicates Serapis; the ram’s horn, Jupiter Ammon; the three-pronged fork, Father Dis and also Neptune; the serpent coiled around it, Aesculapius; the radiant hair, the Sun or Osiris; and the horn of plenty, the Nile.

I once saw a gem engraved with a similar design. They call that a Pantheon.

Marcus Agrippa, Augustus’s son-in-law, either raised the Pantheon from its foundations or completed what had been begun; certainly he adorned it with a portico, as the inscription placed on the front of the building teaches us:

> M. AGRIPPA, SON OF LUCIUS, THREE TIMES CONSUL, MADE THIS.

Dio speaks of it as follows in book LIII: “Agrippa also completed the Pantheon.” It is perhaps so called because, among the statues of Mars and Venus, it contained many images of the gods; or, as it seems to me, it received this name because its convex form displayed the likeness of the vaulted sky.

The very learned Ludovicus Demontiosius, in a booklet entitled *A Gaul as a Guest in Rome*, printed in Roman type in 1585 and of no little value, offers an original conjecture concerning the construction of the Pantheon.

He denies that the Pantheon had the form it now displays. Since, he says, it rose high above the level ground, one now descends by thirteen steps—today by two, thanks to Alexander VII, the Supreme Pontiff, who removed the earth and splendidly restored part of the portico on the right, which had collapsed—into the portico, where many ornaments are buried beneath the ground, and with them Pliny’s passage, which has been buried in almost the same way.

For this reason, he undertook to aid both matters: to display the temple itself so that it could be seen from its foundations, and to bring Pliny’s passage into the light from the dense darkness that has long oppressed it.

I shall briefly review what Caius describes clearly and abundantly, in order to demonstrate what the Pantheon’s former form was.

First, it must be observed that the ancient symmetry now appears greatly altered. Since the width of the temple now equals its height, the structure turns out to be square-shaped, that is, of the Doric order, whereas the double portico, the temple entrance, the door-jambs, the lintel, the window, and the columns are all of the Corinthian order.

Here, then, is a hermaphroditic kind of architecture: the whole work is masculine, but its parts are feminine. Thus there is no symmetry here, for symmetry is nothing other than the proportion of the parts to one another and of those same parts to the whole.

Will anyone disapprove of so celebrated a work, which Pliny counts among the outstanding monuments of the world? Certainly not. But it must be restored to the exact form of its architecture. We must judge that as much lies beneath the ground as is lacking for the proper symmetry of the Corinthian order, and that the present pavement must therefore be excavated to the depth corresponding to the difference between the Doric and Corinthian proportions.

Second, Pliny mentions the Caryatids of the Pantheon. In book XXXV, chapter 5, he says: “Diogenes of Athens decorated Agrippa’s Pantheon, and the Caryatids on the columns of his temple are judged among the few outstanding works.”

Four of them, dug out from the earth beneath which they lay hidden, can still be seen: two in the Capitol and two in the Chigi palace, inhabited by the duke of Bracciano.

What, then, was their position in the temple?

The column plinths are narrower than the proportion of the columns requires. Therefore part of the plinth is concealed by the marble pavement. But the column stylobates are likewise concealed. Vitruvius teaches, in book III, chapter 3, that stylobates ought to be placed in works of this kind.

The breadth of the Caryatids’ marble, however, is the same as that of the plinths and stylobates, and the kind of marble is also the same.

The earth should therefore be removed so that the plinths and stylobates emerge intact, and the Caryatids should be restored to their stylobates, from which ignorant hands had torn them away.

### Third

The Pantheon embraced images of all the gods; but where and in what arrangement were they placed? For sacred rites were not performed for all the gods in the same place. Sextus Pompeius states that the ancients performed rites for the celestial gods in buildings raised above the ground, for the terrestrial gods on the ground, and for the infernal gods in excavated ground. Accordingly, Jupiter was placed in an elevated position in the tribunal; the other celestial gods were in those little shrines that project from the solid part of the wall around the circuit of the temple; the gods were situated in the spaces between the columns; while the infernal gods were in the excavated ground, within the vault that lay beneath the steps.

The steps, moreover, beginning at the threshold of the door, descended to such a depth that they completely absorbed the difference in the proportions of the Doric and Corinthian orders mentioned above. Since the entire diameter of the temple’s width is 178 palms, if the diameter is divided into four parts, and a quarter is assigned on each side to the steps, extending from the outermost point to the innermost, two quarters remain empty in the middle for the temple’s area. Thus, anyone standing on the innermost step and looking up at the dome would see the innermost square circuit of the dome correspond to the innermost circuit of the steps.

From this you can easily infer that the architect intended to shape the lower part of the temple, in a certain manner, in the form of the upper hemisphere, so that the lower parts would correspond to the upper. Otherwise, the builder would have extended the pyramids of the dome, as in other rounded roofs, where they converge at the apex, which is, as it were, the navel of the roof. But, in addition, the proportions of this temple were so arranged that, on the outside, in the convex part of the roof, the same symmetry of the steps was maintained, so that not only the lower parts corresponded to the upper, but also the exterior to the interior.

Thus, by the rules of the art, the most ingenious Gaul divined the form of the Pantheon; Ammianus Marcellinus does not seem to differ from him when, in Book XVI, he calls the Pantheon “a circular region vaulted with splendid elevation.” I hope I shall give pleasure to my readers by placing before their eyes a diagram drawn by the most distinguished author; and this will be all the more useful because the praised book is not readily available to everyone, and the description of the temple will become clearer from viewing the diagram. BALDINUS.

---

### 4

When Boniface saw that the emperor Phocas was favorably disposed toward the Roman pontiffs, he asked him to give him the Pantheon, the famous shrine at Rome, celebrated in the praises of so many ancient writers. It had been erected by Marcus Agrippa, three times consul, during the reign of Augustus, and consecrated to Jupiter the Avenger; it had remained intact while the Romans, after becoming Christians, demolished the dwelling places of demons.

When he had obtained it, he cleansed it of the pollutions of ancient idolatry and consecrated it in honor of Mary, the Mother of God, and of all the holy martyrs, whose relics, for the most part, were transferred there from the cemeteries outside the City. Anastasius and Bede, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4, relate these events.

This church is still seen at Rome and is called Saint Mary Rotunda, on account of the form of the building. Its dedication is entered in the Roman Martyrology under 13 May, where it is called “The Dedication of the Church of Saint Mary at the Martyrs.” Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, assigns this dedication to the first year of Boniface and says that he instituted there, on the Kalends of November, the solemnity of all the martyrs; later, as the Christian religion grew, it was decreed that the solemnity should be celebrated in honor of all the saints.

On this subject Baronius should be read in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 13 May and 1 November. He nevertheless failed to notice that Pope Gregory III had decreed that this solemnity, originally consecrated to the holy martyrs, should subsequently be observed by the whole Church in honor of all the saints, as Usuard records in his Martyrology. See also what will be said under Gregory IV. PAGIUS.

---

### 5

He cleansed this temple of the pollution of idolatry and consecrated it to the true God under the invocation of the most blessed Virgin Mary and all the holy martyrs. On that occasion he instituted a solemnity to be celebrated annually in the City on the Kalends of November in honor of the same blessed Virgin Mary and all the holy martyrs; Gregory IV later ordered it to be celebrated by the whole Church on the same fixed day in honor of all the saints. (Bede, Book II, *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4; Roman Martyrology, 13 May and 1 November.)

This temple was built by Marcus Agrippa, son-in-law of the emperor Augustus, after the Actian victory—today called Capo Figulo—over Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Agrippa dedicated it to Jupiter the Avenger (Pliny, Book XXXVI of the *Natural History*, chapter 15), and it was called the Pantheon, either because images of all the gods worshiped at Rome had been placed in it, or because its vaulted structure displayed the appearance of heaven, which is the dwelling of God (Dio, *Roman History*, Book LIII).

Although, after the conversion of the emperors, the other temples of the idols were destroyed by Christians with immense zeal, this temple remained intact, as is believed, because of the law of the emperor Honorius, which reads: “Just as we prohibit sacrifices, so we wish the ornaments of public works to be preserved” (*Theodosian Code*, Book XVI, title 10, law 15). Even today it stands intact at Rome and is called the Rotunda Church. SOMMIER.]

---3. The most holy Boniface, detesting the worship of idols, expelled Jupiter and all the gods from it, so that the building might deservedly be consecrated to the Virgin Mary and all the saints; it is now called Rotunda by the Romans from its circular form. Bede, a weighty authority, committed to memory that this church was given to the Church of Christ by the emperor Phocas; after him did Valafridus in his book *On the Beginnings and Growth of Ecclesiastical Matters*, and others. This most illustrious temple was dedicated by Boniface IV in the year 610, on 13 May. On that same day many bodies of holy martyrs were transported in twenty-eight laden carts from the various cemeteries of the city of Rome and deposited there beside the high altar. Nearly six hundred and thirty-two years after it had been founded for the worship of idols, it was transferred to Christian religion and named Saint Mary at the Martyrs. This day was a most festive and celebrated one for the Romans, with people gathering from every direction, so that they brought famine upon the Roman people, since the supply of grain was then rather scant. Therefore Gregory IV, Roman pontiff, judged that it should be transferred to the Kalends of November, when the grain supply is usually more abundant. CIACONIUS.

Marcus Agrippa, Augustus’ son-in-law, distinguished for his naval victory over Sextus Pompey, built this temple, a structure of solid mass, for Jupiter the Avenger—or for Mars and Venus—and, since images of all the gods were placed in it, it could be called τὸ τῶν θεῶν κοινὸν ἱερὸν, “the common sanctuary of the gods.” This building was held in such high repute that it was counted among the City’s most outstanding works, and the Roman Caesars diligently labored to preserve it for posterity. “The emperors Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus . . . and Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Pius . . . restored the Pantheon, decayed through age, with all its adornment.”
