## Roman Council under Boniface IV

Held at Rome in the affair of the Church of England, in the eighth year of the emperor Phocas, the thirteenth indiction, and on the third day before the Kalends of March, with Mellitus, the first bishop of London, advancing the English cause and sitting in the council.

(The canons or decree of this council are not extant. [Note: [Col. 0103]

These are the words of Binius. Below, however, you have the decree published by Mansi.] But after completing what he writes concerning Laurence, archbishop of Canterbury, Bede proceeds as follows, Book II, chapter 4.)

In those days Mellitus, bishop of London, came to Rome to discuss with Pope Boniface matters necessary for the Church of the English. When that most reverend pope was convening a synod of the bishops of Italy, in order to establish regulations concerning the life and peace of monks, Mellitus himself also sat among them, in the eighth year of the reign of the ruler Phocas, in the thirteenth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of March. He subscribed and confirmed by his own authority whatever had been regularly decreed, so that, on returning to Britain, he might carry with him the instructions and regulations of the Church of the English, together with the letters that the same pontiff sent to Laurence, beloved of God, archbishop, and to all the clergy, and likewise to King Æthelberht and the people of the English. This was Boniface, fourth after Saint Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0103D]

We reproduce here the same synodal decree promulgated by Pope Boniface IV in the Roman Council of the year 610, from an old codex of Saint Symphorianus of Metz, now found in the library of the highly learned senator of Paris, Claudius Hardy. Since I noticed that it differs considerably in certain places from the Holstenian version, I thought I ought not to hesitate to offer it to you also, reader:

**From the council of Saint Boniface the pope, who was fourth after Saint Gregory: that monks may celebrate everywhere with priestly office.**

There are some people of foolish doctrine, inflamed more by the zeal of bitterness than by love, who assert that monks, because they are dead to the world and live for God, are unworthy of priestly office and cannot bestow penance, Christianity, or absolution through the grace conferred by priestly office. But they are wholly mistaken. For if the ancient opponents were speaking truth on this point, blessed Gregory, the equal of the Apostolic See, distinguished by monastic discipline, would never have ascended to the highest dignity, although the power of binding and loosing was granted to him.

Augustine also, disciple of that same most holy Gregory and outstanding preacher to the English, and Martin of Pannonia, together with very many other most holy men resplendent in the precious habit of monks, would not have been raised to the pontifical ring. Nor was Benedict, the teacher of monks, in any way a prohibitor of this matter; he merely said that monks ought to be free from worldly affairs. This is emphatically commanded by apostolic writings and the institutions of the holy Fathers, not only for everyone but also for canons. For both are clearly commanded, by the examples of the holy Fathers, to be dead to the world.

We therefore believe that the office of binding and loosing is worthily administered by monk-priests, provided that they have worthily been elevated to this ministry. Anyone who considers the status and habit of monks clearly affirms this. For *angel* is called *angelos* in Greek and *nuntius*—“messenger”—in Latin. Monk-priests, therefore, and canons who proclaim God’s commandments are called angels. But each angelic order is established in a dignity all the more exalted the more closely it contemplates the Lord.

Are not monks, like the cherubim, veiled with six wings? Two are shown in the hood, by which the head is covered, according to sound assertions. We say that the garment stretched over the arms represents two wings, and that which covers the body represents two wings. Thus the number of six wings is most certainly completed.

We therefore decree that those who contend against monks in this matter are to be barred from the exercise of priestly power, so that in future they may be restrained from such wicked attempts, since the higher anyone is, the more powerful he is. LABBAEUS.]

## Decree of the Synod

Promulgated in the Roman Council on the third day before the Kalends of March in the year of Christ 610.

### How monks may minister everywhere with priestly office

There are certain people, supported by no doctrine whatsoever, who, inflamed most audaciously by the zeal of bitterness rather than by love, assert that monks, because they are dead to the world and live for God, are unworthy of the power of priestly office and cannot bestow penance or Christianity, nor absolve through the power divinely entrusted to priestly office. But they are entirely in error.

For if the ancient opponents were speaking truth on this account, blessed Gregory, equal to the Apostolic See and distinguished by monastic discipline, would never have ascended to the highest dignity. For the power of administering these things publicly, of binding and loosing, is granted in its fullness by God.

Augustine also, disciple of that same most holy Gregory and outstanding preacher to the English, and the most blessed Martin of Pannonia, whose reputation for holiness, spread far and wide, resounds throughout the whole world, as well as many other most holy men shining in the most precious monastic habit, would not have been raised to the pontifical ring if monks were forbidden to use the powers mentioned above.

Nor was Benedict, the gracious teacher of monks, in any way a prohibitor of such a matter. He merely declared that monks should be free from worldly affairs. This is emphatically commanded by apostolic writings and the institutions of all the holy Fathers, not only for monks but also for canons. No one who serves God involves himself in worldly affairs. The clearest examples of the aforesaid Fathers likewise command everywhere, with evident reasoning, that both groups should be dead to the world.

Therefore, following the examples of so many Fathers—against whose institutions it is most dangerous to rebel—we believe that, by God’s command, the office of binding and loosing is not unworthily administered by monk-priests, provided that they have been worthily elevated to this ministry.

Anyone who clearly considers the status, habit, and power of monks unhesitatingly affirms this. For example, *angel* is called *angelos* in Greek and *nuntius*—“messenger”—in Latin. Monk-priests and canons, who daily proclaim God’s holy commandments, are therefore, by no incongruous reasoning, called angels. But each angelic order is affirmed to be more exalted in dignity the more closely it contemplates the glory of God.

For, like the cherubim, monks are veiled with six wings. Two, by which the head is covered, are shown in the hood through plausible arguments. The part of the tunic stretched over the arms, we say, represents two wings; and that by which the body is covered is likewise asserted most certainly to complete the number of six wings.

We therefore command in every way that those who strive to exclude priests of the monastic profession from the office of priestly authority be restrained in future from such wicked attempts, since the higher anyone is, the more powerful he is.

## Letter Sent from the Same Council to Æthelberht, King of the English

To the most excellent and pre-eminent lord, Æthelberht, king of the English, Boniface, bishop and servant of the servants of God.

Since the integrity of your Christianity has grown so greatly in the worship of its Creator that it shines far and wide, and since, proclaimed throughout the whole world, it reports the increase of your God-worthy works, we render immense thanks to God, the giver of all good things, who has looked upon you from on high and raised you to so great a summit of virtues.

Therefore, glorious son, we willingly grant what you requested from the Apostolic See through our fellow bishop Mellitus: namely, that your kindness may freely establish in the monastery situated in the city of Canterbury—which your holy teacher Augustine, the disciple of Gregory of blessed memory, consecrated to the name of the holy Savior, and over which our most beloved brother Laurence is presently known to preside—a residence in every respect for monks living according to the rule.

By apostolic authority we decree that those monk-preachers of your salvation associate with themselves a community of monks and adorn their holy life with good conduct.

If any of your successor kings, or any bishops, clerics, or laymen, should attempt to invalidate these decrees, let him be subject to the bond of anathema from the prince of the apostles, Peter, and all his successors, until he repents of what he has undertaken by rash audacity with a satisfaction pleasing to God and makes a genuine correction of this disturbance.

May you prosper in Christ, lord son.

## In the Year of the Lord 610. Count Bulgaranus

## Historical Notice Concerning Bulgaranus

*(Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, vol. I, p. 368, no. 218.) (C)*

Count Bulgaranus, prefect of Narbonese Gaul under King Gundemar—who ruled the Goths for two years, up to the year 612—sent several letters to different people. These remained unpublished down to our own time in a parchment codex of the Church of Oviedo, written five hundred years ago by order of Bishop Pelagius for the use of Alfonso VI, king of Castile and León. They were also preserved in another codex of the college of Saint Ildephonsus at Alcalá, older than the Oviedo codex.

In these letters, one of which is addressed to a king, two to a certain bishop named Illustrius, [Note: [Col. 0107A]

Moralius called this Illustrius a bishop of France, or rather of Austrasia, as though that were his proper name, having been misled, as I believe, by the common abbreviation *Ill.*, which he had seen in the Complutensian codex—now Escurialensis, Digramm. et Plut. I, no. 14. In ancient codices written before the year 1000, however, this abbreviation is used to indicate an unknown person, whose name we do not know or wish to conceal. Thus among the Greeks there are *δεὶς* (*deis*) and *δεῖνα* (*deina*), among the Hebrews *pelonî*, and the contracted form *plonî*, whence the Spanish *fulano*, all with precisely the meaning “a certain person,” “an unknown person,” or “an unnamed person.” The Latins express this by *quidam*. More recent codices substitute *N.* in that passage.

Something different must be said about the abbreviation *INL*, especially when the L is crossed in this way: *INL*. In Gothic codices, or codices of Gothic character, it means *inluster* or *illuster*, as I have often learned by testing the matter.] 

and others addressed to other persons, there are also found six letters of Bulgaranus, copied by us from the Oviedo codex: the first is addressed to a certain bishop of France; the second to the same man; the third to an unknown bishop; the fourth and fifth to Bishop Agapius; and the sixth to King Gundemar.

We shall eventually publish all of them, together with other letters by various authors that we preserve among the *inedita*. Cardinal DE AGUIR. [Note: [Col. 0108A]

## Three Letters of Count Bulgaranus Addressed to a Bishop of France

[Note: [Col. 0107C] Scattered errors, as will be evident to the reader. EDITOR.]

*(Mariana, *History of Spain*, Valencian edition, vol. III, appendix.)*

### Letter I

. . . . Meanwhile, we inform your holiness that it has come to us through widespread report that Brunhild, the virgin, and King Theuderic, spreading the most bitter poisons according to their accustomed policy, have stirred up the most atrocious barbarian king to wage war against the glorious King Theudebert, for the destruction of the united people.

If the matter is indeed proceeding in this particular way, what is necessary except that, before military action, the whole people on this side should labor in prayer, imploring divine assistance? We therefore ask that the truth of the matter be made known to us, so that, made participants in it, we may rise with equal fervor of faith and, together with all the priests, the clergy, and the entire Christian people of this province, approach the Lord, Redeemer of all, with supplications through appointed litanies.

May he extend the invincible right hand of his power in defense of the Catholics and, in accordance with the enemy’s deserved merits, bring about the fitting destruction of the hostile undertaking. May the authors of these quarrels, stripped bare by the machinations of the ancient serpent, be exposed as an example to all and, by the manifest and just vengeance of our Lord, be seen lying prostrate all around. This is what we ask.

If you have taken care, as you promised, to send the letters recently addressed to the glorious King Theudebert; or if your messengers have already returned, whether with the reply they received, or whether they have brought back agreements reached there; or if, at any rate, they have come here to prepare themselves for the presence of my glorious lord, King Gundemar, we wish to know this more certainly, so that you may order us, as we trust, together with your holiness, to shape our reciprocal concern faithfully and to arrange how the money is to be prepared for you.

### Letter II

. . . . Although the entire boundary of the lands beneath the heavenly vault is seen by the Lord Creator to have been established by him, and although it is clearly divided, by the wondrous arrangement of him who possesses power over all things, it is necessary that we who keep his evangelical word either seek out those whom one faith in Christ unites or love them; and although we are separated from one another by temporal imperial rule, it is fitting that we not be separated from the commandments of the eternal Prince.

Accordingly, to your holiness, flourishing through the outpouring of heavenly grace and abounding in spiritual generosity—which, with the Lord’s favor, we wish to make bound to us in charity through the exchange of letters—we send these letters with the greatest desire. We not only make inquiry, but also impart a greeting of salvation together with the due discussion of necessary matters.

For Christ rightly dedicated you as a distinguished shepherd to his fold, so that, just as, most blessed Father, you surpass me as though by nobility of blood, you might likewise bear concern for the innumerable souls of his sheep.

Those to whom either greater or lesser care for peoples is entrusted ought to persist in such a practice: the more exalted they become in divine service, the more continually watchful they ought to be over those placed under them.

I do not think it is unknown to your holiness that your son, Lord Theudebert, together with the Gothic people, exists as one joined to the princes who have descended, as it were, from former times, and that he has now vowed, through the envoys of that same people, to strengthen perpetual peace by means of the representations of experienced men. As a result, he has promised to give the Franks some sum of money—[Note: perhaps “of the people of the Avars”]—as a reward of grace.

It is therefore already known to me that I have sent letters to the aforesaid son of yours, Lord Theudebert, through your venerable brother, my true father in Christ, the bishop, making known that money has now been sent by your son, my lord King Gundemar. It is understood to be here with me in Gaul, so that he may dispatch prudent envoys from his presence and that we may at least deliver to the men who bring the agreements all that the Gothic people as a whole hopes for and promises.

For this reason I earnestly entreat your holiness, with due humility, that, as much as you love the Lord Jesus, who left peace for future ages after former ages, you may graciously be willing to devote yourself to confirming this peace.

If you know that the letter we sent to Lord Theudebert has reached him; or whether the arrangements made through the Gothic envoys under the agreed terms will truly remain as represented; or how far the aforesaid son of yours has triumphed over the [Note: perhaps Avars] in battle—we ask to be informed by your affection.

For it has also come to our knowledge through popular report that Brunhild, the queen, and King Theuderic summoned those same [Note: “Abates”; perhaps Avars] to wage war against Lord Theudebert and to migrate from their own settlements into the province. It is a dreadful thing for Catholic ears to hear that people truly placed far from the Lord under Christian religion should have incited others to rage against Christians.

Nor do we believe them to be better than those people; rather, we clearly recognize them as associates of those who supply the world with the necessary instruments of crimes. If, therefore, your holiness has clearly learned that, by the counsel of the aforesaid kings, an impious host has poured forth with hostility against the region of the orthodox prince, order us to be informed by your writing, so that, in the province belonging to the arrangements of your glorious son, my lord King Gundemar, the priests may proclaim, together with the people, the solemn rites of fasting.

May he shatter, by the power of heaven, the hearts of those who approach unjustly and are far from the Lord, even as they wage war; and may you order that he grant a glorious victory, through heavenly mercy, to the people who preserve the doctrine of the Christian faith . . . .

### Letter III

To the most beloved and most reverend Father in Christ, the bishop, from Bulgaranus.

[lacuna]

It is known to Almighty God, who declares the servant just and destroys the unjust with a fitting punishment of condemnation, that a few days ago—as I do not think your Blessedness has failed to learn—the charters of the most glorious kings, and likewise of your sons, Queen Brunhild and King Theuderic, were transmitted to us through the same intermediary. And when we ordered him to deliver them personally, the aforesaid series of documents announced that he had brought to us the writings of his lords together with his own petition, and that, so that he might gain access to us, he humbly requested our decision in writing.

For we had no desire to seek him out, nor do we need to examine any such matters; and even if he had come to announce the reply of his lords, we would not have consented. Since, however, he did not hasten at all—an utterly wicked man—your mind ought to waste away at the very beginning of your argument concerning the man of yours whose access to the presence of your son, my glorious lord King Gundemar, you appear to be demanding, while truth shines upon you with experienced clarity and you conceal the justice that you see in your inward mirror beneath an unjust excuse of words.

Who could fail to discern the ingenuity of your Holiness, and how you seek to soften, with the flattering snares of eloquence, matters that you have made harsh by unlawful actions? Such, if you grant pardon, is how we judge your dissimulation: as when some debtor, casting aside human modesty and encouraged by insolence, assails his creditor with presumptuous objections, while the silent creditor covers the truth, and the calumniator is utterly unashamed to speak.

A substantial, not insignificant, claim for the recovery of money remains for your son, my glorious lord King Gundemar, and for the entire Gothic people, because the noble envoys of that people, travelling under your magnificent authority for the sake of truth, were unjustly captured by your prince. Through a doubled abundance of malice they have been made to endure every disgrace of exile and the insult of poverty.

Let it be known, moreover, that you shut up the illustrious men Totila and Gundrimer, sent by my most serene lord King Gundemar, in your territories, at a place called Irapina, after inflicting contempt upon them, and that you emphatically denied them access to proceed as far as you. Behold what your side has done; these things are not unknown to your minds. Yet although you bear the bitterness of such injuries, you complain that the way to the presence of the envoys of my renowned lord has been opened to you, while you pretend otherwise in your letters.

May the Most High, the Prince from his heavenly throne, judge this case, and may he pierce with divine vengeance the one who appears unjustly to have inflicted trouble upon the other party, and the one who, deceitfully rejecting charity, has violated the peace beloved by the Most High.

Although, when I received the letters of the kings who are your sons, I immediately prepared their reply, we have learned from no informant whether those glorious princes received it or whether it was brought to your knowledge. We therefore also declare to your Honour that, if—having removed the appearance of pretence—you desire to preserve peace, which is recognized as the greatest share of dominion, and if you are resolved to remain in concord with the Goths, loving Christ with a devoted heart, you ought not merely to utter these things with lying lips. Rather, by completed deeds you must show that you yourselves first invaded the peace which we were preserving.

It is fitting that the Gothic envoys first be restored to their proper dignity; and, among kindred peoples maintaining peace, with the Lord’s help, the liberty of your envoys’ journey to the presence of my glorious lord should remain, if necessary.

As for the places concerning which you wrote to us—Jubiniana and Corneliana, which are known to have been possessed in the Gothic province by Queen Brunhild—we are astonished that your Blessedness should urge us to arrange that we grant access to them, after her right, for her own men. For those places were assigned by our lord King Reccared, of holy memory, by right to the aforesaid lady—as though, because your side fosters scandals, the bond of charity ought to be broken and the party that unlawfully provokes conflict ought to possess the rights of the Gothic people.

For I judge that, if you prefer to correct what your side is known to have unjustly done, the same Queen Brunhild will be able to defend those places by her lawful right, together with your people, joined to her in charity.

How, most blessed man, can you care for this matter, when we remember you as one who has until now been awake to kindly purposes and secular affairs, and as one who greatly fears Almighty God? You are a bishop dedicated to God by princes. How can you allow the charity of both sides to remain unharmed for so long, while the peace once joined between the peoples of the two nations by their predecessors now remains dissolved, although through your counsel it ought to have endured forever, strengthened?

**In the Year of the Lord 610. Paul of Mérida, Deacon.**

[Col. 0111]

**Historical Notice on Paul of Mérida**

*(Antonio, Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus, vol. I, p. 373, no. 211.)*

[Col. 0111C] This Paul was a deacon of Mérida in that period, and he left us a book on the Life and Miracles of the Fathers of Mérida. The first to publish it, long desired by many, was Barnabas Moreno de Vargas, a member of the municipal senate of Mérida, who also wrote the history of that city, printed at Madrid in 1631 in quarto. It was subsequently published again by Don Thomas Tamayo de Vargas, a most distinguished man, collated with ancient parchment manuscripts both in Gothic and Latin script and furnished with his own notes, at Antwerp, by John Meursius, in 1638, in quarto. He had eight copies at his disposal: four written in Gothic letters and four in Latin.

Ambrosius Morales, in his scholia on the first chapter of Book II of the Memorial of the Saints by Saint Eulogius, bishop and martyr of Toledo, also mentions another work of the same author. [Col. 0111D] This Paul of Mérida, after writing a history of the Church of Mérida and its bishops, also added certain material about other holy men. His Catholic Confession also survives.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] I carefully examined the excerpts of the distinguished Andrés Marcos Burriel from the Toledo library, which were transferred to the royal library at Madrid, as well as our own catalogues and those of the Escorial manuscripts, in case I might encounter this Catholic Confession of Paul of Mérida. But I searched in vain.]

These two works are preserved in manuscripts of considerable antiquity in the library of the Holy Church of Toledo; we have seen them still more ancient in certain other libraries. Morales praises this history in several places—*In the Prolegomena*, volume II, under the heading “The Aids He Had,” and in Book XI, chapter 72—as do other writers, both Spanish and foreign: Baronius, under the year 589, volume VII; Mariana, Book V, chapter 13; Padilla, century VII, chapter 17; and many others whom Tamayo collected at the beginning of his Notes.

Among them, Jerome Romanus the Augustinian, writing about the Christian Commonwealth in Book I, chapter 15 of his *World’s Republics*, says that he purchased a manuscript copy of this work and, as it were, rescued it from the jaws of Orcus from a bookseller at Alcalá, who was already intending to destroy it; he then donated it, together with other books, to the Church of Toledo.

The work appears to have been composed by its author for the purpose of confirming, by examples of events miraculously performed at home—that is, in the city of Mérida—the credibility of what Saint Gregory had collected in the four books of his *Dialogues* concerning miracles in his own Italy. That those books had no other author than Gregory, besides other arguments—Labbe, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume I, p. 391; Mabillon, preface to the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictines*, §2, volume I—is admirably confirmed not only by Isidore in his little book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, but also in the prologue of our Paul, a contemporary of that holy pontiff. He discusses at length the deeds of several bishops of Mérida, especially Paul, Fidelis, and Masona.

[Col. 0113]

**To a Foreigner Who Loves Spanish Affairs**

I do not think anyone so dull as not to know that our Spain has been, throughout all ages, a nurse of intellectual talent; nor anyone so envious as to dare deny, against the acknowledged and unshaken testimony of so many monuments, that this is so.

I pass over the most ancient peoples, who, according to Strabo (*Geography* III), were thought to excel among the peoples of Spain in wisdom, practiced literary studies, and possessed volumes of venerable antiquity—poems and even laws written in verse, they say, extending over six thousand years. The other Spaniards, for their part, used writing, though not of one single kind, nor did they all possess one language.

It is certainly remarkable in a people among whom, as the Spanish poet Italicus testifies (*Punica* III),

[lacuna]

“Everything in arms

Was centered on the cause of life,

And living in peace was condemned.”

To flourish in peaceful and civil arts amid the use of the military cloak and the din of arms was implanted by nature, not acquired by imitation.

I also pass over that exceptionally fruitful harvest of Spanish writers which, from the Augustan age to the Neronian, so impressed the Romans themselves, those masters of the world and the toga-bearing nation, because Spain produced for them eloquent orators and illustrious poets, as Latinus Pacatus says in his *Panegyric to Our Emperor Theodosius Augustus*, while admiring Spain for her command of every kind of eloquence.

Thus, together with the leading intellect Augustine (*City of God* VIII, 11), we may always call the Spaniards wise. Although many of their splendid monuments of genius have perished through the jealousy of fate, most of them, by the favor of their good genius, can nevertheless be compared with the more fortunate literary yield of any nation whatsoever—envy itself being compelled to admit it.

Besides the many thousands that are valued and useful among all peoples, not a few works still lie hidden in the oldest and rarest libraries. Once known and praised by the learned, they have awakened in others a greater desire to see them. Several distinguished men—García Loaysa, Ambrosius Morales, Juan Mariana, and others—made some of them common property for the sake of the republic of letters. I too have brought several out of darkness, where they were still fighting with worms and cockroaches to the incredible loss of literary scholarship; I have compared them with the oldest parchments, furnished them with notes, and prepared them for publication.

I would readily and deservedly draw up a catalogue of them here, were I not afraid of the pitch-black and grasping hands of certain busybodies who, like Harpies, fly into the chests of the modest and those unlike themselves,

“It pleases them to carry off their spoils and live by plunder; for theirs is

[lacuna]

the foulest filth of the belly

and hooked hands.”  
(Virgil, *Aeneid* III.)

[lacuna]

“Beaks suited to plunder,

[lacuna]

with a hook in their claws.”  
(Ovid, *Fasti* VI.)

Yet I shall appease Carna, or Cardea, the nymph, on the Kalends of June with old pork fat according to the ancient rite (Ovid, *Fasti* VI), so that she may drive away these Fidentines (Martial I, epigrams 30, 54, 73), Autolycuses (Homer, *Iliad* κ, *Odyssey* λ, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV), Gleptae (Plautus, *Truculentus*), Aesop’s jackdaws (Horace, *Epistle to the Pisones*), and

“the evil Lares of good poems”  
(Ausonius, *To Thalassius*),

or at least impose upon the boldest plagiarists

“the shame of the present moment.”  
(Martial I, epigram 53.)

Certainly, although for harmless liberty in books there is

“no monster more grievous to them, nor any fiercer

pest or wrath of the gods rising from the Stygian waters”  
(Virgil, *Aeneid* III),

we are nevertheless, by the benefit of a better nature, so constituted that whenever this

“noisy crowd circles its prey with hooked feet,”

and, having brazenly harpooned what belongs to others,

“pollutes the feast with its shameless mouth,”

[lacuna]

the ugliness of the edition itself and the harvest of errors immediately expose, by their own evidence,

[lacuna]

“the poems stolen in plain sight.”

[Note: [Col. 0113] Another reading: “the crimes.” Both are found in the copies of Martial, Book I, epigram 54, and our plunderers commit both.]

We learned this by experience yesterday and the day before yesterday; today we fear it as well. But while they parade about wearing the mask of fabricated and begged-for fame, we shall not cease, with God’s help, to serve the republic of letters and our native land by genuine merit—indeed, to deserve well of both, as perhaps we have until now done without being useless.

[Col. 0113]

Yet his pious ashes are adorned by no monument and distinguished by no inscription. Nor is this necessary: for heaven was the reward of that incomparable man, the world his tomb, and fame his inscription.

Rudericus Carus, in his notes on the *Chronicle of Maximus*, under the years 576–590.]

**Of Paul of Mérida**

[Note: [Col. 0115D] Deacon of Mérida. This is rightly added to distinguish him from another Paul of Mérida, a bishop, whom our Paul mentions in chapter 5. Moreover, Paul himself declares that he is distinguished by the honour of this diaconate in chapter 1, when he says: “I, unworthy and the foremost of all sinners, a levite of Christ,” etc.]

**Deacon**

[Note: [Col. 0115D] *Book on the Life and Miracles of the Fathers of Mérida.* Thus in almost all the manuscripts; in some, *Lives of the Fathers of Mérida*. But the first title is preferable, since it represents the title that Saint Gregory the Great prefixed to his *Dialogues*, whom Paul testified at the beginning of this work that he was especially imitating.

Gregory’s title reads: “On the Life and Miracles of the Italian Fathers.” But is it *de vita* or *de vitis*? Gregory of Tours, in the preface to his book on the *Life of the Fathers of His Age*, writes concerning *vita*:

“Some ask whether we should say *vita* of the saints or *vitae*. Aulus Gellius and other grammarians preferred to say *vitas*. For Pliny, in Book III of *The Art of Grammar*, says: ‘The ancients used *vitas* for each one of us.’ But the grammarians do not think that *vita* has a plural. Hence it is clearer and more correct to say *the life of the fathers* rather than *the lives*, because, although their merits and virtues are diverse, one bodily life alone nourishes them all in the world.”

This opinion appears to have been followed by the monk Evagrius, who, according to Honorius of Autun, chapter 40 of *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, wrote much that was necessary for monks, namely *The Life of the Fathers*; and also by the deacon Pelagius, who, according to Sigebert, chapter 116 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, translated into Latin sixteen books *On the Life and Teaching of the Fathers*; likewise by John the subdeacon, who, according to the same author, chapter 17, translated one book from Greek into Latin *On the Life and Teaching of the Fathers*.

Nevertheless, usage has prevailed in favour of *vitis* in *Vitis Patrum* (“Lives of the Fathers”). Concerning this subject, our most learned friend, who deserved well—if anyone ever did—of the Church of God and of the republic of letters, and whose departure to join the majority was long mourned at the incalculable loss of both, H. Rosweyde, S.J., has written more fully in the first *Prolegomena* to the *Lives of the Fathers*.]

**On the Life of the Fathers of Mérida** (C)

[Note: [Col. 0116D] Preface. In the manuscripts this division of the preface and chapters is entirely absent. The continuous sequence of this little book was read, as all who have worked through ancient manuscripts testify happened with the works of Pliny and other ancient writers; we ourselves have experienced it more than once.

Learned men later divided the works of the ancients into chapters or sections, partly to relieve tedium and partly to assist studious youth, sometimes successfully and sometimes otherwise. This often provided an opening for errors born from the mutilation of the true reading; the sharp, lynx-like vision of the learned has frequently been profitably directed toward recognizing and removing them.

The first person, I believe, to perform this service for Paul of Mérida was whoever copied this work. For in two copies that I possessed, written in a recent hand, I found the following added at the beginning of the work: “Table of Chapters in the Book of Paul the Deacon of Mérida on the Life and Miracles of the Fathers of Mérida. For we have divided it into chapters for the sake of distinction.”

I too divided the work into chapters for the sake of distinction. The division is precisely the one that I have prefixed and reproduced. I did not wish to alter it, both because I saw that it was confirmed by the authority of those copies and because I judged that it was not inelegantly arranged.

So much for the title. As for the subject, Paul followed almost all writers in prefacing this little work with a preface. Thus the martyr Eulogius began his *Memorial of the Saints* with a preface, his *Apology of the Martyrs* with a prologue, and his *Martyrial Document* with a preamble. Whoever reads the work through will understand the rest; I should not burden a familiar matter with unnecessary testimony.

I shall discuss the date of our writer at the end of chapter 12. I now continue with the remaining matters contained in the preface.]

**Preface**

No one should doubt that the miracles of orthodox men, and especially of Catholics, are true. [Note: [Col. 0117A] Let no one doubt that the miracles of the most holy men, and so forth. Listen, innovator, to the judgment of an ancient writer concerning Gregory’s *Dialogues*. Prefer antiquity to novelty, and at last fall silent, centuriator—or whoever you may be from that company of Alastors—

“who, beside Lake Timarus, thinking himself the leader of frogs, is honoured every day”—

let Lemannus, who near a pond of frogs is honoured as leader on every day, be silent.]

Nor did the authority of the books of the *Dialogues* receive little reinforcement from the authority of Pope John Zacharias, who presented them to Greek ears, as John the Deacon records in chapter 75 of Book IV of the *Life of Gregory*. Because of these books, John of Damascus, Euthymius, and the other Greek writers call their author “Gregory the Dialogist.” On this, see Sixtus of Siena, Book IV of the *Holy Library*; concerning the whole work, Melchior Cano, Book IX of *Theological Places*, chapter 6; and Gerardus Joannes Vossius, Book II of *Latin Writers*, chapter 23.]

No one should doubt that the miracles which Gregory, the most holy and excellent prophet, bishop of the city of Rome, inflamed by the grace of the Spirit the Paraclete, truthfully published in the books of the *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 0117C] In the style of preliminary headings. Gregory himself writes in the preface to Book I of the *Dialogues*: “I explain better what has already been brought forward if I distinguish what must be said through inquiry and response by the mere preliminary notation of names.” John the Deacon, chapter 75 of Book IV of his *Life*, quotes the same passage: “Thus Gregory, strengthened, interrupted the deeper work of exposition and distinguished, by the mere preliminary notation of names, the holy miracles of the fathers that he had related through inquiry and response with his deacon Peter.”], which Almighty God formerly deigned to perform through his servants, who pleased him, for the honor of his name.

No one should, on this account, be troubled in mind because these events appear to have taken place in ancient times and perhaps he does not grant them complete faith, or suppose that this most sacred man, the vessel of election (Acts 9:15), [Note: [Col. 0118A] Shrine of the Holy Spirit. The same designation is used by Honorius of Autun, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1000: “Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome, organ of the Holy Spirit.” Nor is this surprising, since his deacon Peter confirmed under oath that he had seen the Holy Spirit, like a dove, seated above Gregory’s head and inserting its beak into his mouth. According to Sigebert, chapter 41 of *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, this event was also confirmed by a prodigy.]

the shrine of the Holy Spirit, darkened them with vain and clouded words, while [Note: [Col. 0118A] While it is made clearer than daylight by the voice of evangelical authority that the Lord has always worked, and so forth. Christ says in John 5:17: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” Therefore let the brood of vipers again depart to the place they deserve, and let them measure the divine and omnipotent majesty by the smallness of a wretched little man; let them remove miracles even from our own times.

God has always and everywhere provided the material for his wonders, as the divine Psalmist says. And what does John of the golden mouth ask in his commentary on Psalm 110: “He has made a memorial of his wonders”? He says: “He never ceased to perform miracles. This is what ‘he made a memorial’ means: he did not cease, he did not stop performing miracles throughout every generation and awakening the duller minds through wondrous events.” Many miracles, he adds, may be seen both privately, at home, and in cities.

The excellent saying of Basil of Seleucia against those who estimate divine power as unbelievers appears in Book II, *On Saint Thecla*: “For as long as human beings exist, miracles will always pour forth like a spring, always gush forth, always bloom, and always be altogether healing.” In a matter so well known,

[lacuna]

I shall add no more.]

the evangelical authority makes it clearer than daylight to all that the Lord has always worked and continues to work to the present (John 5:17).

Therefore, so that the faith of all who read or hear may be strengthened with greater force of belief, we relate that these things occurred in our own times in the city of Mérida. [Note: [Col. 0118B] In the city of Mérida. See the *Excerpt* at the end of the notes.] We did not learn them from the reports of others, nor did we discover them through fabricated tales; rather, [Note: [Col. 0118B] Which we ourselves heard with our own ears from the person who reported it, and so forth. There are two grounds for stabilizing belief: that a man beyond all exception saw the event, and that we heard it reported in good faith by him. For although, as Plautus says in *Truculentus*,

“One eyewitness is worth more than ten who merely hear:

Those who hear report what they have heard; those who see know plainly,”

that very true saying of Strabo in Book II of the *Geography* is apt: “He who claims that only those who have seen know, removes the judgment of hearing, which is much better than the eye for acquiring knowledge.”

We ourselves heard these things from the person who reported them, whom we do not doubt miraculously departed from the body and reached the heavenly realms.]

**THE LITTLE WORK BEGINS IN THE NAME OF THE LORD**

[Col. 0117]

**CHAPTER ONE. Augustus, a boy and minister of the Church of Saint Eulalia of Mérida, is taken in a vision, at the point of death, to the tribunal of glory**

[Col. 0117D]

[Note: [Col. 0117D] “A little boy … while with his other contemporaries and companions … in the house of the distinguished virgin Eulalia.” This follows the ancient custom clearly taught by the Fathers of the Second Council of Toledo, chapter 1, when they say: “Concerning those whom the will of their parents has dedicated to the office of the clergy from the first years of infancy, we decree that, as soon as they have been tonsured or entrusted to a monastery of the elect, they must be instructed in the house of the church under episcopal supervision by the superior appointed over them.” This is also reported in Distinction 18 concerning those who desire it.

Likewise, the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 24, says: “Every age from adolescence is inclined to evil, for nothing is more uncertain than the life of adolescents. Therefore it was necessary to establish that, if there are any adults or adolescents in the clergy, all should live in one chamber of the atrium, so that they may spend the years of slippery age not in luxury but in ecclesiastical disciplines, assigned to a most approved elder whom they may have as teacher of doctrine and witness of life.” From this arose the institution of clerical seminaries, which Alexander IV and the First Lateran Council, chapter 11, regulated.]

A certain little boy, not yet of advanced age—or, to speak more fully, an adolescent—named Augustus, innocent, simple, and ignorant of letters, was faithfully performing, with a devout mind, the service assigned to him by the superior of the cell, a venerable man, among the other boys of his own age and companions, in the house of the distinguished virgin Eulalia, to whose service he belonged. [Col. 0119A] Suddenly he fell ill.

[Note: [Col. 0119C] “By the superior.” Thus he is called by the Second Council of Toledo, chapter 1; in the Fourth Council, chapter 14, he is also called an elder and teacher.]

When many people, as is customary, went to visit him, and I myself went more frequently, it happened one night, after the solemn offices of the vigils had been completed—for in that holy Church it is customary that, during winter, after a short interval, the Matins office should be celebrated separately, with the Lord permitting— [Note: [Col. 0119D] “The Matins office.” Isidore, *Etymologies* VI, 19: “The Matins office is named from the morning light and from Lucifer, the star that rises as morning begins.” Rabanus Maurus says much the same in Book I, *Institutions*, chapter 11.

For this there is the very ancient custom of Christian assemblies, also observed by pagans. Pliny, Letter 97 of Book X to Trajan, and after him Tertullian, chapter 2 of the *Apology*; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 33; and Nicephorus, Book III, chapter 17, testify that Christians were accustomed to gather on a fixed day before dawn and sing responsively to Christ as to God.

But ancient witnesses also testify that this took place in the middle of the night: Hilary on Psalm 18; Bernard, *Sermon on the Two Disciples*; Chrysologus, sermon 39; Ephraem, *On Blessed Abraham*; Palladius, *On the Monk Adolius*, chapter 30; the *Paradise of Heraclides*; Basil, *On the Monks Living in the Time of Chrysostom*, sermon 20; and others.

For, as the most devout Spanish poet Prudentius testifies:

“After the rising of the shining sun

it is late to forsake one’s bed,

unless, adding a portion of the night,

you have devoted time to labor.”

That this custom was observed by the Fathers of the Church of Mérida is therefore perfectly clear.]

At that interval, then, when I went to see him, I entered the cell in which he was lying and found all who were there so overcome by sleep that none of them had been awakened by the miracles. I entered; but I found the light that had been burning there extinguished. I immediately ordered all those lying before him to rise and commanded that the light that had gone out be lit again.

Once the light had been restored, I asked the aforesaid Augustus how he was. He replied:

“As far as concerns the hope of the present life, I confess that all the limbs of my body are already so relaxed that no strength whatsoever remains. But as far as concerns the hope of eternal life, I rejoice to say not only that I possess hope, but also that I have seen the author of eternal life, the Lord Jesus Christ, with companies of angels and innumerable multitudes of all the saints.”

When I heard him say what he had seen, I was immediately struck with astonishment and trembled violently. I begged him to tell me in detail everything that he had seen. [Note: [Col. 0120C] “I begged.” Just above, “I asked”; the same form occurs in all the manuscripts, and I have not altered it, since I noticed that it follows a manner of writing frequently found in ancient authors.

Afranius:

“They swore falsely, cursing themselves and their own people.”  
Titennius:

“I praise the fact that I kissed my stepdaughter’s head.”  
Plautus:]

I invoke you, Lares Diales, to protect me. And six hundred examples of this kind may be found in Festus, Nonius, and others. Unless we interpret this more simply, and listen to our author speaking, together with Saint Prosper in the *Common Rules*, Letter to Map., no. 15, and other ecclesiastical writers, as follows: “I do not trouble myself over painstaking precision of diction; nor am I ashamed if my disputation, which perhaps has merit in substance, offends certain devotees of empty words by the roughness of its unpolished expression. For”—as Gregory the Great says in the preface to Book I of the *Moralia*—“I consider it exceedingly unworthy to confine the words of the heavenly oracle beneath the rules of Donatus.” Many of the ancient Fathers held this opinion. Each person has his own genius; each age, too, has its own manner.] I begged him.

To this he replied: “I call the Lord of heaven and earth to witness that I am reporting to you no fantastic vision; but, so that you may believe more fully, I confess also that I did not sleep at all this night.” And when he had said this, he began as follows:

“I was in a pleasant place where there were many fragrant flowers, the greenest grasses, roses and lilies, many crowns made of gems and gold, innumerable silk curtains, and a delicate breeze whose cool breath refreshed everything. There too I saw innumerable seats placed on the right and left; in the middle, however, one set much higher than the rest stood out. Innumerable boys were standing there, all adorned and beautiful, preparing tables and an excellent banquet—not of just any animal, but with an abundance of every dish prepared solely from fattened creatures. Everything that was being prepared was white like snow, and they were awaiting the arrival of their king.

“Then I, unworthy as I was—thinking it worthwhile, as a marvel of such importance, to hear him who was telling it describe the matter more fully—said to him: ‘Tell me, I beg you: while that which you describe was being prepared, what were you doing?’

“He replied: ‘I was kissing the feet of them all, and they said to me: “Blessed be God, who has brought you here safely.”’

“While they were saying this and preparing all the service, suddenly there arrived a great multitude of men dressed in white, all adorned with gold and precious stones and crowned with shining wreaths. One line of the multitude advanced on the right and another on the left. In their midst came a most splendid and exceedingly beautiful man, handsome in form and glorious in appearance, taller than all the rest, brighter than the sun and whiter than snow. When they had reached the prepared seats, that more beautiful man sat in the highest place; the others, falling down and adoring him, took their seats. Immediately he blessed them all; and they adored him once, then again, and a third time. Afterward the prepared dishes were set before him.

“When they had begun to feast, that handsome man who sat in the higher place said to those standing around: ‘Is there some rustic here?’

“They replied: ‘He is present, Lord.’

“Then he said: ‘Let him be brought before me.’

“I was standing far away and looking on, observing what was happening. When I had been brought before his gaze, I began to tremble violently. But he said to me: ‘Do not be afraid, son. Pass behind my shoulder and stand here.’ And he added: ‘Do not be afraid. Know that I shall be your protector. You will never lack anything. I shall always feed you; I shall always clothe you; I shall protect you at all times; and I shall never abandon you.’

“Immediately he ordered that food and a cup from the same banquet—such as I had never seen—be given to me. I received it and partook of it with complete joy. Indeed, I confess that I remained so refreshed by his grace that thereafter I desired no food other than that.

“When the banquet had ended, he said to me: ‘Let this multitude go by another road; you shall depart with me, so that I may show you

[Note: [Col. 0121C] my little garden that I possess. Thus in all the manuscripts. Or perhaps, ‘my little green garden that I possess’? One of these alternatives must be demanded by the grammarians; the other seems to be supported by the words added shortly afterward: ‘and, taking my hand, he led me out into a most pleasant garden.’]

my little garden that I possess.’

[Col. 0121B] “Then, when the banquet had been completed, they all went forth again and adored him. The king blessed them and permitted them to depart. As they were leaving, however, they dragged certain men to his tribunal; these men were shouting and lamenting with great howls. When he heard their voices, he said: ‘Drag the wicked servants outside. They are not worthy to see my face.’ When he had said this, they were pulled away so quickly that I could neither see them clearly nor recognize them.

“I asked again: ‘I beg you, son, tell me whether you recognized anyone there among those who had been known to me in this world and had already departed from this life.’

“To this he replied: ‘The men whom I saw there were far unlike all those whom we see now, for they were all adorned with another form and another appearance.’

“Then he continued: ‘After they had dragged those men outside, that Lord who was more beautiful than the others rose from his seat. Taking my hand, he led me out into a most pleasant garden, where there was a stream containing water the color of glass. Along the stream was a grove of spices, and many fragrant flowers exhaled various sweet scents. Proceeding beside the stream, we came at last to the place which I now see while lying on my bed.’”

The boy whom I have mentioned reported all this to me while many people were present. Therefore I, unworthy as I am and the first of all sinners, a Levite of Christ, preferred to write down what he related, in different words indeed, but with the same meaning.

After this I took care to report everything I had heard to the most holy man, the Lord and

[Note: [Col. 0121C] my abbot. Could this be the man called at the beginning the provost of the cell? I should think so. Concerning the word “Lord,” see what I noted regarding F. L. Dexter’s letter to Orosius.

[Col. 0121D] I find the name of a certain abbot of this monastery in the subscriptions to the Eleventh Council of Toledo, in these words: “Florentinus, abbot of the church of the monastery of Saint Eulalia, consenting to these synodal acts determined by us, signed them.” For nowhere among the Spaniards do I find, in these times, any other monastery of Saint Eulalia besides that at Mérida.]

my abbot. When he learned of it—for he is always filled with compassion and piety—he hastened as quickly as possible to the same Augustus, eagerly desiring to hear from his own mouth what he had seen, and asked him about it. The Augustus, repeating none the less what he had said before, disclosed it to his holy ears.

Finally, when a certain holy and blessed Levite and all the brothers asked him what he had said shortly before, he repeated it. For immediately

[Note: [Col. 0121D] his spirit began to burn with the desire to receive penance, and so forth. The ancient Fathers like to speak in this way of the dying. The Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 76: “Let him receive penance; and if he is believed to be immediately dying, let him be reconciled by the laying on of hands, and let the Eucharist be poured into his mouth.” The First Council of Orange, chapter 3: “Those who depart from the body after receiving penance—it has been decided that they should receive communion without the reconciling imposition of hands,” and so forth. The Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 12: “If the danger of death presses, after penance has been received through the laying on of hands”; and immediately afterward: “But concerning those who, having received penance, have departed from this life.”

Yet the grammarian-theologians Valla, in his commentary on chapter 7 of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, Erasmus, in his commentary on chapter 3 of Matthew, and others of the same workshop or kiln—as they call it—try to banish this expression from Christian usage, not so much because they do not find it in Cicero as because it is particularly suitable to ecclesiastical institutions. In its defense, consult the true lights of religion and theology: R. Bellarmine, Book I *On Penance*, chapter 7; A. Salmeron, treatise 4, volume IV; and M. Sandaeus, commentary X, *Profane Grammar*.]

his spirit began to burn with the desire to receive penance. Having received it immediately, while I had gone away and hastened for the sake of prayer to the basilica of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin—which lies five miles from the city of Mérida and which the common people still call the basilica of Saint Quintilina—I returned from there as evening was falling and found him dead. Since it was already evening, he was not buried that day.

On the following night, while his little body lay unburied in the cell

[Note: [Col. 0122D] “In a little cell.” One belonging to clerics. Codinus, *On the Origin of Constantinople*: “The cells around it belonged to the clerics,” as also to monks; Theodorus Anagnostes, *Eclogue* I: “At night, going about among the cells of the monks, he called each one by name.” But these were their proper dwellings; hence that place received the name Cellia, as in Sozomenus, Book VI, chapter 31: “There is another place, almost seventy stadia distant—namely, from Nitria; its name is Cellia. In it are many monastic dwellings scattered about, and for this reason it received such a name.”]

in which the deceased man had been laid, in the dead of night the same Augustus called from outside, in a very loud voice, for another boy of his own age named Quintiliar. Hearing and recognizing his voice, a simple and truthful boy named Veranianus immediately rose and went outside. He was privileged to see the Augustus standing in white; but, terrified by fear, he did not dare approach him more closely. He testified under oath that he had seen his face shining with snowy brightness. On the following day his little body was, according to custom, committed to burial in the basilica of the most holy virgin, my lady Eulalia.

## CHAPTER II

A monk of the Caulinian monastery near Mérida, close to death, is converted from drunkenness and theft to the Lord.

Several capable men lived not very many years ago, by the mercy of God, in the

[Note: [Col. 0122D] province of Lusitania. Thus Mérida was formerly

the chief city of the Lusitanians,

a city.]

province of Lusitania, who mercifully relate the miracle performed by our Savior. While in the monastery called Cauliana,

[Note: [Col. 0123C] “In the monastery called Cauliana.” In some copies it is called Colona, but corruptly; for in the Gothic manuscripts it is clearly written *Cauliniana*. So it is also in those seen by Morales and in the Alcoracense manuscript, written five hundred years ago, which Britto used.

The antiquity of this monastery may be inferred not only from the letter of the monk Tarra to King Reccared, which, although not yet published, has remained hidden until now in the libraries of Spain, and concerning which see Morales, Book XII, chapter 22, and Padilla, century VII, chapter 17, but also from the testament of Don Fua Roupinus, a vigorous and ancient leader of the Lusitanians, found by B. Britto in the Alcohacense archive and published in chapter 4 of Book VII of the *Monarchia Lusitana*. Since its words contain a distinctive part of our history, I gladly transcribe them. After reporting that he had found an image of the Virgin Mother of God, he adds:

“We did not know where this image came from or from where it had arrived. But behold, when the altar was being demolished by *albanires*—as the Spaniards call builders of structures—there was found an ancient ivory box, and in it, in a wrapping—for the Spaniards also use this word for a covering—were the bones of certain saints and a little document with this inscription:

‘Here are the relics of the holy ones, and so forth, which the monk Romanus brought from the monastery of Cauliniana together with the venerable image of the Virgin Mary of Nazareth. In former times it had become renowned in the city of Nazareth for many miracles. It was carried away from there by a Greek monk named Cyriacus and, in the time of the Gothic kings, remained for a long period in the aforesaid monastery, until Spain was conquered by the Moors and King Roderic was defeated in battle. Alone, tearful, rejected, and almost exhausted, he reached the aforesaid monastery of Cauliniana. There he received from the aforementioned Romanus the sacraments of penance and the Eucharist and, together with him, the image and the relics, reached Mount Seano on the tenth day before the Kalends of December. There the king remained alone for a full year in a church where an image of Christ crucified and an unknown tomb had been found. Romanus, however, remained with this sacred image of the Virgin between these two rocks until the end of his life. And lest ignorance hold anyone in future times, we have deposited these things, together with the sacred relics, in this farthest part of the world. May God preserve all these things from the hands of the Moors. Amen,’ and so forth.

For anyone who wishes to know more about this monastery, let him consult Morales and Padilla at the places already cited, Britto in the same work and in chapter 21 of Book VI, Ludovicus de Angelis, Book IV *On the Praise of Saint Augustine*, chapter 20, and Joan Marquez, chapter 12 *On the Origin of the Hermits of Saint Augustine*, section 8.]

which lies not far from the city of Mérida, about eight miles distant, the most reverend man, the abbot Renovatus,

[Note: [Col. 0124C] Renovatus, abbot … later also bishop of the city of Mérida. More about him may be found in the note to chapter 21.]

was in charge. He afterward became a remarkable bishop of the city of Mérida. With wise diligence—for he was a perceptive man of exceedingly keen intelligence and extremely zealous in every discipline and in the fear of the Lord—he earnestly summoned all the monks living there to the heavenly homeland through good conduct and examples of holy works, and the whole flock followed its shepherd as he led them along the narrow heavenly paths and byways.

A ravenous wolf tried with all its strength and biting mouth to tear apart one little sheep belonging to him. While the whole assembly of the holy congregation persevered in the praises of the Lord and lived in the fear of the Lord by the rule’s appointed path, a certain monk, differing from their most holy way of life, surrendered himself immeasurably to gluttony and drunkenness. Then, turning to a still graver course, he began to steal whatever he could find. The aforesaid man often admonished him gently; and when he could not easily restrain him, he repeatedly endeavored to rebuke him with verbal reprimands. But even so he did not free him from his seductive delight in excessive eating or from his intent on theft and rapacity. He ordered him to be beaten with lashes, punished with restrictions on food, and handed over to prison. Yet the man persisted in his former sins. Not only did he in no way cease from his vices, but day after day, promising to consign himself to the Tartarean caves of Avernus,

[Col. 0124A] he hastened more and more toward them.

When he saw him pursuing the path of such an evil purpose, so that neither the force of repeated reprimands nor the many beatings induced him to reform, he was touched by inward grief of heart. He allowed him to go according to the desires of his heart (Judges 16), and he ordered those in charge of the monastery’s storerooms that, at whatever hour he wished to enter, no one should prevent him from eating or drinking, even to the point of vomiting, whatever excellent or sweet things he found in the cellars. If he wished, as usual, to carry anything away or cut off a portion, he was to have complete freedom, so that it might be more fully recognized what he would do after satisfying his appetite or belly.

In accordance with the command, he opened the unlocked gates and secretly entered the well-stocked cellars of the extremely wealthy

[Col. 0124B] monastery—as the story relates. The guards, however, were posted all around at a distance, watching with clever concealment while he remained unaware and waiting to see what he would do. He devoured and drank indiscriminately whatever sweet and pleasant food and drink he found, until, with his mind deranged, he could scarcely walk. Afterward he secretly carried off various dishes and also wine vessels, which in the customary language are called

[Note: [Col. 0124C] guillones. Isidore’s glossary has *gello*, *baucalis*; the Latin-Greek glossaries have *gillo*, βαυκάλιον. The word is known to Cassian, *Institutes* IV, chapter 16, Rufinus III, no. 14, and other writers. On this matter see the most learned Horatius Rosweydus, *Onomasticon* under the *Lives of the Fathers*, and P. Scriverius on epigram 85 of Book II of Martial, *Schidiasma* at the end of decade 6 of the *Horæ Subsecivæ*. There he explains what *guillonarius* means in the Visigothic laws. From this word P. Ciaconius, my fellow citizen and extraordinarily learned man, derives the Spanish *cangilón* in his notes on Cassian and Rosweydus—more plausibly than from *congius*, as my fellow countryman Don Sebastián de Covarrubias proposes in the *Thesaurus of the Castilian Language*.]

guillones, or

[Note: [Col. 0124D] flasks. The word is common to Spaniards, Italians, and French, with only a slight change of letters: *frasco*, *fiasco*, *flacon*, and so forth. Gregory II, *Dialogues*, chapter 18: “Two linen vessels full of wine, which are commonly called flasks … do not drink from the flask that you concealed … when he tilted the flask, a serpent immediately came out of it.” Flodoard, Book I of the *History of the Roman Church*, chapter 15: “He gave him a vessel commonly called a flask, full of wine blessed by him.” Hesychius: Φλάσκων δὲ εἶδος ποτηρίου, “a flask is a kind of drinking vessel.” Thus also medieval writers: Thwrocz in the *Chronicle of Hungary*, chapter 78; Andrew the priest in the *Bavarian Chronicle*; Florence of Worcester in the *Chronicle*. Hence Papias, in his glossary: “Flasks were first made for storing phials, and from this they are also named.”]

flasks. He carried them away and hid them in the adjoining monastery garden, among leafy shrubs or dense reeds, in the most concealed place.

Then, bloated from excessive food and satisfied by his drunken cups, he spread himself out to sleep. Although the things he had stolen no longer gave him pleasure and his heavily burdened stomach caused him to belch excessively, he still desired to eat and drink. But while, with his belly exceedingly weighed down, he languished rather than ate,

[Perhaps *lingeret*—“licked”—rather than *manducaret*, “ate”?]

sleep suddenly overcame him and he fell asleep. Then dogs came and ate everything he had carried away. The guards, watching from the opposite side, retrieved the vessels he had brought and returned them to the cellars while he slept. When this had been repeated many times over long intervals, and no one any longer believed that he would ever reform, the good Shepherd and Savior (John 10:11), by this example, snatched him from the lion’s mouth.

It happened one day that, as usual, he came drunkenly out of the cellar at first light. When the little boys saw him drunk—the boys who, under the discipline of tutors, were studying letters in the schools—they immediately cried out:

“Consider the Lord’s terrible judgment; consider the sentence to be feared at the dread tribunal; consider the terrifying and horrifying avenging severity of that judgment. Consider also the years of your life, and at last change your conduct for the better. Correct your life at least one day before your death, because what you do is not permitted to us children; how much less is it permitted to you, who are plainly already advanced in age.”

When he heard this, he was covered with overwhelming shame and blushed. Immediately he was pierced with remorse, and, weeping with many tears and raising his eyes to heaven, he said:

“Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of souls, who do not desire the death of a sinner but that he should turn from his iniquity and live (Ezekiel 18:24; 33:11), I beg you to correct me and remove this disgraceful reproach from my face. Or, if it pleases you, take me now from this miserable life, so that I may no longer hear reproach directed against me.”

Divine mercy did not delay in hearing him. Instead, striking him with affliction in the same place, it made him burn with the violence of fever. Indeed, the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High (Psalm 76:11) transformed him so thoroughly for the better that, recoiling from all bodily pleasures, he immediately sought with ardent spirit the remedy of penance; specifically, he desired the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

But when the aforesaid gracious Father thought that he was demanding this with a deranged or wicked mind, he postponed granting him full penance. He bestowed on him only the grace of the viaticum, and for three days and as many nights the man made satisfaction with tears and an extraordinary confession.

On the third day after this he departed from the body. Bidding farewell to all the brothers, he said:

“Know that all my sins have been forgiven me. Behold, before the doors are the most holy apostles Peter and Paul, and also the most blessed Lawrence, archdeacon and martyr, with an innumerable throng of men in white, awaiting me. With them I must go to the Lord.”

And saying this, he departed from the body.

After fifteen years or somewhat more,

[Note: [Col. 0125C] The memorable river Anas. From Prudentius, hymn on Saint Eulalia of Mérida:

“Now Mérida is the place of the tomb,
the famous colony of the Vettones,
which the MEMORABLE RIVER ANAS
passes by; and with its green
whirlpool it washes the beautiful walls.”

Today, retaining its ancient name but adding the Arabic word *Guid* or *Guada*, which in Arabic means “water” or “river,” it is called Guadiana. Like another Alpheus of the Greeks, it is often seen to delight in being born again through a new miracle. For more about it, see Rui-Gonzales de Clavijo, in the *Itinerary of the Embassy to Tamerlane* during the reign of Henry III of Castile; Hieronymus Paulus, *On Rivers*; Pedro de Medina, Book II, chapter 33, *On Spanish Affairs*; Mariana I, chapter 3; Garibay IV, chapter 19; and others.]

the memorable river Anas, rising enormously and overflowing the banks of its channel, spread its waters widely and caused the ruins of many houses in the villages near its shore. It likewise overturned the cells of the Caulinian monastery. When the monks wished to restore them, it happened that, while they were laying the foundations, they opened the very tomb in the cell where the man mentioned above had lain. Immediately a nectarous fragrance burst forth from it. He himself was found whole and incorrupt, as though he had been buried at that very hour; neither his clothing nor his hair showed any sign of decay.

## CHAPTER III

Nunctus, an African abbot, comes to Mérida and is killed by wicked men, who are immediately seized by a devil.

While we endeavor to relate recent events, we had omitted the ancient deeds of our forefathers. Many therefore relate that, many years ago,

[Note: [Col. 0125D] In the time of Leovigild. He began to reign while his brother Liuvva was still alive, in the year 568, and died in the year 586, according to the more reliable chronological reckoning of Isidore and Wulsa. Some call him Leovegild, others Liwigild; we have followed the inscriptions on coins.]

in the time of Leovigild, king of the Visigoths,

[Note: [Col. 0125D] From the African regions into the province of Lusitania. Not without precedent. Baronius, under the year 95, testifies that Paulinus crossed from Africa into Spain out of a desire for a stricter life; so do Romanus in Book III of the *Chronicle of the Order of Saint Augustine*, Ludovicus de Angelis, Book IV *On the Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 20, and Marquez, chapter 10 *On the Origin of the Hermits of Saint Augustine*, section 5. Ausonius, in Letter 24 to him, also indicates, not obscurely, that he lived in Mérida, the capital of Lusitania, among other places:

“Paulinus and Ausonius, men whom the sacred
purple of Quirinus and the gold-covered cloak
of the consular robe enveloped,
ought not to yield to the snares of a foreign goddess.

Why do I complain? Why do I pursue the crimes
of the monster of the East?
The bank of the setting Tagus wounds me;
Punic Barcelona wounds me;
the snowy peaks of the two-sea Pyrenees wound me.

Perhaps too a province, by its long expanse,
separates each man from his native city walls, dress, and speech,
beyond mountains and beneath another sun, beyond rivers and cities,

and all that extends between the lands and sky,
between the rivers of Mérida and the broad waters
of the Garonne, wounds me.”]

our abbot Nunctus came from the African regions into the province of Lusitania.

[Note: [Col. 0126D] Abbot Nunctus. More about him may be found in Baronius under the year 589; Morales, Book II, chapter 62; Padilla, century 6, chapter 50; Ludovicus de Angelis, Book IV *On the Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 20; Romanus, Book II *Church History*, chapter 27; Lancilottus, Book II *On the Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 18; and Marquez, chapter 12 *On the Origin of the Hermits of Saint Augustine*, section 8. But all of them derive their account from one source, Paul of Mérida, whose words they transcribe because they relate the deeds nobly performed by Nunctus.]

After he had lived there for some time, he eagerly went, out of devotion, to the basilica of the most holy virgin Eulalia, in which her most sacred little body rests. But, as the story goes, he avoided the sight of women in every way, as though it were the bite of a viper—not because he despised the female sex, but because, seeing temptation in physical beauty, he feared falling into vice. Thus, wherever he went, he ordered one monk to walk some distance ahead of him and another some distance behind, so that no woman might see him on any occasion.

As we have said, when he came to the basilica of Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr, he earnestly begged the reverend man Redemptus, the deacon in charge there, that whenever he left his cell to pray in the church at night, he should arrange the watch in such a way that no woman could see him at all.

After he had spent several days in that holy church, a most noble and holy widow named Eusebia greatly desired to see him. But he absolutely refused to be seen by her. When various people repeatedly asked him to allow her to see him, and he would in no way consent, she took counsel and begged the aforementioned deacon Redemptus that, after the morning praises had been completed, when he was returning from the church to his cell, he should order a very bright light from candles to be made around the most holy man, while she stood in a very secluded place, so that she might at least see him from a distance. This was done.

But when, without his knowledge, the female gaze fell upon him, he immediately threw himself to the ground with a great groan, as though he had been struck violently by a huge stone, and began to say to the deacon Redemptus:

“May the Lord forgive you, brother. What have you done?”

After this he immediately left that place and reached a wilderness with a few brothers. There he built himself a very humble dwelling. But as he shone there through frequent miracles, the report of him returned by word of mouth and reached Prince Leovigild,

[Note: [Col. 0127C] Although he was an Arian. From this act of Leovigild’s piety toward Saint Nunctus, Joan Marquez, chapter 12, section 8, infers his future repentance. We have treated that repentance more fully in the notes to Maximus of Zaragoza’s *Chronicle*.]

who, although he was an Arian, nevertheless wished to commend himself to the Lord through the man’s prayers. He therefore sent that man a written authorization, from a certain important estate of the royal treasury, so that he might obtain food or clothing from it for himself and his brothers. The man of God utterly refused to accept it. But when he persisted in refusing and the person sent by the king said to him, “You must not despise the offering of your son,” he finally accepted it under compulsion.

After several days, the people living in that place began saying to one another: “Let us go and see what sort of man this is, our lord, to whom we have been given.” When they had gone and seen him dirty in clothing and ugly in appearance, they despised him and said to one another: “It is better for us to die than to serve such a lord.”

Then, after some days, when the holy man of God had gone into the forests to pasture a few sheep, they found him alone

[Note: [Col. 0127D] They cruelly killed him by breaking his neck. Ludovicus de Angelis, Book IV *On the Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 20, calls Nunctus “the most holy martyr, a monk by profession”; Lancilottus, Book II, chapter 18, calls him an “invincible martyr.” Nor is this surprising, since he was killed by wicked men for the sake of justice, which Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 14, and Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 124, article 5, response to objection 1, identify as an effective cause of martyrdom. Marquez confirms the matter with examples in chapter 12, section 8.]

and cruelly killed him by breaking his neck.

After no long interval, the murderers were captured and brought in chains before King Leovigild. He was told that these were the men who had killed the servant of God. Although he was not of the orthodox faith, he nevertheless issued a righteous sentence, saying:

“Release them from their chains and let them go. If they truly killed the servant of God, let the Lord avenge the death of his servant without our vengeance.”

When this had been said and they had been released, demons immediately seized them and afflicted them for many days, until they drove their souls from their bodies by a cruel death.

## CHAPTER IV

Paul, a physician by profession and a Greek by nationality, becomes bishop of Mérida and heals a woman suffering in childbirth.

Leaving aside

[Note: [Col. 0127D] the ostentatious finery of words. Thus Ambrose, in the later book against Symmachus’s *Report*, calls speeches “adorned with trappings,” and likewise in Book II on Luke, chapter 2. For when the orator of those who pursue the trappings of speech denies that the fortunes of Greece depend on whether one uses this or that word, see Saint Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 34. Wise men do not approve of speech decked out with ornaments, but of speech that is vigorous, since words were instituted not to be exchanged for things but to express things. Cerippus the African, Book IV *On the Praise of Justice*, similarly says: “To add trappings to trappings and praises to praises,” using the same figure.]

the ostentatious finery of words, and passing over

[Note: [Col. 0128D] the chattering froth of eloquence. That is, hollow words, swelling like bladders, in Jerome, Letter 100; “bubble-blown trifles” in Persius, Satire 5; “windy loquacity” in Petronius, at the beginning of the *Satire*; “inflated phrases” and “words a foot and a half long” in Horace’s *Epistle to the Pisones*; and six hundred expressions of this kind in the authors. For these, see the learned Ludovicus Cressulius, Book III of the *Ancient Theater of Rhetoric*, chapter 23.]

the chattering froth of eloquence, we now relate simply and truthfully those matters that are true in every respect. For if we try to wrap in obscure language things known to be clearer than daylight, we do not instruct the minds of our hearers but weary them, since, when the understanding of many uneducated people grasps less, their hearing is wearied. Therefore, as we promised above

[Note: [Col. 0128D] “As we promised above.” In the very preface to the work.]

, we communicate simply the miracles once performed by the holy Fathers, just as they have reached us through the reports of many.

Many relate that a holy man named Paul,

[Note: [Col. 0128D] “A holy man named Paul.” Concerning him, our writers Morales, Book II, chapter 71, and Padilla, Century VI, chapter 50, write with no little commendation of our author.]

a Greek by nationality,

a physician by profession,

[Note: [Col. 0128D] A physician by profession. May our Paul increase the number of physicians who excel in holiness, a number elegantly assembled by the pious diligence of John Molanus in his *Ecclesiastical Diary of Physicians*.]
