came from the regions of the East to the city of Mérida. After living there for a long time, he became distinguished by holiness and many virtues, and surpassed everyone in humility and kindness. It was granted by the Lord that he should be deemed worthy of the bishopric of that city.

When he had been ordained bishop by the Lord’s choice, God immediately removed all the storms of disturbance that had troubled the same Church during the time of his predecessor and granted it profound peace through Paul’s prayers. While he governed all his fellow citizens peacefully and kindly, with God’s favor, and displayed to everyone through his conduct the sweet-flowing affection of his sacred heart, it happened that the wife of a certain leading citizen, a most noble man of senatorial family, fell ill. She herself, born of an illustrious lineage, traced a noble ancestry. Shortly after her marriage she had conceived, but the tiny infant in her womb had been injured. Although many physicians applied various treatments to her, she felt no relief from their medical care and, placed in grave danger, drew nearer to death each day.

The aforementioned illustrious man, because nothing was dearer to him than the wife whom he had only recently taken in marriage, disregarded all the physicians and, hoping to recover her health, ran to the most holy man. Falling at his feet with tears, he begged him to pray to the Lord through his prayers for the health of his wife, since he was a servant of God; or, since he was a physician, not to consider it unworthy to offer healing to the sick woman with his own hand.

But the man of God immediately replied:

“I may not do what you urge me to do. Although I am an unworthy priest of the Lord and offer sacrifice to the Lord with my hands, I cannot fulfill what you ask, lest afterward I bring polluted hands to the sacred altars and immediately incur the anger of divine power.”

And he added:

“We shall go in the Lord’s name, visit her, and provide physicians of the Church to administer medicine to her. Insofar as we know, we shall show how the treatment may be carried out; but we ourselves cannot perform it with our own hands.”

The man, however, knowing that the care of no other physician would be effective, and that his wife was already almost dead, began with great weeping to implore him earnestly not to send anyone there but to go himself and administer what he knew with his own hand.

But while Paul neither agreed nor gave his full consent, all the brothers who were present also begged him with tears to go. He said:

“I know that the Lord is rich in mercy (Psalm 50:5), and I believe that, when I have gone there, the sick woman will recover her former health, and that he will immediately grant me pardon for my presumption. But I have no doubt that evil men will afterward bring this charge against me.”

When all his brothers replied, “None of us will say anything of the kind because of this; go, lord, and with all speed

[Note: [Col. 0129D] Do that which will profit your reward. This is a pure and unmistakable Hispanism: “for your reward.” The almost universal Spanish custom of addressing someone by *vuestra merced*—“your mercy”—is well known. From this excessively flattering form of address arose the other forms of address familiar in common usage. Traces of Hispanisms remain more than once in our Paul, as learned men have observed in other writers of Spain. Orientius of Illiberis, in the *Commonitorium*:

“Hence the harmony of peace restrains the whole world,”]

do that which will profit your reward.”
which is given even to irrational creatures with reason. [Col. 0130D] In the manuscripts, *co rone*, which the Spaniards call *con mucha racon*—that is, “with much reason,” “deservedly,” “justly,” “not without cause”—as the distinguished M. A. Del Rio notes. Eulogius of Córdoba similarly writes in Book I of the *Memorials of the Saints*: “But in truth it must be admitted that it is a crime to lie hidden.” For we frequently begin an assertion with *en verdad*, as Moral observes in his note to Eulogius, no. 20, and Book II, chapter 1. This expression is also partly known from the Arabic language, where he likewise recognizes a Hispanicism; for we frequently say *por parte de su virtud era mui buen querido*—“on account of his virtue he was very well loved”—and many expressions of that kind.]

Do what will profit your reward. At last, compelled by their entreaties, [Col. 0129D] he promised to set out, but only on the condition that he first seek the Lord’s will, lest by proceeding rashly he easily undertake something for which, if punished by God’s judgment, he would have to return with difficulty to forgiveness. Immediately, therefore, he went to the basilica of the most holy virgin Eulalia, and, prostrate on the pavement, [Col. 0130A] lay there throughout the whole day; persevering tirelessly in prayer, he continued through the following night as well. Then, at once, he was admonished there by a divine oracle. He immediately rose and went without delay to the sick woman’s house. Hastening quickly, he offered a prayer and laid his hands upon the invalid in the name of the Lord. Trusting in God, with marvelous precision he made a very fine incision with a delicate instrument and removed the already putrefied infant, limb by limb and piece by piece. By God’s help he immediately restored the nearly dead, half-alive woman to health for her husband. He also ordered her never again to know her husband sexually, for whenever she recognized marital intercourse, worse dangers would immediately befall her.

But they, falling at his feet, nevertheless gave thanks [Col. 0130B] and promised that they would observe in every respect everything that the man of God had commanded, beseeching the Lord that, if they did not keep it, worse things might later come upon them. Thus an immeasurable joy and immense gladness arose among them; and all, acclaiming God’s praises, praying and rejoicing, said that the Lord had truly sent his angel, who had taken pity on them.

Then they drew up such a written agreement concerning their property that the holy man would immediately receive half of everything they possessed, while the other half, whole and untouched, would belong to his control after their death. They possessed such an abundance of goods that no senator in the province of Lusitania could be found richer than they. He entirely refused and rejected this arrangement and did not wish to accept it. [Col. 0130C] But when they implored him and offered it with excessive insistence, he was at last compelled to receive it. Having accepted it, he ordered it to be devoted not so much to his own uses as to the needs of the poor.

Those from whom it had been offered to him, persevering in chastity with fear of God, were soon afterward summoned by divine calling to the heavenly homeland. After their death, the most holy bishop Paul acquired all their patrimony; and he who had arrived as a stranger possessing nothing became more powerful than all the powerful, to such an extent that the entire wealth of the Church was considered nothing in comparison with his resources.

## CHAPTER V. Fidelis, a Greek by nationality and the son of the sister of Paul, bishop of Mérida, is appointed to the episcopate while his uncle is still alive.

[Col. 0130D]

Finally, after he had enjoyed many years of prosperity with his people and, living joyfully for God, had always flourished, full of virtues, it happened one day that [Col. 0131A] Greek merchants from the region of his own origin arrived by ship from the East and reached the shores of Spain. When they came to the city of Mérida, they paid the customary visit to the bishop. After he had received them kindly and they had left his courtyard and returned to the house where they were lodging, on the following day they sent him a small gift in thanks, carried by a boy named Fidelis, whom they had brought from their region as a hired servant to receive his wages.

When the boy had been brought before him and the holy man had gratefully accepted what he had brought as a gift from a thankful heart, he began to question him individually: what was his name, and from what province or city did he come? When the boy stated his name and city [Col. 0131B], the bishop, seeing that he was of good character, questioned him in detail and asked the names of his parents. In answer to each question, the boy simply disclosed his homeland, city, village, and the names of his parents. As he spoke, the bishop recognized the name of his own sister. Immediately leaping up from his seat, he embraced the boy before everyone; for his heart had been deeply moved toward him. Throwing his arms around his neck and kissing him for a very long time, he wept abundantly for joy. He immediately ordered the merchants named above to be summoned and said to them:

“Give me this boy, and ask whatever you wish from me.”

But they replied:

“We certainly cannot do this, because he is a freeborn man, and we received him from his parents as a hired companion. Without him we cannot [Col. 0131C] return to his parents at all, nor shall we have permission ever again to see their faces if we leave him in so distant a province.”

He, on the other hand, said:

“Know for certain that, if you do not leave him to me, you will not return to your homeland. But accept abundant money from me and go safely on your way in peace.”

Hearing this, and no longer able to resist such authority, they said to him:

“Tell us, lord, what is the reason that you deign to love a man unknown to you with such affection?”

He replied that the boy was his kinsman and very closely related to him; and he added:

“Go in the name of the Lord without any hesitation, and tell my sister that I have kept her son with me for the consolation of my captivity.”

He sent various gifts to his sister through them and bestowed many presents upon the sailors. Thus, enriched by his gifts, they entered their homeland with great joy.

When they had departed, he immediately ordered the aforementioned youth [Col. 0131D] to be tonsured, and offered him for the service of almighty God. [Note: He ordered the youth to be tonsured and offered him for the service of almighty God. This was appropriate, for, as Blessed Jerome testifies—as stated in *Decretum* 12, question 1, chapter “Duo sunt”—the shaving of the head signifies the abandonment of all temporal things, so that the tonsured man, that is, the cleric, may serve God. According to Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, Book II, chapter 4, the tonsure originated with the Nazirites, from whom the apostles introduced it into the Church.]

Like another Samuel in the temple of the Lord, he diligently instructed him day and night [Col. 0132A], so that within the course of a few years he had taught him most perfectly the entire ecclesiastical office and the whole library of the divine Scriptures. Then, leading him through each rank in turn, he ordained him deacon. As soon as he had become a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, he was so illumined by every virtue that in holiness, charity, patience, and humility he surpassed the entire clergy. He presented himself so safely and courteously before God and men that people thought him to be one of the company of angels.

Meanwhile, while he served God blamelessly for many years, obeyed his aforementioned foster-father in everything with loving service, and gently gladdened his old age without causing any offense, the same most blessed Father, after many years had passed [Col. 0132B] and as he declined into extreme old age, chose him as his successor. He soon ordained him in his own place while still alive and appointed him heir to all his goods. He also decreed by testamentary sanction that, if the clergy of Mérida wished to have him as bishop, all the possessions he had bestowed upon him would, after his death, be left to the aforesaid church; but otherwise he would have free authority to dispose of or determine whatever he wished concerning those possessions.

The holy man promulgated this decree after the Holy Spirit had revealed it to him. By the grace of prophecy, he foresaw that many jealousies of wicked men would assail that man, and that afterward they would bark at him from every side like dogs and savagely tear at his succession with the jaws [alternative reading: *facibus*, “torches”] of envy. [Col. 0132C]

Meanwhile, after appointing him bishop with the Lord’s favor, he wished to stand beside him and serve him just as he had been accustomed to minister during the time of his diaconate. Thus, removing his *casula* [Note: *Casula*. The same word occurs in the old interpreter of Philotheus, bishop of Constantinople, in *Commentary on the Sacred Office*, vol. IV of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, col. 528: “The priest goes out at the rear, wearing a lowered *casula*, in Greek *phainolion* (φαινόλιον), for the same interpreter himself uses that word below. It is pleasing to find among ancient writers the terms used by the Roman Church. See Amalarius Fortunatus, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, Book VI, chapter 19, and Book III, chapter 15; and Rabanus Maurus, *The Instruction of Clerics*, Book I, chapter 21.] and standing before him in the manner of a servant, he would perform every service. But the bishop forbade him to do this and admonished him henceforth to hold firmly to the authority of his episcopate; he also ordered him rather to take care of his brothers.

The most holy old man himself then immediately left the courtyard and all the privileges of his honor, and withdrew to the basilica of Saint Eulalia, into a most humble cell. While he was living there, freed from the storms of this world and established in great tranquillity, lying in sackcloth and ashes and praying to the Lord for the offenses of the whole world, he departed from the body.

## CHAPTER VI. Bishop Fidelis leaves his possessions to the church of Saint Eulalia and rescues the clergy from the danger of collapse.

[Col. 0132D]

After his departure, certain pestilential men, just as the man of God had foretold, began to mutter malicious words against the most blessed bishop Fidelis [Note: Bishop Fidelis. Our same writers discuss him: Moral, Book II, chapter 72, and Padilla, century VI, chapter 50.], seeking to drive him by some pretext from the position to which he had been appointed. When he perceived this, he wished to withdraw from their persecution together with his possessions. [Col. 0133A] But they discovered that, if he separated himself from them after removing his estates from the Church’s ownership, nothing at all would remain for them. More unwillingly than willingly, therefore, they fell at his feet. He did not altogether resist them, but consented that he should continue to exercise the care of government and afterward leave his entire patrimony to the Church.

This was done, and at that time the Church itself was so enriched that there was no wealthier church anywhere within the borders of Spain. With the Lord’s cooperation, the pure and sincere affection of everyone toward him was so firmly established that all, burning with the same mind [Col. 0133B] and aflame with immense charity, seethed with an immense love for him in the holy fire. They became one heart and one mouth with him, differing in no way at all through any interruption of mutual affection.

Since we have mentioned the name of so great a prophet, it seems worthwhile to preserve a brief portion in memory of his many virtues, by which he frequently shone forth.

When, therefore, on the Lord’s Day he was going with many sons of the Church into the courtyard, as was customary, the archdeacon and the clergy, coming from the church dressed in white, stood before him. [Note: “The archdeacon with the clergy in white,” and so forth. Moral and Padilla observe this as a distinctive custom of the Spanish Church, drawing on our Paul. One may also add what Isidore wrote in his letter to Laufredus, bishop of Córdoba, concerning the office of the archdeacon, together with the fragments collected by Bernard, provost of Pavia, in *Collection of Decretals*, Book I, title 15, chapter 3, from the Council of Toledo concerning the same office.]

Then he rose and proceeded to the church with the deacons carrying censers according to custom and walking before him, together with all who were present, so that, with God’s help, they might celebrate the solemnities of the Mass. But when they had gone with him only about ten paces from the courtyard, suddenly the entire structure of the very spacious courtyard collapsed from its deepest foundations, and no one there was crushed, by God’s command [perhaps “with God’s help”?].

From this one must consider what merit this man possessed, since by his prayers he obtained such favor with God that the ancient enemy was not granted power to bring about the collapse of so great a structure until he had first led everyone outside in safety, God showing mercy. Yet no one should doubt that, in such great danger, this was especially accomplished through the merits of the most holy virgin Eulalia.

When he carefully investigated and found that no one had perished, he was not at all disturbed in spirit. Rather, he gave thanks to God, gladly offered him a sacrifice, and joyfully enjoyed that day in the Lord with all his people [Col. 0133D; perhaps *partitus*, “shared”].

After a considerable interval of time, he restored the structure of the ruined seat and, with God’s help, completed it more beautifully than before: [Col. 0134A] [Note: He raised the spaces of the building far and wide on taller columns, hung precious ornaments from the columns of the courtyard, and clothed the entire pavement and all the walls with shining marbles, and so forth. In precisely this manner Prudentius vividly described the temple of Saint Eulalia in his hymn:

Here, where the gleam of polished marble  
lights the lofty courts,  
the revered earth preserves in her bosom  
for stranger and native alike  
the sacred relics and ashes.

Above, the shining roofs glitter  
from their golden ceilings;  
cut stones diversify the floor,  
so that you might think  
rose-covered meadows were reddening  
with flowers of many kinds.]

He raised the spaces of the building far and wide upon taller columns, hung precious ornaments from the columns of the courtyard, clothed the entire pavement and all the walls with gleaming marble, and covered the structure above with marvelous roofs. Then, restoring the basilica of the most blessed virgin Eulalia in a wondrous arrangement, he improved it and raised the lofty summits of its towers to a sublime height within that most sacred temple.

This blessed man is said often to have been seen, while still in the body, standing and singing in the church choir with companies of saints. Many other things are also related, which, because of their length and lest they weary the readers, we have omitted from writing.

## CHAPTER VII. Bishop Fidelis is seen taking part in the choirs of the saints.

[Col. 0134B]

One day he sent a servant-boy to a place called Capsiana, sixteen miles from the city of Mérida, and ordered him to return with all speed. When the boy had arrived there but was unable to return that same day, he remained there. At the beginning of the night, when he was already asleep, he seemed to hear the roosters crow. Immediately he awoke, mounted his horse, and hurried rapidly onward. Before midnight he reached the gate of that city called the Bridge Gate.

After sitting there for a very long time, he realized that he had risen before the proper hour and that, although he had shouted loudly, no one would open the gate for him. It occurred to him to give his horse a little grass while he waited for someone perhaps to unlock the gate.

Suddenly, in the dead of night, [Col. 0134C] he raised his eyes and saw in the distance a globe of fire proceeding from the church of Saint Faustus [Note: Saint Faustus. He was evidently the Spanish martyr who suffered at Córdoba, as related by Saint Eulogius, *Memorials of the Saints*, Book II, chapter 9, and by Isidore in the hymn of the Gothic office.], which was about a mile from the city, and advancing toward the basilica of Saint Leocritia [Note: Saint Leocritia. She too was a martyr of Córdoba, mentioned by Alvarus, Paul’s associate, in the account of the passion of Saint Eulogius and in the hymn for her anniversary.].

While he silently watched to see what it might be, suddenly—behold!—a multitude of saints, preceded by that light, came across the bridge and reached the gate. Among them also walked the most holy bishop Fidelis. When they reached the gate, the boy saw the ranks of those dressed in white increase, and he saw Saint Fidelis himself, clothed in a snow-white cloak, hastening in their midst. He was astounded and, overcome with terror and trembling from fear, became like a dead man.

The bishop divinely unlocked the bars of the gate, and they immediately entered the city. After they had entered, the boy rose and wished to follow them inside, but he could not, because he found the gate closed just as it had been before.

At first light, when he arrived at the courtyard [Col. 0135A], the holy man immediately asked him at what hour he had departed from the place mentioned above. The boy told him both the hour at which he had risen and the delay he had experienced at the gate. When the man of God asked whether he had seen anything, the boy admitted that he had. The bishop warned him to tell no one as long as he himself remained in the body, lest it bring him grave danger.

On another occasion, a certain religious man likewise saw him one night leaving the church of Saint Eulalia with a multitude of saints and passing through the Basilica of the Martyrs. Acting imprudently, he immediately told many people. At last he came to the man of God and reported what he had seen. The bishop said to him:

“Have you already told anyone somewhere what you saw, or not?”

He immediately answered simply that he had told it. [Col. 0135B] Then the bishop said:

“May the Lord forgive you, brother; you have not acted rightly. Yet I know that this will not be counted against you at the future judgment. For now, go, receive Communion, and give us a kiss. Take leave of everyone, for you are nevertheless about to depart; put your household in order with all speed, and, if you desire the remedy of penance, receive it.”

Having immediately received penance and put his household in order, he took leave of everyone and departed from the body the following night.

## CHAPTER VIII. Bishop Fidelis, warned by a vision, distributes his goods among the poor and departs to the Lord.

Again, a certain religious man, returning to the ecclesiastical office, was lying one night in his little bed, overcome by sleep in the deep silence of the night. He saw [Col. 0135C] [Note: that he had given the signal for Matins. The same expression occurs below: “Behold, the hour has come when the signal ought to be given.” From the most ancient times, it was customary in the Church, when the signal was given, to gather the clergy for the hours. I observe that this was done in four ways according to the varying periods: by wood, bronze, the voice, and a messenger.

Concerning wood, see Amalarius, *On the Divine Offices*, Book IV, chapter 25: “In ancient times the Roman Church used the sound of a wooden instrument when, because of persecution, it was hiding in crypts.” The *Book of the Miracles of the Martyr Anastasius*, recited in the Seventh Synod, session 4, says: “Striking the sacred pieces of wood, they met one another.”

Concerning bronze, the matter is too well known to require examples here. See further in John Stephen Durandus, *On the Rites of the Catholic Church*, Book I, chapter 22.

Concerning the voice, Jerome writes in Letter 27: “After the Alleluia had been sung, by which signal they were summoned to the gathering,” and so forth, concerning Paula’s monastery.

Concerning messengers, see Ignatius the Martyr’s Letter to Polycarp. Christians used them, like the wooden signal, because of persecution, but this was at the beginning of the nascent Church.

The signals, whether bells or other signs, were always placed in an elevated position. Einhard, *On the Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter*, Book III, chapter 15, says: “The little tower containing the signals of the basilica could have been seen by them.” Malaxus calls it a bell tower. See J. C. Bucenger, *On Temples*, Book IV, chapter 37.]

When he immediately rose and hastened to the church with all speed, lest the time of the sacrifice pass him by, he arrived there breathless after a very rapid run. But [Note: When he entered the church of Saint Mary, which is still called Saint Jerusalem. The same is found in chapter 12: “In the treasury of the older church, which is called Saint Jerusalem.” The Council of Mérida in the time of King Recceswinth says at its beginning: “When we, all the bishops of the province of Lusitania, had gathered in the name of the Lord and were seated in the church of Jerusalem, which is in the city of Mérida, known to be the head of this province and which remains dedicated under its principal name,” and so forth.

Likewise, in the Seventy-Second Council of Toledo, assembled by order of King Reccared in the great church of Saint Mary, in the place called Jerusalem, according to M. Maximus under the year 590; and in the Council of Seville—thus the ancient manuscripts read—under King Sisebut: “We were seated in the place called Jerusalem of the most holy church of Seville,” and so forth. The same appears in the First Council, if that gathering was indeed a council, or rather in the letter of the bishops to Pegasius, chapter 1. This was doubtless a prerogative of metropolitan churches. See Padilla, century 7, chapters 12 and 47.]

When he entered the church of Saint Mary, which is still called Saint Jerusalem, he heard voices singing with marvelous melody. Looking toward the choir, he saw a multitude of saints standing there. Shaken by great fear and trembling, he silently withdrew into a corner of the basilica. Watching quietly and listening attentively, he heard them complete the entire office according to the customary order. [Col. 0136A]

When it was finished, shortly before cockcrow, they came with praises to the church of Saint Mary and to the little basilica of Saint John, in which the baptistery is located. It is extremely close to the aforementioned basilica, the two buildings being separated only by a wall and covered by a single roof. When the praises had been completed, they began to say to one another:

“Behold, the hour has now come when the signal ought to be given. Therefore it is first necessary for us to arrange what we have been sent to accomplish.”

When they had said this, Ethiopians appeared before them, exceedingly gloomy and terrifying. Their stature seemed gigantic, their blackness utterly dreadful, so that from their whole appearance and especially their very dark faces it was plainly evident to the observer that they were undoubtedly infernal ministers. They also carried extremely sharp [Col. 0136B] swords [*romphaeae*] in their hands.

The saints then said to them:

“Go with all speed to the courtyard, enter the cell in which Bishop Fidelis lies, and strike him with a grievous wound in the body, so that his soul may quickly depart from its bodily chain and reach with us our Lord Jesus Christ and the crown prepared for it.”

They immediately obeyed the command and went. But they did not strike him; instead they returned and said:

“We cannot enter his cell, because he is not asleep but lies prostrate on the ground and prays. Moreover, the cell itself is filled with so sweet a fragrance of incense that the brilliance of the perfume offered by him to the Lord does not allow us to enter there at all.”

Again they ordered them:

“Go and [Col. 0136C] strike him, for the Lord’s command must be fulfilled.”

When they went but could not enter, they returned again and said:

“Prayer gives way when the summons comes.” But go and fulfill the Lord’s command, which, once given, cannot in any way be transgressed.”

When they went a third time, God permitting it, they entered. With such a strong and cruel hand they struck him that the religious man standing in the church clearly heard the voice he uttered amid grievous pain and groaning.

At daybreak the religious man approached the holy bishop and disclosed everything he had seen and heard. The bishop said to him:

“I know, my son, I know; nothing is hidden from me.” [Col. 0137A]

After saying this, he suddenly felt himself wholly dissolving, his limbs already failing under the impending illness. He ordered himself to be carried from there to the basilica of the most holy virgin Eulalia. There, first of all, he wept over his sins with many tears of repentance. Then he distributed abundant alms to many captives and needy people. Finally, after returning the written acknowledgments of debt, he released the debts of many.

But after he had returned everything, the written obligation of a certain widow remained, for it had not yet been returned. He was waiting to give it back to her, but the woman could not approach because of the dense crowd surrounding him. She came each day, but could find no place to enter. Greatly saddened and anxious, she accomplished nothing and returned in grief to her lodging. [Col. 0137B]

One night the most holy Cyprian and Laurence appeared to her in a vision and said:

“Do you know why you cannot find a place?”

She replied:

“I do not know.”

They said:

“And tell us why you frequently hasten through the other basilicas of our fellow martyrs, but disdain to come to us.”

She immediately arose and hurried to their basilicas. She offered a tearful prayer and sought forgiveness for her negligence in the past. From there she returned to the basilica of Saint Eulalia and found a place with remarkable speed. Without difficulty she received her written obligation and gave marvelous thanks to God and his saint.

By this she deserved not only to find a place prepared for her to enter, but, through the arrangement of God’s saints, it also happened that when she entered, the holy bishop was waiting with the document in his own hand [Col. 0137C], ready to return it to the person to whom it belonged.

Thus, when he kindly returned it and she joyfully received what she had long desired, the holy man shortly afterward departed, amid companies of saints going before him and angelic choirs awaiting him, rejoicing toward the heavenly realms. Joined to the heavenly ranks, he merited, with perpetual exultation, to be gathered forever among them in the starry dwellings, while Jesus the Lord received him.

His little body was honorably buried beside the body of his most holy predecessor in one and the same sarcophagus, as though in a single bed.

## CHAPTER IX. Massona, a Goth by nationality and raised in the church of Saint Eulalia, succeeds Fidelis in the episcopate and builds a hospice and monasteries.

[Col. 0137D]

To this aforesaid holy man, as he migrated to the heavenly homeland, divine providence in its mercy appointed as successor a man equal in the glory of every virtue, orthodox, whose name was Massona.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] Massona. In other authors he is Mausona. Concerning him, see our writers John, abbot of Biclaro, in the *Chronicle*; Maximus, under the years 579, 586, 588, and 597; Roderick of Toledo, II, chapter 14; the *General History of Spain*, collected by order of Alfonso surnamed the Wise, part II, chapter 40; Vasaeus, under the years 571 and 589; Gariu, book VIII, chapter 83; Morales, book XII, chapter 6; Mariana, book V, chapters 13 and 14; Loaysa, notes on the Third Council of Toledo; Padilla, *Century VI*, chapters 45 and 53; and others—though the more recent writers derive their accounts from a single Paul, whom one may use to illuminate the others. To these add the distinguished Caesar Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 589, and what we note below at chapter 20.],

that is, blessed succeeding the blessed, [Col. 0138A] holy succeeding the holy, pious succeeding the pious, good succeeding the kindly, and shining with every spiritual gift. Massona, resplendent with immeasurable virtues and radiant in priestly rank, succeeded Fidelis.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Massona succeeded Fidelis. Maximus reverses the order under the year 560, saying: “Saint Massona succeeded Paul in the Emeritensian see”; and under the year 566: “Paul, bishop of Emerita, succeeded the bishop Fidelis.” This must be corrected from our account: Fidelis succeeded Paul, and Massona Fidelis. See Morales, book II, chapter 72, and Padilla, *Century VI*, chapter 50.]

Since his predecessor had plainly been joined to the starry citizens in heaven, the sweetness of his successor remained on earth, and his distinguished merit softened the grief of all the citizens. Thus, at the death of the holy bishop, grief was not only dispelled from everyone, but it also seemed evident to all that, after the manner of the ancient fathers Elijah and Elisha (4 Kings 2:15), the doubled grace of the Spirit of the Paraclete had openly rested upon Massona, the holy bishop, as it had upon Saint Fidelis. The people, with their shepherd restored, were not altogether wearied by the affliction of their languor, but rejoiced together with doubled joy, by divine mercy: for God had sent the former to heaven as a reward for his own merits, and had joyfully received this man of outstanding virtue on earth.

Finally, Saint Massona the bishop,

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Born in this world of noble origin. Morales, book XII, chapter 6.]

was born in this world of noble lineage, but by the merits of his life he proved far nobler still. In lineage indeed he was a Goth, but in mind exceedingly ready and wholly devoted to the Lord, manfully girded with the strength of the Most High, adorned with holy conduct, and beautified by a character of great dignity. From his earliest age he was wrapped about with the shining robe of charity and humility, firmly girded with the belt of faith, conspicuously surrounded by prudence and justice, wonderfully adorned with love of the supreme God and of his neighbor. He was beloved by God and human beings, a man of astonishing renown, a lover of the brethren, praying greatly for the people; and his name, gleaming through many miracles, passed throughout the whole land.

In his time the Lord, through his prayers, drove far away the plague of disease and the scarcity caused by famine from the city of Emerita and from all Lusitania, and through the merits of the most holy virgin Eulalia repelled them even farther. He deigned to grant such health and such abundance of every delight to the entire people that no one, however poor, seemed ever to lack anything or to be oppressed by any necessity. Rather, rich and poor alike abounded in all good things, and, in a manner resembling heavenly joy, rejoiced on earth through the merit of so great a bishop.

Joy was present in everyone, peace attended all, happiness was absent from no one; perfect charity blossomed in every heart, and cheerful tranquility prevailed in every mind. Indeed, after the most ancient enemy had been conquered and the aged dragon overcome, no one was overcome by grief, no one afflicted by distress, no one struck by any terror, and no one was shaken by the poisonous goads of the crafty serpent through jealousy or envy. All, filled with perfect charity, rejoiced in the grace of the pious Father, by God’s favor; undaunted, without fear or anguish, they persevered steadfastly in the praises of God.

Nor did his immense charity burn only in the secret hearts of all the faithful; it also drew the minds of all Jews and Gentiles toward the grace of Christ by the marvelous sweetness of its affection. What and how great a man he was, our sluggish tongue cannot explain in every detail. Yet, though we remain silent about the greatest things, let us at least recall the final among the greatest.

Indeed, the aforesaid man,

[Note: [Col. 0139D] Before he was ordained bishop. Padilla, *Century VI*, chapter 68.]

before he was ordained bishop, is said to have lived with the greatest diligence in the basilica of the most holy virgin Eulalia, and there to have served God irreproachably for many years. But after, by God’s inspiration, he had come to dwell in the mouths, eyes, and minds of human beings, he was taken from there and appointed bishop. Immediately, at the beginning of his episcopate, he founded many monasteries, enriched them with great estates, constructed several basilicas with marvelous workmanship, and consecrated many souls to God there.

Then he built a hospice and endowed it with great patrimonies. After appointing attendants and physicians, he ordered them to serve the needs of travelers and the sick. He gave the following command: physicians were to travel continually through the entire circuit of the city, and whenever they found any sick person—slave or free, Christian or Jew—they were to carry him in their arms to the hospice. Having likewise prepared beds of straw, they were to lay the sick person upon them there and prepare delicate and clean food for him until, with God’s help, they restored his former health.

Although the hospice was supplied with an abundance of delicacies from the many estates assigned to it,

[Col. 0139C] it still seemed too little to the holy man. Adding greater benefits to all these, he ordered the physicians to take vigilant care that from all the choicest things brought into the courtyard from every sanctuary and from the whole patrimony of the Church, they should receive half and carry it to the same sick people.

For if any townsman, or any peasant from the countryside, came to the courtyard because of some need and asked the dispensers for oil, wine, or honey, and presented a small vessel into which he might raise it,

[Note: [Col. 0139D] A small vessel into which he might raise it, and so forth. A Hispanism. For us, *tollere* is *llevar*, with the doubled *l*, according to our usage, but it is derived from the Latin *levare*.]

the holy man, whose appearance was always gracious and whose countenance was cheerful, immediately ordered the little vessel itself to be broken and the petitioner to bring a larger one.

But how generous he was in alms for the poor, God alone knows. Nevertheless, let us recount some small part of this matter as well. He was so concerned for the sufferings of all the wretched that he gave two thousand solidi to the deacon Redemptus, a venerable man,

[Note: [Col. 0140D] Redemptus. He is also mentioned in chapters 3 and 18.]

who was in charge of the basilica of the most holy virgin Eulalia. From this sum, as soon as anyone came in urgent need and had given security,

[al. “after an inquiry”]

he could receive as much as he wished without any delay or difficulty and provide for his necessities.

Nor do I think this should be passed over in silence: how generous he was in gifts. For he was most restrained with what belonged to others, more generous with what belonged to himself, and excelled not in the greatness of receiving but of giving. He had learned to be more eager to give than to seek, and to regard the fortune of giving as better than that of receiving. He gave much and took away nothing; of his own accord he granted everything to all. He bestowed many gifts, distributed very many, enriched everyone with benefits, and was regarded as great in generosity.

Everyone was increased by him and enriched with gifts and wealth. He showed himself extraordinarily generous in his gifts not only to brothers and friends but even to the servants of the Church themselves. They were so enriched in his time that, on the most holy day of Easter, when he proceeded to the church, many boys wearing silk cloaks walked before him as though before a king. What no one in those times could or dared do, they did: clothed in such garments, they went before him, offering the service due to him.

Yet this gift of such merit had rightly been bestowed upon him by almighty God: although his heart possessed such abundance and the joy of transient prosperity and glory, it was never swollen or inflated. His humble spirit, founded upon the solid rock, with the sincere thought of an unstained conscience and ignorant of cunning, was humble in prosperity and exceedingly strong in adversity. Prosperity did not exalt him, nor adversity break him; his constancy was changed by no loss or increase. He was constant in everything and exceedingly ready to face all things, most patient and firm in strength. In every adversity he remained constant; in every distress he persevered undaunted. He changed his expression neither in joy nor in sorrow. His countenance was always the same, adorned with a single cheerfulness, and he met everyone with it.

[Col. 0140C] He was always unchanged; his face was never altered by the changing circumstances of life. The hostile elevation of pride did not raise him above all virtues; rather, with the most sacred affection of his heart, he sincerely consecrated genuine humility in all things. And while he excelled in such virtues by divine favor, his reputation grew as the good opinion of him increased, and the works of light, bestowed by the true Light, shone forth in many regions.

## CHAPTER X. King Leovigild, an Arian king of the Visigoths, endeavors to turn Massona, bishop of Emerita, away from the Catholic faith

Thus it happened that this reputation reached the hearing of Leovigild, the most savage and cruel king of the Visigoths. The immense dragon of his envy, always hostile to good works, provoked by sharper goads, filled the mind of that prince with viperous venom and poured the poisoned cup into his entrails. Having drunk this deadly cup, he was immediately armed with a plan; with the devil’s envy urging him on, he repeatedly sent messages through envoys to the aforesaid most holy man, commanding him to abandon the Catholic faith and, together with the whole people entrusted to him, turn to the Arian heresy.

But when the man devoted to God replied with the utmost constancy, and when the messengers returned twice and three times, he told the king that he would never abandon the true faith which he had once recognized. He reproached the recently Arian king as he ought, and repelled his treachery toward him with deserved rebukes.

When the messengers had returned to him, the aforesaid king began, through various arguments and promises of rewards, to entice Massona’s mind, in the hope that by some opportunity he might bend him to the will of his superstition. But Massona despised his crafty persuasions; he rejected gifts and rewards as refuse. He most manfully defended the Catholic faith.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] The man vigorously defended the Catholic faith. Concerning Massona, see John of Biclaro: “Massona, bishop of the Emeritensian Church, is renowned for the doctrine of the faith of Christ.”]

Nor did he wish to remain silent against the treachery, lest by silence he might perhaps seem to consent. Rather, resisting the king’s madness with all his strength, he sounded out the trumpet of truth. When the king saw that his labor was failing in vain, he was carried away into fury and began to assail Massona with many terrors, thinking that threats might shake the man whom he had been unable to overcome with blandishments. But the holy man was neither broken by terrors nor persuaded by blandishments. Fighting in a strong encounter against the most atrocious tyrant, he remained unconquered in defense of justice.

## CHAPTER XI. Sunna, an Arian pseudo-bishop of Emerita, defeated by Massona in a public disputation

[Note: [Col. 0141D] Sunna. Not only was this pseudo-bishop substituted in Massona’s place, but another was substituted as well. Maximus of Zaragoza, under the year 681, among those who, while Leovigild was persecuting them, had assembled a council for Hermenegild, lists Sunna—not Sumnia, as in the common editions—and Nepotianus as intruded bishops of the Emeritensian Church. I believe this Nepotianus to be Nepopis, on the evidence of chapters 13 and 15 of our Paul. On Sunna, see Morales, book XI, chapter 6; Mariana, book V, chapter 34; and Padilla, chapter 68, *Century VI*.]

Thereafter, when the most cruel tyrant learned that he could not make the man of God apostatize from the true faith into his own treachery either by threats or by gifts, he—being wholly a vessel of wrath (Romans 4:22), a smoky mass of vices, and a shrub of damnation, with a savage heresy occupying his breast and the most crafty serpent holding him captive in its power (Genesis 37:6)—offered the citizens bitter things instead of sweet, harsh things instead of gentle, deadly medicines instead of salvation.

He established in that same city a certain pestilential man, named Sunna, who defended the depravity of the Arian heresy in every respect, as bishop of the Arian party, in order to stir up seditious quarrels and disturb the holy man and the whole people. He was a supporter of a perverse doctrine, a baleful man, hideous in appearance: his brow was grim, his eyes fierce, his look hateful, his movements dreadful. In mind he was sinister, in conduct depraved, in tongue biting, obscene in speech, swollen outwardly but empty within, proud externally but inwardly vain, inflated outwardly but inwardly emptied of every virtue. Deformed on both sides, unworthy of good things and wealthy in the worst, bound to sins and exceedingly eager for eternal death—

this aforesaid author of treachery, when he came into the city of Emerita and, by the king’s command, certain basilicas with all their privileges had been taken away, attempted with reckless boldness to seize them for himself from the authority of their own bishop. Bound by the tighter chains of that baleful robber and filled with his deadly cups, he began to bark furious words against the servant of God and, with clamorous speech, vomit forth filthy threats.

[Col. 0142A] But neither did threats from the executioner break the proven servant of God, nor did the turbulent anger of the pestilent man soften him, nor did the storm of the raging madman bend him. Like a most powerful wall (Proverbs 18:11), he stood immovable against every storm in defense of the holy faith.

When this infidel, with all his strength, wished to drive the servant of God and all the faithful from their position by carefully devised torments, but could not, he relied on royal favor and tried openly to attack the basilica of the most holy virgin Eulalia, intending, after removing it from the authority of its own bishop, to dedicate it to the Arian heresy.

When the holy bishop Massona and the whole people with him fiercely resisted and vigorously opposed him, the aforesaid pseudo-bishop Sunna wrote many accusations against the holy man to the aforementioned prince. He suggested that the very sacred basilica which he had desired to enter should be taken from the power of the Catholics and handed over to his own authority by royal command.

In response, the king is said to have pronounced the following judgment: judges should sit in the courtyard of the Church, and each bishop should have judges selected by him present. With both parties before them, the bishops should contend in disputation, defending their respective positions; fighting against one another in alternating encounters, they should establish and support everything they said by producing testimonies from the books of Sacred Scripture. The party that won the triumph and prize should nevertheless claim the church of Saint Eulalia for itself.

When such a decree, as the rumor grew, resounded in the ears of the holy man Massona, he immediately hastened to the basilica of Saint Eulalia the virgin. For three days and as many nights he persevered in abstinence and tears, lying prostrate on the pavement before the altar beneath which the venerable body of the holy Martyr lies.

On the third day at last he returned to the courtyard founded within the walls of the city itself. He entered with such eagerness and firmness of mind that none of the faithful could doubt that he was proceeding to the assistance of the one who had said: “Do not think beforehand what you shall speak, for it shall be given you in that hour what you shall speak; for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 10:19–20).

When he had reached the city, entered the courtyard, and taken his seat, he removed the sorrow from the countenances of all the faithful by the cheerfulness of his own face and warned them not to doubt in any way his victory. He then waited a very long time for the wicked Arian bishop and the judges.

[Col. 0142D] At last the Arian bishop entered together with the judges, surrounded by crowds of people and swollen with the arrogance of pride. Then the bishops sat down, and the judges also sat down, especially those who supported the Arian party and the impious king.

After they had taken their seats, the holy bishop Massona, being a man of the greatest gravity and wisdom, kept his eyes fixed upon heaven in silence for a long time. While he remained silent,

[Note: [Col. 0143D] The bishop Sunna of the heretics began speaking first, and so forth. Here, pious reader, you have a vivid description of the spirit of the Catholic and of the heretic. Just as truth is always celebrated as one and the same, so heresy has never changed the color of its wickedness. Here you see the intemperance and arrogance of a false mouth; you contemplate the restraint and solidity of a Christian breast. However many encounters between Catholics and heretics, ancient and modern, we read, we admire how closely they resemble one another, like milk resembles milk. Thus I shall dispense with examples.]

the bishop Sunna of the heretics began speaking first. From his wicked mouth he began to produce, with great clamor, harsh, rough, and obscene words. The man of God answered him patiently, gently, and sweetly; but Sunna, like one hissing through the mouth of a dragon, responded with increasingly insolent words. Thus the two began to engage in a great contest of words against one another.

But in no way could the mass of flesh resist the wisdom of God and the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the mouth of his servant, Bishop Massona. What more is there to say? Convicted and overcome in every respect, Sunna fell silent and blushed, covered with profound shame. Not only he, but also the perverse mediators who were importunately striving to support his party, were thrown into confusion and shame.

[Col. 0143B] When they heard the speech of an incomparable doctrine proceeding from Massona’s mouth in a honey-sweet discourse, they were stricken in mind and turned into utter astonishment. With great admiration they praised the man whom they had come to defeat. For on that day the Lord deigned to bestow such grace upon his lips that no one had ever before seen him eloquent with such clear expression. Although he had always taught with a fluent tongue, on that occasion he proved more eloquent than on all other days.

Then “the upright saw and rejoiced, and all iniquity stopped its mouth” (Psalm 106:42), because “the Lord stopped the mouth of those who speak wickedness” (Psalm 63:12).

All the faithful therefore marveled greatly. Although they had previously known this man to be most eloquent, they did not remember ever hearing him speak in such a learned style, so polished, or with such sweet-flowing eloquence.

Then immediately all the orthodox and all the Catholics, when their enemies had been thrown down and defeated, cried out in praise, saying: “Who is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you? And there is none according to your works” (Psalms 86:6; 71:19; 82:2).

Afterward they all proceeded together to the basilica of the glorious virgin Eulalia with the victorious bishop Massona. Rejoicing as they went in the praises of God, they entered her most sacred temple with immense shouts of jubilation and returned infinite thanks to almighty God, who, through the prayers of his holy virgin, had raised his servants on high and reduced their enemies to nothing.

## CHAPTER XII. Massona is summoned to Toledo by the king; refusing to give up Saint Eulalia’s tunic, he is sent into exile and tames a fierce horse

[Col. 0143D]

Thus the aforesaid heretic Sunna, although convicted in every respect by reason and truth, stubbornly persisted in his former faith. He could not freely hasten toward the harbor of salvation, because, with God permitting it, the ancient enemy had hardened his stony heart like that of Pharaoh.

After seeing himself defeated in everything, he began more and more, with a savage mind, to devise accusations and charges against the servant of God by cunning schemes. Surrounded by every kind of weapon against the soldier of Christ, he advanced toward his own destruction and secretly accused the most blessed bishop Massona to the ears of the prince Leovigild the Arian with many charges.

The cunning of his opponent achieved nothing; his calamitous wickedness harmed the man of God not at all, for the grace of the Redeemer had armed him with spiritual weapons.

At last the evil spirit compelled the often-mentioned Arian king to remove the holy man from his own see and order him to appear before the king. The king’s ministers, companions in crime, quickly fulfilled the command. Coming to the city of Emerita, they compelled the blessed man, with all haste,

[Note: [Col. 0144D] To the city of Toledo. On the summons of Saint Massona to that city, see Morales, book XII, chapter 6, and Padilla, *Century VI*, chapter 68. On the city itself, see our work on the antiquities of the city of Toledo, at length.]

to hasten to the city of Toledo, where the king was.

When suddenly the most holy man, Bishop Massona, was snatched from the bosom of the Church and led unharmed into exile as though he were guilty, the voice of all the citizens of Emerita resounded with immense lamentation and intolerable tears. With enormous groans and ululations they cried out that the remedies provided by so great a patron were being taken away from them, shouting these words:

“Why do you abandon your sheepfold, holy Father? Why do you leave your flock to perish? Do not cast us into the jaws of wolves, lest your sheep, hitherto refreshed by nectar-bearing flowers, be torn by the mortal teeth of ravenous wolves!”

Moved by so many tears—for he was always stirred by the inward compassion of the Lord—he is said to have wept. Then he addressed them in many words and deigned to console them with marvelous subtlety. Afterward, bidding farewell to all, and accompanied by divine assistance, he departed with a tranquil mind, steadfast spirit, and cheerful face, as was always his custom.

When he reached the city of Toledo and stood before the most savage tyrant, the king assailed him with many insults and struck him with many terrors, striving with every effort of his wicked purpose to draw him into the Arian heresy. But while the man of God willingly endured all the insults inflicted upon him, he nevertheless began to answer without hesitation, with complete gentleness, the things the rabid dog was barking. He set aside his personal insults and, grieving over the injuries done to the Catholic faith, boldly resisted the tyrant.

His steadfastness moved the insane king more and more, and the king began to roar against the servant of God with increasingly rabid barking from his rabid mouth. Then he began to drive Massona by threats and terrors to present the tunic of the most holy virgin Eulalia, which was supposed to be kept in Toledo, in the basilica of the Arian depravity there.

The man of God answered:

“It is known to you that I shall never stain my heart with the filth of Arian superstition. I shall never pollute my mind with such a perverse doctrine. I shall never hand over the tunic of my lady Eulalia to be defiled by the sacrilegious hands of heretics, or even touched with their fingertips; nor can you ever possess it, however you may seek it.”

When the profane tyrant heard this, he was turned into a frenzy of madness. He promptly sent men to the city of Emerita to search carefully everywhere for the holy tunic itself. They were to investigate both the treasury of Saint Eulalia and the treasury of the older church called Holy Jerusalem, searching diligently until they found it and brought it to him. When they arrived and searched everywhere energetically, they did not find it at all, and thus returned empty-handed to their king.

When they reported this to him, the devil began to gnash his teeth more fiercely against the man of God. When Massona was brought before him, the king said:

“Tell me where the thing I seek is. If you do not tell me, know that you will be subjected to still heavier insults and afterward sent into exile in a distant region, where, afflicted by many troubles and intolerably tormented by every necessity, you will perish by a cruel death.”

To this the man of God is said to have replied:

“You threaten me with exile. Know that I do not fear your threats; I do not fear exile in the least. Therefore I beg you: if you know of any region where God is not, order me to be sent into exile there.”

The king said to him:

“And in what place is God not?”

[Note: [Col. 0145C] *Biotenate*. Perhaps *βιοθάνατε*? Or from the word *βροτός*, so that he may call him wretched, or from *βρότος*, so that he may call him bloody? Perhaps. But I would rather believe that we should read *Burdonate*, both because I think Greek words could scarcely be found in the mouth of Leovigild and because the most ancient Spaniards called *Borde* the man whom Statius calls “crooked from his father” and degenerate. J. C. In Euripides’ *Phoenician Women* one finds *μητρὶ λόχευμα, μάσμα πατρός*, “a shameful birth to the mother and a disgrace and pollution to the father.” I also know that in many parts of Spain bastards and illegitimate children are still called by similar names, and rightly so, since *Borde* is like *βόρδος* or *βόρδων*, from which we commonly call a stupid person *burdo*, while *burdones* are mules born from a she-ass. Thus, where the burden of *burdones* occurs in 4 Kings 5, the Vulgate translator reads “of mules,” whereas the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Septuagint have “of mules.” Therefore the impious king either fashioned *Bordonatus* or *Burdonatus* in order to mark him as a bastard or to call the pious bishop a fool, as though “bastard-born.”]

*biotenate* [perhaps *biodonate*]?”

The man of God answered:

“If you know that God is everywhere, why do you threaten me with exile? For wherever you send me, I know that God’s mercy will never abandon me. I am also certain that the more cruelly you rage against me, the more his mercy will follow me, and his clemency will console me.”

Because of this steadfastness, the mad tyrant, inwardly afflicted by the greater punishment of his evil mind and stirred by excessive gall and bitterness, said to him:

“Either present to me the tunic itself, which you fraudulently stole, or, if you do not present it, I shall have your limbs stretched apart by various tortures.”

[Note: [Col. 0145D] *Divaricari*. Cicero, *On Signs*: “He orders Sopatrus, a man of the highest magistracy, to be stretched apart and bound”; that is, to be extended. Cato used the word of trees: “the branches are spread apart.”]

The soldier of God answered him without fear:

“I have already told you once and again that I shall not fear your threats. But if your perverse mind has any power, let it devise something greater against me. I neither fear you nor, terrified by fear, shall I present what you demand. But know this: I burned that tunic in fire, reduced it to ashes, mixed the ashes with water, and drank them. By the touch of your hand”—and he touched his stomach—“know clearly that I drank it after it had been reduced to ashes, and here it is inside my belly; I shall never return it to you.”

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Behold, it is here in my belly. This was the tunic of Saint Eulalia which Leovigild demanded. On it, see Morales, book XII, chapter 6; Mariana, book V, chapter 13; and Padilla, *Century VI*, chapter 68.]

He said this because, without anyone knowing, he had folded it against his stomach beneath his clothing, wrapped in linen, and girded it around himself. Thus, with God alone aware of it, he carried it. For God so blinded the eyes of that king and of all who were present that no one understood how the man of God was carrying out these words.

While they were saying these and similar things to one another, and the sky was perfectly clear, the divine majesty suddenly thundered from heaven with a great crash, so that King Leovigild, trembling, fell from his throne to the ground in great fear.

Then the man of God said with great exultation:

“If you are a king, behold the King whom one must fear—for he is not such as you are.”

Immediately the evil spirit opened the sacrilegious tyrant’s mouth, always armed with insults against the holy, and set it loose to bark this judgment of its impiety:

“Massona, who is always hostile to us in his conduct, an enemy of our faith and opposed to our religion, is to be removed from our sight immediately and sent into exile.”

[Note: [Col. 0146C] We order him to be removed from our presence and relegated to exile. Roderick of Toledo, II, chapter 14. “Finally, filled with Arian treachery, Leovigild stirred up a persecution against the Catholics and sent Leander of Hispalis and Massona of Emerita, most holy bishops, together with many others, into exile. What followed? He confiscated the revenues returned to the churches and took away their privileges; he subjected many to the terror of the Arian plague, and deceived many others without persecution by means of gold and property. Among the other contagions of his heresy, he even dared to rebaptize Catholics, along with other things that would take too long to recount.” The *General History of Spain*, part II, chapter 39, gives the same account in its customary manner. Isidore says similarly in his account of Leovigild: “Filled with the fury of treachery, he stirred up a persecution against the Catholics, sent many bishops into exile, and took away the revenues and privileges of the churches.” On the others, see Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, V, chapter 38: “That year there was a great persecution of Christians in Spain; many were condemned to exile, deprived of their property, and killed by various tortures.” Biclaro, Maximus, and others agree.]

When the most impious king, this enemy, had pronounced such an evil sentence against an innocent man, all his ministers and accomplices in crime dragged Massona from his presence.

At the king’s command they prepared for him a fierce horse to ride,

[Note: [Col. 0146D] The fierce horse. Morales, Mariana, and Padilla recount the matter in greater detail.]

intending that it should throw him so violently that, when he fell with his neck broken, he would die a cruel death. The horse was of such ferocity that no rider dared mount it, since it had already caused many men to fall headlong.

When it was prepared for the man of God to mount, the most cruel king watched from a distance through a window of the palace, waiting for the holy man to fall from the horse and provide him with a great spectacle.

Immediately,

[Note: [Col. 0147C] After raising the banner of the cross in the name of the Lord. Ambrose calls the cross the divine banner in his *Funeral Oration for Theodosius*; so does the Church in its hymn, and so do others. On the ancient use of signing the forehead with the cross for every action, see Tertullian, books III and IV *On the Crown*; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 13; and almost all the Fathers. For, following Jerome’s counsel to Eustochium, why should one not trace the cross with the hand at every action and every step, and therefore also in dangers? The most devout and learned Alanus Copus confirms this with examples resembling the present one in *Dialogue* IV, from chapter 6, against the Centuriators.]

having raised the banner of the cross in the name of the Lord, the most holy priest mounted the fierce horse. The Lord made it as gentle as a lamb. It began to proceed along its way with complete gentleness and caution, although a little earlier, with immense snorting, continual neighing, and movement of its entire body, it had refused, as though scorning another rider, to carry anyone.

When everyone saw this miracle, they were astonished and marveled greatly; even the king himself was shaken by enormous amazement. But what could the most brilliant radiance of the sun profit a blind man whose savage enemy had darkened all his inner faculties?

## CHAPTER XIII. Nepopis, an Arian pseudo-bishop, substituted at Emerita; Massona, exiled in a monastery for three years, shines through miracles

[Col. 0147B]

Therefore the holy man of God, Bishop Massona, arrived at the appointed place with only three boys from among his attendants. [Note: He reached the appointed place. Where this place once was, Moral and Padilla admit that they do not know. M. Maximus, under the year 586, explicitly identifies Complutum: “Massona, who was exiled at Complutum, grieves greatly over the death of the holy martyr and prince” (Hermenegild).] The men who had been sent by the king to punish him immediately confined him in exile at a monastery; yet his exile was supreme elevation, his insult manifest holiness, and his wandering immense happiness.

After this, a pseudo-priest named Nepopis [Note: Named Nepopis. Maxim. under the year 581 calls him Nepotianus; see the notes at chapter 9.] was appointed in his place and installed in the city of Emerita. He was an impious man, truly a servant of the devil, an angel of Satan, and a herald of Antichrist; moreover, he too was bishop of another city. [Col. 0147C] But while the man of God grew through abundant virtues, the other, by contrast, was defiled by wicked deeds.

When the blessed man Massona had lived a blessed life there for three years and more, and excelled there in many virtues, he distributed to the poor everything that he could possess there for his own needs and those of his servants. When almost nothing remained that he could give away, a poor little widow, weighed down by many troubles, came to him begging for alms. But since the man of God had already spent everything on similar works and was earnestly searching for something to give her, yet could find nothing, he began to ask the boys who were with him that, if any one of them possessed anything, he should faithfully present it to him so that he might give it to the woman mentioned above.

One of them, named Sagatus, who was in charge of the others, replied: “I do have one solidus, but if I give it away, we shall have absolutely nothing left with which to buy anything later for ourselves or even for our little animals.” [Note: One solidus. Among the Spaniards, a sueldo. Paul himself explains its value shortly afterward, saying that Sagatus asked the woman to return to him from the sum he had lent her at least one tremissis, and so forth. She immediately returned one, but carried two away with her in a joyful spirit. Thus a solidus then consisted of three tremisses.

“But I see”—to use the words of the great Mariana, alas, formerly my foremost friend among the foremost, chapter 8, *On Weights and Measures*—“that the same solidi, as I conjecture, diminished over the course of time, all the more because there was a smaller supply of silver and gold; yet, although their weight was reduced, they retained their former names and value, so that a silver solidus was worth twelve asses, and a gold one twelve denarii. This is still commonly retained today, since a solidus, although it is almost entirely made of bronze, contains twelve denarii wherever solidi are used; in this it differs from the maravedi, which was worth only ten denarii. But the bronze maravedi should have been exceeded by one-sixth by the bronze solidus, the silver maravedi by the silver solidus, and the gold maravedi by the gold solidus.

“Anyone who wishes to know more about our solidi should consult the most learned book on the comparison of ancient coins with those now in use by the illustrious D. Diego de Covarruvias y Leyva, a member and most distinguished president of our Spanish supreme senate, whose name no one has ever mentioned without praise.”]

The man of the Lord ordered him, without any hesitation, to give it all away and reserve nothing for himself, confident that the Lord would come to his aid and immediately supply him with every good thing. When, in obedience to his command, he had given the solidus itself to the woman, the aforementioned Sagatus shortly afterward ran back to the same woman and begged her that, since he had no means of buying food for himself, she would return to him at least one tremissis from the money he had lent her, so that he might meet his need. She immediately returned one without sadness, but carried two away with her in a joyful spirit.

Without delay, suddenly, two hundred asses loaded with provisions were found standing before the monastery gates. They had been sent to the same man with various supplies by various Catholic men. When this was announced to the man of God and the men who had come offered the supplies to him, he gave immense thanks to almighty God and immediately ordered Sagatus to be summoned.

When Sagatus arrived, the man of God said to him: “How much did you give the woman who was asking for alms?”

He replied: “In accordance with your command, I gave her the whole solidus I had. But because necessity pressed me, I afterward received one tremissis back from her.”

And the man of the Lord said: “May the Lord forgive you, brother, because you proved doubtful and despaired of the Lord’s mercy; moreover, you have sinned against many poor people. [Note: You gave two tremisses; behold, you have received two thousand solidi. [Col. 0149D] For if you had not taken away the third tremissis, without doubt you would have received three hundred. This follows from Christ’s generous and certain promise in Matthew 19:29 and Mark 10:30.] You gave two tremisses; behold, you have received two thousand solidi and two hundred asses loaded with many provisions. For if you had not taken away the third tremissis, without doubt you would have received three hundred loaded asses.”

Afterward, giving thanks and returning the grace of his blessing in acknowledgment of their gratitude, he refreshed all those who had sought him with sacred eulogies and letters alike. But he immediately distributed almost everything that had been sent to him among the poor.

## CHAPTER XIV. King Leovigild, struck by Saint Eulalia, restores Massona to the Church of Emerita.

[Col. 0149A]

Several days later, when he had entered the basilica of the monastery for the sake of prayer, suddenly, above the altar of that same holy basilica, the most sacred virgin Eulalia appeared in the form of a dove of snowy whiteness. Addressing him gently, as a most compassionate mistress, she deemed her most faithful servant worthy of consolation. Then she said to him: “Behold, the time has now come for you to return to your own city and render me your former service.” Saying this, she vanished from his sight in a swift flight.

Thus, although the man of God rejoiced greatly in the grace of so great a vision and so great a consolation, he began to weep bitterly because, abandoning the quiet of his poverty and exile, he would return to the world’s storms and tempests. For he had no doubt that what he had heard would immediately be fulfilled in him.

Then, without any intervening delay, the glorious virgin mentioned above avenged the injuries done to her servant with the severest punishment. [Note: The glorious virgin mentioned above avenged the injuries done to her servant with the severest punishment, and so forth. Eulalia, the patroness of the city and Church of Emerita, freed both from hostile tyranny more than once. Isidore, *Chronicle of the Goths*, under the year 491: “Theodoric, advancing victoriously from Galicia into Lusitania, while preparing to plunder the city of Emerita, was terrified by apparitions of the most blessed martyr Eulalia; immediately, frightened by unfavorable reports, he left Emerita and returned to Gaul,” and so forth. See Rodrigo of Toledo, II, chapter 9.]

One night, while the impious tyrant Leovigild was lying in his bed, she stood before him and for a long time struck both his sides repeatedly with whips, saying: “Give me back my servant; for if you delay, know that you will be tortured with harsher punishments.”

The wretched man was flogged so severely that, when he awoke, he showed all those attending him the many bruises inflicted upon him amid great weeping. He therefore cried out that he had been flogged because he had inflicted injuries upon the most holy bishop. For he described in detail the name, clothing, and beauty of the face of the one who had beaten him, and disclosed everything most clearly with loud lamentations.

Immediately, fearing that he might be punished with a harsher penalty [Note: “With a harsher punishment.” I believe this is the correct reading, not “lest he be punished more severely by judgment,” as it appears in the manuscripts], he—being, as in all matters, a most consummate pretender and an exceedingly ready dissembler—ordered, under the pretense of piety, that the man of God, who had been removed from his city without cause, should return again to govern his Church.

When the most holy man Massona was reluctant to comply with what the deranged king demanded and asserted that he would remain where he had been exiled, the king again presented his requests and asked him to deign to return to his own city. The piety of the most high God immediately softened the sincere heart, and abundant goodwill opened the way for his servant to return.

When, with God now lending his aid, he was returning, the most cruel king tried to make him favorable by prayers and gifts—the very king who had previously condemned him to exile through deceit. But Massona rejected the gifts and refused the presents; with a merciful spirit he released the perpetrated crime, and, in accordance with the Lord’s command [Note: “In accordance with the Lord’s command,” in Matthew 6:12], he did not retain the offenses of those who owed a debt, but forgave them.

## CHAPTER XV. When the pseudo-bishop Nepopis fled, Massona recovers the Church’s possessions.

[Col. 0150A]

Thereafter he returned with a very large retinue from the place where he had been exiled to the city of Emerita. When Nepopis, who had been appointed in his place, heard of his return, he was suddenly terrified by divine fear and attempted to flee to his own city, where he had previously been bishop.

Before leaving, however, he secretly sent to his own city, by men of the Church of Emerita and at night, many wagons loaded with the abundant silver, distinguished ornaments, and whatever better things he saw in the Church of Emerita. Nepopis himself, unhappily driven from Emerita by all the clergy and people, hurried toward his own city. Fearing that the man of God Massona might find him in his Church and drive him out with every disgrace, he hastened to depart as quickly as possible.

While he himself was fleeing with a few companions, all those belonging to him afterward left the city disgracefully, scattered and troubled; wandering about in different directions, they made their way toward their own city.

While these things were happening, by God’s will and through the merits of Saint Eulalia, it happened that on that very day holy Massona suddenly came out with an immense multitude along the road to the city of Emerita—the very road along which the wagons loaded with his possessions were hastening.

When the men and wagons met him on the road not far from the city, the holy man ordered them to say whose men and wagons they were. Recognizing their rightful lord, they replied, filled with great joy: “We are your servants, lord.”

He again asked them what they were carrying in the wagons. They answered: “The possessions of the holy Church and of you, which the hostile plunderer Nepopis seized and carried away. We wretched men are ourselves being led into captivity, separated from our possessions and children and wives, and expelled from the homeland in which we were born.”

When the man of the Lord heard this, he was filled with great joy and said: “I give thanks to you, good Lord Jesus, because great is the abundance of your sweetness, since you have deigned to care so greatly in all things for your servants, though unworthy, and to restore us safely, rescued from every evil, and not to deliver your possessions into the power of your enemies.”

Having said this, he ordered everyone to be recalled to his own city. Thus he reached the city amid immense joy, while all rejoiced. Just as a thirsty person in the heat of the burning season longs for flowing springs, so he, with a fervent heart and eager spirit, by God’s help, was privileged to reach the basilica of Saint Eulalia. There, having gathered the fulfillment of his desire with the whole feeling of his mind, he entered the city exulting in the Lord, while everyone exulted with him. [The source has a lacuna here.]

In this way the Church of Emerita, exulting with the greatest joy, received its governor back. It rejoiced because the sick man had found healing, the oppressed consolation, and the needy sustenance. Why say more? The Lord restored abundant assistance to the Church of Emerita. For, in his mercy, the presence of the holy man suspended the poverty of its calamities, the frequent disasters of pestilence, and the insolent storms of the entire city—troubles that had unquestionably overwhelmed it when the shepherd had been removed on account of his absence.

## CHAPTER XVI. After King Leovigild died in heresy, his Catholic son Reccared succeeded him.

[Col. 0151B]

Thus, since Leovigild did not rule but harm Spain, and since he destroyed rather than governed it, while no disgrace or crime remained that he did not claim as his own, abandoning God in every way—indeed, himself abandoned by God—he disastrously lost his kingdom together with his life. Struck down by a most serious illness through God’s judgment, he lost his utterly shameful life and acquired eternal death for himself. His soul was cruelly torn from his body and, held in everlasting punishments, was perpetually delivered over to the abysses of Erebus and deservedly confined in Tartarus, destined always to burn amid boiling waves of pitch. [Note: “He miserably lost the kingdom together with his life.” Leovigild’s repentance and true, public renunciation of his errors are doubted, together with our author and Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* III, chapter 31, by others among our writers as well. In his favor, however, stand another Gregory, Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* VIII, final chapter, and M. Maximus under the year 585, who noted his repentance and tears, as he himself confessed.]

After his most cruel death, the venerable prince Reccared, his son, lawfully obtained the administration of the kingdom and was deservedly raised to the height of principate owed to him. By outstanding merits, with God’s grant, he legitimately and solemnly earned the royal dignity.
