He was, in fact, an orthodox man and wholly Catholic; following not his faithless father but Christ the Lord, he was converted from the depravity of the Arian heresy and brought the entire nation of the Visigoths to the true faith through his remarkable preaching.

For he was an advocate of divine religion, a preacher and defender of true glory, proclaiming in every way the Catholic faith [Note: Proclaiming the Holy Trinity, coeternal and of one power and substance, and distinguishing it according to the properties of the persons; affirming one God in nature; declaring the Father unbegotten; asserting that the Son was begotten from the Father; and believing that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both.

Reccared himself states this distinctly at the beginning of the Third Council of Toledo:

“As the Lord God wished to be understood through the sacred Scriptures and commanded to be believed, so we must confess that there is a Father who begot from his own substance a Son equal and coeternal with himself—not, however, so that the same person should be both begotten and begetter, but that the Father who begot should be one person and the Son who was begotten another; yet both subsist in the divinity of one substance. The Father is the source from whom the Son exists; he himself is from no other. The Son has a Father, yet without beginning and without diminution he subsists in that divinity in which he is equal and coeternal with the Father.

“Likewise, the Holy Spirit must be confessed and proclaimed by us to proceed from the Father and the Son and to be of one substance with the Father and the Son. He is the third person in the Trinity, yet he possesses with the Father and the Son the common essence of divinity. For this Holy Trinity is one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Although every created thing was established good by his goodness, nevertheless, through the form of human nature assumed by the Son, we are restored from the condemned race to our former blessedness.”

After this formula of the true faith he adds:

“Therefore I anathematize Arius, with all his doctrines and accomplices, who asserts that the only-begotten Son of God is degenerate from the substance of the Father, and who said that he was not begotten from the Father but created from nothing,” and so forth.

“Accordingly, I embrace and hold the faith of the illustrious bishops assembled at Constantinople, which destroyed Macedonius, who diminished the substance of the Holy Spirit and separated him from the unity and essence of the Father and the Son, by the sword of truth.”

This is what he says of himself. You may consult the leading figure among the Scholastics, Gabriel Vázquez, volume II, on the First Part, from disputation 127 to 171, if you are attracted by ingenious, learned, and refined discussions.]

He proclaimed the Holy Trinity, coeternal and of one power and substance, distinguishing it according to the properties of the persons, affirming one God in nature, declaring the Father unbegotten, asserting the Son to be begotten from the Father, and believing the Holy Spirit to proceed from both.

Adorned with these virtues, he began to love all whom he perceived to be dear to God, to abhor utterly and detest all whom he knew to be hateful to God, and to condemn the error of the heretics’ unspeakable impiety. As this was earnestly carried out, and, with God’s favor, much tranquility was restored to the Catholic Church, while the error of the Arian calamity was shaken from almost every mind, and, every quarrel having been driven away, the city of Emerita together with the holy bishop Massona rejoiced over so great a tranquility and continually gave thanks to the Lord, the ancient enemy, stirred by his habitual envy, again brought renewed battles against God’s servant through his ministers.

## CHAPTER XVII. When the pseudo-bishop Sunna, through deceit, sought Massona with the sword by means of Count Wittericus, Massona was freed by a miracle.

Sunna, the Gothic bishop of whom we spoke above, incited by the devil, persuaded certain Goths noble by birth and exceedingly rich in possessions; among them were several counts appointed by the king in certain cities. [Note: In certain cities, counts appointed by the king. Titus, *Those Who Govern Provinces*, book II, title 14, attests that counts were also called governors of provinces and cities in Roman times. Concerning the Visigoths, their legal code more than once calls someone a count of a city; compare law 3, title 4, book XVII, such as Count Waldric of the city of Toledo, who signed the Third Council of Toledo. Servandus the count, in the same period, bears witness that traces of this practice remained among the Hispano-Arabs who ruled the Moors, in the second book of Samson, abbot of Córdoba, *Apology*. From this arose the custom among our kings of choosing counts, a practice that has now grown excessively and is too well known to need repetition here.]

He separated them from the company of the Catholics and the bosom of the Catholic Church together with an innumerable multitude of the people, and devised treacherous plans against God’s servant, Bishop Massona, concerning how they might kill him. [Note: Treacherous plans against God’s servant Massona, the bishop. Moral, book XII, chapter 2; Padilla, century VI, chapter 53; and Mariana, book V, chapter 14, narrate the matter carefully, though they borrowed Paul’s words.]

Then he sent his own servants to Massona and, as though out of affection, asked him to come to his house for their sake, so that he might kill the man of God there by a most cruel death. When they came and conveyed this request to him, the man of God, filled with the Spirit of God, immediately understood their plan and said: “I cannot go there now, because I have matters to arrange for the benefit of the Catholic Church. But if he wishes to see me, let him come here into the Church atrium, and he will see me as he wishes.”

Those who had been sent returned and reported what they had heard. When Sunna heard this, he immediately summoned the counts mentioned above, with whom he had planned to kill the holy man, to his house and told them to go with him to the atrium. He first arranged with them, however, that as they entered the atrium, one of them named Wittericus [Note: Wittericus. I read it this way from the coins I possess, although in other copies it is written, corruptly, as Witiricus or Victericus.]—who afterward also became king of the Goths [Note: He later became king of the Goths. After Liwa, the son of Reccared, Wittericus, having seized power as a tyrant, deprived the innocent young man of the kingdom and killed him after cutting off his right hand, according to Isidore under the year 611 in the *Chronicle of the Goths.]—should draw his sword and strike the most blessed man with a single blow, so that a second would not be necessary.

After he had instructed the aforementioned Wittericus in this plan, they all proceeded together, of one mind and with the same purpose, to the atrium of the holy bishop. When they arrived and immediately wished to enter, they were stopped and told to wait for a short while outside, until Saint Massona sent for the illustrious Claudius, [Note: To Claudius, an illustrious man and duke of the city of Emerita. Paulus Aemilius, in his account of Cherebert, says that Longinus, who chose Ravenna as his seat according to Gothic custom, gave each city its own magistrate, whom they called dukes. Among the Goths, the duke was one of the principal palace officials; thus, in the time of Wamba, Paulus was duke of Narbonne according to Tudensis and Bishop Roderick, and Claudius was duke of the city of Emerita under Reccared, according to our author. See what I shall say at chapter 19.] duke of the city of Emerita, so that in his presence they might meet and look upon one another.

Claudius himself was born of noble lineage and descended from Roman parents. He was thoroughly Catholic in faith and strongly bound by the ties of religion; vigorous in battle, exceedingly ready in the fear of God, trained in military pursuits, and likewise experienced in warlike undertakings. When he was informed of this—for his house was very close to the atrium—he immediately came with a large multitude and arrived alertly.

When the illustrious Claudius entered the atrium, the men mentioned above also entered immediately with great crowds of people. After greeting the man according to custom, they sat down. While they sat for a long time and conversed extensively with one another, the aforementioned Wittericus, a very brave young man, stood behind the shoulders of the distinguished duke Claudius, fulfilling his duty to his elder, indeed to his foster-father, since he was still younger in age.

He tried with all his strength to draw from its sheath the sword with which he was girded, so that he might slaughter both Saint Massona and Claudius, as had been arranged. But by God’s will the sword was fastened so tightly in its sheath that it seemed to have been nailed to it with iron nails. Although he tried for a long time and with great effort to draw the sword, he could not do so at all.

The authors of this wicked plan began silently to wonder why Wittericus was not fulfilling what he had promised. Watching him closely with their eyes, they urged him more and more to commit without delay so great a crime and such an enormous sacrilege, and not to fear striking down the men mentioned above with the sword. [Perhaps: “or whether he dared.”]

Thus, at their most cruel urging, again and again he tried with all his strength to draw his sword from its sheath [Note: The *spatha*. As a count, Wittericus was required by the Gothic laws to be equipped with one. Book IX, title 2, final law of the Visigoths: “Let the duke, count, and gardingus be equipped with shields, swords, *spathae*, spears, and arrows.” Some think the Latin word is used by Isidore, *Etymologies* XVIII.6, because it is broad—that is, wide and ample. Vegetius uses it in books II, chapter 15, and III, chapter 14; Apuleius, books I and X of *The Golden Ass*; Spartianus in *Hadrian*; Claudius in his letter to Eborus preserved by Trebellius Pollio; and others. Hence, with the Spanish change of *t* to *d* and the addition of an initial vowel according to our custom, we now say *espada*. Isidore himself says in the same place: “The *framea* is a sword sharpened on both sides, which the common people call a *spatha*.] but was never able to do so.

When the aforementioned young man saw this, he realized that the sword had been fastened by divine favor, so that he could not draw the weapon he had always kept ready for his own purposes. He was overcome with great astonishment and turned pale.

When the authors of this unspeakable crime saw that the contrivances of their most wicked plan had been frustrated by divine judgment [Note: “The contrivances of their wicked plan.” Thus in the sacred books: Psalm 49:19, “Your tongue contrived deceit”; Psalm 57:3, “Your hands contrive iniquities”; Isaiah 32:7, “For he contrived schemes to destroy the humble through lying speech”], they immediately rose, bade farewell, and returned bitterly to their homes.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Massona is again freed from Sunna’s ambushes through the help of Claudius, duke of Emerita; the obstinate Sunna dies in exile in Mauretania; Vacrila, his accomplice in the crime, becomes the Church’s slave.

After the others had returned, Wittericus did not go away with them. Instead, trembling, he immediately fell at the feet of the most holy bishop Massona, disclosed the entire plan, and truthfully recounted how he had wanted to strike him but had been unable to draw his sword.

After this he said with tears: “I confess my sin, because I intended with all my purpose to perpetrate this evil, but God did not permit me.” He added: “They have also devised another plan against you, so that, since they have not prevailed in the atrium just now, they may at least prevail on the most sacred day of Easter.

“This is their arrangement: when, according to the custom of Easter, you have celebrated Mass in the older church, and after Mass you have proceeded, as is customary, with all the Catholic people to the basilica of Saint Eulalia while singing psalms, their men are to be stationed at the city gate with many wagons loaded with swords and clubs, concealed under a deceptive pretext as though they were carrying grain. When you proceed simply and unarmed, their entire multitude is to rush upon you in formation; seizing the swords and clubs, they are to kill all the men and women, the old and the little ones alike, by a cruel death.

“But I, wretched man, who involved myself in so great a crime, ask forgiveness from you, my most merciful lord, and pray that through your prayers the Lord may grant me pardon. I faithfully report and disclose everything I have learned, in complete sincerity, and behold, I am in your hands. Do with me what is good and right in your eyes.

“And lest your holiness perhaps think me deceitful or a mocker, do not permit me to leave, but deliver me into whatever custody you order until you investigate everything thoroughly or learn it with absolute certainty. If you discover that I have lied, I do not wish to live.” [Note: “Your holiness.” An address proper to priests even among the pagans, as Plutarch attests at the end of *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*. See what I note at the very beginning concerning Dexter.]

When the man of the Lord Massona, who had always shone through the virtue of piety, heard this, he gently urged him to fear nothing. He gave thanks to almighty God, who had freed his servants from such great dangers, and then sent for Duke Claudius, to whom he disclosed everything.

When Claudius heard this, he ordered the matter to be concealed for a short time, in case those men, learning that their plan had been betrayed, should take flight. But while he investigated shrewdly, he discovered most clearly that what had been reported was true.

When the aforementioned Arian counts had furnished what they had laid out, and a multitude had been positioned all around in ambush for the encounter, as customary, Duke Claudius suddenly fell upon them. Some were captured; others, who tried to use their swords, immediately perished by the sword.

Thereupon he went to the house of Sunna the Arian. [Note: Paul always calls him Sunna. Did our author deliberately fashion “Sinon” from *Sunna*, alluding to the one who—

> Confident in spirit, and prepared for either outcome … ]

Whether to contrive deceits, or to meet certain death—according to the divine poet, was this the downfall of the Trojan empire, that eternal work? [Col. 0156D]

[Note: Should we read *Sunnanis*, with the Gothic declension, as in *Wambanis*, *Egicanis*, *Chintilanis*, *Suintilanis*, and many others of that kind?]

Duke Claudius proceeded with a vast multitude to the house of Sunna, the Arian bishop, and likewise seized the heretic bishop himself, who suspected nothing of all this; he entrusted him to Saint Massona the bishop for strict custody, and in the same way committed all his associates to custody. But Witteric, who had disclosed the impious plot, he ordered to depart free. Claudius the duke therefore reported to the orthodox prince Reccared everything that had been done, and suggested that, once the sentence of the decree had been presented, he should immediately order what ought to be done with the enemies of the Lord Jesus Christ.

The king, accepting this recommendation, issued the following sentence: all of them, deprived of all their estates and honors, were to be sent into exile, bound with many iron chains; but they were to exhort Sunna, the false bishop, to convert to the Catholic faith. If he converted, then—and only then—he was to be ordered to do penance and, by the satisfaction of tears, to mourn his sins; once he had completed his penance and they recognized him as a perfect Catholic, they were afterward to ordain him bishop in any other city.

When they repeatedly told him to do penance for such enormous offenses and, by mourning, to appease the Lord’s anger which he had aroused by sinning, he refused to do so. Without abandoning his former tyranny, he replied:

“I do not know what penance is. Let this therefore be known to you: I do not know penance, and I shall never be a Catholic; but in the rite in which I have lived, I shall live—or I shall gladly die for the religion in which I have remained from the beginning of my life.”

When they saw that his mind was obstinate and stubborn in evil, they immediately expelled him miserably and with the greatest disgrace from the territory of Spain, lest he infect others with his pestilential disease. They ignominiously placed him on a small boat and, threatening him, ordered him to have free choice to cross over to whatever place or region he wished; but if he were ever found in Spain, he was to know that he would be punished with a more severe sentence.

He then sailed and reached the shore of the region of Mauretania. After remaining for some time in that province, he stained many people with the treachery of his impious doctrine; then, swiftly punished by the judgment of Avernus, he ended his life by a cruel death.

The basilicas of which Saint Massona had long been unjustly deprived he deserved to receive back justly, together with all their privileges, and, with the permission of the most merciful prince Reccared, he also obtained the entire patrimony of the aforesaid heretic.

[Note: Most Clement Prince Reccared. Because of this notable clemency of King Reccared toward rebels, a gold coin was struck bearing his likeness and name, with the letters: “RECCAREDUS. EMERITA. PIUS,” as Moral thinks, book XII, chapter 2.]

The other wicked men—whom we mentioned above—they banished into exile in accordance with the king’s command. One of them was called Vacrila.

[Note: Vacrila. Concerning him see also Moral, in the same place, and Mariana, book V, chapter 2.]

Escaping from their hands, Vacrila fled to the basilica of Saint Eulalia to receive a remedy. When the aforesaid Claudius had reported this to Prince Reccared, he is said to have spoken as follows:

“An enemy of the Most High God! I wonder with what face he has dared to enter His holy courts—he who until now, in his madness, has persecuted Him in vain, and now takes refuge with Him in order to obtain protection. But because we know that God is rich in mercy and despises no one, we do not doubt that He receives one who, though sinful, turns to Him. Therefore we decree that Vacrila himself, with his wife, children, and entire patrimony, shall serve the most holy virgin Eulalia forever. We further sanction by this present decree that, just as the lowest-ranking slaves are accustomed to walk before their masters’ horses without the aid of any vehicle, so he shall walk before the horse of the lord who presides over Saint Eulalia’s monastery. He shall perform before him, with his cothurnus or pride laid aside, every service which a lowly slave was accustomed to perform, with all humility.”

[Note: *Caballum* (“horse”). Long ago, almost as schoolboys, we said much on this word in our commentary on Persius’s opening poem; it would be superfluous to repeat it.]

Saint Massona therefore received the authority and immediately ordered him to leave the basilica and come into his presence. Since he always abounded in compassion, he gently admonished him not to fear anything further. Nevertheless, in order to obey the prince’s command, he arranged that, as an act of obedience, Vacrila should proceed from the church of Saint Eulalia to the court founded within the city walls, before the horse of the deacon Redemptus. When Vacrila had taken the aforesaid deacon’s staff in his hands and, carrying it, had reached the court, Massona at once permitted him to depart free, with his wife and children and all his estates. He imposed on him only this command: that he should in every respect guard the Catholic faith whole and undefiled [Col. 0157C] throughout all the days of his life.

[Note: “The Catholic faith whole and inviolate,” etc. This corresponds exactly to the standard of the Athanasian Creed. For: “Whoever wishes to be saved, before all things it is necessary that he hold the Catholic faith; and unless each person keeps it whole and undefiled, without doubt he will perish forever” (from the accurate and anciently received interpretation of the Catholic Church). “Whoever wishes to be saved must, above all, hold the Catholic faith; and unless he keeps it whole and inviolate, he will undoubtedly perish eternally.” See the learned notes of the most pious and learned Gilbert Genebrard at the end of book III, *On the Holy Trinity*, which bear on this matter.]

## CHAPTER XIX. The disturbance at Narbonne, stirred up by the Arians under Bishop Athalocus, is suppressed through the efforts of King Reccared.

[Col. 0158A]

At that time, in the distinguished city of Narbonne in Gaul, the devil stirred up such a sedition against the Catholic faith. It would be extremely long to recount the sequence of its causes; for if we wished to pursue the matter in order, we would seem to be weaving a tragedy rather than a history. We shall therefore relate briefly and in summary a small portion of it.

Two counts, Granista and Wildigernus, illustrious indeed in wealth and noble by birth, but profane in mind and ignoble in character—

[Note: Granista and Wildigernus. Concerning both, see Moral, XII, chapter 1, and Padilla, century VI, chapter 52, on the authority of Paul, who alone mentions these counts.]

—together with the Arian bishop Athalocus—

[Note: With Athalocus, an Arian bishop. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* IX.5, from whom you may learn much about Reccared and the events of his time, says: “He sends messengers to the province of Narbonne, who, by reporting what he had done, brought that people to a similar belief. For at that time Athalocus was a bishop of the Arian sect, and by vain premises and false interpretations of Scripture he so disturbed the churches of God that it was thought he himself was Arius,” and so forth. Through error, and through death.]

—and several other companions in their errors—

[Note: Or several others. Such as the bishops Sunna and Uldila, Queen Gosiuntha, Count Sega, and Duke Argimundus. John of Biclaro writes in his *Chronicle*: “Some of the Arians—namely Bishop Sunna and Sega, who with certain others desired to assume tyranny—were exposed. Sunna was punished with exile; Sega, with his hands cut off, was sent into exile in Gallaecia. Bishop Uldila and Queen Gosiuntha, plotting against Reccared, were exposed, and it was made public that they had cast away the communion of the Catholic faith which they had taken on, as it were, under a Christian pretext. When this evil had thus been brought to the knowledge of men, Uldila was punished with exile. Gosiuntha, always hostile to the Catholics, at last yielded to fate. A certain chamberlain of hers and duke of the province, named Argimundus, aspiring to tyranny, conspired against the king, intending, if he could, to deprive him both of his kingdom and of his life. But when the plot of his impious plan was discovered, he was arrested and bound with iron chains; after an inquiry, his associates confessed their wicked designs and were put to death with deserved punishment. Argimundus himself, who had coveted the kingdom, was first beaten with whips, then shamefully shaved; afterward his right hand was cut off, and, riding on a donkey at Toledo, he was made an example to all, so that servants might not rise against their masters.” This was written by a contemporary.]

—caused an even greater disturbance in that same region. For, rising against the Catholic faith, they brought an immense multitude of Franks into Gaul, in order by force to defend the depravity of the Arian party and, if it could be accomplished, to seize the kingdom from the Catholic Reccared. Meanwhile they killed an immeasurable multitude of clergy, religious persons, and all [Al.: people] the Catholics, making an immense slaughter. Our Savior Jesus Christ received their souls, purer than refined gold and more precious than every precious stone, like holocausts, and placed them among the choirs of martyrs in the heavenly treasury.

After this, without any delay, the exalted and almighty God, resisting His enemies with a heavenly arm and avenging the innocent blood through the prayers of the most excellent prince Reccared, immediately inflicted a marvelous vengeance on them by the judgment of the sword.

[Note: He immediately wrought a marvelous vengeance on the enemies by a sword-like judgment. An example was that victory, of which Isidore testifies in his *Chronicle of the Goths* that no greater or similar victory had occurred in Spain. For, according to John of Biclaro, an army of Franks sent by King Gontran under Duke Basso invaded Narbonese Gaul and pitched camp near Carcassonne. Claudius, duke of Lusitania, sent against them by Reccared, put them to flight—and, astonishingly, killed or routed nearly sixty thousand men with little more than three hundred soldiers, after stripping their camp. Isidore says: “When the Franks invaded with forces of nearly sixty thousand armed men, Claudius was sent as duke against them and triumphed with glorious success,” and so forth. “Many thousands were thrown down and captured; the remainder of the army was put to flight, and the Goths pursued them from behind, killing them as far as the borders of their kingdom.” Reccared is praised here in connection with Claudius. Through Reccared’s authority, Claudius’s glory spread so far and wide that he was celebrated not only by historians but also extolled with the highest praises by Pope Gregory the Great in a letter which we read in book VII, letter 124 of the *Register*, with this heading: “Gregory to Claudius in Spain, concerning the intimacy [or household?] of the king of the Goths.” Among other things: “Because the reputation of good men gives off fragrance like ointment, the scent of your glory has reached here from the western regions.” And shortly afterward: “A great testimony to your praise is given by the report that your glory is diligently attached to the excellent king of the Goths; for since good men always displease the wicked, it is certain that we are good because you have pleased the good man.” Therefore, fulfilling the duty of a greeting, I wish you to continue in the undertakings you have begun, and so forth. Claudius is frequently mentioned by our historians. At the Seventy-Second Council of Toledo, Claudius, count and duke of the frontier district, subscribed for the bishops of Spain and Narbonese Gaul, according to M. Maximus under the year 590. Eutrandus, or Luitprandus, in the *Chronicle* which we first published, under era 647 celebrates him with his son: “Flavius Claudius, son of Saint Massona, bishop of Emerita, by his sister, and of Claudius of Emerita, the most illustrious man and duke, flourishes.” You will find more in Moral, book XII, chapter 5; Vaseus under the year 588; Mariana, book V, chapter 14; and Padilla, century VI, chapter 64.]

When all the enemies of the Catholic faith had finally been thrown down and scattered—

[Note: Saint Massona the bishop began a psalmody with all his people. Since these events had been accomplished through the courage of Claudius, duke of Emerita, it was fitting that Emerita’s praises should be added; hence on Reccared’s gold coins we read: “RECCAREDUS. EMERITA. VICTOR,” even though Toledo, the seat of the Gothic empire, received him in triumph. M. Maximus under the year 686: “The people of Toledo gladly welcome Reccared returning victorious from Gaul, praying joyfully for the victor.”]

—Saint Massona the bishop began a song of psalmody with all his people.

[Note: “He sang mystical praises to the Lord, . . . praising and hymning with the people.” I would suppose these praises were not unlike those which the Fathers sing to Reccared at the Third Council of Toledo: “Then there was an acclamation in praise of God and in favor of the prince by the whole clergy: Glory to God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whose care it is to provide for the peace and unity of His holy Catholic Church [lacuna]. To whom is everlasting merit given by God, if not to Reccared, the true Catholic king? To whom is an eternal crown given by God, if not to Reccared, the true orthodox king? To whom belong present and eternal glory, if not to Reccared, the lover of God? He is the winner of new peoples for the Catholic Church; may he truly deserve apostolic merit, who has fulfilled an apostolic office,” etc.]

They sang mystical praises to the Lord and, praising and hymning Him, came with all the people to the court of the blessed virgin Eulalia. Then all the citizens, celebrating the Paschal solemnity with him most joyfully, shouted through the streets with great noise, rejoicing according to ancient custom in the glory of the Lord, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for He has been gloriously magnified.” And again: “Your right hand, Lord, has been glorified; by the strength of your right hand He has shattered the enemies, and by the greatness of your majesty you have crushed your adversaries” (Exodus XV.1, 6–7).

After this, when the storms had been removed from every side, the Lord deigned to grant abundant peace to the Catholic people.

## CHAPTER XX. Massona, extremely old, dies after performing works of charity; the archdeacon Eleutherius dies before him, as the holy man had foretold.

[Col. 0159B]

Thus, while Saint Massona governed the Church of Emerita for many years with divine assistance, he was overcome by extreme old age and fell ill with a fever. The strength of his entire body suddenly began to fail. He then summoned his archdeacon, named Eleutherius, and said to him:

“Know, my son, that the time of my release is at hand” (2 Timothy IV.6). “Therefore I beg and admonish you to care for the holy Church and the entire holy congregation from now on so diligently that you may make me secure in every respect, and that I may be permitted, in a secluded place, to mourn the sins of my soul before I depart.”

When he heard this, the aforesaid archdeacon showed no compassion for his illness and old age, nor did he grieve at being deprived of the consolation of so great a father. Rather, he rejoiced with great joy at his death and inflated his heart with the happiness of transitory power. Thus, proud, he hurried here and there on horseback with a large company of boys.

After some days, however, it happened that Saint Massona the bishop began to write deeds of freedom for the boys who faithfully served him—

[Note: For the boys who faithfully served him, he wrote documents of liberty. In the First Council of Seville, era 628, there is a canon concerning slaves freed by bishops, which bears on this matter; and it is also known from the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 12.]

—and, in confirming their liberty, to give them a small amount of money or, at any rate, to grant them little estates. But when the aforesaid archdeacon was informed of this, he immediately went to the court and asked how the holy bishop was. When he was told that, as his illness grew stronger, he was already very near death, he at once summoned the aforesaid boys and asked them truthfully what the holy bishop had given them. When they truthfully told him, he was roused to anger and began turbulently to threaten them, saying:

“See what you have received, and guard it carefully. For if, whenever I demand them, you do not present everything to me intact, know that you will be tortured with the gravest punishments.”

Having said this, he returned angrily to his house.

The aforesaid boys then entered the cell in which the most holy bishop Massona lay sick on his little bed, and began to weep most bitterly before him, saying:

“You showed mercy to us unworthy men because of your goodness. It would have been better for us if you had not done so. Behold, you are still alive, and they threaten us with such terrible things; once you are dead, who among us will be able to free us from their hands?”

They addressed many words of this kind to him tearfully. But when he heard them, he did not readily believe them. First, as befitted his dignity, he carefully investigated whether what they said was true or false. When he discovered that what he had heard was true, he wept and immediately ordered himself to be carried into a small room and taken to the basilica of the holy virgin Eulalia, whom he had always served with devoted mind.

When the most holy old man had arrived there, he stretched out his hands before the sacred altar, raised his venerable eyes toward heaven with tears, and, with a great groan, prostrated himself on the ground. For a long time he poured out his prayers before the Lord. When his prayer had been completed, he said in a clear voice, with everyone listening:

“I give thanks to you, Lord, because you have heard me. Blessed are you throughout the ages of ages, because you have not removed my supplication and your mercy from me.”

Having said this, he returned to the episcopal residence.

[Note: *Episcopium*. Elsewhere he calls it the *atrium*, for *ἐπισκοπεῖον* (*episkopeion*) is the tabernacle itself and the bishop’s dwelling.]

He was restored to his former strength to such a degree that you would have thought he was neither sick nor old, but had recovered his vigor as one returned from the dead and had become a very robust young man. When, as usual, he wished to proceed to the evening office—

[Note: To the evening office. According to Isidore, *Etymologies* VI.19, it occurs at the beginning of the night and is named from the evening star, which rises as night begins. Concerning its antiquity and institution, I thought it worthwhile to advise the reader to consult the notes of our learned and most pious friend Don Antonio Caraccioli on the chapter *Constitutions of the Clergy* of the rule of religion, which, under the leadership of Don Placido Myrto Frangipane, a most illustrious man and also our friend, has already begun to bless Spain with new growth, greatly benefiting the Christian commonwealth; Spain will be eternally indebted to him for so singular a benefit.]

—all rejoiced wonderfully. When the archdeacon heard this, overwhelmed by guilt, he was struck with astonishment: he had expected the man whom he thought would die that very day to proceed to vespers. Covered with confusion and shame, he came according to custom with all the clergy and stood before the bishop, offering him incense in the customary manner. The man of God said to him:

“You shall precede me.”

But they, not understanding the reason, replied:

“It was said to you for no other reason than that you will precede him to the church.”

When he had begun to perform the evening office, the aforesaid archdeacon was immediately struck in the choir of the psalm-singers by a most severe pain and returned to his house in grave illness. When his mother, a most holy woman, learned this, she hastened at once to the venerable man and began to entreat him with tears and great weeping to pray to the Lord for her son.

To this he replied only:

“What I have prayed, I have prayed.”

From that time, on the third day, the archdeacon died.

Saint Massona the bishop, however, lived on for many days, distributing abundant alms to the needy and, bestowing greater benefits of his favor upon faithful servants, deigning to grant more generous payments and gifts.

[Note: Then, extremely decrepit with age and after many days, the old man peacefully breathed out his final spirit amid words of prayer. M. Maximus assigns the day to the year 602: “Saint Massona, metropolitan of Emerita, dies on the first day of November, is regarded as a saint, and is buried in the church of Saint Eulalia.” I shall not hesitate to append to his praises an epigram corrected from our manuscripts, by Saint Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, in Julian, archpriest of that same church, with the following heading:

“Poem for Saint Leander and Massona, metropolitans: the former of Seville, the latter of Emerita.”

Leander, excellent father, whom heaven receives,  
Adorned with praises, conspicuous in titles,  
The grove of the Arian race, and likewise the healer,  
The teacher of Isidore, whom he begot for the Lord—

You too, three times happy glory of the Emeritan people,  
Massona, in counsel, heart, and renowned faith.

Equal in courage, both equal in piety and praise,  
Each a wall in the house of the great God.

You conquered by enduring threats and the rebellious spirit  
Of the king; they say that he repented of his crime.

You opened the twofold Olympus to the king’s offspring;  
Through us one of them flies as a martyr to the stars;  
The other rises to the rosy airs of light,  
And where light is absent, there he has his radiance.

They say that you granted salvation to the Gothic people,  
When he abandoned the hated doctrine and embraced the pious one.

Rightly the victorious laurel follows you,  
And everlasting glory, owed to such magnificent merits.

Your honor and illustrious fame will always remain;  
The peoples will sing of you, but the stars sing still more.

For you are girded with an eternal crown of leaves,  
In a more splendid place among the teachers.”]

Then, extremely decrepit with age and after many days, he peacefully breathed out his final spirit amid words of prayer.

## CHAPTER XXI. After Massona, the deacon Innocentius becomes bishop of Emerita, and after him Renovatus; both are renowned for miracles.

[Col. 0161C]

After the departure of the aforesaid most holy and venerable Bishop Massona, a man of the greatest humility and simplicity, named Innocentius, was appointed in his place.

[Note: Innocentius. In the decree of King Gundemar, era 648, he subscribed as follows: “I, Innocentius, metropolitan bishop of the province of Lusitania at Emerita, having come to the city of Toledo for the royal reception, after learning those constitutions, gave my assent and subscribed.” Concerning him see also Moral, book XII, chapter 22, and Padilla, century VII, chapter 17.]

The merit of his name was indicated by the name itself: truly innocent and simple, judging no one, condemning no one, harming no one, he was always harmless and kind throughout all the days of his life. At the same time in which he was ordained, he was, as is reported, last in the order of deacons. Finally, he is said to have possessed such holiness and such contrition that whenever rain was lacking and the earth dried out under excessive heat and prolonged drought, the citizens of that place gathered together with him and went through the basilicas of the saints, beseeching the Lord in prayer. Whenever they went out with him, rain was suddenly and abundantly granted from heaven, enough to saturate the earth completely. Hence there was no doubt that his tears, issuing from so humble and simple a mind, could obtain from the almighty Lord not only these things but also greater ones.

After his death, Renovatus, adorned with every virtue, deservedly attained the summit of the priesthood.

[Note: Renovatus. See what we noted concerning him at chapter 2.]

He was a Goth by nation, born of a noble lineage and distinguished by the splendor of his family. He was tall in body, remarkable in appearance, graceful in stature, pleasing in his bearing, handsome of countenance, beautiful of face, and extraordinarily admirable to behold. But although outwardly he was adorned by the glory of his appearance, inwardly he was considered more beautiful, illumined by the light of the Holy Spirit. He was learned in many disciplines and arts, and possessed many different kinds of virtues. He was outstanding in all his works, exceedingly fair and just, of exceptionally keen intelligence, thoroughly instructed in all ecclesiastical disciplines, and deeply practiced in the divine books.

While he shone with many virtues, teaching certain disciples sacred doctrine and forming them by the most holy example of his life—namely, by prudence, holiness, patience, gentleness, and mercy—he made many people like himself, leading them to the thresholds of justice and to the preaching of the doctrine to be followed. Through his teaching, the Church still gleams and shines like the sun and moon.

After he had governed the Church irreproachably for many years, he deserved, when his limbs had been wondrously loosened, to depart from the body and enter the palace of the heavenly kingdom, to remain forever with Christ and reign without end, being joined to the angelic choirs and united with all the heavenly legions of the higher realms.

The bodies of these aforesaid saints rest honorably buried in one and the same small cell, not far from the altar of the most holy virgin Eulalia.

[Note: “In one and the same cell,” etc. The bodies of these Emeritan fathers, renowned for holiness, which rested together, were found during the time of the Catholic kings not far from the sacred altar of the Blessed Virgin Eulalia, as Moral repeatedly testifies, book X and chapter 10, and book XII, chapter 22.

From the end of this little book the end of Paul’s life must also unquestionably be inferred. Where Renovatus rests, Paul rests. After Renovatus had governed the Church irreproachably for many years, according to Paul himself, the man who succeeded him was Stephen, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Emerita, who subscribed at the Fourth Council of Toledo. The council was held in era 571, during the reign of Sisenand. We have established without difficulty that Paul died around this time, if we observe that he mentions Renovatus as already dead. He therefore lived while Stephen, the successor of Renovatus, was alive; perhaps he does not mention Stephen because Stephen was still living. That Stephen outlived Paul is also clear, since Paul closed his writing with the death of Renovatus, as is known; he would have acted otherwise if Stephen had not yet been alive. But concerning these matters see Francisco Padilla, century VII of the *Ecclesiastical History of Spain*, chapter 17.]

At their venerable tombs, Christ bestows daily such an abundant grace of charity that, whatever illness may have afflicted someone or whatever sickness may have oppressed him, as soon as he earnestly implores the divine power there with all his heart, he immediately feels that all diseases have been driven away and every stain divinely removed, and he reaches the desired health cheerful and sound by the grace of God.

The narrative of Christ’s soldiers, hampered at once by the multitude of miracles and deaths, has recounted them as best it could. Although, through excessive stylistic coloring, it may ineptly displease the learned, with verbal pomp omitted it ennobles those who think and believe humbly, and adds a certain increase of good reward for readers and hearers.

I, the most humble of all, ask disdainful readers first to read the little works of this book and afterward to despise them, lest they seem to presume not from judgment but from hatred, and condemn what they have not understood. Let them nevertheless recognize most clearly that I, moved by love of Christ and devotion to the most holy Eulalia, have reported manifest things and set forth truths with complete sincerity.

To the Lord, who always remains one in the Trinity and reigns eternally, be glory, honor, strength, thanksgiving, power, might, and blessing, now and always, and throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0163]

# EXCERPT (*Apospasmation*) ON THE AFFAIRS OF EMERITA IN ANCIENT SPAIN, BY THE ROYAL HISTORIOGRAPHER DON THOMAS TAMAYO DE VARGAS

“Fame remains; fortune perishes. The very ashes of the dead man are visited, and even now he is hallowed in his own tomb. What is small retains traces of great fame, and the unhappy great man has nothing but a name.”  
(From an ancient inscription.)

## Dedication

To the most illustrious lord, Don Fernando de Vera y Vargas, archbishop of Santo Domingo, bishop of Cuzco, and counselor of the Catholic king.

To whom, most illustrious Prelate, should I have consecrated and dedicated the praises of ancient Emerita—by me, L. M. [probably *libens merito*, “gladly and deservedly”]—rather than to you? You were once its finest and most distinguished praise through your goodwill; you will be its eternal fame. In the former case, you defended Emerita when, in the very flower of your age, you were standard-bearer of its own senate; in the latter, the glory of your many merits causes the name of Emerita to be celebrated everywhere.

To you, I say, by whom the longing for that great city can, if not be extinguished, at least be lessened. For if we venerate in her antiquity and excellence of origin, in you we behold the image of both, since you derive the antiquity of your lineage and the nobility of your family from the Roman emperors themselves, to whom the surname *Verus* belonged, and from that hero of ours, García Pérez de Vargas, founder of so many illustrious families in Spain.

If we grieve over the ruin of ancient monuments in her, we shall recognize that they have revived in your breast, capable of containing every branch of learning, and have endured in your mind, extraordinarily fertile in all things.

If Emerita can boast bishops distinguished in piety, commanders in military skill, writers in learning, and other men outstanding in greatness of spirit, it must also boast you, whose religion the churches of both the western and eastern worlds proclaim; whose—

[lacuna]

—quick intelligence and practical wisdom, proven before the hair had appeared, not only by the people of Emerita, of whose senate you were once a great part, but also by the maritime coast of Compostela, where your counsel—

[lacuna]

—and spirit in turn either devoted care to the peoples or leisure to the Muses.

Your learning is so universally known above all others that, throughout the entire realm of the encyclopedic kingdom of the Muses, there is nothing under their hand and authority which, by the common agreement of the learned, does not likewise obey you. You pursue learned men with such honor and affection that, pouring out every resource of emotion and humanity, you seek out anyone marked by any reputation for learning, receive him with extraordinary courtesy, and never dismiss him without an honorable gift, a token of your remarkable generosity and goodwill.

You offer a rare and enviable example to other nobles of your rank: even when you possessed less, you were able, in your disposition toward men of letters, to do everything, with events afterward following your intention.

Finally, to include all the adornments of your generous heart in a single phrase, you are one—

“Who match the lofty name of birth with virtues  
And do not permit talent to be weighed down by nobility.”

But although these things are deservedly owed to you, most illustrious and most friendly Fernando, they are owed by me above all, since so many individual merits of yours toward me are evident that I should rightly be judged to have worn my forehead bare if I allowed them to grow obsolete through some neglect of unworthy forgetfulness, and did not appease the humanity of your genius with some offering of grateful affection.

Therefore, since I feel bound to you by such great obligations that I can in no way repay them equally, I think I must at least strive with every effort not to seem to have confused so great an account and merely overturned the balance of gratitude. I earnestly wish you to regard favorably and kindly the grateful remembrance of so many benefits, while we meditate on repaying our duties—if God shortly grants us the opportunity.

Meanwhile I pray to immortal God that He may soon restore you safe to your family, your country, your friends, and to us; and that we may welcome with equal joy your return, after having followed your departure, undertaken for the sake of the commonwealth, with incredible sorrow, so that you may discharge the honors due to you there.

## THE EXCERPT (*APOSPASMATION*) BEGINS

[Col. 0165]

[Col. 0165A] I have thought that I would do something worthwhile for learned men and students of antiquity if, while illuminating Paul, who committed the affairs of Emerita to writing a thousand years ago, I were to present here, as though on a small tablet and in a concise summary suited to the study of brevity, without sacrificing truth, some things from *Ancient Spain* that concern the antiquity and distinction of the city and Church of Emerita—things neither obvious nor useless—which I assemble with laborious effort from ancient sources.

Those who provided the occasion for founding Emerita itself also gave it its name. Dio, book LIII, after reporting that Augustus had come to Spain while the Cantabrians and Asturians were in revolt, and that, after falling ill at Tarragona, he immediately sent the general Antistius against them, adds:

“Once this war had ended, Augustus discharged the older soldiers and granted them permission to found in Lusitania a city called Augusta Emerita.”

Finishing that war, Augustus discharged the veteran soldiers and ordered them to found a city in Lusitania, named Augusta Emerita.

[Note: The same is said by John, bishop of Gerona, chapter 20. We pass over it. Concerning Spain, however, he inserts many things in his customary manner that are not true.]

This occurred, as it seems, in the year 728 after the founding of Rome, twenty-three years before the birth of Christ, when Augustus Caesar was consul for the ninth time with Marcus Silanus.

From this Isidore our countryman, *Etymologies*, book XV, chapter 1. [Note: According to the very accurate reckoning of the distinguished Antoninus Augustinus, *Dialogue on Coins*, which Joan Mariana seems to have followed, *On the Affairs of Spain*, book III, chapter 25, and G. Genebrard, *Chronicle*, book II. Jacobus Salianus, however, volume VI of the *Annals*, under the year 24 before Christ—that is, year 4029 of the world—says that Emerita was given by Augustus to the veteran soldiers, but that its construction was assigned by Dio to the following year, namely 23 before the birth of Christ.] Caesar Augustus built Emerita after he had conquered Lusitania and certain islands of the Ocean, giving it its name from the fact that he settled veteran soldiers there. For veterans are called *emeriti*, men released from military service. Both statements are true; for, as Suidas testifies, “Among the Romans, a veteran is one who has been released from military service.” This is the sense of the old glosses, in which *emeritus* is rendered ἀπολειτουργήσας ἢ ἀποστρατευσάμενος, “one who has completed his service or been discharged from the army,” and also ἔντιμος κατὰ στρατιωτικοὺς καμάτους, “honored for military labors”—clearly according to the custom of Roman service, in which veterans were rewarded both with a prize and with an *emeritum*. The prize was reckoned in money; the *emeritum*, in the allotment of land.

Tacitus speaks of the prize in book I of the *Annals*, in that seditious speech of Percennius: “The sixteenth year of service should bring an end to their terms, so that they would not be kept any longer under the standards, but that in the same camp the prize should be paid to them in money.” Modestinus, the jurist, speaks of the *emeritum* in book III, *On Military Affairs*: “A veteran will receive his discharge allowance . . . . He is deprived of his discharge allowance.” Hyginus Augustus, *On the Establishment of Boundaries*: “At that time the reward was land, and it was regarded as the discharge allowance.” Arius Menander, the jurist, speaks of both in book V, final section, *Digest*, under the same title: “A veteran will receive both the rewards and the discharge allowance”—namely, the benefits of honorable military service, as Suetonius calls them in his *Life of Vitellius*, chapter 15. For the *emeritus* enjoyed both the discharge allowance and the reward, and, so that he might live more comfortably,

> Weary, the soldier is led away to the allotted fields,

as Ovid says, *Amores* II, elegy 9. Hence Caesar’s wish in our Lucan, that poet of immense spirit, addressed to the soldiers in book VII of the *Pharsalia*:

> This is that day . . . . .  
>   
> . . . . . which will restore pledges and household gods,  
>   
> and make you colonists after your warfare is finished.

More distinctly in book I:

> What dwelling will there be for the discharged veterans, what fields will be given,  
> what land will our veteran plow? What walls for the weary?

Thus Augustus, according to Suetonius, book XIII: “He decided that the veterans should be led back to Italy and settled on municipal lands.” In a similar way he gave lands in Spain to veterans and discharged soldiers. Significantly, an ancient coin recorded by A. Occonus among the Spanish inscriptions, folio 20, number 3, reads:

> EMERITA AVGVSTA VETERANORVM DOMICILIVM  
> EMERITA AUGUSTA, THE HOME OF THE VETERANS.

From those men, therefore, it received its name. Antoninus calls it Emerita, but together with its own name; Ptolemy and Strabo have Αὐγοῦστα ἀμέρητα, “Augusta Emerita,” while Pliny and Mela have *Augusta Emerita*. Both forms occur on coins. On some, the letters IMP. CAESAR. AVGVST. surround the image of Augustus, while in the center, within a representation of walls and gates, is EMERITA. [Note: The insignia now used by Emerita seem to represent the most ancient forms of the coins, since they are decorated with walls and gates. They may be seen in discourse 24, *On Nobility*, in Barnabas Moreno de Vargas, *Emeritensis*.] On others, on one side there is a face with the letters PERMISSV. CAESARIS AVG., and on the reverse a yoke of oxen followed by a farmer with a whip, with EMERITA beneath; on others still, beside the image: CAESAR. AVGVSTVS. PONT. MAX. IMP., and around the walls and gates: AVGVSTA. EMERITA. COL. Likewise on a coin of Tiberius, very similar to this one: on one side TI. CAESAR AVGVSTVS. PONT. MAX. IMP.; on the other AVGVSTA. EMERITA. So too on the stones, which I shall present in their proper place.

Thus it is clear from these coins, and from others in Goltzius’s *Thesaurus*, that the colony was founded under this name. Prudentius expresses the matter more distinctly:

> Now the place is Emerita,  
>   
> the famous colony of Vettonia.

Pliny, book IV, chapter 13: “The colonies: Augusta Emerita.” The coins show that the care of founding and establishing it was entrusted to P. Carisius, the legate and propraetor; on one side are the names of Augustus, and on the other those of Carisius and Emerita, namely:

> IMP. CAESAR. AVGVST. EMERITA. P. CARISIVS. LEG. PR. PR.  
> IMPERATOR CAESAR AUGUSTUS. EMERITA. P. CARISIUS, LEGATE AND PROPRAETOR.

Here, then, you have the true account of the founding of Emerita and the reason for the name bestowed upon it—both not only honorable but also sufficiently ancient. Some prefer an older origin, sought elsewhere: for example, the Arab Tariphius Abentaquirius, published from Arabic by Michael de Luna (in a year which many consider fictitious?), in part II of *The Destruction of Spain*. There he describes Emerita through a confused circuit of badly connected words, absurdly imagining that a city called MORAT—said in Chaldaic to mean “a town of the highest rank”—was erected by Sem Tophail, son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, and that the Christians later corrupted the name into Merida. Likewise Didacus de Valera, who in chapter 2 of part II of his *History of Spain* says that it was founded by Hercules after he had conquered Geryon; and Franciscus Tarapha, who, in his customary manner of dreaming, imagines that it was either built and named by the Myrmidons or called Memorida in memory of Hercules.

These, however, are the waking dreams and most foolish trifles of men—things I would have passed over prudently, had I not known that the customary fables always serve, alongside true proofs of great things, as testimony to their very greatness. [Note: Peter de Medina likewise babbles in book II, chapter 67, *On the Affairs of Spain*; but Florianus Ocampo, book I, chapter 14 of the *Chronicle of Spain*, Didacus Perez de Mesa in his notes on Peter de Medina, and Ludovicus Nonnius, chapter 31 of his *Spain*, learnedly demonstrate what ought to be thought of these matters.]

I return once more to Emerita. Among which peoples in Spain it was situated is not yet clear, if we consider the variety of the ancient writers. Ptolemy, book II, chapter 5, places it among the cities of the Celtici; Strabo, among the Turduli, in book III; Hyginus Augustus, in Baeturia; Prudentius, in Vettonia. Yet no one disagrees with the others, since the provinces were very often changed as time passed.

This circumstance, as Pliny testifies in book III, chapter 1, frequently produces great errors in calculations of distance and measurement: in one place the arrangement of the provinces has been altered, in another the miles of the roads have been increased or reduced; over so long an age the seas have encroached in some places, elsewhere they have pressed back the shores, and rivers have twisted, straightened, or corrected their bends. It will therefore not be surprising—as our distinguished friend, and in Spanish matters deservedly the best of all, Ludovicus Nonnius, observes in chapter 31 of his *Spain*—that in the time of Strabo, who flourished under Tiberius Caesar, the Turduli were distinguished in strength and wealth, whereas in the age of Prudentius, who flourished under Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius, the Vettones had gained the upper hand, occupied part of the territory of the Turduli, and thus caused Emerita to be reckoned among the Vettones, although it had previously belonged to the Turduli.

The matter concerning Baeturia in Hyginus is easily explained from Pliny, book III, chapter 1:

> The region that extends from the Baetis to the river Anas, outside the Baeturia mentioned above, is called Baeturia and is divided into two parts and as many peoples: the Celtici, who touch Lusitania and belong to the judicial district of Hispalis; and the Turduli, who border Lusitania and Tarraconensis and seek justice at Corduba.

Pliny joins the Vettones to these peoples in book IV, chapter 22:

> From the Anas, by which we have separated Lusitania from Baetica, 226,000 paces. From Gades, with 102,000 paces added: the peoples are the Celtici, the Turduli (so the ancient manuscripts read, not *Varduli*), and, around the Tagus, the Vettones.

Hence the three are repeatedly found together on inscriptions.

At Emerita:

> P. AENOVITALVS AVG. LIB. TABVL. PROVINCIAE. LVSITANIAE ET. VETTONIAE.  
> P. AENOVITALUS, AUGUSTUS’S FREEDMAN, RECORDS-CLERK OF THE PROVINCE OF LUSITANIA AND VETTONIA.

At Hispalis:

> M. CALPVRNIO. M. F. PROC. PROVINCIAE LVSITANIAE. ET. VETTONIAE.  
> TO M. CALPURNIUS, SON OF MARCUS, PROCURATOR OF THE PROVINCE OF LUSITANIA AND VETTONIA.

And elsewhere there are others, which will help to clarify the statement of Prudentius, who assigns Emerita to Vettonia—even though another stone, from the district of Oliva and formed from the ruins of Cappara, seems to distinguish the Emeritenses from the Vettones:

> L. PVBLICIO. L. F. PAP. THIAMVS. EMERIT. ANN. XXVII N.S.E.S.T.T.L. CAECILIVS. VETTO SODALI. CIPPVM D. S. P.  
> TO L. PUBLICIUS THIAMUS, SON OF LUCIUS, OF THE PAPIRIAN TRIBE, AN EMERITAN, AGED TWENTY-SEVEN. MAY THE EARTH LIE LIGHTLY UPON HIM. CAECILIUS VETTO, TO HIS COMPANION, SET UP THIS STONE AT HIS OWN EXPENSE.

That Emerita was always enlarged and honored by the Romans is demonstrated by the honors conferred upon it. To establish the colony more advantageously, Augustus assigned the Emeritenses a generous number of *jugera*. Hyginus gives a particularly clear account in *On the Establishment of Boundaries*, folio 164 of the edition of Rigaltius:

> Some determine the measure of a centuria according to the extent of the land. In Italy the triumvirs assigned fifty *jugera*, and in some places two hundred. At Cremona, 210 *jugera*. The deified Augustus assigned 400 *jugera* in Emerita of Baeturia. In these divisions the *decumani* have forty *actus* in length, the *kardines* twenty *actus*. The *decumanus* runs eastward. In certain colonies, moreover, the boundaries are contained by the *perticae*—that is, the first allotments—by other boundary lines, and by prefectures. Within the territory of the Emeritenses there are some prefectures, whose *decumani* likewise run eastward and whose *kardines* run southward.

With so many *jugera* assigned, it was a Latin colony, that is, one enjoying the privileges of Italian law. The jurist Paulus says in book II, *On the Census*, final law, *Digest*, under the same title: “In Lusitania, the Pacenses and the Emeritenses possess Italian law.”

It was also a judicial district of Lusitania. Pliny, book IV, chapter 22, on the Lusitanians:

> The entire province is divided into three judicial districts: the Emeritan, the Pacensian, and the Scallabitan.

I add that the rites of the entire order flourished at Emerita, since the stones themselves record an Emeritan woman serving as *Flaminica*, that is, the wife of the *Flamen Dialis*, as Festus and Aulus Gellius testify in book X, chapter 15.

Above Exarrama, a river two thousand paces below the town of Tenanum in Lusitania:

> IOVI. O. M. FLAVIA. L. F. RVFINA EMERITENSIS. FLAMINICA. PROVINC. LUSITANIAE. ITEM. COL. EMERITENSIS. PERPET ET. MVNICIPI. SALACIEN. D. D.  
> TO JUPITER, BEST AND GREATEST. FLAVIA RUFINA, DAUGHTER OF LUCIUS, AN EMERITAN, FLAMINICA OF THE PROVINCE OF LUSITANIA, AND ALSO PERPETUAL FLAMINICA OF THE COLONY OF EMERITA AND OF THE MUNICIPALITY OF SALACIA, GAVE [THIS] AS A GIFT.

The praises of Emerita must also include the fact that, from the time of the consuls under Augustus, a road was ordered to be paved as far as that city. An ancient stone at Cappara reads:

> T. VICTVRIO. ET. C. SEMPRONIO. COSS. POPVLIS PROVINCIAE. ARENAT. OB. SVPERIORVM. TEMPORVM. BELLA. AD. SVMMAM. INOPIAM. REDACTIS. IMMVNITAS. DATA EST. QVOAD. QVIDQVID. TERRARVM. AD. EMERITAM. VSQVE. AVGVSTAM. INTERIACET. LAPIDIBVS. STERNERETVR. CENSVERE. SIQVIDEM. E. MAIESTATE. AVGUSTI. DIVI. F. AC. S. P. Q. R. DIGNITATE. ET. AMPLITVDINE. HOC. ESSE. VT. PROVINCIAE. PORRO. AB. ITALIA CONSTITVTAE. QVAE. DE. REPVBLICA. RO. BENE. MERITAE. ESSENT. IN. MELIOREM. CVLTVM. REDVCERENTVR. ITAQVE. TITO. MVRTIO. PROVINCIAE. HISP. CITERIORIS. PRAETORI. DEMANDATVM. EST. VT. CCCCX. PONDO. ARGENTI. E. PVBLICIS. POPVLI. RO. EMOLVMENTIS. QVAE. PRAETERITIS. TEMPOR. QVAESTORES. RECEPISSENT. PROVINCIAM. SVBLEVARET. ET. PONDO. E. PROVINCIALIBVS. QVAE. AD. PHILIPPOS. QVAE. AD. ACTIACVM. SVPERERANT. AVT. QVAE. IN. AERARIVM. NONDVM. RELATA. FVERANT. CLX.

> Under the consulship of T. Victurius and C. Sempronius, exemption was granted to the peoples of the province of the Arenates, who had been reduced to the utmost poverty by the wars of former times, until all the territory extending as far as Augusta Emerita should be paved with stones. They judged this appropriate because of the majesty of Augustus, son of the deified one, and because of the dignity and greatness of the Roman Senate and People, so that the provinces established beyond Italy, which had deserved well of the Roman state, might be brought into a better condition. Accordingly, Titus Murtius, praetor of the province of Nearer Spain, was commissioned to relieve the province with 410 pounds of silver from the public revenues of the Roman people, which the quaestors had received in former times, and with 160 pounds from the provincial funds remaining from the payments made for the Philippi and for Actium, or not yet reported into the treasury.

Likewise, from Cappara to Emerita, a stone of Vespasian from the notebooks of Zurita and Scoto reads:

> IMP. CAES. VESPASIANVS AVG. PONT. MAX. TRIB. P. II. IMP. VII. COS. III. DESIG. IIII P. P. VIAM. A. CAPPARA. VRBE AD. EMERITAM. VSQ. AVG. IMP. SVA RESTITV LXXIII.  
> THE EMPEROR CAESAR VESPASIAN AUGUSTUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, IN HIS SECOND TRIBUNICIAN POWER, ACCLAIMED IMPERATOR FOR THE SEVENTH TIME, CONSUL FOR THE THIRD TIME, DESIGNATED FOR THE FOURTH, FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY, RESTORED AT HIS OWN EXPENSE THE ROAD FROM THE CITY OF CAPPARA AS FAR AS EMERITA AUGUSTA, 73 MILES.

The emperor Otho further enlarged Emerita by adding families. Tacitus, book I of the *Histories*: “With the same generosity he also sought the goodwill of cities and provinces, granting the Hispalenses and Emeritenses additions of families.” [Note: This is most correctly emended by the distinguished J. Lipsius.] “To all the Lusitanians he granted Roman citizenship, and he gave the cities of the Moors as a gift to the province of Baetica.”

And deservedly so, for Emerita is counted by Pomponius Mela, book I, chapter 6, among the most distinguished inland cities of Lusitania:

> The capital of the towns of the Lusitanians.

Prudentius calls it a city:

> The city . . . .

Ausonius, in the eighth poem of his *Catalogue of Noble Cities*, under the title “On Emerita,” writes:

> After these, Emerita, you will rightly be remembered by me as an Iberian name,  
>   
> Emerita, past which the sea-like river flows,  
>   
> to which all Spain submits her fasces.  
>   
> Corduba does not contend with you, nor Tarraco, powerful in its citadel,  
>   
> nor wealthy Bracara, which tosses itself upon the curve of the sea.

E. Vinetus, in his commentary on Ausonius, and P. Merula, book II, part II, chapter 24 of his *Cosmography*, vainly attempt to attribute this passage to Hispalis because it occurs in certain manuscripts and because *Iberum* and *Hispanum* are names appropriate to Hispalis, whereas *Emerita* is Latin. As though they did not know that Hispalis had a Latin origin! Isidore, *Etymologies* XV.1: “Hispalis received its name from its location, because it was set in marshy ground upon piles driven deep into the earth.” Rasis also had this etymology in mind when he says: “When Hercules populated Seville, he founded it on wood and gave it this name because of the piles.” [Note: Rodrigo of Toledo says likewise, book I, chapter 5, concerning Hispalis, because its first dwellings were supported upon piles.]

I do not see, however, why Hispalis or Hispal should be a Spanish name. The great man Blessed Arias Montanus was not far wrong in arguing that it was rather Phoenician or Punic. Nor do I see why the distinguished Merula should consider this a very powerful argument, when it is not only fragile but also empty. He has nevertheless found other supporters—though Baeticans—who accuse Joseph Scaliger of negligence because in book I of his *Ausonian Readings*, chapter 23, and book II, chapter 30, he learnedly defends the common reading of Ausonius.

I know that the Baetis was deservedly celebrated by the ancients and was rich in navigable commerce; but I also know that by *Hispalis* or *Spalis* they did not chiefly designate the Baetis River, any more than by Emerita they designated the Anas. Pliny, book IV, chapter 13, says of the latter: “Augusta Emerita, situated beside the river Anas.” Prudentius writes of the same river:

> The memorable river Anas  
>   
> flows past . . . .

Our Paul of Emerita expressed the same thought in chapter 2: “The memorable river Anas, swelling excessively.” Thus Ausonius writes here:

> Emerita, past which the sea-like river flows,

and in his letter to Paulinus:

> and the rivers of Emerita . . . .

[Note: Rodrigo de Cunha, archbishop and primate of the Church of Braga, a great ornament of Spain and a singular model for all prelates, adds his authority to the praise of Emerita in chapter 2 of his treatise *On the Primacy of the Church of Braga*. His learning equals the nobility that is first among the Lusitanians, although nobility itself is surpassed by humanity; so many are the outstanding qualities in that hero. So too does the distinguished Ludovicus Nonnius, chapter 31 of his *Spain*, not to mention writers of lesser stature.]

I add that Ausonius must have been more familiar with Emerita and the Anas than with Hispalis and the Baetis, since he mentions the former twice each, but never the latter. Therefore this matter should be judged more from Ausonius’s greater familiarity with the subject than from any other consideration.

I do not deny that the Baetis is “sea-like,” since its character in relation to the ebb and flow of the tides is made clear by Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* V.2:

> Hispalis, famous upon the Ocean and amid alternating tides,

as our Silius writes in *Punica* III.

What, then? Is the Anas not sea-like, when we know its size to be attested by monuments of every age? The Baetis, according to Pliny, book III, chapter 1, is at first moderate in size, but receives many rivers, by which it takes away both their fame and their waters. Isidore our countryman was therefore unjustly criticized by the critics when, in *Etymologies* XIII.21, he says that the Baetis was so called because it flows through low-lying land: for the Greeks call something low or submerged βαθύ, *bathý*.

The Anas, however, rises in the territory of Laminium in Nearer Spain; now spreading itself into pools, now being swallowed into narrow channels, now being completely concealed in underground passages, and rejoicing in being born again repeatedly, it pours into the Atlantic Ocean, always and everywhere through an immense channel.

What could be more ingenious? Strabo, at the beginning of book III, when discussing the Turdetani and joining the Anas with the Baetis, places the Baetis below the Anas:

> This region of the Turdetani extends eastward between the Anas and as far as Oretania; to the south, from its mouth as far as the maritime tract of the Anas and as far as the Pillars, etc.

Into this maritime region both the Baetis and the Anas flow; from there the last region of Mauretania, entering the Atlantic Sea, forms the strait at the Pillars, by which the outer sea is joined to the Mediterranean. A little earlier he says:

> The beginning of the southern side of Spain extends as far as another river, the Anas, and its outlet. From the eastern regions both rivers descend. One of them flows backward toward the west, the other being much greater. The Anas, however, bends toward the south, dividing the region lying between the rivers, which is inhabited for the most part by the Celts and by many of the Lusitanians whom the Romans transferred into a colony from beyond the Tagus. In the upper regions the Carpetani, the Oretani, and numerous Vettones dwell, etc.

And finally:

> This is the river which the Baetis washes, rising in the same places as the Anas and the Tagus, being of a size intermediate between the two. From its source it flows westward like the Anas, then turns southward and reaches the same coast.

This conjecture must be derived not only from the rivers but also from the cities. Hispalis was once great and famous, but Emerita was not inferior to it in greatness and renown. I have discussed Hispalis at length not only in my *Ancient Spain* but also in the notes to our Festus Avienus’s *Maritime Description*. As for Emerita, I shall now show that it was once so great that, although Corduba, Tarraco, and Barcino would scarcely have been willing to compete with it, as Ausonius writes, it was certainly once of such size that it gave occasion to legends—stories greater than the credibility of all historical fact, not only among the Arabs but also among our own writers.

If these accounts could safely be believed, its walls were nearly three leagues in circumference, seventeen cubits thick and forty-five cubits high; it was distinguished by 1,500 towers and opened by forty-four gates besides the principal one. The number of its fighting citizens supposedly filled out this vast extent. From its fame the celebrated Spanish verse arose:

> MERIDA, which in Spain  
>   
> once was another Rome,

and this passed down to later generations.

Hence, not without reason, Joseph Moletius, the distinguished mathematician of his age, when illustrating Ptolemy, book II, chapter 5, says: “Augusta Emerita, commonly Merida, once another Rome.” For when other cities, which were considered worthy and thought comparable to the greatness of Rome, uselessly competed with those inferior to Rome,

> to which all Spain submits her fasces,

Emerita, by contrast, was not ungrateful to Rome and to the Romans. As far as it could, it fashioned itself entirely after the model not only of the city but also of its citizens—in speech, dress, and manners.

Strabo, book III, on the Turdetani:

> They completely adopted Roman customs, no longer even remembering their native language; most became Latins, received Roman colonists, and came very near to becoming entirely Roman. The cities now founded are Pez Augusta among the Celtici, Augusta Emerita among the Turduli, etc. Spaniards who follow this form are called *Stolati* or *Togati*.

The Emeritenses took no less care to construct their public buildings on the model of Rome. The city was renowned for its theater, its triumphal arch or trophy, its Naumachia, and its very long bridge of Roman workmanship—all of which are much discussed by our writers.

I shall insert here only the words of the learned Ludovicus Nonnius, which contain a summary of many matters, from chapter 31 of his *Spain*:

> Emerita is situated on level ground beside the river Anas, commonly called the Guadiana. The river is crossed by a most beautiful bridge, which, judging from the harmony of its architecture, reflects Roman magnificence. This city had two aqueducts, whose scattered arches are still visible here and there and display the splendor of their workmanship. There is also a structure adjoining the city which the inhabitants call the Septisolium, because they report that at a fixed time the seven kings of the Carthaginians were accustomed to assemble in this city and sit in these seats. But these are genuine absurdities, since the structure does not even resemble the shadow of a seat. Gaspar Barrerius says that it was a theater: its arches have plainly collapsed, but its walls remain intact in various places, though the whole has been disfigured by heaps of rubble.

> An arch is also seen here near the church of St. James, which the inhabitants and most writers believe to have been a triumphal arch. But besides the fact that it is false that triumphal arches existed anywhere but Rome, such arches are of more distinguished and elaborate construction; they bear carved representations of achievements, defeated enemies, and victories, together with the title of the emperor, as may be seen at Rome in the arches of the emperors Septimius Severus and Titus Vespasianus. The Emeritan arch displays none of these features. Barrerius therefore reasonably suspects that it was some kind of trophy.

> Another notable work of antiquity is also visible here, the Naumachia. Its ground plan is oval, extending 1,400 feet in length; its width corresponds to its length. It is surrounded by a great wall arranged in arches and vaults, as traces still show in several places.

This once most illustrious city has declined into a great scarcity of inhabitants and displays nothing except the ruins of its former splendor. Thus I may rightly exclaim, and complain, with the ingenious poet Naso, *Metamorphoses* XV:

> Devouring Time, and envious old age,  
>   
> you destroy all things, and with the teeth of time  
>   
> slowly consume everything in lingering death.

I shall add three matters that I have found in writers concerning Emerita, so that nothing relevant to the city—whose affairs will be treated individually—may be omitted.

That there was once frequent commerce between the Emeritenses and the Caesaraugustani is shown by the three routes assigned by Antoninus from Emerita to Caesaraugusta, namely—as I shall give them after correcting them, if you will accept me as an emender:

I find the same commercial connections between the Hispalenses, Cordubenses, Salacienses, Olisipponenses, and others with the Emeritenses. The routes themselves make this clear; as I have noted previously in the account of the coast, I shall add them after correcting them.

Carmona, 22 miles.

[Note: Incorrectly printed in the common editions as *Osto et Ani*.]

To the Red Places, 17 miles.

Curica, 49 miles.  
Contributa, 24 miles. [Note: Ptolemy has Κουντριβοῦτα. It abounded in *coccum* and in exceedingly sweet olives, though they were rare.]  
Perviana, 20 miles.  
Emerita, 24 miles.

A further observation about Emerita follows in the writers. Second, the finest *coccum* for dyeing was found around Emerita. Pliny, book IX, chapter 41: “The red grain of Galatian *coccum*, etc., or that around Emerita of Lusitania, is held in the highest esteem.”

Third, its olives were of exceptional flavor. The same author, that most excellent and refined investigator of nature, book XV, chapter 3:

> There are also olives that are naturally very sweet when dried and sweeter than raisins, exceedingly rare in Africa and around Emerita of Lusitania.

Among these matters—as our cook says, as is customary at banquets, when

> the olive ends the feast.

[Note: Perhaps it was called by the ancients from the preparation or cooking of savory delicacies, as I once discussed fully in *Schidiasma* 10 of the *Hours of Leisure*, Decade 4.] I shall now stop, to ward off distaste.

Hitherto concerning those matters that relate to the size of the city of Emerita [Col. 0173C]; now concerning those that relate to religion. From the very beginnings of the Catholic faith, Emerita was illumined by the presence of two apostles, Peter, their chief, and James, the sole patron of the Spains, and gloried in that presence. For Blessed James, after departing from the port of Jaffa, penetrated as far as the island of Sardinia, and from there went to Spain, where he disembarked at the city of Carthage. From there he proceeded toward Granada; after sowing the seeds of the divine word, he stood by at the martyrdom of his disciple. Afterwards he went to Mentesa, thence to Córdoba and EMERITA, and through Lusitania and Braga came into Galicia, etc., as says the Armenian Breviary in Ferdinand de Oxeda the Dominican, chapter 6 of his *History of St. James*, no. 2.

The teaching of Blessed Peter of Rates, disciple of James and bishop of Braga, was added to this. For when he was in Spain as St. James’s vicar, following his master’s example, he did not remain in one city only, but, animated by zeal for the faith, traversed the regions on both sides of the Tagus and, visiting the peoples entrusted to him, disseminated the word of God through Aegitania, Callensia (thus the manuscript codices read), EMERITA, Ambracia [Col. 0173D], and the other cities of the Vettones and Lusitanians. This is attested by Caledonius, Peter’s successor in the see of Braga, in his life, preserved in Hugo, bishop of Porto, in a letter to Maurice of Braga, written in Gothic letters and extant in the monastery of Santa Cruz at Coimbra.

Thus, around the year 40 after Christ’s birth, the first light of the Gospel shone upon Emerita. For in the year 37 James appointed Peter to Braga, and in the year 45 Peter was crowned with martyrdom, as we have elsewhere asserted from Dexter, son of D. Pacianus. Emerita must therefore boast of such great antiquity in religion [Col. 0174A].
