Blessed Peter, the apostle of the Lusitanians, laid the foundations of its Church, either himself exercising pontifical functions there or appointing another to exercise them, according to his own custom and that of the apostles. Hence we may not unjustly recognize as the first bishop of the Emeritans this St. PETER, in whom the people of Braga also formerly gloried as their first bishop.

Although the succession of the others has been diminished by the changes and interruptions of circumstances and time, I am pleased to append it from ancient records. After the rays of evangelical light had been scattered by Blessed Peter of Rates, or of Braga, the first bishop to preside at Emerita was perhaps ST. EPITACIUS, when the apostle Peter visited Emerita. Dexter, under the year 48, writes:

> Peter came to the Spains and visited them; he left shepherds there, appointed Sextifirmus bishop of Epennetum, and Epitacius at Emerita—as is read in certain manuscripts, and as I note there.

Concerning Epitacius, see the Roman Martyrology, 23 May.

Following him, though after a considerable interval, was MARTIALIS, around the Christian year 258, whom Vasaeus under the year 256, Moral, book IX, [Col. 0174B] chapter 45, and Padilla, century 3, chapter 10, claim to have been Emeritan (although Baronius under the year 258, and following him Severinus Binius in volume I of the Councils, fol. 139, call him Asturicensian). Misled by the misfortune of the times, he fell with Basilides into various errors. Against these Blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, wrote a letter to Felix the presbyter and to the communities residing by the legion and at Asturica, and likewise to Aelius the deacon and to the community of Emerita, brothers residing in the Lord; it appears as no. 68 in the Pamelian edition.

Around the year 312 LIBERIUS succeeded him. He signed in tenth place at the Council of Iliberis: “the Emeritan or Emeritanus bishop” (for both forms are read in the manuscripts); and at the first Council of Arles, under Silvester and Constantine I, in the year 314: “Liberius, bishop from the city of Emerita.” Concerning him, see Moral, book X, chapter 31.

Around the year 347 came FLORENTIUS or FLORENTINUS (both names likewise occur in the autograph manuscripts), who, together with Bishop Liberius, had attended the Council of Arles as deacon from the city of Emerita. Afterwards, at the general Council of Sardica, an appendix, so to speak, of Nicaea, he signed as follows: “Florentinus [Col. 0174C], from Spain, of Emerita.”

Around the year 380 Severus Sulpicius assigns ITACIUS or IDACIUS (I found both forms in the manuscripts) as bishop of Emerita when, in book II of his *Sacred History*, he was treating Priscillian—but corruptly. For in the common editions one reads “Idacius, a priest of Emerita,” where “of the city of Emerita” should stand, as I formerly pointed out in my commentary on the year 429 of Dexter, where there is much material concerning those in Spain who are distinguished by the name Idacius, Ithatius, Ithacius, or Idalius, as well as much that is not commonplace. Idacius of Emerita signed at the First Council of Zaragoza, convened in the era 418.

After this, the writers are profoundly silent about the bishops of Emerita. The next to appear after a long interval of time—namely, during the reign of Leovigild, that is, in 570—is PAUL, concerning whom our Paul writes in chapter 4. He was succeeded by FIDELIS, concerning whom the same author writes in chapters 5, 6, 7, and 8.

A fuller record is found of MASSONA. At the two Councils of Toledo held in the time of Reccared, namely in the era 627, that is, in the year 589, he subscribed as follows:

> In the name of Christ, the metropolitan bishop of the Catholic Church of Emerita, of the province of Carpetania, assenting to the constitutions in which he took part in the city of Toledo, subscribed.

And likewise in the era 635, that is, in the year 597. Concerning him our Paul writes from chapter 9 through chapter 21: while Massona was staying at Toledo on account of the council, he attended the purification of the church of Toledo.

Julian, archpresbyter of Toledo, writes in his *Chronicle*:

> The church of St. Mary of Toledo, begun by the apostle James and consecrated to the Assumption of Blessed Mary by M. Marcellus Eugenius, was repeatedly profaned by Arian bishops who compelled the kings of the Visigoths, and was restored by the Catholic king Reccared of blessed memory in a solemn rite on 13 April, by Euphemius or Euphemianus, archbishop of Toledo and primate of the Spains, in the presence of Massona, metropolitan of Emerita, Benignus of Braga, and the other metropolitans, etc.

But where did the bishop of Emerita reside at Toledo during the council? The same Julian writes in his *Adversaria*:

> Bracarensis resided at the palace of St. Leocadia during the councils of Toledo; the bishop of Seville in the church in its suburb; the Emeritan in that of St. Eulalia; etc.

After Massona had been exiled, SUNNA and NEPOTIS, pseudo-bishops, were intruded in his place; concerning them see Paul, chapters 11, 12, 13, and 14.

INNOCENTIUS succeeded Massona as the true bishop, according to Paul, chapter 2. In the era 648, that is, in the year 610, by decree of King Gundemar, he was metropolitan bishop of the province of Lusitania at Emerita. When he had come to the city of Toledo for the royal assembly, he gave his assent and subscribed. Not long afterward came RENOVATUS, concerning whom Paul writes in chapter 21. I have shown in the note to chapter 21 that STEPHANUS succeeded him; he subscribed in the year 619 at the Fourth Council of Toledo as metropolitan bishop of the Church of Emerita.

After him came ORONTIUS [Col. 0175B], mentioned in the Sixth Council of Toledo, era 676, year 636. In the subscriptions, the presbyter Guntiscus acts in the place of Orontius, bishop of the Church of Emerita. And in the Seventh Council of Toledo, era 684, year 646, Orontius, “in the name of Christ, bishop of the metropolitan Holy Church of Emerita,” subscribed while defining the statutes. He also attended the Eighth Council, era 691, year 653.

After him came PROFICIUS, “by the mercy of God bishop of the metropolitan see of the Holy Church of Emerita in the province of Lusitania.” In the era 704, year 666, at the council assembled at Emerita under King Recceswinth, he confirmed the synodal acts established with his neighboring bishops.

I find that FESTUS succeeded him at the beginning of Wamba’s reign, around the year 675. I read no other mention of him except in a letter of King Egica:

> While all the holy fathers were residing in the Sixteenth Holy Synod of Toledo, our predecessor, King Wamba of divine memory, at the very beginning of his reign, appointed our sword-bearer Theudemund, contrary to the custom of his birth and rank, solely through the exercise of royal power, to hold the office of treasurer in that same city of Emerita, at the instigation of the former Festus [Col. 0175C], bishop of Emerita, etc.

STEPHANUS, another bishop, in the era 719, year 681, confirmed the metropolitan bishop of the Church of Emerita at the Twelfth Council of Toledo; likewise in the era 721, year 683, under Ervig, at the Thirteenth Council; and at the Fourteenth, era 722, year 684, under the same king, Maximus the abbot likewise acted in the place of Lord Stephanus of the Church of Emerita.

This MAXIMUS is identified as metropolitan of Emerita under Egica, in the era 726, year 688, at the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, and in the era 731, year 693, at the Sixteenth.

I also find ANDREAS as bishop of Emerita around the year 910. Julian records in his *Chronicle*:

> Blasius, bishop of Toledo, convenes a council this year in the city of Toledo. The bishops who assemble for it are Egas of Valencia, Andreas of Emerita, Theodominus of Braga, Adelphius of Elbora from Carpetania, and thirty others. The reform of the clergy and a change in the office are discussed.

This is the succession of the bishops of Emerita, extracted from ancient records of councils and writers; no fuller information about them can be drawn from elsewhere. For the circumstances of the Church of Emerita underwent many changes. No one doubts that from the earliest times it was the metropolitan church of all Lusitania. For when, under the direction of Constantine the Great, Spain was divided into six archbishoprics or primatial sees—namely Narbonne, Toledo, Tarragona, Braga, Seville, and Emerita—each metropolitan was assigned his suffragans.

To the metropolitan church of Emerita in the province of Lusitania belonged Avela, Salamanca, Évora, Coria, Ossonoba, and Lisbon, as an ancient manuscript of Seville belonging to D. Laurence, written nearly a thousand years ago, records in its division of the provinces of Spain and their sees [Col. 0176A]. In another Gothic manuscript from Oviedo, however, more are assigned, namely Merida (I reproduce the ancient spelling), Pace, Olisipo, Ossonoba, Aegitania, Coimbra, Viseu, Lamego, Caliabria, Abela, Coria, Elbora, Abela, Salamanca, and Numantia, that is, Zamora. The arrangement was no different in the division carried out by King Wamba at the Eleventh Council of Toledo, according to Itacius.

With the authority of these suffragans, the metropolitan Church of Emerita proceeded in glory until the fatal destruction of Spain. At that time Muza, commander of the Arabs, went to Emerita—in the words of Rodrigo of Toledo, chapter 23 of book III—which displayed through many ancient buildings the glory of its former dignity. Its inhabitants, relying on their numbers, went out to battle against him, but on that day Muza could not prevail.

Seeing that he could not obtain the city by force, he concealed an ambush in a quarry near the city. On the following day, as they had done the day before, the citizens advanced to battle; but caught between the concealed troops and the battle lines, many of the citizens were killed, and those who escaped fled to the circuit of the city walls [Col. 0176B]. For the strength of the walls had been constructed with marvelous workmanship.

The faint-hearted Christians, despairing, sought a parley the next day. When they were permitted to approach Muza’s presence, they noticed the whiteness of his hair, returned to their own people after the interview, and, reporting the age of the besieger, supposed that he would soon die. Therefore on that day they withdrew from negotiations for an agreement.

Then Muza ordered the wall to be undermined all around. The besieged, however, making sallies from within, killed many of the diggers. On the third day they again requested a parley and returned to Muza’s presence. Those whom they had observed the previous day to be gray-haired they now found, through the application of dye, to be of a contrasting color. Struck by this folly, they regarded it as a miracle. Returning immediately to their own people, they announced that he was a man endowed with power, who changed at will from youthful to elderly appearance and back again. Troubled by this miracle, they immediately surrendered the city, but on the condition that they might depart with their property and persons unharmed.

Thus he captured the city in the ninety-third year of the Arabs, on the last day of the month of Ramadan [Col. 0176C]. Rasis the Arab, Dalharab, historiographer of the Miramolin of Morocco and of the king of Córdoba, relates this more fully in his *Description of Spain*. Eleastras also relates it, if this is a genuine rather than an invented name—the writer said to be the author of the history of Rodrigo and of the destruction of Spain, in which there is much material about Emerita—from chapter 141 through chapter 143. See also Moral, book X, chapter 73, and Mariana, book VI, chapter 20.

[Note: [Col. 0175D] Concerning this, Mariana, book III, chapter 25, *On the Affairs of Spain*, writes: “Rasis the Arab, with the lavish resources of his imagination, praises in many and almost incredible ways the magnificence and elegance of that city, Emerita, affirming that it was overthrown by the Moors when they subjected Spain to their rule.” [Col. 0176D]]

Thus, while Emerita lay prostrate among the barbarians, its metropolitan dignity lay without a see and without a name until approximately the year 1122 of our salvation, when Callixtus II raised the Church of Compostela to metropolitan dignity and transferred to it all the rights of the Church of Emerita, ordering all its suffragans to obey the archbishop of Compostela, as Vasaeus says in chapter 21 of his *Chronicle*.

It is worthwhile to repeat this in the words of Innocent III, Supreme Pontiff, in his letter to Peter of Compostela, from book II of the *Register*:

> For the Apostolic See, wishing to adorn the Church of Compostela with a special privilege out of reverence for the blessed apostle James, whose venerable body lies buried and rests there, generously bestowed upon that Church, in its entirety, the dignity of the metropolitan church of Emerita, which, by reason of sins demanding punishment, has for a long time in the past and down to the present been held captive by barbarian savagery, together with the whole province of Lusitania, as the privileges of our predecessor, Pope Callixtus of blessed memory, clearly testify.

From that time nothing but fame remained to Emerita from its ecclesiastical dignity. For no source will acquaint you better with the oppression suffered by the Emeritans under the Arabs than the letter of Louis the Pious Augustus to the Emeritans of Spain, composed by Einhard, in whose letters it is inserted, and published among the *Miscellanies of Minor Writings of Various Kinds*, following the notes of the most learned Jacques Sirmond, S.J., on the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald and His Successors*, fol. [Col. 0177A] 123.

Although war provides the occasion here, I shall insert it both because our writers have silently passed it over and because it contains an account both of the oppressed condition of the Emeritans and of their spirits, most ready for every venture of military valor. Here it is:

## Louis’s Letter to the Citizens of Emerita

> LOUIS, by the providence of God Augustus Emperor, to all the primates and the entire people of Emerita, greeting in the Lord.
>
> We have heard of your tribulation and the manifold troubles that you suffer through the cruelty of King Abdiraman, who, driven by excessive greed for your possessions, which he has repeatedly attempted to seize from us, has very often violently oppressed you—as we have also learned that his father Abolaz did. By unjust impositions he compelled you to pay him a tax to which you were not liable, and because of this he turned friends into enemies and those obedient to him into opponents and disobedient subjects. For he also attempted to take away our liberty, burden us with unjust taxes and tributes, and humble us.
>
> But, as we have heard, you have always, like brave men, vigorously repelled the injuries inflicted upon you by unjust kings and manfully resisted their cruelty and greed. We have learned from the reports of many that you are doing the same now. Therefore it has pleased us to send you this letter, to console and exhort you, so that you may persevere in defending the liberty you have begun to defend against the most cruel king, and may not, as you have not done hitherto, yield to his fury and savagery.
>
> Since this same king is a most certain adversary and enemy both of us and of you, let us fight by common counsel against his savagery. For, with the help of almighty God, we intend to send our army next summer to our frontier, so that it may remain prepared there and await your instructions concerning when it should advance—if this seems good to you, so that, for your assistance, we may direct that same army against our common enemies who are residing on our frontier.
>
> The purpose is that, if Abdiraman or his army wishes to come against you, they may be hindered by our army, so that he and his army may not be able to come against you with aid. For we assure you that, if you wish to turn away from him and turn toward us, we grant you full use of your ancient liberty, without any diminution, and permit you to remain free from tax and tribute. We command you to observe no law other than the one by which you yourselves wish to live. Nor do we wish to act toward you otherwise than by honorably treating you as friends and allies in the defense of our kingdom.
>
> We desire that you may always prosper in the Lord.
>
> Thus far Louis to the citizens of Emerita.

To return to the point from which I digressed: among the honors of Emerita, the authority it acquired through the teaching of councils, the glory of martyrs, and the memory of illustrious men must rightly be counted. I shall treat each briefly, in my customary manner.

We know from the testimony of writers that several synods were once held at Emerita, of which the injuries of time have scarcely preserved even the names.

[Col. 0177D] Around the year 254, just as frequent synods were held at Tarragona, Seville, Carthage, Braga, and Toledo, so also at Emerita, concerning the question whether baptism conferred by heretics, with the intention of doing what the Church intends, is valid. It was concluded that it is valid and that those baptized by heretics should not be baptized again. This is attested by Julian, archpresbyter of Toledo, who lived in the year of Our Lord 1050, in his *Chronicle*. Baronius discusses the matter at length under the years 217 and 258; I shall not compile his material here.

Around the year 306 there was another synod of the three metropolitans at Emerita Augusta, concerning the question then greatly agitated in Spain: whether baptism or confirmation was the greater sacrament. The Apostolic See was consulted on this matter, according to the same authority. Pope Melchiades, also a Spaniard, answers this question in his letter to the Spanish bishops, written during the consulship of Volusianus and Rufinus, which is extant in volume I of the Councils, fol. 188, Roman edition.

Around the year 354 there was another synod at Emerita, as also at Toledo, Braga, Seville, and Tarragona, with a numerous gathering of provincials, concerning the reception of the lapsed who had already done penance [Col. 0178A]. The same authority reports this.

Around the year 385, Idacius, metropolitan bishop of the province of Lusitania (this is how it must be read, not “pontiff”), convened a council against Priscillian at Emerita Augusta in Spain. This is reported by Flavius Lucius Dexter in his *Chronicle*, with the agreement of Severus Sulpicius in book II of his *Sacred History*. I formerly asserted in my notes to Dexter that this council differed from the one extant in the collection of the most illustrious G. de Loaisa, archbishop of Toledo and primate of Spain, fol. 108.

The heading (*epigraphē*) of the council reads as follows:

> In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The synod held in the province of Lusitania, at the city of Emerita, which is recognized as its capital, with twelve bishops gathered together on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the eighteenth year of the most serene and pious King Recceswinth, era 701, that is, the year 667.

Concerning this, see Innocent III, Supreme Pontiff, in his letter to Peter of Compostela, volume II of the *Letters of the Pontiffs*.

So much concerning the councils. Concerning the martyrs, briefly: among them the chief place belongs to

[Col. 0178B]

> Noble by birth, Eulalia,
>
> Nobler still in the manner of her death,
>
> The sacred virgin adorns her own Emerita,
>
> From whose bosom she was born,
>
> With her bones and cherishes her with love.

Thus sings our poet Prudentius, both devout and learned, in his hymn in praise of her.

[Col. 0178C]

Hence Venantius Fortunatus writes in his *Book on Virgins*, book VIII:

> Eulalia raises her head from the city of Emerita.

Equilinus, book I, chapter 54, Mavinaeus the Sicilian, and others confuse her with the virgin of the same name and age from Barcelona who suffered martyrdom in the same persecution. This is not surprising, since in the Gothic Breviary of Barcelona the virgin is credited with deeds that belong to the Emeritan, as I have discussed at greater length in my notes to Dexter under the year 300.

Eulalia’s companion was Julia, her fellow virgin. The words are those of the ancient Breviary of the Church of Astorga:

> Julia, her fellow virgin, accompanied her. As they were traveling, Blessed Eulalia said to her: “Know this, lady sister: I am going last, but I shall suffer first.”

Therefore in the Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Ado, and the Roman Martyrology, on 10 December, Blessed Eulalia is said to have been accompanied by her companion, who remained inseparably beside her as she hastened to martyrdom—at Emerita, not at Barcelona, as Bishop Equilinus thinks in book I, chapter 55, and Volaterranus in book XVI of his *Antiquities*. These passages should be corrected from Vasaeus under the year 306.

Also at Emerita in Spain occurred the passion of St. Lucretia, virgin and martyr, who completed her martyrdom in the persecution of Diocletian under the governor Datianus, according to the Martyrologies of Usuard and Rome, 23 November.

Likewise, at Emerita in Spain is celebrated the feast of St. Victor the soldier, who, together with his two brothers Stercatius and Antinogenus, was subjected to various tortures and completed his martyrdom, as Ado of Vienne says on 24 July, and the Roman Martyrology. Thomas Trugillus, volume II of the *Treasury of Sermons*, and Ambrose, Moral, book X, chapter 20, attribute to Emerita the holy martyrs Hermogenes and Donatus, together with twenty-two others, concerning whom Bede, Usuard, the Roman Martyrology, and Wandalbert write on 12 December. Tradition says that they completed their martyrdom after being cast into a deep marsh; among the Emeritans the marsh itself is commonly called the Marsh of the Martyrs, and bears witness to the event.

[Col. 0178D] Similarly, Fides and Sabina suffered at Emerita, if we are to believe Diego Rodríguez de Almela—or Fernando Pérez de Guzmán—in chapter 5, title 3, book III, as well as Valerius Scholasticus and Vasaeus under the year 306.

Nor unjustly do we count among them the holy martyrs of Christ, Servandus and Germanus, sons of the martyr Marcellus and brothers of other martyrs, who were seized and led to martyrdom, as Isidore testifies in the Breviary. Concerning them, see Athanasius Lobera, chapter 26, part II of the *History of León*.

I shall not pass over in silence Decianus, concerning whom Julian writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 388:

> The memory of St. Dacianus or Decianus, a man of rank, Stoic philosopher, and citizen of Emerita, is still celebrated; Martial praises him greatly. He suffered at Rome under Hadrian, with four others, on the fourth day of July.

The old and new Martyrologies of the Roman Church likewise testify that Decianus suffered at Rome on the same day. He was a friend of Martial, to whom other Christians also were dear on account of their learning and influence, such as Marcellus Eugenius, Vitalis, [Col. 0179A] Pudens, and Claudia, together with others, as I have shown in my notes to Dexter. This is known from Martial himself, epigrams 9 and 39 of book I and epigram 59 of book II.

We also know from Martial himself, in epigram 39 of book I, that Decianus was a Stoic, when he says that Decianus followed

> The doctrines of mighty Thrasea and consummate Cato.

He also calls him an Emeritan in the same book, epigram 58:

> Gades rejoice in my delightful Canio,
>
> Emerita in my Decianus.

Among the purple laurels of the martyrs there also shines the radiant crown of the confessors Felix, who accompanied Eulalia and Julia on the estate of Rutianus, and Donatus the presbyter, by whom Eulalia was instructed from her infancy in the rudiments [of faith], that she might confess Christ, as the ancient Breviaries of Palencia and Salamanca testify. Concerning these men, see Moral, book X, chapter 20; Marietus, part I, book I, chapter 40; and Padilla, century IV, chapter 14.

Why name more? We owe many more to our Paul, whom I shall not repeat here. I shall add only the special love and devotion that the Emeritans have shown toward the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, from the earliest times. Julian writes in his *Adversaria*:

> From apostolic times there has been throughout the Spains the greatest devotion and singular love toward the Blessed Virgin. While she was still alive, pilgrims visited her every year with gifts, and there was a very frequent and celebrated pilgrimage to her from every part of the world. The following cities especially sent their pilgrims: Tarragona, Pamplona, Barcelona, Ilerda, Zaragoza, Braga, Clunia, Astorga, Toledo, and Emerita. The most holy Virgin blessed them and their cities, received them into her protection, and sent them home joyful and devout.

Emerita also produced others illustrious for military valor and literary renown. Although I shall now pass over them in silence,

[Col. 0180A]

> The fearless pen will bring to light
>
> The fame that survives.

Among the men distinguished by military glory was the illustrious Claudius, commander of Emerita:

> Let Fame speak of one for all.

Concerning him, see more in chapter 19 of Paul.

Among writers,

> If anyone, steeped in Cecropian and Latin Minerva’s arts,
>
> Adorns Emerita,

> I should perish if this were not Decianus.

Thus I borrow the words of his friend in epigram 40 of book I, by whom Decianus too is celebrated among Catullus, Maro, Livy, Naso, the Senecas, Lucan, and other men distinguished in writing, in epigram 62 of the same book.

Nor is Idacius, the Spanish bishop, worthy of no lesser fame, distinguished both by his name and by his eloquence—according to Isidore of Seville, chapter 2, and Honorius of Autun [Col. 0180B], where “Idatius” should be restored in place of “Anicius,” in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*. He wrote a certain book in the form of an *Apologeticus*, in which he exposed the detestable doctrines of the Priscillianists, together with the practices of their magic and the shamefulness of their lusts. He showed that a certain Marcus of Memphis, highly skilled in magical arts, had been a disciple of Mani and the teacher of Priscillian.

This man, together with the bishop Ursacius, was deprived of communion with the Church and condemned to exile on account of the death of Priscillian, whose accusers they had been; there he died on the final day of his life, while Theodosius the Elder and Valentinian were reigning. Concerning him, see what has already been said above, when we were discussing the bishops.

Let our Paul close the procession of learned men. He was long desired and praised by many; we now publish him, so that in him—for whose sake this little book, whatever it may be, has been undertaken—we may rest with God.

# In the Year of Our Lord 610–612. Gundemar, King of the Goths

[Col. 0179]

## Historical Notice Concerning Gundemar

*(Mariana, History of Spain)*

[Col. 0179B] Gundemar immediately obtained the kingdom of the Goths after Witteric was killed, in the year of salvation 610. Did the leader of the conspiracy undertake so great a crime merely in hope of reigning? Or did he do so with the support of the nobles, since he possessed singular prudence in war [Col. 0179C] and peace? I suppose that he was made king with the assistance of the Franks—although in matters so uncertain it is permissible to be mistaken—for they were hostile to Witteric. An annual tribute was customarily paid to the Franks by Gundemar, as is sufficiently clear from the letters of Count Bulgaranus, who at that time governed Gothic Gaul for the king. These letters are preserved to this day at Alcalá and Oviedo among old papers and books.

From this it may also be understood that Gundemar’s envoys were once violated by the Frankish kings, although ambassadors are sacred even among barbarian nations. Although it appeared that they had acted in such a way that they should be treated as enemies, when a new embassy was sent, the Spanish envoys were not even granted permission to meet the kings. Moved by these injuries, Bulgaranus prevented Theodoric’s ambassadors from entering Spain. Then, [Col. 0180B] when war was contemplated, he suddenly took up arms and recovered for the Goths the towns of Jubinianum and Corneliacum in Narbonnese Gaul. These towns had been ceded to Brunhild under the treaty made between Reccared and the Franks; after the Frankish garrison was expelled, they were restored to Gothic power [Col. 0180C].

We believe that Brunhild’s death, which followed not long afterward, made it impossible for the Franks to recover them by force of arms, since she left no surviving offspring. In Spain, Gundemar harassed the Vascones, who had again rebelled against his authority, as well as the commanders and forces charged with guarding the Roman frontier in Spain; the outcome of the war was favorable to him, in the year of salvation 612. He died at Toledo of an illness.

He reigned one year, ten months, and thirteen days. He left no known offspring by his wife Hilduara. At that time Heraclius, successor to Phocas, held the Roman Empire in the East. After Gregory, Sabinianus, Boniface III, and Boniface, the Roman Church was governed by Boniface IV. The Church of Toledo was governed by Aurasius, successor to Euphemius, Tonantius, and Adelphius [Col. 0181A], a man comparable with any of his predecessors in literary studies, learning, greatness of spirit, and integrity.

During his pontificate, and indeed in the first year of Gundemar’s reign, twenty-five bishops from various parts of Spain were summoned to Toledo in the matter of the bishop of Toledo and the bishops of the province of Carthage. The assembly was held in the presence of the king and at his command.

For Euphemius, bishop of Toledo, had imprudently called himself metropolitan of the province of Carpetania in the acts of the preceding Council of Toledo. The other bishops of the province of Carthage, which was much larger in extent, twisting Euphemius’s subscription into an opportunity for liberty, refused to obey the Church of Toledo. They were summoned to give an account and compelled to alter their decision. This was done both according to the rights of Aurasius and because judgment had been pronounced by the king and by the bishops, among whom were Isidore of Seville, successor to his deceased brother Leander; Innocentius of Emerita; Eusebius of Tarragona; and, unless the manuscripts are corrupt, Benjamin of Dumium [Col. 0181B].

The bishops of the province of Carthage concerned in the matter—fifteen in number—confirmed this judgment in a separate document:

[Col. 0182A]

> Protogenes, of the holy Church of Segontia; Theodorus of Castulo; Minicianus of Segovia; Stephanus of Oretum; Jacobus of Mentesa; Magnentius of Valencia; Theodosius of Ercavica; Martinus of Valencia; Tonentius of Palencia; Portarius of Segobriga; Vincentius of Bigastrum; Eterius of Basti; Gregorius of Ossonoba; Praesidius of Complutum; Senabilis of Elota.

From this it is understood that the metropolitan jurisdiction of Toledo once included many more churches than in our own age. For we are neither now discussing the primacy that it holds over all the Churches of Spain, nor was that the subject of the dispute then undertaken.

It is beyond doubt that in the time of Montanus, formerly bishop of Toledo, a council was held in that city by which the right over all [Col. 0182B] the Churches of the province of Carthage was granted to the bishops of Toledo. The very bishops whose case was being considered acknowledge this, as the acts of that assembly and the decree of these bishops plainly demonstrate.

[Col. 0181]

## Decree of Flavius Gundemar, King of the Goths, Concerning the Church of Toledo

*(Mansi, Councils, vol. X.)* (C)

[Col. 0181B]

> Flavius Gundemar, king, to our venerable fathers, the priests of Carthage [Col. 0181C].
>
> Although the care of our kingdom appears to be wholly occupied with arranging and governing the affairs of the human race, our majesty is then adorned with the most glorious reputation for virtue when matters belonging to the order of Divinity and religion are arranged according to the equity of the straightest path. We know that by this our piety obtains not only the title of a long-lasting temporal empire but also the glory of eternal merits.
>
> For certain men, in ecclesiastical disciplines, contrary to the authority of the canons, have used the delays of earlier times to claim for themselves license based on the usurpation of a former ruler. Thus some bishops of the province of Carthage are not ashamed, contrary to the judgment of canonical authority, to advance everywhere and freely into the episcopal office, through certain fraternities and conspiracies, men of unexamined character; and, having been elevated to that office, to despise the dignity of the aforesaid Church, which was itself exalted by the throne of our empire. In doing so they disturb the truth of ecclesiastical order and abuse the authority of that see, which the ancient judgment of the canons declares.
>
> We shall by no means permit this to continue from now and forever. Rather, according to the ancient authority of the synodal council, we establish that the bishop of the see of the Church of Toledo shall possess the honor of primacy throughout all the churches of the province of Carthage. Among his fellow bishops he shall surpass them both in the dignity of honor and in the distinction of his title, in accordance with what ancient canonical tradition has decreed concerning metropolitans in each province and what ancient authority has permitted.
>
> [Col. 0182B] Nor do we permit the province of Carthage to be divided between the rule of two metropolitans, contrary to the decrees of the fathers, thereby producing a diversity of schisms through which the faith might be overthrown and unity divided. Rather, as has been stated, this same see shall possess the dignity of the Church of the entire province and shall surpass it in authority, just as it is distinguished by the antiquity of its name and by the devotion of our imperial power [Col. 0182C].
>
> 
> [Col. 0182D] But concerning what was formerly recorded in the general synod of the Council of Toledo by the venerable Bishop Euphemius, namely that Toledo was the metropolitan see of the province of Carpetania, we correct the judgment of that same ignorance. We know beyond doubt that the region of Carpetania is not a province but a part of the province of Carthage, as the ancient records of events also make clear.
>
> Therefore, because it is one and the same province, we decree that, just as Baetica, Lusitania, and the province of Tarragona, as well as the other provinces belonging to the administration of our kingdom, are known, according to the ancient decrees of the fathers, to have their several metropolitans, so also the province of Carthage shall recognize and revere one and the same primate, whom ancient synodal authority declares, and shall honor him among all his fellow provincials as its supreme bishop. Let nothing further be done in contempt of him, such as the proud presumption of arrogant priests has hitherto attempted.
>
> Through this edict of our authority we now establish both a rule of conduct and a law of religion and innocence. Henceforth we shall not permit bishops to commit similar acts through disordered license. But through our clemency, out of regard for piety, we grant pardon for past negligence and extend the aid of indulgence [Col. 0183A].
>
> Although it is a great fault to have transgressed up to now, a more severe and inexpiable judgment will nevertheless hold those liable who hereafter attempt to violate this decree of ours, which proceeds from the authority of the ancient fathers, by rash presumption. We shall grant no further pardon for an offense once committed [the printed text here reads *admissi, adempti*, apparently corrupt]. If from now on any priest of the province of Carthage despises the honor of that same Church, he will surely undergo both the sentence of ecclesiastical degradation or excommunication and the judgment of our severity [Col. 0184A].
>
> For when we arrange such matters in the divine Churches, we faithfully believe that the kingdom of our empire is governed by divine guidance in the same way that, inflamed by zeal for justice, we strive both to correct the order of worship and to ensure that it endures forever.

# In the Year of Our Lord 612. Marcus of Cassino, Disciple of Saint Benedict

[Col. 0183]

## Historical Notice on Marcus of Cassino

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis.)*

[Col. 0183B] Marcus the poet, a disciple and intimate of Saint Benedict of Cassino around the year 610, according to Sigebert, chapter 33, abridged into a brief heroic poem the Life of Saint Benedict described by Gregory the Great *(Book II of the Dialogues)*, and added a few things concerning Saint Benedict’s miracles. It appeared in the third volume of Prosper Martinengo of Brescia’s *Ancient Poems*, edited by Arnold Wion, Rome, 1590, quarto, and in Mabillon’s *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, volume I, page 28. It had already been read by Paul the Deacon and Aldevrald, as John Baptist Maurus noted on chapter 3 of Peter the Deacon. The same Peter teaches that Marcus wrote about the situation and construction of the monastery of Cassino. Angelus a Nuce published it at the end of the *Chronicle of Leo of Ostia*, who mentions this poem at III.20. It is also found in volume IV of Muratori’s *Thesaurus Italiae*, page 605.

[Col. 0183]

## The Poem of Marcus of Cassino, Monk, on Saint Benedict

*(From Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti, vol. I.)* (C)

[Col. 0183C]

While the blind crowd was worshiping profaned images  
and believing that gods were those made by human hands,  
it had once built these temples on ruined altars,  
to which it offered bloody rites to obscene Jove.  
But, summoned and coming from the lofty desert,  
the holy Benedict cleansed this soil.  
He cast down the sculpted marble with its broken images  
and made the temple a dwelling for the living God.  

Let him hasten here who longs to see the heavens opened,  
nor does the difficult path remove a pious desire.  
Great things are always sought with difficult labor;  
the blessed life always has a narrow way.  
Therefore, when I entered here, weighed down by the burden of sins,  
I felt that the burden laid upon me had departed.  
I believe that I shall also enjoy that blessed life,  

[Col. 0183D]  
if you pray for Marcus, your own, O Benedict.

This place the foolish populace had once called a fortress  
and had made it sacred to marble gods.  
If someone had then designated it by its true name,  
he could rightly have called it Tartarean Chaos.  
To it, wandering with blinded minds, they went  

[Col. 0184C]  
to offer wicked vows to death-dealing Jove.  
But I think that it marked the summit of a foreseen hall,  
when it called the modern temples by the name “fortress.”  
Within them the gate of eternal Gehenna is condemned,  
and the fortress is now one of life, though formerly it was one of death.  
From it the door of the star-bearing heaven is struck,  
while the blessed crowd sings in angelic melodies.  
From it you converse with the true Thunderer, Benedict,  
guide of the little hill and leader of the sacred hermit choir.  
When, instructed from another mountain, you came to it,  
Christ was your guide, O leader, through the wilderness.  
For he led two young men to every fork in the road,  
that they might strengthen you in the path you were following.  
Here, too, he had foretold to one righteous man who was still alive:  
“Spare these places; another friend is present.”  
When you were taken away from it, the mountain shudders in darkness,  

[Col. 0184D]  
and itself grows pale, matching its own mists.  
The caves mourn and drip with abundant tears,  
and the decaying retreats grieve together with their hearths.  
The pools of clear water wept for you with genuine sorrow,  
and the loosened forest scattered its disheveled hair.  

[Col. 0185A]  
I would be thought to speak falsely unless, lest you depart alone,  
three ravens suddenly offered themselves to follow you.  
Here, too, the people seek you, shut away, with you as their witness,  
when they await the pious festivals of the sacred night.  
Like people deprived of someone, they persist in weeping for you with hoarse complaints,  
because they have been deprived of your companionship.  
But when you were brought here, the rocks gave way, and the brambles,  
and the dry earth uncovered wondrous waters.  
It is certain that the mountain of Christ commands the mountains themselves;  
the mountain itself subjected its head to your feet.  
And so that you might rise above its summit, holy one,  
it smooths the swelling ground with its bowed crest.  

[Col. 0186A]  
And so that those who seek you, Benedict, may not be wearied,  
it everywhere gently bends its sloping side.  
Yet the mountain itself rightly returns this honor to you,  
who, by adorning it, earned so great a blessing.  
You make gardens of pleasantness from what was arid,  
and cover bare rocks with fruitful vines.  
The rocks marvel at crops and fruits not their own,  
and the forest grows green with fruit-bearing foliage.  
Thus you direct the sterile deeds of human beings toward fruitfulness,  
thus watering dry hearts with a saving stream.  
So, I ask, now turn the malignant thorns into fruit,  
the thorns that lacerate the brutish heart of your Marcus.

# In the Year of Our Lord 615. Saint Warnaharius, Priest of Langres

[Col. 0185]

## Historical Notice on Saint Warnaharius

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis.)*

[Col. 0185B] Warnaharius, or Warnacharius, a priest of the Church of Langres in Gaul, was asked by Ceraunius, bishop of Paris, at the beginning of the seventh century to write the Acts of the Martyrs. The following still survive: the *Acts of the Threefold Martyrs*, that is, Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus, published by Surius on 17 January, page 392, and by Bollandus, volume II of January, page 76; see also page 73. Likewise, the *Acts of Saint Desiderius, Bishop of Langres*, who suffered martyrdom in the second century; these survive in the *Acta Sanctorum* for May, volume V, page 244. The preface of these Acts, addressed to Ceraunius, is also found in Gerard Dubois’s *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, III.6, no. 12. See the *Literary History of France*, volume III, page 524.

[Col. 0185]

## The Acts of the Holy Martyrs Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus, Threefold, by Warnaharius, Priest of Langres

*(From Bollandus, Acta Sanctorum, January, vol. II.)* (C)

## Prologue of the Author

[Col. 0185C]

### 1

To the holy Pope Ceraunius, whom I prefer to myself by the summit of the pontifical dignity, Warnaharius sends greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0185C] We shall discuss him on 27 September. We stated above, in the *Prolegomena*, §1, no. 3, when he lived.]

You never cease to be continually equal in merit to the persons of the most blessed bishops; hastening daily to adorn every aspect of priestly conduct with holy religion, you have traversed all the teachings of divine Scripture in your zeal for reading it. Now, to increase your praise and out of love for religion, you devote yourself to gathering in the city of Paris the deeds of the holy martyrs. Therefore,

[Note: [Col. 0185C] He is incorrectly called “saint” here and in many martyrologies on 21 June: Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, who, although he was not without merit toward the Church when he wrote the deeds of the saints, was nevertheless a defender of the Arian heresy. But when some people found the name of Saint Eusebius the bishop in the sacred calendars, they supposed him to be Eusebius of Caesarea, whereas he was Eusebius of Samosata, as we state on 21 June. Perhaps some, suspecting the name “Samosatan” because of Paul the heresiarch, dared to correct it as though it were an error. Consult Baronius in his notes on the martyrology for that day, and X.3, year 340, no. 42, where he sharply rebukes Sixtus of Siena, who dared to excuse Eusebius of Caesarea from heresy.]

you should be equated with the holy Eusebius of Caesarea in your zeal for emulation and be remembered forever with an equal gift of glory. Forgive our incompetence, since we are not sufficient to praise you as much as you would deserve in our affection, if eloquence were available to us. As you devotedly commanded, so receive the deeds of the three holy twin brothers, who attained their precious consummation of martyrdom in the suburb of the city of Langres, and also those of the most blessed martyr and bishop Desiderius of that same city, as the eager obedience of my service has desired.

[Note: [Col. 0187D] We shall give the Life of Saint Desiderius, Bishop and Martyr of Langres, on 23 May.]

## Chapter I. Saint Benignus’s Arrival at Langres

### 2

With Christ as our author, we are compelled to unfold more diligently the glorious contests of the martyrs, and we unquestionably confess that they were undertaken out of love for his faith. Therefore, it is fitting to explain rather than pass over in silence, with the fullest account, how the three twin brothers, the saints Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus, reached the rewards by which they attained the dignity of martyrdom. It is a matter sufficiently worthy of wonder and, by the predestination of almighty God, worthy of being set forth in many ways. Accordingly, as we pursue the sequence of this event and carefully weigh the benefits of the giver’s graces, let us publish its beginning.

### 3

Finally, Saint Polycarp, bishop of the city of Ephesus,

[Note: [Col. 0187D] Saint Polycarp was not bishop of Ephesus but of Smyrna, as we shall state in his Life on 26 January.]

perfectly instructed in the teaching of the most blessed apostle and evangelist John and filled with the Holy Spirit, desiring under the guidance of faith to enlarge Christ’s army, was sending his disciples through various parts of the world to preach confidently to the nations the word of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When he heard that, after the departure of Severus,

[Note: [Col. 0187D] Aurelian began to reign fifty-nine years after the death of Severus. Saint Polycarp lived during neither of their reigns.]

Aurelian the emperor had once again revived the most savage persecution of the wicked persecutor Severus, and that one ruler worse than the evil one had succeeded another in the kingdom, and that he had proclaimed before himself and his governors, and generally among the entire people subject to him, an edict and decree that Christians everywhere should be punished with various tortures, blessed Polycarp sent there for the sake of preaching the holy priests of God, namely Andochius and Benignus,

[Note: [Col. 0187D] We shall discuss Saints Andochius and Thyrsus on 24 September.]

presbyters, and Thyrsus, a deacon—men outstanding in virtues, overflowing with the love of God, eager for the contest, wholly devoted to undertaking the hardships of travel for Christ’s name, not slow to endure the dangers of the sea, gladly and eagerly desiring pilgrimages, and willingly leaving parents for the sake of Christ’s religion, desiring rather than fearing the punishments of torture and the suffering of blessed death.

[Note: [Col. 0187D] We shall give the Life of Saint Benignus on 1 November; but it too was written by a careless author, who states that Benignus was sent into Gaul by Saint Polycarp under Marcus Antoninus and, while Severus was raging against Christians, reached Lyons and finally completed his martyrdom under Aurelian. That Life also mentions Saint Leonilla and her three grandsons.]

[Col. 0187D]

### 4

These three men, obedient to the holy commands, boarded a small ship. Polycarp, holy among the saints, bade them farewell and gave them this charge:

“Go, brave men, fighting bravely in the strength of Christ. Through the holy confession of Christ, acquire many fellow soldiers, with whom, triumphing in victory, you may attain the glory of an everlasting name and dignity. May the fruits of your labor be filled with manifold abundance; through your acquisition of holy souls, may the seats of the paradise of the just rejoice greatly.”

With these and many other prayers Saint Polycarp accompanied them.

### 5

They sailed successfully and, by divine guidance, quickly reached the shores of Massilia. Going ashore, and traveling prosperously with the angel of God preceding them, they entered the city of the Aedui.

[Note: [Col. 0188D] That city is called Augustodunum or Augustodunus. In the Celtic language, as Ericus interprets it in the Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, it means “Augustus’s mountain.” Hence correct what Cornelius Grasius writes, namely that the saints proceeded to Aedua Augustodunum.]

There, by the Lord’s providence, they found Faustus, a man of the noblest family, distinguished by senatorial rank and elevated to the praetorian fasces. He received them most graciously as guests. When he learned that they were priests, he humbly requested that they make his friends or household Christians through the washing of baptism. He himself, because of the severe persecution, secretly worshiped Christ.

He also offered his son, the adolescent Symphorian,

[Note: [Col. 0188D] We shall discuss Saint Symphorian on 22 August.]

who, through the preaching of the saints and by divine predestination, was in due time to become a famous martyr. He earnestly begged that, placing him in the hands of the saints, he should be baptized by Saint Benignus and received from the sacred baptismal font by Saint Andochius. They, eagerly carrying out the work for which they had come and obeying the prayers of so great a man, fulfilled all the desires of his will through the grace of baptism.

### 6

After this, when the aforesaid Faustus had investigated more carefully the reason for his request through conversation with the holy priests, divine piety brought his sister and her grandsons to his mind. Then he said to them:

“I have a full sister named Leonilla, an illustrious matron and citizen of the city of Langres. She has, through her son, three twin grandsons, brothers born together at a single birth, educated in the liberal arts but still living in pagan error according to their paternal tradition. Their mother desires to join them to Christ’s army. Help, most holy priests, her devout purpose, and the family most noble in lineage, which you have begun.”

When he had said this, the holy men carefully considered the matter for which they had come. It pleased both of them that Saint Benignus should hasten, in accordance with God’s will, to illuminate the territory of Langres. Saint Andochius and Thyrsus, meanwhile, greatly increasing the village of Augustodunum through their divine preaching, were soon afterward crowned with a blessed martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian.

The aforesaid Faustus therefore sent Saint Benignus to his sister as a divine gift, just as he was. She received him with every reverence, as though he were manna descended from heaven.

## Chapter II. The Threefold Brothers Invited to the Faith by Their Grandmother’s Admonition and by Dreams

### 7

On that same day, therefore, the aforementioned grandsons were offering the customary profane sacrifices in a field called Palmasius before the image of the goddess Nemesis,

[Note: [Col. 0189D] The *Menaea* report that the Threefold Brothers sacrificed to Jupiter Nemesius, who is unknown to mythographers—unless the name refers to the fact that he possessed Nemesis in the form of a swan, when she herself had either been changed into a goose or transformed into an eagle by Venus’s deception. See Lilius in the *Castores*.]

and they had saved for their grandmother the remains of the superstitious libations. Inviting her to the banquet, they brought out what had been reserved. But she threw everything to the dogs and rejected it as dung.

Then she approached them from a distance together with Saint Benignus and began to speak as follows:

“Dearest grandsons, acknowledge that our Lord Jesus Christ is the true God, to whom the angels and every creature offer fitting service. He established the whole world and, by the sudden ordering of his word, arranged all the substance of things in due balance. By the same act he extended the height of heaven; he broadened the varied expanses of the earth farther and farther; by an instantaneous command he ordered the boundless ocean of the abyss to be gathered together and confined within shores. He adorned the sky with stars and, establishing two chief lights, decreed that they should adorn all that he had made in successive alternation and reveal everything clothed in light. He granted the whole sea as a dwelling for fish to roam. He clothed the entire earth with various trees and grasses. By that same ordinance he created all the creatures of the world, everything that grows and everything that lives.

“Finally, he formed the human being in his own image and likeness, enriching him with the singular gift of wisdom and understanding for this purpose: that he might carefully investigate the immense structure of the world and everything he had made, distinguish good from evil, and not put off the Creator through the negligence of ignorance. He must not offer worship to images made by human hands from various metals, devoid of sensation and deprived of every living breath, fashioned by diabolical invention for the deception of humankind. Indeed, he must not merely refrain from offering them the worship of veneration; he must also flee them, despising them as unclean in every abuse.

“For the devil’s perverse invention fashioned idols in this world; it deceived Adam, the first human being, who had been placed in paradise, through transgression. Therefore, dearest grandsons, abandon all idols consecrated to demons and confess without any uncertainty our Lord Jesus Christ, the Creator of all things.

“Believe that this holy man Benignus, whom you see standing before you, was sent to you from a distant region by divine mercy. Therefore attend to the words of his mouth, for the commandments that proceed from his mouth are God’s. Learn from him a doctrine richer than every gift and above all advantageous to your salvation.”

### 8

While holy Leonilla was preaching these most salutary words to her grandsons together with Saint Benignus, and the grace already inspired in their hearts was growing strong by divine power, they stood together, fixed in great amazement. Looking at one another and considering everything that had been said to them, they turned to their grandmother and unanimously said with one voice:

“Why have you kept so great and so excellent a matter concealed in silence for so long? Why have you hidden from us for so many years the way of truth and the splendid light?”

She answered them in gentle speech, raising her eyes and extending her hands toward heaven, and giving thanks to God:

“My son, your father, persisted in such hardness of heart that, plunged into a Tartarean seat and overshadowed by the darkness of sins, deprived of all wisdom and understanding and blinded by the counsel of perversity, he neither believed in nor ever wished to confess Christ the Lord. What benefit could divine speech have brought him, when the wickedness of unbelief possessed his heart completely and, surrounded by the darkness of idols, he could not see the true light? He himself made me maintain this silence until now, while I feared that, through his hostile persuasion, he might cause you continually to stray from the straight path.

“But when he had departed by God’s will, every obstacle was removed. Behold, now is the acceptable time. Open, therefore, the eyes of your hearts and bodies, looking rather toward heaven. Filled with the grace of the Lord Christ, root out from your souls the worship of idols, which is hostile to your salvation, so that you may reach eternal joys.”

### 9

When blessed Leonilla had told her grandsons these and many other things together with Saint Benignus, so that divine mercy might reveal in them the signs of faith, they recalled the visions they had seen the previous night.

First Speusippus said:

“In the vision of the previous night I saw myself in my grandmother’s lap. She poured milk from her full breast into my lips and said: ‘Speusippus, drink the milk, for when you enter the contest and struggle, the more you drink, the more strongly and swiftly you will conquer.’”

When Speusippus had said this, Eleusippus replied:

“Believe me also: I saw a vision of this kind. I saw someone seated in heaven upon a great throne, as though made of amber and gems, radiant with the power of majesty. His immeasurable splendor overshadowed my sight, and excessive amazement terrified my understanding with dread of heart. Then he called me to himself with a serene face and said: ‘Do not fear; you will earn the crown of victory.’”

In the third place Meleusippus explained his vision:

“I too saw some very great king holding extraordinary scepters. He summoned the three of us together to his service, girded us with splendid belts, redeemed us at a great price from the bond of captivity, wrote the rewards of our perpetual freedom in golden letters, and rewarded us all with unfailing gifts. In addition, to encourage me, he said: ‘Meleusippus, I have decided to place you three brothers in my palace and crown you together with eternal rewards. Your grandmother pours out humble prayers for your salvation every day and night, so that, walking along the straight path and freed from gloomy darkness, you may behold the true light and pass from condemnation to eternal life.’”

The king whom I mentioned told me these and many other words of encouragement in the vision.

O how wondrous, how harmonious, and how clearly indicating one single reality—and worthy of being kept in perpetual memory—were the visions that the three twin brothers, still placed in the darkness of night but already illuminated by the predestination of the grace of the Holy Spirit, deserved to see! Through their grandmother’s intercession, the Trinity was revealed by grace to these three boys before they had received the full teaching of Christ. With eyes partly illumined, they saw the Lord God before they fully recognized the Savior through the confession of their mouths.

## Chapter III. The Idols Overthrown and the Faith Publicly Professed

### 10

Finally, carefully considering the agreement among their visions, the preaching of Saint Benignus, and the prayers of blessed Leonilla, the holy Threefold Brothers, constantly instructed, considered attentively what they should undertake. They also desired, with the darkness wiped away, to behold visibly the pure light of radiance in the sight of daylight and to know the living and true God without any uncertainty.

Then they said to their grandmother:

“Tell us what we should do, so that your preaching, after all errors have been driven away, may advance us toward salvation.”

At this, blessed Leonilla rejoiced over the holy confession of her grandsons, gave thanks to God, and said to them together with Saint Benignus:

“Therefore keep all the divine commandments, believe without doubt that Christ, the King of kings, is God, and, separated from the abominable idols, offer yourselves to your Creator God.”

Saint Benignus taught them all holy doctrine and the perfect confession of faith in Christ, a true and manifest belief. When he recognized that they had received it completely through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, he likewise consecrated them through the grace of baptism.

Then Saint Benignus went to the fortress of Divio,

[Note: [Col. 0191] Divio, in French Dijon, the principal city of the duchy of Burgundy, is described at length by Claudius Robert in *Gallia Christiana*.]

where he gathered many fruits of his labor and, not long afterward, earned a martyr’s crown worthy of his many merits.

[Col. 0191D]

### 11

The three holy twin brothers, confirmed in every belief in Christ, ordered their servants to break the image of Nemesis and utterly overthrow the twelve temples that had been erected in their house. They also ordered the statues of the idols themselves, reduced to fragments, to be immediately scattered. The servants did everything their masters had commanded.

### 12

Meanwhile, swiftly spreading throughout the entire territory of the city of Langres, the report traveled everywhere, announcing that the three twin brothers, grandsons of blessed Leonilla and born of illustrious ancestry, had very openly turned toward the worship of Christ out of devotion. Trusting in Jesus Christ almighty, they considered the images of the gods worthless, despised them in every abuse, and had ordered them overthrown from their foundations together with the idols themselves.

The immense rumor grew among the people. The leading men, judges, and priests of the idols were provoked to anger, and, inflamed by extreme fury, they came from every direction to the children of God. Gathering together, the leaders said to them:

“What sudden madness has seized you? Who persuaded you to abandon the worship of our gods, which our ancestors and yours are known to have practiced from ancient times, thereby overturning the decrees of the emperors? The Christ whom you worship as God was crucified by the Jews under a sentence of death.”

Then the saints, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them:

“O madmen sunk in profound darkness, overshadowed by perpetual gloom, weighed down by the enormous burden of sins, condemned to the perpetual death of unending punishments, deceived by the error of the ancient enemy—why do you compel us to worship stones and other metals fashioned by human beings into human likenesses, which appear to possess no breath of life? They are nothing, they perceive nothing, and they are worshiped altogether for nothing by fools.

“The true and living God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, must be believed to be one in the Trinity of the Godhead and three in the unity of majesty. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself is God from God, Light from Light, Splendor proceeding from Splendor, who always is, always was, and will always remain himself without end. He made everything that exists in this world.”

[Col. 0192C]

### 13

Then the leaders of the people, the judges, and the priests who had come to the spectacle were deeply angered against the holy servants of God.

Quadratus, rising and filled with anger, struck Speusippus and Eleusippus in the face with his fist, because only those two had spoken.

Meleusippus, grieving, cried out:

“Why have you not made me share with my brothers in this gift of a blow? In them you displayed the desirable beginning of suffering, while, as though honoring me for your unbelieving deeds, you have separated me from the holy company. We are united in the confession of Christ; equally, through your faithlessness, we rejoice in Christ’s reward.”

Quadratus said:

“Today we intend to punish you for your contempt of our gods with various tortures.”

Eleusippus said:

“The greater the torments you prepare for us, the more greatly you strengthen us by God’s grace.”

Palmatius said:

“Unless we cut out their tongues at the roots, they will not cease speaking insult against us or our gods.”

Speusippus said:

“If your cruelty cuts out our bodily tongues, we shall proclaim the great deeds of God within our hearts, and your wickedness will never separate us from the holy faith in Christ.”

Again Palmatius and Hermogenes said:

“Unhappy men, you are rushing together toward the destruction of your death.”

Speusippus said:

“To die for Christ’s name is glorious. From there we shall reach eternal life more swiftly,

[Col. 0193A] where there is no sadness, but joys that never end.”

## Chapter IV. They Are Crowned After Various Tortures

### 14

When Palmatius, Quadratus, and Hermogenes saw that the saints continued steadfastly in the confession of Christ, they considered carefully what they should do and by what most grievous punishments they should afflict them, and by what kind of death they should condemn them, because of the merit of those who had gathered there, with the utmost cruelty.

[Note: [Col. 0193D] The Ripot manuscript reads: “because of fear of the Jews.”]

While they were carefully deliberating these matters, they ordered blessed Leonilla to be summoned privately, in case she might be able through her parental tenderness and persuasion to recall them to the worship of the gods, so that they would deny the majesty and divinity of Christ in every respect.

When blessed Leonilla had come to them, the judges said to her:

“Go to your grandsons. If you wish to save them and free them from the punishments of torture and the destruction of death, persuade them to restore the temples they destroyed and, worshiping our gods, offer the customary sacrifices.”

After they had said these and many other things, blessed Leonilla answered them:

“I will go and persuade them of everything that is fitting for their salvation.”

### 15

At last blessed Leonilla came to her grandsons. When she learned that they were persevering in the holy confession, she rejoiced with great exultation. She gave everyone sweet kisses, weeping for joy, and poured out many prayers to almighty God. Giving thanks to Christ, she said to her grandsons:

“No one in your family is found nobler, richer, or more pleasing in Christ than you. By your splendid confession of Christ you have forever illumined your entire lineage. Although placed in tender youth, by your wisdom you have surpassed all the elders of your ancestry. Through the service of Christ you have acquired an immense treasure richer than every price.

“Therefore persevere manfully in the holy religion of Christ. Let no adversity break you; let no threats or tortures frighten your minds, which are bravely armed in the faith of Christ. The kingdoms of this world, which are visible and end together with temporal life, are nothing. To desire the kingdom of God, invisible and everlasting, is perpetual, perfect, and above all advantageous fullness of wisdom. Through these temporal labors and suddenly passing punishments you will reach eternal joys.”

When she saw that they remained full of Christ’s grace and firm in their steadfastness, and that they were bravely keeping the faith they had promised, she commended her grandsons to God with complete devotion and departed from them.

### 16

When the judges asked whether they wished to agree with them and publicly confess the images of the gods, the brothers nevertheless persisted stubbornly in their love of Christ and absolutely refused to grant the petitioners’ request. Their hands were tied above and their feet below, and they were suspended from a tree. They were stretched by such an accumulation of tortures that they were almost thought to be torn apart from the very structure of their limbs.

Strengthened by Christ, however, so that divine endurance was inwardly supplied to them, they remained manfully in the confession and faith of Christ. While hanging amid those tortures with his brothers, Meleusippus taunted the judges, saying:

“Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, fastened with nails and to be worshiped in the Trinity, hung upon the holy wood for our redemption. From this we have merited receiving the sign of the cross. We three, his servants, hanging from this single trunk for his name, shall also become glorious martyrs. O blessed fruit of that tree which bore three martyrs consecrated in the name of the Trinity!”

### 17

When the judges saw that the saints were strengthened rather than saddened by their punishments, they said to them:

“You will not die on this tree as you claim you wish to do; you will perish in consuming fire.”

Meleusippus answered them again:

“Our increase in blessedness will be greater if, tested through fire, we pass to God and through this fire come from darkness into perpetual light.”

Then the judges, because of the fear of the people who were present, brought out wood and the other materials usually used to feed fires, and a great fire was kindled. With their hands and feet bound, the holy Threefold Brothers were thrown into the fire.

Christ the Savior was present in their midst. The bonds were broken, and the holy martyrs rejoiced in the fire; yet no burning touched them.

O blessed fire, which so cleansed original sin

[Note: [Col. 0193D] How did it cleanse original sin if they had already been baptized by Saint Benignus? Warnaharius transferred this account from the earlier Acts and did not consider what he had previously added concerning their baptism.]

and inflicted no loss or harm through its burning upon the limbs of the saints! Rather, the fire aided the saints. Through it the enemy wished to cause harm but could not. The unbelievers fed the fire more fiercely so that the bodies of the saints might be burned without delay; but divine mercy, turning the matter toward something better, prepared there an unquenchable light for the saints.

The burning flames rose higher, but, serving Christ’s work, they displayed the saints’ extraordinary glory, although the persecutors had wickedly prepared the flames for their destruction. The fire could not retain the strength to consume the limbs of the saints, because God’s power, out of its loving concern for his saints, tempered the heat of the vapor.

### 18

The wicked and unjust persecutors saw the holy Threefold Brothers exulting amid immense flames and remaining unharmed, although they had thought that they would see them consumed at once by so great a fire.

Christ granted the saints permission to walk in the fire, so that, when the unbelievers saw the divine mysteries, the sadness of their confusion might increase.

The wood and all the materials feeding the fire were therefore exhausted. The holy Threefold Brothers, standing in the middle as the flames died out, mocked the malice of the persecutors, saying:

“We have been given the power, if we wish, to depart from this present life to Christ. And if we still desire to remain, we have been permitted to mock your madness while living in this age. For it is better for us to hasten to his banquets, where the generosity of the giver never fails.”

[Note: [Col. 0194D] Other manuscripts read: “if we still deliberate.”]

After the fire had been extinguished, when the unbelievers approached the holy Threefold Brothers from a distance, they could not see any scars from the fire on the saints’ limbs.

But, so that those who desired it might not endure a longer delay before the martyrdom, and so that the saints might now receive from Christ, their rewarder, the imperishable crowns prepared long before, they saw choirs of angels ready to receive them and standing before their eyes. Then, immediately bending their knees to the ground and prostrate in prayer, invited by Christ’s blessed summons, they together breathed forth the holy spirit and are known to have departed together to heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0195C] Peter de Natalibus: “And angels were seen gathering their souls with much light.”]

### 19

Their bodies were carried away and buried by the devout at the second mile from the city of Langres, in a village called Urbatus, where two major roads join and other roads meet them from different directions.

[Note: [Col. 0195C] The Bruges manuscript of the martyrology reads: “in one.”]

Thus a ready devotion of the will and a very convenient gathering-place for travelers might always be present there, with crowds continually hastening from every direction to their threshold for prayer. There, too, whatever the devout pray for is granted daily by God’s generosity through the intercession of the holy brothers. Through them, assistance in healing is diligently supplied there to the sick; consolation that strengthens the sorrowful is granted without delay; and around their basilica a special worship is always offered, while the generosity of resources is daily increased for the better by the devout.

## Chapter V. The Grandmother and the Other Companions of the Martyrdom
20. It is also rationally fitting to add that which is recognized as contributing to the increase of the praise of the holy Twins and to the practice of religious devotion: through their holy acquisition, the number of martyrs was enlarged, by God’s inspiration. Finally, when a certain woman named Jonilla saw so precious a consummation of the martyrdom of the holy Twins, she rejected marital companionship, abandoned the sweet embrace of her little and only son, and, hastening at a swift pace amid the unbelieving crowds still stirred by the heat of persecution, cried out, saying:

“I too am a handmaid of Christ. Without any ambiguity I proclaim Christ, the living and true God. I utterly despise worshiping your shameful and vain idols.”

Immediately she was seized; and, because of the fear inspired by the surrounding crowds, she was suspended by her hair and afflicted with many tortures. Since she absolutely refused to be compelled to deny Christ, she was led together with Blessed Leonilla, the grandmother of the saints, to the place of martyrdom; at the aforementioned village of Urbatum, both women were likewise slain by the persecutors’ sword.

[Note: Saussay, in the *Supplementum Martyrologii Gallicani*, 9 January, writes that Saint Leonilla was buried at Dijon in the same crypt in which Saint Benignus had been buried by her.]

21. Neon, also the recorder and writer of this event, entered the midst of the persecutors’ crowds while handing the book to Turbon. Desiring to be associated with the most blessed military service of the holy Twins, he confessed the name of Christ. Immediately afflicted by the persecutors with various tortures and stripped of his temporal life, he deserved to be honored at once with martyrdom. Turbon likewise, not long afterward, perfectly instructed in the teaching of the most blessed Twins, was captured by the persecutors and himself enriched by the reward of martyrdom.

22. These events took place under the emperor Aurelian, with Palmatius, Quadratus, and Hermogenes as governors, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February. The finding of the holy bodies of the Twins, or the dedication of the basilica of the holy Twins, is to be celebrated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October.

[Note: Mombritius has “the fourth day before the Kalends.”]

Christ our God reigning forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0195]

# LIFE OF SAINT DESIDERIUS, BISHOP OF LINGONUM, BY SAINT WARNAHARIUS

*(Bollandist, Acts of the Saints, May, vol. V.)* (C)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0195D]

1. The testimonies of the most blessed Desiderius, martyr and bishop of the city of Lingonum, whose solemn feast we customarily celebrate as the yearly cycle returns, make manifest how great are the virtues found in God almighty’s elect and predestined priests. Although the rustic inexperience of the place is unable to publish his deeds in due order, he himself nevertheless, with God’s assistance, does not cease to reveal himself through his illustrious virtues.

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Maximinus is extremely confused and reads approximately as follows: “How great is the grace, bestowed by God almighty through the gifts of the blessed Desiderius, martyr and pontiff of Lingonum, which is made known as the yearly cycle returns and we celebrate his customary feast; the matter suggested . . . cannot be republished, yet he makes himself renowned through his eminent virtues, with God’s help, by which he does not cease to be made manifest.”]

[Note: The Swedish Royal manuscripts read: “For the works of goodness are innumerable.”]

For innumerable are the signs of his virtuous goodness; nevertheless, our slight eloquence can appropriately pluck only a few of them for expression.

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Maximinus has “in the abundance of speech.” The Swedish Royal manuscript has “our eloquence, poor in expression”; the Arras manuscript, “the poverty of our feeble eloquence in expression.”]

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Maximinus and Bellon read: “Because, inasmuch as the aforesaid martyr [is glorious] by divine rite in the office . . .”]

For in proportion as the aforesaid martyr is glorious through the divine gift, so much more does the writer appear, through ignorance, reluctant to recount his virtues.

[Note: Thus the Swedish Royal manuscript; other manuscripts have “entirely sluggish.”]

## CHAPTER I. THE INCURSION OF THE VANDALS. THE MARTYRDOM OF SAINT DESIDERIUS AND HIS COMPANIONS

2. At that time, when the barbarous and pagan ferocity of the Vandals had come to wage war against the provinces of Gaul, and, after conquering and overcoming the Gauls, was devastating the cities of Gaul exceedingly through military attacks and, driven by the desire for plunder, was ruthlessly laying everything waste, God’s will, together with the outcome of the event and of the journey, brought that wicked people, with their king Croscus, as far as the city of Lingonum.

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Maximinus has “Croco”; other manuscripts, cited by Vignier, have “Chroco” and “Caroco.” He was discussed above.]

At that time the most blessed Desiderius was exercising the episcopal office in that city, a priest preeminent in virtues. And although, because of the mountain rising opposite it, the city is for the most part naturally fortified in a lofty position, and the carefully constructed joining of squared stones makes its walls more secure, nevertheless, to test the faith of the aforementioned bishop and of those who, remaining steadfast in the holy confession of Christ, are known to have attained glorious martyrdom together with him, the multitude of Vandals surrounded the city on every side, and the city was enclosed on all sides in a siege of destruction.

[Note: The same manuscript has “oppositione montis”; other manuscripts have “opposito montis.” In the breviary, with these words omitted, it reads: “Although [the city] is fortified by its natural situation”; etc.]

Without delay the Vandals, attacking with greater ferocity, pressed on relentlessly in their cruelty to overthrow the walls with missiles, slings, arrows, and various weapons. In response, the most blessed bishop Desiderius, together with his priests and the other citizens, shouted from the wall:

“We are servants of Christ. We worship Christ our Lord, the living and true God, who established the whole world. Do not commit a cruel crime against us, by which you may provoke God’s power to anger against you.”

3. But since, by God’s predestination, the appointed day of martyrdom had arrived, terror and fear suddenly seized all the citizens together, and they no longer attempted to defend themselves with any boldness. Driven back, they fled within the walls, each ignorant of where he should go. The Vandals, however, bursting in at a headlong pace, entered the walls after breaking through the gates.

Others, having set up ladders, rushed upon the walls from different sides and sent fire down upon the citadel.

[Note: “Pergama” was the name of the Trojan citadel, and was also used for Troy itself; hence it is transferred here to any citadels and fortified places.]
