With swords and various javelins they struck down all the citizens in impious slaughter. No one’s age helped him; impiety spared no sex or stage of life. Its cruelty slaughtered infants hanging at their mothers’ breasts together with their mothers. One groan and lamentation of the dying resounded throughout the entire circuit of the walls.

4. Finally, the most blessed bishop Desiderius was found engaged in prayer and was brought before the gaze of the king together with the other Christians. Filled with pastoral grief at the destruction of the citizens, he did not wish to plead for himself before the ruler, but earnestly implored him to aid the perishing citizens, saying:

“If you are merciful, now spare them, I beg you, excellent ruler: spare the wretched citizens, and I humbly beseech you in every way to restrain the hostile hands of your men from such a slaughter of cruelty.”

To this the savage barbarian ruler, hardened by the harshness of his natural cruelty and swollen with the outcome of victory, gave the holy Desiderius a contemptuous reply in barbarous speech, which the blessed bishop could not understand in any way. Therefore the most cruel king also remained unaware of what the priest of God had previously asked.

The pious shepherd offered himself for his citizens, his neck prepared for sacrifice, so that the destruction of the perishing citizens might at least cease for a little. The impious ruler was moved by no compassion. Rather, inflamed by his persistence in cruelty, he ordered the priest’s head to be cut off; and at the same hour and by the same sentence he ordered many other Christians to perish.

[Note: Some manuscripts have “priests,” that is, together with others.]

For throughout all the citadels, those who persevered in the confession of Christ were struck down here and there in various slaughter on that same day. When questioned about religious devotion, no one throughout the entire city who said that he believed and confessed Christ was able to escape.

O city of Lingonum, which then suddenly remained desolate, why do you lament your citizens? You have greater reason to rejoice in them, since at that time you acquired so many martyrs for your protection. Do not reckon as anything the temporal loss that you mourn, while, without any price being assessed, you now possess—and will continue to possess—profits that will endure without end, in which you may rejoice.

[Note: Some manuscripts have “do not mourn.”]

You were then saddened by fires, swords, and plunder, when, with every example of humiliation, you were reduced to ashes; but from that very ruin you are now adorned and illumined with courage and fortified by the support of protection. From that cause you are and remain forever more glorious than other cities.

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Maximinus has “You were burned.”]

## CHAPTER II. THE PUNISHMENT OF THE SLAYER AND THE KING; THE MIRACLES AND MEMORY OF SAINT DESIDERIUS

5. The beginning of the blessedness of so illustrious a martyr, Desiderius, and the chief grace of his perfect love, shown in the shedding of his blood, divine mercy disclosed through sudden signs among his persecutors.

His slayer, immediately condemned in the sense of madness and seized by the fury of impatience, ran through the walls shouting terrifying cries and, at a full run, drove his head against the city gate. His brain was emptied by repeated blows, and his lifeless body was observed there by his terrified companions. When this was heard, fear and trembling penetrated the minds of all the astonished enemies, and for a little while they ceased to shed blood.

[Note: The Swedish Royal manuscript reads, “the barbarian impiety caused them for a little while to cease from shedding blood.”]

Finally, God, the just judge, compelled to avenge his holy martyr Desiderius and the other martyrs of that city, delivered the ruler Croscus to his enemies in the city of Arles.

[Note: Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book I, chapter 32, writes: “Crocus, having been captured at the Gallic city of Arles, was afflicted with various tortures and died after being beaten with a sword, deservedly paying the penalties that he had inflicted upon the saints of God.” Many similar accounts are reported from Aimon.]

After he had been captured and chained, he was afflicted for a long time by various tortures, until, through the most cruel and continual slaughter, he reached death according to his deserts.

6. The most blessed bishop Desiderius earned the worthy crown of martyrdom through his preceding way of life and devotion to good works, because he had first been found and proved righteous. The beginning of his life was marked by chastity, sobriety, generosity in almsgiving, mercy toward the poor, piety, uprightness of conduct, and steadfast patience. In all things he was found so acceptable to God that, joined to the company of many martyrs, he reached the kingdom of heaven with the greatest blessedness through his own acquisition.

In his own city the holy bishop was especially enriched by the gift of martyrdom; in that same city he was buried with the other martyrs in due veneration, on account of the benefits of salvation. How greatly he had been honored and loved by his fellow citizens in former times seems clearly shown by the signs at his burial place: so great was the love of the people within the walls that they received for burial the body of the priest whom they had loved greatly while he was alive, because of his goodness, gentleness, and steadfast holiness.

For if a sick person comes to his threshold, he returns from there, with God’s assistance, strengthened. If someone comes terrified by grief, through the intercession of the holy martyr he immediately returns from there rejoicing. If a blind, lame, deaf, or mute person, or one troubled by an adverse power, comes there, each receives without delay the appropriate healing and the remedies restored to him.

7. Among the many other distinguished signs of his virtues, the martyr does not permit treachery committed in his name to go unpunished. If anyone within the enclosure of his church, after invoking the name of Christ over his holy altar, attempts under the guise of falsehood to perform a lying oath, he is immediately condemned by the sentence of divine retribution.

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Maximinus has, “divine vengeance pursues him.”]

Faith is preserved through the faithful martyr. With divine grace assisting there, no one dares invoke or mention the name of this martyr in false oaths.

O martyr worthy to be preferred above blessedness, who has obtained such favor with God that even after death he can show that he hates iniquity and loves truth, detests perjury, and condemns falsehood. The pious shepherd, dead yet still caring for his sheep, urges good citizens to preserve the integrity of faith entirely without stain, for the salvation of their souls. He detests the wicked, exposes treachery, and gives particular examples of destruction so that they may amend.

8. Finally, illustrious priests, primates, and all the people of Lingonum: you possess within the city the outstanding protection of the illustrious martyr and of the multitude of martyrs joined to him, and a special guardianship of the city through him; outside it, you have the singular defense of the city placed before you through the three twin martyr brothers, and the city’s greatest adornment through divine reward.

[Note: As stated above, the three pairs of martyr brothers are honored on 17 January.]

Indeed, enough has been said in praise of this holy martyr Desiderius concerning his virtues; greater length of speech, however, produces weariness in the hearer. To confirm the truth of the testimony concerning the illustrious martyr, the gate where his slayer, guilty of the crime, killed himself by striking his head, has from that time provided no service to travelers entering, nor has it afterward opened to the people the customary passage for leaving the city. Rather, closed with stones, it remains condemned as a sign of the offense.

Finally, when the swordsman cut off the sacred body of the priest, the stroke of the sword penetrated into an open divine book.

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Maximinus has, “the stroke of the one striking, received in the divine book as an approach.”]

Although it pierced many leaves, the outpouring of blood did not injure the course of the letters by bringing destruction upon them.

[Note: The Swedish Royal manuscript has “the literary course”; the manuscript of Saint Maximinus has “the extremity of the letters.” The learned Ferrarius explains the whole matter somewhat differently and much more clearly from the Genoese records: “The book in which Desiderius was accustomed to recite prayers was so sprinkled with his blood that, although several leaves were stained by it, the characters nevertheless remained unharmed. This book is still shown to the present day.”]

The stain in the book reveals a certain sign of the blessed martyr’s passion and in no way disturbs the sequence of the writing for those who read it. The truth of the testimony, living in both things, is displayed to the people of the present and, by God’s ordinance, preserved for those yet to come to see.

The sword was permitted to possess its own sharp edge for enlarging the blessedness of this martyr and piercing the leaves of the book; but the omnipotence of the Lord did not permit the divine words inserted there in the written letters to be violated, for the glory of his martyr, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom are honor and glory, might and power, forever and ever. Amen.

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 615: SAINT COLUMBANUS, ABBOT AND CONFESSOR

[Col. 0201]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT COLUMBANUS

*(Fabricius, Library of the Middle and Later Ages.)*

[Col. 0201A]

Columba, or Columbanus the Irishman, founder of many monasteries, abbot in Gaul at Luxeuil and finally in Italy at Bobbio, of the Benedictine order, died in the year 615.

[Note: John Trithemius makes him a Benedictine in chapter 223 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and in book II, chapter 5, of *On Illustrious Benedictines*; Constantine Cajetan argues this vigorously in a book published in 1627, although Antonio Gallonio held otherwise in an unpublished work. On this, Richard Simon’s *Selected Letters*, volume III, letter 29, p. 67 ff., is worth consulting.]

Besides the writer of his *Life*, Jonas the Scot, in Surius under 21 November, and Vincent Barralis in part II of the *Chronology of Lérins*, the following authors speak of him: the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon*, volume I of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 377 ff.; Bernard in the *Life of Saint Malachy*, chapter 6, p. 670; and, among more recent writers, besides the editors and James Ussher, p. 18, on Irish writers, James Basnage in volume I of Canisius, p. 772 ff.; Mabillon in the second century of the Benedictines; and writers on the saints of Ireland, Thomas Messingham, John Colgan, and others.

Charles Le Cointe, in volume II of the *Annals of the Franks*, p. 98 ff., also discusses him. It is worthwhile to list separately the writings of Columbanus, published together at Louvain in 1667 by Patrick Fleming of the Order of Friars Minor.

[Note: See Wadding, *Bibliotheca Ordinis Minorum*, p. 272.]

**Monastic Rule.** Ten chapters, and a penitential book concerning the daily penances of monks, fifteen chapters, pp. 3 and 6; also in Luke Holstenius’s *Codex Regularum*, part II, pp. 88, 98.

[Note: These are also in Thomas Messingham’s *Florilegium of the Saints of Ireland*, p. 403; but in Goldast’s *Paraenetics*, pp. 166 ff., the final chapter is absent, although the Rule is there divided into fourteen chapters.]

The distinguished Cave was mistaken when he wrote that Columbanus’s Rule had been published by Canisius. It was published by Charles Stengel, with a fuller preface by Columbanus, in the *Corona Lucida of the Benedictine Order*, Augsburg, 1622, octavo, p. 128. The penitential book is likewise absent from Goldast and Messingham.

Abbot Eustasius defended the Rule of Columbanus against the accusations of Agrestius at the Synod of Mâcon, as Jonas the Scot relates in the *Life of Eustasius* in Surius and Henschenius under 29 March, and Sirmond in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 477. Some assign the Synod of Mâcon to the year 627; Mabillon, in the second century of the Benedictines, p. 119, assigns it to 624; Cointius, volume II of the *Annals*, p. 730 ff., to 623.

2. **Sixteen Instructions on the Faith and Duties of a Christian**, p. 9. In a manuscript a seventeenth is also added, but it is found after the two books on free will under the name of Faustus of Riez, volume XVIII of the Lyon edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 545. The fifth is also found in Messingham, p. 407, and was published under the title of an epistle by Ussher in the *Irish Epistles*, p. 7; Dublin, 1632, quarto; Paris, 1665, quarto.

3. **On Determining the Measure of Penances**, forty-two chapters, p. 21.

4. **On the Eight Principal Vices**, p. 23.

5. **Five Epistles**, p. 24: I and IV to Pope Boniface IV; II to the fathers of the Gallican synod assembled concerning the question of Easter; III to his disciples and monks; and V to Pope Gregory I, likewise concerning Easter. Mabillon rightly values these epistles highly in the *Italian Journey*, p. 216 ff.

6. [Note: Polycarp Leyser, *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, p. 177 ff.]

**Poems.**

a. An acrostic, “Columbanus to Hunald,” p. 33, beginning: “The times of life run through countless vicissitudes.”

A poem to Seth, in which he detests greed, begins: “Receive willingly, Seth.” In George Fabricius, *Christian Poets*, p. 779; Canisius, volume I, p. 779; Messingham, p. 411; Vincent Barralis, volume II, p. 113; and Ussher, p. 11, it reads: “Receive willingly, Hunald.” But in Sirmond, appended to Eugenius of Toledo, Paris, 1619, octavo, and volume II of his works, p. 908, it reads: “Receive, I beg, willingly.”

v. To Fedolius, an Adonic poem, p. 34, beginning: “Receive, I beg, what has now been composed in two-foot verse.” At its conclusion he indicates that he was seventy-two years old: “Now we have reached three times six years of the Olympiad.”

An epigram on a woman. Monostichs, p. 35, beginning: “Let her read these precepts devoutly and fulfill them in action.”

Goldast published these poems together and supplied them with notes in the *Ancient Paraenetics*, p. 47 ff., Insel, 1604, quarto. The learned Christian Daumius likewise presents them with his notes at the end of the *Distichs of Cato*, Zwickau, 1672, octavo.

Ussher had also published them in the *Irish Epistles*, p. 10 ff., except for the monostichs and the epigram. The monostichs are also found in Canisius, volume I of the new edition, p. 175, and thence in the Cologne and Paris *Libraries of the Fathers*, and in Messingham, p. 408. Among them are several pieces resembling Cato’s distichs, which Goldast attributes to some Roman named Octavian.

The same monostichs are read under the name of Alcuin in his works, p. 1715, and were published under the name of Aldhelm by Detrion, as stated above.

7. **A Rhythm on the Vanity and Misery of Mortal Life**, p. 36 ff., beginning: “This world passes away and diminishes every day.” It was first published by Ussher in the *Irish Epistles*, p. 9 ff.

Allatius notes in the *Urban Bees*, p. 74, that Constantine Cajetan intended to publish the writings of Saint Columbanus furnished with notes and arguments.

The following works of Columbanus are missing: a book of psalms or hymns, which Sigebert of Gembloux, chapter 60, testifies was written in polished language while Columbanus was still a young man. From this it might seem that Trithemius made a book of commentaries on the entire Psalter, which he says in chapter 223 was written by Columbanus in an elegant style. Goldast also mentions Columbanus’s exposition of all the psalms in the *Paraenetics*, p. 72.

Hartmotus, who was abbot of Saint Gall around the year 880, lists among the books preserved in the library of Saint Gall in his own time a **Book against the Arians**, mentioned by Jonas in chapter 29 of his *Life* and by Columbanus himself in Epistle 4. See Mabillon’s *Italian Journey*, p. 216 ff.

**Against the Adulterous King**, mentioned by Baleus XIV, 12, refers to Theodoric, king of Austrasia. Jonas reports in chapter 18 of Columbanus’s *Life* that Columbanus strongly rebuked him, both in person and by letter, on account of his relationship with Brunhild.

[Col. 0203]

# INTRODUCTION TO SAINT COLUMBANUS

*(Galland, Library of the Fathers, vol. XII.)*

[Col. 0203B]

I. Columbanus, father of very many monks, is said to have been born in Lagena, a province of Ireland, around the middle of the sixth century, as we learn from his deeds by Jonas, a monk of Bobbio, almost his contemporary.

[Note: Jonas, *Life of Saint Columbanus*, in Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, volume II, p. 3 ff.]

After studying the liberal arts, he devoted himself to cultivating the Sacred Scriptures.

[Note: Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book VIII, volume I, p. 191 ff.]

Soon afterward he went to the monastery of Bangor in Ulster and embraced the monastic discipline. After spending several years there, he departed from Ireland and went to Gaul, then being thirty years of age. In the kingdom of Burgundy, where Guntram held power, he founded the distinguished monastery of Luxeuil.

The date of his arrival at Luxeuil is not entirely certain. Cointius, however,

[Note: Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume II, p. 370.]

and after him Mabillon

[Note: Mabillon, cited work, p. 192.]

place it in the year 590.

Driven from Luxeuil, he withdrew to Italy and founded the famous monastery of Bobbio. After completing one year there, he died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, as Jonas writes.

[Note: Jonas, in Mabillon, cited work, p. 26.]

This date is also recorded in the ecclesiastical calendars, namely in the year of Christ 615, as Mabillon teaches after Cointius.

[Note: Cointius, cited work, p. 679. Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, p. 26, note b.]

In what year of his life the blessed man departed from the living, however, we do not know with sufficient certainty. We know only that, while writing a poem to Fedolius, he sang the following about himself:

[Note: Columbanus, *Poem* III, lines 160 ff., below, p. 360.]

> I would dictate these words to you, oppressed by grievous illnesses  
> Which I suffer in my fragile body and sorrowful old age.  
> For while the times glide onward in headlong course,  
> Now we have reached three times six years of the Olympiad.

“Thus,” says Ussher,

[Note: Ussher, *Collection of Ancient Irish Epistles*, p. 17.]

“Columbanus must have written this when he was either seventy-two, if we define the Olympiadic period as four years, or forty, if we define it as a period of five years, following the practice of certain Latins.”

Mabillon preferred to follow the latter calculation. For he says concerning the same passage:

[Note: Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, book XI, § 17, volume I, p. 281.]

“If an Olympiad is reckoned as five years, as it commonly is, Columbanus had then reached the age of ninety when he wrote the verses in question.”

I would be less inclined to accept this and would prefer the former method of calculation, together with the majority of learned men. The authors of the *Literary History of France* likewise held this view and therefore concluded from the words quoted that the blessed man was then seventy-two years old.

[Note: *Literary History of France*, volume III, p. 509.]

His sacred body was buried in the monastery of Bobbio. Mabillon, who visited Bobbio, recorded the following:

[Note: Mabillon, *Italian Journey*, p. 214.]

“In the basilica of the monastery scarcely anything remains of the original antiquity of the monastery except the underground crypts, where there are four altars, formerly five. In the principal one the body of Saint Columbanus is preserved inside a stone sarcophagus, which was fashioned in crude workmanship in the year 1480. Indeed, this is that splendid mausoleum of the once great abbot Columbanus, but it is preferable to any little golden shrine.”

II. The surviving writings of Saint Columbanus were published together at Louvain in 1667 by Patrick Fleming. First among them, therefore, is his **Cenobitic Rule**. Apart from Fleming’s edition, however, we have taken it from the excellent Holstenian *Codex Regularum*. The learned men recently mentioned rightly praise this distinguished exemplar and value it above the others.

[Note: *Literary History of France*, cited work, p. 511.]

This Rule comprises ten chapters, both in Thomas Messingham’s *Florilegium of Ireland* and in Luke Holstenius’s *Codex Regularum*. Here one should observe with Cointius that chapter 10, which is missing from the manuscript codices and from the exemplar of Saint Gall, exists in the Bobbio Codex; in Messingham it bears the title **On the Perfection of the Monk**.

[Note: Cointius, cited work, p. 371.]

In Holstenius, however, it is appended to chapter 9 as an appendix, while chapter 10 is entitled **On the Diversity of Faults**. This is what others call the *Penitential of Saint Columbanus* and distinguish from his Rule.

Both little works are further illustrated and supplemented in places by Cointius.

[Note: Cointius, cited work, pp. 371, 379.]

Nor should one omit what Mabillon observed: the Rule of Columbanus, as it has been published in print, is not complete if the chapter cited in the *Concordia Regularum*, chapter 74, § 10, from Rule of Columbanus chapter 33, belongs to Columbanus’s Rule.

[Note: Mabillon, note c to the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, volume I, p. 26.]

Others, however, observe that the chapter cited in the *Concordia* should be attributed not to Columbanus but to an earlier author.

[Note: *Literary History of France*, cited work, p. 510, no. 1.]

The same eminent scholar also says something about the *Penitential* of Saint Columbanus in the *Analecta*. The reader may consult the passage if he wishes.

[Note: Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 19, new edition, § 8, at the end.]

The Rule and the *Penitential* just discussed are followed by a book of the same holy abbot, **On Determining the Measure of Penances**, which Fleming first brought to light from an ancient manuscript codex. The same very learned men mentioned above make several observations concerning this work.

[Note: *Literary History of France*, cited work, p. 512, no. 3.]

III. Next come **Sixteen Sermons or Instructions**, together with the little book **On the Eight Principal Vices**, transcribed by the same Fleming from the celebrated Bobbio Codex. They are certainly most worthy of reading and everywhere breathe an extraordinary piety joined with equally fine eloquence.

The following words of Jonas in his *Life* seem to concern these works:

[Note: Jonas, in Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, volume II, p. 7, no. 11.]

“The venerable man acted so that, wherever he traveled, he proclaimed the evangelical word. For it was pleasing to people that what cultivated eloquence adorned, the doctrine of his laboriously prepared preaching, and likewise examples of virtues, should confirm . . . . . . Such grace overflowed upon the blessed man that, whenever he stayed for any length of time in anyone’s house, he fixed the minds of all upon the practice of religion.”

It is also worth noting that Mabillon read Instruction V, which begins, “O you life, how many you have deceived!”, under the title **Epistle V** in a manuscript codex of Saint Gall.

[Note: Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 19, § 9, at the end.]

Goldast had long before published it under the same title from that codex.

[Note: Goldast, *Ancient Paraenetics*, part I, p. 145, edition of Insel, 1604.]

Nevertheless, he acknowledged that no trace of an epistolary character appeared in it, while also declaring that he did not think he should depart from the authority of the very ancient codex, whose title read: “Here begins the epistle of Saint Columbanus, abbot.” Ussher likewise noted this and included the same Instruction V under the name of an epistle in his collection of ancient Irish epistles.

[Note: Ussher, *Collection of Ancient Irish Epistles*, p. 5 ff.]

IV. Following the aforesaid instructions are **Five Epistles of Saint Columbanus**, all marked by fervent zeal and written in Christian freedom. Fleming transcribed them from a very ancient but sufficiently corrupt codex of the Bobbio library. In his published edition, however, they are placed together without any indication of their dates.

The most learned men whom we have repeatedly mentioned pointed out this confusion.

[Note: *Literary History of France*, cited work, p. 513, no. 3.]

Accordingly, following their guidance, we arranged the same epistles according to their chronology.

The first in order is addressed to Gregory the Great; it was subsequently included among the letters of the latest edition.

[Note: Gregory, book IX, epistle 127, works, volume II, p. 1036 ff.]

Yet there is no letter among Gregory’s letters addressed to Columbanus, although a very ancient author of the little book on the life of Saint Salaberga, abbess of Laon, testifies that the same holy pontiff sent honey-sweet writings to the aforementioned father, Columbanus.

[Note: *Acts of the Benedictine Order*, volume II, p. 406, no. 3.]

The principal subject of the epistle concerns the celebration of Easter, which the holy abbot, together with his companions, insists should be celebrated according to the rite of the Britons—that is, according to the custom of the Easterners.

The learned editors of the works of Saint Gregory think that this epistle should be assigned at least to the year 599, because Columbanus refers to it in his second epistle to the Gallican bishops assembled on his account to settle the question of the celebration of Easter. No other memory of this council survives.

Mabillon says that the epistle was written in the twelfth year after Columbanus had begun living in the Vosges forests—that is, in the year of Christ 602.

[Note: Mabillon, *Italian Journey*, p. 214.]

V. Meanwhile, Abbot Columbanus of Luxeuil, in order to settle the dispute raised against him by the Gallican bishops concerning the celebration of Easter, wrote the third epistle in order, in the year 606, to Boniface III, Gregory’s successor. He humbly asked him to afford the solace of his pious judgment to one laboring in exile, so that, if it was not contrary to the faith, he might confirm the tradition of their elders and enable them to observe during their pilgrimage the Easter rite as they had received it.

“Whether Columbanus obtained a reply from the pontiff,” Mabillon says,

[Note: Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book X, § 36, volume I, p. 361.]

“we do not know. But it is clear that he retained his ancestral rite in the celebration of Easter, from his Epistle IV to his people at Luxeuil, written at Nantes when he was preparing to cross over to Ireland.

“Nevertheless, he seems at least to have abandoned this tradition when he came to Italy. This is suggested both by his Epistle V to Boniface IV, written from the monastery of Bobbio, and by the Synod of Mâcon of the Gallican bishops, convened at the urging of the monk Agrestius against certain distinctive rites of the monks of Luxeuil, in which there is no further mention of Easter.”

[Col. 0206D] VI. While Columbanus was staying at Nantes for three days [Note: [Col. 0206D] The same, loc. cit., § 50, p. 268 ff.], intending shortly to proceed to Ireland—as stated above—he wrote Letter IV in the year 610 to his Luxovian monks, whom he had left unwillingly, wishing them peace, health, and everlasting charity. When Attala received this letter, he preferred to follow Columbanus rather than remain at Luxeuil; he was later to succeed Columbanus [Col. 0207A] in the governance of the monastery of Bobbio. Finally, Abbot Columbanus wrote Letter V from the Bobbio monastery to Pope Boniface IV in the year 613, prompted by King Agilulf of the Lombards and Queen Theodelinda, concerning the Three Chapters. In this letter the holy man sends greetings to the supreme pontiff, the head of all the churches throughout Europe and the shepherd of shepherds. Mabillon discusses it at greater length both in the Benedictine Annals [Note: [Col. 0207B] The same, ibid., Book XI, § 4, p. 273 ff.] and in the Italian Journey [Note: [Col. 0207C] The same, *Italian Journey*, p. 215 ff.].

To these five Letters we have added a sixth, which Goldastus published [Note: [Col. 0207C] Goldastus, loc. cit., p. 153.] from two copies in the library of the monastery of Saint Gall. One of them is fairly ancient, but anonymous (*ἀνώνυμον*); the other is no less ancient, yet is more valuable because its editor was shown the author by its own index. Goldastus, however, did not perceive—and neither did the authors of the *Literary History of France* [Note: [Col. 0207C] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 520.]—that this letter corresponds exactly to that poem which the Lyon Library of the Fathers presents as added to other works of this kind [Note: [Col. 0207C] *Library of the Fathers of Lyon*, vol. XII, p. 36 ff.]. We ourselves discovered this later; for that reason we refrained from printing the poem.

VII. Four of his poems conclude the collection of the works of Saint Abbot Columbanus.

I. The first is entitled *Letter to Hunald*. Goldastus was the first to publish it [Note: [Col. 0207C] Goldastus, loc. cit., p. 47.]; but he wrongly divided it into two, supposing that one had been sent to Hunald and the other to Seth. In reality it is one poem, as learned men have observed [Note: [Col. 0207C] *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 518 ff.], and is inscribed to Hunald alone. Its first part is enclosed by an acrostic, which gives the names of both persons in the form: **COLUMBANUS HUNALDO**. This is correctly found in Sirmond [Note: [Col. 0207C] Sirmond, *Works*, vol. II, p. 908, Paris edition.] and Usserius [Note: [Col. 0207C] Usserius, *Collection of Ancient Irish Letters*, pp. 10–12.]. The acrostic is absent from the Canisian copy [Note: [Col. 0208B] Canisius, *Thesaurus*, vol. I, p. 779.].

II. Canisius took the poem entitled *Monostichon*, or *Monosticha*, from a manuscript of Freising [Note: [Col. 0208B] The same, ibid., p. 775 ff.]. Basnagius doubts whether it is genuinely a work of Columbanus, but without justification, as the most distinguished scholars judge [Note: [Col. 0208C] *Literary History of France*, loc. cit., p. 519.], and they also enumerate its various editions. On this matter, however, Fabricius should be consulted above all [Note: [Col. 0208C] Fabricius, *Medieval Latin Bibliography*, vol. I, p. 1129.].

III. The third poem is the *Letter to Fedolius*, brought to light by Goldastus from a Saint Gall manuscript [Note: [Col. 0208C] Goldastus, loc. cit., p. 52.] and incorporated by Usserius into his Irish Letters. In presenting it, he writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0208C] Usserius, loc. cit., p. 13.]:

> “It is composed in two-foot Adonic verses, with every opportunity for elision of syllables carefully avoided, so that the poem might consistently consist of five syllables (*πεντασύλλαβον*). Six hexameters are also appended, in the third from the end of which the author reveals his age.”

We ourselves noted this above, in § 1.

IV. Finally, there is an *Epigram on Women*, which we likewise acknowledge as received from Goldastus.

There also exists a *Rhythm of the same Saint Columbanus on the Vanity and Misery of Mortal Life*. It begins: “This world passes away,” and so forth. It appears in Usserius [Note: [Col. 0208C] Usserius, loc. cit., pp. 6–7.] and in the Lyon Library of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0208C] *Library of the Fathers of Lyon*, vol. XII, p. 36.]. In fact, however, this rhythm is altogether identical with Letter VI and has therefore been omitted by us, as we noted above concerning that letter.

For the rest, we have done our best to arrange in a better order the works of Saint Columbanus that we have so far reviewed, and occasionally either to restore or to elucidate them with annotations.

[Col. 0207]

# CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

*(Brokie, Book of Rules, vol. I)*

Among the other propagators of monastic life who flourished in the sixth century, Saint Abbot Columbanus held a most celebrated name. He was a Scot by nation and was educated in the monastery of Bangor; but whether he came from Irish Bangor or from one of the Bangor monasteries of modern Scotland is vigorously disputed by the inhabitants of the two peoples.

For we find several monasteries called Bangor. The first was situated in modern Wales and was celebrated by the Venerable Bede in his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*; perhaps the others derived their origin from it. Nevertheless, the modern Scots contend for the antiquity of their own Bangor monastery, situated on the bank of the River Dee and founded by Saint Ternan, a disciple of Saint Palladius, as we are informed by the *Scottish Monastic History*.

As for Irish Bangor, we likewise consider it to have been the true monastery of Saint Columbanus, since Saint Bernard testifies in the *Life of Saint Malachy* that he laid the foundations of his monastic life there. Yet that most holy abbot does not distinguish the two peoples very precisely and often confuses the Scots with the Irish.

Whatever the truth may be, Saint Columbanus withdrew into Gaul with a company of Scottish and Irish monks around the year 590, at the age of thirty. There he built the monastery of Luxeuil, into which he introduced the strict discipline of the Scottish monks, as an uncompromising defender of the traditions of his fathers.

When, therefore, he saw many monks gathering at Luxeuil from neighboring regions, he composed this present Rule for them and somewhat moderated the severe Scottish discipline. Nevertheless, he commanded his monks to maintain perpetual fasting and silence and complete obedience, since he wished the governance of the monastery to depend solely upon the abbot’s will.

This Rule is primitive and original, having no connection with other rules, although the Benedictine Rule had already been promulgated among the Gauls by Saint Maurus several years before Saint Columbanus’s arrival. For nowhere does it mention the ancient rules; only in chapter 7 does it speak of a thousand Catholic monks under one archimandrite, who uniformly, whenever they assemble at night, sing twelve psalms, whether the nights are long or short.

There he plainly speaks of the psalmody practiced in the Columbanian monasteries founded throughout modern Scotland and Ireland by Saint Columba the Great, patriarch of the Scottish monks. To him also we attribute the Rule of a certain Father.

Meanwhile, this Rule of Saint Columbanus, consisting of nine chapters—to which Holstenius added a tenth—does not provide all the precepts necessary for the perfection of monastic life, but prescribes only general statutes. Thus he seems to have directed his monks more by living speech than by a written Rule.

Despite these limitations, the monastic discipline propagated by Saint Columbanus among the Gauls made remarkable progress even after his expulsion from Luxeuil and his withdrawal into Italy, where he again founded the monastery of Bobbio and died there in great holiness, leaving his monks the sacred relic of his remains as a token of love and reverence.

This monastic Rule flourished and was observed for many years not only in the monasteries founded by him at Luxeuil, Bobbio, Anegray, Fontaine, and elsewhere, but also in other monasteries established by his most holy disciples Gallus and Magnoaldus.

Nor did these monasteries embrace the Rule of Saint Benedict alone very quickly, but only gradually. Old statutes do not suddenly fall into disuse among monks. Thus, in the writings of the renowned Benedictine scholars Mabillon and Calmet, we find that this Rule of Saint Columbanus continued to be observed, even toward the end of the seventh century, together with the Rule of Saint Benedict in the monasteries mentioned above and in many others. Eventually, however, it was compelled to yield to the Benedictine Rule alone as the more perfect rule, so that at the beginning of the eighth century no rule other than that of Saint Benedict was observed in any monastery.

Appended to this Rule is also Saint Columbanus’s *Penitential Book*, which prescribes regular penalties for every, even the slightest, fault committed against the Rule and the custom of the monastery. These penalties, although quite severe for such minor offenses, seem to have no connection with the Rule itself or with other written norms of monastic life. Accordingly, the penalties inflicted upon the monks arose from the strict Scottish discipline, as will be evident from the *Monastic Order* of the Scottish monks, or Culdees, at Culross, included among the additions.

That this *Penitential Book* was taken from the common discipline of the Scottish monks may be obvious to anyone even slightly acquainted with monastic history, since this very book is usually called in ancient manuscripts *The Coenobitic Rule of the Scottish Fathers*, and sometimes *The Rule of the Irish Brothers*. For the monks of both peoples shared the practice of inflicting strict penalties for the smallest faults.

[Col. 0209]

# THE COENOBITIC RULE OF SAINT COLUMBANUS, ABBOT AND CONFESSOR

*(Galland’s Library of the Fathers, vol. XII.) (C, S)*

## CHAPTER ONE. On Obedience

[Col. 0209A]

First of all we are taught to love God with all our heart and with all our mind (Matthew 22:37) and with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. Next, at the first word of an elder, everyone who hears must rise to obey, because obedience is offered to God, as our Lord Jesus Christ says: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke 10:28).

Therefore, if anyone hears a word and does not rise immediately, he is to be judged disobedient. Whoever contradicts incurs the crime of stubbornness; and therefore he is guilty not only of disobedience but also, by opening the way to contradiction for others, is to be regarded as the destroyer of many.

[Col. 0209B] But if anyone murmurs, he too is to be considered disobedient, as though he were not obeying willingly. For this reason his work is to be rejected until his good will becomes known.

But to what extent is obedience defined? Certainly, it is commanded even unto death, because Christ obeyed the Father for us unto death, as he himself makes known to us through the Apostle, saying:

> “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

Therefore nothing is to be refused by the obedient, the true disciples of Christ, however hard and difficult it may be; rather, it must be accepted with fervor and [Col. 0209C] joy. For if obedience is not of this kind, it will not be acceptable to God, who says: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:27). And therefore he says of the worthy disciple: “Where I am, there also will my servant be with me” (John 12:25).

## CHAPTER TWO. On Silence

The rule of silence is to be carefully observed, because it is written: “The cultivation of justice is silence and peace” (Isaiah 32:27). Therefore, so that guilt may not be incurred through talkativeness, except in matters of usefulness and necessity, one must keep silent, because according to Scripture, “In much speaking there will not be lacking sin” (Proverbs 10:19).

For this reason the Savior says: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12:37). Those who refused to speak what was right when they could have done so will rightly be condemned; but they preferred to speak, with babbling verbosity, things evil, unjust, impious, vain, insulting, uncertain, [Col. 0210B] false, contentious, abusive, disgraceful, fanciful, blasphemous, harsh, and devious.

Monks must therefore be silent about such matters and such people, and speak with caution and judgment, lest either slander or inflated contradiction break forth into vicious loquacity.

## CHAPTER THREE. On Food and Drink

The monks’ food should be poor and taken in the evening, avoiding satiety; and their drink should avoid drunkenness, so that it may sustain without harming. Vegetables, legumes, flour mixed with water, with a little bread baked in ashes, should be used so that the belly is not burdened and the mind suffocated.

For those who desire eternal rewards should be concerned only with utility and necessity. The use of food must therefore be moderated just as labor must be moderated; for this is true discretion: that the possibility of spiritual progress be maintained together with abstinence that mortifies the flesh.

If abstinence exceeds the proper measure, it will be vice, not virtue. Virtue endures and contains many good things. Therefore one must fast daily, just as one must pray daily, labor daily, and read daily.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On Poverty and on Trampling Down Greed

The monks for whom the world has been crucified through Christ, and they themselves to the world (Galatians 6:14), must trample down greed. Indeed, it is blameworthy for them not only to possess superfluous things but even to desire them. What is sought in them is not wealth but intention. They have left everything and follow Christ the Lord with the cross of fear each day; in heaven they have treasures (Matthew 16:34).

Since, therefore, they are to possess much in heaven, they ought to be content on earth with the small and meager allotment of necessity, [Col. 0211B] knowing that greed is leprosy for monks, who imitate the sons of the prophets, and betrayal and destruction for the disciples of Christ; it is also death for those who follow the apostles with divided loyalty.

Thus nakedness and contempt for possessions are the monks’ first perfection; the second is the cleansing of vices; the third, and most perfect, is continual love of God and constant love of divine things, which takes the place of forgetfulness of earthly things.

Since this is so, we need few things, according to the Lord’s word (Luke 10:42), or even one. For few things are truly necessary, without which life cannot be carried on—or even one, as food, literally speaking. But by God’s grace we need purity of understanding, so that we may spiritually comprehend what those few things of charity are which the Lord proposes to Martha.

## CHAPTER FIVE. On Trampling Down Vanity

[Col. 0211C]

How dangerous vanity is is shown in a few words of the Savior. When his disciples were rejoicing in vanity, he said to them: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). And to the Jews who were at one time justifying themselves he said: “What is exalted among human beings is an abomination in the sight of the Lord” (Luke 16:15).

From these words and from the example of that famous Pharisee who justified himself (Luke 18:11 ff.), it is inferred that vanity and elevated boasting destroy all good things. The Pharisee’s virtues, praised vainly, perished, while the publican’s confessed sins disappeared.

Therefore let no grand word come from a monk’s mouth, lest his great labor perish.

## CHAPTER SIX. On Chastity

[Col. 0211D]

A monk’s chastity is judged in his thoughts. To the disciples who approached to hear him, the Lord said: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:18).

When the man consecrated to God considers her face, he must fear that he may find in his soul what he ought to abhor; otherwise, according to Saint Peter’s judgment, he may have “eyes full of lust and adultery” (2 Peter 2:14).

What does bodily virginity profit if the mind is not virgin? For God is spirit (John 4:24), and he dwells in the spirit and in the mind when he sees it undefiled: when there is in it no adulterous [Col. 0212A] thought, no stain of a polluted spirit, and no blemish of sin.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. On the Course of the Psalms

Concerning the synaxis—that is, the course of psalms and prayers according to the canonical order—certain distinctions must be made, because different traditions have been handed down by different people concerning it. Therefore I too shall set forth the same matter in writing in various ways, according to the character of life and the succession of seasons.

It ought not to be uniform with the alternating seasons. It should be longer during long nights and shorter during short nights. Thus, according to the tradition of our elders, beginning on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, when the nights gradually begin to lengthen, the course increases from twelve choirs of the shortest form, on the night of Saturday or Sunday, until the beginning of winter, that is, the Kalends of November. At that time they sing twenty-five antiphons of the psalms, of the same number; three singers always take the place of two psalmists.

Thus, across the two nights just mentioned, they sing the whole Psalter in twelve choirs, moderating the remaining nights throughout the winter. When winter has ended, through spring three psalms are gradually withdrawn each week, so that only twelve antiphons remain for each night. This is the winter daily course of thirty-six psalms; twenty-four are used throughout spring and summer and until the autumnal equinox, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of October. At that time the form of the synaxis is like that of the spring equinox, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, while through reciprocal changes it gradually increases and decreases.

Therefore the vigil must be considered according to one’s strength, especially since the author of our salvation commands us to watch and pray at all times (Luke 21:36), and Paul commands us to pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17).

But since the order of the canonical prayers must be known—at which all should assemble together at the appointed hours for prayer, and after those hours have been completed each should pray in his own cell—during the day three psalms have been assigned by our elders to each hour, with intervening verses increasing according to the work being done: first for our own sins, then for all Christian people; next for priests and the other orders of the sacred people consecrated to God; finally for those who give alms; afterward for the peace of kings; and lastly for enemies, so that God may not count against them as sin the fact that they persecute and slander us, because they do not know what they are doing (Acts 7:59).

At the beginning of the night twelve psalms are sung, and likewise twelve at midnight. At matins, twenty-four are arranged for the shorter nights, as has been said; more are always assigned to the vigils of Sunday and Saturday night. During these, seventy-five are sung individually in one course.

This has been said according to the common synaxis. But the true tradition of prayer is that the capacity of the person appointed to it should prevail without weariness of desire, whether his own degree of perfection permits it, or the capacity of his mind, with consideration of his needs, or the quality of his life can accommodate it.

The amount should vary according to what each person’s fervor demands—if he is free and alone, or if the extent of his learning requires it, or if leisure, the greatness of his study, the nature of his work, or the differences of age permit it. Thus the perfection of one and the same thing must be assessed in different ways, because it is divided with the labor of worship.

Therefore, although the length of standing or singing may vary, there will nevertheless be equality in the perfection of prayer in the heart and in the mind’s continual attention to God.

There are, however, certain Catholics for whom the same canonical number of twelve psalms applies in short and long nights alike. But they render this canon in four periods during the night: at the beginning of the night, at midnight, at cockcrow, and at matins.

This course, just as it appears small to some in winter, is found sufficiently burdensome and even heavier in summer, when the frequent services during the shortness of the night cause not so much weariness as exhaustion.

On the most reverend nights—that is, Sunday and Saturday—thirty-six psalms are appointed at matins. Their large number has imposed this canonical number upon many for holy conduct with a kind of sweet delight, as well as the rest of the discipline. Under their rule, no one is found to be weary.

Although their number is so great that a thousand abbots are said to have lived under one archimandrite, no quarrel between two monks is reported to have appeared there from the beginning of the coenobium. It is clear that this could not have been so without God dwelling there, who says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (2 Corinthians 6:16; Leviticus 26:12).

Therefore they rightly increased, and every day, thanks be to God, they increase—among whom God dwells. May we deserve through their merits to be saved by our Savior. Amen.

## CHAPTER EIGHT. On Discernment

The necessity of discernment for monks is shown by the error of many and demonstrated by the downfall of some. Those who began without discernment and lived without guiding knowledge were unable to bring their lives to a praiseworthy end.

For just as error occurs when people travel without a road, so excess is immediately present in those who live without discernment. It is always opposed to the virtues, which are placed in the middle between either extreme.

The impact of this danger is evident, since along the straight path of discernment hostile perversity places obstacles and the stumbling blocks of various [Col. 0213D] errors.

God must therefore be asked to grant the light of true discernment for the illumination of this life, surrounded on both sides by the deepest darkness of the world, so that his true worshipers may escape these darknesses and reach him without error.

The word “discernment” (*discretio*) derives from “to discern” (*discernere*), because it itself distinguishes within us between good and evil and also between what is intermediate and what is perfect.

From the beginning these were divided, like light and darkness—both good and evil—after evil began through the devil by the corruption of good; but first through God’s illumination and afterward through his division.

Thus Abel first chose good, while the impious Cain fell into evils [Note: [Col. 0213D] “Evils.” It seems that the reading should be: “into evils” (*in mala*).]

God made all the good things that he created, but the devil sowed evil over them by deceitful cunning and the underhanded persuasion of reckless ambition.

What, then, are those good things? They are those that remained whole and incorrupt, as they were created: those which God alone created and prepared, according to the Apostle (Ephesians 2:10), so that we might walk in them. They are the good works in which we were created in Christ Jesus: goodness, integrity, piety, justice, truth, mercy, charity, saving peace, spiritual joy, and the fruit of the Spirit.

All these things, together with their fruits, are good. Their opposites are evil: wickedness, corruption, impiety, injustice, falsehood, avarice, hatred, discord, bitterness, and their many fruits, which arise from them.

For innumerable things are generated from both opposing classes, that is, from good and evil. Whatever departs from created goodness and integrity is the first evil, as pride is the first form of wickedness. Opposed to it is the humble recognition of pious goodness, which acknowledges and glorifies its Creator; this is the first good of a rational creature.

So too the other things gradually grew through their twofold divisions into an immense forest of names.

Since this is so, those who have God’s help must hold firmly to good things, praying always through prosperity and adversity, lest in prosperity we be exalted into vanity or in adversity cast down into despair.

We must therefore restrain ourselves from both dangers—that is, from every excess—through glorious moderation and true discernment. Discernment clings to Christian humility and opens the way of perfection to the true soldiers of Christ and to those who fear God.

We must always discern rightly in doubtful matters and divide justly between good and evil everywhere: whether between the two externally, or within, between body and soul; between works and habits; between care and repose; or between public and private matters.

Evil must likewise be avoided: pride, envy, falsehood, corruption, impiety, evil conduct, transgression, gluttony, fornication, greed, anger, sadness, instability, vainglory, arrogance, and slander.

The good of the virtues must also be pursued: humility, kindness, purity, obedience, abstinence, chastity, generosity, patience, joy, stability, fervor, diligence, watchfulness, and silence.

These must be established in the action of accustomed work through the fortitude that endures and the moderation that governs, seeking everywhere what is sufficient according to the capacity of our effort.

For when what is sufficient is not enough for someone, it is beyond doubt that he has exceeded the measure of discernment. Whatever exceeds that measure is plainly a vice.

Thus, between the small and the excessive there is a rational measure in the middle. It always recalls us from every excess on either side; it is placed in every matter, securing everywhere what necessity requires and avoiding what irrational desire makes superfluous.

This measure of true discernment, weighing all our actions in a just balance, will never allow us to depart from what is right. If we always follow it directly as a guide, we will not fall into error.

Since we must always restrain ourselves on both sides, according to the saying: “Keep yourselves to the right and to the left” (Deuteronomy 5:32; 2 Corinthians 6:7), we must always proceed straight ahead through discernment—that is, by the light of God—frequently saying and singing the victorious verse of the Psalmist:

> “My God, enlighten my darkness, for in you I shall be delivered from temptation” (Psalm 18:29–30).

“For human life upon the earth is a temptation” (Job 7:1).

## CHAPTER NINE. On Mortification

[Col. 0215A]

A very large part of the monks’ Rule is mortification. Through sacred Scripture they are commanded: “Do nothing without counsel” (Ecclesiasticus 32:24).

Therefore, if nothing is to be done without counsel, everything must be referred to counsel. Moses likewise commands: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you” (Deuteronomy 32:7).

Although this discipline may seem harsh to those who are harsh—that a person should always depend upon another’s word—it will nevertheless be found sweet and secure by those who fear God, if it is preserved entirely and not partially. For nothing is sweeter than security of conscience, and nothing is safer than freedom from punishment of soul.

No one can give this to himself independently, because it properly belongs to the examination of others. This protects a person from fear of judgment: the judgment of the judge has already examined him, and the burden of another’s weight is imposed upon the judge, who bears the whole danger of what he undertakes.

For, as it is written, the danger of the judge is greater than that of the person judged (Wisdom 6:6–7).

Therefore whoever always asks and preserves the answer will never err. For even if the answer of the other should be mistaken, the faith of the believer and the labor of the obedient will not err, nor will they be deprived of the reward of the one who asks.

If the person who ought to have asked examines something on his own, he is thereby proved to have erred, because he presumed to judge when he ought to have asked. Even if his decision was correct, it will be reckoned wrong to him, because by this he departed from what was right: he whose duty is only to obey dares to judge nothing by himself.

Since this is so, monks must everywhere avoid proud liberty and learn true humility, obeying without murmuring and hesitation, so that, according to the Lord’s word, they may experience that Christ’s yoke is easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:30).

Otherwise, until they learn Christ’s humility, they will not feel the sweetness of his yoke or the lightness of his burden.

Humility of heart is rest for the soul wearied by vices and labors, and its one refreshment amid so many evils. To the extent that a person draws himself away from so many external, wandering, and vain concerns, to that extent he rests and is refreshed within, so that even bitter things become sweet to him, and what he previously regarded as hard and difficult he feels to be smooth and easy.

Mortification, intolerable to the proud and harsh, is consolation to the person who delights only in what is humble and gentle.

It must be understood, however, that no one can perfectly fulfill either this blessedness of martyrdom or any other useful undertaking that comes upon him unless he has devoted himself to this single aim: not to be found unprepared.

For if, in accordance with this aim, he wishes to pursue or nourish some personal intentions, he will immediately be detained by the occupations placed in his way. Completely disturbed, he will not always be able to follow where the command leads with gratitude; nor can one who is agitated and ungrateful fulfill it as he ought.

Mortification therefore has three forms: not to disagree in spirit, not to speak freely with the tongue, and not to go anywhere on one’s own authority.

One’s constant saying to the elder, even when he commands what is contrary, should be: “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39), following the example of the Savior, who said: “I came down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 6:38).

*(Up to this point the manuscript copies and the Saint Gall exemplar read as above; the Bobbio copy adds the following passage.)*

[Col. 0216B] **On the Perfection of a Monk**

A monk should live in a monastery under the discipline of one Father and in the company of many, so that from one he may learn humility and from another patience; one should teach him silence, another gentleness.

He should not do what he wishes. He should eat what he is commanded; have as much as he receives; pay the assigned measure of his work; submit to one to whom he does not wish to submit; come to bed tired; and, walking, fall asleep, without being compelled to rise until his sleep is complete.

Having suffered an injury, he should remain silent. He should fear the superior of the monastery as a lord and love him as a parent. He should believe that whatever the superior commands is salutary for him, and should not judge the decision of his elders; his own duty is to obey and fulfill what is right, as Moses says: “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4), and so forth.

## CHAPTER TEN. On the Various Kinds of Faults

[Col. 0216C]

Different kinds of faults must be healed by the remedy of different kinds of penance.

Therefore, brothers, the holy Fathers established that we should confess everything—not only capital crimes but also serious negligences—because confession and penance deliver from death.

Even small sins must not be neglected in confession, because, as it is written: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall away” (Ecclesiasticus 19). Confession should therefore be made before the meal, before entering one’s bed, or whenever it is easy to make it.

Accordingly, whoever fails to observe the blessing at table and does not answer “Amen” is to be corrected with six strokes.

If anyone speaks while eating, when it is not required by another brother, six strokes.

Whoever says something belonging to himself, six strokes. Whoever does not make the sign over the spoon which he licks, six strokes.

If anyone speaks in a loud voice—that is, louder than usual—six strokes.

If the lamp is not signed—that is, when it has been lit by a younger brother and is not presented to the elder for signing—six strokes.

If anyone performs some useless task, let him be corrected with six strokes.

Whoever among the brothers has been entrusted with cooking or serving, if he spills even a little, is to be corrected by prayer in the church after the course has been completed, with the brothers praying for him.

Whoever forgets the humiliation in the synaxis, that is, during the course [Col. 0217A]—this is the humiliation in the church after the end of each psalm—should likewise do penance.

In the same way, whoever loses crumbs is to be corrected by prayer in the church.

This small penance is to be imposed only if he has spilled something small. If through negligence, forgetfulness, or a breach of carefulness he has lost more than usual, whether liquids or dry goods, he must do penance in the church for a long period of pardon, prostrated while the twelve psalms are sung at the twelfth hour, moving no limb.

Or certainly, if what he spilled was much—if through negligence he spilled and lost four *quadrants* of beer or measures of any kind of goods—he should calculate how many days’ provisions he ordinarily received for his own expenses and should know that he has lost that amount, so that he may drink water instead of beer.

If something is spilled onto the table and falls outside it, pardon at table is sufficient.

[Col. 0217B] Whoever leaves the house to ask for prayer and does not humble himself, and after receiving the blessing does not make the sign of the cross or approach the cross, is to be corrected with twelve strokes.

Likewise, whoever forgets the prayer before work or after work, twelve strokes.

Whoever eats without a blessing, twelve strokes.

Whoever returns to the house seeking prayer and does not bow within the house is to be corrected with twelve strokes.

But if a brother confesses all these things, and the other matters up to prostration for half-penance—that is, half the penance—he should be treated with corresponding moderation.

Meanwhile, whoever fails to guard against coughing at the beginning of the psalm is to be corrected with six blows; likewise whoever strikes the chalice of salvation with his teeth, six blows. Whoever does not observe the order of the sacrifice when coming forward to offer it, six blows. A priest offering who has not removed his fingernails, and a deacon whose beard has not been shaved—those receiving the sacrifice from the grate (rastro) and approaching the chalice—six blows. Whoever smiles during the synaxis, that is, during the course, six blows; if laughter breaks out audibly, a prostration, unless it happened in a pardonable circumstance. The priest offering and the deacon guarding the sacrifice must take care that their eyes do not wander aimlessly; if they neglect this, they are to be corrected with six blows.

Whoever forgets the chrismal while going a long distance for some task, twenty-five blows. If he leaves it on the ground in the field and finds it immediately, fifty blows; if he lifts it onto wood, thirty blows; if it remains there overnight, a prostration. Whoever receives the eulogiae while unclean, twelve blows. Whoever forgets to make the offering, until he goes forward to offer it, one hundred blows. Whoever utters idle stories to another, then immediately reproves himself, only a pardon; but if he does not reprove himself and instead makes excuses, explaining how he ought to excuse them, a prostration of silence, or fifty blows. Whoever offers an excuse straightforwardly when he is being questioned about something, and does not immediately say while asking pardon, “My fault; I regret what I did,” fifty blows. Whoever straightforwardly advances one counsel against another counsel, fifty blows. Whoever shakes the altar, fifty blows. Whoever speaks in a loud voice without restraint, except where necessity requires it, a prostration of silence, or fifty blows; whoever makes an excuse in order to obtain pardon, fifty blows.

Whoever, when a brother points something out, answers, “It is not as you say,” except for elders speaking simply to juniors, is to undergo a prostration of silence or fifty blows. This is permitted only to an equal brother, if he remembers that something is more accurately stated than the other has said: “If you recall it correctly, brother.” The other, on hearing this, must not affirm his own statement, but must say humbly: “I hope that you remember better; I exceeded in my speech through forgetfulness. I regret that I spoke wrongly.” These are the words of the children of God: “Do nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility of spirit let each regard the other as superior to himself” (Philippians II, 3). But whoever excuses himself is to be judged not a spiritual son of God, but a carnal Adam. If he does not quickly take refuge in the harbor of the rest of the Lord’s humility, opening an entrance to excessive contradictions for others and persisting in pride, he is to be separated from the freedom of the holy Church and confined in a cell to perform penance, until his good will becomes known and through humility he is again inserted into the holy congregation. Whoever speaks even a little to criticize the work of the doorkeeper, or if the doorkeeper has not properly observed the hours, a prostration of silence or fifty blows.

Whoever offers a correction against a correction—that is, rebukes one who is rebuking him—three prostrations. Whoever conceals a fault he sees in his brother until he has been corrected for another fault or for that very one, and then brings it forward against his brother, three prostrations. Whoever criticizes or disparages the work of other brothers, three prostrations. Whoever disparages a brother, or hears someone disparaging him without immediately correcting the speaker, three prostrations. Whoever expresses any contention with sadness is likewise to do penance with three prostrations. Whoever criticizes something to his superior but does not wish it to be disclosed until he tells the abbot, three prostrations—unless all these things are done with a shamefaced confession. If a brother is sad, he should receive consolation if this is possible; if he can endure it, he should meanwhile suppress his confession, so that he may speak more shamefacedly. When the sadness has ceased, let the brothers pray for him.

If someone says to his kinsman, urging him who lives elsewhere, “It is better for you to live with us or with some others,” three prostrations. Whoever reproaches a brother who is rendering service, three prostrations. Whoever teaches a kinsman some art or anything else assigned by the elders, so that he may learn the lesson better, three prostrations.

Whoever dares say to his superior, “You will not judge my case, but our abbot or the other brothers,” or, “We shall all go to the abbot,” must be corrected for forty days in penance on bread and water—unless he himself, prostrate before the brothers, says, “I regret that I spoke wrongly.” Any brother occupied in some task, however tired he may be, must nevertheless say to the steward in his own case: “If it pleases you, I will tell the abbot; otherwise I will not”; in another’s case: “If you repeat this, do not think it burdensome if I perhaps tell the abbot, so that obedience may be preserved.”

Whoever does not return something he has borrowed by the following day, if he returns it after remembering, six blows; if he forgets until it is requested, twelve. Whoever forgets to ask about a penitential obligation until the following day, six blows. Whoever murmurs or says, “I will not do it unless the abbot or the second-in-command says so,” three prostrations. An unnecessary running or jumping, twelve blows. It is forbidden for anyone to hold another’s hand.

The steward shall see to the humane reception of those who arrive, both strangers and the other brothers; and all the brothers must be ready to serve with complete devotion for God’s sake. Even if the steward has not judged the matter or is not present, the others must diligently do what is necessary and guard their utensils until they can assign them to a prepared custodian. If they neglect this, penance for it is to be imposed according to the priest’s judgment.

Whoever does not ask pardon when corrected, a prostration. Whoever visits other brothers separately in a cell without asking permission is likewise to do penance; or whoever goes into the kitchen after None without arrangement or command, a prostration; or whoever goes outside the enclosure—that is, outside the monastery’s boundary—without asking permission, a prostration. The youths who have been given the rule that they are not to call one another, if they transgress, are to undergo three prostrations. They are to say only: “You know that we are not permitted to speak with you.” If someone commands them to do what is not permitted, they are to say: “You know that we are not permitted to do so.” If he commands them further, he is to be condemned to three prostrations; they, however, are to say: “We will do what you say, so that the good of obedience may be preserved.” This must be especially guarded: just as they do not speak to one another directly, so they must not speak through another’s mouth. If they knowingly transgress, they are to do penance in the same way as though they had spoken directly to one another.

If someone’s chrismal falls, without breaking anything, twelve blows. Whoever utters an idle word is to be condemned to silence for the next two hours, or to twelve blows. Penitent brothers, even when they perform difficult and dirty tasks, are not to wash their heads except on Sunday, that is, on the eighth day. Otherwise, on the fifteenth day, or certainly because of the growth of flowing hair, each person may wash according to the elder’s judgment. Turning aside from the road without asking permission or receiving a blessing, six blows.

If the superior imposes short penances beside the table, he should impose them at the table; and no more than twenty-five blows are to be given at once.

Penitent brothers, and those who require the psalms of penance—that is, anyone who must still chant psalms because of a nocturnal vision—must chant, according to the diabolical illusion and the character of the vision, twenty-four psalms in sequence, or fifteen, or twelve. Nevertheless, on Sunday night and during the season of Pentecost, penitents are to bend their knees.

If the abbot or superior assigns one of the brothers to make a journey, this is to be observed: the junior must obey the senior, provided that he strives to observe what the senior has indicated if it is right. If the abbot or chief steward gives an order and another, more subordinate steward repeats it, he must obey while quietly indicating what the other superior had ordered. Within the monastery, however, no one is to command another by a superior authority except the one who presides.

From the beginning of the day until night there is to be a change of clothing, and at night the two are to be questioned separately. Whoever serves on Sunday or another solemn day, whether at the bath or for any other need, requires one prayer before going out and entering; nevertheless, if he does not go far, he requires the sign of the cross. Although while walking he should sign himself, it is not [perhaps, nevertheless] necessary for him to turn toward the east. Anyone hurrying out of the house and signing himself likewise does not need to turn toward the east. Thus, while walking, he should do whatever is fitting if he is hurrying to ask for prayer; and when humbling himself in a house where kneeling is not appropriate, only a bow is prescribed. If anyone wishes, on Saturday he may prepare the offering for Sunday; once the bath has been completed, the priests may change, if this is convenient. The deacons, either before the command or after the command, are to perform the appropriate ministry.

If anyone has seen an unclean dream, or has been defiled, or is a penitent, he is commanded to stand when the command is given. On great solemnities, when they hear the sound, they are to sit; at the daily command, they are ordered to sit when nearly halfway through. Then, when all hear the sound summoning them to the synaxis, the assembly of the day, they are to wash before entering the oratory, unless they have washed earlier.

The first-ranking brother is to be appointed to chant first, and the second-ranking brother likewise; the knee is not to be bent, but only a bow is to be made. Those of the first ranks are to stand in the middle of the oratory; the others are to stand on the right and left, except the one offering and the one attached to him. At every Sunday solemnity, the hymn of the Lord’s day is to be sung, and likewise on the day beginning Easter. Whoever begins at the altar is to humble himself three times while receiving the sacrifice. The newly admitted and the unlearned, and anyone of that sort, are not to approach the chalice. When the offering is presented, no one is to be forced to receive the sacrifice, except in necessity. On every Sunday and solemnity, whoever has not been among the assembly of the brothers pouring out prayers to the Lord is to pray individually if necessity compels him; and while the offering is being made, he is not to move about excessively. A penitent occupied by the necessity of travel, walking with others who are using permitted foods, if the third hour arrives and they are traveling a long distance, may also receive some food according to his circumstances, and should receive what he lacks wherever he rests.

In general, all the brothers, every night at the times of prayer, are to bend their knees in prayer at the end of all the psalms, with an even disposition unless bodily weakness prevents it, saying silently: “O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me” (Psalm LXIX, 2). After they have silently chanted this verse three times in prayer, they are to rise together from kneeling in prayer, except on Sundays and from the first day of holy Easter until the fiftieth day. During these days, humbling themselves moderately during the time of psalmody, they are not to bend their knees, but are to pray to God diligently.

If a brother is disobedient, two days with one paximatium and water. If anyone says, “I will not do it,” two days with one paximatium and water. If anyone murmurs, two days with one paximatium and water. If anyone does not ask pardon or offers an excuse, two days with one paximatium and water. If two brothers contend about something and become enraged, two days with one paximatium and water. If someone, while contending, confirms a lie and a distinction, two days with one paximatium and water. If anyone contradicts a brother and does not ask his pardon, two days with one paximatium and water. If anyone contradicts, breaks a command or rule, two days with one paximatium. If someone assigns him a task and he performs it negligently, two days with one paximatium. If anyone disparages his abbot, seven days with one paximatium; if his brother, twenty-four psalms; if a layperson, twelve psalms.

If anyone forgets something outside, if it is a small thing, twelve psalms; if a greater thing, thirty psalms. If anyone loses or drops something, his penance is to correspond to its value. If anyone converses with a layperson without permission, twenty-four psalms. If anyone, when he has completed his task and has no other task to seek, does something without permission, let him chant twenty-four psalms.

If anyone is double-tongued and disturbs the brothers, two days with one paximatium. If anyone eats in another’s house without permission and then comes to his own house, one day with a paximatium. If anyone recounts a past sin, one day with a paximatium. Or whoever has walked in the world and speaks of the world’s sin, one day on bread and water. A lukewarm person who hears someone murmuring and disparaging, or doing something against the rule, and consents rather than confessing, one day with a paximatium.

If anyone provokes his brother to anger, then satisfies him afterward, but he himself does not forgive him and instead leaves the matter to his superior, twenty-four psalms and that day on bread and water. If someone wants something and the steward forbids it, but the abbot orders it, five days. If anyone does not come to prayer before the table and after the meal, let him chant twelve psalms. If anyone sleeps while prayer is being offered, if this happens frequently, twelve psalms; if not frequently, six psalms. If anyone does not say “Amen,” thirty lashes. If he has passed the hour, twelve psalms; if it is the Song of Ascents, unless it is winter matins, twelve psalms. Whoever does not hear the sound of the prayer, twelve psalms. If anyone comes to the sacrifice wearing a nocturnal belt or a garment wrapped around him, twelve psalms.

If anyone eats before None on Wednesday or Friday, unless he is ill, he is to live for two days on bread and water. If anyone tells a lie unknowingly, fifty lashes; if knowingly and boldly, bread and water. If his lie is denied and he persists in arguing, seven days on bread and water. If a monk sleeps in one house with a woman, three days on bread and water; if he did not know that he ought not to do so, one day.

If anyone does not lock the church, twelve psalms. If anyone spits and it touches the altar, twenty-four psalms; if it touches the wall, six. If anyone forgets while chanting or during the readings, four psalms. If anyone comes late to prayer, fifty blows, or fifty lashes; or if he carries out more sluggishly what is commanded to him, fifty. If he makes a sound after the peace, fifty. If he answers defiantly, fifty.

If anyone enters the house with his head covered, fifty lashes. If anyone does not ask for prayer when he enters the house, fifty. If anyone eats without prayer, fifty. If anyone speaks something in his mouth, fifty. If anyone makes a sound while prayer is being offered, fifty lashes. If anyone holds anger, sadness, or envy against his brother, the penance is to correspond to the length of time he has held it, on bread and water; but if he confesses on the first day, twenty-four psalms.

Whoever loses the sacrifice and does not know where it is, one year of penance. Whoever is negligent with regard to the sacrifice so that it dries out and is consumed by worms, until it comes to nothing, half a year of penance. Whoever is negligent with regard to the sacrifice so that a worm is found in it, but it is nevertheless still whole, is to burn it in the fire beside the altar and hide its ashes beneath the altar; he himself is to do penance for forty days. Whoever neglects the sacrifice and it becomes altered, so that the bread loses its taste: if it is red in color, let him do penance for twenty days; if blue, fifteen days.
