But if its color has not changed and it has merely become stuck together, seven days of penance. Whoever submerges the sacrifice is immediately to drink water. Whoever spills the sacrifice into the chrismal is to eat it. If it falls from a boat, or from a bridge, or from wood, not through negligence but by some accident, one day of penance.

Whoever knows that his brother is committing a sin unto death and does not rebuke him is to be marked as a transgressor of the law of the Gospel (John V, 16), until he rebukes the one whose evil he concealed and confesses to the priest; for as long as he concealed the evil conscience, so long is he to do penance in affliction. Whoever concealed a small sin is to do penance with a similar correction, but not the same affliction: thirty blows, or fifteen psalms. If thereafter he contemptuously neglects small matters, he is to do penance on bread and water, so that the sinner may be rebuked according to the Lord’s command (Matthew XVIII, 15). Whoever rebukes not gently is to be marked until he asks pardon from the brother he rebuked, and is to receive thirty blows or chant fifteen psalms. Whoever reproaches someone with a shameful sin before rebuking him privately between himself and that person, is to be corrected, as the Lord says (Matthew XVIII), until he makes satisfaction to the person reproached, and is to do penance for three days on bread and water.

Whoever transgresses a rule, command, or general discipline is to remain expelled without food, so that he may be received again on the following day. Whoever speaks familiarly alone with a lone woman, without reliable witnesses, is to remain without food, or spend two days on bread and water, or receive two hundred blows. Whoever presumes to carry a message without the permission of the one in charge, proceeding freely and without restraint without necessity, is to be restrained by fifty blows. Presumption in undertaking a private task, one hundred blows. Possession of any object which general necessity has not granted to the brothers is to be restrained by the loss of that object and one hundred blows. To do, give, or receive something necessary and permitted without permission, twelve blows—unless some circumstance provides a defense, so that submissive satisfaction may cancel the penalty.

Whoever speaks while eating, six blows. Whoever’s voice carries from one table to another, six blows. If it sounds from the house outside, or from outside into the house, twelve blows. To leave or enter a house, or perform a task, without prayer and the sign of the cross, twelve blows. If it happens otherwise, five blows. To say “mine” or “yours,” six blows. Word against word, if said simply, six blows; if out of contention, one hundred blows or a prostration of silence. If he has not kept the order of chanting, six blows. If he presumes to speak during the appointed time of silence without necessity, seventeen blows.

If anyone, through contempt, loses or dissipates anything from the monastery’s possessions, he is to restore it by his own sweat and additional labor, or, according to its valuation and the priest’s judgment, do penance by a prostration, or spend one day on bread and water. If he lost or broke it not through contempt but by some accident, he is to cleanse his negligence only through public penance: with all the brothers gathered in the synaxis, he must remain prostrate on the ground and ask pardon until the solemnity of the prayers is completed; he is to obtain it when, by the abbot’s judgment, he is ordered to rise from the ground. In the same way, whoever has been summoned to prayer or some task and arrives late is to make satisfaction.

If, while chanting a psalm, he stumbles; if he is excessively severe; if he answers defiantly, a prostration. If he fulfills assigned services negligently, a prostration. If he murmurs even slightly, a prostration. If he prefers reading to the work of obedience, a prostration. If he carries out the appointed duties sluggishly, a prostration. If, after the synaxis has been dismissed, he does not immediately return to his cell, a prostration. If he stops briefly with someone, a prostration. If he withdraws somewhere for a short time, a prostration. If he presumes to converse, however briefly, with anyone who is not his cellmate, a prostration. If he holds another’s hand, a prostration. If he prays with someone who has been suspended from prayer, a prostration.

If he sees one of his parents or secular friends, or speaks with him without permission; if he receives anyone’s letter; if he presumes to give anything without his abbot, a prostration. If he pushes someone away from completing a necessary task, a prostration. If, through ardor of mind, he exceeds the lawful measure of religious life, a prostration. If he presumes to hold back another who is fervent in a lawful task for the sake of his own timing, a prostration.

Up to this point, and in offenses of a similar kind, spiritual correction proceeds so that the rebuke made by many may benefit the sinner for salvation, and so that, with God’s favor, he may thereafter be found saved, more cautious and more diligent in correcting his conduct.

Whoever has engaged in a quarrel is to do penance for seven days. Whoever has despised his superior or blasphemed the rule is to be driven out, unless he says, “I regret what I said.” But if he does not humble himself, he is to do penance for forty days, because he is held by the disease of pride. The talkative is to be condemned to silence, the restless person to gentleness, the glutton to fasting, the sleepy person to wakefulness, the proud person to confinement, and the deserter to expulsion. Let each one experience what corresponds to his deserts, so that the just may live justly. Amen.

In every place and task, the rule of silence is considered worthy of the greatest care, so that, as far as human frailty can manage—frailty that is prone to vices and from which it is accustomed to fall—we may be cleansed from vice, and may utter from our mouths the edification of our neighbors, for whom our Savior Jesus poured out his holy blood, rather than the tearing apart of those who are absent, conceived in our hearts, and idle words scattered everywhere, for which we shall render an account to the just Requiter.

This path, tending upward to the highest summits, we have established for those who wish to attain the things above, leaving the earth with its vices and freely desiring to cling to the one God sent into this world; they will surely receive immortal rewards, with the greatest joy that never declines throughout eternity.

[Col. 0223]

# Book of Saint Columban, Abbot and Confessor, on Determining the Measure of Penances (C, S)

[Col. 0223D] I. True penance is not to commit what must be repented of, but to mourn what has been committed. But because the frailty of many—not to say of all—breaks this rule, the measures of penance must be known. Their order is handed down by the holy Fathers as follows: the length of penances is to be established according to the magnitude of the faults.

II. If, therefore, anyone sins in thought—that is, desires to kill someone, commit fornication, steal, eat secretly, or become drunk; or indeed to strike someone, depart, or do other things like these—and has been ready in heart to carry them out, let him do penance for the greater offenses for half a year, and for the lesser offenses for forty days, on bread and water.

III. If anyone sins in deed, overcome by sins: if he commits homicide or the sin of sodomy, let him do penance for ten years; if he commits fornication only once, let the monk do penance for three years; if more often, seven years. If he departs and breaks his vows, but returns quickly as a penitent, three forty-day periods; but if after years, let him do penance for three years.

IV. If anyone steals, let him do penance for a year.

V. If anyone strikes his brother in a quarrel and sheds blood, let him do penance for three years.

VI. If anyone makes himself drunk and vomits, or, having overeaten, vomits the sacrifice because of it, let him do penance for forty days; but if he is forced to vomit the sacrifice because of illness, let him do penance for seven days. If anyone loses the sacrifice itself, let him do penance for a year.

VII. If anyone defiles himself, let him do penance for a year, if he is a junior.

VIII. If anyone knowingly gives false testimony, let him do penance for two years, with the loss or restoration of the matter involved.

[Col. 0225C] These matters concern accidental causes; the following concern the minor matters of undisciplined conduct.

IX. Whoever does something on his own without asking permission, or contradicts and says, “I will not do it,” or murmurs: if the matter is serious, three prostrations; if minor, let him do penance for one year. A word simply uttered against a word is to be punished by fifty blows; or, if it arises from an intention to maintain silence, by a prostration; but if it is a quarrel, let him do penance for a week.

X. Whoever disparages someone, or willingly listens to someone disparaging another, let him do penance with three prostrations; if the person disparaged is the one in charge, let him do penance for a week.

XI. Whoever, through pride, despises his superior or blasphemes the rule is to be driven out, unless he immediately says, “I regret what I said.” But if he does not humble himself properly, let him do penance for forty days, because he is held by the disease of pride.

XII. The talkative is to be condemned to silence, the restless person to gentleness, the glutton to fasting, the sleepy person to wakefulness, the proud person to confinement, and the deserter to expulsion. Let each one experience what corresponds to his deserts, so that the just may live justly.

The diversity of faults produces a diversity of penances. Physicians of the body likewise compound medicines from different kinds of remedies: they treat wounds differently from diseases, diseases differently from swellings, swellings differently from bruises, bruises differently from putrefactions, putrefactions differently from dimness, dimness differently from fractures, and fractures differently from burns. Thus spiritual physicians, too, must heal the wounds, diseases, faults, pains, illnesses, and weaknesses of souls by different kinds of treatment. But since these matters belong to only a few—namely, to those who know how to understand everything purely, to cure completely, to restore the weak to a sound state—let us propose a few things according to the traditions of the elders and according in part to our own understanding (“For we prophesy in part, and we know in part,” I Corinthians XIII, 9). First, concerning the capital crimes that are also punished by the sanction of the law, the following must be established.

XIII. If a cleric commits homicide and kills his neighbor, let him do penance as an exile for ten years. After this, let him be received back into his homeland if he has performed penance well on bread and water, as attested by the bishop or priest with whom he did penance and to whom he was entrusted, so that he may make satisfaction to the parents of the person he killed, making repayment to them and saying: “Whatever you wish, I will do for you.” But if he does not make satisfaction to that person’s parents, he is never to be received back into his homeland; instead, like Cain, let him be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth.

XIV. If anyone falls into the greatest ruin and fathers a son, let him live as an exile for seven years and do penance on bread and water; only then, by the priest’s judgment, may he be joined to the altar.

XV. If anyone commits fornication as the Sodomites did, let him do penance for ten years: three on bread and water; for the other seven let him abstain from wine and meat, and never remain with another person.

XVI. If anyone commits fornication with women but does not father a son and the matter has not become known among people: if he is a cleric, three years; if a monk or deacon, five years; if a priest, seven; if a bishop, twelve years.

XVII. If anyone commits perjury, let him do penance for seven years, and never swear afterward.

XVIII. If anyone destroys someone by his sorcery, let him do penance for three years on bread and water in measured amounts, and for three further years abstain from wine and meat; only then, in the seventh year, is he to be received into communion. But if someone practices magic out of love and has destroyed no one, let the cleric do penance for a full year on bread and water, the layman for half a year, the deacon for two years, and the priest for three—especially if by this means he has harmed a woman's pregnancy. For this reason, let each add six forty-day periods, lest he be guilty of homicide.

XIX. If a cleric commits theft—that is, steals his neighbor’s ox, horse, sheep, or any animal—if he has done this once or twice, let him first repay his neighbor, and do penance for a full year on bread and water. If he has made a habit of it and cannot repay what he took, let him do penance for three years on bread and water.

XX. If a cleric, deacon, or person of any rank who was a layman in the world with sons and daughters, after his conversion again has intercourse with his former dependent woman (clientela [perhaps, clientula]) and fathers a son by her, let him know that he has committed adultery and sinned no less than if he had been a cleric from his youth and sinned with another man’s girl. For he sinned after his vow, after consecrating himself to the Lord, and made his vow void. Therefore let him likewise do penance for seven years on bread and water.

XXI. If a cleric strikes his neighbor in a quarrel and sheds blood, let him do penance for a full year; if a layman, forty days.

XXII. If anyone commits fornication by himself, or with an animal, let him do penance for two years if he has no rank; but if he has a rank or vow, let him do penance for three years, unless age provides an exemption.

XXIII. If anyone desires a woman but cannot carry it out—that is, the woman does not receive him—let him do penance for half a year on bread and water, and abstain for a whole year from wine, meat, and communion at the altar.

XXIV. If anyone loses the sacrifice, let him do penance for a year; if he vomits it because of drunkenness or gluttony and negligently leaves it, let him do penance for three forty-day periods on bread and water; but if because of illness, let him do penance for seven days.

These matters have been stated indiscriminately concerning clerics and monks. The following concern laypeople.

XXV. Whoever commits homicide—that is, kills his neighbor—let him do penance for three years as an unarmed exile, on bread and water; after three years let him return to his own people, making repayment to the parents of the slain person as an act of compassion and duty; and after satisfaction, by the priest’s judgment, let him be joined to the altar.

XXVI. If a layman fathers a son by another man’s wife—that is, commits adultery by violating his neighbor’s marriage bed—let him do penance for three years, abstaining from richer foods and from his own wife, and additionally giving the husband of the violated wife a payment for her chastity; thus let the priest wipe away his fault.

XXVII. If a layman commits fornication in the Sodomite manner—that is, sins with a male in a woman’s sexual role—let him do penance for seven years: for the first three on bread, water, salt, and dry garden fruits; for the remaining four let him abstain from wine and meat. Thus his fault is to be forgiven him; the priest is to pray for him, and then he is to be joined to the altar.

XXVIII. If a layman commits fornication with women free from marriage—that is, widows or girls: with a widow, one year; with a girl, two years—let him do penance, provided that he has paid the price of his humiliation to her parents. But if he has no wife, but a virgin man is joined to a virgin woman, if her parents wish, let her be his wife; nevertheless, both are first to do penance for a year, and thus let them be married.

XXIX. If a layman commits fornication with an animal, let him do penance for a year if he has a wife; if he does not have one, for half a year. Likewise, let the man who has a wife and violates himself with his own limbs do penance.

XXX. If a layman, or a woman, suffocates his or her own infant, let them do penance for a full year on bread and water, and for two further years abstain from wine and meat. Thus they are first to be joined to the altar by the priest’s judgment, and that husband may lawfully have intercourse with his wife. For laypeople must know that during the time of penance assigned to them by priests, they are not permitted to have intercourse with their wives until the penance has been completed; for the penance is half [perhaps, “for he divides the penance”].

XXXI. If a layman commits theft—that is, steals his neighbor’s ox, horse, sheep, or any animal—if he has done so once or twice, let him first repay his neighbor the damage he caused, and do penance for three forty-day periods on bread and water. But if he has made a habit of stealing and cannot repay what he took, let him do penance for a year and three forty-day periods, and thereafter promise never to do it again. Thus he may communicate at Easter of the following year—that is, after two years—provided that he has first given alms to the poor from his labor and a meal to the priest who judges the penance; thus the guilt of his evil habit may be forgiven him.

XXXII. If a layman commits perjury: if he did so out of greed, let him sell all his possessions, give them to the poor, turn wholly to the Lord, be tonsured after abandoning the entire world, and serve God in a monastery until death. But if he did this not out of greed but from fear of death, let him do penance as an unarmed exile for three years on bread and water, and for two further years abstain from wine and meat. Thus, giving a life in his place—that is, freeing a male or female slave from the yoke of servitude—and giving many alms for two years (during which he may freely use all permitted foods except meat), let him communicate after the seventh year.

XXXIII. If any layman sheds blood through a scandalous incident, or wounds or disables his neighbor, he must be compelled to repay as much as he caused harm: but if he has no means of payment, let him first perform work for his neighbor for as long as the latter is ill, and seek a physician; after the neighbor’s recovery, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water.

XXXIV. If a layman makes himself drunk, or eats or drinks to the point of vomiting, let him do penance for a week on bread and water.

XXXV. If any layman wishes to commit adultery, or to fornicate with a betrothed woman, and lusts after his neighbor’s wife but does not do so—that is, is unable to, because the woman did not receive him—although he was nevertheless prepared to fornicate, let him confess his guilt to a priest and then do penance for forty days on bread and water.

XXXVI. If any layman eats or drinks beside pagan shrines, and does so through ignorance, let him promise thereafter never to repeat it, and do penance for forty days on bread and water. But if he does this contemptuously—that is, after the priest has preached to him that it was sacrilege, and afterward he has shared in the demons’ tables—if he has done or repeated this merely through the vice of gluttony, let him do penance for three Lents on bread and water. But if he has done this for the worship of demons or the honoring of idols, let him do penance for three years.

XXXVII. If any layman through ignorance has communicated with the Bonosians or other heretics, let him remain among the catechumens—that is, separated from the other Christians—for forty days, and for two further Lents let him lament the guilt of his unsound communion at the very end of the Christian order, that is, among the penitents. But if he has done this contemptuously—that is, after it had been announced and forbidden to him by the priest that he should not defile himself by communion with the party of the left—let him do penance for a full year, and throughout three Lents and two further years abstain from wine and meat. Then, after the laying on of hands by a Catholic bishop, let him be joined to the altar.

Finally, the lesser sanctions of the monks must be addressed.

XXXVIII. If anyone leaves an open fence or enclosure during the night, let him do penance by an additional imposition. But if during the day, let him make amends with twenty-four blows if he left it open while no others were coming upon it. If someone has gone before this same person unaccompanied (*absolute*), let him do penance by an additional imposition.

XXXIX. If anyone, while seeking a beast, washes alone *absolute* [read: “without mud”], let him do penance by an additional imposition. But if, while washing lawfully and standing before the brothers, he has done this—not from the necessity of removing abundant mud—let him make amends with twenty-four blows.

XL. But if anyone, even while sitting on a beast, uncovers his knees or arms without the necessity of washing off mud, let him not wash for six days; that is, until the following Sunday, that dishonorable washer shall not wash his feet. A monk alone may wash his feet privately while standing. An elder, however, may also be washed publicly, provided that he stands while another washes his feet.

XLI. Before the preaching on Sunday, everyone, except in cases of specific necessity, must be gathered together, so that none of those commanded to hear may be absent from the number, except the cook and the porter. They too, if they can, must make every effort to be present when the thunder of the Gospel is heard.

XLII. Confessions must be given with particular diligence, especially concerning disturbances of the soul, before going to Mass, lest anyone perhaps approach the altar unworthily—that is, if he does not have a clean heart. For it is better to wait until the heart has become sound and free from scandal and envy than to approach boldly for judgment at the tribunal. The tribunal is Christ’s altar, and there he judges, with his body and blood, those who approach unworthily. Therefore, just as one must beware of capital and carnal sins before receiving Communion, so also one must abstain from and cleanse away the more hidden vices and illnesses of the languishing soul before entering into the union of true peace and the bond of eternal salvation.

[Col. 0229]

THE VARIOUS INSTRUCTIONS OF SAINT COLUMBANUS, ABBOT AND CONFESSOR, COMMONLY CALLED SERMONS. (C, G, S)*

INSTRUCTION ONE. On the One and Triune God.

[Col. 0229C]

I. Taking up the care of an instruction of great necessity, I may first briefly say what everyone must know above all: I wish that what is the foundation of everyone’s salvation should be the threshold of our discourse, and that our teaching should begin from where everything that exists arises and what did not exist comes into being. Let the faith of the heart open the door of our speech, the faith that has opened the mouths of all Christians who rightly believe for the confession of salvation. Let our words, therefore, with Christ’s help, rightly take their beginning from the origin of human salvation.

Let everyone who wishes to be saved first believe in the one and triune God, the first and the last: one in subsistence, three in substance; one in power, three in persons; one in nature, three in name; one in divinity, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one God, wholly invisible, incomprehensible, ineffable. In him there is always being, because God the Trinity is eternal. Do not seek his beginning: he has no end, and he always was what he is and will be, because in God there is no repetition, but always the perfection of the Trinity.

That God is one Trinity, God himself testifies concerning himself in the Law, saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. VI, 4). But that this one God is Trinity, the Savior taught in the Gospel, saying: “Go now, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). By these two testimonies of the two Laws, as by two very firm supports, the faith of believers has been strengthened. Here you have the Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity.

Because of the greatness of the matter, then, we have briefly stated what we believe, and the faith of the heart has brought forth the confession of the mouth. This must be held firmly against all heresies: God cannot be divided or separated, because what he was wholly, he has always been as he is. Let the poisonous and insane madness of all heretics therefore cease, when we hear and believe God himself testifying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one.” For he who is one has always been what he is. Yet, so that you may know how great he is, he spoke in the plural at the creation of the world: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26).

But lest you go astray concerning the number, Christ points out to you the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in whose name—as the name of the one God—the whole human race must be baptized. What more need be said about the coeternity of the Trinity? The fact that he is One teaches us sufficiently. Concerning the reality of the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Christ’s distinction, supported by the authority of his command, has abundantly instructed those who hear. From these testimonies, I say, every perverse error has been excluded; by naming them, the Trinity is approved, and by their testimony, unity is affirmed.

II. Since the greatness of the matter prevents us from speaking more fully about these things, as about ineffable realities, let us preserve with firm faith what has been said above. For if these few things about God the Trinity are not sufficient for someone, more things according to Scripture will not benefit him. We have said only that he is One in Trinity and Triune in unity.

But who could speak of his essence? How is he present everywhere while invisible, or how does he fill heaven and earth and every creature, according to the saying: “Do I not fill heaven and earth?” says the Lord (Jer. XXIII, 24). And elsewhere: “The Spirit of God,” according to the prophet, “has filled the world” (Wis. I, 7). Again: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI, 1).

God, therefore, is everywhere: wholly immeasurable and everywhere near, according to his own testimony concerning himself: “I am,” he says, “God who is near, and not God who is far away” (Jer. XXIII, 23). We do not seek a God who remains far from us, whom we are to receive within us. For he dwells in us as the soul dwells in the body, provided that we are his sound members; provided that we are not dead through sins; provided that we are free from the corruption of a rotting will. Then indeed he dwells in us, who said: “I will dwell in them, and walk among them” (II Cor. VI, 16; Lev. XXVI, 12).

If we are worthy that he be in us, then in truth we are brought to life by him, as his living members: “For in him,” as the Apostle says, “we live and move and have our being” (Acts XVII, 28). Who, I ask, in accordance with the ineffable and incomprehensible greatness of his essence, will investigate its height [perhaps: “its height” is masculine in the source]? Who will search out the depths of God? Who will dare to consider the eternal beginning of the universe? Who will boast that he knows the infinite God, who fills and surrounds everything, penetrates everything and surpasses everything, contains everything and eludes everything? “No one has ever seen him” (I Tim. VI, 16) as he is.

Let no one therefore presume to seek out the things that cannot be investigated concerning God: what he was, how he was, or where he was. These things are ineffable, inscrutable, unsearchable. Simply—but nevertheless firmly—believe that God is so and will be so, as he was, because God is unchangeable.

III. Who, then, is God? The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one God. Seek nothing further concerning God, because for those who wish to know the profound depth of realities concerning God, nature must first be considered. Knowledge of the Trinity is rightly compared with the depth of the sea, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “And the deep depth—who will find it?” (Eccl. VII, 25).

If anyone therefore wishes to know the deepest ocean of divine knowledge, let him first, if he can, examine this visible world. The less he knows that he can understand of what lies within the sea, the more he should understand that he can know only lesser things of the depth of its Creator. As he ought and as is fitting, let him presume to discuss less about the Creator than about the creature. For one cannot be competent in greater matters who has not first investigated lesser ones; and if someone is not trusted in lesser matters, how can he be trusted in greater ones?

Who, I ask, ignores earthly things and yet scrutinizes heavenly things? Oh, those who speak vainly without understanding either what they say or about what they make assertions, as the Apostle says (I Tim. I, 7). How many there are—woe to them—who, though equipped with a fragile wing, strive to fly on high and set their mouths against heaven, and who, without first gathering any rational account of the creature—or, not to say all of it, of its parts—presume to teach first about the supreme depth with an impure heart and unclean mouth [Codex, erroneously: “enim coli”]. They do not understand that God the Trinity is recognized not by words but by faith, and that he is understood by the pious faith of a pure heart, not by impure idle talk.

The great Trinity must therefore be believed piously, not impiously scrutinized. For God the one Trinity is an abyss that cannot be crossed or investigated. High heaven, broad earth, deep sea, and long ages (Job VIII, 9)—but higher, broader, deeper, and longer is the knowledge by which he who created nature from nothing has encompassed it.

IV. If you wish to know the Creator, understand the creature. If you do not understand even that, be silent about the Creator, but believe in the Creator. Pious silence is better and knows more than impious talk. It is utterly foolish and impious to pass from faith to empty words about the invisible, immeasurable, unseen Lord who is being discussed.

“For the deep depth,” as it is written, “who will find it?” (Eccl. VII, 25). Just as the depth of the sea is invisible to human eyes, so the divinity of the Trinity is likewise found to be incomprehensible to human senses. Therefore, if anyone wishes to know what he ought to believe, let him not think that by speaking he can understand more than by believing. The wisdom of divinity that is sought will flee much farther away than it was.

Seek, then, the highest knowledge not through verbal disputation but through the perfection of good conduct. It proceeds not from the tongue but from faith, from simplicity of heart, not from deductions drawn from learned impiety. If you seek the ineffable through discussions, it will withdraw farther from you than it was (ibid., 24). If through faith, it will stand where it dwells, at the gates of Wisdom (Prov. I, 21), and where it moves about it will be seen, at least in part.

But it is touched in truth, to some extent, when the invisible is believed to be incomprehensible. God must be believed invisible as he is, although he may be seen in part by a pure heart. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us beseech our invisible God, who is present everywhere, that either fear of him or charity—which does not know how to fall—may persevere in us. Joined to charity, that fear will make us wise in all things. May piety persuade us to be silent about what is greater than can be spoken, since to know God as he is is something inscrutable and indescribable.

Who he is and how great he is is known to him alone. But because he is our God, although invisible to us, he must nevertheless be sought by us—sought often and held always: the deep, immeasurable, hidden, exalted, almighty God. Through the merits and intercessions of his saints he must be entreated to grant our darkness at least some fragment of his light, so that it may shine for us, foolish and ignorant as we are, upon the dark road of this world and lead us to him. This he may grant through our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, there is glory forever and ever.

INSTRUCTION II. On the Mortification of Vices and the Acquisition of Virtues.

I. The greatness of divine depth has been sampled, as it were, by a measured discourse and touched with due honor, rather than narrated, because that ineffable thing of God ought to be meditated upon rather than expressed. Apart from what the Law, the prophets, the Gospel, or the apostles say, there ought to be profound silence concerning the Trinity.

For only God’s testimony concerning God—that is, concerning himself—is to be believed: the testimony he has given either in the Law, in a prophet, in the Gospel, in an Apostle, or individually to someone concerning himself, through himself or through an angel. Human argument, human ingenuity, or any proud wisdom that is deceived in its reasoning about the world cannot be a teacher concerning God; it must instead be regarded as sacrilegious and impious presumption against God.

For where, I ask, brothers, could those vain, exceedingly wicked, and impious men—who either do not know themselves or do not understand that they are alive—have learned to know, even to the point of discussing, the invisible one God, the coeternal Trinity embracing everything beneath, above, within, and outside, not to mention defining God?

Having therefore kept silent about these matters, as though they were inexpressible, with the honor due to them, let us begin to speak about what is manifest and pleasing concerning the ineffable God. Let us not presume, like others of whom one ought to be ashamed, to inquire into higher things, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Do not seek what is higher than you” (Ecclus. III, 22). Rather, speaking about the edification of our souls, we do not presume first to lay the foundations of our own littleness, but seek the authority of a greater teacher—namely, the most lucid and elegant teaching of Saint Faustus.

From his sayings we have selected a few passages sufficiently suitable for our work of imitation, since, in the very admonitions about which we wish to speak, he taught us, however unworthy we may be, who were entrusted to him. As though he were prior to me in time, merit, and knowledge, and as though he were to fight on my behalf against the ignorant and sluggish, let him speak first.

II. He says [Note: [Col. 0233] “He says.” Perhaps *enim* is missing. What follows are the words of Congall, the first abbot of Bangor, who was also called Faustus]:

“If a cultivator of the countryside and farmer of the earth, because he prepares his field for the seeds to be sown, does not think it sufficient merely to cut up the earth with a strong plow and subdue the hard clods with repeated plowing, but also takes care to cleanse the field itself of barren grasses, to empty it of harmful refuse, and to pull out by the roots the fuel of thorns and shrubs, never believing that his land will produce a good crop unless it is free of harmful grass, applying to himself the prophetic saying, ‘Break up new ground for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns’ (Jer. IV, 3)—how much more ought we to cleanse the field of our heart from the passions of vices, and not think it sufficient for us to wear down the soil of our body through the labor of fasts and vigils, unless we first take care to correct our vices and order our conduct, since we believe the hope of fruits to be stored not in earth but in heaven?

Let us therefore first strive to uproot vices and plant virtues. Let us uproot pride and plant humility; let us tear out anger and pour in patience; let us cut away envy and introduce benevolence.

Otherwise, if the flesh is beaten down but the soul bears no fruit, it is as though a field were continually being plowed and yet no harvest ever appeared; or as though someone built a statue golden on the outside but clay within. What does it profit if war is waged outside the city while destruction is suffered within? Or as if someone dug outside and around a vineyard while leaving the inside uncultivated, full of thorns and thistles.

What does outward religious observance profit unless the inner person’s correction is also applied [read: ‘if … is not also applied’]? Anyone who displays one thing in dress and another in conduct is false and hypocritical, and can also be a thief. Let us not therefore be like whitewashed tombs. Let us strive to appear beautiful and adorned within, not without, for true religion consists not in humility of the body but in humility of the heart.

In what other place does the Lord dwell except in the heart of the truly humble, according to Isaiah’s saying: ‘Upon whom shall I look, and with whom shall I rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?’ (Isa. LXVI, 2).

Whoever therefore wishes to become a dwelling place of God must strive to make himself humble and quiet, so that he may be recognized as a worshiper of God not by eagerness for words [perhaps: ‘dryness’] or bodily flexibility, but by the truth of humility. The goodness of the heart does not need religion falsified by words.

Outward religion, colored by gestures, is therefore vain; bodily affliction alone is likewise vain, and the diligence of the external person is empty unless fruitful self-restraint of the spirit accompanies it. What does it profit for a servant to attack passions that are found to be at peace with their master?

Therefore, lest we labor without fruit, let us give our efforts, with God’s help, to being freed from vices, so that afterward we may be adorned with virtues. Let us cleanse ourselves, as far as we are able, from every stain of vice: first from pride, envy, anger, blasphemy, wickedness, malice, sadness, vainglory, greed, malignity, and every bitterness, so that we may be possessed by humility, gentleness, kindness, meekness, self-restraint, mercy, justice, joy, and charity.”

III. But what are we doing? We recite these things as though they were familiar and leave them, as though they were likewise harmless, uncultivated, and undiscerned. We delight in reading them but grow lax in driving them out. Will hearing things that we are proved not to possess within us save us? If they are always read to us but never corrected by us, will frequent reading of things that we slowly expel help us?

Will anyone cleanse his house of any filth by speech alone, or remove dusty heaps of unclean refuse by words alone? Or can anyone accomplish even the things belonging to daily life without sweat? Patience, diligence, labor, and tireless effort are therefore necessary for us as we cleanse the house of the inner person, so that we may show patience in injuries, diligence in religious practice, labor in works, and zeal in progress.

Though we preach frequently, we are slow to amend; though frequently offended, we are rarely patient; though frequently defeated, we are rarely victorious; though frequently led astray, we are rarely understanding. What, then, will help us as weak and unlearned fighters, whose weapons are turned into wounds, since praise consists not in hearing these things but in fulfilling them?

The Law sanctifies not by hearing but unquestionably by doing. Let each person honor the Lord not merely with words and bodily labor, but with maturity of conduct and purity of heart. Let it not be said of us: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX, 13; Matt. XV, 8; Mark VII, 6).

And when you hear of battle, believe that wounds and flight are involved [perhaps: “that you should take part in wounds and flight”]. While no one can possess peace against the seven hostile nations attacking him, he must not cease fighting, girded for battle, until, by fighting manfully through God’s gift, he emerges as king and ruler of the seven nations.

For no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully (II Tim. II, 5), and no one competes lawfully in the first contest. One must first fight, then take one’s stand, and labor in the battle, so that afterward one may fight lawfully.

Would that we too might fight lawfully, so that we might deserve to be crowned; and just as we are in the same equipment and under the same arms, so might we fight daily against our enemies, directing our weapons not against ourselves but against our adversaries.

Long practice in warfare, together with God’s grace, will grant this through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor, glory, and power forever and ever. Amen.

INSTRUCTION III. On Pursuing Contempt for the World and Love of Heavenly Goods.

[Col. 0235D]

I. What is best in the world? To please its Creator. What is his will? To please him by doing what he has commanded—that is, to live rightly and piously seek what is eternal. For piety and justice are the will of the pious and upright.

How does one reach this? Through zeal. One must therefore be zealous in piety and justice. What helps preserve these? Understanding, which examines all other things and, finding nothing to which it can cling firmly, turns by reason from what the world possesses toward the one thing that is eternal.

For the world will pass away; it passes away daily and rolls toward its end—for what does it possess that it does not assign to an end?—and in a certain sense it is supported by pillars of vanity. When the end of vanity arrives, it will fall and not remain. Whatever does not come to an end cannot be said to belong to the world.

Everything therefore passes away through death and decay and does not stand. What, then, ought a wise person to love? A dead image, partly mute and partly vocal, which he sees but does not understand? If he understood it, perhaps he would love it; but he also stumbles in this, in which he does not reveal himself.

For who understands either himself or another—the flower of the earth and earth made from earth—how, by what dignity, earth and dust, soon to become [otherwise?] and never to be of use unless the soul mediates, makes [one] a son of God and a denizen of heaven? [The transmitted syntax is corrupt.]

II. If anyone understands this, through the gift of God, what sort of life must he live so that he may be eternal from mortal, wise from foolish, and heavenly from earthly? Let him first have a pure sense with which to live well, and let him see not what is, but what will be.

What will be is what is not yet. Through the things he sees, let him think about the things he does not see; let him strive to be what he was created to be, and call upon God’s grace through his own effort. For no one can attain by himself alone what he lost in Adam.

What does it profit to receive understanding and not use it well? He uses it well who lives so that he never either regrets or has cause to regret. Late repentance proves that something was used badly; a good conscience praises life.

What, then, does a pure mind wisely love? Certainly that which made it love, and made all other things, and always remains and never grows old. According to true reason, nothing external should be loved except what is eternal, and the eternal will that is inspired and animated by the eternal, marvelous, ineffable, invisible, incomprehensible one who fills and surpasses all things, is present everywhere and eludes all things.

The wise person ought to love nothing here that does not last. For eternal things are there with the Eternal, and perishable things here with the mortal. It is dangerous to dwell among deceiving and false things and not to see the true things that you ought to love, while also seeing those things which, by fleeing, provoke you and persuade you to sin with them as though in a dream, and which flatter you with what is hateful in reality, while withdrawing what ought rightly to be loved as though it did not exist.

III. It is therefore clear that someone who dwells among deceivers ought to be watchful, like one who will not escape unless he flees from them and acts cautiously and well.

How will we flee from the world, which we ought not to love, when we are in the world and are taught to die to it, while conversely we enclose within ourselves, through a kind of livid desire, the one whom we ought to have trampled beneath our feet as though beneath our own?

He tramples upon the world who conquers himself, who dies to vices in mind rather than in body before dying by nature. No one who spares himself can hate the world; in himself alone he either loves or hates the world. Whoever has died to the pleasures of the body has nothing to love from the world.

Let us die such a death, because bodily death holds everyone, whereas this death holds only a few. It belongs to the few to live daily as though dead [perhaps: “as though about to die”]. Since one has not always existed and cannot remain in the world, but exists only in a brief interval, each person ought to live as though he were dying every day, so that, mindful of this death, he may think only of eternal and heavenly things—things in which, if he deserves it, he will become eternal and heavenly.

The things that existed before the world will themselves exist after the world, forever; and they still exist, but do not appear. They are hidden from us to such an extent that human beings are not permitted to speak of them. They do not rise into the human heart or ears, nor enter them, nor can they be discerned by human sight (Isa. LXIV, 4; I Cor. II, 9).

O condition deserving of lament! The things we ought to have loved have been so removed from us, undiscovered and unknown, that as long as we are human beings and confined in this prison of the body, it is altogether impossible for us to see, hear, or contemplate the true and eternal goods.

What, then, shall we do? Let us at least love and seek what is unknown, lest perhaps we remain ignorant of and lose it forever. He was born without purpose who will remain ignorant of those perpetual things forever, and who will fail to know those eternal things eternally.

O miserable human being! You ought to hate what you see, and you are ignorant of what it is fitting for you to love. While your life speaks to you, you are ensnared, whether you wish it or not. Within you is what fetters you; within you is not what sets you free. Will you beware of yourself, wretched one, and not trust yourself, since you are ensnared by yourself and cannot be freed by yourself? Though you have eyes, you are bound blind, and willingly led to death.

IV. O intolerable blindness! O incomparable grief! O most unhappy misery! One who favors his adversaries, who willingly hands himself over to persecutors who never spare him, who gladly consents to those who bind him and hand him over to death.

Who has ever gone joyfully to death? Who is willingly led to be slaughtered or beheaded? Woe to you, human misery! Would that you were merely slaughtered or beheaded and not tortured forever.

What is blinder than you, wretched humanity? You err while seeing—although you see as far as heaven, not beyond it. You understand what is below heaven; beyond heaven you do not understand.

Hard and incomprehensible ignorance—who will tell you things that cannot be told? Unhappy humanity, what will help you? Hear what the Wise Man said: “For one to whom a few things are not sufficient, more will not help.”

You have heard, I believe, the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41). And you know, miserable human being, why one goes into the fire. Be merciful. Perhaps you will be able in this way to draw yourself away from the son of perdition. Do not spare food; do not spare fragile clothing; do not put your possessions before yourself. Love yourself more than your possessions, and your soul more than your property. You alone are miserable, not your possessions; you ought to love yourself more than what belongs to another.

For what is yours except your soul? Do not therefore destroy your soul for nothing. Do not spare perishable things lest you lose eternal things. The whole world is foreign to you: you were born naked, and naked you are buried [source reads *sepeliris*; perhaps *sepelieris*].

O irremediable madness! What perishable thing belonging to another do you love with such great love that you lose what is eternally your own forever? Think, then, of death, which puts an end to the world’s pleasures [perhaps: “desires”], and see where the pleasant joy of the rich has gone.

Luxury, amusement, lust, and extravagance have fallen silent; and the naked corpse, to be dissolved by worms and decay, has been received by mud, while the most wretched soul has been handed over to eternal punishments.

What is more tearfully pitiable than this condition? What is more unhappy than this misery: to pursue the vanities of this life until corruption and perpetual destruction?

Truly, the patience of a single hour was better than late repentance after an eternity of time. Fear, then, death on this side of heaven and eternal fire beyond heaven. Fear this which you see, and that which you do not see but nevertheless believe on the testimony of him who saw it.

For our Lord Jesus Christ is truthful. To him are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

INSTRUCTION IV. That We Must Labor in the Present Life So That We May Rest in the Future.

I. Every discipline, according to the Apostle, seems in the present not to be joyful but sorrowful; afterward, however, it yields a pleasing fruit and a peaceful return on one’s reward to those who have been trained by it (Hebr. XII, 2).

For what, in truth, is learned here without sorrow or labor, in a time of our great foolishness and fragility? If the temporal kinds of discipline take away the sweetness of present joy, what should we expect from the discipline of our school? This is the discipline of disciplines, which exchanges the delight of eternal time and the loveliness of eternal joy for present sorrow.

For what kind of discipline is free from the sorrow of correction? How much sadness or sorrow is present in the crafts of artisans? How much labor? How much effort weighs upon those who manufacture or even build? With how many blows and pains are students of music [Note: [Col. 0237] “Students of music.” Perhaps *musicorum*, “of musicians,” as shortly afterward *medicorum*, “of physicians.” *Discentes* means “students” or “disciples.”] instructed? With what weariness and how many sorrows are the students of physicians troubled? With what kinds of anxieties, and with how many hardships of poverty, are lovers of wisdom—or philosophers [perhaps: “philosophers”]—confined?

Finally, with how many dangers are the helms sought? In all these pursuits, after the labors of countless hardships, a very peaceful end is patiently awaited. In consideration of it, the aforesaid calamities are endured, though not without sorrow and with much bitterness.

For although discipline is accompanied by sorrow, its end nevertheless proceeds in joy; labor is turned toward security; and, in a wondrous way, sorrow is patiently endured in place of joy, bitterness in place of sweetness, labor in place of security, and unrest in place of rest.

Although they do not know whether they will reach the end of whichever discipline they are pursuing, they nevertheless endure present sorrow for the uncertain hope of future joy; they do not reject it, and while they labor, they attain it through perseverance.

For which of them is certain whether the teacher of the discipline whose labor he endures will ever be his teacher [perhaps: “even be the teacher of that discipline”]? Or whether he will share in the joy for which he tolerates sorrow?

II. If, then, such great and difficult things are tirelessly endured for temporal and uncertain matters, what ought we to endure for eternal, true, and certain things whose end is eternal?

For although it is uncertain, among those who pursue temporal disciplines, how long they will be able to enjoy the discipline they have attained, they are not undone by any sluggishness in pursuing it. Thus they are doubly uncertain and yet more persistent than we are: uncertain, as I said, whether they will reach the end of the discipline, because life is uncertain and understanding is foolish; and, after attaining the discipline, they are again uncertain how long they will use it. For the more uncertain they are about making progress, the more certain they are that they will soon lose the discipline.

Therefore, when it is clear that temporal studies, defective abilities, sorrows and sadnesses, hardships and labors, dangers and wanderings, injuries and wearinesses are uncertain and fragile—even though such great calamities are endured for their sake—will the discipline of our school, if it contains tribulations, difficulties, sorrows, and bitterness, be surprising or be thought worthy of avoidance? Is it not impossible to acquire any perfected mastery without discipline [source: *magistratio*], or any kind of warfare [read: *militia*]? Or can discipline be attained without bitterness?

Since these things are so, let us prepare our minds not for joy or security, as the Wise Man says (Ecclus. II, 1), but for temptations and tribulations, for sadnesses and labors. Christ was troubled, insulted, reviled, and suffered. Do you expect security on earth? See and understand how difficult it is to conquer the world, since no one is freed from it as a saint except through Christ’s death: “If the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (I Pet. IV, 18).

Hear the Lord saying to his disciples: “In the world you will have distress” (John XVI, 33). And again: “But you will weep and lament, while the world will rejoice, and you will be sorrowful” (ibid., 20).

III. Consider the sorrow of our discipline; understand that one passes not from joy to joy, nor from security to security, but from mourning to joy and from tribulation to security. The brief sorrow must therefore be patiently endured, so that eternal joy may be acquired; and the light burden of our tribulation must be borne with eagerness, so that we may attain the eternal life of immeasurable glory.

For if such things happen on account of perishable matters—as we have very often said—and do not conquer us, what will weary or overcome us, who are merchants of the heavenly kingdoms? We must yield to neither pleasant nor sorrowful things, to flatterers nor to friends: the world is full of both kinds, and each kind overcomes the leader of our battle. Let us see how perilously the unclean person yields to those things to which the pure and spotless person did not yield: with Christ, let us regard the honors of the world and the kingdoms of the devil with all their glory.

Whatever belongs to the devil, let us disdain to accept, and let us say to that king of brief joy: “Let your possessions be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8:20). Let us be sorrowful with Christ unto death, so that our sorrow may be changed into joy. Let the world laugh with the devil; may their joy be far from us. If we wish to rejoice now, let us rejoice partly in hope, while later possessing true joy in reality: sorrowful because of our sins, joyful because of the hope of eternal life; sorrowful because of Christ’s absence, yet likewise exulting because we read: “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Although we are filled with the sorrows of present miseries, although we are saddened by the multitude of our sins, the generous victory over both is joy and noble gladness. And although for a time we are pilgrims away from the Lord, so that after the battle of a brief time we may be crowned forever, we must not be excessively sorrowful, knowing that we shall soon go to God and remain with him always. For he created us for this purpose: that, reigning with him forever and ever, we might praise him and persevere in giving him thanks.

Knowing these things, let us not fail through any labors or tribulations; let us not be overcome by any sorrows; let us not be wearied by any battles; let us not be abandoned by any anxieties of discipline; let us not again be dissolved by any pleasures; let us not be deceived by any flatteries. And, to speak in the Apostle’s words (Romans 8:38–39), let nothing separate us from the love of Christ: no tribulation, no distress, no persecution, no famine, no nakedness, no danger, no death—whether by sword, fire, cross, or slaughter. Let nothing sorrowful, nothing pleasant, nothing harsh, nothing flattering, nothing of the world’s true things [perhaps “vain things”] separate us from Christ, so that here and throughout the eternal ages of ages we may cling to him. Amen.

# INSTRUCTION V. That the present life should not be called life, but a way

## I

O life, how many you have deceived, how many you have led astray, how many you have blinded! While you flee, you are nothing; while you appear, you are a shadow; while you are exalted, you are smoke. You flee each day and come each day; by coming you flee, and by fleeing you come. Unlike in your outcome, like in your origin; unlike in your splendor, like in your flow; sweet to fools, bitter to the wise.

Those who love you do not know you; those who despise you understand you. Therefore you are not truthful but deceptive: you present yourself as though true, and withdraw yourself as though deceptive. What, then, are you, human life? You are the way of mortals, and not life—from sin beginning and continuing until death. You would indeed be true if the sin of humanity’s first transgression had not interrupted you; but then you became [Note: “Cassabunda.” Perhaps *casabunda*: perishable, slippery, unstable.] perishable and mortal, when you consigned all your travelers to death.

You are therefore a way to life, and not life. You are not true; you are a way, but not a level one: long for some, short for others; broad for some, narrow for others; joyful for some, sorrowful for others; hastening equally for all, and irreversible.

You are a way, I say—you are a way—but you are not evident to everyone. Many see you, but few understand that you are a way. For you are so subtle and so seductive that only a few know you as a way. You must therefore be questioned, not trusted or claimed; passed through, not inhabited—you miserable human life. No one dwells on a road; one walks upon it, so that those who walk on the road may dwell in their homeland.

## II

Why, then, mortal life, are you inhabited, loved, and claimed? You are loved and claimed by fools and the lost; you are despised by the sensible and avoided by those being saved. You must therefore be feared and greatly avoided, human life, since you are so fleeting, so slippery, so dangerous, so brief, and so uncertain that you dissolve like a shadow, an image, a cloud, nothing, or emptiness.

Since, then, you are nothing, mortal life—or an image, fleeting like a bird, uncertain like a cloud, and fragile like a shadow or a dream—we must travel through you so attentively, cautiously, and swiftly that, in the manner of travelers, all who understand may hasten toward the true homeland. [Note: “[The text is defective from ‘all who understand . . .’ to ‘attentive.’ Goldastus, *Paraeneticorum veterum*, part I, p. 153, restores the passage—certainly corrupt—as follows: ‘Every intelligent person should hasten, secure concerning what has passed, and attentive to what remains.’”]

Secure concerning what has passed, attentive to what remains: it does you no good to climb what you have climbed unless you escape what remains. For this way must be considered a kind of road and ascent [perhaps “life”]. Let us not seek on the road what will be found in the homeland. Labor and weariness belong to the journey; rest and security are prepared in the homeland.

We must therefore beware lest we be secure on the road and fail to reach our true homeland. For there are indeed some on this journey who are idle, secure, and envious, so that they seem to be not on the road but in the homeland; and they go to the homeland not so much willingly as unwillingly—indeed, to one already lost. Here on the road they have enjoyed their homeland in advance, and for a brief life they have purchased eternal death.

Unhappy people, they rejoice in a frustrated exchange; they have loved what belongs to others and is perishable, and have neglected what is their own and eternal. Therefore, however joyful, flattering, or beautiful earthly things belonging to others may be, let us avoid them, lest we lose what is our own and eternal. Let us be found faithful in what belongs to others, so that in what is our own and ours we may become heirs, through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# INSTRUCTION VI. That the present life is like a shadow

## I

By the gift of the Lord we have spoken about human life, saying that it resembles a road, on which each person, journeying toward eternal things, should remain free from alien desires and content—as though with only the poverty of a traveler’s provisions—so that, clinging to no enticements, he may understand that all earthly things are foreign to him.

Now let us show that this same life is a shadow, as we said earlier. Does human life on earth not seem to you to be a shadow and an image? It is so doubtful and uncertain in its duration that it resembles a shadow. You see and do not see; let us say, it is itself and yet not itself. What has been, you do not see; what will be, you cannot see either. You see only what is, what remains for a while. Remove what you are [perhaps “what is”], and you see nothing; it is unseen, as though it did not exist.

Thus everyone sees his life as a shadow, and from morning until evening, as though in a mirror, he looks upon the vanity of his life. [Col. 0241D] But each person sees such other likenesses only in dreams: for he likewise observes false things in place of true ones, and is enclosed [perhaps “mocked”] by empty things in place of the image of truth. [Note: “*Includitur.* Perhaps *illuditur* (‘is mocked’). Thus a little later, *illudunt* (‘they mock’) seems to be required instead of *includunt*.”]

For what, I ask, is the difference between what you saw yesterday and what you dreamed at night? Do they not likewise seem empty to you today? Indeed, what flees while I see it does not satisfy me more as something true than what encloses me in dreams. I find both to be empty.

What I am, I was not, and I will not be; and each hour I am something else, and never do I remain still. I am always running from the day of my birth to the day of my death, and each day I am changed throughout my life. I do not see whatever is changed, or how it is changed; nor can I ever see my whole life all at once in a single view.

What I was yesterday, I am not today; just so, what I am today, I will not be tomorrow. And so I shall remain ever mobile and changeable throughout the remaining spaces of my life, as from moment to moment, from moments to hours, and from hours to days, I run together with the uncertain spans of my age toward death, so that there I may see what is certain and true, and all at once in a single view—that which is impossible for me here.

## II

O miserable me! If there I do not see the life that I never see as true here—for it must be true there, where eternity acts. Flee, then, flee, O shadow of mortal life! Flee from us, and let us flee from you. You flee as you do, for you always flee, so that true life may come quickly. Let us flee from you, lest you deceive us; for you are accustomed to deceive the slow through alluring impediments.

Flee, I say, and hasten—you who have led many astray, who are pressing to lead us astray, and who will lead others after us and consign them to death. O how blind you are, how seductive, uncertain life! You await me in order to seize me; you summon me in order to persuade me; you entreat me in order to lead me astray; you persuade me in order to deceive me.

Who is so foolish as to believe you, when you deceive those who love you and lead believers astray? Those who love you have been deceived; those who believe you have been led astray. But those who neglect you have been enriched, and those who flee you have been saved. Those who despise you seek God.

Let us therefore flee from you before you flee from us. And because you are mortal, brief, perishable, uncertain, unstable, mobile, changeable, and mutable, let us be regarded as lovers and merchants of God and eternal life rather than of you. Let us flee from you as you flow and flee, lest you claim us along with your lovers.

For we must flee what flees, and live in it as though we had to die every day. What difference does it make to us whether we die today or tomorrow? Since we must die, death should be considered by us as though it had already long since passed away. Since nothing lasts before death, we must hasten toward death, so that after death we may be able to see the true and eternal things.

Therefore we must not delay but hasten from the shadow of imagined life to the truth of true life. And because the way of bodily life is one thing and the way of spiritual progress another, let the mind run in progress as life runs in its courses, and let the maturity of the mind increase to the fullness of age. As the circles of life diminish, so let the number of vices decrease, so that, when we leave the world, we may leave its ways behind and carry none of its customs with us to the Lord, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# INSTRUCTION VII. On the blindness of the human being who, neglecting the spirit, serves the body

## I

O blind madness! O blind pit, human will, which conceals what it has received and does not return what has been given! You are appeased in vain; though fed, you are ungrateful; you devour in vain, you who exact the revenue [perhaps “capital”] of your greed so opportunely.

O utterly shameless one, impatient leech, harsh yet satiated, flattering yet fasting, voracious, shameless, ravenous—what is right in you? What is honorable? Nothing.

You seek what has been frustrated; you repeat what has been reproved; you adorn what is shameful. Why do you not consider yourself, miserable humanity—rotten within, full of bile, moisture, fluid, blood, and phlegm; without, a washed skin [perhaps “a skin washed”], but never cleansed [perhaps “purified”]? For you are always defiled and polluted by the innermost filth of the mire. Although you wash yourself every day, every day you are violated.

O soiled skin! You are washed in vain, since by nature you are unclean. O inverted blindness! What you wash and adorn is by nature rot; what you violate and pollute is by nature splendor. Why do you pollute what is clean and wash what is unclean, when you corrupt the soul and adorn the body?

Do you love yourself enough, or do you know yourself too little? If you know yourself, why do you love the horrible and unclean dwellings of phlegm and filth? If you see uncleanness on your clothing, if you recoil from phlegm and turn your gaze away, why do you not flee or detest yourself as an unclean dung heap and foul, rotting wallow in your own garments?

Do you not see what your tubelike skin harbors through its openings? It is shameful to mention what it is not shameful to love. Why do we not recoil from what is horrible? Why do we not detest what is shameful? Why do we not flee what is foul? Is it not because we lack understanding and are not clean?

Therefore the unclean seek what is unclean, the shameful what is shameful, and the dishonorable what is dishonorable; and because we are blind and dishonorable, we avoid nothing shameful. If we are not blind, why do we not despise our original uncleanness? Why do we not despise either our shamefulness or our disgrace?

Do not things that are shameful seem honorable to you—things that require repeated lamentations and varied adornments, things that are not satisfied with the expenses lavished upon them, and, once satisfied, do not help with what is to come, while desire already passed does not satisfy the present or repel the future? [Note: “*Repellit.* Perhaps *esuriem* (‘hunger’), *famem* (‘famine’), or something similar is missing.”]

## II

He therefore labors in vain who nourishes such things, and sows in the wind who serves this empty will, where the service expended produces no benefit. Let these things hunger, then, since they are so ungrateful and troublesome that they seem always to be hungry. Those who nourish them deceive themselves.

O dishonorable servitude, in which the flesh is enjoyed [perhaps “the flesh is served”]! O harsh, inexorable, savage domination, even though domesticated! It is discharged every day and demanded every day; it goes and comes during the day; satiated it departs, hungry it returns.

Woe to those who are nourished here, where hunger rules and is not conquered even by riches; while one demand is discharged, another is made. If you pay the first, you are compelled to pay the second. Feed the throat, and you will be required to satisfy lust.

With Susanna, therefore, we must cry out: “I am distressed on every side” (Daniel 13:22). And with Paul we must wail and say: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24).

If you pay what is necessary, you are compelled to pay what is unnecessary. If, then, miserable human being, you fear paying the second, refuse the first if you can; if not, pay sparingly and discharge it grudgingly. Pay nothing except unwillingly; give nothing willingly. But you cannot. I see what is worse and more grievous: you love your exactors. Your enemy is your friend.

What shall I say? I do not know. What shall I advise? I am at a loss. I shall say one thing that I know: whoever is nourished here, satiated here, takes pleasure here, laughs here, becomes drunk here, and plays here will hunger there, thirst there, mourn there, lament there, and howl there, as the Lord said: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall mourn”; and: “Woe to you who are filled, for you shall hunger” (Luke 6:25).

For two times follow one another, and there are two lives and two ages: one life is brief and the other long. Whoever hungers in one will be nourished in the other; but whoever here devours, is satiated, and is consoled in the one will hunger and thirst in the other, according to the word of Isaiah: “Therefore the Lord says: Behold, those who serve me shall eat and drink, but you shall hunger and thirst” (Isaiah 65:13). And shortly afterward: “Behold, those who serve me shall exult in gladness, but you shall cry out because of sorrow of heart, and because of contrition of spirit you shall howl” (Isaiah 65:14).

Since these things are so, let us be sparing with riches and serve the brief will [perhaps “pleasure”] not at all, lest we be nourished unto hunger, lest we perhaps be satiated unto famine and drink unto thirst. For we see that we must necessarily experience one of the two, either here or there.

Therefore, if we are filled and drink—O miserable us!—let us eat here only in part, what is necessary and not what is pleasant. Let us eat with the poor, drink with the poor, and share with the poor, so that in this way we may deserve to share with the poor there, where those who hunger and thirst for righteousness here for Christ’s sake shall be filled (Matthew 5:6).

For whose is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:3), if not the poor—those who are humble in spirit and poor in riches for Christ’s sake? To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# INSTRUCTION VIII. That we must hasten toward the heavenly homeland, the end of the present way

## I

Now, behold, we must speak about the end of life. We have already said that human life is a way, and we have shown by its likeness to a shadow how doubtful and uncertain it is, and that it is not what it is. We likewise said earlier how unforeseen and how blind it is. With the Holy Spirit’s help, our discourse must now proceed concerning the end of our life.

It belongs to travelers to hasten toward the homeland; likewise, concern belongs to them on the road, and security in the homeland. Let us therefore hasten toward the homeland, we who are on the road, for our whole life is like the journey of a single day.

Our first duty is to love nothing here; rather, let us love above, desire above, understand above, and seek the homeland above. For the Father is there. We have no homeland on earth, because our Father is in heaven (Matthew 6:9).

Indeed, by the power of his dominion and the greatness of his divinity he is everywhere—deeper than the sea, more stable than the earth, broader than the world, purer than the air, higher than heaven, brighter than the sun (Job 11:8–9). Yet he is manifestly in heaven, where there is the bread of angels, who, as inhabitants of the first heavenly kingdom in their own home, enjoy the sight of God.

But because a nature more infirm could not bear the pure nature of God, which cannot be seen [perhaps “the nature of God, which cannot be seen”], the merciful God—within whom all things exist and outside whom nothing exists—enclosed the first region of his knowledge within the first heaven, which he tempered with raised waters, and assigned it to the heavenly powers. For unless the nature of that first heaven were tempered by the waters mentioned above, it could never have been endured by the lower natures, being kindled by the power of the heavenly God. Thus God, present everywhere, is invisible.

For he is greater than the whole can comprehend and greater than all things, since he created all things from nothing. Therefore, when he is seen, he is invisible, because who and how great he is is known to him alone.

Nevertheless, let us knock upon him, for, although invisible and beyond estimation, God the Trinity is present and known to each person according to the merit of his purity. Let us knock, I say, either from here or from there more familiarly; let us enter, or let us understand more clearly. Let us say, singing on the road:

“After you, we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1:3);

and: “My soul has clung to you” (Psalm 62:9);

and: “Draw me after you” (Song of Songs 1:3).

Thus, hastening through the world with these songs, guided by heavenly things, let us neglect the present. Thinking always about heavenly things, let us despise earthly things; for unless we long ardently with impatient heavenly desires, we must cling to earthly things.

## II

Let us therefore occupy ourselves with divine things, lest perhaps with human things. Like pilgrims, let us always sigh for the homeland and always desire the homeland; for the end of the road is always welcome and desirable to travelers.

Since we are travelers and pilgrims in the world, let us always think about the end of the road—that is, of our life—for the end of our road is our homeland. But there all who travel through the world [perhaps “all who journey through the world”] receive different destinies according to their merits, and good travelers rest in the homeland; the wicked, however, will perish from it.

Many lose the true homeland because they love the road more. Let us not love the road more than the homeland, lest we lose the eternal homeland. For we have such a homeland as we ought to love.

Let this definition therefore endure among us: that here we live on the road, as travelers, pilgrims, and guests of the world, clinging to no desires and longing for no earthly things, but filling our minds with heavenly and spiritual forms, singing in virtue and deed:

“When shall I come and appear before the face of my God? For my soul has thirsted for the strong and living God” (Psalm 41:3);

and:

“My soul is like land without water before you” (Psalm 142:6).

And let us say with Paul: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). Let us know that although we are pilgrims away from the Lord as long as we are in the body (2 Corinthians 5:6–8), we are nevertheless present before the eyes of God.

Therefore, having trampled down all sloth and laid aside all lukewarmness, let us strive to please him who is present everywhere, so that with a good conscience we may pass successfully from the way of this age into the blessed and eternal homeland of our Father, the Eternal One: from present things to absent things, from sorrowful things to joyful things, from perishable things to eternal things, from earthly things to heavenly things, from the region of death to the region of the living.

There, face to face, we shall see heavenly things, and the King of kings, the Lord our Jesus Christ, governing kingdoms by righteous rule. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# INSTRUCTION IX. On the final judgment

## I

Let us speak further about the end, dearest brothers. The end of our road, as we have said, is our homeland. But because some possess a homeland here and will not have the end of their road there in the homeland, they go from road to road—that is, they will be changed from punishment to punishment with a gnawing heart—and will have no rest.

Therefore the end of their road, that is, of their life, is not a homeland but punishment; it is not rest but disquiet. For the righteous, however, the end of life is eternal life, rest, everlasting peace, the heavenly homeland, blessed eternity, and infinite joy.

The end of human life’s road is therefore different, because although the way of human life is similar in fragility, slippery instability, and uncertain fugitiveness, it is dissimilar in its pursuits and progress. Yet a similar lot weighs down this dissimilar life here, and the course of the uncertain journey reveals it.

All are likewise born, grow, decline, become weak, suffer tribulation, and die. But when they come to the end, they are distinguished there. Those whom a similar course has wearied are separated by a different order. There the true testing and careful examination of a similar misery will take place—the misery that all travelers on the road endure as mortals upon the earth.

For there, as the Apostle says: “The fire will test what sort of work each one has done” (1 Corinthians 3:13).

Observe the order of the misery of human life: from earth, upon earth, into earth; from earth into fire; from fire into judgment; from judgment either into Gehenna or into life. For you were created from earth, you tread upon earth, you will go into earth, you will rise from earth, you will be tested in fire, and you will await judgment. After these things you will possess either eternal punishment or a kingdom.

For there, as the Apostle says, we must be revealed before the tribunal of Christ, so that each person may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10). The Lord likewise declares this in the Gospel: “The Son of Man will come in his glory, and then he will repay each according to his works” (Matthew 16:27).
