Consider, I ask, the weight of these words, and with fear and trembling keep that dreadful coming of divine judgment constantly in your anxious mind. Before that terrifying tribunal of Christ the Judge, the fire will test what sort of work each person has done, and each will report what belongs to his own body, whether good or evil, according to what he has done. There the Son of Man, when he comes, will repay each according to his works.

## II

The sentence is sufficiently terrifying, brothers, because he did not say, “He will repay each according to his mercy,” but “according to his works.” Here he is merciful; there he is a just judge.

Therefore we must fear; we must greatly tremble, dearest ones, when, as God proclaims, we learn that each person will be repaid according to his works. What harsher thing could he have said? What hope did he leave to humanity? Who can be justified through fire and not need the Judge’s mercy, when he dwells in a body of sin?

Who, I ask, bearing the flesh of the human race, would not fear these things, when it is proclaimed that we shall all be revealed and, so to speak, assigned before the tribunal of Christ, and that our works will there be tested by fire?

With sorrow for the lost it must be said: “Why does clay receive understanding? Why has understanding been made from dust?” We who were created from earth, standing upon it for a little while and soon to enter it again, will finally be tested by fire when God once more returns and casts us into it by his command, so that fire may, as it were, dissolve the earth and mud by its art; and if it contains any gold or silver, or any other useful elements of the earth, it may reveal them when the [*paracarassimo* / *paracaximo*] has been melted.

It belongs to dead and despairing souls not to fear these things. For hearing them even once should have been sufficient warning for anyone.

Therefore let us know that nothing is more useful to us than to review our precarious life throughout all the days of our life, examining ourselves daily, giving an account of our words and thoughts, and shuddering at human life. Let us think without interruption about the end of this road—that is, of our life—despising all the pleasures of this world.

We see life, but we recognize it as a fleeing and deceiving shadow and image. Therefore let not deceptive and seductive, brief and temporal, perishable and fragile, bitter and sorrowful life deceive us. Let us always think about the true and eternal life, which will possess the righteous as immortals after death.

Observe the reversal of things: life before death, and life after death. The righteous first possesses two lives, but the sinful and wicked person unhappily had one and lost the other, the blessed one. After the brief life, he goes from death into death, into destruction. May the goodness of the merciful God deign to rescue us from it through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# INSTRUCTION X. On avoiding the terrible wrath of the Judge who is to come

## I

In the preceding passages, dearest brothers, the Lord instilled great fear of the end in us through the Gospel and Paul. After such terrifying testimonies of the divine canon, what refuge remains for us? What tears, how many sighs, are required? By what kinds of compunction must the hard and stony heart be crushed, so that we may escape so great a Judge’s wrath?

The Creator and Lord of the universe threatens this wrath through himself, through the Apostle, and through the prophets, who do not conceal these same threats when they say:

“Behold, the day of the Lord comes, burning like a furnace, and it will consume them. All foreigners and all who commit iniquity will be like straw; and that day which is coming will set them ablaze, says the Lord almighty, and will leave them neither root nor shoot” (Malachi 4:1).

Likewise another prophet says:

“Behold, the Lord almighty comes; and who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will withstand the sight of him? For he himself will enter like a refiner’s fire” (Malachi 3:1–2).

Isaiah also says:

“Behold, the day of the Lord will come, incurable, a day of wrath and fury, a day of cloud and darkness” (Zephaniah 1:15).

And shortly afterward:

“For heaven will be shaken, and the earth will be moved from its foundations, because of the fury of the wrath of the Lord of hosts on the day when his fury comes upon it” (Isaiah 13:13).

Again he says:

“The foundations of the earth will be moved; the earth will be utterly troubled; the earth will be utterly astonished; the earth will be utterly bent; the earth will be utterly shaken. Like a drunkard and one overcome by wine, it will be shaken off” (Isaiah 24:19–20).

Asaph also speaks similarly:

“God will come manifestly; our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and around him there will be a mighty tempest” (Psalm 49:3).

And David speaks in agreement with this, saying:

“Fire will burn before him, and it will inflame his enemies round about” (Psalm 96:3).

## II

After such terrifying proclamations of the Old and New Testaments—the few that we recalled yesterday and today—let us consider by what satisfaction we may escape the wrath of so great a Judge.

We must remember the words of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ:

“Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; for whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:25).

Whatever we love apart from Christ must therefore be willingly lost for Christ’s sake. First, life itself, by which the body is given life through its union with the soul, must be surrendered for Christ by those who suffer martyrdom, if such a necessity arises. Or, if the opportunity for such blessedness is lacking, there will nevertheless be the mortification of the will, so that whoever lives may live not for himself but for him who died for him (2 Corinthians 5:15).

Let us therefore live for him who, when he dies for us, is life; and let us die to ourselves, so that we may live for Christ. For we cannot live for him unless we first die to ourselves—that is, to our own wills.

Let us belong to Christ, not to ourselves: “We are not our own, for we were bought with a great price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)—truly a great price, since the Lord was given for the servant, the King for the minister, and God for humanity.

What ought we to return, if the Creator of the universe died undeservedly for us wicked people, though we are nevertheless his creatures? Do you think you ought not to die to sin? Indeed, you ought.

Let us therefore die—let us die for life, because Life dies for the dead—so that with Paul we may say: “I live, yet it is no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20), he who died for me. This is the voice of the elect.

No one, however, can die to himself unless Christ lives in him. If Christ is in him, he cannot live for himself. Live in Christ, so that Christ may live in you.

## III

But you ask how the understanding may live in him, so that he may teach you to die to yourself and live for Christ—or, more truly expressed, to live for you. For whoever dies for Christ lives, while whoever lives for himself dies.

He is mortal if he lives according to his own wills, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die” (Romans 8:13).

You see, dearest ones, that we dwell in what belongs to another, since even our life is not our own. We ought not to live for ourselves. Great violence is required to seek through labor and possess through diligence what corrupted nature did not preserve.

Nevertheless, although blessedness has been lost, the freedom of choice has not been lost. Hence we now seize the kingdom of heaven by force and violence. We are, as it were, drawn out from the midst of our enemies’ hands, from the middle of the field of combat and its bloody ground, while we are attacked more harshly not only by our adversaries but by ourselves.

Each person loves himself wrongly and harms himself in the very thing that he loves. He loves himself well who hates himself in a salutary way—that is, afflicts himself. But whoever consents to his adversaries is not rightly said to love himself.

Great, therefore, is the misery of the person who does not perceive that he is harming himself. Since a human being is opposed to himself, it is not possible for everyone to pacify him in such a way that he truly loves himself.

Here, therefore, we must fight and contend against our vices, so that elsewhere we may be crowned. This is a time of war; therefore no one should imagine security in war, because no one sleeps in war and no one enters the battle line securely.

Our battle line must therefore be directed against everything vicious, pleasure-loving, and wrongly flattering. It is enough for combatants to conquer their adversaries. If you conquer yourself, you are victor over all. But if you are conqueror of yourself and dead to yourself, you are shown to be alive to God.

When you hear “dead,” with what boldness will each person enter Christ’s judgment, making himself—[the syntax is corrupt]—the advocate of his own case, the proponent of his own desire, and the avenger of his own contempt, while martyrizing himself for Christ?

For if he had truly taken up Christ’s cross, he would recognize that none of these things were permitted to him, since Christ also gave this example: that no one should seek what is his own, saying, “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39), and: “I came down not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

## IV

Let each person consider himself, lest he be found free and alive in the place of a servant and one crucified. Let each person remain with God in the calling in which he was called, and, as the Apostle said, “whether free or subject” (1 Corinthians 12:13), let them be servants in Christ beneath the yoke of humility.

Therefore, dearest ones, let each of us come against himself. For if we live not against ourselves but against our brothers, and if we speak as we please, our religion is not true but false.

Nothing free, then, ought to exist in Christ’s servants, and nothing lofty ought to exist in Christ’s humility. Let us not be proud, insolent, or free; let us be humble, gentle, approachable, and companionable, so that the humble King—another, yet Christ—may reign in us.

But in order that we may love this salutary death with a certain sweetness of hope, let us hear its end. Who, in truth, is happier than the one whose death is life, whose life is Christ, and whose reward is the Savior; for whom heaven is humbled and paradise lies open; for whom earth is heavenly and hell is closed; for whom the door is opened and life does not end; for whom God is Father and an angel is minister?

He acquires, in a blessed exchange, the long from the brief, the blessed from the wretched, the eternal from the perishable, the joyful from the sorrowful, the exalted from the humble, heaven from earth, and God from being mortal.

If, therefore, we despise present things and seek only future things, we exchange all the things mentioned above for better ones. But if, God forbid, we place the superior after the inferior, we shall undoubtedly lose both.

Therefore, if we seek life with Jesus, let us first have his mortification in us. [Note: “*Ut mortif.* Something such as *opus est* (‘it is necessary’) must be supplied at the beginning, or something similar that completes the sense.”]

May God Christ deign to grant this to us, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one God forever and ever. Amen.

# INSTRUCTION XI. On the love of God and of one’s neighbor
## I

Moses wrote in the Law: “God made man in his own image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Consider, I beg you, the dignity of this statement. Almighty, invisible, incomprehensible, ineffable, and inestimable God, fashioning man from clay [perhaps: “the clay”], ennobled him with the dignity of his own image. What does man have in common with God? What does one made of clay have in common with spirit? For God is spirit (John 4:24). Great is the condescension by which God gave man the image of his eternity and the likeness of his character. Great is man’s dignity in being like God, if that likeness is preserved; but great also is the condemnation incurred by violating God’s image.

For if man corrupts what he receives from God’s breath by turning its use toward the opposite, and contaminates nature’s gift, then he corrupts the likeness of God and, so far as lies in him, erases it. But if he rightly uses the virtues implanted in his soul, then he will be like God. Whatever virtues, therefore, God sowed in us at our first creation, he taught us by his commandments to return to him.

This is the first commandment: to love our God with all our heart (Matt. 22:37; Mark 12:30), because he first loved us (1 John 4:10), from the beginning and before we existed. For love of God is the renewal of his image. The person who keeps God’s commandments loves God. For he said: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15). His commandment is love for one another, according to the words: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34). True love is not only in word, but in deed and truth (1 John 3:28).

Let us therefore return to our God, our Father, his image inviolate: in holiness, because he is holy, according to the words, “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 11:44; 1 Pet. 1:16); in charity, because he is charity, according to John’s words, “God is charity” (1 John 4:8); and in piety and truth, because he is pious and true.

## II

Let us not be painters of another’s image. For the painter of a tyrannical image is the one who is savage, angry, or proud. Just as false knowledge is read about, so also a false, shadowy image is detected. Truth is divided from falsehood, justice from wickedness, charity from malice, diligence from carelessness, equity from perversity, and love from pretense; and these two sets paint within us images that oppose one another. Devotion and impiety, peace and discord, are contrary to one another.

Therefore, lest we introduce tyrannical images into ourselves, may Christ paint his own image in us—he who painted it by saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

But what good is it to know that peace is good if it is not carefully preserved? Whatever is best tends to be most fragile, and precious things require greater caution and more diligent protection. For what is lost through a light word, and perishes through the slightest injury to a brother, is exceedingly fragile. You injure no one when you flatter him, nor do you flatter anyone when you despise him. Say “Fool” (Matt. 5:22), and you have violated peace and become liable to hellfire.

Those who strive to fulfill fraternal love must therefore beware of speaking as they please and moving their tongues according to the impulse of their spirit, since we shall give an account not only of injurious words but also of idle ones (Matt. 12:36). Accordingly, we must take care not to linger over many words, but to speak whatever is necessary.

Nothing is more agreeable to people than speaking about others, concerning themselves with others, uttering idle words indiscriminately, and slandering those who are absent. Therefore, those who cannot say, “The Lord has given me a learned tongue, so that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word” (Isa. 50:4), should remain silent; and if they say anything, let it be peaceful.

Even a wise person offends fewer people with few words than with many. For whenever someone lies, curses, or slanders, he cuts his own throat with his own sword. What else would our enemies have wished for us except that we should fall by our own weapons? “Do not slander,” Scripture says, “lest you be uprooted” (Ps. 36:8–9).

See how much labor is expended upon works of impiety: the dwelling and planting that we scarcely establish through great and divine labor is uprooted by a single word of slander; and what can scarcely be made firm through long toil is overthrown by the force of one utterance. Let everyone therefore beware lest, because of slander born of hatred, his own root be uprooted from the land of the living. No one ever slanders one whom he loves; for slander is hatred’s firstborn, and therefore the child of such a father will rightly be uprooted.

## III

A dangerous dwelling-place, beloved, is one in which these things are not avoided. For if, as the Apostle says, you envy and bite one another, and slander one another, I say, take care lest you be consumed by one another (Gal. 5:15). If the one who does not love is in death (1 John 3:14), where will the one who slanders be?

These matters require tears more than words. For what has God’s law commanded with greater diligence or abundance than love? And rarely do you find anyone acting in this way. What shall we say in our defense? Can we say, “It is difficult”? “It is harsh”? Love is not laborious; love is more pleasant, more healing, and more wholesome for the heart. For if the heart is not weakened by vices, its very health is love, and nothing is dearer to God than love—especially spiritual love—since it is the sum of his law and all his commandments, according to the Apostle’s words: “The one who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law” (Rom. 13:8).

Whoever fulfills the law through the practice of love possesses eternal life, just as John says: “Brothers, we know that we have passed from death to life because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love remains in death. Whoever hates is a murderer; and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3:14–15).

Either, then, nothing should be done except love, or nothing should be hoped for except punishment. For “love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13:8). May our merciful Lord and Savior Jesus Christ abundantly inspire this love in us—he who, as the author of peace and God of charity, deigned to give it. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# Instruction XII: On Compunction and Vigilance, by Which the Judge’s Coming Is to Be Awaited

## I

In our preceding discourses we have attempted, however inadequately, to suggest the necessity of compunction; and, as though in a soliloquy—though one of our own—we have wished to rouse the sluggishness of every heart. But because poverty of faith and the will of the flesh, together with worldly desires, listen coldly to these lessons of correction and despise them, the same things must very often be repeated. For if faith were not doubtful, even one of the testimonies of the divine oracle mentioned above would be sufficient.

Those who disregard what they have heard both believe and do not believe. Otherwise, if someone said to you today—“Utare” [uncertain; perhaps a proper name]—that the judge of this world wished to burn you alive tomorrow, what anxiety, I ask, and what fear would threaten you? Having heard this, if you had one day of freedom, how much would you do? How would you cry out? Through whom would you run about? How humbly, mournfully, and miserably would you wander? Would you not pour out all your money upon those through whose intercession you believed you could escape? Would you not make all your possessions the ransom of your soul and reserve nothing, even if you were frugal and greedy, but squander and give everything for your life?

And if someone attempted to delay or hinder you, would you not say: “Let everything perish for my salvation, so that [perhaps: “nor”] nothing may remain—only let me live”? Why would you do this? Because you would not doubt [read: “but that”] that, according to the sentence of the most severe Judge, you were to burn.

Here, however, you doubt because you do not know how soon it will happen; yet you do not fail to know that it will happen, although you neglect it. Therefore we must awaken, keep watch, and pray, according to the command of our Savior Jesus Christ, our God, who says:

“Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with overeating and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly. For it will come like a snare upon all who dwell upon the face of the whole earth. Keep watch, therefore, at all times, that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21:34–36).

## II

If we hear and believe these things, our vigilance will display our faith. Once the filthy and sluggish torpor of deadly tepidity has been shaken off, let the sentence of the Lord our Savior stir our senses, so that, having laid aside all mortal cares, we may always be ready—awaiting, that is, the coming of the final day, when either punishment or glory will receive us.

Let the foregoing word of the Lord sharpen the sight of our minds. It taught us to be continually watchful and prayerful, so that we may not be like people who both believe and do not believe, or who both hear and do not hear. Let us unweariedly implore, ask, and pray from the depths of our hearts, through Jesus Christ his Son, for the ineffable mercy of the gracious and good God: may he deign to inspire his love in us so that he may unite us to himself forever, bind us inseparably to himself, raise us from the earth, and meanwhile join our minds to heaven, as long as we remain established in this body of death; and thus may we await his coming without complaint, so that when he appears we may meet him with joy and great confidence of love, pleasing to him.

How blessed, how happy are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, will find watching (Luke 12:37)! Blessed is the watchfulness by which one watches for God, the author of the universe, who fills all things and surpasses all things.

Would that he might also deign to awaken me, though vile, yet still his little servant, from the sleep of inertia, and kindle me with that fire of divine love, by which the flame of his love—the longing for his immeasurable affection—might blaze above the stars, and the divine fire might always burn within me.

Would that I had that wood which this fire might continually be [nourished—perhaps “fed”], sustained, and kindled; and that the flame might be nourished which knew neither extinction nor increase. Would that I were such in merit that my lamp might always burn at night in the temple of my Lord, shining for all who entered the house of my God.

## III

Lord, I beg you, in the name of Jesus Christ, your Son and my God, give me that love which knows no falling: let my lamp know how to be kindled but not how to be extinguished; let it burn for me and shine for others.

You, Christ, most sweet Savior of us all, deign to kindle our lamps, so that they may shine perpetually in your temple and receive everlasting light from you, the everlasting Light; thus may our darkness be illuminated, while the world’s darkness flees from us.

I beg you, my Jesus, to grant your light to my lamp, so that by its light that holy of holies may appear to me, which has you, the eternal High Priest of eternal things, entering the inner chambers of that great temple of yours; there may I continually see, behold, and desire only you. May I behold you in love alone, desire and await you, and may my lamp always shine and burn before you.

May it be yours, I beg you, most loving Savior, to show yourself to us when we knock, so that, understanding you, we may love only you, desire only you, meditate upon only you day and night, and always think of you. Deign to inspire your love in us to the degree that it is fitting for you, God, to be loved and cherished, so that your love may occupy all our inward parts, your love possess us wholly, and your charity fill all our senses. Thus may we know how to love nothing besides you, who are eternal; and may such great charity never be extinguished in us by the many waters of this air, this earth, and this sea, according to the words: “Many waters could not extinguish love” (Song 8:7).

May this also be fulfilled in us, even if only in part, through your gift, Lord our God Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# Instruction XIII: On Approaching and Drinking from Christ Jesus, the Living Fountain

## I

Having gathered the misery of human life from the reasonings of daily experience and having also been terrified by divine perils, we have for a long time, though rashly, displayed above the smallness of our limited intelligence. Although this loquacity of ours may perhaps seem superfluous to others, we nevertheless consider the speech to have arisen appropriately for us. For we are trying to rouse not so much another person’s sluggishness as our own. And although this wisdom, devised in part, may perhaps satisfy more perfect sages, it will nevertheless seem necessary and sufficiently suitable to beginners and to those who are lukewarm according to our measure.

For what is harmful to conceal, and harmful to keep silent, ought not to be hidden or left unspoken. It therefore seemed better to us to speak about these matters, however inelegantly, than to remain silent. Indeed, we judged it safer to speak of them than either of frivolous matters or of idle subjects.

Therefore, dearest brothers, continue to lend your ears to our words as though you were about to hear something necessary. Refresh the thirst of your souls with the waters of the divine fountain about which we now wish to speak, but do not extinguish that thirst. Drink, but do not become satisfied; for the Living Fountain, the Fountain of Life, is already calling us to himself and saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

Understand what you should drink. Let Isaiah [read: Jeremiah] speak to you; let the Fountain itself speak to you: “They have forsaken me, says the Lord, the fountain of living water” (Jer. 2:13). The Lord himself, therefore, our God Jesus Christ, is the Fountain of Life, and for this reason he invites us to himself, the Fountain, so that we may drink him.

The one who loves drinks him; the one who is satisfied with God’s word drinks him; the one who loves and desires sufficiently drinks him; the one who burns with love of wisdom drinks him. Let us therefore, we Gentiles, drink eagerly what the Jews abandoned.

For perhaps this was said concerning us Gentiles: “He cut off in the stupor of the mind; the heads of the mighty will be shaken,” and not toward those opening their jaws, like a poor man eating in secret; and perhaps it was also said concerning us together with all the perfect, about whom this was written.

Let us open the jaws of our inner person, as though eating that bread which descended from heaven, so that we may eat voraciously and, as it were, quickly, lest anyone see us, consuming it in secret.

Let us therefore eat the bread and drink the fountain—our same Lord Jesus Christ, who calls himself the living bread to be taken by us, the bread that gives life to this world (John 6:33). Likewise, showing himself to be the fountain, he says: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink” (John 7:37). Of this fountain the Prophet also says: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:10).

## II

See from where this fountain flows, for it flows from the same place from which the bread descended. The one who is both Bread and Fountain is the same: the only Son, our God Christ the Lord. We must always hunger for him, even though we eat him by loving and devour him by desiring; still, as though hungry, we must desire him.

In the same way, let us drink him as the fountain, always with an excess of love; let us drink him always with the fullness of desire, and delight in a certain sweetness of his pleasantness. For the Lord is sweet and gracious.

Although we eat and drink him, let us nevertheless always hunger and thirst, because our food and drink can never be wholly consumed and drunk. Though it is taken, it is not consumed; though it is drunk, it is not diminished. For our bread is eternal, our fountain everlasting, and our fountain sweet. Hence the Prophet says: “You who thirst, go to the Fountain” (Isa. 55:2). This Fountain is for those who thirst, not for those who are satisfied; and therefore it calls to itself those who hunger, whom it blessed elsewhere. They can never have drunk enough; rather, the more they draw, the more they thirst.

Rightly, brothers, the Fountain of Wisdom, the Word of God on high (Ecclus. 1:5), is to be desired, sought, and always loved by us. In him are hidden, according to the Apostle’s saying, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3), and he calls those who thirst to draw from them.

If you thirst, drink the Fountain of Life; if you hunger, eat the Bread of Life. Blessed are those who hunger for this Bread and thirst for this Fountain. For while they are always eating and drinking, they still desire to eat and drink more.

What is always eaten and drunk, always hungered for and thirsted for, always tasted and always desired, is exceedingly sweet. Hence the prophetic king says: “Taste and see how sweet, how gracious, the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9).

Therefore, brothers, let us follow this call by which Life calls us to the Fountain of Life—him who is not only the Fountain of living water, but also the Fountain of eternal life, the Fountain of light, and likewise the Fountain of illumination. All these things come from him: wisdom, life, and eternal light.

The author of life is the Fountain of life; the creator of light is the Fountain of illumination. Therefore, rejecting the things that are seen and passing by an ascent into the heights of heaven, let us seek the Fountain of light, the Fountain of life, the Fountain of living water, as rational and very discerning fish, so that we may drink living water springing up into eternal life (John 4:14).

## III

Would that you might deign to admit me there, merciful God and gracious Lord, to that Fountain, so that there I too, together with your thirsty ones, might drink the living stream of the living Fountain’s water. Delighted by its immeasurable sweetness, may I always cling upward to it and say: “How sweet is the Fountain of living water, whose springing water does not fail into eternal life” (ibid.)!

O Lord, you yourself are this Fountain, always and always to be desired, always indeed to be drawn from [perhaps add: “to be drunk”]. “Lord Christ, give us this water always” (ibid. 15), so that in us too it may be a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life.

I am asking for great things—who does not know it? But you, King of glory, know how to give great things, and you have promised great things. Nothing is greater than you, and you gave yourself to us; you gave yourself for us.

Therefore we ask you to let us know what we love, since we ask that nothing other than you be given to us. For you are everything to us: our life, our light, our salvation, our food, our drink, and our God.

I beg you, our Jesus, inspire our hearts with that breath of your Spirit, and wound our souls with your love, so that each one of our souls may truly say: “Show me the one whom my soul has loved” (Song 1:6), for I am wounded by love.

I desire those wounds to be in me, Lord. Blessed is the soul that is wounded in this way by love. Such a soul seeks the Fountain; such a soul drinks, yet always thirsts while drinking; it always draws while desiring, and always drinks while thirsting. Thus it always seeks by loving, and is healed by being wounded.

May God and our Lord Jesus Christ, that gracious and healing physician, deign to wound the innermost parts of our souls with this saving wound. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belongs unity forever and ever. Amen.

# Instruction XIV: Various Lessons for the Spiritual Life

## I

Although I have spoken for a long time about conduct and moral disciplines, you ask again, my son who must be instructed, to be taught. You have heard what is written: “For one to whom a little is not sufficient, more will not be beneficial.”

I previously wrote to you about seriousness and chastity, concerning which, as someone aptly put it, I fear even what is safe. But because admonition becomes, for some, protection; for others, consolation; and for others, perfection—provided, of course, that they understand and fulfill it—therefore the dearest sons must frequently be taught and instructed, so that through certain delights of reading they may be able to overcome the bitterness of their inward battle.

Conquer, therefore, war and what is beastly: namely, desires and haughtiness; and be useful [perhaps: manly] in humility, weak in authority, simple in faith, learned in conduct, sharp in others’ affairs, lenient in your own, pure in friendship, shrewd against ambushes, hard in soft things, soft in hard things.

Be varied in plain matters and plain in varied matters; cheerful in bitter things and sad in cheerful things; discordant in necessary matters and even-tempered in truthful ones; severe in pleasant things and gentle in bitterness; strong in tribulations and weak in quarrels; slow to anger, quick to learn, and also slow to speak (James 1:19), as Saint James says, but likewise quick to hear.

Be effective in progress, dull in revenge, cautious in speech, prompt in action; lovable to the upright, unkempt toward the dishonorable, gentle toward the weak, hard toward the foolish, upright toward the upright, humble toward the dejected.

Be sober everywhere, chaste everywhere, modest always, patient even in zeal, never covetous, always generous, whether in material help or in intention. Be timely in fasts, untimely [that is, persistent] in vigils; discerning in duties, steadfast in studies, constant amid uproars, joyful amid sorrows.

Be bold in the cause of truth, timid in disputes, submissive toward the good, unconquerable by evil, gentle in generosity, tireless in charity, just in all things, devout toward the worthy, merciful toward the poor.

Remember benefits; forget injuries. Be a lover of moderation, one who does not desire riches, a humbler of the spirit, a publicizer of thoughts. Obey elders, cooperate with the younger, and make yourself equal to your peers.

Strive with the perfect; do not envy those better than you; do not grieve over those who precede you; do not slander those who lag behind; agree with those who provoke you. Though weary, do not fail; weep and rejoice at once, according to fervor and hope; always fear concerning the end, even while making progress, because the outcome is uncertain.

## II

Here is your reminder, O beloved boy and sweet servant: if you are such, you will be exceedingly blessed, because you will remain the same through prosperity and adversity, ready for everything, meeting each circumstance, moderating your behavior, nourishing what is growing, destroying what is declining, smoothing what is desperate [perhaps: rough], making what is blameworthy more severe.

Always be concerned, always growing, always acquiring, always reaching toward heavenly things, always running toward the prize, always desiring celestial things, always thirsting for divine things.

Behold the teaching: give it adherence, if you can, so that you may possess happiness and power. Fleeing childish desires, bring the body under the power of the spirit in such a way that you may hand yourself over as a surety for your sins, a soldier in the short present life for eternal wages.

O how happy, how blessed, and how remarkable a boy you will be if you fulfill all these things! For if you are diligently occupied in all these matters, in thought and deed, you will have no leisure for vain and wandering or shameful thoughts. Rather, as one always beginning, you will continually gather for yourself the things that you will enjoy forever. You will be called a man of single purpose, a seeker of singular profit, an excellent merchant of the eternal kingdom.

Turn yourself wholly to these things, therefore, because you have here the means to exercise your youth, virtue, effectiveness, and diligence. Otherwise, if these qualities are exercised in contrary pursuits, they will perish—those qualities that by force seize the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 11:12).

# Instruction XV: On Fervor in Serving God

## I

In the Church of God, my brothers, by God’s mercy we occupy the highest position. We must take the greatest care that we hold firmly, with watchful purpose, what we have once resolved, and that what we promise outwardly we demonstrate through the practice of good works.

In this matter it is necessary that, having removed foolish and inept thoughts from our hearts, we enter upon God’s way according to the rule of a perfect life. Forgetting what lies behind—that is, temporal things—we must, with the Apostle (Phil. 3:13), stretch ourselves toward what lies ahead as we advance along it, saying to our Creator: “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1:3).

By ourselves we cannot reach the way of truth or make progress along it. Therefore let us ask for prevenient grace, saying: “Draw us after you, so that we may run to you.” It is fitting that “Draw us after you” is said first, and “we shall run” follows, because without divine grace preceding us we cannot begin a good work, nor complete it without that same grace following us. Hence that prayer says: “May your grace, O Lord, both precede and follow us” (Collect, Sixteenth Sunday after Pentecost).

It is also fitting that it says, “we shall run.” For in God’s way we must not proceed at a slow pace, but run with great rejoicing and haste. The Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Run in such a way that you may obtain the prize” (1 Cor. 9:24).

The one who advances toward God with all his strength runs; the one who does not grow weary in good works runs. Thus the Prophet says of Christ: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6). Christ ran [perhaps: “ran” rather than “runs”] the way of God, because he did not stand in the way of sinners (Ps. 1:1); that is, he was delayed by no burden of sin.

## II

We must run—but how must we run? Hear how. Let us run, I say, in the fragrance of your perfumes.

What are the perfumes whose fragrance we pursue as we run after Christ? They are the examples of the saints who preceded us. Perfumes are made from various flowers or spices mixed together. The various spices are the various virtues of the saints, which, like fragrant aromatics, are brought together through the power of charity and prepared cleanly for our use.

Of such perfume it is said: “Dead flies ruin the sweetness of the perfume” (Eccl. 10:1). The dead flies are vain thoughts rushing upon our hearts. Through the practice of prayer we must drive them away, as with a kind of fan, lest they destroy for us the sweetness of the perfume.

Dead flies destroy the sweetness in the fragrance of the perfume when vain thoughts extinguish the delight of the virtues and the rules of divine service that we learned from the ancient fathers.

Let us therefore look most diligently upon the examples of the saints who preceded us, and hasten to enter that rest (Heb. 4:11). Let us run and not fail in what we have begun, so that with the Apostle we may be able to say: “We have fought the good fight; we have finished the course; henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for us, which Christ the righteous Judge will award us on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7–8). He is blessed above all forever and ever. Amen.

# Instruction XVI: What Is, or What Will Be?

## I

Consider [Note: “[Col. 0257D] *Nunquid.* Perhaps *non quid* (‘not what’), for *sed* follows]: are you a miserable man? But what will you be? For what you are is momentary, whereas what you will be is everlasting. Therefore do not be lazy with yourself; practice in this brief life what you will possess forever. Let the desire for rewards drive away reluctance toward temporary labor.

Be spiritual, if you are not lazy. But if the world provokes you, consider what you should flee, what you should pursue, and why you do not pursue what never flees. Why are you impatient over lesser things, when you could be more precious in better ones? Do not be uncertain about better things that are certain, nor certain about things that perish.

You see in others what others will see in you. What good is it to take pleasure in seeing a shadow in the waters? What benefit is there for you in exulting or rejoicing through dreams? Yet these dreams, however long they may be, are brief for everyone; for the day [perhaps: “and the days”] of the whole world is like that of a single, exceedingly dark night, and nights are dreams.

Awaken, therefore, O son, from the night. Seek the light, so that you may be seen and may see. Light a lamp and read. Beware lest you sleep, lest you be led astray by dreams and deceived by imagined falsehood, so that you believe false things to be true and later, rising, grieve that you have been deceived.

Your life is a wheel; it runs every day and does not wait for you. Go with it.

Therefore prepare provisions for yourself here. You are ordered to withdraw from another’s field; take care not to sell your own. Here, O man, you possess nothing on the earth from which you were born naked and in which you will dissolve into dust. Do not sell heaven, where there is an eternal inheritance—provided you have not lost it.

Otherwise, if you have lost it, sell yourself so that you may recover it. What did I say—sell yourself? Sell your vices and buy life.

Perhaps you ask what they are. First sell pride, as the first vice before all others, and thereby happily buy humility, by which you may be like Christ, who says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

By a shorter method these things, sold entire, will be sold all at once, and lesser things will be despised through the desire of possessing. For when the root of any tree has been cut out, its branches are not highly valued.

Know what you must sell for the destruction of this flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 5:5): gluttony, greed, fornication, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory, and envy—things it would have been better for you to have lost, even if you had received nothing in return.

# Instruction XVII: On the Eight Principal Vices

There are eight principal vices that plunge a person into destruction: gluttony, fornication, greed, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory, and pride.

Concerning the correction of gluttony it is said: “Do not be led by the fullness of the belly” (Ecclus. 36:20). Concerning fornication: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13:4). Concerning greed we read: “The desire for money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10). Concerning anger: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to the judgment of hellfire” (Matt. 5:22). Concerning sadness: “The sadness of the world produces death” (2 Cor. 7:10). Concerning acedia: “Idleness has taught many evils” (Ecclus. 33:29). Concerning vainglory: “The stench of the one who magnifies his works will rise” (Joel 2:20). Concerning pride: “God turns away from the proud” (James 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5). And: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Matt. 23:12).

These, therefore, are the origins and causes of all evils, and they must be healed through their opposites.

Gluttony, which is threefold, must be overcome by abstinence from fasting from the ninth hour to the ninth hour, and by moderation and usefulness of food [read: “lowliness” or “plainness” of food]. Fornication and every impurity must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints (Eph. 5:3); they must be overcome through chastity and vigilant, ever-fearful continence.

Greed is conquered by possessing nothing as one’s own and holding everything in common. Anger must be overcome by patience and gentle meekness. Sadness must be conquered by spiritual joy and hope of future blessedness.

The instability of acedia must be corrected by stable gentleness and dwelling in one place, through sobriety, as Scripture says: “If the spirit of one who rules rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4). Vainglory, elevation, impurity, and pride are likewise conquered by true humility and contrition of heart through fear of God.

---

# The Six Letters of Saint Columbanus, Abbot and Confessor, Arranged According to the Circumstances of the Times (C.S.)

## First Letter: To Saint Pope Gregory

To the holy lord and Father in Christ, the most beautiful Roman ornament of the Church [Note: “[Col. 0259D] *Romano.* Perhaps, through a copyist’s error, *papae* (‘pope’) has been omitted], the most august flower, as it were, of all languishing Europe, an eminent watchman, possessed of the divine contemplation of *castulitas* [Note: “*Castulitatis.* Thus the manuscript reads”], I, Columba in Christ, a lowly *bargoma* [Note: “*Bargoma.* Thus Fleming prints it from the manuscript. Cangius, in his Glossary under this word, thinks that *barginna* should be read, that is, ‘pilgrim’; consult him under *BARGINNA*”], send greetings.

I. Grace and peace to you from God our Father in Jesus Christ. I would gladly, holy pope, not have to question you hyperbolically about Easter, in accordance with that verse from the Song: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32:7). For although I am merely a petty speaker, I may apply to you the fine saying of a certain distinguished wise man, which he is said to have uttered when he saw a certain woman [Note: *Contupictam*. The editor conjectures *compte pictam*, “elegantly painted.” Cangius, however, understands either *comptam* or *acu comptam*, “adorned with a needle,” i.e. embroidered.] richly adorned: “I do not admire the workmanship, but I admire the face” [Col. 0259D]. This may be inscribed by my wretched writing to you, illustrious as you are. Nevertheless, trusting in your evangelical humility, I venture to write to you and to entrust you with the matter of my grief.

For there is no vanity in writing when necessity compels one to write even to superiors. What, then, do you say about Easter on the twenty-first or twenty-second day of the moon, which—as many [Note: *Calcalenteris*. If Cangius is followed, the reading might perhaps be *calculatoribus*, “calculators,” unless one prefers *chalcenteris*, that is, “learned men,” by which title we know Origen was called. Neither conjecture, however, satisfies the learned Benedictines, who would prefer *calendariis*, “calendar-computists,” who calculate the Kalends and the seasons.] have decisively established—is not Easter, being darkened [Col. 0260C] (though I say this with your permission)?

For, as I believe, your efficacy is not unaware how Anatolius, a man of remarkable learning—as Saint Jerome says, whose work Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, inserted in the *Ecclesiastical History* under the heading “Extracts” [sic], and whom Saint Jerome praised for this same work on Easter in his *Catalogue*—argues reprovingly about this age of the moon. Against the Gallican computists, whom he calls mistaken concerning Easter, he delivered this dreadful judgment:

“Certainly, if the rising of the moon is delayed until the end of the second watch, which marks the middle of the night, then darkness does not overcome light, but light is overcome by darkness. It is certain that this cannot be considered appropriate for Easter: that any portion of darkness should dominate the light, because the solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection is light, and there is no fellowship between light and darkness. And if the moon shines forth in the third watch, there is no doubt that the twenty-first or twenty-second moon has risen; and in that moon it is impossible for the true Pasch to be sacrificed. For those who determine that Easter can be celebrated at this age of the moon cannot affirm it by the authority of divine Scripture; rather, they incur the charge of sacrilege and obstinacy, and endanger souls, while asserting that true light can be sacrificed together with some domination of darkness, though it dominates all darkness.”

Moreover, we read in the book of the holy teaching: “Easter, that is, the solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection, cannot be celebrated before the beginning of the sixteenth [day] after the passing of the vernal equinox, so that the equinox does not precede it.” This, of course, Victorius transgressed in his *Cycle*, and through it long ago introduced—or, to speak more humbly, confirmed—the established error in Gaul. For how can both of these positions stand: that the Lord’s resurrection should be celebrated before his passion—which is plainly absurd even to imagine—or that the seven days sanctioned by the Lord’s commandment in the Law, during which alone the Lord’s Passover was ordered to be eaten lawfully (days which are to be counted from the fourteenth moon through the twentieth), should be exceeded contrary to right and justice [Col. 0261B]?

The twenty-first or twenty-second moon, however, lies outside the proper order of light, since it rises at that season after midnight; and when darkness overcomes light, it is impious, they say, to celebrate the solemnity of light.

II. Why, then, do you, so wise a man—whose brilliant lights of sacred intellect, as in ancient times, have been diffused throughout the world—honor a dark Easter? I confess that I marvel that this error of Gaul has not long ago been removed by you, as though it were a Schyntenean error, unless I should perhaps think—something I can scarcely believe—that, since you have not corrected it, you have approved it.

Yet your expertise can be excused in another and more honorable way: perhaps you fear incurring the stigma of Hermagorean novelty, and are content with the authority of your predecessors, especially Pope Leo. [Col. 0261C] Do not, I beg you, rely in such a question solely upon humility or dignity, which are often deceived. “A living dog is better in a matter of inquiry than a dead lion” (Eccl. 9:4). A living saint can correct what was not corrected by another who was greater.

Know that Victorius was not accepted by our teachers and by the ancient Irish—philosophers and wisest computists in the composition of the calculation—but was considered more deserving of laughter or pardon than of authority. Therefore, to me, a timid man and more a pilgrim than a pedant, do not disdain to send the support of your judgment and, in due time, the point of your gracious moderation to restrain this storm surrounding us [Col. 0261D]. For, after reading so many authorities, I am not satisfied with the single opinion of those bishops who say only: “We must not celebrate Easter with the Jews” [Note: *Facere*, “to celebrate,” is absent from the manuscript.].

Victor, the bishop, said this long ago as well; but none of the Easterners accepted his argument. Rather, this sleeping thorn of Dagon absorbed this lump of error. What, I ask, is this frivolous and so uncultivated opinion, supported by no testimonies of divine Scripture: “We must not celebrate Easter with the Jews”? What bearing does it have on the matter? Are we to believe that the rejected Jews now celebrate Easter, seeing that they are without a temple, outside Jerusalem, and that Christ, who was prefigured in it, was crucified by them? Or should we rightly believe that the fourteenth moon is theirs and that it is their Easter [Note: “The moon and Easter.” Perhaps *lunae Pascha*, “the moon’s Easter,” or *luna et Pascha*, “the moon and Easter.” The reading is not satisfactory.] [Col. 0262A], rather than confess that the Passover was instituted by God himself, who alone knows with perfect understanding why the fourteenth moon was chosen for the passage?

Perhaps this will shed some light for the wise and for those like you. Those who advance this objection, although they reproach God without authority, should ask why, if he did not want us to celebrate Easter with the Jews, he did not beforehand, in his foreknowledge, prevent the Jews’ obstinacy by prescribing nine days of unleavened bread in the Law, so that the beginning of our solemnity would at least not exceed the end of theirs. For if Easter is to be celebrated on the twenty-first or twenty-second day, nine days will be counted from the fourteenth through the twenty-second: namely, the seven commanded by God and two added by human beings.

But if human beings may of themselves add something to the divine decree, I ask whether this might not appear contrary to that saying of Deuteronomy: “Behold,” he says, “the word that I give you: you shall neither add to it nor take away from it” (Deut. 4:2).

III. But in writing these things more boldly than humbly, I know that I have bound myself in the most difficult net of presumption, which I shall have to navigate [perhaps *ignorans*, “being unaware”]. For it is neither appropriate to the place nor to the order of things that anything should be brought forward for discussion against your great authority, and that Western writings should absurdly trouble you—sitting lawfully upon the chair of Peter the apostle and keeper of the keys—with the question of Easter.

Yet you should consider that in this matter I am not merely a worthless man, but also the many teachers, both dead and living, who affirm the same things I have noted; and imagine that you are entering into conversation with them. Know that, though intermittently and hyperbolically, I have opened my bilious mouth in piety. Therefore either excuse or condemn Victorius, knowing that if you praise him, a dispute of faith will arise between you and the aforementioned Jerome, who praised Anatolius, the contrary authority, so that whoever follows one will be unable to accept the other.

Let your vigilance therefore consider how, in testing the faith of the two authorities mentioned above, who contradict one another, there may be no disagreement between you and Jerome in the judgment you pronounce; otherwise we shall be trapped on every side, compelled to agree either with you or with him. Spare the weak in this matter, lest you display the scandal of disagreement.

For I frankly confess to you that anyone who comes against the authority of Saint Jerome will be regarded among the churches of the West as a heretic or as one to be rejected. They grant him unquestioned faith in all matters of the divine Scriptures. But enough concerning Easter.

[Col. 0262D] IV. As for those bishops who are ordained contrary to the canons—that is, through bribery—I ask what you judge concerning them. You have written that simoniacs and *Giltas* are pestilences. May communion be held with such men? For, what is more serious, many in this province are known to be of this kind.

And what of others who, having been violated in the diaconate, are afterward chosen for the episcopal rank? We know the consciences of some in these matters; and, consulting our own smallness, they wished to know with certainty whether, after this, they can minister without danger [Note: *Possint*. Something seems to be missing to complete the sentence, perhaps “minister.”]—that is, either after purchasing their rank with solidi, or after adultery in the diaconate [Col. 0263A]. I mean adultery concealed, together with its accomplices; among our teachers this is judged no less a crime.

Third, as the subject of my inquiry, answer me still, I beg you, if it is not burdensome: what should be done concerning those monks who, inflamed by regard for God and by a desire for the perfection of life, go against their vows, leave the places of their first conversion, and, against the will of their abbots, compelled by monastic fervor, either are released or flee into the deserts? Vennianus, the author, questioned Giltas about these matters, and Giltas replied to him most elegantly; nevertheless, the more eager one is to learn, the more fear continually increases.

V. All these matters, and many more that the brevity of a letter does not allow, ought to have been asked in person, more humbly and more purely, unless bodily weakness and the care of my fellow pilgrims had kept me bound at home [Col. 0263B], eager to go to you [Note: Something is missing here, perhaps *teneret, cupidum ad te*, “kept me, eager to come to you.”], so that I might drink from that spiritual vein of the living fountain and from the living wave of knowledge flowing down from heaven and springing up into eternal life [Note: *Haurire*, “to drink.” Perhaps *possem*, “I might be able,” should be added.].

And if the body followed the mind, Rome would once again endure contempt of itself, so that, just as we read—according to the learned account of Jerome—that some once came to Rome from the furthest shores of the Heulian sea and, wonderful to say, sought something other than Rome, so I too would now seek you, not Rome, with due reverence for the ashes of the saints. Although I confess that I am not wise but thirsting, I would do this if I had the opportunity.

I have read your book containing the *Pastoral Rule*: brief in style, expansive in teaching, filled with mysteries, and sweeter than honey—a work, I confess, for one in need. Therefore, I beg you, in your generosity to me, who thirsts, send me the little works that, as I have heard, you composed with marvelous genius on Ezekiel.

I have read Jerome’s six books on that prophet, but he did not expound even half of him. If you are willing, send us some of your rereadings, expounded in the city—namely, the final portions of the book. Send us also your exposition of the *Song of Songs* from the place where he says, “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense” (Song 4:16), through the end; or else a brief treatment of other passages in your own words. And, I ask, disclose the whole obscurity of Zechariah, bring to light what is hidden, so that the blindness of the West may thank you for these things.

I ask importunately and inquire about great matters—who does not know it? Yet you possess great things, because you know how to lend well from little and better from much [perhaps, “because you have great things and know how to lend…”]. Charity urges you to reply; let the roughness of paper not hinder you from explaining, for the bronze belonged to error, while the honor owed to the heart must be given by me to you.

It was my part to provoke, inquire, and ask; yours, if you accept these requests graciously, not to refuse, to put the talent out at interest, and, at Christ’s command, to give the petitioner the bread of instruction.

Peace to you and to yours. Forgive, I beg you, blessed pope, the boldness with which I have written, and pray, at least once, for me, the lowliest of sinners, in your holy prayers to the common Lord.

I consider it entirely unnecessary to commend to you my companions, whom the Savior declares must be received as walking in his name. And if, as I heard from your holy man Candidus, you wish to reply that what has been strengthened by the antiquity of time cannot be changed, this is plainly an ancient error; for truth, which reproves it, is always more ancient.

EPISTOLA II. TO THE FATHERS OF A CERTAIN GALLICAN SYNOD CONVENED CONCERNING THE QUESTION OF EASTER

To the holy lords and fathers in Christ—or brothers—bishops, priests, and all the other orders of the holy Church, Columba the sinner sends greeting in Christ.

I. I give thanks to my God that, on my account, so many holy men have gathered together to deliberate concerning the truth of faith and good works and, as befits such men, with trained faculties to distinguish good from evil and to judge matters under discussion with righteous judgment.

Would that you did this more often! Although, according to the canons, it may not always be possible for you to preserve this practice once or twice a year amid the turbulent disputes of this age, nevertheless this zeal ought to be present in you, however rarely, as quickly as possible: so that the negligent might acquire fear, and the zealous be provoked to greater progress.

Behold, I say, thanks be to God, that an opportunity has been given you, in holy synod, to discuss Easter, at least on my account. May our Lord Jesus Christ, that chief of shepherds, grant that your counsel may benefit his Church. And may God himself, who is accustomed to stand in the assembly of the gods (Ps. 81:1), present among you, inspire the hearts of his people to follow his will completely by the strength of his commandments.

May you deliberate not only about the matter of Easter—which has long been debated and judged variously by different authorities—but also about all the necessary canonical observances that have been corrupted by many, which is more serious. And since the day of judgment is now nearer than it was then, may you still undertake a stricter counsel concerning evangelical religion and apostolic tradition.

For if you carefully investigate the evangelical commandments, I am not surprised that among the conduct of some you find things contrary to them. But it is enough to have indicated that each person must be shaped according to the example of his Redeemer and the form of the true shepherd. He preached humility first, and joined to it the seven beatitudes beginning with poverty of spirit. He taught a person to follow his footsteps so fully that, by pursuing righteousness, he might arrive at the true circumcision of the eighth day [Col. 0264D], because the eighth beatitude culminates in martyrdom: one is crowned not only for acting justly, but also for enduring for the sake of justice, eager for the heavenly kingdom—or, [perhaps read] “together with those who contend in the same way.”

II. Since, as it is written, “Whoever says that he believes in Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked” (1 John 2:6)—that is, poor, humble, and always proclaiming the truth amid human persecution—and again, “All who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12); and since “faith without works is dead in itself” (James 2:17, 20, 26), while the Lord answers those foolish people who are content with faith alone, “I do not know you” (Matt. 7:23), and has promised those who believe well and say, “Lord, Lord” (ibid., 21), that they will not enter the kingdom of heaven—let each person examine himself.

Since they cannot be his disciples, nor worthy of him, if they have not renounced everything they possess, let each person consider whether he has firmly fulfilled or endured these things, lest he be alien to the disciples of our Lord Jesus Christ. For a son must not be degenerate, and a disciple must not preach what is contrary to his Teacher.

“Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). And whoever flees the labor of correction and resistance to vice is a hired man, not a son who will remain always in the Church.

I have touched on these things briefly so that, if you are willing to teach us who are as inferiors, you fathers may have this voice of the true Shepherd both in deed and in word, which his sheep recognize: “They do not hear the voice of strangers, but flee from him” (ibid., 5), whose voice they do not recognize—and unless it is put into practice, it does not agree with the voice of the true shepherd.

Nor can a word spoken from the mouth of a hireling effectively penetrate the minds of those under discipline, when it bears this sign: that he himself is the first not to hear what is not heard from him. What the Teacher first despised in his actions, he cannot transmit by bare words as an example to be preserved.

III. Let us all, therefore—clerics and monks alike—first fulfill these true and singular canons of our Lord Jesus Christ in the same way, and then, laying aside the swelling of pride, write as one in all other matters [Col. 0265C].

If we are all humble and voluntary poor for Christ, who became poor for us although he was rich (2 Cor. 8:9), then, through humility, rising from the earth of vices, and through the voluntary poverty of evangelical admonition, laying aside various desires and driving away mortal cares, as though the causes of difference and discord had been cut off, all the children of God will possess true peace and complete charity among themselves through likeness of conduct and equality of one will.

Difference of conduct and variety of traditions have greatly harmed, and continue to harm, ecclesiastical peace. Yet if, as I said, we first hasten to heal the poisons of pride, envy, and vainglory through the commandment of our Savior—who gives himself as an example, saying, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29)—and through the other exercises of true humility [Col. 0265D], then, without any further scandal, all of us, made perfect and with hatred destroyed [perhaps “hatred having been destroyed”], will love one another with all our hearts as disciples of our Lord Jesus Christ.

And even if there is some diversity of traditions, as there is concerning Easter, humble people cannot contend, nor does the Church have such a custom (1 Cor. 11:16). Those who seek in the same purpose and with the same desire to recognize the truth will quickly recognize what is more correct to follow, when no one is conquered except error and when no one glories in himself but in the Lord.

Let us therefore seek together, I beg you, most beloved fathers and brothers, and let us see which tradition is more correct: yours or that of your brothers in the West. For all the churches of the entire West—as I indicated in the volume of my reply that I have now sent you, although it was written three years ago—do not accept that the Resurrection should take place before the Passion, that is, before the equinox, and they do not exceed the twentieth moon, lest they celebrate the sacrament of the New Testament without the authority of the Old Testament.

But these matters belong elsewhere. Otherwise, what those people think about Easter, whether of the pope or others, I have made known in three volumes, and I have also ventured to write the same thing in a short book to your holy brother Arigius.

IV. I ask one thing of your holiness: receive with peace and charity my ignorance and, as some say, my proud presumption in writing [Col. 0266B], which necessity, not vanity, extorted, as my very lowliness [perhaps “usefulness”] proves [An. *utilitas?*].

And because I am not the author of this disagreement, but have come as a pilgrim into these lands for Christ the Savior, our common Lord and God, I beseech you by our common Lord and adjure you by him who will judge the living and the dead (2 Tim. 4:1)—if you are worthy to be acknowledged by him, who will say to many, “Amen, I say to you, I never knew you” (Matt. 7:23)—to allow me, with your peace and charity, to be silent and live in these woods beside the bones of our seventeen deceased brothers, just as until now we have been permitted to live among you for twelve years, so that, as we have done until now, we may pray for you as we ought.

May Gaul, I beg you, receive us together, whom the kingdom of heaven will receive if we are of good merit [Col. 0266C]. For one kingdom has been promised to us, and one hope of calling in Christ, with whom we shall reign (2 Tim. 2:11–12), provided that we first suffer here with him, so that we may also be glorified with him.

I know that many will consider this loquacity of mine superfluous. But I judged it better that you should know what we discuss and think among ourselves here as well. For these are our canons, the commandments of the Lord and of the apostles [Note: “In faith.” The word *in* is inappropriate. I think *haec*, “these things,” should be read, as the following words indicate.]: this is our faith; these are our weapons, shield, and sword; this is our defense; these things moved us from our homeland; these things we strive to preserve here, though tepidly. In these things we both pray and desire to persevere until death, just as we have seen our elders do.

V. But you, holy fathers, consider what you do to these veteran poor men and aged pilgrims. As I think, it will be better for you to comfort than to disturb them.

I did not dare go to you, lest perhaps I should contend in person against the Apostle’s saying: “Do not contend with words” (ibid., 14); and again: “If anyone is contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11:16).

But I confess the secrets of my conscience: I believe more in the tradition of my homeland, according to the Do[lacuna], and the eighty-four-year calculation, and in Anatolius, praised by Eusebius, the author and bishop of the *Ecclesiastical History*, and by Jerome, the holy writer of the *Catalogue*, than in Victorius, who wrote recently and hesitantly and, where it was necessary, defined nothing, as he himself testified in his preface [Col. 0267A]. He wrote after the times of Saint Martin, Saint Jerome, and Pope Damasus, under Hilary, one hundred and three years later.

You yourselves, however, choose whom you would rather follow and whom you should trust more, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thess. 5:21).

Far be it from me to contend against you, so that our enemies might rejoice in the dispute of us Christians—namely, the Jews, heretics, or pagan gentiles. Far be it, far be it! Otherwise, we can agree in another way: either let each person remain with the Lord in the calling in which he was called (1 Cor. 7:20), if both traditions are good; or let both books be read with peace and humility, without any contention, and let what agrees more closely with the Old and New Testaments be observed without anyone’s envy [Col. 0267B].

For if it is from God that you drive me from this desert place, which I sought across the sea for the sake of my Lord Jesus Christ, it will be mine to utter that prophetic saying: “If this storm is upon you because of me, take me up and cast me into the sea, so that this disturbance may cease for you” (Jon. 1:12).

Yet first it should be yours, after the example of those sailors, to attempt to rescue the shipwrecked man with compassionate hearts and draw the vessel to land, as those men did—even though they were pagans—as Scripture relates: “The men tried to return to the land,” he says, “but they could not, because the sea grew increasingly turbulent and the waves rose higher” (ibid., 13).

Finally, at the end of this statement, though presumptuously, I suggest that, since the road of this world is spacious (Matt. 7:13–14), broad, and crowded with many who run toward the crossroads [more correctly, *compita*, “crossroads”] [Col. 0267C], if a few are found who walk through the narrow gate and along the narrow way that leads to life, according to the Lord’s command, you should send them onward to life rather than forbid them.

Otherwise, perhaps the Lord’s saying will also rebuke you with the Pharisees: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before people; for you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to go in” (Matt. 23:13).

VI. But someone may say: “Are we not entering the kingdom of heaven?” Why can you not, by the Lord’s grace, become like little children (Matt. 18:3)—humble, that is, and chaste; simple and innocent in evil, yet prudent in good (Rom. 16:19), gentle, and not holding anger in your hearts?

Yet women, often seeing [such things] and more frequently quarrelling and becoming angry over the possessions of the world, can scarcely fulfill all these things. Therefore our people, renouncing the world once and for all and first cutting away the causes and tinder of vices and quarrels, believe that naked men can fulfill the Lord’s word more easily than the rich.

For without these four things the kingdom of heaven is not entered. Saint Jerome bears witness to three of them, and Basil to the fourth; they explain the conduct of infants according to the force of the evangelical saying. An infant is humble; he does not remember having been injured; when he sees a woman, he does not lust; he does not have one thing in his mouth and another in his heart.

As I said, a person who is free and sees that God himself is Lord will preserve these things better than one who sees and hears diverse matters. Let no one disparage the blessings of silence. Unless they grow lukewarm, those who live in secret live better than those who live in public, except for the still more austere life [Note: Something seems to be missing after *quae*, perhaps “which receives a greater reward.”] [Col. 0268A]. For where the battle is harder, there the crown is found to be more glorious.

Accordingly, as Saint Gregory says, those who do not avoid public evils do not believe in hidden virtues. Knowing this, Saint Jerome ordered bishops to imitate the apostles, while he taught monks to follow the perfect Fathers. The instructions of clerics and monks are different and far separated from one another.

Let each person preserve what he has undertaken; but let all, and both groups alike, as members of one body, follow Christ, the head of all, in one harmony through their particular commandments. He has shown that these commandments are to be perfected in peace and complete charity.

These two things cannot be perfectly accomplished except by those who are truly humble and by those who, united in spirit, fulfill Christ’s commandments, as the Lord himself testifies: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15). “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15:12). “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35).

Then there can be a firm union of souls, and peace and charity poured out by the Holy Spirit into the hearts of believers, when all desire alike to fulfill the divine commandments. For to the extent that the measure of dissimilarity in practical pursuits is great, so great will be the counterfeit of peace and charity among the imperfect.

Therefore, so that we may love one another in unfeigned charity, let us carefully consider the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ and hasten to fulfill them once understood, so that through his teaching the whole Church may hasten heavenward with one surge of fervent zeal.

May his freely given grace grant this to us: that we may all dread the world, love him alone, and desire him together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

For the rest, fathers, pray for us, just as we, though worthless, pray for you. Do not regard us as strangers to you, for we are members of one body, whether Gauls, Britons, Iberians, or whatever the nations may be.

Therefore let us all rejoice, all nations, in knowledge of the faith and recognition of the Son of God (Eph. 4:13), and let us all hasten to attain mature manhood, to the measure of the fullness of the age of Jesus Christ. In him let us love one another, praise one another, correct one another, visit one another, and pray for one another, so that together we may reign and rejoice with him.

I beg you, most patient and holy fathers and brothers, grant pardon to my loquacity and presumption, which labor beyond their strength.

EPISTOLA III. TO BONIFACE IV

To the holy and apostolic lord, the father and pope in Christ, Columba the sinner sends greeting in Christ.

For a long time I have desired to visit in spirit and console all those presiding over the apostolic see, those dearest to all, faithful prelates, and fathers most worthy of reverence by reason of their apostolic honor. Until now, however, because of the chill of this age and the tumultuous rebellions of intervening peoples, I have been unable to fulfill my desire, as though shut off by a sea-beam, by the back of a sea that is not so much visible as intelligible, which, as you know well, has been set against us and is harsh and unnavigable.

For this reason Satan has once and twice hindered the bearers of our writings to Pope Gregory of blessed memory. These writings, composed long ago and placed below, are now sent from our lowliness to be offered to you as well for examination—not so much through the proud, as the words demonstrate, diabolical presumption of our region, as through the observance of our region’s customs [perhaps *observantia*, “observance”], which would trample upon the necessary testing of the true computation, since the books of our province do not ascend to the same limits as the book of these Gauls, which is not accepted by our men in two places by the teachers [Col. 0269B].

We have tried, as far as we could, to indicate this in the letters of our lowliness to the blessed pope mentioned above, though presumptuously. Therefore, lest repeating the same things in writing to you should produce weariness rather than allow you, as is fitting, to test the skill of both authorities, I send you only prayers, together with the salutations due to you.

I beseech you by our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, and by the unity of our faith that we share—through which we believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths that there is one Father of us all who is in heaven, from whom are all things, and one Redeemer, the Son of God, through whom are all things, and one Holy Spirit in whom are all things (1 Cor. 8:6; Rom. 11:36); that there is one Lord in the Trinity and the Trinity in Unity; that each person is fully Lord, and that all three persons together are one Lord—to grant us pilgrims laboring here the consolation of your pious judgment.

Thus, if it is not contrary to the faith, may you strengthen the tradition of our elders, so that by your judgment we may observe, in our pilgrimage, the rite of Easter as we received it from our ancestors.

For it is evident that we remain in our homeland when we accept none of these Gallican rules. Sitting in the deserts, troubling no one, we remain with the rules of our elders. To defend these rules, we have written these letters either to you, as I said, apostolic fathers, or to these neighboring brothers of ours, our fathers in Christ; this little document commends them to you.

Since we have been unable to satisfy them by our merits, as they are more turbulent than rational, we ask for the point of your mature authority, so that, with judgment among the just, we may live in the peace of ecclesiastical unity. Thus did the holy fathers Polycarp and Pope Anicetus teach, separating without scandal to the faith, indeed with complete charity: each preserving what he had received [perhaps *accepit*, “received”] and remaining in the calling in which he had been called.

Farewell, most beloved pope in Christ. Remember us in your holy prayers beside the ashes of the saints, and in your most pious decrees remember the churches of God established among barbarian peoples, judging—according to the one hundred and fifty authorities of the Council of Constantinople—that they should live by their own laws, as they were taught by the Fathers [Col. 0270A].

EPISTOLA IV. TO HIS DISCIPLES AND MONKS

To his sweetest sons, most beloved learners, frugal brothers, and all his monks together, Columba the sinner sends greeting in Christ.

## I.

“Peace be with you” (John 20:19–21), as the Lord said in wishing it to his disciples; may there also be salvation and everlasting charity. May the Trinity grant you these three things with him [perhaps: “with it”], and preserve them among you together with my prayer. He alone who bestowed it knows the greatness of my concern for your salvation, and my desire for your progress in doctrine.
