But since, in accordance with the Lord’s word, tribulation and persecution have arisen on account of the word, no other admonition is now suitable for you except that you beware lest you be that rocky soil which, because of the thinness of its turf, cannot nourish the seeds it has received; lest the Lord say of you also: “When tribulation and persecution arise on account of the word, immediately they are scandalized” (Matthew 13:21).

We ourselves know that we received [MS: “receive”] the word of the Lord with joy and fervor. Let us beware now lest we be temporary [hearers] (ibid.; Mark 4:17). We need patience (Hebrews 10:36), so that the testing of our faith may be, as it is written, more precious than gold (1 Peter 1:7). Know that contention concerns perishable things and the kingdom of heaven [Note: “Concerning perishable things. Read not *concerning perishable things*. And immediately: ‘that there should be battle’”]; it is no new thing that there should be battle and contention concerning the kingdom. Nor should you suppose that human beings themselves are persecuting you: demons are in those who envy your blessings. Against them take up the armor of God, which the Apostle displays (Ephesians 6:13, 17), and make your way toward heaven, slaughtering them with the ardent prayers that are like arrows.

For whatever you ask with faith and unanimity will be given to you. But see to it that you are of one heart and one soul, so that you may receive as your present reward whatever salutary thing you ask of the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of our common Father of all, according to the promise of our Lord, who says: “If two of you agree on earth concerning any matter whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:19). Otherwise, if you do not have one will and one refusal, it is better that you not live together.

Therefore I command you that all those who wish to agree with me from the heart, and who recognize and love my mind, should remain with my true follower Attala. Whether he is there or wishes to come after me is his own choice; for the danger to your souls lies in his own judgment, and you must obey him. But if he wishes to come, Valdolenus shall be superior, because, with God’s help, he will soon be able to understand what is certain. Meanwhile, beware lest there be among you anyone—whoever he may be—who holds a single vote among you [Note: “Either ‘let there be . . .’ or ‘afterward.’ Instead of *aut*, perhaps in both places *utrobique* should be read.”]. For those who were not unanimous among us have harmed us most.

## II.

You know, most beloved Attala, who are burdensome to your judgment. Remove them immediately, provided that you remove them in peace and with the unity of the Rule. Honor only Libranus [Col. 0271A], and always retain Valdolenus, if he is there with the congregation. May God deal well with him; let him become humble, and give him my kiss, which, when he was hurrying away, he did not receive.

You know how long my desire has been to form a character worthy of cultivation. If you see progress there in the souls, remain there; if you see dangers, come away from there. By dangers I mean dangers of discord. For I fear that there too, because of Easter, there may be discord; perhaps, while the devil lies in ambush, they may wish to alienate you if you do not maintain peace with them. For without me you now seem weaker in standing there.

Therefore be cautious, considering the time in which they do not endure sound doctrine (2 Timothy 4:3). Teach yourselves, and those who wish to listen. Only let there be no one among you who is not one with the others. Above all, provide for peace, always diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3).

For what does it profit to have a body and not have a heart? I have been broken, I confess, by this matter, while I wished to help everyone—those who, when I spoke to them, attacked me without cause (Psalm 119:7)—and while I trusted everyone, I nearly became a fool. Therefore be more prudent. I do not want you to undertake so great a burden, beneath which I myself have sweated. You already know the drop—or, rather, the smallness—of my knowledge. You have learned that different admonitions suit different people, because human characters are diverse and their qualities differ greatly among themselves.

But what am I doing? I am now going to call you to that immense labor from which I myself flee. If I disclose the diversity of doctrine, I shall moderate it. Therefore be diverse and many-sided in your care for those who obey you with faith and love. But fear their very love as well, because it will be dangerous for you.

## III.

But there are dangers on every side, dearest one: danger if they hate you, danger if they love you. Know that both are true; hence they either hate or love. In hatred peace perishes; in love integrity perishes.

Hold yourself, therefore, to the impulse of the one desire that you know my heart longs for. You know that I love the salvation of many, and solitude for myself: the one desire is for the advancement of the Lord, that is, of his Church; the other is for its own fulfillment. But these wishes are rather present in me than accomplished. In you, however, let them be perfected, I beg, because, in my absence, you can recognize both of them, at least in part. Yet I do not write as one commanding.

Know, then, my command concerning everyone: because I perceived the diverse wishes of many for maintaining the firmness of the Rule, I have bound branches to the root—those who, through their own fragility, have departed from my small firmness [Al.: “have departed”], that is, have withdrawn from the truth of doctrine. Let those who preserve my judgment serve God in this way: always choosing for themselves those who are wiser and more religious, provided that they are humble and merciful.

Whoever is rebellious, let him go outside; whoever is obedient, let him become an heir. Observe these things. And let all who belong wholly to me, through unity and humility—however many you may be, as Christ enlarges and multiplies you—look toward him who has served God beside the altar blessed by the holy bishop Aedus. Therefore you also, if the persecution of these people has made me . . . .

## IV.

I have written these things because the outcomes of affairs are uncertain. It was my wish to visit the nations and have the Gospel preached to them by us. But, since their lukewarmness is now reported to me, it has almost taken my spirit away from that undertaking. I wanted to write you a tearful letter; but [Leg.: “yet because”] I know your heart, and therefore, by adducing only what was necessary—things hard and themselves arduous—I have used another style, preferring to close the fountain rather than provoke tears.

Thus my speech is gentle outwardly, while grief is enclosed within. See, the tears are welling up [perhaps: “streaming forth”]. But it is better to stop the spring; for it is not the mark of a brave soldier to weep in battle.

What has happened to us is not new. This is precisely what we used to proclaim every day. Long ago a certain philosopher, wiser than the rest because he had said, contrary to everyone’s opinion, that there is one God, was thrown into prison. The Gospels are full of this subject, and were written especially for this reason. For this is the truth of the Gospel: that the true disciples of the crucified Christ follow it with the cross.

A great example has been displayed; a great mystery has been revealed. The Son of God, offering himself willingly—for he was offered because he himself willed it (Isaiah 53:7), ascended the cross as one accused, leaving us, as it is written, an example so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Peter 2:21).

Blessed, therefore, is the one who becomes a participant in this passion and this shame. For something marvelous lies hidden within it: “What is foolishness in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weakness in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25). In a wondrous manner an immeasurable wisdom is seen in foolishness, and incomparable strength in weakness.

Therefore all desirable refreshment and the mysteries of salvation are hidden there. Yet they are hard, so that they may be precious; they are obscure, so that they may be worthy of the few; and worthy of the few because they are exceedingly wondrous. Let us therefore patiently endure every adversity for the sake of truth, so that we may share in the Lord’s sufferings: “For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Timothy 2:12).

What must be added to these things except perseverance? “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). Judgment rests at the end, and praise is sung at the outcome. But, in order that one may persevere, let each person continually pray for God’s help with complete humility of mind. For, he says, it is “not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16), because “God’s mercy is greater and better than life” (Psalm 63:4), however good a person’s life may be.

For no one is worthy of mercy except those who confess before God that they are wretched and recognize themselves as unworthy of salvation by their own power, unless the Lord’s mercy alone rescues them from such dangers. Even if they are conscious of good works, they nevertheless fear God’s judgments and groan that they have committed many injustices; they humbly trust in God’s compassion alone. Their perfect fear pleases him all the more because it devotes itself more fully to humility: “The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope in his mercy” (Psalm 147:11).

## V.

No one, therefore, will save himself by his own right hand, according to the Lord’s word to Job, by which he mocked Job’s justification through certain demonstrations of power, saying: “And then I will confess that your right hand can save you” (Job 40:9)—except the one who humbly exercises his own ability, which itself has been given, with fear and trembling according to God’s will, praying frequently: “Do not cast me away from your presence” (Psalm 51:13); and, “Do not repel me from your commandments” (Psalm 119:10).

For, as someone has said, greatness of virtue has often been an occasion of destruction for some; once they become more beautiful through virtues, they descend from the level of humility. Hence it is written: “You are more beautiful; descend, rise, and sleep with the uncircumcised” (Ezekiel 32:19), as though the words were addressed in another form to a proud soul: “Because you have raised yourself up through your holiness into pride, descend from there now and be counted among sinners, because nothing is acceptable to me that is accomplished with pride.”

You see that the gate is narrow, and that the way of perfection is entered by few; it turns away from vices on the left and from the evils of vanity and pride on the right. We must therefore walk by the royal road to the city of the living God: through affliction of the flesh and contrition of heart; through bodily labor and humiliation of spirit; through our diligent performance of legitimate duty, not through the dignity of merit; and, greater than all these, through the grace, faith, hope, and charity of Christ.

There are many dangers in the flesh. Recognize the cause of the battle, the greatness of the glory; do not fail to recognize the powerful enemy and the freedom of the will in the midst of all this—the gate opened to the enemy from the north. Therefore Jerusalem too is opened from the north; from that side the enemy who dwells in the north watches. Hence it is written: “From the north evils are kindled over the whole earth” (Jeremiah 1:14).

If you remove the enemy, you remove the battle; if you remove the battle, you remove the crown. If these things exist, then wherever they exist there must necessarily be virtue, vigilance, fervor, patience, faithfulness, wisdom, steadfastness, and prudence; otherwise, there is slaughter. And to put it plainly: if you remove freedom, you remove dignity.

## VI.

See the diversities by which we are surrounded and with which we are inundated—as though by the crashes of whirlpools [Al.: “eddies”], dearest learner—apart from those things that lie hidden within and fight against us daily inside ourselves.

Therefore, amid such dangers, to will and to run—although it is yours—is not yours. Human weakness is not sufficient, amid so many opposing forces, to reach what it desires, unless the Lord’s mercy causes the wishes of the one who rejoices to be fulfilled, and enables the runner to finish his course successfully, escaping falls, obstacles, and adverse mishaps.

Consequently, humility of mind is the cause of merit; without assistance it cannot be helped. The proud person does not deserve it and, once abandoned, is hardened. The ungrateful person who does not pray is an undevout servant. The lazy person is scourged in this life, and his service is despised. The despairing person is also treated with disdain and is in no way considered worthy to be counted among men.

What, then, shall we say to these things, wretched as we are? Before we deserve to be free from evils, we flatter ourselves with our virtues; before laying aside our vices, we hope to possess perfection. We wish to know everything, yet we are reluctant to do everything we know, hoping to repay words for deeds. Perhaps this may be so here; but there it is plainly impossible before the Lord, because there the one who speaks will not be saved, but the one who acts.

## VII.

As I am now writing, a messenger has arrived, telling me that a ship is being prepared on which I shall be carried unwillingly to my own region. But if I flee, no guard prevents me, for they seem to want me to flee.

If I am thrown into the sea like Jonah—who is himself called “dove” (*columba*) in Hebrew—pray that, in place of the whale, there may be some safe protector who, with fortunate returning oarage, may restore your Jonah to the desired land.

But now the end of the letter is forced to come to the parchment [*pergamenae*], although the greatness of the subject compels it to extend farther [Al.: “may compel it”]. Love does not preserve order; hence the letter has been sent in confusion. I wanted to say everything briefly; I could not say everything. What I wished to write, I did not wish to write because of the diversity of wills.

Perhaps my will is not without the lure of flattery. May God’s will be done in all things; if he wills it, let that be my desire. Examine your consciences, and see whether they are purer and holier in my absence. Do not seek me out through love, but only through necessity.

Do not use this occasion to abandon one another, nor seek through this separation a freedom that may reduce you to slavery under vices. He is mine who loves unity; he is not mine who separates. “For whoever does not gather with me,” my Lord says, “scatters” (Luke 11:23).

Otherwise, if you see perfection withdrawing farther from you than before, and if chance separates me from you, and Attala is not sufficient to govern you because your brothers are here near the Britons, gather all together in one place that is better, so that you may fight more easily against vices and the devil’s snares. Let the one whom you all choose preside over you for the time being; for, if I am free to do so, it will belong to me, God willing, to concern myself with you.

But if you are pleased with the places and God is building with you there, grow there by his blessing into a thousand thousands (Genesis 24:60). Pray for me, my inmost ones, that I may live for God.

# EPISTLE V. TO POPE BONIFACE IV

To the most beautiful of all, the head of the churches of all Europe, the exceedingly dear pope, the exalted prelate, the Pastor of pastors, the most reverend watchman: the most humble to the most exalted, the rustic to the urbane, the writer of trifles (*micrologus*) to the most eloquent, the last to the first, the pilgrim to the native, the very poor to the most powerful—“a strange thing to say! a new occurrence!”—the rare bird, Columba, dares to write to Father Boniface.

## I.

Who could hear such a bald-faced address? Who would not immediately say: “Who is this chatterbox, this presumptuous man, who dares to write such things without being asked?” Who, as an instigator of retaliation, would not at once burst into that ancient reproachful saying with which the Hebrew who was wronging his brother replied to Moses: “Who appointed you ruler or judge over us?” (Exodus 2:14).

I answer him first: there is no presumption where necessity for the building up of the Church is evident. And if he quibbles about my person, let him consider not who I am, but what I say.

For what will a Christian pilgrim keep silent about when a neighboring Arian has long been proclaiming it? “The wounds of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6). Others secretly slander with delight; I shall reprove publicly, grieving and sorrowful—not the good of impious peacemakers, but the evils of those guilty of schism.

I do not therefore presume, out of vanity or insolence, to write to men so exalted, being a little man of the lowest station. Pain, rather than arrogance, compels me to point out to you, with the most humble suggestion, as is fitting, that the name of God is blasphemed among the nations by those who contend against one another through you.

## II.

For I grieve, I confess, over the disgrace of the chair of Saint Peter. Yet I know that the matter lies above me, and that at the very outset I am, as they say, putting my face under the coals. But what is a human face to me, when zeal for the faith must be disclosed? Before God and the angels I shall not be put to shame. To be put to shame before human beings for God’s sake is praise; if I am heard, there will be a common gain; if I am despised, my reward will be mine.

I shall speak as your friend, as your disciple, as your attendant—not as a stranger. Therefore I shall speak freely to our teachers, as it were, and to the helmsmen of the spiritual ship and its mystical pilots:

“Watch, because the sea is stormy and is provoked by savage whips. For it is not merely the threatening wave—which, even when the sea is stirred, rises continually over the cautious through the foaming whirlpools of the hollow sea, swelling and lifting itself hyperbolically from afar, and driving before it the roaring surge over eight thousand furrowed [perhaps: “furious”] waters—but the storm of the entire element, rising and stirred up from every side, threatens the shipwreck of the mystical ship. Therefore, as a fearful sailor, I add this cry: Watch, because water has already entered the ship of the Church, and the ship is in danger.”

For we are disciples of Saints Peter and Paul and of all the disciples, who wrote the divine canon by the Holy Spirit [Note: “*By the Holy Spirit.* *Dictating* or something similar is missing]. We are all Hibernians, the final inhabitants of the world, accepting nothing outside evangelical and apostolic doctrine. There was no heretic, no Jew, no schismatic; but the Catholic faith, as it was first handed down by you, that is, by the successors of the holy apostles, is held unshaken.

Strengthened by this confidence, and as though spurred on, I have dared to rouse you against those who blaspheme your people, and who cry out that you receive heretics and call you schismatics. Thus my boast, in which I faithfully spoke in answer to him on your behalf, will not be empty, and they—not we—will be put to shame.

For I promised on your behalf that the Roman Church would defend no heretic against the Catholic faith, as it is fitting for disciples to think concerning their teacher. Therefore receive with willing spirit and pious ears the necessary suggestion of my presumption. Whatever I say will be counted to you either useful or orthodox. For the teacher’s praise lies in the doctrine of his disciples. Thus, if the son speaks wisely, the father will rejoice, and your praise will be present, because, as I said, it proceeded from you; purity is attributed not to the stream but to the spring.

But if you find in this letter, or in the other one against Agripp[ina?—the text breaks off] who moved me to write, any words that seem to exceed the proper measure of zeal, attribute them to my indiscretion, not to arrogance.

## III.

Watch, therefore, for the peace of the Church. Come to the aid of your sheep, already fearful as though terrified by wolves, who fear that you yourselves, driven about by excessive fear, may turn against one another.

Therefore, being uncertain, some come and others withdraw; as they come, so they return, and they are always in fear. Hence use the whistle of a true shepherd, O pope, and your familiar voice. Stand between them and the wolves, so that, once their fear has been put aside, they may recognize you for the first time as their complete shepherd.

For the people whom I see, while enduring many heretics, are zealous and are quickly disturbed like a frightened flock; and therefore they are not quickly secure, because Italy has had so many wolves, whose cubs can scarcely all be crushed, since they have been nourished among so many caves.

May God destroy the caves and such seed, nourish them with his flock, and pierce your heart. Apply yourself vigilantly to your pastoral office, standing upon your watch day and night, so that you may be worthy afterward to see that nut-shaped staff which is a hook (Amos 8:1–2), at the time of gathering the true fruits.

Therefore, so that you may not lack apostolic honor, preserve the apostolic faith, confirm it by testimony, strengthen it in writing, fortify it by a synod, so that no one may rightly resist you. Do not despise the little counsel of a foreigner, as though he were a teacher zealous on your behalf.

The world is already declining; the Prince of shepherds is drawing near. Beware lest he find you negligent, striking your fellow servants with blows of bad example, eating and drinking with the Hebrews, lest the following come upon you in your security: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14:38). It is not enough for you to be concerned for yourself, since you have undertaken the care of many: to whom more has been entrusted, from him more is required.

## IV.

Watch, therefore, I beg you, pope—watch. And again I say: watch. For perhaps Vigilius did not watch well, whom those who accuse you proclaim to be the head of the scandal.

Watch first for the faith, then for the works that must be commanded in accordance with the faith and for the vices that must be trampled down. For your vigilance will be the salvation of many, just as, conversely, your security will be the destruction of many.

Let Isaiah send you to the mountain where you proclaim good news to Zion (Isaiah 40:9); or rather, through Isaiah, may God, according to the interpretation of your name, place you upon the watchtower of true contemplation. From there, set higher than all mortals and made near to heavenly things, raise your voice like a trumpet and announce to the people of your Lord, entrusted to you by him, their sins, and to the house of Jacob their iniquities (Isaiah 58:1).

Do not fear the charge of lying. You have something that you ought to announce. Many, what is more serious, have been cast down in these regions through the security of shepherds, and many have been deceived through the prosperity of a most wretched abundance.

Since, according to the Lord’s threats, the blood of the saints will be required from the hands of the shepherds, watchfulness is necessary—namely, the word of the Lord must frequently be preached by the shepherds, that is, by the Church’s watchmen and teachers, so that no one may perish through ignorance. For if anyone perishes through negligence, his blood will be reckoned upon his own head.

## V.

But why I have recalled these matters so sharply, though they have long been known to everyone, I shall append below. They also belong to the first categories of the proposed admonition, for both matters are bound together: the one depends on the other. Therefore these things must first be cut away.

For the one who does not care about religion does not care about error. Here the entire struggle consists; here the whole case stands; here is that two-edged sword (Revelation 1:16) that reaches to the division of flesh and soul, joints and marrow, and is the discerner of heart and thoughts (Hebrews 4:12). It must cut the sinews down to the mouth.

Hence our speech has been seasoned with divine salt (Colossians 4:6), for every sacrifice was commanded to be sprinkled with salt. Hence sparks descend from that divine [fire supplied] which the Lord came to cast upon the earth (Luke 12:49), consuming the wood, hay, and straw (1 Corinthians 3:12) that many wrongly build upon the foundation.

This is astonishing: how often we Christians are built up, when no one can lay another foundation besides what has been laid, which is Jesus Christ (ibid., 11). Alas, how many fuels for Gehenna are prepared everywhere from these wretched buildings! Upon them the Lord’s sparkling word, descending from the immensity of that ever-living fire, has fallen in order to burn them, saying:

“Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly. For like a snare it will come upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth” (Luke 21:34–35).

## VI.

You see with what terror the Lord rouses our sleep and harmful lukewarmness to vigilance, lest we be found unprepared. Therefore I said: “Pope, watch.” It is time to rise from sleep (Romans 13:11). The Lord is near, and we are already standing close to the end, amid perilous times.

Behold, the nations are troubled and kingdoms are bending. Therefore the Most High will soon give his voice, and the earth will be moved. I, like a fearful man, since I am not a strong warrior and see that the hostile enemies have surrounded us, try to rouse you with importunate cries, as the chief of commanders. For the danger of the entire army of the Lord concerns you—the army lying inert in the field rather than fighting, and partly, what is more lamentable, offering its hands to its adversaries rather than resisting.

The whole army awaits you: you have the power to organize everything, begin the war, rouse the commanders, order the weapons to be seized, form the battle line, sound the trumpets everywhere, and finally enter the contest with yourself marching at the front.

For woe has long been appearing in this region. In this spiritual war we Christians too have been defeated: first by carnal vices and pompous conduct; then by the lukewarmness of wavering faith. Once that faith had been weakened, we were surrounded, without realizing it, by three enemies given to us as punishment for our luxurious security.

For the cause of every evil is the security of blind prosperity.

## VII.

I am astonished, I confess, at such security, and I do not know what hearts, ears, or understanding this deadly sleep almost entirely covers—hearts, ears, and understanding that the Lord’s own fiery words have in no way roused to the vigilance of continually burning zeal, to contempt for the world, and to Christ’s poverty, as they have affirmed in the case of many nations.

I have come from the end of the world, where I saw spiritual commanders wage the Lord’s battles, and I hoped afterward to see commanders stronger and more experienced in this holy conflict. Finding you as I do, I am as one who gazes after battle upon a dewy field of war, wet with corpses. I am amazed, grieving, and afraid; and, looking toward you alone, who are the one hope among rulers, powerful through the honor of the holy apostle Peter, I lament the slaughter of so great an army.

But because the boat of my frail intellect has not been led out into the deep, in accordance with the Lord’s word (Luke 5:4), so much as it still clings to one place—for a sheet of paper cannot contain everything that my mind, amid changing circumstances, wished to confine within the limits of a letter—I am asked by the king to set forth one by one to your pious ears the matter of his grief.

For his grief is the people’s schism concerning the queen, the son, and perhaps himself also; for he is reported to have said that, if he knew it for certain, he too would believe it.

## VIII.

Let us return to the book that we left beside the bank. Therefore, lest the ancient thief bind human beings with this very long rope of error, let the cause of the schism, I beg you, be cut at once by you with a sort of knife of Saint Peter—that is, by a true confession of the faith in a synod, and by the abomination and anathematization of all heretics—so that, if its purity is acknowledged by everyone, the world may recognize the chair of Peter as free from every error—and from any “horror,” if, as they say, one has been admitted [Note: “*Horror.* This word seems to have entered through an error.”].

For it must be mourned and lamented if the Catholic faith is not held in the apostolic see. But, to say everything, lest I seem to flatter you beyond what is permitted, it must also be lamented that you did not first, out of zeal for the faith, immediately condemn and excommunicate—after displaying the purity of your faith—those who had for so long departed from you, since you possessed legitimate authority, so that no one would dare to accuse or defame the principal seat of orthodox faith [Note: “*Why?* Because—or: ‘that not why.’—It is not acceptable.”].

For you know with what savage punishment the accusers of the innocent were condemned by the fathers at the holy Council of Nicaea. In saying this I do not fail to recognize that there are many causes amid the clamorous, sharp, and tumultuous multitude, which do not permit these matters to be investigated thoroughly. I have said this not because I believed it, but because I believed it ought now to be done.

If any of your provincial associates are rebellious against the truth, let guilt be confined to them. For a mouth filled with meal or any other material cannot blow fire; everything is harmed by a neighboring contrary force.

Therefore I beg you for Christ’s sake: come to the aid of your reputation, which is being torn apart among the nations, lest your opponents count it as treachery on your part if you remain silent any longer. Do not therefore continue to dissemble; do not remain silent. Rather, utter the voice of the true Shepherd, whom his sheep recognize. They do not hear the voice of strangers, but flee from it (John 10:4–5).

## IX.

I urge you, my fathers and personal patrons, to drive confusion from the faces of your sons and disciples, who are put to shame on your account—and, greater than this, to remove the shadow of suspicion from the chair of Saint Peter.

Therefore summon an assembly, so that you may purge yourselves of the charges brought against you. For what is alleged against you is no trivial game. The reception of heretics, as I hear, is attributed to you—God forbid that it should be believed to have been, be, or ever become true.

For they say that Eutyches, Nestorius, and Dioscorus, ancient heretics as we know, were received by Vigilius in some fifth synod [perhaps: “in the fifth synod”]. Behold the cause of the whole scandal, as they say. If you too receive them in this way, as is alleged—or if you know that Vigilius himself died infected with this error—why do you recite him against your conscience? For everything that is not from faith is sin (Romans 14:23).

The fault is now yours if you have departed from true confidence and made your first faith void (1 Timothy 5:12). Your juniors rightly resist you, and rightly do not communicate with you until the memory of the lost has been erased and consigned to oblivion.

For if these matters are more certain than fabulous, your sons have been turned into the head, while you have been turned into the tail (Deuteronomy 28:44)—a thing painful even to say. Therefore your judges will be those who have always preserved the orthodox faith, whoever they may be, even if they seem to be your juniors.

They are orthodox and true Catholics who have never received or defended either heretics or persons under suspicion, but have remained in zeal for the true faith. If these men are not your elders in rank, let those who are nevertheless greater in fault judge justly, each side eagerly asking pardon for so long a discord, and neither side defending anything contrary to reason—neither you, the heretics, nor they, the persons under suspicion—so that both may more quickly come to agreement.

## X.

Forgive me as I cross such rugged places [Note: “*While crossing.* We have emended thus for the printed *tranctanti*”], if some words from outside have offended pious ears, because the logic of the consequent history permits me to omit nothing from the question, and the freedom of paternal familiarity, so to speak, makes me venture to do so in part.

For among us it is not the person but reason that carries weight. But love of evangelical peace compels me to say everything, so that the greatness of my concern for concord and your peace may be a wonder to you both, who ought to have been one choir [Note: “*Greatness.* And *greatness.* Likewise below, *and your peace*”]. “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26).

For, as I said earlier, we are bound to the chair of Saint Peter. Although Rome is great and renowned, it is great and illustrious among us through this chair alone. For although the name of the city once founded—of Ausonian splendor, as though something most august, set far apart from the heavens amid diverse climates—has, through the excessive favor of almost all peoples, been widely proclaimed throughout the world as far as the western regions beyond the limits of the world, with the whirlpools of the sea rising everywhere in triple waves and leaping intermittently, though hyperbolically—“a wondrous thing to say!”—nevertheless, from the time when God and the Son of God deigned to exist, and when he rode across the sea of the nations upon those two most fervent horses of the Spirit of God, namely the apostles Peter and Paul, whose dear pledges made you blessed, stirring up many waters and multiplying the chariots of innumerable peoples by thousands, he himself, the supreme charioteer of that chariot, who is Christ, the true Father, the Driver of Israel, passed across the current of the Euripus, across the backs of the dolphin, across the swelling nine-inch measure [*dodrans*], and reached us.

From that time you have been great and renowned, and Rome itself has become nobler and more illustrious. And, if it may be said, because of Christ’s twin apostles—I mean those very heavens said by the Holy Spirit to declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1), concerning whom it is added: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (ibid., 5)—you are almost heavenly, and Rome is the head of the churches of the whole world, apart from the unique prerogative of the place of the Lord’s resurrection.

Therefore, just as your honor is great in proportion to the dignity of the chair, so great care is necessary for you, lest you lose your dignity through any perversity. For power will remain with you only as long as right reason remains. The true keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven is the one who opens to the worthy through true knowledge and closes to the unworthy. Otherwise, if he does the contrary, he will be able neither to open nor to close.

### XI

Since these things are therefore true, and have been accepted without any contradiction as true by all wise people—although it is known to everyone, and no one is unaware of how our Savior bestowed the keys of the kingdom of heaven upon holy Peter—and since perhaps on this account you claim for yourselves, with a certain lofty arrogance, some authority and power in divine matters greater than that of others, know that your power before the Lord will be the lesser if you even entertain this thought in your hearts: that the unity of faith throughout the world has produced unity of power and privilege, so that liberty is everywhere granted to truth by all, and access is likewise everywhere denied to error. For right confession also granted a privilege to the holy common keeper of the keys, the universal Nonno. Let it therefore be permitted even to your juniors to admonish you out of zeal for the faith, love of peace, and unity of the Church, our common mother—who, like Rebecca within her womb (Gen. 25:22), is being torn apart maternally, and grieves over the quarrel and civil war of her children, and mournfully laments the division of her own members. Here tears are needed more than words.

How has the enemy prevailed against the Christian name after the living words of the Son of God, after the fullness of the Gospels, after apostolic teaching, after the recent writings of orthodox authors, who have disclosed the sacraments of faith concerning the Old and New Testaments in varied language? To divide the body of Christ, to separate its members, and to tear the very tunic of the Son of God, the Savior of the world—which is unity: whose handiwork is this? Yours, devil; may Christ, our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2:14), conquer you.

### XII

Therefore, dearest ones, make haste to agree and come together as one, and do not contend over ancient disputes; rather, be silent and consign them to eternal silence and oblivion. If there are matters of doubt, reserve them for divine judgment. But whatever is manifest, about which human beings can judge, judge justly and without partiality. Let your judgment be peaceful within your gates, and recognize one another, so that there may be joy in heaven and on earth because of your peace and union.

What else have you to defend besides the catholic faith, if both of you are true Christians? I cannot understand how one Christian can contend with another concerning the faith. Whatever an orthodox Christian says—one who rightly glorifies the Lord—the other will answer, “Amen,” since he likewise loves and believes. Let all of you therefore say one thing and think one thing, so that, as Christians in their entirety, you may both be one (1 Cor. 1:10).

For if, as I have heard, some do not believe that Christ has two substances, they should be regarded as heretics rather than Christians. Christ our Savior is true God, eternal and beyond time, and true man, existing in time without sin. According to his divinity he is coeternal with the Father, and according to his humanity he is younger than his mother. Born in the flesh, he was nevertheless not absent from heaven; remaining in the Trinity, he lived in the world.

And therefore, if it is written in the Fifth Synod, as someone told me, that whoever worships two substances has his prayer divided, that person is divided from the saints and separated from God—the one who wrote this. For, because of the unity of the person in whom the fullness of divinity was pleased to dwell bodily (Col. 2:9), we believe in one Christ, both his divinity and his humanity, because the one who descended is himself the one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fulfill all things (Eph. 4:10).

If anyone thinks otherwise concerning the Lord’s Incarnation, he is an enemy of the faith and must be abominated by all Christians and anathematized, whatever his order, status, or rank may be. No one ought to honor a human being to the injury of God. Therefore, I beg you, for Christ’s sake, spare no one who attempts to separate you from Christ; rather, resist him openly if anyone unwilling to believe rightly tries to turn you away from the catholic faith.

### XIII

Grant pardon, I beg you, to me, excessively offensive, harsh, and somewhat loquacious, who could not write otherwise about such a matter. Since I wished in every respect to please the truth, and knew that unleavened bread must be eaten with bitterness, I served God alone, who is blessed forever.

I have proved my kinship and my zeal for the faith, since in such a cause I preferred to give my critics an opportunity rather than leave my mouth, however unlearned, unopened. Therefore, although a three-forked scorpion may rise up with an arched wound, stretching out its tongue like the bow of falsehood against those matters of which it is written—those who judge every new thing, however “epicrocan” [the reading is uncertain], having become exceedingly rich, in hyperbolic fashion, and those who always bring forward their deceitful opposition to envy against writings of every kind that are not elegant—still, when a gentile king asks a wandering Lombard to write, and a Scot to write who is dull, when the wave of the ancient torrent flows backward, who would not marvel rather than bring an accusation?

Nevertheless, I shall not tremble, nor fear human tongues in God’s cause—tongues that more often lie than speak truth—since, wherever necessity compels, modesty must be resisted rather than cowardice obeyed.

### XIV

Therefore, to return to the point from which I digressed, I beg you—since many doubt the purity of your faith—to remove quickly this blemish from the splendor of the holy chair. Such a report of present frivolity is unworthy of the dignity of the Roman Church: that it could be moved by any force from the firmness of the true faith, for which so many of its martyrs poured out their blood, preferring to die rather than be shaken.

For if persecution should come in our time—the final scale of that loathsome creature whose hide all the ships in the world could scarcely carry—shall we not resist unto blood while struggling against sin (Heb. 12:4), as our fathers did, that is, the apostles and so many martyrs? If persecution was severe at the beginning of the faith, how much more will it be at the end, concerning which the Lord says: “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8). And again: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matt. 24:22).

Blessed is the one whom death takes before he, in weakness, denies. Yet he says that the elect will be present there; of them he plainly foretold to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Since therefore the elect who will live in those days—more dangerous than all others and unparalleled both before and after—will endure greater things, with the Lord strengthening them, why should we not, with the Lord’s help, endure lesser things in times that are still safer and more secure, even for the sake of our faith, by which we differ from pagans, Jews, and heretics?

### XV

But since I am urging such things while myself inactive in deed, and speaking rather than acting, grant pardon, I beg you, as I have often asked, to me—Jonah in Hebrew, *Peristera* in Greek, *Columba* in Latin, or rather bearing this name in your own language, although almost shipwrecked under the ancient Hebrew name—because I was compelled to write more by necessity than by vainglory.

For someone, in a letter by which he seized me almost at my first entry into the borders of this region, informed me that you should be avoided as falling into the sect of Nestorius. Astonished, I replied briefly, as best I could, not believing his allegation. But, so that I might in no way be opposed to the truth, I altered my response in accordance with his letter and with my good opinion of you—for I always believe that the pillar of the Church is firm upon its branch—and sent it to you to reread and dispute wherever it departs from the truth. For I do not dare to profess myself among the irreproachable.

### XVI

After this occasion for writing, moreover, the command of King Agilulf was added. His request placed me in astonishment and in manifold anxiety, since I consider what I see to be something not without miracle. Kings established this Arian stain in this region for a long time by trampling upon the catholic faith; now they ask that our faith be strengthened.

Perhaps Christ now looks upon us with a gracious eye [the reading may be *pio nos oculo*, “with a gracious eye”], through whose favor every good thing comes into being. We are most wretched if, on our side, the breach becomes greater.

The king therefore asks, and the queen asks, and all ask you, that as quickly as possible everything may become one: that peace may be made in the fatherland, that peace may immediately be made for the faith, and that henceforth the whole people may become one flock of Christ. King of kings, may all Italy follow you, Peter.

What is sweeter than peace after wars? What is more delightful than the union of brothers long separated? How eagerly does a father arrive after many years? How sweetly is his arrival announced to a mother who has long been waiting? Thus the peace of the children will be joy to God the Father throughout the ages of ages, and the happiness of the mother Church will become an everlasting celebration.

For the rest, holy pope and brothers, pray for me, the most worthless sinner, and for my fellow pilgrims, beside the holy places and the ashes of the saints, and especially beside Peter and Paul, likewise great men and commanders of the great King, most valiant warriors in the happiest field, following the crucified Lord with his blood; so that we may deserve to cling to Christ, please him, give him thanks, and praise him without end, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with you and with all the saints, here and throughout the eternal ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0283C] This letter was first and only published by Goldast from a manuscript codex of the library of the monastery of St. Gall; it appears in Part I of his *Paraenetici veteres*, pp. 146–148.]

## LETTER VI. TO A CERTAIN DISCIPLE OF HIS

### I

This world is passing, and every day it grows less. No living person will remain; no living person has remained. The whole human race follows the same course in birth and falls at the end of life in the same way. Death uncertainly steals away the lives of those who are passing onward. Sorrowful death seizes all the proud wanderers.

What all the greedy refuse to give generously for Christ, they lose at an inopportune time. Others gather their possessions afterward. While alive, they scarcely dare to give anything small to God; they leave everything to death and have nothing from it themselves.

Every day the present life they love grows smaller; the punishment they prepare for themselves will remain without end. While they attempt to gather what slips away, they are less afraid to believe in this thing that carries them onward.

They loved the gloomy darkness more than the light (John 3:19). They disdain imitating the Lord and guide of life. As though they ruled in dreams, they rejoice for a single hour; but eternal torments are still being prepared for them. The blind do not see what remains after death for sinners, nor what impiety provides for the ungodly [perhaps, “what remains for the ungodly after impiety”].

[Note: [Col. 0283C] *Deferentibus.* Goldast reads *differentibus*, “those who differ,” which is less satisfactory.]

[Note: [Col. 0283C] *Vagos.* “Wanderers on this earth.” Or perhaps *divagos*? Goldast reads this way.]

### II

It is fitting for you, my friend, to consider all these things. Keep far from you any love for this pattern of life. “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40:6), even though it burns and flowers; thus all human glory is like the flower of grass. When the sun rises, the grass dries up and the flower withers (Jas. 1:11); so it is with all youth when strength has failed.

The beauty of human beings, growing old, slips away. The radiance of Christ’s face, lovable above all things, is more worthy of love than the fragile flower of the flesh. Take care, little son, not to sow appearances which death enters with no small destruction.

Many have endured the fires of punishments because they refused the losses of a slippery will. Never drink the cup of the most impious person. From it you often see many laughing happily; for whoever you see laughing vainly, know that at the end they will weep bitterly.

[Note: [Col. 0284C] *Conantes.* The manuscript has *conantur*, which ought not to have been changed.]

[Note: [Col. 0284C] *Timent credere.* “They distrust.” Goldast.]

### III

Observe, dearest, that lust is like a deadly bite, one that overcomes sweetness.

[Note: [Col. 0284C] *Quod vincit dulcedinem.* Goldast emends this to *qui vincit dulcedine*, “which overcomes by sweetness.” In my judgment, that is less correct.]

Do not proceed headlong along the ways of mortals; consider how many have suffered shipwreck.

[Note: [Col. 0284C] *Quam multis.* Goldast corrects this to *per quas multis*, “through which many.” I change nothing, reading *quammultis* continuously.]

Proceed among snares with your feet suspended, through which we discover that the other careless people have been caught. Lift the eyes of your heart above earthly things; love the most loving peoples of the angels.

Blessed is the household that dwells on high, where no old man groans and no infant cries; where no voice restrains the praises of the Lord [perhaps, “is silent”]; where there is no hunger and never any thirst; where the heavenly people are fed with food from above; where no one dies, because no one is born; where the heavenly royal court is nourished, in which no discordant voice has been heard; where green and true life will be, which neither fear of death nor sorrow will consume.

When death has been passed, they will joyfully see the joyful King. They will reign with the One who reigns; they will rejoice with the One who rejoices. Then pain, weariness, and labor will be erased; then the King of kings, the King pure among the pure, will be seen.

[Col. 0285]

# THE POEMS OF SAINT COLUMBANUS, ABBOT

*(Galland, Library, vol. X.)* (C, G, S)*

## TO THE READER

Since I could not make better things, I use old words in place of my own;

For to alter ancient sayings is sheer impiety.

## I. LETTER TO HUNALD

[Col. 0285A]

[Note: [Col. 0285D]

Verse 2. *Et anni.* Thus Sirmond. But Goldast, *Paraenetici veteres*, p. 47, has *in annis*, less correctly.

Verse 12. *Admittas.* Goldast rightly reads this. In Sirmond it is incorrectly *admittens*.

Verse 13. *Nec te.* Sirmond’s reading. But Goldast has *Ne te*.

Verse 18. *Suscipe, Hunalde.* Thus Canisius; for it is one and the same letter as the preceding acrostic. Instead of *Humalde*, Goldast has *quaeso, Sethe*, and divided the poem into two letters: one, namely the acrostic, addressed to Hunald; the other, beginning here, addressed to Sethus. See the note at column 296. EDITOR.

Verse 29. This verse is absent from Goldast.

Verse 30. *Carmine vates.* Thus Sirmond. Goldast and Canisius have *ante magistri*.

Verse 70. *Nudos quos.* Goldast has *nudos quoque*.]

In countless changes the times of life run on;

All things pass away: months and years roll on.

Age slips toward old age at every moment,

So that you may be permitted to grasp everlasting life.

[5] Now despise the soft enticements of perishable life.

Pleasant luxury overcomes honorable virtue.

Avarice burns, and blind desire consumes the heart.

A mind devoted to empty cares knows no limit.

Silver is base beside gold, and gold beside virtues.

[10] The highest peace is to desire nothing beyond what use requires.

I have often sent you these little verses to read:

I beg you to admit my words to your ears.

Let neither vain nor perishing pleasure deceive you.

See how brief is the power of nobles and kings.

[15] The slippery glory of mortal life quickly passes.

Pardon these words: perhaps we have been too loquacious.

Remember always to avoid whatever is excessive.

Receive gladly, Hunald, and read with a serene mind

The words of Columbanus, faithfully admonishing you:

[20] Though they lack the adornment of polished speech,

They nevertheless testify to the love of a pious heart.

Live trusting in God, following Christ’s commandments,

While life remains, while the appointed time of salvation lasts.

Time and the hour fly; age slips away in moments.

[25] Despise the joys of fleeting life, which pass away.

Do not pursue fragile wealth and empty gains,

And do not let overflowing abundance trouble you.

Let the teachings of the divine law be your riches,

And the chaste rules of life taught by the holy Fathers,

[30] All that learned poets have written for the teachable in verse.

Take these riches; always despise perishable things,

And let trembling old age come to your mind,

Followed at last by the icy violence of death.

The wise person now meditates upon the final seasons of life:

[35] Strengths grown numb with age, frequent illnesses,

The uncertain day of death, and certain pains.

Many hardships of the fragile flesh torment the old.

For languid limbs waste away in shameful emaciation.

Then the joints of the knees grow stiff, and through all his veins

[40] The blood grows cold throughout his body.

Thus, leaning on a staff, he supports his inert limbs.

Why should I recall the sad groans? Why the weariness of the mind?

Sleep is absent from his eyes; every sound awakens him.

What then will silver accomplish, or yellow gold,

[45] The wicked hoard accumulated over many years?

What will the gifts of nobles accomplish? What the meals of a rich table?

What joy is there in remembering the pleasures of a life now past,

When at last the end of life has come?

While this life flies away, whoever reviews these things with a watchful mind

[50] Despises avarice and rejects empty honors.

[Col. 0286B] Why do mortals wish to fix their minds upon earthly cares?

Why do they pursue shameful profits?

The miser is always in need of money, as the poet testifies:

“Love of money grows as the money itself grows.”

[55] He is needy amid wealth, and does not possess what he seems to possess.

Alone at home, he hides his money in a chest,

Piling up riches while failing to love himself;

He loves his heir more, the one who faithfully preserves everything.

O exceedingly happy is the one for whom modest use is sufficient,

[60] So that he may temper care for the body with a balanced restraint.

He is not ensnared by miserable and blind desire for possessions,

Nor does he desire more than nature requires.

[Col. 0286C] He does not, desiring profit, fill his purses with money,

Nor heap up soft clothing as food for moths.

[65] He does not provide fat grain to feed horses,

Nor turn such anxious thoughts over in his troubled heart:

That the money gathered might perish in sudden flames,

Or that a wicked thief might break the chest and carry off the coins.

One can live without silver now, and live without gold.

[70] Naked they are born, and naked the earth receives them.

For the rich, the black thresholds of Dis are opened;

For the pious poor, the heavenly kingdoms are laid open.

The Savior warned the greedy to despise riches.

Whoever loves Christ follows Christ’s footsteps.

[75] For the brief and fragile glory of the flesh destined to die—

Whatever it possesses, the swift flight of rushing time carries away.

Beautifully the voice of the truthful poet sang such things,

[Col. 0287A]

Counting the seasons of age and of perishable life:

Time drives all things, and with time all things are dragged along.

[80] The elements alternate their changes, and the seasons change:

Days receive increase, and nights in turn do likewise.

There is a season for flowers, and harvest retains its season;

So again the field is clothed in thick grass.

There are seasons for rejoicing, and definite seasons for sorrow.

[85] There are seasons of life, and sorrowful seasons of death.

Swift time gives, takes away, and diminishes all things.

Spring, summer, autumn, winter: the year returns to the year.

Although everything returns, a person’s age does not return.

The wise person remembers this at every hour,

[90] And prefers the house of mourning to sumptuous feasts.

[Col. 0287B] Now, in a final humble prayer, I shall conclude my words.

Remember me yourself when you read these verses.

May you thus have a long old age of your desire.

## II. SINGLE-LINE VERSES (*MONOSTICHA*)

[Note: [Col. 0287D]

Verse 9. *Divitias*, etc. This verse is repeated below at verse 97. Goldast did not read it in his own codex, p. 60, in the same place.

Verse 21. *Non possis.* The Leodien manuscript apud Goldast has *non cogites*.

Verse 25. *Qui prod.* This verse is absent from Goldast.

Verse 27. *Repleta salutis.* The reading of the Leodien manuscript, *repleta triumphis*, seems preferable to Goldast’s reading.

Verse 29. *Qui fiet omn.* The Leodien manuscript has *qui sit in omnibus*. But, in Goldast’s judgment, the archaism should not be rashly rejected.

Verse 35. *Largire vid.* The verb *largio* is among those which signify one and the same thing in both active and passive voice, says Priscian, Book VI. GOLD.

Verse 53. *Faciet.* Goldast has *faciat*. Likewise in the following verse.

Verse 63. *Perdit.* The manuscript of St. Gall apud Goldast has *pendit*. I would change nothing.

Verse 67. *Torquentis.* Goldast suspects that *torquendo* should be read.

Verse 68. *Severa.* The Leodien manuscript has *te vera*.

Verse 70. *Noli tu.* Goldast reads *nolito*.]

Let the devout person read these precepts and fulfill them in action,

Whoever seeks an honorable life adorned with the titles of virtues,

Whether he desires to be esteemed among human beings,

Or to earn the heavenly kingdom by the merits of his character,

[5] And to be seen forever as a companion of God Christ.

Let the one who wishes his prayers to come true fulfill God’s will.

Live trusting in God, following Christ’s commandments.

Let the teachings of the divine law be your riches.

The blessing of the Lord will make his riches glorious.

[10] The prudence of the mind surpasses the strength of the body.

Wisdom is better than all the treasures of the world.

The knowledge of good things is always worthy of love.

The best spirit is clothed in the love of Christ.

Against demons, virtue is a great prayer.

[15] Do not cease to admonish your dear friend.

Whatever pleasure there is, excessive pleasure is the cause of sickness and evil.

Do not close your hands in giving, nor open them in taking.

Let good words of salvation always resound in your mouth.

I beg you, let your mind not meditate bitter vengeance.

[20] Let your character be peaceful, with great sweetness.

Take care lest you regret your victory over yourself.

Endure your father’s authority while his words proceed into anger.

Let every day of life be regarded as though it were the last.

[Col. 0287D] Do not promise in words what you cannot give.

[25] Do not shun a friend who can be useful.

Strive to conquer the eightfold armies of vices.

[Col. 0288A] Let a chariot filled with salvation carry you to heaven.

Let the tongue have its reins tied within the heart.

No one can be a good man unless he becomes fair to everyone.

Whoever conceals crimes will perhaps not deserve forgiveness.

Whoever abandons good practices soon becomes accustomed to evil.

[30] I beg you, do not injure anyone by jokes or by verse.

You will more often be instructed by listening than benefit from speaking.

Let the belly be servant to the mind; let lust be its servant.

Piety does not lose whatever it seems to give generously.

Good reputation is not bestowed by wealth, but by noble character.

[35] Take care that another does not rightly mock you in words.

For a wretched companion, in pity, pour forth tears.

If you can, rescue the enraged man; do not supply him with weapons.

Compassionate indulgence by a teacher often harms a boy.

Never prefer an unknown person to a known friend.

[Col. 0288B] Do not believe everything that people say.

Let no one live for himself, but everywhere let him live for Christ.

Do not seek what is yours, but what is Christ’s, if you love him.

Do not love yourself, nor the world, but Christ alone.

[45] When speaking with a wise man, use very few words.

Eyes are of no use when the mind is blind to seeing.

The reproach of the rich is the immense groaning of the poor.

Wisdom always grows greatly in one who is learning.

Judgment most certainly awaits all deeds.

[50] The Judge will come, who will repay everyone with justice.

Famed patience bestows everlasting life.

Self-restraint will make you more renowned than ferocity.

Steadfastness of mind will produce outstanding character.

I beg you, let whatever must be done be done with deliberation.

[55] For every age labors under some burden.

Young man, consider carefully the true models of the ancients.

Blessed is the one who speaks a prudent cause into a prudent ear.

Words have as much power as the mind that utters them feels.

He is rich for everyone who abounds in honorable things.

[60] A new friend must not be preferred before an old one.

Perhaps you will find it difficult to discover a true friend.

Make an honorable name for yourself by outstanding character.

No one has had more friends than the one who has lost them.

What benefit is there to the companion who is shown not to be useful?

[65] Faith alone will be enriched by the gracious gift of faith.

Let a light concern not weary the soul that is being tormented.

A serious matter always declares itself honorably.

What is worse than for an unjust inhabitant to join himself to another?

[70] Do not accustom yourself to wicked deeds or words.

It is better not to be than to live wickedly.

[Col. 0288D] A good mind surpasses all treasures in the gift it offers.

Guard your life with complete virtue.

Everything must be lost in order to preserve life.

[75]

[Col. 0289A]

[Note: [Col. 0289D]

Verse 79. *Cujus doc.* Goldast reads, with the Leodien manuscript, *cui sunt doc.*

Verse 86. *Hoc alii.* The manuscript of St. Gall has *hoc alio*. Goldast prefers this reading. Nor are examples lacking that use *alio* for *alii*.

Verse 106. *Censes.* Goldast has *causes*.

Verse 109. *Qui prod.* This verse is given above at verse 25.

Verse 112. *Cathegita.* A female teacher, instructress.

Verse 114. *Conditus.* “So then, you see no distinction between *condere* and *condire*?” GOLD.

[Col. 0290D] Verse 136. *Constat.* Read *conflat*.

Verse 153. *Omnis.* Goldast more aptly and conveniently reads *omnia*.

Verse 154. *Permitte.* Read *commit­te*.

Verse 157. *Dimittis.* Read *dimittito*.

Verse 158. *Fidelis amicus.* Canisius reads *fidelis ubique*. Goldast judges that nothing should be changed: the expression is by repetition (*κατ’ ἐπανάληψιν*), in the same manner as Juvenal’s:

“Love of money grows as the money itself grows.”

Verse 174 (following column). *In ore.* Canisius reads *more*. Goldast thinks the reading should not be disturbed. See above, verse 153.]

Those who have considered such things beforehand will be able to endure them more lightly.

Things that arrive suddenly seem much more burdensome.

A pious and kindly ruler is the people’s joy.

Another’s death warns us everywhere of our own death.

Happy is the one who learns from another’s scourges.

[80] He will receive no reward who gives good things to an ungrateful person.

Let a human being be dear to you as a brother, and God as a gracious father.

Every hour gradually brings us nearer to death.

Before the day of death, no one is found praiseworthy.

Every tree is recognized by its own fruit.

[85] He will be a great teacher by his deeds who fulfills what he teaches.

Remember to do for another what you wish to be done for you.

Heavenly glory remains for the just poor.

What you would not wish for yourself, do not do to anyone else.

Have an even weight, and hold a just balance.

[90] Let there be neither a double measure nor a double balance for you.

Reprove the prudent person; gratitude will be returned for your words.

If you do what is right, do not worry about the words of the wicked.

Do not despise useful counsel because it comes from a servant.

Among fellow guests, see that your speech is modest.

[95] When you have sinned, punish yourself thereafter.

While you heal wounds, pain is the medicine of pain.

The blessing of the Lord will make his riches glorious.

Happy mercy grants everlasting life.

Use the wealth you have acquired; flee the name of miser.

[100] Learn, but from the learned; teach the unlearned yourself.

Do not contend with the wordy by words.

Speech is given to many, but wisdom of mind to few.

Let joys not lift your spirit, nor sorrows break it.

Be near the good, if you cannot be the best.

[105] The greater you are, the more cautious you should be.

When you judge another, first examine your own life.

As a judge, condemn your own crimes more than another’s.

Be good, and be good to the good; when injured, do not injure the wrongdoer.

Do not shun a friend who can be useful.

[110] When you are fortunate, beware of what is adverse.

What you are accustomed to condemn, do not do yourself.

Let another’s life be a guide for your own life.

Anger produces hatred; concord nourishes love.

Let all your speech be seasoned with the salt of wisdom.

[115] Great indeed is the virtue of restraint in our speech.

Trust in God, and then direct your own steps for yourself.

The light of the heart is the fear of the Lord; always love this fear.

No one who hopes in the Lord is ever confounded.

A prudent man is better in spirit than a strong man in arms.

[120] Wisdom of mind surpasses the strength of the body.

Do not set your mind upon unjust riches.

A sweet word will indeed multiply your friends.

Do not delay turning to the Lord by the straight path.

Do not be swayed even by varied teachings.

[125] For may the firmest way of the Lord always hold you.

May the words of justice and peace please you as you speak.

May gracious peace, I beg, always please you in your mouth.

Let pious words of salvation always resound in your mouth.

A wise king defends his people better against the enemy.

[130] A foolish ruler will scatter his entire people.

A just wisdom is indeed great glory for a king.

Do not avenge your injuries upon your brother.

The miser always loves lies, thefts, and robberies.

Let what God himself has given you be sufficient in worldly things.

[135] Why does an earthly man, dust and earth, boast?

Alas, dreadful pride stands at the beginning of crime.

[Col. 0290B] Take care of your salvation with complete virtue.

A single day reveals what sort of friends people have been.

If you have sinned alone, do not forgive yourself.

Commit what you wish kept secret to a silent companion.

[140] Remember to avoid envy through excessive display.

The evil plague of envy stains an honorable reputation.

Do nothing without deliberation; thus deeds are approved.

Whoever trusts in the Lord keeps the commandments of salvation.

The wise person always fears the anger of the Judge.

[145] Do promptly whatever task chance assigns to you.

Do not frequently remain with an unjust man.

Neither does flowing water return, nor does our time return through the years.

Devouring ending destroys all the joys of the world.

The Lord will have mercy on the one who is pious and kind.

[150] Bring no complaints of mind against good deeds.

Never reproach someone if you have given any little gifts.

Let the mind first work through every word before speaking.

Entrust the care of the body to a faithful physician.

While you can, always do good, dear one, for your friend.

[155] Thus let a friend grow old, new and new wine alike.

In adversity, never abandon a friend.

A friend always loves, and a faithful friend endures.

The gracious day follows the night; so gifts follow labors.

While times change, let the mind always remain honorable.

[160] Foresee in advance, by the counsel of your mind, whatever threatens.

While life is strong within you, cleanse evil crimes with tears.

Do not repeat a crime while washing it away with tears.

Do not serve wicked luxuries with your mind.

[165] Whoever despises small things diminishes greater things hour by hour.

Every faithless person is removed from the number of the saints.

Let the foolish hate the words of the wise teacher.

The talkative man rouses bitter laughter among his brothers.

Nothing is worse than one who rejoices in wicked crime.

[Col. 0291A]

[Note: [Col. 0291D]

Verse 184. *Diligit Sophia.* The manuscript of St. Gall has *Diligit en Sophia*. Nothing is truer. Christ the Wisdom (*Sophia*) always loves again the one who loves him. Proverbs 8:17: “I love those who love me.” GOLD.

Verse 187. *Divitias*, etc. See above, verse 9.

Verse 193. *Exsuperat*, etc. The Leodien manuscript has:

“By number the company of the righteous powerfully exalts kingdoms.”

Verse 207. *Corrigit.* The manuscript of St. Gall has *corripit*.]

See with the greatest care to whom you entrust secrets.

Reprove the sinner; do not abandon your friend.

It is better to reprove a known friend than to lose a friend.

Whoever forgives his brother, Christ also forgives him.

The wise person observes the proper time for speaking.

[175] The foolish person speaks a despised word at the wrong time.

The excessively talkative person strips the soul of honorable merits.

It is great glory to fear God the Lord.

The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord from the heart.

Fire tests gold; temptation tests righteous people.

[180] Hope in the Lord, and mercy will come to you.

Love Christ, if you desire the joyful blessings of heaven.

The father’s blessing will make children happy.

Never afflict the mind of the poor and wretched.

[Col. 0291B] Christ the Wisdom always loves the one who loves him.

[185] Do not be quick with your tongue, nor sluggish in action.

A false witness is not harmless through his words.

The blessing of the Lord adds many riches.

Now return a great gift to your friend for a small one.

A friend always loves; love is more precious than gold.

[190] He will be rich who always works hard in the field.

The one who pursues leisure will always come to poverty.

A faithful man in mind is better than all riches.

The number of the righteous surpasses the kingdoms of the powerful.

Behold, the one who fears the Lord will live through happy years.

[195] The righteous joyfully awaits heavenly happiness.

The wicked looks upon dreadful punishments for his crime.

A people under a wicked ruler falls headlong.

Gentle mercy prepares eternal life.

Whoever pursues good things rises well at the first hour.

[200] The tongue of the wise brings salvation to many.

In war, a strong right hand rules over enemies.

The sluggish man will also serve beneath the harsh burden of labor.

A tongue at peace acquires many friends for itself.

Place bars and bolts upon your words and speech.

[205] Whoever fears God’s commandments dwells in peace.

For good teaching will grant everlasting salvation.

He loves the son who corrects him with the rod.

## III. LETTER TO FEDOLIUS

[Note: [Col. 0292D]

Verse 39. *Aurea pellis.* Most manuscripts have *aureum vellus*, “the golden fleece.”

Verse 46. *Populavit.* An archaism.

Verse 66. *Adulter.* The Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* has *ad inter*, very badly.

Verse 67. *Obtulit aurum.* In the same edition this verse is carelessly omitted.]

Receive, I beg you,

Now composed in two-foot

Verse,

These little poetic gifts,

[5] Small presents;

And you, frequently,

Return to us

The due

Of mutual services.

[10] For just as fields dry

Rejoice in rains

When the South winds

Are blowing in the heat,

So your page,

[15] Frequently sent,

Will gladden

Our minds.

I do not now ask

For gifts of perishing

[20] Treasure;

Not the gold

Which the miser

Always gathers by his activity,

Gold which blinds

[25] The eyes of the wise,

And, like fire,

Burns through its flame

Wicked hearts.

Often the dreadful desire

[30] For gold suggests

Unspeakable crimes

To many.

Of these things

I shall now unfold

A few to you,

[35] Deeds performed

In ancient times.

The golden fleece

Was the great

Cause of evils.

[40] Because of a small gift

Of gold,

The banquet of the goddesses

Collapsed,

And a great dispute

Arose among those three goddesses.

[45] From this, the wealthy kingdoms

Of the Trojan-born people

Were ravaged

By the Dorian youth.

[50] The laws of the law,

divine right, and faith

are broken by gold.

For the impious deeds

Of King Pygmalion

[55] Are recorded

As having been done

Because of gold.

Thus the avaricious host,

Incited by gold,

Deceitfully killed

[60] His guest Polydorus.

Often a woman

Loses her chastity

Because of gold.

It was not Jupiter’s gold

That flowed in the rain;

[65] But the gold which the adulterer

Offered

Is represented

As that golden rain.

[Col. 0292D] Gold betrayed

Amphiaraus

Through his faithless wife.

Achilles sold

The heroic body

[75] Of Hector for gold.

And the black thresholds

Of Dis

Are said to be opened

By a certain gift.

[80] I could now recount

More things,

If concern for brevity

Did not forbid it.

Sending these little gifts

Of letters to you,

[85] Illustrious brother,
I urge you to leave vain cares.

[90] Cease, I beg you, now to feed spirited horses with rich grain,

[Col. 0292B] and cease, by piling gain upon gain, to add coins to coins.

Why do you associate with the unjust, whose frequent gifts you receive?

Christ hates the gifts of the unjust.

These things the wise man ought to despise,

[105] who must recognize the fleeting and perishable seasons of life.

[Col. 0292C] Yet it is enough now to have sung these things in eloquent verse.

For this poetic formula may perhaps seem new to the reader.

But that illustrious poetess of the Trojan-born peoples,

[120] Sappho by name,

used to produce sweet poetry in verses of this kind.

[Col. 0292D] If you happen to desire to compose poems in such a verse,

so that one dactyl may always begin

[130] in a fixed sequence,

[Col. 0293] [Note: Verse 163: *ter senos* (“three times six”). Another manuscript: *ter senae*.]

then a trochee should properly be placed immediately after it

in the following part.

Often it will be permissible, by right,

[140] to close the final verses with two long syllables.

Only, loving brother Fedoli,

sweeter to us than every nectar,

leaving the more flowery poems

[145] of eloquent writers behind,

receive our trifles gladly.

Thus may Christ, judge of the world,

[150] the only offspring of the Almighty,

restore to you the sweet joys of life:

he who, ruling all things without end

in the name of the Father,

reigns forever.

[160] [Col. 0294] These verses are dictated to you while oppressed by severe illnesses,

which I suffer in my frail body and in my sorrowful old age;

for, while the seasons slip by in their headlong course,

we have now reached three times six years of the Olympiad.

All things pass away; irretrievable time flees.

[165] Live, and farewell in joy; remember sorrowful old age.

## IV. AGAINST WOMEN

Let every person devout in mind flee the mortal poison

which the proud tongue of a woman wickedly possesses.

A woman destroyed the summit bestowed upon life;

but a woman also gave life its enduring joys.

## V. ON THE VANITY AND MISERY OF MORTAL LIFE

*(Bibliotheca Patrum of Lyon, vol. XII)*

[Col. 0293]

[1] [Note: [Col. 0293]

Verse 9: “for those who differ.”

Verse 15: The manuscript incorrectly has *inopportune*.

Verse 17: Perhaps *parum* (“too little”).

Verse 23: Perhaps *manet* (“remains”).

Verse 26: Perhaps *conantur* (“they endeavor”).

Verse 33: Read *regnant* (“they reign”).

[Col. 0293] Verse 45: Job 13.

Verse 47: Psalm 103.

Verse 48: The manuscript has *est* (“is”).

Verse 49: Isaiah 40; James 7.

Verse 55: Something seems to be missing here.
