This world passes away, and

every day grows smaller;

no living person will remain,

no living person has remained.

[5] The whole human race

is joined by a similar birth

and falls from a similar life

to an equal end.

Death uncertainly snatches away life

[10] from those who prolong it.

Sorrow of death seizes

all the proud and wandering.

What all misers refuse

to give generously for Christ,

[15] they lose at an inopportune time;

others gather it after them.

While alive, they scarcely dare

to give even a little to God;

they leave everything to death,

[20] and have nothing of them afterward.

Every day the present life,

which they love, grows shorter;

the punishment they prepare for themselves

will remain without end.

The slippery thing that slips away,

[25] as they endeavor to gather it,

and this which deceives them,

they are less afraid to believe.

They loved the dark

more than the light;

they disdain to imitate

[30] the Lord, the guide of life.

Like people in dreams, they reign;

for one hour they rejoice;

but eternal torments

are still being prepared for them.

The blind can in no way see

[35] what remains after death

for wicked sinners,

which their wickedness supplies.

It is fitting for you to consider

all these things, my friend;

let it be far from you to love

[40] the pattern of this life.

All flesh, though flourishing, is like grass,

and, like the flower of grass,

so too is all its glory.

When the sun has risen,

[45] the hay dries up and the flower withers;

so is all youth,

when its strength has failed.

The beauty of human beings,

growing old, slips away.

The radiance of Christ’s face,

[50] more lovable than all else,

is to be loved more

than the frail flower of flesh.

Beware, little son,

of sowing outward appearances

which death will enter

[60] with no small destruction.

Many have endured

the fires of punishment,

unwilling to pay the cost

of slippery desire.

Never drink the cup

[65] of utter wickedness,

from which you often see many

laughing joyfully.

For whoever you see

laughing vainly,

know that at the last

[70] they will weep bitterly.

Look, dearest one,

at how lust is

like a deadly disease

that conquers sweetness.

Do not proceed headlong

[80] along the ways of mortals:

how many do you see

suffering shipwreck?

Proceed among snares

with your feet suspended,

through which we discover

[85] that the other heedless people have been captured.

Lift the eyes of your heart

above earthly things.

Love the most loving

peoples of the angels.

Blessed is the family

[90] that dwells in the heights,

where no old man groans,

nor does an infant keep watch;

where no voice restrains

the praises of the Lord;

where no one ever hungers,

[95] where no one ever thirsts;

where the heavenly people

are fed with food from above;

where no one dies,

because no one is born;

where the royal court [the text is corrupt; perhaps: “and is fed with heavenly food”],

[Col. 0295] [Note: [Col. 0295]

Verse 106: Perhaps “and heavenly.”

[Col. 0295] Verse 111: Alternatively, *mors* (“death”).

[Col. 0296] Verse 112: Alternatively, “about to consume.”]

q Perhaps “is fed with heavenly food,”

in which no badly sounding

voice is ever heard;

where life is green

[110] and truly future,

which neither the fear of death nor of sorrow has consumed.

When death has passed,

they will joyfully see the joyful king;

[115] they will reign with him as he reigns,

they will rejoice with him as he rejoices.

Then pain, then weariness,

then toil will be destroyed;

will be seen by the pure.

## GOLDAS T’S NOTES ON THE POEMS OF SAINT COLUMBANUS

### PREFACE

[Col. 0295A]

Those ancient Christians were so devoted to the writings of their Fathers that they not only did not handle the books of the pagans, but even kept their sacred hands away from them as from forbidden things. Thus I think that the monks became exceedingly barbarous in this discipline, because they had neither heard nor seen anything from which the elegance of good literature is obtained.

But, with the Bible translated into a semi-Latin idiom, writers stammering in an unknown language, and the noisy inflections of Greek and vernacular words—if, with their leave, I may say so—they were the first of all to lose the wisdom which the Fathers of the greater nations labored to retain in its ancestral possession.

The writings of Basil and Augustine on reading pagan books still exist; but in vain. Therefore they followed another path: they commended, under the designation of the Christian name, those writers who shape human minds by the precepts of wisdom. We read that this was done in Seneca, Claudian, and the Pythagorean [Col. 0295B] or Stoic writers; Saint Jerome considers their school very similar to the Christian religion.

Others labored to extract better sayings and deeds and to impose them upon Christians in the guise of maxims and proverbs. A very ancient book of such proverbs is preserved among us, excerpted from Ovid, Virgil, Horace, Lucretius, Statius, Lucan, Juvenal, Persius, and others.

There were also others who built their own books out of the sayings of the ancients, as if from building stones and material, silently concealing the names of their architects—silently, because those architects were hateful to them. In this category Columbanus is especially conspicuous, and we present his miscellany, or, in a manner of speaking, his stitched-together cento.

The deception is not impious, if one considers the end for which the deception was employed. He touches on it in the letter to Hunaldus: after producing verses of Horace, he adds:

> I have often sent you these little verses to read;

namely, because Horace’s books had been hateful to him, and Hunaldus had asked for them.

This empty piety—or, more truly and certainly, superstition—had spread beyond the Britons and through many nations; [Col. 0295C] for among them good writers in both languages were read by adults and assigned to boys at school.

Under the emperor Charlemagne, the Franks at last began to be freed from this condition through the work and teaching of John, Clement, and Alcuin. From Britain the very best books were brought and imported by them: among the poets, to speak plainly, Virgil, Ovid, Horace, Juvenal, Persius, Lucan, Statius, Nemesianus, Calpurnius, Maximianus, and others.

As for Valerius Martial, one may reasonably doubt whether the testimony of Lupus and Hincmar establishes his presence among them. His work, like that of the others, was offered to the Franks as a model for imitation, with greater—if only it had been equally fortunate—enthusiasm than success; for what those Fathers had rarely done, for the reason I have mentioned, these men turned into a custom.

Indeed, it became customary for some people of that age always to append to their verses something from an ancient poet, and thus to compose a rhyme. This kind of game is said to have been customary for a certain Raymond, whose verses circulate. Consider this example:

> So that the mind may see itself once the smoke of darkness has been set aside,

[Col. 0295D]

> who forbids a light to be taken from a light that has been set beside it?

> And if I cannot bring forth everything perfectly,

> though strength is lacking, nevertheless the will should be praised.

A nobler and more highly esteemed imitation was that by which among the Greeks Eudocia reproduced Homer, and among the Latins Proba Faltonia reproduced Virgil. Isidore adds to them a certain Pomponius, who, among his other literary pastimes, composed *Tityrus* in honor of Christ, and likewise *Aeneids*, *Etymologies*, book I, chapter 38. Concerning Proba, see the same author, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 5; Honorius, chapter 43; Sigebertus, chapter 52.

## IN THE LETTER TO HUNALDUS

Verse 2. “Months roll into years.” Some read “and years,” less correctly. In the *Monostich*: “Nor does our time remain in years.”

3. “It slips into old age.” An imitation of the ancients. Ovid, *Fasti* VI:

> Time slips away, and we grow old through silent years.

Ausonius, *Epigrams*:

> We grow old; age escapes.

Fortunatus, book VII:

> Time that has slipped away flies; we are deceived by fugitive hours,

[Col. 0296B]

> and slippery life leads men into old age.

4. “Perpetual life.” “Eternal,” *perpetual*. The Greek-Latin Lexicon: *aionios* (αἰώνιος), everlasting, eternal, perpetual, and so forth.

Solomon of Constance, in his Lexicon: perpetual, enduring, eternal, immortal, everlasting.

Valerianus of Cimiez, *On Good Learning*: “to exclude the presumption of perpetual death.” The forms *perpes* and *comperpetus* are also used by Prudentius in the *Apotheosis*.

*Perpetuity*, eternity, *perpétuité*. The same Solomon: “Perpetuity pertains to angels or to the soul; eternity, however, to God.”

To perpetuate, to make eternal. Ennius, *Annals*, book IX, concerning the Romans: “and so that liberty may be most enduring.” Arator, *History of the Apostles*, book I:

> For by these chains, Rome, you alone have been made perpetual.

Malthaeus of Vindonissa explains Columbanus in *Tobias*:

> He makes life perpetual and grants the honor that is to come.

7. “Avarice burns with blind desire.” In the following letter: “and with blind desire for possessions.” Raymond Astucius, in his book *The Struggle of Man*: “Blind desire binds everyone.” In Horace, book I, letter 1:

> Avarice seethes, and wretched desire burns in the breast.

In an ancient manuscript of Schobinger, the glosses explain *cupido* as “love.”

9. “Silver is worth less than gold.” From Horace, the same letter, book I, to Maecenas.

10. “The highest peace is to desire nothing more.” From Prudentius’ *Psychomachia*, where *super* is used absolutely. Solomon in the Lexicon: *super* is sometimes understood as “too much” or “enough.” Dositheus, book I: *super* in place of “in addition” and “more.”

16. “Forgive my words.” An Ovidian imitation: “Forgive my faults,” and so forth, in *Letters from Pontus*.

## IN THE LETTER TO SETHUS

2. “The sayings of Columbanus.” Admonitions, *paraineseis* (παραινέσεις). In the letter to Hunaldus:

> I beg you to admit my sayings to your ears.

Lucilius, book XXVII:

> At the same time, understand and attend both to the meaning and to the words.

I therefore thought that this verse should be restored, since it commonly circulates in an unfinished and unmetrical form.

[Col. 0297A] Ovid, book III of *The Art of Love*:

> This part too must be instructed by my words.

Thus in the old reading and in the manuscript of Paul Stephen. Gratian accordingly calls the *Sentences of Isidore* “sayings,” *Decretum* XXIII, question V, chapter CXX: “from the sayings of Isidore”; and distinction IX, chapter CII: “from the words of Isidore.”

“Words” are proverbs, *gnomai* (γνῶμαι). Hence the books of the ancient wise men on morals were called proverbs. There are the Proverbs of Solomon, the Proverbs of Seneca, the Proverbs of Publius and Laberius, the Proverbs of Saint Evagrius the abbot, the Proverbs of Varro, who was highly regarded in the *Sophologus* and by the author of the *Destroyer of Vices*; Pharo or Faro, sometimes Baro; the Proverbs of the Wise, the Proverbs of the Ancient Poets, and the Proverbs of Marcus Seilo.

To indicate this meaning, Cyril the bishop, an author of no account, entitled the moral conclusions of his fables “proverbs” in a four-part apologetic work. Master Odo, preface to the *Moral Philosophy of the Philosophers*: “It was also lawful for me to insert among their proverbs whatever I had heard either from them—Cicero, Seneca, and so forth—or from others.”

The *Proverbs of the Wise* attributed to Demetrius—not to Demetrius of Phalerum, as the title falsely claims, but to some Greek schoolman—are *apophthegms* (ἀποφθέγματα) and “precepts” (*hypothekai*, ὑποθῆκαι) of Sotiades. Ausonius calls them *sententiae*, commonly *gnomai of the wise*. Aristobulus, preface to the *Galeomyomachia*:

> For proverbs, maxims, precepts, and apophthegms are sisters to one another.

3. “Of honorable speech.” *Kalos* (καλός), elegant and ornamented. Plautus, Terence, and Cicero often use it in this way. It is opposed to what is inept. Symphosius, preface to the *Riddles*:

> Then came the verbose company, eager for inept speech.

5. “Live, trusting in God.” In the *Monostich*, *secutus* (“having followed”) is read instead of *sequendo* (“by following”). As far as the sense is concerned, it makes no difference which way one reads it.

6. “While the appointed seasons of salvation last.” Some read *cepta* (“begun”), contrary to the sense. Bede, *On the Day of Judgment*:

> Do not despise the appointed times of pardon given to you.

In the *Monostich*:

[Col. 0297C]

> While life remains vigorous in you, cleanse your evil crimes with tears.

For every hope of pardon is denied to sinners after this life. The author of *On Contempt of the World*, published sixty-eight years ago by Focaudus Monierus:

> And he who has once gone there never returns here,

> nor are their punishments released from prison

> by prayer, by payment, or by the passage of days.

Go now, mortals, and place your hope in your little possessions. Prepare the good works of others; purchase indulgences, purifications, and other things. What next? Fire and torments.

7. “Time and the hour fly.” A verse of an ancient poet, certainly written in imitation. Silius Italicus, book XV: “the hour flies and snatches away.” Likewise, verse 100 of Seneca’s *Hippolytus*:

> The hour, a mobile winged thing, flies amid uncertainties.

Ovid, book I of the *Elegies*, according to the reading of Paul Stephen:

> Age slips away secretly, and the flying years deceive us.

10. “Nor should it trouble you.” From Prudentius’ *Psychomachia*. “Overflowing.” Curtius, book VIII: “Avarice is insatiable: it still wishes to fill what is already overflowing.”

13. “Teachers capable of teaching.” *Didaktikoi* or *didaskaloi* (διδακτικοί / διδάσκαλοι). Solomon in the Lexicon: “teachable, learned.” Isidore, in the *Synonyms*: “Teachability is the wisdom of instructing the unlearned”; for the same, *docibilis*. Placidus in the Glosses: *docibilis* is taken for *docilis*. For we use both *indocibilis* and *docibilis*.

In an ancient Pontifical: “We choose a presbyter imbued with apostolic and ecclesiastical discipline, catholic in faith, prudent by nature, teachable,” and so forth.

Abbot Benedict interprets it in the Rule: “learned in divine law, so that he may know and have from which to bring forth new and old,” from Paul’s Second Letter to Timothy, chapter II, where the old translator rendered *didaktikon* (διδακτικόν) as *docibilem* (“teachable”).

This meaning of the word is indeed very rare, but was transmitted in imitation of the ancients. Pylades, in the Glosses, on the word *docibilis*: “Verbal adjectives in *-bilis* derived from absolute verbs signify an action and the ability to perform it: for example, *risibilis*, that is, capable of laughing; *gressibilis*, that is, capable of walking.”

We shall append examples from the Fathers. Prudentius has “a forgetfulness-producing cup,” in hymn VI of the *Cathemerinon*; Synesius has *poma letheon* (πόμα ληθαῖον), “a drink of forgetfulness.”

The same author has “a tormenting destruction,” *basanizon* (βασανίζων), in *Peristephanon*; in this form *exitiabilis dies* (“a destructive day”) occurs in Plautus for *exitiosus* (“ruinous”).

Elsewhere he has “a triumphal cross,” *thriambeutes* (θριαμβευτής), “one who triumphs.” Ambrose has “triumphal commanders of war,” in the hymn on the apostles. Guntherus has *suasibilis vox*, “a persuasive voice,” book I; *peithanos* (πειθανός), “persuasive,” in Quintilian.

21. “The troubles of the flesh torment.” Pope Innocent III, in *On the Worthlessness of the Human Condition*, lists these troubles as follows: “An old man,” he says, “is easily provoked and difficult to recall; he believes quickly and disbelieves slowly; he is tenacious and greedy; sad and complaining; quick to speak and slow to hear; he praises the ancients and despises the moderns; he blames the present and commends the past; he sighs and is anxious; he grows numb and becomes weak.”

Hear the poet:

> Many troubles surround an old man.

This is a verse of Horace from the *Art of Poetry*.

25. “Thus leaning on a staff, supporting his inactive limbs.” For old men assist their steps with staffs. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII:

> They raise their limbs with staffs, slow through their aged years.

Titus Calpurnius, *Eclogue* V:

> Do you see how for a long time now old age, bent over, brings us

> a thousand complaints and presses upon a staff?

Seneca, *Hercules Furens*:

> Inactive old age assists its steps with a staff.

See whether Columbanus had this passage before his eyes. Certainly both poets are playing on the proverb. They think that *inertes* (“inactive”) is said as though it meant “without limbs.” “Inactive limbs” is a kind of Hellenism, *artha anarthra* (ἄρθα ἄναρθρα), just as *philos aphilos* (φίλος ἄφιλος), “a friendless friend,” and *charis acharis* (χάρις ἄχαρις), “graceless grace.”

30. “What are the banquets of Dis’s table?” Papias in the Glosses: *dis*, rich, wealthy. Solomon in the Lexicon: *ditis*, “of the rich,” singular; *dites*, “rich,” plural.

Below, in the poem to Fedoli: “rich kingdoms.” The same Solomon: “rich gifts,” “very rich gifts.” From a verse of Statius: “you will give rich gifts,” which Priscian praises in book VI.

Again Solomon: Titius observed in *Controversies*, book IV, chapter 18, that the ancients said *ditior* (“richer”), *plus dives* (“more wealthy”), *ditiores* (“richer”), and *ditias* for *divitias* (“riches”).

34. “And rejects empty honors.” Solomon’s Lexicon: *refuto*, “I refuse.” In the *Hermeneumata*: “he rejects, repudiates, refuses.” Cicero, *For Rabirius*: “You ought not merely to disdain and reject, but also to embrace and increase.”

Sallust, in a fragment: “They devote themselves to kings and afterward reject life.” Servius and Philargyrius, in their notes on *Georgics* IV, are ignorant of the history and have interpreted this passage differently.

Amoenus, in the *Enchiridion*: “He values what he receives alive and rejects what is earthly.” The author of *On Contempt of the World*:

> But do not reject my gifts.

Anonymous glosses: “In the Egyptian language, *Sarabaitae* are called *Rennuitae* in Latin; they refuse to have an abbot.” Jerome, *In the Agon*:

> For me you sweated precious blood; do not reject me.

37. “The miser is always in need.” A half-verse of Horace, book I, letter 2 to Lollius. The author of *On Contempt of the World*:

> Flaccus bears witness that the miser always has too little.

Columbanus clearly had these words before his eyes.

38. “Love of money grows.” A verse of Juvenal, satire XIV, which both the author of *On Contempt of the World* and Raymond Astucius, in his book *The Struggle of Man*, chapter against usurers, transcribed. Ovid, *Fasti* I:

> In time the love of possessing, now at its height, grew.

Sulpicius Servatus:

> If greater concern for the growing coin is present.

[Col. 0299A]

41. “While he does not know how to love himself.” Juvenal, satire XII, concerning the miser:

> Let him neither love anyone nor be loved by anyone.

42. “For whom he keeps it.” Habakkuk II, verses 6, 9, and 10.

47. “He fills the moneybag.” Solomon in the Lexicon: *marsuppium*, a money pouch.

This Solomon came from the illustrious and very ancient family of the Ramsuvagii. He laid the foundations of a very pleasant town, which he named Cella of the Bishop after himself, between Saint Gall and Constance; for he ruled the territories of both. That town lies less than half a mile from the castle of Ramsuvag, in whose immediate neighborhood I first began to see the light of day in these regions; this is why I praise him so often, and not without affection—he was indeed numbered among the saints, and his family touches families related to us.

That Lexicon was compiled from various glosses of various writers more than eight hundred years ago. In this work, as they testify, he used the work and teaching of his teacher Iso, as well as those of the very learned men Notker and Tutilo.

But as for Columbanus, did he express this passage of Varro? And does he rather empty the lord’s moneybag than fill it? See Varro, *On Agriculture* III, chapter 16.

49. “To feed the horses with grain.” In the poem to Fedoli:

> To feed horses with rich grain.

In the *Hermeneumata*: *cavo*, *caballus*. Virgil—perhaps the bishop of Juvavum who was enrolled among the saints?—in Solomon’s Glosses: “A *cabo* is a gelded horse, which we call a *caballus*.”

Hugutio: *caballus* is said to derive diminutively from *cabo*, that is, “an inferior horse.” Papias: “A *caballus* is so called because its hoof hollows out the earth, or from its hollow feet.” This is from Isidore, book XII, chapter 1 of the *Etymologies*.

John of Genoa, from the ancient Glosses: “*Cabiare*, that is, to pierce, is said to derive from *cabo*. *Cabo*, that is, horse, from *cavare*, as though *cavo*.”

50. “He turns cares beneath his breast.” Fabricius read *doluit* (“he suffered”), very badly. Solomon: *voluit*, “he wishes, considers.” Virgil’s Glosses: “he turns over with himself, he considers with himself.” Placidus’ Glosses: *volvere*, “to consider, arrange, suffer, endure.” In the *Hermeneumata*: “He turns over in his breast; he considers.”

55. “The black gates of Dis are opened.” Matthew 19, 25 and following. Below, in the poem to Fedoli:

> And it is said that the black gates of Dis are opened.

In this way Theognis, in the *Sentences*:

> He descended into the dark house of Hades.

*Niger*, “black,” and *Ditis*, “of Dis.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV:

> Where is the savage palace of black Dis?

Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> Day and night the door of dark Dis stands open.

Seneca, *Agamemnon*:

> What are the features of black Acheron? and so forth.

Statius, *Thebaid* II:

> And he enriches the empty halls of black Jupiter

> with the dead.

Greek-Latin Lexicon: *Plouton* (Πλούτων), Dis. Solomon: “to the Stygian Jupiter, to Dis.” The same author: “to Dis, the god of the underworld.”

Hugutio in the Glosses: “*Dis*, *ditis*, that is, Pluto, from *ditare* (‘to enrich’), because he enriches his realm through our deaths.” The word is usually accompanied by *pater*. Philoxenus in the Glosses and Solomon: “Father Dis, Dis, who is also Pluto, whom the poets say—or intend—to have been king of the underworld.”

In ancient times *Dispiter* was used; because grammarians could not understand it, they changed it to *Diespiter*, as I demonstrate elsewhere by many arguments concerning the subject.

56. “And the pious poor.” Matthew 5, 3; Luke 6, 20; the Letter of James, chapter II, 5.

57. “To despise riches.” Luke 12, 15 and following.

58. “Whoever loves Christ.” John 13, 15 and 21. Below, in the *Monostich*.

61. “The poet’s voice sang such things.” It is not clear who this poet was. The illustrious Scaliger testifies that he found these verses on an old sheet of Jacques Cujas, as though they had been excerpted from a complete work; Ausonius, *Readings* I, II, chapter 29.

He correctly indicated that they are not by Ausonius, nor by Priscian. For Columbanus either seems not to have read the latest poets or not to have seen them. Yet we owe the first publication not to Scaliger but to Georg Fabricius, a man who rendered outstanding service to literature. He was the first among Christians to publish the poets.

From him Magarinus de la Bigne inserted them into the library of the Holy Fathers, from whom Canisius received them. The thread of the error was drawn from the fact that they attributed to Hunaldus what had been sent to Sethus.

63. “As all things are dragged along by time.” He imitates Maximianus in the *Elegies*:

> Time carries and turns everything along with itself.

A corruption has entered this verse [the following OCR reading is unclear: *luen la*]. For *vertit* (“turns”), one should read *verrit* (“sweeps”), so that it corresponds to *trahit* (“drags”).

64. “The elements alternate their changes.” Fabricius incorrectly read *alimenta* (“nourishments”) for *elementa* (“elements”). Rusticus Helpidius, *On the Benefits of Christ Jesus*:

> The elements preserve their changes.

Arnulf of Lisieux, *On the Renewal of Spring*:

> Both work and resources alternate, and the elements in turn.

[Col. 0300B] Ancient Glosses: “*alternandis*, in alternating turns.”

66. “There are seasons of flowers.” Scaliger read and punctuated: “and the nights in turn.”

“Seasons, but flowering, retain their own …,” contrary to the testimony of our manuscripts.

68. “The seasons of rejoicing.” From the divine precepts of Solomon, *Ecclesiastes*, chapter III. Therefore the poet was a Christian and read Solomon? I do not affirm this, but conjecture it; compare the passages, and you will call me a conjecturer.

71. “Spring, summer.” Jerome cites this as if it came from an ancient poet, in his commentary on Ezekiel; we owe this observation to the foremost jurist Jacques Cujas. In *Epigrams* IV there is a verse modeled on it:

> Spring, summer, autumn, winter are the four seasons

> of the year …

72. “When all things return.” Scaliger does not have this verse, but only the preceding ten. I do not know whether it belongs to this poet or to another of the ancients, for it is not Columbanus’.

74. “And the house of mourning.” Solomon, *Ecclesiastes*, chapter VII, 2.

## IN THE LETTER TO FEDOLIUS

8. “The obligations of services.” Solomon of Constance: *obsequia*, services, duties, benefits, thanks, remembrances. Agraetius: “We obtain through effort; we serve through duty.” Isidore transcribed these words, as he did the others, in *Differences*, book II.

Afranius Privignus: “How agreeable his service is to me.” Basil, bishop of Ammon: “Whatever service parents render toward us is Christ’s benefit, for he prepared parents for us beforehand, so that we might be nourished by their service.”

10. “For just as in the heat of summer.” He used *aestus* (“heat”) in place of summer, contrary to Fontonius’ distinction, though not without precedent. Eusthenius, *Description of the Four Seasons*:

> And the fields bristle with the gifts of Ceres through the heat.

Vitalis, in the same work:

> And in the heat the reaping goddess’s sickles are held back.

Here, from two manuscripts of the monastery, *messes* (“harvests”) would be a better reading. For it is the harvests, not the sickles, that are said to hold back Ceres.

Guntherus, *Ligurinus*, book I:

> He might say that he had heard thunder amid the heats.

16. “The page will bring joy.” A letter. Strabo to Fulgentius:

> Rather, the page of holy Paul gave warning.

Sometimes *pagina* means “book.” Prudentius, hymn “Born from the Heart”:

> Which the faithful pages

> of the Prophets had promised.

This is Prudentius, not that Aurelius Clemens, the consular and most honeyed man; nor that bishop of Troyes, but, as I persuade myself, the teacher of Walafrid Strabo, abbot of Reichenau. I learned this from Walafrid himself.

[Col. 0301A]

20. “Gifts of treasure.” Cyril, in the Lexicon of Scripture: *gaza* (γάζα), “possessions”; *gazophylakion* (γαζοφυλάκειον), “treasury.”

Solomon in the Lexicon: *gaza*, “treasure.” Riches are called *gaza* in the Persian language, from Gaza, a Greek city in which the king of Persia once amassed all his wealth.

In Ezekiel, *gazophylacia* are small chambers where treasures are stored. In the old translation, however, *pastoria* (“shepherding places”) is found in place of *gazophylacia*.

24. “Which blinds the lights of the wise.” Moses, Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19; Solomon, Proverbs 12:11 and 28:19; Sirach 20:29 and 41:16.

Alexander, an ancient poet:

> The unjust censor is convicted by the gift he has received:

> for a gift bends the judgment of the judge away from the rule of right

> and envelops his mind in dreadful darkness.

Claudian somewhere:

> Treacherous gifts estrange your senses.

From this one may learn that “lights” is used metaphorically of the intellect, just as “to see” means “to understand”; thus the eyes are called lights, and Alexander calls judgment “keenness.”

Solomon: “Lights. They are called eyes because light flows from them, or because at their beginning they hold enclosed light within—or, correctly, intrinsically—or because they pour back into sight the light received from outside.”

Augustine writes in his commentary on John that among the ancients it was customary to swear, “So may my lights live”; among the Greeks, *phae* (φάεα) is used for “eyes.” Homer, *Odyssey*:

> And he kissed his head, the two beautiful eyes.

See Eustathius and Didymus on seeing. Synesius, hymn:

> But you, shining forth, O lord, are the upward-leading lights.

26. “Fire’s flame.” The Hebrews commonly join words that have the same meaning. Hosea, chapter VII, 6: “In the morning he himself is kindled like the flame of fire.” Both Greek and Latin writers imitated them: “in a flame of fire” in Acts 7:30; “in a fiery flame” in the Second Letter to the Thessalonians 1:8.

Likewise, Lucretius and Apuleius use expressions such as “the path of the road,” “the weapons of arrows,” “the breeze of air,” and so forth; the same is true of Apuleius. Columbanus uses *jura legum* shortly afterward.

30. “He suggests to many.” Columbanus below:

> I suggest that you leave vain cares.

Solomon in the Lexicon: *suggerit*, “he supplies, provides, places beneath, offers, furnishes, presents, grants, performs, ministers, or insinuates.” The *Interpretation of Words from the Rules*: “suggestion, supplication, indication, assistance.”

37. “There arose a great cause of evils.” This is a well-known subject; see Orpheus, Apollonius, Flaccus, and Catullus in the *Argonautica*; Dares Phrygius, *On the Destruction of Troy*; Justin, book XLII; Apollodorus of Athens, book I of the *Library*; Eusebius’ *Chronicle*; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, 13; Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History* VII, chapter 50; and the Greek commentators everywhere, especially those on Aeschylus, Sophocles, Lycophron, and Pindar.

Columbanus presents it to Fedolius as a historical event. Palaephatus interprets the story in *On Incredible Tales* (*Peri apiston*, περὶ ἀπίστων), as do Diodorus Siculus, book V; Pliny; Strabo; Hyginus; and Albricus in *Images of the Gods*.

39. “The golden fleece.” Most authors have “golden fleece”; Manilius, “gilded fleece”; Catullus, “gilded hide”; Propertius, “golden wool”; Ovid, “Phrixian fleeces”; Apollonius, *chryseion koas* (χρύσειον κῶας), “golden fleece”; Callistratus, *chrysomallon deras* (χρυσόμαλλον δέρας), “golden-fleeced hide.”

In three manuscript books, *ariete* (“ram”) was read most consistently. This was inserted by a pedantic corrector, lest he seem unaware that the hide belonged to a ram. The passage gave rise to the proverb: among the Greeks, “the golden-fleeced ram”; among the Latins, “the golden sheep,” which Euphorbus calls “the golden flock” in *On Celestial Signs*.

For it was placed among the stars, together with Helle, an ill-omened constellation for sailors. Theodolus, *Eclogues*:

> A sorrowful sight for those carried on the sea is Helle’s appearance among the stars.

I restored this reading, whereas the common text had *Helenae*. That is an inept example, for Helle gave her name to the sea, just as Icarus did in another case.

44. “The three goddesses.” Juno, Pallas, and Venus, because of the golden apple sent by Eris to their banquet, on which she had written: “Let the beautiful one take it” (*He kale labeto*, Η ΚΑΛΗ ΛΑΒΕΤΩ).

The author Lucian, *Dialogues*, “The Assembly of the Gods,” and Galen. One should consult Dares Phrygius, *On the Destruction of Troy*; Euripides, *Hecuba* and *The Trojan Women*; Ovid, *The Letter of Paris*; Strabo, book XIII; Augustine, *City of God* III, 25; Cyril of Alexandria, preface to Evoptius against Theodore of Cyrrhus; Coluthus, *The Rape of Helen*; besides innumerable others.

Tanhuser, a German knight, learned as well as energetic, celebrated among us in poems and stories. I shall add these words for the sake of German antiquity.

In an elegant and golden poem:

> Venus, an apple was given to her;

> from it arose great trouble.

> Because of it Paris gave his life,

> and there Menelaus also lay dead.

46. “He ravaged.” An archaic inflection, not uncommon in this period. Solomon: “they ravage, take away, plunder.” Cicero, *On Expressions That Are Said in Several Ways*: “he afflicted, overthrew, oppressed, crushed, overturned, ravaged.”

This is not an inept little book, nor the work of a recent writer. Three ancient manuscripts attribute it to Cicero, as does Solomon in the Lexicon.

Accius, *Astyanax*:

> He demanded our country’s goods by force.

Caecilius, *Asotus*:

> For a long time now he has been ravaging the market.

Plautus and Virgil use the word similarly, as do Marcellus, Diomedes, Priscian, and Eutyches.

49. “The Doric youth.” Solomon: “Doric camp,” the camp of the Greeks. Doric is one of the languages of the Greeks, spoken by the Egyptians and Syrians.

53. “For the impious deeds of Pygmalion.” He killed his paternal cousin Sichaeus before the altars. Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> That impious man, blind with love of gold,

> overcame Sichaeus, unsuspecting, secretly with the sword

> before the altars, and so forth.

Consult Servius, Tiberius Donatus, and Sabinus; Justin, book XVIII; Lupus of Ferrières, letter 34 to Alcuin.

57. “Thus the greedy guest killed Polydorus.” Polymestor, Virgil, *Aeneid* III; Euripides, *Hecuba*; Plutarch, *Parallel Lives*.

64. “Not Jupiter’s gold.” Columbanus appears to have been exceptionally devoted to antiquity, since he continually preserves archaic forms. The nominative *Jovis* was used by Caecilius, Accius, and Ennius. Nevertheless, Cassellius Vindex labored to preserve it, and Priscian followed him in book VI.

Suidas: “*Iobis* among the Italians is Zeus.” Hugutio in the Glosses: “*Jovis* is derived from *juvo* (‘I help’), with the genitive *Jovis*; and *Jupiter* has the genitive *Jupiteris* or *Jupitris*. In ancient times these names were declined in this way.”

It is ignorantly derived from *juvo*, whereas it is from the Hebrew [term omitted in the supplied text], *Jehova*, by the same contraction as *Josua* from *Jehoschua* and *Judaeus* from *Jehudaeus*.

Nor does *Jupiter* mean “helping father”; rather, it means “father Jovis,” corresponding to the Greek *Zeus pater* (Ζεὺς πατήρ). An example is *Marspiter*, “Mars father”; likewise *Dispiter*, that is, “Dis father.”

Some ancient Christians, considering the force and power of the name, did not reject it. A Roman inscription reads:

> To one who, led by the desire for a quieter and more perfect life, had withdrawn from civic affairs in which he had conducted himself honorably, by the great favour of Jovis: this place was publicly granted to him as he rests in the hope of resurrection.

See Gruter, page 1050.

65. “He flowed down in a shower.” There are two approaches to this story, the popular and the philosophical.

The popular one arose from ordinary usage, since we call great riches “showers”; Cresconius Corippus, a poet of no little elegance, spoke of “golden showers.” Synesius, hymn:

> Do not pour upon me earthly

> showers of ungrudging wealth.

Then many philosophers, especially the Stoics, thought that the air was the medium from which rain or showers fall. Hence Jupiter was identified with rain.

Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> And now Jupiter must be feared by the ripening grapes.

Here is the explanation of the fiction. Jupiter, who corrupted Danae with gold, is imagined as changed into a golden shower because rain is generated in the air. This is why Zeus was called *chrysorroes* (χρυσορρόης), “golden-flowing,” by Hedylus in Athenaeus, book VIII; he is commonly called *Ombrios* (Ὄμβριος) and *Hyetios* (Ὑέτιος), “Rainy,” and by the Latins *Pluvius*.

Cyprian also mentions the story, letter II to Donatus: “They represent that Jupiter of theirs now flowing down in a golden shower.”

Donatus on Terence’s *Eunuch*, act III, scene 5, should be consulted. Augustine praises the verse in *Confessions* I, 15. Servatus parodies it in the *Catalecton*:

> Thus once, through the barriers, adultery flowed in golden form

> into Acrisius’ daughter’s lap, corrupting the maiden.

Theodolus, *Eclogues*:

> Even above the roof the dripping adulterer poured down;

> the gold had corrupted Danae in her lap.

### 66. But that adulterer.

The same mythological account, apart from the detail just mentioned, is related by Horace, Book III, Ode 16; by Acron and Porphyry in their commentaries there; by Ovid, *Amores* III.7; by Paulus Silentiarius in the *Anthology*; by Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*; by Lactantius, Book I of the *Institutes*; by Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.13; by Natalis Comes, Book II, chapter 1; and by Petrus Victorius, *Various Readings* I.15.

### 70. And the rights of laws.

Cyprian wrote *jura legesque* (“the rights and laws”), *Epistle* II to Donatus: “To see, contrary to right and law, patience fashioned by incestuous shame” [Col. 0303B]. I therefore think that the reading should be restored from the Aconian variant reading. Cato, in Charisius, Book I: “cultivators of rights and laws.” Plautus, *Epidicus*, Act III, scene 6:

> … He is reputed the maker and founder  
> Of all laws and rights.

Cornelius Severus, in *The Death of Cicero*:

> That champion of the forum, of law, of right, and of the toga.

Thus in the old book quoted by Seneca the Elder, *Suasoriae* I; Gunther, Book I:

> Let him avenge so great a ruin of right and morals.

### 71. And sacred law and good faith.

Some read the formula *jus fasque* (“right and sacred law”); Savaro noted this in his annotations on Sidonius, Book II, Epistle 13.

### 72. The treacherous wife.

Eriphyle. Sulpicius Servastus:

> Thus Eriphyle exposed her husband’s hiding place, when the shameful mother  
> Received the gold, the material of her crime. [Col. 0303C]

Theodulus, *Eclogue*:

> You pay the price of the goads of your wife, priest Amphiaraus,  
> While the jewel gleams upon your burning breast [the reading *molinis* is uncertain].

See, if you wish to know the story, Stephanus of Byzantium, Pausanias in *Boeotia*, Plutarch in the *Parallel Lives*, Diodorus Siculus IV.6, the commentator on Juvenal’s sixth satire, Lactantius in his commentary on Statius’ *Thebaid* II, and Jerome, *Against Jovinian* I.

### 73. Hector’s hero.

Homer, *Iliad* XXII; Virgil, *Aeneid* I; Dictys Cretensis III; Justin Martyr, *Oration to the Greeks*.

### 78. The black threshold of Dis is said to be—

Charon’s. Philoxenus in his *Glosses*: “Dis, Χάροντος [Charon’s].” An old glossary: “Carus, the name of a greedy man who is said to transport people into hell.”

Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VI:

> “Then does greed live even among the dead? And does that Charon, the father of Dis, so great a god, do nothing for free? Even the poor man, when dying, must seek travel money, and so forth.”

Isidore, *Etymologies* VIII, must by all means be consulted. The superstitious rite of the Gentiles was to place a coin in the mouths of the dead as passage money and ferry fare for Charon. On this subject see Lucian’s dialogue *Mercury and Charon*, and also Plutarch, *On Grief*, the *Collections*, Juvenal’s third satire and its commentator, Plautus’ *Poenulus*, and Arnobius V.

An inscription from Camerina reads:

> TO INFERNAL PLUTO, TO HIS DEAR WIFE PROSERPINA,  
> AND TO THREE-HEADED CERBERUS:  
> CARRYING A GIFT WITH ME, I GIVE UP  
> MY CONDEMNED SOUL.

This passage money was sometimes simply called *ναῦλον* (“fare”). Hesychius: “*Ναῦλον*: the little coin placed into the mouth of the dead.” Sometimes it was called *δανάκη* (“danake”). The same author: “*Δανάκη*: a certain barbarian coin, worth only a little more than an obol.” It was also said to be the obol given to the dead. I restored this word from Plutarch and Suidas, since the common reading was *Δανάη*, “concerning an obol.” Suidas writes:

> “Honey-cake was given to the dead, as though for Cerberus; and an obol, a payment for the ferryman.”

Antiphanes:

> You will die, leaving behind a great and wealthy will,  
> Having brought with you only one obol out of many.

[Col. 0304A] In Stobaeus, *Sermon* 1, we find *μοῦνον* (“only”): “Behold, he says *only*,” though everyone repeats the passage. What, then, is the meaning of Aristophanes, for whom two obols are the price for crossing Acheron? In the *Frogs*:

> In such a tiny boat an old man,  
> A ferryman, will transport you, receiving two obols as his wage.

The scholiast says:

> “Because they place two obols upon the mouths of the dead, and because the judicial fee was two obols.”

I cannot explain the matter unless he perhaps confused the honey-cake with the obol. It was a most disgusting superstition, remnants of which still survive today among the Allobroges, for they put gold into the mouths of the dead as a ransom (*λύτρον*) for purgatorial punishment. Albert of Bukuwka, lord of Eywanowic and Jornsdorf, likewise confirmed to me that the Moravians had been endowed with the same superstition; I knew him very intimately when I was among the Allobroges.

### 96. Stop adding coins to coins.

If Saint Columbanus were to rise from the dead and now see the luxury and avarice of priests, what, do you think, would he say? Surely what Blessed Wolkuinus, abbot of Scidichenbach, says in his homily *On the Weeds and the Seed*, against the vices of the clergy [Col. 0304B]:

> “Rare nowadays on earth is a canon who is a canon according to the rule of life. Why is this? Listen to why. There is, as has been said, a canon of life; and there is also a canon of money, namely, some fixed payment, from which it is customary to say: ‘Pay me my canon,’ that is, my pension, my fixed sum of money. Come, then, O canon, let us discover your canon, from which you derive your name: from the canon of money, not from the canon of life; from the canon of the region, not from the canon of religion, and so forth.”

Their avarice has been noted in every age, and likewise that of monks, whose institution and profession were once the same. The history of the emperor Conrad—Conrad I, that is—is memorable. I found it in the annals of the monastery of St. Gall.

After leaving Italy, he had turned aside across the Rhaetian Alps toward the monastery. He ordered that the sons of noblemen be brought before him; then, putting his hand into his purse as though he were taking out sweets, he slipped a gold coin into each boy’s mouth. While the others picked the coins out with their fingers, one boy, not sufficiently trusting the emperor and offended by the roughness of the coin, immediately spat it out. When the emperor noticed this, he said: “If this boy lives, he will make a good monk.”

The saying was shrewd: it implied that monks do not count themselves among those attracted by love of gold.

Chunradus of Fabaria reports something similar in his *Cases of the Monastery*. Since it leads to the same point, I shall include it. Chunradus, abbot of the monastery, had been summoned to the court by the emperor Frederick and excused himself on account of a tertian fever. When King Henry, son of the emperor Frederick, happened to encounter him, he uttered some joking words to this effect:

> “My lord abbot, I have discovered the medicine your illness requires. Take four hundred marks of silver as an antidote. I believe that, once you have received such a restorative, you will immediately be freed from your tertian fevers, and so forth.”

In this rather amusing remark the king unquestionably intended to criticize the abbot’s avarice.

### 119. Of Trojan descent.

The Lesbians, who once held dominion over the whole of Troy. The authority is Strabo.

### 120. The poetess named Sappho, bending down.

Salomo, in the *Lexicon*: “Sapphic meters, which the woman Sappho composed and which were therefore so called.” Terentianus, Atilius Fortunatianus, Diomedes, and Hephaestion should be consulted.

In the manuscripts of Diomedes, Rufinianus, Servius, and Clement, the meter is called *Adonium*; in the printed editions of Priscian and Maurus, *Adonicum*. A poem of this kind occurs in Boethius, Book I of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, and another among the ecclesiastical hymns, in Alcuin’s letter to Eulalia, in Walafrid, Notker Balbulus, and finally Metellus of Tegernsee, in the *Quirinal*.

Its use was once very widespread among Greek comic poets, but also among other poets. The Latins generally append an epichoriambic line, almost trimeter; this may explain why the verse itself too was taken as choriambic. Examples are common in Horace and in Seneca the tragedian.

Furthermore, after Fulvius Ursinus, Henry Stephanus collected Sappho’s lyric poems and gave them to Latin readers. We possess other poems, not yet, so far as I know, publicly published; with God’s will, we shall eventually bring them forth for use, together with those of Alcaeus.

[Col. 0305A] ### 131. There let the foot begin with a dactyl.

Hephaestion: “Coinciding with the dactylic foot that proceeds into a second trochee.” Above is a two-foot verse, called by grammarians a catalectic dimeter, and by the Greeks a *πεντασύλλαβον* (“five-syllable verse”) and a five-part choriambic, as Hephaestion Terentianus writes in Book II.

It is called the meter *δίμοιρον ἐπικόν* (“epic of two parts”), because it admits only two heroic feet, a dactyl and a spondee. Sappho is said to have composed a poem in continuous meter of syllables, that is, a *πεντασύλλαβον*.

Alcuin calls it a poem “noble in the senary rhythm,” not because it consists of six syllables, but because it is frequently used in a hexameter line. His words in his letter to Eulalia, daughter of Charlemagne, are:

> “I have sung this poem to you, noble in the senary rhythm, which is a perfect number in its parts; and I wish you to be perfect in your understanding.”

From this you may learn why he sent these verses to Fedolius. He then adds:

> “The wisest emperor can very easily explain to your intelligence the nature of this rhythm, as also of the others; the nobility of his mind is wondrous,” and so forth.

For Charlemagne was a distinguished poet in his age and is said to have written many verses in Latin, Greek, and German, which fate has begrudged our age.

### 156. He who is without end, eternal.

An ecclesiastical hymn:

> You who stand forth as the beginning  
> Of all things, without end.

Theodulus, *Eclogue*:

> To whom three persons have three names without end.

Prosper of Aquitaine, Book I, Epigram 5:

> Lest guilty men endure punishment without end.

Ambrose—or Gregory the Great, if the hymn is his—uses *omni fine* (“with every end”) in the hymn for Friday at Matins:

> And at the end of every age  
> He preserves purified hearts.

Among the Hebrews, *in finem* (“to the end”) occurs in a certain psalm:

> Arise, and do not reject me forever.

### 163. Now to three times six Olympiads.

Another manuscript has “three times six” in the feminine form. An Olympiad is a lustrum, that is, a period of five years. Sidonius Apollinaris, Book IX, Epistle 12: “After I had passed three Olympiads in silence.” Rabanus, *Martyrology*, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, concerning a solemn bishop: “Having completed three Olympiads in the episcopate, he departed from this light to Christ.”

Ovid:

> In Scythia a five-year Olympiad was completed for us,  
> And the period of the lustrum passes into another.

Salomo, in the *Lexicon*:

> “An Olympiad was established among the Greeks at Elis, a city of Greece, its inhabitants conducting a contest and a five-year competition, with four intervening years left free. For this reason they called the period of the Eleans’ contest an Olympiad, reckoning four years in one Olympiad.”

Demetrius Triclinius, on Pindar’s second Olympian ode:

> “The Olympiad took place every five years.”

And an exceedingly old scholiast—whether Victorinus or Didymus—on Pindar’s tenth ode, at the words:

> and five—  
> year—

adds:

> “And thus he established a five-year festival and ordained the assembly of the Olympic games.”

If, therefore, you suppose Columbanus to have reached his ninetieth year, you will find that he composed these verses then. Thus the oldest of authors, always accompanied both by the greatest gravity and by remarkable holiness, died in extreme old age.

The Roman Martyrology, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December:

> “Famous for many virtues, he rested in a good old age.”

The *Violet of the Saints*:

> “In a good and holy old age he fell asleep in peace.”

### 164. Irrecoverable time flees.

A Virgilian half-line from *Aeneid* X.

### 165. Live, and farewell joyfully.

Was this borrowed from Persius, Satire V, “Live mindful of death,” and from Horace, Satire VI, Book II? Or is it a Horatian formula, “Live, farewell,” in the *Epistles*? “And remember your sad old age.”

Ovid, *The Art of Love* III:

> Already remember the old age that will come,  
> So that no time may pass away uselessly for you.

[Col. 0306A] A golden saying spoken by another poet would have a different meaning. It would resemble the saying of Sirach: “Remember the last things, and you will never sin.”

The adjective *triste* (“sad”) belongs naturally and properly to old age. Hence Juvenal, Satire II:

> But old age is more to be feared than death.

Why, then, does Columbanus call old age desirable in the preceding final epistle?

## Against Women

Unless I am seriously mistaken, this epigram was written against Brunhild, the most criminal queen of the Burgundians. For through her machinations and false complaints Columbanus was expelled both from the monastery of Bobbio and from the whole of Burgundy, far away.

### 1. Mortal poison.

*Θανατηφόρον φάρμακον* (“a death-bearing poison”).

The author of *On Contempt of the World*:

> He avoids earthly beauty and mortal poison.

Glosses on the *Ecclesiastical History*: “deadly, mortal.” And in the gloss on Cassian: “Lethean, mortal.”

Theganus, *On the Deeds of Emperor Louis*:

> “That mortal judgment which had been imposed on the others, the emperor refused to exercise.”

For all the others had been sentenced to death. Gunther, Book V:

> … He pierces their mortal bodies  
> With iron.

Here *mortalia* (“mortal things”) has hitherto been printed incorrectly; Christoph Pflugius also observed this. In this sense Virgil has “a mortal wound” in *Aeneid* XII; Apollonius, “mortal Enyo,” in Book III of *The Destruction of Jerusalem*; and Cyprian, “a mortal crime,” which later became “mortal sin” in the Church.

In Book XI of the *Meditations*: “Preserve me from every mortal sin.” Those who attribute this book to Augustine of Hippo certainly do not know that African bishop. Trithemius assigns it to Anselm of Canterbury. I cannot guess on what grounds, since the manuscripts of our work clearly prove that it is not his. In one manuscript the author’s name is not written; in another, recent and late, the name of Augustine appears.

But we possess Anselm’s *Meditations*, in whose preface he declares that he has gathered all his prayers there. He writes:

> “Anselm, unworthy bishop, sends greetings to the reverend Countess Matilda. It pleased Your Highness that I should send you all the prayers which I had composed for various brothers according to each one’s request,” and so forth.

In the Cologne edition, the poem *On the Glory and Joys of Paradise*, which is chapter 26, is attributed to Peter Damian, Anselm’s peer, as its author; the writings reveal him to be a pious and learned man. Is he the fabricator and founder of the entire book? Or is he Augustine, the apostle of the English, as some maintain? The latter is more likely.

### 2. What belongs to a woman.

Euripides, *Phoenician Women*:

> The female sex is a lover of blame;  
> If they obtain small beginnings for reproaches,  
> They introduce more and more.

Seneca, *Hippolytus*:

> But woman is the leader of evils and the contriver of crimes.

Propertius, Book II, Elegy 8:

> But for you it is easy to devise words and contrive deceptions;  
> This one task woman has always learned.

Tibullus, Book III, Elegy 4:

> Ah, cruel race, and the name of woman is not faithful!

### 3. Conferred upon life.

Saint Paul, First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 15, verse 21:

> “Since through a man came death, and through a man came the resurrection of the dead; for just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.”

What now? Does Columbanus convict Paul of falsehood? Take care—take great care that you do not think so. Did he have Genesis chapter 1 in mind? No more than that. What, then? The Song of Solomon? Much less indeed.

Yet he says the same thing as Paul, and with him nearly all the Fathers. Listen, so that we do not go farther afield: hear the author of *On Contempt of the World*, a holy and thoroughly devout man. Comparing sinful Adam with Christ the Redeemer, he finally says:

> Woman was the cause of human destruction;  
> Woman was the cause by whom mankind is restored.
>
> Woman was the cause that man fell from paradise;  
> Woman was the cause by whom he returns to life.
>
> The first mother, hated, evil, proud, was a woman;  
> The virgin mother, chaste, kind, and devout, was a woman.
>
> The first mother made him angry;  
> The virgin mother makes him gracious.
>
> Eve was the means by which man was left without a protector;  
> The Virgin was the means by which God became man.
>
> If God is man, he wishes and is able to show mercy;  
> What he gave—[the corrupt text continues:] “to man, to confer, the power [of] God.”

The last verse is corrupt. We have attempted to restore it as follows:

> What he gave, God himself will confer upon man.

What God gave to man in Christ, Christ—God—confers upon the human race, namely mercy.

The other distich comes from the presbyter Sedulius, in the edition published by Turcius Rufus and wrongly attributed to Claudianus Mamertus:

> Woman alone was the one through whom the door to death was opened,  
> And woman alone was the one through whom life returns.

## In Monostichs

If you ask what my own judgment is concerning these Monostichs, I shall explain to you the matter which is closest to the truth.

There was a time when I had scarcely taken them into my hands before I would have thrown them down again, judging them unworthy of so great a man. I could give many arguments for that view, if it were worth the effort. For what do these idle particles—*quidem*, *quippe*, *etiam*, *-que*, *enim*, *nam*—do in Monostichs that already complete their meaning, particles which he so often repeats merely to fill out the verses? Do they not, I ask you, magnificent Volserus, mark their author as a poor and wretched poetaster?

What of the many repetitions of the same thoughts, when verses are frequently repeated twice, three times, and sometimes four times, with scarcely any change in the form of the words? Those were indeed among the things—and there were others I do not mention—that would not allow me to be diverted from the opinion I had once adopted.

For the argument of Canisius seemed far too *ἀσυλλόγιστον* (“illogical”): “There are two verses here that are read in Columbanus; therefore these are Columbanus’ verses.” I could argue in the same way: “In the *Monostichs on Morals* published by Pierre Pithou, there are three verses that are read here; therefore those Monostichs are Columbanus’.” How decisive that is, those who know anything about Zeno or Chrysippus understand.

But when I examined the parchment more carefully, its authority ought not to have been disregarded. It is so ancient and of such good character that Hartmotus and Ratpertus, writers eight centuries older than us, also praised it.

In it, although cautiously yet quite explicitly, the name of Columbanus is written before the work in these words:

> “Here begins the little book of a certain man and, as it is said, of Blessed Columbanus.”

The same title is borne by the Freising manuscript, which was copied from our parchment.

Moreover, when I compared these poems with those addressed to Hunaldus and Sethus, I scarcely found “milk like milk and egg like egg,” as the saying goes—that is, anything more alike. They, like these, borrowed from ancient poets, except that these are more inelegant because they were composed hastily and not polished with exactness.

Clearly, each man copied extracts from his *Hypomnemata* for the use of his brothers, as the material presented itself, and shaped them into Monostichs. Hence it happened that, in this heap of verses by different authors, he unwittingly repeated thoughts that often expressed the same meaning, just as he had inferred from the Gentile poets.

We see the same thing happening to Octavianus, the compiler of the distichs called Cato’s, a poet whom Columbanus studied carefully; Columbanus copied many of his verses with the same form and words.

As for the particles, we have seen poets who considered themselves fortunate in their own judgment abuse them quite often. Octavianus himself provides an example; you will not be mistaken if you call him Columbanus’ teacher. A verse in Cato, or the *Distichs*, Book I:

> And when you admonish someone …

I shall not say more; I have stated the essential point.

[Col. 0308A] ### 1. Let him read these precepts.

Octavianus, at the beginning of Book IV:

> These precepts must always be read again by you,

and at the beginning of Book III:

> You will carry these precepts, and so forth.

Do these examples not prove to you that Columbanus published his Monostichs in imitation of Octavianus’ distichs?

### 2. In the titles of virtues.

Isambardus the deacon, in the charter of a donation by which Wago transferred property to the monastery:

> “He was distinguished by the titles of the virtues of his life.”

Arnulf of Lisieux, in the epitaph of the empress Matilda:

> By the titles of her virtues this woman surpassed  
> The summit of human honor.

The following verse likewise:

> Shining with the outstanding glory of her virtues.

Papias, *Glossary*: “A title is an inscription or a sign of praise and honor, or praise itself.”

### 5. To be seen forever as Christ’s companion.

Salomo interprets the phrase in the *Lexicon*: “Without end, without limit, without interruption.” Sidonius, Book VI, Epistle 4:

> “Your apostolate is owed to you without end, even if it is paid without interruption.”

Marcellus: “Infinity, as though without end and without definition.”

An ancient poet—whether Petronius, as Binetus thinks, or another—writes in a Phalaecian verse:

> But thus, thus, let us rejoice without end.

Ovid, in the *Heroides*:

> If I do harm because I love, I confess that I shall do harm without end.

And in *Letters from Pontus*:

> … And my sorrows watch without end.

Petrus Diaconus, *On Notations*:

> “In this monument there is money without end.”

### 6. May God himself fulfill it, and so forth.

No one can explain the meaning of this verse more suitably than an old German saying:

> What we always did, what we always ought to do,  
> So also may the Lord do what we wish.

Xystus, *Sentences*: “You ought to desire what God also desires.”

*Votum* means *βούλησις*, “desire” or “will.” Isidore, *Sentences on the Highest Good* III.51:

> “Many people become evil under wicked rulers more from necessity than from choice.”

Persius, Satire V:

> Each person has his own desire; one does not live by a single wish.

The author of *On Contempt of the World*:

> Therefore, despising lowly things with all your desires …

The “desire of God” means the will, command, or ordinance of God. Human desires mean prayers.

Xystus, *Sentences*, in Rufinus’ translation:

> “The prayer or desires of the lazy are empty speech.”

Avianus, in the edition of the manuscripts of his *Fables*:

> Learn, nevertheless, that the gods are not bent by lazy prayers,  
> And, while you act, summon the gods themselves to your aid.

Ambrose, hymn for Advent at Vespers:

> Hear the prayers of those who plead.

Thus the old manuscripts read; those who wanted to assist the meter rashly altered the wording.

The hymn attributed to Hilary—not Hilary of Poitiers, in my view, but Hilary of Arles—on the Purification of the Virgin Mary:

> You who willingly receive the prayers of petitioners,  
> Mother of the eternal King, favor us.

Waldrammus to Bishop Salomo:

> If two of you, he says, with united prayers  
> Ask something, the Father himself will give it.

### 10. Wisdom of mind surpasses the strength of the body.

Salomo, Proverbs XXI.22; the author of *Wisdom* VI.50; below, verses 117 and following. Phocylides, *Nuthētika*. Titinnius of Setia:

> Wisdom turns the ship as pilot; strength does not.

### 14. Against demons.

A confused and hyperbatonical verse, whose order is: “Prayer is a great virtue against demons.” Verse 46 suffers from a similar hyperbaton.

[Col. 0309A] ### 16. Excessive and every pleasure.

The text is now corrupt in Octavianus. Columbanus followed the better manuscripts, as did Planudes, who translated it:

> For every luxury is the beginning of a dreadful disease.

### 17. Do not close your hand when giving.

Jesus Sirach IV, final verse; Pope Innocent III, *On the Misery of the Human Condition*, chapter 42. Because of their wording, this passage is corrupt.

The Liège manuscript, from which Delrio published the first edition ascribed to Bishop Aldhelm, has *in dare* (“in giving”), and I consider this preferable, in imitation of the Greeks, who lack gerund forms—if I may use the grammarians’ term. *In dare*, *ἐν τῷ δοῦναι* (“in giving”); *in prendere*, *ἐν τῷ λαβεῖν* (“in taking”).

The meaning is: “Do not keep your hands closed when giving, or carry them open when receiving.” The Greeks use words—especially infinitives—in place of nouns more readily than the Romans.

Terence, *Phormio*, Act IV, scene 4:

> The soothsayer forbade beginning a new  
> Business before winter.

Thus the variant readings have *pro inceptionem novi negotii* (“for the beginning of a new business”). Persius: “Your knowing is nothing.” The same author: “Each person has his own desire.”

The ecclesiastical writers imitated these expressions, continually adopting Greek usage. Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, in his prayer to God:

> Thus may I be able to will what is good, so that the power to do evil may withdraw.

Juvencus, Book I:

> May your willingness be sufficient.

Dracontius, *Hexaemeron*:

> To will and not to will equally, one steadfast intention.

Columbanus, Epistle 1:

> It does you no good to ascend what you have ascended.

### 18. Always in your mouth.

He says the same thing, and nothing else, in verses 124 and 125.

### 23. Every day of life is one day.

From Octavianus, Book I, Distich 33. Horace, Book I of the *Epistles*, addressed to Albius:

> Believe that every day has dawned for you as your last.

[Col. 0309C] Boethius, from Seneca:

> Let every day be judged as though it were the last.

Alcuin, Epistle 36, to Altapetra.

### 24. What you cannot give.

The Liège manuscript has *non cogites* (“do not consider”), a verse sketched from Octavianus’ Distich 25, Book I.

### 26. Strive for eight.

Today only seven principal vices are counted, but the ancients counted eight. Theodulf of Orléans, in his letter to the clergy:

> “There are eight principal vices, without which scarcely anyone can be found. The first is *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony; second, fornication; third, *acedia* or sadness; fourth, avarice; fifth, vainglory; sixth, envy; seventh, anger; eighth, pride,” and so forth.

Likewise Evagrius to Anatolius: “He wrote on the eight vicious thoughts”; Saint Nilus, *On the Eight Vicious Affections*; Abbot Serapion, *On the Eight Principal Vices*, in Cassian, *Conferences* V; John Climacus, *The Ladder of Paradise*, steps 13, 14, and following.

Finally, Nicolaus Dinkelspühl preferred to imitate the ancients rather than the moderns. For two hundred years ago he composed a book *On the Eight Capital Vices*, with a corresponding work *On the Eight Beatitudes*, concerning which a sermon of Bishop Chromatius also circulates.

We have now prevailed, Canisius, and have closed our pugilistic and athletic contest after the challenge of the great Delrio.

### 27. A chariot filled with salvation.

This is a Hellenism: *ἀναπλησθεῖσα τῆς σωτηρίας* (“filled with salvation”). Such a manner of speaking is not unknown among the Latins.

Symmachus, Book I, Epistle 13:

> “Our lord Gratian’s heavenly address filled him with good hope and cheerfulness.”

But I prefer the reading of the Le Mans manuscript, “filled with triumphs.” Christians, having conquered death and defeated the devil with his minions, are said to triumph: preceded by angels, they ascend to the heavenly Capitol, where, after their white victim has been sacrificed, they remain glorious in the palace.

Augustine, *Sermon on the Words of the Apostle* 3:

> “Let the struggle first be completed, so that victory may finally exist; for death, the last enemy, will be destroyed when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality. Consider beforehand the words of those who triumph: ‘Where, O death, is your contention?’ This is the voice of those who triumph, not of those who fight,” and so forth.

Jerome, Book IV on Matthew, chapter 27:

> “The angel came as guardian of the Lord’s tomb; and in his white clothing he signifies the glory of the one who triumphs.”

Plutarch and Pliny teach in more than one place that after sacrificing a white bull they returned home from the temple.

### 28. The tongue has its own reins.

A similar maxim occurs in verse 113. Ambrose, hymn 5, for Prime:

> Let him restrain and govern his tongue,  
> Lest the dread of strife resound.

### 29. Unless he be for everyone.

The Liège manuscript has “who is in all things.” But this archaism should not be rashly despised; sometimes the Fathers deliberately adopt an ancient form.

Marius Victorinus, *Genesis* III:

> There is nothing for you to fear: your heir, that Damascus,  
> Will be.

I shall speak elsewhere.

[Col. 0310B] ### 30. He perhaps did not deserve pardon.

The Liège manuscript has, with an interrogative, *ne forte meretur?* (“perhaps does he deserve it?”), with *ne* meaning “whether.” Mamertinus, *Panegyric for Julian*:

> “Can it be that one God gave many harvests in one year to a single field?”

I have corrected it thus; the common reading is *nec quis* (“nor anyone”). Columbanus denies while asking the question. Thus below:

> Of what use is the associate who is proved not to be useful?  
> That is, of no one.

And later:

> What is worse than for a solitary inhabitant to join himself to another?  
> That is, nothing.

Machales, in his *Interpretations*: “A question occurs when nothing is answered or understood as the answer, as in the Apostle’s Epistle: ‘Who will accuse God’s elect?’ The implied answer is: heretics or Jews.”

The Hebrews also commonly ask questions in affirmations. Following them, both the ancient Romans and the writers of the New Testament did likewise. John IV.70:

> “Did I not choose you twelve? And one of you is a devil?”

The commentators should be consulted.

### 31. Whoever abandons good habits—

“He who abandons good things”—*ὃς ἀγαθὰ ἀπεθίζει*—“accustoms himself actively to evil,” just as the Hebrews form such expressions in the Hiphil.

Isidore, *Differences* II:

> “We become accustomed to good things, become unaccustomed to evil things, and become accustomed to both.”

The same is found in Uguition’s *Glossary* and in the author of *On Ancient Differences of Expression*. Cicero, in a letter to Metellus:

> “I ask from you what you have been accustomed to do.”

Basil, bishop, in his *Admonition*:

> “Do not grow accustomed to the worst habits.”

As for the paronomasia, Maximus, in his sermon on John the Baptist, writes:

> “One of the wise men said: Those who have become well accustomed will be ashamed to abandon their habits.”

Bernard of Clairvaux:

> “When he begins to become unaccustomed to these things and little by little accustomed to those.”

The barbarous form *dissuescere* (“to become unaccustomed”) is no more correct, and *diffinire* should be *definire*.

### 32. Do not, I beg you, do so in jest.

Jests, derisive remarks, and taunts—Sirach calls them “words of reproach” in the final verse of chapter 31. A “jocular evil.” For Terence, the word is *scommaticus* and *sycophanticus*.

Ambrose, *On Duties* I.23:

> “Jokes seem sweet and pleasant, although they are foreign to Christian discipline.”

Publius, *Mimes*:

> One may not injure a friend even in jest.

Macrobius lists several examples of this kind in *Saturnalia* VII.3, as does Aristophanes in his play against Euripides. Pliny, *Natural History* XXII.22.

A poem is also called a psalter or song. Paulus, *Sentences* V, title 4:

> “A psalter, commonly called a song, composed to disgrace another,” and so forth.

And in the preceding section:

> “He composes a poem not only who writes satires and epigrams, but also one who composes an illegitimate cause for attacking someone, or anything else in another genre.”

Arianus comments on these words:

> “He who composes or sings a song for another’s blasphemy is punished extraordinarily.”

These remarks accord with Columbanus’ meaning.

### 33. You will be instructed more often by hearing.

The Liège manuscript reads: “You will enjoy hearing rather than the voice of salvation,” which has no meaning. He wishes us to be fully informed and instructed in the truth of the matter before we report it to others. For things that are easily said and believed are full of emptiness and extreme frivolity.

Therefore Nigidius, quoted by Aulus Gellius, says:

> “A good man ought to ensure that he does not lie; a prudent man, that he does not tell a falsehood.”

Accordingly, I would contend on any wager that, instead of *instrueris* (“you will be instructed”), Columbanus wrote *instruere* (“to instruct”), in the imperative mood. The *e* is long.

Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II:

> It is useless to criticize; we are now accustomed to the Taurian rites.

The same author, *Psychomachia*:

> To imbue men, fragile …

Again, *Apotheosis*:

> Whenever it pleases him to blow upon the cold wind …

Hubert Giphanius, the foremost jurist of our age, restored the text from a variant reading, and two of the oldest manuscripts of St. Gall support him.

Juvencus, Book IV:

> Look upon the scribes, proud in their lofty seat.

Octavianus, Book I, Distich 21:

> It is not foolish to ask for what may rightly be denied.

Again, Distich 26:

> You also do something similar; thus craft is deceived by craft.

Terence, *The Self-Tormentor*:

> It is a wise practice to learn from others a danger  
> That may stand you in good stead.

Pope Damasus, on the Apostle Paul:

> To deny that the holy prophets praised Christ.

Thus among the Greeks, Orpheus, *Argonautica*:

> And concealing the wedding garments, the work deserving of reverence.

### 35. Whatever he seems to give—that is, he gives.

Canisius ought not to have changed the text. It is expressed according to Hebrew usage, for among the Hebrews such words refer not only to thought but also to action.

Genesis XXXI: “He considered us as strangers,” that is, “he treated us as foreigners.” Fourth Ezra VII: “Do not be angry with those who have been judged worse than beasts.” Paul, Hebrews IV, at the beginning: *δοκῇ τις ἐξ ὑμῶν ὑστερηκέναι*—that is, “should seem to be lacking and to have come late.”

The verb *largior* belongs to those verbs which, in both active and passive voice, signify the same thing, as Priscian says in Book VII. He and Caper supply examples.

The same form occurs in *populavit* (“he ravaged”) in the *Causes* addressed to Fedolius, verse 104, and in *ulciscere* (“avenge”) in verse 129:

> Do not avenge your injuries upon your brother.

Lucilius, Book XIV, used *largi* for *largire* (“give”). Accius, according to Diomedes, has *largito*. Cato, in the Baebian law, has *inlargibo*. Not Marcellus, chapter 7.

### 36. Not by riches.

The great Scaliger restored this verse to Octavianus; see him in Book II. He published *pro almis* (“for nourishing things”) instead of *ipsis*. But the correct reading is *aptis* (“suitable”), that is, “freely.”

[Col. 0311D] ### 37. Let another mock him.

The Liège manuscript has *derideat* (“let him deride”), taken from Distich 7, Book III:

> By a similar example, let another not deride you.

### 40. Gentle pity, indulgence.

Quintilian, Book II, chapter 3:

> “That soft upbringing which we call indulgence weakens every sinew both of mind and body.”

### 41. You will never put anyone before a friend.

I have restored *praepones* (“you will put before”) from Distich 32, Book I, and verse 59. Likewise verse 154: “You will never abandon a friend,” where there was a similar corruption. See verse 95.

### 42. Everything they say.

Phaedrus, Book III, Fable 49:

> Let him despise nothing, yet let him not immediately believe everything.

Seneca:

> It is a vice to believe everything; it is a vice to believe nothing.

Romulus, Book II of the *Fables*:

> Do not trust everything to everyone at every time.

And what follows.

### 43. No one should live for himself alone.

*Non quis* means “no one,” just as *nequis* means “no one” in Plautus. Salomo, in the *Lexicon*: “*Non quis*: not anyone, no one, nobody.”

### 44. Not for yourself, but for Christ.

Paul, Epistle to the Philippians, chapter 2, verse 21.

### 45. Not yourself, not the world.

Matthew X and XVI; Mark VIII; Luke IX and XVII; John XII and XVII.

### 48. The rich man’s reproach.

The amphiboly of the syntax makes the meaning obscure. Construe it thus: “The poor man’s groaning is the rich man’s great reproach.” See verse 14.

### 52. Patience is preferable to life and martyrdom.

Second Maccabees VII.36. Perseverance amid adversity, Sirach II.1 and following. Steadfastness through to the final end of all things, Matthew X.22; Mark XIII.13; Luke XXI.9.

### 53. Make yourself gentler rather than fierce.

I cite the commentator at verse 8:

> Let your ways be peaceful, with great sweetness.

Moderation is humanity joined with gravity. Salomo: “Moderation, restraint, fellowship.” Old glosses: “Gravity, modesty.”

Its opposite is fierceness, which is the proud and barbarous savagery of a contemptuous person. Augustine the Englishman—or Peter Damian—*Meditations*, chapter 8:

> “To his piety, my impiety; to his modesty, my perversity; and to his gentleness, let fierceness be attributed.”

“Rather by fierceness” means that it will make you more distinguished or more commendable than austerity and inhumanity.

Basil, bishop, *Admonition*:

> “Therefore let us love God more than all things.”

*Μᾶλλον πάντων* (“more than all”) occurs in Demosthenes.

Walafrid, *On Wettin’s Vision*, chapter 30:

> … He benefited that place more than all the others.

### 55. Act with counsel.

Jesus Sirach XXXII.23. Below, verse 140, which Antoninus of Florence cites almost as from an ancient poet, Book II, title 5, verse 110.

This is a common and widely disseminated maxim, taught by the earliest teachers of wisdom: Pythagoras in the *Golden Verses*; Theognis in the *Sentences*; Bias in Stobaeus, *Sermon* 3, and Demetrius in the *Apophthegms*; Isocrates, *To Demonicus*, and Agapetus, in his *Exhortation to the Emperor Justinian*, following him; Thucydides, Book I; Demosthenes, *First Philippic*; and Sallust, the preface to the *Catiline*.

From Sallust it was taken by Jerome, Lupus of Ferrières, Epistles 33 and 93, and Fulbert, in the preface to the *Life of Autbert* in Surius, December 13.

### 57. Young man, consider the examples.

A corresponding verse occurs in the poem to Sethus:

> And the chaste disciplines of the life of the holy Fathers.

He warns us not to disregard the examples of the holy Fathers, who made a path for us toward piety both by teaching and by doing.

*Παράδειγμα* means “example.” Thucydides:

> “To be regarded by the majority of the Greeks as an example of manly virtue.”

The word *μέσον* (“neutral”) is also applied to reproach and crime. Alcimus Avitus, to his sister:

> A paradigm of old-age luxury.

Isocrates, *To Demonicus*:

> “What example of injustice, false accusation, and wickedness could one find greater than this?”

Are *paradigms* parables? For these figures are related among rhetoricians and are even confused by Quintilian and Cicero. Indeed, the Hebrew word *mischlii* (*mishlê*), by which Salomo titled his maxims, signifies both, so that Columbanus may mean what Basil advises in a more serious matter in his *Admonition*:

> “Do not regard the commandments of God as fables, but let your heart always be attentive to them.”

### 59. Words have great force

Celsus expresses this elegantly, and thus also in *Digest* 7, § final, *On legacies of household goods*: “The thought of the speaker is prior and more powerful than his voice.” Hilary of Poitiers: “The meaning of what is said must be derived from the speaker’s reason for saying it”—that is, from his purpose and intention. Nicholas of Lyra cites this exceptionally elegant passage in his commentary on Deuteronomy, chapter XVIII. The Scholastics say: “Words must be understood not in the sense they produce, but in the sense in which they are produced.” Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “The meaning must be directed by the subject matter of the words.” Thomas Aquinas: “In words one must consider not so much from what they are taken as toward what they are directed.” Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book III: “When, with Plato affirming it, you have learned that the words spoken ought to be kindred to the things of which they speak.” More simply from Plato: “Things must be understood according to the understanding that follows the things” (*κατὰ τὴν ἀκολουθοῦσαν τοῖς πράγμασι νόησιν*).

### 62. You will find it difficult

Alcuin, letter 11 to Charlemagne: “The proverbial saying of the ancients shines forth: a friend is sought for a long time, found with difficulty, and preserved with difficulty.” He repeats the same in letter 2 to King Æthelred, in letter 35, and in his letter to Cangyth addressed to the martyr Boniface.

### 64. How he loses friends

The manuscript of St Gall has *pendit*; the Liège manuscript, *expedit*. Most truly, no one has ever had too many friends, just as the name itself declares. *Expedit* means “it is advantageous” (*συμφέρει*). Petronius, *Satyricon*:

> If the name of friendship clings only so far as it is advantageous, etc.

Thus the verse is metrically defective. Yet I see that Columbanus and the versifiers of his age either knew the laws of meter imperfectly or certainly neglected them. Thus Romulus lengthened the middle syllable of *vindicat* in book I of the *Fables*:

> Often sluggishness vindicates faith with a false witness.

Gunther in *The Exile*, book III:

> Behold, a pitiful crowd driven from the citadel.

Alanus thought that he had lengthened the first syllable of *trahere* in the following verse of the *Parables*:

> The dog’s hide will not easily be pulled off when smeared with oil.

But he understood that the verse was corrupted through error. It should be restored as follows: “it will be driven away from the oiled hide.” Horace, *Satires* II.5:

> As a dog will never be driven away from an oiled hide.

Others have sinned in the opposite direction. For Damasus shortened the middle syllable of *beatus* in his poem on Paul the Apostle:
