> In these verses, most blessed teacher, I briefly confess.

In Gunther’s *Theatre*, book VIII:

> Caesar looks from afar upon the citadel of the ancient theater.

Likewise in *Infidelity*, book VI:

> Because of whose treachery his brothers, with rebellious necks,  
> Cast off the yoke.

Pain rages in my heart whenever I take this poet into my hands; he is so badly treated and badly composed. From the examples already given, perhaps one may defend the common reading of verse 31: “You will be instructed more often by what you hear,” *ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι*—a phrase which among the Hebrews has the force of an imperative.

### 66. Faith will be enriched with a gracious gift

The glossary in the *Ecclesiastical History* has “affected, enriched.” The Liège manuscript has “will be approved,” [or] “disapproved.” For faith alone will receive the reward of faith, not the work performed. Saint Cyriacus to Theophanes: “I tell you that if a man performs all the virtues but does not believe rightly, he will be tormented in this place,” in Sophronius or John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 27.

### 67. Light, not tormenting the soul

The verse is corrupt. Liège has: “Light things, not tormenting the mind.” That reading is no easier. I suspect it was: *Torquendo cura fat.* [reading materially uncertain], in the manner of verse 124:

> May the words of justice and peace please you as you speak.

Thus the sense will be perfectly clear. *Levis* makes a spondee. Octavian, book I, distinction 7:

> Be steadfast and light, as circumstances require.

They do not distinguish between *levis*, “light” (*ἐλαφρός*), and *levis*, “smooth” (*λεῖος*). See above, *expedit*, verse 62, and below, *conditus*, verse 112. Gunther lengthened the first syllable of *Ligur* in *The Theatre*, book IX:

> Ligur and immense …

In *well*, Wipo, *Panegyric to Emperor Henry III*:

> May you come here prosperously; here may you see all things favorable.

Unless the particle *si* was omitted by the scribe and must be restored, the reading should be: “May you prosperously arrive here.”

### 68. A serious matter indeed

In the same place: “A truly serious matter.” The meaning is: “Conduct yourself modestly with people, and do not rashly display your birth or wealth; the matter itself will always reveal who you are. That will be much more honorable for you than feeding harsh spirits with your tongue”—something boastful.

### 68. Do not accustom yourself

I write *nolito* (“do not accustom yourself”), rather than *noli tu*. It imitates Octavian, verse 110 of book IV:

> Do not often remain with an unjust man.

This is a common manner of expression among biblical interpreters.

### 71. It is better not to be

It is better to be dead than to lead a bad life. “To be” signifies living; “not to be” signifies having lived. Thus *εἶναι ἀντὶ τοῦ ζῆν*—“to be” in place of “to live.” Hence the frequent Latin formula *pro mortuus est* (“he is dead”).

### 72. A good mind is a treasure

That is, wisdom. Above, verse 11:

> Wisdom is better for everyone than all the treasures of the world.

See the temple of Good Sense at Rome.

### 73. Protect with all your strength

Both this verse from the following one and the following verse from this one must be explained. Florentinus, *Digest* on Justice and Law: “It rightly follows that whatever a person has done for the protection of his body is considered rightly done.” Brasidas’ celebrated saying in Plutarch: “How could anyone perceive, etc., that nothing is small or weak, who will not live by daring to defend himself?”

Therefore there is no such endurance; rather, it is self-murder not to repel force and injury inflicted upon one’s life. Whoever unjustly lays an ambush may be killed with impunity. This is Draco’s law, cited by Demosthenes, by Cicero in the speech *For Milo*, and by Paulus, *Opinions* V.23.

From these statements it is clear that *tota virtute* means “with all one’s strength” (*πάσῃ ἀρετῇ*), for among the Greeks *ἀρετή* also means the same as *δύναμις*, “power,” and *ἰσχύς*, “strength.” Philoxenus’ glossary: “Virtue: *ἀρετή*, courage, power, strength.” It is also properly related to the original force derived *ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἄρεος*, that is, from Mars. Salomo, *Lexicon*: “Virtue, steadfastness, firmness, vigor of the sinews, strength, strength of mind.” Below, verse 134:

> Let the care of your salvation be yours with all your strength.

Gunther, book VII:

> Resist with all your strength, even unto death.

Columbanus, letter 2:

> When the sun rises, the hay dries up, and the flower perishes. So it is with every discovery: its virtue fails.

Cyprian, letter V, joins “strength” and “virtue” as though they signified the same thing. Augustine, *Soliloquies*, chapter 18: “In your will lies the virtue of our salvation.” What Columbanus said in the *Rule*, chapter 1, “with all your strength,” the old translator rendered “with all your virtue,” in Greek *ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος σου*, Mark XII.30.

Isidore, *Etymologies* XVIII.22 and VII.2, on the synonyms of the Savior, should be consulted. He seems to have copied these from the *Confession of the Catholic Faith* which Blessed Armenius and Honorius addressed to the illustrious Theophilus.

### 73. They will be able to be endured

That is, “They will be able to be endured.” The following verse is set in opposition: “which suddenly arrive.” It was extremely common among Christian writers, especially those of this period, to use active forms in place of passive ones. In this they seem to have imitated the Hebrews, among whom verbs in the *niphal* and *hithpael*, though passive in form, are gladly used reciprocally. Synesius, hymn III:

> Around whom a chorus will dance about the glorious body.

That is: “around whom the minds will be made to dance about the glorious body.”

In a church hymn:

> Who, lest the mingled streams of water should be confused,  
> Dividing them,  
> Gave a boundary to heaven.

Lucretius, an ancient poet and therefore closer to the mother of languages, Hebrew, book IV:

> Thin, which cannot fasten itself to places where it has adhered.

This is found in all old and printed books. The conjecture by which Giphanius was guided seems to me no conjecture at all, since the figure occurs elsewhere, and I know that a considerable number of corruptions have arisen from conjecture. It is worth seeing what the most learned interpreter noted on Matthew II.13 and XXI; Mark IV.6 and XXXVII; and 1 Peter II; as well as Casaubon on Matthew II and Acts VII.

### 79. Whose lessons are scourges

The manuscript of St Gall has: “Whose lessons are.” I read, with the Liège manuscript, “to whom they are,” following the familiar and celebrated verse:

> Happy is the man whom the dangers of others make cautious.

And Tibullus:

> … Happy is whoever, through another’s grief,  
> Has learned that his own danger can be avoided.

“Scourges” means dangers and afflictions. Augustine, *Sentences*, when he counsels a person both by indulgence and by the scourge. Prosper of Aquitaine, book I, epigram 4:

> Sometimes chastising with a father’s heart by blows,  
> Lest cruel scourges quickly consume the guilty.

To scourge means to chastise and afflict. Waldrammus to Dado:

> They fight for the Lord, who scourges us in this manner.

This Waldrammus was a monk and dean of St Gall, who wrote this poem to Dado in the name of Salomo, bishop and abbot alike. The epigrams absent from the Freising manuscript bear witness to this. Therefore the work should be restored to its rightful possession, from which Canisius expelled it after erasing its title, according to the judgment of the abbot of St Gall.

### 80. Everything gradually moves toward death

From that verse of Horace, *Epistles* II, to Florus:

> Each year as it passes plunders something from us, etc.

### 81. Before the day of death

This is taken from Ovid:

> … The final day must always  
> Be awaited by a human being; no one should be called blessed  
> Before death and the final funeral rites.

Perhaps Eusebius had this in mind in *Life of Constantine the Great* I.7: “We are forbidden by the commandment of the ancients to consider anyone completely blessed before death, because of the various and uncertain changes of life.”

### 84. Every tree is known by its fruit

Luke VI:

> For every tree is known by its own fruit (*Ἕκαστον γὰρ δένδρον ἐκ τοῦ ἰδίου καρποῦ γινώσκεται*).

Therefore nothing should be changed.

### 86. What you wish to happen to you

Matthew VII; Luke VI; Tobit IV; Obadiah XV. This saying was thoroughly familiar among the Hebrews, and the rabbis incorporated it into their Talmud. Alexander the Emperor loved it so much that he ordered it to be inscribed both in the palace and on public buildings, as Lampridius reports. Lactantius VI.23 and the *Epitome* III should be consulted.

The author of *On the Lives of the Philosophers* ascribes it to Socrates; Demetrius ascribes it to Cleobulus of Lindus. It was the foundation from which the title of the *Digest* was constructed: “Whatever right one establishes for another, let him himself use the same right.”

Moreover, a certain monk of St Gall attempted to parody Columbanus’ verses in an old parchment manuscript:

> What you yourself do not wish to happen to you, do not do to anyone.  
> What you wish to happen to you, do this also for others.

Another manuscript reads *alio praestare* (“to do good to another”) in place of *facere*. Thus it stands in the St Gall manuscript, from which the Freising copy was taken; it is autograph. The reading is correct, and so also in the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 4: “Do not do to another,” and chapter 70: “Do not do to another.” In two copies of Schobinger, than which I dare deny that any older survive, this is supported by the accompanying German translation and by the translations of Otfrid of Weissenburg and Saint Notker—translations the more remote from us because their language is more difficult.

Octavian, book I, distinction 14:

> Do not trust another more about you than you trust yourself.

Thus it appears in four old manuscripts and in Schobinger’s excerpts.

### 89. Keep a just balance

*Στατήρα.* For Columbanus, *stater* is a weight; *statera* is a measure. The distinction is remarkable and unwelcome.

Salomo, *Lexicon*: “The balance, called in Hebrew *mozene* (*moznaiim*), is understood of things that are weighed. It consists of two pans of the balance, weighing with equal equilibrium, and derives its name from the number [perhaps ‘function’] by which it hangs balanced from two pans and one central rod.”

The same is *trutina* in the Greek-Latin lexicon: “A yoke, *stater*, pound, examination, balance.” Thus *stater* is *statera*, just as *αἰθήρ* gives *aethera*, and by syncope *aethra*; *κρατήρ*, *cratera*; *κλιμακτήρ*, *climactera*.

Old glosses on Ezra: “A *cratera*: a dish or cup.” On Clement: “*Climacteres*: parts of the sky.” Virgil, *Aeneid* XI:

> … And a golden  
> Helmet for the prophet …

On these words Servius says: “The accusative is used by the Greeks in place of the Latin nominative *cassis*.”

Moreover, Columbanus reverses the accentuation (*προσῳδία*), since *statera* shortens the first syllable and lengthens the second. Examples occur in Statius and Martial.

### 90. Let there not be one measure for you

From Solomon, Proverbs XX.10.

### 92. If you do what is right, do not worry

Octavian, book III, distinction 2: “When you live rightly, do not worry.” Hence it is clear that *recte facis* (“you do rightly”) should be read, following the model of *bene facere*, *male facere*, and so forth.

People commonly think that the ancients always lengthened the *e* in such adverbs. Hence many passages have been corrupted, in restoring which our learned teacher Giphanius performed excellent work. Ennius, *Annals* IX:

> … And that they might perpetuate freedom  
> Most greatly …

Walafrid to King Lothar:

> May you rightly and powerfully govern noble peoples.

Columbanus, verse 48:

> Judgment most certainly remains for all deeds.

And verse 167:

> Carefully discern to whom you entrust your secrets.

Metellus of Tegernsee, *Quirinalia*:

> How badly he had acted, impiously denying it.

Terence, *Hecyra*, act III, scene 5:

> Here he ordered Philumena to be summoned to him; say that he ordered you to do so.

*Here* is used for *yesterday*, and the verse is metrically sound if the final syllable is shortened; thus no emendation is needed.

### 97. The Lord’s riches will make him

Verse 179:

> The father’s blessing will make his children happy.

And verse 184, nearly identical:

> The Lord’s blessing will add greater riches.

Yet in all the books *addit* (“adds”) is read, which is more emphatic.

### 98. Happy is mercy

Verse 196: “Gentle mercy.” Verse 147: “Pious and merciful.” See Solomon, Proverbs VI.6 ff. and XXI.21.

### 103. Let them not exalt what is broad

In the *Proverbs of the Ancient Poets* this is attributed to Ovid; it occurs in the old epigram *On Morals*, book I.

### 104. Be nearest to the good

In old manuscripts it is included among Octavian’s verses, although he found it in no copy. Nevertheless, Jacobus Magnus quotes it from the same source in *Sophologium* III.6 and in Schobinger’s very ancient excerpts. That writer of the *Monostichs* claimed it for himself.

### 105. The greater you are

You will also read this verse in the *Monostichs* just mentioned.

### 106. And when you accuse another

Add verse 83 and Octavian, book I, distinction 30. The word *causari* properly belongs to the forum and the courtroom. Papias: “To accuse, to plead a case, or to rebuke, slander, or blame.” Pacuvius, *The Judgment of Aemilius*:

> I give all those who wish to bring a charge concerning virtue the opportunity to examine the matter.

The passage in Nonius is extremely corrupt; through my efforts it has been restored as I have cited it.

Jerome, preface to Habakkuk: “The prophet brings a charge against God,” that is, he argues and in a certain way litigates with God.

For Columbanus it means “to blame” or “to rebuke.” For Seneca it means “to accuse,” as in the saying: “You should praise no one and accuse no one too quickly.”

Salomo, *Lexicon*: “To bring a charge, to terrify; to accuse, to consume, hinder, exact, detain, frustrate, deceive, evade.”

### 108. Be good, and good to the good

Octavian: “Be good in this way to the good.” *Atque* is a particle of comparison. “Be good to the good in the same way,” that is, equally or similarly. See verse 153.

### 110. When you have been happy

Octavian, book I, distich 18. It is a half-line from Ovid’s *Tristia*.

### 112. Life is the guide

*Cathegita* means “female teacher”; in Octavian, *magistra*, “teacher,” book III, distinction 13. “Life is our teacher from without.”

*Καθηγητής*: teacher, adviser. Gregory Nazianzen on Basil:

> A good counselor, an able attendant, interpreter of divine things, and guide in things that must be done.

Cyril, *Lexicon of Scripture*:

> *Καθηγητής*: teacher, instructor, leader.

Pollux should be consulted. Thus *mathita* (*μαθητής*)—“disciple.” Waldrammus to Dado:

> Be present as a faithful teacher to the disciple;

> Let him be present as a teacher to a faithful disciple (*Μαθητῇ πιστῷ παρὼν διδάσκαλος ἔστω*).

That is: “Life, the guide,” by apposition. Ennodius uses the same manner of expression in a letter: “Application is the teacher of the arts.” Valerian, *On Good Discipline*: “Discipline is the teacher of religion, the teacher of true piety.”

Thus in an old manuscript of Schobinger, Gregory Nazianzen, *On Virtue*:

> Of whom some use sight as their teacher.

The same work:

> Well, O Fortune, teacher of good things for me.

### 114. Let it now be seasoned with the salt of wisdom

Eucherius, *Formulae of Spiritual Understanding*: salt, the seasoning of wisdom. Verianus:

> If you call this salt what wisdom signifies.

Old glosses on Ezra: “Rememberful of salt”: *salt* is put for food or instruction. Salomo, *Lexicon*: “Seasoned with salt: wise, or ordered, or tempered.” In the Apostle: “Let your speech always be seasoned with grace.” Coelestinus, in Salomo: “Seasoned with salt, or moderated.”

Augustine on Psalm LIX: “In the valley of salt”: the valley signifies humility; the saltworks signify taste. For many humble themselves, but vainly and foolishly they are humbled in empty antiquity, etc. It is therefore good to humble oneself wisely, etc.

Matthew V: “You are the salt of the earth,” etc. Jerome, book IV on Ezekiel, chapter XVI, on the words “not salted with salt,” after reciting the words of Matthew and Paul adds: “Hence in common speech wise people are called ‘salty,’ and fools ‘unsalted.’”

In the same place: “I know that I have read in a certain volume concerning the Lord Savior that he himself is heavenly salt,” that is, the wisdom of the heavenly Father.

“Everything seasoned.” Do you really make no distinction between *condere* (“to compose, store”) and *condire* (“to season”)? *Condita oratio*, “composed speech,” shortens the penultimate syllable. Above, addressed to Fedol: *condita versu*. In the same place: *condere versu*. *Condita*, metaphorically, “sprinkled as though with certain seasonings,” lengthens it.

Cicero, *On the Orator* II:

> Neither weighty speech nor speech more seasoned with wit and charm.

Augustine, *Confessions* I.11: “I was marked with the sign of his cross and seasoned with his salt,” namely, the Lord’s.

An old verse, not inelegant, in the otherwise inept author of the *Mamotrectus*, on Luke XIV:

> Salt makes learned, salt seasons, salt reproves.

Brito, who lived under Charlemagne, in his *Synonyms*:

> A city is founded, a vegetable is seasoned, but gold is buried.

Verse 116: “Believe in God, and then direct your own steps.” Solomon, Proverbs III.6. Menander:

> Whenever you do something holy, place before yourself  
> Good hope, knowing this:  
> With righteous courage even God lends his aid.

The manuscript of St Gall:

> Believe in the true God, and direct your own steps;

this wording appears to be written by a reader’s hand.

### 117. Light is the fear of the Lord

David, Psalm CXI.10; Solomon, Proverbs I.7; Sirach I.13. Below, verse 175:

> The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord in one’s mind.

### 118. Hoping in the Lord

David, Psalm XXXI.1.

### 122. A sweet word indeed

Below, verse 201:

> A gentle tongue acquires many friends for itself.

Rabbi Joseph of Hysopolis, *Silver Dish*:

> Acquire friends through kind words.  
> You will purchase their souls without bronze or gold.

### 131. Wisdom rightly belongs to a king

Tutilo, monk of St Gall, under the image of Wisdom:

> O glory of empire, most worthy ruler of the world.

Wipo, *Panegyric to Emperor Henry III*:

> It is sufficiently well known how much wisdom can accomplish,  
> Which by the power of speech bends the reins of government.

Martinus of Braga, book addressed to King Miro, should be consulted.

### 135. What is an earthly human being? Dust

From Ovid:

> We are dust and shadow.

Hence Primas constructed his own little verses:

> Since we are filth, clay, and the vilest substance,  
> Why are we proud? As earth, we return to earth.

Hence “earth” is used for the human being himself. Eucherius, *Formulae of Spiritual Understanding*, chapter 3:

> “Earth: the human being himself. Dry land: unfruitful people. Dust: sinners.”

Hilary of Poitiers on Psalm LX, knowing that he dwells in the flesh, which is earth.

Junilius Africanus, *On the Parts of Divine Law*, chapter 4: “And in Jeremiah, when he says, ‘Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord,’ he calls those who inhabit the earth ‘earth’ proverbially, using the earth for the people dwelling upon it.”

Augustine, book II, *Expressions in Genesis*: “And the land of Egypt failed”: “land” is put for the people who were in the land. In the same work: “Let all the earth worship you”: “all the earth” is said for the people who are on the earth.

The same on Psalm XLVI: “Those who were mighty gods of the earth, presuming upon earth—which earth? Upon themselves, because every human being is earth. For it was said to the human being: ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go.’”

Jerome, book I on Isaiah, chapter I: “By heaven he signifies the higher and angelic powers; by earth, the race of mortals,” by metonymy, using the container for what it contains. The same, book II on Habakkuk, chapter 3: “In this way we also understand ‘earth’: those who were first called earth because of the image of the earthly one, and to whom it was said, ‘You are earth,’ etc.”

Walafrid Strabo, *On the Lust of the Flesh*:

> O you who by your gift have healed  
> The earths lost through vices,  
> Through your begotten Son.

Thus Christ’s words to the disciples in Matthew V must be understood: “You are the salt of the earth,” etc. And in John’s *Apocalypse* VI.11:

> You avenge our blood upon the earth (*Ἐκδικεῖς τὸ αἷμα ἡμῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς*),

where the correct interpretation is: “upon those who dwell on the earth.”

### 136. Pride is the dire beginning of every sin

Sirach X.15. Grimoaldus, *On the Condemnation of Pride*:

> From which every head of sin sprang and increased,  
> And is believed to have led Lucifer, the first prince,  
> The criminal who acquired his name from the nature of evil,  
> Into destruction and to have disturbed heaven.

Even today every evil of the human race flows, in a certain sense, from him as from a fountain.

Primas in the *Great Sophologium*:

> If you are given wealth, wisdom, and beauty,  
> Pride alone destroys everything if it accompanies them.

Raymundus Astucius, *On the Battle of Man*:

> Blind pride destroys every height of moral character.

Partly from Primas, partly from Claudian, *On the Fourth Consulship of Honorius*:

> When added, pride stains excellent morals.

### 144. Whoever believes in the Lord preserves

The manuscript of St Gall has *credat, servet* (“let him believe, let him preserve”), in the manner of the verse following this one:

> … The lot that will assign you what must be done.

See, nevertheless, John XIV.15 and XXI.23.

### 116. Do it diligently

Modianus, in his *Synonyms*: attentively, accurately, carefully, intently, diligently. Theodore, *Life of Saint Magnus*: “He performed his work diligently.” Ennodius in a letter: “Application is the teacher of the arts; negligence is the stepmother of learning.”

### 145. The flowing wave does not return

Ovid, *The Art of Love*:

> … The years go on like flowing water;  
> Nor can the wave that has passed be called back again;  
> Nor can the hour that has passed return.

### 149. Death devours everything

Death, which for Horace is “the final line of things,” book I, letter 16. Cicero, *Letters to Friends* VI.21: “Especially since death is the end of all things.” Octavian paraphrases it thus: “That which is the final end of life.”

### 150. The Lord will have mercy on him

This is barbarous, and unknown among ecclesiastical writers. The old translation of Proverbs XIV has: “He who will have mercy on the poor.” Jeremiah XXX: “I will have mercy on his dwellings.” Psalm CIII: “The Lord has had mercy on those who fear him.” In the old liturgy: “Have mercy on us.”

From this Alcuin: “You are my mercy; have mercy on me.” Old glosses: *Kyrie eleison*, “Lord, have mercy on us.”

The author of *On Contempt of the World*: “He has mercy on no one”; and “over someone,” though this is excessively barbarous, in Augustine or Damian, *Meditations*, chapter 6: “And have mercy upon the weakness of the frail creature.”

Gregory the Great sinned in the contrary direction by using *miserari*, in the hymn at dawn:

> So that God, having had mercy on us,  
> May drive away every sickness.

### 151. Do not complain about benefits

You must not complain in any way about benefits, however small, or inwardly grumble about them. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*:

> For it is not my nature maliciously  
> To disparage good deeds.

### 156. Thus a new friend and new wine

Cicero, *Laelius on Friendship*: “The oldest things, like wines that have endured age, ought to be the sweetest.” A certain wise man in the *Great Sophologium*: “New wine, a new friend.”

*Atque* is a particle of comparison. Ulpian, *Digest*, title “On the Sullan Decree of the Senate”: “Thus it should be avenged, and so the Senate decreed concerning their own slaves.” Paulus, *Digest* XXXVI.3, *On Claims to an Inheritance*: “Thus he is condemned, and as though he possessed it.”

It is sometimes used absolutely, verse 106: “Be good, and good to the good.” Unless *atque* has been established in place of another connective to mean “also.”

### 158. A friend is always a friend

Nothing should be changed. It is a saying formed by repetition (*καθ’ ἐπανάληψιν*), like Juvenal:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.

And that verse of some unknown poet:

> Let the poor man love cautiously; let the poor man fear to curse.

The figure is not unknown to Virgil. Sulpicius Victor, *On Figures*; Rutilius Lupus; Rufinianus; and especially Bede, *On Tropes*, should be consulted.

### 161. And whatever lies ahead

A half-line from Octavian, book II, distich 28. *Quodque* means “whatever.” Alcinous on Virgil:

> Whoever is second will be far from the first.

Ausonius, *Sentences of Pittacus*:

> Obey the law; whoever you are, establish the law.

### 168. He who rejoices in wicked crime

The verse will scan if we read *scelere* (“in crime”). The *e* in ablatives of this kind was customarily lengthened. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 19:

> O new miracle of a wound through a wondrous slaughter.

Lucretius, book III:

> So that he knows each of the other senses in its own part.

Thus the superior manuscripts. Book V:

> To press the air upon us from both sides of the pole.

Thus all manuscripts, both old and recent. Book VI:

> Moreover, the sea from the great mountain presses upon it on one side.

Thus also here, in all manuscripts written by hand and in print. In all similar places Hubert Giphanius thought *parti* should be restored.

I do not agree with him, since his reading rests on no authority, and the authority of Priscian which he cited actually disagrees with his opinion.

Gregory the Great, hymn for Ascension Day:

> The lot of mortals being changed.

Grimoaldus, *On the Condemnation of Pride*:

> And, with his loose knee, he leaped after shaking off his foot.

### 170. Correct the sinner

He teaches that a friend should indeed be corrected if he sins; but immediately, if he refuses to obey, one should neither abandon nor cease to help him. Solomon, Proverbs XXVII.10; Octavian, book I, distinction 9. Above, verse 14; below, verse 139.

### 172. Whoever forgives his brother

Matthew IV.14; Mark XI.25.

### 173. The wise person observes the time in speaking

The reading is good and should not be disturbed. Above, verse 150:

> Let every mind first consider the words of speech.

There it would be more suitable and convenient to read *omnia* (“all things”) for *omnis* (“every”), which does not fit very well.

### 174. A word despised without regard to time

The fool pays no attention to what, when, or how he speaks.

> If the fool reports anything, I think he reports nothing true.  
> His words themselves are worthy of no weight.

Seneca: “Speech is the image of the mind; as the man is, so is his speech.”

Hence Socrates, when he saw an attractive young man remaining silent for a long time, said: “Speak, so that I may see you.” Socrates plainly did not see the silent man, for he believed that human beings should be considered not by the sharpness of the eyes but by the acuity of the mind and the gaze of the spirit. Apuleius, at the beginning of the *Florida*.

### 178. Gold is tested by fire

David, Psalm XII.7; Solomon, Proverbs XVII.3; Sirach II.5; Ovid, *Tristia*:

> Just as bright gold is inspected in the fires,  
> So faith must be examined in difficult times.

Seneca, *On Divine Providence*, near the end: “Fire itself tests gold; adversity tests strong men.” Matthew of Vendôme, on Tobit:

> Fortune’s die examines the brave; gold in the furnace,  
> And faith shines through anxiety.

### 179. Hope in the Lord

Sirach II.6 ff.; David, Psalm XXXI.1; Isaiah XXVI.8.

### 180. Of the poor and afflicted

From the saying of Dionysius, *On Morals to His Son*: “Do not mock the unfortunate.” In an old epigram, *Monostichs*:

> He who mocks the unfortunate should know that everything future is uncertain.

The saying is attributed to Pittacus by Demetrius, Ausonius, and Sosiades.

### 183. He loves in Wisdom

The autograph manuscript of St Gall has: “He loves in Sophia.” Nothing is truer. Christ, Wisdom, never fails to love the person who loves him, as he himself testifies in Proverbs VIII.17: “I love those who love me.”

The Fathers also use Wisdom for Christ. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*: “This power and this ordering of the divine sense is also shown in the Scriptures under the name of Wisdom. For what is wiser than the reason or speech of God? Therefore understand Wisdom also as the second person, created.”

See Isidore, *Etymologies* VII.2; Silvius, *On the Titles of the Savior*, wrongly attributed to Damasus; Armenius in the *Confession of Faith*; and Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*: “Who knows what belongs to God and what is in God, except the spirit who is in him? But Wisdom was his spirit; she was his counselor; she herself is the way of understanding and knowledge.”

The Canisian manuscript has this meaning in *Sophia*: “Christ loves all who love him wisely (*σοφῶς*), that is, wisely rather than superstitiously, truly rather than falsely.” The Deltian manuscript does not have *ἠθική*.

### 184. Nor swift upon the tongue

James, chapter 1; Solomon, Proverbs XVII; Sirach V. Octavian:

> What you are able to provide, do not promise twice to anyone.

Or does he mean that we should be slow to speak and quick to work? Hildebert of Le Mans, in a letter.

### 185. A false witness through utterances

A witness who speaks falsehoods will not escape punishment. Exodus XX.16; Deuteronomy V.21 and XXIX.16; Solomon repeatedly in Proverbs; Daniel XIII.62.

*Innocuus* means “unpunished” (*ἀτιμώρητος*, *ἀζήμιος*). *Famina*: *φήματα*, *ῥήματα*, “utterances”; Hesychius has *φάσματα*, where *φράσματα* should be read.

Papias: *famen* derives from *for* (“to speak”) and means “speech.” An old glossary in the *Book of Wheels*: *faria*, “utterances.” Read *famina*.

Waldrammus to Dado:

> When we speak mutual words.

The same work:

> Heaven and earth pass away, but these firm words endure.

And poem III:

> The aforesaid writer set down these same words.

Hymn on Saint John the Baptist:

> Lest you should stain your life  
> Even slightly with a word.

### 187. You will make it great

The thought is expressed in a distich of Octavian, book I:

> When a poor friend gives you a small gift,  
> Return a great one.

If a poor friend offers you a small gift, return a great one; in this you will equal the highest princes, who, when offered water drawn from a hollow vessel, an apple, or a turnip, accepted them eagerly and repaid them as though they were the greatest gifts.

The Liège copyist corrupted this very beautiful maxim.

### 190. He who pursues leisure

Solomon, Proverbs XXIII.21.

### 193. He surpasses in number

The Liège manuscript:

> The number of the righteous exalts kingdoms powerfully.

But my reading is preferable in many respects. Although the righteous may be very few in number, they nevertheless conquer the kingdoms of the most powerful and surpass them. See the author of the *Book of Wisdom* III.6 and V.1.

### 195. He falls headlong

Isidore, *Sentences on the Highest Good* III.2: “Kings, unless they are restrained by the fear of God alone and by fear of Gehenna, freely rush headlong.”

### 202. And the idle man will serve

The lazy and sluggish man, who consumes all his possessions in idleness, will finally be forced to work under a greater burden, and will serve someone whom he least wished to serve—or even someone whom he might have been able to rule.

You make a yoke (*ζυγόν*). Euripides, *Hecuba*:

> For whoever is not accustomed to tasting labor  
> Bears it, but suffers when he places his neck beneath the yoke;  
> And he would be happier if dead  
> Than if alive.

### 204. Put bars upon your words

That is, make yourself a Harpocrates, the god of silence. The words are from Jesus Sirach XXVIII.28 ff. Add David, Psalm CXLI.3; the same Sirach XXI.1; Solomon, Proverbs XXI.23 and XXX.30.

Rabbi Joseph of Hysopolis, *Silver Dish*:

> Close the door of your lips; shut  
> Your enclosure. If it should melt,  
> You will be bound in its chains.

Last verse: “He loves the child he has begotten.” Solomon, Proverbs XIX.18; Seneca, *On Clemency* I: “The duty of good parents, who sometimes rebuke their children gently, sometimes threateningly, and sometimes even admonish them with blows.”

Rabbi Hai, in an educational poem:

> If you beget sons and daughters,  
> Correct them at all times, but with mercy.

“Correct him.” The manuscript of St Gall has “rebukes him.” Sergius, *Differentiae*, in Salomo: “We rebuke with words; we correct with blows.” See verses 89 and 168, and *deinceps* (“what follows”).

Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* II:

> You rebuke the sins of your foolish companion as you ought.

Sidonius, book VI, letter 9: “If anyone has not departed from the orbit of your correction.” Many others use the same distinction, though not in such a way that Sergius’ difference is observed, except insofar as—something I have so far shown to have been practiced—the words have yielded place to one another.

## Appendix

### Certain Documents (C, S)

### I. Privilege, or first donation, of Flavius Agilulf, king of the Lombards, granted to the venerable Saint Columbanus from the territory of Bobbio, extending four miles on every side (C)

Flavius Agilulf, most excellent man and king, to the venerable Columbanus and his companions.

We believe that a pious recompense will be repaid to us by the almighty Lord if priests in our kingdom are able, through salutary governance, to fulfill their vows to the Lord. Therefore, to the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, situated in the place called Bobbio, by this general decree of ours we grant to your holy fatherhood, there in the name of God, permission to dwell and possess property everywhere, as we determine, extending four miles in every direction around the whole territory, whether cultivated or uncultivated, except only half of the well which, by the decree of our donation, we have granted and caused to be founded.

For all the other boundaries which we named above—whether belonging to the basilica of the blessed Peter, to you, or to whoever there serves you and your officials, castellans, or our agents—we command in every respect that none of them ever presume to act against this decree of our document, so that you may be able to pray to the Lord day and night for the salvation and stability of our kingdom.

Issued at Milan, in the palace, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, in the eighth year of our most fortunate reign, in the fifth indiction.

At the command of the lord king and at the command of Agiderius, the notary, I, Liunus, wrote this.

### II. Charter recording how the lord Columbanus handed over the monastery of Bobbio to the Apostolic See

In the name of the Lord and of Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, our Lord, ruler of all.

In the year pleasing to God, during the pontificate of the lord Gregory, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most holy see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in the fourth indiction, year 13, I, Columbanus, servant of the servants of God, born in the regions of Ireland, said to the pope:

“For it is clear that the human race was formed from the beginning together with divine mercy; but the ancient rival and author devised deadly poisons for destroying the joys of the human race, so that the whole human mass might be held subject to the bond of sin. Therefore our Creator, the Lord Jesus Christ, coming into the world through the Virgin’s womb to restore the freedom of his image, bestowed upon those who believe in him the renewed joys of Paradise.

“Therefore, considering the guardian of eternal recompense, whom we wish to be our gracious rewarder, we decree with the readiest spirit and establish that all those properties which came to us through the charter of the most glorious King Agilulf—which lie beside the river Trebbia in the valley called Bobbio and extend, according to legitimate measurement, for four miles on every side—as well as whatever we and our successors may acquire, shall be subject to the protection and immunity of the most holy apostolic see and shall be held under the judgment of you and your successors, without prejudice.

“If at any time after the construction of the monastery any dispute should arise, from whatever quarter, involving a person of high or low rank, let it be evident that these matters have now been settled in the presence of your most holy heart, so that they may remain firm for all future time. For if anyone acts otherwise than has been written above, we commit him to the one who said: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.’ Therefore we wish two charters, subscribed in identical form and made for the most certain truth: one of them we deliver to be preserved in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; the other we have retained for ourselves and for our successors to retain, so that, as we have said, every dispute may be removed and destroyed. These charters of my offering we delivered to the most reverend deacon Peter, with a formal stipulation duly inserted.”

Done in the palace of Constantinople, on the third day of the month of November, in the above-mentioned indiction, successfully.

I, Columbanus: these charters of my offering have been made by me and delivered.

I, Bubulenus, monk and priest.

I, Eunochus, priest and monk.

I, Domitialis, humble deacon, Scot, and monk.

[Col. 0323C] I, Evonenus, priest and monk.

I, Bobulenus, monk and priest.

I, Gurgazus, of Breton origin.

I, Boniface, chief examiner.

I, Attalus, priest of Frankish descent.

I, Deusdedit, examiner.

I, Meliaderus, presbyter and monk.

I, Romanus, deacon. Sign: [three marks].

Leoni, Simeoni, and Audo, witnesses. Sign: [three marks].

Leoni and Zachariah, Epiphoni, witnesses.

I, Peter, deacon and notary of the holy apostolic see, wrote, published, completed, and delivered these charters of offering.

### III. Confirmation of the aforesaid privilege by King Adivaldus (C)

[Col. 0323D]

Flavius Adivaldus, most excellent king, to the monastery of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul situated at Bobbio, and to the venerable brother Attala, abbot, and all his monks.

“When we had come, for the sake of devotion concerning our sins, to pray at the hall of the blessed apostles, at Bobbio, where our revered father, the lord Columbanus, rests in body, your veneration and the entire holy congregation of the servants of God together petitioned us. You displayed before us the charter of the Lord and our father, King Agilulf, and it was contained in it that our father had handed this place over to blessed Columbanus for inhabiting and possessing, both for himself and for those who, after him, would serve the Lord there perpetually in their appointed time. Your holy fatherhood as a whole likewise requested us to do this now.

“Therefore, awaiting eternal recompense, we have determined to proclaim the present things so that we may be worthy of eternal things that will endure without end. And so, hearing the petition of all of you, we confirm and grant to you, in the name of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the basilica situated at Bobbio, with permission, in God’s name, to inhabit and possess it.

“We accordingly establish boundaries extending four miles on every side of that basilica, just as the Lord our father instituted by his charter that blessed Columbanus should possess them. Except only for half of the well, which the same father, a man of venerable memory, founded and granted, and for the timber used to boil salt—this too we grant and confirm for possession.

“Likewise, [we grant] the little mountain called Pennice, where our lady and mother, the most glorious Queen Theodelinda, out of love for our father Columbanus, ascended to inspect this place. She requested us to grant that little mountain to your holy monastery; and we, hearing her petition, have gladly decided to give it. We wish it to remain perpetually given to you and to those who after you will serve God there.

“Therefore, considering eternal recompense, by this charter of our authority we confirm in your holy monastery both the boundaries already established above for your veneration and the mountain Pennice with its boundaries, extending along those same boundaries as far as the rock of Gragio, and from there returning below the rock of Pedenna, along the slope before one reaches the rock of Digna; and from there, along that already mentioned slope, as far as the river Trebbia. By our most recent letters we firmly establish this as a gift of ours for possession.

“So henceforth let no one of our judges, counts, gastalds, or agents presume to diminish anything from it. Rather, may that holy and venerable place, and your blessedness, or whoever in due time succeeds you, be able to possess inviolate, both during our most fortunate times and in the future, those things which, with God’s favor, we have conferred upon that holy and venerable place.”

“At the command of the lord king and at the command of Agiderius the notary, I, [unreadable abbreviation: *pron.*], subscribed.”

Given at Ticinum, in the palace, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the sixth year of our most fortunate reign, in the ninth indiction, successfully.

### IV. Another confirmation of the aforesaid privilege (C)

Flavius Adjuvaldus, most excellent king, to the venerable Bertulf, abbot, and all his monks.

“We believe that recompense will be returned to us by the almighty Lord if priests in our kingdom are able, through salutary governance, to fulfill their vows to God. Therefore, just as our father, King Agilulf, of holy memory, in his piety granted you and your predecessors, the lords Columbanus and Attala, abbots of Bobbio, permission to dwell at the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by this general charter of ours we grant you, at the threshold of blessed Peter, permission, in God’s name, to inhabit and possess it.

“We establish the boundaries on every side as they were granted or handed over by the Lord and our father, the lord Columbanus of holy memory, or by Attala: four miles around on every side, cultivated or uncultivated, except only for half of the well, which our predecessor and father, King Agilulf, granted, and the timber for burning there to boil salt.

“Moreover, whatever came to you from Russone by gift and with legal authority, we confirm as a gift of ours in your monastery. We also grant to the basilica of blessed Peter, or to you, for possession, those boundaries which we named above, as far as the rock of Gragio; from there below the rock of Pedena, along the slope before one reaches Digna; and along that same slope as far as the river Trebbia.

“Therefore we give orders to all our dukes, gastalds, and agents that none of them should ever presume to act against this page of our charter. Thus may you be able to pray day and night to the Lord for the safety and stability of our kingdom.”

I, Bonus, the notary, wrote this.

Given at Pavia, in the palace, on the sixteenth day of the month of August, in the seventh year of our reign, successfully, in the tenth indiction.

## In the year of the Lord 615. Saint Alphanus, Bishop of Benevento

[Col. 0325]

### Historical Notice on Alphanus

(Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VIII, p. 18.) (C)

[Col. 0325B] Alphanus, bishop of the church of Benevento, lived in the year of Christ 615, in the twenty-fourth year of the rule of Arichis, first duke of the Beneventans. This can be understood from a document of that same Alphanus renouncing the rights of the church of Saint Martin, whose words, set out below, are preserved in the *Chronicle of Saint Sophia*.

The indiction and the reckoning of the years of Duke Arichis in this document appropriately fall in the year 615. Arichis the First began to reign after Zotto in the year of salvation 591. Moreover, that church of Saint Martin, after being freed from Alphanus’s jurisdiction, passed many years later into the ownership of the monastery of Saint Sophia. Hence Alphanus’s document was copied among other materials into the Sophian Chronicle, which preserved his memory for posterity.

[Col. 0325]

## Charter of Renunciation of the Rights of the Church of Saint Martin by Saint Alphanus, Bishop of Benevento (C)

[Col. 0325C] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his most holy Mother.

In the time of the lord Arichis, most glorious man and supreme duke of the people of the Lombards, in the twenty-fourth year of his most glorious dukedom, confirmed in the month of March, in the fourth indiction.

We, the lord Alphanus, most blessed man, reverend bishop of this most holy see of Benevento, concerning the release of the church of Saint Martin, hereby free that aforesaid church for you, Trasemundus Schuldachis, inasmuch as you, the aforementioned Trasemundus, have been seen to bring that oft-mentioned church, from a new foundation to the height of consecration, upon your own territory, in the place called Monsbonionis, which appears to be in the locality of Buente.

We free it according to canonical law, so that no priest, deacon, or subdeacon may have authority to give it away or cause it to belong to a parish, or to withdraw it under any title, except the priest whom you, the aforementioned Trasemundus, or your heirs, may from time to time appoint. Once the church has been completed, it shall come to us or to our successors in this named holy see for consecration, according to canonical ordinance.

For no one else may have authority to give away any of its property—not I, Alphanus, bishop by the grace of God, nor any of my successors—and you shall never at any time have any claim or reproach against me concerning this release of mine. Rather, from now and for all perpetuity, let the named church remain in the condition described above.

[Col. 0327A] We ordered this written record of release to be written for you by Nicolaus, our notary; and, so that it might possess legal force, we affixed the image of the holy cross.

Done successfully at Benevento, in the episcopal residence, in the month and indiction named above.

[Col. 0328A] I, Majorachus, presbyter, wrote myself as witness, with our priests and the entire clergy present.

I, Aripaldus, ordered this to be written and the witnesses to be entered.

## In the year of the Lord 615. Saint Aileranus, a Scot-Irish abbot

[Col. 0327]

### Historical Notice on Aileranus

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis*.) (C)

[Col. 0327B] Aileranus—more accurately Aireranus or Ereranus—called the Wise, a Scot-Irish presbyter and schoolmaster, or teacher, of the school of Cluainerard in Ireland, apparently lived in the eighth century, after Columba, Ultanus, and Adamnanus. He wrote the deeds of Saint Patrick and, the only work of his that has survived, a mystical interpretation of the ancestors of Christ. This was published together with the writings of Columbanus by Patrick Fleming, O.F.M., at Louvain in 1667, and reprinted in volume XII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon edition, 1677, p. 37.

[Col. 0327]

## The Mystical Interpretation of the Ancestors of Christ by Saint Aileranus, a Scot-Irish Abbot

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XII, p. 39.) (C, S)

[Col. 0327C] **Note:** [Col. 0327C] [Col. 0063] This note is printed at the foot of column 327, but its callout letter, “a,” does not appear in the text.

Before this little work there is the following notice in volume XII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 39:

> “Although, kind reader, the treatise of our Aileranus placed below is not by Columbanus, and therefore, according to the purpose of the present undertaking, does not seem in itself to belong to this collection, nevertheless, since it is so short that it cannot suitably be published separately, and since it draws from the sacred Scriptures meanings of such fertile and learned ingenuity that its publication will be as useful as it will be welcome to all students of sacred letters, and especially to preachers of the divine word, I thought it advisable, lest the distinguished memorial of this excellent man remain hidden any longer, to append it to this present booklet, which contains the sermons of Columbanus, for the benefit of the reader.

> “Concerning Aileranus himself—Aireranus or Ereranus, for the name is found in various forms among ancient Latin and Irish writers, although the latter form is more frequently found written in the ancient Irish martyrologies—it should be observed that two most holy men of this name once flourished in Ireland.

> “One was Ereranus, abbot of Tamlacht in Leinster, successor of Saint Mailruan, the most famous archimandrite and founder of a monastic rule and order. The *Compilation of the Ancient Martyrologies of Ireland*—that is, of Saint Aeneas or Aengus, bishop and son of Obelen, of blessed Marianus the abbot, and of Lord Charles Maguire—places his feast on 11 August.

> “But since this Ereranus, although wise (and he is also recorded under this surname), is said to have written nothing apart from his monastic rule, and since he was an abbot, he should not be considered the author of the present little work, which was written by a celebrated writer who was nevertheless not an abbot.

> “The other was Aireranus, surnamed the Wise, a presbyter and schoolmaster, or teacher, of the celebrated school of Cluainerard, which nurtured many thousands of disciples distinguished for holiness and learning. To him this work placed below seems truly to be attributable. In addition, he is read to have published, among other things, a life of Saint Patrick.

> “For in the Irish manuscript epitome of the deeds of Saint Patrick, which begins, ‘The people who sat in darkness saw a great light,’ reliable authorities among our people, near the end, list Aireranus among the writers of Saint Patrick’s life. Thus it reads:

> “‘These are the holy elders and wise men of Ireland who wrote and handed down to us the signs and wonders of Patrick: Saint Columba of Kells, Saint Ultanus—another than the one of Fosses in Belgium—Saint Adomnanus, Saint Areranus the Wise, Saint Chieranus, and others.’

> “The aforementioned Saint Aeneas, a bishop who flourished at the end of the eighth century with outstanding praise for holiness and learning, also mentions this same Areranus in his most elegant and reliable metrical martyrology. Under 29 December, during the reign of Hugh the Honored, or Ordnith, son of Niall of the Clouds, monarch of all Ireland, he writes:

> “‘Aireran of the wise men’—that is, Aireranus, the Wise.

> “The Martyrology of Subiaco in Bavaria agrees with him, where one reads: ‘On the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in Ireland, Saint Areranus, Averanus, confessor.’

> “There is no doubt that this Areranus belonged to the second order of the saints of Ireland, and perhaps not long after Saint Finnian’s departure to heaven he took over the administration of the school mentioned above—that is, as I suppose, around the time of Columba, Comgall, Brendan, and the other fathers, under whose governance the most famous schools of sacred letters flourished in Ireland.

> “Among these, the college of Cluainerard, greatly distinguished by the teaching of this holy doctor, must certainly be believed to have held no inferior place. From this little work itself, small though it is, the prudent reader will recognize Aileranus as one recognizes a lion from its claw, and, after reading it through, will judge how truly the surname ‘Wise’ adhered to him.

> “Would that earlier centuries had not begrudged us the many other monuments of his great genius and learning that he doubtless published. From these and from the wisest writings of other teachers of our people, suppressed by the injury of time or the envy of certain persons, Ireland might today find consolation in her affliction and restrain the impious mouths of certain detractors.

> “This treatise, moreover—alas, incomplete—has been transcribed from a very ancient manuscript codex of the celebrated monastery of Saint Gall in Switzerland. In that codex it bears above it the title ‘Mystical Interpretation, etc.’ and it is also added that it was customarily read there on the feast of the Nativity of the holy Mother of God.

> “The monks of Saint Gall, who were themselves most learned, evidently valued that golden treatise greatly and rightly. Henceforth, reader, kindly enjoy it; and if any other works of that man should come to light, you may expect them from me as soon as possible. Farewell.”

It seems appropriate to explain the meanings of the names in the genealogy of the Lord according to the mystical interpretations received chiefly from the authority of the Fathers. The primary purpose is to establish, through suitable testimonies of sacred Scripture, how the interpretation of each name is to be referred to our Lord Jesus Christ [the text has *hominis*, perhaps *nominis*], and to show that all the generations of the genealogy prefigured and prophesied the Savior, into whose genealogy they were inserted by divine providence.

The Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, who is Priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 109), and King according to the election of David, whom Samuel anointed king and prophet before his brothers (1 Sam. 16:18), just as the Father also anointed Jesus Christ with the oil of gladness above his companions (Heb. 1:9), is called Patriarch among the patriarchs, Priest among the priests, Judge among the judges, Prophet among the prophets, Leader among leaders, Apostle among the apostles, and, among the angels, the Angel of great counsel.

[Col. 0329B] In Abraham, “Exalted Father” is understood (Jerome, *Book on the Interpretation of Hebrew Names*, on Genesis), concerning whom Isaiah says, among other things: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6). And David says: “But if his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. 88). For when the sons of our Lord Jesus Christ fall—those whom he begot through the word of life and caused to be born again through baptism—they will not be dashed to pieces, because the Lord extends the hand of his mercy (Ps. 36:24), which he stretched out to Peter when Peter was in danger (Matt. 14:30).

In Isaac, “joy” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Hebrew Names*, on Genesis; Origen, Homily 7 on Genesis), as the angel said to the shepherds: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people” (Luke 2:10). For he had said concerning John the Baptist to Zechariah: “And many will rejoice at his birth” (Luke 1:14). When prophets, holy men, and those born through divine promise were born, joy arose for their parents and relatives; but when the Redeemer of all and Lord of the whole world was born, it was rightly announced that incomparable and greatest joy had arisen for all the people—that is, for the whole human race.

In Jacob, “supplanter” (Gen. 27:36; Origen, Homily 11 on Exodus; Arnobius, on Psalm 52). For he himself says: “No one can enter the house of a strong man and seize his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. 12:29). The Lord had indeed been the supplanter of Satan when he said: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:31); for he thrusts back the rear foot [*plantam*, “sole” or “foot”; perhaps *planta*, “plant”].

In Judah, “confessing” (Jerome, on chapter 3 of Mark, and *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Matthew; Origen, Homily 17 on Genesis), who said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 12:25).

In Phares, “divider” (Origen, Homily 23 on Matthew), who separates the sheep from the goats (Matt. 25:32), that is, the fruitful from the unfruitful.

In Zara, “rising one” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Genesis), concerning whom the prophetic spirit says: “Behold, a Man whose name is Rising.” Of him Zechariah likewise says: “The Rising from on high has visited us” (Zech. 6:12; Luke 1:78). And elsewhere: “For those who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Mal. 4:2). Abraham desired to see the rising and setting of his day, and he saw it (John 8:56). By the rising we should understand his birth, through which the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14); by the setting, the death on the cross which he suffered for us (Phil. 2:8). For that eternal and ineffable day of the Godhead, of which it is said, “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 109:4), is always a beginning but knows no rising; it is always an end but has no setting. The name *Coccineus* [perhaps *Coccinus*, “scarlet”] is derived from the Lord in such a way that it signifies either the red blood of the Passion or the unquenchable ardor of fiery love, the example of which he gave.

In Esdron, “he saw an arrow” (Origen, Homily 35 on Matthew; Augustine, on Psalm 87; Hesychius, on Leviticus 14), or “his court” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Joshua), to whom it is said: “The arrows of the mighty are sharp” (Ps. 119:4). His arrows are the Lord’s commandments, or the judgments of the Judge. But “court,” that is, a spacious house open to all, is said of him because, inviting everyone to himself, he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28); and again: “Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit” (John 15:5); and again: “Go out,” he says, “to the crossroads, and compel everyone to enter” (Luke 14:23).

In Aram, “chosen,” concerning whom he speaks thus: “Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my chosen one; I have placed my spirit upon him” (Matt. 12:18). And truly, who is the chosen child except the one who from childhood rejected evil and chose what is good (Isa. 7:13)? This is not common to all children, except for the one child who was born from sin without sin, like an incorrupt worm born from corruption.

In Aminadab, “my spontaneous people” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Exodus, Numbers, and Judges), who says: “No one takes my life from me” (John 10:18); and: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17).

In Naasson, “foretelling” (Jerome, *Book on the Interpretation of Hebrew Names*, on Acts of the Apostles and Matthew), who promises, saying: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty” (Luke 9:26). His prophecy looked toward three times of prophecy: the past, as in “Abraham saw my day, and rejoiced”; the present, as in “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (John 8:56); and the future, as in “For they will be like the angels in heaven” (Matt. 9:4), and: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it” (John 2:19).

In Solomon, “perceptive” (Jerome, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Matthew; Mark 12:25), who says: “Someone touched me, for I perceived power had gone out from me” (Luke 8:46). And: “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4). Truly he is perceptive who sees thoughts as deeds and future things as present, as it is written concerning him: “He made the things that are to be” (Wis. 8:8).

In Boaz, “in whom there is strength” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Judges and Ruth), who says: “I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). The strength of every human being fails in death, but the Word who became flesh became stronger through weakness, more living through death, and more exalted through humility.

In Obed, “serving” (Josephus, *Antiquities*, book V, chapter 14), who did not come to be served but to serve (Matt. 20:28). Likewise the Apostle says: “He took the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7).

[Col. 0331C] In Jesse, “incense” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on 1 and 3 Kings), who says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). And John says: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11; Luke 3).

In David, “desirable” (Jerome, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Matthew and Acts of the Apostles), concerning whom the Evangelist says: “His face shone like the sun” (Matt. 17:2). Hence the Prophet had also said: “Beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3).

In Solomon, “peaceful” (Origen, Homily 6 on John), who says: “I give you my peace” (John 14:27). By adding “my,” he shows that he hates the peace that is not his own; concerning that peace it is said: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). And the Apostle says of Christ: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14).

[Col. 0331D] In Rehoboam, “breadth of the people” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on 2 Kings; Jerome, in the same work, on Matthew), when he says: “Many will come from the east and the west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8). Likewise elsewhere: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28). He is called the impetus of the people because, just as lightning comes forth from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man (Matt. 24:27).

In Abijah, “the Lord is Father” (Jerome, as above, on Matthew), who says: “Do not call anyone your father on earth” (Matt. 23:9)—not because we say that there are two in the divinity, but because even a human being can be the father of the human being whom he teaches, as Paul says: “Even if you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you” (1 Cor. 4). If the disciple deserved to be called a father, how much more his Teacher.

In Asa, “taking away” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on 3 Kings and Jeremiah), concerning whom John says: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away sins” (John 1:29).

In Jehoshaphat, “he himself judging” (Philo, in the same work, on 2 and 3 Kings), as he says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

In Joram, “where there is exaltation” (Philo, in the same work, on 3 Kings; Jerome, in the same work, on Matthew), as he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John 3:13).

In Uzziah, “the strength of the Lord” (Philo, in the same work, on Isaiah), who said: “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43). Then the voice of the Lord was in power, when he recalled the soul of the four-day dead man from the underworld and his body from the tomb.

In Jotham, “completed” (Jerome, *Book on the Interpretation of Hebrew Names*, on Matthew), concerning whom it is said: “When every temptation had been completed” (Luke 4:13). And at the end of everything prophesied about him it is said: “And when he had finished all these words, he said to his disciples: You know that after two days the Passover will take place” (Matt. 26:2). And while hanging on the cross and having drunk vinegar, he said: “It is completed,” and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30).

If he is called “perfect” (Author of the *Opus imperfectum*, Homily 1 on Matthew), it is explained in this way: since he commands his own to be perfect, saying, “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48), Jesus ought to be called perfect above all others, since he began to do and to teach (Acts 1:1) things that are perfect.

In Ahaz, “turning” (Author of the *Opus imperfectum*, Homily 1 on Matthew; Origen, on Exodus), who says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2); or “grasping” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Micah), who grasped Peter’s mother-in-law by the hand and healed her of fever (Luke 4:38), and raised the dead daughter of the ruler (Matt. 9:23). Paul likewise says: “If somehow I may grasp that for which I have been grasped” (Phil. 3:12). And elsewhere: “For he did not grasp angels, but he grasped the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16).

In Hezekiah, “the Lord has strengthened” (Anonymous Author, Homily 1 on Matthew), who says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:31). And Paul says: “But we preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24).

In Manasseh, “forgetful” (Philo, as above, on Genesis), who says: “Her many sins are forgiven because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). For love covers a multitude of sins (James 5:20). And Ezekiel says: “On whatever day the unjust person turns from his injustice, all his iniquities will be handed over to oblivion” (Ezek. 18).

In Amon, “faithful” (Philo, in the same work, on Jeremiah), who says: “Ask, and it will be given to you” (Matt. 7:7). And Paul says: “That he might become a merciful and faithful High Priest before God” (Heb. 2:17). And John in the Apocalypse: “And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness” (Rev. 1:5). He is called faithful because his promises are always trustworthy; they are equally to be hoped for and feared in both respects.

In Josiah, “where there is the incense of the Lord” (Jerome, *Book on the Interpretation of Hebrew Names*), concerning whom it is said: “And he prayed more earnestly” (Luke 22:44). How prayer is called incense, the Psalmist bears witness, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, O Lord” (Ps. 140:2).

In Jeconiah, “preparing” (Jerome, in the same work; and Philo, *Fourth Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on 1 Kings and Jeremiah), as he says: “If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again to you and take you to myself” (John 14:3).

But if Joachim and Joachin are properly distinguished—“Father,” that is—then in Joachin “the resurrection of the Lord” is meant (Jerome, in the same work, on Matthew), as he says: “But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee” (Matt. 26:2). In Joachim, “the preparation of the Lord” (Author of the *Opus imperfectum*, Homily 1 on Matthew), who said: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

In Salathiel, “my petition is God” (Jerome, in the same work, on Matthew; Philo, in the same work, on Haggai), who said: “Holy Father, preserve those whom you have given me” (John 17:11).

In Zerubbabel, “he himself the master of confusion” (Jerome, in the same work), as he says: “Many will come from the east and the west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8:11). And of him it is said: “Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” (Mark 2:16).

In Abiud, “this one is my Father” (Philo, in the same work, on Exodus), who says: “I and my Father are one” (John 10:30).

In Eliakim, “the Lord will raise up” (Philo, in the same work, on the Book of Kings), as he says: “Whoever believes in me will not die forever, but I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6:40).

In Azor, “helped” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on 3 Kings and Jeremiah), as he says: “I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 8:19).

[Col. 0334A] In Zadok, “justified” (Jerome, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Luke), as he says: “I speak the truth, because the one who sent me is truthful” (John 8:26). To him it is also said: “You are justified in your words” (Ps. 50:6). And John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

In Achim, “my brother” (Origen, Homily 20 on Joshua), as he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father is my brother, my mother, and my sister” (Matt. 12:50), or “the brother of the mother.” For the Lord is called the brother of the mother because he has one Father, to whom all, at Christ’s command, say: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (ibid.).

In Eliud, “this is my God” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on 1 Kings), to whom Thomas says: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). But what else does the pronoun “this” signify except the marks of the nails and the spear, which display the true knowledge of the body?

In Eleazar, “my God is helper” (Philo, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Genesis and Exodus), as he says: “The Father who sent me is with me” (John 8:16).

In Matthan, “giving” (Jerome, *Book on the Interpretation of Names*, on Matthew), as he says: “Every debt is forgiven you because you asked me” (Matt. 18:32).

In Jacob, “supplanter” (Origen, Homily 11 on Exodus), as he says: “I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

In Joseph, “increased” or “adding” (Philo, in the same work, on Genesis; Josephus, book I, chapter 17, *Antiquities*), as he says: “I have come so that they may have life and have it more abundantly” (John 10:10). And elsewhere: “I have other sheep that are not from this fold; these too I must bring, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10).

Thus far, as we have been able, we have established by examples from sacred Scripture how Christ was prefigured and prophesied in all the genealogies, or in the generations [perhaps “degrees of the genealogy”].

[Col. 0333]

## A Moral Explanation of the Same Names, Compiled by the Same Author (C)

[Col. 0333D] It also seems appropriate to extend the names of the same genealogy, through interpretation and broader figures, toward a moral understanding, insofar as we can.

In holy Abraham, therefore, let us understand this and strive to become fathers of holy nations—that is, of perfect souls and virtues. After evil nations, that is, deadly vices, have been uprooted, destroyed, dispersed, and scattered, holy Jeremiah is commanded by the Lord to build and plant these virtues. In the figure of these vices, the seven nations of the Canaanites, like so many principal vices, were destroyed by the Israelite people (Cassian, *Conferences*, 5, chapter 22), and the same land was possessed by that people by hereditary right [perhaps “and their land”].

Let us also be strangers in this world, in the likeness of Abraham, and pilgrims, as all our fathers were. Let us likewise offer to God all the joy of the present life, like Isaac, the most beloved son, at the Lord’s command, so that we may rejoice eternally with Christ, who himself says: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted” (Matt. 5).

In Isaac, may we become rich a hundredfold in fruit, rejoice in trials, and take Rebecca as our second wife—that is, possess patience—as the Apostle James says: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience” [Col. 0335A] “so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope,” according to Paul’s words (Rom. 15; Jas. 1). Let us rejoice in the Lord always; for even if we have rejoiced without God, we cannot rejoice forever. For this is eternal and true joy: what begins here through faith is brought to perfection there through sight. The joy of the present age is brought to an end and erased by mourning, whereas the joy to come knows no limit and is not interrupted by sorrows.

In Jacob, let us overthrow our old, Idumean—that is, earthly—man by means of the new man, so that the spirit of our mind, renewed according to the Lord, may receive the name of the overthrower. For, according to the Apostle, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” [Col. 0335B] (Gal. 5): the elder brother against the younger, and the younger against the elder, because “the spiritual was not first, but the animal” (1 Cor. 15). Whoever emerges victorious from this struggle, having overcome the carnal and old man and mortified his members that are upon the earth, becomes pure in heart—emptied, that is, of vices and filled with virtues—and, passing from the active life into the contemplative, deserves to be called by the name Israel: that is, either “a man who sees God,” or “a prince with God,” or “the directed [beloved] of the Lord.” In the present life he will see Him through faith, and in the future will contemplate Him face to face: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 0335C] In Judah, let us praise and continually glorify the Lord, and confess to Him while praising His name. In the divine Scriptures confession has two forms: it either concerns the satisfaction of repentance—as in, “they were baptized by him, confessing their sins” (Matt. 3), and again, “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5)—or it refers to thanksgiving and praise, as with the holy Daniel: “To You, God of our fathers, I confess, and I praise You” (Dan. 2); and again in the Gospel, He who committed no sin like a sheep says, “I confess to You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11), that is, “I give You thanks,” or “I glorify You” (St. Augustine, Sermon 8, *On the Words of the Lord*). Therefore, let us come before the face [of the Lord] in confession and confess our sins; for we have an advocate with the Father, [Col. 0335D] Jesus Christ the righteous, and He is the expiation for our sins (1 John 2). Let us expose our wounds to the physician; for whoever conceals his wounds nourishes them. Let hidden offenses be disclosed to the Lord; once revealed, let them be covered through repentance by the Lord’s mercy. In adversity and prosperity alike, let us praise Christ, giving thanks to the Lord the Father for everything through Him.

In Phares, let us divide rightly and offer rightly to the Lord, avoiding the worst example of that parricide; let us divide our possessions among the needy and return to our parents what belongs to our parents. Moreover, let us strive to become dividers of the upper waters from the lower—that is, with the firmament of patience intervening, let us separate virtues from vices. Having become clean animals, let us be taken into Noah’s ark, dividing the intellectual hoof [Col. 0336A]—that is, distinguishing the letter from the spirit—and, as we said earlier, distinguishing vices from virtues. Let us approve everything according to the Apostle [perhaps: “test everything”], and hold fast only to what is good, so that when the day of that dreadful judgment arrives, we who have judged ourselves may not be judged by the Lord, nor condemned with the evil world (1 Thess. 5).

In Zara [another reading: Zaram], let the morning star arise in our hearts (2 Pet. 1), and let the sun of righteousness—which rises for those who fear the Lord and sets for the negligent—illumine us: the true light, namely, which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). Nor let any deadly vice set upon our anger, or upon anything else [the wording is corrupt/uncertain]. Illumined by its radiance, may we ourselves shine like stars for everlasting ages (Dan. 12), and rise [Col. 0336B] like lights for this world, holding the word of life, so that our light may shine before human beings and they may glorify our Father who is in heaven through our works (Matt. 5). Nor should it be enough for us merely to believe in Christ; if necessity so requires, we must also be ready to pour out our blood for His name and undergo the fellowship of martyrdom. Let our scarlet thread [another reading: *coccus*, “scarlet dye”] also be twice dyed—that is, let it be filled with love of God and of our neighbor, kindled by the Holy Spirit. Of this it is said: “Many waters could not extinguish love; its lamps are lamps of fire and flame” (Song 8).

In Esron, let us foresee the devil’s burning arrows and the enemy’s fiery darts with the watchful gaze of a perceptive heart, so that with the Apostle Paul we may say, “For we are not unaware of his devices” [Col. 0336C] (2 Cor. 2). To see these, we need the eyes of the heart to be vigilant. “Our struggle,” says the Apostle, “is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). Therefore, as the same Apostle says elsewhere, “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but spiritual” (2 Cor. 10). With spiritual and invisible weapons, the invisible soul must fight against invisible enemies.

Let us therefore take up, according to the Apostle (Eph. 6; 1 Thess. 5), so that we may be able to resist on the evil day, in every circumstance, the shield of faith, by which we can extinguish the enemy’s fiery darts, the helmet of hope, the breastplate of love, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word [“of God” omitted]. We must understand the name Esron in both ways: either because, as was said above, we must beware of the devil’s arrows, or because, seeing the Lord’s arrows—which according to the Psalmist are sharp—we must oppose them with His arrows. For no one who competes in the contest will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully (2 Tim. 2).

Let us also become an atrium, so that He may dwell in us as in His holy atrium [Col. 0336D], for He says: “I will dwell in them.” Let us also stand in the house of our Lord, in the courts of the house of our God (Ps. 115), praising the Lord. Because He is good, let us enter His gates with rejoicing and His courts with hymns (Ps. 99). For those planted in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, will flourish (Ps. 91), so that after flourishing in the courts of the present Church, they may be planted, steadfast, in the house of the eternal kingdom.

[Col. 0337A] In Aram, let us be counted among the Lord’s elect, against whom no accuser can stand. For the Father chose us in Christ so that we might be holy and blameless before Him (2 Pet. 1). Let us therefore make our calling and election sure through good works, so that, although many are called, we may be found among the few elect. For all who obey the Lord’s will are called “a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2). Let us also be exalted and sublime, raised above earthly things to heavenly ones by the dignity of our merits; whoever clings to these from the lofty dwelling of heaven despises all transitory things.

In Aminadab, let us be the Lord’s willing people. For in the construction of the tabernacle of testimony—which plainly signifies the whole Church—each person offered willingly whatever he wished [Col. 0337B]. Hence Truth itself says: “If anyone wishes to come after Me” (Matt. 16); and elsewhere: “If you wish to be perfect” (Matt. 19). Again, concerning the choice of virginity, He left free choice, saying: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (1 Cor. 7). For just as the Lord acquired our life through a voluntary passion, so He also wishes us voluntarily to sacrifice ourselves to Him, so that He may make the willing offerings of our mouths pleasing to Him. Thus, knowing the will of the blind, He asked them, “What do you want Me to do for you?” (Mark 10); and at once the faithful will obtained the result of healing.

In Naason, having abandoned the worldly omens of the Gentiles, let us put faith in the divine promises, and place the prosperity of all things in the will of the Lord alone, not [Col. 0337C] in false divinations. Thus Paul says: “If somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you” (Rom. 1).
