See: he placed the prosperity of his journey not in fate or augury, but in the Lord’s will. David likewise says of the blessed man: “Everything that he does shall prosper” (Ps. 1); and the Apostle John says: “Beloved, I pray that in all things you may prosper” (3 John). Having therefore despised all worldly omens, let us prosper in God’s will, believe the divine oracles, and attend solely to the Lord’s promises. For “love believes all things, hopes all things” (1 Cor. 13). As the highest culmination of praise, it is said of the people of Israel: “There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel” (Num. 23).

[Col. 0337D] In Salmon, let us test all things with sound judgment in the Lord and hold fast only to those that are good (1 Thess. 5), and, perfect in our understanding, be infants in wickedness (1 Cor. 14). Let us have within us the same mind that was in Christ Jesus, who, “though He was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2), and so forth. Being of one mind and having one understanding, let us honor the Lord with one voice. Instructed by the understanding of sacred Scripture, let us become teachable by the Lord, as the holy Isaiah says: “They shall all be taught by God” (Isa. 54; John 3).

In Booz, let us be strengthened in the Lord and act manfully, with Christ strengthening our hands for battle and our fingers for war. Thus, fortified by the strength of patience, may we be able to endure every kind of temptation and triumph over [Col. 0338A] our enemies, while also fearing the Apostle’s warning: “How have you become such that you need milk, not solid food?” (Heb. 5). Solid food belongs to mature men, who have their faculties trained for the discernment of good and evil. Strengthened by such fortitude was the one who said: “I can do everything through Him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4).

In Obed, let us serve the Lord with gladness (Ps. 99), with that service by which the Lord is served not through the spirit of fear but through the spirit of adoption as sons (Rom. 5). For just as there are two fears that produce two kinds of people who fear, so there are two services that produce two kinds of servants. One fear is penal and belongs to servitude; the other [perhaps: “and is”] is the beginning of wisdom; the other is the fullness of the divine law. Let us therefore present ourselves to the Lord as perfect servants through perfect service, so that when the time of servitude has ended, we may be called by the Lord into the eternal kingdom.

In Jesse, let the incense of our prayers rise upon the altar of our heart. “Let my prayer,” David says, “be directed like incense in Your sight” (Ps. 140). Let us burn with the fire of the Spirit, setting everything ablaze, offering to the Lord a contrite spirit and sacrificing to God an offering of praise (Ps. 115), burning with the fire of God, of which it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

In David, let us forgive personal injuries, become desirable to the Lord, and have a longing for God—that is, loving the Lord so that we may be loved by the Lord: “Whoever loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him” [Col. 0338C] (John 14). Let us also be strong-handed: that is, by perfect action, let us wound the intellectual giant with his own sword and rescue from the jaws of the ancient robber the souls both of ourselves and of our neighbors. Thus, when the final judgment arrives, may we, desirable to the Lord, shine like the sun in the kingdom of our Father and, having fought the good fight, receive from the just Judge the crown of righteousness laid up for us in heaven.

In Solomon, let us, as far as depends on us, live at peace with everyone. Having conquered the internal war of the vices through spiritual virtues, and reconciled our two selves into one heavenly person, let us have peace with the Lord and with our neighbor. Let us not merely be at peace with everyone [Col. 0338D], but also be peacemakers for everyone, recalling even hostile brothers to unity of spirit and concord. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5).

In Roboam, fulfilling the Lord’s broad commandment—that is, showing brotherly love to all without respect of persons—let us, according to Paul, enlarge our hearts, and let the sons of Israel multiply and increase in our land: that is, let them be filled with spiritual virtues opposed to the race of vices. When such a people has been enlarged within us, may the rush of spiritual desire break the spiritual surge; for “the river’s rushing waters make glad the city of God” (Ps. 56).

In Abia, let us have the Lord as our Father and be in [Col. 0339A] the Lord, so that we may truly say, “Our Father” (Matt. 6). Let us be sons of God and heirs—heirs indeed of God, but fellow heirs with Christ (Rom. 8)—provided that we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified together.

In Asaph, let us lift our mind from earthly things to heavenly ones. According to the prophet, let us also remove stones from the road (Jer. 50)—that is, let us take sins away from the path of holy conduct.

In Josaphat, let us judge rightly, examining our sins as though they were subject to us. For, as the Apostle says, “if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged by the Lord” (1 Cor. 11).

In Joram, when we have risen with Christ, let us seek the things that are above and think upon the things that are above, not those upon the earth. Made exalted in the Lord, let us have our way of life [Col. 0339B] in heaven (Col. 3).

In Ozia, let us henceforth be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of His might, so that, while we fight in this way, Satan may swiftly be crushed beneath our feet (Eph. 6).

In Joatham, let us do perfect works and thereby be perfect and whole, failing in no kind of temptation, since Truth itself says: “You must be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5).

In Achas, let us grasp that for which we have been grasped, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, so that we may apprehend the true life, which is Christ. “I am,” He says, “the light and the life [Col. 0339C] of the world” (John 8).

In Ezechia, having been freed from every sickness of the soul, let us ascend into the temple of God and do His will. Strengthened by the Lord’s power, may we deserve to have the sun of righteousness rise for us, though it sets for the wicked (Mal. 4). Wherever sin, and death from sin, have drawn near [“and” appears redundant], let us turn to the Lord and implore Him with tears in repentance until, moved by mercy, He raises us up and makes us live with spiritual life.

In Manasse, having forgotten past evils, let us always, during the night of this present age, remember the name of the Lord. Let us not seek vengeance, nor remember the injuries inflicted by our neighbors; rather, forgiving [Col. 0339D] everyone’s debts, may we deserve to have our own sins released by the Lord, who says: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6).

In Amon, let us stand in faith and cling faithfully to the faithful Lord. For “love believes all things” (1 Cor. 13), while “faith is the substance of things hoped for and the proof of things not seen”; for what does someone hope for if he sees it? (Heb. 6). Faith, therefore, makes us children of Abraham, who “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4). Through faith all our fathers likewise obtained testimony that they were righteous. Let us therefore live by faith, so that we may be justified by faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1).

In Josia, let us seek where we ought to burn incense to the Lord—namely, ourselves—presenting our bodies [Col. 0340A] as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice to God (Rom. 12), offering the sacrifice of praise to the Lord through our words (Ps. 115), and sacrificing through our thoughts contrite and humbled hearts and contrite spirits. Dedicated to God in these three things—thought, word, and deed—let us be found to be unblemished sacrifices. Having become hearers who are not fruitless, let us repent for those things that the divine law reproves in us, going before His face in confession (Ps. 94), so that, having received our satisfaction, He may turn His anger away from us.

In Jechonia, let us be prepared for the Lord’s coming and always watchful (Luke 21), lest our hearts be weighed down with feasting, drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and that day come upon us suddenly. For it will come like a snare [Col. 0340B] upon all who dwell upon the face of the earth. Avoiding being evil and useless and, by the example of the foolish virgins [the second “and” is an apparent scribal error], watching and preparing ourselves, so that when the Lord comes we may enter as a bride into the Lord’s joy and be admitted to the eternal wedding feast.

In Joachim, let us deserve to become the Lord’s resurrection, rising from the death of sin to the life of righteousness. For in baptism we were buried with Christ so that we might live with Him through righteousness. This is the first resurrection, in which only the righteous are raised. In the second, however, both the ungodly and sinners, as well as the faithful and perfect, will rise: some to the resurrection of life, others to the resurrection of judgment (John 5). “Blessed,” John says, “and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection [Col. 0340C]; over such the second death has no power” (Rev. 20).

In Joachim, let us deserve to be called with the righteous into the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world, at the right hand (Matt. 25).

In Zalathiel, let us ask one petition of the Lord: that we may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of our life and behold His will (Ps. 22). For everyone who asks receives (Luke 11). Let us always ask the Lord in the name of the Savior—that is, let us ask for what pertains to true salvation—for the Savior says: “Whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you” (John 14). Let our requests be just, lest our prayer turn into sin.

In Zorobabel, let us strive with every effort to become both disciples [Col. 0340D] of the heavenly and true Teacher and teachers of disciples, so that whatever we have learned we may fulfill in practice and teach to others. “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 21). Whoever has been invited to the spiritual banquet should invite others as well, so that the house may be filled with those reclining at table (Luke 14).

In Abiud, may God be our Father and may we be sons and daughters to Him. Giving birth to spiritual children in Christ, let us be their fathers, at once disciples and teachers; being both fathers and sons, taught and begotten by the Lord, let us teach and beget a people for the Lord, so that such offspring may reign eternally with the Father.

In Eliachim, let us rise here in spirit, and there, raised up, live in a holy and spiritual body [Col. 0341A]. For the one death of our Redeemer brought salvation through our two deaths, and His one resurrection provided two resurrections: in the present time, the soul’s vivification from the death of sin, and in the future [Col. 0342A], the incorruptible resurrection of the body.

In Assur, with the Lord’s help . . . (The rest is missing.)

## In the Year of the Lord 616. Ethelbert, King of the Angles

[Col. 0341]

## Historical Notice on Ethelbert

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca of the Middle and Later Ages.)* (C)

[Col. 0341B] Ethelbert, or Edilbert, the first Christian king of the Kentish people in England, died on February 24, 616. No writing of his survives, but Bale, p. 73, and Priscus, p. 105, citing Bede, note that he wrote the *Decrees of Judgments*, or that first great Charter, also approved by the other kings of the Heptarchy in England. Concerning it, besides David Wilkins, volume I of the *Collection of the Ancient Laws of the English*, London, [Col. 0342B] 1721, folio, see what Thornagh Gourdon recently noted in his *History of Parliament*, published in English at London in 1731. He also wrote a book of letters, chiefly to Saint Gregory the Pope and to Saint Augustine, apostle of the English and first archbishop of Canterbury. Concerning this Ethelbert, see Baronius and the *Acts of the Saints* under February 24; concerning that Augustine, under May 26.

[Col. 0341]

## Donations of Ethelbert, King of the Angles, to Various Churches

*(Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, pp. 110, 126, 167.) (C, S)

### I. Donation of King Ethelbert of the Land on Which the Monastery of the Apostles Peter and Paul Is Situated, with the Adjacent Lands

[Col. 0341C]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let it be known to all, present and future, that I, Athelbert, by the grace of God king of the Angles, having been converted from an idolater into a worshiper of Christ through my spiritual father Augustine, have through that bishop handed over to God a certain portion of my own land, beneath the eastern wall of the city of Dorobernia, where, through that same founder in Christ, I established a monastery in honor of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. Together with that land and everything belonging to the monastery, I have granted it perpetual freedom, [so that neither] [Col. 0341D] I, nor any of my successors who are kings, nor any authority, ecclesiastical or secular, may ever usurp anything from it; rather, everything shall remain under the free jurisdiction of its abbot. If anyone should attempt to diminish or invalidate anything of this donation of ours, let him, by the authority of the blessed Pope Gregory and of our apostle Augustine, and by our own curse, be separated here from all communion with the holy Church and, on the day of judgment, from the fellowship of all the elect.

The land on which the monastery of the apostles [Col. 0342C] Peter and Paul is situated, together with the adjacent land, is enclosed by these boundaries: on the east, the church of Saint Martin, and from there eastward to Be Siwenidoune; then northward to Be Wykyngmearch; again eastward and southward to Be Bureyaremearch; then southward and westward to Be Kyngesmearch; again northward and eastward to Be Kingesmearch; then westward to Ritherchepe, and so northward to Dryttingstrete.

This was enacted in the city of Dorobernia in the year from the incarnation of Christ 605, in the sixth indiction. I, Athelbert, king of the Angles, confirmed this donation with the sign of the holy cross in my own hand. I, Augustine, archbishop by the grace of God, willingly subscribed. I, Aswald, the king’s son, performed this. I, Hanugi, the son, a duke, approved. I, Hocca, the count, consented. I, Andemund, the referendary, approved. [Col. 0342D] I, Graphio, the count, blessed it. I, Tangi, the king’s son and a nobleman, confirmed it. I, Pinca, consented. I, Geddi, strengthened it.

### II. Charter of Athelbert

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let it be known to all, present and future, that I, Athelbert, by the grace of God king of the Angles, having been made a worshiper of Christ from an idolater through my spiritual father Augustine, [Col. 0343A] have through that bishop handed over to God a certain portion of my own land beneath the eastern wall of the city of Dorobernia, where, through that same founder in Christ, I established a monastery in honor of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. Together with that land and everything belonging to the monastery, I have granted it perpetual freedom, so that neither I, nor any of my successors who are kings, nor any authority, ecclesiastical or secular, may ever usurp anything from it; rather, everything shall remain under the free jurisdiction of its abbot. If anyone should attempt to diminish or invalidate anything of this donation of ours, let him, by the authority of the blessed Pope Gregory and of our apostle Augustine, and by our own curse, be separated here from all communion with the holy Church [Col. 0343B] and, on the day of judgment, from the fellowship of all the elect.

This land is enclosed by these boundaries: on the east, the church of Saint Martin, and from there eastward to Be Siwenidoune; then northward to Be Wgkyngmearch; again eastward and southward to Be Bureyaremearch; then southward and westward to Be Kyngesmearch; again northward to Be Kyngesmearch; then westward to Ritherechepe, and so northward to Dryttingstrete. This was enacted in the city of Dorobernia in the year from the incarnation of Christ 605, in the sixth indiction.

I, Athelbert, king of the Angles, confirmed this donation with the sign of the holy cross in my own hand. I, Augustine, archbishop by the grace of God, willingly subscribed. I, Edbald, the king’s son, performed this. I, Hamigisilus, the duke, approved. I, Hocca, the count, consented. [Col. 0343C] I, Angemund, the referendary, approved. I, Graphio, the count, blessed it. I, Tangisilus, the king’s nobleman, confirmed it. I, Pinca, consented. I, Geddy, strengthened it.

Athelbert, king of the Angles, a Catholic through the mercy of almighty God, to all the faithful of his people who await in blessed hope the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ: greetings and the blessedness of eternal life, granted by the clemency of the highest King.

I, Athelbert, established upon my father’s throne and granted peace by divine favor, having now held royal power for ten five-year periods, and having been illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit through venerable teachers of the holy faith, turned with all my heart from the error of false gods to the worship of the one true God. In order that I not appear ungrateful to Him from whose holy seat the light of truth shone upon us who were sitting in the region of the shadow of death, among the other churches that I built at the instruction and urging of the most blessed Pope Gregory and our holy father Augustine, I constructed from the foundations a monastery for the most blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, and for Paul, the teacher of the nations. I strove to adorn it with lands and various gifts of property, and I caused God-fearing monks to be gathered there. With the counsel of that most reverend archbishop Augustine, I chose from his holy community a venerable man, Peter the monk, who had been sent with him from the apostolic see, and appointed him abbot over them, as ecclesiastical order requires.

Desiring to advance this monastery toward the fitting height of its dignity [Col. 0344A] and eager to enlarge the boundaries of its possessions, with sound mind and unimpaired judgment, and with the consent of my son Edbald and of my other nobles and chief men, for the redemption of my soul and in hope of eternal reward, I also offered it a village called Sturiga, otherwise called Cistelei, with all revenues rightfully belonging to it, together with slaves, cultivated and uncultivated woods, meadows, pastures, marshes, rivers, and the adjacent maritime boundaries enclosing it on one side. I granted everything, movable and immovable, for the use of the brothers serving God there under the regular discipline and monastic way of life. I also offered a silver vessel [*missurum*; the reading is uncertain], [Col. 0344B] a golden scepter, another saddle with a golden bridle and adorned with gems, a silver mirror, an *armilcaisia closerica* [an uncertain garment or textile term], an ornamented shirt, which had been sent to me as a gift from the lord Pope Gregory of the apostolic see—all of these I gladly offered to the aforesaid monastery.

That monastery the servant of God Augustine also richly furnished with relics of the holy apostles and martyrs and with various ecclesiastical ornaments sent to him from the apostolic see. He ordered that he himself and all his successors be buried there by apostolic authority, since Scripture says that it is “not a city of the dead, but of the living.” There I also provided burial for myself and my successors, hoping that one day I might be freed from the bonds of sins by that chief of the apostolic order to whom the Lord gave the power of binding and loosing and entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and that I might be admitted through the gate of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0344C] Let no bishop, nor any of my royal successors, presume to injure or disturb this monastery in any way, nor dare to usurp any subjection over it whatsoever. Rather, the abbot appointed there shall freely govern and order it, within and without, with the counsel of the brothers and according to the fear of God, so that on the day of the Lord he may deserve to hear that sweet voice of our most merciful Redeemer saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

I established this donation in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, through divine generosity, so that the forgiveness of sins might be granted to me in all things, with the counsel of the most reverend father Augustine; and I commissioned Augemund the presbyter to write it. Therefore [Col. 0344D], concerning everything written here, if anyone should presume to diminish anything thereof, let him know that he will have to render an account before God, the most just Judge, and before the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

This donation was confirmed in the presence of these witnesses: the most reverend father Augustine, first archbishop of the Church of Dorobernia; Mellitus and Justus, prelates of London and Rochester; the religious servant of Christ, Laurence the presbyter; Edbald, my son; Hamigisilus, the duke; Augemund, the referendary; Hocca and Graphio, counts; Tangesilus, Pinca, Geddi, and Aldhun, the king’s chief men; and many other persons of various ranks. It was enacted in the forty-fifth year of our reign, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

### III

[Col. 0345A]

Aedelbearht, king of the West Saxons or of the Kentish people, sold to Bishop Waermund twenty acres of land, one and a half *vincula* [a land measure] in the city of Strobi, and one *mansus*, for his money: fifteen pounds and thirty *mancuses* (as it is written in the charter), in the year 790. The subscribers are: Aerdelbearht, king; Crolnolth, archbishop; [Col. 0346A] Eulhstan, Swithun, Guthheard, and Dioruull, bishops; Ettheldred and Aelfred, the king’s sons; Uullaf and Uurseth, abbots; Uulthem, presbyter; Uuerenberth and Celmund, ministers; Eannulf, Oric, Uulfhere, Aetheluulf; Humbearht, Uullaf, Aldred, Aethelred; Dryhtwald and Biorhtuulf, dukes.

[Col. 0345]

## Decree Concerning the Non-Removal of the Property of God and the Church

*(Wilkins, Collection of the Ancient Laws of the English, vol. I, p. 1.)*

These are the judgments which [Note: [Col. 0345B] Aethelbirhtus. According to the Savilian Chronicles, King Aethelbirht began to reign in the year of Christ 561 and ceased in 616. Malmesbury and Bede write that he died in the twenty-first year after receiving the Christian faith. Bede says that he died in the year 613—which is 616 according to Saxon chronology—in Book II, chapter 5 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, where, among other things, he says of him: “Among the other good things that he provided for his people, he also established, with the counsel of the wise, judicial decrees for them according to Roman examples. These were written in the language of the Angles and have remained to this day, being observed by them. Among these [Col. 0345C] he first established how the person who should steal anything belonging either to the church, or to a bishop, or to any of the other orders, ought to make compensation, clearly wishing to provide protection for those whose persons and teaching they had received.”] King Ethelbert established these laws in the days of Augustine.

[Col. 0345B] **I.** [Note: [Col. 0345C] **God’s property and the Church’s.** The first part of this law is to be understood of sacrilege and theft: namely, that things dedicated to God, the Church, and so forth, if taken secretly, must be compensated. King Alfred below, in law 6, wishes sacrilege to be compensated by a fine (*mulcta*) according to the value, and in addition either the thief’s hand to be cut off or redeemed according to the man’s assessed value. In civil law, the jurist Paulus, *L. Sacrilegii* 9, ad *l. Jul. pec.*, book XLIII of the *Pandects*, title 13, says: “Sacrilegious persons who have plundered public sacred property are punished capitally; but those who have violated private sacred property or entered unguarded shrines deserve more than thieves and less than sacrilegious persons.” He says that the punishment for sacrilege ought to be established according to the status of the person and the condition of the thing, as well as according to time, age, and sex—more severely or more leniently—and immediately reports various punishments formerly imposed: some sacrilegious persons, he says, were condemned to the beasts, others burned alive, and others hanged on the gallows. In canon law, anyone who removed ecclesiastical property dedicated to God was judged infamous and struck with anathema or excommunicated. *Decretum* of Gregory, Causa 12, Question 2. In Gothic and Scanian law the most severe punishment was inflicted on thieves—namely, hanging without the defense ordinarily allowed to a person accused of theft—whereas no special punishment was established for sacrilegious persons. See Stiernhook, *De jure Sueonum et Gothorum vetusto*, p. 368 ff. In the provincial laws of the present kingdom of Sweden, a sacrilegious person pays the bishop a fine of three marks for violating the peace of the Church; for theft, however, he is punished according to the provincial laws. He enjoys no protection in a temple or cemetery, because he has offended against that peace. Loccenius, *Leges civiles regni Sueciae*, title “On ecclesiastical law,” chapter 18, p. 301. Among the Danes a light punishment is prescribed for thieves, as is read in book VI of the *Danish Law*, chapter 17, under “Theft”: beating with rods, simple or double restitution of the thing secretly taken, and *Bremmerholm*, that is, the naval workhouse. But a breaker-in and plunderer of a money chest, box, or cupboard found in a church is punished as a robber, by wheel and stake; whoever plunders from a church things not secured by locks is hanged on the gallows; and whoever carries off less valuable things is beaten with rods at the stake and punished with perpetual bonds and labor. See book VI of the *Danish Law*, chapter 16, § 4. Concerning sacrilege, King Theodoric says in his edict, chapter 126: “If anyone drags people from churches—that is, from sacred places—or presumes to carry anything away by force, he shall be punished capitally.” According to the twelfth law of the Frisians, whoever breaks into a shrine and takes anything sacred from it is led to the sea; on the sandbank normally covered by the incoming tide, his ears are split, he is castrated, and he is sacrificed to the gods whose temples he violated. See Lindenbrog, *Codex legum antiquarum*, vol. I, p. 508. In King Childebert’s constitution, sacrilege committed by a servile person is punished by one hundred lashes. See Baluze, *Capitularia regum Francorum*, vol. I, p. 7. In the capitularies of the emperors Charles and Louis, book VI, chapter 304, the following is stated concerning sacrilegious persons: “If anyone, breaking into churches and their property, brings or inflicts any injury upon priests and ministers, or upon worship itself and the place, or does anything injurious to divine worship, he shall know that convicted or confessing offenders are to be punished by capital sentence.” And in the Canons of Isaac, bishop of Langres, title 7, sacrilegious persons are called infamous and are not to be admitted either to accusation or testimony. See Baluze, *Capitularia regum Francorum*, vol. I, p. 1267 ff. Compare Droco’s judgment on this matter in the appendix to the *Acts of the Ancients*, chapter 146, vol. II of Baluze’s *Capitularies*, p. 1549.] 

God’s property and the Church’s shall be compensated twelvefold; a bishop’s property elevenfold; a priest’s property ninefold; a deacon’s property sixfold; a cleric’s property threefold; the Church’s peace shall be compensated twofold; the monastery’s peace [Note: [Col. 0346D] **The monastery’s peace.** What we said concerning the peace of the Church must likewise be said concerning the peace of the monastery: namely, that every violation of the peace is to be compensated twice over according to its dignity and value. In the Constitutions issued under Aethelred in the year 1015, the following law is established concerning violation of the monastery’s peace: “Violation of the peace of a chief monastery shall be atoned for with compensations worthy of the matter, according to the king’s peace—that is, with five pounds according to English law; and violation of the peace of a middle-ranking monastery with 120 shillings, that is, according to the king’s fine; and of a lesser monastery with 60 shillings, and of a rural church with 30 shillings.”] shall be compensated twofold.

[Col. 0346B] [Note: [Col. 0346D] **The peace of the Church.** That is, if quarrels or disputes arise in a church, a double fine is to be paid according to the dignity of the church. Withraed, at the beginning of his laws, says that violation of ecclesiastical peace is to be compensated by 50 shillings. In the laws of Aethelred, violation of the peace of the Church was punished in the same way as violation of the king’s peace; and among the Southern English, whoever fought in a church forfeited everything he possessed, and it was at the king’s discretion whether he should live or not. Homicide within the walls of a church, however, is said to be inexpiable. King Cnut, in law 3, concerning the peace of the Church, says: “Not all churches are equally worthy of earthly honor, although they possess the same ecclesiastical consecration. Violation of the peace of a chief church is compensated in the same way as the compensation for property protected by the king’s peace—that is, by five pounds according to English law; and in Kent, for violation of the peace, five pounds were paid to the king and three to the archbishop; for a middle-ranking church, 120 shillings, which is the same as the king’s fine; for a lesser church, 60; and for a rural church, 30 shillings. Among the ancient Swedes and Goths, judgments and punishments for violation of ecclesiastical peace consisted of a double assessment, and all capital crimes that the bishops brought before the ecclesiastical court were punished not with sword and fire but by monetary fine; indeed, there was absolutely no case in that episcopal court from which some legally prescribed payment did not return to the bishop. See Stiernhook, *De jure Sueonum et Gothorum vetusto*, final chapter. Today, violation of ecclesiastical peace among the Swedes is punished by a fine of three marks. See Loccenius, *Leges Civiles Suecicae*, p. 301. Among the Danes, violation of sacred or ecclesiastical peace was punished according to age: the younger were beaten with rods and whips, while adults were put in the stocks if the crime was not capital. See *Danish Law*, book VI, chapter 3. Ecclesiastical peace was held sacred among the ancient Alemanni and Franks, as is asserted in a thousand places in the capitularies and in Lindenbrog’s *Code of Ancient Laws*. See the capitularies of the emperors Charles and Louis, book IV, chapter 13, and book V, chapter 185; the capitulary of King Charles, title 15; the capitulary of Charles the Bald, Baluze edition, p. 177, and elsewhere throughout. Concerning the preservation of public peace, Emperor Frederick established an edict with a penalty against its violators. *Feudal Customs*, book II, title 27. Nevertheless, Charles humanely enacted that the children of those who had been outlawed under the imperial ban for violating the peace should again be admitted by their patrons to dependent estates. See Tholosanus, *Syntagma juris universi*, book XXXV, chapter 1, § 33.] 

[Col. 0347A] **II.** If the king summons his people to him, and anyone harms them there, he shall make double compensation, and 50 shillings shall be paid to the king.

**III.** If the king feasts in someone’s house and anyone causes damage there, double compensation shall be made.

**IV.** If a free man secretly takes anything from the king [Note: [Col. 0347D] Theft committed against the king has no special punishment in the older laws, so far as I know, apart from this law. Theft committed by a free man, however, was punished more severely than theft committed by a slave. Thus in the Burgundian Laws, title 70: “If a free man and a slave commit theft together, the free man shall pay three times the amount stolen, provided it was not a capital crime; but the slave shall be assigned to punishment by the cudgel.” Emperor Louis permits a free man accused of theft to defend himself by surety and oath; but if two or three persons accuse him of theft a second time, he may contend against one of them with shield and club. See the Lombard Laws, book I, title 25, law 76.] he shall compensate ninefold.

**V.** If anyone kills a man in the king’s estate, he shall compensate with 50 shillings [Note: [Col. 0348B] Namely, for violation of the king’s peace, which was held sacred among the Anglo-Saxons, like the peace of God. See the treaty of Eadmund and Guthrum, and the laws of Aethelred and Cnut. A separate punishment was also established for homicide. The same is observed in the following law, 6.]

**VI.** If anyone kills a free man, the king shall receive 50 shillings as his lordly compensation.

[Col. 0348A] **VII.** If anyone kills a servant of the king’s chief smith or cupbearer, he shall pay the ordinary moderate fine (*leod-geld*) [Note: [Col. 0348B] *Leod-geld* signifies the ordinary fine: namely, that for the killing of servants of the king’s cupbearer or chief smith the same penalty is established as compensates for the life of other slaves, according to the *were*, that is, the assessed value of each person’s life. The reason is that those servants are under the protection not of the king but of the king’s officials.] 

**VIII.** Violation of the king’s protection [Note: [Col. 0348B] The meaning of this law is that if anyone mistreats a person under the king’s protection—that is, a person under his own jurisdiction or a private person—he shall pay the king 50 shillings for contempt of a privilege that ought to be regarded by all as sacred.] shall be compensated by 50 shillings.

**IX.** If a free man steals from a free man, he shall make threefold compensation, and the king shall have the fine and all the thief’s property.

**X.** If anyone has intercourse with a virgin who is the king’s female slave [Note: [Col. 0348B] In this and the following laws a fine is assigned for fornication with female slaves of the king and of a nobleman. Alfred below, in law 29, orders that, in addition to monetary compensation, if the father consents, the man shall take the woman as his wife. Among the ancient Swedes, a fornicating woman was always held infamous unless she married the man with whom she had had intercourse. Monetary punishment was imposed only on men, varying according to the circumstances; such is the rule in Uplandic law, where the censure of the Church is scarcely avoided, since the guilt is diminished and the penalty removed by the frequency of illicit intercourse. For a girl on the first occasion, four and a half marks are owed; for a widow, three marks; on the second occasion, three marks for the girl and one and a half for the widow; thereafter nothing is owed. The Frisians, ancient Goths in Spain, expelled fornicating women from the province or city after flogging them, and if they returned, assigned them to some poor man in perpetual servitude. Today, among the Swedes, six marks are paid to the bishop or to the holder of episcopal jurisdiction for illicit intercourse. See Loccenius, *Swedish Civil Law*, p. 291. Among the Danes, whoever violates a woman pays twelve ounces of silver to her master, while the woman pays six ounces, and both atone publicly through absolution. If anyone commits rape upon a woman or virgin in the king’s hall, he is punished by the loss of two fingers. If the woman has been entrusted with keys to the stores where beer, food, clothing, money, or other objects are kept, her violator is punished like a manifest thief against his fellow servant. See *Danish Law*, book VI, chapter 13. Among the Bavarians there is a law of King Theodoric, title 7, law 13: “If anyone has intercourse with a virgin slave, he shall settle the matter with four shillings.” Among the Lombards, King Rothari established that if anyone fornicates with a Gentile slave woman, he shall pay her master 20 shillings, and if with a Roman woman, 12 shillings. See Lindenbrog, *Code of Ancient Laws*, vol. I, pp. 416 and 579. See also book XLVIII, § “On the Julian Law concerning adulterers,” and book IX of the *Code*, title 9.] he shall compensate with 50 shillings.

**XI.** If she is a mill-servant [the reading *molens serva* is uncertain], he shall compensate with 25 shillings; if she is of the third rank, with 12 shillings.

**XII.** The king’s female purveyor shall be compensated with 20 shillings.

[Col. 0349A] **XIII.** If anyone kills someone in the estate of a count, he shall compensate with 12 shillings [Note: [Col. 0349B] Namely, for violation of the peace within the count’s territory; for the homicide itself, however, another fine according to the assessed value of the life must be paid.]

**XIV.** If anyone has intercourse with the count’s female cupbearer, he shall compensate with 12 shillings.

**XV.** Violation of the protection of a commoner shall be compensated by 6 shillings.

**XVI.** If anyone has intercourse with a commoner’s female cupbearer, he shall compensate with 6 shillings; for another female slave, he shall pay 50 *sceattas*; for one of the third rank, 30 *sceattas*.

**XVII.** If anyone enters another’s house first, he shall compensate with 6 shillings; whoever enters second, with 3 shillings; thereafter, each person with one shilling [Note: [Col. 0349B] The legislator does not state what wrongdoing someone is presumed to be plotting when entering another’s house; the preceding laws suggest that it is fornication.]

**XVIII.** If anyone lends weapons to another [Note: [Col. 0349B] Alfred says that the author of the damage and the owner of the weapons are liable to equal punishment; but if the owner of the weapons wishes to prove that he knew of no fraud in their transfer, he is free from blame. See Alfred’s Laws, chapter 19. Cnut, in law 73, assigns compensation for damage caused by another’s weapons, which had been placed at the door, to the person who handled the weapons, after the owner of the weapons has cleared himself by proving that the damage occurred without his knowledge and against his will. See what Henry I says below, chapter 87, concerning an offense committed with borrowed weapons. Among the ancient Swedes, according to West Gothic law, homicides committed through the lending of another’s weapon were punished in the same way as voluntary homicides; indeed, the owner of the weapon was also fined, because he was regarded as having possessed something that contributed to the man’s death and thus shared in the misfortune. See Stiernhook, *On Ancient Swedish Law*, p. 357. Today, among the Swedes, the borrower is liable not only for fraud and malicious intent but also for fault committed through carelessness and negligence. See Loccenius, *Synopsis of Swedish Public Law*, p. 353. Among the Danes there is the following law: “If anyone lends another person his weapon—sword, knife, spear, club, or any other weapon of that kind capable of causing greater harm—to one who is quarreling with someone else, knowing that the recipient will certainly abuse it to another’s destruction, and if the lender is convicted of this, then, if injury has resulted, he shall pay a fine one-half smaller than that of the person who injured the other with the weapons supplied to him.” See *Danish Law*, book VI, chapter 10. The Lombard law states: “If anyone simply lends his weapons to another, and the recipient does some evil with them, the blame shall not be attributed to the person who lent them but to the one who committed the evil with them. Conversely, if the lender consented to the evil being done, he shall be his accomplice in making good that evil.” See Lindenbrog, *Code of Ancient Laws*, vol. I, p. 550.] where there is a quarrel, and no harm is done, he shall compensate with 6 shillings.

[Col. 0349B] **XIX.** If a robbery has been committed, he shall compensate with 6 shillings.

**XX.** If anyone kills someone, he shall compensate with 20 shillings.

**XXI.** If anyone kills someone, he shall pay the ordinary moderate fine of 100 shillings.

**XXII.** If anyone kills someone at an open grave, he shall compensate with 20 shillings and, within 40 days, pay the entire ordinary fine.

**XXIII.** If the killer leaves the country, his kinsmen shall pay half the ordinary fine.

**XXIV.** If anyone binds a free man, he shall compensate with 20 shillings.

**XXV.** If anyone kills a commoner’s table-companion, he shall compensate with 6 shillings.

**XXVI.** If a guest kills the chief fellow-drinker, he shall compensate with 80 shillings.

**XXVII.** If he kills the second, he shall compensate with 60 shillings; for the third, he shall compensate with 40 shillings.

**XXVIII.** If a free man violates an enclosure, he shall compensate with 6 shillings.

**XXIX.** If anyone takes away something kept inside, he shall make triple compensation.

[Col. 0350B] **XXX.** If a free man climbs over an enclosure, he shall compensate with 4 shillings.

**XXXI.** If anyone kills someone, he shall compensate every person according to the proper assessment (*agene scaete*) and in sound money [Note: [Col. 0349D] *Agene scaette*, properly understood, denotes the true assessed value of anyone’s life.]

**XXXII.** If a free man has intercourse with the wife of a free man, he shall redeem the value of her life, purchase another wife with his own money, and bring her to the other man [Note: [Col. 0349D] King Cnut wishes adultery to be compensated by what has been done; namely, as he explains in the following law, 50 [Col. 0350B], if a wife has intercourse with another man while her husband is alive, she shall thereafter become an object of universal infamy, and her true husband shall have everything she possessed; moreover, she shall lose both her nose and her ears. William the Conqueror, in law 14, wishes adultery to be compensated according to the assessed value of the life. The laws of the ancient Goths in Spain permit a husband to kill a wife caught with her adulterer immediately; they likewise permit a wife to kill her husband when caught with another woman. Norwegian and Icelandic law allows this not only in the case of one’s own wife but also in that of one’s mother, sister, daughter, or brother’s wife, as though the family’s disgrace were to be avenged by him. The laws of the Spanish Goths and Burgundians require precisely that both be put to death, or neither. Under Scanian law, a person accused of adultery had to appeal to the red-hot iron; if he failed in the case, the man was sent into exile and the woman dismissed from the marriage bed. The Swedish Goths, sparing women’s lives in all crimes, prescribed disgrace or some bodily punishment for adultery. Westmannic law orders that either the adulteress’s ears or her nose be cut off. Uplandic law, under the eminent author Ladislaus, removes her ears, nose, and hair together. Swedish municipal law orders a husband who catches his wife in adultery to strip her of her dowry and gives him power over her life. If the husband is content with a fine, the law fines the adulterer and adulteress separately 40 marks each. But if the adulterer cannot pay the fines, public or civic stones, *Stadzens Stena*, are placed upon the adulteress’s shoulders, and a cord is tied to the adulterer’s genitals, so that, burdened in this way, she may publicly drag her weary companion through the town. This law is now obsolete and no longer in force; today the adulteress is deprived only of her dowry and all her property. See Stiernhook and Loccenius in the works cited above. Among the Danes, the adulterer and adulteress are fined all their property and money; if they offend again, they are expelled from the country; and when they break marital fidelity a third time, the adulterer is punished capitally, while the adulteress is drowned. See *Danish Law*, book VI, chapter 23, §§ 24. According to Visigothic law, whoever kills an adulterer together with the adulteress is not regarded as a homicide, book III, title 4, “On adulteries.” Slaves and female slaves, however, are to be beaten or tortured with one or two hundred lashes, as often as necessary, so that the truth may be discovered and recognized with certainty. King Theodoric, in his edict, law 61, wishes a man who commits adultery with a widow to be burned in avenging flames. Among the Lombards, children born of adultery were excluded from inheritance, book I, title 32, law 3. See the Salic law concerning adulteries with female slaves, title 27. In the capitularies of the emperors Charles and Louis, book VI, § 325, adulteries are punished by capital penalty. See book VII, § 298. In civil law, the punishment of the Julian law was the ultimate penalty, *l. Quamvis* 30, final paragraph, *Code*, “On the Julian Law concerning adultery”; likewise the Julian law concerning adulteries, under public prosecutions, in Justinian; and, concerning the time when Octavian Caesar issued the law under the name of Julius, laws 1 and 2, “On the Julian Law concerning adultery,” in Suetonius, *Augustus*. In later times Roman law allowed a husband to kill an adulterer of low and base status caught in his own house with his wife in the act. *L. Marito* and *l. Si adulterium*, § “The Emperors,” on the Julian Law concerning adultery; *P.* [probably *Pandects*], *l. Gracchus* 4, *Code*, same title, book III, § “If a husband,” against Sulla, in the *Pandects*. Under the Novels the punishment of women is milder, namely, confinement in a monastery. *Authentic*, “But today,” concerning the Julian Law on adultery, chapter [uncertain], § “But if at any time,” “so that no one may be permitted by law,” in the *Authentic Collection*, title 9. The cutting off of the nose is likewise prescribed as a punishment for adultery, Novel in the Constitution of Emperor Leo, Constitution 32. Under pontifical law, suffering adultery is not considered as serious a crime as killing one’s wife. See *Causa* 33, Question 2, “If there is something true,” where the reasons are given. Thus, in the court of conscience, a husband may not kill an adulterer or his adulterous wife: canon “Among these things,” together with the gloss, and canon “To admonish,” Causa 33, Question 2; for only a judge, or a prince who possesses the power of the sword, may kill.] 

[Col. 0351A] **XXXIII.** If anyone pierces the right thigh with a spear, he shall compensate it according to its value [Note: [Col. 0351D] In the following 39 laws compensation is established for various wounds, most of which are contained in Alfred’s law 40 and William the Conqueror’s laws 12 and 13. Among the Visigoths compensation formerly existed for limbs that had been amputated or mutilated. If a hand was amputated, 9 marks were paid for the wound and 3 marks for the mutilation. For the fingers of hand and foot, 9 marks were paid for each wound; for mutilation, 12 shillings for the thumb, 6 shillings for the adjacent finger, half a mark for the longest finger, 2 shillings for the next, and 1 shilling for the smallest. Amputation of the nose was compensated by 9 marks for the wound and 3 for the mutilation. [Col. 0352B] The same compensation was made for an eye, hair, and teeth. If someone was castrated, 9 marks were paid for the wound and the same amount for the mutilation. See the Visigothic laws, edited by Olaus Rudbeck, p. 44 ff. Modern Swedish civil law differs little from Visigothic law in its compensation for amputation of the fingers of hand and foot. See Loccenius in the *Civil Laws of Sweden*, p. 233 ff., and in the *Provincial Laws*, p. 310. A wound in the skin, chest, or arm, in the loins, or in the leg is compensated by 20 marks according to Swedish law. The four front upper or lower teeth are compensated by 3 marks for mutilation and 9 marks for a wound. See Loccenius, *Civil and Provincial Laws*, title 13, “On voluntary wounds.” Among the Danes, if anyone cuts off or amputates another’s nose, ear, tongue, hand, foot, finger, or similar limb, or knocks out or excavates an eye, he is punished by perpetual confinement in the naval workhouse at Copenhagen or by exile; he loses all his property, which is divided equally between the injured person and his master. See *Danish Law*, books VI and VII. In the Sicilian Constitutions, if anyone strikes another with forbidden weapons—namely, sword, spear, or shield—so that the person does not die, the striker loses the hand with which he struck. See Lindenbrog, *Code of Ancient Laws*, vol. I, p. 706. Among the Lombards, an eye is compensated at half the value of a homicide; an ear, by 2 shillings; a lip, by 6 shillings; each front tooth, by 4 shillings; an arm, by 6 shillings; a hand, by half its own value; the thumb of the hand, by 8 shillings; the great toe, by 4; the second finger of the hand, by 6, of the foot, by 2; the third finger of hand and foot, by 3 shillings; the fourth finger of the hand, by 2, of the foot, by 1; and the fifth finger of the hand, by 4, of the foot, by 1 shilling. See further concerning the kinds of blows and wounds and their punishments among the Lombards, book I of the Lombard Laws, vol. I of Lindenbrog’s *Code of Ancient Laws*, p. 522 ff. See concerning compensation for wounds the Burgundian Laws, titles 11 and 48; the Salic Law, title 19; the Alamannic Law, titles 59 and 65; the Bavarian Law, title 3, chapter 1; the Ripuarian Law, titles 1 and 2 ff.; and the Frisian Law, title 22, where penalties and fines not very different from those we have enumerated are prescribed for mutilation, amputation, and fracture of bodily limbs.]

**XXXIV.** If someone seizes the hair, 50 *sceattas* shall be paid as compensation.

**XXXV.** If the bone appears, he shall compensate with 3 shillings.

**XXXVI.** If the bone is injured, he shall compensate with 4 shillings.

**XXXVII.** If it is completely broken, he shall compensate with 10 shillings.

**XXXVIII.** If both occur, he shall compensate with 20 shillings.

**XXXIX.** If the shoulder is made lame, he shall compensate with 20 shillings.

**XL.** If one ear hears nothing, he shall compensate with 25 shillings.

**XLI.** If the ear is cut off, 12 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**XLII.** If the ear is pierced, he shall compensate with 3 shillings.

[Col. 0351B] **XLIII.** If the ear is cut short, 6 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**XLIV.** If the eye is knocked out, he shall compensate with 50 shillings.

**XLV.** If the bone or eye is injured, 20 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**XLVI.** If the nose is pierced, 9 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**XLVII.** If one membrane is pierced, he shall compensate with 3 shillings.

**XLVIII.** If both are pierced, 6 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**XLIX.** If each nostril is cut short, each shall be compensated by 6 shillings.

[Col. 0352A] **L.** If they are pierced, 6 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**LI.** Whoever cuts off the bone of the chin shall compensate with 20 shillings.

**LII.** For the four front teeth, 6 shillings for each; for the tooth next to them, 4 shillings; for the one next after that, 3 shillings; and thereafter 1 shilling for each. If speech becomes worse, 12 shillings; if the jaw is broken, 6 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**LIII.** Whoever pierces the arm shall compensate with 6 shillings. If the arm is broken, 6 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**LIV.** If the thumb is cut off, 20 shillings; if the thumb’s nail is cut off, 3 shillings shall be paid as compensation. If anyone cuts off the index finger, he shall compensate with 8 shillings; if the middle finger, with 4 shillings; [Col. 0352B] if the ring finger, with 6 shillings; but if the little finger, with 11 shillings.

**LV.** For each nail, 1 shilling shall be paid as compensation.

**LVI.** For a small mole, 3 shillings; for larger ones, 6 shillings.

**LVII.** If anyone strikes another’s nose with his fist, 3 shillings.

**LVIII.** If there is a wound, 1 shilling; if he receives the wound with a raised hand, he shall compensate with 1 shilling.

**LIX.** If the wound is black outside the clothing, he shall compensate with 30 *sceattas* [Col. 0353A]; if it is beneath the clothing, each shall be compensated by 20 *sceattas*.

**LX.** If the diaphragm is wounded, he shall compensate with 12 shillings; if it is pierced, he shall compensate with 20 shillings.

**LXI.** If anyone is made lame, 30 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**LXII.** If anyone wounds the callus, he shall compensate with 3 shillings.

**LXIII.** If anyone’s genitals are cut off, they shall be compensated by three times the ordinary fine; if they are pierced, he shall compensate with 6 shillings; if anyone makes an incision, he shall compensate with 6 shillings.

**LXIV.** If the thigh is broken, 12 shillings shall be paid as compensation; if the person becomes lame, his friends must judge the matter there.

**LXV.** If a rib is broken, he shall compensate with 3 shillings.

[Col. 0353B] **LXVI.** If anyone pierces the thigh, each incision shall be compensated by 6 shillings; if it penetrates above one thumb’s breadth, 1 shilling; above two thumbbreadths, 2; above that, 3 shillings shall be paid.

**LXVII.** If a vertebra is wounded, 3 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**LXVIII.** If the foot is amputated, 50 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**LXIX.** If the great toe is amputated, 10 shillings shall be paid as compensation.

**LXX.** For each of the other toes, half the value prescribed above for the fingers shall be paid.

**LXXI.** If the nail of the great toe is amputated, 30 *sceattas* shall be paid as compensation; for each of the others, 10 *sceattas*.

[Col. 0353C] **LXXII.** If anyone does something dishonorable to a free-haired woman [Note: [Col. 0353C] **Free-haired woman.** The Saxons always held hair in great reverence, as appears from Gregory of Tours, book V of the *History*, chapter 15, and Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book III, chapter 7. Hence above, in law 34, seizure of the hair is counted among injuries or wounds and compensated by 50 *sceattas*. Here I believe that by “free-haired woman,” following Lombard custom, a virgin is meant, as appears in book II of the Lombard Laws, title 20: “If a Lombard, while alive, gives his daughters in marriage, and leaves others after his death at home unmarried, all are to succeed equally to his estate as heirs, like legitimate male children.” See also the following title, 22. When Diceneus Boroista came to the Goths, he called the priests “wearers of caps,” but ordered the rest of the people to be called “free-haired”; the Goths, adopting the name with great pride, still recall it today in their songs. See Jordanes, *On Gothic Affairs*, chapter 11, and Spelman, *Glossary*, under “Hair.” Hair was a sign of free birth; hence in the Burgundian Laws, title 6, § 4, “to make hair for a slave” means to let his hair grow so that he appears free-born; cutting a person’s hair against his will is counted among crimes.] he shall compensate with 30 shillings.

**LXXIII.** The compensation for a virgin shall be the same as for a free man.

**LXXIV.** Violation of the protection of a superior widow of noble family [Col. 0354A] shall be compensated by 50 shillings; of a second-ranking widow, by 20 shillings; of a third-ranking widow, by 12 shillings; of a fourth-ranking widow, by 6 shillings.

**LXXV.** If anyone takes a widow who is not under her own authority, he shall compensate twice for violating her protection.

**LXXVI.** If a man purchases a virgin for a price, she shall belong to him if the transaction was without fraud; but if fraud is involved, she shall afterward be taken back to her home, and her property shall be returned to her.

**LXXVII.** If she gives birth to a living child, she shall have half the property if the man dies first.

**LXXVIII.** If she wishes to depart with her children, she shall have half the possessions.

**LXXIX.** If the husband wishes to have the children, they shall be reckoned as one child.

**LXXX.** If she does not bear offspring, her kinsmen shall have the property [Col. 0354B]; she shall have maintenance and her dowry.

**LXXXI.** If anyone seizes a virgin by force, he shall give 50 shillings to her owner and afterward redeem her according to the owner’s wishes.

**LXXXII.** If she has been betrothed to another for a price, he shall compensate with 20 shillings.

**LXXXIII.** If she is pregnant, he shall pay 35 shillings, and 15 shillings to the king.

**LXXXIV.** If anyone has intercourse with a slave’s wife while her husband is alive, he shall make double compensation.

**LXXXV.** If a slave kills another innocent person, he shall compensate with all his possessions.

**LXXXVI.** If a slave’s eye and foot are knocked out, they shall be compensated at their entire value.

**LXXXVII.** If anyone binds another person’s slave, he shall compensate with 6 [Col. 0354C] shillings.

**LXXXVIII.** A slave’s robbery shall be compensated by 3 shillings [Note: [Col. 0354C] This law is to be understood of robbery committed against a slave, which is to be compensated by three shillings.]

**LXXXIX.** If a slave steals, he shall make double compensation.

**IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 617. SAINT DEUSDEDIT, ROMAN PONTIFF.**

[Col. 0355]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON POPE DEUSDEDIT

*(From the Pontifical Book, Blanchinius edition, vol. IV.)*

[Col. 0355A] [Note: [Col. 0355A]

**Deusdedit.**—1. After the death of Boniface IV, when the apostolic see had been vacant for five months and twelve days, Deusdedit, distinguished by outstanding virtues and holiness, was created pontiff. It is publicly attested concerning him in the Church on 8 November that he possessed such great merit that, when visiting the sick, he healed a leper by a kiss and cleansed him of leprosy. BINIUS.

**2. Fabrotti’s chronology:** Saint Deusdedit, [Col. 0355B] in the year of Christ 614, in the fifth year of the emperor Heraclius. BLANCH.]

### 3

Although the commonly circulated manuscripts of Anastasius show no vacancy of the see—and the Catalogue of Lucca does likewise—the first Freherian manuscript gives six months and five days. The second Thuanus gives six months and twenty-five days. The Membranaceus-Ambrosianus and the royal Mazarinus agree with it, while the first Thuanus and the second Ambrosianus give seven months and twenty-five days. Finally, the Farfa catalogue indicates an interregnum of thirteen days, both after Boniface IV and after his two successors, Deusdedit and Boniface—incorrect everywhere, and with serious damage to the chronology.

It is plainly evident that none of the interregna just cited is correct. For, whatever point is chosen as the beginning of the enumeration of days—whether the day of death or the day of deposition—one never arrives at a Sunday, unless the reckoning begins from the day of deposition at the Vatican, 25 May. This is indeed often found after Honorius, though with less discrepancy when reckoning from the day of death. Moreover, the definite day of the death and of the accession to the see of Saint Deusdedit cannot be removed; consequently, one must either devise a new interregnum or resort to conjecture.

As for the duration of the see, both the manuscripts and the catalogues establish it as three years and either twenty-three or twenty-four days. Other catalogues, however—such as the fifth of Antonius Pagius, our previously unpublished Blanchinian catalogue, and the second of Mabillon—give three years and twenty days. Their opinion is supported by Martin of Troppau, the author of the *Fasciculus temporum*, and Godfrey of Viterbo, who incorrectly made Deusdedit contemporary with the reign of Phocas.

Following their authority, I reckon backward from the day of death, or deposition, 8 November 618, three years and twenty days, and arrive at 19 October 615, marked by the letter F, which in that year coincided with a Sunday. I therefore seem to have found the very day of his ordination, and Pagius likewise recognized it as such. Then, ascending from this day of ordination to the day of Boniface IV’s death, 7 May, I count five months and thirteen days—not twelve, as Pagius has it, for he includes the day of death itself.

Thus the Farfa catalogue, which gives thirteen days, errs less than the other catalogues and manuscripts, in which an interregnum has been invented at will. Here I cannot sufficiently marvel at Garnerius’s negligence. In his learned notes on the *Book of the Pontiffs*, he places the beginning of the pontificate of Boniface V, the successor of Saint Deusdedit, in the year 617; accordingly, he adds Indiction 5 to the decree of the pope’s election, although that indiction belongs to the same year only after September, and he admits with Anastasius that Saint Deusdedit died in November. Yet, being wholly occupied with determining the age of the collection of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, he did not read in that same Anastasius the clearest indication of the pope’s date. Anastasius says that a great earthquake followed—in August of Indiction 6, before the pope’s death—and John the Deacon likewise affirms this in his *Chronicle*, namely in the year 618, which was followed by the disease of scabies, or elephantiasis.

Saint Deusdedit’s death must therefore necessarily be assigned to that year. Nor may the election of his successor Boniface be placed earlier in that same year as it came to an end, nor, with Pagius, be postponed to the following year, since the murder of Eleutherius and other arguments demonstrate the contrary; I shall present these in the notes on that same Boniface.

Since this is so, Saint Deusdedit was ordained after a vacancy of five months and thirteen days, on 19 October 615. After occupying the see for three years and twenty days, he died on 7 November and was buried on the following day, as Anastasius rightly states, together with the Roman Martyrology corrected by Baronius—namely, on the day of his deposition itself, 8 November.

*Cennus.*

### 4

A cardinal priest of the church of Saints John and Paul, the title of Pammachius, appointed by Pope Saint Gregory, he obtained the pontificate by the unanimous vote of all. He sat during the reign of the emperor Flavius Heraclius Augustus for three years and nineteen days, having been consecrated on Sunday, the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the year of the Lord 613.

“Deusdedit” was a compound name formed from a noun and a verb, customary in those times. Marcus Aurelius Cassiodorus, for example, writes to Deusdedit, a Ravenna scribe, and Saint Augustine writes to Quodvultdeus.

*Ciaconus.*

Deusdedit, by nation a Roman,

**Note:** From his father Stephen, a subdeacon. In the copy of Anastasius used by Baronius, the text read: “Deusdedit, son of Stephen, having been a subdeacon, sat for three years.” He writes the passage as follows: “That a Roman subdeacon should be created pontiff happened for the first time, without precedent among his ancestors; and this plainly shows that great disturbances had been stirred up in the clergy. But, leaving the other matters aside, the reason Deusdedit was elected was his outstanding holiness, by which he shone forth wonderfully, illuminated amid so much darkness.”

Since learned men had hitherto been persuaded, on the basis of the royal edition of Anastasius and various manuscript copies, that subdeacons had never been elected Roman pontiffs, the passage in question was restored in this form: “Deusdedit, from his father Stephen, a subdeacon”—so that Deusdedit was not himself a subdeacon, but the son of a subdeacon.

Yet, since it is clear from chapter 22 of the *Breviary* of the deacon Liberatus that Silverius was called a Roman pontiff from the rank of subdeacon, and since Liberatus lived at the very time when Silverius was elected, it remains uncertain which of the two readings should be preferred, since the correction of the former rests on a false foundation. I believe, moreover, that subdeacons could be elected until the time of Stephen III—called Stephen IV by others—at whose Roman synod, held in 769, it was forbidden under anathema that anyone should ever presume to promote to the sacred honor of the pontificate either a layman or anyone from another order, unless, ascending through the distinct grades, he had become a cardinal deacon or priest.

From these words it seems to me possible to infer that subdeacons were excluded from the pontificate only at that time. For from the Liberatus just cited we know that Silverius was taken into the pontificate from that order, and no one objected that he was disqualified on that account. From Anastasius, meanwhile, it remains uncertain whether Deusdedit himself had also been only a subdeacon before his election. This seems more probable, for the later reading indeed says that he was the son of a subdeacon, but does not deny that he himself was also a subdeacon, whereas the former reading explicitly says so.

*Pagius.*

from his father Stephen, a subdeacon,

He sat for three years and twenty-four days.

**1.** Three years less five days. For his anniversary is commemorated in the Church on 8 November, and thus, when the calculation is made from the beginning of his pontificate, he is found to have held the see for the period stated.

*Binius and Labbe.*

**2.** The Codex Farnesianus reads: “He sat three years and twenty days.” The Codex of Valla: “twenty-three days.”

*Blanch.*

He sat for three years and twenty-four days. He greatly loved the clergy and restored priests and clerics to their former places.

At that time,

**Note:** “Coming,” and so forth. The Codex Farnesianus reads: “He came to Ravenna and killed all those who had been involved in the killing of John the exarch and in the affairs of the commonwealth.” The Codex of Vallicella reads: “And those involved in the affairs of the commonwealth were killed. And, coming to Rome, he was received most favorably by the most holy pope.”

coming—Eleutherius, the patrician,

**Note:** Eleutherius the patrician. Anastasius, again copying the words of Paul, once more confuses the events. It should therefore be corrected from the same source, which writes in chapter 31: “At this time John Compsinus seized Naples; not many days afterward Eleutherius, the patrician eunuch, assumed the imperial authority from that city.” Compsinus—or, as Anastasius calls him, Compsinus—invaded Naples together with the surrounding cities and called himself king.

Batillus, in his *History of Bari*, maintains that this John Compsinus was crowned with an iron crown in the city of Bari and subsequently crowned with a golden one among the Neapolitans, so that he might prove himself king to the peoples of Italy. Eleutherius, however, brought him back into submission. Paul adds concerning Eleutherius: “After this, Eleutherius the patrician eunuch assumed the imperial authority. While he was traveling from Ravenna to Rome, he was killed by soldiers in the fortress of Luceoli, and his head was brought to the emperor at Constantinople.”

Anastasius inserted this episode among the deeds of Boniface V.

*Bencinus.*

Eleutherius, the patrician and chamberlain, came to Ravenna and killed all those who had been involved in the killing of John the exarch and in the affairs of the commonwealth.

He came to Rome.

**Note:** “He came here to Rome.” The Codex Farnesianus reads: “He came to Rome.”

He was received most favorably by the most holy Pope Deusdedit. Having gone out

**Note:** From Rome. The Codex of Vallicella reads: “from Rome.”

from Rome, he came to Naples, which was held by John

**Note:** Compsinus Intarta. The Codex of Vallicella reads: “Campsivo Arcata.”

Compsinus Intarta.

**Note:** “Intarta.” Hesychius says: “*Intarta*, a tyrant, a rebel against the king.” The term derives from *ἀρταίρω*, “I contend, I quarrel.” Festus likewise says: “*Antarium* is a battle fought before the city, namely by citizens in revolt.”

In the acts of the virgin Martina we likewise read: “O Alexander, and *intarta* of the Christians.” And in the chronicle of Fontenelle, chapter 3: “A war was fought between Charles the exarch and Regenfrid the *Intarta*.” From this arose the verb *intartarizare*, which occurs more than once later in these acts.

*Bencinus.*

Eleutherius the patrician entered Naples by force of arms, killed the tyrant, and returned to Ravenna.

And, after a *roga* had been given to the soldiers, peace was made throughout all Italy.

**Note:**

**1.** A *roga* is a distribution made by a prince in place of a gift and given to soldiers. Anastasius, in the life of Severinus, says: “And where are your *rogae*, which the lord emperor has repeatedly ordered to be given to you, when they have been stored up by the holy man?” Gregory, Book II, Letter 32, writes: “The Theodosians who remained here, receiving no *roga*, scarcely apply themselves to guarding the walls.” I discussed this above.

A *roga* also means a distribution made by Roman pontiffs to the clergy or the people. Anastasius, below, in this same codex, says: “He left one full *roga* for his services and for all the clergy.” The same author, in the life of Boniface V, writes: “He loved the clergy and gave a full *roga* to his clergy. He left one full *roga* to all the clergy for their services.” Likewise, in the life of John IV: “He left a full *roga* for all the clergy.” In the life of Eugene: “He granted a solid *roga* to the clergy.” In the life of Leo III: “He greatly increased the *roga* for his clergy in the presbytery.”

*Altaserra.*

**2.** A *roga* is a gift, so called from its distribution.

*Binius and Labbe.*

And, after a *roga* had been given to the soldiers, peace was made throughout all

Italy.

### Note

He instituted a second Mass among the clergy.

**1.** It was customary for only one public—that is, solemn—Mass to be celebrated on Sundays, according to canon “And this,” *On Consecration*, distinction 1. See concerning this Dionysius the Areopagite, in his letter to Demophilus; John Moschus, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 27; and others.

Leo I instituted the celebration of a second Mass so that the people would not be too greatly confined while the custom of one Mass was preserved, according to the canon *Necesse*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1. After him, Pope Deusdedit instituted a second Mass among the clergy, that is, in the Roman Church, as Anastasius testifies here. Perhaps the custom of one public Mass had not yet ceased in the Roman Church, which was always more tenacious of antiquity.

*Altaserra.*

**2.** Among those who have written treatises on liturgical matters, there is no one who does not struggle with this passage of Anastasius when the question arises of repeating Mass in the same church.

Cardinal Bona, whose name should never be mentioned without praise, in his golden treatise on liturgical matters, Book I, chapter 14, no. 4, had attempted to prove from Leo the Great’s letter to Dioscorus of Alexandria—where Leo ordered the sacrifice to be repeated when the multitude of the faithful was so great that the basilica could not receive everyone at once—that from Leo’s time onward the custom prevailed at Rome of offering the sacrifice several times on the same day.

He then adduces the text in question, saying: “Concerning Pope Deusdedit, the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* writes as follows: ‘He instituted a second Mass among the clergy.’ To these words Peter of Orvieto says in his scholia: ‘For at that time perhaps, following the custom of the Greeks, only one Mass was sung in the church, which, according to the ancients, was more edifying.’”

He immediately adds: “But from the testimony of Leo just cited it is clear that the custom of repeating the sacrifice had been introduced into the Roman Church much earlier.”

Yet, with due respect to this eminent writer, if one wishes to accept the interpretation of Peter of Orvieto—namely, that the practice of celebrating only one Mass in each church continued until the time of blessed Deusdedit—the authority of Leo’s letter can easily be weakened by explaining that Leo ordered the sacrifice to be repeated only in the case of a new congregation filling the basilica, in places where there was only one basilica, and by the same priest.

Blessed Deusdedit, however, appears to have instituted for the first time that, after the solemn Mass, another private Mass should be celebrated by another member of the clergy, whether a new congregation had assembled in the basilica or not, and whether there was one basilica or several. It was then, apparently, that the practice was first introduced into the Latin Church of celebrating several Masses in the same church and constructing several altars for their celebration.

It is beyond dispute that during the first centuries of the Church there was one altar in each basilica and that only one Mass was celebrated upon it. Both customs are retained by the Greek Church. All who attended that Mass were nourished by the sacred assembly, especially those who served at the solemn Mass. Thus the Fourth Council of Toledo, in the year of Christ 635, decreed in canon 17 that priests and Levites should receive Communion before the altar, the clergy in the choir, and the people outside the choir.

All the priests who were present, however, together with the celebrating priest or bishop, performed the sacred rite, offering and receiving Communion together. It is the custom of the Roman Church that priests should be present at the offering of Christ’s sacrifice and should, together with the pontiff, complete it by word and gesture, as Mabillon reports in Part II of the *Museum Italicum*, page 4, citing Amalarius, Book I, chapter 12.

Moreover, history teaches us that ancient monks were accustomed to celebrate one Mass, and that only on Sundays and feast days, when all the monks assembled. “Certainly during the days of Lent, except Sundays, Mass was not sung in the time of Saint Benedict,” says Hildemar in his commentary on chapter 48 of the Rule, as found in Mabillon’s first preface to the fourth century of the Order of Saint Benedict, no. 168.

Peter of Cluny, Book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 28; Abbot Guibert, Book I of his *Life*, chapter 11; and Peter of Blois, Letter 86, report that in former times the Carthusians celebrated Masses only on Sundays and feast days.

Thus Cardinal Bona, Book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 18, no. 3. He adds in no. 8: “Palladius relates in the Life of blessed Arsisius that there were eight priests in the church of the mountain of Nitria. The first among them alone offered the sacrifice; and as long as he lived, the others neither offered, nor judged, nor delivered a sermon.”

For this reason blessed Francis, according to Álvaro Pelagius, Book II of *The Lament of the Church*, article 5, “wished the brothers to be content with one Mass in whatever place they lived, knowing that the brothers would wish to justify themselves by Masses and reduce them to a source of profit, as we see happening today.”

Pelagius wrote this around the year 1330, about a hundred years after the death of blessed Francis, clearly directing his attention and reference to a letter written by blessed Francis to his brothers, in which we read:

“Moreover, I admonish and exhort you in the Lord that, in places where the brothers reside, only one Mass should be celebrated each day, according to the practice of the holy Roman Church. If there are several priests in a place, let one, out of the love of charity, be content to hear the celebration of the other priest.”

I know that modern sectarians abuse this authority in order to abolish the private Mass, which they intensely hate. But their response does not seem convincing to me when they declare the letter of blessed Francis apocryphal. The testimony of Pelagius stands against them, since he uses that letter; his testimony cannot be rejected, for he was both an ancient witness and a member of the same order.

It must therefore be said that the ancient discipline of celebrating only one Mass was relaxed by blessed Deusdedit to the extent that, after the solemn Mass, only one additional Mass was sung among the clergy. It was not relaxed so far that Masses were multiplied according to the number of priests, as perhaps began to happen in the time of blessed Francis and as later became customary.

There was one cause of this development. As the same Cardinal Bona says, Book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 18, no. 9: “When the Mendicant Orders were founded and spread far and wide, the obligations of Masses multiplied, and therefore it became necessary for each priest to celebrate privately every day in order to satisfy them.”

From this we can easily understand the origin of the multitude of altars with which the churches of the Mendicants are filled, a phenomenon not seen in other basilicas, whether of monks or clerics.

*Baldinus.*

**3.** The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* commends Deusdedit’s love and generosity toward the clergy, and also writes: “He instituted a second Mass among the clergy.”

To these words Peter of Orvieto says in his scholia, as quoted by Cardinal Bona, Book I, chapter 14, no. 4, *On Liturgical Matters*: “For at that time perhaps, following the custom of the Greeks, only one Mass was sung in the Church, which, according to the ancients, was more edifying.”

Yet it is clear from Leo the Great’s Letter 81 to Dioscorus of Alexandria that the custom of repeating the sacrifice had been introduced into the Roman Church long before Deusdedit. In that letter Leo orders the sacrifice to be repeated when the multitude of the faithful is so great that the basilica cannot receive them all at once. Otherwise one part of the people would be deprived of its devotion if the custom of only one Mass were to be preserved.

He says that it is entirely consistent with piety and reason that whenever the presence of a new congregation has filled the basilica, the sacrifice should be offered again. The holy pontiff gave this command on the basis of the custom then prevailing at Rome, “so that,” he says, “our observance may agree in all things.” Further on he writes: “So that what has become established in our custom through the form of our fathers’ tradition may not be neglected by your care.”

Cardinal Bona, already cited, discusses these matters at greater length. What Anastasius understands by these words I leave to others to examine.

*Pagius.*

**4.** It is not sufficiently clear what the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* means by these words.
