Some believe that he permitted the sacrifice of the Mass to be repeated on the same day in places where the churches could not hold the people because of their narrowness. But Saint Leo the Great had already established this, as we said in the account of his pontificate.

*Sommier.*

He instituted a second Mass among the clergy.

**Note:** “At the same time.” The words of Anastasius must be illustrated by what Paul writes in chapter 42, where he speaks of Rothari, king of the Lombards:

“He waged war against the people of Ravenna and the Romans at the river Aemilia, which is called the Scultenna. In this battle, when the rest of the Roman side turned their backs, eight thousand fell. At that time a great earthquake occurred at Rome, and there was a great inundation of waters. After this came the scourge of scabies, so that no one could recognize his dead, because of the excessive swelling.”

But the ignorant compiler of the pontifical acts mixes together both the dates and the events. While Deusdedit was pope, Adaloaldus the Lombard was ruling. Therefore, if the inundation and the scourge of scabies occurred during the reign of Rothari, the narrative of Anastasius may perhaps have to be transferred to the deeds of John IV or of Pope Theodore, since Rothari did not take up the Lombard kingdom before the year 636.

After winning this victory and gaining greater dominion and wealth, Rothari strengthened the Lombard kingdom in Italy and was the first to apply himself to issuing Lombard laws and committing them to written record. Thus Paul writes in the same work, chapter 44:

“This Rothari, king of the Lombards, arranged in written sequence the laws which they had previously retained only by memory and custom, and ordered the code itself to be called an edict.”

It was already the seventy-seventh year since the Lombards had entered Italy, as the same king testified in the prologue to his edict. It is preserved at the very beginning of the Lombard Laws.

*Bencinus.*

At the same time there was a great earthquake in the month of August, in the eleventh indiction.

**Note:** “A great earthquake … eleventh indiction.” The Codex of Vallicella reads: “A greater earthquake … in the sixth indiction.” After this, the Codex Farnesianus adds: “sixth indiction.”

*Blanch.*

### Note

After this, a disaster struck the people.

**1.** In the year 613, in the month of August, the earth trembled with a mighty convulsion, and an exceedingly foul disease followed the earthquake. This was the disease called elephantiasis, which so disfigured the faces of those afflicted that the living could scarcely be distinguished from the dead, nor could they be recognized. At that time the holiness of the pontiff displayed itself conspicuously among men. For when the pontiff offered a kiss to a man afflicted with elephantiasis whom he met, he immediately restored him to his former health.

*Ciaconus.*

**2.** After this the disaster followed. Pliny states in Book XXVI of his *Natural History* that the disease elephantiasis, which the Greeks call *σατυριασμός*—“satyrism,” because it makes the face of the sufferer resemble the face of a satyr—was not present in Italy before the time of Gnaeus Pompey.

But while Saint Deusdedit occupied the pontificate, elephantiasis raged in the city with such violence that, as our author says, no one could recognize his own dead. In such a great calamity among the people, the charitable care of the pontiff, aiding those afflicted by the disease, was glorified by divine power. For when Saint Deusdedit kissed an elephantiasis sufferer whom he met, he immediately restored him to his former health through the divine power working through him.

This remarkable deed, praised in the very ancient records of the Church, is commemorated annually on the sixth day before the Ides of November, his feast day, in the Roman Martyrology, in these words: “At Rome, Saint Deusdedit, pope, who was of such merit that by a kiss he healed a leper from leprosy.”

*Mafeus.*

After this a disaster struck the people, the scourge of scabies, so that no one could recognize his own dead.

**Note:** “The deceased.” Anastasius writes of this holy pontiff: “He died and was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the eighth day of the month of November.” Marianus Scotus likewise has this in his *Chronicle*.

Since, on the other hand, Godfrey of Viterbo, Martin of Troppau in his *Chronicle*, the author of the *Fasciculus temporum*, and several catalogues of the Roman pontiffs state that Deusdedit occupied the see for three years and twenty days, it follows that we have correctly assigned his ordination to 19 October of the year 615 and his death to 8 November of the year 618.

His name is not found in the Martyrology of Galesinius or in the older martyrologies, but Baronius, because of his outstanding virtues, entered it in the Roman Martyrology, which he corrected by apostolic authority, under 8 November.

*Pagius.*

He died and was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the eighth day of the month of November. He left one full *roga* for his services and for all the clergy. He held three ordinations: nine priests, five deacons, and twenty-nine bishops in various places. The see then remained vacant for one month and sixteen days.

## Deusdedit

**Note:** We have received only one letter of Pope Deusdedit from Labbe, and I have found no others in the manuscript codices. Yet I consider it worthy of notice that the heading is sometimes transmitted differently. For where the printed editions address the letter to Gordian, bishop of Seville, the Pistoian manuscript, at least eight hundred years old and containing the collection of Isidore Mercator, reads: “To Gordian, fellow bishop of the Church of the Spains.”

This reading is of some importance, since Labbe derived an argument against the authenticity of the letter from the common heading. He observed that during this period the Church of Seville was governed not by Gordian but by Isidore. This correction therefore overturns that argument, although other features make the letter itself suspicious—for example, its very style, which is wholly foreign to the usage of the period.

None of the preceding or immediately subsequent pontiffs adorns himself with this title: “Deusdedit, bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic Church”—and “apostolic” is absent from the manuscript codex. After Saint Gregory, scarcely any other title was used by the Roman pontiffs than “Servant of the servants of God,” as we learn from the letters of Boniface V.

Add to this that the discipline concerning the dissolution of a marriage, in the event that a man unknowingly and imprudently lifted from the sacred font a son born of his wife, is absurd and plainly contrary to the decision of Pope Nicholas I in a fragment of his letter to Salemon, perhaps Solomon, which I shall produce from my manuscript codex in its proper place.

### Letter of Pope Deusdedit to Gordian, Bishop of Seville

Those who receive their own children from the sacred font are to separate from their wives; and no one is permitted to take his godmother as a wife.

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, vol. X.)*

Deusdedit, bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, to Gordian, fellow bishop of the Church of Seville and most beloved brother.

Your deacon has come to us bearing a letter from Your Holiness, reporting that certain men and women, on the preceding Easter Saturday, because of the great rush of the crowds, unknowingly received their own children from the holy font. You therefore wish to know whether, in consequence of such an accident, men and women ought to return to their proper marital relations or not.

We, distressed by this matter, examined the statements of our earlier fathers. We found in the archives of this apostolic see that such things had already occurred in the churches of Dauria, Ephesus, Jerusalem, and other cities as well. When the bishops of those cities wished to know from this apostolic see whether the men and women should return to their proper marriage beds, the most holy Fathers of blessed memory—Julius, Innocent, and Celestine—together with the agreement of many bishops and priests, wrote and confirmed the following in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles:

Those men or women who, for whatever reason, have received their own children must in no way thereafter take one another back in marriage. Rather, they must separate, lest, with the devil’s persuasion, such a sinful vice grow throughout the world and universal error increase.

You know that, just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so there are seven gifts of baptism, beginning with the first nourishment of consecrated salt and entry into the holy Church and continuing to the confirmation—or perfection—of the Holy Spirit through chrism.

From this first gift of the Holy Spirit to the seventh, no Christian may take his godmother in marriage. Whoever presumes to do so shall be bound forever by the bond of anathema, unless he performs worthy penance.

When women have been separated from their husbands because of this unlawful matter, we command them to receive from their former husbands the entire dowry which they received on the day of their marriage. After the completion of one year, they may take another husband, and likewise the husband may take another wife.

**Note:** Human law has permitted marriages to be dissolved, but divine law has forbidden it. Truth itself said: “What God has joined together,” and so forth.

*(Saint Gregory, Letter 39, Book IX, chapter 2.)*

## Appendix

Udalric of Bamberg inserted in his collection a decree on the election of the Roman pontiff, issued under the name of Pope Deusdedit. Eccard published its codex in the *Corpus Historicorum Medii Aevi*, vol. II, column 188.

Let others debate whether it is genuine. For me, it is enough to present it exactly as it is found there. I should not, however, omit the fact that other writers attribute this same decree, in identical words, to Stephen IV, to Stephen VI, or to some impostor.

Deusdedit, Roman pontiff, established the following by his decree:

Because the holy Roman Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, suffers many acts of violence when a pontiff dies—violence arising because the pontiff’s consecration takes place without the knowledge of the emperor and the presence of his legates, and because messengers are not sent by the emperor according to canonical rite and custom to prevent violence and scandals from occurring at his consecration—we wish this practice henceforth to be forbidden [the manuscript reads *obdicetur*, apparently corrupt].

When a pontiff is to be appointed, let him be elected by the assembled bishops and the entire clergy, with the senate and people requesting the one who is to be ordained. Once he has been solemnly elected in the presence of all, let him be consecrated in the presence of the imperial legates. Let no one, at his own peril, dare by some new invention to exact oaths or promises, except those required by ancient custom, lest the Church be scandalized or the honor of the emperor diminished.

## In the Year of the Lord 621: Sisebut, King of the Goths

## Historical Notice on Sisebut

*(Antonio, Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus, vol. I, p. 320, nos. 220–222.)*

Sisebut, too, the king of the Goths, illustrious not less for the height of his dignity and the excellence of his arms than for his literary culture, learning, and mastery of the Latin language, deserves to be assigned his proper place among writers.

For he was, as Isidore says in his *History of the Goths* (Era 650), “brilliant in eloquence, learned in judgment, and to a considerable extent imbued with literary knowledge.” Therefore the same Isidore, in his work *On the Nature of Things*, addressed to Sisebut, begins as follows:

“Although I know you to be outstanding in talent and eloquence and adorned with the varied flowers of learning, you nevertheless devote still greater care and ask me to provide you with support concerning certain matters of nature and their causes.”

The other Isidore, bishop of Badajoz, in his *Chronicle*, or *Epitome of the Emperors and the Arabs*—under Heraclius, Era 650—calls him “a wise man and exceedingly devoted to learning.” Rodrigo of Toledo copied these words in Book II, chapter 17.

An anonymous Benedictine, in the *Chronicle of the Abbey of Saint Remigius at Dijon*, published by d’Achery in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, page 377, under the twelfth year of King Theuderic—although he calls him Sisebut—commends him as “a wise man, praiseworthy throughout all Spain, and very full of piety.”

Sisebut succeeded Gundemar and held the Gothic kingdom for eight and a half years, until 621. He was distinguished among few men for the arts of war and peace, religion, justice, kindness, and clemency. It is not the present subject to investigate his deeds further.

As for his library, the preservation among us of one or two ancient codices, containing several works and letters written by him, provides the evidence. These are the frequently praised books of the Church of Oviedo and of the College of Alcalá, which Morales saw and discussed in Book XII, chapter 3, and in his letter to Andrés Resende, in volume II of *Hispania Illustrata*, page 1022. He also discusses them in the prologue to the second volume of his history, where ancient books are treated.

I add a third, said to be found in the library of the Church of Toledo, according to Martín Ximena, *Annals of the Church of Jaén*, page 35.

In all these books are found letters of King Sisebut: to Caecilius, bishop of Mentesa; to Caesarius the Roman patrician, under whom, it seems, whatever belonged to the Roman imperial authority within Spain was then situated; to Eusebius, bishop of Barcelona; and to certain Theudila and Sandrimerus. Their subjects may meanwhile be seen in the same Morales, until someone, avenging our former negligence, allows these sacred monuments of antiquity to come fully into the light.

I retain the hope that, if it should ever be possible, these texts might be more carefully compared with the Gothic manuscripts of the Toledo library, from which they have reached us disfigured by defects and errors through the gross ignorance of copyists.

The headings of the letters are:

1. To the bishop of Mentesa, who withdrew into a monastery.
2. To Caesarius the patrician, the reply being sent through Ausemundus.
3. To Eusebius the bishop.
4. To Tudila, after he had received the monastic habit from the lay state.
5. To Advalic, king of the Lombards, and Queen Theudolinda, concerning the faith of Christ, sent through Totila.

*Cardinal de Aguirre.*

## Letters of Sisebut, King of the Goths

*(Flórez, España Sagrada, vol. VII.)*

### First Letter: King Sisebut to Caecilius, Bishop of Mentesa

While Caecilius had withdrawn into a monastery.

#### 1

I wished, most beloved father, that, after you had first kept your flock safe and unharmed, our immense sins—which are not exposed by our own merits—might at least be washed away through your prayers.

But who can bring aid to another’s suffering if he has denied himself the medicine of healing? Nor can anyone watch over wandering sheep in the Lord’s folds who, through neglect, has delivered his own into the jaws of wolves and, denying them grassy and fragrant fields, preferred to wound their companions among thistles and thorn bushes, amid the cubs of raging lions.

Thus, while the care of the watchful shepherd has withered, they tear apart the harmless flock with ravenous jaws and savage mouths, no one resisting; and, through hidden winding passages, the beasts kill their victims, with no one defending them.

I should say how mournful this is and how worthy of lamentation from every source of tears, were it not that so grievous an event has occurred that I prefer to weep over it rather than find it necessary to recount it.

#### 2

If the Lord carried one wandering little sheep upon his shoulders until he placed it among the hundred, how much more ought human frailty to exercise care, so that, if it could not produce gain, it should at least not lose what it had received!

### 3

[Col. 0365B] Nevertheless, lest what we assert seem to you to remain far from reason, hear with what arrows the Lord in the Gospel strikes the hearts of sinners, and with what rewards he enriches the aforesaid faithful—[Note: [Col. 0365D] Asi la Real. Gimena, “endowed”]—so that he made the one who increased the talents entrusted to him remain with him in joy, established in the greatest honors—[Note: [Col. 0365D] Missing in the Real.] But concerning the contrary case, namely, what punishment overtakes the man who hid the money by preserving it, and with what loss the divine utterances show that burning wrath rages against him, you will be able to investigate more fully. And if the man who produced no profit brought forth the sum—[Note: [Col. 0365D] Gimena, “bore.”]—and was condemned with such punishment—[Note: [Col. 0365D] Real, “with such foreknowledge.”]—with what sentence will he be punished who acquired nothing and, by neglecting what he had, cruelly lost it?

### 4

The innumerable examinations of the divine books lie open [Col. 0365C], and they do not allow you to remain innocent in this matter. Yet if small things are useful—[Note: [Col. 0365D] Gimena, “even if.”]—I believe that many will suffice as well. If today someone entangled in worldly affairs and polluted by the foulness of every crime should pay the debt of nature, yet wish to obtain a single reward of repentance; if healing is denied to the sick man, and death thus swallows him in eternity, from whose hand, I ask, will the Lord seek his soul?

Likewise, when a pagan has been brought to the holy fonts, but, because the bishop has withdrawn—[Note: [Col. 0365D] Gimena, “because he has failed.”]—has not yet been baptized, so that death forestalls the rite, I ask: who will be able to render an account for him? It seems to me that, when the One to whom all things are open comes, they will say: “We were awaiting both repentance and baptism together; but we have found this man a murderer, who did not grant the wishes of the penitent, but rather, through negligence, denied them.” I think that another will suffer their punishments. And since no one is found worthy concerning himself who can judge himself clean from sin, how much more so the man to whom the crimes of another are added? I believe him worthy of a thousand deaths—[Note: [Col. 0365D] The same witness, “bites.”]

### 5

But since we have learned from your letters that you entered the monastery for no other reason than that you might be able to bring aid to your own infirmities, I am amazed that, at the cost of many, you are still happy, and that you do not rather immediately correct those things which lately you chose cruelly—[Note: [Col. 0366D] The same witness, “credulously.”] to commit.

Therefore, since you await our pronouncements, having summoned a notary at once, we have chosen what is to be read aloud. When these words have been made public by your own hands, lay aside every deceit, and swiftly direct your steps into the presence of us and your brothers, so that, rebuked by a living voice and corrected by the written word, you may at last come to your senses and return to the growth of virtues.

## LETTER II. OF THE PATRICIAN CAESARIUS TO KING SISEBUT, SENT ON BEHALF OF THE AFORESAID CAECILIUS WHILE HE HAD BEEN CAPTURED BY SOLDIERS (C)

To the most glorious and most merciful lord, lord Sisebut, king: Caesarius, by the will of God your patrician, sends reverence.

### 1

Our frequent petition has been before your Eminence, but it has been wholly unable to achieve its purpose. Yet now may the unconquerable cry of those who groan prevail upon your royal exaltation, and may God’s inspiration prepare your heart to restore the condition of peace—[Note: [Col. 0366D] Gimena, “impulsion.”] May God at last be appeased by the lamentation of so many, if, looking upon the streams, he extinguishes the rivers of tears.

For the earth, which, as its heat failed, was awaiting rain in order to produce its fruit, has been sated by the immense flood of Catholic blood pouring forth, and has completed the work of an inundation. Indeed, captivity multiplied throughout our regions and yours has almost filled the whole world, and the land groans, crowded with the habitation of nobles.

### 2

For such a multitude of deaths inflicted, therefore, I do not cease to urge your Eminence with my entreaty: do not disdain humility; hear our prayers; do not cease to grant what is requested. Show yourself, after God—[Note: [Col. 0366D] Gimena, “the Lord.”]—to be the giver of peace, so that he who, having assumed a body, ascended into heaven and left peace to humanity may number your kingdom among the peaceful and place you, as a son of peace, among the company of the saints.

Since I ask for the peace of which all are in need, grant it to me, with the Lord inspiring you, so that, even if I dwell in foreign lands, I may nevertheless carry the love that has been stored up in my heart, always hold the name of your kingdom as especially dear, and may it never depart from your mind—[Note: [Col. 0366D] Perhaps, “may you never depart.”]

### 3

We released our most blessed father Caecilius, who had been detained by our men, out of regard for God and for your kingdom, hastening in every way to satisfy the will of God and of your kingdom—[Note: [Col. 0366D] The Real, “our father.”]—and we took evident care that he be presented to his holy Church and to your most Christian eyes—[Note: [Col. 0366D] Gimena, “we took care evidently.”]

### 4

Now, just as without any admonition from your kingdom we released that most holy man, hastening in every way to benefit the condition of your kingdom, so may your most eminent power not disdain to fulfill our petition, which is approved by the counsel of many souls, showing yourself in all things a cultivator of good endeavors.

If our will does not remain sorrowful in its supplication, recognize that before the most serene lord of the city, your father, we shall acknowledge your Eminence to be in every respect the author of what is especially useful to him. We have discharged the rights of the duty owed by us; and, wishing to know the health of your Clemency, we inquire through the service of writing, so that your Clemency’s spirit may be moved to return an answer to those who inquire and show care.

## LETTER III. OF KING SISEBUT TO CAESARIUS, SENT THROUGH ANSEMUNDUS (C)

### 1

If the Searcher of hearts were to pour our affection into your feelings; if he were to insert our love into your secret thoughts; if he were to disclose to the sight of your mind whatever I think about you—[Col. 0367B] (I cannot reveal it by striking the metal)—[Note: [Col. 0367D] The Toledo Codex has “would disclose … to reveal”; we add the punctuation of the parenthesis.] I believe that, once the restraints of circumstances had been removed, the business of perishing causes dismissed, and the delays arising from hesitation banished, you would long ago have become our companion, and that the exchange of affection could have enjoyed a pure spirit in both of us—[Note: [Col. 0367D] Toledo, “companionship.”]

But, as I understand, I write these things to myself because of my sin, so that no fruits may be returned to my realms by the one whom I love above all others [nor may an equal recompense be reciprocated to my lot—[Note: [Col. 0367D] Missing in the Real.]]. For what do you hesitate, dearest friend? If faith is given to Christians, accept the covenant; if rewards are offered, receive gifts—what is worthless in your estimation. I profess, with God himself looking favorably upon it, to preserve my promise in all things and to hold the purpose of sacred devotion with an undefiled mind.

For the days which, if we lived well, ought to lead us in abundant joy and exultation—why should disasters and deaths, why continual pestilence, why ruinous calamity consuming all things, mutilate them? It is indeed not unworthy of us to await counsel, but it is our task to disclose fully what we love and our entire wish, for however many—[Note: [Col. 0367D] The Real copy, “for whatever.”]—are the days of our life, though we know them not. For, while there is time, our intention ought to direct itself toward what may benefit the one for whom, trusting in God’s mercy, we ask that matters stand in all perpetuity, justly and in the most upright manner, by the gift of God.

As the most watchful examiner of the matter itself, you can perceive this: if wars arise, if the hot sword rages anywhere, if human life does not pass through a time of warfare, whom do you think will render an account to God for such crimes, for the disasters inflicted, for the most grievous wounds brought upon us—[Col. 0367D]—[Note: [Col. 0367D] Toledo, “inflicted upon us.”]?

It seems to me—and rightly so—that the man who refused to accept the remedy offered with deepest piety should be held answerable for so many evils. But why should we reopen these matters, when it is enough merely to admonish him? Let us return to your most ample affection and our purest devotion.

Trust Ansemundus confidently; receive him after setting aside cavilling; once suspicion has been removed, let whatever you command be mild in his breast. For he is ours: though unpolished in speech, he is not unpolished in his zeal for purity. I have chosen—[Note: [Col. 0367D] The Real, “I shall love.”]—with sincere affection whatever things were appropriate; I have equipped them as they seemed suitable; I have polished them as I could. Therefore I entrust his sincerity to your guidance, and whatever he may have obtained less elegantly through you, dearest friend, I shall defend in your presence—[Note: [Col. 0367D] Toledo, “here.”]

I find nothing further to disclose to your Experience, to whom I desire to offer my whole self—[Note: [Col. 0368D] The Real, “to whom I desire to offer myself wholly.”] This bearer, however, is so fully furnished in every respect—[Note: [Col. 0368D] Perhaps, “instructed.”]—and so finally prepared that, whatever your Clemency asks of him, I think he will give you a completely satisfactory answer—[Note: [Col. 0368D] The Real, “give you.”]

The letters which he will present to you publicly express the rectitude of justice and preserve the boundary of truth; for they do not obstruct your glory if things more expedient for us are granted and, by God’s mercy, the desires for which alone we plead come to fulfillment.

Ansemundus has brought us the bow sent by your Glory. For this we offer you the greater thanks, because we are enriched by you both in words and by the gift.

## LETTER IV. OF THE PATRICIAN CAESARIUS TO KING SISEBUT, SENT THROUGH URSELLUS—[Note: [Col. 0368D] Toledo, “Urselus.”] (C)

We have read sincerely the noble letter by which your message became known to us, by which it decided to insinuate itself in various ways, and by which its deliberate arrangement became evident—[we have treated it at length—[Note: [Col. 0368D] Absent in Toledo.]]; we have observed it carefully and ordered a notary to be summoned and to take it down immediately.

He now knows what he learned long ago, and we rightly give thanks: namely, that we have knowingly recognized those things previously understood by you with a merciful spirit—[Note: [Col. 0368D] The Real, “recognizing.”]—but just as your Clemency preferred to make us informed about many matters, so we render your most noble minds more certain about everything that has happened.

I believe that Theodoricus and our envoys, with the help of him to whom all things are subject, are already united with us in our territories, and that, after being honored by the most merciful and—an incomparable distinction—most lordly emperor, and having recovered cheerful spirits, they were sent back to us. I believe that they make known to our minds those things which speech once demanded, which a pious mind earnestly desired, and which a sincere spirit longed for. It is impious to believe otherwise; nor can imperial majesty offend a royal spirit in a way that accords with what is fitting, except by granting the desired benefit more abundantly.

Finally, while life remains with Christ accompanying us, until these men, so long desired here—[Note: [Col. 0368D] Toledo, “there”]—arrive, we reserve for your senses a full account of whatever their complete report leads our conscience to understand. Some matters are held in your words: part is conveyed figuratively, part historically, and some occupies the place of tropical narrative. The matter itself demands more leisure for speaking about these genres; nevertheless, I shall touch upon it with whatever brevity I can, in a fitting and orderly manner.

According to the sacred writings, it is fitting to wage spiritual warfare against spiritual wickedness—[Note: [Col. 0369D] Toledo, “wickedness” singular]—but your goodness has previously instructed us not to permit this in these matters. In such affairs, divine rather than human aid must be sought. May he who was the death of death and the life of the living himself crush the war on behalf of both parties.

If, however, your judgment pronounces this to concern human beings, we formerly made you aware—and have agreed repeatedly—of those whom your father’s agreement—[Note: [Col. 0369D] Toledo, “father”]—does not at all avenge or defend by its intention. But while the time of delay is prolonged, while an opportunity is granted, and while the mind is scattered in different directions, our party has by no means received what it requested, to such an extent that our intention followed a man given over to the gravest crime and prostrated by every disease, for the sake of discipline—[Note: [Col. 0369D] Toledo, “discussion”]—for the sake of chastity, and for the sake of abstinence.

Our petition could not reach its fulfillment. For this reason we thought this pseudo-presbyter ought to be introduced, so that, among other matters, we might make you aware of things you certainly do not fail to know—[Note: [Col. 0369D] Toledo, “which.”]

Nevertheless, your goodness has made known to us that you have issued such sanctions to our judges that they hold and demand from us things owed to us, from which they have no claim whatsoever, while they do not delay returning those things which are justly owed to your side. May your Clemency know that this pleases me; for it is enough for us to defend what is ours and not to demand what belongs to another.

With a most devoted mind I return the proper signs of your well-being and the rights due to your happiness; and again, through an epistolary greeting, I reserve for a future time the expectation that, by God’s grace, I shall receive an abundance of words concerning your health—[Note: [Col. 0369D] The Real, “concerning your health.”]

## LETTER V. OF THE PATRICIAN CAESARIUS TO KING SISEBUT, SENT THROUGH THEODORICUS BY AMELIUS—[Note: [Col. 0369D] The Real, “Umelius.”] (C)

We gladly received, with exceedingly grateful devotion, the most venerable letter graciously offered by the most lordly emperor, whom we hold in paternal embrace. Its most noble sequence, ennobled by its radiant distinction, deserved the highest honor, since, written by the hand of illustrious power in fitting places—[Note: [Col. 0369D] Toledo, “in suitable passages.”]—it saw itself entrusted to the most potent faith.

Refreshed by such gifts, we preferred that your benevolence should share in them, since, as I believe, you willingly carry the commands of illustrious power into effect. Finally, it is certain that the glorious and most friendly-to-truth Theodoricus was sent to your Glory in accordance with the instruction of the most merciful emperor, who is outstanding in all things beyond all men. We considered it fitting to join with him the venerable presbyter Amelius, so that the happy journey which made them united—[Note: [Col. 0370D] Toledo, “among friends”]—might not allow any circumstance of their return to separate them.

These men can disclose everything to you in faithful words and lively speech—[Note: [Col. 0370D] The Real, “conversation.”]—for their faith is reliable, their sincerity abundant, and their diligence exceedingly careful. Therefore, out of regard for your friendship, it was appropriate to convey through them to your incorruptible understanding whatever has been brought to your knowledge, so that, with superfluous causes finally removed far away, the imperial—[Note: [Col. 0370D] Toledo, “removed from the imperial.”]—sanction, which must be preferred to all mortal things, may persist in bringing your changeable tranquility to a glorious fulfillment.

As far as I can, I return to you the duties of greeting, and with pious devotion I commend to you our dearest men, who, because of the immeasurable excellence of the emperor’s love, are present and privately exalted above others.

## LETTER VI. SENT BY KING SISEBUT TO EUSEBIUS THE BISHOP (C)

To the holy and venerable father, Bishop Eusebius.

We have scarcely touched with our extremities a letter more dead than dying, risen from ashen tombs, however polluted and stained with every contagion—[Note: [Col. 0370D] Toledo, “from the end, the word is *cinosam*.”]—and we have seen it rather panting, as it were—not dead, but never destined to live.

From those very smoky ashes we perceived that you are followers of empty causes and that you agree not with the firmest realities, but with wretched and vainly inflated men. No one can doubt the charge that you obtained your office through theatrical games of bulls—[Note: [Col. 0370D] Toledo, “theatrical games of phantoms.”]—as a ministry; who does not see this, though he also regrets seeing it?

Before blessed men you carry stinking corpses, and by your reprehensible judgment you reproach men who are constantly devoted to divine worship. Therefore do not henceforth expect any address from our perpetuity. Rather, entrust the Church of Barcelona to this man, who pleases God more than pitiable human beings, to govern and direct it, so that, under Christ’s auspices, the glorious solemnity of Easter may be revealed—[Note: [Col. 0370D] The Real, “at Easter”]—and we may rejoice in the desirability of his episcopate and, at last, in your agreement, even if it comes late.

## LETTER VII. SENT BY KING SISEBUT TO THEUDILA WHEN HE HAD TURNED FROM A LAYMAN’S CONDITION TO THE MONASTERY (C)

Who, indeed, could fail to return immense thanks to you, since the kindling of the Holy Spirit has made you his worshipers? Who could fail to raise you up with the most faithful praises, knowing that you hasten onward into the everlasting regions?

For faith is proved by action, when good work is completed from faith; and we confess without hesitation that those attain heavenly things whom we know willingly and effectively to leave earthly things behind.

Therefore, you, the pledges of my character and the most splendid beginnings of my eyes and my inmost being, must make this work, which we recognize as unworthy in ourselves, worthy through the firmness or faith that is suitable in you. For we expect to gather abundant returns from our crops, trusting that from our seeds we have sent forth abundant fruits toward the blessed region, amid the commandments proclaimed by the saints [the transmitted wording is materially corrupt].

“Blessed [are] those who place their sons in Zion and their household members in Jerusalem.” The meaning conveyed is that paternal affection is remembered in children when they remember how they were raised—[Note: [Col. 0371D] The Real, “instructed”—]—in the care of the household.

And although, in accordance with the sacred proclamations of the author, I do not judge you as subjects but as more precious friends, I nevertheless do not doubt that greater assistance will come to me from you, whom I trust have passed from the rank of subjection to a friendly purpose—[Note: [Col. 0371D] Toledo, “submission”; the Real, “to the one placed in charge.”]

Nevertheless, since the wicked often hate the good and the faithless oppose the faithful, I earnestly entreat you, as far as the weakness of my understanding permits, to live with greater steadfastness and care, you who are my offspring in the flesh. And I trust that those whom I know to be bound together in the Lord by the bond of charity will rejoice, while avoiding the waves of this world, to have reached the harbor of victory—[Col. 0371B]—through the divine assistance expressed in the judgments set forth below—[Note: [Col. 0371D] The same copy adds “below” here.]

I could have gathered a few things at the outset concerning universal greed—[Note: [Col. 0371D] The Real, “greed”]—the nurse of evils; but it would have been superfluous ever to embrace what belongs to another, when we know that those who joyfully abandon what is owed to themselves have been destined for a profitable rest.

Pride, the sister of envy—[Note: [Col. 0371D] Toledo, “and its sister”]—which must be guarded against more and more, made its wicked origin the beginning of death. The apostle Peter, wiser than all, declares: “Through the envy of the devil,” he says, “death entered the world.”

By these virtues, both vices are put to death—or are believed to be put to death—[Note: [Col. 0371D] The Real, “are believed”—]—when frequent humility overcomes pride and love tramples down envy, which separates brothers. Let there be, then, fitting and sincere prayer without interruption, constant reading, moderate eating, measured abstinence, abundant humility, steadfast hope, most certain faith, and above all these, charity, which covers a multitude of sins, increasingly generous.

When grace has surrounded you with all these things—[Note: [Col. 0371D] Toledo, “when grace has been received”]—you must resist firmly the thousandfold cunning of the most crafty deceiver, lest, God forbid, the kind of hostile exaltation—[Note: [Col. 0371D] The Real, “infected”]—should make virtues appear to be not virtues but vices. Rather, the greater the gifts of the Giver that have been bestowed upon you, the more ready your mind ought to be in the holy work, without anyone’s praise.

For he who, seized by envy and exaltation from the lofty heights of virtues, was cast down—not undeservedly, but disastrously—in the form of this air, still appears to bear ancient hatred—[Note: [Col. 0372D] Toledo, “today”]—against the human race. And lamenting frailty cries out that, through the grace of humility, we acquire what he lost through ill-fated pride.

His purpose is easily crushed with Christ accompanying us, when the Lord, being asked, has come to our aid. For the Creator of all creatures, in pious compassion, ordered himself to descend to earth, so that through the abundance of his goodness he might lead the human race to the heavenly seats, in order that, when the structure of all the members had reached the Head in the heavens, the fullness of Christ’s body might be believed to be with Christ.

Thus, dearest ones, instructed faithfully and begotten with a sincere mind without deceit, recognize that those from whom the precious blood of the Lord was poured out are subject to eternal punishments. But lest we seem, through a circuit of words, to have introduced something far from reason—[Note: [Col. 0372D] The Real, “from the discourse”—]—let us bring forward commandments clearer than the light of the Gospel. There the righteous are embraced and the impious terrified; it reveals the paradise prepared for us all, shows the unquenchable fire prepared for the devil and his angels, and teaches that he will come for the rewards of the faithful and the punishments of the impious.

These things I ask with sincere petition of you whom I trust to be united in the Lord’s grace. And I adjure you by the Lord not to hesitate to pray with unceasing prayer to our Redeemer and Lord, who came to save sinners, not to destroy them, for our crimes and immense offenses, so that he may lead me, liberated from eternal punishments, with the holy angels to the eternal kingdom in common with them.

Indeed, I think there will be forgiveness for us before God if your prayer intercedes for us. Otherwise, how will the Lord strengthen in holy virtues your purpose, which he foresaw to be blessed? Or how will you, having attained the monastic life, make paternal desires joyful through letters expressing the affection of sons—[Note: [Col. 0372D] The Real, “you look back upon them”?]

Great everywhere is God, the never-changing Creator.

[long lacuna]

Dear to me forever, may you remain well, Theudila,

and with grateful heart love the name of one who loves.

[Col. 0372C] May he who commanded you to grant the divine vow

himself grant you Sandrimer—[Note: [Col. 0372D] Toledo, “Sundrimer”—] Almavia.

May the true Lord preserve you with true grace,

so that you yourself may vindicate the name through your merits.

May the Lion from the tribe of Judah be your helper everywhere;

may Christ, life and light, be gracious to you everywhere.

Amen.

## LETTER VIII. OF SISEBUT, KING OF THE GOTHS, TO ADVALVALD, KING OF THE LONGOBARDS, AND THEODOLINDA—[Note: [Col. 0372D] Toledo, “Terdolinda”; the text writes “Theodolinda”—] THEIR QUEEN. CONCERNING THE FAITH OF CHRIST, SENT THROUGH TOTILA (C)

To the most eminent and most venerable lords, joined to me by brotherly affection, my brother Advalvald, king of the people of the Longobards, and Theodolinda, queen: Sisebut, king of the Visigoths, in the name of the Lord.

Charity is recognized through sincere action when the untainted rule of faith is demonstrated by a Catholic mouth. A pure profession gives birth to immense joys for the other party when the detestable Arian destruction is expelled from a noble lineage and, dug out or suffocated from the root in the body of Christ, is judged to have been deprived of Christ’s grace.

Meanwhile, just as we are lifted up in abundant rejoicing over those who have been converted, so, in like manner amid adversities, bending beneath an immense burden of grief, we are afflicted, when a distinguished offspring, sprung from a glorious stock, is held captive by a serpent’s bite and, having been devoured by bloody jaws, voluntarily permits itself to perish.

It is not merely a matter for wonder but rather for lamentation: to receive saving commandments and yet rush headlong toward the gate of death, to pursue things that perish and diminish eternal things. We grieve over these remedies, and not without reason produce streams of tears under a great burden, recognizing that the kinship of our blood is now polluted by Arian contagion and that brotherly relationship is severed by the virulent discharge of a cancer.

We see rustic men, plainly less capable of reason, daily serving in the heavenly armies through the mother Church. Why, then, should a noble race and noble appearance, innate virtue and natural prudence, elegance of conduct and the discipline of a good life, conspicuous dignity and the outstanding glory of dignity, shamefully remain beneath dead and buried heresies—or, to speak more truly, while they themselves still live, submit their necks in misery?

Let them at last be ashamed to follow the blasphemies of this sect wickedly; let them be ashamed to travel the intolerable road of the smoky path; let them finally be ashamed to reach the punishment of eternal death. Let this also move such people: what is sung daily throughout almost the whole world concerning the heresiarch of their heresy—[Note: [Col. 0373D] Toledo, “of the heresies”; it should be read “heresiarch”—]—who, with his foul entrails torn out, consigned a horrifying soul to eternal fires.

I think that an eternal punishment will likewise receive his followers unless they believe rightly. This was once a disease spread by a most bitter pestilence; it secretly mingled the souls of the unfortunate with the dwellings of hell and offered deadly antidotes in cups smeared with sweetness.

At that time immense calamities and various shortages, most bitter and frequent wars, daily misery, want of crops, and pestilential wounds oppressed this insolent people in times past. After the starry radiance flashed upon the hearts of the faithful and orthodox faith shone upon blinded minds, the empire of the Goths flourishes, with the peace of Catholics increased by the Lord’s favor.

Those who once were torn by the hooked blades of sickle-shaped thorns, wounded by the curved stings of scorpions, and through the serpent’s threefold [uncertain: *trivida venetio*] mouths—these the Catholic Church tends, having cleansed them with maternal affections. It tends them as they profess without guile of heart and tongue, the immutable, indivisible, uncreated, creator of all, eternal Trinity herself sustaining them.

Therefore we beseech your Clemency with words, we beseech you with vows, and we beseech you with pure minds: may your people become participants in such great rewards and, united in the body of Christ, become your companions in them.

It is utterly intolerable, detestable, and not to be endured—[Note: [Col. 0373D] Toledo, “not to be deferred”—] that a head raised to such an abundance of virtues should have even its smallest members become torpid. Rather, the fact that you have acquired Catholic inward parts and are seen to have been reborn in a Catholic font has given us confidence to act without hesitation in these matters.

I think that, through the divine gift, your Glory may be raised to greater distinction by both titles, if you preserve gloriously the path of your mother and extend, with every effort you possess, the gift of election that has been bestowed upon you to all others—[Note: [Col. 0373D] The Real, “with every effort,” rather than “with every means.”]

How much glory of the future kingdom awaits you, most merciful king, as heir; how many gifts of generosity divine virtue is prepared to confer upon you; how many marks and rewards of happiness the same Author desires you to receive, if you are willing—I could say; but mortals are not permitted to know what is prepared for immortals.

Nor can human senses or the human mind attain what the Lord has rightly promised to grant to believers—[Note: [Col. 0374D] Toledo, “the things which the Lord has promised”; the printed reading is corrupt.]

But if your mind should perhaps falter at converting heretics, which it would be wicked to say, because it has failed to cut away errors by the putrid knife of experience—[Note: [Col. 0374D] Toledo, “by preserving rather than cutting away”—]—we speak among those who recognize the matter—consider what loss it will feel in itself and in its own people, or what account it will render to the shepherd of shepherds. We have committed these matters to your judgment. If he should prefer to gather his conclusions in learned and gracious words, I think that time will run out before examples do.

Therefore do not doubt. With Christ as helper, all mortal things yield. There you have a mother worthy of honor in every respect: a teacher most firm in the faith, illustrious in works, sincere in humility, contrite in prayer, devoted to gracious pursuits, bound by the bond of charity, prudent in counsel, rich in acts of mercy, outstanding in honor, laden with every virtue—[Note: [Col. 0374D] Toledo, “honorable”—]—gentle in speech, keen in intellect, generous in gift, just in judgment, merciful in word, Christ’s closest friend, a friend to the Catholic flock, always hostile to the devil, and always most hostile to his heretical body.

Justice calls forth her virtues and makes her persevere with greater balance; prudence urges her to attend to the force of reason. Not undeservedly is she ennobled by the title of so great a name, for she is recognized as fortified by so many rewards under the starry Author.

Therefore, if we wish to consider the force of this name, in clear Argive (Greek) words: “Theodolinda …”

*(In the manuscript of the Church of Toledo, the letter ends here.)*
They should be bent by the promise of what they desire: some, when they are inflamed, must for a time be subjected to the gentle warning of discipline; others must be moved by a sterner rebuke. For the covetous man is easily attracted by an extended gift, while the obstinate man is driven from his perverse course by the severity of strictness. These things must indeed be done with equanimity, according to place, time, and person, [Col. 0374D] until the strengthening ardor of faith, shining with Catholic vigor like a lamp, makes the hearts of believers radiant with light and, burning the rotten remains of heretics—arising from smoky materials—reduces them to ash.

By this reasoning, lest perhaps the mere rigor of charity, which our defender extorted, and so forth. But unpolished confidence, driven by love, put presumption first; may it convey to its hearers that, in the service of religion, prayer touches everything with less flourishing words. Let those who will rightly say these things hear that the kingdom [Col. 0375A] of God consists not only in words but in power. Since the strong please the prudent more than the embellished, and remedies are more useful to the sick than pleasant things, we have not assumed the form of a teacher but have shown fraternal affection; and just as we share an affinity by origin, so let us share the character of holy faith.

Therefore, whatever the brilliance of measured grammatical art lacked, whatever the eloquence of rhetorical acclaim lacked, whatever the argumentation of dialectical discipline lacked, poverty did not deny us abundance of speech; rather, the divine word withdrew from such a discourse the eloquence with which to open its treasures to believers. For, as he says through Solomon, the sophistical speaker is hateful; and again through the Apostle he says: “Where is the wise man, where the scribe, where the investigator? Has God not made foolish the wisdom of this world?” [Note: “Through Solomon” apparently ought to be placed before “sophistically,” after “withdrew.”] He sufficiently showed that the proofs of faith should be asserted in simple words and that orthodox profession should be displayed in ordinary speech. Hence it was that he removed worldly literary studies and refused to preserve the acclamations of the Gentiles in their errors.

But from the radiance of the heavenly library we have tasted examples and marked upon a tablet the connected teachings of the faithful Fathers, so that the authority of the sayings may make faith unimpaired and the apostolic rule, handed down by the Fathers and darkened by no shadows, may reach you.

“The one who confesses me,” says the Lord, “before men, him I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven.” And again: “The one who denies me before men, him I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.” But such must be the confession that makes you and your people followers of the apostles. Build the foundation of faith upon the rock, so that, driven from the caves of heretics by the blast of the winds, it may look upon them and, with the most secure fullness of strength, despise the turbulent drops falling from the faithless.

“You are Peter,” says the Lord, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and to you I give the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against you. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

It is clearly shown that no one can be released from guilt—whether past, present, or future—unless he has maintained the apostolic profession without blemish. The heavenly entrance will remain closed and hardened to him whose heart remains hardened in defending errors. [Note: The manuscript reads *clausum … introitum* and *erroris*.]

The quality of faith is compared with a mustard seed, as the Lord says: “If you have faith like a mustard seed and say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ it will move.” Just as a mustard seed does not admit of being cut, but, extending itself in fruitfulness and thickening through the growth of its branches, becomes a lofty tree, so the purity of the Catholic faith, as though incapable of being cut, multiplies with such noble fruit and raises its supporters to such height that it reaches heaven; and those who merit heavenly gifts enjoy Christ, who never fails. [Note: Apparently the same as *sic*.]

Here he shows the death of the heretical cultivator, the enemy of faith: terrified by the standard of the cross and disturbed by orthodox profession, unable to inflict the most wicked injury upon Catholics, he is carried headlong, uprooted, toward his everlasting destruction.

The Lord spoke to his disciples, saying: “Go and baptize the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” He says not “in the names” but “in the name,” so that the distinction of the Trinity may appear in three persons and the ineffable divinity of one substance may shine forth. Thus the teacher of the Gentiles, following in the footsteps of his master, declares in these words: “One God, one faith, one baptism.”

He clearly and brightly admonished us that there is one confession for the worship and veneration of believers. The Roman Church, faithful in its following, received it from the apostles and, after rightly uprooting the crops of heretics, entrusted it to those who rightly sought it with maternal affection.

Other testimonies of divine law also lie open across the fields, abundantly flower-bearing; like keys or lamps, they illuminate dark things and disclose what has been shut. Meanwhile, we have selected the passages in which Arian presumption, barking in defense of its perverse doctrine, clamors and perversely twists the examples of the divine books through impious interpretations. We have chosen these sayings in order to expose their detestable nonsense, joining beneath them the most sacred words of undefiled faith, so that, once the condition of both sides has been examined and heretical presumption confuted, it may more readily know both how to teach what is good and how perfectly to unteach what is evil.

Finally, wishing in its rash audacity to exclude the Son from the Father’s substance, it brings forward, in support of the subjection of our Redeemer, those statements that pertain to human nature. [Col. 0376C] “The Father is greater than I.” [Note: The manuscript reads *malorum est*.] And: “He who sent me himself gave me a commandment.” And: “I did not come of myself, but he sent me.” And again: “I did not come to do my own will.” Again: “As the Father said to me, so I speak”; and: “What he gave me I have kept,” and “No one will take from me all that he has given me.”

After introducing such passages, they add: “I will ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve thousand legions of angels”; and: “If this cup cannot pass unless I drink it”; and: “If it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will.” They also add: “Whatever is pleasing to him, that I always do”; and: “To sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you.”

In their madness they connect these statements: “He gave him the name that is above every name”; and: “He exalted his servant”; and: “The Lord your God has blessed you”; and: “He raised him from the dead and made him sit at his right hand”; along with many similar passages. The most upright faith receives these in such a way that it knows which belong to divinity and which to humanity.

By these arguments the unhappy are convicted even by examples accepted by the faithful. In the Son of God we most certainly confess two natures: one divine, and the other human. Christ, therefore, is said to have been subject to the Father in the form of a servant which he assumed from the Virgin. The apostle, confirming the teacher of the Gentiles, says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law.” He is said to be subject in that nature in which he was generated, born from a woman under the law.

If anything is indeed found in the divine utterances that makes Christ’s person more subject to the Father, it does not empty the nature of his divinity, but affirms that the true man is subject to the divinity of God. [Note: Some words are missing: “something.”]

Therefore, where God the Son is shown to be equal to God the Father, we have selected the heads of the flowers from the treasures of sacred law, gathered them together, and, drawing from the gifts of the eternal King, presented them under one heading.

For the Son says to the Father: “All that is mine is yours.” And again the evangelist says: “Making himself equal to God in every power.” And: “I and the Father are one.” And in what follows: “That they may be one in us, as you and I are one.” And: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” “My Father works, and I work.” And: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whomever he wills.” And: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” And: “Whoever hates me hates my Father.” And: “Glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you.” And: “I have glorified you on earth and have manifested your name to men.”

Now, so that every effort at quibbling may be silenced, let them accept and defend this sentence of John, foreseen and proclaimed in this manner, as he narrates the most sacred words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” [Col. 0378A]

Let the tongues of the mad be silent from pronouncing judgment through their pompous speech, as they pantingly strive to separate the Son from the Father’s substance.

Concerning the Holy Spirit, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Son in equal unity of power, they suppose and bark out a wretched opinion worthy of being mourned with every fountain of tears. Blinded, they proclaim this view in a funeral-like discourse, wounded by impious madness: they separate him from the Father and the Son and, with criminal voices, declare him not to be God—which is impious to say—but a creature.

Yet sacred authority, rich in divine utterances, has demonstrated in the clearest words that the Holy Spirit is God and Creator with the Father and the Son: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power.” Again, the one who above disclosed beautiful things through his utterances said: “Send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.” That king wiser than all, and also a prophet, says: “He himself created them through the Holy Spirit.” Job, more patient under suffering than all men, says: “The divine Spirit who created me.” And the warrior Judith says: “Every creature serves you, for you spoke and they were made; you sent forth your Spirit, and they were created.”

# The Life and Passion of Saint Desiderius, by Sisebut, King of the Goths

*(Flórez, España Sagrada, vol. XXX.) (C)*

**1.** For the imitation of those now living, for the edification of future generations, and for the exercise of the holy studies of succeeding ages, I have resolved to write the life of the holy martyr Desiderius. I shall report faithfully what reliable fame has made known to our understanding, in a rather plain style than one burdened with ornate words. As I beg the Lord, who is to be present with us, and who not undeservedly granted him power for the performance of virtues, to dispel the dullness of our mind and tongue, may he grant us, unworthy as we are, the ability to recount the order of his deeds.

**2.** This man, born of distinguished Roman parents and consecrated to God from his very cradle, came from a sufficiently noble ancestry. When he reached the proper age at which boys may be taught, he was handed over to literary studies. Before much time had passed, his understanding grew strong; already learned and surpassing others, he mastered grammar completely and, retaining the divine authorities with remarkable speed, explained them. He was energetic in capacity, retentive in memory, keen in intellectual ability, distinguished in speech, and—greater than all these qualities—devout in every action.

According to the Gospel, he gave food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty; he offered assistance to the sick and imprisoned, hospitality to the stranger, and clothing to the naked. Haughty arrogance, hostile to all virtues, did not exalt him; languid drunkenness did not wound him; excessive indulgence in food did not burden him; voracious lust did not corrupt him; deceitful falsehood did not alter him; harmful greed did not persuade him.

When he flourished in such virtues by divine favor, passed beyond the years of youth, and did not embrace youthful desires, his reputation for goodness increased. He spread abroad his works, granted by the true light, and they shone in many regions. Finally, the peoples of many cities, because of his benefactions, asked that he be their bishop. He resisted, confessing according to his humility that he was unequal to so great a mystery. [Note: The manuscript reads *poposcerit*. Toledo reads *studium*, “study,” instead of *studia*, “studies.” The text at this point is corrupt: *sensus si vigore*. He was fully trained in grammar.]

**3.** At last the Church of Vienne obtained the bishop whom it had long desired—not so much willingly volunteering as compelled by many prayers. Once he had assumed this office, by very cautious preaching he removed the quarrelsome from anger, the deceitful from falsehood, the greedy from rapacity, and the lustful from disgraceful acts. He subdued drunkenness by sobriety, overcame gluttony by abstinence, conquered discord through the gift of charity, restrained pride by sincere humility, and shook the uncertain from sluggishness through vigilance.

He taught them to be more generous in almsgiving, grateful and contrite in prayer, steadfast in friendship, careful in judging matters, and always discerning in every action. But he taught all these things more by example than by words, knowing that the Lord, who would come, would seek not so much speeches as deeds.

**4.** While these things were being accomplished by Christ’s permission, the inventor and friend of death groaned against those who had turned back and those who had turned away; surrounded by every kind of weapon, he threw himself into battle against the soldier of Christ. Yet the adversary’s cunning achieved nothing, nor did its disastrous wickedness teach the man of God anything; the grace of the Redeemer had armed him with special weapons.

At last the evil spirit wounded with viperous poison a man of pestilential mind and poured into his entrails the poisoned cups of carefully composed accusations, so that the impious mouth, which he had enlarged with malicious thoughts, might equally defame the athlete of the Lord. The deceiver persuaded certain men, his accomplices in his own name, and contrived such proofs of fraud against the Savior’s servant.

At the same time there reigned Theuderic, a man worthy of every kind of folly, and Brunigild, the patroness of the worst arts and the closest friend of evil. [Note: From *virus* onward the Latin is corrupt.] They also approached a certain matron who was noble in ancestry but deformed in mind: named Justa, disgraceful in conduct; an ornament in name but more a dishonor in deed; unworthy of good things and, naturally, laden with evils; outwardly separated from truth but never separated from crime.

In council she was instructed to accuse the most blessed Desiderius, claiming that he had once committed sexual violence against her. Everyone marveled that the servant of God could be entangled in such matters, and they thought that a fabricated accusation had been brought against him. The presiding authorities pronounced sentence against the innocent, according to the plots previously prepared, and with reckless boldness issued an evil judgment against the good man. Immediately, those who were to punish him deprived him of his office and confined him in exile to a monastery on an island.

His rejection was supreme happiness; his conspicuous humiliation was holiness; his degradation was everlasting felicity. A pseudo-priest was substituted for him, Domnolus by name but truly a servant of the devil. As the man of God grew through abundant virtues, the other was correspondingly defiled by wicked deeds.

**5.** While the blessed martyr was leading a blessed life in that monastery, a poor man arrived begging for alms. Innate silence had closed his mouth, and perpetual muteness had obscured the function of articulated speech. The almighty Father did not disregard the prayer of his soldier: by a gift he made the man at once capable of speech.

What had happened could not be concealed by favorable public report; rather, as the story traveled everywhere, it reached the knowledge of many. Consequently, a multitude of sick people hastened to him in hope of recovering health, and the Lord’s benefits were not lacking in healing those for whom the servant of God implored the Savior.

As I think, a general account of the grace of healings has sufficiently emerged. But lest the composition of this speech, by guarding the entrance through excessive brevity, close the door on the reader seeking further details, I have tried to record individually, with whatever continuity I could manage, certain events belonging to this work.

Certain old men, always darkened by shadows, possessed a nocturnal condition and faces without light. The soldier of the Lord, by prayer, removed the horrible veil of darkness and restored them through God’s grace to the shining light of their heads.

### Where three lepers were healed by Saint Desiderius

**6.** After these events, three lepers afflicted by the disease came to him seeking the grace of healing. A disfiguring whiteness had invaded their bodies, and black sores covered the limbs of the unfortunate. Their stench was intolerable, and the swollen condition of their faces was exceedingly and abundantly dreadful. A dark fluid consumed them and dragged almost all their hair, together with the festering contagion, shamefully from its roots after the hairs had been cut away.

The servant of God removed the diseased sufferings of these afflicted men and restored them healthy and joyful to their proper well-being.

When the Lord had granted this according to his customary mercy, popular rumor brought the matter to the ears of Theuderic and Brunigild: the servant of God had been exalted by abundant virtues and had received from the gift of almighty power a special gift of healing.

Immediately, terrified and struck with the greatest fear, they searched out the matter beforehand, asking whether the honor due to the man unjustly expelled should be restored or whether his exile should be prolonged despite his undeserved condemnation. While cunning investigation struggled to discover the cause of the whole affair, divine vengeance, not undeservedly and fittingly, seized the inventor of magical arts and wicked counsel who had earlier seemed to condemn Christ’s soldier. I have recorded his detestable end in a continuous narrative written by my pen.

This pestilential and unhappily memorable person was held liable to many vices and crimes. Yet his distinctive crimes among his wicked acts were greed for wealth and accusation, and these provoked a great multitude to kill the monstrous disgrace. For at a certain time, while he stood before the gaze of his patron Theuderic, he was seized by the hand of the Burbundians amid a tumult of destruction; his body was butchered limb from limb and left scattered and bloody.

Thus the wretched man lost both life and soul in a horrible manner and voluntarily joined himself, destined to perish, to the infernal prisons, where he would burn forever. [Note: What follows is very barbarous and corrupt.]

What shall I say of her—unjustly just and justly unjust—whom the bloody man seized as his own possession? At the same time in which the aforementioned man was deservedly killed, the evil spirit deservedly entered her.

The same fatal domestic servant again demanded from her all the stores of falsehood which he had earlier prepared. His exaction was expressed in this manner:

“I acknowledge the crime contrived against the servant of God; I acknowledge the cause; I acknowledge, with even greater awareness, the deserved punishment. May the almighty avenger answer this inventor, Brunigild; may the avenger restore these punishments; may the avenging hand of torment inflict sufferings upon the one whose persuasion dragged me, smoky, to destruction; whose accursed gift led to death; whose promise led to no salvation that could survive.” [Note: The Real manuscript reads *peritura* for *perituram*.]

When he had finished speaking, the master of all vices killed the woman, strangling and suffocating her. He carried her with him, destined to burn forever in flames blazing for vengeance. When Brunigild and Theodoric heard of the deaths of those mentioned above, they were terrified.

**7.** Believing that these things had occurred by divine judgment, they were profoundly frightened. So that they might not be punished by a sentence of similar retribution, they feigned piety and ordered that the man of God, who had been unjustly removed from the episcopal office, should return once more, as they desired, to govern his Church.

When he was slow to agree to their request and firmly declared that he would remain where he had been exiled, they repeatedly asked him, with prayers repeatedly offered, not to deny them his presence and to forgive their fraudulent schemes with a merciful heart. Genuine piety moved the sincere heart, and abundant goodwill opened the way for the servant of God to return. [Note: Toledo reads *vitam*, “life,” for *viam*, “way.”]

When the most blessed man appeared before the faces of the unhappy rulers, they fell prostrate at his feet and tried to make favorable to themselves the man whom they had previously exiled by a fraudulent condemnation. They sought to make themselves free from the guilt of so great a crime, though their fatal contagion had entangled them in crimes.

He, however, forgave the deed committed with a merciful heart and, according to the Lord’s command, did not retain the offenses of those who owed satisfaction but released them.

Thereafter, with great ceremony, and with Domnolus unhappily expelled, the rejoicing Church of Vienne received its own governor. The sick rejoiced that they had found a physician; the oppressed, that they had found consolation; the needy, that they now possessed sustenance.

Why say more? The Lord restored abundant aid to the Church of Vienne. Through the presence of the holy man, with the Lord showing mercy, he suspended the shortages caused by calamities, the frequent disasters of pestilence, and the extraordinary storms afflicting the whole city—troubles which, when the shepherd was removed, had undoubtedly been pressed upon it because of his absence.

**8.** Although my speech is weakened by the disease of sluggishness, I have undertaken to relate three things concerning his virtues.

When a great multitude once came to him to visit him, he ordered that they be refreshed, as usual, with food and drink. A servant reported that the supply of wine so greatly desired had run out. He immediately ordered the vessel in which the liquid had run dry to be brought before him. Marked beforehand with the protection of the cross, it was filled by the grace of the Savior with fragrant wine of excellent quality. Thus the assembled crowd was refreshed at once by the blessing and by the mystical drink.

Again, when he was wasting his body through prolonged abstinence and abstained from eating meat at intervals, not because he considered it unclean but as an exercise of moderation, one of his fellow priests came to visit him from not far outside the city. Among other things, they were engaged in familiar conversation about divine oracles.

The sun had already passed beyond the daily course of the hours, and the customary time for refreshment was approaching. Suddenly, with the air breaking beneath beating wings and with swift flight, an eagle—the queen of birds—appeared from the regions of the shining sky. Carrying an aquatic dish, a creature of the sea, it set it down before their faces. They received it with great joy and, giving thanks to the Lord the giver, gratefully and cheerfully ate it. [The following words are corrupt: *ante quoddam suae nobilis secta*.]

At the time of his Passion it happened that he filled a lamp with his own hands and lit it beside the altar. It gave less illumination than the extended rays of light, but, without anyone’s objection, it grew beyond the measure of its capacity, [lacuna] the liquid of overflowing oil. With supreme reason, he embraces the one who, by God’s grace, drives away the illnesses of suffering and removes human diseases by granting health. [Note: Perhaps *hominum*, “of human beings.” The reading is obscure.]

Let it suffice that I have said briefly what I have been able to touch upon concerning his life in this diminished speech. Now I shall explain, with his support, how he entrusted his holy soul to the almighty Lord in his Passion, as these events have been handed down to our knowledge.

**9.** When Theuderic and Brunigild were seen to be harmful rather than beneficial, and more destructive than governing, hostile to virtue, and when, released from the stain of perjury and having abandoned their sworn agreements, they persisted sacrilegiously in betrayal until they were nothing, leaving no disgrace or crime undone, this martyr of God, as inspector and bishop, sounded forth like a prophet’s trumpet against their evils. He threw himself entirely into removing their errors, so that he might make them God’s own, though the devil had made them strangers.

The eminent divine utterance says: “He who converts the wicked saves his soul and covers a multitude of sins.” But they were vessels of wrath, fuel and bushes of vices, bitter condemnation in place of sweet things. They offered harsh things in place of gentle ones and deadly medicines in place of salvation. A more savage enemy besieged their breasts, and the most cunning serpent held them captive under his power. They could not reach the harbor of salvation with free steps, for the fatal robber had subjected them to tighter chains.

Nevertheless, having been satisfied with his mild cups, they began to bark rabid words against the servant of God. With clamorous speech they threatened and vomited the foulest words. But neither the threat of mortals broke God’s martyr, nor the anger of the faithless softened him, nor the storm of the raging bent him. He offered himself immovable in persecution, ready to be struck for justice, so that through these things he might receive from the Lord the promised heavenly kingdom. [Note: Toledo reads *anode quod*.]

When the enemy of humankind saw his unblemished steadfastness, he who never abandoned the breasts of Brunigild and Theuderic mingled himself entirely with them as in his own dwelling. [Note: The manuscripts read *illibatum*; the Real manuscript reads *quae*, and Toledo *que*.] In an imperative tone he impelled them to exact the right he claimed for himself, promising to assign them the first place in punishments if they could tear the soul of Christ’s soldier from its bodily bonds.

Immediately, with harmful words, the sacrilegious mouth, always armed with insults, proclaimed a sentence in the following form: [Col. 0383A]

“It has pleased us that Desiderius, hostile to our morals and an enemy of our deeds, should be beaten with stones and afflicted by many kinds of punishment.”

The accomplices and ministers of the crime quickly promised to carry out the wicked edict of so vile a command, saying to the ears of the ruler what they had wickedly received.

The struggles of his labor did not escape the martyr of God. He had been predestined—or rather forewarned—by the Lord to receive the rewards of the crown.

When he saw that the appointed day had arrived, he was suddenly snatched from the midst of the Church by the hands of the faithless and taken away. As though he were guilty—[the corrupt text reads *indemnes occisurus*, “about to kill the innocent”]—he was led to punishment. There was an unbearable lamentation from the immense crowd, deprived of the remedies of so great a shepherd. They cried out:

“Why, merciful father, do you abandon your sheepfold? Why do you leave the flock to perish? Do not, we beg you, cast us into the jaws of wolves. Do not let us, your sheep, who until now have been refreshed by the sweetness of nectar-bearing flowers, be torn by biting thistles and sharpened thorns while the bishop provides us no protection.”

It is certain, and the voice agrees with the divine Scriptures, that the shepherd’s absence is the scattering of the sheep, while his presence among them is the greatest benefit. We cannot endure in any way that you should be torn from us. If we are denied the life we desire, at least let us be permitted to undergo a glorious death with you.

Finally, to these words the blessed martyr answered gently:

“Your intention is admirable, but your devotion is not to be praised. If the caverns of Tartarus surrounded us, if the gates of hell strove to close us in, if the crackling flame of the abyss attempted to invade us, it would be more fitting to attack the enemy more fiercely with spiritual weapons. But now, since I am invited to serve in the heavenly camp with the radiant ranks of angels, with the apostles and apostolic men, and with the shining hosts of martyrs, the whole of our community is restored to you. Permit your shepherd, I beg you, to return to the Shepherd of all shepherds, so that, with the bishop going before, the undefiled flock may more easily reach the place prepared for it.”

He spoke, and suddenly a raging crowd, packed together and raging, arrived: men of death, with terrifying faces, savage brows, fierce eyes, and hateful expressions; their movements were dreadful. They were sinister in mind, evil in conduct, lying in speech, obscene in words, swollen outwardly but empty within, deformed in both respects, unworthy of good things, rich in the worst, liable to crimes, enemies of God, and constant friends of the devil, exceedingly ready for death.

Their accursed violence, with fury providing its weapons, seized the most wicked arms and poured a shower of stones from its stony heart upon Christ’s martyr. When the terrible missiles of the raging men passed beyond the [text corrupt: *marsiliam*] and bent their course elsewhere; when the exceedingly hard nature of the flints and the very crash of the stoning offered service to the servant of God; and when even lifeless things, though not living, obeyed God according to the divine laws, only the human breast remained hardened—though it could have been inclined to mercy and compassion.

When he breathed out his soul, one man seized the staff of the blessed man and broke his neck. Thus, when the soul abandoned its fleshly material and stripped itself of bodily bonds, victorious, it mingled with the company of the star-bearing airs.

**10.** With an unpolished speech, I have recounted as best I could both the life and death of the soldier of Christ.
