Although this account may displease those skilled in such matters because of its excessive roughness, it ennobles those who think and believe humbly, having omitted the pomp of words.

Therefore, just as we have described his life, virtues, and exceedingly glorious end, it remains for us to recount the destruction and death of the lost.

When Theuderic [Note: Toledo reads *Theciderius*], having abandoned God—or rather, having been abandoned by God—rejoiced upon receiving the news concerning Christ’s servant, he was seized by dysentery, lost his most shameful life, and acquired the everlasting death he had befriended.

The ruined Brunigild lost her perishable consolations and was tortured inwardly by the accusing witness of conscience, so that the quality of her guilt, which had raised her up in the commission of crime, might be fed more harshly by the ensuing vengeance in torment.

While she revolved these things in her dark mind, she declared war against a neighboring people. When the time for battle arrived and the armies, gathered in different groups, clashed, divine terror indeed seized the wicked woman’s side. Thus it happened that her diseased head followed her stiffening limbs to the refuge of flight.

As they wandered everywhere before the faces of the enemy, the first to be captured was the enemy of Christian discipline and the architect of every crime. I shall not hesitate to relate what we have learned by common report concerning her death.

There is an animal of twisted shape, possessing a huge body and naturally having certain curves. Although the top of its back is more swollen, it occupies a higher position than the remaining limbs and is exceedingly well suited to bearing burdens, surpassing other animals in carrying both creatures and other objects.

Upon the raised center of this animal the woman mentioned above was lifted, her garments removed, and she was disgracefully led before the faces of the enemy. For a while she provided the spectators with a most disgraceful spectacle. Then she was fastened to untamed, hoofed beasts and dragged through pathless and rugged places.

Thus her body, already weakened by old age, was torn limb from limb by the raging horses, and her scattered, nameless limbs and bloody remains were loosened in every direction. In this way, her soul, released from its earthly matter, is deservedly held bound in everlasting punishments, amid black, boiling waves destined to burn her.

This account has grown longer and broader because of the matters that arose. But lest its length displease the fastidious, let us now join together a shorter account and bring it to its end. Let us collectively entreat everyone not to receive with excessive reluctance what our Lord Jesus Christ did not disdain to grant through his martyr, whose most venerable body Christ will endow with such abundant healings. [Note: Toledo reads *condemnare*, “to condemn,” rather than *condonare*, “to grant.”]

Whatever illness may afflict anyone, or whatever bodily weakness may cast him down, if he immediately invokes the divine name there with all his heart, he will drive every disease from himself, remove every stain, and by God’s grace arrive healthy and joyful at the healing he desires.

May the Lord, one in the Trinity and everlasting, grant eternal life to me, most unworthy as I am, who recount these things, and grant abundant grace to you who hear them.

# In the Year of Our Lord 623: Saint Bertichramnus, Bishop of Le Mans

# Historical Notice Concerning Bertichramnus

*(Mabillon, Vetera Analecta, vol. I, p. 254.)*

[Col. 0385A] The deeds of Lord Bertichramnus, bishop of the city of Le Mans, who lived in the final period of Chilperic, son of Chlothar, and in the time of Chlothar, son of that same Chilperic—illustrious men who were kings of the Franks.

Domnus Bertichramnus, bishop of the city of Cenomannum, noble by birth, partly Aquitanian and partly Frankish by nation, was tonsured at Tours. Later he spent some time with Domnus Germanus, the distinguished bishop of the city of Paris, and was instructed by him; he was ordained through certain priestly grades and spiritually educated. The aforementioned Domnus Bertichramnus built a certain cell beyond the River Sarthe in honor of his holy master, Domnus [Col. 0385B] Germanus, the distinguished bishop of the city of Paris. He endowed it from the property of Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius, namely from certain estates belonging to that same Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius, as well as from other possessions which he deserved to acquire through his good ability, and endowed it according to ecclesiastical law. In the aforesaid cell, which he had built, consecrated, and endowed in honor of the aforementioned Saint Germanus, he established certain monks living under a rule, and instituted there a hospice for the poor and the noble. He subjected this cell to the church of his see, Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius, and left it perpetually to his successors and to the canons of Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius, to be possessed and governed according to the regular order. [Col. 0385C]

To the aforementioned Bertichramnus, moreover, a cell within that fifth estate which is now called the monastery of Stivale was legally transferred, by instruments of charters, from a certain cleric named Bertigisellus, who had twice seized his see and episcopate by tyrannical authority against canonical law, on account of certain negligences which he had committed through his negligence during the episcopate of Domnus Bertichramnus and in the possessions of Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius. It was transferred under the right and lordship of Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, as can still be found in the testament of Domnus Bertichramnus. Domnus Bertichramnus himself, receiving it under firm conveyance, as we have said, for the restoration of ecclesiastical property, nobly enlarged and improved it, established there nuns living under a rule, subjected it to the church of his see, Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius, and left it perpetually to his successors to be possessed and governed under the firmest legal title. [Col. 0385D]

For he also built from the foundations, in the territory of the mother church and city church of Saint Mary and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, on an estate called Vivereus, a monastery beside the city in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. An angel had shown him the place while he was keeping vigil in prayer in the church of Saint Michael, within the city, in a tower belonging to that city constructed beside the aforementioned mother church; at dawn on the Lord’s Day the angel appeared visibly to him and indicated the place. He nobly constructed the monastery and, after the church of the Apostles had been completed, endowed it with the property of Saint Mary and Saint [Col. 0386B] Gervasius, the mother and city church, and also with other possessions which he was able lawfully and legally to obtain or discover from anywhere, both from the property of his inheritance and from other things purchased or acquired. He endowed it magnificently, with the consent of Domnus Clotharius the king and of many bishops. He also built from the foundations, around the church, the monastery with cloisters and other buildings, established in it a community of many monks living according to a rule, and most devoutly provided, and decreed that there should perpetually be provided, reception and refreshment for the poor, newcomers, pilgrims, and those registered for support.

Not far from that same monastery [Col. 0386C] he built a church in honor of the holy Cross, established servants of God there to perform the divine office, and magnificently arranged there the reception of the poor and of guests. He subjected the aforementioned monastery of the apostles Peter and Paul, together with the church of the said holy Cross and everything belonging to them, to the church of his see, Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius. He named and constituted that mother and city church of Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius heir to all his possessions, both personal and ecclesiastical or hereditary. He assigned and left to his successors and to the priests and canons of that senior church, perpetually and under the firmest legal title, the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, with its entire ecclesiastical property, to be possessed and governed.

The same Domnus Bertichramnus also built or restored on the River Idonia a certain [Col. 0387A] monastery or hospice in honor of Saint Martin, called Pontileuva, and endowed it with property from his episcopate and with other possessions which he was able lawfully and legally to find or acquire. He ordained that all who arrived there should receive everything necessary. He established monks to live there according to a rule, as well as registered dependents, in the number and under the terms contained in his testament. He subjected that hospice to the church of his see and left it to his successors for future possession according to canonical and ecclesiastical custom, as has until now been decreed under oath with us in his testament. We have thought it useful to copy an example of it below. [Col. 0388A]

The aforementioned Domnus Bertichramnus was an archbishop, and he bore the pallium, as is customary for metropolitans. He presided over and served all the bishops of the entire kingdom. Full of days, he died peacefully in good old age, on the … Kalends of July, and was honorably and fittingly buried in the church which he himself had built in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, by his fellow priests and disciples. He lives with the saints of God in heaven; may we also, through his prayers and those of all these saints, deserve to reach and live there, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0387]

## FORTUNATUS’S VERSES TO BERTICHRAMNUS

*(Book of Poems, III, nos. 22, 23.) (S)*

### I. To Bishop Bertichramnus, when he was lifted into a carriage

[Col. 0387B]

There is a kind of carriage which Gaul calls a *rheda*,  
moving gently as its wheel-track cuts the ground.

Leaping forward, it flies on a double yoke with swift axle,  
and the joined team of four horses drives its rapid wheels.

While I, serving, joined the same retinue,  
and my limbs were soon to be carried by the horse,

honoring the deeds of the holy bishop Bertichramnus,  
as he seized me by the hand, I was lifted into the carriage.

As the devoted mother swallow  
cherishes her featherless young and gently guides their outstretched wings,

so he, powerful in goodness and rich in generous affection,  
as shepherd places me tenderly in his own seat.

[Col. 0387C]

Nor does his loving spirit embrace only one, but it loves everyone;  
therefore he stands forth as the people’s one and only love.

### II. To the same man, concerning his little works

I undertook lofty epigrams, sending my sheets,  
and words rolled forth in Sappho’s cothurnus.

Running through poems foaming in swelling verse,  
I thought that I was spreading sails upon a billowing sea.

The smooth page belched forth stormy waves,  
and, like Oceanus (or *Oceanas*), poured out waters from its source.

Only now does Rome, reverend in the Forum of Trajan,  
hear poems so splendidly adorned.

What if the Senate’s ear had heard such an ornament?  
Golden threads would have been strewn for your delights.

Through places, through peoples, through every crossroads, you would see  
your little verses running, with the common people applauding.

Yet I noticed something in your speech:  
in an old poem you speak of new thefts.

Among these, in a few places, an added syllable broke the meter;  
the music, wounded in its own foot, lies limping.

[Col. 0388C]

Now, venerable Father, I greet you with prayer, vow, and voice,  
commending my spirit to you with a suppliant heart.

May your life be long; through your singing muse  
we are compelled to return words in answer to our wished-for pleasures.

[Col. 0387]

## TESTAMENT OF SAINT BERTICHRAMNUS, BISHOP OF CENOMANNUM

*(Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. I, p. 255.)*

[Col. 0387D]

The following is a copy of the aforesaid testament of Domnus Bertichramnus, which he made jointly for the mother church of Cenomannum and the monastery of Saint Peter, as it is inserted here. We have therefore included it in these pontifical acts so that, if anything should unfortunately be lost, it may be found here, and by it one may know how the matter was conducted.

[Col. 0388D]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit. On the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirty-second year of the reign of the most glorious Lord King Clotharius, I, Bertrannus, though unworthy, a sinner and bishop of the holy Church of Cenomannum, sound in mind and body by God’s favor and of sound judgment, fearing the accidents of human frailty, drew up my testament and asked my son Ebbo, the notary, to write and dictate it. If, for any reason, this testament of mine should not be valid under civil law, praetorian law, or through the intervention of any new law, I nevertheless wish it to be valid as though I had died intestate, in place of a codicil, and let it be valid.

Therefore, when I, the aforesaid Bertrannus the sinner, have departed from human affairs or completed the term owed by nature, then you, the sacred Church of Cenomannum, together with the holy and venerable basilica of Domnus Peter and [Col. 0389A] Paul the apostles, which I built before the city for the defense of the city and the welfare of the people, shall be my heirs. I constitute and command you to be my heirs, and let all others be entirely disinherited. Whatever I have given, bequeathed, or ordered to be given by this testament of mine, I entrust to my heirs in good faith, so that it may be given, done, and fulfilled. If I have ordered any persons to be free, let all of them be free, male or female.

And because the illustrious and exalted Lord King Clotharius—may God grant him eternal blessedness in abundance—gave me a precept confirmed by the authority of his own hand, granting me free discretion to assign, for the remedy of my soul, or to my relatives or faithful dependents, whatever I possess from the succession of my parents, whatever I have received as his gift, whatever I have purchased or, with God’s help, may be able to purchase, and whatever increase I may be able to obtain in any possessions or property, therefore I wish and command you, the sacred Church of Cenomannum, my heir, to possess the estate belonging to me called Bonalfa, situated in the territory of Stampense or in the Aequaline Forest. The exalted Lord King Clotharius, together with the exalted Lady Queen Fredegund, once his mother, granted it to me as their humble servant, after Lord Vaedola had rendered justice to them, in return for my faithful service, which I have always been seen to maintain inviolate toward that prince.

I wish you perpetually to possess that estate after my death, with its houses, dependents, vineyards, woods, fields, and everything else, with all its rights and appurtenances, both movable and immovable, except those persons whom I may wish to free from it. Likewise, I wish and decree that you, my Lady Church and heir, possess the cultivated land acquired at that time. From this land the Lady Ingoberga of blessed memory, formerly queen, left one half to Saint Mary at my urging and through the demands of my service; the other half I purchased for a stated price from her brother Magnulfus, so that the whole field might come into the possession of the holy church.

Also, concerning the estate of Celonica, situated in the territory of Tricurinus, of which Bobelenus of blessed memory had assigned one half to the Church, and for which half I endured many troubles, I acted through my own efforts so that it would not be removed from the ownership of the holy Church. [Col. 0389D] Later I purchased for a stated price the other half, which he had assigned to his wife or heirs for possession, and it came into my ownership. I wish you, the sacred Church, my heir, to possess that estate in complete security, together with the shrine of Vicinonia, whatever I purchased for myself or established for the dependents through my own efforts, and whatever, with God’s favor, I may still be able to improve in those fields, with all their integrity and with the dependents residing there.

Likewise, the estate of Brea, which Daulfus transferred to me by a deed of gift and which I later purchased for myself, together with whatever I have attached to it—in short, the estate itself with all its entirety, as it is possessed by me at the present time—shall remain under the ownership of the holy Church of Cenomannum, my heir. I have also acquired through my efforts for you, holy Church, very many things which I am unable to enumerate [F., “which I cannot enumerate”].

Although it is known to everyone, with Christ’s favor, how faithfully I have labored in the holy Church, in the monasteries, and in all affairs, nevertheless you too, my lord bishop, whom God may wish to be there after me, can learn how much God was pleased to confer there through my efforts and labor during my time. If you undertake to inquire with complete faith, you will learn that I labored for your Church to no small extent.

Therefore it should not seem improper to you if I leave in usufruct something from the possessions of Saint Mary to any of our brothers—that is, priests, deacons, or readers—or to my relatives, friends, or servants, whether of the holy Church or my own household. I do not remove the ownership of the holy Church, and I constitute that Church heir to the little substance involved.

And because Domnus Domnolus, a bishop of holy memory, assigned certain small properties from the Church’s fields to his own basilica, where he appears to rest, it displeased us that we should again remove or diminish anything from the Church’s fields under a similar condition in order to transfer it to the basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which I built in honor of their name. But after deliberating more fully with the counsel of our venerable brothers, the priests, deacons, and all the clergy, it seemed fitting to assign one small property from the Church’s estate to that holy basilica—not only out of necessity, but for the first fruits and reverence of those lords the apostles.

The holy mother Church, which nurtures and enriches all the basilicas belonging to it, agreed with the bishops concerning the day on which the heavenly blessing, or the relics of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, were placed in that basilica, and on which, through the assistance of divine grace, it was consecrated twice over by the holy priests in honor of the holy apostles and for the consecration of that place. The estate of Umbriacus, which Basilius and Baudegundus had once transferred by a deed of gift to the holy Church, to be possessed after their death, was the property concerned. We too thereafter labored continually so that it would not be removed from the Church. Therefore, all the foregoing which through me, humble servant of the holy Church, benefits or comes to the Church—both the aforesaid Umbriacus and the suburban basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which is known to have been built through my efforts—must, with Christ’s favor, remain perpetually with that holy Church. [Col. 0390D]

I have decided to assign the following: the estate of Nimione, situated in the territory of Paris, with the vineyards at Frontanitus known to belong to the *palastriae* and to the winegrowers, which Lord King Clotharius gave me and which, while I was still a layman, I possessed partly from the fisc and partly from purchases. I wish the whole of it to be donated to the Church of Paris, under whose favor I was raised.

As for the basilica of the holy and blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which above I constituted heir together with the Church of Cenomannum, since it is my devotion—and since I desire, when God wills, to place my little body there—I give to that holy basilica, in honor of the holy apostles, so that, for the crime which I appear continually to have committed here in this world, those apostles may deign to free me from infernal punishment through their intercessions, and, if not glory—which I do not deserve, may I at least deserve to obtain forgiveness through their patronage or intercession.

Therefore I give to that holy basilica estates situated both in the territory of Cenomannum and in Stampense or Burdigalense, or wherever else, both those which I have already given to that basilica by deed of gift on the day of its dedication and those which I shall still give through the document of this testament. These are estates which glorious Lord Clotharius has granted me through his munificence, or concerning which, for the preservation of my loyalty, he has granted me complete authority by his precepts confirmed by his own hand, so that I may transfer to the aforesaid place, for the remedy of my soul or the stability of his kingdom, the estates which I have deserved to receive from his gift.

These are the estates: the estate of Thedone; the estate called Telate; and other estates, Buresacum, and dwellings in the territory of Wastinum, which we received from the illustrious Varnacharius the Mayor in exchange for the estate of Columbaria.

I ask and command the abbots who, at each period, remain there as divine power or the grace of the lord apostles shall direct them, to observe this above all throughout their lives: that from the estates named above, whatever can come from them each year as tribute or assistance, one half, whenever my commemoration is held, be distributed to the poor, either for clothing or in gold. The other half shall be used to keep lamps burning sufficiently in the holy basilica at all times, so that the holy basilica may never be without a lamp for even one hour of the night. A worthy sign of light, in honor of the aforementioned apostles, shall shine continually both at the basilica of the holy apostles and at the holy Cross which I later built, and at the basilica of Domnus Martinus at the hospice which is at Pontileuga.

Apart from the produce and other revenues expected from the aforesaid fields for the uses of the holy basilica and its monastery, sufficient food and clothing shall be supplied each year for the nourishment of the canons and the poor who appear to sit at the *matricula* of that holy basilica. They shall continually pray to the Lord for the expiation of my sins, and for the prince who bestowed these things, so that the heavenly King may grant him a long-lasting kingdom and that he may deserve to receive a hundredfold in eternal recompense.

To you, holy Church, my heir, I assign the estate of Dolus, which I built through my efforts and which came to me from every direction through my own ability. After the day of my death, whatever I shall have labored to establish there, with houses, dependents, vineyards, fields, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated land, and all its rights and boundaries, whatever I have lawfully withdrawn there, I assign to you, holy Church, in its entirety. [Col. 0392A]

To the basilica of Saint Peter and Saint Paul I assign the estates which I purchased for a price: Gaviacum, Colonica, Landolenae, and Ferrenae, acquired everywhere through my efforts; whatever there was at Cellis or at Samarciacum near the city of Cenomannum; whatever there was at Portithorengum, which I received for protection; and whatever Ceta, Mancia, and Guntha appeared to have possessed there by right and which came into my control, including their entire share of lands, vineyards, tenants, and slaves.

Likewise, I assign the estates which I purchased for the honor of the basilica of Domnus Peter and Paul with money that glorious Lord King Clotharius gave us, or which we gathered from every direction for the preservation of our loyalty. These estates are Campocunanae, Ludina, Comariacum, and Cambariacum, as the deeds of sale make clear. I wish them to be possessed by that basilica, just as we have already transferred them there, together with the estate called Piciniacum, which Gondobaldus, once a deacon, held, and likewise Iliacum, which we received from the illustrious Babisus.

I also establish and decree that whatever has been given to me in small possessions or in any manner, or whatever is known to have been written in my charters, all of it in its entirety—which perhaps has escaped me in this written testament—shall be divided by you, holy Church, and the venerable basilica of Domnus Peter and Paul, and possessed between you in equal measure.

As for the estate of Morenacum, which I acquired through my own efforts and with great labor, and which afterward, when I was absent and at war for the preservation of my loyalty, was wrongfully seized by the evil Modeghiselus, when God restored justice to Lord King Clotharius it came again under the ownership of the holy Church and of me. I constitute you, holy Church, its possessor, with all its rights and boundaries.

As for the portion which I appear to possess in the basilica of Saint Peter and Paul, together with the estate which Leodaldus transferred to me by deed of gift, and whatever I later purchased there from every direction, in the estate of Mechense and Voligione, with its entire integrity, its portions and their boundaries, its dependents, and movable and immovable property, may you, holy basilica, possess it perpetually.

Although no one is unaware of how, after the death of a certain King Guntrannus, I gave my lord King Clotharius an unbreakable oath concerning the fact that the city of Cenomannum ought lawfully to have come, after the death of Lord Guntrannus, from the inheritance of his father, Chilpericus of blessed memory, once king, yet through greed the city itself was taken from him, and he suffered great loss in the remainder of his kingdom.

But when my oath bound me completely, so that I could in no way abandon him, it was easy for me, according to my means, both to leave the holy Church and my own property, rather than be found—God forbid—a perjurer. Since, however, I stood with that prince wholeheartedly out of love for him, and since he had unjustly suffered both his earlier and his later dispossession, it was necessary for that prince to add something to our possessions, from which we and our poor might sustain the substance of life, so that the heavenly King might prove a recompense for us.

For we are poor and have neither gold nor silver with which to repay you, most glorious Lord Clotharius. Nevertheless, from what Your Glory has bestowed upon us, we presume in this testament of ours to commemorate your exaltedness.

We therefore offer to your kingdom gifts from your own benefactions, concerning which you granted us permission, through a precept confirmed by the strength of your hand, to do what we wished: namely, the estates of Neolone and Walionnum, with all their boundaries and appurtenances, and whatever was afterward improved by us. May Your Exaltedness receive these under your own authority.

Likewise, we give you, most glorious Lady Queen Berchirudis, an estate called Penpina, which is named Cella, and which our glorious lord, your husband, granted us as his gift. After my death, under your administration, may you receive that estate without any impediment, with its houses, dependents, and boundaries.

Let my dearest nephew Sigechelmus and my great-nephew Thoringus divide equally between them, if they survive me, the estate of Seuvacum and the estate of Villare Ripariola.

In like manner, the estate of Briomilia, which was justly owed to us from the succession of our parents, had been taken from us for a long time during the interregnum. Later, when God restored his kingdom in its entirety to Lord Clotharius, his piety returned that estate to us and confirmed it by his precept. I wish that estate to be donated to my dearest great-nephews, the sons of Sigechelmus, Leutrannus and Sichrannus.

Likewise, the estate of Castalio, situated in the territory of Saintes, which belonged to my parents and to the illustrious man Sigelenus, and which glorious Lord King Clotharius granted to us by his precept—because it had long been taken from both me and the aforementioned relative of mine, Sigelenus—if Sigelenus survives me, let him reclaim it under his authority. But if not, I wish it to be donated to his sons, namely Sichelecus and Berchelaicus.

The estates of Crisciacum and Botilum, which are justly owed to us from the succession of our father, and which I ought to have divided with my brothers had death not preceded them, I now command my dearest nephew Sigechelmus and my nephew Thoringus to divide equally between them.

The estate of Bualo, situated in Stampense beside Aequalina, which I gave by deed of gift to my dearest great-nephew Leuthrannus on the day of his wedding, as the gift itself declares, I wish by this testament of mine also to be donated to him.

The small estate called Fontanidum, which glorious Lord King Clotharius granted me as his gift, where Eusebius, once a layman, planted vineyards and where we later placed dependents, let the holy basilica of Domnus Peter and Paul reclaim that small estate under its authority, whole and entire, with everything that appears to be there. Let my great-nephew Leuthrannus and his wife be able to possess half of its vineyards in perpetuity.

To the basilica of my lord and special godfather, Bishop Germanus, who brought me up with the greatest affection and through his holy prayer led me, unworthy as I was, to the honor of the priesthood: if he survives, I give there, at the basilica of Domnus Vincentius, where his holy little body rests, the estate of Bobana, which is in the territory of Stampense on the River Calla, and which most glorious Lord King Clotharius granted me as his gift.

If it should be decided that his body is transferred to the new basilica which the illustrious King Chilpericus once built, let that estate always serve the place where his body shall be. May that holy bishop deign to pray for my crimes. I ask the illustrious abbot of that place that my name be recited in the book of life.

My estate which is in the territory of Cramtenum at Summa Vedantia, as it is possessed by me at the present time, and which was lawfully restored to me from the succession of my lord and father, I wish to be donated after my death to the basilica of Domnus Peter and Paul for the benefit of my soul.

To my dearest great-nephew Thoringus I give the estate called Villa Nova, which I purchased for a price from the son of Papolenus. Let him hold and possess it perpetually.

I wish the estate of Idguinum to be donated to my dearest nephew Sigechelmus for as long as he lives. After his death, I command that it be possessed, without participation by his brothers, by his sons who are known to have been born from Bertichildis, daughter of Leutramnus, if he has other sons.

The small vineyards or meadows at Riulionum, adjoining the vineyards of the holy Church and lying within the boundary of Calimarcum, which I purchased for a price, I wish to be donated to the holy Church.

Likewise, the tenant-estate of Satovera, which Vulfarius once held, and which Aiga afterward gave us together with the deeds of sale that she had received from that same Vulfarius, I wish you, holy Church, my heir, to receive, together with that small estate, its vineyards, and all its rights.

As for the small estate called Condomas, which I received in exchange for my property and afterward granted by deed of gift to the most faithful Cotta, I wish that the aforesaid Cotta or her sons be able to possess that small estate in its entirety and perpetually.

As for the house within the walls of the city of Paris, which Eusebius once built or possessed and which is known to have been granted to me by the exalted Lord King Clotharius, I decree that it be possessed equally between the holy Church of Cenomannum and the holy basilica, as my heirs. Likewise, from the shops known to be within the house, the rent expected from them each year shall be brought as a light-offering into the sacred Church of Cenomannum and the aforesaid basilica of Domnus Peter and Paul. The plots outside the city shall likewise be possessed jointly by them.

We establish that the following must be observed: whatever on the day of my death is found in the house mentioned above at Paris, whether in one place or in any of the possessions known to be our property, shall be divided equally between my heirs, the holy Church of Cenomannum and the basilica of Domnus Peter and Paul.

This had almost slipped from my memory, but by the inspiration of divine grace I remembered it. The small vineyards beside the sands, insofar as I recovered or gathered them from the wilderness, from that sand as far as the road enclosed by the same boundary, which the holy basilica of Domnus Peter and Paul appears to possess at the present time, shall likewise belong to it. [Col. 0395A]

Likewise, the small vineyards, meadows, and territory on the right-hand side of the road that goes to Pontileuga, which I purchased from my venerable brother Eoladius the abbot and which are known to be within the town of that basilica, together with the brushwood which I redeemed from my brother Leusius the abbot for forty solidi, and the small fields which we exchanged with that abbot, lying by the channel of the Sarthe, together with the meadow at the confluence, all of it in its entirety, with the servants whom I placed there or whom, with Christ’s favor, I may still be able to place there, and which is now possessed in God’s name by that holy basilica, shall be possessed by it perpetually.

Likewise, the half of the tenant-estate of Vatilonnum which I purchased from Bero in the name of that holy basilica, and the other half which the illustrious matron Egydia transferred to that holy place by deed of gift, I command to remain there in its entirety, just as it is now possessed by that basilica under Christ’s protection, and to continue there perpetually.

And since no one is unaware of how Berthegisellus had illegally attacked his own see against the decrees of the canons, and caused great loss to the possessions of Saint Mary and to my own property, and did not restore them as he should have, except in part through my personal possessions—which he had wrongfully alienated—he gave certain small estates with a deed of sale. That is, he sold us his entire portion, with houses, at Bariacum and Vivale.

Later, when glorious Lord Clotharius suffered another ambush from his kingdom, and I was again held captive for his sake, that same Berthegisellus—whose name ought not even to be mentioned—returned as a despoiler of the Church. He found in the Church archive the deed which he had previously made and ordered it to be burned by fire. May the judge who is fearful and terrible place him with himself in judgment on account of his possessions.

Afterward, when our Lord, by God’s will, entered into friendship with his exalted cousin King Teudobert and willingly received a portion of his kingdom, we reclaimed those small estates, despite opposition, under our authority.

As for Campariaca and Estivale, with their houses, dependents, vineyards, woods, meadows, waters and watercourses, their rights, and every possession, I assign them to the holy basilica of Domnus Peter and Paul.

I completed the house within the walls, on the right-hand side after the little gate, which I built through my efforts, where a small oratory has been constructed in honor of Saint Michael the archangel. I wished those houses to belong to the basilica of Saint Peter and Paul. [Col. 0395D]

While we were detained with Lord King Clotharius for the sake of our loyalty and love for him, a bakery was built by the Church in front of that house. Therefore, in these places, the Church’s allowance and the *matricula* which I established there, I humbly ask my lord bishop who shall be my successor to ensure that, at all times, that *matricula* be maintained, just as until now it has earned an allowance at those times, and that it henceforth always be supported by the holy Church. Let that house serve as a reception place for bishops and for the religious who serve at that oratory, since miracles have also been displayed there, and it ought to be honored [Col. 0396A] and venerated in every respect.

We implore our lord and successor bishop, and adjure him by the God of the Trinity, that from the estates which I have assigned to the holy Church through this page of my testament, or which were acquired during my time, or which came to the holy Church by donation, all the tithes of grain, wine, cheese, and bacon—in short, all tithes—be gathered each year in the house of Saint Michael the archangel, as was done in our time, and distributed for the nourishment of the poor and pilgrims.

For the holy Church will suffer no loss, and what we, though unworthy, who appeared to occupy some kind of priestly office, endeavored, with God’s assent, to distribute among the poor, you must preserve continually.

To the basilica of Saint [Col. 0396B] Peter and Paul I assign that court with the houses which Romolus of blessed memory, once a priest of Cenomannum, held in the city, and that house which he built above the walls in our time, to which we also extended a hand, and which we later purchased from his niece. The houses themselves, as they are now possessed in God’s name by that holy basilica, together with everything that has been worked there, or was attached to it before or in my time, the aforesaid Church shall be able to possess, wholly and entirely, perpetually and without anyone’s impediment.

I give to Holy Church, my heir, the estate called Grandefontana, which I purchased for a price from Vaddolenus, my kinsman, son of Bavo, together with all its rights and boundaries.

To you, holy basilica of the Lord Peter and Paul, I give the estate of Conadacum, which I purchased for a price from Belletrudis, or Bettana, the widow of the late Maurinus, together with the estates of Colicas, which I later purchased for a price from Betholenus and Mantharigus, with their woods and every appurtenance belonging to them, with houses and slaves, just as I have already transferred them into your possession. I wish the whole to be donated, with movable and immovable property, together with that small estate called Timiagum, which I possess in usufruct with my son and kinsman Berulfus, and which after my death you shall recall to your authority.

Although in earlier times I had already conferred upon my most beloved nephew Sigechelmus, by a deed of gift, the estate of Murocinctum, which had lawfully come to me by succession from my lord and father, [Col. 0396D] and although later, through my sins, my brother Berthulfus was killed on the expedition of the lord King Chlothar, and his portion lawfully came to me, I have wished it to be included in this testament of mine. Thus, both what I formerly gave him and what later came to me from my brother shall belong wholly and entirely to my nephew himself: the estate itself, with houses, slaves, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, just as he now appears to possess it. He and his descendants shall possess it in perpetuity.

The third portion of the same estate of Murocinctum, which my brother Ermenulfus of good memory held and gave to me, I wish, after my death, to be donated to my beloved great-nephew Leodefredus, son of Sigechelmus. [Col. 0397A] Except for those whom he set free, or whom I redeemed from captivity: let those persons remain free.

The house situated within the walls of the city of Cenomannis, which my lord and brother Bishop Chaimoaldus built while he was serving in the office of archdeacon, together with the small house held by the deacon Malaricus, I wish to belong to my beloved nephew Sigechelmus, to whom I gave them, so that he and his sons may possess them in perpetuity. For it is known that the new house was built on those plots that had been purchased.

The estate of Patriliacum, situated beside Pontochiuggane, which I formerly purchased from Dolenus, and which I sold in the name of the saints Peter and Paul, or of their basilica, which we already saw being built at that time, and later transferred to that holy basilica, [Col. 0397B] I wish it to possess in perpetuity, together with the tenant farms belonging to it.

The estate of Monciacum, together with the tenant farm that I acquired and added, whether it was established there or purchased everywhere in the territory of Condacum or Monciacum, I wish you, holy Church, my heir, to receive in full.

As for the vineyards which the lord Bishop Licinius of blessed memory gave me as a gift out of affection, beside the vineyards of Cariliacum, and which we previously purchased, together with the land, from Sargitus, formerly a merchant, through divine providence, and afterward planted vineyards there and joined them within one enclosure with the vineyards of the holy church, we wish the holy church of Cenomannis to possess them for the salvation of our souls.

Although previously that estate possessed only a few little vineyards, and my lord bishops, my predecessors, had wished to add nothing there, we [Col. 0397C] nevertheless, for love of the holy Church and its increase, expanded it greatly, both by purchases from merchants and by acquiring other holdings, and paid the price, so that they might advance into the right and dominion of the holy Church, as we desire.

Likewise, the little vineyards situated in Saboranum, which I added everywhere through my own labor, whether by gift or purchase, and whatever more I may still be able to add, together with their cultivators and households, I order you, holy Church of the lords Peter and Paul, to possess at the estate that is more firmly established there.

Concerning Ponteleugua: this is from the register and hospice in honor of Saint Martin; these are the miracles of Saints Peter and Paul, which are at Pontemleugua. If we weigh each matter carefully, it is clear how many crimes we committed in this world while we were held captive. We do not possess enough means of redemption to match the number of sins committed. But almighty God, who wishes no one to perish, may, through the abundant grace of his mercy, grant some forgiveness for the small gifts which we seem to offer to our Redeemer amid great tears and remembrance of the soul, in the person of the poor.

Therefore, since it is my vow, liberation, and considered decision that the basilica built at Ponteleugua in honor of our most blessed and special patron, Saint Martin the bishop, where, by God’s favor, I have placed his holy remains, should receive these gifts, I transfer and assign to that holy place the estates called Longiagae, Nogintum, Novavilla, Antoniacum, and Monasteriolum; the portion which I purchased for a price from Leodelenus; and Avanto, whatever I purchased there [Col. 0398A] or whatever came to me from there, together with slaves, movable and immovable property, and all their rights. Whatever more I may still be able to add or purchase for those places, I order and decree shall remain under the authority of the abbot or of the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul.

Although it may seem presumptuous for us to call it a hospice when we have contributed only a small amount there, God and that holy athlete of Christ himself are able to provide many things there, so that the poor may be clothed and fed, and all our friends and pilgrims may appear to have a lodging there in memory of us.

For the present we order that sixteen little souls devoted to God—that is, poor men, blind men, or disabled men—be placed in that place, and that sufficient food be provided for them each day according to an established allowance.

And, as we mentioned above, concerning the tax from Taletum and the subsidy from Criscianum or Cambariacum, just as we have already ordered above, both for clothing, bedding, and footwear, and for these brothers of ours and the matricularii of Saint Peter who are known to be under his rule: you, abbot of the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, must take the greatest possible care to fulfill all this for them.

If you should appear negligent in any respect in this matter—which God forbid—you shall give an account before the tribunal of Christ, together with Saints Peter and Paul the apostles and Saint Martin the bishop.

Let none of our episcopal successors presume to remove anything that has been assigned to the aforesaid place or to the poor. Rather, on the feast itself, both the bishop and the entire clergy shall receive a worthy meal. If anyone withdraws anything else from the aforesaid little estates, let him be judged before the divine presence as a murderer of the poor. [Col. 0398C]

You, venerable abbot, and your successors, shall take the same care of the course of the holy church of the lord Martin as of that of Saints Peter and Paul. Let sufficient light for the night be purchased from the tax of those estates, and let whatever remains benefit the poor and needy of that basilica.

The estate of Blacciacum, situated in the territory of Bordeaux beside the fortress of Blavit, above the river Garonne, although it had long been possessed by my parents, was removed from their lawful ownership during the interregna or during the youth of my mother. It was then occupied by Aunulfus, son of Maurilio. In the pages of his testament, while he was unlawfully assigning it to the holy Churches—namely, those of Bordeaux, Tours, and Equilium—two parts of the estate were transferred to them, while Arnulfus, brother of Aunulfus, possessed the third.

On this account we had disputes with them concerning the aforesaid estate. But when he acknowledged that what was owed to us lawfully belonged to us, he returned to us, in the presence of those bishops who appeared to possess two parts of it, the present third of the whole estate. He delivered to us a letter, confirmed by his own hand and ratified by the aforesaid priests, so that we might possess it.

But since divine love now constrains us not to act against the holy Church, perhaps, with the favor of my lords and brothers, we may be able to redeem that property. Since, however, the lord Bishop Agericus [of Tours] sold us the portion that belonged to Saint Martin, and made the sale to us with his canons, and since we paid at once sixty solidi, according to his valuation, and added that disputed portion to our holding, we wish you, holy Church of Cenomannis, my heir, to possess it. If we can still redeem anything of that property from the house of the bishop of Bordeaux or of Equilium, recall the whole and entire property to your authority.

The tenant farm of Vincentiana, which my lady and mother possessed, and which we now appear to possess in God’s name, situated beside the same estate of Blaviacum, I wish to be donated to the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, together with its slaves, vineyards, and lands.

The estate of Floriacum, situated between two seas, which belonged to my parents, and which my mother later lost through orphanhood, and which had been unjustly possessed by Childegernus: half of that estate, with its slaves, houses, vineyards, woods, all its boundaries and appurtenances, I redeemed for a price from Berthranus, or Betto, son of Childegernus. I wish that estate, which belonged to my parents, to be possessed in perpetuity by the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul.

The house within the walls of the city of Bordeaux, which my brother Ermenulfus and I recovered by our own labor, the stone-built house itself with its appurtenances, we order to pass into the possession of our beloved nephew Sigechelmus, so that he may have and possess it and leave it to his descendants for possession.

We further order that, throughout their lifetime, whenever messengers of the lords and venerable men of the holy [Col. 0399C] Church of Cenomannis or of the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul come there to trade in fish, they shall always have lodging in that house and shall purchase there whatever they need.

The place called Bresetum, in the territory of Bordeaux, where we appear to hold precarial grants [alternative reading: pitch-works], and which we purchased for a price together with Arennoaldus, I transfer after my death to you, holy and venerable basilica of the lords Peter and Paul, with the precarial grants [or pitch-works] remaining there, their households, and the pitch, just as it is possessed by me at the present time, so that you may recall it to your authority and receive pitch from it each year.

It is known to all how twice or three times I endured the plundering of the property of the holy Church and of my own possessions. [Col. 0399D] God knows that I suffered this not on account of our sins, but because I wished to preserve the faith undefiled; and at that time the holy Church suffered grievous loss in its resources, while I became very poor and reduced to my own meager substance.

Therefore I am ashamed to write how little remains to offer. I give the silver which God, or the lord king, or friends later bestowed upon us, as the memorandum written by my hand records. I have arranged that you, holy Church, receive two parts of the silver which I appear to have acquired through my own labor. Of the other portion, which I recorded in that memorandum, I order you, basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, whom I appointed my heir as I appointed you, holy Church, to possess it.

I adjure, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, both you, lord bishop [Col. 0400A] who shall be my successor, and you, abbot, who shall be in office when God orders me to depart from this world, as well as your successors, that no one presume to remove or sell anything from these small gifts which I give to the holy Church or to the holy basilica in remembrance of my name and from these materials. Rather, they shall remain forever for the adornment of the holy Church or basilica and upon their tables.

As for the remaining silver, whatever may be found after my death in my little treasury, except the silver reserved for the holy Church, and whatever I now appear to possess or may still acquire that has not been assigned, I order to be divided equally between the holy Church and the holy basilica of the lords Peter and Paul. If necessary, let the abbot use the portion he has received to adorn something for my burial; and if I have not done this beforehand, let him take from what he received from the bishop and diligently arrange it for my burial. If Christ should permit us to remain in this light beforehand, let that silver be brought into the service of the basilica for whatever is necessary.

In like manner I order that from the damask garments [Alternative: brooches], you, most beloved archdeacon, whoever you are at that time, reverently offer two of the best pieces of my own damask clothing to my lord and successor the bishop. To you, holy archdeacon, I prescribe that you take one good horse and one little pair from my property.

Whatever belonging to my property or arising from military service is found in my little treasury after my death, as well as goods or garments which I have made or acquired, except what belongs to the holy Church, I order to be divided into three portions. One shall be received by my lord and successor the bishop; another by the basilica of the lords Peter and Paul; and the third I order to be distributed immediately to the poor.

Likewise I prescribe to you, archdeacon, and I testify before God, that from the fruits which I leave that year, when I have breathed my last, one third shall be distributed to the poor by your hand without fraud.

Likewise I wish and order that all the servants of the holy Church who are known to be officials, or my own servants, both clerical and secular, who appear to live with me, receive immediately one horse each, whether they are freeborn, freed, or servants.

The remaining horses—Warannones, stallions [the text reads spadas], or fillies—which are found and which bear the mark of the holy Church, shall all be received by the bishop or the Church. But those which bore my personal mark, or which my relatives or friends gave me, shall be divided: the holy Church shall receive half, and the basilica or the abbot who is there shall collect the other half.

I wished this to be attached to this testament: of the herds of horses which my small resources have gathered or increased from every quarter, except the old beasts of burden, two portions shall be made of those herds which appear to be my own and which graze upon the land of the holy Church, as we have said. One shall be received by the holy Church, and the other by the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul.

The herd whose shares of horses appear to be held upon the property of the holy basilica of Bishop Victurius I wish to be donated to that holy basilica.

The beasts of burden which were Gallimera’s personal property I wish to be given to my faithful Elopodia.

I give and transfer, in perpetual possession, to my beloved great-nephew Leodochrannus the estate of Marciliacum, situated beside the village of Diablanta, which I purchased for a price from Medighiselus and Ebretrudis, or added from elsewhere, or may still be able to add, together with houses and slaves, its appurtenances, meadows, pastures, waters, and watercourses.

Likewise, the estate situated beside the village of Pacilena, which Bladus, father of Victribernus [Alternative: Bladovic, the tribune], sold to us for our solidi, I order my beloved great-nephew Sigramnus to possess, together with all its appurtenances.

Likewise, the estate of Pauliacum, which I purchased for a price—that is, for three hundred gold solidi—from the venerable Abbot Bobenus of the basilica of the lord Albinus, I order my beloved great-nephew Leodochrannus to possess, so that he may hold it in perpetuity.

If either the basilica of the lord Albinus or the abbot who succeeds Bobenus should thereafter attempt anything against him, let him repay the aforesaid Leodochrannus double compensation. Even if that estate should wish to act against the decision of its predecessor, it shall not thereby be able to claim it; rather, it shall be claimed in perpetuity by my great-nephew himself.

The estate which is known to be beside the village of Berulfus, and in that estate whatever Berulfus formerly lost that I purchased there, whether from the son of Enulfus or from Remoaldus and his wife, I wish to be donated in full and divided equally between my beloved great-nephews Leutfredus and Thoringus, if they outlive me. After my death, let each recall his share wholly to his own authority.

For the basilica of the holy and most blessed Bishop Germanus of Paris, who lovingly nourished me and, through his intercession, brought me to the priestly burden, although I did not deserve it, I built in the city of Cenomannis [the text reads obedum civitatis; proposed reading: “death in the city”] in his honor; I also built houses there and established monks who, with Christ’s favor, may carry out worship and service there for all time.

To that basilica, in honor of that bishop, I give the following estates: Charisagum, together with the vineyards situated in the village of Silviacum; the little estate called Stirpiacum, with the little vineyards and little slaves known to be there; Landolena, Graciacum, and Manciacum, which I purchased for a price from every quarter and which came under my authority. Both what I appear to possess at the present time and whatever I may still be able to improve, I wish to be donated to that holy basilica in honor of the most blessed lord Germanus.

The vineyards at Ruilio, which the deacon Aunigiselus held, and whatever else I later purchased from every quarter, together with half the meadow at Ruilio, I prescribe for possession by that holy basilica.

The estate of Comancium, which I purchased from Ebroaldus, son and kinsman of mine, and where I later built houses and vineyards, together with what I found there and with all its rights and appurtenances, I decree that you, basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, which I built in your honor and immediately constituted as my heir in all things, shall possess.

The little estate called Fontana, within the boundary of Alaunum, which the magnificent man Baudhegiselus and his wife Saucia granted and donated to me, and to whom we gave much assistance insofar as we could, you, holy Church and venerable basilica of the lords Peter and Paul, shall recall to your authority after our death, just as it was possessed by Baudhegiselus. Let their names likewise be recited in the book of life in that basilica.

The estate of Redonatiacum, which has always belonged to Bonalfa, together with the lands and woods which we later purchased there for a price from Chargarius and Ragnaricus, and everything else, wholly and entirely, just as the estate of Redonatiacum has always belonged to Bonalfa and ought to belong there, I assign so that you, holy Church, my heir, may benefit from it in perpetuity.

Although we wished everything that had been worked by us, both in fields and in movable and immovable property, to be assigned wholly and entirely in one testament, just as our earlier testament contained it, afterward God ordered the glorious lord our King Chlothar to bring the whole kingdom of the Franks under his authority, and afterward his abundant [Col. 0402C] mercy took some account of our services. We must not pass over this matter.

Therefore, the estates which Avitus of good memory, son of the late Bishop Felix, who had married our kinswoman and relative, possessed, and all the property of Avitus which his mercy granted between me and the illustrious man Gundolandus, mayor of the palace, and which I now appear to possess against him, my entire portion—both what is in the territory of Bourges and what is in the territory of Albi, Cahors, and Agen—everything, wholly and entirely, whatever half of that estate belongs to my account, I release for the remission and lessening of my sins. After my death, you, basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, whom I appointed my heir, shall receive those estates in their entirety.

The estate of Nogiogilum, which both the illustrious man Gundolandus and I had granted in usufruct to my daughter and kinswoman Dundana, you, holy Church and basilica, shall, after her death, jointly recall to your authority in equal halves, as is proper for the precarial grant of the aforesaid woman, so that it may be divided equally.

The estate of Vocriomnum, which the glorious lord King Chlothar granted me as a gift in return for our property, which Egulfus and Arnoaldus had unjustly held and devastated—although the pious king had already given us more of it—I relinquished, at his command, to the Church of Metz in honor of the lord Stephen. I asked, together with my lord and brother Bishop Arnulfus, for this estate and for the estates that had belonged to Egulfus and Arnoaldus, which he had received, so that we might hold the estate of Vocrionnum in perpetuity and have free discretion to do with it whatever we wished.

Therefore, for the benefit of the lord king and for our own benefit, since the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul possesses few vineyards, I wish this estate, with all its rights and appurtenances, wholly and entirely, to be donated in perpetuity to you, holy basilica of the lords Peter and Paul, where I desire my body to be buried.

The estate of Nociogilum, situated in the territory of Poitiers above the river Loire, which Beatus, nephew of the late Bavo and son of Theudaldus, granted there by a deed of gift from his maternal property, I order you, holy basilica of the lords Peter and Paul, to possess after my death.

Of the estates of Marogilum, Rufiniacum and Marigilum, which came to me from the property of Nunciana, after she had greatly devastated the property of the holy Church, and which the glorious lord King Chlothar granted to us after Nunciana’s death, I order you, holy Church, my heir, to possess.

As for the little estate called Lucianus, whatever is owed there to Hisigilo; and the little estate situated above the river Ledo, called Bauciallum, which I purchased from Bestingiselus of the territory of Vendôme, from his wife, and from their stepsons, I wish to be donated to the basilica of Saint Victurius in the city of Cenomannis, together with its slaves and everything that has been improved there.

The estate called Tauriaci, the portion which Nuncia held there, which we now hold by the command of our lord, just as we hold Marogilum and Rufiniacum, and the estate of Tauriaci itself—both Nuncia’s former portion, which has now come to us by our transfer, and the portion which Audericus and his nephew, the son of his sister and of his female relative, sold to us, which we joined together—I order you, holy Church, my heir, to possess.

The little estate called Luciacum, whatever I purchased there from Berthigisilus, his wife, and their sons, and which I appear to possess at present, together with whatever I have added there or may still be able to add, I assign to the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, my heir, for possession.

As for the estates situated in the territory of Duno, namely the estate of Pannonium, which I purchased from John the abbot for a price of one hundred and forty solidi, and the estate of Marciriae, which I likewise appear to have purchased from Betto, son of the late Baddo, you, my beloved nephew Sigechelmus, shall receive after my death. After your death, let your sons divide them equally among themselves.

The little estates which Suadria, sister of the late Bishop Theoderus, gave to the holy Church by her testament—namely Luciniacum and Monte—and which I later claimed through my own efforts; and the estate which I purchased from Dudo, nephew of Romonus, above the Loire, for one hundred solidi: I order you, holy Church, my heir, to possess that property, together with whatever I now appear to possess there, with houses, vineyards, lands, slaves, and the whole of that portion.

Likewise, the estate of Brea, which Theudoaldus sold to me, you shall recall to your authority, together with its vineyards, slaves, and all its rights.

The estate of Kairacum, which I purchased from Comerius the deacon for three hundred solidi and which is now known to be in my possession in God’s name, I decree that you, holy basilica of the lords Peter and Paul, whom I named my heir together with the Church, shall possess, with houses, slaves, vineyards, meadows, woods, and all its rights. If I should still be able to improve anything there, recall the whole and entire property to your authority.

The estate of Sitriacum, which I purchased for a price from Leugadia, together with the other little estate called Blaciaci, with their appurtenances, houses, slaves, vineyards, lands, meadows, woods, and all their rights, I order you, holy Church of Cenomannis, my heir, to possess.

The estates of Cresciacum and Vallis, as was agreed by letters between me and the lord Bishop Arnulfus of the Church of Metz, I previously decreed by our letter for the honor of the lord Stephen and his Church. After my death, let that holy Church in honor of Saint Stephen recall them to its authority, and let it order my name to be written in the book of life there by whichever bishop is in office at that time.

I order the basilica of the lord Peter and of our special patron, Bishop Medardus, to possess after my death the three parts of the tenant farm which we held from the property of Arngaldus.

The estate of Montiniacum, which the late Bishop Giboaldus held and which later came under our authority, I now assign and decree to be the property of the holy Church, together with all its rights.

As for the estates situated in Burgundy, which our glorious lord King Chlothar and the illustrious men Bradonus and Warneharius, mayors of the palace, gave us—estates which had belonged to the late Leudegiselus—I do not wish you, holy Church of Cenomannis and basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, my heirs, to possess equally with those illustrious men the third portion which is lawfully owed to me from those estates together with those men.

As for the estates in Provence which that pious king granted between me and the illustrious men Gondolaidus and Chugo from the property of Aureliana, whatever we might lawfully claim from them without sin, namely my portion of those estates, you, my heirs, shall recall to your authority together with those illustrious men.

As for the estate derived from the property of Nunciana, both in Poitiers and in Erbaticola, and those other estates which, together with my kinsman Chiso, we lawfully received from Nunciana’s portion in Cahors, Limoges, or anywhere in Gaul, I order you, my dearest kinsman Chiso, to possess them for the sake of affection and purchase, to be divided equally with your nephew and ours, Thoringus.

The estates which I purchased for a price from Dracoaldus, bishop [of Auch], and which are known to be in the city [Reading: territory] where the aforesaid bishop was killed, I prescribe for possession by you, my beloved nephew Sigechelmus, together with your sons.

My most faithful men Warneharius and Walco, son of the late Tedemondus, who are known to have served me faithfully from their youth, and the holy Church with complete faith, as is known to all, shall receive in full whatever lands, slaves, or vineyards I have given them or which they appear to have acquired during my time. I wish them and their sons and daughters to possess these things as long as they live, and I order and decree that no one remove anything from them.

Whatever we formerly gave to our faithful Cherulfus or to his sons, we confirm in full.

As for my most faithful friend Chadelenus, whatever I gave him here and in the territory of Cenomannis, I wish him and his sons to possess it in perpetuity, since it is known to all that he served faithfully and continually in the ministries of the holy Church and intends to do so throughout his life. It is just that whatever came to him lawfully from the Church, or whatever came to the Church through my labor, should remain with him forever.

As for my faithful Betolenus, son of the late Cundelenus, whatever was given to his father, or whatever was afterward granted to Betolenus from our generosity, I wish to be donated in perpetuity to Betolenus, his wife, and their sons. His mother, too, shall possess in usufruct whatever she has received from it for as long as she lives. After the death of the aforesaid Betolenus, his sons shall receive it in full, and may they always remain friends of the Church.

Therefore I ask and order that, whoever my friends or faithful servants may be, they should always remember my upbringing and the benefaction which I bestowed upon them, so that after my death they may take care to be present there whenever the day of my commemoration arrives. Let them offer assistance to the abbot of that place, and let them say: “Blessed is the man who leaves behind good friends.”

I prescribe to you, my beloved nephew Sigechelmus, and I ask and adjure you and your sons by almighty God: as long as he wishes you to survive in this world, you and your wives and children, if health permits, shall visit my little tomb twice or three times each year.

I also adjure the abbot of that place to refresh you fully and honor your sons, just as he knows that the holy Church found me to be a comforter, so that it may please you and your sons to visit that holy place frequently and commemorate my memory.

I adjure and ask my lord Bishop Cabimoaldus [below: Bishop Chaimaldus of Poitiers], who is known to be my kinsman and whom divine mercy has brought to the priestly summit, always to remember my upbringing and the patronage of Saint Peter, through which, under Christ the bishop, he advanced to that burden.

When God eventually orders me to depart from this light, I ask that they honorably bury my body with his own hands, together with his other lords and brothers, in a suitable burial place, so that they may gain the Lord’s reward from it and praise may spread among the people.

I order the archdeacon at that time to give those lords who are gracious enough to bury a sinner two paired horses [F.: two pairs] and two foals from the herd, and let each of those lords receive one little pair (pariocolum). You, lord Chaimaldus, shall graciously do this together with the archdeacon; and we order you to receive a similar share, just as your brothers do.

As long as God wishes you to survive in this world, I ask you to come for my commemoration, and let the lord abbot or the community of Saints Peter and Paul offer you fitting honor.

I order the following persons, male and female, to be free: Libigiselo with his wife and sons; Chinemundus; Chrodosindus with his wife and children; Theodogundi with son Lopo and daughter; Emmane with wife and sons; Ebrelenus with his wife and sons; Gariulfus; Julianus; Picoaldus with his wife and sons; and the son and daughter of Maurellus.

Likewise, I order my household servants who appear to serve there, whether of Roman or barbarian origin, to be free: Teodana, Bajona, Baudasinda, Mauro, Austreharius, Audisgisilus, Vetesigilus, Bercehanus, Quotana, Alagisa, Leodegisilus, and the sons of Theodonivia.

I order all these to be free, with all their personal property which they have or may thereafter acquire through their labor. May we deserve to have the protection of the holy basilica of the lords Peter and Paul the Apostles, where I desire my body to rest in God’s name.

Thus, at the time of my burial, each of them shall assemble and offer or recite before the holy altar only offerings made in my name. Each shall observe, in God’s name, on the aforesaid day, the service which he appears to have performed. They shall offer assistance to the abbot of that place; and on the following day the abbot shall give them a most worthy meal. Then each shall return to his own house—both those whose names are recorded here and those whom I later purchased from the barbarian people or may still be able to purchase, whether boys or girls, who are known to have been bought by me and for whom I made deeds.

Let them remain in complete freedom and observe what many of them observe, and let all remain under the protection and defense of Saint Peter. The dasgastaldus [title uncertain], and those among them who wish to remain with that abbot or serve the basilica, may be enriched from the property of the holy basilica, so that they may take greater pleasure in honoring my little tomb and serving the holy basilica.

Those who are known to remain in the territory of Cenomannis are likewise known to have the protection of the holy basilica of the lords Apostles Peter and Paul.

If necessary, the abbot to whom the holy basilica has been entrusted for its governance and administration shall always use what I have bestowed there to celebrate my burial and the light of my little tomb each year, taking such care that others may be encouraged to enrich the holy places with great gifts.

If that abbot should prove negligent in this matter, let him know that he will suffer vengeance for it before the tribunal of Christ with the lords Peter and Paul the apostles, and receive everlasting condemnation.

As for those whom I have released, or may release, from the property of the Church for the individual festivals during the period of white garments, let them, as their letters declare, be restored under the protection and defense of the holy Church.

And because human circumstance renders many things uncertain, and I fear lest—God forbid—unrighteous greed, which is the root of evils, should in any respect break my devotion, I adjure you, lord priest, whom God may will to exist after me, by that dread judgment and day, so that you may attain the eternal reward of blessedness and not acquire a share in condemnation with Judas: fulfill every determination of my will; or, for as long as God wills you to survive me, intend to guard everything. He who firmly desires the judgment of his will to remain in force ought to weigh this freedom.

I ask that, when my testament has been opened before all and before my fellow provincials, one hundred solidi be sent through the hand of the archdeacon, by the bishop of the city of Tours, to the tomb of the lord and particular patron, Saint Martin the bishop, where I laid down my hair and where year by year I paid my tribute. Likewise, fifty solidi are to be sent to the basilica of Saint Albinus the bishop through the hand of the bishop of Angers. I entrusted these solidi to a faithful dispenser, separately in small purses with sealed notes for each place, as I mentioned above, to be distributed as the page of my testament declares.

To you, archdeacon, I command and order that throughout all the basilicas known to be situated around our city—that is, at the basilica of Saint Victurius, my particular patron, you shall give twenty solidi; at the basilica of the lord Vincentius, where Saint Domnolus the bishop rests, in honor of that martyr and of the lord bishop, you shall give twenty solidi; at the basilica of Saint Mary or of the Holy Cross, you shall give ten solidi; at the basilica of Saint Julian the bishop, either a horse or five solidi in gold; likewise at the basilica of Saint Richomer, ten solidi; at the basilica of Saint Hilary, five solidi. At the oratories of the lord Martin, the lord Victurius, or Saint Peter within the walls, you shall give five solidi in gold or horses. At the basilica of Saint Stephen the martyr, either in gold or in horses, you shall give five solidi.

Likewise I wish and order that you give each of all our clerics who are known to serve here in the church fifty solidi, whether from these funds or in any kinds of property. I especially ask this: in the places written above, where I have assigned something not as it ought to have been assigned but insofar as my ability prevailed, let them order my name and the names of their priests to be entered in the book of life and recited at each festival.

Although I ought to have stated above what they should do for my ashes, since I had not fully investigated which members of my household I should entrust with this task, it is therefore fitting that, from however many estates of the holy basilica of the lord Peter and Paul I have assigned to be possessed as my hereditary property, we should wish to have written in one letter the names of the individual householders (*condomae*) from each estate who are known to be the most orderly and who faithfully serve us and the holy basilica, and to confirm it with our hand, so that they may be wholly released from service. Together with the abbot, they and their offspring who shall be born from them must have complete care of my tomb, both of its lighting and of my ashes, until the last day of their lives; and they must serve perpetually with complete diligence, while the free status of their condition must endure forever under the protection of that abbot.

But because we presume that nothing from the household of the holy Church may be imposed upon or released for our ashes or for any disposition to be made, as our lords and predecessors did, I likewise order that, if anything concerning my servants, or those of my late brother Bertulf, has escaped my mind, and if they are seen to remain in the territory of Le Mans, all of them shall be entirely freed from service and shall deserve to have the protection and guardianship of the holy basilica of the lord Peter and Paul, like my other free people. Those whom I redeemed from captivity, who had previously been free but now appear to serve for a price—both men and women from the estate of Boalcha—shall all be released from service. To the principal recipients of alms in the city, and to those attached to the small basilicas, I order five solidi to be given through the hands of the archdeacon.

Because I desire the determination of my deliberation to be firmly preserved through this testament, I therefore adjure you, lords and bishops, by the holy apostolate which you have received through divine tradition: wherever necessary, always provide assistance to my basilica or to the abbot of that place, and instruct my lord and successor with such counsel that he diminish nothing from what I have assigned to the holy basilica in honor of the lord apostles Peter and Paul as a remedy for my soul, nor defraud it of anything for any reason. For I know that I have caused no loss to the holy Church.

Likewise I adjure all of you, by the victories of the most merciful princes—since in the world you possess influence to act with those lords and our princes—that, whenever necessary, you never deny the little document the help of your protection.

I have still mentioned little of what I committed to great forgetfulness. The house of Diablentes, which I built by my own labor, with its courtyard and stable, garden and farm buildings, and everything that I acquired everywhere from the priest Boso, from the heirs of Etolenus and Trilono, at the place called Calviac, or everywhere in the town of Diablentes beside the bank of the little river Aroena—lands, dependents, woods, meadows, and everything with its lawful rights—together with the Taxonaria which I claimed against Leuttherus and his heirs, I wish you, holy Church, my heir, to possess wholly and entirely, except for the ancient property of the Church of Diablentes.

Likewise, those shares which Guntherus transferred to me by gifts in all his possessions, together with Guntherus himself attached to that house of Diablentes, I decree that you, holy mother Church, my heir, shall possess.

Those little houses which the deacon Domnigisilus of blessed memory received from our gift, and which he, poor man, built there; and which, after his death, we granted to our most beloved nephew Leudochramnus—with all the little houses, small fortresses, little vineyards, small fields, and whatever that deacon himself appeared to possess there, together with the little dependents who appear to belong there—we wish our nephew himself, whenever he decides to come frequently to the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul out of love for us, to possess them always with the favor of our episcopal successor, just as we wrote in our testament; and likewise, after his death, they are to return to the right of the holy Church.

[Col. 0409A] For I now declare that if anyone attempts to act against this will of mine, he shall be struck with perpetual excommunication, and may God display such judgment against him that, struck with the leprosy of Naaman, the earth may swallow him as it swallowed Dathan and Abiron; and may divine vengeance appear against him in such a way that he recognizes his wrongdoing in the present age and never obtains the remission of pardon at the future judgment.

If there are any erasures, if there are any overwritings, if any letters have been added or removed, I made them, and ordered them to be made, while I repeatedly read my will aloud to myself; and I recognize and correct everything individually.
