As the law teaches, I have entrusted this document to be secured by the subscriptions and seals of seven honorable men, and I ordered these to be appended for the firmness and ratification of the whole matter.

Executed at Le Mans, in the city, on the day and in the year stated above.

Bertichramnus, in the name of Christ, although an unworthy bishop, reread and subscribed my testament, which I dictated for writing to my son Ebbo the notary.

I, Guntinus Honoratus, subscribed, at the request of the lord Bertichramnus.

I, Dado, subscribed, at the request of the lord Bertichramnus.

The sign of Gerinus: I subscribed, at the request of the lord Bertichramnus.

I, Ibbolenus, subscribed, at the request of the lord Bertichramnus.

I, Gaddo, subscribed, at the request of the lord Bertichramnus.

I, Hugo Honoratus, subscribed.

I, Ebbo the notary, at the command of my lord Bertichramnus the bishop, with him present, wrote, reread, and subscribed this testament, and recorded the day.

Likewise I, Bertichramnus the bishop, ask my son the archdeacon that, when my testament has been opened, he himself, pursuing the matter, cause it to be attached to the municipal records according to law, so that it may always remain firmly in force.

**In the year of the Lord 624. Saint Protadius, archbishop of Besançon.**

[Col. 0409]

## Historical Notice on Protadius

*(Dunod, History of the Church, City, and Diocese of Besançon, vol. I.)*

[Col. 0409A] This bishop’s name appears in our catalogues after that of Saint Nicetius, and in our ancient litanies among the holy confessors. His legend states that he was of illustrious birth, *nobilissimus*, loved and esteemed by King Chlothar II, and that the prince often sought his advice; that he wrote a book on the rites of his Church at the request of Stephen and Aymin, heads of the cathedrals of Saint John and Saint Stephen; that he died on 12 February and was buried in the Church of Saint Peter. He may have been the brother or son of Protade, who belonged to a Roman family and was mayor of the palace of Burgundy under Theuderic II. He succeeded Nicetius at the beginning of the seventh century and had died by 625. His successor, Donatus, attended the Council of Reims.

[Col. 0409B] His body was raised from the earth and exposed for public veneration in the church of Saint Peter, where he had been buried. The chaplains of this church [Col. 0410A] had a silver bust made, and the citizens a reliquary, into which his head and his other relics were transferred on 9 February 1614. His memory is held in great veneration in this city, where his feast is celebrated on 10 February with a double office.

The magistrate customarily invites the clergy of the Church of Saint Peter to expose the relics of Saint Protadius, so as to encourage the people to ask, through the intercession of this holy pontiff, to be delivered from public calamities when threatened by them. The records of the metropolitan church state that in 1529 and 1642 the archbishops ordered general processions from the Church of Saint John to beyond the bridge, in which the reliquary of Saint Protadius was to be carried.

[Col. 0410B] Saint Protadius is regarded as the author of the first written Ritual of the Church of Besançon, later interpolated and enlarged over time.

[Col. 0411]

## Liturgy of Saint Protadius, Bishop of Besançon

### I. Praises or Acclamations Transcribed from an Ancient Book of Epistles (S)

These were sung in the pontifical Mass, according to the ancient Ordinal of the Church of Besançon, p. 62, between the prayer and the epistle. They are still in use in the most renowned churches of France, namely those of Vienne, Lyon, Rouen, and others.

[Col. 0411A] Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands. Hear us, O Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0411] See Roman Ordinal 12, by Censius, no. 2, in volume LXXVIII of the *Patrologia*, from the Ralico Museum. EDIT.]

For N., the supreme pontiff and universal pope: life! Savior of the world, help him. Saint Peter, help him. Saint Paul, help him. Saint Andrew, help him. Hear us, O Christ.

For N., the pontiff, and the clergy and people entrusted to him: salvation and glory! Redeemer of the world, help him. Saint Ferreolus, help him. Saint Antidius, help him. Saint Desideratus, help him. Hear us, O Christ.

For N., the most excellent emperor, great and peaceful, crowned by God: life and victory! Protector of the world, help him. Saint Maurice, help him. Saint Sigismund, help him. Saint Victor, help him. Hear us, O Christ.

For N., the illustrious queen: light and grace! Light of the world, help her. Saint Perpetua, help her. Saint Lucy, help her. Saint Walburgis, help her.

Hear us, O Christ.

For all judges and the entire army of Christians: life and victory! Our salvation, help them. Saint George, help them. Saint Theodore, help them. Saint Mercury, help them.

Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands.

[Col. 0412A] Our King: Christ conquers.

Our hope, our mercy, our help, our deliverance and redemption, our victory, our weapons and our unconquerable one, our impregnable wall, our defense and exaltation, our light, way, and life: to him alone be dominion, glory, and power through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

To him alone be honor, praise, and jubilation through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

To him alone be strength, might, and victory through all ages [Col. 0412B] of ages. Amen.

Christ, hear us. Christ, hear us. Christ, hear us.

Kyrie eleison. Christ, have mercy. Christ, have mercy.

The following were sung before the deacons said, “Go, the Mass is ended,” as may be gathered from the same Ordinal, pp. 11 and 12:

God has chosen you as shepherd. May God preserve you in this see.

May God multiply the years of your life.

Happily, happily, happily. Three times.

May you have good times. Having good times, may you have good times. Three times.

Many years. Amen.

### Note

What follows the Martyrology in Dunod.

[Col. 0421C] I have a letter from M. Abbé Leboeuf, canon of Auxerre, in which he greatly esteems the Praises of the Church of Besançon as a rare work of good antiquity. Referring to the fact that M. Du Cange transcribed them from a manuscript of the Church of Arles, he observes that the ancient Pontifical of the Church of Besançon is also among the ancient manuscripts of Tours. Concerning the Martyrology, or Calendar, he says that it is extremely curious. In it one finds, on 10 May, the feast of Silvester, first bishop of Besançon, whose memory is no longer celebrated; and on 5 June, the translation of his body and that of Saint Anianus, another bishop of Besançon, both of them belonging to the fourth century. In their Lives I stated that their bodies had been placed in the chapel of Saint Agapitus, in a particular tomb, where they were seen in 1625, according to the testimony that I transcribed on page 44 of what I wrote about the Church of Besançon in volume I of the civil history [Col. 0422C] of the county of Burgundy. From this, and from the fact that Saint Anianus is named in our ancient litanies among our holy bishops, I conclude that he, like Saint Silvester, should be counted among our holy bishops and confessors. One could not cite a more enlightened judge of the documents printed here than M. Abbé Leboeuf. It appears, moreover, from the notes added to the calendar concerning the obits of several persons who died in the eleventh century, that it belongs to an earlier period.

The proper Mass of the holy martyrs Ferreolus and Ferrucius, taken from the Gallican Liturgy or Gothic Missal, book III, p. 269, and the Ritual of the Church of Besançon, composed by Saint Protadius, its archbishop, at the beginning of the seventh century, have been printed in the Proofs appended to the first volume on the Church of Besançon. There they may be seen, together with the documents of an ancient rule for the canons of the metropolitan church of that city.]

[Col. 0421]

# Appendix

## I. Charter of the Restoration of the Chapter of Saint Stephen

### [Charter]

[Col. 0421D] Since it appears exceedingly shameful to cover the lower parts of the body with splendid garments while making the upper parts contemptible by leaving their surface exposed, I have considered it worthwhile first to adorn the whole body in its entirety and then to provide what follows with fitting garments.

Let the faithful people of the Catholic Church therefore learn that I, Hugo, archbishop of Chrysopolis, both out of love for the heavenly judgment, in which the beginning of good will is known to consist, and out of fear of that same judgment, in which the beginning of wisdom consists, and also for the sake of my soul, as well as for the sake of my predecessor, the lord Valcherius, who received me renewed in the waters of holy baptism and afterward devoted himself wholly to me in affection, have considered how I might give to the church of the protomartyr Stephen, and to the canons of that place who dwell there and serve daily, part of what was held in my dominion and what I was able to acquire from alien hands, for their common support.

That place itself, now deprived of the assistance of the clergy—indeed, of the entire company of canons—while the blessed John the Evangelist serves Christ under his rule, seemed to me an intolerable neglect: the head of the whole archbishopric, [Note: [Col. 0421] This term gave the Chapter of Saint Stephen occasion to contest the motherhood of the Chapter of Saint John.] exalted by the most precious gift of Saint Stephen’s relics, adorned with the head of Saint Agapitus, and strengthened by the aid of many saints, was through forgetfulness failing in its daily praises, while poverty pressed the brothers because of their common expenses.

I therefore appointed canons to the service of the aforesaid place, so that, living a fraternal life under the rule of ecclesiastical religion, they might there render worthy services to the supreme King and to the blessed protomartyr Stephen, for the praise and glory of all the saints, with commemoration of us and of my predecessor Valtherius, and of all who rest there.

I gave for the support of the common table, from property which I possessed in my own dominion, one church dedicated in honor of Saint Leodegarius, situated in the county of Port, in a village called Villiacus [Vieilley], with its altar and all its appurtenances, namely vineyards and fields.

I also transferred to them one church constructed in the city in honor of Saint Quintinus, and I arranged that the archbishop’s tithes and the burial rights of pilgrims should belong to it.

I also gave them another church consecrated in honor of Saint Martin, situated in the district of Varas, in a village called Terceniacus [Tarcenay]. Since this church had been given to blessed Stephen by the archbishop Berengarius from ancient times, but was later granted by his successor Girfredus, by way of a lease, to a certain soldier named Furcardus, and had been possessed by his heirs for many years, I finally obtained it, through my own labor and ingenuity, from a certain cleric named Rodulphus, who then presided over it, and delivered it to the clergy of the aforesaid place to possess, together with its altar and all its appurtenances.

The mill, too, situated within our city—namely at the foot of the mountain on the western side, not far from the church of Blessed Mary of Jussanum Monastery—was not established on boats but founded upon rock. Having received it from the hands of the aforementioned cleric, I decreed that it should be joined to the earlier gift.

I also granted as a demesne one of my fields, which in the vernacular they call a *condamina* [Held in outright ownership], surrounded on every side by mountain and river [Col. 0423C]. Although it is adorned with a spacious plain, it opens only a narrow passage for entrance or exit at its two gorges, one of which provides the easiest access to the city. [The Prairie of Vaux, or the meadow of the Tower.]

Likewise, I subjected to the dominion of the aforesaid canons one mill upon the Lignon River, situated in the village called Cussiacus, namely beneath the bridge by which the river is crossed, together with the *naulum* [toll right] collected there when the river rises, along with all the things written above.

Therefore I, Hugh, archbishop, in the name of the Lord and of the entire heavenly Hierarchy, admonish—and, as one possessing the power of binding, I have forbidden under the pontifical sword—that none of my successors presume in any way, or dare, to violate this gift of mine. But if anyone should wish to overthrow it, may he become like Midian, Sisera, Oreb, Zeb, and so forth, and like any of those who overwhelmed Blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, with hurled stones [Col. 0423D], and without repentance stripped off the outer man in their unbelief.

But so that this donation may remain more firmly in the future, I confirmed it with my own hand and marked it with the impression of my seal.

I, HUGH, archbishop, confirmed this with my own hand.

[Note: [Col. 0423] See M. Du Cange, under the word *Signum*, concerning what these S.’s signify.]

Sign of Gibuin, archdeacon and cantor. Sign of Wido, archdeacon. Sign of Raaldi, archdeacon. Sign of Manegaud, dean. Sign of Albert, abbot. Sign of Husico, canon. Sign of Dudin, canon. Sign of Beroald, vassal. Sign of Warner, vassal. Sign of Rainer, viscount. Sign of Theodoric, chancellor. [Col. 0424A] Sign of Gotbert, the scribe who wrote this charter.

I, HUGH, bishop of Langres, confirmed this charter with my own hand; and lest anyone attempt to corrupt this gift, I forbade it under the sword of excommunication. Done at Besançon, on the Ides of August, in the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[CHARTER.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, archbishop of the sacred Church of Chrysopolis, and to his successors forever.

We give thanks to God and to our Lord Jesus Christ, who, without any preceding merits of ours, nevertheless raised us to the summit of the apostolic see. Hence it seems to belong to the charge of our apostleship to exercise care over all the Churches and to increase their honor. Since, therefore, you requested from the Roman See, most blessed brother, that the goods which the clemency of the Almighty has provided in your time for the Church divinely entrusted to you should be fortified by our authority, it pleased us to consent to your petition as you desired, especially since the same sacred place over which, by God’s disposition, you appear to preside shines with such dignity that it has been exalted not only by the authority of an archiepiscopal see but also strengthened by the privileges of many apostolic Fathers, and remains distinguished while preserving its rightful honor. To this we are also invited by the joy of a greater title, because the aforesaid place is adorned by the patronage of Stephen the protomartyr, whose priceless relic—the desired gift of his arm—it preserves. And, to speak more truthfully, with our own eyes we saw the bone of that most sacred relic shattered by the blows of the stoning Jews, when we placed it beneath the altar which we consecrated in your presence, with our brother bishops and fellow bishops standing by: Alinard, archbishop of Lyons; George, archbishop of the Church of Kalocsa among the Hungarians; Kilinus, bishop of Sutri; Frederick of Geneva; Wido of Chalon; and Walter of Mâcon; together with abbots and reverend clergy of holy character, and with an innumerable multitude of laypeople present. In the course of your prayers you also added that, since the altar had been consecrated by our hands, it should receive some dignity from the apostolic see. Therefore, moved by your just prayers, we did not delay in extending to you the ascent of our piety.

Accordingly, by this page of our decree, we confirm all the goods that have been given either through your industry or through the devotion of any of the faithful. Finally, in honor of our protomartyr, we establish that upon the holy altar mentioned above Mass may be celebrated only once a day. No one may presume to approach it for the celebration of the sacrifice except one whom the archbishop of the place has appointed for this purpose with the consent of the brethren—namely, seven of the brothers of that congregation, chosen for their better way of life and called cardinals. One of them shall be the dean of that Church, and, just as he is senior in the congregation, so shall he excel in dignity.

Whoever among these celebrates Mass there shall put on a dalmatic, and only then may he dare to celebrate with all reverence and devotion. They shall also use sandals and the mitre—the priest himself, as well as the deacon and subdeacon—on the feasts of our Lord and Savior, of Blessed Mary the Mother of God, and of the archangel Saint Michael; on the birthdays of the apostles and of the holy martyrs Stephen, Vincent, and Agapitus (whose head we placed with the arm of Saint Stephen in the same altar); of the blessed Ferreolus and Ferrucius; and on the feast of All Saints and the dedication of that place. We likewise deny these privileges to all bishops and abbots, unless perhaps they have been invited, and we decree by apostolic censure that no one of ecclesiastical rank dare violate any of these provisions.

We confirm under our apostolic protection that no emperor, king, duke, count, viscount, archbishop, bishop, or power of any rank whatsoever may dare to act against this shield of apostolic defense or diminish anything from the goods of the Church belonging to the provision of the brethren [Col. 0425A] or grant anything from them as a benefice. If anyone should declare that any of the things it possesses is subject to dispute, no one may seize it before the matter itself has been judicially settled. But if anyone should attempt with reckless boldness to come against this apostolic protection, let him be struck by the sword of our anathema unless he repents. Whoever guards this command, however, shall deserve an abundance of our blessing.

Given on the third day before the Ides of January, through the hands of Wido of Toul, first secretary and chancellor of the holy apostolic see. In the second year of the pontificate of Pope Leo IX, indiction three. [1049.]

[CHARTER.]

Henry, by the favor of divine mercy, Augustus, emperor of the Romans.

If we incline our ears to the just petitions of our faithful, we undoubtedly believe that this will benefit the condition of the state and also our honor. Whenever we are asked by petitions to extend the favor of equity, we ought to offer the ascent of our piety. Therefore let the diligence of all those now living and of those who will live through the ages know [Col. 0425B] how Hugh, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Chrysopolis and most dear to us, approached our clemency, humbly begging that the goods which he had bestowed upon and acquired for his Church, in honor of Christ’s protomartyr shining upon the mountain, should be confirmed by our imperial authority. Considering his petition as useful as it was honorable, we thought it wrong not to satisfy him according to his desire. For such a great Church, deserving veneration in every religious observance, had been held almost universally in the lowest condition through the carelessness and negligence of its badly living predecessors. But after divine mercy advanced the archbishop of the aforesaid place, he began to grieve over such great miseries and to utter tearful sighs, because he had a wrinkled and aged, deserted and prostrate Bride. Immediately, after invoking the heavenly Name, he began to gather from various regions the means by which he might cast off the wrinkled garments of the widowed Bride of the Church. At last, having assembled resources from his patrimony and his own right, or from the goods of the Church, he raised up a community for fifty [Col. 0425C] brothers. He did not appoint a provost for them, but ordered them to choose a dean from among themselves, one who would prefer to preside for the benefit of the canons rather than to advance his own household interests.

Therefore, at the intercession of our beloved consort Agnes, Augusta, empress of the Romans, and of our most faithful archbishop of the aforesaid Church, we commend and confirm whatever he has bestowed upon it or may henceforth acquire from anyone.

We confirm to them half of the offerings made at the altar of Saint Stephen and at the Arm; the archbishop shall have the other half for the restoration of the church.

The church of Saint Hippolytus of Villetta and the entire altar, with tithes, lands, and all appurtenances.

The church of Saint Quintin in the city, to which all the archbishop’s tithes in every respect and the burial places of pilgrims belong.

The church of Saint Leodegarius of Villiacus, with the altar, [Col. 0425D] tithes, vineyards, fields, meadows, and all appurtenances.

The chapel of Saint Justin of Camborniacus, with the altar and the allod which Archbishop Hector acquired there for Saint Stephen.

The estate of Vico, with the altar, church, tithes, fields, meadows, woods, mills, waters, watercourses, and all appurtenances.

The church of Saint Stephen of Noiret, half the tithes and the entire altar.

The church of Saint Martin of Terceniacus, with the altar, tithes, and all appurtenances.

At Mont Rond, whatever Saint Stephen appears to possess there.

Likewise the church of Saint Anatolius of Salins, with the altar, tithes, vineyards, fields, woods, mills, male and female servants, and everything that he had acquired during the time of the canons and afterward of the monks. In this church of Saint Anatolius the aforesaid archbishop established an order of canons before becoming bishop. Later, after becoming bishop, at the request of his mother, who lived at the said church, he changed the order and granted it to the monks of Dijon. When we heard that the estate of our Church had been transferred to the church of another kingdom and bishopric, we rightly took it ill, ordering under threat of our favor that, as was just, it should return to the altar to which it belonged. From now on, let the church possess what it has lawfully recovered.

The church of Saint John of Salins, with the altar and all appurtenances. The archbishop himself held these churches as a benefice from his predecessor Walcher. Let no one believe that they had come to him as a paternal benefice, although they had come to him from a certain Odilo, a canon of Besançon, who appointed him his heir, and thus, while still a boy, he received them from the hand of the archbishop.

The little estate of Arlo in the same valley, with its small wood, vineyards, and all appurtenances; four cauldrons for making salt, with their own sites, which are commonly called *Rauches*; the jurisdiction which Herpin held by precarious tenure, with male and female servants and cultivated and uncultivated lands; the church dedicated to Saint Stephen at Chamblay, with the altar, tithes, fishing rights, and lands. His father gave this to him as an estate, so that he might possess it during his lifetime, but after his father’s death he would grant it to the Church for his father’s soul.

At Grozon, the altar and whatever the protomartyr appears to possess there, in lands, meadows, male and female servants, and cauldrons with their sites. Two *mansi* in the village of Capey, with all appurtenances. Two others at Vorge, with vineyards, lands, and all appurtenances. The mill in the city called Terragniolum; the vineyards of Odo of Capey; one *mansus* at Majodorum; the new and old vineyards beside the Arch; one mill at Cussiacus, with the toll collected whenever the river rises; two *mansi* at Noiret and at Judicium.

These and the other things which the Church possessed we confirm, and we ratify whatever it may acquire in the future, whether from its own resources or from another source. We decree that neither the bishop nor any power of any rank may grant anything as a benefice, but that everything shall come to the table of the brethren. We commend and confirm that they shall have the power to leave their houses to whatever canon of the place they wish, to give, sell, or exchange them. But if a brother dies intestate, the house shall be given by common consent to whichever of the brethren needs it.

So that this may remain ratified and firm, we ordered it to be marked by the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry, most invincible king, third of the Germans, second Augustus, emperor of the Romans, first of the Burgundians. Hugh, archchancellor of Burgundy and archbishop, has authenticated it. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1049, indiction two, in the twenty-first year of his appointment, in the first year of the reign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king. Done successfully at Aachen. Amen.

[CHARTER.]

In the year 1053, Hugh, archbishop, transferred the bones of the holy martyrs Ferreolus and Ferrucius from the monastery situated outside the city to the metropolitan church of Saint John, although part of them was left in the church of the said monastery and decently placed in a stone reliquary of the high altar, as is related in the charter of the translation in these words.

Thus, while the monastery long remained in its former condition, through the sins of the people and by God’s permission, whose judgments are hidden, the negligence of the guardians of its rights brought about the result that, just as it had been a dwelling of the highest religion, so it became a gathering-place of irreligion. For after the estates belonging to that place had been handed over as benefices of laymen at the will of an ill-advised administrator, it soon declined so completely that, after the congregation had been destroyed, no one remained for the service of the blessed martyrs except a very few ignorant and unteachable priests.

When, therefore, in the common destruction of the whole region, the holy martyrs lay exposed in the open—for thieves from France were attempting to carry them away to the ruin of Burgundy—Christ’s everlasting mercy, unwilling to deprive his people of such great protection, preserved them for us for so long, not by human guardianship, nor by the enclosure of walls, nor finally by any strength of that place, but by its own marvelous grace. In the time of the emperor Henry II, the lord Hugh, archbishop, to whom the diligence of friends had disclosed this grave danger, secretly resolved to transfer them to the city, although he was seeking a suitable opportunity to accomplish it.

Finally, on the third day before the Kalends of June, which was the day after the Ascension of the Lord, the archbishop ordered the clergy and people to come for the sake of prayer, as was their custom. He himself arrived, celebrated Mass, and then they went to the tomb where rested the two illustrious lights of heaven, twin brothers illuminating their homeland, bringing peace to the peoples, and delivering God’s people. When the sarcophagus was opened, a fragrance of incomparable sweetness spread throughout the whole church [Col. 0427B], signifying that God’s presence was there. Some of those present who saw this, when they beheld their bones [Col. 0428A], were held by divine fear as though placed in ecstasy. It was possible to see clergy and people mingled together, wet with a shower of tears for joy and rejoicing together in the praises of God.

It was marvelous to behold: such a multitude was suddenly present there, although no one had been informed, that no one remembered so many ever having gathered in so short a space of time—not only citizens, not only inhabitants of neighboring places, but also people streaming in from distant regions.

Of these most sacred bodies, the metropolitan lord, by prudent counsel in this matter, placed the smaller portion beneath the principal altar there, for the preservation of the place dedicated in their honor. The larger portion, which would always be a protection for him, he carried to the city with hymns and praises and deposited it at the altar of the Blessed Mother of God Mary in the church of Blessed John the Evangelist. There the glorious martyrs offer divine refuge to those who flee to them and protection to those who ask it, to the praise of the Lord, to whom honor and glory belong forever and ever. Amen.

## III. Another Catalogue of the Bishops of the Church of Besançon

Except for those whom a disreputable life or accession caused to be erased from the catalogue, such as Chelmesigelus, Tetradius, Felix, Hayminius, and certain others.

[Col. 0427]

1. LINUS (Saint). He first built the Besançon church of Saint Stephen, which remained until the time of Hilary.

2. MAXIMINUS (Saint). He led the life of a hermit six miles from the city, where he also rests.

3. PAULINUS (Saint). He was a disciple of Blessed Maximinus. After Maximinus’s death, he hid in the same wilderness during the persecution of Maximian. He rests in the church of Saint Stephen, before the altar.

4. EUSEBIUS (Saint). He was a disciple of Pope Melchiades. He held the bishopric for two years.

5. HILARY (Saint). In his time the church of Saint Stephen was rebuilt by Queen Helena, the mother of Constantine, since there was not yet any church at Besançon.

6. PANCRATIUS (Saint). He was a contemporary of Pope Julius, by whom he was also ordained bishop.

7. JUSTUS (Saint). In the time of Julian the Apostate, he is said to have had much intimacy with Eusebius the martyr, bishop of Vercelli.

8. ANIANUS (Saint). In the time of Valentinian and Valens, he built the church of Saints Ferreolus and Ferrucius, a mile and a half from the city.

9. SILVESTER (Saint). He built the church of Saint Maurice.

10. FRONIMIUS (Saint).

11. DESIDERATUS (Saint). He ended his most holy life near the village of Ledon, where he also rests.

12. GERMANUS (Saint). Through him the Lord performed a very great miracle at Saint Vitus.

13. LEONTIUS (Saint).

14. CELIDONIUS (Saint). In his time the arm of Saint Stephen came to the city of Besançon.

15. ANTIDIUS (Saint). Ten miles from the city, where he was buried, he received the capital sentence under Croscus, king of the Vandals.

16. NICETIUS (Saint). He was a contemporary and intimate associate of Blessed Pope Gregory. Another, somewhat more recent, hand added: “He built the church of Saint Peter.”

17. PROTADIUS (Saint).

18. DONATUS (Saint). Through him the Church received the estates of Domblingum and Arflatum. He built the church of Saint Paul, in which he also rested in the Lord, and Jussanum Monastery with his mother Flavia, who was buried there.

19. MIGETIUS (Saint).

20. TERNATIUS (Saint).

21. GERVASIUS (Saint).

22. CLAUDIUS (Saint).

23. ABBO. He was a man of great abstinence, through which he obtained the bishopric.

24. GUADALBERTUS.

25. EVRARDUS.

26. AURULEUS.

27. ERVEUS.

28. GEDEON (Saint).

29. BERNUINUS. He built the church of Saint John the Evangelist.

30. AMALWINUS.

31. ARDUICUS. He acquired for the Church of Saint Stephen, for the preparation of lamps, the saltworks of Ledon from Chlothar, nephew of King Charles. He obtained the abbey of Bergill and the toll of Besançon from King Charles.

32. THEODORICUS. Through him King Zwentibald restored the village of Pauliacus to the church of Saint Stephen.

33. BERENGARIUS. He was Theodericus’s nephew and succeeded him in the archbishopric. He was seized and enthroned by common election before the altar of Saint Stephen, of which he was a canon. But because of Haguinus the heretic, he was blinded. He had as his deputy in the pontifical office Stephen, bishop of Belley.

34. GIRFREDUS.

35. GUIDO.

36. GUICHARDUS.

37. LEOTOLDUS.

48. HECTOR.

59. GUALTERIUS. He began once more to rebuild the church of Saint Stephen after the model of the Roman church of Saint Peter.

40. HUGO. He completed it, though after much delay.

## In the Year of the Lord 625: Boniface V, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0429]

## Historical Notice on Pope Boniface V

*(From the Pontifical Book, edition of Blanchard, vol. IV.)*

[Col. 0429A] [Note: [Col. 0429B]

Boniface.—1. On the fourteenth—or, according to another reading, the twenty-fourth—of December in the year of the Lord 617, after a vacancy of one month and six or sixteen days, Boniface V, of that name, a Neapolitan by birth, was created pontiff. In his time lived the Arab Muhammad, a false prophet and plague of the world, from whom the sect of the Muslims took its origin. To attract all peoples to his sect, he adopted something from nearly every sect: from the Jews, circumcision, worship of one God, and abstinence from pork; from the Christians, Christ; but, with the Arians, as created; with the Nestorians, a mere man; with the Manichaeans, not truly crucified but only apparently so; and from the pagans, worship of the moon or of some star. He taught that the law he proposed, utterly foolish as it was, should be propagated by arms, and prohibited its examination through disputation. See John of Damascus, *On Heresies*; Theophanes and Cedrenus, under Heraclius; Baronius, year 630. Binius and Labbe.]

—2. The vacancy of the see from the burial of Saint Deusdedit is correctly stated by the commonly circulated Anastasius and by many other manuscripts, both manuscript and printed, as one month and sixteen days, although some—including two Freherian manuscripts together with the Farfa Catalogue—give thirteen days, omitting the month. The Royal manuscript and Thuanus give one month and fifteen days; another Thuanus gives only sixteen days.

The reason why the see remained vacant for so short a period is clear. Heraclius, from whom authorization had to be sought, was being oppressed by the Persians, who were holding his ambassadors, badly treated, in chains in prison. The city of Constantinople was suffering from famine and pestilence. The exarch Eleutherius, taking advantage both of the emperor’s extraordinary distress and of the papal vacancy, had seized tyrannical power and had therefore been slaughtered by the people of Ravenna. Meanwhile Rome was being ravaged by the elephantine plague that had recently arisen and was spreading. For these serious reasons, authorization appears neither to have been requested nor awaited.

Hence, apart from the manuscripts and catalogues mentioned above, Hermannus Contractus, Marianus Scotus, and Sigebert place the creation of Boniface V in the year 618 and understand the vacancy not to have been prolonged. Finally, Bede, an eighth-century writer, says in book II, chapter 7, of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*: “Boniface, who governed the Church after Deusdedit, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation six hundred and eighteen.” Pagius maintains that this passage, indeed the whole edition of Bede used by Baronius, is corrupt, and recommends returning to the Chiffletian and Cambridge manuscripts, which have nineteen. Yet, with due respect to that most learned man, I carefully examined several editions of Bede: the old Basel edition of 1563, the Antwerp edition printed at Cologne under the care of Gravius in 1612, and another edition published there in 1688, the most carefully corrected of all. Everywhere I found the year 618. Since so many manuscripts and catalogues of Anastasius agree, I preferred to give them greater credit than the two editions corrected at the discretion of recent editors, especially the Chiffletian attempt to reconcile Bede with Fredegarius.

Antonio Pagius, however, favors the following view. Setting aside the authority of five of the seven older catalogues displayed in Baronius’s *Critica*, and of the most serious writers, he embraces above all a sixth catalogue, copied at the end of the twelfth century, which gives: “Vacancy of the see: one year, six days.” Since that interval does not fill the period of vacancy after Deusdedit, he extracts forty days from his own repositories, thereby reaching the day of the ordination of Boniface V. His certain tenure of the see, and the certain beginning of Honorius’s pontificate, persuaded him that the latter could not be extended beyond Sunday, 23 December, of the aforesaid year 619.

I cannot deny that I was almost carried away into Pagius’s conjecture when I saw that, to prevent the whole chronology from collapsing, a full year had to be added between Deusdedit and Honorius. The fact that this year should not, with Baronius, be added to the see of Boniface was made clear by the excellent manuscripts Farnesianus and Ambrosianus 3 (while the others either are silent or indicate a corrupt passage in the commonly circulated text by giving ten rather than thirteen days), as well as by catalogue 2 of Mabillon. All these agree with the epitaph written before Boniface was buried, cited by Baronius, volume XII, appendix to volume VIII, and Aringhus, *Rome Subterranean*, book II, chapter 8, which reads:

> For five years and ten months  
> He ruled the apostolic summit, and departed to the summit of great honor.

That is, according to the interpretation of Papebrochius, Pagius, and all learned men, Boniface sat for five years and ten months. Therefore I acknowledged that the extra year had necessarily to be added to one or the other of the periods between pontificates—either after Deusdedit or after Boniface V.

The reason why I departed from the learned Pagius, preferring to add it after Boniface without damage to the chronology of Anastasius, was both the authorities cited in support of Boniface’s ordination and the shortness of the interval between his death and the ordination of Honorius. These plainly show that Pagius incorrectly placed the beginning of Honorius’s pontificate too late, as I shall say under Honorius. To this may be added the reasons recently mentioned, by which much lesser circumstances advised that the imperial authorization should be disregarded at the consecration of Pelagius II (Anastasius, vol. III, p. 30).

The chief reason that moved Pagius, however, was the two letters of Boniface to Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, and to his wife Ethelburg, which Bede recites after the ordination of Saint Paulinus, the first bishop of York. He says that Paulinus was ordained on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, that is, 21 July of the year 625 (book II of the *History of the English*, chapter 9). Lest anyone suppose this to be an error—since in the *Epitome* the year is given as 622—Bede also records Paulinus’s death on the sixth day before the Ides, that is, 10 October 644 (book III, chapter 14), after he had held the bishopric, he says, for nineteen years, two months, and twenty-one days. Nothing more exact could be desired in this chronology.

This is especially so because the same Paulinus was ordained by Justus, archbishop of Canterbury, who succeeded Mellitus after the latter was called to heaven in the year 624, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. Before that, while administering the church of Rochester, Justus had not possessed the power to ordain bishops.

Nevertheless, although Paulinus’s ordination is certain, we do not consider it necessary to place the date of Boniface’s letters after Paulinus’s ordination, since no chronological indication compels us to do so. We learn from Bede himself, in several places in his *History of the English*, that he was accustomed to relate matters belonging to the same subject without regard to temporal order. Examples above all are chapters 17 and 18 of book II, where he first relates that the pallium was sent to Honorius, archbishop of Canterbury, and only afterward reports the death of Justus, whom Honorius succeeded.

For this reason I am certain that Boniface gave the two letters before Ethelburg and Paulinus departed for York. Everything contained in them had been arranged through messengers sent back and forth, as will be evident to the reader. I have no doubt that the exhortation to Edwin and the letter to Ethelburg were carefully arranged by her most devout brother, King Eadbald, while negotiations were taking place concerning the marriage, the dispatch of a Catholic retinue for Ethelburg, and the ordination of a bishop for the Northumbrian people, so that they might carry the exhortation to Edwin with them. In it there is no mention of Saint Paulinus—or even of a bishop—but only of evangelical preaching.

Moreover, since Bede was a very ancient writer who committed these things to writing more than a hundred years after they occurred, I do not see why I should regard his chronology as preferable to all others. Indeed, it seems highly suspicious to me. For Bede says in the same chapter 9 that on the night of Holy Easter in the year 626, which fell on 20 April, Ethelburg’s daughter Eanfleda was born. What are we to make of this? Paulinus was ordained on 21 July of the preceding year, in order to escort Ethelburg. They still had to travel from Canterbury to York. Then Ethelburg herself, together with the new bishop and the whole royal retinue, undertook a journey that certainly lasted many days. Yet in the following year, on 20 April, Eanfleda was born, before nine full months had passed. Believe it, posterity.

Therefore, lest we affirm something absurd while pressed by so many difficulties on every side, we reject the year of vacancy after Boniface and arrange the chronology of that pontiff together with Anastasius as follows.

After Saint Deusdedit was buried at Saint Peter’s on 8 November 618, and after a vacancy of one month and sixteen days, his successor Boniface V was ordained on 24 December of that year—a date which the A-letter of the dominical cycle shows to have fallen on a Sunday. He was to comfort his sheep, who were shamefully perishing day by day amid the raging disease of scabies. After sitting for five years and ten months, he died on 24 October 624 and was buried the next day at Saint Peter’s, as the manuscripts of Anastasius, both printed and manuscript, correctly testify. His death was followed by a particularly long vacancy, as I shall say under Honorius. Cennus.]

—3. Boniface, of Campanian nationality and Neapolitan birthplace, son of John Fumminus, was the ninth native Roman pope. Under the emperor Flavius Heraclius, he sat for five years and ten months and was consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, at the beginning of the year of the Lord 617. During this period Boniface wrote to Edwin, king of the English, and to Queen Ethelburg, earnestly urging them to keep the peoples subject to them away from idols and their worship. A copy of these letters, in which Boniface introduces himself as “bishop, servant of the servants of God,” is preserved in Bede, book II of the *Ecclesiastical History of His People*. Ciaconius.]

Boniface, a Campanian by nationality, [Note: [Col. 0432C] From the city of Naples. Vallicellian manuscript: “From the city of Naples, from his father John; he sat for five years and ten days. He was extremely gentle, kind, humble, mild [this word is superfluous], and merciful. He established that no one should be dragged out of a church and that an acolyte should not …” Blanchard.]

from the city of Naples, [Note: [Col. 0432C] “He sat for five years and thirteen days.” Farnesian manuscript: “He sat for five years [Col. 0432D] and ten months.” Blanchard.]

sat for five years and thirteen days. [Note: [Col. 0432D]

He established that a testament should be valid according to the command of the prince.—1. By a decree of Boniface V it was enacted that testaments made according to the command of the prince—that is, according to the laws—should be valid. Altaserra.]

### 2. That a will should be valid according to the sovereign’s command

Why Boniface established this, what law concerning wills he had in mind, and which emperor the author of these *Deeds*—whoever he may be—intended, is not certainly clear to me. Did he mean the Roman laws of the ancient emperors, or some recent law promulgated by the emperor Heraclius concerning this matter? Certainly neither. For under Roman law all citizens were unquestionably governed by the same rules in making wills, and no one could affirm on any grounds that new laws concerning wills had been enacted at this time by the emperor Heraclius.

Or had there actually been doubt whether wills written according to the emperors’ laws remained valid, so that the pontiff had to confirm in writing that they did? Nothing could be less likely. Could we perhaps suppose that Pope Boniface had turned his attention to Lombard law and had declared a will made under it valid? But what connection at this time did the Romans have with Lombard law, when they were governed by the Greek emperors and the exarch of Ravenna solely according to Roman laws?

Moreover, no written law was published among the Lombards until the year 643, when King Rotharis published his edict, in which he makes several provisions concerning wills in sections 157 and following—that is, in the year 613 or 644. For, according to Paul the Deacon, Rotharis’s edict appeared in the seventy-seventh year of the Lombard kingdom. According to his chronology—which Pagius vainly shortens in the *Critica* on the authority of Segeber­tus—Alboin reigned from the year 568 for three years and seven months, Cleph for one year and six months, and, after an interregnum of ten years, Authari for six years, Agilulf for twenty-five, Adalwald for ten, and Arioald for twelve; Rotharis came afterward. His election therefore fell in the year 636, while the Lombard kingdom was in its sixty-eighth year. Consequently, the eight years remaining until the completion of the seventy-sixth year were Rotharis’s own years, coinciding with indiction 2. Those chronological markers are contained in the very preface to the edict.

Thus, one or another charter of the Cassinese *Bullarium* is not of such weight as Pagius thought, in the year 626, that it could overturn Paul the Deacon’s account distinguishing the periods of Adalwald and Arioald, and moreover force one to tamper with the royal edict and read “the eighteenth year” instead of “the eighth year of my reign.” When A. Muratori­us saw this, in the preface to the Lombard Laws, volume I, part II of the *Rerum Italicarum*, I do not know why he postponed the promulgation of the edict to the year 638, despite the chronology of the Lombard kingdom, which Paul the Deacon and the royal edict itself record, with a discrepancy of only one year.

But this is by the way. To return to our subject: since laws of this sort appeared a full eighteen years after Boniface’s death, the pontiff could not possibly have had them in mind. Either, then, the author of the papal *Deeds* is again suffering from an anachronism and attributes to Boniface a decree belonging to one of his successors—for it later happened that Lombard law, like Roman law, prevailed throughout Italy, and at that time I have no doubt that similar declarations could have been issued by the pontiffs—or, if one prefers to maintain complete confidence in Anastasius, one may conjecturally suppose that the pontiff approved one of the customs which the Lombards used as law up to the time of Rotharis, namely, the custom they employed in making wills.

Alternatively, perhaps Agilulf or Adalwald had promulgated some special law concerning these matters for his own people and for the peoples of Italy, and, while minds were wavering between Roman law and these new laws, the pontiff confirmed it by his decree—so that in those same places, where Lombards were administering their estates and where the patrimony of Saint Peter lay, wills made according to their customs or laws would be valid once confirmed by recognition of the royal chancellery.

Examples of this recognition occur in a deed of donation made by Beringarius, preserved by Bacchinius; and the matter is well established by the diplomas published by Baronius, Mabillon, and others. Which of these explanations is the more accurate, I do not wish to decide. Let the judgment rest with someone else.

**BENCINUS.**

He established that a will should be valid according to the sovereign’s command. [Note: “He established that no one should be dragged out of a church.” This is a decree of Boniface V, that no one should be forcibly removed from a church. The same had already been enacted by the constitution of Theodosius, book III, title *De his qui ad ecclesias confugiunt*. Augustine, on Psalm 149: “Such fetters consolidate for you—and the hands of the bishops. Do not those in chains flee into the church, and are they not freed here?” **ALTASERRA.**]

But the ravages of time have so leveled it to the ground that in our age scarcely any of its walls can be seen. As for the cemetery, since it was unknown before Bosio, Bosio first discovered it in 1601 near the walls of the City, on the Nomentan Way. It includes three or four corridors and the same number of chambers. **MAFEUS.**]

[Note: “When he had died, he was buried.” After Boniface sent those letters to England, he did not live long afterward; for in that same year, 625, on 22 October, he died, and, according to Anastasius, was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 25 October, after he had occupied the see for five years and ten months. This is reported by Gotfridus of Viterbo in his *Chronicle*, Liutprand, the *Catalogue of Apostolic Names*, the Colbertine manuscript of Anastasius, and four of the catalogues prefixed to Baronius’s *Critica*. The matter is placed beyond doubt by his epitaph, quoted by Baronius, which ends with these two verses:

> He ruled the apostolic height for five years and twice as many months,  
> And departed to the height of great honor.

## THREE LETTERS OF BONIFACE V, ROMAN PONTIFF

*(Mansi, Collection of the Councils, vol. X.)* (C)*

### FIRST LETTER. BONIFACE THE POPE TO JUSTUS, RECENTLY BISHOP OF ROCHFESTER, NOW THE SUCCESSOR OF MELLITUS IN THE ARCHBISHOPRIC OF CANTERBURY

He praises him for having brought King Adelvald to the faith, and hopes that he will bring others as well. He sends him the pallium and grants him the right to ordain bishops.

[Col. 0435A]

**Boniface to his dearest brother Justus.**

How devoutly [Note: Bede, book II, chapter 8] and how diligently your Fraternity has labored for the Gospel of Christ has been shown not only by the content of the letter you sent us, but also by the success granted from above to your work. For almighty God has not abandoned either the mystery of his name or the fruit of your labor, since he faithfully promised the preachers of the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). His clemency has demonstrated this especially through the ministry entrusted to you, opening the hearts of the nations to receive the unique mystery of your preaching.

For he has adorned the pleasant course of your virtues with the support of his goodness through a great reward, preparing for the talents entrusted to you, through the most faithful exercise of your office, an abundant profit that you may present to him, multiplied in many forms. This too has been bestowed upon you as a recompense: remaining steadfast in the ministry entrusted to you with praiseworthy patience, you await the redemption of that people, and through your merits their salvation has been brought near, as the Lord says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10; 24). You have therefore been saved through the hope produced by patience and endurance, so that the hearts of unbelievers, cleansed of their natural and superstitious disease, might obtain the mercy of the Savior.

For, having received the letter of our son King Adelvald, we learned with what instruction in sacred speech your Fraternity had led his mind to the belief of true conversion and unwavering faith. From this we draw certain confidence in the long-suffering clemency of heaven, and we believe that not only the fullest salvation of the peoples subject to him, but also that of neighboring peoples, will follow through the ministry of your preaching. Thus, as it is written, may the reward of your completed work be granted by the Lord, the rewarder of all good things. “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18): the universal confession of the nations [Col. 0436A], having received the sacrament of Christian faith, bears witness to this.

Moreover, prompted by our goodwill toward your Fraternity, we have sent you the pallium by the bearer of this letter. We have granted you permission to use it only in the celebration of the sacred mysteries; and we also grant you the right, whenever necessity requires and the Lord’s mercy goes before you, to celebrate the ordination of bishops, so that the Gospel of Christ may be spread among all the nations that have not yet been converted through the preaching of many.

Let your Fraternity therefore strive to preserve, with the undefiled sincerity of your mind, what you have received through the kindness of the Apostolic See, reflecting on the likeness of that for which you have undertaken to carry so distinguished a garment upon your shoulders. Strive to present yourself, while imploring the Lord’s clemency, in such a manner that you may bring the rewards of the gift granted to you before the tribunal of the supreme and coming Judge—not with guilt, but with the benefit of souls. May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

### SECOND LETTER. TO EDWIN, KING OF THE ENGLISH

He exhorts him to the Christian faith.

**To the glorious man Edwin, king of the English, Boniface, bishop and servant of the servants of God.**

Although the power of the supreme divinity cannot be explained through the offices of human speech [Note: Bede, book II, chapter 10], since by its greatness it abides in an invisible and incomprehensible eternity, so that no keenness of intellect, however great, is sufficient to grasp and express what it is; nevertheless, because his mercy, opening the doors of the heart, graciously pours into human minds by inspiration the secrets that are to be disclosed concerning himself, we have taken care to exercise the pastoral office in announcing to you the fullness of the Christian faith. In this way, implanting in your minds the Gospel of Christ, which our Savior commanded to be preached to all nations, we may offer you the remedies of salvation.

The clemency of the heavenly Majesty, which created and fashioned all things by the mere word of its command—namely, heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them—ordering and sustaining them according to the arrangements by which they were to subsist, disposed all things through the counsel of its coeternal Word and the unity of the Holy Spirit. It formed the human being from the clay of the earth in its own image and likeness, and granted him so great a privilege of reward that it placed him above all things and, provided he observed the limit of its command, fortified him with the permanence of eternity.

Therefore the human race, from the rising of the sun to its setting, venerates and worships God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the indivisible Trinity—as its creator and maker of all. To him even the highest powers of empire and the authorities of earthly affairs are subject, because by his ordinance authority over all kingdoms is granted.

Through the aids by which his entire creation is to be enlarged, the mercy of his goodness has also graciously deigned to enter, by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, into the recognition of himself by the cold hearts of nations situated at the ends of the earth. What the clemency of the Redeemer has accomplished in the enlightenment of our glorious son King Audubald and of the nations subject to him, we infer that your Glory has learned more fully because of the proximity of the regions. We therefore trust that his marvelous gift will also be bestowed upon you through the steadfastness of a sure hope in heaven. We have indeed learned that your glorious wife, who is recognized as being part of your body, has been illumined by the reward of eternity through the regeneration of holy baptism.

Therefore, by this letter, we have taken care to exhort you with the greatest dignity and with all the affection of intimate charity: abominate idols and their worship; reject the foolishness of shrines and the deceptive allurements of auguries; and believe in God the almighty Father, in his Son Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit. Thus, by believing, and through the power of the holy and indivisible Trinity, you may be freed from the bonds of devilish captivity and become partakers of eternal life.

How great is the guilt of condemnation by which those who embrace and practice the most destructive superstition of idolatry are bound is shown by the examples of those whom they worship. Therefore the Psalmist says of them: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm 95). And again: “They have eyes, but they do not see; they have ears, but they do not hear; they have nostrils, but they will not smell. They have hands, but they will not touch; they have feet, but they will not walk. Those who place the hope of their confidence in them therefore become like them” (Psalm 113).

For how could those beings possess any power to help, when they are made from corruptible material by the hands of those inferior beings who are subject to you? By applying human craftsmanship to them, you have given them an inanimate likeness of limbs. Unless they are moved by you, they cannot walk; but, like a stone placed in one spot, once constructed they remain there, understanding nothing and overwhelmed by their very insensibility. They have acquired no power either to harm or to help. We cannot, therefore, discern by what deception of mind you worship and follow as gods those to whom you yourselves have given the image of a body.

You must therefore receive the sign of the holy cross, through which the human race was redeemed, and, cursing the subversion of the devil’s cunning—for he remains envious and hostile to the works of divine goodness—cast it out from your hearts. Then, laying hands upon the gods whom until now you have fashioned for yourselves by joining pieces of material, take the greatest care to break and destroy them.

For their very dissolution and decay—things that never possessed a living spirit and could in no way receive sensation from their makers—plainly reveal to you that what you worshiped until now was nothing. Indeed, you who have received a living spirit from the Lord are nonetheless superior to them as their makers; for almighty God ordained that you, descended from the lineage of the first man whom he fashioned, should multiply through the ages in innumerable generations.

Approach, then, the knowledge of him who created you, who breathed into you the spirit of life, and who sent his only-begotten Son for your redemption, so that he might rescue you from original sin and, once rescued, reward you with heavenly gifts from the power of devilish wickedness.

Receive the words of the preachers and the Gospel of God that they announce to you, so that, believing—as has often been said—in God the almighty Father, in Jesus Christ his Son, in the Holy Spirit, and in the inseparable Trinity, you may put the powers of demons to flight. Once the enticement of the poisonous and deceitful enemy has been driven from you, may you, reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, be enabled, by his help and generosity, to dwell with the one in whom you have believed in the splendor of eternal glory.

Moreover, we have sent you a blessing from your protector, blessed Peter, chief of the apostles: namely, one shirt with gold ornamentation and one Ancyrian cloak [*laena Anciriana*]. We ask that your Glory receive these with the same kindly disposition with which you know them to have been sent by us.

### THIRD LETTER. TO EDELBURGA, WIFE OF EDWIN, KING OF THE ENGLISH

He congratulates her on having received the faith and urges her to render this service to her husband as a benefit arising from her own merit. He also sends her small gifts: a silver mirror and an ivory comb.

**To the glorious lady, his daughter, Queen Edelburga, Boniface, bishop and servant of the servants of God.**

The goodness of our Redeemer [Note: Bede, book II, chapter 18], which rescued the human race from the bonds of devilish captivity by the outpouring of his precious blood, supplied it in great providence with many remedies for its salvation. By making the knowledge of his name known to the nations in various ways, he enabled them to acknowledge their Creator by receiving the sacrament of the Christian faith. That this has been granted to the understanding of your Glory as a heavenly gift is plainly indicated by the mystical regeneration of your purification.

Our mind therefore exulted with great joy at the great benefit of the Lord’s generosity, because he deigned to kindle in your conversion a spark of orthodox religion. Through this, he would more easily inflame not only the understanding of your glorious husband, but also that of the entire people subject to you, with love for himself.

We have learned, from those who came to us announcing the praiseworthy conversion of our glorious son King Audubald, that your Glory also, having received the wondrous sacrament of the Christian faith, shines continually through pious deeds pleasing to God. Let her carefully abstain from the worship of idols and from the allurements of shrines and auguries, and let her remain steadfast in the love of her Redeemer with unchanging devotion, so that she may not cease to contribute her efforts continually to the spread of the Christian faith.

When paternal charity had carefully inquired about your glorious husband, we learned that, until now, while serving abominable idols, he had delayed offering obedience to the voice of the preachers. This has caused us no small bitterness, because one who is part of your body has remained alien to the knowledge of the supreme and indivisible Trinity.

Therefore, in the exercise of our paternal duties, we have not delayed conveying our admonition to your glorious Christianity. We exhort you not to delay acting, in season and out of season, strengthened by the aids of divine inspiration, so that he too, through the cooperating power of our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, may be joined to the number of Christians, and so that you may hold the rights of marital fellowship in an undefiled bond of union. For it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Matthew 19).

How can the unity of your union be said to exist if he remains alienated from the splendor of your faith by the intervening darkness of detestable error? Therefore, persist continually in prayer and do not cease to seek from the long-suffering clemency of heaven the gift of his illumination. Thus, those whom the bond of bodily affection is shown to have made one body in some manner may also be preserved by the unity of faith in perpetual fellowship after the passage of this life.

Persist, then, glorious daughter, and strive with the greatest efforts to soften the hardness of his heart through the devout instruction of the divine commandments. Pour into his understanding how splendid is the mystery that you have received by believing, and how marvelous is the reward that, through your rebirth, you have merited to attain.

Kindle the coldness of his heart through the proclamation of the Holy Spirit, so that, once the torpor of the most destructive worship has been removed, he may kindle the understanding of divine faith through the warmth of your frequent exhortations. Thus the testimony of sacred Scripture may be shown unmistakably to have been fulfilled through you: “The unbelieving husband will be saved through the believing wife” (1 Corinthians 7).

For you have obtained the mercy of the Lord’s kindness for this purpose: that you might return to your Redeemer an abundant fruit of faith and of the benefits entrusted to you. With the support of his goodness, we do not cease to ask in continual prayers that you may accomplish this.

Having said these things, and showing you the duties of paternal affection, we exhort you, whenever you find an opportunity to send a bearer, to report to us as quickly as possible what the power of heaven has deigned to accomplish through you in the conversion of your husband and of the people subject to you. In this way our concern—which eagerly awaits good news concerning the salvation of your soul and of all those who belong to you—may be relieved by your report; and, recognizing more abundantly the illumination of divine favor poured out upon you, we may rightly offer abundant thanks with joyful confession to God, the giver of all good things, and to blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.

Moreover, we have sent you a blessing from your protector, blessed Peter, chief of the apostles: namely, a silver mirror and a gilded ivory comb. We ask that your Glory receive these with the same kindly disposition with which you know them to have been sent by us.

## APPENDIX

[Col. 0439]

### LETTER TO JUSTUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY (C)*

[Col. 0439C]

**To his dearest brother Justus, Boniface, bishop and servant of the servants of God.**

Having received the letters of your affection [Note: Mansi, *Supplement*, vol. I, p. 470, from Wilkins, vol. I, p. 32], in which we learned, among other things, that many of the pagans living there had been converted with the help of God almighty and our Lord Jesus Christ, and especially that in the regions of Kent they had been brought to faith in our true God through your labors, we rejoiced greatly.

We also praised the almighty Lord because the mind of King Eadbald had been corrected toward the path of true knowledge, and because he had not abandoned the sacrament of his name or the fruit of your labor, just as he himself truthfully promised the preachers of the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

Great is the clemency of God, which has been greatly demonstrated among us, since the hearts of barbarian nations are opened to receive the unique mystery of your preaching. So that they might advance through your merits, their salvation has been brought near, the Lord saying: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved”; and elsewhere: “The reward of your completed work will be granted by the Lord, the rewarder of all good things.”

I have learned from your letter that our predecessor of holy memory, Gregory, established for Augustine and all his successors that henceforth the metropolitan and primatial see should be in the city of Dorobernia, where the head of the entire English people has been located since pagan times.

But now, through the revelation of Jesus Christ, who is the origin and head of all Christianity, that same city is exalted, and the orthodox faith, which is the noblest root, is established there, so that from that seedbed they may measure throughout the whole island an abundant harvest of good works as food for the heavenly homeland.

O how happy is that city which has deserved to have Christ dwelling within it, once the snares of the ancient enemy have been expelled! Happy that city, and happy the entire people, since that heavenly mercy has not disdained to visit those whom it had predestined before the creation of the world to join itself!

Therefore, let it be far from every Christian that anything should now or in future be diminished or changed in that city of Dorobernia which was established by our predecessor, the lord Pope Gregory, whatever shocks may befall human affairs. Rather, by the authority of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, we confirm the same provision, ordering that the metropolitan see of all Britain should always in future remain in the city of Dorobernia, and we decree with perpetual and unimpaired stability that all the provinces of the kingdom of the English should be subject to the metropolitan church of that place.

But if anyone should attempt to diminish this church, which exists in a special manner under the power and protection of the holy Roman Church, or should remove anything from it by right of the authority granted to it, may God remove him from the book of life, and may he know that he has been marked by the bonds of anathema. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

## In the year of the Lord 625: Saint Sonnatius, Archbishop of Rheims

[Col. 0441]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT SONNATIUS

*(Gal­lia Christiana, vol. IX, p. 18.)*

[Col. 0441A]

Sonnatius was archdeacon of Rheims when he became bishop of Rheims, before the year 613. For, according to Flodoard, he exchanged certain properties with Queen Brunhilda, who did not die before that year. Cointius supposes that he was elected at the beginning of the year 594. If this is true, there is nothing to prevent his having transferred the body of Saint Remigius to a new crypt around the year 600, as some maintain.

Moreover, Flodoard writes that he probably put the affairs of his church in good order. He enlarged the bishop’s estate by purchasing, at a stated price, lands and serfs; some records of these purchases are still found. Certain properties which unscrupulous men had seized he recovered and duly restored to the Church through the royal authority, both personally and through his agents, with the priest Marcus, his legate, also conducting the cases.

He arranged the colonists of certain estates belonging to the bishopric according to their assigned services. He also obtained royal privileges concerning the immunity of ecclesiastical property, as well as confirmation of certain transfers. In the year 625 he celebrated the Council of Rheims with more than forty other bishops of Gaul; many useful regulations were enacted at that council, as Flodoard records.

Finally, he made a will concerning his property, in which, according to the same writer, he bestowed several gifts upon various churches. He made the basilica of blessed Remigius his principal heir, choosing to be buried there and assigning to it a gilded silver vessel. He also assigned twelve spoons, a silver saltcellar, and his share of a certain Villaris, together with its serfs, vineyards, meadows, and everything else adjoining it, as well as several other properties which he remembered having purchased at a stated price.

To the basilica of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris he assigned certain houses, both beside the church itself and within the city. To the basilica of Saint Martin, whom he calls his personal patron, he gave in full the estate called Mutation, which he had purchased, just as he had possessed it. In addition, he gave gold from which a chalice was to be made there.

To the basilica of Saint John he gave five gold solidi; likewise, to the basilica of Saint Sixtus three gold solidi; to the basilica of Saint Medard three solidi; and to the monastery of women a vineyard situated at Germaniacum, together with certain vessels useful to that basilica.

To the basilica called *Ad Apostolos* he gave three gold solidi, together with other small gifts from which a chalice was to be made. To the basilica of Saint Peter in the city he gave three gold solidi. To the basilica of Saint Theodore he gave his share of the estate at Germaniacum, together with its serfs, vineyards, and everything belonging to it, as well as silver for making or adorning the tomb of Lord Theodulf.

To the basilica of Saint Vitus he gave a certain silver vessel for making a chalice, and fifteen solidi each year. He also gave several gifts to the matricular body of the holy Church of Rheims, and assigned various gifts to the other matricular bodies and religious communities.

To certain persons among his heirs he left various estates on the condition that, after their death, they should return to the holy places he had designated. He granted freedom to a number of serfs and enriched them by adding personal property. This testament of the man of God is found confirmed by a document of royal authority.

The most worthy bishop is believed to have died on 20 October in the year 631, if Cointius is to be trusted. Demochares reports that, after a lapse of many years, God revealed his holiness to the world through miracles shining at his tomb, especially in the time of the archbishops Rainald II, Sanson, and Henry I—that is, in the twelfth century. His sacred bones were then transferred from the church of Saint Remigius to the cathedral on 4 November 1204, with the solemn elevation celebrated by Wido, cardinal-bishop of Palestrina.

Shortly afterward, however, they were destroyed by an accidental fire in which the church was disfigured and its immense furnishings perished. Certain synodal statutes are attributed to this holy bishop; see Labbe and Marlot.

[Col. 0443]

## STATUTES OF SAINT SONNATIUS, BISHOP OF RHEIMS

[Note: **Statutes.** These statutes, taken from the major monastery—called Marmoutier in French—founded by Saint Martin in the suburbs of the city of Tours, reached our hands only later, and it seemed appropriate to add them in the form of an appendix. Although some features in them do not seem to bear the stamp of such great antiquity—for example, that they give parish priests the title of “pastor,” when in Sonnatius’s time and for long afterward they were usually called merely priests or presbyters; and likewise that they place the feast of the Nativity of blessed Mary among the feasts to be celebrated, although in these regions it does not seem to have been so ancient, since Fulbert of Chartres, who lived in the year 1017, is said to have first celebrated it in Gaul, if we believe Demochares—nevertheless, it could easily have happened that the word “pastor” was substituted for “priest” by some more recent writer, and that the feast was perhaps added by someone later.

Saint Ildefonsus, however, who lived at the same time as Sonnatius, writes in his book *On the Virginity and Childbirth of Blessed Mary* that her Nativity was celebrated and venerated on the authority of the whole Church.]

Similar things are written by Jesse, bishop of Amiens, in his letter to the priests of his diocese, as well as in the constitution of Riculfus, bishop of Soissons, which Jean Cordes published together with the minor works of Hincmar. (Colvenerius in his notes to Flodoard.)]

# STATUTES

*(From Flodoard, History of the Church of Rheims.)*

## Chapter One

Without faith, as the Apostle testifies (Hebrews 11), it is impossible to please God; therefore we command everyone to hold and follow exactly the doctrine of faith, according to the word of God and the tradition of the holy Roman Church. And whoever are pastors must learn and know the matters pertaining to the instruction of the people and flock, and must rouse their own people to the practice of virtue.

### II

Let them administer the sacraments devoutly to the faithful, and let them always provide what pertains to explaining the sacrament’s usefulness and its institution.

### III

Let them accept no payment, but trust in God, who gives food to the young ravens that call upon him (Psalm 146).

### IV

The person who is going to baptize must be sober, and must perform the task honorably; he must pronounce the words attentively and properly inquire about the sponsors.

### V

The sacrament of confirmation contains the gift of the strengthening Holy Spirit and conveys more abundant grace; therefore it must not be neglected.

### VI

The remission of sins and expiation rests chiefly upon, and depends upon, the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### VII

Let the pastor care for his sheep and not neglect it. Let him instruct it to attend the sacrifice of the Mass on solemn days and Sundays; let him recognize its face. If it is absent twice in a year, let it be forbidden to enter that same church, and let it be deprived of pastoral burial and consolation.

### VIII

During Lent, no one except the pastor is to hear the confessions of penitents. For it is his responsibility to recognize the sheep for which he has pledged his own life to the Lord.

### IX

The priest who is going to celebrate the most holy Eucharist must prepare and examine himself, and must do so at least twice each month.

### X

Let the Eucharist be carried to the sick in a proper vessel, with a light going before it and preceding the procession. And whoever wishes to travel should receive it as viaticum.

### XI

And why is it refused to those condemned to death, when it is especially useful to them for the hope and assurance of a certain death and of their present struggle?

### XII

Those who wish to be promoted to orders must possess a benefice sufficient for their support, and must be subjected to examination by trustworthy and sworn men.

### XIII

Let the tonsure be given to no one except a suitable person who may thereafter plausibly rise to the sacred orders. For what need is there to throw the children’s bread to dogs, or spiritual things to lovers of the world?

### XIV

In marriage there exists an image of the most holy union brought forth between Christ and the Church. Therefore it is a bond divinely strengthened, which greatly contributes to the happiness of the household, to peace between the parties, and to the begetting of children (Ephesians 5).

### XV

Let extreme unction be brought to the suffering person who requests it; and let the pastor visit him frequently in his own home and visit him devoutly, encouraging him toward future glory and preparing him properly.

### XVI

As for clerics, let them shine like stars and perpetual lights in the firmament of the Church. Let them not be drunkards, frivolous, or mixed up with secular affairs.

### XVII

Nor should they converse with women or keep them in their homes. Let them live in common and inhabit houses open to the poor.

### XVIII

We command that the suffrages for all the dead be preserved, and that the solemn celebrations of Mass not be diverted in any other way contrary to the intention of the founders.

### XIX

Let bishops be faithful and diligent dispensers of the word of God. For their charity is recognized in this: that they feed the flock by example and by word.

### XX

The feasts to be observed and celebrated with due veneration, without any secular labor, are these: the Nativity of the Lord; the Circumcision; the Epiphany; the Annunciation of blessed Mary; the Resurrection of the Lord together with the following day; the Ascension of the Lord; the day of Pentecost; the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist; the feasts of the apostles Peter and Paul; the Assumption of blessed Mary; her Nativity; the feast of the apostle Andrew; and all Sundays.

### XXI

Let churches be properly endowed for the support of the pastor and clergy, so that they may watch more securely over the flock and be anxious and concerned for its salvation.

# In the Year of the Lord 625: Verus, Bishop of Rodez

## Historical Notice Concerning Verus

*(Fabricius, Library of the Middle and Later Ages.)*

Verus, bishop of Rodez in Gaul, attended the Council of Rheims in the year 625. Two of his letters to Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, were published by Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, vol. I, pp. 648–649. Letters addressed to him by Sulpicius Severus, bishop of Bourges, are found in the same work, p. 645, as well as one by Ruricius of Limoges II, 22. Add *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 201.

## Two Letters of Verus, Bishop of Rodez

*(Canisius, Ancient Readings, vol. I.)*

### I

To his ever-lord Desiderius, pope, Verus the sinner.
