We have received your command together with a copy of the letter of Lord Sulpitius, in which the lord made known that your brother, Lord Sulpitius, appeared at another time to have altered this arrangement concerning this synod. We had already made this known to Your Grace through your servant, the deacon Becobenus, and afterward through your messenger. But since, God willing, the lord made known that my suggestion was contained in it, we rejoiced that through your felicity we had deserved to learn of these desired joys.

Meanwhile we render the full service of our obedience, begging you to deign to implore the Lord’s mercy for us and to command that we be frequently consoled by news of your happiness. For the almighty Lord knows that we always desire to hear and see from you those things that are good. May I deserve to serve you for many years, apostolic Father.

### II

To the illustrious lord, and one especially deserving of our respect, the worshiper of God, Lord Desiderius, Verus the sinner.

Since our son Leodoaldus the deacon is approaching, we thought it appropriate that I should inquire into the lordship of Your Charity, since we know that the devotion of your holy soul always desires good things on our behalf. Above all, we enjoy your patronage before that of anyone else.

Therefore, greeting Your Eminence, we ask that, just as we chose your patronage and your protective defense has until now notably fortified us, so now also, concerning the circumstances of our nephews—about which we ask you to make the foregoing request to them—you should apply such care and persistence that, just as we are indebted to you, you may likewise acquire them as debtors to you in every respect.

Also, by sending back the aforesaid man with a written response from the height of your happiness, deign to relieve our anxiety. May our Lord Jesus Christ guard your body and soul on the day of his judgment! Amen.

# In the Year of the Lord 628: Chlothar II, King of the Franks

## Historical Notice Concerning Chlothar II

*(Literary History of France, vol. III, p. 541.)*

Chlothar, second of that name, was the son of Chilperic I, whom we discussed in his proper place, and of the celebrated Fredegund. He was born four months before the death of his father, which occurred around the autumn of the year 584. He immediately began to reign in Neustria under the direction of his mother the queen; and this is why the years of his reign are counted by the years of his age. Fredegund skillfully secured for him the favor of Gontran, his paternal uncle, who always protected him and even lifted him from the sacred baptismal font, with wishes for a prosperity still greater than that of his grandfather, whose name he bore.

*[Note: Gregory of Tours, History, book VI, chapter 41; book VII, chapter 7; book VIII, chapters 1 and 18; book IX, chapter 20; book X, chapter 28.]*

Care was taken to have this young prince educated, and all our historians agree in bearing witness that he was well instructed in letters. Hence the inclination and honor he showed toward those who cultivated them. He esteemed good men no less than learned men, and had at his court several holy persons who were raised to the highest dignities of the Church. Among them were Saint Arnulf, Saint Goeric, Saint Faro, Saint Desiderius, Saint Romaric, and several others.

One cannot give a just picture of his reign except by saying that he caused all the virtues that make great kings to reign together with him. His piety shone forth in his affection for the bishops and his generosity toward the churches; his goodness and humanity in the care he took to aid the poor and in his attention to providing for the needs of all the orders of his kingdom; his generosity in remitting to the Lombards the annual tribute they paid to the Frankish kings; his valor in the notable victory he won over the Saxons; and his love of peace in the preference he gave to wise and peaceful government over the ambition of conquering provinces and winning battles.

He is reproached only for having shown too much tenderness and indulgence toward women, and for having used too much cruelty toward Brunhilda, upon whom he inflicted the horrible punishment known to everyone.

*[Note: Fredegar, Chronicle, no. 42; Aimoin, book IV, chapters 1, 6, 7, and 16.]*

After Gontran’s death, Chlothar had some disputes with Theuderic and Theudebert, his cousins, one king of Burgundy and the other of Austrasia, in which he did not always have the advantage. But he finally defeated them and reunited under his rule the three kingdoms that formed the Frankish monarchy. This monarch lived another fifteen years thereafter and died at the beginning of the year 628, in the forty-fifth year of his age and reign. He was buried in the church of Saint Vincent—that is, Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

*[Note: Fredegar, same work, no. 56; Aimoin, same work, chapter 16.]*

Chlothar had married three women, two of whom each bore him a son. From Bertrude he had Dagobert I, whom he associated with the kingship as early as 622; from Sichilde he had Charibert, who died two years after his father.

*[Note: Fredegar, Chronicle, nos. 46–47; Aimoin, same work, chapter 8.]*

Chlothar’s love of good order, both in ecclesiastical and civil matters, led him to issue various regulations to maintain it in his states.

1. Under his name there is an ordinance issued around the year 595, when he was only eleven years old. It is divided into eighteen titles or articles and is directed especially toward suppressing theft and the disloyalty of serfs, and toward prescribing the manner in which they were to be prosecuted and punished. But it forbids violating sanctuaries in their case or in the case of any other criminal, and forbids forcibly dragging them from churches in which they had taken refuge. The final article of this ordinance is extremely severe toward judges who are declared liable to death if they violate the regulations it contains. This document strongly reflects the rusticity of the period in which it was composed, as is shown by the large number of barbarous words found in it. Besides the collection of the capitularies of our kings, this ordinance is found at the end of the Salic Law in the 1602 edition.

*[Note: Baluze, Capitularies, vol. I, pp. 19–22.]*

2. We also possess from Chlothar another, more substantial edict, much better written than the preceding ordinance, and in which he had a greater share, since he was then reigning in his own right. It is dated the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November—that is, 18 October—in the thirty-first year of his reign, consequently on the same day and in the same year as the Sixth Council of Paris discussed above. It was therefore intended to confirm what had been established by the bishops of that assembly. The prince carried this out in twenty-four articles, in which he repeats nearly all the decrees of the council, explains some of them, and makes various additions concerning civil affairs. This document has not been preserved for us in its entirety, although it is in every respect worthy of a most Christian king. Nothing remains of the fourteenth and fifteenth articles, and something is missing from the thirteenth.

*[Note: p. 21–24.]*

It was applauded and confirmed, together with the canons of the Sixth Council of Paris, in another council held shortly afterward at a place that is still unknown.

*[Note: Councils, vol. V, p. 1655.]*

This edict was inserted into the collection of ancient monuments containing the proofs of the liberties of the Gallican Church. It is also found, together with the preceding ordinance, among the capitularies of our kings of the first dynasty. From there it passed into the collections of councils and into the history of the Church of Paris.

*[Note: pp. 1653–1655; Gallia Christiana, vol. I, pp. 474–476; Dubois, Ecclesiastical History, part III, chapter 7, no. 4.]*

3. Goldast, who inserted Chlothar’s ordinance into his collection of imperial constitutions, also gave us there a fragment of a letter from the same prince to Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, attempting to draw him from his retirement and make him return to his church. This fragment is indeed read under Chlothar’s name in the life of Saint Arnulf, where the original author incorporated it. Several features of the prince’s attachment to this great prelate can be seen in it. But Goldast places it ten years too early, dating it to 615.

*[Note: Goldast, Imperial Constitutions, vol. III, pp. 115–637; Mabillon, Acts of the Saints, vol. II, p. 154.]*

# Ecclesiastical Ordinances of Chlothar II, King of the Franks  
## Decree concerning Serfs and Sanctuaries, Issued around the Year 595

*(Baluze, Capitularies, vol. I.)*

### I

It has been decreed that, since nocturnal thieves were not being caught at the established watches because, through various forms of collusion, crimes were being overlooked while guards were being maintained, hundreds should be formed. If anything is lost in such a hundred, the person who lost it shall receive the principal compensation, and the thief shall be pursued. Or, if the matter appears in another hundred and, even after being warned, they neglect it, they shall be condemned to five solidi. Nevertheless, the person who suffered the loss shall undoubtedly receive the principal compensation from that hundred—that is, from the second or third watch.

### II

If the thief’s track is established, nevertheless [the following corrupt phrase is uncertain: *praesentia nihil longe multando*]. Or, if the person pursuing his thief captures him, let him receive the full composition for himself.

### III

But if the thief is found within a trustis, let the trustis acquire half the composition and demand the principal compensation from the thief.

### IV

If anyone finds a theft in another person’s house where there is a locked door, the master of the house shall pay compensation for his life.

### V

If anyone is caught with stolen goods, he shall be subject to the aforementioned law.

### VI

If anyone is accused on suspicion, let him come to the ordeal.

### VII

If the ordeal should go badly, the thief nevertheless—[the text is corrupt]. Let three persons be chosen on each side, so that collusion may not occur.

### VIII

Concerning the serfs of the Church, of the fisc, or of anyone else: whoever is accused shall come to the ordeal, or be brought before the people, or the price of the serf himself shall be restored by his master. For they will be subject to the danger of proof.

### IX

If anyone is suspected of a crime concerning the serfs of one of the more powerful men, who possess them in various places, let notice be given privately to the master with witnesses, so that he must present the man before the judge within twenty nights. If he does not do so within the appointed time because of collusion, the master, according to the measure of his guilt, shall compensate from the *fredum* and the *faidus* of his status.

### X

If a serf disappears before his master has been warned, the master shall restore the principal compensation and renounce his claim to the serf. When the serf is found, he shall be surrendered for punishment.

### XI

If anyone secretly accepts composition from any thief for property stolen from him, he shall be subject to both offenses of the thief. The thief, however, must be presented to the judge.

### XII

Let him hasten immediately to restore the principal compensation to the person who suffered the loss and pursue the thief. If he finds him within a trustis, let him claim for himself half the compensation or the *delatura*. If it is within the thief’s means and the person who suffered the loss is satisfied, then, if the pursuer captures the thief, he shall recover for himself the full composition together with the payment, or whatever the loss may have been; but the *fredus* shall be reserved for the judge in whose district it is.

### XIII

No one may presume to drag a thief or any guilty person from a church atrium, as is appropriate according to the highest bishops. But if there are churches whose atria are not enclosed, a space of land measuring an *aripennis* on both sides of the walls shall be preserved as the atrium.

### XIV

No one who has taken refuge outside the aforesaid places may claim that he has left them out of desire for work. If they do so and are captured, let them be condemned to a punishment appropriate to them.

### XV

If a serf of anyone, abandoning his master, takes refuge in churches, and his master arrives there first, the dispute is excused; let the theft be returned so that the serf may redeem himself by his price.

### XVI

If anyone, having been summoned to mark the tracks or pursue the thief, refuses to come, let him be condemned to five solidi.

### XVII

What we have established in the name of God under the guarantee of peace, we wish to be observed forever.

### XVIII

In establishing this, we decree that if any judge presumes to violate this decree, he should know that he is subject to the danger of his life.

# Edict Concerning the Synod of Paris

*(Bréquigny, Diplomata, vol. I.)* (C)

There is no doubt that the prosperity of our kingdom increases more and more, with divine assistance, if we diligently strive in our time to preserve inviolably whatever has been rightly done, established, and decreed in our kingdom, God being favorable; and if, through Christ our protector, we resolve generally to correct whatever has been done or ordered contrary to the order of reason, lest such things occur again in the future, which may God avert. Therefore it is our determination that the statutes of the canons be preserved in all respects, and that whatever has been omitted over time be observed perpetually henceforth.

### I

Thus, when a bishop dies, the person who is to be ordained in his place by the metropolitan together with the provincials must be chosen by the clergy and people; and, if he is a suitable person, he is to be ordained by the prince’s order. Or, if he is chosen from the palace, he is to be ordained on account of the merit of his character and learning.

*[Note: Sirmond first made this constitution publicly available, Councils of Ancient Gaul, vol. I, p. 374, from the Rheims Church Codex. From there it passed to Baluze, Capitularies, vol. I, col. 21; Hardouin, Councils, vol. III, col. 55; Cointius, Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks, vol. II, p. 674; the author of Proofs of the Liberties of the Gallican Church, part II, p. 66; Dubois, Ecclesiastical History of Paris, vol. I, p. 143; D. Bouquet, Historians of Gaul and France, vol. IV, p. 118; Mansi, Great Collection of Councils, vol. X, col. 543; and finally Pertz, Monuments of German History, vol. III, p. 14. Sirmond notes that this constitution is inscribed in the Codex before the council; nevertheless, the learned man placed it afterward, not without reason, since it mentions a council whose decrees were partly fortified by royal sanction.]*

### II

No bishop, while he is alive, is to choose his successor; rather, another is to be substituted for him only when he has become so incapacitated that he can govern neither his Church nor his clergy. Likewise, no one may presume, while a bishop is alive, to assume his place. If anyone requests this, it must not be granted to him.

*[Note: It cannot be inferred from this that the prince had permission to promote anyone to the episcopate according to his own judgment and without canonical rules; the author of the book entitled *Theory of the Political Laws of France*, vol. IV, part II, pp. 82 ff., proved this at length.]*

### III

If any cleric, invested with whatever dignity, despising or bypassing his bishop, goes to the prince or to any of the more powerful persons, or seeks to choose their patronage for himself, he is not to be received—unless he appears to be seeking pardon. And if he has sought the prince for any cause and has returned to his own bishop with a letter from the prince himself, he is to be received with his excuse. Whoever, after being warned by his bishop, presumes to retain him shall be deprived of holy communion.

*[Note: See canon II of the Council of Paris.]*

### IV

No judge, concerning clerics of any rank, may presume personally to constrain or condemn them in civil matters, apart from criminal cases, unless they are manifestly convicted, except in the case of a priest or deacon. Those who have been convicted of a capital crime are to be constrained according to the canons and examined together with the bishops.

*[Note: Compare canon III of the Council of Paris.]*

### V

If a case arises between a public person and people of the Church, the heads of the churches and the public judge, placed together in a public hearing by both sides, must judge the matter.

*[Note: This had already been established by several councils and, much earlier, by an imperial constitution of the year 425.]*

### VI

If any deceased person dies intestate, his relatives shall succeed to his property according to the law, without judicial opposition.

*[Note: The decree of the council mentioned in the preceding chapter adds a certain law and, in the case foreseen there, establishes a mixed tribunal.]*

### VII

The freedmen of any freeborn persons are to be defended by the priests in their freedom, according to the wording of the charters; they are not to be judged, or recalled to public service, without the presence of the bishop or head of the Church.

*[Note: This chapter agrees with chapter 2 of Chlothar I’s constitution of the year 560.]*

### VIII

Wherever a new tax has been impiously added and the people protest against it, let it be mercifully corrected through a just inquiry.

### IX

Concerning the toll: it is to be collected at those places, or from those very commodities, from which it was collected in the time of the preceding princes—that is, up to the death of our good-memory lords and parents, the kings Guntran, Chilperic, and Sigebert.

*[Note: Compare canon 5 of the Council of Paris.]*

### X

Jews are not to bring public actions against Christians. Therefore whoever presumes to associate himself with the money-making order shall incur the most severe penalty according to canonical judgment.

*[Note: This agrees with canon 15 of the Council of Paris.]*

### XI

So that peace and discipline may be perpetual in our kingdom, Christ being favorable, the rebellion or insolence of wicked men is to be suppressed with the utmost severity.

*[Note: This chapter confirms the pact and decrees of Childebert and Chlothar, which may be seen on p. 166 and following.]*

### XII

No judge is to be appointed from other provinces or regions to another place; so that if he perpetrates any wrongdoing concerning people of whatever condition, he must restore, according to the order of the law, from his own property whatever he wrongfully took from them.

*[Note: Compare chapter 6 of Chlothar’s constitution of the year 560.]*

### XIII

Our commands are to be fulfilled in every respect.

*[Note: The remainder of this chapter, together with the following two, is missing; therefore the next is numbered 16.] (The end of the chapter is lost.)*

### XIV

*(The text is lost.)*

### XV

*(The text is lost.)*

### XVI

Whatever our earlier princely ancestors, or we ourselves, appear to have granted and confirmed by justice must be confirmed in all respects.

### XVII

And whatever one of the faithful and *leudes*, while preserving his faith toward his rightful lord during an interregnum, appears to have lost, we order generally to be restored to him without any inconvenience, from the possessions justly owed to him.

### XVIII

No one may presume, whether by our command or by any other authority, to molest, drag away, or entirely presume to marry girls, religious widows, or nuns who have devoted themselves to God, whether they reside in their own houses or are placed in monasteries. And if anyone has obtained a command concerning this, it shall have no effect.

*[Note: The same had already been enacted in chapter 7 of Chlothar’s constitution of the year 560.]*

And if anyone, by force or through any office, presumes to abduct them or marry them to himself, he shall be struck with a capital sentence. And if they have contracted marriage in a church, and the woman who was abducted—or was to be abducted—appears to have consented to it, they shall be separated from one another and transported into exile, and their property shall be transferred to their near heirs.

*[Note: The same had been established by canon 13 of the Council of Paris. Compare chapter 4 of Childebert’s edict of the year 595.]*

### XIX

Bishops or powerful men who possess property in other regions are not to appoint judges or investigating commissioners from other provinces, except from the locality, so that they may receive justice and render it to others.

### XX

Therefore the agents of bishops or powerful men must not, by force of their authority, seize collected payments for anything, nor presume personally to show contempt toward anyone.

### XXI

Fiscal swineherds must not presume to enter the forests of churches or private persons without the consent of the possessors.

### XXII

Neither a freeborn person nor a serf who has not been caught with stolen property is to be killed by judges or by anyone else without being heard.

*[Note: See chapter 7 of Childebert’s decree of the year 595.]*

### XXIII

And whenever there has not been pasture sufficient for pigs to be fattened, no *cellarinsis* is to be exacted publicly.

*[Note: The order of the chapters appears to be disturbed, for this belongs to chapter 21.]*

### XXIV

Whoever presumes to violate this deliberation, which we established with the bishops and with such great noblemen and our faithful in a synodal council, is to be judged by a capital sentence, so that others may not perpetrate similar acts.

We have decreed that this authority or edict, which is to remain valid for all time, be strengthened by the signatures of our hands.

—Hamingus.  
—Chlothar, king in the name of Christ, have subscribed this determination.

Given at Paris, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the thirty-first year of our reign.

# Grant for the Monastery of Saint-Denis

*(In Mabillon, Supplement on Diplomatic Matters, p. 92.)*

[Lacuna] … to the illustrious men Chrodegarius … of sound mind, [lacuna] through basilicas from his own property he wished to be legally assigned by a page of testament, by our authorities [lacuna] our abbot Dodo of the basilica of the holy lord Dionysius the Martyr, our special patron, [lacuna] a page of testament from John, formerly a merchant, son of Hid… [lacuna] whatever from his property to the basilica of that Saint Dionysius, or to the remaining holy places within the town of the city of Paris, and also to some of his relatives, we ought generally to confirm. Since Your Greatness, as to every rightful petitioner, or for the benefit of our rewards, has not refused this favour [lacuna] the often-mentioned John is known justly to have assigned to the aforesaid basilicas of Saint Dionysius, or the remaining holy places, or his relatives, that is, lands, houses, slaves [lacuna] or remaining benefit; confirmed by the force of this authority of ours and by general favour, let it benefit those basilicas or his relatives forever [lacuna] likewise, secured by this grant, may remain safe. And that this authority [lacuna] under unshaken law [lacuna] in our enlarged titles and future times [lacuna] Ursinus died [lacuna] Chlothar, king in the name of Christ, subscribed this grant [lacuna] of ours, at Stirpiniacum, happy in the Lord, at the old palace.

# Letter to Arnulf

*(Bréquigny, Diplomata, vol. I.)*

Arnulf, whose life may be read in the Bollandists under 18 July, and concerning whom Mabillon, cited below, should be consulted, repeatedly and urgently begged King Chlothar to give him a successor. He sent letters through intermediaries, declared himself unworthy of the episcopal office, and asked that another bishop be chosen in his place to sow the word of preaching among the people.

When the content of the letters became known, Chlothar was tormented by anxieties, declaring that he would be deprived of all assistance if Arnulf withdrew from the frequenting of the palace. Accordingly, he wrote him a letter in which he urged the bishop to continue performing his office.

Neither the day nor the year is certain. Mabillon, in the work cited below, appears to indicate the year 640, but this conflicts with the letter itself, since it is addressed to Chlothar, who died in the year 628. Goldast incorrectly gives the year 615. For when Chlothar had established his son Dagobert as king of Austrasia in 622, he entrusted the kingdom to Arnulf to govern and Dagobert to educate. D. Bouquet, *Historians of Gaul and France*, vol. III, p. 508, assigned the year 625; I have followed his view.

… Lord and Father, what you wrote in your letter, that we ought to choose another successor in your place, our presumption in no way presumes to do this. Meanwhile, among other things, he says:

As much as we rejoiced in your devotion, which we are confident proceeds from divine admonition, so much again, grieving, did we consider that we did not wish to be absent from your presence. Indeed, Lord and Father, if, compelled by any devotion, you are considering setting out somewhere for the sake of a good work, we ask that, for the love of God, you in no way leave us without your peace or communion.

# Appendix

*(Bréquigny, Diplomata, vol. I.)*

Charter by which Lonegisilus donates to Hadoindus, bishop of Le Mans, and to his Church, the little monastery he founded at Bussiacum, together with everything he has acquired or may acquire.

*[Note: Printed by Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 265, among the acts of the bishops of Le Mans; reprinted by the same author in the *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. I, p. 330. Mabillon, in the work cited above, Cointius, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 769, Corvaisier, and Bondonnet commonly regarded it as genuine, but we judge that it should nevertheless be counted among the spurious documents. We find no slight ground for suspicion in the fact that it appears to have been entirely fabricated on the model of the charter of Carileph, which we published above, p. 98, and demonstrated to be forged; the chronological notes, which we shall examine shortly, reveal its falsity. [A distinguished scholar discussed this argument at length in the prolegomena; I ask the reader to consult them.]]*

*(Year 625)*
In the name of God and our Lord Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit.

It is fitting for every person to prepare the day of his death by good works, lest the final day of his life find him unprepared and without the fruit of good work. Therefore I, Lonegisilus, in God’s name an unworthy priest and, though not in deed, nevertheless a monk in intention, considering the condition of human frailty, left Alamannia, my homeland, and my noble and wealthy parents, who were forcing me to live as a pagan, joining me to royal military service, training me in arms, and withdrawing me from Christ’s service; they urged me to serve mortal gods. But, as I believe, under divine inspiration I rejected them, because they seemed vain to me, and I endeavored to unite myself to almighty God.

Then I began to seek Christians, so that I might learn from them how I ought to live. Instructed by them in letters and baptized, I became a Christian. Afterwards I began to frequent the places of the saints and monasteries, and to seek a place where I might build some small cell. Thus, with the Lord leading me, I came to the territory of Le Mans, where I was kindly received by Lord Hadoind, my master. I disclosed my intention to him and explained how I had lived from my infancy. Strengthened by him, I began, with his assistance and exhortation, to seek in that territory a place where I might establish some small cell for the winning of souls.

One day I came to Busiacum, a canonical village, where I was detained by the priests and inhabitants of that place. When I disclosed my intention to them, they began to urge me to build a small cell in that same place, because it is a populous locality, and much alms comes there; and our people love God and would provide for me sufficiently, to such an extent that I might obtain the place from the bishop. They immediately gave me their inheritances and granted many possessions.

When I reported these things to my lord Hadoind, he gave thanks to God, ordained me a priest, and gave me the aforesaid village of Busiacum together with its remaining estates and appurtenances, on the following condition: that I should remain subject to the mother church of Le Mans, and that whatever I could gather and attract from every quarter I should hand over to him; and that the aforesaid monastery, with everything belonging to it, should remain with the aforesaid church in the future as it had previously been, together with everything that I might be able to acquire there.

I willingly placed myself in his hands, and by this charter I perpetually assigned for possession to him and his successors all the property that I had been able to acquire or might be able to acquire in the future. With the permission and authorization, or grant, of Lord King Chlotar, together with his agent, the count Buccellinus, I legally transferred and confirmed it.

From that same lord Hadoind, bishop, I received from the property of his see, the church of Saint Mary and of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, a portion of the estate of Lucdunum together with the aforesaid village of Buxidum, as well as other property for which I had petitioned him, and many ecclesiastical ornaments. Through these I was greatly enriched, so that I could complete the small monastery. With his assistance, and supported by workmen and craftsmen, I was able to build the monastery there.

Afterwards I was accused and brought before King Chlotar. But the Lord, who always helps those who hope in him, himself helped me and turned that accusation to good. Through his mercy I found favor with King Chlotar, and was enriched by him with many gifts. He also assessed for that monastery an annual payment of silver, by which I might complete it, and he granted me protection.

Having returned, I transferred all these things by these instruments to my aforesaid lord Hadoind, bishop, and to his church, to be held perpetually. At the command and exhortation of Lord Chlotar, we transferred and confirmed them in such a manner that in future monks, always living there according to the rule, should remain under the authority of the bishop; specifically, so that the property given to the bishop might be held not according to judicial custom but according to ecclesiastical law, under complete immunity, just as it has until now been possessed by us, in the oratory of Saint Peter.

By God’s grant, I was worthy to find a tooth of Saint Peter in Rome, upon the body and altar of that same Saint Peter, when the prince of the apostles himself revealed it; I was worthy to bring it to my lord Hadoind, bishop, who commended it to the Lord by his prayers and solemnly placed it in our aforesaid oratory.

By this testamentary document I restore our aforesaid small monastery to my lord Hadoind, bishop, and whatever I have acquired or may henceforth be able to acquire, in every kind of property, both movable and immovable, I transfer and convey into the right, power, and dominion of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, so that, with God protecting and aiding them, it may belong to their rectors and bishops.

Although it is not necessary to attach a penalty to transfers, nevertheless, for the sake of complete security, we have decided that one should be inserted. If anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, God forbid, or any of our heirs, or any other person, moved or induced by cunning, should at any time attempt to revoke the written deed of our transfer, which we have decided to make voluntarily for the name of the Lord and out of reverence for that holy place, or should attempt to do anything against it, or should become a resister, let him be anathema. Both the one who does this and the one who consents to its being done shall be anathema.

Together with the aforesaid holy apostle, let him render an account before the tribunal of Christ. Moreover, under the penalty of this world, let the treasury compel him to pay to the church itself or its rectors one hundred pounds of gold and two hundred weights of silver, and let him in no way be able to vindicate what he claims. Rather, this present transfer and our will shall remain inviolate for all time, supported by formal stipulation.

And so that this transfer might be held more firmly and preserved inviolably, we have affixed our hands below and have decided that it be strengthened by the hands of other good men.

Executed at Sagonna, at the public assembly. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, in the fifty-second year of King Chlotar’s reign.

[Note: Lonegisilus lived in the time of Hadoind, bishop of Le Mans, who governed the church of Le Mans toward the end of the reign of Chlotar II. Bondonnet, *Lives of the Bishops of Le Mans*, p. 324. Therefore this refers to the years of the reign of Chlotar II. No one is unaware that he reigned no more than forty-five years; yet the charter of Lonegisilus is represented as having been issued in the fifty-second year of Chlotar’s reign. Let us see whether an error of this kind could have entered a genuine charter. Critics’ conjecture is at first sight sufficiently plausible: Mabillon, Cointius, Corvaisier, Bondonnet, and others think that the number LII should be corrected, and read the forty-second year of Chlotar’s reign. We admit that the numeral X might be believed to have been omitted through a copyist’s negligence or obliterated by the ravages of time. But when we detect the same error in two other documents to be produced shortly, on pp. 224 and 225, drawn from the same source—one of which is likewise attributed to Lonegisilus and is dated to this same year LII, while the other is a diploma of Chlotar confirming the charter of Lonegisilus and is dated to year LIII—who could persuade himself that this happened by chance in three documents so closely connected with one another? Who would not attribute it to the ignorance of the forger who fabricated these three documents rather than to a copyist’s negligence or the damage caused by time? Add what we shall say in the following note concerning the subscriptions. Since these documents ought not to be placed beyond the reign of Chlotar, we have assigned them a place according to the conjectures of the critics.]

I, Lonegisilus, an unworthy priest and a monk in intention, have subscribed this donation made by me and have asked that it be confirmed.

In God’s name, I, Medegiselus, archbishop of the city of Tours, a sinner, at the request of Lonegisilus, have subscribed.

[Note: The subscriptions seem to agree with the dates, according to Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 331. Madegisilus was indeed presiding over the church of Tours in 625, when he attended the synod held by Sonnatius, bishop of Reims; Flodoard, *History of Reims*, book II, chapter 5. But the title of archbishop was unusual at this period. Mabillon considers Magnobonus to have been the bishop of Angers, though he ought properly to have called him Magnebodus. He conjectures that Abbo governed the church of Meaux, an unfortunate conjecture: for Arnulfus was then presiding over that church and attended the synod mentioned above. It seems quite plausible to us that the forger borrowed Abbo’s name from the subscriptions of the spurious charter of Carilephus, which he had taken as his model. For that charter is subscribed in precisely the same words: “Abbo, bishop by the mercy of Christ.” These considerations, together with those noted above, lead us to think that all credibility must be denied to the charter of Lonegisilus.]

In God’s name, Magnobonus, a sinner and bishop, at the request of Lonegisilus, have subscribed.

In God’s name, I, Abbo, bishop by the mercy of Christ, have subscribed.

The mark of Odilard, count.

The mark of Leobad, count.

The mark of Ratgaud, count.

I, Benedict, abbot, have subscribed.

I, Siagrius, abbot, have subscribed.

I, Leutfridus, abbot, have subscribed.

The mark of Leutramnus.

The mark of Turingo.

The mark of Teutbert.

The mark of Paternus.

The mark of Babo.

The mark of Ibbolenus.

Agatho Honoratus has subscribed.

Gheirinus, at the request of my lord King Chlotar, have subscribed.

Guntinus Honoratus has subscribed.

Ibbo, notary, have subscribed, reread, and recorded the day and year.

## II. Charter by which Lonegisilus received from the Church of Le Mans the small monastery founded by him at Busiacum and donated to that church, to possess under the right of usufruct

[Note: Published in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 266, among the acts of the bishops of Le Mans, which are of very slight reliability. It displays the same indications of falsity as the charter of the same Lonegisilus published immediately before it, p. 221: namely, the same error in the chronological notices and the same, indeed even greater, similarity to the other spurious charter of Carilephus, which may be seen above, p. 98, taken from the same *Analecta* of Mabillon. If the two are compared carefully, one will scarcely recognize a single word that differs, except for the names of places and persons; hence everyone will judge that this charter was copied from the other word for word. Such features plainly seem to reveal the offspring of forgers. Add what we said in our notes to the immediately preceding charter of Lonegisilus, above, p. 222.]

In the year 625.

To Lord Hadoind, holy and venerable apostolic bishop of Le Mans, together with the holy congregation residing in that city: I, Lonegisilus, in God’s name an unworthy priest and a monk in intention, approach you as a petitioner.

Since my request and your will have agreed that the small monastery which has been constructed in honor of Saint Peter and is situated in the territory of Saint Mary, holy Mother of God, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, the mother and senior church of the city of Le Mans in the territory of Le Mans, in the place called Busiacum, a canonical village—which I, Lonegisilus, once received through your generosity and, with your assistance, rebuilt through your benefaction under the right of usufruct for the duration of my life—you permitted me to hold, with all the property belonging or pertaining to it, and assessed me annually to pay to the mother church of the city and to its bishops and rectors, namely, for the church-light, four large pounds of wax; six pounds and two *treantes* of oil; for the bishop’s use, one staff and one fur garment; and one-half pound of silver in public coin; and for the use of the canons, two *modii* of wine for charitable distribution.

If I should appear negligent or slow in paying this rent, I shall provide assurance concerning it, and I shall not lose the small monastery during my lifetime. Nor shall I have the right anywhere to sell, give away, or alienate it, unless it remains under the right, power, and dominion of Saint Mary and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, or of their bishops and rectors.

After my departure from this light, when the Lord so directs, without the authorization of a judge or the opposition of our heirs, you or your succeeding rectors shall cause the aforesaid monastery, with its full integrity and with the property belonging or pertaining to it, to be recalled into your power or dominion.

[Note: Several charters of this kind exist, drawn up in the same words, and scholars recognize all of them as genuine. Since provision had been made by both canon and civil laws that church property could not be alienated, it became customary for such property to be granted for usufruct. On this subject one should consult especially the Council of Agde of 506, above, p. 52. The petitioner requested that the church’s property be granted for his use; the bishop, or the abbot of the monastery, assenting to his petitions, granted the property; and often the donor or seller retained usufruct for himself. Hence these charters were variously called *precariae* or *praestariae*. Their forms may be found among the Marculfian formulas, book II, forms 5, 39, and 40; the Appendix to Marculf, 27, 28, 41, and 42; the Bignonian collection, 20, 21, and 22; the Sirmondian collection, 6, 7, and 38; the Mabillonian, or Angevin, collection, 7; and Lindenbrog, 19, 20, 25, and 26. Cangius should also be consulted under the words “Praestaria” and “Precaria.” In the other charters, as also in the formulas, there is almost always a clause “without renewal after five years”; see what will be said below, vol. II, p. 369, note 2.]

And so that these *precariae*, written in one consistent form,

[Note: These were called *pariclae*, and sometimes *paricolae*, because they were almost always written in one and the same form. Some are found in this collection. Numerous formulas composed on the same subject and in the same manner occur in Marculf, book II, forms 23, 24, 29, and 40; Appendix to Marculf, 27 and 28; Bignon, 20 and 21; Sirmond, 26 and 44; Mabillon, 8. Compare Cangius, under “Paricla.”]

one copy, deposited in the treasury of the city church, and another which I, Lonegisilus, shall receive from you, may remain firm and stable for all time.

Executed publicly in the city of Le Mans. Given on the Kalends of December, in the fifty-second year of the reign of King Chlotar.

I, Hadoind, a sinner and bishop, have subscribed this *precaria* made by me.

I, Winomannus, an unworthy abbot, have subscribed.

I, Christianus, an unworthy abbot, have subscribed.

I, Bodilo, an unworthy abbot, have subscribed.

I, Benedictus, an unworthy archdeacon, have subscribed.

I, Innocens, an unworthy archpriest, have subscribed.

I, Berto, an unworthy priest, have subscribed.

I, Winegaudus, an unworthy priest, have subscribed.

I, Ratgaudus, an unworthy priest, have subscribed.

I, Brichius, an unworthy priest, have subscribed.

I, Wallisius, an unworthy deacon, have subscribed.

I, Aldabertus, an unworthy deacon, have subscribed.

The mark of Hartgaudus.

The mark of Requisitus.

The mark of Sigemarus.

The mark of Walandus.

The mark of Sigebodus.

The mark of Sigefredus.

I, Walefredus, deacon, at the request of my lord Hadoind, bishop, wrote and subscribed this *precaria*.

## III. Diploma of Chlotar II, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the donation of the small monastery made by Lonegisilus to the Church of Le Mans and the transfer of that same monastery from the church to Lonegisilus under the law of usufruct

[Note: Published in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 266; reprinted in the *Collection of Writings on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 625. No one known to us has hitherto suspected it, yet we judge it wholly spurious, as are the two charters of Lonegisilus immediately preceding it, which are confirmed by this very diploma. We establish this by the same arguments.

First, the same error occurs in the chronological notices of all three documents. For since the charters of Lonegisilus are falsely represented as dated in November and December of year LII of Chlotar’s reign, contrary to the evidence of history, the confirming diploma is likewise assigned the month of January of year LIII of that reign.

Second, just as the charters of Lonegisilus have been fabricated word for word after the model of the false charters of Carilephus, which may be seen above, pp. 96 and 98, so the diploma of Chlotar has been copied word for word from the spurious diploma of Childebert I, which we published above, p. 100. Indeed, the forger was so careless in concealing the fraud that he used the very subscription of Childebert I’s notary, namely Adogrimus, who had served as notary almost a full century earlier. It is astonishing that all this seems to have escaped critics of such keen eyesight.

Nor should it be omitted that these three documents exist nowhere else than among the acts of the bishops of Le Mans, a collection so full of spurious instruments, as is evident from what we have drawn from this thoroughly impure source and will repeatedly become evident from what follows.]

In the year 627.

Chlotar, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

If we grant increase to the petitions of servants of God or good men that have been reported to our ears, and bring them to fulfillment, we trust that this will, in God’s name, contribute to us as a reward and stability of eternal salvation.

Therefore the illustrious man, Lord Lonegisilus, by a petition addressed to us, asserting the clemency of our kingship, informed us that previously, in the territory of Saint Mary and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, the mother and senior church of the city of Le Mans, with the consent of Hadoind, bishop of the city of Le Mans, and of his congregation, he had constructed or rebuilt a certain small monastery in honor of Saint Peter, with the consent and considerable assistance of the aforesaid bishop; and that he had improved it with silver which we had given him.

After he came there and acquired it through the generosity of the aforesaid bishop, as is contained in their instruments and *precariae*, he transferred and assigned, by our permission or through our license and authority, to the aforesaid mother church of the city, which is in honor of Saint Mary and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and to the aforesaid Lord Hadoind, bishop, who presently appears to preside there as guardian and rector, the property and dependents that had been given to that monastery by good and God-fearing men, both in the territory of Le Mans and in other territories and districts, with all their appurtenances and dependencies, together with every unspecified property.

Therefore he petitioned our highness that we should cause these things to be more fully confirmed by our authority. We gladly assented to his petitions and confirmed everything.

For we command and order that, just as the aforesaid Lonegisilus, priest and monk, transferred and assigned by his instruments to the house of God the small monastery that he built in the territory of Saint Mary and of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, together with lands, houses, buildings, dependents, vineyards, forests, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, livestock, money, movable and immovable property, and every other benefit, and whatever may be transferred to that same place in our time or in the future, and whatever presently appears to be rightly possessed or held in dominion there, so henceforth also, upon examination of the deed of donation and the *precaria* of reception, by this decree we more fully confirm in God’s name the monastery named above, with complete integrity, so that it may accrue as a most firmly established possession to the aforesaid house of Saint Mary and of the holy martyr Saints Gervasius and Protasius, in our time and in future times.

And so that this decree may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect, we have decided to strengthen it below with the subscriptions of our hand and to seal it with our seal.

Chlotar, king of the Franks, have subscribed.

Adogrimus, ordered to present it, have subscribed.

Given on the eighth day of January, in the fifty-third year of our reign, at our palace of Compiègne, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## IV. Charter by which Romaricus founded a monastery for women near the fortress of Avendi

[Note: This charter has been published several times: first in the *Sacred Antiquities of the Vosges*, p. 51; second in the *Holy Monarchy of France*, vol. II, p. 26; and third in the *History of the Church of Metz*, p. 97, by Meurisius. It has been regarded by everyone as false, to use the words of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. XIII, col. 1488. Cointius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 712, considered it a work of modern times; Mabillon argues this more fully in a letter published at Paris in 1687, quarto, concerning the original foundation of the monastery of Romaricus. It will be sufficient to indicate some signs of falsity in the following notes.]

In the year 620.

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Since the world, placed in wickedness, impiously attempts to violate the legitimate donations of the faithful, reason therefore demands that we too take care to confirm reasonably those things that have been donated for the increase of the churches.

Let it therefore be known to all the community of Catholics, present and future, that I, Romaricus, count of Avendi,

[Note: Romaricus had already become a monk of Luxeuil three years earlier, after distributing his possessions among the poor, before he founded the convent in the Vosges, as his Life testifies, published by Mabillon among the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, second century, p. 416. Therefore in this charter Romaricus should by no means have been called a count.]

seeing men of virtue bear upon their bodies, through voluntary poverty, the marks of poor Jesus, and dwell in deserts and thorny places so that they might proclaim for all ages the bitterness of the cross and the austerity of holy penance, according to my desire prepared a place for them on Mount Rombech, beside my fortress, on a sufficiently wild and rugged mountain, not far from the bank of the Moselle River.

Thus, where previously the roar and howling of wild beasts frequently resounded in human ears, thereafter thanksgiving and the voice of praise might more often resound in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs in the ears of angels; and that wild mountain became the dwelling of these holy women, who live in knowledge and desire in the heavens.

After clearing away the thorns and brambles, I built there a monastery for nuns of the Benedictine order, in honor of the most holy Trinity, of the blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints.

That monastery, having received a name appropriate to the nature of the place, is called Holy Mount. Then, with the common consent of my people, I summoned a congregation of holy nuns, to whom I freely and purely granted the aforesaid monastery: Gertrude,

[Note: It is established from the Life of Saint Amatus (*Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, second century, pp. 124 and 133), written by an anonymous contemporary of Romaricus, that Magdefleda was the first abbess of the monastery of Romaricus. Amatus assisted his disciple Romaricus in founding this monastery. Therefore the statements found here concerning Gertrude, Romaricus’s first-born daughter, whom he supposedly placed over this monastery when he founded it, are false. No abbess of this name appears in the succession of abbesses of Romaricus that is presented in the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. XIII, cited above. Compare Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 313.]

my first-born daughter, and her sister Clara, my daughter, together with the other nuns, so that they might serve God securely and freely, without fear or concern for earthly goods. Because I desire to serve God, I give and freely grant them my entire patrimony, namely, the whole county of Avendi,

[Note: Avendunum, a fortress in the Vosges, which is also designated here by the names Avendum and Habendum as a county. Valesius, *Notice of Gaul*, p. 480. It is falsely represented that this county came to Romaricus by hereditary right, as though counties had been hereditary at this period.]

the same way, form, authority, and ownership by which my father and I held it.

This donation was made on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the year 620 from the Incarnation of the Lord,

[Note: It is universally known that the years of the Incarnation were not used as chronological markers in charters of this period.]

while the glorious Frankish king Chlotar was reigning.

The witnesses are:

[Note: The names of the bishops subscribed do not fit the year 620. Arnoaldus, bishop of Metz, had died in 607. Dodo did not obtain the church of Toul until the beginning of the eighth century. Paul was unwillingly forced into the bishopric of Verdun in 625. We shall pass over the others. We shall note, however, with Cointius, that the year assigned to this charter by the forger agrees sufficiently with the time when the monastery was founded; see Cointius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 712. It is worth noting that the monastery in question was, before 1789, the celebrated convent called Remiremont, from the corrupted name of its founder Romaricus and from its situation at the foot of the Vosges mountain.]

Arnoaldus, bishop of Metz;

Dodo, bishop of Toul;

Paul, bishop of Verdun;

Arnulfus, my kinsman, duke of Austrasia Mosellana;

Brunulphus, count of Templa;

Waubertus, duke of Lower Austrasia and count of Salm.

And so that no one might ever dare rashly to slander this almsgiving or inflict any injury upon the nuns serving God in this place, I confirmed it by the authority of my seal and by that of the aforesaid king, bishops, dukes, and counts.

ANNO DOMINI 638. HONORIUS I, ROMAN PONTIFF.

## Historical Notice on Pope Honorius I

(*Liber Pontificalis*, Blanchini edition, vol. IV.)

[Note:

---1. Honorius. What necessity and the calamity of the times had once persuaded the Roman clergy and people to dare in the election and consecration of Boniface V, is shown by Anastasius himself and by the unanimous agreement of all the catalogues and manuscripts not to have been done in the case of his successor Honorius. For if Honorius sat for twelve years, eleven months, and sixteen days, and was buried on 12 October, as all most consistently maintain, he was ordained on 27 October; thus, counting both endpoints, there are to the day of his burial as many years, months, and days as Honorius reigned. Since, moreover, the aforesaid 27 October was a Sunday in the year 623, as the dominical letter F indicates, the interpontificate was therefore one year and three days, not merely thirteen days, as almost all manuscripts and catalogues have, except the vulgate, which, wholly without reason, assigns a vacancy of six months and eighteen days.

Antoine Pagi rightly observed that the beginning of Honorius’s pontificate cannot be placed later than the aforesaid year 625, and proves this from the pontiff’s letters to the bishops of Epirus, dated on the Ides of December, indiction 14, which are found in Holste’s Roman Collection, p. 248. Papebroch considers these letters corrupt because they contradict him by taking a year from Honorius, whose beginnings he places in 626; Pagi accordingly attacks him under the year 625, no. 16, as though he had not seen that collection. Here, however, the great error of Pagi—otherwise a most learned man—is evident. Having fixed the burial, with Anastasius, on 25 October, although he puts the death two days earlier, he admits that Honorius was ordained on the 27th of the same month and year. Yet what ears can endure a pontiff being elected and ordained with only a single intervening day between burial and ordination, especially at a time when the emperor’s command had to be awaited from Constantinople, without any canonical election and, above all, contrary to the decree of Boniface III issued a few years earlier, that a pontiff was not to be elected until the third day after the burial?

To this is added the authority of the *Liber Diurnus* of the pontiffs, contemporary with those times, where, in the chapter on the election of a pontiff, addressed to the Exarch, the following is read: “When he of pontifical memory had been called from the cares of the present to eternal rest, as is wont to happen in human affairs, a great weight of grief bound us, deprived of our own steward. But the accustomed goodness of our God did not long abandon those who hoped in him to affliction. For while we insignificant persons remained in prayer for three days, that heavenly condescension might show to the minds of all who was worthy,” etc.

Certainly Pagi would not now be caught in these straits if, misled by Bede, he had not extended Boniface V’s tenure beyond measure. This being so, the vacancy of the see between Boniface and Honorius is evident of itself: one year and three days; and consequently the error of nearly all the manuscripts and catalogues that give thirteen days arose, I think, from the Arabic numeral 13 written without dots, according to the ancient and barbarous practice of a later age. Honorius’s day of death, or burial, is clear from Anastasius; and as for the year, namely 638, all scholars agree, especially Papebroch in the *Historical Attempt*, Sirmond in the *Synopsis* to the Collection, Anastasius, and Antoine Pagi. I therefore thought that this uncertain year, variously displaced by others, ought to be restored; if this restoration does not please, let the risk of the matter be undertaken more successfully. CENNUS.

---2. Honorius. In the year of our Redeemer 626, on the thirteenth day of May, Honorius of Campania was made Roman pontiff. In his time the heresy of the Monothelites arose and spread. Whether Honorius was a Monothelite is a serious question. But the truer opinion of nearly all orthodox writers of our time is that by which Honorius is cleared of every stain and suspicion of heresy. The Monothelites stood against him, asserting that he was theirs. But Maximus, in his dispute against Pyrrhus, John IV, Martin I, Agatho, and several other Roman pontiffs who claimed Honorius as their own, fought for him. See the most learned annotation of Severinus Binius in vol. V of the *Councils*, on the Life of Honorius; Bellarmine, book IV *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 11; and Baronius, under the year 633. BIN. AND LABB.

---3. Honorius. Son of Petronius de la Marca, a man of consular rank, a Campanian, the tenth pope who was a native of the kingdom, under the emperor Flavius Heraclius, he sat in Peter’s chair for twelve years, eleven months, and seven days, having been created and consecrated on Sunday, the seventh day before the Ides of November, in the year 622. In the published codices of the third Sixth Synod of Constantinople, the charge of the Monothelite heresy is brought against this most holy man; yet it is utterly false that he ever subscribed to that heresy, indeed it is certain that he condemned it, as is sufficiently clear from the Greek letters of Maximus the monk, his contemporary, who lived under Pope Martin, and from his dialogue against Pyrrhus, the heretical Monothelite patriarch of Constantinople, which survives in the Palatine Library.

That this same pontiff was always Catholic was also confirmed in writing by Emmanuel Calles the Greek, Cardinal John of Torquemada in his book *On the Primacy of the Holy Roman Church*, and, in our own times, Albert Pighius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Moreover, Anastasius the Librarian teaches in his Latin history, which he compiled from the same Theophanes, Nicephorus, and George the abbot, that the published copies of the Sixth Synod were corrupted by the Greeks and that its canons, in which Honorius is condemned, are spurious; he relies on Theophanes the Isaurian, a Greek writer of ecclesiastical history. William Sirleto, a Calabrian, observed these things while he was protonotary of the Apostolic See; being most richly endowed with learning, piety, and every kind of virtue, he deserved promotion to the college of cardinals, and his memory is now blessed. CIACONIUS.]

Honorius, a Campanian by birth, son of the consul Petronius, occupied the see for eleven years, eleven months, and seventeen days. [Note: Codex Luc. 494: eleven years, eleven months, less three days.] In his time he did many good works. He instructed the clergy. [Note: In his time he renewed, etc. Anastasius contains many remarkable accounts of Honorius’s reverence toward divine worship in arranging ecclesiastical affairs, and of his generosity in building, adorning, and endowing churches. For he renewed almost the entire clergy; he covered the basilica of blessed Peter with bronze tiles taken from the Capitol, and sheathed Saint Peter’s altar with silver, adding many other ornaments. He rebuilt from the foundations the church of Saint Agnes the martyr. He restored the church of Saint Pancratius on the Via Aurelia, as well as the church of Anastasius at the Aquae Salvias and the church of the Four Crowned Martyrs; he built the church of Saint Severinus near the city of Tibur with magnificent workmanship, and decorated it with silver, gold, porphyry, and marble inlays, with stucco and mosaic work. He also restored the cemetery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter; he restored many other churches and built many anew. He was the first to establish that every Saturday the people should go with litanies from Saint Apollinaris to Saint Peter. But still more remarkable is what his epitaph and an ancient inscription reported by Canisius, volume VI of *Antiquae Lectiones*, attest: namely, that he extinguished the schism of Istria concerning the Three Chapters—no small distinction. Yet since we have shown from Saint Gregory that this schism lasted until the time of Pope Sergius, either it was not entirely suppressed under Honorius, or the schismatics fell back again after Honorius’s death. PAGIUS.]

In his time he renewed the entire household [Note: Codex Luc.: *cimiliam*; others: *cimeliam* or *supellectilem*.] of blessed Peter the apostle, and revested blessed Peter’s confessio with pure silver, weighing 187 pounds. [Note: He revested the royal doors at the entrance of the great church, [Col. 0465C] which are called the Median doors, with silver. “Royal” means the larger doors of churches. John the Monk, in the *Life of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny*, uses the expression of a boar which he calls exceptional: “But he, laying aside his fierceness so that entrance might be granted to whoever entered, beat for a long time upon the aforesaid royal doors and smeared them with the foam of his mouth wherever he could make it adhere.” A basilica-door means the same thing. Frodoard, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 820: “At Rheims, in the monastery of Saint Peter, at the basilica-door.” The same author, book IV of the *History of Rheims*, chapter 46, calls the main door of Saint Peter’s basilica “royal.” Paulinus, Letter 33: “Into the spacious basilica of glorious Peter, through that venerable royal door, smiling from afar with its blue façade.” Anastasius, in his Life of Conon: “Those who had been sent from the army to guard the royal doors of the basilica kept them closed.” The same, in Gregory III: “From the arch of the altar to the royal doors.” The same, in Leo III: “In the basilica of the Mother of God at the Manger, at the entrance of the manger, he made royal doors covered with the purest silver.” ALTASERRA.] He revested the royal doors at the entrance of the great church, which are called the Median doors, with silver; they weighed 975 pounds. He also made two pairs of large silver *cerostata* (candelabra) [Note: Codex Luc.: “larger *cerostata*.”] standing before the body of blessed Peter the apostle; each of the four weighed 272 pounds. [Note: Other copies omit “of silver.”] He also made for blessed Andrew the apostle, at the same place, before the confessio, silver panels [Note: Other copies: “a silver panel weighing,” etc.] weighing 73 pounds. During his time sixteen beams were raised in the Church of blessed Peter the apostle. [Note: Here he covered the church. He covered Saint Peter’s basilica with bronze tiles taken from the Capitol. CIACONIUS.]

He covered the entire church [Note: Other copies: “his church with bronze tiles.”] with bronze plates [Note: Codex Luc.: “tiles.”] which he removed [Note: Concerning the temple. This temple, from which Honorius, with the consent of the emperor Heraclius, removed the bronze plates—or, as the Royal, Freher, Mazarin, and both Thuane manuscripts read, the bronze tiles—and covered the entire church of blessed Peter, is called the Temple of Rome in some manuscripts, and the Temple of Romulus in others. The former temple, in Rome—which was impiously worshiped as a goddess—was built by Hadrian and joined to the temple of Venus. Dio, book 69, says of it: “Hadrian himself, sending Apollodorus the architect a plan of the temple of Venus and Rome, thereby indicating that even immense buildings could be erected without his work and assistance, asked whether the structure was satisfactory. Apollodorus replied that the temple ought to be made lofty and concave, so that from an elevated position there might be a more distinguished and conspicuous view all the way to the Sacred Way; the concavity was needed to receive the stage machinery for the games, which could be assembled there secretly and then brought out from concealment into the theater.” Anastasius himself can show where this temple stood. In the Life of Felix IV he wrote: “He built the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian in the city of Rome, in the place called the Sacred Way, beside the Temple of Rome.” It therefore stood not far from the Amphitheater, since, according to the plan of the mathematician Apollodorus, the machinery for the games was to be taken from there and returned there. Many have therefore been persuaded that the two enclosures still surviving in the gardens of Santa Maria Nova are the ruins of this temple. It was so famous that the imperial coins themselves were marked with its image, such as those recently excavated in our Piedmontese territory near Mondovì and preserved in the Royal Treasury, perhaps destined someday to come before the eyes of scholars. If, however, one prefers the Temple of Romulus mentioned by Anastasius, that too enjoyed no small veneration among the Romans. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I, when discussing the Lupercal, says: “Along the road leading to the Circus, and near it, a temple is shown in which is the she-wolf giving suck to two boys.” It therefore stood at the Lupercal in the eighth region, beyond the Curia, or at the Basilica Porcia, where the church of Santa Maria Liberatrice now stands. From these papal records we meanwhile learn that one or the other of those temples still survived in the seventh Christian century, rich in panels and statues, perhaps preserved so long by the rulers because it contained images of the ancient Caesars. BENCINUS.] from the temple called [Note: Codex Luc.: “of Romulus.”] Rome’s temple [Col. 0466A] with the consent of the most devout emperor Heraclius.

At the same time [Note: “He built the church of blessed Agnes,” as the verse in the apse indicates. CIACONIUS.] he built from the foundations the church of blessed Agnes the martyr, three miles from the city of Rome on the Nomentan Way, where she rests. He adorned and embellished it on every side [Note: Other copies omit “and embellished it.”], and placed many gifts there. He adorned her tomb with silver weighing 252 pounds. Above it he also placed a gilded bronze canopy of marvelous size. He also made four golden bowls [Note: Codex Luc.: “bowls”; other copies: “three.”], each weighing one pound. He made the apse of the same basilica in mosaic [Note: Codex Luc.: “mosaic work.”], where he also offered many gifts [Note: Codex Luc. and others: “good things.”] Likewise he built the basilica of blessed Apollinaris the martyr in the city of Rome, in the portico of blessed Peter the apostle, called [Note: Codex Luc.: “Palmaria.”] *ad Palmata*, from the foundations, where he bestowed many gifts.

[Col. 0467A] He established a regulation in the Church and decreed that every week, on Saturday, a litany should go forth, and that all the people should proceed with hymns and songs to blessed Apollinaris and to blessed Peter the apostle. [Note: Other copies: “from blessed Apollinaris to blessed Peter,” etc.] He also built from the foundations a church for blessed Cyriacus the martyr on the Ostian Way, seven miles away, where he also offered a gift. At the same time he built the church of the Four Crowned Martyrs, dedicated it, and offered a gift. He built from the foundations a church for blessed Severinus near the city of Tibur, twenty miles from the city of Rome; he himself dedicated it and offered many gifts. He also renewed the cemetery of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter on the Lavican Way. At the same time he built from the foundations the basilica of blessed Pancratius [Col. 0467B] the martyr on the Aurelian Way, two miles [Note: Other copies: “from the city of Rome.”] away, and adorned his tomb with silver weighing 120 pounds. [The words enclosed in brackets are absent from Codex Luc.] And there he established a mill [or *mola*] in the wall at Trajan’s place beside the city wall, [Note: “And an aqueduct-channel that brings water to Lake Sabbatenus, and beneath it another channel that conducts the water of the Tiber. Honorius led a *forma*, that is, an aqueduct, from Lake Sabathenus into the city, to the atrium of the church of blessed Peter the apostle. Adrian I restored the same, as Anastasius says in his Life: ‘The channel called Sabbatena, being greatly broken, through which water flowed by the Centenarius into the atrium of the church of blessed Peter the apostle,’ etc. Gregory IV likewise restored it. Anastasius, in his Life: ‘The channel called Sabbatena,’ etc. The Sabbatena channel is led from Lake Sabatenus, called Angularius, in *Digest*, “Rutilia Polla,” concerning contracts of sale. Its name comes from the three angles presented by the Aurelian Way as it leads to the Vatican, as Platina taught us in his Life of Adrian. In the atria of churches there were *canthari*, or water fountains; water was brought from outside through pipes at great expense for the churches’ use. Anastasius, in Gregory II: ‘He likewise repaired the church of Saint Laurence outside the walls and, after a long interval, brought water back into that church through joined pipes.’ ALTASERRA.] and [Col. 0468A] a channel bringing water to Lake Sabbatenus, and beneath it another channel conducting the water of the Tiber.]

He also made a silver canopy over the altar, weighing 287 pounds. [Note: Codex Luc. and others: 187 pounds.] He also made five silver arches, each weighing fifteen pounds. He also made three golden candelabra, each weighing [Note: Other copies add: “good things.”] pounds, and offered many gifts at the same time. He built the church of blessed Lucia in the city of Rome near Saint Silvester; he dedicated it and offered many gifts. [Note: He built the church of blessed Adrian the martyr at the Three Fates and dedicated it. The Three Fates was a place in the city mentioned by Procopius, *Gothic War*, book IX, toward the end. This is confirmed by another passage in Anastasius’s Life of Adrian: “In the church of the blessed Cosmas and Damian at the Three Fates he made a vestment of *stauracin*.” And again: “He restored the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian situated at the Three Fates.” I do not claim as my own what belongs to another; Lacerda has already noted this, *Adversaria*, chapter 149, no. 27. Perhaps one should instead read “at the Three Sowings,” that is, “three years,” according to the rustic usage of counting years by sowings or crops. Virgil, *Eclogue* 1: “After several years, seeing my realm’s ears of grain, I shall marvel.” ALTASERRA.] He built the church of blessed Adrian [Note: Codex Luc.: “Aeriano”; another copy later has “Martin.”] the martyr at the Three [Note: Codex Luc.: “outside.”] Fates; he dedicated it and offered many gifts.

[Note: But also many others. Among the many things performed by Pope Honorius was this: he brought peoples who did not know the Christian religion to faith in Christ by sending ministers of the word to teach them. Bede testifies (*Book III*, chapter 7) that Bishop Birinus was sent to Britain by Honorius, through whom the West Saxons received the Christian faith: “At that time,” he says, “the people of the West Saxons, who were anciently called Gewissae, under King Cynegils, received the faith of Christ when Bishop Birinus preached the word to them. He had come to Britain at the advice of Pope Honorius, promising that, while he was present, he would sow the seeds of the holy faith in the innermost regions beyond the Angles, where no teacher had preceded him. By the command of that same pontiff, he was therefore consecrated to the episcopal office by Asterius, bishop of Genoa.” MAFEUS.]

But he also performed many other works, which it would be tedious to enumerate. He held three ordinations during the month of December [Note: Other copies omit “during the month of December”]: thirteen priests [Note: Codex Luc., Labbe, and Mansi: thirty-one priests], twelve deacons [Note: Codex Luc.: eleven deacons], and eighty-one bishops in various places. [Col. 0468B]

[Note: He was also buried. Pope Honorius finally died on 12 October 638, after having sat—as Anastasius records—for twelve years, eleven months, and seventeen days. This total apparently combines the day of his ordination with the day of his death or burial, as often happens. It therefore becomes clear that, according to Anastasius’s intention, we have correctly connected his accession with 27 October 625, since, according to the same witness, he died and was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle on the fourth day before the Ides of October. PACIUS.]

He was also buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle on the fourth day before the Ides of October. The episcopate then remained vacant for one year, seven months, and seventeen days.

[Col. 0469]

## Letters of Pope Honorius I

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, volume XII.) (C,S)*

### First Letter: Pope Honorius I to Isacius, Exarch of Ravenna

He asks that Adalwald, the Catholic king of the Lombards, be restored to the kingdom, and that Ariwald, an Arian and treacherous man who had been substituted for him, be expelled; he requests that the Cisalpine bishops, through whose agency the crime had been committed, be sent to him for punishment.

**Honorius to the Exarch Isacius.**

It has been reported to us that the bishops beyond the Po tried to persuade Peter, son of Paul, to abandon King Adalwald [Note: Concerning Adalwald, Paul the Deacon says in book IV, chapter 5: “But when Adalwald, deranged in mind, became insane, after reigning ten years with his mother, he was expelled from the kingdom, and Ariwald was substituted in his place by the Lombards.” If this were true, it should hardly be thought that Honorius labored so strenuously to restore an insane and utterly demented man to the kingdom. SEVERINUS BIN.] and attach himself to the tyrant Ariwald. Since Peter rejected obedience to their wicked counsels and devoutly desired to preserve the oaths of allegiance sworn to Agilulf—namely, to Adalwald’s father—and since it is displeasing to God and to men that those who ought to punish such a crime should themselves be its instigators, we ask you, after you have restored Adalwald to the kingdom by divine assistance, as we hope, to send the aforesaid bishops to Rome, so that we may not leave such a crime unpunished.

### Second Letter: To the Bishops of Venetia and Istria

Concerning Fortunatus, the deposed patriarch of Grado, and Primogenius, substituted in his place.

**Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Venetia and Istria.**

We exhort you, and we send decretal letters to your fraternity, by which we request that, in place of Judas, another man of approved life be promoted to govern the Lord’s flock. And rightly so: the man who has been deposed resembles Judas both in deeds and in character. For what Judas appears to have exercised in the head, this man seems to have exercised in the body.

We have therefore sent Primogenius, subdeacon and regionary of our see, to be consecrated to the episcopal order for the Church of Grado, with the blessing of the pallium. It will therefore be necessary for your fraternity to arrange everything according to ecclesiastical law and to display sincere obedience to your head. For, when sending our men to the most excellent king of the Lombards, we instructed them to seek out Fortunatus himself—who had abandoned the commonwealth, fallen in with foreign peoples, rebelled against God by renouncing the unity of concord, and shown himself treacherous—and also to demand whatever goods he is shown to have carried away with him, without delaying to reclaim them, so that those from whom they are demanded may obtain equal justice from the fathers of the most Christian commonwealth. [Note: “The most Christian commonwealth.” He rightly adorns the Venetian commonwealth with this title, because it had abandoned the schismatics and adhered to the Roman Church, and was accustomed to request a bishop from the Roman Church so that it might not become entangled in the snares of the schismatics. SEVERINUS BIN.]

### Third Letter: Of Sergius, Bishop of Constantinople, to Pope Honorius

[Note: Concerning Sergius’s letter. When Sophronius had sent Sergius a letter asking that the passage of the Alexandrian synod asserting one will in Christ be deleted, and insisting that two wills and operations must altogether be acknowledged, the two men eventually agreed concerning the matter and truth of the orthodox faith. Each acknowledged two natures, wills, and operations in Christ according to the letter of Leo and the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. On Sergius’s advice they therefore agreed that, to avoid scandal and the danger of heresy, which often arises from novel terminology, they should refrain from the expressions “one will” and “two wills.” The bishop of Constantinople reports the matter to Pope Honorius in this letter. Since the letter contains nothing contrary to the orthodox faith or to the Council of Chalcedon, defends Leo’s letter, and asserts two natures in Christ, Honorius could do nothing other than answer him as a Catholic bishop, especially because at the end of the letter Sergius submits himself and all that belonged to him to the judgment of the Church and the apostolic see. It is therefore most evident—and this must be particularly noted and repeatedly emphasized—that although Sergius was later exposed and condemned as a heretic, at the time when he wrote this letter to Honorius, namely in the year of Christ 633, the eighth year of Honorius’s pontificate, he was not only considered orthodox by Easterners and Westerners alike but was also held to be a bishop of great reputation, as is clear from Sophronius’s letter to Sergius. SEVERINUS BIN.]

He explains to him the origin of the controversy concerning one or two wills, professes the true faith concerning Christ’s nature according to Leo’s letter and the Council of Chalcedon, and states that Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, who had opposed Cyrus of Alexandria, had agreed at his urging that the new and dangerous controversy should be avoided and silence maintained.

“To such an extent, to you most holy ones, etc.” *(This appears in Session 12 of the Sixth Synod.)*
