[Note: “The letter,” etc. This letter of Honorius is a stumbling block and rock of offense to earlier and modern heretics, who try, on Bede’s authority, to fasten upon the pontiff—who was most holy—and upon the apostolic see itself the grave crime of heresy. And indeed without any just cause. For he could not rightly be blamed for writing back to Sergius, who at that time was still regarded by everyone as Catholic, had not yet said or written anything heretical, and had submitted all his affairs to the judgment of the Church, as is clear above. If this is counted as a crime against Honorius, what, I ask, will you bring forward in defense of Sophronius, who, even before Honorius, not only communicated with Sergius by letter but plainly agreed with him when he prescribed silence concerning one or two wills for the reasons stated above? If you think no crime of heresy should be imputed to Sophronius, I do not see how you can judge that Honorius should be numbered among the Monothelites except by calumny. At the beginning of the controversy, prescribing silence concerning novel terms cannot be regarded as suspicious, since disputes over new expressions have sometimes stirred up the gravest heresies, as we have seen above.

In this letter Honorius confesses both the matter and the true faith concerning Christ; he prudently warns that the terms should be avoided because of the danger of scandal and of greater controversy. Surely no one but an imprudent person could count this as a fault or crime in a most holy man. How his statement should be understood—“Therefore we confess one will of our Lord Jesus Christ, because our nature was assumed by divinity, not guilt”—is explained by Honorius’s secretary, at the command of Pope John IV, in Maximus’s disputation with Pyrrhus; I have also explained it above in the notes to the Life of Honorius and below in the cited disputation. See further Baronius, under the year 635, no. 25 and the following number. SEVERINUS BIN.]

### Fourth Letter: To Sergius, Bishop of Constantinople

After asserting the true doctrine of the orthodox faith concerning Christ’s two wills, he explains why he judges that Sergius should be followed in prescribing silence concerning the new terms.

**Honorius to Sergius, bishop of Constantinople.**

We have received the writings of your fraternity, through which we learned that certain disputes and novel questions concerning words had been introduced by a certain Sophronius, then a monk but, as we have heard, now established as bishop of the city of Jerusalem, against our brother Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, who was preaching, after conversion from heresy, one operation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When this Sophronius came to your fraternity and presented such a complaint, after receiving instruction in many ways he asked that the matters about which you had instructed him be disclosed to him in written words. We received a copy of the letter sent to Sophronius, and, observing that your fraternity had written with sufficient prudence and care, we commend you for removing the novel term, which could generate scandal among the simple.

For we must walk in that which we have understood. Indeed, with God as our guide, we shall arrive at the measure of the right faith which the apostles of truth extended like a cord of the sacred Scriptures, confessing that the Lord Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings, performed divine works through the humanity naturally united to the Word of God [Note: Greek: “hypostatically.”], and that the same person performed human works ineffably and uniquely through assumed flesh [Note: Greek: “indivisibly, without confusion, and fully by divinity.”], distinctly, without confusion, and without change, in full divinity. He who shone forth in the flesh [Note: Another Greek reading: “in the flesh perfected by divine miracles, he himself is the one who also performed the affections of the flesh amid insults, perfect God and one human mediator.”] full of divine miracles is himself the one who, in his fleshly effects [*carneus effectus*], is fully God and human. One mediator between God and human beings, the Word made flesh, suffers passions and insults in both natures, and dwelt among us. He himself is the Son of Man descending from heaven, one and the same, as it is written: “The Lord of majesty was crucified,” although it is certain that divinity cannot undergo any human passions. And the flesh was assumed not from heaven but from the holy Mother of God. For Truth itself says in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3), clearly instructing us that passible flesh was ineffably and uniquely united to divinity, so that it might be seen to be joined distinctly, without confusion, and indivisibly.

Thus, while the differences between the two natures remain wondrously and astonishingly, their union is recognized. In agreement with this, the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “We speak wisdom among the mature, but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are passing away. We speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom hidden and predestined by God before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age understood. For if they had understood it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2).

Certainly divinity could neither be crucified nor experience or endure human passions. But because of the ineffable union of the human and divine natures, God is therefore said to suffer everywhere, and humanity to have descended from heaven together with divinity. Hence we confess one will of our Lord Jesus Christ, because our nature was assumed by divinity [Note: Another Greek reading: “there was no guilt in it, certainly.”], not guilt—specifically the nature created before sin, not the nature corrupted after transgression.

For Christ the Lord, coming in the likeness of sinful flesh, removed the sin of the world, and from his fullness we have all received. Taking the form of a servant, he was found in appearance as a human being (Philippians 2), because, conceived without sin by the Holy Spirit, he was also born without sin from the holy and immaculate Virgin, the Mother of God, experiencing no contagion of corrupted nature.

We know from the sacred Scriptures that the word “flesh” is used in two ways, for good and for evil. Thus it is written: “My Spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6). And the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 5). Again: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin. I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans 7). Many other such passages are plainly understood or spoken in the evil sense.

In the good sense, however, the prophet Isaiah says: “All flesh shall come to Jerusalem, and they shall worship before me” (Isaiah 66). Job says: “In my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19). Another passage says: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3). There are many other examples.

Therefore, as we have said, the Savior did not assume a corrupted nature that would oppose the law of his mind. Rather, he came to seek and save what had been lost (Luke 16), that is, the corrupted nature of the human race. There was no other law in his members, nor a different will opposed to the Savior, because he was born above the law of human condition.

And although it is written, “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 7), and, “Not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Mark 26), and other statements of this kind, these do not concern different wills but the dispensation of the assumed humanity. They were said for our sake, for he gave us an example to follow his footsteps, the merciful teacher instructing his disciples that each of us should prefer not his own will but the Lord’s will in all things.

Therefore, walking along the royal road and avoiding on the right and left the hunters’ snares set around us, lest we strike our foot against a stone, leaving to the Idumeans—that is, to earthly and heretical people—their own things, and not even treading the soil, that is, their perverse doctrine, with the trace of our foot, so that we may reach the goal toward which we strive, namely, our ancestral borders, let us walk in the path of our leaders.

And if certain people, so to speak, stammering and unable to explain what they utter, fashion themselves after the model of teachers [Note: Greek: “of teachers.”] so that they might instruct the minds of their hearers, these matters ought not to be twisted into ecclesiastical dogmas. Neither synodal decrees examining this question nor canonical authorities appear to have explained it, so that anyone should presume to preach one or two energies [operations] of Christ God. Neither the evangelical nor apostolic writings, nor the synodal examination held concerning these matters, appear to have defined them—unless, as we said above, certain people, stammering, taught something in condescension to form the minds and understanding of children. Such statements should not be drawn into ecclesiastical dogmas, since each person, abounding in his own understanding, appears to explain them according to his own opinion.

For the sacred Scriptures clearly and brilliantly demonstrate that the Lord Jesus Christ, Son and Word of God, through whom all things were made, is one operator of divinity and humanity [Note: Greek: “one and the same, performing divine and human works”; the sacred Scriptures show this most clearly.].

Whether, on account of the works of divinity and humanity, one operation or two operations ought to be said or understood as proceeding from them does not concern us. Let us leave such matters to grammarians, who are accustomed to sell refined names to children by deriving them.

For we have not learned from the sacred Scriptures that the Lord Jesus Christ and his Holy Spirit have one operation or two, but we have learned in many ways that he operated. For it is written: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him” (Romans 8). And elsewhere: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit. There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of operations, but the same God who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12).

If there are many varieties of operations, and God performs all of them in all the members of the complete body, how much more may these things be applied in their fullness to our head, Christ the Lord? Thus the head and the body may be one perfect whole, so that, as it is written, it may indeed come together “into a perfect human being, into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4).

If the Spirit of Christ operates in many ways in others, that is, in his members, in whom they live, move, and exist, how much more fitting is it that we should confess that, through himself, the mediator between God and human beings, he operated fully and perfectly, in many and ineffable ways, through the communion of both natures?

We must think or breathe according to the ordinances of the divine utterances, rejecting those things that are recognized as novel expressions capable of generating scandals for the holy churches of God. Otherwise, the simple, offended by the term “two operations,” might think that, by following Nestorians, we are entertaining madness; or, if we should judge that one operation of our Lord Jesus Christ must be confessed, we might appear to confess, to the astonished ears of the Eutychianists, their foolish insanity.

Let us take care that the ashes of those whose empty weapons have been burned may not revive into flames and renew the fire-breathing controversies. Let us confess simply and truthfully that the Lord Jesus Christ is one operator of the divine and human nature. Let vain assessors of natures, idle busybodies, and swollen philosophers shout against us with the voices of frogs, rather than allow the simple and humble Christian people to remain without nourishment.

No one will deceive the disciples of the fishermen through philosophy and empty deceit, since they follow the fishermen’s teaching. All the rugged arguments of crafty and wave-tossed disputation have been shattered against their nets.

Let your fraternity preach these things with us, just as we unanimously preach them with you. We exhort you, fleeing from the newly introduced term “one operation” or “two operations,” to preach with us one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, very God, who in two natures operated divinely and humanly, in orthodox faith and Catholic unity.

**Subscription.** May God keep you safe, my most beloved and most holy brother.

### Fifth Letter: To the Same

The same subject.

*(From Session 13 of the Sixth Synod.)*
And this Latin letter of Honorius was produced together with its translation, bearing the following superscription: “To his most beloved brother Sergius, Honorius”; its opening was: “The writings of our most beloved son, the deacon Syricus.” [Col. 0474D] The same letter contains shortly afterward the following:

“Likewise, to our brother Cyrus, bishop of the city of Alexandria: once the newly devised expression ‘one or two operations’ has been rejected, the clear proclamation of God’s Churches must not be clouded or obscured by the darkness of contentious disputes, so that the expression ‘one operation’ or ‘two operations,’ newly introduced into the profession of faith, may be removed. For those who say these things—what else do they suppose than that, just as there is one or two natures of Christ God, so also there is one or two operations? On this point the divine testimonies are clear. But it is exceedingly foolish to think and declare that the Lord Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings, is or was the mediator of one operation or of two.” [Col. 0475A]

The same letter has the following near its end. [Note: [Col. 0475D] Another version: “And these matters, indeed, we judge must be made clear to your most holy fraternity by the present letter.” HARDUINUS.]

“And indeed, insofar as it concerns instructing the understanding of those who are uncertain, we have foreseen that this should be conveyed to your most holy fraternity. But insofar as ecclesiastical doctrine is concerned, what we ought to hold and preach for the sake of simple people and to cut off the inextricable tangles of disputes, as we said above, we must not define one or two operations in the mediator between God and human beings; rather, we must confess that the two natures, joined together in the one Christ by natural unity, operate and are operative through the communion of the other: the divine nature performing what belongs to God, and the human nature carrying out what belongs to the flesh. We do not teach that the nature of God was changed into man, nor the human nature into God, either separately, confusedly, or convertibly; rather, we confess the distinctions of the natures intact. For the one and the same person is both humble and exalted, equal to the Father and less than the Father; he himself existed before the ages and was born in time. Through him the ages were made, and he was made within the age. He who gave the law was made subject to the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law. He himself was crucified; he himself, by emptying on the cross the bond that stood against us, triumphed over the powers and principalities.

“Therefore, removing—as we said—the stumbling block of this novel invention, we ought not to preach by defining one or two operations. In place of the one operation that some people speak of, we ought truthfully to confess one operative Christ the Lord in both natures. In place of two operations, after removing the expression ‘two operations,’ we ought instead to preach with you the two natures themselves—namely, divinity and the assumed flesh—operating according to their own properties, without confusion, division, or change, in the one person of the only-begotten Son of God the Father.

“We have foreseen that this should be communicated to your most blessed fraternity, so that we may show your holiness the purpose of our one confession and, breathing together in one spirit, join in agreement with an equal confession of faith. We have also written to our common brothers, the bishops Cyrus and Sophronius, so that they may not appear to insist upon or linger over the expression of a novel term, namely, ‘one operation’ or ‘two operations,’ but, after erasing the designation of this novel term, may preach with us that the one Christ the Lord operates divinely and humanly in both natures. Although we have instructed those whom the aforesaid brother and our fellow bishop Sophronius sent to us not thereafter to attempt to preach the expression ‘two operations,’ they have most earnestly promised that the aforesaid man would do so if our brother and fellow bishop Cyrus also withdrew from the expression ‘one operation.’”

A book was likewise produced containing a letter of Pyrrhus, formerly bishop of this royal city, to John of holy memory, who was Roman pope. Its opening is: “Our Lord and God Christ, being destined to ascend into the heavens.” [Col. 0476A] The same letter contains the following after some intervening material:

“For who, seeing that we are thus set against one another, and that we who exercise the priesthood are subjected to reproaches by those appointed to the king, would not mock and despise our counsel, making our instability an opportunity for his own impiety? The war concerning the two natures has not yet been destroyed, and we are introducing another disturbance among ourselves.”

## LETTER VI. TO EDWIN, KING OF THE ENGLISH

He exhorts him to persevere in the faith and, at his request, sends two pallia to the metropolitans Paulinus and Honorius, so that, when either one dies, the survivor may ordain another in the place of the deceased.

[Col. 0476B] “To the most excellent and most distinguished son Edwin, king of the Angles: Honorius, bishop and servant of the servants of God, sends greetings.

“The integrity of your Christianity has been so inflamed by the ardor of faith toward the worship of its Creator [Note: [Col. 0476D] From Bede, Book II of the History of the English, chapter 17.] that it shines far and wide, and, proclaimed throughout the whole world, bears abundant fruit from your work. For you recognize that you are kings when, instructed by orthodox preaching, you believe in reverence for God, your king and creator, and offer him the sincere devotion of your mind, insofar as human nature is capable.

“What else can we offer our God except that, persevering in good works and trusting in the author of the human race, we hasten to worship him and render our vows to him? Therefore, most excellent son, [Col. 0476C] we exhort you with the paternal love that is fitting, so that you may diligently and through continual prayers strive in every way to preserve what divine mercy has deigned to call you to—that he who has deigned in the present age to lead you, freed from every error, to the knowledge of his name, may prepare for you a dwelling in the heavenly homeland.

“Therefore occupy yourselves frequently with the reading of your preacher, my lord Gregory of apostolic memory, and keep before your eyes the affection of his teaching, which he willingly exercised for the sake of your souls, so that his prayer may increase your kingdom and its people and present you blameless before almighty God.

“As for what you hoped would be arranged by us for your priests, in view of the sincerity of your faith—which has been commendably made known to us through many reports by the bearers of the present letter—we have decided, without any delay, freely to grant it to them. We have sent two pallia for both metropolitans, namely Honorius and Paulinus, so that, when either of them is summoned from this world to his Creator, the other may, by authority from us, appoint another bishop in his place. We have been persuaded to grant this both by our affection for your charity and by the great distance of the provinces known to lie between us and you, so that in all things we might provide our cooperation for your devotion and act according to your wishes. [Col. 0477A] May heavenly grace preserve your Excellency in safety.”

[Note: [Col. 0477D] Pagius proves that this and the following letter were issued in the year 634; see Pagius, under the year of Christ 633, no. 20 and following. MANSI.]

## LETTER VII. TO HONORIUS, BISHOP OF DOROVERNUM

He urges him to persevere in preaching the Gospel and sends the pallium mentioned in the preceding letter.

“To his most beloved brother Honorius: Honorius.

“Among the many gifts of good things that the mercy of our Redeemer deigns to bestow upon his servants [Note: [Col. 0477D] From Bede, Book II, chapter 18.], that mercy also kindly grants this through the munificence of its goodness: whenever, through fraternal words, it represents united love by a kind of mutual contemplation and reciprocal regard. For these things we continually render thanks to his majesty, and we entreat him with suppliant prayers [Col. 0477B] to strengthen your affection, laboring and bearing fruit in the preaching of the Gospel and following the rule of your teacher and head, Saint Gregory, with enduring stability. May he raise up through you still greater growth for the increase of his Church, so that, in faith and works, in the fear of God and in charity, the acquisition of your predecessors—which has begun through the work of the lord Gregory—may grow stronger and extend farther, until the promises of the Lord’s word themselves address you in the future, and this voice summon you to eternal festivity: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matthew 11); and again: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord’ (Matthew 25). [Col. 0477C]

“And indeed, dearest brothers, having first addressed to you these words of exhortation for eternal charity, which we see may again be appropriate for the privileges of your Churches, we do not cease to bestow them.

“And now, in accordance with your petition—the transmitted phrase “quam filiorum nostrorum regum vobis praesenti” is syntactically corrupt or uncertain—by this present command, in the stead of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we confer authority upon you, so that, whenever divine grace orders one of you to be called to itself, the one who survives may ordain another bishop in the place of the deceased. For this reason also we have sent to each of your affections a pallium for the celebration of this ordination, so that by the authority of our command you may carry out an ordination pleasing to God. For the long intervals of land and sea that stand between us and you compelled us to yield to this request, so that no loss of your Churches might in any way result under cover of any pretext, but rather that you might more fully extend the devotion of the people entrusted to you. [Col. 0477D] May God preserve you in safety, most beloved brother.

“Given on the third day before the Ides of June, while our most pious lords the Augusti Heraclius were reigning, in the twenty-fourth year, in the twenty-third year of his proconsulate [Note: [Col. 0478D] Read ‘after the consulship’; and below, ‘in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 634.’ See Pagius, at the place cited immediately above, no. 21. MANSI.], and in the third year of his consulship; and also in the third year of Heraclius Constantine, the most fortunate Caesar, that is, his son; in the seventh indiction, that is, in the year 633 of the Lord’s Incarnation.”

## LETTER VIII. OF POPE HONORIUS I TO JOHN AND THE OTHER BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGH EPIRUS

(From the collection of Cardinal Deusdedit.)

“Honorius to John, Andrew, Stephen, and Donatus, bishops established throughout Epirus.

“The bearers of the present letter (Book II, chapter 188) have earnestly requested us, in accordance with ecclesiastical discipline, to send the pallium to Hypatius, deacon of the Church of Nicopolis, whom you ordained bishop in the sacred orders. Since his person causes us anxious uncertainty, lest he perhaps appear to have been involved in the killing of Sotericus, bishop of the aforesaid city, we have deemed it appropriate to give the bearers of this letter the following reply: once he has assumed the dignity, especially since times of peace permit it, he should hasten to come to these Roman regions and offer an oath at the confession of blessed Peter the apostle that he gave no consent whatsoever, through any deceit or scheme devised by himself or by others plotting such things, so that, with every suspicion of guilt removed, we may be able, according to ecclesiastical order, to grant what is requested. For when the aforesaid Sotericus had been suspected concerning certain matters, he came to this city and nevertheless gave an oath before blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, concerning the purity of his conscience. Given on the Ides of December, in the fourteenth indiction.”

## LETTER IX. OF POPE HONORIUS I TO SERGIUS THE SUBDEACON

[Col. 0478C]

(Fragment from the same collection.)

“Honorius to Sergius the subdeacon.

“After a short interval, certain charges were reported to us against the archbishop of the city of Caralis and his clergy. In order that these might be investigated and discussed with canonical discernment in this Roman city, we ordered not only the bishop of the aforesaid city, by an issued command, but also those of his clergy who were reported to have committed some offense, to be summoned. Since the aforementioned bishop took care to come to this city, as he had been ordered, while his clergy, fearing to come because they were convicted of their own guilt, appeared to have been deprived of sacred communion and bound by the bond of anathema, [Col. 0478D] Barbarus, regional defender of our holy Church, was afterward sent to the same city of Caralis to bring the aforesaid clergy. But it happened that a certain Theodore, a perverse governor of Sardinia, seized by diabolical intent, prevented them from coming after they had already been placed on a ship, and, having forcibly removed them, sent them to the province of Africa.

“We therefore wrote to our son Gregory, the prefect, ordering him to have Theodore, governor of that island, correct so great a crime and to send to us in this Roman city the persons subject to our jurisdiction. [Col. 0479A] Therefore let your Experience hasten to press the same most eminent prefect, so that he may strive to avenge the crime of so great a man and not fail to send those persons to us. Know that not only those who are held liable for the crime have been deprived of sacred communion and punished with the penalty of anathema, but also those who appear to be associated with them.

“We have taken care to send a copy of the imperial law of Theodosius and Valentinian to your Experience, and through your Experience to forward it to the same most eminent prefect. Its contents can instruct not only his Eminence but also all those who attempt in any way to depart from the authority of the apostolic see. The most serene princes have hitherto renewed all the privileges of the apostolic see, and those once granted to it may be confirmed by the very reading of the document. For we trust in the mercy of our Lord God that we shall seek the rights and privileges of blessed Peter and defend them, once sought and granted, with unimpaired purpose.

“Strengthened by reading the contents of this imperial law with the greatest attention, let your Experience not delay to make these matters known not only to the most eminent prefect but also to others. As for us, concerning all these matters, as divine favor directs, it will unquestionably be our care and concern to deliberate according to the path of equity and to bring them to a more useful canonical conclusion. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the fifteenth indiction.”

## LETTER X. OF POPE HONORIUS I TO HONORIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

He grants him primacy over all the Churches of Britain.

[Col. 0479C]

“To his most beloved brother Honorius: Honorius, bishop and servant of the servants of God.

“Having received the letters of your affection [Note: [Col. 0479D] From Wilkins, *Concilia Magnae Britanniae et Hiberniae*, vol. I, p. 35; from the Supplement to Mansi, p. 471.], we found in them that your concern for the flock entrusted to us is occupied with great fatigue, and that, amid increasing evils and worldly demands, you frequently endure the burden of mental difficulty with much labor and distress.

“We exhort your affection to hold fast to the work of the Gospel that you have begun, because in this work you must labor and persevere rather than abandon it. Remember the Gospel command, how it says: ‘I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers’; and again, in the Apostle: ‘Brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.’ Therefore we earnestly admonish your affection that, in faith and works, in the fear of God and in charity, the acquisition of your predecessors—which has sprung up through the beginnings of the lord Gregory—may grow stronger and extend farther, until the promises of the Lord’s word themselves summon you to eternal festivity: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’; and again: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord.’

“In the meantime, you requested that the authority of your see be strengthened by the privilege of our authority. We, freely consenting without any delay, have granted this, since it is right that what we know to have once been established and arranged by our predecessors should also be confirmed by us. Therefore, following in their footsteps and according to the rite of ancient custom, which your Church has maintained from the time of your predecessor Augustine of holy memory down to the present, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we grant to you, Honorius, and to your successors in perpetuity the primacy over all the Churches of Britain.

“We therefore command that all the Churches and regions of England be subject to your jurisdiction, and that the metropolitan see and dignity of the archbishopric at the city of Dorovernum, as the head of all the Churches of the English peoples, always be preserved in the future and be moved to no other place by any person through evil persuasion. But if anyone should act otherwise, driven by the arrogance of pride, disobedient to our command, and should attempt to resist the grants made to the aforesaid Church and its dignity, let him know that he is separated from participation in the body and blood of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ. May God preserve you in safety, most beloved brother.”

## LETTER XI. OF POPE HONORIUS I TO GRATIOSUS THE SUBDEACON

(Fragment copied from his register, from the collection of Deusdedit.)

[Col. 0480C] “Lest the labor and diligence that anyone applies to the affairs of the Church [Note: [Col. 0480D] Published by the Ballerini in vol. III of the works of Saint Leo the Great, p. 306.] prove harmful to him, arrangements must be made [Col. 0480C] so that his labor may be useful to him and the ecclesiastical affairs suffer no loss.

“Therefore we grant you possession for twenty-nine years of a house with its garden, situated in this city of Rome near the Baths of Diocletian, in the district, together with everything belonging to it, at an annual payment of one gold solidus, to be paid each year to the ecclesiastical treasury by way of rent. Nor shall you thereafter be expelled from it, nor shall we impose an increase of rent there. You must, however, take care of the repair of the same house in all respects, like a diligent head of a household.

“After the completion of twenty-nine years, the same house with its garden shall without doubt return to the right of the holy Roman Church, whose property it is. Nor shall you or your heirs have any license to reclaim anything spent on its improvement, since the order of reason does not permit one who received no increase in the rent to reclaim expenses incurred for the improvement of the property. Given on the Ides of December, in the fourteenth indiction.”

## LETTER XII. OF POPE HONORIUS I TO SERVUSDEI THE NOTARY

(Fragment from the same collection.)

“Whenever something is requested from us that is known to accord with reason, it is fitting for us to grant it willingly. Therefore, because you requested from us that we should grant you for a fixed period the estate called Aurelianum, situated in its entirety with its vineyards on the Portuensian Way, near Saints Abdon and Sennen, yielding two and a half gold solidi, belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, we have consequently issued this command and grant you the aforementioned estate, with everything belonging to it, from this present fourteenth indiction for the days of your life. You must, however, pay each year without delay to the ecclesiastical treasury, by way of rent, two gold solidi and one tremissis, so that you may thereby have some relief and the usefulness of our Church may not diminish. After your death, the aforesaid estate shall without doubt return to the right of our holy Church, whose property it is. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the fourteenth indiction.”

## LETTER XIII

[Col. 0481B]

(Fragment from Ivo, part VII, chapter 132.)

“The bearer of the present letter began his supplication to us with a broken voice, sighs, groans, and unceasing tears, because a certain foster-son there deceived the daughter of the supplicant, who had been placed in sacred garments, through his constant attentions, until she fell into the defilement of the body through the commission of adultery. Thus, after the crime became known, that utterly depraved man continues to live there in the disgrace of the entire community residing in that place, while, through the patronage perhaps of certain people, the matter has so far been left unpursued and he himself has been kept unpunished.

“Therefore, your affection, kindled by zeal for God, must not cease to press the competent jurisdiction until the perpetrator of the crime, brought before a public inquiry [Col. 0481C] and the most severe examination, receives the punishment of ultimate death, lest, if retribution against him is delayed, the sentence of divine judgment spread to many.”

## LETTER XIV. OF POPE HONORIUS I TO PETER, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

(Fragment from Ivo, part VIII, chapter 309.)

“We have learned from the report of certain people that your fraternity is becoming involved in criminal cases, and that you are being constrained not merely by readings but also by daily practice to know what the sacred canons forbid. For we have likewise heard that this was done by you rather carelessly: when almost the hour of dining had passed, you went with more than three hundred prostitutes [Col. 0481D] to our most eminent son, the prefect, who was in a bathhouse, and the crowd of those aforesaid women of evil life pressed upon him with their pestilential cries, so that the man who had previously been appointed their overseer might by every means be removed by them and another nevertheless appointed in his place.

“If this is so, it would have been more fitting to lament than to correct such conduct. But lest so great and shameful a crime appear to remain unpunished for long—for it was both contrary to the priestly office and inimical to the conduct of life—we have instructed our son Cyriacus the deacon, once the truth has been disclosed, what must be done concerning this matter, so that those things committed there that are unlawful and contrary to reverence for modesty may be cut off at the root by the canonical sword (*ense canonico*; the text prints “[F. ense]”), in accordance with ecclesiastical discipline.”

## LETTER XV. OF POPE HONORIUS I TO ANATHOLIUS, MASTER OF THE MILITARY

[Col. 0482A]

(Fragment from Ivo, part X, chapter 187.)

“The bearer of the present letter has tearfully entreated us, asserting that his brother was killed by a certain soldier of the fortress of Salerno and, moreover, robbed of his own property after his death. It is therefore evident to all from the very documents of the case how impious and contrary to the provisions of the laws it is that innocent blood shed should in no way be avenged upon the perpetrator.

“Those who can avenge these things but neglect to do so through connivance must surely know that, if they neglect to defend innocent blood, at the future and fearful judgment such a crime will be demanded of them as participants in this deed. Therefore let your Glory remove from the military ranks the man entangled in the deadly crime of murder, and hasten, under the impulse of justice, to hand him over to the provincial judge for punishment. The property that he seized by the force of robbery must unquestionably be restored to the aforesaid petitioner, if he was indeed his brother, so that, with discipline pressing upon us, the one who committed the crime may always expect and unhesitatingly receive his punishment, and the integrity of the military may in no way be subjected to the contagion of murderous guilt because of the offense of one man.”

## LETTER XVI. OF POPE HONORIUS I TO ISAAC, PATRICIAN AND EXARCH OF ITALY

(Fragment from Ivo, part XII, chapter 25.)

“From the writings of certain people we have learned that certain bishops in the regions beyond the Po pronounced to Peter, the son of Paul, certain words hostile to episcopal conduct and suggested an impious persuasion to him. They asserted that he ought to assume the guilt of perjury and consent not to King Adalubald but rather to the tyrant Ariopalt, because the aforesaid glorious Peter refused to yield to their wicked—if it may be said so—priestly persuasions, preferring firmly to keep the oaths that he had given to King Cono, the father of the aforesaid Adalubald.

“Since such a crime is hostile to God and to pious minds—so much so that those who ought to have prevented it from being committed instead urged that it be done—now that, through the favor of heavenly power and your efforts, the aforesaid Adalubald has been restored to his kingdom, may you deign, with God’s help, to send the aforesaid bishops to these Roman regions, since we shall in no way allow such a crime to remain unpunished.”

## TWO FRAGMENTS FROM THE DECRETALS

(Burchard, Book XI, chapter 40; Gratian, XI, question 3.)

“It should be the concern of all bishops to make known the names of excommunicated persons both to neighboring bishops and to their own parishioners, and, having posted them in a public place before the doors of the church, to impress them upon all who assemble, so that through both forms of diligence ecclesiastical access may everywhere be denied to the excommunicated and the cause of their excommunication may be made known to all.”

(Ivo, part V, chapter 325.)

“Any metropolitan who dares to use the pallium through the streets or in litanies, rather than only on the principal festivals and at the times appointed by the apostolic see, solely for the solemn celebrations of Mass, shall lose that honor. And, as blessed Pope Gregory says to John, bishop of Palermo, since he defends a heavy yoke and a bond upon his neck not for ecclesiastical but for some secular dignity, let him lose the dignity that he abuses by the permission granted to him, because by right he deserves to lose the privilege who boldly usurps what is unlawful.”

## EPIGRAM: ON THE APOSTLES, ASTONISHED AT CHRIST’S ASCENSION INTO HEAVEN

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon, vol. XII.)

Peter sees Christ by daylight, whom he denied at night;

and he sang that his Lord was proceeding to the stars.

[Col. 0483B] Terrified, Andrew prays: “Have mercy, Master;

gather your disciple into the kingdom of the Father.”

James was astonished that a man was carried through the clouds;

he offers his shoulders and gives holy vows to God.

John, trembling in every limb, clings to the sight,

and, bewildered, still stood there in a manner pleasing to him.

“Why do we not follow you, Christ?” Philip calls without a voice:

“Am I cast aside, free and yet entangled?”

Bartholomew, you tremble to see Christ’s feet hanging,

and you wish, if you can grasp them, to extend your hands in peace.

Thomas, not yet wholly satisfied with love,

thinks that he is touching the wounds, the limbs, the side.

Matthew, like one who is mute, spoke through his writings;

for fear seized the old man and made him silent.

James son of Alphaeus grows pale, buried without dying:

[Col. 0483C] giving his companions eyes to return what he could.

Here Simon, stunned, marvels that the Thunderer has departed,

and flees, desiring to endure the lightning.

Matthias clings fixed to the gate of heaven,

thinking that everything has departed with Christ as witness.

Judas, lifted from all the others, his body without a face,

sees the slain God living throughout the world.

## PRIVILEGE GRANTED TO THE MONASTERY OF BOBBIO

(Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV.)

“Honorius, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his brother Bertulf, abbot and priest.

“If things that accord with pious desires are always to be granted, how much more must those things not be wholly denied which are known to arise from the prerogative of religious worship—things that should not only be requested from those who bestow them but which, by the force of charity, must unquestionably be demanded. You therefore ask us [Col. 0484A] to grant the privileges of the apostolic see to the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul established at Bobbio, over which you are known to preside, so that the monastery, constituted under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, may not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church.

“For this reason, in response to your pious prayers, we readily commit to your desire by our authority what you have requested from your affection. Therefore we entirely forbid any priest of any Church to extend authority of any kind over the aforesaid monastery or, by his own authority, celebrate the solemnities of Mass there unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery.

“Let it therefore be your concern to adorn the brothers of the monastery, as far as you can, with excellent morals and an irreproachable life, so that, in accordance with that which [lacuna] preferred to be endowed immovably with apostolic privileges, they may rather desire and yearn to be adorned by the inviolable abundance of heavenly grace through the daily prayers of holy discipline. Let their life be communal and sincere; let there be sober, communal sincerity, so that those for whom the world has died and been buried may not be [uncertain text] incited to the vices of contention. For one is known to labor in vain and fruitlessly if he feels that he must submit his neck to pride, the mother of vices. Let humility therefore be exalted, because through this heavenly art one may possess heavenly gifts.

“Let the rule of our fathers’ traditions therefore be before the eyes of mind and body, and let every superior know how he ought to command his subjects, lest, while harsh things and matters not suited to every brother are demanded to be fulfilled to completion [lacuna] those commanding the things of God should be subject to discretion. Let there accordingly be moderated vigor; let there be, among the brothers, an outstanding earnestness in solicitude, so that, while all who are wholly devoted to God present themselves as good servants through the path of obedience and offer temporal things, they may arrive at the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland.

“Let what we have said concerning matters belonging to solicitude suffice. Above all, we more earnestly await with sobs and groans the mercy of our Redeemer, while awaiting our redemption with sighing, so that the frailty of the human condition may sufficiently and confidently fulfill what piety requires through the support of its Creator. Farewell.

“Given on the third day before the Ides of January, in the eighth year of the reign of our most pious lord Augustus Heraclius, in the eighteenth year after the consulship of that same emperor, and in the sixteenth year of Heraclius Constantine, his new son, in the first indiction.”

## APPENDIX

[Col. 0483]

[VARIOUS DOCUMENTS. (C,S)*]

### I. EXCERPT FROM THE LETTER OF SAINT MAXIMUS TO THE PRIEST MARINUS, WHO AMONG OTHER THINGS MAKES AN APOLOGY FOR HONORIUS

(Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. XII.)

I believe that Pope Honorius the Roman did not deny the natural duality of wills in Christ in the letter which he wrote to Sergius, because he said that there was one will; rather, I think that he confessed it and perhaps even firmly established it. For he did not say this in rejection of the human and natural will of the Savior, but because in no way did a carnal will or vicious thought precede his conception, which was without seed, or his incorrupt birth. For it was solely the divine and paternal will, working through the only-begotten Son by its own operation, that effected his incarnation and the coming together of the Holy Spirit; and that this was his meaning is clear from what follows.

For when he had said that, on account of the ineffable unity of the human and divine natures, God is said to suffer, and humanity to have descended from heaven with humanity [read: divinity], and had thus shown that the attributes naturally belonging to each nature are wholly ascribed, by a supreme exchange, to the one Christ and Son of God, he adds:

> “Therefore,” he says, “we also confess one will of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

How does he say this? “Because assuredly our nature was assumed by the divinity, not our guilt”—that is, not from sin—almost speaking with the great Athanasius, who writes the following against the impious Apollinarius:

> “He was born of a woman, raising up for himself, from the first fashioning of humanity, the human form in the manifestation of the flesh, without carnal wills and human thoughts in the image of newness. For the will is solely that of the divinity, since the whole nature is divinity. Finally, the advance of the Word’s birth for our sake according to the flesh was made above us. For no vicious will or thought of the flesh preceded it, as is seen in us on account of the desire of our race, which it acquired through the deception of the first parent. Rather, the will of the divinity alone, through the Son who, according to the Father’s good pleasure and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, effected by himself his own incorporation—as I have said—bore in himself and through himself the newly discovered mode of nature’s birth and accomplished his own conception without seed from holy Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of God.”

Having therefore considered this ineffable manner of his birth, the former said that there was in him only the will of the divinity, whereas the latter said that there was one will of our Lord Jesus Christ. “For assuredly,” he says, “our nature was assumed by the divinity, not our guilt, without carnal wills and human thoughts,” as the most sacred Athanasius says.

He did not, however, assert that, as a human being—for he is also God by nature—Christ lacked a human and natural will, just as he possessed a divine and paternal will. He indicates the same thing in what follows, asserting:

> “He was conceived without sin from the Holy Spirit and from holy, immaculate, ever-virgin Mary, the Mother of God, and without defilement was born from her according to the flesh.”

He also adduces divine Scripture in praise and condemnation as making mention of the flesh, indicating that the flesh of the Lord is to be understood as neither another nature nor another substance than ours. He knew that this flesh too had been assumed from our substance—that is, from the holy womb of the ever-virgin and Mother of God, who was congenitally related to us—but that it was free from vice and in no way possessed, as it does in us, the law of transgression resisting the law of the spirit in the members.

“For,” he says, “flesh corrupted by sin was not assumed by the Savior, flesh that would resist the law of his mind. For the law of generation did not precede the sowing of that which is brought about through sin; therefore such a law is altogether absent from his members. Rather, the law of divine justice was shown to us in an image, and it completely destroys that which was introduced through the transgression of nature. For he came without sin to seek and save what had perished—that is, the nature of the human race which had sinned. There was no other law in his members, nor any different or contrary will, in the Savior.”

From this he shows—not that Christ did not possess a human and natural will (for he does not seem to have said this), but that, just as a human being has no operation through the members of the body beyond the laws of nature, so likewise, according to the soul, he did not possess a contrary, irrational, or opposing movement of the will, as we do, because he was also born above the law of human nature.

He establishes even more explicitly in what follows that his purpose was only to distinguish from the Savior the will that was corrupted and contrary to nature, and that the natural and human will was indeed conformed to the paternal and divine will, but had no difference from it arising through opposition.

Giving us himself as a model, he voluntarily subjected what was properly his own, while commending what was paternal, so that we too, imitating him, may reject what is ours and fulfill with all zeal what is divine. He says:

> “Although it is written, ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me’ (John 6), and, ‘Not what I will, but what you will, Father,’ these do not indicate different wills—that is, contrary and opposing wills—but the dispensation of the humanity assumed, which compassionately performed its own things, which are ours. For he said these things for our sake, giving us an example of piety as a teacher, so that each of us may follow his footsteps and prefer in all things not his own will, but rather the Lord’s.”

Thus, as I have said, he does not abolish the natural and human will, but the vicious will, that which is outside nature. Let us confess entirely that God is free from every sin, he who became incarnate according to our condition and for our sake.

To put it briefly, I infer that by “one will” he indicates that only the divine will preceded his birth according to the flesh. But by saying that there was no difference of will in him, he does not assert that he lacked anything contrary or opposing, but that what he possessed was wholly concordant and completely united. Therefore, when he says that our nature was assumed from the will of the divinity, he mentions one will.

But when he introduces the words, “I have not come to do my own will,” he places the saying in the middle without specifying the number. “These,” he says, “are not different wills, that is, contrary and adversarial wills.” From this it is manifestly inferred that there exist in the Savior two wills according to nature. For if he did not have a contrary will, he had a natural one, as a human being. Whatever is not contrary is certainly natural, and no one disputes this. For nothing in nature, or among the things that are according to nature, is altogether contrary.

It is therefore rash to suppose that something is written in his words which is not actually there, and to make that man's writings a covering for an unsound opinion, falsely interpreting them in both respects contrary to his intention. The discourse of reason stands as an advocate, driving away every attack of the calumniator. This, at least, is how I understand his meaning, cleansed of every suspicion.

The most holy presbyter, namely the lord Anastasius, the abbot who had recently returned from elder Rome, made this clearer to me. He is an incomparable man, adorned with divine virtue and prudence. He reported that he had raised the matter at length with the most sacred men of that great Church, asking for what reason, or in what manner, “one will” had been inserted in the letter which Honorius had written to Sergius. He found them hesitant about this and giving an explanation.

Moreover, he affirmed that the man who, at Honorius’s command, had dictated the letter in Latin words—namely the lord abbot John, the most holy secretary—said that he had in no way mentioned in it, by number, “one will” in any absolute sense. Although this is now fabricated by those who translated it into the Greek language, the letter did not contain any emptying out or abolition of the Savior’s natural will according to his humanity. Rather, it spoke of the complete casting down and destruction of the will that is ours and has become blameworthy.

Accordingly, among things of the same kind, conflict also arises against one another. He wished to show that the flesh assumed was wholly free from sin, in accordance with the tradition of the most sacred writings and the teachings of the Fathers.

It is evident how such statements harmonize with those which I have just recited from my own small store, and how they serve as supporters of the defense made on behalf of Honorius.

When he had answered these matters by reasoning, I was amazed, recognizing very clearly the subtlety of those men. I was, in a way, stupefied at the craftiness of those who impiously dare and wish vainly to do everything for one thing, as has long been—and still is—their custom: by clandestine and false narratives to draw to themselves in this manner those who contend courageously against them, even without any rational basis, and to deceive their understanding, which in no way follows them.

Therefore, when I had learned this as well, I necessarily informed you, my lord and venerable father, so that, fully armed in every respect, you might know how to pursue the adversaries’ phalanxes, casting words at them without weariness, overcoming them powerfully by faith, and having the glory of the Only-begotten as your proclamation and the diadem of this communion through grace and unity.

## II. EXCERPT FROM THE LETTER OF SAINT MAXIMUS TO PETER THE ILLUSTRIOUS

He mentions Pyrrhus, Saint Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, and Pope Honorius, proceeding as follows after some preliminary remarks.

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, vol. X.)*

You have deigned to signify to your unworthy servant, in commendable words, your concern regarding the abbot Pyrrhus. A little later:

It would certainly have been appropriate for me, perhaps for this reason, to hasten to rebuke him and all who follow, without distinction, the impious novelty associated with him, and to hasten toward the preservation of your divinely protected and most renowned footsteps, so that all who, according to you, love piety might know their excessive abundance of impiety together with their utter ignorance.

But I feared that I might be thought to be acting outside the sacred laws, doing this against the will of the most holy apostolic men of the see, who rightly govern the whole fullness of the Catholic Church and lead it in orderly fashion according to divine law. For heavenly and earthly things subsist by this divine law, and one must in no way deviate from it. Those who have resolved to live holily according to you ought to do the divine things according to God, so that they may have God as the guardian of their actions, though their reception may be without success.

For, most renowned lord, even worse than these—as I mentioned earlier—is a new faith and exposition, more wicked than those of the ancient heretics. He sustained this for many years in the episcopate, revealing his depraved mind. For God often knows how to endure wickedness patiently even for its disclosure—not in order to make it greater through delay, but so that, once it has become greater, he may punish it more justly. His predecessor impiously nourished it in the womb; this man begot it still more impiously; and the successors of these men, in contempt of divinity, cultivate it anew.

A little later:

Their practice is even worse, and as it were a special mark of all perverse heretics: they describe those who are guilty of their own impiety as innocent. They whisper here and there that Sophronius, who wisely taught and proclaimed the divine dogmas of the Catholic Church, had led them into error.

A little later:

For, as you yourselves testify, the divine Sophronius was staying in the region of Africa with me and with all the monks living abroad, while they were fabricating those perversities against everyone.

After a short interval:

The whole house, through divine harmony and unanimity, had become one peaceful and tranquil community under the favor of God, with the Churches fortified by the faith that exists beneath the sun. But those who envied their concord and their confession of Christ God, as though no one had stirred them except the demon who loves disturbance and incited the human race to mutual strife, suddenly devised a new *ecthesis* against the true faith of Christians, like a dark cloud or a shrieking and oppressive wave of the sea and of the barbarians. Then they produced opinions and unjust compositions in its favor; next, acts of councils; then robber synods and gatherings of bishops who had not come together by consent but had been compelled by force, who had not hastened through exhortation but had gone abroad in flight from the barbarians; and then commands and threats sent here and there against the devout.

For they cunningly reduced the man who was then emperor to servitude through gifts.

A little later:

They persuaded him to issue an *ecthesis* under his own name.

Shortly afterward:

He became both their enemy and their defender—or rather, it must be said, their supporter and accuser—making their argument public and revealing that he himself had not been moved by his own initiative, but had been compelled by them to produce the most impious *ecthesis*. In writing it on his own behalf, he said these things and gave an account to John of holy memory, formerly the senior pope of Rome.

A little later:

They convict themselves, for these men, who are very manifestly the strongest, produced this document, and he did so not at all. For he had no particular interest in this matter, being occupied with other things.

After a brief interval:

In all these matters the wretched men did not even understand the mind of the apostolic see. What is laughable—or, to speak more accurately, most deserving of lamentation, as demonstrating their audacity—is that they were not even reluctant to lie recklessly against the apostolic see itself. As though they had become its counselors, and as though they had received some decree from it, they included the great Honorius with themselves in their written proceedings on behalf of the impious *ecthesis*, presenting to others the display of their presumption concerning a man of the greatest distinction in the cause of piety.

Who, then, most renowned lord, and what sort of Sophronius, persuaded these men to do such things, so atrociously and for so long? What Church did he not ask them? What pious and orthodox bishop did not entreat them, crying out and adjuring them to cease from their heresy?

Indeed, the holy Arcadius was breathing his last and surrendering his spirit to God, yet even up to that hour he did not cease entreating them.

A little later:

And what of the divine Honorius? What of the aged Severinus after him? What finally of the holy John who succeeded him? Moreover, did the most blessed pope who now presides omit anything appropriate to entreaty? Did not the whole East and West bring tears, lamentations, pleas, and supplications alike before God through prayers and before these men through letters?

God indeed accepted the faith of those blessed men and preserved a return for it forever. But those men, scorning the Lord’s forbearance, which kindly urged them to conversion, and becoming sluggish in the face of the distinguished supplication made for so long by these men, were in no way willing to prefer the heavenly faith.

After some further remarks:

The divine and great Sophronius, coming then to Alexandria, immediately upon the first reading—for Cyrus had also given him those nine chapters of impiety to reconsider—uttered something mournful and immense, pouring forth fountains of tears. He fervently entreated, begged, and pleaded with him, falling prostrate on the pavement at his feet, that he should preach none of these things from the ambo against the Catholic Church of God, since these were plainly the impious doctrines of Apollinarius.

A little later:

In this way, my head whom I revere above all others, those men tore one another apart with insults directed against God and with theatrical mockeries of one another, as it were. Yet they did not console the most holy Sophronius, who lamented so miserably, mourning the broken condition of the Catholic Church like a second Jeremiah and deploring, with the greatest goodness and compassion, so great a fall of the divine dogmas.

After a number of further remarks:

For if the Roman see knows not only the rejected Pyrrhus but also those who think and believe wrongly, it is entirely clear that whoever anathematizes those who rejected Pyrrhus anathematizes the Roman see—that is, the Catholic Church. I omit saying that such a person also anathematizes himself, if at least he communicates with the Roman see and with the Catholic Church of God.

I therefore beseech you, my blessed lord, to order everyone not to call Pyrrhus “most holy” or “most beneficent.” For the sacred rule does not permit him to be called anything of the kind. He has fallen from all holiness, since he voluntarily leapt out of the Catholic Church.

It is not lawful to give any honorable title to one who was long ago condemned and rejected by the apostolic see of the city of Rome because of the content of his foreign opinion, until he is received back by that see after converting to it—or rather to our Lord—through pious confession and orthodox faith, by which he may receive sanctification and the holy name.

Thus, if he wishes neither to be a heretic nor to be heard as one, let him not satisfy this or that individual; for that is superfluous and irrational. Just as when one person is scandalized against him, all are scandalized, so when one person has been satisfied, all are undoubtedly satisfied. Let him hasten to satisfy the Roman see on behalf of all. Once that see has been satisfied, everyone everywhere will together proclaim him pious and orthodox.

For the man speaks in vain who thinks that people like me can be persuaded and secretly won over, while he does not satisfy and implore the most holy pope of the Roman Church—that is, the apostolic see—which has received and possesses, from the incarnate Word of God himself and from all the holy synods, according to the sacred canons and definitions, authority and power in all things and through all things over all the holy Churches of God throughout the whole world, including the authority and power to bind and loose.

For when it binds and looses, the Word, which rules over the heavenly powers, also binds and looses in heaven.

If he seeks to satisfy others but does not implore the most blessed Roman pope, he acts like someone accused of homicide or some other crime who hastens not to prove himself innocent before the one who has received judicial authority according to the laws, but uselessly and fruitlessly strives to display the purity of his conduct to other private individuals who have no power to release him from the crime.

Therefore, my blessed lord, extend still further the command which is recognized to have seemed good to you and according to God’s pleasure, so that this man may have permission to speak or dispute with no one concerning doctrine.

But learn his will clearly by investigating it more fully: whether he wishes to assent completely to the truth. If he should desire to do this and hastens toward it rationally, urge him to make an appropriate appeal to the most blessed Roman pope, so that, through that man’s divine command, the matters concerning him may be regulated according to the rule and most suitably, to the glory of God and the praise of your eminence.

## III. OBSERVATION OF PHILIPPE LABBÉ, S.J.

Nor should the royal collector have omitted the letter which appears at the beginning of the collection edited by Sirmond, in place of a preface: the letter of Anastasius, librarian of the apostolic see, to John, deacon of the city of Rome. In it he explains not only the plan of the work undertaken but also contains a defense of Pope Honorius against the censure of the Sixth Synod, by which he seemed to have been branded among the Monothelites, as Sirmond teaches.

Receive it, then, in a few words, as entirely necessary both in view of what has just been said about Honorius and of what will follow in the next volume.

## LETTER OF ANASTASIUS, LIBRARIAN OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, TO JOHN THE DEACON

To his dearest brother John, worthy Levite of Christ, Anastasius, the least of the servants, sends greetings in the Lord.

I had promised your diligence that, for the instruction of many, I would translate from the Greek language into Latin a certain ecclesiastical historical work. For you had said—and truth itself, as the highest teacher, had confirmed—that you could not confidently begin an ecclesiastical history unless a written sequence of events in both languages had reached your knowledge.

Therefore, because I recognize myself to be so ignorant that I am not capable of penetrating even the force of my own language, in which I was born—not to mention a foreign language—and because of this I would never have presumed to undertake the task of translation in any manner, I have hastened, with the consent and correction of my teachers, to satisfy you as far as my abilities allow. I plainly believe that you will correct whatever in my work is distorted and polish whatever you find unpolished.

I confess that, with my conscience bearing witness, I would rather have had these things and similar matters done by others—not so much because I shrink from the labor as because of my unlearned knowledge in every respect, if it is to be called knowledge rather than ignorance. I do not know whether, without violating the peace of your brotherly affection or your purpose of writing the history, I could have omitted these matters.

You shine, in fact, with so great a light of wisdom that it might seem that I have undertaken not something necessary but something rash. Let it therefore be enough for me, through obedience, to gather what others have sown with a rustic sickle and carry it faithfully on my shoulders to the threshing-floor of Latin, adding or subtracting nothing.

It will be your task, by adding judgments as though with a winnowing fan of discernment, to enlarge the work of history and to cleanse our words, which you decide should be inserted into it, like grains of wheat.

We have undertaken this and our other translations in such a way that we may be recognized as having departed neither altogether from the precise circumstances of the words nor, insofar as possible, from the truth of their meaning.

Furthermore, I translated certain brief works concerning the most recent times, because the deeds of earlier times have already been translated by our predecessors—or rather by our greater forebears—who anticipated us in this kind of work and surpassed us by far more excellent achievements.

Therefore, after the tripartite chronicle which, at your urging, we translated, and after certain other very brief works which we interpreted at the request of various fathers and brothers, there came into our hands a defense of the fourth John, Roman pontiff, on behalf of Pope Honorius, who had been attacked by his calumniators because he had supposedly written that our Lord Jesus Christ had only one will.

This defense, as I believe, renders him sufficiently excusable, although the holy Sixth Synod pronounced an anathema against him as though he were a heretic and pierced him with the weapon of condemnation, placing him already in the judgment of God alone. For a heretic is generated not so much from the deception of error as from an incorrect choice and contentious obstinacy.

Who, meanwhile, will tell us whether he himself certainly dictated the letter from which the calumniators took the pretext for anathematizing him, when such a thing could have arisen from the writer’s lack of discipline or from hatred of the pontiff? Although we do not fail to know, as Saint Maximus teaches in his letter to the presbyter Marinus, that the most holy abbot John wrote it.

Let it be so: he himself was the dictator. Who questioned him about this? Who investigated his intention? Who wished to correct him, and did he resist the person asking questions or attempting to amend the text, or did he reply contentiously? This is especially relevant since, in the Gospel where it is said, “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Luke 6:37), and in what follows, the great teachers of the Church seem to have been given no other command than that we should interpret for the better those deeds whose motive is uncertain.

There are indeed certain intermediate actions whose motive we do not know, since they can be done with good or evil intent. It is rash to judge them, especially in order to condemn them.

In the end, there are two circumstances in which we must avoid rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what motive something was done, or when it is uncertain what sort of person someone who now appears evil or good will become.

How rash judgment must be avoided, the Lord plainly indicates when he speaks of the Sodomites in our human manner, saying:

> “I will go down and see whether they have fully acted according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Genesis 18:21).

And again through Moses:

> “You shall not curse the deaf,” he says, “nor place a stumbling-block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14).

The Apostle teaches the same thing in nearly the same words:

> “Each of us will give an account of himself to God. Therefore let us no longer judge one another, but judge this instead: that you do not place a stumbling-block or scandal before your brother” (Romans 14:12–13).

Who, however, should be called more deaf or mute than one who lies lifeless and disintegrating in a tomb, whose ear is not open to hear the charges formally brought against him and whose mouth is not opened to refute them rationally?

But concerning judgments of this kind, what the venerable Anastasius, bishop of the apostolic see, teaches in writing to the emperor Anastasius is sufficient: his teaching is laden with the weight of the authority of sacred Scripture.

Yet, so that we may not seem to accuse or rashly criticize the synod, we believe that we may hold concerning it the opinion which we know that our holy fathers held concerning the great Synod of Chalcedon.

One of them, namely Saint Pope Gregory, indicated that it should be accepted only insofar as the canons were promulgated. The equally blessed Pope Gelasius, in his volume on the bond of anathema, showed through lucid examples and several divine testimonies how that same synod should be received. There he concludes the matter with this deliberation:

> “These and similar examples teach us, and the divine testimonies confirm, that we must not indiscriminately accept everything said by anyone or written anywhere, but, retaining what is good, reject what may cause harm.”

The writings of the Greeks also testify that this holy synod promulgated certain canonical chapters, although nearly all of them—which the apostolic see did not approve—the whole Latin world rejected.

But why speak only of this synod, when the apostolic see does not accept even the Second Ecumenical Synod, which was first celebrated at Constantinople, in the matter of the primacy of the Churches? Indeed, it decrees that all synods are to be received in such a way that the aforementioned Pope Gelasius describes the Synod of Chalcedon as deserving acceptance on account of the communion of faith and Catholic and apostolic truth, for the sake of which the apostolic see commissioned that synod and confirmed it once it had been held.

Yet if we wished to gather together everything that we can collect in defense of Pope Honorius, the paper would run out more readily than speech, and our purpose of translating would certainly be turned into a work of composition.

We shall say only one thing, which we surely ought not to conceal: Honorius has been declared to be what he was. If he was not such, the sentence affixed to him will certainly not stand, for, as it is written, “Man sees the face, but God sees the heart.”

But behold: while our preface is being addressed to you at excessive length, we have wandered far from the task of translation, eager to show that on the rock of the apostolic see, as far as faith is concerned, not even in the case of Honorius has there ever been found a trace of the serpent—that is, of a poisonous sect.

Take, then, the aforementioned defense of Pope John on behalf of Honorius. Take also the defense of that same man from the letter of the monk Maximus—truly a philosopher and martyr of Christ our God—which was sent to the presbyter Marinus, here excerpted.

For the most blessed Maximus defends the aforementioned Honorius not only in the letter already mentioned but also in the letter which he wrote to the abbot Thalassius. Moreover, in his dogmatic letter to Peter the Illustrious, he calls him great and divine. From this letter we bring you certain excerpts and translations concerning Pope Honorius, and concerning Sophronius of Jerusalem—whom we have often mentioned in the writings translated by us—as well as concerning Pyrrhus, the heretical patriarch of Constantinople.

Furthermore, from the letter of the same Saint Maximus written to the presbyter Marinus, we translated the discussion concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. In it he indicates that the Greeks argue against us in vain, since we do not say, as they suppose, that the Son is the cause or principle of the Holy Spirit. Rather, recognizing the unity of substance of the Father and the Son, we confess that, just as the Spirit proceeds from the Father, so he proceeds from the Son, understanding “mission” as “procession.”

He interprets this piously and teaches those who know both languages toward peace, showing that both we and the Greeks teach that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son in one respect and does not proceed from the Son in another, expressing the difficulty of conveying the property of one language in the other.

Indeed, through a pious interpretation of this kind, Saint Athanasius once united Easterners and Westerners who were divided over the name of subsistence or person. He taught that both groups believed and retained one and the same thing in their hearts and understanding, although, because of the variety of language, they confessed it orally in different ways and raged in untimely disputes.

We also translated certain letters of Pope Theodore, the successor of the aforementioned Pope John, written, as the order of events required, to Paul, the successor of Pyrrhus, and to those who consecrated him. The style of the letters of these distinguished bishops of the apostolic see, John and Theodore, clearly breathes Latin eloquence. From this it is evident that they were not dictated in Greek but in Latin.

It should therefore be noted that some works originally produced in Latin would have been utterly buried beneath the mass of oblivion, had the Latins not drawn them again, with thirsty hearts, from the spring of Greek books, as happened with the letter of blessed Pope Felix pronouncing a sentence of condemnation against Peter of Antioch.

Indeed, this is also shown by Clement himself, whom Rufinus indicates, in writing to Gaudentius, to have been rendered into our language, restored, and brought back—clearly showing that he had been written in Latin, lost, and then recovered.

I have also excerpted and now present to you in translation a certain account from the letter of Saint Maximus to the abbot: what the Roman legates accomplished at Constantinople, to encourage steadfastness in the cause of the greatest piety, to rebuke the fainthearted, and to acknowledge the power of the apostolic see against those who attempt to extort anything from it by force.

Furthermore, I also present to you the account of the exile of Saint Pope Martin, which I published at the request of the venerable Martin, bishop of Narni, together with the *Hypomnesticon*, which briefly relates the deeds of Saints Maximus the philosopher and both Anastasii, as well as Theodore, Euprepius, and others.

## IV. EPITAPH OF POPE HONORIUS I

*(Baronius, Annals, under the year 638.)*

In the apse—which the illustrious pope constructed—the following verses are read, inscribed in mosaic beneath the images woven in the same material, in a rough style, as the age generally produced:

> A golden painting rises in cut metal,  
> And, embracing it, the very day is enclosed.  
> You would believe, Aurora, that from snowy fountains  
> You rise, having seized the clouds and watering the fields with rain.

In the same semicircle of the apse, the following verses were placed in a straight line:

> What kind of rainbow will he display among the stars,  
> And the purple peacock itself, gleaming in color?  
> He who was able to restore the end of night and of light  
> Drove the chaos away from the tombs of the martyrs.  
> What is seen above, turned by a single nod toward all,  
> Bishop Honorius gave these vows as a dedication.  
> His face is marked by his garments and his deeds,  
> And he shines in appearance, bearing a radiant heart.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 638: DAGOBERT I, KING OF THE FRANKS

[Col. 0495]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON DAGOBERT

*(Literary History of France, vol. III.)*

### § I. History of his life

A reign first directed by prudence, moderation, justice, and equity, and then darkened by a chain of excessive debaucheries, sums up in two words the character of this prince. [Note: [Col. 0495C] Fredegar, *Chronicle*, nos. 46, 47, 58, 60; Mabillon, same work, vol. II, pp. 425, 715.]

He was the son of Clotaire II and Berthrude, and was born around the year 603. He brought into the world excellent natural qualities, much intelligence, gentleness, and humanity, and became one of the most skillful, best-formed, and most vigorous princes of his age.
