He was not yet twenty years old when, in 622, Clotaire established him as king of Austrasia, giving him as his principal counselors the illustrious Pepin of Landen and Saint Arnoul, bishop of Metz. [Note: [Col. 0495C] Fredegar, same work, nos. 58, 61; Mabillon, same work, p. 154, no. 16; p. 425, no. 8.]

The latter took exceptional care to train him in the art of reigning as a most Christian king, and succeeded so happily that Dagobert was regarded as the prince best instructed in the knowledge appropriate to a sovereign ever yet seen among the Frankish kings.

While he followed the counsel of these two wise ministers, and that of Saint Cunibert of Cologne, who succeeded Saint Arnoul, his reign was prosperous and flourishing, to such a degree that no other had been more so [Note: [Col. 0495D] Ibid.]. He became an object of admiration, esteem, and respect to foreign nations as well as to his own subjects. Indeed, nothing was more charming than to see a young prince display extraordinary attentiveness and personally take tireless care to administer justice. Neither gifts nor consideration for persons had any influence [Col. 0495C] upon his mind. He followed only what accorded with order and equity.

But such fine beginnings were soon horribly darkened by conduct full of debauchery [Note: [Col. 0495D] Fred., ibid., no. 58–60; Mab., ibid., p. 715, no. 15.]. Not only did he abandon Gomatrude, whom he had married, and take Nantilde, one of her ladies-in-waiting, in her place, but he carried his love of women to such an excess that he had three of them simultaneously as queens, along with a great number of concubines. To incontinence he added avarice; and this led him to seize the property of his subjects, and [Col. 0496A] even of churches, in order to fill his treasuries. Neither the salutary advice of Saint Cunibert of Cologne nor the moving remonstrances of Saint Amand of Maastricht were capable of restraining the passions of this young prince.

It was after the death of his father, Clotaire, in 628, that he began to turn away from justice, seeing himself master of almost the whole of France [Note: [Col. 0495D] Fred., ibid., no. 60.]. He became entirely so two years later, upon the death of his brother Charibert and of a son whom he had named Childeric, who followed him almost immediately [Note: [Col. 0496C] No. 67.]. Despite his debauchery, Dagobert nevertheless did good to several churches, specifically those of Verdun, Rebais, Aumont, Aninsole or Saint-Calais, and especially Saint-Denis in France, of which he [Col. 0496B] is regarded as the founder [Note: [Col. 0496C] Mab., ibid., p. 274, no. 12.]. He also took care to provide some others with good bishops; and, following the example of his father the king, he enjoyed having holy men at his court, such as Saint Didier of Cahors, Saint Eligius, Saint Ouen—then known by the name of Dadon—Saint Wandregisel, and several others [Note: [Col. 0496C] P. 560, no. 4; Bal., Capit., vol. I, pp. 141–142.]. As for his acts of valor, the most remarkable thing he did was to bring the Gascons and the Bretons, who had abandoned their duty, back into obedience [Note: [Col. 0496C] Fred., ibid., no. 78.].

This monarch died of dysentery on 19 January 638, or only in 637 if the year at that time began at Easter [Note: [Col. 0496D] Nos. 79; Mab., Dipl. supp., ch. 7, no. 2; Ana. vol. III, pp. 514–528; An. book XII, nos. 1–3.]. He was only thirty-five or thirty-six years old, and had reigned sixteen years, counting from 622, when Clotaire established him as king of Austrasia, and ten years from the death [Col. 0496C] of his father. The years of this prince’s reign long caused our writers difficulty in their calculations; but there is no longer any problem since Dom Mabillon took care to clarify the matter in a dissertation composed specifically for that purpose, as well as in the other places in his writings cited in the margin.

Dagobert was buried in the church of Saint-Denis, which he had enriched and in which he had established perpetual psalmody [Note: [Col. 0496D] Fred., ibid.; Mab., An., ibid.]. His tomb may still be seen there near the altar on the Epistle side; and each year, on the day of his death, his anniversary is still celebrated [Col. 0497A] there with a royal splendor. Du Chêne gave us his acts, filled with fables, after which his epitaph is read; we shall not reproduce it, because it is scarcely better [Note: [Col. 0497D] Du Chê., vol. I, pp. 574–590.]. He left two sons, Sigebert and Clovis, whom during his lifetime he had established, one as king of Austrasia and the other of Neustria [Note: [Col. 0497D] Fred., ibid., nos. 75–76.].

## II. His Laws and Other Monuments

It has been observed elsewhere that the laws which we must discuss here were first drawn up under the care of Thierry I, king of the Franks, and then revised and enlarged by some of his successors; but that it was Dagobert I who, after revising them, published them in the form in which they are read today, both in manuscripts and in [Col. 0497B] printed editions [Note: [Col. 0497D] Bal., Capit., vol. I, pp. 25–26.]. On this basis, people agree in attributing them to him, as belonging more legitimately to him than to the other kings who preceded him. These are the laws of the Ripuarians, the Alemanni, and the Bavarians—all ancient peoples who inhabited the upper Rhine region. It is commonly believed that Dagobert published them around the year 630. But perhaps one would have better grounds for placing this date a few years earlier, during the period when this prince governed the kingdom of Austrasia, before Clotaire’s death, administering justice and equity there.

**1. The law of the Ripuarians** is contained in eighty-nine titles, most of them subdivided into several articles [Note: [Col. 0497D] P. 27, 52.]. It has much in common with the Salic Law, which was discussed in its proper place; but it retains [Col. 0497C] more from Roman law, and its style is much less barbarous, although it still contains several expressions bearing the mark of the former rusticity of these peoples. Apart from this, like the Salic Law, it seeks to repress theft, murder, abduction, and other crimes and injuries, distinguishing free men from serfs and clerics from laymen; to regulate the penalties due from the guilty, which consist almost entirely of monetary fines or arbitrary compositions; to prescribe the duties of office to judges, forbidding them to accept any gift so as to prevent corruption; and finally to determine the manner of settling various disputes between the parties.

We have an edition of this law published separately from the following two; and it is the best that has appeared [Col. 0497D] to date [Note: [Col. 0497D] Journal des Savants, 1721, pp. 591, 393.]. We owe it to M. Eccard, who published it together with the Salic Law and several other works, both ancient and modern, from a manuscript which he says is from the ninth century and came from the city of Tours. This collection appeared in 1720 at Frankfurt and Leipzig in one folio volume. The editor enriched this law of the Ripuarians with learned and curious notes.

**2. The law of the Alemanni** contains ninety-nine titles, almost all divided into several articles [Col. 0498A] or chapters [Note: [Col. 0497D] Bal., ibid., pp. 53, 90.]. This law deals much more extensively than the preceding one with matters concerning clerics and ecclesiastical affairs, and presupposes that the peoples for whom it was made were more civilized than the Ripuarians. It gives considerable detail concerning injuries inflicted upon a bishop, a priest, an ordinary cleric, or a monk, and proportionates the penalty to the dignity of the person offended. These penalties, moreover, are monetary or arbitrary compensations, as in the law of the Ripuarians. The death penalty is mentioned only for murder committed against a duke. Few laws provide more detailed treatment of the various matters in dispute between parties. In addition to the ninety-nine titles contained in this law in the earliest editions, M. Baluze [Col. 0498B] found in an ancient manuscript from Reims two additions made to explain certain points more fully, and had them printed after the law. One of these additions contains forty-four articles, with some lacunae, and the other only three.

**3. The law of the Bavarians** (*Bajuvariorum*) has only twenty-one titles, yet it is more extensive than the preceding laws because each title contains several chapters, sometimes as many as twenty, and each chapter contains several articles [Note: [Col. 0498D] P. 91–140.]. It is composed in roughly the same manner as the others, with this difference, however: several articles have been inserted that concern subjects treated in various conciliar canons. Among these are those concerning the right of asylum granted to churches, incestuous marriages, the sanctification of Sunday, and the residence of priests and deacons with women. The penalty prescribed for anyone who killed a bishop is particularly remarkable [Note: [Col. 0498D] P. 99, ch. 11, no. 1.]. A lead tunic would be made for him according to his size, and he would pay its weight in gold, or its value from his property. If these were insufficient, he, his wife, and his children would surrender themselves to the service of the Church. In general, although these laws are filled with barbarous words, they are important for understanding the character and customs of the ancient peoples for whom they were drawn up.

We have several editions of them, produced at different times and in different places. They are printed together with the Salic Law and the laws of the Burgundians [Col. 0498D] and Saxons in a small duodecimo volume without date or indication of place or printer [Note: [Col. 0498D] Bib. S. Alb. And.]. They were also collected in the *Code of Ancient Laws*, which first appeared at Basel in 1557 in one folio volume, and then at Frankfurt in the same format in 1613, through the efforts of Frideric Lindenbrog [Note: [Col. 0498D] *Cod. reg. ant.*, pp. 399–470]. They also form part of another collection of ancient laws, printed in duodecimo at Paris by Jacques du Puy in 1573 [Note: [Col. 0498D] Bib. D. de Lorch.]. In all these editions the law of the Alemanni occupies [Col. 0499A] first place, that of the Bavarians second, and that of the Ripuarians last. In 1677, M. Baluze had them reprinted at the beginning of the *Capitularies of Our Kings*, placing them in the order in which we have discussed them [Note: [Col. 0499B] Bal., ibid., pp. 27–140]. The text of these laws in that edition is more correct and more complete than in the earlier ones. As early as 1720, M. Eccard led us to hope that he would publish a new edition of the laws of the Alemanni and Bavarians, as he had then published one of the law of the Ripuarians [Note: [Col. 0499B] *Journal des Savants*, ibid., p. 397]. He had already examined them against ancient manuscripts and enriched them with notes.

**4.** In addition to several diplomas of Dagobert in favor of various churches, though these are of lesser importance, two other monuments of this prince have been preserved [Col. 0499B] which are important for the history [Col. 0500A] of Saint Didier, bishop of Cahors, and highly honorable to his memory [Note: [Col. 0499B] Bal., ibid., pp. 141–144.]. One is a manifesto, or letters patent, announcing the election of this prelate and the reasons that led the prince to consent to it. The other is a letter to Saint Sulpicius of Bourges, urging him to go to Cahors to consecrate the new prelate and summon the bishops of his province for the ceremony. These two documents are dated 6 April, in the eighth year of Dagobert’s reign, corresponding to 8 April 629 before Easter, since this prince began to reign with his father in 622. The letter has been included in the general collection of councils; and the author of the *Life of Saint Didier* inserted both documents into his work [Note: [Col. 0500B] *Conc.*, vol. V, pp. 1855–1856; Lab., *Bib. nov.*, vol. I, pp. 703–704.].

[Col. 0499]

# ECCLESIASTICAL ORDINANCES OF DAGOBERT I, KING OF THE FRANKS

(Brequigny, *Diplomata*, vol. II, new edition, from which the notes are also taken.)

## I. Diploma of Dagobert I by which he transfers the Abbey of Saint Maurice, or the Thielogian Monastery, to the Church of Saint Peter of Trier [Note: [Col. 0499C] Published among the *Genealogies of the Dukes of Lorraine and Bar* by François Rosier, Paris, 1580, fol. 2 recto, who pretended that he had taken it from the monastery of Saint Maurice of Toledo; but he himself forged it, along with several other documents, in order to establish a genealogy of the dukes of Lorraine descended from the Merovingian and Carolingian kings. His ignorance of diplomatic matters was so great that it was easy to expose the fraud; he was therefore condemned by a solemn judgment and punished, Thuan., *History*, year 1583. His book, publicly denounced, should thereafter have deceived no one; nevertheless, the forger’s system was revived in our own century in the *Musaeum Lotharingicum vetus et recens* and in Hugo’s work, under the fictitious name of Baleicourt, and was again solemnly condemned in 1712. We reprint these spurious documents deliberately. Although their falsity must be regarded as a matter judicially settled, we nevertheless think it useful to set out briefly the principal indications [Col. 0500C] of it. On these matters, see the censorious notes of the highly learned Baron de Zur-Lauben in the *History of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions*, vol. XXIV, p. 180 and following.] (year 622).

[Col. 0499B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity [Note: [Col. 0500C] This initial formula is unusual for this period, as Mabillon and other masters of the diplomatic art attest, *Dipt.*, book II, chapter 2; *Chron. Gotwicense*, book II, p. 112, etc.]. Amen. [Col. 0499C] Dagobert, by the divinely ordained clemency, king of the Franks. Prudence requires that the memory of holy dispositions or exchanges be committed to writing, since through the representation of writing the cloud of forgetfulness is removed and the perversity of those who plot evil is destroyed. Therefore, let the diligence of all the faithful of God’s holy Church, both present and future, know that the apostolic man, our father, the lord Modoaldus, archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0500C] Modoaldus was elevated to the see of Trier in this very year, 622; see *Nov. Gall. Christ.*, vol. XIII, cols. 384 and 561. He did not authorize Dagobert to establish the Thielogian monastery until 623, which conflicts with the diploma under discussion, in which this monastery is falsely represented as having been constructed, endowed, and donated to the Church of Trier in 622. We pass over the title “archbishop,” by which Modoaldus and, below, Cunibertus are designated contrary to customary usage. Certainly, this title was in use at the beginning of the eighth century.], approached the summit of our serenity, requesting that we transfer a certain abbey of Saint Maurice [Col. 0500B] the martyr, called the Thielogian monastery, built by us and situated beside the River Saar, in the duchy called Mosellan Austrasia, to the church of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, which is known to have been built in the city of Trier, where the principal [Col. 0500C] seat of his bishopric is recognized to be, for the honor of God and of his saints resting there. Immediately, wishing gratefully to satisfy his suitable request out of reverence for him, we decreed that this should be done.

We have likewise given the same abbey, with its entire integrity, to the church of the aforesaid see, for the perpetual commemoration of the blessed memory of King Chilperic, our grandfather, as well as of Clotaire, our father, and of our paternal ancestors, namely Chilperic and Clotaire, most Christian kings, and for the perpetual commemoration of our own soul, together with its churches, vineyards, fields, people, roads, things acquired and to be acquired, movables and immovables, and all its appurtenances and dependencies. And for the aforesaid churches, and for the Father of the brothers of the aforesaid cell of Saint Maurice built upon the River Saar, we have appointed as protector, rector, and advocate the illustrious lord Clodulf, duke of Mosellan Austrasia [Note: [Col. 0501C] In the two diplomas that follow, forged by the same forger and purportedly dated 623, the duke of Mosellan Austrasia is called Arnulfus, Clodulf’s father.], son of Duke Arnulfus, born of royal blood.

Therefore, by this present decree of our authority, we donate and transfer all these things so that they may belong eternally to the frequently mentioned see, namely under the condition that the aforesaid bishop and his successors may possess perpetual authority over the aforesaid abbey, just as over the other affairs of that bishopric, and may securely dispose of everything according to the usefulness of that church and as they deem appropriate, so that the rulers of that see, together with all the clergy subject to their governance, may always delight in imploring the mercy of God for us, for our aforesaid predecessors, and for the protector appointed.

May this authority of our donation, never violated by any successor of ours, possess the firmest stability in the name of God throughout all the ages as the world turns. Having strengthened it by our protection, we confirmed it below with our own hand together with Duke Clodulf, and ordered it sealed by the impressions of our rings; so too did Cunibertus, archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0501C] Cunibertus did not yet preside over the Church of Cologne [Col. 0501D] on 1 May 622; he obtained the insignia of the Church of Cologne on 26 September of that year; see *Nova Gall. Christ.*, vol. III, col. 626.]. Given on the Kalends of May, in the year 622 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0501D] The years of the Incarnation attached to Merovingian diplomas prove them to be spurious products, as we have noted more than once. See *Dipl. nov.*, vol. IV, p. 695, etc. Rosier adds an enumeration of the seals and describes with great display the heraldic coats they supposedly exhibit; this clearly reveals both the forger’s ignorance and the falsity of the document.]. Executed at Metz, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God.

Dagobert, king of the Franks. Cunibertus, archbishop [Col. 0501C] of Cologne. Clodulf, duke of Mosellan Austrasia.

## II. Diploma of Dagobert I by which he confirms the property of the Church of Saint Peter of Trier, orders the cell of Saint Hilary, or Saint Maximinus, to remain under that church’s jurisdiction, and appoints Arnulfus, duke of Mosellan Austrasia, as advocate for both [Note: [Col. 0501D] Rosier published it among the *Genealogies of the Dukes of Lorraine and Bar*, fol. 1, claiming to have found it in the monastery of Saint Hilary, but in reality he composed it himself, after another diploma published by Brower in the *Annals of Trier*, vol. I, p. 351, which we shall reprint below. Rosier, however, adulterated Brower’s document in many ways and enlarged it with a lengthy interpolation, in order to lend some credibility to his fable about the dukes of Lorraine descended from the royal blood of the Franks, which was the principal object of his frauds. We distinguish the discrepancies, and especially the interpolations, by brackets. Rosier’s false diploma is rejected, among others, by Brower, p. 351, whom see, and also by Masenius in his notes to Brower, note 13, p. 608.] (year 623).

[In the name of the Lord, amen [Note: [Col. 0502D] This initial formula is absent from Brower. “Who,” asks Brower, p. 352, “with any knowledge whatever of ancient history, has heard of dukes being called dukes of Mosellan Austrasia in this period?”].] Dagobert, king of the Franks, to the illustrious [duke Arnulfus of Mosellan Austrasia [Note: [Col. 0502D] The diploma published by Brower contains nothing about Arnulfus.], and to the other] dukes, counts, household officers, and all administrators both beyond and on this side of [Col. 0502A] the Rhine, Loire, and Moselle, both absent and present.

We believe without doubt, in the name of our God, that this will remain for the increase and stability of our kingdom if we bring to fulfillment what priests request and what the rightful petitions of churches have made known to our ears. Therefore the apostolic man, our father, the lord Modoaldus, archbishop of Trier, presented to our sight a decree of our predecessors, earlier kings and our relatives—Sigibert, Theodebert, Theodoric, and especially the glorious king Lothar, of good memory and remembrance, our father—confirmed by their hands. It contained the statement that not only our father himself but also the aforesaid kings who preceded him, namely the kings of the Franks, had assigned to the Church of Saint Peter of Trier whatever property good and holy men, out of devotion to God, had given to it, and had confirmed it by the authority of their seals, so that their kingdom might be protected by heavenly assistance and that afterward, in the heavenly kingdom, they might rejoice with Christ in a blessed end.

For the firmness of the matter, the aforesaid prelate Modoaldus petitioned our sublimity to follow the custom of our father and predecessors and order such a decree of authority concerning these same properties, out of love for God and reverence for Saint Peter. We willingly granted his request and decreed that this decree of our authority should be made for that church, out of love for divine worship and for the remedy of our soul.

By it we command and order that all properties or resources belonging to the Church of Saint Peter of the city of Trier—namely, the cell of Saint Hilary, now called the cell of Saint Maximinus, which was built on the estate of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0502D] Here Brower mentions other cells belonging to the Church of Trier besides the cell of Saint Maximinus, namely those of Saint Paulinus, Saint Eucharius, and Saint Mary. Rosier took this as an opportunity to fabricate a separate diploma, see below (Col. 504, note h) for the cell of Saint Eucharius, closely resembling this one in many respects, and in which he revived his fable about Arnulfus in order to support it with several documents.], castles, villages, estates, vineyards, forests, people, and whatever, through the gracious clemency of God, may henceforth be added to enlarge that church, situated around the Rhine, Loire, [or Moselle] [Note: [Col. 0502D] The name “Moselle” is absent from Brower’s diploma and was inserted by Rosier so that the text would better accord with Arnulfus of Mosellan Austrasia, whom he pretends was appointed advocate of the Church of Saint Maximinus.]—shall all remain perpetually subject to the right and power of the Church of Saint Peter of Trier and of its bishop.

[For better observance of this matter, and so that the property of the aforesaid churches [Col. 0503A]—namely, of blessed Peter and blessed Maximinus—may be preserved prosperously, and so that no further harm may be inflicted upon them by plunderers, we give to the aforesaid Church of Saint Peter of the city of Trier and to the brothers of the aforementioned cell of blessed Hilary, now called the cell of Saint Maximinus, built on the estate of Saint Peter, as protector, rector, and advocate the illustrious lord Arnulfus, born of royal blood, our kinsman and instructor, duke of Mosellan Austrasia; and we command him faithfully to observe all these things [Note: [Col. 0503C] This lengthy clause, entirely absent from Brower, was inserted by Rosier and exposes the whole contrivance of his fable.].]

For this reason we likewise decree that no one of the [dukes], public judges, or anyone exercising judicial authority shall place any impediment in the monastery, around the churches, cells, villages, fields, people, or other places [Note: [Col. 0503C] Rosier omits much here that is found in Brower concerning the immunities of the properties belonging to the churches mentioned there.]. Rather, let the aforesaid prelate and his [Col. 0503B] successors be permitted to possess all the aforesaid things in their entirety forever, for the remedy of our soul or those of our relatives, as is contained in the decree of our most pious father, in quiet order, and faithfully to obey our command [and that of our lord Arnulfus] [Note: [Col. 0503C] The repeated mention of Arnulfus, added by Rosier, was intended to lend greater credibility to the fictitious interpolation.].

But so that this decree of our authority may possess fuller force in the name of God, and may be more truly believed by the faithful of holy God’s Church, namely those of the present and future times, and more diligently preserved by our successors, we confirmed it below with our own hand [together with our princes [Note: [Col. 0503D] Brower reads *luidis* instead of *principibus*. Rosier evidently thought this word less suitable alongside the name of Duke Arnulfus, which he intended to append to the subscriptions.]], and ordered it sealed [by the impressions of our rings]. [Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the year 623 from the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0503D] The diploma published by Brower speaks only of the king’s ring and contains no chronological notation. Brower nevertheless writes in the margin the twelfth year of Dagobert’s reign, namely among the Austrasians, which corresponds to the year 634 of Christ. We shall discuss this below, when we examine Brower’s diploma.].]

Dagobert, king of the Franks. Cunibertus, archbishop [Col. 0503C] of Cologne. Atto, bishop of Metz. Principius, bishop of Speyer [Note: [Col. 0503D] The episcopal subscriptions in Brower differ slightly; but since they do not agree with the year 623 of Christ, Principius did not preside over the Church of Speyer before 642, *Nova Gall. Christ.*, vol. V, p. 716; Atto is not listed among the bishops of Metz unless by this name Abbo is meant, who did not obtain the insignia of Metz until 625, ibid., vol. XII, col. 699. Brower acknowledges the subscription of Pippin the mayor of the palace, but omits the title “duke of Hasbania,” which Rosier freely bestows upon Pippin.]. [Arnulfus, duke of Mosellan Austrasia.] Pippin, mayor of the palace, [duke of Hasbania] [Note: [Col. 0504C] Rosier appends a note to the diploma in which he describes heraldic coats, the same as those in the preceding diploma—coats entirely unknown in this period, as we observed above (Col. 501, note c).].

## III. Diploma of Dagobert I by which he confirms the property of the Church of Saint Peter of Trier, orders the cell of Saint Eucharius, or Saint Matthias, to remain under that church’s jurisdiction, and appoints Arnulfus, duke of Mosellan Austrasia, as advocate for both [Note: [Col. 0504C] Another production of the notorious forger Rosier; see what we mentioned above (Col. 502). This spurious diploma exists only among the *Genealogies of the Dukes of Lorraine and Bar*, fol. 1 verso. Rosier says that he found it in the archives of Saint Eucharius of Trier, but he composed the whole of it himself in order to lend some authority to his fable concerning Arnulfus, duke of Mosellan Austrasia and descended from the royal blood of the Franks. It is rife with the same signs of falsity as the other diploma that he likewise fabricated for the Church of Trier and the cell of Saint Maximinus, published above by us (Col. 502). In both, Modoaldus is given the title of archbishop; the years of the Incarnation are used as chronological notations; Atto’s name at Metz is corrupted and does not fit the period; we admit that the name Pippin, bishop of Speyer, was written by a copyist’s carelessness in place of Principius, who truly was bishop of Speyer, but not before 642, *Nov. Gall. Chr.*, vol. V, p. 716. We spoke above (note g) of the heraldic coats which Rosier falsely and absurdly claims existed in both diplomas. We should be ashamed to dwell on these matters any longer.] (year 623).

[Col. 0504A]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Dagobert, by the favor and ordinance of divine providence, king of the Franks. It is fitting for every person in authority, and especially for princes—royal, humble, and moderate—to obey the prayers of those living under religion, and, according to their ability, to foster and thereafter secure their quiet and peace.

Therefore, let the discernment of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable and apostolic man, our father, the lord Modoaldus, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, presented before us a decree of the earlier kings of the Franks. It contained the statement that our predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had assigned to the Church of Saint Peter of Trier whatever properties good and holy men, out of devotion to God, had given to it; that they had confirmed them by the authority of their decrees; and that they had appointed worthy dukes as protectors and advocates, so that their kingdom might be defended by heavenly assistance and that afterward, with Christ the King of kings, they might reign in heaven.

For the truth and firmness of the matter, the aforesaid prelate Modoaldus petitioned our highness to follow the custom of our father and of the preceding kings and order such a decree of authority concerning these same properties, out of love for God and reverence for Saint Peter, and to provide them with a protector or advocate. We willingly consented to his petition and decreed that this decree of our authority and protection should be made for that church, out of love for divine worship and for the remedy of our soul.

By it we command and order that all the resources or properties belonging to the Church of Saint Peter of the city of Trier—namely, the cell of Saint Eucharius, now called the cell of the apostle Saint Matthias, built in the territory of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, together with castles, villages, estates, vineyards, forests, people, and whatever, through the gracious clemency of God, may henceforth be added to enlarge that church, situated around the rivers Rhine, Loire, or Moselle in our kingdom—shall all remain perpetually subject to the right and power of the Church of Saint Peter of Trier and of its bishop [Col. 0505A] [Note: [Col. 0505D] Everything that follows is found in precisely the same words in the preceding diploma. See our notes to that diploma (Cols. 501–503).].

For better observance of this matter, and so that the property of the aforesaid churches may be preserved prosperously—namely, so that no further harm may be inflicted by plunderers upon the churches of blessed Peter and blessed Eucharius—we give to the aforesaid Church of Saint Peter of the city of Trier and to the brothers of the aforementioned cell of blessed Eucharius, now called the cell of the apostle Saint Matthias and built on the estate of Saint Peter, as protector, rector, and advocate the illustrious lord Arnulfus, born of royal blood and our [Col. 0505B] instructor, duke of Mosellan Austrasia; and we command him faithfully to observe all these things.

Furthermore, we likewise decree that no one of the dukes, public judges, or anyone exercising judicial authority shall place any impediment in the monastery, around the churches, cells, villages, fields, people, or other places. Rather, let the aforesaid prelate and his successors be permitted to possess all the aforesaid things in their entirety forever, for the remedy of our soul or those of our relatives, as is contained in the decree of our most pious predecessors, in quiet order, and faithfully to obey our command and that of Lord Arnulfus.

But so that this decree of our authority may possess fuller force in the name of God, and may be more truly believed by the faithful of holy God’s Church, namely those of the present and future times, and more diligently observed by our successors, we confirmed it below with our own hand together with our princes and ordered it sealed by the impressions of our rings. Given on the third day before the Ides of November, in the year 623 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

Dagobert, king of the Franks. Cunibertus, archbishop of Cologne. Atto, bishop of Metz. Pippin, bishop of Speyer. Arnulfus, duke of Mosellan Austrasia. Pippin, duke of Hasbania, mayor of the palace.

## IV. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he transfers to the basilica of Worms property belonging to him in the district of Ladenburg and confirms its possessions, together with their immunities (year 627).

[Col. 0505D] Dagobert (Dagebert), king of the Franks. We wish all to know how, reflecting upon the salvation of our soul and future recompense, we have resolved entirely in our mind [sign] to make the churches of God co-heirs with us from our hereditary possessions and to increase the sites of the saints. Concerning this we took good counsel with our nobles, Pippin, who is mayor of the palace, Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and Hunibert, archbishop of Cologne (bishop), and from this we confidently hope to obtain the Lord’s mercy and to merit the intercession of his saints [Note: [Col. 0505D] Cointius, in the place cited above, judges the words from “Concerning this” through “we hope” to be interpolated, both because Hunibert is adorned with the title of archbishop, then still unusual, and because that same Hunibert is said to have given the king good counsel together with the nobles, at the same time as Arnulf, bishop of Metz, who did not begin to participate in royal counsels until after Arnulf had renounced the episcopate and withdrawn into the wilderness. The authors of the New Gallia Christiana do not recognize the words that have rashly crept into the diploma.]. Therefore, all faithful people of God and of us, present and future, recognize (know) how we hand over in its entirety all possessions (omnes res; variant *omnis res*) of our right in the district of Ladenburg (Lobedungowe), and whatever appears to belong to our city [Note: [Col. 0506D] See annotation e below.], and everything that has hitherto belonged to our fisc, except the stipend and the county, leaving nothing out of it (*nihil*; variant *nichil ex eo*), great and small, to the basilica of Saint Peter (with the addition “and Paul”) the apostle (with the addition “or of the other lords”), built in the city of Worms, [Col. 0506B] over which the lord, the apostolic man Amandus, presides.

This is what we hand over: our city of Ladenburg (Lobedunburg), our palace (the word “our” omitted), buildings, slaves, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields, meadows, open country, all the woodland (*omne sylvaticum*; variant *omnem*) in the Odenwald forests, with every appurtenance throughout the district of Ladenburg (Lobedungowe), and everywhere along the Intraha (Jutraha) [Note: [Col. 0506D] Schannat writes *intrantia*, as in the confirmation of this privilege granted by Charlemagne. The text of the Academy of the Palatinate at Heidelberg has *Jutraha*, which is a river.], in pastures, timber, waters and watercourses, fisheries, those already sought and those to be sought, every toll (*omne theloneum*; variant *omnem*), market, and whatever can be said or named, just as it previously appeared to be assigned to our use [Note: [Col. 0506D] From this it may be inferred that the words “assigned to our use” should more properly be written above, in place of “belonging to our city.”], so henceforth we have granted it to the aforesaid basilica to possess, for the increase of eternal reward. And under complete *communitas* (“immunity”; variant *immunitate*) we newly reconfirm by our writ everything belonging to that [Col. 0506C] basilica, just as (*sicuti*; variant *sicut*) in the preceding year we granted the protection of *communitas* (“immunity”) to all (variant “and all”) villas, properties, or abbeys, and whatever appears to pertain to the city of Worms itself, so that no public judge may dare (variant plural, “may dare”) to cause any hindrance—whether by hearing lawsuits (variant: “nor for hearing lawsuits”), exacting fines, or distraining the men of that church, both freeborn and servants—unless this has been granted and conceded for the benefit of (variant: “to”) that church, or Bishop Amandus himself or his successors have (variant: “are held to have”) it granted and conceded, so that they may possess and exercise lordship (variant *dominare*) in peace over what it was customary to render to the fisc.

And so that this charter may be more firmly established, we have decreed that it be strengthened by our hand and by the subscriptions appended below [Col. 0506D]. Dagobert (Dagebert), king of the Franks. Godefrid (Odefrid) examined it. Given (the word “given” omitted) on the second (eleventh) day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth year of our reign [Note: [Col. 0506D] Dagobert’s sixth regnal year agrees with the year of Christ 627, counting the beginning of his reign from 622, when Dagobert began to reign among the Austrasians. See what is said below (Col. 509, note b, and Col. 511, note c).]. Executed at Mainz, in our palace, very happily.

## V. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the division of property between Ursinus and his brother Beppolenus [Note: [Col. 0507C] Mabillon recovered this document, written in Merovingian letters on Egyptian papyrus, from the Dionysian archive, now in the royal archive, K, tab. IV; he reproduced it engraved in copper in the *Supplement to De re diplomatica*, tab. II, p. 70, and there, p. 92, had it printed in ordinary letters. It was published again in the *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. I, appendix II, p. 685; finally it was transferred (reprinted), from Mabillon’s edition, into the *Collection of Writers on Gallic Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 631, and also by Marini, *Diplomatic Papyri*, no. 60. We reprint it after collating it most carefully with the plate published by Mabillon. Certain spaces occupied in the autograph by obliterated letters [Col. 0507D] have been marked with dots, and, as far as possible, the extent of the spaces has been indicated by numerals in parentheses. The signs prefixed to Dagobert’s name at the beginning of the diploma, and to Burgundofaro’s name at the end, can be seen in the copper engraving made by Mabillon.] (year 628).

[Col. 0507A]

Dagobercthus, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

Whenever the petitions of faithful persons, in which our interests are disclosed, have been made known to us, we willingly wish to hear them individually and, in God’s name, bring them to fulfillment. And therefore, illustrious and faithful man, by God’s favor our Ursinus [Note: [Col. 0507D] According to Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 343, this Ursinus was the same person who subscribed to the diploma of Chlothar, about which we have spoken elsewhere.] petitioned the clemency of our kingdom that, from what he and his brother Beppolenus had received in a deed of division—both from the inheritance of his father Chrodolenus and from his late brother Chaimedes—the places called Ferrarias, Leubaredo Villare, and Eudoncovilla, together with the remaining property, [Col. 0507B] or those villas which are known to have come to them at Rotenecus through an agreement concerning their mother’s hereditary property—that is, with lands, buildings, slaves, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, and the remaining things or appurtenances belonging to . . . [space of three or four letters], as stated, and which had come to his share, and which they presently held in rightful possession.

He further affirms that, by a fuller agreement concerning the places and the remaining property, subscribed by his aforesaid brother Beppolenus, or by a strengthening of the property . . . [approximately four syllables missing] [Note: [Col. 0507D] At this point Mabillon, in the specimen printed in ordinary characters, inserted the syllable *cta*, which is absent from the copper engraving.], he has them in his possession; and likewise he affirms that he has in his possession the deeds of sale by which he appears to have pur. . . chased (*con. . . rasse*) certain shares from some people in the places written above [thus in the copper engraving. [Col. 0507C] Mabillon reads *comparasse*]. The aforesaid man therefore petitioned that our full grant concerning him should be confirmed by a charter.

Because of his petition, for the more secure confirmation of the matter, we did not wish to refuse it. We therefore command that whatever he is known to have received in the aforesaid places or in the remaining property, in proper order [one-letter lacuna], as his share, after examination of the agreement made with his aforesaid brother in the division, and whatever he is known to possess in those places by virtue of the purchases, so that he appears presently to possess it by rightful title, is confirmed to him generally by our authority in God’s name; and that this be held by him [space of four syllables] . . . ndat, and be left to him and his descendants to possess perpetually.

And so that this authority may endure with firm stability for all time, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand [Note: [Col. 0507D] This diploma contains no chronological notes. Mabillon, in the places cited above, pp. 343 and 685, assigns it to the year 628, and we follow him. In the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs* it is placed after another diploma of the same Dagobert, issued in the fourteenth year of his reign, that is, in A.D. 635 or 636.].

Burgundofaro [Note: [Col. 0507D] Burgundofaro, who here performs the office of referendary, is, according to Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 343, the same person elsewhere called Faro, brother of the virgin Fara, who was also called Bungundofara. First married, then having dismissed his wife and received the veil, he became a cleric and eventually obtained the insignia of the Church of Meaux in the year 626, according to the *New Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1600. He was called Burgundofaro, as though “the Burgundian Faro,” that is, a man of noble Burgundian descent. That he was both bishop and referendary is not at all contradictory. On these matters see Plessaeus in his notes to the *History of the Church of Meaux*, vol. I, p. 654, note 23.] requested. Dagobercthus, king, subscribed.

## VI. Writ of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, ordering that Desiderius receive the bishopric of Cahors [Note: [Col. 0508D] It is inserted in the *Life of Saint Desiderius*, written by an almost contemporary author according to Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 358, or in the eighth century according to Pagius, *Annals of Baronius*, vol. II, under the year 629, no. 11. It has been published several times: first by Labbe, *Manuscript Library*, vol. I, p. 703, in the *Life of Saint Desiderius* from the Herouvall manuscript; then by Cointius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 808, and Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. I, col. 141, from the Moissiac manuscript. We follow Baluze’s edition, who says, vol. II, col. 1020, that he compared this diploma more carefully with the manuscript. Nevertheless, we have placed in angle brackets various readings of some importance from Labbe’s edition. This writ was also reprinted in the *Supplement to the Councils* by Lallande, p. 64, etc.; in Ruinart’s appendix to Gregory of Tours, col. 1314; again by Labbe, *Curious Miscellanies*, vol. II, p. 420; among the *Documents Relating to the Liberties of the Gallican Church*, vol. II, part II, chap. 15, p. 66; and in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. III, p. 520. It has been printed so often because its chronological notes, many of them disputed and full of controversy, have prompted discussions concerning the succession of the bishops of Cahors and the chronology of Dagobert’s reign. See below (note b).] (year 629).

[Col. 0508B]

Dagobert, king of the Franks, to the bishops and dukes and to all the people established within the boundaries of Gaul.

It is fitting for the clemency of our rule [the word “our” is absent in Labbe] to pursue with careful investigation and to consider with vigilant concern that our choice or arrangement should agree in all things with God’s will; and while, by the Lord’s generosity, regions and kingdoms are known to have been entrusted to us for governing, the privileges of office should be committed to those whom praiseworthy life, upright conduct, or noble birth elevates.

And because we have learned that the illustrious man Desiderius, our treasurer, has from the very time of his boyhood preserved religious observance in all things, [Col. 0508C] and, beneath secular dress, served as a soldier of Christ, possessing angelic ways and priestly conduct, so that the fame of his goodness has spread and grown not only in neighboring regions but also in distant lands, therefore we believe that he rightly ought to be advanced to the priesthood [Col. 0509A] whom, as we have said, we continually see striving toward the heavenly homeland, adorned with virtuous conduct. And since the agreement of the citizens and abbots of Cahors emphatically demands that they have him as bishop, and our devotion likewise consents, we undoubtedly believe that this is being done by God’s will: although he is very necessary to us in our palace, we are, in a certain sense, compelling ourselves to remove him from our own household and to provide him, for the public good, from our own residence [Labbe: “to provide him from our houses for your public benefit”].

But since, as we have said, we remove him from our own household, we who have received regions and kingdoms from God, although we suffer loss by doing so, ought to provide such shepherds as can govern according to God and in accordance with apostolic teaching the peoples entrusted to them and to us [better in Labbe: “entrusted by us”], [Col. 0509B] so that a greater reward may accrue to us. Therefore, in accordance with the petition of the citizens and our will, which agrees with it in all things, we decree and command that, with the Lord’s assistance and with the clergy and people acclaiming his praise, the illustrious man and true worshiper of God, Desiderius the bishop, be consecrated in the city of Cahors; and that the will of our citizens and ourselves, which has been decreed, be fulfilled in all things in God’s name and be exalted by episcopal blessing—provided that, with Christ’s favor, we profess this true religion: that his life and conduct are regarded by all as worthy and approved, so that he ought to pray for us and for all the orders of the Church and diligently offer acceptable sacrifices to God. For we believe that by this our life will be prolonged to a greater age, with the Lord as author, [Col. 0509C] if he is chosen and exalted in the priesthood who may confidently offer prayers for us, for you, and for those entrusted to him before Christ’s tribunal, and who may stand as an intercessor at the future judgment to excuse our faults [Labbe: “the faults of sinners”].

Therefore, by the present authority we decree that the aforementioned Desiderius presently receive the bishopric in the city of Cahors and, with Christ’s favor, hold it throughout his lifetime. And so that this decision of our will may be regarded as firmer, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscription of our hand. Chrodobertus presented it. King Dagobert subscribed. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of April [Labbe: “on the Ides of April”] [Note: [Col. 0509C] According to Labbe’s edition, *Manuscript Library*, vol. I, p. 703, the writ was issued on the Ides of April, that is, on the thirteenth day; according to the Moissiac codex, on the sixth day before the Ides, that is, on the eighth. Everyone will judge that the numeral VI was more likely omitted by scribes than deliberately inserted.], in the eighth year [Note: [Col. 0509C] Critics disagree greatly as to which year of Christ corresponds to the eighth year of Dagobert’s reign. Some count the years of this reign from Dagobert’s assumption of the kingdom of Austrasia, others from the death of his father Chlothar. Even those who agree on one or the other method of computation do not therefore agree among themselves as to the year of Christ to which Dagobert’s eighth regnal year should be assigned. See what Mabillon, at the end of his *Analecta*, p. 520; Cointius; Pagius, in the places cited above; and, more recently, Vaissette, note 78, pp. 679 ff., in his notes to the *History of Occitania*, have discussed on this subject. We would be detained too long in examining the various opinions. It is enough to say that Mabillon, in his dissertation cited above on the year and day of Desiderius’s ordination, and Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. II, p. 809 ff., proved that the eighth year of Dagobert’s reign in the writ under discussion should be counted from the beginning of his reign among the Austrasians, that is, from the beginning of spring 622. Vaissette, in the place cited above, refers the beginning of the reign to October of that same year and consequently argues that April of the eighth year falls in A.D. 630. We, however, counting the beginning of Dagobert’s reign from the beginning of spring 622 with Mabillon, Pagius, and even Valesius, *Frankish Affairs*, book XVIII, p. 21, place the diploma under the year 629. We shall discuss this again and more fully in our notes to Dagobert’s brief concerning the consecration of Desiderius. See below (Col. 512).] of King Dagobert.

## VII. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he establishes the market of Saint Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0510C] Published by Dublet in the *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, p. 655, from an original parchment; reprinted by Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, vol. I, p. 241, and by the editors of the *Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 627. Foppens, in his notes to Miraeus, in the place cited above, p. 342, says that this instrument was published by Félibien in the *History of the Royal Monastery of Saint Dionysius*: incorrectly, for Félibien neither published nor even cited it; what he relates about the fairs of Saint Dionysius in his *History of Saint Dionysius*, p. 14, he supports from the *Chronicle of Fredegar* and the *Deeds of Dagobert*, passing over Dagobert’s diploma, perhaps because he suspected it. Cointius openly declared it false, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. II, p. 824; but Mabillon regarded it as of excellent quality, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 345, and refuted Cointius’s accusations. The original no longer exists in the archive of Saint Dionysius. We publish it from a thirteenth-century manuscript cartulary preserved in that same archive and most generously communicated by Dom Poirier, to whom our Collection owes much. It also exists in the Colbert Codex of the Royal Library, no. 5415. Marini also published the same diploma, *Diplomatic Papyri*, no. 61.] (year 629).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to Leuthon, Vulfion, and Rauco, counts, and to all our agents, [Col. 0510B] vicars, centenaries, and other officials of our public authority.

Let your diligence and prudence know how we have wished and established, in honor of our lord and glorious patron Dionysius, that a market be founded for the very feast that occurs on the seventh day before the Ides of October, once each year, for all merchants residing in our kingdom or coming from overseas, on the road that leads to the city of Paris, at the place called Pasellus of Saint Martin.

And know that our messengers and all the cities in our kingdom, especially the ports of Rouen and Wicus, which come from overseas to buy wine, honey, or *garantia*, shall have this toll remitted this year and the next, and previously, until the third year. Thereafter, from each *quarrada* [a measure] of honey they shall pay two solidi to the representatives of Saint Dionysius, and likewise two solidi for each *quarrada* of *garantia*. And those Saxons and Vicars [Note: [Col. 0510D] For *Vicarii*, the editions have *Ungarii*. Labbe says that he read *Vigarii* in an old manuscript, perhaps the same from which we took this instrument; he orders it corrected in this way and supposes that the vicars were so called from Vicarius Portus, whence there was a frequent gathering at the market of Saint Dionysius, as is said at the beginning of this diploma.], and the Rouennais, [Col. 0511A] and the other provincials from other cities shall pay, for those ships, twelve denarii for each *quarrada*, as well as *vultatici* and *passionatici*, through all their successions and generations, according to ancient custom.

We also order that the market extend for four weeks, so that merchants from Lombardy, Spain, Provence, and other regions may be able to arrive there. And we expressly wish and command that no merchant dare conduct business in the Parisian district except in the market that we have established and arranged in honor of Saint Dionysius; and if anyone does so, let him pay our ban for this to the representatives of Saint Dionysius.

Finally, we expressly command and instruct you and all your agents, whether present or future [Note: [Col. 0511C] For *vestros* the more recent copy preserved in the archives of Saint Dionysius, copied from the Colbert manuscript, reads *nostros*.], that the party of Saint Dionysius shall never suffer any hindrance from us or from you in connection with this market, either within the city of Paris or outside it in the district, with respect to those tolls, ships, port dues, bridge dues, river dues, road dues, *vultatici*, *themonatici*, *chespetatici*, *pulveratici*, *foratici*, *mestatici*, *laudatici*, *saumatici*, *salutatici*—all of them and from all sources, whatever the party of Saint Dionysius or its agents could exact from this market, from the merchandise itself, on behalf of us or the public fisc—so that the party of Saint Dionysius or its agents may possess it perpetually by this our favor and authority.

And so that this writ of ours may be regarded as firmer for that holy place in our times and in those to come, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand [Col. 0511C] and have ordered it sealed with our ring. Dagobert [Note: [Col. 0511C] The word *ego* before Dagobert’s name is found in the printed editions. Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 627, rightly considers that it has intruded rashly and should be entirely removed. For this word is not prefixed to Dagobert’s subscriptions in the authentic diplomas of this king that we have been able to examine; this had led critics to suspect forgery. The old cartulary before us does not recognize the word, nor does the Colbert manuscript copy mentioned above (note a).] the king, subscribed. Dado presented it. Given on the third day before the Kalends of August, in the second year of Dagobert’s reign [Note: [Col. 0511D] Cointius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 824, argues from these chronological notes that the diploma in question is false. For, he says, in the second year of his reign Dagobert did not possess Neustria, and therefore the establishment of the fair of Saint Dionysius did not belong to him. This is true if Dagobert’s regnal years are counted from his assumption of the kingdom of Austrasia in A.D. 622. But Mabillon observes, *On Diplomatic Matters*, pp. 626 ff., that the computation should begin with the death of Chlothar II and Dagobert’s assumption of the kingdom of Neustria in 628. Cointius adds that in Dionysian charters Dagobert’s regnal years were sometimes counted from the beginning of his reign in Austrasia. Why, then, should Dagobert’s years of reign not have been counted in some documents from his Austrasian reign and in others from his Neustrasian reign? Different systems of this kind of computation occur in other royal documents, as Cointius himself admits, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 803, in connection with a diploma of King Childeric. Thus Mabillon dissolves Cointius’s charge of forgery. It should also be noted that this writ of Dagobert was confirmed by diplomas of subsequent kings, which will be published in their proper place.], at Compiègne, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## VIII. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he orders Sigibert, his paternal cousin, to restore to Otho a fortress situated in the Alps [Note: [Col. 0512C] Published by Labbe in the *Curious Miscellanies*, vol. II, p. 407, from manuscript papers whose reliability he admits he regarded with suspicion. But we are astonished that a man wholly devoted to handling and copying ancient charters should have given a place in his collection to an instrument of such foul falsity that it could offend even the eyes of the blind. We would be ashamed to spend any time examining this monster of audacity—not to say ignorance.] (year 630).

[Col. 0512A]

In the six hundred and thirtieth year of salvation, the eighth year of Lothar II, king of Gaul, our father, the one hundred and fifty-ninth year since the collapse of the western empire, the nineteenth year of Heraclius, eastern emperor, and the sixty-ninth of Honorius, Roman pontiff, on the fourth day of the month of May.

We, Dagobert the Great, king of Austrasia and of the Burgundians, at the request of our mother Beretrude, queen of the Franks, having first examined ancient tablets prepared by Roman emperors, while always preserving fidelity, and having also considered our origin from the most noble patrician Fabian stock, restore, grant, and confirm [Col. 0512B] the fortress situated in the Curian Alps of Rhaetia, in Praevalitana, called Castrum-Altum of the village of Praevanus, with all revenues and rights belonging to it, including the tithes from Mount Julius as far as the town of Oscela on Lake Larius in the said Praevalitana, to Otho, a brave man of the equestrian order, our military commander against Ariovaldus, the sixteenth king of the Lombards.

Therefore, to you, Sigibert, our beloved paternal cousin and first duke of Alemania, we order, command, and expressly require that you restore the aforesaid fortress to the aforesaid Otho, our commander, with all the things that belonged to it when it was seized from him, and establish him as vassal of all the property previously held by his ancestors. In witness whereof, etc. Given [Col. 0512C] in our fortress of Isenburg.

## IX. Brief of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, ordering that Desiderius be consecrated bishop of Cahors at the solemnity of Easter [Note: [Col. 0512D] There are many kinds of briefs, all written in epistolary form; on them see Du Cange’s *Glossary* and the *New Treatise on the Art of Diplomatics*, vol. I, pp. 270 ff. Briefs were especially common under the Merovingian dynasty, as is clear from the old formulas of Marculf and others. The brief we reprint here differs little from the royal diplomas called writs. This charter, taken from the *Life of Saint Desiderius*, where it followed Dagobert’s writ issued in the same year and presented above, has often been printed. Besides the books in which we stated that Dagobert’s writ was published (see the preceding page, note c), the brief was inserted without the writ in Hardouin’s *Collection of Councils*, vol. III, col. 2085. We follow Baluze’s edition, adding in angle brackets variants of some importance from Labbe’s edition.] (year 630).

To the holy lord and apostolic lord, my father Pope Sulpicius, King Dagobert.

Since we believe that it is already well known to Your Holiness how our faithful man, the illustrious Desiderius (Labbe: “truly illustrious”), our treasurer (Labbe omits “our”), has faithfully served us from the time of his adolescence, and that we have become well acquainted with his most devout and monastic way of life, know therefore that we have decreed the following: in the city of Cahors, where his brother, Lord Rusticus, previously served as bishop, he ought in God’s name to receive the honor of the episcopate in his place.

For, under divine inspiration, our devotion remains such that those whom we perceive to be adorned with good conduct and devoted to holy works—such as this most faithful servant of God and of ours, Desiderius—we ought to advance to the episcopal height. [Col. 0513B] It is fitting for royal majesty to strive to promote to such an office those whom it knows to conduct themselves in the fear of God, to preserve the Catholic faith intact, and to observe the evangelical commandments in every respect.

Therefore, since we know that you hold the metropolitan dignity (Labbe: “we know that you hold the position of arch-metropolitan” [Note: [Col. 0513B] See Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. II, col. 1020.]), we have taken care to send this present letter, with the proper duty of greeting, to Your Holiness, asking that you hasten to bless him and direct letters to your provincial brothers, so that they too may be present, in order that canonically and according to apostolic [Col. 0514A] institution, in our presence [Note: [Col. 0513B] All printed editions except Baluze have “in your presence.” Baluze’s reading seems preferable to us. For when the king had commanded Sulpicius to hasten to bless Desiderius, it was surely superfluous to order him also to have the blessing take place in his own presence. It is therefore probable that this was written not concerning Sulpicius’s presence but the king’s. Baluze copied the brief from the same Moissiac manuscript from which Cointius copied it; but in ancient instruments the reading of *vestri* and *nostri* is often ambiguous. From Baluze’s reading it follows that Dagobert was present in the city of Cahors at the solemnity of Easter. It is therefore not surprising that he wished to display such care in consecrating Desiderius, his treasurer, whom he greatly loved and whose blessing he wished to attend.] at the holy solemnity of Easter, he may be confirmed by episcopal blessing (Labbe: “may be consecrated”).

We also earnestly ask above all that you commend us to the Lord in your holy and God-pleasing prayers, and that you make no delay in completing the task we impose upon you.

We have decreed that this brief be strengthened by the subscription of our hand, as is customary. King Dagobert subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0513C] Cointius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 808, and certain others engaged in textual criticism think that the brief preceded the writ by a considerable interval; others conjecture that both were issued on the same day. A full discussion would detain us if we entered into the matter in detail. Those who argue that the brief preceded it take their principal argument from the fact that, if the writ is said to have preceded the brief, the time available is too short: the writ by which Desiderius’s election was approved was issued in April of the eighth year of Dagobert’s reign; this must be understood as referring to his reign in Austrasia—see Cointius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 809. Some, including the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. III, p. 585, note 713, maintain that this reign began in October of A.D. 622. Therefore April of the eighth year of that reign was A.D. 630. In that year Easter fell on the sixth day before the Nones of April, the very day on which the writ was issued; consequently the brief ordering the consecration to take place at the solemnity of Easter must have been sent earlier.

It should be observed, however, that the solemnity of Easter extends for eight days from Easter Day itself, according to Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 345. Eight days would have been sufficient for the brief to reach Sulpicius, for him to notify his provincial bishops, and for them to travel to Cahors—difficult, certainly, but not impossible. [Col. 0514B] The words of the brief, which command the bishops to hasten and again not to delay in completing this task, imply that the greatest diligence was required.

But if the beginning of Dagobert’s reign is reckoned not from the end of 622 but from the spring of that year, as many assert—for example Mabillon, *On the Year and Day of Desiderius’s Ordination*, no. 4; Pagius, under the year 629, no. 9; Valesius, and others—then April of the eighth regnal year falls in A.D. 629, when Easter was on the sixteenth day of that month, leaving a longer interval from the eighth day. Why should we not say that the brief was sent only at the beginning of the following year, 630? This certainly seems more probable, and we are no longer pressed by the narrowness of the time.

As for why so long an interval elapsed between the writ and the brief, one may conjecture the reason: namely, that the consecration might take place in the king’s presence, since he had decided to attend it, as may be inferred from the words of the brief itself. (See above, note b.)

What chiefly moved us not to place the brief before the writ was the order of events stated in Desiderius’s Life in these words: “The king’s decision having been published, and Desiderius having been elected to the episcopate by the unanimous voice of the citizens, authority was given to Sulpicius . . . he himself invites the provincial bishops,” and so forth. Thus, preserving this order, the brief follows the writ in the Life itself; and we have thought we should do the same.]

## X. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, concerning the many churches he built in honor of Saint Dionysius and subjected to the principal church of Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0514D] Hiretius published this diploma in his *Antiquities of Anjou*, p. 95. Cointius had it reprinted, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 860, not because he placed any confidence in it, but rather to demonstrate that it deserved no confidence whatsoever. He shows its falsity by several indications. The word “archbishop,” then unusual in Gaul (see, nevertheless, vol. I, p. 147, note 3), suggests a later age; the indiction is not consistent with the fourth year of Dagobert’s reign among the Neustrians; the names of the subscribers do not at all agree with that same year; and the forger’s ignorance is revealed by the mention of a church dedicated to Saint Leodegarius, who was not appointed bishop of Autun until the reign of Chlothar III, Dagobert’s grandson. We omit the rest.] (year 631).

[Col. 0514B] Dagobert, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man, to archbishops, bishops, record-keepers. Not unmindful of the benefits which the generosity of the supreme King has bestowed upon the merits of the most blessed Dionysius, our special patron and protector, and also keeping before our eyes the condition of human frailty—indeed, cherishing in heart and mind a heartfelt love for that same blessed Dionysius and the fitting fulfillment of that love—among the many things which we have bestowed upon his church, in which we desire to be buried, we have built many churches in our kingdom. We caused these, dedicated in his honor and name, [Col. 0515A] to be subjected to his principal church.

One of these we built near the fortress of Doe, on the border of the Poitevin territory and in the diocese of Angers, and, after consecrating it to the name of that most blessed martyr, we subjected it to his aforesaid principal church, together with two other churches built within the same fortress: one in honor of Saint John the Baptist, and the other in veneration of blessed Leodegarius. We also gave two estates situated in the same diocese of Angers, namely Sisiacum and Albiniacum, together with the two churches built in those estates and dedicated in honor and memory of the aforesaid most excellent martyr.

We have also granted to blessed Dionysius whatever adjoins those five churches, together with the income from all their possessions. Therefore we ordered this precept of our Highness to be drawn up [Col. 0515B] and given to the aforesaid Saint Dionysius and to the brothers serving the Lord there, so that they may hold and possess the said churches perpetually, without anyone’s opposition. And so that everything might be preserved unaltered for all time, we have confirmed this authority of ours with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with our ring.

Dagobert, most glorious king; Louis, son of Dagobert; Arnulf, bishop of Metz; Aurifalus, most learned bishop of Nomen. Given through the hand of Dado, chancellor of royal dignity. Done successfully at Paris, in the name of God. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of April, in the twelfth indiction, in the fourth year [Note: [Col. 0515C] The fourth year of Dagobert’s reign among the Neustrians began at the beginning of spring in the Christian year 631, according to Cointius, Mabillon, Longuerue, and Pagi, whom we follow. Thus the abbot of Longuerue expressly says, in the Annals of the Franks, under the year 628, at the end of volume III, p. 686, col. 1, of the Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs published there: “I believe that Clotaire died at the beginning of spring.” We entirely agree with him.], while Dagobert was reigning.

## XI. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants the monastery of Saint Dionysius the right of asylum

[Note: [Col. 0515D] Printed by Dublet, History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius, p. 657. It exists in a fourteenth-century chartulary, marked 5415, in the Royal Library. Valesius rightly regarded it as spurious and disfigured by a fictitious story drawn from the Deeds of Dagobert, which are full of fables. The unusual privilege which this charter pretends was granted to the church of Dionysius proves it to be a spurious production. Nevertheless, Sirmond, Labbe, and Mansi placed some confidence in this document and, relying on its authority alone, believed that a synod had been held at Clichy in Dagobert’s fifth year. Hence, in Hardouin’s Collection of Councils, at the end of volume III, p. 2685, there is a notice of this synod, and a fragment of the charter in question is copied from Sirmond’s papers. See Mansi, General Collection of Councils, vol. X, col. 591. Dom Labbe will show that no synod of Clichy was held in this year, in the new edition of the Councils of Gaul, eagerly desired by the Gallican Church and soon to be committed to the press; we acknowledge that we owe him much.] (year 632).

[Col. 0515C]

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, counts, centenarii, vicars, and our other officials. Whatever we presently decree and bring into effect for the welfare of the holy Church of God and for the sake of honor, we confidently believe to be of the greatest necessity to us against visible and invisible enemies. Therefore, in the name of God, while seated in a general synod at our palace at Clichy, we deliberated together with the venerable bishops, abbots, counts, and our other faithful men about how the honor and praise of the church of the blessed martyrs—namely, of our special patron, the lord Dionysius, [Col. 0516A] and his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius—might be maintained and observed.

That is, if any fugitive, fleeing to the aforesaid basilica of the blessed martyrs because of any crime, should reach the Tricenna bridge, or, coming from the direction of Paris, should pass Montmartre, or, leaving our palace, should cross the public road that leads to Louvres, then, just as God delivered us through those holy martyrs from the hands of our enemies and from the fury of our lord father, so all who take refuge there shall be released and saved.

But if Almighty God, through the intercession of those holy men, clearly delivered a brute animal—namely, a stag—[Note: [Col. 0516D] This is the fable sung by the anonymous and wholly untrustworthy author of the Deeds of Dagobert, and long ago rejected by all learned men: the story of a stag taking refuge in the church of Saint Dionysius, while the dogs were excluded and barked at it. See Valesius, On Frankish Affairs, book XVIII, pp. 18 ff.] there in that sacred place, how much more is it fitting that rational human beings, whatever offense or crime they may have committed, whether against us, against succeeding kings of the Franks, or against any other faithful member of the holy Church of God, should be released and set free.

For we solemnly charge and earnestly adjure all our successors, kings or princes, by the holy and undivided Trinity and by the coming of the just Judge, that the honor and reverence of the holy mother church, where our lord and patron, the most holy Dionysius, rests, be preserved in every respect, just as the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul at Rome is known to possess it by virtue of the privilege of the emperor Constantine. Whoever does not observe this, let him be anathema both here and in the future.

But so that this authority of ours might obtain fuller and firmer force in the name of God, we and our holy synod [Col. 0516C] have decided to confirm it below with our signatures.

Landeric presented it. Dagobert the king subscribed. Laudomerus the bishop consented and subscribed. Crodobertus the bishop consented and subscribed. Acterius, sinful bishop, subscribed. In the name of Christ, Eligius the bishop subscribed. Rannemundus the bishop subscribed. In the name of Christ, Sylvinus the bishop subscribed. Dado, [Note: [Col. 0516D] Dado, also called Audoenus, was not raised to the see of Rouen before the year 639. It would be tedious and unnecessary to examine the individual episcopal subscriptions, since they are attached to a spurious charter.] bishop of the church of Rouen, consented and subscribed. Lorado the bishop consented. Mauricius the bishop consented. Palladius, sinful bishop, subscribed. Aegynayvi [Note: [Col. 0516D] In the royal chartulary this word is written in separate capital letters: A. E. G. Y. N. A. V. I.] subscribed. Clarus subscribed in the name of God. Ermenricus, illustrious man, subscribed. Hubertus, consenting, subscribed. Dado the sinner consented.

[Col. 0517A] Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, in the fifth year of the reign [Note: [Col. 0517C] Since Dagobert’s reign among the Neustrians began at the beginning of spring in 628, May of the fifth year of this reign was the Christian year 632.] at Clichy, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## XII. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he declares and confirms all the possessions belonging to the church of Saint Peter of Trier

[Note: [Col. 0517C] Published by Brower in the Annals of Trier, vol. I, p. 351, and from him by Miraeus, Diplomatic Works, vol. I, p. 242; by Calmet, History of Lorraine, vol. I, p. 250; and finally by Hontheim, in his Diplomatic and Pragmatic History of Trier, vol. I, p. 76. This is the same charter which the notorious forger Roserius printed after adulterating it with new additions; we previously had it reprinted (col. 501), with a mark of disgrace prefixed. Roserius inserted the chronological note “year of the Incarnation 623,” which plainly exposes its falsity. In Brower, there is no chronological note in the text, but a blank space is left after Dagobert’s subscription, while the regnal year 12 is written in the margin. Zyllesius vigorously attacked this document, generally regarded as genuine, in Defense of the Abbey of Saint Maximin, part II, section 2; Hontheim gives his arguments and declares that they completely destroy the credibility of the charter. The authors of the New Gallia Christiana, vol. XIII, cols. 383 and 523, appear to agree with them. See the following note for the indications of forgery brought forward by Zyllesius.] (year 632).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, to the illustrious men, dukes, counts, household officers, and all our officials both beyond and on this side of the Rhine, and beyond the Loire, both absent and present. We undoubtedly believe, in the name of God, that the increase and stability of our kingdom will endure if, assenting to the just petitions of priests and the churches of God, we bring to completion what they have made known to our ears.

Therefore the apostolic man, our father, the lord Modoaldus, archbishop of the church of Trier, brought us a charter confirmed by the hands of the earlier kings, our predecessors and relatives—Sigebert, Theodobert, Theoderic, and, indeed, the glorious king of blessed memory, our father Chlothar. It contained the statement that not only that same father of ours but also his aforesaid predecessors, the kings of the Franks, had confirmed by the authority of their charters all the possessions which good and holy men had assigned to Saint Peter’s church of Trier for the sake of divine contemplation, so that their kingdom might be protected by heavenly aid and that afterward they themselves might rejoice with Christ in the heavenly kingdom, in an everlasting end.

Accordingly, for the security of the matter, the aforesaid bishop Modoaldus [Col. 0517C] begged our Sublimity, following the custom of our father and predecessors, to order a charter of this kind, expressing our authority, to be made concerning those same possessions, for the love of God and in reverence for Saint Peter. We gladly granted his petition and decreed that this charter of our authority be made for that church, out of love for divine worship and for the remedy of our soul.

By it we command and order that all possessions or estates belonging to the church of Saint Peter of the city of Trier—namely, the cell of Saint Hilary [Note: [Col. 0518C]

Zyllesius argues, in the work cited above, that the cell of Saint Maximin was nowhere called by the name of Saint Hilary; this is the principal argument he makes against the authenticity of the charter, though it is merely an argument from denial and does not diminish the force of the opposing evidence. Zyllesius maintains that the monastery of Saint Maximin was first dedicated by Saint Agritius to Saint John the Evangelist, according to a charter which we shall publish below under the year 633 (col. 522). But, together with Mabillon, Cointius, Hontheim, and others, we shall show that this charter is spurious. Thus Zyllesius’s argument collapses. He is no more successful when he wonders that Dagobert expressed his name in letters appended to the charter. For this was Dagobert’s practice, since he was skilled in writing. See the subscriptions which he affixed to the excellent charter reproduced by Mabillon in copper engraving, On Diplomatics, supplement, p. 70, and which we published above (col. 507).

Another argument, no less important, is drawn from the judgment delivered in the year 953 in the dispute of Robert, bishop of Trier; this may be seen in the Collection of the Councils of Gaul, vol. XIII, cols. 937 and 524.]

[Col. 0518A] which is now called Saint Maximin and which was built on the estate of Saint Peter; the cell of Saint Paulinus and Saint Eucharius; and the monastery of Saint Mary, which the aforesaid bishop Modoaldus recently built from its foundations in the territory of Saint Peter and which is called Horrea; the basilica of Saint Martin, situated in the district of Maiginum; and the other basilicas, fortresses, villages, estates, vineyards, woods, people, and whatever else, by the generosity of divine clemency, may henceforth be granted for the enlargement of that church, situated around the Rhine and Loire rivers within our kingdom—all these possessions shall remain perpetually assigned under the right and power of Saint Peter, the church of Trier, and its bishop.
