Moreover, we establish in like manner that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall dare, in our time or in that of our successors, to enter the monasteries, churches, fortresses, villages, fields, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid church, whether beyond or on this side of the Rhine or Loire, in the districts or territories within the power of our kingdom which the aforesaid church possesses or which divine power may henceforth increase under the right of that holy place, for the hearing of cases, the collection of fines, tributes, or any other taxes, the provision of lodging or supplies, the taking of sureties, the coercion of the church’s people, the investigation of unjust exactions, or the collection of tolls; nor may they presume at all to exact any of the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess all the monasteries, estates, villages, and fortresses mentioned above, with their appurtenances, wholly and perpetually, for the remedy of our soul and those of our parents, in peaceful order, just as is contained in the charter of our most pious father, and faithfully to obey our command.

But so that this charter of our authority might obtain fuller force in the name of God, might be more truly believed by the faithful of the holy Church of God, namely by those of our present and future times, and might be more carefully preserved by our successors, we have confirmed it below with our own hand together with our leudes (luides), [Col. 0519A] and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Dagobert, king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0519C] A blank space is left here. Brower wrote in the margin: “Given in the twelfth year of the reign,” which coincides with the Christian years 632 and 633, if Dagobert’s reign is reckoned as beginning in the spring of 622, as we have often stated. Several of the subscriptions that follow do not fit Dagobert’s twelfth year. Principius became bishop of Speyer in 642; Abbo became bishop of Metz in 690. The bishop of Cologne is called an archbishop, contrary to usage. From these facts we suspect that the subscriptions were added by modern writers.], … Cunnibertus, by the grace of God archbishop of Cologne. Abbo, bishop of Metz. Principius, bishop of Speyer. Pipin, mayor of the palace.

## XIII. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants Sigirannus the estate of Longoretus for the construction of a monastery, and Milepecum for the construction of a basilica

[Note: [Col. 0519D] This charter was published by Choppinus, Monasticon, book II, p. 261, and by the Sammarthani, Gallia Christiana, vol. IV, p. 828, who recovered it from an old parchment codex, though they nevertheless regarded it as suspect. Labbe later published fragments of it in Miscellanea, vol. II, p. 413, from manuscript papers which he too admits were suspect. He apparently did not know that the complete document had been printed sixty years earlier—something we certainly find surprising, since Labbe was a diligent investigator of ancient monuments and highly skilled in bibliographical matters. We are committing it to the press again [Col. 0520C] from a copy said to have been compared with the original and communicated to us in this collection by the highly deserving Dom Turpin of the congregation of Saint Maur. [Col. 0520D] We have enclosed Labbe’s fragments in parentheses; readings of some importance from the printed editions have been placed between brackets. Dom Turpin informs us that the autograph has perished; he also notes that the old copies are interpolated. Yet throughout the text of the charter we detect so many and such substantial indications of forgery that we judge the whole to have been fabricated by a forger, as the following notes will show. Mabillon did not deign to mention this document even once in his Annals; and the authors of the New Gallia Christiana rejected it, vol. II, p. 130.] (year 632).

When throughout the whole world the Christian faith [Sammarthani: “of the Christian religion”], to be dispensed by the holy apostles, was being spread, with teachers, prodigies, and signs of miracles going before it [Sammarthani: “pressing forward”], and the name of Christ having been proclaimed, an innumerable multitude [Col. 0519B] of people of every condition flocked to the sacrament of baptism, to be cleansed from the guilt of their former fault. Therefore Clovis, king of the Franks, received through the preaching of Saint Remigius [Sammarthani: “of Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims, through divine inspiration breathed by him; from him, the first of the Frankish kings, [he received] the baptism”] the bath of baptism and sacred purification.

From that Clovis—who was the first of our people to be imbued with the faith of Christ—I, Dagobert, son of King Chlothar, son of Chilperic, son of Chlothar, son of Childebert [Sammarthani: “son of King Chlothar, from that same Clovis”], am the fifth in descent. Drawing the life of my blood from him, I am a true worshiper of the faith of Christ and of the undivided Trinity, at whose command not even the stars resist, and everything that exists in heaven serves. Preferring the dwelling-place of the heavenly homeland, I desire to increase the sacred places founded with relics of the saints and built by holy imitators of the apostles, through the possessions granted to me by God [Choppinus: “by divine will”], and also to build foundations in places where the memory of Christ has not been established, without delay [Choppinus: “wherever the memory of Christ has not yet been established, without delay”].

There is a place not far from the borders of the Poitevin and Touraine districts, extremely rich in pastures for cattle and beasts of burden [Choppinus adds: “innumerable”], watered by flowing streams and pleasant for the hunting of wild animals. I often wished to stay there; and because of the frequent presence of kings, for the sake of delight, the inhabitants call it Longoretus [Note: [Col. 0520D] Here the grant of Longoretus is being discussed, as though it preceded the grant of Milepecum. This conflicts with the Life of Sigirannus; see it in Labbe, Manuscript Library, vol. II, p. 443, and Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, second age, p. 437. We shall return to this matter below (col. 521, note c).], [Col. 0520A] which I am pleased to give to Sigirannus, my kinsman, who, desiring to enjoy a more fortunate life than that of the archdeaconate of Tours, has withdrawn under the monastic rule and declares to me that he wishes to spend his life with the brothers already joined to him.

Therefore I, Dagobert, king of the Franks, living in tranquil peace by the divine clemency’s preordination, together with my son Clovis and with many of my nobles present, give and grant the aforesaid place, situated along the course of the Clasia [Choppinus: “Clasis”] and marked out in honor of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary [Choppinus: “marked out in honor”], together with the entire court and all the rights belonging to that court: churches with their tithes, namely, and their dues, and every ecclesiastical payment [Choppinus: “jurisdiction”]; whatever land, cultivated or uncultivated; tolls on the public roads; the pasturage of the forests; and also the poll-tax from all the people belonging to that court [Choppinus: “the taxes and everything”; Sammarthani: “the tax and from all”]. In short, everything which appears to exist—from the course of the Andria to the course of the Crouse, around the boundaries of the territory of Berry and the Poitevin border—which remain under my dominion and proper lordly power [Choppinus and Sammarthani: “under my lordship”], I give, grant, and confirm as perpetual possession, with royal power and dignity, to Sigirannus, son of Sigelaicus, count and bishop of Tours, so that he, renouncing secular pomp as the son of the count of Berry, and striving to please God through chastity, guardian of the virtues, may be permitted there to build, from my own possessions and resources, a coenobitic [Col. 0520C] monastery, as he conceives in his mind], and, together with the company of brothers who have vowed to live for God under the regular order of monks [Choppinus: “to vow themselves to God under the protection”; Sammarthani: “to devote themselves to him in life”], may gladly keep watch, under the protection of the Mother of God, who is more powerful than we are, with devoted service to the mysteries of God, for his own salvation and ours.

This place, therefore, which I regard as especially important from the beginning of its construction [Sammarthani: “constructing”], we adorn with a portion of the life-giving wood on which Christ suffered, enclosed in gold; with a portion of the garment of the Mother of God; with a portion of John the Baptist’s chin; and with relics of other saints, which we possess from religious [Col. 0521A] men. We adorn it also with the reverent service of the most honorable men—namely, clerics and monks singing praises to God [the word “sacred” is absent in Sammarthani]—so that the faithful people who come here devotedly to pray may know whose intercessions they ought, with God’s favor, to implore.

(For I commend, admonish, and command Clovis my son, whom I establish as my successor in the kingdom of all France in peace and tranquility [Note: [Col. 0521C] What Dagobert says here—that he established Clovis as successor to the entire kingdom of France after his death—cannot be reconciled with the histories. For from the Chronicle of Fredegar, chapter 76, we learn that, although the kingdom of the Neustrians was assigned by Dagobert to Clovis when he was scarcely born, the kingdom of the Austrasians was at the same time assigned to his elder son Sigebert. This reveals both the falsity of the document and the ignorance of its forger.], to refuse no expense, out of paternal love [Choppinus and Sammarthani: “my love”], with God rewarding him, if, as the number of monks living in this place increases, it should be necessary to add something from our possessions or resources beyond what we have given. And if any of our heirs, collateral relatives, kinsmen, or outsiders, unable to restrain himself through envious fury, should presume to disturb or alienate any part of this, whether great or small), he shall perish in the infernal fire with the devil, or, having opposed Sigirannus or the monks who follow him and serve God and his holy mother Mary forever [Sammarthani: “him”], he shall await royal vengeance and, in addition, shall be worthy of the wrath of God, together with those to whom on the day of judgment he will say: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his ministers.” With the two sons of Korah, namely Dathan and Abiram, may he be swallowed alive by the opening of the earth; or, hated by heaven and earth like Judas the traitor, may he be reduced to dust and perish, exposed to the whirlwinds of the winds [Note: [Col. 0521C] In Choppinus, everything preceding the words “and if anyone” is absent.].)

Therefore, for the firmness of the perpetual tenure of this gift of ours, we command that the place which Sigirannus now says he has foreseen [Choppinus: “provided”] as suitable for the construction of a basilica in honor of Saint Peter, and which he also calls Millepecum [Choppinus: “Mollepecum”], [Col. 0522A] be designated, together with all the churches already built or yet to be built, and with all tithes, tolls, pasturages, and taxes, and with all revenues from the lands and forests—whatever, namely, is seen to be cultivated or uncultivated there, as has been said—within the boundaries of the aforesaid territories, so that succeeding kings may acknowledge that they ought to be protectors and patrons of this royal monastery against every attack by persecutors, if anyone should presume to seize anything, as though from our gift or grant [Choppinus: “fee”; Sammarthani: “fief”], or by any fraudulent device [Note: [Col. 0521D] Choppinus ends here.].

I, Dagobert, and my son Clovis, by royal power and dignity, confirm, authorize, and ratify this gift with our own hands, in honor of the holy Mother of God and perpetual virgin Mary [Sammarthani: “this gift, through devotion to the holy…”]. In her honor I order an altar to be made in my royal residence, for the celebration of the solemn sacrifice, until a larger building is constructed.

In the year 632 from the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0521D] The chronological notes based on the year of the Incarnation are absent in the Sammarthani. Whether they existed in certain copies unseen by the Sammarthani and were later removed by editorial care, or whether they subsequently entered other copies, is difficult—and unnecessary—to investigate. Other chronological markers, which the fabricator seems to have heaped together to give greater credibility to the fictitious document, destroy all confidence in it. The indiction, epact, and lunar date added here do not agree with one another, nor were such notes appended to charters at that time. The year reckoned from the episcopate of Vulfoldus is likewise demonstrably false, since Vulfoldus could not have assumed the title of bishop until three years after Dagobert’s death: he was appointed coadjutor bishop of Bourges in 641, Gallia Christiana, second edition, vol. II, p. 130. It would be tedious and unnecessary to adduce further indications of forgery from the style and formulas. We place this charter under the year 632 because it expressly gives that year. In fact, its synchronisms seem to assign it to later years, for Dagobert’s son Clovis had not yet been born in 632. But it is not our task to determine the year in which this charter was given, since we have shown it to be spurious; we must attach it to the year in which it is pretended to have been given.], with Vusseodus [Sammarthani: “Vulfoldus”] occupying the episcopal see of the city of Bourges; in the sixth indiction, epact XI, lunar day VII.

The sign of Lord Dagobert. The sign of Pipin, duke of the royal household. The sign of Ebroin. The sign of Clovis. The sign of Count Odo [Sammarthani: “The sign of Ebroin. The sign of Count Dodo”; likewise Labbe]. The sign of Boso, chief keeper of the keys. The sign of Theodoric, precentor.

It was confirmed at the dictation of Sigirannus [Note: [Col. 0522D] Labbe here has: “The sign of Clovis.”]

## XIV. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which, after an inquiry into the origins of the monastery of Saint Maximin of Trier, he confirms its gifts, privileges, and grants, and himself makes new gifts

[Note: [Col. 0522D] Published by Miraeus among the Belgian charters, vol. I, p. 124, who noted that the autograph preserved in the archive of Saint Maximin was shown to Rosweyde in 1624. Zyllesius likewise had the same charter printed from that autograph in 1638, Defense of the Abbey of Saint Maximin, part I, p. 8, and part III, p. 9, together with Dagobert’s monogram engraved in copper and the seal of the same king, by which he says it was enclosed; he testifies that it remained complete and undamaged. We have had it reprinted several times: in Cointius’s Ecclesiastical Annals, vol. III, p. 6; [Col. 0523C] in Brusch’s Annals of the Monasteries of Germany, fol. 125 verso; in Calmet’s History of Lorraine, vol. II, p. 70; and in Nic. ab Hontheim’s Diplomatic History of Trier, vol. I, p. 78. We follow Zyllesius’s edition, since it was copied from the archetype itself. Papebrochius regarded this charter not merely as genuine but as a model of genuine charters, in the Propylaeum, no. 22. Mabillon, however, attacked it so forcefully, On Diplomatics, p. 218, that Papebrochius afterward admitted that he had been defeated. Cointius had preceded Mabillon in attacking this document; Nic. ab Hontheim supports them. We shall review their principal arguments in the notes that follow.] (year 633).

[Col. 0522C]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0522D] Mabillon derives the first ground for suspicion from this invocation, which was unusual under the Merovingian kings.].

[Col. 0523A] Let all Christian diligence know how I, Dagobert, most powerful king [Note: [Col. 0523C] Mabillon, in the work cited above and more fully on p. 88, and Cointius, Annals, vol. I, p. 7, maintain that Dagobert never spoke of himself in the singular number in the text of his charters, nor with any complimentary title, but only with the designation “illustrious man.” They mention several other features altogether unsuited to this age, which we pass over.], after a suitable council with my bishops and counts, sent envoys on my behalf to the abbot Memilianus, instructing him to investigate carefully and report to me personally by whose authority that monastery of Saint Maximin had been built, or to whose command it had been subject from ancient times.

The abbot, having diligently received this embassy together with the brothers, and having read certain very ancient documents found in that place, discovered that the monastery had been the royal temple of the emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0523D] Cointius and Mabillon reject this fable; see them in the works cited above.], and that by his command it had been dedicated by Saint Agritius, the venerable bishop, in honor of Saint John the Evangelist.

In that temple, as the same father of the monastery explained to our Royal Highness in a trustworthy account, the aforesaid emperor, at the request and with the favor of the holy servant Helena, gathered the poor of Christ and placed over them a man of God named John, so that they might devote themselves continually to God’s service and persist in prayers for him. Moreover, he did not wish the habitation of that place to be subject to any other persons except to his own authority and that of succeeding emperors.

Having firmly understood that these matters were so, I establish according to royal custom and command by an exceedingly firm order that no one should ever presumptuously enter that monastery, over which the aforesaid abbot appears to preside, or violently inflict any inhuman treatment upon it.

Therefore, so that constant remembrance of me and my parents might remain in the aforesaid monastery, I took care to enlarge the provisions of the prebendaries of Saint Maximin, which had been established under the aforementioned emperor, by adding estates on my behalf. Their names are these: [Col. 0524A] Kannis, Cressiacum, Lunewich, Regiodola, Vallis Poliche, Baudeliacum, Talevant, and Loavia.

These places belong to the royal estate called Decima [Note: [Col. 0523D] Calmet, History of Lorraine, in the work cited above, shows that the estates or royal courts of the Merovingian kings were designated by numerical names. See also Dom Germanus’s dissertation on Royal Estates.]. I have transferred that estate, with all the possessions belonging to it—that is, whatever estate I appear to possess from the river called the Rubera as far as the forest called Leder—to Saint Maximin the bishop as a perpetual inheritance.

Furthermore, with the advice and request of my chief men, I have firmly and perpetually decreed for the future, concerning the groups serving God there, that the full and undisturbed number of one hundred monks shall always remain there, except if the benevolence of emperors [Note: [Col. 0523D] This manner of speaking suggests at least the tenth or eleventh century.] or princes succeeding one another throughout the ages should enlarge the estates or treasures.

And if, because of the devastation caused by pagans, unbelievers, or Christians, extreme want should befall those same servants of Christ, and it could not be driven away by the expenditure of treasure, they shall have permission from Almighty God and from me and my successors to give or sell the allod, together with its dependents, which has been transferred to them by the faithful, before the services of God are destroyed.

And so that the confirmation of this document might remain firm forever, I ordered it to be written out and confirmed it thereafter with our seal [Note: [Col. 0523D] This formula, Mabillon says, is entirely different from Merovingian formulas.].

Given on the day before the Nones of April [Note: [Col. 0523D] April of Dagobert’s twelfth regnal year corresponds to the Christian year 633, if the beginning of his reign is reckoned from the beginning of spring in 622.], in the twelfth year of our reign, successfully at Mainz. Amen.

The sign of Dagobert the king [Note: [Col. 0523D] Zyllesius had a monogram engraved here. But the Merovingian kings placed a sign and their name on charters before the chronological notes, and used a monogram only when they did not know how to write, as Mabillon shows, On Diplomatics, p. 110. Dagobert, however, was skilled in writing, as is clear from the charter which Mabillon had engraved in copper, Supplement to On Diplomatics, plate 2, where Dagobert’s name may be seen subscribed in reasonably elegant letters.]. Henry, chancellor, examined this in place of Ricolfus, archchaplain [Note: [Col. 0524C] The title “archchaplain,” as Mabillon teaches, On Diplomatics, p. 114, was not used for the chief chancellor before the tenth century and under the second dynasty of our kings. The subscriptions attached to this charter, which Zyllesius published twice, differ in some respects; we reprint them following the example of part III.]

## XV. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, concerning the foundation of the monastery of Haslach

**[Note: [Col. 0524C]** Coccius first published it, p. 158, in *Dagobertus episcopatus Argentinensis fundator*, from Haslach documents. Vorburg followed Coccius in *Historia rerum Germanicarum*, vol. VIII, p. 257; Cointius in *Annales ecclesiastici*, vol. III, p. 768; Schoepflinus in *Alsatia illustrata*, vol. I, p. 36; Henschenius in *De tribus Dagobertis*, p. 88; and Berain in his commentary on the Dagoberts, part IV, p. 72. More accurately, however, Abbé Grandidier, a man highly skilled in diplomatic scholarship, had it reprinted in *Historia ecclesiae Argentinensis*, vol. II, proofs, p. 35, from a shapeless parchment written in the sixteenth century and preserved in the archives of the collegiate church of Haslach—the same document that Coccius had transcribed; no other copy survives. Cointius, Mabillonius (*Annales Benedictini*, vol. I, p. 533), and Schoepflinus declared the instrument spurious in every respect; D. Grandidier agrees with them in *Historia ecclesiae Argentinensis*, vol. II, dissertation IV, p. 88, where he examines it carefully. Anyone who turns his eyes to this spurious offspring will marvel alike at the audacity and ignorance of the forger, for its style in no way suits the age of Dagobert. The childish story of Dagobert’s being severely struck down by Saint Michael so embarrassed Henschenius that he removed it entirely from the charter. He also removed the chronological notes and the names of the witnesses, hoping thereby to lend the instrument some credibility, as though it had been cleansed of interpolations; but he did not remove all the indications of forgery, as the following notes show.]** (year 633).

**[Col. 0524C]**

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

**[Col. 0525A]** Dagobert **[Note: [Col. 0525D]** This charter confuses two Dagoberts, as Cointius perceptively observed, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 768. Certainly, the statements about Dagobert as an outstanding devotee of Saint Dionysius, about his wife Nanthild, and about his sons Sigebert and Clovis belong to the first king of that name. But Florentius, at whose request Dagobert is alleged to have founded the monastery of Haslach, belongs to the age of Dagobert II; hence Mabillonius, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. I, p. 533, judges, with better reason, that this monastery was founded by Dagobert II in the year 676, rejecting the charter published by Coccius. The names of the witnesses, moreover, indicate partly the reign of the elder and partly that of the younger Dagobert, as Cointius teaches; see him.]**, by the favor of divine clemency, king of the Franks. To all the leading men of his kingdom, indeed to all who profess the Christian faith, both present and future: grace to you and peace from him who is, who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.

A vow by which anyone has bound himself to God and the saints cannot be rendered void without the stain of guilt; and the greater and more worthy is he to whom the vow is made, the heavier the judgment that will strike the presumption of one who vows and does not fulfill it. We therefore ought and wish also to render what we vowed to the terrible Lord God, and to him who takes away the breath of princes, terrible among all the kings of the earth. We have thought it worthy that all should be informed, as an example of correction, how he terrified us by the power of his arm, and how, striking and healing, he visited us again—especially so that every faithful person, having heard of our danger, might refrain from laying waste the churches of God and might show due honor to things dedicated to God.

First, therefore, we shall briefly explain the terrifying divine examination that took place against us; afterward, the vow and the fulfillment of our vow. When my father Clothar, of blessed memory, died, I assumed responsibility for my father’s kingdom. But, led by youthful frivolity and distracted by a desire to rule, I neglected the obligations of royal office, showing neither the diligence nor the care required by the charge entrusted to me, and doing or judging nothing with gentleness or zeal for justice.

Among my other transgressions, I had begun to be a destroyer and despoiler of churches, although I ought to have been their defender and promoter, fearing neither the eyes of the divine majesty nor the outcry of men. At last, the goodness of God, crushing the pride of my obstinate mind, visited my iniquities with the rod of correction, and, after chastising me, did not deny me forgiveness.

For I was carried aloft and presented before the divine Majesty, seated among the choirs of the saints in the appearance of a judge. I was gravely and persistently accused by the most holy patrons of the churches because of the ecclesiastical property that I had seized and squandered by robbery, especially by Mary, the most holy Mother of God, and by the holy archangel Michael, receiver of souls, and by the most blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles.

Since, burdened by conscience, I did not dare defend my crimes, I was condemned to punishment at the judge’s discretion. After I had long been beaten and exhausted by savage torments, the aforesaid archangel appeared, holding a fiery sword over me and wishing to exact vengeance from me for the goods I had usurped from him and from the saints named above, and because of the outcry of the needy and the poor, against whom I had been hostile with the material sword, judging no judgments rightly.

At last my special patron, the martyr Dionysius, came to my aid, making satisfaction for me to the holy archangel Michael. By his prayers he obtained for me both a respite from the punishment that was pressing upon me and time for repentance. He himself, as though establishing the terms of my penance, placed in me the hope of complete indulgence on this condition: that I should build, in honor of God and of the saints whom I had most offended, a house suitable for divine service.

Rejoicing at this promise, I willingly made my vow, and, released, returned from the heavenly realms **[Note: [Col. 0526D]** The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from Henschenius and his followers.]**.

Therefore, under the certain hope of indulgence and remission of our sins, fulfilling with eager devotion the vow that we made, I built a monastery in honor of the holy Trinity and of holy Mary, perpetual virgin, in a place called Haslach, situated in my kingdom and in the diocese of Strasbourg. We resolved to exalt this monastery and enrich it with royal munificence for the honorable Florentius, a friend of God, then dwelling there in solitude, who, moved by divine inspiration, had obtained it from us.

We therefore give to the aforesaid monastery, and wish it to be given in perpetuity, from the property of our fisc lying there, whatever belongs to us, both in villages and in slaves, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters, and courses of waters; and we assign all these things by free donation for the use of the aforesaid monastery and of the brothers serving and ministering to God there, while nevertheless living under a canonical rule.

We also hand over to the venerable worshiper of God Florentius and to his church the place and valley within the boundaries of the Vosges, which he faithfully chose for solitude or hermitage, and also for rest and expectation of the general resurrection, for himself and his followers.

But so that the servants of divine worship there, both in the aforesaid place and in the aforesaid church, might suffer no poverty or lack of material resources, we handed over to them our well-ordered or well-provisioned royal residence of Kirchheim, with the suburbs of Marley; the valley of Corona; Virdenheim; the village of Vege; the fortress situated on the mountain beside the road to Tabernis, as far as the Moselle stream, with all its adjoining hides, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters, and watercourses.

As for the place itself, which we embrace with singular affection, we wish it now and henceforth to be free from every oppression of servitude and to remain under royal protection. Thus no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, may presume to exercise any power or conduct any business there; nor may anyone compel the inhabitants of the aforesaid places to appear for hearings, pay fines or tribute, or, finally, dare to exact anything whatever from them.

But so that this transfer of ours, and the establishment of its legal status and granted dignity, may remain stable and unshaken forever, we ordered this charter to be drawn up and signed it, strengthened by the addition and hanging of our seal **[Note: [Col. 0526D]** The mention of a hanging seal takes us back to a much later age **[Col. 0527C]** and exposes the forger’s ignorance.]**.

**[Col. 0527A]** (This donation was made by us, together with our sons, namely Clovis and Sigebert, in the aforesaid monastery of Haslach, among the brothers devotedly engaged there in divine service. Nanthild, queen of the Franks, our lawful wife, was present at this transfer, together with our daughter Rathild. Archbishops, bishops, abbots, provosts, dukes, marquises, palatines, counts, and many other princes of our kingdom also assembled. This was enacted in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord **[Note: [Col. 0527C]** The year of the Incarnation is here added contrary to the custom of the Merovingian kings. Moreover, the year 613 suits neither Dagobert: the elder was not called to share the kingdom until 622. This instrument may be attributed to the elder Dagobert, that is, the son of Clothar I, at less cost if the chronological note is corrected and the year 613 restored, so that at least the spurious offspring may accord with the times of Dagobert I.]** six hundred thirteen, in the month of April, on the sixteenth day, in the place often named **[Note: [Col. 0527D]** Henschenius removed the material enclosed in parentheses as though it were an interpolation.]**.)

## XVI. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants gifts and privileges to the church he founded at Weissenburg

**[Note: [Col. 0527D]** Published by Trithemius, *Opera*, part I, p. 51; Coccius, *Dagobertus rex*, p. 172; Nauclerus, *Chronographia*, generation 21, vol. I, pp. 757–758; Vorburg, *Historia Germanica*, vol. VIII, p. 241; Heda, *De episcopis Ultrajectinis*, p. 20; Magerus, *De advocatis*, book 5, p. 124; Lunig, *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, part III, p. 185; Cointius, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 164; and Schoepflinus, *Alsatia diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 22. It is said to have been taken from an old parchment of the collegiate church of Weissenburg, *Historia ecclesiae Argentinensis*, vol. I, proofs, p. 34. It also exists among the *Monumenta Boica*, vol. XXXI, new series, vol. IV, p. 1, from a transcript made at Vienna in 1582 by order of the emperor Rudolf II; that version assigns the charter to the year 623. Cointius demonstrated the charter’s spuriousness by irrefutable arguments; see him. Mabillonius, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 384, and all others skilled in diplomatic matters agree with him. It has the same indications of forgery as the charter fabricated under the same king’s name for the monastery of Haslach, which we exposed in its proper place, p. 23. It is composed in exactly the same words, with only the final clauses added, which we have enclosed in parentheses. The chronological notes suit no Frankish king named Dagobert, for none reigned for twenty-three years; above all, Dagobert, son of Clothar II, who began to reign jointly with his father in 622. Since this document concerns the beginnings of the monastery of Weissenburg, we think it should suitably be placed around the year 633. At that time this place began to be inhabited by monks, as is attested by the *Chronicle of the Abbey of Münster in the Valley of Saint Gregory*, written in 1194 and published among Martène’s *Anecdota*, vol. III, col. 1435, and more accurately from the original by D. Grandidier, *Historia ecclesiae Argentinensis*, vol. I, proofs, p. 22; see below the notes to the charter of Childeric II, of the year 661. Some recognize Dagobert II as the founder of the monastery of Weissenburg; Cointius refuted them in the passage cited above, and the chronicle just mentioned, which Cointius did not know, agrees with him. Schannat nevertheless published in *Vindemiae* 5, 11, a catalogue of the abbots of Weissenburg in which the foundation of the monastery is attributed to Dagobert I in the year 623. I have inserted in the text, within brackets and marked “M. B.,” the variant readings drawn from the *Monumenta Boica*.]** (year 633).

**[Col. 0527B]**

Dagobert, by the favor of divine clemency, king of the Franks, to all the leading men of his kingdom, indeed to all who profess the Christian faith, both present and future.

A vow by which anyone has bound himself to God or to his saints cannot be rendered void without the stain of guilt; and the greater and more worthy is he to whom the vow is made, the heavier the judgment that will strike the presumption of one who vows and does not fulfill it. We therefore ought and wish also to render what we vowed to the terrible Lord God, and to him who takes away the breath of princes, terrible among all the kings of the earth. We have thought it worthy that all should be informed, as an example of correction, how he terrified us by the power of his arm, and how, striking and healing, he visited us again **[M. B.: *exemplem* for *exemplum* (“example”); adds *dignum* (“worthy”)]**, especially so that every faithful person, having heard of our danger, might refrain from laying waste the churches of God and might show due honor to things dedicated to God.

First, therefore, we shall briefly explain the terrifying divine examination that took place against us; afterward **[M. B.: “in addition”]**, the vow and the fulfillment of our vow. When my father Lothar **[M. B.: Clothar]**, of blessed memory, died, I assumed responsibility for my father’s kingdom. But, led by frivolity in living and distracted by a desire to rule, I neglected the obligations of royal office, showing neither the diligence nor the care required by the charge entrusted to me, and doing or judging nothing with gentleness or zeal for justice.

Among my other transgressions, I had begun to be a destroyer and despoiler of the churches of God, although I ought to have been their defender and promoter, fearing neither the eyes of the divine Majesty nor the outcry of men. At last, the goodness of God, crushing the pride of my obstinate mind, visited my iniquities with the rod of correction, and, after chastising me, did not deny me forgiveness.

For I was carried aloft and presented before the divine Majesty, seated among the choirs of the saints in the appearance of a judge. I was gravely and persistently accused by the most holy patrons of the churches because of the ecclesiastical property that I had seized and squandered by robbery, especially by Mary, the most holy Mother of God, and by the most blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles.

Since, burdened by conscience, I did not dare defend my crimes, I was condemned to punishment at the judge’s discretion. After I had long been beaten and exhausted by savage torments, my special patron, the martyr Dionysius, finally appeared **[M. B.: *succurrit*, “came to my aid,” for *occurrit*]**. By his prayers he obtained for me a respite from the punishment that was pressing upon me and time for repentance. He himself, as though establishing the terms of my penance, placed in me the hope of complete indulgence on this condition: that I should build, in honor of God and of the aforesaid saints whom I had most offended, a house suitable for divine service.

At this promise I willingly made my vow **[M. B. adds: *laetatus*, “rejoicing”]**, and, released, returned from the heavenly realms.

Therefore, under the certain hope of remission and indulgence of our sins, fulfilling with eager devotion the vow that we made, we built a church in honor of the holy Trinity, of holy Mary, perpetual virgin, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in a place called Weissenburg. We resolved to exalt it and enrich it with royal munificence.

We therefore give to it, and wish it to be given in perpetuity, from the property of our fisc lying there, whatever belongs to us, both in villages and in slaves, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters, and courses of waters; and we assign all these things by free donation for the use of the brothers serving God there under a monastic profession.

And so that the authority of this donation of ours may remain stable and firm for all time, we have caused the boundaries and names of the surrounding places to be set down.

Toward the east, the boundary of the territory we have granted extends as far as Marchenhofen **[M. B.: Morchenhevenum]** and Aldenherden, and thence to Geboldeswege, and thence below the ford (*vadum*) of Lutra **[M. B.: *vatum Lutere*, for *vadum Lutrae*]**, and thence to Buozdingeshorste **[M. B.: Buezdingershurst]**, and thence to the boundary-marker standing at the summit of the valley of Invenesdal **[M. B.: Invensdal]**. From there it runs toward the south over Warspach, and thence to Bodemlosestompha **[M. B.: Bodemelosemstamph]**, and thence to Sebach, and thence to Kirchdale **[M. B.: Kirchendale]**, and thence to Ingoldeshare **[M. B.: Ingeldeshoche]**, and thence through the wooded mountains as far as Bedebur.

Toward the west it extends as far as Lautenbach **[M. B.: Lutenbach]** and Bernbach **[M. B.: Berenbach]**, and thence to Belebach **[M. B.: Erlibach]**, and thence to Gruneburnen **[M. B.: Grünenbrunnen]**, and thence to Otterichescheyt **[M. B.: Otterichschritt]**. Toward the north it extends as far as Eichenberg **[M. B.: Eychenberc]**.

As for the place itself, which we embrace with singular affection, we wish it now and henceforth to be free from every oppression of servitude and to remain under royal protection. Thus no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, may presume to exercise or hold any power or conduct any business in that territory without the permission of the abbot of the monastery; nor may anyone compel the inhabitants of that place to appear for hearings or to pay fines or tribute, or, finally, dare to exact anything whatever from them.

(We have also decreed with equal authority that none of the bishops of the city of Speyer, or of the other bishops, shall have the power to exercise any lordship there or to conduct any legal proceedings of any kind; rather, under the protection of our immunity **[M. B. omits “under”]**, the abbot of the monastery with his brothers shall freely and peacefully possess everything belonging there **[M. B.: “shall possess”]**.

Furthermore, we grant to that place a mint bearing images and letters and displaying an exact likeness of the coinage of Speyer **[Note: [Col. 0529D]** What is added here concerning the establishment of a mint and the rights of advocates is absent from the charter for the monastery of Haslach. It is a new indication of forgery, since it reflects an age much later than that of King Dagobert.]**. By an equal donation of our authority, we decree and wish it to be ratified and confirmed that the people of this church may conduct their business freely throughout all the boundaries of our kingdom, so that they pay no toll owed to any persons **[M. B.: *nulli* for *nullis*, “to no one”]**, and no judge or person of whatever rank may presume to inflict any violence upon them in such a matter.

To the brothers serving God there **[M. B.: *aut* for *autem*]**, so that they may observe the order of their sacred way of life with greater devotion and tranquility **[M. B.: *sanctae* for *sacratae*, “holy” for “sacred”]**, we grant the free power to choose an abbot for themselves. To that abbot, and to all succeeding him (*sibi*) **[M. B.: *ei* for *sibi*]**, we grant this special privilege of dignity: that he may promote to the rank and legal status of ministeriales anyone from the household whom he judges worthy of such an honor.

All the ministeriales of the same church shall also receive a benefice from the abbot **[M. B.: “from the said abbot”]**, and shall serve the abbot alone; nor may the advocate dare exercise any authority over them, unless perhaps, because of some disobedience, the abbot should summon the advocate to compel those ministeriales as rebels **[M. B. omits “to” and reads “those”]**.

The rest of the household must assemble, at the proper place and time, three times a year at the advocate’s court to render justice **[M. B.: *debent* for singular *debet*]**, and, if the advocate is present, each shall pay one denarius for his service, except those who are under immunity **[M. B.: *immunitate* for *emunitate*]**. But if the advocate is absent from one of these courts **[M. B.: “from”]**, nothing from these denarii is owed to him unless he is shown to be engaged in the king’s service **[M. B.: “services”]**.

To ensure that this transfer of ours, and the establishment of its legal status and granted dignity, may remain stable and unshaken forever, we have signed this charter, drawn up and strengthened by the addition of our seal. Done by us in the monastery itself, in the month of May, on the eleventh day, in the twenty-third year of our reign, prosperously in the name of Christ. Amen.)

## XVII. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, concerning the foundation of the church of the Holy Cross of Saint Audoenus

**[Note: [Col. 0529D]** Domnus de Vaines, of the Congregation of Saint Maur, a man highly skilled in diplomatic matters, accurately transcribed this charter in 1772 from an authentic transcript of the letters of Charles IV, king of the Franks, by which it was confirmed in November 1325. Those letters were themselves inserted into other letters of Charles VI, dated 20 August 1382. From the same transcript, preserved in the archives of the church of Saint Cornelius at Compiègne, Labbaeus published it in *Miscellanea*, collection II, p. 414, and Marlotus in *Historia Remensis*, vol. I, p. 265.

Although the instrument was confirmed twice by royal letters, its spuriousness will be clear from the following indications. The original parchment presented to Charles IV had been badly worn, as he himself testifies in his letters in these words: “We therefore caused the privilege itself to be copied and transcribed, wishing, out of reverence and honor for the saints who signed such a privilege, and because of the antiquity of the said privilege, which can scarcely be handled, carried, or moved without danger of damage, that full credibility should be given to the said copy and transcript as though it were the original.” From this it may certainly be inferred that Charles was reluctant to violate this charter by suspecting it of forgery. We publish it from the copy of Domnus de Vaines, as being the more accurate; it is preserved in the archive established for our collection.]** (year 633).

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity **[Note: [Col. 0530D]** This instrument teems with indications of forgery: the formula of invocation is unusual for this period; the title of archchaplain is applied to Audoenus, although it was unknown under the first dynasty; fifteen subscriptions are included, although such a number was not then used; the names of the subscribers themselves do not at all accord with the times of Dagobert; the word *miles*, as though a title, is added to the names of several subscribers; and there are other features that it is not worth bringing forward here.]**.

I, Dagobert, son of the younger Clothar, king of the Franks, when, after the death of my father, the most glorious and excellent **[Supplement: “of blessed memory”]** king of the Franks, I was flourishing in the kingdom and everything round about lay silent under our rule, on a certain day in the month of May, together with the nobles and chief officers of the palace, in the Cusiacus forest, according to the customary manner . . . . **[As in the copy.]**

But while we were all eagerly occupied in taking the wild animal, and each person was running here and there through the shadowy thickets in pursuit, suddenly Domnus Audoenus, our archchaplain, entered a pleasant but narrow clearing. There he found the image of the Lord’s cross impressed upon ground unblemished by snow. For the sky had been perfectly clear yesterday and the day before yesterday, and the sun, driving its unrestrained chariots, had also illuminated the earth with its bright light.

He saw it, stopped, and stood stunned. Then, running back, he hurried to us and reported it. “Let us hasten,” he said. We also saw it, marveled, and confessed that so great a prodigy had occurred.

Therefore the same Domnus Audoenus, being most prudent and knowing that the same place was visited and frequented by the Lord, threw himself at our knees and asked that it be given to him for the building of a basilica. He succeeded in obtaining it from the river Yser, opposite Gallis-Villa, with a broad stretch of the forest and the lands lying far and wide around it, as far as Bellumvillare and as far as the bank of that same river—opposite, namely, the estate of Riparius. There he built a church in honor of the holy Cross and also established a small village.

Finally, with our permission and consent, he donated it to Saint Medard, out of love for the brothers with whom he had been brought up there from the earliest beginnings of childhood and had been educated in the liberal arts, not merely to a moderate degree but thoroughly. At his earnest request, we freed it from every lordship, advocacy, ban, and customary due.

And so that this might remain firm, we ordered these letters to be made as a testimony and, in the presence of bishops, counts, and palatines, marked them with our name and confirmed them by the impression of our ring.

Sign of the illustrious Dagobert, king of the Franks.

S. Flavius, archbishop of Rheims.

S. Sulpicius, archbishop of Bourges.

S. Ambrose, bishop of Javols.

S. Faro, bishop of Meaux.

S. Amandus, bishop of Utrecht.

S. Eligius, bishop of Noyon.

S. Lebuinus, bishop of Chartres.

S. Amalarius, bishop.

S. Maurinus, bishop.

S. Erchinoald, mayor of the palace **[Note: [Col. 0531D]** That Flavius did not preside over the church of Rheims during Dagobert’s reign is proved by Marlotus, *Historia Remensis*, vol. I, p. 266. There was indeed a Flavius who was archbishop of Rheims, but, after a full century had elapsed, he subscribed to the Council of Auvergne. Eligius became bishop of Noyon only after Dagobert’s death. Lebuinus is not counted among the bishops of Chartres. Erchinoald was not raised to the office of mayor of the palace until after Dagobert’s death.

In Dagobert’s genuine charters, Audoenus subscribes under no name other than Dado, although he was known by both names, as everyone knows; nor did he ever claim to be chancellor, but rather referendary. See Mabillonius, *De re diplomatica*, on the chief chancellors under the Merovingian dynasty. We are surprised that the authors of *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IX, col. 390, cited as evidence an instrument so disfigured by defects and suspected even by the editors themselves, when discussing the foundation of the monastery of the Holy Cross of Saint Audoenus.]**

S. Beroaldus, nobleman of the palace.

S. Aygulfus, count.

S. Bertinus, knight.

S. Verchemarius, knight.

S. Autharius, knight.

S. Rado, knight.

I, Audoenus, chancellor, wrote and subscribed **[Note: [Col. 0532D]** The chronological notes are absent, and no year can be assigned to this charter with certainty. We follow the chronological order in which Labbaeus published it.]**

---

## XVIII. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives the castle of Saint-Denis to the monastery of Saint-Denis

**[Note: [Col. 0532D]** Published by Dubletus, *Historia abbatiae Sancti Dionysii*, book III, p. 661, from a copy checked against the original in 1612, now in the royal archive, K, no. 1. Everyone will rightly judge it spurious, since it makes an extravagant mention of the Constantinian Donation, which all agree was fabricated long after Dagobert’s time.]** (year 633).

**[Col. 0531D]**

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to Mummolus, prefect; Gondoenus, Werpenus, Dructoaldus, Auclinus, Charimundus, and Chariulphus, counts; and to all present and future officials.

In these matters we ought especially to be vigilant which concern the glory of God and the honor of his Church, and to bring them to a good conclusion, so that from them we may deserve to attain our salvation.

Since, therefore, we often had our residence in the castle of Saint-Denis, and, residing there as in our own palace, held our solemn court on feast days, and since this was an impediment to the brother monks serving God there, it pleased our serenity, after consultation with our faithful men, to withdraw from that castle and henceforth to transfer our court on those same festivals—not far from the same castle, however, but to our palace at Clichy—so that the church of our great patron Dionysius might remain undisturbed by every disturbance, and no secular noise prevent the brothers from continually praying more attentively for the Lord’s mercy on our behalf.

Having therefore followed sound counsel, with the agreement of the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the great men and nobles of our kingdom, we have decreed and ordained, calling upon the holy and undivided Trinity and upon the coming of the just Judge, that from this day forward neither we nor our successors shall in any way take up residence in the aforesaid castle or holy place, where, as I have said, Domnus Dionysius rests in body and where we desire to be buried; nor shall we celebrate or hold our solemn court there on the feasts of Easter, Pentecost, Christmas, or Epiphany.

But just as Constantine the Great, ever-august emperor and most steadfast defender of the holy Catholic Church, under whom it flourished and grew wonderfully, offered to blessed Peter the citadel of the Roman Empire in its entirety and conferred it upon Saint Sylvester through his lawful documents, so we too, by our royal munificence, grant and donate in perpetuity to God and to blessed Dionysius, our special protector, this castle with all its appurtenances and dependencies, without any challenge.

Whatever our fisc could hope to derive from it, we establish by this decree for that holy place and for the brother monks serving God there. We decree that those who presume to attempt anything against this authority of ours and against our decree shall be subjected and struck by the bond of anathema through the archbishops and bishops **[Col. 0532D]**.

So that this may obtain perpetual strength, we have decreed that it be strengthened by our hand and ordered it to be countersigned with the impression of our ring.

King Dagobert subscribed.

Dado, referendary, presented it.

Given at the palace of Clichy, in the eleventh year of our reign **[Note: [Col. 0533D]** The eleventh year of Dagobert’s reign falls around the year 633, counting from his acquisition of the Austrasian kingdom. If it were counted from the Neustrian kingdom, it would extend beyond Dagobert’s reign, since he died at the beginning of 638, before ten years had yet been completed from his father’s death.]**, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

---

## XIX. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives the villages of Vallis and Argenterias to the monastery of Saint-Denis

**[Note: [Col. 0533D]** Dubletus alone brought this charter to light, *Historia abbatiae Sancti Dionysii*, p. 669, having transcribed it from a copy of no reliability. For several defects are found in it that prove it false: the unusual invocation and the indictional note, which it was not then customary to add to royal charters; this is observed by Germonius, *De veteribus regum Francorum diplomatibus*, vol. II, p. 108; see Mabillonius, *De re diplomatica*, p. 68.

We add, with Cointius, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 21, that Arnulfus, who is falsely represented as having subscribed with the title of bishop of Metz, had already laid down the see of Metz eight years earlier, *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XIII, col. 694, and for that reason had withdrawn into solitude after being badly treated by Dagobert. We pass over the unusual formulas of the subscriptions, “of the most glorious King Dagobert” and “Dado, chancellor of royal dignity.”]** (year 634).

In the name of the eternal Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

If we lavish the munificence of our generosity upon holy places and those dedicated to divine worship, we have no doubt that this will greatly assist us in passing more easily through the present life and in obtaining the future life more happily **[Col. 0533B]**.

Let the prudence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, know that, for eternal recompense, we grant to Saint Dionysius, outstanding among the martyrs, and to the brothers serving God there, certain villages belonging to us and situated in the district of Berry: namely, the village called Vallis, situated on the river Cher, and the village called Argenterias, situated on the river Magneuria, with all their appurtenances.

For this reason we ordered this command of our high authority to be drawn up and given to the aforesaid Saint Dionysius and to the brothers serving the Lord there, so that they may hold and possess the said villages in perpetuity, without anyone’s opposition **[Col. 0533C]**.

And so that this may be preserved inviolate for all time, we have confirmed this authority of ours with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with our ring.

S. Dagobert, most glorious king.

S. Clovis, son of Dagobert.

S. Arnulfus, bishop of Metz.

Given through the hands of Dado, chancellor of royal dignity.

This was enacted at Paris, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of April, in the twelfth indiction, in the thirteenth year **[Note: [Col. 0534D]** That is, indiction 12, year 13]**, while King Dagobert reigns.

---

## XX. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants the estate of Wallare in the forest of Fania, with many appurtenances, to Landelinus for the construction of a monastery there

**[Note: [Col. 0534D]** Published by Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 489, from a copy of a later period, as he admits on p. 490, in the notes to the charter of Authbertus below, p. 31. The charter is spurious, as is evident from the invocation formula, then unusual; from the indictional note, used contrary to custom; from the title “king of the Austrasians” assigned to Dagobert, who had already been king of all France for eight years; from the chronological notes reckoned from the Incarnation; and finally from the very subject of the charter, namely the foundation by Landelinus under Dagobert of the monastery of Wallare, which was not founded until 657, almost twenty years after Dagobert’s death. See Cointius, *Annales*, vol. III, pp. 447 ff.; Mabillonius, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 428; *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. III, p. 77.]** (year 634).

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 0534A] It is not fitting that the excellence of royal majesty should be unaware that there is one, sole, and everlasting King of kings and Lord of lords, from whom all power also is, was, and shall be forever; to whom belongs everything that we are and can be, in whom we live and move, and whom, according to the strength granted us by him, we ought to serve. We ought also, with special devotion, continually to enlarge the worship and dignity of his one, holy bride, the sacred Church, by royal munificence, insofar as we are able.

Therefore I, Dagobert, king of the Austrasians, moved by persuasion and salutary admonitions of the venerable man Authbert, bishop of Cambrai, for the sake of the soul of my most pious father, King Lothar, who reigned in Francia for forty-five years, grant and give to Landelinus Maurosus, a converted robber, my estate in the Fania, called Wallare, with the following villages, lands, woods, meadows, waters, and watercourses, assigned with fixed boundaries, so that he may build there a monastery in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and establish persons who shall serve the Lord God perpetually:

The village of Bavia with all its territory; the water itself and its course, as it flows through that territory, beginning at the place called Railhiez and continuing until it descends into the river Elpra; the whole wood called Aetimundus, with all its territory, tithe, pannage, jurisdiction, and ban, from the wood of Baileporis to the aforesaid water between Bavia and Wallare; and from that same water, the entire wood called Brolium, Fania, Mansilium, Clarus Voionus, and Wiellemanus; the wood near [Col. 0534C] Wilheis, from Mount Gomundus and Merdosus Voionus as far as the village of Wilheis; and the wood of Ducion, as a dowry for the church to be built on the aforesaid estate of mine.

Whatever, in whatever manner, may bring advantage or benefit within the boundaries of the aforesaid woods, I give by my munificence to the aforesaid Landelinus to possess perpetually, with the approval of the princes and nobles of my palace, Arnulf and Pippin.

But so that this royal grant may obtain the perpetual strength of legal firmness, I confirm the aforesaid document with my own hand and decree that it be secured by the attachment of my seal.

Sign of the lord Dagobert, king of the Austrasians.  
Signatures of Arnulf of Metz and Pippin of Neustria, elders of the palace.  
I, Anso the chancellor, acting in place of Cunibert the archchancellor, have recognized it.

Given at Cambrai, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May [Col. 0535A], in the six hundred and fortieth year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0535C] The year 640 of the Incarnation is incorrectly written here, since Dagobert died in 638; nor was it customary among Merovingian kings to use an indiction, but rather the year of the reign. If one wishes to investigate in which regnal year the forger intended this diploma to have been issued, we may determine it from the following charter, which, although of no better quality, was devised to lend credibility to the diploma under discussion and confirms Dagobert’s gift on the authority of the bishop of Cambrai. This charter, however, is falsely dated to the thirteenth year of Dagobert’s reign, which began in early spring of the year 634.], in the thirteenth indiction.

## XXI. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives the estate of Sarclidas to the poor matricularii of Saint-Denis

[Note: [Col. 0535D] It appears in Dubletus, *History of the Abbots of Saint-Denis*, p. 669; it was reprinted in Cointius’s *Annals*, vol. III, p. 23, and in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 629. We compared it with a later copy in the Colbertine chartulary, p. 13, preserved in the archive of Saint-Denis, and with the fourteenth-century chartulary now in the Royal Library, no. 5415, and found no discrepancy of any importance. This document was suspected by no one; even Germonius, the merciless opponent of the charters edited by Dubletus, admits in *On the Diplomas of the Ancient Frankish Kings*, vol. II, p. 11, that he found nothing in this diploma that would discredit it.] (A.D. 635).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to Wandelbert, duke.

Whatever we contribute with complete devotion for the support of the poor, we trust that for this we shall receive the reward of recompense in the future. Therefore let your diligence know that we have exchanged the estate called Sarclidas [The editions read *Sarclitas*], situated on the river Joina in the district of Étampes, which we exchanged with Lord Ferreolus, bishop of the city of Autun, or with Abbot Deodatus, or with the clergy and church or basilica of Lord Symphorianus, [Col. 0535B] where they are known to serve, for another estate called Amica, located in the territory of Marseille.

For the benefit of our reward, we have granted Sarclidas in its entirety, with all its rights and appurtenances, to the matricularii [Note: [Col. 0535D] Who the poor matricularii of Saint-Denis were is explained by Cangius, *Glossary*, under “Matricula”; Felibianus, *History of the Abbots of Saint-Denis*, p. 13; Mabillon, *Annals*, [Col. 0536C] vol. I, p. 342; and others. They were poor persons enrolled in a *matricula*, or register, who had devoted themselves to the service of the monastery and had been assigned lodging in the church’s atrium.] of Lord Dionysius the martyr, where that precious lord rests bodily, and who appear to reside at that basilica, or within its atrium, among the matricularii. Whatever they may thereafter wish to enlarge for their support, we have granted to them with complete devotion.

Therefore we command that, from the present day, they should possess the aforesaid estate of Sarclidas, with its houses, slaves, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, mills, flocks with their shepherds, appurtenances, and everything belonging to it within its boundaries, just as it was possessed in complete ownership by the aforesaid holy church of Autun or by Lord Symphorianus, when, as we have said, we exchanged it by mutual agreement upon giving another estate.

Accordingly, that which by our generosity, for the salvation of our soul, has been perpetually granted, with God’s favor, to those matricularii of Lord Dionysius, without the intervention of judges, no abbot nor any other person shall ever presume to remove from their donation. Rather, through the hand of their abbot, in whom lies the continual provision of food for those poor persons, it shall be administered in the name of God; and whatever the treasury might be able to gain from its fees or residual proceeds shall benefit those poor persons by way of increase. Thus may they, and those who succeed them, take delight in praying more frequently for the stability of our kingdom and the salvation of our soul.

And so that this decree may endure undisturbed through the ages, we have determined to strengthen it with our own hand.

Ursinus presented it. King Dagobert subscribed.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth year of our reign, at Clichy, prosperously. Amen.

## XXII. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives the estate of Aquaputa to the monastery of Saint-Denis

[Note: [Col. 0536C] Dubletus first published it in *History of the Abbots of Saint-Denis*, p. 670; it was reprinted by Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. III, p. 24, and in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, [Col. 0536D] vol. IV, p. 630.] (A.D. 635).

[Col. 0536B] Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

A person, whether always healthy and safe or as though placed in illness, must continually keep watch more attentively for the salvation of his soul, so that he may be able to seek a reward in the future. Therefore, for God’s sake and as a remedy for our soul, we give to the monastery of Saint-Denis, where that precious lord rests bodily and where we desire to be buried, and we wish it to be given in perpetuity, our estate called Aquaputa, situated in the district of Paris, with all its rights and full ownership.

Accordingly, by this present transfer we decree that, under God’s protection, it shall remain perpetually, so that the estate itself, with all its entirety and appurtenances, may by this authority come with the strongest legal force to the aforesaid [Col. 0536C] monastery or to Dodo [Note: [Col. 0536D] Mabillon doubts whether Dodo presided over the monastery of Saint-Denis in this year, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 341, and *On Diplomatics*, p. 627. He mentions Dodo under Clotaire II, and Chunaldus and Aigulf as abbots of Saint-Denis under Dagobert, though he admits that this list of abbots is highly uncertain. Another diploma, dated to the tenth year of Dagobert’s reign, states that Chunaldus, Dodo having already died, presided over the monastery of Saint-Denis. But this tenth year seems to have been reckoned from the death of Clotaire, and therefore we shall place that diploma below, under the year 637 (Col. 561). Consequently, the argument drawn from that other diploma should have aroused no suspicion in Cointius, above, in Germonius, *On the Ancient Diplomas of the Frankish Kings*, vol. II, p. 110, or in the authors of *New Christian Gaul*, vol. VII, col. 339, against the authenticity of the diploma presented here, since it cannot be challenged on any other ground.] the abbot, who appears to preside there as rector.

Thus, in time to come, with its lands, houses, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, flocks with their shepherds, appurtenances, additions, and every other benefit, just as it has until now been possessed by our treasury, so by our indulgence, for the salvation of our soul and the stability of our sons, it shall increase for that holy place and for those brothers [Col. 0537A] who serve God there, in our time and in the times to come.

And so that this transfer may be held more firmly and remain unharmed through long ages with our successors, we have strengthened it below as best we could and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

Ursinus presented it. King Dagobert subscribed.

Given on the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth year of our reign, at Clichy [Note: [Col. 0537C] It is rightly said to have been given at Clichy. See below (Col. 540), note c to Dagobert’s diploma concerning the estates of Tauriaco and others, given to the monastery of Saint-Denis. We compared Dubletus’s edition with the fourteenth-century chartulary in the Royal Library, no. 5415, in which the chronological note reads “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August” (that is, July 18); there is no other discrepancy of any importance.], prosperously. Amen.

## XXIII. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, concerning the foundation of the monastery of Rebais and the immunities granted to it

[Note: [Col. 0537D] We publish it from Mabillon’s *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, appendix, p. 687. Plessaeus reprinted it among the documents relating to the history of the Church of Meaux, vol. II, p. 3, but with part of it truncated, taken from that church’s cartulary. It appears in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 630, copied from Mabillon. It was suspected by no one known to us.] (A.D. 635).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to our apostolic fathers, namely the bishops and abbots, and to the remaining priests established anywhere in our kingdom in the name of God, both now and in future times; and to the illustrious men, the dukes, as well as to the magnificent Count Chanulf.

Among other petitions, princely clemency ought to receive with favorable hearing, and without doubt bring to completion, whatever is offered for salvation or requested through fear of the divine name, so that recompense may be made when a suitable request is granted for the peace of God’s servants. For perfect faith does not doubt that something belongs to the grace of the Most High if, according to his word, something is devoted with a faithful mind especially to those of the household of faith, since it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Therefore, since the illustrious man Dado, our referendary, and his brothers Ado and Rado [Note: [Col. 0537D] Mabillon considers the name Rado to be interpolated; see, however, Aimoinus, cited below.], [Col. 0537C] have devoutly built, with God’s help, the monastery of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0537D] Aimoinus, book IV, chapter 41, testifies that this monastery was called by that name by its founder; in his own time, however, it was called the monastery of Rebais, after the little river flowing past it. These are Aimoinus’s words: “Moreover, blessed Audoin . . . built a monastery within the forest of Brie, which he indeed named Jerusalem; but now, from the little river on which it is situated, it is called the monastery of Rebais.” This name prevailed so completely that it is the only one surviving today.] in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Paul and Saint Antony, commonly called Rebais, situated in the territory of Meaux, for monks and pilgrims to inhabit and to enjoy a solitary life in the name of God, and since they have earned this through our generosity as well, therefore, in accordance with their petition and for the peace of God’s servants, it has pleased us to promulgate a decree of our authority.

By it, since the monastery appears to have been built upon our estate, which we have granted for the remedy of our soul, and to have been endowed in part, the monks, under the tranquility of peace and with the Lord’s protection, may continually remain there according to the rule of their religion.

We choose that this document should declare more fully [Col. 0538A] that nothing is taken away from canonical authority if, as we have said, something is granted to those of the household of faith for the tranquility of peace. Nor should anyone, by disparaging us, think that we are making new decrees in this matter, since from ancient times, according to the constitutions of the pontiffs and by royal sanction, the monasteries of the holy men of Agaunum [Note: [Col. 0538D] Concerning the monastery of Agaunum, see the diploma of Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, from the year 523, above, vol. I, pp. 66ff.], of Lérins, and of Luxeuil, and even the monks of Lord Marcellus [Note: [Col. 0538D] This is to be understood of the monks of Saint-Marcel of Chalon, whose monastery was founded by Guntram in the year 579, Fredegar, *Chronicle*, chapter 1. This is also attested by Aimoinus, book III, chapter 80; Hermannus Contractus, *Chronicle*, under the year 584; the *Chronicle of Saint-Benignus of Dijon* in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 370; and the Bollandists, in the *Life of Saint Sorus*, February 1. Compare Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 173.] appear to exist under the privilege of liberty.

Therefore, if anything there—villages, slaves, or any other possessions and livestock—has been assigned either by royal gift or by the aforesaid men or by anyone else, or if anything thereafter is added, since, as we have said, it has been built through our generosity, no bishop, neither those now present nor their successors, nor their administrators, nor any person whatsoever, shall be able in any manner to remove it from that place, claim any authority for himself in that monastery, diminish anything under the pretext of an exchange, or take away any of the ornaments of the sacred rites or anything offered upon the altar.

Nor shall anyone presume to enter that monastery or its cells except to gain the benefit of prayer; and a bishop shall not enter unless it is with the consent of the abbot himself or of his congregation, and then without serious burden to them. Thus it may more easily be permitted to the monks, established there regularly in the name of God, to possess their rightful endowment in peace throughout the ages.

When that abbot has been called from this world, the congregation itself shall choose one from among its members and, according to the holy rule, appoint the senior in every respect and from among all the members, in accordance with the vote concerning the endowment and with the authority of this document, so that everything there may increase for him without any disturbance.

We add that no judge or any other person whatsoever shall have permission, without the consent of God’s servants, to defraud the aforesaid monastery of anything belonging to it or, in a rash spirit, to divert anything from it to his own uses, lest what was established at the beginning incur divine and our displeasure [lacuna] [As in the editions] suffer serious loss from the treasury [lacuna] [As in the editions].

And, considering the merits of those aforesaid men, it has pleased us to add, for the sake of our complete recompense, that whatever has been or shall at any time be transferred there, whether from our generosity or from the endowment of Dado and his brothers, their parents, or anyone else, no public judicial authority, neither present nor future, shall presume to enter there to hear cases or exact anything.

Rather, under complete immunity, this monastery and its congregation shall possess for themselves all the fines granted to them. Whatever the treasury might perhaps have hoped to receive from their people, whether free persons, dependants, servants, or those dwelling on their lands, or from any other source, shall, by our indulgence, all benefit the lights of that holy place and the stipends of God’s servants, both while we live in the name of God and in the times of our successors, as an advantage of recompense. Thus may the monks continually delight in imploring God’s immense mercy for eternal salvation, everlasting happiness, and the stability of the kingdom.

So that this decree of our authority may be held more firmly, with Christ assisting in all things, we have taken care to inscribe below our handwritten subscription.

King Dagobert subscribed.  
Dado presented it.

Given on the Kalends of October, in the fourteenth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0539C] Cointius dates the beginnings of the monastery of Rebais to A.D. 634, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 16. The fourteenth year of Dagobert’s reign began in the year 635, and indeed at the beginning of spring, as we have said more than once. See below, col. 597, note a.]

## XXIV. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives the estates of Tauriaco, Tibernion, Rubridum, Monarvilla, and Vasconis Vallis to the monks of Saint-Denis

[Note: [Col. 0539C] Dubletus printed it in *Antiquities of Saint-Denis*, p. 658, from what he calls the original of Saint-Denis, which, he says, was enclosed with a seal bearing the king’s image. It was reprinted by the compilers of the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 628, from Dubletus. The original is not extant in the archive of Saint-Denis; but this diploma is found in the so-called “white” chartulary, written in the thirteenth century, in part by the hand of William of Nangis, and preserved in the archives of Saint-Denis. We compared Dubletus’s edition with it and have placed the discrepancies in parentheses. Germonius, *On the Ancient Diplomas of the Frankish Kings*, vol. II, p. 102, attacks this document on several grounds: first, because the day is omitted from the chronological notes [Col. 0539D]; second, because the name “monks” is given to the clerics then serving in the basilica of Saint-Denis; and third, because the king grants “jurisdictions,” which is not characteristic of this period. These objections do not overturn the authority of the diploma. First, although the law of the Alemanni, which Germonius cites, orders the day to be added to documents, the Salic law, renewed by Dagobert, does not; moreover, the notation of the day could have escaped the copyist’s eye or been omitted through a scribe’s negligence. Second, who does not know that in Dagobert’s time the name “monks” was applied indiscriminately to clerics and monks, as Ruinart, drawing on Thomassin, teaches in his preface to Gregory of Tours, *Collection of Frankish History*, vol. II, p. 87? Third, what is said here about *justitiae* should be understood not as jurisdictions in the later sense, but as rights; for the ancient use of the word in that sense, see Cangius’s glossary. Add that the word itself appears to have been interpolated in this place: it was absent from the text of the chartulary mentioned above and was written between the lines [Col. 0540C] in an old hand, but in a later correction and with paler ink. This diploma is also included in the fourteenth-century chartulary preserved in the Royal Library, no. 5415. It presents discrepancies which may be read between brackets and which will be discussed in notes c and d.] (A.D. 635).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

While we remain in this perishable life, it ought to be considered desirable to raise up, for an eternal reward, the holy places from transitory possessions [Royal Chartulary: “in place of”], for the nourishment and support of God’s servants, so that from perishable things we may earn eternal ones.

Therefore, considering this, we give estates belonging to our right, namely Tauriaco, Tibernion, and Rubridum, situated in the district of Orléans, and also Monarvilla [“and Monarvilla” is absent in the Royal Chartulary], and Vasconis Vallis in the district of Étampes, to the monk-brothers serving at the basilica of Lord Dionysius, our special patron, where Abbot Aigulf appears to preside and where we desire to be buried, to be administered perpetually especially for their sustenance.

We grant the aforesaid estates, with all their rights and lordships [these three words are absent in the chartulary], lands, houses, slaves, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and all appurtenances, to the aforesaid holy place and to the monks [Col. 0540B] serving God there, by our munificence and as a special donation for their sustenance, so that, using the aforesaid estates, they may pray daily to God for us and for our offspring, that he may protect us by his mercy, for whose love we have bestowed these things upon them.
