And so that this donation of our authority may retain inviolable firmness through succeeding ages, we have decreed to strengthen it below by the subscription of our hand and the impression of our ring [Note: [Col. 0540C] The words concerning the impression of the ring, which appear to be evidence of forgery, are absent from the chartularies before us and may therefore be judged interpolated. But even if they were present in the original, this should disturb no one, since mention of an impressed ring is not unusual in Merovingian diplomas, as Mabillon testifies, *On Diplomatics*, p. 107, and *New Diplomas*, vol. V, p. 665, even before Dagobert’s time.]

King Dagobert subscribed.  
Dado presented it.

Given in the month of October, in the eighth year [Note: [Col. 0540C] The eighth year of Dagobert’s reign, reckoned from the death of Clotaire, was in October of the year 635. Fredegar records that Tibernion, which is granted by this diploma to the people of Saint-Denis, was given to them in Dagobert’s fourteenth year [Col. 0540D]; but this amounts to the same thing if the fourteenth year is counted from Dagobert’s being called to share in the kingdom. Thus Fredegar agrees with the diploma, which weakens Cointius’s argument, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 23, drawn from Fredegar. Greater suspicion is raised by the name of Abbot Aigulf, whom we do not yet believe to have presided over the monastery of Saint-Denis at this time; but on this sole suspicion we do not dare to brand it as false.] of our reign, in the name of God, at the palace of Clichy [Note: [Col. 0540D] The place-name was added between the lines in the chartulary of Saint-Denis, in the same ink and, apparently, in the same hand in which the entire diploma was written; it appears in the text of the Royal Chartulary. Fredegar, chapter 78, testifies that in the year in question Dagobert stayed at Clichy while he initiated a war against the Basques through envoys.], prosperously. Amen.

## XXV. Diploma of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives Molliacum to the monks of Saint-Denis

[Note: [Col. 0540D] Dubletus alone published it, *History of the Abbots of Saint-Denis*, p. 671, and does not say that he copied it from any authentic source. At least today, no copy is extant in the archive of Saint-Denis [Col. 0541C]. Germonius successfully attacks this diploma, *On the Ancient Diplomas of the Frankish Kings*, vol. II, p. 110, using arguments based on the subscriptions of Arnulf and Eligius. The former was indeed bishop of Metz, but after abandoning the episcopate he withdrew into solitude against Dagobert’s will long before the year in which this document is supposed to have been issued, *New Christian Gaul*, vol. XIII, col. 695. The latter, who is called bishop of Noviomagus, did not obtain the bishopric of Noviomagus until after Dagobert’s death, ibid., vol. III, col. 982.] (A.D. 635).

[Col. 0540C] Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

While we remain in this perishable life, it ought to be considered desirable to raise up, for an eternal reward, the holy places from transitory possessions, for the nourishment and support of God’s servants, so that from perishable things we may earn eternal ones.

Therefore, considering these things, we give the estate belonging to our right called Malliacum, situated in the district of Bourges, two miles from the river Carus, to the monk-brothers serving at the basilica of Lord Dionysius the martyr, our special patron, where Abbot Aigulf appears to preside and where we desire to be buried, to be administered perpetually especially for their sustenance.

Accordingly, we grant the aforesaid estate, with its lands, lordships, slaves, male and female servants, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and all its appurtenances, to the aforesaid holy place and to the monks [Col. 0541B] serving God there, by our munificence and as a special donation for their sustenance, so that, using the goods of the aforesaid estate, they may pray daily to God for us and for our offspring, that he may protect us by his mercy, for whose love we have bestowed these things upon them.

And so that this donation of our authority may retain inviolable firmness through succeeding ages, we have decreed to strengthen it below by the subscription of our hand.

King Dagobert subscribed.  
Dado the chancellor presented it.  
Sign of Arnulf, bishop of Metz.  
Signature of Eligius, bishop of Noviomagus.  
Signature of Aigulf, abbot of the monastery of Lord Dionysius.

Given in the month of October, in the fourteenth year [Note: [Col. 0541C] Dagobert’s fourteenth year, in the month of October, indicates the year A.D. 635] of our reign. Done, in the name of God, at the palace of Clichy, prosperously. Amen.

## XXVI. Fragment of the testament of Dagobert I, king of the Franks

[Note: [Col. 0541C] We copied this fragment from a manuscript of Aimoinus’s *History*, folio 81 recto, formerly folio 89, preserved in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It appears to have been written at the end of the eleventh or the beginning of the twelfth century. We then compared it with the chartulary into which it was inserted, preserved in the archive of the same abbey, marked with three crosses, which we judge to belong to the later part of the twelfth century [Col. 0541D]. We have distinguished in brackets a single discrepancy below. Breulius published this fragment in his 1603 folio edition of Aimoinus, p. 176, and Bulliardus, p. 4, in the documents appended to the history of the abbey of Saint-Germain, taken from the same chartulary that we have before us. It was included in Cointius’s *Annals*, vol. III, p. 28, and in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. III, p. 133, note, from Aimoinus; nowhere does the complete testament survive. Thus the four copies that Dagobert had ordered to be made and deposited in different places for greater security have perished.

The anonymous author of the *Deeds of Dagobert*, chapter 39, reports everything contained in our fragment in precisely the same words; indeed, he adds several things omitted from the fragment, which he pretends Dagobert said at a general assembly when he spoke about his testament. Hence there is room to conjecture that the Anonymous had before his eyes Dagobert’s testament, which, he says, was deposited in the royal treasury and still reverently kept in the archive of Saint-Denis in his own time.

But what degree of credibility did this document possess, and how much confidence does the anonymous ninth-century writer himself deserve, one branded with the epithet “storyteller” and entirely lacking concern for investigating the truth? The author of the fragment, whoever he was, appears indeed to expose himself as a liar when he makes Dagobert say that he chose to be buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent, although he so often designated the basilica of Saint-Denis as the place of his burial, and it is established that he was buried there. Hence Valesius, *Frankish Affairs*, book XIX, p. 122, and Cointius, cited above, counted these remains among fabricated documents. Mabillon, however, *On Diplomatics*, book I, chapter 7, no. 5, praised Dagobert’s testament as almost genuine. We support the judgment of Valesius and Cointius.] (A.D. 635).

[Col. 0542A]

In the name of the Trinity, the Lord God Almighty.

To the apostolic fathers—namely, the bishops and abbots—and to the remaining priests established in our kingdom: Dagobert, king of the Franks.

As far as the human intellect can consider with an attentive mind and weigh through diligent inquiry, nothing more can be gained in the light of this world and its fleeting joys than that one should strive to devote transitory possessions to venerable places for the support of the poor, so that those who generally suffer the frailty of nature may keep watch for the salvation of their souls before sudden departure [Col. 0542B] occurs, lest anyone be found unprepared or depart from this world without any provision.

Indeed, while he remains established in the right of his own liberty, he should strive to purchase perpetual life from perishable possessions for the eternal tabernacles, so that he may obtain a desirable place among the company of the righteous, and so forth.

[And again, after a few words] [Note: [Col. 0542C] The words distinguished here and below in italic type, indicating omissions, appear both in Aimoinus’s manuscript and in the chartulary. The omissions may be supplied from Dagobert’s speech inserted by the Anonymous in his *Deeds*, chapter 39. The speech continues in one uninterrupted passage as follows: “And let him prepare the Lord as his retributor, and from transitory possessions let him take care to devote offerings to the venerable places of the saints, for the support of the poor, so that from the Lord himself he may earn the fruit of unfailing paradise, to be refreshed among the morning stars. From whose living fountain, when one asks in perfect faith, neither is the cup withheld nor the channel diminished; rather, whoever drinks is watered with heavenly sweetness, and the fragrant odor of paradise’s balsam is sweet to him. And therefore, examining my conscience and the excesses of my heart, considering the judgment of the heavenly King and fearing his judgment, as well as the true punishments of unhappy men, and especially desiring the endless glory of the righteous, and taking care that the last day, according to the Lord’s dispensation, should not find us sluggish in remembering the saints or comforting the needy [Col. 0543C], thus, with sound mind, [lacuna]” as follows in the fragment.]

Therefore, with sound mind and sound counsel, it pleased us—and, as we have said, divine devotion admonished us—to order a testament to be written for our salvation and eternal recompense. For an immutable benefit, we confirmed four copies in one form, and whatever we have bestowed anywhere upon the holy places, we set down in them with similar notation. Of these, we sent one to Lyon in Gaul, and another we entrusted to the archives of the church at Paris [Col. 0543A].

[As stated above] [Note: [Col. 0543C] Here again we shall supply the omission from the *Deeds of Dagobert*: “The third we give at Metz for safekeeping to Lord Abbo; but the fourth, which we hold in our hands, we order to be placed in our treasury.” For the remainder, see the cited passage. What follows, however, is absent from the *Deeds*.]

Then follows:

Therefore, we give to the basilica of Lord Vincent at Paris, where we have decided to have our burial whenever God shall command it, and we decree that it be given in perpetuity, the estate called Cumbis [Note: [Col. 0543C] That Cumbis was given by Dagobert to the church of Saint Vincent is attested by the diploma of Philip I, issued in the year 1061, which we shall present in its proper place], in the district of Paris, which Ursa, daughter of Alderic, held.

Likewise, to the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle at Paris, where Saint Genevieve rests bodily, the estate of Dravernum in Brie.

(To the basilica of Lord Dionysius, likewise at Paris, where he rests with his companions, the estate of Braunata [Note: [Col. 0543C] Of the gifts of Dagobert specifically listed here, the Anonymous author of the *Deeds of Dagobert*, a monk of Saint-Denis, mentions only Braunadum as having been given to the church of Saint-Denis; in the fragment of the testament it is called Braunata. The words enclosed here in parentheses are absent from the chartulary of Saint-Germain.], in Brie.)

To the basilica of Lady Columba and of Lord Lupus at Sens, the estate of Grande-Camp in the Gâtinais, and so forth [where several further items are included].

Finally he added [Note: [Col. 0543D] The *Deeds of Dagobert* offer no help in supplying what the copyist of the fragment indicates is missing here.]:

But you, good sons, considering first the reverence due to nature, whose power binds even beasts, remain brothers; do not cast off what you have been burdened with.

Next, revere me, your father. I prefer to ask, though I could command, that you preserve our decrees undisturbed, just as you wish your own decrees to be preserved by your successors, knowing certainly that if you hold what we have sanctioned in contempt—which I do not think you will do—your own decrees likewise will be despised by posterity.

[Note: [Col. 0543D] There are no chronological notes. But the *Deeds of Dagobert* and Aimoinus place the assembly at which that king spoke about the testament then being composed in the fourteenth year of his reign, in April or May: the *Deeds* say the tenth day before the Kalends of May, Aimoinus the tenth day before the Kalends of June. For this reason we have prefixed the year A.D. 635 to this fragment.

As we reread these materials, a considerable suspicion arises that, after Dagobert’s genuine testament had been lost—perhaps the testament seen by the author of the *Deeds*—another was fabricated from his narrative when the estate of Cumbis was being restored by Philip I. Hence fragments of the reconstructed document were inserted at the beginning of the twelfth century into Aimoinus’s manuscripts, and, later in that same century, copied into chartularies. We have discussed this conjecture more fully in the prolegomena, so that our note here would not grow beyond measure.]

## XXVII. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants numerous estates in the Limousin and Berry frontier district to the monastery of Saint Dionysius

[Note: This appears in Dublet, *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, p. 672; no one subsequently reprinted it, and everyone regarded it as spurious, especially Germonius, *On the Charters of the Ancient Kings of the Franks*, vol. II, p. 113—and rightly so. Its style is entirely different from that of Dagobert’s charters, and its formulas are unusual. The abbot of Saint Dionysius is designated by the fictitious name Leobafarius, who, according to Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 500, is found only in instruments of doubtful reliability; or at least, according to Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. III, p. 625, he did not perform the office of abbot until many years after Dagobert’s death, namely when Theodoric was deprived of the kingdom by his brother Childeric. Several of the subscribing bishops are given the title of archbishop, contrary to the custom of the period. Godinus is called archbishop of Lyon, although he had governed that church no earlier than fifty years before; Dado subscribed not as referendary but as archbishop of Rouen, although he obtained the Rouen dignity only after Dagobert’s death. Who would not be revolted by so many indications of forgery? The forger seems to have taken the basis for composing this instrument from the *Deeds of Dagobert*, chapter 35, where he had read that this king inserted, under the conclusion of a single charter, a grant of twenty-seven estates to the monastery of Saint Dionysius. But the estates heaped together in this charter, though very numerous, are not the same as those mentioned by the author of the *Deeds*, nor are they situated in the same provinces. Consequently, that author’s authority lends the instrument no credibility.] (A.D. 636).

**Dagobert, illustrious man, king of the Franks.**

Since clear and daily indications show that what is true of all matter and of the condition of those who are born—that it returns in a moment of time to nothingness—our souls’ salvation demands that each person, whom the negligence of the first man has made an exile and a stranger, examine daily the course of his entire life and thereafter, while the final lot has not yet taken away his living spirit, train himself to obtain by his merits a place there from which he first fell and to which his soul, after his departure, will return under angelic guidance.

Therefore I, Dagobert, king of the Franks, crowned by God, to whom, by the permission of the highest King and by the concession of both our predecessors and ourselves, Francia obeys and renders service, now considering the salvation of my soul and following sounder counsel, have deliberated within myself how I might make one of Christ’s soldiers my helper and neighbor by a donation of certain possessions of mine.

This is the illustrious and precious witness Dionysius, who once, stripped of fear but girded with the fervor of faith, came to Gaul and there, while the perfidy of the pagans was spreading, resisted manfully, steadfast in faith, preaching and making known the teaching of the holy law. Since he is known to sit at the right hand of God through the shedding of his own blood, and continually to obtain whatever he asks for those for whom he wishes to ask, the whole world ought to venerate him with the highest devotion. I, indeed, have greatly experienced that his grace was not absent from me when I was turning aside my father’s anger.

Therefore, although the aforesaid Dionysius lacks nothing for the glory that he happily possesses with God, nevertheless, so that he may become for me, my wife, and my children a most faithful intercessor before the just Judge and also an excuser of our sins on the day of judgment, we decree that the monks of that monastery, in which sinners approach him as he rests there bodily, with groans, confessing their sins, and where Abbot Leobafarius is seen to preside, shall quietly possess throughout succeeding ages certain properties situated in the frontier district of Limousin and Berry, properties hitherto assigned to royal ownership.

To make their names certainly known, we list them all below. First, we transfer from this day forward, into the right and dominion of the brothers of the monastery of that same martyr of Christ, Dionysius, our fortress called Patriagus, with its churches, and also the estates belonging to that fortress, together with the churches and everything known to have hitherto been under its authority.

Next, our estate called Patriacus, situated on the river Jugie, with our chapel consecrated in honor of Saint Savior, with the three churches existing in the same estate, and with all its appurtenances. We further add two other estates, with their churches, situated on the river Vulsie: Petra-Ficta and Patriacum, with the lord’s meadow and all their appurtenances; and our estate called Fornolis, with male and female servants; Nigromons, with its church; and Campaniacum, with its church.

We also give the cell of Larundum and the parish church, with all the churches belonging to that fortress, both within and outside it.

In the district of Berry we further add and grant the estate of Casimansi, with its church; the estate of Lanatidum, with its church; the estate of Giureti, with its church; the estate of Archiniacum, with its church; the estate of Maniacum, with its church; the estate of Stivaliculi, with its church and the five holdings belonging to that church; the estate of Guierlaicum, with its church; the estate of Vernidum, with its church; the estate of the Two Houses, with its church; the estate of Vicoplenum, with its church; the estate of Perolium, with its church and the lord’s field; the estate of Vallum, with its church; the estate of Argenteria, with its church; the estate of Notum, with its church; the estate of Umreziacum, with its church; and the estate of Napsiniacum, with its church.

Everything that appears to belong to these estates is included: male and female servants, lands, meadows, woods, mills, waters, and watercourses.

Moreover, we give the entire land lying between two waters, from the river Conus to the river of the spring Moer, with all its churches—namely, the church of Saint Martial of Salviacum, the church of Cursiacum, and the church of Mosaycum—and also all the properties belonging to those churches, both within and outside them, up to the place where these two waters join.

Outside this grant is our chapel consecrated in honor of blessed Martin, with the two estates belonging to that church, namely Golaocum and the other called Longavilla, which Lord Godinus, an apostolic man and archbishop of Lyon, held from the royal majesty.

Behold the things I offer to blessed Dionysius and to those who serve him. If anyone should ever—God forbid—of those who succeed us on the royal throne, or any powerful person, inflict harm upon them and bring them back under his own dominion, then, just as I hope to be saved by the support of Dionysius when I give these things, so may that invader, by retaining them, be condemned to the worst death.

To ensure that this gift does not appear apocryphal to posterity but remains stable, and that this charter may be firmer through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened and confirmed by the sign of our hand.

Sign of Dagobert, illustrious king.  
Sign of Palladius, archbishop.  
Sign of Landeric, bishop.  
Sign of Laudomer, bishop.  
Sign of Fraudobert, bishop.  
Sign of Asterius, bishop.  
Sign of Eligius, bishop.  
Sign of Franemund, bishop.  
Sign of Sylvinus, bishop.  
Sign of Lauradus, bishop.  
Sign of Maurinus, bishop.  
Sign of Clarus, bishop.  
Sign of Grado, bishop.  
Sign of John, bishop.  
Sign of Burgundophar, abbot.  
Sign of Leobafarius, abbot of Saint Dionysius.  
Sign of Mummolus, prefect.  
Sign of Gundoenus, count.  
Sign of Chariulf, count.  
Sign of Audinus, count.  
Sign of Dructoald, count.  
Sign of Charimund, count.

Dado, archbishop of the church of Rouen, subscribed with his consent.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of August, in the fifteenth year of our reign. Enacted happily at the palace of Compiègne. Amen.

[Note: Dagobert’s fifteenth year began at the opening of spring in the year 636.]

## XXVIII. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants the estates of Noth and Pascellarius to the monks of Saint Dionysius

[Note: This spurious charter is found only in Dublet, *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, p. 671. Germonius, *On the Charters of the Ancient Kings of the Franks*, vol. II, p. 3, exposes its falsity from its style, its subscriptions, and the clause by which Dagobert provides that the abbot of Saint Dionysius should not presume to take away from the monks the estates there granted to them—as though at that time one part of the monastery’s possessions were assigned to the monks and another to the abbot.

Dagobert, whose sign is used in this instrument in place of a subscription, was accustomed to authenticate his charters by writing his name with his own hand, as may be seen in the autographs reproduced by Mabillon, *Supplement to Diplomatic Art*, engraved plates. Abbot Geremarus, who appears among the subscribers, is certainly the man whom the maker of the instrument knew to have lived for a long time in Dagobert’s palace and to have taken part in his councils; but he did not know that Geremarus became a monk only in 648 (see Cointius, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 234), and afterward became abbot. We pass over the remaining points.]

(A.D. 636).

**Dagobert, illustrious man, king of the Franks.**

Before a person dies a sudden death, he ought to keep watch for the salvation of his soul, lest death, taking away the present light without any warning, find him unprepared and so hand him over to everlasting darkness and eternal torments. Therefore, while he remains by the right of his own freedom, he ought from perishable possessions to seek to purchase life in the eternal tabernacles.

Accordingly, for the remedy of my soul, I grant to the monks of the basilica of our special patron, Lord Dionysius, in which that precious martyr rests bodily with his companions and where we wish also to be buried, and where Abbot Aigulfus appears to preside, the estate called Noth and another called Pascellarius, with their appurtenances, situated in the district of Berry, together with slaves of both sexes, meadows, fields, woods, waters, and watercourses.

Just as these possessions have hitherto been held by our treasury, so, by our indulgence, for the acquisition of the salvation of our soul and for the stability of our sons, may they profit and remain in perpetuity for the present and future time. Let none of our sons, nor our successors as kings of the Franks, nor any bishop, nor the abbot of that monastery, nor any powerful person presume to take away the aforesaid estates that we have granted to that holy place, if he does not wish to incur the anger of God and the displeasure of Lord Dionysius.

To make this grant more secure and preserve it through the ages, and so that it may possess firmer force, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Sign of Dagobert the king.  
Sign of his son Chlodoveus.  
Sign of Eligius, his goldsmith.  
Sign of Dado, his chancellor.  
Sign of Geremarus, abbot.  
Sign of Aigulfus, abbot.

Given on the Kalends of November, in the fifteenth year of our reign.

[Note: That is, in the year 636; see above.]

Enacted happily at the palace of Clichy. Amen.

[Note: In the charter immediately preceding, which is falsely said to have been issued in this same year, Leobafarius is called abbot of Saint Dionysius—a fictitious abbot, as Mabillon appears to think. See above, column 544, note f. Aigulfus is more appropriately brought into this context: he presided over the abbey of Saint Dionysius under Dagobert’s son, and perhaps under Dagobert himself.]

## XXIX. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants the estate of Iticinascoam to the church of Saint Dionysius

[Note: Mabillon first brought this charter out of the Dionysian archive, written on Egyptian papyrus and now preserved in the royal archives, table V. It was almost entirely obliterated. He made part of it public in *On Diplomatic Art*, p. 374, engraved in Merovingian letters with an interlinear reading expressed in ordinary letters; afterward he presented the whole in ordinary script in the same work, p. 465. Certain passages remained defective, however, and in some places he supplied a few letters obliterated in the original, which the sequence of the text plainly indicated.

We have transcribed the first part from the engraved Merovingian autograph; the remainder from Mabillon’s reading, distinguishing it in italics. Mabillon published the instrument again in *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. I, p. 685; after him Germonius, *On the Charters of the Ancient Kings of the Franks*, vol. I, p. 275; Felibianus, *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, documents, p. 5; the collectors of the historians of Frankish affairs, vol. VI, p. 628; and Marini, *Diplomatic Papyri*, p. 98.

The authenticity of this instrument was vigorously attacked by Germonius, in the work cited above, pp. 116 ff. Suspicion was aroused by the complete silence concerning this charter both in the ancient author of the *Deeds of Dagobert* and in Dublet, who had thoroughly examined the archive of Saint Dionysius. Mabillon, *Supplement to Diplomatic Art*, p. 7, and the authors of the *New Diplomatic Art*, vol. III, p. 654, weakened this argument.

Certainly, the anonymous author of the *Deeds of Dagobert* did not intend to recount individually all the gifts of this king to monasteries, as he himself testifies in chapter 30. Why should it be surprising if Dublet, who often used previously prepared copies and was unable to read Merovingian script, overlooked or disregarded a Merovingian charter?

Germonius, in the same work, p. 120, derives another argument from the similarity of this charter to another charter of the younger Chlodoveus, which he argues is false. But why could not a false instrument have been made to resemble a genuine one? Finally, he censures the spelling error in Dagobert’s name, which, he says, should have been written *Dagobertus* or *Dagoberthus*. But *Dagoberchtus* is plainly read in the autograph charter of the same king that we reproduced above from the engraved plate, p. 2. See Mabillon’s supplement to diplomatic art.] (A.D. 637).

[Column 0547B]

…rcthus [Note: That is, *Dagobercthus*, as it is distinctly read in the subscription], king of the Franks. To the illustrious men Vandelbert, duke; Raganric, domesticus; and all present and future officials …

[Eight syllables left blank]

…eternal, and that from perishable substance eternal joys should be gained. Therefore, we, considering in reality how we may deserve, even in eternity or to some small degree, to be companions of the just, [we grant] the estates … [three syllables left blank] called Iticinascoam, in the district of Paris, which belonged to Landeric and Gan … [one letter left blank] brothers, and with additions … [four syllables left blank] or the revenues to the basilica of Lord Dionysius, martyr and our special patron, where that precious lord appears to rest bodily … We have been devoted through the ages, and, with the Lord’s favor, we shall be seen to have granted them at present with complete devotion.

For we command that … properties, woods, meadows, pastures, waters, and watercourses, from the present day, just as they are … held by them … or are now possessed in the name of God by our treasury, be granted by our indulgence to that holy basilica, so that … may receive from our jurisdiction more particularly … for the poor residing there, for the stability of the kingdom and the remedy of our soul, without any later opposition, they ought to prosper through the ages; and so that, while we are … to the clergy, the poor, and those residing in that holy place … or … or to some small degree … every … inconvenience may arise.

And so that this … [four syllables left blank; Mabillon partly supplies: “And so that … may receive … through all ages an inviolable …”] may possess firm stability, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand …

**Dagobercthus, king, subscribed.**

**Dado, offered** [seal-space].

… fifteen days [Note: This charter is said to have been given on the fifteenth day of the tenth year of Dagobert’s reign, namely 15 April. If we reckon the beginning of his reign from the opening of spring—that is, from the division of the kingdom among the Neustrians—we place the charter in the year 637. The mention of Duke Wandelbert, to whom Dagobert addresses the charter, agrees with this calculation. For Wandelbert is known to have still been alive under King Chlodoveus, Dagobert’s son and successor, from a charter of that Chlodoveus which we shall publish below.]

… of the tenth year of our reign, in God’s … At Clichy, happily …

## XXX. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants Bishop Amandus the place between the rivers Elnon and Scarpe, suitable for establishing those who serve God there

[Note: In 1772 Lord Queinsert, of the congregation of Saint Maur, copied this from a parchment roll containing several charters written in the fourteenth century and from a chartulary attributed to the beginning of the twelfth century; both are preserved in the archives of the monastery of Elnon. We follow his copy, deposited in the archive established for our collection.

This charter was published by Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, vol. I, p. 123; by the Bollandists, under 6 February, in the preliminary commentary on the *Life of Saint Amandus*; by the Sammarthani, *Gaul Christian*, vol. IV, p. 37, in fragmentary form; by Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. III, p. 89; and also by Boxhornius, *Authors of the Republic of Liège*, 1633 edition, p. 437.

The authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. III, p. 254, and the collectors of the historians of Frankish affairs rejected it. Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 372, considered it corrupted; Cointius regarded it as fictitious.

Arguments for its falsity may be drawn: first, from formulas mostly different from those used in the reputable charters of this king. The initial invocation “In the name of the Lord” is unusual for this period, as is the formula “by divine-ordaining clemency, king”; the customary title of Dagobert, “illustrious man,” is absent. Second, another indication of falsity is supplied by the chronological data, about which see the note that follows.] (A.D. 637).

**In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Dagobert, king by divinely ordained clemency.**

We believe that God will be favorable to us if we devote special care to restoring and confirming the practice of religion and open the hand of our generosity and liberality to those who serve religion. Therefore we wish the diligence of both present and future generations to know that the venerable Bishop Amandus, who by God’s grace baptized our son Sigebert, having already built and well organized certain churches and monasteries for the advancement of divine worship, approached our excellence and, as a cultivator of the Lord’s vineyard who did not grow weary, yet confident in the benefit of our generosity, humbly requested that a place situated between the two rivers, the Scarpe and the Elnon, be granted to him by our liberality.

Although the place was difficult to clear because of the great density of the forest, it nevertheless appeared suitable for his labor—or rather, after his labor, for the rest and use of those serving God, whom he was already piously planning, by God’s grace, to establish there.

Therefore, considering the worthy petition of the reverend bishop, both for the stability and peace of our entire kingdom and our offspring and for the salvation of our souls, we granted with willing devotion of mind the place he had requested, together with both waters and the forest growing all around it, and we establish the grant with the binding sanction of law.

Therefore we command, and by royal authority order, that no secular or ecclesiastical person attempt to cause the aforesaid bishop or his successors any disturbance, opposition, prejudice, or violence concerning the aforesaid place, with its water and forest, granted to that bishop by our liberality.

Rather, both that bishop and those whom he establishes there, as well as his successors, shall securely and perpetually have and possess this benefit of royal generosity, without any diminution, accusation, or contradiction.

If divine mercy should wish that this place be improved and enlarged through the industry of this beloved man and his successors and through the devout generosity of good people, whatever the treasury might thereafter have been able to claim from it—whether in dues, fines, meadows, divisions and restitutions of lands, or in any other way—we grant in full to the aforesaid Father and his successors.

We also wish the place itself and the properties belonging to it, together with anything that the generosity of princes or the devotion of any of the faithful may subsequently add, to remain under the protection and defense of our safeguard and immunity.

And so that this royal authority may remain firm, unshaken, and perpetual, we confirm this present charter below with our own hand and seal it with the impression of our ring. We also admonish our successors to imitate our practice in this matter.

Given on the Kalends of May, in the seventh indiction, in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord Dagobert.

[Note: If Dagobert’s regnal years are reckoned from A.D. 622, when he was proclaimed king of Austrasia, his eleventh year would give A.D. 633 or thereabouts. But Mabillon, in the work cited above, proves that the monastery of Elnon was not founded until near the end of Dagobert’s reign.

If, however, Dagobert’s years are reckoned from Chlothar’s death, May of Dagobert’s eleventh regnal year falls in A.D. 638, when Dagobert was already dead, having died in January of that year. Thus, under either method of calculation, the chronological data used here cannot stand.

A more accurate calculation, in fact, seems to refer this charter to the final year of Dagobert, when the monastery of Elnon was founded. The instrument’s maker should therefore have written the tenth rather than the eleventh year of the reign, namely A.D. 637, which is why we place that year before the charter. But correcting the chronological data of a fictitious instrument is to waste time and effort.]

Enacted happily in the city of Paris. Amen.

## XXXI. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants the monastery of Saint Dionysius immunity from every authority

[Note: We took this from the chartulary of the Royal Library, numbered 5415, p. 6, already cited several times. It is the only one missing from Dublet among the fourteen charters of Dagobert contained in this chartulary.

Certain features of this charter arouse suspicion of falsity. First, so many and such extensive immunities are granted to the monastery of Saint Dionysius that they scarcely appear credible, although examples of them are supplied by formulas 3 and 4 of Marculf, book I. Second, the monetary penalty imposed on violators is exaggerated beyond measure. Third, the charter is said to have been given in the second year of Dagobert’s reign, yet Aigulfus is mentioned as abbot of Saint Dionysius, although he seems to have presided over that monastery only at the very end of Dagobert’s reign.

These considerations prevent us from regarding the instrument as genuine. Without taking account of the chronological data, however, we think it should be assigned to the year 637 because of the mention of Abbot Aigulfus. For more details, see our notes on the other charter very similar to this one, which follows immediately.] (A.D. 637).

[Column 0550B]

**Dagobert, illustrious man, king of the Franks, to Mummolus the prefect, Gondoenus, Werpenus, Dructoald, Audinus, Charimund, and Chariulf, counts, and to all present and future officials.**

Among other petitions, royal clemency ought to receive with favorable hearing what is offered for salvation and requested in the name of God, and without doubt bring it to effect [read: “bring it to effect,” as in the following instrument], so that eternal things may be acquired from the perishable things of the present age, according to the Lord’s command: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.”

Therefore, according to his saying, we ought to purchase eternal and heavenly things with the mammon of iniquity, so that, while we grant suitable benefits to the priests of Christ, we may thereby deserve to have the Lord as our rewarder in the eternal tabernacles.

Accordingly, the venerable Aigulfus, abbot of the basilica of our special patron, Lord Dionysius the martyr, where that precious lord rests bodily, petitioned the clemency of our kingdom that, in accordance with what we recently discussed at Compiègne in our general assembly, we should now, by our own authority and again for the security of the matter, grant and confirm in the name of our immunity, concerning that holy place and the people who, with their property and possessions, may wish to give and devote themselves to that holy basilica, what we should deign to provide and confirm in God’s name concerning that holy place.

Therefore let your greatness or prudence know that, out of reverence for those saints and for the peace of the monks serving God there, we have again granted and confirmed everything with the greatest willingness, as your diligence may perceive [in another charter: “we have appeared to”].

Accordingly, by this charter, which we establish more particularly and wish to remain perpetual, we order and decree that neither you, your juniors [another charter reads “we and ours,” omitting “juniors”], nor your successors in perpetuity, nor anyone invested with judicial authority, may ever enter the estates of the aforesaid basilica of Lord Dionysius, wherever they may be, in whatever regions or districts of our kingdom, which by God’s favor the monastery’s portion appears to possess and govern at the present day, or which has been granted there to God-fearing people by lawful documentary instruments, or may hereafter be added or assigned there, either to hear cases, take sureties, impose fines or levies, provide lodging or transport services, or demand any payments.

No one may at any time enter or make demands within the immunity of Saint Dionysius [this negation is absent from another charter], except that whatever our treasury could have exacted from those possessions, in every respect and in full, for the increase of our reward, we grant from the present day under complete and firm immunity.

If anyone should wish to violate this authority or immunity of ours, and should hire others for this purpose, each person shall be compelled to pay thirty pounds of the purest gold, each on his own behalf, to the share of Saint Dionysius. Moreover, as stated, whatever our treasury might perhaps have hoped to receive from those possessions for our share shall be granted and bestowed in full forever for the lights and support of the monks, and also for the sustenance of the poor of that monastery [in another charter: “for the alms of the poor”], so that we may be more eager to pray attentively for the stability of our kingdom, for peace, and for all our dependents, seeking the Lord’s mercy.

So that this authority may remain perpetually firm and inviolate concerning that holy place in our time and in the time of our successors, and may be guarded and preserved unharmed through all ages, and so that you may believe it more fully and securely, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Dagobert the king subscribed.  
Dado offered it.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the second year of our reign. At Compiègne, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## XXXII. Another charter on the same subject, with additions

[Note: We transcribed this charter from the same chartulary from which we took the preceding one, Royal Library no. 5415. It is composed in almost exactly the same words from beginning to end, but with several additions inserted, which we have enclosed in brackets so that they may be more easily distinguished.

Dublet published it in *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, p. 659, claiming to have taken it from bark. We have placed within brackets its variant readings of some importance. It suffers from the same defects as the preceding charter, and indeed from more. The immunities granted beyond measure and the monstrous gold penalty imposed on violators appeared to Germonius, *On the Ancient Charters of the Kings of the Franks*, vol. II, p. 103, to be the clearest indications of forgery.

Add to this the subscriptions, from which the fraud is demonstrated. Eligius and Taurinus subscribe with episcopal titles, although neither obtained his episcopal dignity before Dagobert’s death: Eligius became bishop of Noyon and Taurinus bishop of Nantes. See *New Christian Gaul*, vol. VIII, column 982.

Mabillon offers some defense of this instrument, discussing both charters at length in *On Diplomatic Art*, pp. 224 ff., but he is silent about the subscriptions. If we may state our opinion, we think that neither should be accepted as genuine. We judge the first to have been more successfully modeled on a reputable charter but adulterated in certain respects, especially in its chronological data; the second to have been fabricated in imitation of the first, enlarged by interpolations to increase the scope of its immunities, and fortified by a large number of subscriptions in the hope of winning credibility, though defiled by spurious ones.

The chronological data of the first instrument are partly retained in the second—namely, the fourth day before the Kalends of August—and partly altered; we do not know whether this was done so that the later charter might appear to confirm the earlier one. Some interval between the two was necessary. Hence the forger, perhaps the same person who had assigned the second year of Dagobert’s reign to the first charter, attached to the second the tenth year of the same reign. In both instruments he carelessly used the name of Aigulfus, abbot of Saint Dionysius, although that name certainly does not suit the first.

In Dublet the year and place are the same as in the first charter. But so as not to linger any longer over fictitious instruments …] (A.D. 637).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, centenarians, and our other officials, both present and future.

Among other petitions, the principal clemency ought to receive with gracious hearing whatever is recorded for the salvation of the soul and requested in the name of God, and without doubt bring it to effect, so that eternal life may be acquired from the perishable goods of the present age, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.” Therefore, from the mammon of iniquity, according to his own saying, we ought to purchase eternal and heavenly things, so that, while we bestow suitable benefits upon the churches of Christ, we may deserve thereby to have the Lord as our rewarder in the eternal dwellings.

Accordingly, let your greatness or authority know that the venerable Aygulfus, abbot of the basilica of our special patron, the lord and martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily, petitioned our royal clemency that, in accordance with what we discussed a few days ago at Compiègne in our general assembly, we should now, at our universal synod convened at Paris, by our own authority and under the name of immunity, renew and confirm for the security of the matter, concerning that holy place itself and the persons who, with their substance and possessions, have wished to give and devote themselves to that holy basilica, what we might graciously grant and confirm in God’s name concerning that holy place.

Therefore, in reverence for those saints and for the peace of the monks serving God there, we appear to have granted and confirmed all this anew with the greatest readiness. Accordingly, by this charter, which we more specifically decree and wish to remain permanently in force, we command and establish that neither we nor our successors [in the earlier diploma: “you and yours”], nor any person, nor any archbishop [Dubletus: “any bishop or archbishop”], nor anyone invested with judicial authority, shall ever have any power over that holy basilica or over those dwelling in it, except with the consent of the abbot and his monks. Rather, the holy mother Church—namely, the basilica of our special patron, the lord and great Dionysius—shall be free and exempt from every invasion or disturbance by all persons, whatever their rank or authority may appear to be.

As for the estates of the aforesaid basilica of the lord Dionysius, wherever they may be, in whatever regions or districts of our kingdom, with God’s favor, which from this day the portion of that monastery appears to possess and control, or which has been granted there to God-fearing persons through legitimate chartered instruments, or which may hereafter be added or transferred, no one shall at any time presume to enter the immunity of Saint Dionysius or demand anything there for the hearing of cases, the taking of sureties, the collection of fines or royal dues, the provision of lodgings or transport, or the exaction of any payments. Whatever our treasury might have been able to extract from it, all of it and in every respect, for the increase of our reward, we grant from this day under complete and most secure immunity [and confirm in perpetuity for that holy place].

But if anyone should wish to violate this authority or immunity of ours and should enlist others for that purpose, each person individually shall pay thirty pounds of the purest gold to the portion of Saint Dionysius. And, as stated, whatever our treasury might have hoped to receive from it for our portion shall be granted and conceded in full and forever, by our royal command, for the lamps and provisions of the monks and for the alms of the poor of that monastery, so that they may be more pleased to pray attentively for the stability of our kingdom, for its peace, and for all our subjects, imploring the Lord’s mercy.

And so that this authority may remain perpetually firm and inviolate concerning that holy place in our time and in the times to come, and may be preserved and maintained unharmed for all ages, and so that it may be believed more fully and securely by all our nobles and public and private judges, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand and have ordered it sealed with our ring.

Dagobert, king, subscribed.  
Palladius, bishop, subscribed. Taurinus, bishop, subscribed. Eligius, bishop, subscribed. Silvinus, bishop, subscribed. Orado, bishop, subscribed. Clarus, bishop, subscribed. Gondoenus, count, subscribed. Dado presented it. Johannes, bishop, subscribed. Richoaldus, bishop, subscribed. Atherius, bishop, subscribed. Laudomerus, bishop, subscribed. Landericus, bishop, subscribed. Acterius, bishop, subscribed. Mommolus, prefect, subscribed.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the tenth [Dubletus: second] year of our reign, at Paris [Dubletus: Compiègne], prosperously, in God’s name. Amen.

### XXXIII. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants Ruilliacum and many other possessions to the monastery of Saint Dionysius

[Note: We publish this from the chartulary of the Royal Library, marked 5415 and written in the fourteenth century. Dubletus had already published this charter, *History of the Abbots of Saint Dionysius*, p. 677. Two principal indications of forgery are evident here, apart from those that may be inferred from its style and formulas. First, it is purportedly dated to the twenty-fifth year of Dagobert’s reign, although he did not complete his sixteenth year. Second, Leobafarius is called abbot of Saint Dionysius; according to Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 500, his name occurs nowhere except in instruments of doubtful authenticity. For this reason the authors of *Nova Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 339, removed it from the catalogue of the abbots of this monastery, prefixed to Felibien’s catalogue of abbots in the *History of Saint Dionysius*. We place within brackets various readings from Dubletus.] (637.)

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

Since it is made manifest by certain and daily signs that the truth is this: the whole substance and condition of those who are born returns in a moment to nothing, the salvation of our souls requires that each person, whom the negligence of the first man has made an exile and a stranger, examine daily the course of his entire life and thereafter, before the final lot has taken away his living breath, exercise himself in securing for his merits a place there from which he first fell and to which, after his passage, his soul is to return under angelic guidance. For whoever is setting out for any city, perhaps for the sake of commerce or driven by necessity, does not first send ahead some goods by which he may be adequately supplied and remain free from every want.

Thus, since it is clear that the Apostle said, “While we have time, let us do good to all,” this ought to be committed to the memory of every orthodox person who confesses himself to be Christ’s creation and temple: while the laws and ordinances of death grant the appointed intervals of life, let him distribute and bestow his possessions for Christ. In this way, storing up treasure in the heavenly Jerusalem, he will possess a free dwelling there when he returns to it, and hunger and thirst will be denied his spirit forever.

Since it is in no way expedient for me to be excluded from that bridal chamber, I, Dagobert, king of the Franks, crowned by God, to whom, by the permission of the supreme King and through the grant of our predecessors as well, Francia obeys and serves, have now considered the salvation of my soul and, following sounder counsel, have deliberated within myself how I might make one of Christ’s soldiers my helper and neighbor by donating certain possessions of mine.

This illustrious and precious witness is Dionysius, who once, naked of fear and girded with the fervor of faith, came to Gaul and there, while the unbelief of the pagans was spreading, resisted manfully, steadfast in faith, preaching and revealing the teaching of the holy law. He, who through the shedding of his own blood is known to sit at God’s right hand and continually to obtain what he asks for those on whose behalf he petitions, ought to be venerated by the whole world with the highest devotion. I above all owe him much, since, when I sought to avert my father’s anger, I experienced that his grace had been bestowed upon me [Dubletus: “had not been absent from me”].

Therefore, although the aforesaid Dionysius has no need of anything for the glory that he happily enjoys with God, nevertheless, so that he may become for me, my wife, and my children a most faithful intercessor before the righteous Judge and an advocate for our faults on the day of judgment, we decree that the monks of his monastery—in which he rests bodily, where sinners approach him with groans and confess their sins, and where the abbot Leobafarius is seen to preside—shall quietly possess throughout succeeding ages certain properties situated on the borders of the Biturician district, hitherto recorded as belonging to the royal domain.

To make their names certain and clear to all, we list them as follows: first, Ruilliacum; then these villages: Fracillo, Montelliacum [Dubletus: Francillo, Montellicum], Avendelliacum, Noziocum, Morilliacum, Talaicum [Dubletus: Talliacum], Sarmasiacum, Paredum, Ger, Pay, Masnile, Cassinoilum, Cantalupum [Dubletus: Masline, Cassionilum, Cantuplum], Jernacum, Vineolas, the land of Planis, the land of Valle, to which Arnolliacus belongs [these words are absent in Dubletus], the land called Mons Beraldi, and the land called Canehuces, with all their appurtenances, namely woods and vineyards, meadows, waters and their courses, male and female servants.

In addition to these, I grant the royal estate, with the chapel built there in honor of Saint Savior and his apostles Peter and Paul, and of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, together with the enclosed vineyard, seven mills, ten ovens, the port, the market, and the fisheries that I ordered to be established there.

I also give two estates, one called Cirsai, situated on the river Telum, and the other Goyse, which lies near the river Arnon, with all their appurtenances.

Behold the possessions that I offer to blessed Dionysius and to those who serve him. If anyone, which God forbid, among those who succeed us on the royal throne, or any powerful person, should inflict harm upon him and bring these possessions under his own control, may that invader, by retaining them, be condemned to the worst death, just as I hope to be saved by the intercession of Dionysius himself when I give them.

To ensure that this gift may not appear apocryphal to posterity but remain stable, and that this charter may be firmer through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened and confirmed by the sign of our hand.

Sign of Dagobert, the most glorious king. Sign of Clovis, his son. Sign of Eligius, his goldsmith. Sign of Dado, his chancellor. Sign of Geremarus [Dubletus: Geremarus, abbot]. Sign of Leobafarius, abbot.

Given on the Kalends of September, in the twenty-fifth year of our reign. Executed at the city of Orléans, prosperously, in God’s name. Amen.

[Note: The false chronological date appears at least to indicate the final year of Dagobert’s reign.]

### XXXIV. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives the estates Acuciacum, Cosdunum, and several others to the matricularii of the church of Saint Dionysius

[Note: Dubletus published it in *History of the Abbots of Saint Dionysius*, p. 676; we have taken it from the fourteenth-century chartulary in the Royal Library, no. 5415, p. 12. We have placed within brackets Dubletus’s differing readings when they are of some importance. Anyone who compares this charter with the *Deeds of Dagobert*, chapter 42, written anonymously in the ninth century, will judge it to have been compiled from that author’s narrative, whose very words are found in the charter from beginning to end. The forger nevertheless inserted some material of his own and omitted other material, facts that indicate a spurious product. The charter is falsely dated to the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the sixteenth year of Dagobert’s reign—that is, 15 September 637, four months before Dagobert’s death—whereas the anonymous author of the *Deeds* says that it was issued a few days before the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, that is, before 19 January 638, the day on which Dagobert died. The author of the *Deeds* clearly had before his eyes a genuine charter and copied most of it; therefore the person responsible for renewing the charter was mistaken in assigning the chronological dates. We do not deny that an authentic charter of Dagobert concerning the estates Acuciacum and the others granted here to Saint Dionysius may have existed and that those whose interests were involved perhaps attempted to renew the lost instrument. We possess an autograph charter of Clotaire III by which this charter of Dagobert is legitimately confirmed. From this another argument against the authenticity of the instrument before us follows: Clotaire III testifies that his grandmother Nantechild subscribed Dagobert’s charter, yet no trace of her subscription appears in the charter under discussion.] (637.)

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

Every person, while healthy and safe, and even as though placed in illness, ought always to watch attentively over the salvation of his soul, so that he may be able in the future to acquire the profit of rewards.

Accordingly, for the sake of God and as a remedy for our soul, we grant to the matricularii of the lord Dionysius, our special patron, where that lord rests bodily and where we wish to be buried, the estates called Acuciacum and Cosdunum, situated in the district of Beauvais, as well as Magnino villa and Mediano villare [Dubletus: Magnovillare, Mediovillare], Gellis, and Averciacum. These estates, namely Acuciacum, Cosdunum, Magnino villa, Mediano villare [Dubletus: Magnovillare, Mediovillare], Gellis, and Averciacum, with all their rights and boundaries, shall presently come to those matricularii, for their property and administration [Dubletus: “we have granted them as property”].

Thus, with their lands, houses, dependents, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, flocks with their shepherds, appurtenances, and all other benefits, just as they have until now been possessed by our treasury, by our indulgence they shall, for the acquisition of the salvation of our soul and the stability of our children, benefit perpetually in the present and future ages the matricularii who reside at the aforesaid holy basilica or within its atrium.

We have already commanded this transfer to be made while suffering severely in illness. No one among our children, or anyone else on this account, shall have an opportunity to attempt to oppose or resist our present will. Nor shall any bishop or abbot dare to take this away from those brothers, unless he wishes to incur God’s anger and the displeasure of the lord Dionysius.

If anyone should attempt to overturn this, let him give an account of it before Christ’s tribunal, with those brothers. Since we do not undertake to establish a hospice from these estates, or from Saclitas [Dubletus: Sarclitas], which we formerly assigned to those brothers, and from the remaining revenues of the basilica they receive sustenance, if the account is balanced their annual maintenance from this source, God granting, may well suffice, so that our almsgiving may always sustain the matricularii and their successors on behalf of our soul, and they may be more inclined always to pray for us.

And since we were unable to subscribe to this charter ourselves, because the pen trembled in our hand, we therefore asked our sweetest son, King Clovis, to affirm the charter by the sign of his name, and Dado to present it, and our nobles to subscribe it.

Sign of the glorious lord King Clovis.

Dado, at the command of the aforementioned lord King Dagobert, who was present, confirmed and presented the charter.

Sign of A., illustrious man and seneschal Waldebert, which Ragnegiselus signed [Dubletus: “seneschal; sign of Ragnegisellus”]. Sign of A. Frannegiselus [Note: After the name Frannegiselus, the chartulary displays a sign formed in poorly shaped letters.] Sign of the illustrious man Austrapius, chamberlain [Note: A certain sign appears in the chartulary at this point.]

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the sixteenth year of our reign, at Clichy, prosperously, in God’s name. Amen.

[Dubletus adds: “I, Ermenulfus, wrote this.”]

### XXXV. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives the estate Esterpiniacum to the basilica of Saint Dionysius

[Note: Dubletus alone published it, *History of the Abbots of Saint Dionysius*, p. 674; we have copied it from the chartulary of the Royal Library, written in the fourteenth century, marked 5415, p. 10. This charter is mentioned in the *Deeds of Dagobert*, chapter 22, as follows: “Dagobert presently transferred Stirpiniacum, an estate in the district of Vexin, by a firm charter, to the basilica of Saint Dionysius.” See also the *Chronicle of Saint Dionysius*, book V, chapter 10. It must therefore be believed that in the ninth century, when the *Deeds of Dagobert* were written, the instrument under discussion already existed in the archive of Saint Dionysius; nevertheless, it should still be relegated among the spurious instruments. Esterpiniacum, also called Istirpiniacum and Sterpiniacum, was a royal estate under Dagobert I and did not cease to belong to the number of royal estates before Clotaire III, who was residing there in the fifth year of his reign when he granted immunities to the monks of Corbie in a charter that we shall publish in its proper place. In the acts of the Synod of Soissons of 862 it is listed among the estates of Saint Dionysius; see Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 327. It may therefore be conjectured that, after the legitimate instrument of the grant had been lost, another was perhaps fabricated around the beginning of the ninth century, and that this is the document that survives. Germonius detected other indications of forgery in it, from its style, formulas, and invented place-name in which the charter is purported to have been issued; see *On the Ancient Charters of the Kings of the Franks*, vol. II, p. 414.] (637.)

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all officials [Dubletus: our officials], present and future.

One ought to seek to obtain eternal things from transient things and to gain everlasting joys by distributing perishable substance. Therefore, considering this matter, so that we may deserve to be counted forever, or at least to some degree, among the company of the righteous, we have appeared to grant with complete devotion the estate called Stirpiniacum [Dubletus: Esterpiniacum], situated in the district of Vexin, with all its entirety and rights, to the basilica of the lord Dionysius the martyr, our special patron, where that precious lord rests bodily and where the venerable man Aigulfus, the abbot, appears to preside as custodian; there, with the Lord’s favor, we have appeared to bestow it at present with fullest devotion, for good times.

We specifically order that the aforesaid estate, with all its entirety and integrity—that is, its houses, buildings, equipment, dependents, tenant farmers, resident tenants, inhabitants, freedmen, and slaves, both those born there and those transferred from elsewhere [Dubletus: from another place], rural and urban persons, woods and attached lands, cultivated and uncultivated fields, vineyards, forests, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, animals, livestock, movable and immovable goods, every kind of beast, all rights, appurtenances, and dependencies, both within and beyond its boundaries, and every thing acquired, whatever can be said or named, or whatever at the present time is possessed in God’s name by our treasury—shall, by our indulgence, be granted to that holy basilica.

We specifically order that thereafter it may please to benefit that holy place, or the clergy or poor residing there, for the stability of the kingdom and the remedy of our soul, without anyone thereafter resisting it, in its times; so that, while we assign this substance to the clergy or poor residing at that holy place, or at least some small portion of it, we may, through the intercession of the aforesaid lord Dionysius the martyr, deserve to obtain from the Lord a future reward—[the final words, *quod agerentur*, are corrupt or uncertain].

[Note: Up to this point we have placed within brackets the various readings excerpted from Dubletus. The text at Dubletus now differs entirely; it reads: “By our indulgence, let it remain granted to that holy basilica, so that thereafter both the clergy and the poor residing at that holy place may pray to God for the stability of our kingdom and the remedy of our soul, and so that what we have granted may, without anyone thereafter resisting it, benefit them as an increase throughout perpetual times. Thus may it come about that, while we assign these possessions to the aforesaid clergy or to the substance of the poor of that place, or at least some portion of them, out of reverence for the aforesaid lord Dionysius the martyr, we may through his intercession deserve to obtain everlasting reward from the Lord in the future.”]

And so that this grant of our authority may acquire inviolable firmness throughout the times of the present and those that follow, we have, as stated, decided to outline it by the subscriptions of our hand and by our own notation [Note: From the words “our hand” to the end, Dubletus again differs. In his text it reads: “We have decided to outline it by the subscriptions of our hand and by our own notation. The illustrious man Dagobert, king, subscribed. Given on the Kalends of October, at Sauriciagora.”]

The illustrious man Dagobert subscribed.

Given on the Kalends of October, in the fifth year of our reign, at Sauriciagora.

[Note: Dubletus omits the regnal year, and in the chartulary it is represented by a character of uncertain meaning. For the character does not represent either the letter *q* or the numeral sign for 6, as it may at first glance appear, as is clear from comparison of this character with the forms of letters and numeral signs elsewhere in the same chartulary. Since the charter mentions Aigulfus, abbot of Saint Dionysius, we have assigned this instrument to the final period of Dagobert’s reign.]

### XXXVI. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he gives the estate of Giuretis to the monastery of Saint Dionysius

[Note: Dubletus published it, *History of the Abbots of Saint Dionysius*, p. 679, without stating where he obtained it. We have copied it from the fourteenth-century chartulary of the Royal Library, no. 5415, p. 13. We give Dubletus’s significant variant readings within brackets. As far as we know, no one has accepted this instrument; Germonius, in the work cited above, condemns it as false on the basis of its chronological indications, which extend Dagobert’s reign to the thirtieth year, having been enlarged through about half its text. If this is insufficient, add the title of royal goldsmith given to Eligius, who subscribes, and the sign of the chancellor, placed indiscriminately among the witnesses’ signs. We pass over the remaining matters.] (637.)

Dagobert, by the grace of God king of the Franks.

Before the dissolution of our life overtakes us, and while the dwelling granted to us here under the law of our first parent is still permitted to us, because it is profitable and salutary for our souls, we ought to enlarge the generosity of present goods toward the holy churches of God, which no one possesses permanently but which pass away with slipping time [Note: The words “which no one possesses permanently but which pass away with slipping time” are absent from Dubletus], so that, when our immortal spirit has cast off its mortal body, it may rejoice to obtain a happy and unfading glory [Dubletus: “may exult to obtain glory”].

Therefore, when bodily assistance fails me, so that I may deserve to be placed in perpetual rest, I, together with my children and my wife, grant by perpetual right to the monks of the monastery of our patron Saint Dionysius, where his body rests and where we desire to be placed in the tomb at the time of our burial, the estate called Gyuretis, with its appurtenances. There the abbot Astulfus appears to preside [Dubletus: Aygulfus, abbot]. The estate is situated in the district of Berry, two miles from the river Cher.

And if any powerful person, by laying waste to the estate, should inflict harm upon the precious martyr Dionysius, or if any king succeeding us on the royal throne should wish to reclaim it for his own dominion, may he suffer the anger of God and of the martyr whose Church we enrich by this gift.

To make this gift much firmer and ensure that it may not appear apocryphal to posterity in future times, and that this charter may possess stronger authority, we have decreed that it be strengthened and confirmed by the sign of our hand.

Sign of King Dagobert. Sign of Clovis [Dubletus: Chloudovius], his son. Sign of Eligius, his goldsmith. Sign of Dado, his chancellor. Sign of Geremarus [Dubletus: Geremarus, abbot]. Sign of Aistulfus [Dubletus: Aygulfus], abbot.

Given on the Kalends of December [Dubletus: September], in the thirtieth year of our reign. Executed at the estate of Spinogilus, prosperously, in God’s name. Amen.

### XXXVII. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he orders that the children of the dependents or slaves of the monastery of Saint Dionysius, together with their offspring, be subjected perpetually under the law governing ecclesiastical dependents

[Note: Dubletus printed it, *History of the Abbots of Saint Dionysius*, p. 660, without stating where he obtained it. We have copied it from the frequently cited chartulary of the Royal Library, p. 5. Germonius, *On the Ancient Charters of the Kings of the Franks*, vol. II, p. 105, considers it one of the spurious instruments. Among other arguments, he relies on these: the day, month, and place are absent. In the subscription Dado uses the unusual title “chancellor of royal dignity.” As Mabillon shows, *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 39, the word “majesty,” used by Dagobert in this instrument, is inappropriate to the period. Many things are foolish and ridiculous, including the penalty imposed upon a slave who breaks the king’s decree: ten pounds of the purest gold and twenty pounds of the finest silver. Felibien, usually a more discerning man, cited this charter as authentic in his *History of the Abbots of Saint Dionysius*, p. 13, although he rightly did not reprint it among the proofs of his history.] (637.)

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, counts, dukes, vicars, centenarians, authorities [Dubletus: officials], judges, and everyone exercising authority throughout the entire kingdom of the Franks.

If, by royal judgment, we decree whatever appears to pertain to the reverence of the holy places of God and to the testamentary status of the dependents attached to them, we appear to act justly and therefore undoubtedly hope to obtain from God the reward of eternal recompense.

Therefore, let the wisdom of the present and future know that, at the petition of the lord Chunaldius, venerable abbot, and of the monk-brothers of the monastery of our special patron, the holy and most blessed lord Dionysius the martyr, where that lord rests bodily together with his illustrious companions, the martyrs Rusticus and Eleutherius, concerning the unions of dependents, male slaves, and female slaves belonging to those same venerable holy martyrs, and universally of all other persons residing throughout the whole kingdom entrusted to us by God, whether our own or belonging to any other person, whatever their dignity, rank, or authority may be, we establish and decree by this precept of our dignity that from now on, throughout all future ages of the present world, whenever any person belonging to the aforesaid martyrs—whether a male or female dependent, slave, or maidservant—should, by any union, whether lawful or furtive, beget, bear, and bring forth offspring, those persons shall from that time and forever, without any co-owner or divider, be irrevocably recalled and subjected to the power of the aforesaid holy martyrs together with all their offspring, and shall be perpetually assigned under the law of ecclesiastical dependents to the jurisdiction of the aforesaid abbot and his successors, the monks serving God in the said monastery.

But if anyone should presume to act against this decree of our majesty, violate what we decree out of love of justice, or infringe it in any way, he shall be compelled under the law to pay ten pounds of the purest gold and twenty pounds by weight of the finest silver according to the standard of our palace; and, if he is free, he shall be held as one of those dependents; if he is a slave, he shall pay the same and shall be struck one hundred and fifty times in public before the judges.

To ensure that this decree of our command may remain unshaken, acquire fuller force, and be preserved inviolate in future times, we ordered it to be marked with the ring of our dignity.

Given in the tenth year [Note: If the tenth year of the reign is reckoned from the beginning of Dagobert’s reign among the Austrasians, it was the year 631. Yet Chunaldus, who is called abbot of Saint Dionysius in the charter, does not seem, according to Cointius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 825, to have presided over this monastery before 635. Therefore this tenth regnal year must be reckoned from the death of Clotaire, so that the charter may be assigned to 637. Certainly Dado, whom Chunaldus succeeded, was still presiding over the monastery of Saint Dionysius in the fourteenth year of Dagobert’s reign, that is, in 635, as is clear from the charter published above (col. 536).] of the reign of our lord Dagobert, the most glorious king of the Franks. Dado, chancellor of royal dignity, examined it, read it, and reread it [Dubletus: “read and reread it.”]

### XXXVIII. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, confirming the precarial charter of Sigrannus, abbot of Anisola, and Hadoindus, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the monastery of Anisola

[Note: Inserted by Mabillon among the acts of the bishops of Le Mans, *Analecta*, p. 269. We presented above (col. 546) the precarial charter confirmed by this diploma. Since that charter has been condemned as false, everyone will judge that the charter by which it appears to be confirmed was fabricated to lend it some credibility. We are surprised to find it reprinted in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish History*, vol. IV, p. 632, from which fictitious instruments have generally been excluded. It is not listed among the spurious charters presented in the ninth century by the bishop of Le Mans in the dispute concerning the monastery of Anisola, as stated in vol. I, pp. 96 and 100, and above (col. 546), unless perhaps this charter is the same one whose title, through carelessness, was listed under the name of Clotaire. See Baluze, *Miscellany*, vol. III, p. 127, no. 11.] (637.)

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

If we willingly grant or bring to completion whatever pertains to the needs of churches or priests, we trust that thereby we shall have the Lord as our recompense, and we trust that this will redound, in God’s name, to our reward and to the stability of our kingdom. Therefore let it be known to all our present and future faithful that Hadoindus, venerable bishop of the city of Le Mans, and Sigrannus, abbot of the monastery of Anisola, sent to our Clemency; their messengers made their request known to us, and, through letters from the aforesaid men, confirmed their consent and petition, saying that the aforesaid abbot Sigrannus had petitioned the aforementioned bishop Hadoindus for the aforesaid little monastery of Anisola by a charter of usufruct, in which little monastery the lord Karileffus also rests bodily—he himself built it and, at the dedication of the church, handed it over by written charters to the lord Innocent, bishop of the aforesaid city—and that the aforesaid abbot had also acquired it as a benefice from the aforementioned Hadoindus by precarial tenure.

Accordingly, their messengers showed us the written usufruct charter, in which it was stated how the aforesaid abbot had requested the aforementioned little monastery from the said bishop, and how he had received it from him by beneficiary right for the days of his life, promising, for the security of the matter, to pay him a fixed rent every year: namely, four pounds of wax for the lamp of the mother church; for the work of the canonical brothers serving God in the aforesaid city, on the Lord’s Supper, a full bushel of eggs and full prepared bottles of the best wine; and, for the bishop’s use, one crozier and two under-shoes every year, which he was to pay to the aforesaid bishop or his stewards.

Therefore both men sent letters and messengers to our Highness, asking that, for the sake of securing the usufruct of the aforementioned bishop, we issue a writ by which the aforesaid abbot Sigrannus might safely and securely hold and possess the aforesaid monastery, with complete integrity, for as long as he lived. For this reason we ordered this authority to be made for the aforesaid venerable men, by which we command and decree that the aforesaid little monastery, just as it was granted to the aforesaid abbot by the aforementioned venerable bishop Hadoindus under beneficiary tenure, shall henceforth remain in his beneficiary control, and that he diligently pay the above-written rent to the stewards of the same see of Le Mans, without any delay.

After his death, however, it shall return, without anyone’s detention or opposition, to the right and power of the mother church of the aforesaid city of Le Mans, from which he is known to have received that benefice, so that the stewards of the same holy church may do with it whatever they wish to arrange according to ecclesiastical law. And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved through the ages, we have ordered it to be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

### XXXIX. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which he grants to the church of Saint-Denis the church of Plumbata and many other churches, with their appurtenances, and grants the same church privileges (year 637)

**Note:** Dublet published this charter in *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 675, transcribing it in such a way that he seems to have had the original before his eyes; but Germonius argues that it is spurious. We have copied it from the register of the Royal Library, 5415, p. 19, inserting Dublet’s various readings within brackets.
