The indications of forgery are these: the style is entirely unlike the style of Dagobert’s diplomas; mention is made of Ansoaldus, bishop of Poitiers, with whose consent the charter is said to have been issued, although he did not obtain the see of Poitiers until 673; the year and place notes and the subscriptions are omitted, so that this document appears to be an example of an incomplete diploma, as though it had been attempted in the forger’s first effort and was to be brought into authentic form by later revision. In any event, we certainly judge it to be entirely untrustworthy; and, since the year note is lacking, we have assigned it to the final year of Dagobert’s reign.

We know that our predecessors decreed, in accordance with the fathers, that whatever was done for the benefit of posterity’s memory should be committed to writing, lest it be suppressed by the darkness of oblivion. Therefore I, Dagobert, by the grace of God king of the Franks, wish it to be known to all, future as well as present, that, with the counsel of our nobles and the consent of the lord Ansoaldus, bishop of Poitiers, and of other archbishops and bishops, we give and grant to the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius of France the church of Plumbata—that is, the church which the blessed confessors Ursinus, Martialis, Lucianus [Cacianus], and Julianus established in honor of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, and of the holy angels, and which those same angels consecrated to God.

I mean the church situated between two valleys, near the water called the Vigenna [Vigona]. We grant it to the aforesaid martyrs free of service [free and released from every service]. Again, we make known to those present and future that we have given to the aforesaid martyrs vineyards, lands, and meadows, with waters and woods, male and female slaves, in the same place.

I do not wish you to remain unaware that whoever—whether free, slave, or condemned for any crime—within the boundaries that I established from the place called Aula to the other place called Ternant, as indicated by the aforesaid water, and by the land of Saint Martin and of blessed Radegundis—whoever, I say, whether fleeing from judicial combat or a native, robber, thief, or murderer, should seek refuge there, shall escape free and immune from every harassment by persecutors. Furthermore, let it be manifest to all that those who remain within the aforesaid place owe obedience to no one except God alone and the monks of the church.

We have also given to the aforesaid martyrs the church of Saint Hilary within the Annam [river], with lands, tithes, and waters. Likewise, in the same place called Cursous [Cursona], our churches: namely, the church of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and another in honor of blessed Martin; and, from the spring called Benedicta to the place called Claustrum, all the land and water called Voda, the mill of Cumignech, and the land of Bosnay, with male and female slaves and tithes.

Likewise, the land of Laingniacum [Lingniacum] and the church of blessed Hilary, with lands, meadows, and tithes. On the other side of the Vienne River we gave to the holy martyrs our village of Ingrandisse on the Vigenna [the village of our water, the Vigenna], with the churches of the apostles Peter and Paul and of the holy martyr Apolitus, with lands, tithes, male and female slaves.

Likewise, on the same Vienne, the church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul at Dangeo, with lands, tithes, and slaves. Likewise, our royal estate of Odriacum and the church of Saint Sulpicius, with lands, meadows, tithes, slaves, and vicars. Likewise, the land of Maleredum, with meadows, vineyards, woods, male and female slaves, and vicars; and the other Laingniacum [Lingniacum], and the church of blessed Remigius.

Likewise, in the territory of Tours, Antigniacum and the church of Saint Vincent on the Vigenna, and the land of Selignech, with lands, tithes, and slaves. Likewise, in the same territory, the land of Pleis, with the church of Saint Sylvester, and the land of Buymet.

Therefore, so that every claim of adversaries may be silenced and laid to rest, and every attack of all wicked men may be condemned and driven away, it has pleased us, for the sake of preserving the memory of the matter, to confirm this document with our seal.

### XL. Charter of Dagobert I, king of the Franks, by which, at the request of Aubert, bishop of Cambrai, he grants many gifts to the oratory of blessed Mary (year 637)

**Note:** This charter, much of which has been truncated, is published from a supplement to Miraeus’s *Diplomatic Works*, vol. III, p. 1, and from Carpenter’s *History of Cambrai*, vol. II, proofs, p. 4, which was taken from the archive of the abbey of Saint Aubert. Its spurious character is indicated by the unusual opening invocation; by Dagobert’s title, in which he calls himself king of the Austrasians, whereas in the other diplomas of good authority he is called king of the Franks and, after the death of Charibert in 631, ruled the whole of Francia alone; and by its being dated in the year 640 of the Incarnation, although Dagobert had already surrendered both kingdom and life two years earlier. I have therefore placed it at the end of Dagobert’s reign, under the year 637. We think it unnecessary to enumerate its other indications of forgery.

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, amen. The Son of God warns and says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.” Therefore I, Dagobert, king of the Austrasians, moved, for the sake of the soul of my dearest father Lothair, most august king of the Franks, by the salutary admonitions of the venerable man and my kinsman Aubert, bishop of Cambrai, grant and give to the most devout brothers of the oratory of blessed Mary two royal estates, Oenengium and Karubium, with all their appurtenances—that is, slaves and bondservants of both sexes, villages, lands, woods, meadows, waters and watercourses, and so forth.

Likewise, the village of Buriacum, the village of Haidem, and parts of the villages of Halogin and Glevia, and so forth. I likewise give and hand over to the church of Saint Peter of Cambrai, in which the most holy father Vedastus established canons, the royal estate of Tilletum, and the villages of Vinciacum and Harnam, with their appurtenances, and so forth; these donations being approved by the princes and elders of my palace, Arnulfus and Pippin.

And so that this grant of ours, and so forth.

The sign of Dagobert, king of the Austrasians. Subscription of Arnulfus of Metz. Subscription of Pippin of Neustria, elders of the palace. Subscription of Anso, chancellor, acting in the place of Cunibertus, archchancellor, recognized . . . . Given at Cambrai, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 640, indiction XIV.

## In the year of the Lord 638. Saint Hadoindus, bishop of Le Mans

[Col. 0565]

## Historical Notice on Saint Hadoindus

*(Mabillon, Old Analecta)*

Hadoindus, lord bishop of the city of Le Mans and successor of blessed Bertichramnus, was a Frank or Gaul by nationality, born of noble stock. He restored and renewed many monasteries in the diocese of Le Mans and established those monasteries in regular observance.

In his time there was also a certain man named Alanus, who possessed many properties of his own and had one son, whom he loved as his own soul. One day the aforementioned Alanus’s son was hunting on his father’s estate, whose name is Doliacum—for because of the grief experienced there it was afterward given this name, whereas previously it had another name. While he was driving a doe through the grove of his aforesaid father at Doliacum, his horse became frightened, and Alanus’s son fell dead from the frightened horse.

When the aforesaid Alanus saw this from the upper room where he was standing, he was filled with profound grief. Nevertheless, consoling himself, he announced the death of the young man to his wife, the boy’s mother, considering that such an event had not happened without cause. Then, devoutly entreating the God of heaven, he prayed that he might be permitted to dispose of his possessions in such a way as would accord with God’s good pleasure and by which he might merit the eternal kingdom.

He therefore began, together with his wife, to travel on foot through monasteries and holy places and to seek the bodies of the saints, earnestly beseeching God day and night to inspire him as to which church, in accordance with the will of his Creator, he should give his possessions to the Lord, both for the sake of offering his property on behalf of his aforesaid son and for the remedy of his own soul.

With this devotion, rising and praying and giving alms, he visited the shrines, relics, and churches of many saints, so that, as has been said, the Lord might inspire him where he should give his own property, since he possessed a great inheritance and had no son or daughter as heir.

When, for the aforesaid purpose, he was returning from the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours—although many servants of God had urged him to give his possessions to the holy places where they served, and, if he wished, to receive payment from them, so that he might have both alms from his possessions and gifts—the abbot of the monastery at Tours, where Saint Martin rests bodily, gave him this advice. Likewise the abbot of the monastery called Duo-Gemelensis, and other superiors and abbots, as well as many servants of God, offered similar counsel.

Yet his intention submitted to none of the places mentioned, nor did his devotion incline toward them, because perhaps the Lord did not wish it, and therefore perhaps did not inspire him to do this, since in this matter he was seeking the Lord’s will with the greatest devotion.

While these things were taking place, as the aforesaid man was returning from the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours and proceeding toward the city of Le Mans, intending to visit the holy mother church of the city, that is, the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, in which the Lord worked many miracles through their merits, he was traveling toward the Pontileuval hospice, a mile distant from the aforesaid city.

The servants of God of that Pontileuval hospice and of Bishop Hadoindus came to meet him. They received him in silence, led him with prayers, willingly and carefully supplied everything necessary for him, and served him with great honor. For the aforesaid lord Bertichramnus, bishop of that city, had built that hospice at Pontileuva in honor of Saint Martin precisely so that all travelers, rich and poor alike, might receive hospitality there and obtain abundant food and other necessities.

The next day, the aforementioned Alanus rose from the hospice and hastened barefoot to the mother church just mentioned, intending to pray there with the utmost devotion. During the preceding night, while he had been devotedly engaged in prayer at the aforesaid hospice of Pontileuva, God’s prompting had kindled his heart to hand over all his possessions to the mother and city church, which was built and consecrated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, the apostle Saint Peter, and the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and to which he himself was hastening in order to pray.

That this was accomplished by God’s will no one can doubt. As he was considering carrying out what had been inspired in him, he sent word to the aforementioned lord Hadoindus, the bishop, asking him to come to meet him and to consider with him how he ought to dispose of his property, since the lord Hadoindus was known to him as a trusted friend.

The lord Hadoindus did as the aforementioned Alanus had instructed. He came to meet him, received him kindly, and led him through the churches of the aforesaid city with the highest honor and great reverence.

When they had devoutly reached the aforesaid mother church and entered it, and had begun to pray together, Alanus and his wife began to weep. Through their tears they publicly disclosed their intention. They could not leave that church of Saint Mary, Saint Peter, and the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius before they had legally and firmly handed over all their property, by written charters confirmed under stipulation, to the aforesaid lord Hadoindus, to his fellow priests and ministers, and to the aforesaid mother church.

When this had been done, they were filled with such a joyful spirit and gladness and became so light in body that, by God’s power and through the intercession of the aforesaid saints, they returned to their former youth. All who saw this were astonished and confessed with tears that they had neither seen nor heard of anything like it, and there is no doubt that it was accomplished by God’s will and power.

With this condition, therefore, and moved by God, the aforementioned man, the God-devoted Alanus, gave to the aforesaid bishop and to the mother church twelve excellent villages with their appurtenances: Juliacum, Lucdunum, Ruliacum, Ruppiacum, Sabololium, Quilselidas, Vernum and Vericium, Tanida, the aforesaid Doliacum, where his son had died, and Camariacum. Later, through transferred hands, he gave donkey-estates (*asinarias*) and other little villages, whose names we have not inserted here because of the weariness and tedium of readers. Nevertheless, they are still found fully entered in the polyptychs [read: *polyptychis*] and complete registers of the holy mother church of the aforesaid city.

Moreover, the aforesaid Alanus gave himself and his wife to the aforementioned bishop, lord Hadoindus, and to the servants of God serving the Lord in the aforesaid church, so that they might take great care of their souls and bodies, nourish their bodies, and win their souls for the Lord.

The lord Hadoindus carefully provided for them, supplied them sufficiently, and served them as a servant serves his master. The aforementioned Alanus and his wife, under the authority of the aforesaid bishop, served the Lord most diligently and devoutly day and night. For these devotions, as we believe, they obtained the kingdom of God and, with the Lord’s favor, received eternal life.

For they live with Christ and his saints in blessed glory. May we also, supported by their prayers, merit by the Lord’s gift to live with them there forever. Amen.

In the time of the aforesaid lord Hadoindus there came, under God’s guidance, a certain holy man in monastic habit, named Lonegisilus, seeking places where he might establish some cell for the salvation of souls.

Having heard the reputation of the aforesaid Hadoindus, he came to him and requested from him his canonical village called Buxidum, situated in the pagus of Le Mans, in the district of Sagon. He knew that village, since he was accustomed to come frequently to the same place. It seemed suitable to him for the salvation of souls because of the large population; it also had good and God-fearing men around it who welcomed him warmly and supplied him with everything necessary.

Moreover, they urged him to establish a monastery there, which they wished to enlarge from their own possessions, so that, under his instruction, they too might merit to win their souls for the Lord.

When the lord Hadoindus heard this, he rejoiced greatly and willingly gave him the aforesaid village for the completion of the work just mentioned and for the construction of the aforesaid little monastery for winning souls to God. He also urged him to complete courageously in deed what he held in his heart under the Lord’s inspiration.

Furthermore, the aforementioned lord Hadoindus gave him other small estates and little villages situated around the aforesaid village of Buxidum, which the aforementioned lord Lonegisilus had specifically requested from him.

The lord Hadoindus also gave him, as assistance for completing the work of God just mentioned, the whole tithe of the estate of his see’s church called Lugdunum, so that the servants of God and he himself might have more abundant food and clothing in the aforesaid village and in the same little monastery.

Afterward, both during his lifetime and during that of his successors, many possessions were legally given to the aforesaid little monastery by noblemen and free men. He left that little monastery, together with the aforesaid possessions and everything belonging to it, subject to the church of his see, to be possessed by his successors according to ecclesiastical law and canonically governed.

[Col. 0567]

## Extant Writings of Saint Hadoindus, Bishop of Le Mans

*(Brequigny, Diplomatic Works, etc., new edition, vol. II)*

### I. Testament of Hadoindus, bishop of Le Mans

**Note:** Brissonius was the first to publish this testament, in *Formulae*, book VII, no. CLXI, p. 659 of the new edition, where it was found among the papers of Cruceius. It was reprinted from Brissonius in Baronius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 652; again in the commentaries on the customs of Le Mans; and later, in a more corrected form, Corvaiserius printed it in his *History of the Bishops of Le Mans*, p. 236, from an old pontifical register of the Church of Le Mans. From Corvaiserius it was taken by Cointius, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 135. Finally Mabillon published it, inserted among the *Analecta* in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, p. 267.

Everyone has regarded it as genuine, and it bears not even the slightest suspicion. We follow Corvaiserius’s edition. We place within brackets variant readings of some importance taken from the acts of the bishops of Le Mans; readings absent from Baronius are enclosed in parentheses. It is not surprising that various discrepancies are found in the editions of Hadoindus’s testament, since it may have been revised more than once by later editorial work.

The copy we publish was drawn up in the fifth year of Chlodoveus’s reign—that is, according to Cointius and Mabillon, in 642. Hadoindus did not die before 655, since, according to Cointius, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 409, and Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 383, he died in that very year. Baronius unfortunately assigned this testament to the year 652.

[Col. 0567C]

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit, on the eighth day before the Ides of February, in the fifth year of the reign of the most glorious King Chlodoveus.

I, Hadoindus, although an unworthy sinner [though a sinner], bishop of the holy Church of God in the city of Le Mans, being sound, by God’s favor, in mind and body and of sound judgment, fearing the fall of human frailty, have delivered this testament and dictated it to the deacon Cadulphus to be written.

If this testament of mine should for any reason be unable to stand under civil or praetorian law, or through the intervention of any new law, I nevertheless wish it to stand, and let it stand, as though intestate, in the form of codicils.

Therefore, whenever I, Hadoindus, the aforesaid bishop, shall depart from human affairs and fulfill the debt of the time to come, then you, holy and venerable Church, my heir, be my heir [of Le Mans]; and I constitute you my heir, so that whatever I have given through this testament, bequeathed, or ordered to be given, may be given, done, and provided to your trust. You are my heir.

I give to you, holy and venerable Church of Le Mans, in honor of holy Mary and of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, a village belonging to me called Avesa, which I acquired with my own property, with its houses, buildings, slaves, vineyards, woods, meadows, and pastures, together with everything that appears to belong to that place [those places], with its tenants and its entire boundary, so that it may be restored to your right and dominion [donation] and possessed forever.

Likewise, to the basilica of the lord Victurius, where that lord is known to rest and where, if I should deserve it, I desire to have burial, I give the village called Acerveum, which I purchased for a stated price, with its houses, slaves, vineyards, woods, meadows, and pastures. Except for those whom I have ordered to be made free for the remedy of my soul, let the aforesaid basilica restore the whole property, in its entirety, to its own power after my departure, to possess it in perpetual [Col. 0569C] dominion.

On this condition I give to the holy basilica of the lord apostles Peter and Paul, which the lord Berthicramnus, formerly bishop of Le Mans [at the town of Le Mans], built by his own labor, my hereditary village Iscomodiacum, situated in the pagus of Bellivi [Belim], which I purchased with money from Anserus [Aussorenus] and his mother, so that after my passing its ministers may hold and possess it and leave it for the future to whomever they wish.

Likewise, I give to that same basilica of the lord apostles Peter and Paul the villages called Taudiniacum and Martiniacum, which Lupus formerly appeared to hold through my benefaction. After my [our] departure, let the ministers of the aforesaid basilica immediately receive the whole of what appears to belong to those villages [the aforesaid villages], to possess it as their own.

In the same way I give to the basilica of the lord martyr Vincentius, which Domnolus, of holy memory, built by his own labor, my village Pratellus, with everything belonging to it, whatever Domnola appeared to have possessed for me [there].

Likewise, I give to the basilica of the lady and holy Mary the village of Aurionum [Aureonnum], which Agobertus, abbot of Diablentum [Dixiagens], built, together with the village of Jona, which belonged to the priest Sigulphus and which our faithful Chaddo appears to possess through our benefaction.

Likewise, the dwelling near that Jona which Lupus formerly appeared to hold, we wish to be granted to that same Chaddo. If, however, he has sons, let it remain in their power; but if he has no sons, after his death let it return to the right and dominion of the lady Mary of the village of Aureonnum [let it return, to be possessed in perpetuity].

Likewise, concerning the village Lastemaricum [Lastemariacum], which, through our generosity, we granted to our faithful defender Caddo [our faithful Caddo, defender], it is my will that he possess it in usufruct as long as he lives. After his departure, with every improvement or addition, let it return to the holy basilica of the village of Aureonnum.

Likewise, we decree that Pauliacum, which belonged to Roccolenus [the portion of Roccolenus], shall be possessed by the aforesaid basilica of the lady Mary and its ministers.

Also, let the village Baudiacum, which we recovered by purchase and through our lawful legal actions [the village of Baudriacum, recovered through purchase and our lawful conveyances], with its lands, houses, slaves, woods, meadows, pastures, all its inhabitants, and its entire boundary, be received in perpetual right by the aforesaid basilica of holy Mary and its ministers from the present day.

Likewise, the village Briacum, which is at the town [and the village Driacum, at the town] of that basilica, together with the estate of Hamaricum, which I gave to the aforesaid church of holy Mary, for intercession on behalf of our sins [the estate of Cameriacum, given to the aforesaid holy basilica of Saint Mary for intercession on behalf of our sins].

Likewise, Tusciacum, which belonged to Dondulfus, and the land which we exchanged with Edebertus [Ausciacum, which belonged to Dructulfus, and what we exchanged with Edebertus, I wish to be given].

Likewise, Auliacum, and likewise the fortified places, and the village Cometas, which we purchased with our money from the illustrious matron Modenana, with houses, buildings, lands, slaves, woods, and pastures, we enter in writing for the basilica of the lady Mary of the village of Aureonnum, together with the estate of Appiacum.

In the same way, the village of Frigidus Fons, with everything belonging to it—namely, all its buildings, slaves, inhabitants, servants and free persons, woods, lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and everything acquired there—I wish to be given to the holy basilica of the lady Mary, so that she may intercede for our sins and our Lord Jesus may deign to grant forgiveness for our offenses [with every unsearched-out matter, so that from the present day it may be given to the aforesaid holy basilica of the lady Mary for intercession on behalf of our sins, so that our Lord Jesus Christ may deign to grant forgiveness proportionate to our offenses, and that it may be beneficial there].

Likewise, let Vernicella, with all its rights and boundaries and the estates belonging to it [estate], benefit that holy basilica forever.

And if anyone should produce from this a document supposedly made by us, let it remain void and empty. It is likewise agreed by us, as was stated above, that if anyone should produce any charter concerning our acts from our relatives or heirs, however much it may have been confirmed by the hand of good men, as greed prompts, let it remain void and empty, and let him receive the curse described above.

Let our son and kinsman Bodilo, while he survives, hold and possess the estate of Fontanas in the pagus of Sylviasinum, that little property for the duration of his life.

In Christ’s name, I, Hadoindus, although a sinner, bishop, have reread and subscribed this testament, which I requested to be made out of devotion.

I, Rosindus [Rensidus], have subscribed.  
I, Berteghiselus, have subscribed.  
I, Marsus, have subscribed.  
I, Auffrebertus [Austribertus], have subscribed.  
I, Sigrannus [Seighrannus], have subscribed.  
I, Audobertus, have subscribed.  
I, Cadulphus, having been ordered by the lord Hadoindus, bishop, wrote and subscribed this testament when it was delivered [returned].

**To the magnificent [Note: Baronius shows that this instruction was written above the closed testament; he notes, however, that the codicil in which the manumissions of slaves and other bequests were written is missing] Badilo and Andrannus, sons of the holy Church in Christ:**

I, Hadoindus, bishop, ask and beseech your charity that, when the Lord and Creator of all commands me to depart from this world, you go to Le Mans and, when my testament has been opened, have it formally entered in the public municipal records [acts]. Whatever I appear to have assigned through that testament to the holy citizens or to my relatives [to the faithful], may each person, through your administration, receive according to that assignment.

Whatever you do in this matter must remain valid and utterly firm. We have confirmed this mandate with our hand and ask that it be secured.

*(Done in the city of Le Mans. In Christ’s name, amen. I, Hadoindus, although a sinner, bishop, have reread and subscribed this mandate. I, Rosindus [Rensindus], have subscribed. I, Bertigheselus, have subscribed. I, Marsus, have subscribed. I, Auffrebertus [Audo; Austrebertus], have subscribed. I, Audebertus, have subscribed [missing]. I, Deffensor, have subscribed. I, Ursimannus, have subscribed [missing]. I, Sirannus, have subscribed [missing]. I, Cadulphus, deacon, having been ordered by the lord Hadoindus, bishop, wrote and subscribed this mandate.)*

### II. Charter by which Sigrannus acknowledges that he holds the monastery of Anisola from Hadoindus, bishop of Le Mans, by usufructuary right and subject to a fixed rent

**Note:** This usufruct charter appears in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 268. It is listed among the charters by which the bishops of Le Mans attempted in the ninth century to assert their right over the monastery of Anisola. These charters were condemned as false by both royal and episcopal authority, as we stated above, vol. I, p. 96, note 1, and p. 100, note 2; see Baluzius, *Miscellanea*, vol. III, p. 127, no. 10. Accordingly, by the force of the judgment already rendered, this charter must be counted among the spurious documents. (Year 637.)

To the holy lord and venerable apostolic see, Hadoindus, bishop of the city of Le Mans, together with the entire congregation established in that city: I, Sigrannus, an unworthy priest and monk, approach you as a petitioner in the name of God.

Since there was my petition and your will decreed that the little monastery constructed in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Martin, situated on the estate of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius—the mother and senior church of the city of Le Mans—in the county of Le Mans, at a place once called by the ancients Casa-Gaiano, on the river Anisola and now called Anisola after the name of that river, should be entrusted to me; there Lord Turibius, formerly bishop of that parish, had built a church in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, from the resources of the senior and mother church of the city over which he presided. That church, however, had been destroyed because of the devastations that threatened, although part of its masonry still remained there.

Later Lord Karilefus, with the permission, intercession, and assistance of Lord Innocent, bishop, built it anew on the aforesaid estate of holy Mary and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, from its own resources and those of other good men. By your beneficence, under the arrangement of usufruct, for the duration of my life, you permitted me to possess there all the property belonging or pertaining to it. I have agreed each year to pay to the mother church of the city, or to its bishops and administrators: for the church-lights, four pounds of wax; for the bishop’s use, one *cambutta* [bishop’s staff] and two *subtalares* [sandals]; and for the use of the canons dwelling there in God’s service, two prepared flasks (*buticulas*) filled with the finest wine, and on the Lord’s Supper, one full *modius* of eggs.

If I should appear negligent or late in delivering this census, I shall provide due assurance concerning it, and I shall not lose the little monastery during my lifetime. Nor shall I have the right or power to sell or alienate it anywhere, unless it remains under the law, authority, and lordship of holy Mary and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, or of their bishops and administrators.

After my departure from this life, moreover, with all its property improved or added to it, without the attestation of any judge or opposition from our heirs, you—or your administrators and successors—shall cause the aforesaid monastery, in its entirety, together with the property belonging or pertaining to it, to be restored to your authority and lordship.

And so that these precarial documents, written in one form—one to be deposited in the treasury of the city church and the other to be received by me, Sigrannus, from you—may possess firmer validity, we have affixed our own hands below and have decreed that they be strengthened by the signatures of good men.

Enacted publicly in the city of Le Mans. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the thirty-first year of the reign of King Dagobert.

[Note: The chronological date betrays the forger’s ignorance—or carelessness. For who does not know that Dagobert died in the sixteenth year of his reign? Mabillon conjectures that, as noted above, year 16 should perhaps be corrected to year 31. But this charter, condemned as false, is wholly unworthy of any emendation. To assign it a place, however, it may be attributed to the final year of Dagobert’s reign.]

I, Hadoindus, although an unworthy bishop, have signed this precarial document made by me.  
Wistremandus, abbot, have signed.  
Oduluvinus, priest, have signed.  
Bernericus, an unworthy abbot, have signed.  
Winetharius, priest, have signed.  
Adamalgandus, deacon, have signed.  
Danihel, priest, have signed.  
Helenus, priest, have signed.  
Erigandus, deacon, have signed.  
Ebrenus, priest, have signed.  
Landricus, deacon, have signed.  
Emmo, priest, have signed.  
Albo, deacon, have signed.  
Herifredus, priest, have signed.  
Besto, priest, have signed.  
Urso, deacon, have signed.  

Mark of Landohic, advocate.

# In the Year of Our Lord 640

## Saint Sulpicius, surnamed Pius, Bishop of Bourges

### Life of Saint Sulpicius Pius, by an Almost Contemporary Anonymous Sulpician Monk

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictine Saints, from manuscript codices, and in John Bollandus.)*

## Preliminary Observations

### 1

Besides Sulpicius surnamed Severus, bishop of Bourges—whom some mistakenly confuse with Sulpicius Severus, the disciple of Saint Martin—the Church of Bourges had another bishop named Sulpicius, surnamed Pius, whose Life we present here. The former flourished toward the end of the sixth century; the latter at the beginning of the seventh.

### 2

Two contemporary writers committed the Life of Sulpicius Pius to writing. One wrote at greater length and was a monk of the monastery founded by Sulpicius, whom he repeatedly calls his patron; the other wrote more briefly, and for that reason we shall call him the abridger. John Bollandus published both on 17 January. Here we shall give only the former, noting in its proper place anything worthy of observation in the other.

The Sulpician monk indicates his own period in sections 4, 11, 16, 17, and 32, and appended to the Life he wrote a Book of Miracles, which he had promised at the end of Saint Sulpicius’s Life. Yet the metrically falling and often languid style of the Book of Miracles seems to indicate an entirely different author, as does the preface placed before the Life, which is missing from many parchment copies.

The writer Patriarchius of Bourges [Note: Extant in Philip Labbe, volume II of the *Bibliotheca*.] states that five books on the Life and Miracles of Saint Sulpicius himself were preserved in the archives of the treasury of the cathedral church at Bourges. You should not therefore suppose that he was an author different from ours, whose work we observe to be divided into five books in certain copies, as may be seen from the marginal notation.

### 3

The work of the Sulpician monk was embellished by John Phernandus Casalis, a Benedictine monk praised by Trithemius in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and included by Patriarchius of Bourges in chapter 31. From him we shall borrow a few observations to illuminate the anonymous author. We pass over Vincent of Beauvais and Saint Antoninus, who, together with many modern writers, have dealt with Saint Sulpicius.

### 4

Usuard and Ado commend Sulpicius in their martyrologies on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February. Ado’s words deserve notice:

> At Bourges, the deposition of blessed Sulpicius, bishop and confessor, who, educated in letters from childhood and conspicuous for the radiance of holy conduct, also shone forth in virtues while still a layman. Later, after laying aside his hair, he became Father of monks; thereafter raised to the episcopal chair, illustrious in life, he rested in peace.

For Sulpicius was abbot of the Camp, superintendent of the monks who performed the divine offices night and day in the royal camps.

### 5

Sulpicius was therefore a monk, both before and after his episcopate. Several years before his death he resigned pastoral governance so that he might devote himself more freely to God in the monastery he had founded at Naves. But to what institution did he ultimately belong as a monk?

Those who stubbornly defend throughout that entire century a separation between the rule of Saint Columbanus and that of Saint Benedict will not easily claim Sulpicius for us. In the time of Vualdebert, abbot of Luxeuil, and therefore also in the time of Sulpicius, monasteries were founded solely according to the rule of Saints Benedict and Columbanus, as a serious and contemporary writer, the author of the Life of Saint Salaberga, testifies.

Jonas, a monk of Bobbio, while enumerating the monasteries constructed near Bourges according to the rule of Saint Columbanus in the Life of Saint Eustasius, abbot, related above under the year 625, makes no mention of the then-existing monastery at Naves, or Sulpicius’s monastery—namely, because it obeyed the genuine and pure institutions of Saint Benedict.

## Preface of the Author

### 1

While the bright and glorious assembly with which, by the gift of the eternal Emperor, the palace of the Church is filled on account of the merits of its holy bishop shines with the lamp of virtues, although we are scarcely capable of expressing what is worthy, nevertheless we attempt to bring even our humble speech to the ears of the devout people. This is especially fitting since it benefits those who hear when the deeds of faithful men are recalled in writing for the memory of peoples.

Although the righteous man whose name is already contained on the heavenly page has no need of mortal writing, nevertheless the increase of faith grows when the recent examples of the saints are repeated: when the shepherd, enclosed in an earthly paradise, is represented in writing to the company of Christ’s worshipers; and when the flock, summoned by his example, advances toward heaven, so that, according to Daniel’s prophecy (Dan. 12:3), the people instructed by the teaching of their patron may shine like the brightness of the firmament, and the teacher may gleam with the starlike light accumulated within him.

This is especially so because, as a manifestation of his merit, throughout the vast world of Gaul, amid the abundant material of his virtues, by the remarkable gift of Christ a fountain of oil continually overflows with heavenly dew at his sacred body [Note: Concerning this oil, see below, sections 43 and following]; and thus the perpetual fire receives its nourishment, so that through the infusion of the Holy Spirit the flowing liquid continually increases.

Although death, the debt owed by nature, extinguished the little body of this prudent man, his living miracles nevertheless shine forth in the *polyandrum* [Note: *Polyandrum* or *polyandrium* signifies a common dwelling for men, a monastery—which seems to be its meaning here—and a cemetery.].

## Here Begins the Book

### 1

Blessed Sulpicius was born of distinguished parents [Note: John Phernandus illuminates this passage with these words: “The village of the Bituriges called Vastinium—Vatan—was his native soil; his lineage was illustrious, from the leading and foremost men of that province. He flourished at the same time as Theoderic and afterward as the most Christian king Clotaire II, who wisely guided the fortunes of the Gallic kingdom.”], almost the foremost citizens, and raised amid royal camps. He became the distinguished shepherd of the city of Bourges and has now, through his glorious departure, become its patron.

In the flower of his earliest youth, after breaking the snares of the world, he undertook the service of Christ with steadfast resolve. The blessed man had burned with such zeal for embracing religion while still a very young boy that, so to speak, if the time of persecution had not been lacking, he would have thrust himself voluntarily into dangers.

From that time he began to devote himself to reading the divine books and to exercise himself diligently in the instruction of the faith. Finally, to restrain youthful desires and attain progress in wisdom, he bound himself with the reins of prayer and abstinence. From his very cradle the ecclesiastical rule was so honorable to him in its observance that, when crowds of young and old came to him asking about the religion of our faith, he not only converted them to the faith but also formed them in the disciplines of a perfect life.

### 3

Divine grace was plainly present in him, through which he summoned innumerable people to imitate him in the faith of God. Above all, he judged that the evangelical commandments and the Savior’s word must be fulfilled with the greatest love and zeal. Although he may perhaps have seemed youthful and of less mature understanding, he placed in his soul, as it were, a first foundation containing the sign of the most perfect chastity.

Upon this foundation he then proceeded to build the remaining virtues. In accordance with the faith of the Gospels, from which the Savior’s exhortation is drawn—that there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God (Matt. 19:12)—he rejected marital union and embraced the purpose of chastity.

### 4

Certainly, as we have learned from the testimony of those who were his companions or servants from childhood down to our own times, while he was still in secular dress he seemed to do nothing other than build monasteries, raise basilicas, restore ruined churches through new construction, assist the wretched, supply the poor and needy from his own resources, and liberate many who had been cast down—not only by words and exhortation concerning perfect and spiritual teaching, but by his own services and ministries—from bonds, punishments, and misery.

### 5

There was a church not far from his parents’ house, almost destroyed by enemies, where neither clergy nor people gathered in any number. There the blessed man frequently gained the reward of prayer. Avoiding every occasion for boasting, when the deep silence of night had fallen he would secretly put on the clothing customarily worn by penitents, arm himself with holy prayers, and remain there throughout the night.

After rejecting the idle labor of sleep and passing the night in sweet meditation, when the splendor of rosy light illuminated the world he would again put on secular clothing and thus labor to conceal his holy purpose. These were his first childish exercises, this was the play of his infancy; such was the affection toward the Lord that grew strong in him.

### 6

One night, in the church mentioned above, while he was keeping vigil with two boys and applying himself more fervently to prayer, when his whole delight depended upon the deepest recesses of his mind, two exceedingly dreadful and savage spirits, resembling Ethiopians in appearance, each tried violently to drag one of the boys whom they had seized from the church.

At last the man of God found his companions behind him, crying out with loud lamentations. He looked upon the dreadful beings and raised his hand against the adversaries. As they were already dragging the boys away by force and carrying them outside, the priest of God brought forth the sign of the cross. Immediately, when the dreadful and bloodstained creatures fled, the boys remained unharmed.

From that time, therefore, the ancient enemy of all goodness and of truth, the adversary of human salvation, directing every effort against the soldier of God whom he could not corrupt in mind, attempted to frighten him with phantasmal threats. If anyone wishes to learn more carefully about this, we shall briefly show it in its proper place below.

### 7

Meanwhile he began to become renowned and adorned with signs and miracles of virtue. Although still wearing secular clothing, he cured the sick by prayer and drove out demons by his word, the athlete of Christ laboring with all his strength never to depart from his holy purpose.

He wished what he did to remain hidden from human favor, lest some breeze of worldly applause break forth and stain his ears with the pollution of arrogance. While these things were being done by him, and the truth of our God became known through the silent preaching of his deeds, the splendor of the light often kindled some who believed devoutly, while the dreadful darkness of unbelief covered others who impiously disparaged him.

Thus it seemed that what is written in Genesis had been fulfilled: “For the Egyptians there was thick and palpable darkness, but for the children of Israel there was light in all that belonged to them” (Exod. 10:20). Nevertheless, our God continued to be glorified in his saint and to extend the work of virtue already begun through increasingly favorable successes.

### 8

When his fame had suddenly spread far and wide, flying especially through the region beneath the western sky, Austregisilus, bishop of the city of Bourges, requested from Prince Theoderic permission to entrust him with a share in teaching in the church, since crowds were flocking to him for the sake of his instruction.

Without delay, royal authority was conveyed that he should have his hair cut and assume the burden of the clerical state. Advancing through the grades, after serving for a year and more as superior over the others and receiving the office of the Levitical order, he ministered to the church.

### 9

Meanwhile he was increasingly surrounded by the grace of signs. When the faithful had urged King Clotaire to do so, he immediately asked the bishop to grant permission, for the safety of himself and his army, for the blessed man to serve as abbot in his camps.

When provisions were distributed for himself and all his companions over three days, he kept enough for one day and gave the remainder to the needy. When his companions murmured anxiously about the danger of scarcity, he said:

> Fix the eyes of your minds, my sons, upon the Lord your Savior. Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Remember the prophetic word: “Those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing” (Ps. 33:11).

Indeed, such an abundance of food was suddenly sent to him by the faithful that he could rejoice, without worldly glory, to have received—so to speak—the hundredfold return that the faithful Recompensor had promised his disciples (Matt. 19:29).

### 10

At last, after a few days had passed, the king was afflicted with a cruel illness, and the poison, spreading through his limbs [For *diffuso*, “having spread”], rushed toward death. Meanwhile the queen, struck by sudden grief, threw off her jewelry, tore her clothing, and lacerated her hair and cheeks; she mourned her husband as though he had already been lost.

The household was thrown into confusion, and the tears of the servants joined the lamentations of their mistress. They hastened to the most blessed man, clung to his knees, and watered his feet with holy tears, asking that the pious priest pour out a prayer to the Lord for the king’s recovery.

He, whose hope rested in almighty God, drenched his face with tears, beat his breast, uttered sickly sighs, continued his vigils and fasts, and constantly poured out prayers for the sick man.

After five days had passed, the king slipped ever more rapidly toward death. His fellow priests then asked him, in order to moderate his excessive fasting, to take a modest amount of food. He replied:

> I shall not eat until I am able to obtain the prince’s health from Christ the Lord, whom I serve.

When they saw that the king’s spirit was failing and that he was almost lifeless, they cried out in vain that the priest was cruelly afflicting his innocent body through prolonged fasting. But he, whose salvation remained firmly in God, promised that, once seven days had been completed, the prince—his former strength restored—would eat with him and the other companions.

Thus the day awaited by everyone’s prayers arrived. The priest’s promise was fulfilled, swift healing was granted to the prince, and the priest was raised up in glorious triumph by everyone’s hands and summoned with great honors to the royal banquet. By this deed he became dear and acceptable to all.

### 11

Since we have set down in writing, with the same faithfulness with which they reached us, the deeds of the blessed man that we learned from our elders, who were his contemporaries, we shall now begin from the part belonging to our own time, which we ourselves witnessed, and from the part handed down to us by our fellow disciples, and we shall leave it as a memorial for posterity.

### 12

When the palace of the king was flourishing in beautiful splendor with the flowers of his virtues, the grace of his signs, and his jewels, and when a certain radiance of light had shone upon this world and filled it far and wide with the fragrance of its scent, it happened that the holy bishop—whom we mentioned shortly before—departed gloriously to the Lord.

When the entire people of the Church had gathered together to elect a bishop, and, as usually happens in such circumstances, one person called out one name and another called out another, a certain faction of the frenzied crowd, moved by the favor of its clients, gave its consent to some of the leading men. Through a mortal and arrogant prefect, they brought before the king representations accompanied by immense quantities of gold and silver, seeking his approval so that, in accordance with the sacrilegious sect of that wicked Simon, they might seize heavenly grace contrary to law and justice.

Our people, however, to whom the Savior says, “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32), asked the immortal Christ, perfect God, that the blessed man should be their priest. Nevertheless, they sent a modest embassy consisting of a few words, and through one of those of whom it is said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3), they made their request known to the king.

Since he, as often happens, had been infected with the poison of human greed and had inclined his mind toward the large sum of money brought before him, his wife, inflamed with divine love, warned her husband. She declared that, after the departure of such a great man, it would be worthy and just to allow this man to occupy his see, since he was supported by equal merit, signs of miracles, and the grace of virtues.

The noble woman also recalled to her husband the labor by which, through his prayer, Sulpicius had recently drawn him back from the precipice of death. At last, by heavenly indulgence, the prince drew a higher counsel from his lips. Suppressing the poison of greed and rejecting the persuasions of evil men, he ordered without delay that what had pleased divine providence be fulfilled.

Thus, through the Lord’s providence, he deserved to occupy the first see of Aquitaine. For it was God’s will that the peoples dwelling among one another in discord and divided in spirit should be recalled by a swift conversion to love of the bishop and suddenly united in one accord.

### 13

Having therefore obtained episcopal dignity, blessed Sulpicius bowed beneath the burden, not the honor. He became all things to all people, seeking not what was useful to himself but what was useful to many, so that they might be saved.

The Lord hastened to kindle his priest like a lamp. The blessed man gave himself entirely to extensive abstinence, unceasing fasts, and almost continuous vigils. If natural necessity ever demanded a little sleep, he did not take it upon the softness of a bed, which he had never been accustomed to use, but upon the surface of a simple mat [That is, a straw mat] and a haircloth.

The venerable man, worthy of God, was distinguished in every respect by purity of life and the virtues of his soul. He did not place much value on verbal ornament, since his soul was adorned with divine virtues, together with the grace of signs granted to him by the Lord Jesus Christ. Each day this increased his preaching of the word of God, and he sowed more widely throughout the whole earth the saving seeds of the kingdom of heaven.

### 14

Soon he made such progress in reforming the Jewish people, who were infected with ancient poisons, that they seemed to behold a new light of truth. Although the teacher of religion taught much by words, he taught still more by example; and since his disciples did not see him command anything that he had not first done himself, he permitted no Jew to live in the city without the grace of baptism, which had been entrusted to him from heaven.

He continually prayed to the Lord for their conversion and taught them that through baptism they received remission of sins and that they could not otherwise enter the kingdom of God. As though rays of the true sun had shone into their hearts, they were astonished, and, beholding the glory of God with unveiled faces, repented of their ancient errors. Coming with faithful confession, they were baptized by the bishop himself.

Thus, by divine favor, the outstanding warrior snatched spoil from the enemy, restored it to its Author, and drove the stain of unbelief from the inner chambers of the heart through love of Christ. Some of them still live today under the observance of our faith.

### 15

A short time afterward the grace of virtues increased in him so greatly that signs occurred through him no less than formerly through the apostles. For although we said above that he drove out demons by his word and cured the sick by prayer, our God added to his glory in the saint: as time passed, he restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, life to the dead, right hands to the maimed, and walking to the lame, along with many other things that would take too long to recount individually. If God’s favor assists us, we hope to touch briefly upon a few of them.

Come now, my speech; fulfill what you promise.

### 16

A certain Gunthoald placed before the feet of the blessed man his son, about ten years old. His tongue had adhered so firmly to his throat that no articulate speech had ever been uttered from his mouth. Gunthoald explained the entire matter.

The bishop, moved by human compassion, raised his eyes and hands toward heaven with groans and sighs. With complete faith and tears he invoked Christ, who is God over all. After offering a prayer, he touched the boy’s tongue and impressed upon him the sign of the cross.

Immediately the tongue was released, and from then until today he speaks miraculously in various forms of speech. Astonishing miracles followed these splendid and glorious signs.

### 17

At the time when deadly famine had laid waste to all the provinces, a boy almost dead from hunger fell at the saint’s knees, with only a faint breath remaining, and begged him to pity him.

The man, full of compassion, took pity on him. Looking at the person in charge of the household, he said:

> I commend this boy to you with the utmost care, under Christ’s witness.

The man promised that he would provide the care commanded. But while he was occupied with various matters here and there, he began to look after the needy boy rather carelessly.

Consumed by cold and hunger, the boy threw himself into the furnace of the baths. When he could no longer drag his exhausted limbs along with his faint breath, he finally died.

After some time the servant inquired among everyone, investigated the matter thoroughly, and found no trace of the boy anywhere. But the blessed bishop asked the servant about the boy entrusted to him. The man fell at his knees and confessed that he had lost him.

At once the blessed man entered his cell, prostrated himself on the ground, poured forth abundant tears, redoubled his deep sighs, and begged the Lord Jesus that the boy be restored to his sight. He had taken what he heard so harshly, and uttered such cries amid his tears, as though mourning his own crime, as if the soul of the dead boy were already being demanded from his hands before the tribunal of the eternal Judge.

Meanwhile the man whose duty it was hurried to the furnace to light it, and, finding the corpse, tried to pull out the stiff limbs. Recognizing the dead boy, he reported the matter to the blessed bishop.

Again the bishop prostrated himself on the ground, groaned, poured out prayers, and remained for a long time in sighs. Then, raising his head over the lifeless bones, he ordered hot water to be poured over them.

Meanwhile the priest of God continued without interruption to plead with the Lord for the boy, beating his breast. The dead boy’s limbs began gradually to move, and the bones returned to their former function, ready to serve their uses.

Although still weak, while the blessed man continued in prayer the boy crawled to his feet and, having touched the bishop’s foot, recovered his former strength. He is therefore believed to have survived the deadly famine; indeed, he afterward remained among us for a long time.

### 18

Before many more years had passed, another deed performed by divine power through him was also recorded. In a little field of the people of Vierzon there was a certain deep pool, abundant in its volume of water and consecrated, as it were, to demons. [Note: Virisio, Vierzon, is a town in the territory of Bourges, where there is a monastery of Saint Peter of the Order of Saint Benedict, recently united to the Congregation of Saint Maur. Formerly called Doverense, it was founded by Radulf, archbishop of Bourges, in the ninth century, and was afterward transferred in 903 by Gerontius, bishop of the same see, to the fortress of that town. See the author of the *Patriarchate of Bourges*, volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, chapters 47 and 52, and the *Chronicle of Vierzon*, there, p. 737.] If anyone entered it for any reason, he was suddenly seized by demonic cords and cruelly lost his life.

But God’s help arrived at last through the coming of blessed Sulpicius. The inhabitants of the place clung to his knees and prayed with holy supplication that the priest come to their aid, since they mourned the loss of many relatives and servants there.

As always, he pitied them with his whole heart. He ordered chrism to be mixed with a little oil and water [Some copies read *modicum*, “a little,” instead of *modica*]. After blessing it, he handed it to a disciple and instructed him to say, following the example of the prophet Elisha:

> Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters, and there shall no longer be death or barrenness in them (2 Kings 2:21).

When this had been done, the most wicked enemy was suddenly driven away, so that from then on everyone passed through safely, dragged an abundance of fish to the shore, and felt no danger.

Thus safety was restored to the people, and the water’s deadly power was removed.

### 19

Not long afterward an even more illustrious virtue followed. One of the country people, wishing to lessen the heat of summer, voluntarily threw himself into the river. Immediately bound by Satan’s snares, he violently lost his life.

This place was not far from the house of the basilica, where the saint of God was reclining at table with the brothers in a certain chamber for refreshment. Meanwhile an old woman was standing at a distance. Suddenly she signaled with her hand to the servants who were standing in the bishop’s sight.

They attempted, through one of their fellow servants, to inquire into the meaning of the event. When they reached the place, the woman indicated that someone had been submerged below and had lost his breath.

He then summoned his companions and reported the matter to the bishop, who ordered that the body, once drawn out, be kept until the Ninth Hour. After everyone had eaten, he went to the place of prayer.

Indeed, as soon as he had asked, he had drawn the power of life from the depths of the soul; but for this reason he believed that three hours should intervene from the Sixth Hour, so that no one would doubt that the man had truly been dead.

At last he rose from prayer and ordered the lifeless man to be brought before him. Raising his hand, he impressed upon him the image of the cross. When the breath returned, the dead man’s limbs moved in every direction. Thus, at the bishop’s command, he quickly rose up unharmed and, his strength restored, returned on his own feet.

### 20

At a certain time one of the leading men, named Theodegisilus, came to the blessed bishop to pay him a visit. The bishop showed him the affection that he knew he extended to everyone. Since it was winter, an excessive amount of fuel was piled upon the fire.

Perhaps the servants’ minds were occupied with something else, and no one was concerned about the danger from the fire. At last the flame rapidly devoured the roof; as it spread, everything began to shake, and, with collapse threatening, they confronted powerful flames. The abundant fire had thrown everyone into panic.

Since no one dared to climb onto the roof because of the extreme danger, everyone fled in despair, seeking safety. The priest, carrying the banner of the cross, attempted to resist the flames. To everyone’s amazement, the globes of fire were immediately extinguished before the servant of God withdrew his hand, as though they had been surrounded on every side by the force of a great river’s waters.

[Note: From this and the miracles that follow it appears that Saint Sulpicius’s power was especially manifest in extinguishing fires. In the very year in which we write this, 1668, in October, when a fire accidentally kindled in the Sulpician suburb threatened the danger of an enormous conflagration, it was suddenly extinguished when the head of Saint Sulpicius was brought there.]

### 21

Let us relate a similar deed. Within the walls of the city, one of the distinguished women had filled a large granary with ears of grain. In the dead of night a wicked man secretly entered and set it on fire; soon the flames surrounded it.

What had happened could not remain hidden, as everyone’s grief made clear. An uproar arose while the blessed man was overcome by his customary sleep. At last, learning the cause of the event through a disciple, he hastened swiftly and went around the burning pyre while singing spiritual songs.

In a wondrous manner, with his staff he marked out a boundary that the fire could not cross. Although the flames touched the neighboring houses on every side, they were forced back upon themselves and contracted into one mass; they fled into a chaos beyond which they dared not pass.

The Father returned joyfully to the church, dancing for joy, to offer the appointed praises at the morning hours.

### 22

Let us add a third similar miracle. In the same city the man of God had built a monastery with the greatest effort, in which he enclosed a company of virgins and continent women [Note: In the city of Bourges, the most ancient surviving convent of religious women is the Benedictine nunnery of Saint Lawrence. Its origins are attributed to Charlemagne. Or should its origins rather be attributed to Sulpicius, and its restoration to Charlemagne?]. There he raised a masonry structure into buildings of great size.

Through the carelessness of one of the women, during the silence of night a fire seized the wall and gradually increased and spread. Soon, after the house had been consumed, it prepared to reach the neighboring buildings. The mass of flames had already grown into a great mountain.

At last the priest of God, summoned by his sheep, hurried to the enclosure. He prepared to resist the flames, which had reached an immense height, with the sign of the cross. Immediately, in the middle of the blaze, holy help appeared in the form of a dove—the form in which the Holy Spirit had descended upon the baptized Lord.

Suddenly the flames were restrained and dared not touch the other houses. The shepherd instructed the sheep he had rescued with salutary admonitions. Through his teaching, the purpose of chastity still shines among them today.

While they eagerly devote themselves to the pursuit of wisdom, they consecrate not only their bodies but also their souls through the grace of virginity. They prepare clean vessels for wisdom, from which they seek holy and immortal unions with the divine Word, unions from which offspring may be produced that will in no way be subject to the corruption of mortality.

How brightly the grace of abstinence, sobriety, and modesty shines among them in beautiful splendor exceeds our strength to declare. Now let us return to the course of our narrative.

### 23

Far from the city, at a place called Anatra, he ordered a massive tree to be cut down with axes. When it was cut, it quickly collapsed. One of the boys, distracted in mind and standing there stunned by something else, did not avoid the danger of death.

Immediately the priest raised his hand with the sign of the cross, miraculously turned the tree in another direction, and drew the boy safely away from mortal danger.

### 24

And now, as the miracles shone forth like those of the brightest stars, while the faith by which all alike everywhere had believed in the Lord and Savior was flourishing, that ancient rival of all goodness and deceiver of the human race endeavored, through certain wicked men, to attack the Church resting in peace, together with all the people, by an internal war. He inflamed a certain prince of the Gallic provinces with the ardor of greed and pressed him by secret persuasions to enroll the people of Bourges, together with the priests of the Church, in a wicked assessment. And, like some beast hissing with two mouths and brandishing diabolical poisons with two tongues, he sent one of his agents to agitate the people in question.

[Col. 0582D] [Note: The shorter Life names the king as Dagobert and the assessor as Lullus. Sulpicius is said to have done something similar against Guarnerius, the administrator of King Theodoric, in the *Miracles of Saint Austregisilus*.]

But because divine power and grace, especially in the greatest struggle, never abandons its own, when the impious official was compelling the Christian multitude—free through the ages—to serve under royal cruelty, everyone, unable to endure the wicked oppression, flocked to the devout shepherd. So great was the uproar of those lamenting with raised voices that it seemed to the hearers to be a terrifying thunderclap. All the voices cried out only this:

“Devout shepherd, help the flock whom until now you have cherished with pastoral affection. Act, lest the flock entrusted to you by God perish. Defend from the wolf the one whom he tears with his raging tooth.”

Moved by exceeding compassion, he proclaimed a fast for all and addressed the assessor gently, asking him to desist from pursuing the impious command.

[Col. 0583D] [Note: Others call them *assisores*, those who impose *assisae* or assessments—French *assises*—a term signifying the imposition of a tax.]

But when the hardened mind was not broken by humility, and, scorning the priest’s words, grew ever more fiercely inflamed, the blessed man sought his cell, prostrated himself upon the ground, beat his holy breast, and asked from the Lord what he had been unable to obtain from the governor. Knowing that it is no lesser act of spiritual strength to implore the Lord for an enemy than to prostrate oneself for the Lord, he asked rather for the conversion of his enemies than for their destruction. Indeed, if he had asked for it at once, a fitting and outstanding punishment would have overtaken the immoderate prince and the most savage assessor; but the blessed man was always gentle and compassionate toward his adversaries.

### 25

Meanwhile he sent one of his own solitaries, a certain man named Ebregisilus—who, having renounced everything, that is, the world with all that belonged to it, was superior to the others in life and speech, as an example of the blessed man—to rebuke the prince’s savagery. Unless he changed through the correction of a better life, Ebregisilus was to announce that sudden destruction threatened him.

The blessed man’s follower also warned the prince about the impious crimes he had committed, in case he might be able to repent of his deed, if he could weep over his crime and extinguish the avenging punishments of the flames by an abundance of tears; for God does not desire the death of sinners so much as that they should be converted and live.

When the king heard this, he was struck by overwhelming fear and shaken by such terror that, as soon as he recognized his guilt, he mourned his offense with tears and, without royal haughtiness, undertook his penance. He willingly fulfilled what the great priest had communicated through his disciple.

The previously unheard-of assessment was swiftly abolished; the wicked registration was annulled; safety was granted to the people. And, as though the sun’s radiance had been restored after a violent storm, peace was granted to the Church and the joy of the priests was multiplied.

The king also remarkably added that a general authorization should be issued so that such an impious exaction would never again be repeated against the people. But the savage assessor, who had not agreed to the king’s recommendation, was struck by a deserved vengeance.

[Col. 0584D] [Note: An anonymous author says: “By divine vengeance, it is believed that both the king and his attendant died after a short interval.”]

He immediately lost, with dishonor, the life he had unworthily enjoyed. For the agent of so great a sacrilege could not escape unpunished.

O man blessed in every respect! He never defended himself against the fury of his adversaries with hand or weapon, but by fasts and continual vigils, lying beneath the altar, he prepared God as his defender and that of his Church through supplication. And who could ever have terrified him by schemes or attacks, since he always remained safe and unconquered by the assisting right hand of Christ?

### 26

At that same time the man of God, observing in every respect the apostolic simplicity, inferior to no one and in all things a perfect priest and victim of God, was striving everywhere to complete the work he had long ago undertaken of caring for the poor. But as his age, already advanced, was inclining toward extreme old age, he saw that he was not sufficient for everything: he could neither devote himself to the deeper things of God as he wished, nor remain continually in holy prayer, nor complete the instruction of those who were daily being restored to the faith. From all these duties he was not even given time to breathe, or at least one free hour, since he was always being summoned from one task to another, so that from first light until deep evening he never ceased to be occupied with various responsibilities.

[Col. 0584A] Therefore, when he saw himself weighed down by so great a burden, he judged it more useful to entrust to one of the leading faithful Christians of the region, a man already fully and excellently instructed, Wlfelentus [Al., Vulfolentus], a share in his office and labor, committing to him only the ministry of the divine word. And so, after assembling the clergy, he undertook there the rights and duties of the priesthood.

### 27

Who could relate with what humility and charity he thereafter was content to conduct himself toward his companions and ministers and toward the supports of the poor? He was always turning over in his most pure mouth that evangelical saying and striving with all his strength to fulfill it in deed:

“Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your last; and whoever wishes to be your master, let him be your servant” (Matthew 20:26).

Because he kept the eye of his mind wholly fixed upon God, he unceasingly considered that our Lord Jesus Christ, having become man for our sake, had taught us to struggle against sin unto death. Indeed, he himself “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself unto death.” Following him, the holy Sulpicius of God undertook every labor of struggle and every torment of flesh and mind, lest he stain the purpose of his faith in conscience.

[Col. 0584D]

### 28

For if we now wished to relate the virtues of the most blessed Bishop Sulpicius and set forth the strength of his steadfastness, we would have neither an abundance of words sufficient for so great a subject, nor would we think that such things could appear credible to others except those who saw them with their own eyes. Let our discourse now run on to the matters it had begun earlier, so that we may attempt briefly to recount the miracles which he thereafter wrought by heaven’s aid, with the associate joined to him.

On one occasion, one of the wicked and, as might be expected, needy men forcibly thrust himself by night into the blessed man’s storeroom. At once he tried to seize what his wicked mind had conceived as a crime of theft. But when he hurried to depart, no exit for returning was open to him; and, as though surrounded by a prison built all around him, the guilty man was bound on every side. Thus, after wasting the entire night’s journey in vain, he who had found entry easy could find no exit, however narrow.

Meanwhile the radiance of dawn illumined the world, and the man of God summoned one of the guards, sending him to his companion with instructions to bring out the man whom he had found in the storeroom, exhausted by error and, as though entangled in certain bonds, so ensnared in crime.

### 29

Without delay the minister hurried to the companion. When he had summoned him, they found the criminal inside, and immediately seized him in order to bring him out. But he suddenly slipped from their hands. Seeing himself surrounded by crimes and hemmed in on every side by the crowd, he preferred to undergo a swift death rather than endure the torments of a prolonged crime. He threw himself headlong from a distance into a well nearly eighty cubits deep, believing that he would die.

Nevertheless, when the devouring earth [Possibly: water] had received him, he called for the aid of the blessed bishop. Then the man of God arrived swiftly and ordered one of the boys to be lowered, secured by a rope, after the fallen man, warning him most carefully to draw up the criminal while holding him fast in his embrace.

When everyone cried out that the man whom the chasm of earth at such a depth had swallowed could no longer be alive, and all rather believed that he had already perished, he ordered the boy to obey his command quickly. The servant entered, armed without hesitation with the sign of the holy man, and found alive the one whom everyone believed to be dead. Bound with ropes and held captive, he brought him back to his native ground.

The walls were crowded with throngs of people; nearly the entire city had gathered to witness so great a marvel. Everyone’s voices resounded amid the clapping of hands. They marveled at the man’s survival, whom they had thought dead after being plunged into a chasm of such depth.

At last the criminal, shaken by profound amazement of mind, prostrated himself at the holy man’s feet and asked pardon for his crime. Immediately the man, full of compassion, forgave him and supplied him with what was necessary for his needs, often admonishing him to ask rather than seize, and to desire that a gift be conferred upon him rather than obtained by theft.

Behold how perfect his humility, how ready his mercy, how holy his simplicity! But who could say how great was his patience and long-suffering?

[Col. 0585D]

### 30

When one of the disciples, belonging to the order of the Levites, asked permission to return to his own country, the bishop, out of affection and lest some accident occur during the long journey, did not grant him freedom to depart. But the man, armed with the spirit of pride, scarcely had his first rest loosened the forgetfulness of his cares when, with swift steps and a vehicle, urged on by his criminal purpose, he set out in flight.

He was struck by a fitting punishment for his blindness, so that throughout the entire night he wandered uncertainly here and there in fruitless exertion. When daylight was restored to the earth, after exhausting himself in vain motion, he saw himself standing at the very place from which he had hastily begun his journey.

At last he went to the priest, from whom, I think, nothing could now be hidden, asked pardon for his offense, clung to his holy knees, and confessed everything in order. The bishop, with a mind most ready for compassion, forgave him and immediately granted pardon to the confessed offender.

[Col. 0586A]

### 31

We have taken care to mention briefly, for those who wish to know, with what arts and determination the worst demon, together with his entire army, fought against him, what new assaults he brought forth against all the others who at that time were struggling for Christ’s name, and what weapons of demonic fury he stirred up against him.

Since we have already spoken shortly before about his frequent night vigils, on one occasion, after he had completed the melodious singing of psalms in the baptistery during the deep silence of night, he went with a few companions to the basilica of Saint Martin, so that he might spend the remaining part of the night there feasting upon divine praises until Matins.

When, with a boy carrying a lamp before him, he had already reached the doors of the basilica, the destructive demon presented himself in a powerful form and the appearance of a most dreadful and horrible bird. First he tried to suffocate the light that went before them; then he hurled himself with great force into the face and eyes of the blessed man. Flying around him at a distance here and there in ludicrous assaults, he made himself violent and troublesome again and again.

At this the man of God, treating the spectacle as insignificant, said: “I know who you are, minister of the ancient serpent, and you do not allow yourself to remain concealed, for you almost continually reveal yourself as the wickedest persecutor.” At last, when he raised his hand with the sign of the cross, the demon not only did not dare to interfere any further, but vanished at the very blow [Al., onset] of the impressed cross.

### 32

Since he was shameless and a wretched deceiver, the seditious enemy subsequently inflamed himself with great fury against the holy man. Accordingly, when the bishop had ordered one of the boys, simple in mind and conduct, named Ansulfus, to go to a certain place to procure the provisions necessary for the brothers and the poor, the boy promptly obeyed the command, fulfilled the order, and hastened to return home.

The most savage demon, together with his attendants, confronted him. He threw him from the vehicle, severely beat him with lashes, and left him apparently lifeless. Half-dead, he was carried by his neighbors to the house.

Because no one reported to Saint Sulpicius what had happened as an injury done to him, the bishop at last perceived through the spirit of prophecy, which he had received by the grace of divinity, that his servant had remained mute and blind for ten consecutive days, with all his limbs apparently dead, and with his mouth so tightly closed, his teeth locked together, that no one could pour even a drop of water inside.

Meanwhile the man of God revealed to the brothers, in the order in which they had occurred, what he had perceived in the spirit. Mourning the afflicted man out of compassion and shedding tears from pity, the devout shepherd lamented that the sheep had endured such suffering on his behalf.

Immediately he prostrated his holy limbs upon the ground. After prayer, rising from the earth, he ordered a morsel of bread with wine to be offered to the lifeless man. At once, after the teeth had been opened with an instrument, his neighbors poured into his mouth a drop of the wine that the bishop had sent.

Soon the senses that had been lost were restored to the man, who had been almost entirely dead, and his limbs, which served him, returned to their former strength. We learned these things from the man who suffered them himself, and they have been confirmed by the testimony of the faithful.

### 33
