Not long afterward, when daylight had departed from the earth, Saint Sulpicius entered the church with a few companions to spend the night. When deep silence prevailed, the serpent’s craft first made a soft hissing in the air. Then, when silence was everywhere, he shook the enclosure of the church, the arches, altars, lamps, and other furnishings with a violent assault, so that the disciples already thought that the church was being completely overturned.

Trembling and pale with overwhelming fear, they abandoned their chants, awaited destruction, and clung to the pavement. But the Blessed One, unconquered in every respect, persisted so steadfastly in the divine songs, making little of what the envious one was doing, that he had never been more steadfast or more radiant in times of prosperity.

At last the envious serpent gathered itself with its army into a single mass. Thinking to frighten the undefiled steadfastness with heavier blows and noise, it roared amid an immense tumult and threw itself upon the pavement before the face of the blessed man, so that the disciples thought that their master had been crushed to pieces.

They themselves remained astonished for a long time. But the glorious priest, wounding his adversary with divine darts, continued in the spiritual songs. He rightly rebuked the disciples for abandoning their chants and being frightened by fantastic threats.

But what wonder if this enemy of the human race sought the death of so great a priest, since he was leader and standard-bearer among the people of God—when that enemy once extended his impious and unclean crimes even to an attack upon Divinity itself?

### 34

Because wickedness continually fights against goodness, and the adversary’s rivalry pursues the saints of God, we cannot adequately describe how much the worst enemy, revealing himself through various illusions, is said to have intensified the goads of his fury against Christ’s company, which the right hand of Christ protected through his priest.

Nevertheless, let us recount briefly one of the things he credibly did against one of Christ’s servants, in the presence of so many witnesses.

When one of the group whose office it is continually to sing to God in the Mother Church, a man named Legontius, was proceeding at the appointed pace to spend the night at the church, he encountered the enemy of the human race as an adversary in combat. Grinding his teeth in anger, the enemy tried to turn the servant of God back from the good work on which he had begun his journey. He afflicted him with many blows and left him almost lifeless and apparently dead.

In the morning several people found him lying alone on the ground, and he had lost the use of all his senses and the ability to perform his service.

At that time the saint of God had gone far from the city. When he returned after three days, he found the man half-dead and severely beaten with lashes. Then, prostrating himself beside the brother’s limbs, he groaned bitterly. With force he opened the man’s teeth and, with his own hands, the priest of God poured the sacrifice into his mouth.

To the amazement of all who watched, the man suddenly grasped the priest’s hand and rose up unharmed before his face, as though he had suffered no injury at all. He leapt about everywhere and blessed the Lord.

### 35

Not long afterward, one of the country people, with an axe in his hand, polluted the day of the Lord’s Resurrection with a wicked act. Immediately his sacrilegious hand withered; its skin and sinews dried up, and, adhering to the axe, it was unable to open.

He hurried at once to the holy man of God and fell at the feet of Christ’s athlete. His dry hand disclosed the perpetrator of the sacrilege; and, mourning, the guilty man was admonished instead to go to the church.

The priest continued his prayers beneath the altar, so that at last he might obtain from Christ pardon for the crime he had committed. Meanwhile the saint of God returned to his customary refuge. He entered his cell, covered himself with ashes, and spent the night in prayer, shedding tears.

When, early in the morning, the priest of God came to the church to perform the appointed praises, and the crowd observed the man with the axe, the man of God bent down in prayer. At once the guilty man, unable to endure the torments, began to cry out with such loud screams that the place was thought to be shaken. An immense terror seized everyone.

Meanwhile the sacrilegious hand was suddenly restored to its former function. The bones, skin, and sinews were refilled with their proper fluids, and the axe miraculously sprang away from the same hand. The criminal poured out abundant tears, confessed his sin, was absolved, and returned home pardoned.

Thus divine providence, in its surpassing mercy, cures the diseases of the soul by afflicting the body, in accordance with the saying:

“I will visit their iniquities with the rod, but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Psalm 88:33).

### 36

Since, while still dwelling on earth, our Lord and Savior had said to his disciples, “If you believe in me, you will also do the works that I do, and you will do greater works than these” (John 14:12), the spiritual flame had finally inflamed the blessed man with such love of faith that, if anyone secretly stole from his hands a little water dripping from them while he was washing and touched the body of a sick person with it, many were freed from their illnesses. In particular, those afflicted by tertian and quartan fevers recovered their former health to the amazement of all.

For we think that the signs the Lord performed through him at the end, and the new and astonishing miracles by which he revealed his powers, could be believed by no others except those who saw them with their own eyes.

### 37

And because he was believed to share the life and actions not of other mortals but of immortal angels, he rejected the falsehoods and flatteries of the world to such an extent that he could rightly say with the Apostle:

“For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21);

and:

“I desired to depart and be with Christ” (ibid. 23),

except that he wished to live for the sake of those for whom he would also die.

Finally, he rejected the pomp of the world as dung, despised gold, and rejected silver as mud. He held councils, summoned bishops to synods, and frequently warned them not to neglect the divine commandments, repeatedly citing that command of the Savior:

“Do not possess gold or silver, etc.” (Matthew 10:9).

[Note: Sulpicius subscribed to the Council of Rheims held under Bishop Sonnatius in the year 625, as Charles le Cointe correctly establishes in the *Annals*.]

But, as the Apostle says, “having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Timothy 6:8), and let us shun the things that follow.

He himself labored with all his strength, disciplining his body and bringing it into servitude, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should become disqualified. For a long time Saint Sulpicius possessed no silver vessels and did not use them; everything used for his needs was wooden, earthenware, or marble.

O undefiled steadfastness! By the virtue of patience it trampled underfoot the vices by which human weakness is assailed. And since, according to the Savior’s words (Matthew 5:9), he taught what he himself had first practiced in every respect, no one can doubt that he was great in the kingdom of heaven.

This was the priest of God who wore the priestly *petalum*.

[Note: *Petalum*, from the Greek πέταλον, means a leaf, plate, or thin sheet customarily placed upon the forehead or breast of the pontiff. See Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 19, chapter 21.]

By crucifying his body in himself and persecuting his vices, he attained a new martyrdom—not by death, but by the mortification of the flesh.

### 38

After he had built churches, monasteries, and cells in sufficient and abundant number, and had become the father of innumerable clerics and monks, many renounced their possessions. Devoted to this philosophy, they distributed their goods to those in need, cast aside even the many cares of this life, and lived outside the city in little gardens or on whatever small plots of land they possessed.

Others, like those who are remembered in the Acts of the Apostles as the first believers, sold their possessions and estates, placed the proceeds at the feet of the others, and distributed them to each according to need. Thus he might readily fulfill the evangelical office, having fully instructed in spiritual teachings all whom he desired, and having devoted them to the studies of Christian philosophy in imitation of their master.

Some of them, indeed, after three days, would take not so much the food they desired as that necessary for the body. For many, occupied with a deeper understanding of the sacred volumes and yearning for them as though for abundant banquets, could not be satisfied; as they gazed more intently, they were inflamed, and in continual struggle they fought against the flesh so that they yielded nothing to its pleasure or lust. Instead, they continually advanced the soul, nourishing it with the banquets of wisdom and the food of knowledge.

The Father rejoiced in such zeal among his sons, and at last hastened to demand from the eternal Father the interest that had been stored up. And suddenly the Lord was present to console and reward his faithful servant.

### 39

While he shone with these miracles of virtue, the glorious time of his blessed completion arrived. But as his limbs, already broken by age, grew weak, the burden of abstinence strengthened his afflicted and exhausted body; what nature had neglected, merit confirmed.

Thus, full of days and having completed the span of his life, resplendent with the brilliance of his merits, he entrusted his earthly limbs to the earth.

[Note: Saint Sulpicius died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, as we noted at the beginning from the Martyrologies, around the year 644. We infer this as follows. Sulpicius was placed in the see of Bourges after Austregisilus in the year 624 or the following year, when he subscribed to the Council of Rheims. If we trust the compiler of the Patriarchate of Bourges, he occupied the see for thirteen years, after which he appointed Vulfolentus as his coadjutor and successor. He lived for several years afterward, for Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, in Letter 10 to Dado, also called Audoenus, the newly appointed bishop of Rouen and his friend, boasts that he possessed Sulpicius, outstanding in merits, as a valued friend. Dado certainly was not ordained bishop before the year 641. It is clear enough from the foregoing that Sulpicius survived Vulfolentus’s appointment for some time. He was especially dear to the aforementioned Desiderius, whom, according to the writer of the Life of Saint Desiderius himself, he consecrated at Dagobert’s command in the eighth year of that king’s reign. In chapter 8 the writer reports a letter written by King Dagobert to Sulpicius, in which the king calls Sulpicius “archmetropolitan.” Desiderius himself calls him “holy patriarch” in Letter 12. Sulpicius sent Desiderius two letters, which are placed after Desiderius’s letters in volume 1 of the *History of the Franks* [the printed reading is corrupt: “Ch snii”], as numbers 64 and 72. The relics of Saint Sulpicius are now religiously preserved by our people in his own monastery in the suburb of Bourges, while his head appears there in a separate reliquary. Thus it is plainly necessary to conclude that Antonius Domenecus, in *Saints of the Principality of Catalonia*, and others are mistaken when they assert that it is kept in the town of Villefranche, in the territory of Conflent, at Tethin. Ado, in his authentic Martyrology, records no translation of Sulpicius. In the ancient Martyrology of Saint Lawrence of Bourges, published by Philippe Labbe in volume 2 of the *Bibliotheca*, two translations of Saint Sulpicius are noted. One is on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in these words: “At Bourges, the translation of the body of Saint Sulpicius, bishop and confessor, a man of great holiness”; the other is on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November: “At Bourges, the translation of Saint Sulpicius, bishop and confessor.” Both were solemnly celebrated from ancient times in the monastery of Naves, as is established by an old manuscript *Diurnale*. It is reasonable to believe that they date from the time of the Normans, who devastated the aforementioned monastery. Out of fear of them, the body of Saint Sulpicius was carried to a safer place and afterward brought back, giving occasion for the two celebrations.]

His heavenly spirit ascended among the choirs of angels to the heights of heaven.

### 40

Then, from every side of the city, an innumerable crowd of people suddenly poured together from all directions. The walls, courtyards, and every street became packed, so much so that, unless the aid of the blessed bishop had been present, most of the people would have been crushed beneath their feet and killed by the force of obstructed breath and the press of so great a crowd.

There was immense mourning among all, unbearable grief, and such a groan burst forth from the mourners’ voices that even hearts of stone would have shed tremendous tears. I do not know whether anyone there could have been so cruel and senseless as to restrain himself from tears.

The uproar of their voices was so great that the place seemed to be shaken by a mighty thunderclap. And while everyone’s grief of soul was immeasurable, the clergy’s sobs, wholly broken by lamentation, scarcely allowed them to sing the spiritual hymns. Only these words were wrung from them amid their sobs:

“Alas, desolate flock, what will you do? Behold, with your shepherd lost, you are scattered; and who will ever be able to free you from the rabid teeth of wolves? At your death, O good shepherd, who can doubt that we have all perished?”

### 41

Meanwhile they came to the basilica, where the priest of God now lies buried in glorious triumph, awaiting the time of resurrection. He himself had earlier built it with the greatest effort.

[Note: The Abbreviator says: “That place where the basilica itself is situated, and where the aforementioned man of God was buried, is called NAVIS”—as this author also says below—“because it seems to have been the site of a harbor for ships. It is a most pleasant place, between two rivers, the Euram and the Molum, rich in woods and vineyards, with meadows threaded by streams. It is an immense plain, so that those who live there seem to possess a likeness of paradise.” The words of John Phernandus should also not be omitted: “Among the monasteries that the devout Father raised with very great labor and no small expense, he especially delighted in one situated in the suburb of the city of Bourges and consecrated to the Virgin Mother of God, which he chose to call by the name NAVIS. There he ordered men of proven monastic conduct to live, whose most exact rule of good living might provide the clearest examples to those wishing to work out their salvation. He loved those brothers from the heart, serving them both as abbot and as companion,” and so forth. This monastery, long ago distinguished by the name of Saint Sulpicius and now presided over by one of our regular abbots, is still flourishing.]

When the body had been carried into the tomb, the entire people, unable to endure the absence of their shepherd, lay prostrate on the pavement and gave forth a bellowing beyond human measure, so that even the ministers of the church were not permitted the freedom to perform their office. They lamented him as though he were absent, though they had not lost him but sent him ahead, not knowing that, entering heaven as their ambassador, he was hastening to serve before the divine gaze on behalf of the people: there he would intercede for the people, granting there what he had granted here to the petitioner and the faithful; there he would pour forth prayers, as here he had answered prayers.

### 42

Nor did he permit himself to remain absent for long from those whom he had sustained on earth by unceasing labor. Immediately, in spirit, he hastened to visit those whom he had left in body but not in affection. By restoring health to people afflicted with various illnesses, he suddenly revealed himself to be present, so that it was as though a heavenly light had been displayed, or a ray of the sun had burst forth, illuminating the whole world with the brightness of supernatural light.

From that time immense crowds gathered in every city and village to the churches, as grain is gathered into threshing floors at harvest time. News of the various miracles of healing shone forth with winged flight—not merely through the neighboring cities, but throughout all the kingdoms of the earth.

And unless the basilica itself had been enlarged to a considerable extent, it would not have been able, given its capacity, to receive the multitude of the sick.

[Note: The abbot Domio is said by another contemporary anonymous author to have enlarged that basilica for the most part. Hence John Bollandus suspects that the writer of this Life was Domio himself, who out of modesty concealed his name. But from the following book of the *Miracles*, which Bollandus did not see, it is clear that another abbot was in charge at that time.]

And if I shall have deserved to have God as my guide, I wish still to show in a brief discourse some of the things that the illustrious victor has now accomplished. Rightly, too, the place where these things occur has long been called NAVIS by the ancient predecessors because of its harbor for ships. As though by a prophetic indication of future things, that name once pointed to what it now reveals by divine dispensation.

That is the Ship in which those who cling to it cross the sea of this world and arrive freely at the distant homeland, namely, the kingdom of heaven. There it becomes a harbor of refuge from the threatening storms of visible and invisible evils; there grace is granted for escape from the waves and tempests of the world.

There, every day, they pour the salt of knowledge into the weak and ignorant. There, through the intercession of our blessed Father, healing is freely granted to the sick by the eternal and invisible physician. Through it, shipwrecked and exiled people return completely to their former homeland.

### 43

Leaving aside the other matters to which, as I promised above, I shall shortly devote attention, I shall now speak briefly about the lamp that hangs before the Blessed One’s tomb.

It is said to have been filled once by the ministers with oil and, when the holy liquid overflowed, to have poured forth from above an abundant stream [Possibly: flow], from which many who were anointed are said to have been freed from various illnesses.

[Note: The shorter Life states more clearly: “And when the abundance of oil that flowed down from above overflowed onto the ground, many were anointed and freed from their illnesses.”]

This too must be acknowledged with wonder: once, in the evening, while the priestly assembly was resounding with divine songs, a heavenly flame suddenly struck the lamp’s wick with a lightning-like blow and miraculously provided light in the sight of all. From that time onward it never lost its brightness, and to this day divine agency nourishes its sustaining fuel.

### 44

Having related these deeds of the illustrious man—although in words unworthy of them—we now intend, at the appropriate time, to bring our account to an end. We place our hand upon our mouth and hasten to return inwardly to our conscience.

Let us ask that the one whom we cannot imitate become our patron, so that we may be aided by the merits of him whose feast we celebrate, through the help of him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0591]

## Three Letters of Saint Sulpicius, Bishop of Bourges

(*Canisius, Ancient Readings*, volume 1)

### First Letter

[Col. 0591D]

To the ever-lord and proper master, the lord Desiderius, worthy of reverence as occupying the apostolic see, pontiff of the city of Cahors, Sulpicius, bishop of the city of Bourges [F. Bourges].

The extraordinary sweetness of your greatness has stirred the mind of my littleness, and I have presumed, in however slender a discourse, to set forth the distinguished pontifical praise of your priesthood. But all power suddenly failed in words before a subject of such magnitude, so that, while weighing in my mind the beginnings of such great difficulties [Ms., *anagnusticorum*], I was defeated and sank beneath the weight of its greatness.

Thus I have at least satisfied my own desire, although I was unable to fulfill it with your support, and I do so willingly, since it appears that I can contribute nothing else to your lordship. Yet, in your accustomed compassion, you always value so greatly the inquiry into our affairs that you wish to visit us frequently.

Therefore, first of all, as we inquire after your well-being, what we desire—that we might complete by mutual conversation through the movement of the body rather than the tongue—we fulfill, although the distance between regions prevents our seeing one another, except that the interval of separation alone deceives the sight. Even so, affection sees the very object when it shapes our minds through remembrance [F., the mind remembers]. Thus absence loses nothing that presence has labored to accomplish.

In directing your letters, your blessedness always fulfills its duty, so that you ought to return a greater service of attendance than you consider yourself indebted according to your merits. We presume to ask the Author of heaven to command that your life be prolonged through the courses of many years, and may he deign to preserve it for a long time, since the world is now richly kept in his name. May the wavering heights of affairs long be strengthened, or, having fallen apart, rise again more solidly.

He has done this with his own hand in your times. May I deserve to serve your grace, my special lord.

### Second Letter

To the holy lord and brother worthy of reverence as occupying the apostolic see, Verus, bishop of the city of Rodez [L., the city of Rodez], Sulpicius, a sinner.

As the apostolic man, the lord Desiderius, bishop of the city of Cahors, has informed you by his letters, his men suffered serious injury from Perricius, your deacon, in his parish at Aronnac. And we have heard that he is to have a hearing with you concerning this on the Kalends of April [perhaps, “the Kalends”]. Therefore, greeting your Charity, we ask that you arrange for satisfaction to be made to the lord Desiderius in such a way that, if you recognize what I wrote above—that the deacon has been negligent in this matter and has delayed obedience, as your prudence knows, even if he perhaps says this himself—[the passage is wholly corrupt; perhaps: “if you recognize what I wrote above …”], and if it is not thus remedied as the lord Desiderius wishes, let nothing else be done except at the hearing which the aforesaid bishop has announced to you. [The manuscript has *Meme raverit*, but this was erased and corrected, so that it is uncertain whether *memorato* or *memoratus* is to be read; perhaps read “your aforesaid deacon.”] [lacuna] Your deacon, through sureties, together with your written record, you shall have sent before our lowliness. Meanwhile, we are retaining a copy of the letter with us. We ask your most beloved Holiness to deign to remember us in your holy prayers.

## LETTER III

### [Col. 0594B]

To the lord Desiderius, ever to be revered and to be named venerably with every honor, pope: Sulpicius, a sinner.

You have fittingly fulfilled the pastoral office through singular mysteries, since, by sending solicitude to our lowliness with affection, the pastoral visitation doubled the joy which the principal solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection bestowed upon us. In it, on both sides, blessing shone forth partly in the offerings and affection partly in the written words [perhaps: “on both sides”; for the manuscript reads “each parts”]. [Eulogiae had various meanings: first, the sacrament itself, or the Eucharist; then the bread offered at the altar, part of which was consecrated and sent to absentees. Finally, *eulogiae* were gifts which bishops sent one another, or the king himself, every year at the recurrence of the Paschal feast or on Christ’s Nativity. Marculf preserves formularies or letters then written, both for sending *eulogiae* and for giving thanks by those to whom they had been sent; Bignon explained them for his learned readers. In the following letter, I think, the ten little vessels of Falernian wine must be distinguished from the *eulogiae*. For although wine was often listed among *eulogiae*, I do not know whether so great a quantity ought to have been blessed. **BASNAGE.**]

Therefore, returning the duties of well-being, we desire that, as the courses of the years multiply, we may merit both to receive your eulogies and to be blessed by your words. I shall serve you for innumerable years, and, with prosperity continuing, may you flourish, most blessed pope.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 640. SAINT AUTBERT, BISHOP OF CAMBRAI

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT AUTBERT

*(Gallia Christiana, vol. I.)*

### [Col. 0593D]

Concerning this holy prelate, and concerning the place assigned to him among the bishops of Cambrai and Arras, Alcuin speaks as follows in chapter 5 of the Life of Saint Vedast, which he himself revised:

> “He [Saint Vedast] lay in that same place until the time of blessed Autbert, who succeeded him as the seventh bishop in the pontifical seat.”

That Autbert succeeded Ablebert is taught by Saint Fulbert of Chartres, who wrote the Life of Saint Autbert:

> “It happened,” he says, “that Ablebert, bishop of the see of Cambrai, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, departed from this world. Therefore, while divine providence arranged all things beneficially, Autbert, a distinguished man and worthy successor, advancing from virtue to virtue, obtained the pontifical dignity of that same see.”

His ordination is recorded as having taken place on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the year 633, according to Charles Cointius. He was consecrated by Leudegisel, metropolitan of Rheims, together with Aicharius, bishop of Noyon, and Attila, bishop of Laon. Because of the fame of his virtues, from the beginning of his pontificate he was especially dear to King Dagobert, by whom he was honored with very many gifts; in return, he was received by him as a guest and most lavishly nourished, especially with spiritual banquets. For he gave the ruler salutary admonitions, which the king heard most willingly. Among the other things that Dagobert gave to Autbert, or rather to the church of Cambrai, Saint Fulbert lists Onengia and Quarubium, between Valenciennes and Condé.

A little later Autbert received Landelin from the sacred font. Landelin was born of a most noble Frankish family, in a village called Val, or Vaux, and Autbert later instructed him in the sacred letters. Landelin founded many monasteries: Lobbes, Aulne, Waulsort, and others. In the year 654 Saint Autbert took part in the elevation of the body of Saint Fursa.

He also raised the body of Saint Vedast from the earth, after being warned from heaven, and transferred it to the monastery of Nobiliacum, which is now distinguished by the name of Saint Vedast. For this solemnity he invited Saint Audomar, bishop of the city of the Morini. Although Audomar was blind, he is said to have recovered his sight on that occasion and, shortly afterward, by a greater miracle, to have obtained the restoration of his former blindness through prayer. This is recorded as having occurred in the year 658, although Mabillon postpones the translation to the year 666. Certainly, in the year 658, Landericus, bishop of Paris, is recorded as having subscribed the privilege of Saint-Denis, in Miræus *(Notitia Ecclesiarum Belgicarum*, p. 13).

Autbert subscribed the privilege which the aforementioned Audomar, bishop of the Morini, had granted to the new monastery of Sithiu, in the sixth year of King Chlothar. On this matter Mabillon is to be consulted under the year 660, no. 2. At approximately the same time, Emmo, archbishop of Sens, fortified the monasteries of Sens—Saint Columba and Saint Peter the Living—with a similar privilege, to which our Autbert subscribed as evidence of his agreement. He did the same with the privilege of Bertefrid, bishop of Amiens, for Corbie, granted in the year 662 according to Cointius, in 663 according to Mabillon, and, according to the judgment of the brothers Sammarthanus, in the year 664.

A privilege which Saint Drausius, bishop of Soissons, granted to the nunnery of Saint Mary on the sixth day before the Kalends of July in the year 666 is addressed to him and to other bishops of the province. He blessed the monastery of Celle, constructed by Saint Gislenus, and that of Malbodium, constructed by Saint Aldegund. He also blessed the monastery of Marchiennes in the diocese of Arras. Saint Vincent, founder of the monasteries of Hautmont and Soignies, and his wife Waldetrude, founder of the nunnery in the hills of Hainaut, were instructed by him in the discipline of a stricter life; noble canonesses now reside there. At his urging, King Dagobert granted numerous estates between Valenciennes and Condé to the clerics serving in the church of Cambrai.

He departed to the heavenly realms in the year 668, according to the Sammarthani and Cointius, on 13 December. His life was written by Fulbert, bishop of Chartres. As Autbertus Miraeus estimates in *Notitia Ecclesiarum Belgicarum*, Surius published it in mutilated form under the sixth day of February; a complete copy exists at Cambrai in the abbey which preserves the sacred body of its patron. Autbert is entered in the tables of the Roman Martyrology on 13 December, and he is also commemorated by Molanus and in the additions to Usuard’s Martyrology. See the Life of Saint Waldetrude, second century of the Benedictine edition, p. 869, and the Life of Saint Landelin, abbot of Crespin, in the same work, p. 873, chapters 1, 3, and 4.

## CHARTER OF SAINT AUTBERT, BISHOP OF CAMBRAI, CONCERNING THE MONASTERY OF WALLERS

By this charter Saint Autbert takes under his protection the estate of Wallers, donated by Dagobert to Landelin for the construction of a monastery.

[It occurs in Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 490, together with notes; he copied it from a modern apograph and put it into print, so that no one might seek his diligence in this respect. The charter appears spurious, fabricated to support the spurious diploma immediately preceding it (p. 30) concerning the same monastery of Wallers. Besides the indications of forgery which it shares with that diploma, it has faults of its own: Dagobert’s thirteenth regnal year agrees neither with the year of the Incarnation 642, nor with Sigebert’s fourth year, nor with the time when the monastery in question was founded. See above, Col. 534, note d, and 535, note a.]

### [Col. 0595D]

*(Brequigny, Diplomatic Documents, new edition, vol. II.)*

Autbert, by the grace of God bishop of Cambrai, to all the faithful of Christ, eternal salvation.

We do not doubt that it belongs to our care and solicitude that whatever the faithful of Christ confer and dedicate to the holy Church through pious generosity, we ought to consecrate and confirm by episcopal authority. Accordingly, we have taken under our protection and defense the estate called Wallers, belonging to our most pious king Dagobert, with all its appurtenances, which that same king gave as alms to the servant of God Landelin Maurosus, for the sake of the soul of his father, the illustrious King Lothar, in order that a monastery might be built there.

This includes all the villages, lands, woods, meadows, fields, waters, and courses of waters assigned there and situated in our diocese. We grant in perpetuity all the tithes of these possessions to the aforesaid Landelin and, by God’s gift, to his successors. We also grant and permit him to build a monastery, construct a church, and appoint persons who, according to what the angel of the covenant shall grant him, may be supported from the assigned resources.

Whatever arrangement he makes there, we hold to be ratified and inviolate. By our authority we prohibit anyone from inflicting trouble or burden upon those serving God in all the possessions which the aforesaid king gave to the aforementioned place, Wallers. If any secular or ecclesiastical person should presume to act against this and occupy those same possessions, we strike that person with the sword of eternal anathema, unless he repents and takes care to restore what he has occupied.

So that this aforesaid almsgiving of the illustrious king may endure forever and enjoy ecclesiastical liberty, we have caused our seal to be affixed to this document.

Executed at Castrilocus, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 642, in the fifteenth indiction, in the thirteenth year of the reign of the illustrious lord King Dagobert, and in the fourth year of Sigibert, son of that same king.

### [Col. 0597]

Dagobert had departed this life in the year 638. His thirteenth regnal year had begun at the beginning of spring in the year 634.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 642. JOHN IV, ROMAN PONTIFF

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON POPE JOHN IV

*(The Book of the Pontiffs, from various editions.)*

### [Col. 0597C]

**1.** At the consecration of this pontiff, Papebrochius holds that confirmation began to be sought not from Constantinople but at Ravenna from the exarch. Pagius, in order to support his own opinion concerning the postponement of Boniface V’s ordination, says that this began at the election of Honorius, on account of the troubles brought upon the Church after the death of Saint Deusdedit. Accordingly, he dates the beginning of the authority delegated by the eastern emperors to the exarch of Ravenna to the year 625.

Garnerius, in his notes on the *Book of the Pontiffs*, traces the exarch’s authority to the year 618, at the election of that same Boniface V, since he observes that only a few days intervened between Saint Deusdedit and Boniface. But since much longer vacancies followed later, as we have seen, neither Garnerius’ nor Pagius’ conjectures seem worthy of acceptance.

The matter is different concerning Papebrochius’ opinion. Since it is clearly established that after John IV the emperor’s command was no longer awaited at Constantinople, it is not unreasonable to believe that John’s election too was confirmed by the exarch. This is suggested by the shorter interval between pontificates than in previous cases. Although Blanchinus, in his account of Pelagius II, says that one hundred days were more than sufficient for sending a messenger to Constantinople and receiving him back, the 144 days preceding John’s election seem all the more sufficient.

Whatever may be the truth concerning this matter, which is attested by no documentary records, certainly before the death of John IX the exarch of Ravenna received from the eastern emperor the authority to confirm the pontiff.

John IV, after a vacancy of the see lasting four months and twenty-four days—according to the Freherian Codex 1 and Codex Thuaneus 2, which Pagius testifies that he saw, not twenty-nine days as is incorrectly printed, nor as stated by others, supported by Ordericus—was ordained in the year of Severinus’ death, 640, on 24 December, with the Sunday letter A.

This is clear not only from the interval preceding his pontificate, since the Kalends of August are four months and twenty-four days distant from 24 December, including the day of death, but also from the duration of John IV’s pontificate: one year, nine months, and eighteen days, as recorded in most catalogues and codices, with which the authors in Pagius agree.

The Freherian Codex 2, Codex Thuaneus 2, and the catalogue newly edited by Blanchinus, however, apart from the year and months, give nineteen days, differing by one day. The Royal, Mazarin, and first Thuaneus codices would likewise give nineteen days, unless the inattentive copyist had omitted the numeral and only nine days were written.

Indeed, if one counts one year, nine months, and eighteen days from the day of ordination, 24 December 640, one arrives at 11 October, the day of John IV’s death. If nineteen days are counted, one arrives at 12 October, or the fourth day before the Ides, when Anastasius reports that the pontiff was buried at Saint Peter’s. It is customary for Anastasius and the catalogues sometimes to record the day of death and sometimes the day of burial, as a careful observer will frequently find.

**CENNUS.**

**2. John.** In the year of the Lord 636, John, the fourth of that name, was substituted for Pope Severinus. He was a steadfast and undaunted defender of the orthodox faith. Yielding nothing to the threats of the exarchs and little moved by the exiles of the cardinals, he gathered a council of bishops and, as Theophanes says, anathematized the heresy of the Monothelites in order to defend and free his predecessor, Pope Honorius, from the accusation of the heretics.

For this reason he took great care that the writer who had been secretary to Pope Honorius and had written the letters to Sergius the bishop should interpret their true and genuine meaning and transmit it to the emperor. When that writer faithfully fulfilled the command of blessed Pope John IV and set forth the legitimate meaning of Honorius’ words, he removed every sinister suspicion of heresy from Honorius.

**BIN and LABBE.**

**3. John.** The son of Venantius the schoolmaster, a Dalmatian, and cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church from Jadera, he occupied the see for one year, nine months, and eighteen days. He was consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, at the beginning of the year of Christ 639.

Scarcely had Severinus departed this life when letters from the Scottish people were brought to Rome. John the deacon, elected Roman pontiff but not yet consecrated according to the custom of the city, could not answer them alone. Rather, Hilary the archpriest and John the primicerius, who were maintaining the place of the apostolic see, composed a response together with him; it is found in Bede. From this letter we learn that it was the custom of the Roman Church for those who were prominent among the ministers of the Church to respond in writing to letters received before the legitimate consecration of the bishop.

**CIACONIUS.**

John, a Dalmatian by nation, from his father Venantius the schoolmaster, occupied the see for one year, nine months, and eighteen days [Codex Lucullanus: six days; in another copy eighteen days is absent].

In his time [The following is added in a note: Pope John, as Anastasius testifies, sent throughout Dalmatia, or Istria, much money from the treasuries which Isaac the exarch had squandered, as we related under Severinus, through the most faithful and holy abbot Martin, for the redemption of captives whom the pagans had carried off. Fearing that the relics of the saints in Dalmatia, his native land, might be scattered by the invading barbarian enemies, he ordered the relics of the holy martyrs Venantius, Anastasius, and Maurus to be brought from Dalmatia and Istria, as the same Anastasius testifies, and deposited them in the Lateran church, in a private oratory which he built in their honor beside Constantine’s baptistery. This remains intact to the present day, and, from the year 1575 onward, after an image of the Virgin Mother began to shine there with miracles, it was commonly called “La Madonna di San Giovanni,” as Octavius Pancirolus writes in Augustine Oldoinus’ account of John IV. **PAGIUS.**]

He sent throughout Dalmatia, or Istria, much money through the most holy and faithful abbot Martin, for the redemption of captives who had been carried off by the pagan peoples. [He sent much money throughout Dalmatia, or Istria. Since an immense multitude of captives had been carried off from there by the ravaging Slavs, or Sclavs, John IV, a Dalmatian by nation, took pity on the sufferings of his countrymen and redeemed them with a great sum of money all the more readily because by these works of charity he was placing the Church’s treasure in a safer place—namely, in the bosom of the poor. For he had already seen the ecclesiastical goods amassed by Honorius plundered by the sacrilegious avarice of the emperor’s servants, concerning which Anastasius speaks above under Severinus. **MAFEUS.**]

At the same time he built a church for the blessed martyrs Venantius, Anastasius, and Maurus, and for many other martyrs. He had ordered their relics to be brought from Dalmatia and Istria, and deposited them in the aforementioned church beside the Lateran font, beside the oratory of blessed John the Evangelist [Codex Lucullanus: the Baptist]. He adorned it and offered various gifts.

In the same place he made two silver arches, each weighing fifteen pounds, together with many other silver vessels. He held two ordinations in the month of December: eighteen priests [another copy: twenty-four], five deacons, and eighteen bishops in various places.

Here he gave the entire *roga* to all the clergy [The *roga* may be understood chiefly in two senses: either as a gift or honorarium, which the emperors customarily distributed to nobles and magnates, and even to the people, or which the supreme pontiffs distributed to the clergy—hence the word’s origin—or as an exaction or payment, under the name of a request, which the clergy themselves annually paid to the pontiff. Anastasius’ words may perhaps mean that John remitted and forgave such a tribute to the Roman clergy. Nevertheless, this word frequently occurs in these pontifical records to express distributions.

It is well established from Roman historians that the ancient Caesars distributed gifts to the soldiers. The Greek emperors likewise maintained this custom. When they sent crowned images through the provinces as tokens of their assumption of power, solidi bearing that image were scattered by the imperial officials wherever the new emperor’s image was carried. We shall discuss this later under the emperor Philippicus. The author of the *Miscellany*, under the emperor Tiberius II, writes: “He took Anastasia as his wife, crowned her Augusta, and distributed a great *roga*.”

Gregory of Tours’ account in Book VI of his *History* is relevant here: “Mauricius proceeded to the Circus, and, after acclamations had been offered to him, was confirmed in the empire by distributing gifts to the people.” The *Annals of Fulda*, concerning Charles the Bald, report that he “corrupted and allied the Roman Senate in the manner of Jugurtha, so that even Pope John, after a crown had been placed upon him, ordered that he be called emperor and Augustus.”

It is tedious to copy further documents of this kind concerning imperial generosity, by which rulers are shown to have continued even after the restoration of the Western Empire. The Roman pontiffs likewise distributed such *roga* to the people and clergy at their ordinations and on other solemn days.

Examples are readily available. Anastasius himself, in his account of Vigilius, p. 108, reports that after the solemn celebration of Mass he gave gifts to the people. In his account of Theodore, p. 126, he writes: “After he had completed these things, he had gifts distributed among the people.” He is speaking of Pyrrhus of Constantinople, to whom the pontiff, after Pyrrhus had renounced Monothelitism at Rome, granted the honor of distributing the *roga* to the people according to pontifical custom.

In the account of Leo IV, who had first celebrated the Octave of the Assumption, the Acts, p. 368, say: “A great multitude of the people had also gathered for it, desiring to celebrate the solemnity of the new feast. When this great-hearted bishop saw this, he distributed several silver pieces to all who were present at the celebration.”

The same pontiff, at the dedication of the Leonine city, p. 383: “After the sacred offices had been performed, he honored and enriched all the nobles of Rome with many gifts, not only in gold and silver but also in silk cloaks.”

Concerning this *roga* distributed by elected pontiffs, William the Librarian gives an example in his account of Adrian II, where, after reporting the visions that preceded Adrian’s future election, he writes, p. 425: “Some, according to apostolic custom, distributed gold pieces in the Lateran basilica,” and so forth.

We also read, in the account of Benedict III, p. 493, that rulers journeying to the thresholds of the apostles made such distributions: “In his time the king of the Saxons, hastening to Rome to the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, offered gifts. And when the most holy lord Pope Benedict requested that he make a public *roga* in the church of blessed Peter the apostle, consisting of a weight of pounds of gold or silver, he gave gold to the bishops, priests, deacons, the entire clergy, and the Roman nobles, but small silver coins to the people.”

The pontiffs, however, distributed a fixed sum of money to the clergy: to all the clerics, one complete *roga*, and to those assigned to apostolic service, a second *roga*. Thus we read in the account of Deusdedit: “He gave one complete *roga* to his household and to all the clergy.” This distribution is recorded by Anastasius in almost every pontifical biography.

In other churches, distributions were made to the clergy according to the revenues. A constitution of Felix IV survives in Agnellus’ Life of Ecclesius, bishop of Ravenna, p. 96: “The fourth part of the patrimony of the Church of Ravenna—that is, three thousand solidi—shall be assigned through the customary distributions to all the clerics and to those to whom it is customary to distribute them.”

Sometimes a double *roga* is also recorded, as in the account of Boniface V, p. 119. I think this happened especially when the apostolic see acquired new estates or other goods through the generosity of rulers and the faithful. For Felix the pontiff also established that a fourth part of newly acquired goods was owed to the clergy of Ravenna, adding in the same constitution: “If, however, by the Lord’s will, something should increase from rents or inheritances, then, with the same Lord’s help, it too shall be added to the fourth portion, so that, once the lists have been arranged, what is distributed to each person may not remain concealed … according to the places which God has established entirely according to justice and measure.” **BENCINUS.**]

Here he gave the entire *roga* to all the clergy.

He was also buried at blessed Peter the apostle [Who was also buried there. Finally, after Pope John had occupied the see for one year, nine months, and eighteen days, as Anastasius writes, he fell asleep in the Lord on 11 October of the year 642 and was buried at blessed Peter the apostle on the fourth day before the Ides of October, that is, on 12 October. That Anastasius’ text is sound concerning the duration of his pontificate is shown by the fact that Regino, Liutprand, Ordericus in Book II, and the Vatican-Palatine catalogue assign him the same duration of one year, nine months, and eighteen days. **PAGIUS.**]

He was buried at blessed Peter the apostle on the fourth day before the Ides of October. The episcopal see then remained vacant for one month and thirteen days.

## LETTERS OF POPE JOHN IV, ROMAN PONTIFF

*(Mansi, Collection of Councils, vol. X.)* (C, S)*

### LETTER I OF POPE JOHN IV AND THE ROMAN CLERGY TO THE BISHOPS AND PRIESTS OF SCOTLAND

Concerning the celebration of Easter according to Catholic custom and the careful avoidance of the resurgent Pelagian heresy.

### [Col. 0601B]

To the most beloved and most holy bishops Thomianus, Columbanus, Chromanus, Dimanus, and Bathanus; to Chromanus, Hermanus, Laustranus, Stellanus, and Segianus, priests; to Saranus and the other Scottish teachers or abbots: Hilary the archpriest, and John the deacon, elected in God’s name and maintaining the place of the holy apostolic see; likewise John the primicerius, maintaining the place of the holy apostolic see; and John, servant of God and counselor of the same apostolic see.

The writings which the bearers brought to Pope Severinus of holy memory remained unanswered with respect to the matters that had been requested, since he departed this life. When these writings were opened, lest the darkness of so great a question remain unexamined for long, we discovered that certain people from your province were attempting to renew from an old source a new heresy against the orthodox faith. They were rejecting our Easter, at which Christ was sacrificed, under a cloud of darkness, and striving to celebrate it with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon.

The beginning of the letter clearly declares both that this heresy had arisen among them only recently, in those times, and that not their entire people but only some of them had become entangled in it.

After setting forth the rule of the paschal observance, the same letter adds concerning the Pelagians:

“We have also learned that the poison of the Pelagian heresy is reviving among you. We urge you most earnestly to remove such a poisoned crime of superstition from your minds. For you ought not to be unaware how that detestable heresy was condemned: it has not only been abolished for these two hundred years, but is also daily buried and condemned by us with perpetual anathema. We urge you not to revive among yourselves the ashes of those whose weapons have been burned.

“For who would not abhor their proud and impious attempt, when they say that a human being can exist without sin by his own will and not by the grace of God? In the first place, it is blasphemy and foolish speech to say that a human being can be without sin, which is utterly impossible except for the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who was conceived and born without sin.

“For all other human beings, being born with original sin, are known to bear the testimony of Adam’s transgression, even when they exist without actual sin, according to the prophet’s saying: ‘For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins’” (Psalm 50).

### LETTER II OF POPE JOHN IV TO THE EMPEROR CONSTANTINE, SON OF HERACLIUS

[The fact that Pope John IV’s apology for Honorius was written to the emperor Constantine, whom the Greek annals report to have reigned only four months after the death of his father Heraclius, makes it necessary to understand that it was written in the year of Christ 641, in which Heraclius is said to have died. The occasion for writing arose from the patriarch Pyrrhus and other Monothelites, who were abusing Honorius’ letter to Sergius, Pyrrhus’ predecessor, as though it favored their heresy. John proves that the letter had been dictated in a correct and orthodox sense. Saint Maximus the Confessor used the testimony of this apology in his disputation with Pyrrhus, which took place in Africa a few years later. Honorius’ letter to Sergius, by which he was accused, is recited in the sixth synod, action 12.

Certain excerpts from three letters of Maximus himself are appended to John’s letter. The reason why the first two are inserted here is clear: in one, written to the priest Marinus, he also defends Honorius’ letter to Sergius; in the other, addressed to Peter the Illustrious, he likewise supports Honorius and Sophronius against Pyrrhus. The reason for mentioning the third here is not equally clear, since it is uncertain what it should be related to. **SIRMOND.**]

### Apology for Pope Honorius concerning the one will in Christ, which his accusers claim he mentioned

The Lord, who said that light should shine forth from darkness, who rescued us from the power of darkness into his marvelous light—the light of truth and the truth of light—in whom he was pleased that the whole fullness of divinity should dwell, and through whom he reconciled all things, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things in heaven or the things on earth, looking upon the face of his Church because of the eminent greatness of the riches of his goodness, has deigned to call your kindness, known and predestined by him, to the present integrity of the faith, so that, with every deceptive darkness driven far away, he may make the truth victorious through you.

For, as we have learned from the various reports that have come to us in crowds, and indeed also from direct hearing, all the regions of the West are scandalized and disturbed because our brother Pyrrhus, the patriarch, has been preaching something new and contrary to the rule of faith in letters sent here and there, and hastening to draw our predecessor, Pope Honorius of holy memory, toward his own understanding—something wholly alien to the mind of the Catholic Father.

Therefore, so that your kindness may learn the whole cause of the matter, I shall recount with the most exact truth what happened a short time ago.

Sergius, the patriarch of revered memory, informed the aforesaid pontiff of the Roman city, of holy remembrance, that some people said that there were two contrary wills in our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ. When the aforementioned pope learned this, he wrote back to him that, just as our Savior was one, in a unique manner, so also he had been conceived and born in a wondrous way above the whole human race.

By the sacred dispensation of his Incarnation he also taught that, just as our Redeemer was perfect God, so also he was perfect man, so that, without any sin, being born, he might renew the noble origin of the first image which the first human being lost through transgression.

Thus the second Adam was born, possessing no sin either in his birth or in his association with human beings. For the Word made flesh, in the likeness of sinful flesh, assumed everything that is ours, bearing no sinful fault arising from the transmission of transgression. Therefore we understand the likeness to refer not to his flesh but to sin.

The Lord truly assumed flesh from the undefiled and blessed Virgin, the Mother of God, and became consubstantial with us. Thus the holy apostle speaks of “the likeness of sinful flesh”: he assumed flesh like ours, with a rational soul, yet without sin. For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to have one will, according to the natural first formation of Adam’s humanity, and not two contrary wills, as we are now known to have, since we have been begotten from Adam’s sin.

For when the first human being had been made corruptible through transgression and refused to be subject to his Creator, he experienced the flesh, which had previously been subject to him, nevertheless resisting him. Through his sin he made the entire human race subject to sin, as the Apostle says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans 5).

Therefore we who are born through his transgression and sin are known to have two contrary wills. By two I mean the wills of mind and flesh, struggling against one another, as the same blessed Apostle teaches: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish” (Galatians 5).

Every human race placed under sin suffers this condition, since no one is clean from this sin of transgression, not even an infant, whose life upon earth is said to be but a single day. And as the Holy Spirit says through David: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in transgressions” (Psalm 50).

For just as all sinned in Adam (1 Corinthians 15), according to the Apostle, so all will be justified in Christ. And just as through one human being many were constituted sinners, so through one human being many will be constituted righteous (Romans 5).

Therefore the one and only person without sin is the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who was conceived and born free among the dead. In the dispensation of his holy flesh, therefore, he never had two contrary wills, nor did the will of his flesh resist the will of his mind. For he had no sin whatsoever, since he came to take away the sin of the world, as he himself also said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John 8). And elsewhere he said: “The prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14).

Therefore, knowing that there was absolutely no sin in him when he was born or when he lived among human beings, we rightly say and truly confess that there was one will in the humanity of his holy dispensation. We preach not two contrary wills, those of mind and flesh, as certain heretics are known to rave about him as though he were merely a human being.

Accordingly, our aforesaid predecessor is known to have written to the aforementioned patriarch Sergius, who had questioned him, in the following manner: that in our Savior the two contrary wills—that is, in his members—do not exist at all, since he derived no defect from the transgression of the first man. For what is written, “For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7), applies to us, not to him. Again: “For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I do not will, that I do. But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (ibid.). And afterward: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin which is in my members” (ibid.).

Hence these two contrary wills of mind and flesh, which the Apostle teaches, were in no way present in our Savior, since this stimulus to struggle began with the transgression of the first parent: our Redeemer assumed nature, not the guilt of crime. But lest someone of insufficient understanding should object to why he is known to teach only about human nature and not also about divine nature—for Christ is known, adored, and worshiped as God and perfect man in two natures united in one person—whoever doubts about this should know that the answer was directed to the question of the aforementioned patriarch. Moreover, it is customary that where the wound is, there medicinal assistance should be supplied.

The blessed Apostle, too, is known often to have acted in this way, adapting himself to the disposition of his hearers: sometimes, when teaching about the supreme nature, he is entirely silent about the human; at other times, when discussing the human dispensation, he does not touch upon the mystery of his divinity. For here he says of the divine nature, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1); elsewhere, however, he said of his incarnation: “What is foolish in God is wiser than men, and what is weak in God is stronger than men” (ibid.). Wisdom and foolishness, power and weakness, are without doubt set against one another as contraries.

Does the blessed Apostle, then, teach that there is contradiction within Christ himself? Certainly not. Rather, he wisely adapts himself to his hearers, teaching according to the occasion, like a provident nurse who gives milk to infants but solid food to the perfect. What, then, is meant by his saying, “What is weak in God is stronger than men, and what is foolish in God is wiser than men”? This entire passage appears to teach about Christ’s dispensation, not about his heavenly nature. He wishes to show that God, having become man, possessed a human soul and body, which he calls foolish and weak. Human wisdom, compared with divine wisdom, is foolishness; bodily strength, compared with God’s power, is weakness. For created human wisdom, compared with the wisdom of the Creator, is foolishness.

Thus, by joining both aspects together, we confess Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God according to his divinity, and we confess the nature of his humanity according to the dispensation of his holy flesh—namely, that which is foolish and that which is weak in God—because this weakness and foolishness are stronger and wiser than all human beings. For all human beings, as was also said above, are born under the sin of transgression. Our Lord Jesus Christ, however, existing without sin and bringing with him no defect of the old condition, is not only stronger but also wiser than all human beings, although he deigned, solely out of mercy, to assume what in us is weakness and foolishness.

Those who were born from the sin of the first man are called by the teaching of Holy Scripture sons of wrath and darkness. Christ, however, since he is the true light, deigned to illuminate those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. Let us hear what the Apostle teaches when writing to the Ephesians:

“And you, when you were dead in your transgressions and sins, in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of unbelief, among whom we too once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of our thoughts, and we were by nature sons of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2).

These, then, are the two contrary wills—of mind and flesh—which were entirely absent from our Savior. We are known to possess them because of the sin of our forefather Adam, who made both himself and the whole human race liable to sin. Thus at times the thorn of the flesh appears to resist the mind, while at other times the will of the mind strives to oppose the will of the flesh, so that, groaning in this manner with the Apostle, we may confess: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7).

Our Lord, however, deigned to assume one natural will of humanity, which, in his own flesh, he carried by his sovereign authority as Lord of all, since all things serve God. He neither possessed nor brought any sin derived from transgression, for he alone was born without sin and without the crime of transgression.

Thus my aforesaid predecessor, teaching about the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, said that there were not in Christ, as there are in us sinners, contrary wills of mind and flesh. Certain people, twisting this to suit their own interpretation, supposed that he had taught Christ to possess one will of his divinity and humanity; but this is altogether contrary to the truth.

Nevertheless, I should like them, when questioned, to answer according to which nature they say that Christ the God has one will. If they mean only according to his divine nature, what will they say about his humanity? For he is also perfect man, lest he be condemned together with Manichaeus. But if they say that, according to Christ’s humanity, this will was perfect God, let them beware lest they be judged together with Photinus and Ebion. If, finally, they say that there is one will from both natures, they will confuse not only the natural wills but the natures themselves, so that neither the one nor the other—divine or human—can be understood.

For just as we do not divide the two natures in the union of the one Christ, like the impious Nestorius, so we do not wholly deny the distinction of the natures, nor do we confuse them. Rather, we confess both natures, with the union of the one person of Christ the God, in an ineffable harmony. Since they say that Christ’s divinity and humanity have one will and likewise one operation, what else are they known to be doing than asserting that Christ the God has one nature, according to the Eutychian and Severian division?

Finally, the orthodox Fathers who shone throughout the whole world are shown, by their harmonious teaching, to have taught both the two natures and the wills and operations of Christ. We have learned that a certain document was circulated in which priests were compelled to subscribe against the tome of the blessed pope Leo and against the Council of Chalcedon. In this document certain things were newly composed which are plainly recognized as rejecting ecclesiastical doctrine.

Therefore may divine mercy inspire your most Christian piety and, since you are guardians of our spotless faith, move you to compunction, so that by imperial decrees you may restrain those liable to be corrupted by new inventions. May you order the aforesaid document—which is rushing toward the scandal of the faith and has been posted in public places—to be taken down and torn apart. For all who heard of this in the western regions, as well as the people of your royal city, were struck to the heart when they learned how the aforesaid document had been composed.

By your authority and apostolic perfection, that document, composed against the Council of Chalcedon, will now and forever be useless and void of all force. We pray that the perfection of the faith, which has shone forth until the present, may through you, as also through Constantine of blessed memory, remain firm by divine assistance.

Therefore, most Christian rulers and guardians of the faith of Christ, offer this gift at the beginning of your reign to your mother the Church, whose helpers you are, after God, so that the serpent’s cunning may not dare to violate the faith of her Bridegroom. Offer this salutary sacrifice to the Lord our God at the beginning of your reign, and scatter from his Church every cloud of novelty by the ray of your piety, so that the Lord our God may by his aid crush all the nations that oppose you, and all those that reject peace and the unconquerable God. While you care for the things that belong to God, may God in his kindness deign to accomplish the things that belong to you.

Therefore, with the knee of the mind bent, the whole Church joins me in pleading that he may deign to remove from the integrity of our spotless faith—which the holy Apostles handed down to us and the most holy Fathers committed to us in their lucid teachings—the storm of a new confusion. May God and our Lord, whose spotless faith is guarded, richly and deservedly bestow his mercies upon you. He is almighty and everlasting Lord. May the Creator of all look kindly upon your rule, and by his unconquerable power overthrow the nations that trust in their own truth.

## LETTER III. OF POPE JOHN IV TO BULCRED, KING OF THE SAXONS

(Fragment in Ivo, Part VII, chapter 130)

Since, as we have heard, the sin of fornication reigns among you above all, inasmuch as men of your kingdom presume to take as wives nuns, women already consecrated to God, and women related to them by blood, contrary to the statute of Saint Gregory—a statute then necessarily promulgated for a new people—we admonish, exhort, and command by this letter of our apostolate that all who are under your authority, both laymen and clerics, henceforth and in the future beware of this grave crime and offense, perform worthy penance for their deeds, and never again commit such acts.

But if you perhaps find it difficult to correct this impiety, on account of which you are enduring such adversities, inform our paternal office by letter, so that we may rebuke those who are weakly subject to such a wicked work under the authority of the Apostolic See and punish them with every severity of decree.

## LETTER IV. OF POPE JOHN IV TO ISAAC, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

That priests may be appointed by monks for their churches

Pope John to Isaac, bishop of Syracuse.

Having read the letter of your charity, from which it is sufficiently clear how earnestly you show reverence to this holy see, we rejoiced greatly. Accordingly, concerning what you consulted us about, we now offer kind counsel to our most dear brother.

Your pious gentleness referred to us the question whether churches entrusted by holy and Catholic bishops to monks for the sake of the monks’ peace ought to be staffed by priests ordained and installed by those monks. Your fraternity also added that considerable dispute and sedition had arisen between clerics and monks on this account. No one doubts that this was brought about by the instigation of the crafty enemy, for he has a thousand ways of doing harm, and we are not ignorant of his tricks. From the beginning of his ruin he has tried to sever the unity of the Church, wound charity, and infect the sweetness of holy works with the gall of envy. He grieves and blushes greatly that the charity which he was unable to possess in heaven is maintained on earth by human beings, steadfast though fashioned from clay.

Therefore, as far as our frailty permits, we ought to fortify most diligently every entrance through which his cunning might cause harm, lest death enter our gates. After most carefully seeking the counsel of many brethren, we have decreed that from now on churches entrusted to monks are to be staffed by their own priests.

For both divine and secular laws provide that the institution should belong to the one to whom the possession belongs. If charity was generous in granting the greater thing, let holy generosity be still more generous in granting the lesser. For it was greater to give possession than to grant investiture.

How, however, will the rights of the possessor be recognized, and how will what is owed to him be rendered, when what belongs to him is given through another and taken away whenever that other wishes? It is human custom to respect the one by whose judgment and will a person is now raised up and now cast down. Hence a priest who is in some degree dependent upon bishops becomes more inclined to serve them; and so the bishop who had given the church in holiness and religious devotion withdraws it to himself by a kind of simulated authority.

Thus the bishop is deprived of the reward he would have obtained: first, because under a feigned charity he takes away what he had given; and second, because, having become excessively credulous through the words of wicked priests who love discord and division and sow disputes and dissensions among bishops, he attempts, after the fraud has been exposed, to take back entirely by usurpation what he had previously contrived to obtain deceptively.

Recognizing their cunning and the persuasions of the crafty enemy, we therefore grant monks full permission henceforth to become the installers of their own churches, provided that, if they presume to act against the priesthood, they are punished by the judgment of a synod, and that the bishop cut away the offenses of priests with a salutary sword.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 644: MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF CAESARAUGUSTA

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT MAXIMUS

(Nicholas Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*, vol. I)

The subject now reached is Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta. We are preparing a somewhat longer work on him, and therefore, as the matter requires, some preliminary points must be set forth. Once the true Maximus has been brought forward, we must discard the other material superimposed upon him—entirely fictitious and fabricated in the minds of those who, abusing the sincerity of their readers, are equally accustomed to say and write what is true, false, or flattering.

The true Maximus, then, is the man whom Saint Isidore commended to posterity as still living at the end of his little book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Maximus, bishop of the city of Caesaraugusta, is said to have composed many works in verse and prose. He also wrote, in a brief style, a history of what happened in Spain during the times of the Goths, in historical and carefully composed language. He is also said to have written many other things which have not yet been read.

Thus Isidore.

Maximus’s subscriptions are found in the councils held at Barcelona in 599, at the Council of Gundemar in Toledo in 610, and at Egara in 614. He did not live long afterward. For John, his successor, governed that same Church for twelve years during the reigns of the kings Sisebut and Suinthila; Sisebut began to reign in 612. Braulio, John’s brother and successor, attended the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633 as bishop.

Everything that Isidore taught us Maximus had written in verse and prose has perished, and, what would be more greatly missed by others, so has the *History of the Goths* composed by him—unless that another Chronicle, or continuation of the earlier one, is appended to the fragment of the Chronicle attributed to Dexter—as we noted when discussing it—and preserved in the Codex of Adam Centurion Estepan, marquis: it is complete, nowhere mutilated, and likewise attributed to Maximus of Caesaraugusta.

This work continues an entire history of nearly two centuries year by year, from the year of Christ 430, or era 468, to the year 606—that is, era 644. Its earlier portions, up to the year 456, are taken from the Chronicle of Prosper Tiro, with very few exceptions.

Yet, whatever its nature, it is, as we have said elsewhere, a foundation or ground-plan upon which the common compiler of the Pseudo-Dexter Chronicle, taking up the same thread of rashness and insolence, built a vulgar Chronicle also marked with the name of Maximus.

The work that is placed before our eyes and read in the fragment at the end of this volume, when compared with the common version, will reveal itself to anyone, however stubbornly he resists, as an embryo once conceived which, after additions or alterations to the features of its face and entire body, was finally delivered—still abortive and truly monstrous—by the most audacious desire to deceive and to make sport even of sacred matters.

This is not the place to refute each individual head of falsehood or to explain the extent to which one version is contrary to or different from the other. Such a task requires another time and a work of greater magnitude for its completion.

[Note: As we noted elsewhere, it was published at Valencia under the title *Censure of Fabulous Histories*, edited by the distinguished Gregorio Mayans y Siscar, in the vernacular, folio, 1742.]

Nevertheless, we shall not allow readers who come to this point to be deprived of certain general headings of refutation, which may serve as a sample and foundation of the whole complete and solid argument.

Three matters in particular concerning Maximus himself, entirely germane to the subject treated by this *Bibliotheca*, must necessarily be noted here, lest they be missed.

First, Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, was not a Benedictine monk, as the Pseudo-Maximus of Toledo appeared in our own century. Second, he was not called Marcus Maximus. Third, the Marcus who was a disciple of Saint Benedict and who set forth the virtues of the blessed father in a certain poem was consequently a different person from our Maximus.

First, that he was not a monk is sufficiently suggested by Saint Isidore’s silence regarding monastic profession. It is not recorded that Isidore ever omitted such a detail in the case of the other monks whom he praises, as may be seen in Martin of Dumio, his brother Leander, John of Biclarum, and Eutropius.

Following this example, Saint Ildephonsus likewise did not fail to note the monastic status of Donatus; of John of Caesaraugusta, the brother and predecessor of Maximus; of Helladius; of Justus; of the two Eugeniuses of Toledo; and of Nonnitus of Gerunda, all bishops.

Moreover, John Trithemius, who treated in four books *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, and in the second of these doctors and writers; Arnold Uvion, who rolled the same stone in his *Tree of Life*; and Antonio de Yepes, who in his extraordinarily rich chronicle of the Benedictine order, written in Spanish, carefully collected the deeds and commendable achievements of all the illustrious men of the Benedictines—all these made no mention of him.

Although Trithemius admits somewhere that he did not praise everyone because of their enormous number, it is scarcely possible that he could have passed over a man whom, in Isidore’s most celebrated catalogue of writers, he could not fail to have before his eyes.

Furthermore, all those who praise Maximus, before the Toledan ferment corrupted the entire mass, attribute to him the dignity of bishop, but none attributes to him the profession of monk.

[Note: Matamoros, *Apologeticus*; Morales, book XII, chapter 7; Genebrardus, in the *Chronicle*, year 607; Antonius Augustinus, *To Blanca*, letter, volume III of the *Illustrious Men*; Loaysa, in our edition of the Council of Barcelona, p. 247.]

To all these we rightly prefer Hieronymus Romanus de la Higuera himself, the Toledan whom common opinion regards as the author of this manifold and many-branched fable. [Read: “to all of them, Hieronymus himself.”] He was the first inventor of the Chronicles of Dexter and Maximus. Although he boasts about Maximus and mentions him, he maintains profound silence about his monastic status.

There exists a still unpublished history of the city and kingdom of Toledo, composed in the vernacular and contained in several volumes. When we were illuminating the affairs of Dexter, we gave notice of it. We therefore thought it worthwhile to transfer here, as evidence, certain words in which, while discussing the Third Council of Toledo, its author records all those who attended after the order of bishops:

> The king and queen also attended the council, as did the abbots listed below: Eutropius of Servitanum, of the Augustinian order, as has already been said; Exsuperius of Agali; Aurasius of Saints Cosmas and Damian—or, as others read, of the Holy Cross. These two abbots later became bishops of Toledo. Maximus, abbot of the holy Masses at Caesaraugusta; Emila of Saint Eulalia at Barcelona, later bishop of that same city; and Theochristus, abbot of Saint Eulalia at Toledo. All these abbots were Benedictines. Artuagus, surnamed the Goth, prior of Cîteaux at Toledo, of the order of Saint Augustine, greatly assisted this work with his sermons. Fulgentius also, and Maximus, the one who wrote the Chronicle, archdeacon of Caesaraugusta; Eugenius, deacon of the Church of Toledo; Isidore, deacon of the Church of Seville; and John, a Benedictine monk of the monastery of Agali, later abbot of Biclarum.

These are exactly the words in Spanish—provided here in the vernacular—of the author of the *History of Toledo*, who first received this Chronicle from Germany and published it among us. He thereby made a most explicit distinction between two Maximuses: one, an abbot at Caesaraugusta of the holy Masses and of the Benedictine order; the other, the archdeacon of the same Church of Caesaraugusta who wrote the Chronicle.

But where, you may ask, did the author learn this complete distinction between the two and the entire account of the council? From nowhere else than the Chronicle of Maximus. He also praises John of Biclarum shortly afterward in these words:

> All this is owed to the diligence which Biclarum and Maximus of Caesaraugusta employed in writing.

But which Maximus? Certainly not the common one, whom public usage repeats from mouth to mouth, but the one preserved for us by the Codex of the Marquis Estepan. I would scarcely call him genuine or sincere, or one speaking in his own words; nevertheless, he is the Maximus whom Higuera at that time used as the true Maximus.
