We shall place the testimony of both here, so that it may immediately be recognized to which of the two the author of the *History of Toledo* attributes his knowledge of the Fathers of the Toledan council, and which of the two instructed him—or was instructed by him.

### MAXIMUS

From the Estepan Codex.

> King Reccared and Queen Badda also attended, together with the abbots Eutropius of Servitanum, Exsuperantius [Exsuperius] of Agali, and Aurantius [Aurasius] of Saint Cosmas and Damian, who afterward became bishops of Toledo; Maximus, abbot of the holy Masses at Caesaraugusta; Emila of Saint Eulalia at Barcelona, who afterward became bishop of that same city; Elias, abbot of Saint Leocadia at Toledo, afterward bishop of Salamanca; and Terechristus, abbot of Saint Eulalia at Toledo. All these were of the order of Saint Benedict. Fulgentius the presbyter also attended; Maximus, archdeacon of Caesaraugusta; Eugenius, deacon of Toledo; Isidore, deacon of Seville; and John, a monk of Agali, afterward of Biclarum. Among the Palatine officials were Helladius, and so forth.

### From the Common Edition

> The glorious King Reccared and the glorious Queen Badda likewise attended, together with the abbots, namely Eutropius of Servitanum, Exsuperius of Agali, Aurasius of Saints Cosmas and Damian, M. Maximus, formerly a Benedictine abbot of the holy Masses at Caesaraugusta and now archdeacon of Caesaraugusta, Stephen, abbot of Reate, and Emila of Saint Eulalia at Barcelona, who afterward became bishop of that city. All these were of the order of Saint Benedict. Elias, abbot of Saint Leocadia at Toledo. Fulgentius the presbyter also attended, as did Eugenius, deacon of Toledo; Isidore, deacon of Seville; and John, a monk of Agali, afterward abbot of Biclarum and bishop.

You now see, reader, the incorporation of two men into one archdeacon and also one abbot, Maximus; and the former, whom Higuera considered the author of the Chronicle, suddenly transformed into a Benedictine monk.

From this arose the difference between the letter of Luitprand, prefixed to the fragment or continuation of Maximus’s Chronicle in the Estepan Codex, and the version that was published. In the latter Maximus is praised as a Benedictine monk who afterward became bishop of Caesaraugusta; in the former he is simply an earlier-created Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta.

Likewise, under the year 596, the Estepan Codex has:

> Simplicius of Caesaraugusta was succeeded by the man who wrote this Chronicle.

This testimony concerning the year of Maximus’s consecration is absent from the printed editions.

Nor should you say that this Luitprand of Pavia, in the continuation of this same Chronicle of Maximus, preserved in the fragment mentioned shortly before—our Estepan Codex—has the following under the year 624:

> Maximus, formerly a monk, is celebrated as bishop of Caesaraugusta;

and under the year 624:

> Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, dies.

We rightly turn these statements of his and of the other fig-tree authors produced by the same hen back upon them, to expose and convict the twin defects and lies of their works. We cannot, however, admit them as witnesses to the truth.

Indeed, the very testimony concerning Maximus’s death will once again reveal the difference between the earlier Maximus and the later one produced by the new fabrication. In our Codex, or fragment, as we have seen, the memory of Maximus’s life or distinction and of his death is divided between two years. But in the published Luitprand these words appear once, and in a substantially different form, proclaiming an entirely different work.

Under the year 622 he says:

> Marcus Maximus, formerly a Benedictine monk and afterward bishop of Caesaraugusta, is celebrated after his death.

This is evidently the very man who, according to the testimony of the other Luitprand, died two years later and not before.

It is equally false that he was called Marcus. We shall persuade those who have not been carried over to one side by prejudice, using the same arguments.

In the first place, Maximus is called by no other name, and no other name appears attached to him in the councils where he subscribed, or in the works of Isidore, Ildephonsus, Honorius, and the other writers cited above whose histories were still uncorrupted, including the Benedictine writers, as well as countless others.

Hieronymus Higuera likewise calls him throughout his *History of Toledo* by no other name than this single name, Maximus, as can be established from the words previously quoted and, for those who have access to the work itself through its owners, from nearly every page.

The Estepan Codex agrees in the very title of the Chronicle, which reads:

> Letter of Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, to Argebatus, bishop of Portugal, concerning his Chronicle. To the holy and venerable brother Bishop Argebatus, Maximus. Chronicle of Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, from the year 630.

Nor does the Estepan Codex call either Maximus by any other name when it mentions those who attended the Toledan Fathers, just as Luitprand does not do so in the testimonies of the continuation cited shortly before.

Finally, this name—or rather this praenomen—was nowhere ever heard or found until the Toledan-Fulda nomenclator breathed it into the ears of later generations.

“But upon what monument of antiquity,” you will ask, “did he rely when he suddenly made Marcus appear as the name of a man who, from the age in which he flourished down to us, has come marked only by the bare name Maximus?”

With incredible and insane audacity he imposed this upon his agents, so that they might present to the good and unsuspecting people of their own age a certain Marcus, a disciple of Saint Benedict who shortly after the saint’s death gathered the praises of the blessed father in a brief poem, and Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta and author of the Chronicle under discussion, as one and the same man—fused together by him—and so that the same unfortunate credulity might be passed down from them to their descendants.

This was the third head of our opposition. The witnesses suborned by the impostor in this matter must now be examined individually and entered into the record of history.

The Pseudo-Maximus himself says in the dedicatory letter to Argebatus:

> I shall send to Your Beatitude at the earliest opportunity the life of our holy Father Benedict, polished in heroic verse.

And under the year 612, section 15:

> I too knew by sight Euphemius, a Benedictine monk and, in his youth, dear to Saint Father Benedict, archbishop of Toledo.

None of this is found in our fragment.

A poem about the same Maximus was also attributed to Braulio, who himself was bishop of Caesaraugusta.

[Note: In the Bivar edition of Maximus’s works, in the additions, p. 8.]

> Here lies Maximus, called by the surname Marcus,  
>   
> A noble historian, herald, poet, and vigilant man.  
>   
> A distinguished offspring of the Benedictine race,  
>   
> He was here a shining bishop in Caesar’s city.  
>   
> Far from ambition, enriched by great merits,  
>   
> He unwillingly accepted the pontifical dignity.  
>   
> His grave life, snow-white morals, and distinguished countenance  
>   
> Made him worthy of the office of bishop.  
>   
> A generous hand, fitting learning, and eloquent speech,  
>   
> Outstanding intelligence and weighty eloquence.  
>   
> Worn out by old age, he is recalled to the heavenly citadels,  
>   
> Whose members the house called the Column contains.  
>   
> In that house, having fulfilled the office of a renowned bishop,  
>   
> He will rise rejoicing at the final light of judgment.

> HERE RESTS IN PEACE THE SERVANT OF GOD, M. MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF CAESARAUGUSTA. HE DIED ON THE FOURTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF OCTOBER, IN ERA 654, IN THE FIFTH YEAR OF THE GLORIOUS KING SISEBUT. HE LIVED ABOUT SEVENTY-TWO YEARS.

Another poem, attributed to Heleca, bishop of the same see, was written for the tomb of this same Maximus. It is a deceptive and spurious product, like the similar merchandise frequently sold by John Tamayo de Salazar, the Spanish martyrologist, and it reveals the scribbling style of its author.

[Note: Volume V, under September 18.]

> In this tomb you lie, Marcus—but Maximus in name  
>   
> And epithet among the poets of our western land.  
>   
> Born at Caesaraugusta, you seek the light  
>   
> Of the western desert and undertake sacred offices.  
>   
> You, dear to Father Benedict [lacuna], from his mouth  
>   
> Drank the rule which you yourself also give to your own.  
>   
> Monk, deacon, abbot, and bishop, everywhere  
>   
> Known in verse and prose, you shine among the stars.  
>   
> Heleca, your successor as bishop, asks you  
>   
> To protect our city and never abandon it.

Luitprand and Julian, historians of the same kind, supplied auxiliary forces to support this lie.

The former says in the dedicatory letter to Tractamentus prefixed to his Pseudo-Chronicle—not, however, to the Estepan Codex:

> Let me seek for you the Chronicle of Dexter, which M. Maximus, a Benedictine monk later bishop of Caesaraugusta, continued.

And under the year 616, in the Chronicle itself:

> M. Maximus of Caesaraugusta, formerly a monk of Saint Benedict, an excellent writer of Chronicles and preacher, a pious and learned man who wrote the life of Saint Benedict in verse and many things in prose and verse, died a holy death.

In *Adversaria* 33, elsewhere numbered 32, he calls him Marcus Maximus, a Benedictine monk, a most wise poet, and bishop of Caesaraugusta.

The later writer, Julian, in his Chronicle, sections 304 and 306, twice gives the name Marcus to Maximus. All these twin authors were intent on observing faithfully the law of deception once pronounced to themselves by their common parent and on pursuing with zeal the project of transforming Maximus.

But, good God, when the shadows struck by the single light of truth fall and are driven back into their own darkness!

Almost everyone who once committed anything to writing concerning the deeds of the holy Father Benedict mentions Marcus, the monk of Monte Cassino and disciple of Saint Benedict, praising the poem he composed, by which he added certain material to the history of that same holy patriarch written by Gregory. This poem has already been printed many times.

[Note: In the Floriacum Library of John of Bosco, p. 281; in the edition of Prosper Martinengo’s poems, vol. III, Rome, 1590; in Bivarius’s French commentary on Maximus, p. 89; and in Angelo della Noce’s commentary on the *Chronicle of Leo of Ostia of Monte Cassino*, appendix, p. 3.]

Yet none of these writers ever attributed to him the surname Maximus, or the offices of abbot, archdeacon, or bishop of Caesaraugusta. Consult Paul the Deacon, book I of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 26, whose words Adrevald uses in book I, chapter 4 of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*;

[Note: In the Floriacum Library, p. 18.]

Peter the Deacon, in his little book *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*, chapter 3;

[Note: Published at Rome with notes by Giovanni Battista Mari, 1655.]

and Leo of Marsica, or of Ostia, book III of the *History of Monte Cassino*, chapter 21.

[Note: Finally published at Paris with notes by Angelo della Noce, 1668.]

These men, as alumni of the same monastery—and especially the last, Leo of Ostia, who was devoted to praising its illustrious men—could not have been unaware, nor ought they to have concealed, that this disciple, so dear to his father and such a renowned encomiast of him, had gone to Spain and there been considered worthy of such distinguished honors. For if the matter had really happened in this way, he should have been the first bishop taken from the Benedictine family, which would have brought considerable distinction both to the man and to the order.

Similarly, let us add Aimoinus of Fleury, who speaks only of Marcus as a monk of Cassino, in a certain sermon on Saint Benedict [Note: [Col. 0615D] In the same Library of Fleury, pp. 281 and 283.], into which he wove his poem, and in the preface to Book II of *The Miracles of the Same Holy Father Benedict* [Note: [Col. 0615D] Ibid., p. 80.]; Saint Peter Damian, Sermon 8, *On Saint Benedict*; Sigebert of Gembloux, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 33; and, among writers of more recent centuries, Johannes Trithemius. In his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Trithemius mentions Marcus the monk and Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, separately; but in his other work, *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, he mentions neither Marcus nor Maximus. In the former work, perhaps he thought that a poet of only a few verses scarcely deserved to be numbered among the writers whom he placed in Book II; and he could not praise Marcus among the bishops, whose catalogue is contained in Book IV, since, like all the other writers of his order and of earlier times, he knew nothing of Maximus’s bishopric of Caesaraugusta. As for the latter, Maximus, Trithemius omitted him because it had not yet been pronounced by the fig-tree law that, since no such person had ever been heard of anywhere, Maximus of Caesaraugusta was a monk. Arnold Uvion [Note: [Col. 0616D] In *The Tree of Life*, Book II, chapter 72.] likewise speaks of Benedictine monks; Lilius Gyraldus, when praising poets; Cardinal Baronius [Note: [Col. 0616D] In his notes on the *Martyrology*, 21 March.]; Johannes Gerardus Vossius [Note: [Col. 0616D] *On Latin History*, Book II, chapter 24.]; Antonius Possevinus [Note: [Col. 0616D] In the *Apparatus*]—and who does not?—speak either of one Marcus or distinctly of both.

Shall we then deny credence to the testimony of so many centuries—not merely their silence, but also their clearest indication—in order to surrender ourselves basely to a few pseudonymous writers born yesterday or the day before in Toledo, all of whom plough with the same heifer and can all be learned from a single source? “The ancients are silent,” you say; “they do not deny.” On the contrary, by remaining silent they do deny. For such is the force of silence, when a matter ought not to have been left unmentioned, that we may rightly declare it not to have occurred. What if the author of a Life, or the encomiast of Saints Gregory the Great, Athanasius, Basil, Leander, and others, content with praising their beginnings, had omitted their performance of the greatest offices of the Church? What if a companion had commended to posterity a companion of nearly the same period merely for composing a few verses, while saying nothing of the other virtues by which that man had deservedly risen to some lofty pinnacle of distinction?

Did the memory of a man whose poem, according to Leo of Ostia, was inscribed in letters of gold in the vestibule of the great Cassinese house immediately fade among the Cassinese themselves, so that they spoke of him in no other way than as one of the monks who had died there? A man whom, because of the benefit of his very long life, the honors he held, his presence at councils, his historical labors, and his great virtues, the historians of our age have portrayed as so conspicuous and so renowned? We should be mad if we allowed ourselves to be so mocked and led about like buffaloes with a rope through our noses.

We can also make use of affirmative arguments. Marcus wrote about the affairs of Saint Benedict after Saint Gregory. We must hold this opinion if we trust the older authorities. Sigebert says [Note: [Col. 0616D] Chapter 33.] that Marcus extracted the Life written by Gregory in brief heroic verse and added a few things of his own. Aimoinus likewise plainly teaches that Gregory was the originator of this subject, and that after him Marcus and Paul of Cassino wrote some additional material in verse.

Saint Gregory, however, was writing the Life of Saint Benedict—that is, Book II of the *Dialogues*, which contains it—already as pope, around the fourth year of his office, A.D. 593, as is clear from Book IV, chapters 36, 47, and 55. Therefore, if Marcus was Maximus, he too wrote his poem about Benedict not yet at Cassino, but when, having advanced from monk and abbot to archdeacon of the Church of Caesaraugusta, and perhaps already to the episcopate, he was known throughout Spain. For in the year 599—that is, six years after Saint Gregory the pope had written the Life of Saint Benedict—Maximus was already bishop of Caesaraugusta, as is established by the previously cited subscription to the Council of Barcelona. Everyone can see how poorly this agrees with the Marcus the monk, author of the poem, whom the Cassinese have celebrated in such a dry and meager fashion.

Moreover, according to the same Aimoinus, Marcus was Saint Benedict’s levite—that is, his deacon. That he was likewise a Benedictine monk has only recently been demonstrated by the clearest documents by a man learned and prudent in few things, but always to be honored by me, the lord Angelo della Noce, formerly abbot of Cassino and now archbishop of Rossano, in his most learned notes on the Cassinese history of Leo of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0616D] On the Life of Saint Benedict written by Gregory the Great, p. 45, note 24.]. Aimoinus’s words [Note: [Col. 0616D] In the place cited above, namely, the sermon on Saint Benedict in the Library of Fleury.] are:

> Then a certain poet named Marcus, coming to the same venerable Benedict and entrusting himself to his instruction, wrote in verse some things in his praise, as his levite.

The office of levite, however, is very far removed from the episcopal dignity of Maximus. Finally, these trumpeters of Spanish affairs confuse Marcus with Maximus, so that the Spanish origin of the latter may be called into question. For the man who devoted himself to the discipline of the gracious father who lived at Cassino and remained in that house ought, with stronger probability, to be considered Italian rather than one of our own countrymen.

To the Benedictine monks, who are so eager for such things—though I always except the men of this order whom it continually produces, men of disciplined and purified judgment—the architect of this most mendacious history offered, to use a phrase adapted from Virgil,

> a poppy-cake steeped in honey and drugged deceits,

namely, his Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, as well as Marcus, this monk of the order, so that the most learned men who lived within its cloisters would not taste the things that had been mixed together and offered to them through the flatterer’s deception.

Anyone who wants more on the matter may consult the two-part—or perhaps three-part—commentary of our late friend, D. Joseph Pellicer of Jaca, knight and royal chronicler, *On Two Different Persons, Marcus and Maximus* [Note: [Col. 0617C] The title of the two vernacular Spanish books is: *Maximo obispo de Zaragoza distinguido de Marco levita y monge del Casino* [“Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, distinguished from Marcus, levite and monk of Cassino”]. Madrid, 1671, quarto. D. Lorenzo de Padilla likewise proves the same distinction in the preface to Book I of *The Antiquities of Spain*.]. From that work it was right and proper for me to extract these few points—translated from the vernacular into Latin so that they might become more generally accessible—and thus sufficiently serve my purpose.

Against him a certain masked man once rose up [Note: [Col. 0617C] This was Diego Antonio de Barrientos, an Augustinian, who assumed the name Luis José Aguilar de Losada. His vernacular name, Fray Diego Antonio de Barrientos, is concealed by the Latin anagram: [Col. 0618C] *Do tibi fontes ire: onera grana odi* (“I give you springs to go forth; I hate burdens of grain”). The work is entitled *Censure of the Distinctions between Marcus and Maximus, and between Berossus of Chaldaea and Viterbo; and of the Settlement and Primitive Language of Spain, Published by Don Joseph Pellicer de Tovar y Ossau*, Toledo, 1674, folio.], following the practice of those who, as Seneca elegantly says, prefer a mask to a face, and who, in a little book full more of jeers than arguments, won some reputation as a clever and witty rather than learned man.

By turning up his nose at the principal purpose of that learned little work—as though the cultivator of sandy shores, in Ausonius’s phrase [Note: [Col. 0618C] *To Theon*.], had labored only to establish this distinction between Marcus and Maximus, that is, had pursued a useless and vain undertaking—he surrendered himself entirely to laughter and universal ridicule. For to that hidden Aristarchus, ashamed to reveal himself, it was a useless and vain task to destroy at first encounter the monster of falsehood and, by exposing the falsity of the name he had assumed, overturn all his statements and credibility—he who, passing himself off as the true Maximus, had recently thrust upon us a new history, not only of all secular Spanish affairs but also of sacred matters, a history overflowing with lies.

Pellicer is wasting neither effort nor oil, since he strikes this giant down with one or two blows of a stone. Yet the man who, enraged by resentment at the exposure of certain fabulous origins, bites the stone by which he was struck, like a dog, is indeed making a great show of industry.

This wooden transformer, speaking through the mouth of Pseudo-Julian, next attributes to his Maximus the authorship of the Office of Saint James the Apostle. In a collection of various poems it reads as follows [Note: [Col. 0618C] p. 156.]:

> The Office of Saint James the Apostle was composed by Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta. The preface is by Saint Isidore, as is the hymn.

How worthy it is to insist here that a liar must also be a mindful man! For this very same author says in his *Chronicle*, no. 17, that the Mass of Saint James was corrected by Blessed Isidore, published by Melantius, and enlarged by the bishops of Toledo, Serranus and Asturius. [Col. 0618C] But now let us turn to other matters. Maximus must be examined in other chapters.

# All the Extant Writings of Maximus, Bishop of Caesaraugusta

[Col. 0617]

## Letter of Maximus, Bishop of Caesaraugusta, to Argebatus, Bishop of Portugal, Concerning His Chronicle

[Note: [Col. 0617] In Nicolás Antonio’s *Old Spanish Library*, from which we have taken Maximus’s writings, the following note precedes the two letters: “These two following letters were found after the *Chronicle*, written on very old parchment in Gothic letters.” The editor added in the margin: “One of these letters is missing, perhaps Argebatus’s to Maximus.”] (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0617D] To the holy and venerable brother Argebatus, bishop: Maximus.

When we were in the royal city, summoned to the council by our most glorious lord, King Gundemar, we often met together. Since there was much discussion among us about the histories of the Gothic kings, which I had published not long before, you very modestly entreated me to continue that Chronicle which circulates under the name of Dexter of Barcelona.

Although, because of your goodwill toward me and my respect for you, you could have ordered me to do so, your holiness preferred to obtain by request what you might properly have commanded or demanded as your right. I have done what you ordered, connecting the sequence of times according to our custom by eras and by the years of Christ, and omitting the method of reckoning by the years of the City and of the emperors, which Dexter follows.

Would that I had carried out your command, most blessed Father, as diligently as I tried to carry it out willingly! For I have brought the narrative of events from Era 469—that is, after the year of Christ 431—where Dexter ends, and extended it to Era 644, that is, up to the death of King Gundemar. Father, commend me to Christ in your prayers. Farewell.

[Col. 0619]

## Chronicle of Maximus, Bishop of Caesaraugusta, from the Year 430

(C, G, S)*

The end of the Chronicle of Maximus of Caesaraugusta.

[Col. 0633]

# Chronicle of Eutrandus of Pavia, Deacon and Subdeacon of Toledo

[Col. 0633A] To the holy Father Regimundus, bishop of Eliberis: Eutrandus, an unworthy servant of servants.

It pleased me, most blessed Father and deeply revered lord, that our *Antapodosis*, in which I play now in verse, now in prose, finally reached your hands. Nor was I less pleased that you now order me to search for you in the library of the monastery of Fulda, where I am presently living in exile, for the Chronicle of Dexter, which Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, continued at the request of Bishop Argebatus [Note: [Col. 0633D] “He continued it” is missing.], and, if I had the leisure, to carry it forward to our own times.

For you say that you are suffering from an extreme shortage of certain books. Among the barbarous and inhuman Saracens there is not even an adequate supply of things necessary for life, much less an abundance of good books. I have indeed grieved for your situation, that you should be passing your life in such hardship. Yet, placed amid such great difficulties, you are consoled because, as a good shepherd, you are a consolation and aid to your sheep, daily undergoing death for the sake of all.

I found the Chronicle you requested in this library, copied on ancient parchment, and I added, as I was ordered, the sequence of years up to the present time—that is, up to Era 960. I congratulate myself that, when I traveled from Toledo to Italy, where I had been a subdeacon under the most holy Bishop Bonitus of Toledo, I carried some history books with me. In them was collected, in order, the succession of many bishops of Spain. [These books were] brought from Spain to this library, as I believe, by order of the holy Emperor Charles the Great; they say that the most holy Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, had presented them to him after he had seriously repented of his error concerning the adoption of Christ.

I have done what you ordered, most blessed Father. You, who gave the command, will judge whether my effort has answered your wish. Farewell, and commend this exiled exile-servant to God.

[Note: [Col. 0633D] This observation was read in precisely these words in the manuscript, whether it was written by Scolanus, Fonseca, or someone else.] It would be more accurate to say that this is a fragment, since, although it promises to reach the year of the Lord 922, it extends only to the year 630. Two hundred and ninety-two years are missing, and only twenty-five years of the Chronicle are found in this fragment—namely, from the year 606 to the year 630. Here this author is incorrectly called Eutrandus, as he is also by Trithemius. He should be called Luitprandus. He came to Toledo from Italy and was a subdeacon there. On departing for Italy, he became a deacon; Trithemius writes about him.

# In the Year of the Lord 646: Victor, Bishop of Carthage

[Col. 0635]

## Historical Notice Concerning Victor

(*Baronius, Annals*, under the year 646.)

[Col. 0635B] After Fortunatus had either died or been removed from office on account of heresy, Victor was appointed in his place during this year, in the month of July. As soon as he had been made bishop of Carthage, he considered nothing more urgent than to indicate by his letters that he was a Catholic. Accordingly, following the custom of his predecessors, he wrote a profession of his faith [Note: [Col. 0635D] In his notice concerning Victor, Fabricius writes: “The statement of faith delivered to Huneric, king of the Vandals, is preserved in Sicardus’s *Antidote against Heresies*.” But Fabricius’s words plainly mean only that this statement of faith was attributed to Victor, not that it was his; for King Huneric is known to have lived nearly two centuries before our Victor. EDIT.] and sent it to Theodore, the pontiff. He appointed a suitable embassy to him, delegating Mellosus, bishop of Gippus, or Gisippus, Redemptus, a Carthaginian deacon, and Cresciturus, notary of the same Church. He therefore gave these men a letter to the same Pope Theodore, informing him of his election and at the same time declaring himself a professor of the Catholic faith.

Victor’s own letter is preserved in the Acts of the Roman Council under Pope Martin. [Col. 0635C] We have therefore thought it appropriate to present it to you in its proper place and at the time when it was written.

After giving Victor’s letter, Baronius adds the following:

> Up to this point, it is Victor’s letter to Theodore, the Roman pontiff. But what he says at the end about the African bishops, who had been brought under suspicion of sedition through the report of certain people before the emperor, and on account of which it had not been possible to send an embassy to Constantinople, clearly signifies the Gregorian disturbances of which we spoke, which began in Africa in this year, according to the Greek annals [Note: [Col. 0636D] Theophanes, under this year, the fifth of Constans.], when Governor Gregory rebelled against the emperor.

It had plainly been reported to the ears of the emperor Constans that the African bishops were conspiring with Gregory, and for that reason they became objects of deep hostility to him. But the rebellion of Gregory must be discussed at greater length under the following year.

As for Victor’s own letter, it is found commended by Pope Martin, Theodore’s successor, at the Lateran Council, in these words [Note: [Col. 0636D] Lateran Council under Martin, *Secretarium*, 2.]:

> In his synodical letter, which was read aloud to us some time ago, Victor, the venerable bishop of Carthage, displayed both his most fervent zeal and, with good reason, a humility pleasing to God. He showed his zeal by the fact that he is known to have strongly denounced to our apostolic see the novelty that had been introduced, and to have set down in writing for it the acclamations of almost all Christians, as well as the groans of the most reverend bishops, who—as he wrote—were greatly disturbed by the fabrications and inventions that Paul, bishop of Constantinople, had upheld against the true faith. He showed humility appropriately by not rashly treating that same Paul as deposed, but by calling him a fellow priest until he should learn the judgment of our apostolic authority—that is, of Peter, prince of the apostles—since Peter alone, and before all others, is believed to have received, and deserved to receive, from Christ God, the King of kings, the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so as rightly to open it to those who believe in the same Lord and to close it against unbelievers and heretics.

Clearly, it belongs to him to impart Catholic communion by opening the Church to those who stand outside, or to close it by declaring them heretics. He adds many other things in praise of the letter, but these are sufficient for our purpose.

[Col. 0637]

# Letter of Victor, Bishop of Carthage, to Pope Theodore

(*Mansi, Collection of Councils*, new edition, vol. XII.) (C, S)

[Col. 0637A] To the most blessed and honorable lord, holy brother Theodore, pope: Victor.

The works and glorious conduct of your most blessed fatherhood, acceptable to God, are almost universally known. Since, therefore, the whole earth has been filled with the cultivation of the true faith through apostolic preaching and teaching, the orthodox Church of Christ—founded upon apostolic institution and most firmly strengthened by the faithful Fathers—is built up through instruction in the divine words, under the guidance of your exhortatory admonition.

To this Church all the most blessed apostles, endowed with an equal share of honor and authority, converted throngs of peoples. In a pious and holy manner they led people foreknown by the grace of divine predestination from darkness to light, from falling away to the true faith, and from death to life, through saving precepts and admonitions.

Your venerable fraternity, following more fully the merits of those holy apostles and fulfilling their examples more perfectly, adorns the Church of God by the integrity of its conduct and the holiness of its actions. Alive in sacred faith and Christian morals, it unceasingly performs and completes, through pontifical zeal, the things that it has commanded to be pleasing to God, preserving the commandments of the divine law: “For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God,” as the Apostle says, “but the doers of the law will be justified” (Romans 1).

In this divine law your holy and venerable sincerity meditates day and night, as it is written (Psalm 1). This meditation is not perceived merely through reading the written letters, but, because Christ’s grace overflows in you, it is recognized as firmly implanted in your conscience, with the most sacred law of Christ God our Lord never departing from your heart, as the prophet says in the Psalms: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment” (Psalm 36:30). “The law of his God is in his heart”—written not with ink, but by the Spirit of the living God, secretly within you; and not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of a fleshly heart (2 Corinthians 3:3), as the letter of the most blessed Apostle Paul sent to the Corinthians teaches us.

Having said this, we inform your God-pleasing fraternity that, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth indiction, our humility, by divine grace—which, as he commanded, went before us with its gift—received, in the holy church of the city of Carthage, the consecration and stole of pontifical honor.

In this position of dignity, we ask that we may be governed by almighty God from on high, freed from evil actions, and possess not merely the name but also the merit of a priest, protected by the aid of Christ our Lord and God. Commending ourselves to your holy prayers, acceptable to God, we ask that, fortified by your supplications poured out to God on our behalf and instructed by good teachings, we may be made worthy, together with all the Christian people entrusted to us, to be kept unharmed beneath the divine protection.

Therefore, to salute your holy and venerable fraternity, we have sent in our place Mellosus, your humble brother and our bishop; Redemptus, a deacon; and Cresciturus, the notary of our holy see [Note: [Col. 0637C] Here *vel*, as frequently elsewhere, means “and.” In Greek, καί. HARDUINUS.], your servants. We ask that you send them back to us as quickly as possible, so that, God willing, they may return to their own churches before winter.

Above all, however, I confess that at the very beginning of my advancement our heart was wounded not lightly, so that I desired the fulfillment of that prophetic precept:

> “Who will give water to my head, or a fountain of tears to my eyes? Then I will sit and weep day and night” (Jeremiah 9:1).

For behold, the churches of God are deeply disturbed, and we cannot endure the voices and groans of the most Christian bishops, who complain and cry out that novelties and fabricated compositions, allegedly approved by our venerable fellow priest Paul against the most truthful faith, must be rejected.

But, applying moderation to the matter, we thought it expedient to bear with equanimity the entirely just complaints of the aforementioned most blessed fellow priests of ours, and to bring this very matter, with vigilant care, to the venerable hearing of your fraternity. For they say that certain volumes of writings, in the manner of inscriptions, were recently hung in the sacred buildings of the royal city, wholly contrary to the Catholic religion, to the true faith itself, and to the tradition of the Fathers.

What foolish person would dare, with sacrilegious speech, to proclaim that in our Lord Jesus Christ there exists only one will or only one operation, when the manifest definitions of the Fathers make it abundantly and clearly evident that in our Lord Jesus Christ there are in every respect two natures, and two wills and two operations, or natural properties, belonging to them?

We could confirm the intention of our humble selves with many documents of the Fathers, unless we firmly believed that your most holy fraternity retains all these things in its heart. But, so that we may be confirmed in every respect by the decrees of the apostolic see itself, we have taken care to insert the definition of your most blessed predecessor, Leo, of apostolic memory. It says (Letter 10):

> Each nature acts, in communion with the other, according to what is proper to it. [Note: [Col. 0639B] Here again, in the Greek, “each nature” is in the ablative case. HARD.]

Following the decrees of the Fathers in all things, therefore, we most firmly proclaim that in Christ our Lord there are two natures, and two wills and two operations belonging to them. We truly confess him as true God and true man, without human sins, rejecting the mockeries, vanities, and mendacious insanities of every heresy.

It is therefore your task, most holy brother, according to your customary canonical discernment, to oppose whatever is contrary to the Catholic faith, and not to permit anything to be newly asserted that the authority of the venerable Fathers has wholly rejected.

For we, humble in heart and, with the Lord’s help, wise in what is right, are bound to you by a single bond of charity, defending the true faith and the Catholic religion steadfastly in all things. It is therefore necessary for Catholics to strive more diligently to resist the wicked, lest, overcome by the torpor of indolence, we be held guilty of the sin of silence and be judged to be offering approval while we neglect to repel what is opposed to the Catholic faith.

For Blessed Felix, the predecessor of your holiness, said [Note: [Col. 0639B] Read “apostolic,” rather than “apostle.” HARD.]:

> To neglect, when one is able, to drive out the wicked is nothing other than to encourage them; nor is the one free from the taint of hidden complicity who ceases to oppose an obvious crime. [Note: [Col. 0640B] From Letter 1 of Felix III to Acacius of Constantinople.]

It is clear, most holy teacher, that the poisonous cunning of serpents lacks simplicity, and that the deceitful trickery of heretics is manifest. For what is it to remove the properties of the natures in Christ our Lord, except to introduce a confusion of those same natures? This is utterly contrary to the Catholic Church—that is, to the decrees of the Fathers of the holy Council of Chalcedon—from which the foundation of the faith and its perfection stand all the more certainly established. [Note: [Col. 0640B] He refers to the Gregorian disturbances, of which Theophanes speaks under the fifth year of Constans. Baronius, under the year 646.]

We could also send similar writings to that same most blessed brother and fellow bishop of ours, Paul, bishop of the royal city, unless we knew that our African province had been falsely said, through evil speeches, to be able to undertake certain things that have no basis in truth. But we add this to our request: that you order the matters written by our fellow bishops of our holy council in letters to the most blessed Paul, patriarch, to be sent to that same brother of ours, Paul, through the messengers of your blessedness.

# In the Year of the Lord 646: Saint Braulio, Bishop of Caesaraugusta

[Col. 0639]

## Historical Notice Concerning Saint Braulio

(Nicolás Antonio, *Old Spanish Library*, vol. I, p. 374.)

[Col. 0639C] Braulio is praised by the most holy historical writer Ildephonsus. He was the brother of the John mentioned above; concerning John’s death at Caesaraugusta, Ildephonsus says (chapter 12):

> He obtained his place, a man remembered not only as his blood relation but also as a man of outstanding talent.

Braulio too was distinguished by his knowledge of the canons and by certain short works. He wrote the Life of a certain monk named Aemilianus, which both preserves the memory of this man and commends and illustrates the virtue of that holy man in its own manner. He held the priesthood for nearly twenty years, at the end of which he closed the day of his present life. He governed during the reigns of Sisenand, Chintila, Tulga, and Chindaswinth.

His subscription is read in all the councils of the period in which he is said to have lived, the Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Councils of Toledo. In the Seventh, under Chindaswinth, in the year 646, the name of the bishop of Caesaraugusta is missing. In the Eighth, under Recceswinth, in the year 653, Taio already appears as bishop of Caesaraugusta.

How great his service to the Church was in those assemblies is sufficiently shown by Isidore, bishop of Beja. Speaking of the Fourth Council [Note: [Col. 0639D] In the *Epitome of the Emperors*, or of the Arabs, under Sisenand.], which Sisenand had summoned, he says:

> In this holy synod, among the others, Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, shone forth; Rome, the mother and mistress of cities, later expressed her great admiration for his eloquence through an exchange of letters.

A little farther on, speaking of the Sixth Council of Toledo under Chintila, he says:

> In this synod Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, illustrious above the others, excels, and fittingly pours pious teaching into Christian minds; his work the Church still reads to this day.

Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, combined these two testimonies by copying them in Book II, chapter 19. He writes:

> In this synod—the Sixth according to the order of our editions, although he himself calls it the Fifth—Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, illustrious above the others, shone forth and fittingly poured pious teaching into Christian minds; his short works the Church still venerates. Rome, the mother and mistress of cities, admired his eloquence through an exchange of letters.

I believe that nothing other than the infusion of doctrine can be meant by that expression: namely, that the canons of this Sixth Council were composed in Braulio’s style. For, as is evident from other writings of his, and as Andreas Resendius notes in a letter to Quevedo [Note: [Col. 0641C] The letter is published among Resendius’s works, p. 177, and in *Illustrious Spain*, vol. II, p. 1009.], his style was considerably more polished and refined than that of the others of his age.

He himself also admits near the end of the preface to the Life of Saint Aemilianus, which we shall discuss shortly, that he had to some extent touched upon the study of secular disciplines [Note: [Col. 0641C] That Braulio had not merely touched upon secular studies, and that Virgil, Naso, Flaccus, Juvenal, Terence, and the other poets of the golden age were not unfamiliar to him, is demonstrated by his letter to the priest Taio, preserved in the work of the distinguished H. S. Flórez’s continuator, vol. XXX, p. 331 onward. It belongs to the type that the Greeks call ἀποπομπαίαι [*apopompáiai*, “dismissive or retaliatory compositions”]; for Taio had provoked him in writing. Braulio writes to him: “Keep it fixed in your mind that, if I wish, I can bite back; that, if injured, I can drive in a genuine tooth—κραντήρα [*krantēra*, ‘tooth’]—because we too, following Flaccus, have learned our little letters and have often withdrawn our hand from the schoolmaster’s rod; and it may be said of us: ‘He has hay on his horn; flee far away.’ Indeed, that Virgilian line:

> And we too, Father, scatter darts and no feeble iron  
> from our right hand, and blood follows from our wound, etc.”]

He was an archdeacon when Saint Isidore sent him the letters that are included among the Isidorian letters. As we believe, he was of the city of Caesaraugusta and the blood brother of John. This was the opinion of the author who, against Thomas Truxillo, our own scholar, composed the historical Synopsis of Braulio in the great work *On the Acts of the Saints*, under 18 March.

We are almost prepared to approve that author’s conjecture concerning certain words of this letter of Saint Isidore addressed to Braulio that lie under corruption. Isidore writes:

> I asked you to send me the sixth decade of Saint Augustine;

and immediately adds:

> I ask you to make me known to him in whatever way you can.

Since these words cannot be understood of Saint Augustine, who had died two centuries earlier, it seems necessary to correct them as follows:

> I ask you to make it known to me in whatever way you can.

Nevertheless, I would more willingly leave the text untouched, since Isidore likes to use the verb “to know,” or “to be unknown,” in precisely this sense. Concerning Justus of Urgell, he says in chapter 21:

> His brothers Nebridius and Elpidius are also said to have written certain things; since we are unfamiliar with them—or, better, concerning them—we acknowledge that they should rather be passed over in silence.

For just as he used “unknown” here to mean “not yet learned,” so he asked Braulio to make him “known” to the sixth decade of Saint Augustine. Unless one prefers this lighter alteration in the same sense: “Since we are unknown” in the notice of Justus, or “make me acquainted with it” in the letter to Braulio.

When, therefore, he was already bishop of Caesaraugusta, he wrote:

### Life of Saint Aemilianus the Priest

Saint Aemilianus the priest (who is said to have departed to heaven in the year 564, at an age exceeding one hundred), together with the dedicatory letter to the priest Fruminianus, whom he calls his lord and brother.

> **Note [Col. 0641D].** It survives in the Escorial Codex, written in the year 992 of the Spanish era, or A.D. 954, as the same manuscript records, shelfmark A, pluteus II, no. 9, with this heading: “To the man of God, my lord and brother, the priest Fronimianus, Braulio, bishop, unworthy.” Immediately thereafter: “Here begin the chapters on the life or miracles of the holy and most blessed Aemilianus, priest and confessor of Christ, published by the blessed Braulio, bishop of the See of Caesaraugusta” (sic). It consists of thirty-one chapters, the last of which, together with part of the penultimate, is missing from the manuscript.

From this Bivarius rightly concluded that Braulio had as brothers not only John, his predecessor in the episcopate, but also this Fruminianus.

> **Note [Col. 0642C].** *Ad Maximum*, under the year 562, no. 7, p. 475, in the margin.

Braulio seems to have indicated this at the beginning of the same Life, calling John “the elder brother, common to us,” that is, his own and Fruminianus’s.

> **Note [Col. 0642C].** Others understand this word differently. See Bivarius, in the same work, under the year 578, no. 2, p. 565.

This means that he called John his and Fruminianus’s brother.

> **Note [Col. 0642C].** Fruminianus, or rather Frunimianus, as he is called in the Leonese Codex mentioned shortly, was not Braulio’s brother. This is established by the headings of two letters by Braulio to the same man, in which we read only: “Braulio to Frunimianus, priest and abbot”; whereas in the letters to Bassila and Pomponia we read: “Braulio to Bassila, his sister,” and “Braulio to his kinswoman Pomponia, abbess.” All these letters are found in the distinguished continuator of *Hispania Sacra*, vol. XXX, pp. 335, 337, 339, 343.

This Life was first published, as we believe, by the Benedictine Prudentius Sandoval, later bishop of Tuy and Pamplona and royal chronicler, in his book on the foundations of the Benedictine order in Spain under Gothic rule, or on the Benedictine origins of Spain, when he was treating of the monastery of Saint Aemilianus Cucullatus, commonly called La Cogulla.

> **Note [Col. 0642D].** *Primera parte de las fundaciones de los monasterios de S. Benito*. Madrid, 1601.

The common opinion of the Castilians is that this is the Aemilianus described in Braulio’s history.

> **Note [Col. 0642D].** Venerus, in the *Enchiridion*; Morales, book XI, chapter 58; Mariana, book V, chapter 9; Marieta, *Santos de España*, book VI, chapter 6; Santoro and Villegas; Tamaius cites several others; Bivarius, *Ad Maximum*, under the year 562, p. 468; Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, vol. I, p. 205, in the preliminary observations to this Life; Padilla, century VI, chapter 31, and in the additions to that century, at the beginning of volume II.

The Aragonese, however, maintain that this was not the Aemilianus whose body is preserved in the monastery in question and who gave that monastery its name, but another hermit of the kingdom of Aragon, whose sacred remains lie in the town of Torre-la-Paja in the diocese of Tarazona.

> **Note [Col. 0642D].** Michael Martínez del Villar, *Del patronato, antigüedades, varones ilustres de Calatayud y su arcedianato*, fol. 128; Lanuza, *Historias de Aragón*, vol. II, book IV, chapter 3.

It is not our purpose to appropriate this controversy, which has thus far been fought with such great zeal, or to untie the knot with the sword of Pseudo-Maximus. After the controversy had arisen, its inventor fashioned or distorted the material in order to serve both parties. Not content with praising one Aemilianus and another under the years 562 and 578, he added the following at the latter place, where he discusses the Aemilianus of Aragon—words that openly reveal their novelty:

> “There was also another, still earlier, a priest and abbot of Saint Benedict”—do you really believe that Maximus spoke in this way?—“of whom mention was made above.”

In our fragment, or in Estepanus, Aemilianus is mentioned only once, under the year 553: “Saint Aemilianus, monk and priest, dies in Cantabria.”

I likewise regard Helecanus as a fabrication. He too, intent on settling the question from this side, babbles that he was the bishop of Vercelli whom the Aragonese venerate—or so Bivarius himself, having misunderstood the passage, says.

> **Note [Col. 0643D].** *Ad Maximum*, under the year 578, no. 2, p. 562.

The Martyrologies of Usuard and of Rome do indeed speak of Aemilianus and of the Life written by Braulio. It appeared a second time in the commentary of Francis Bivarius on the *Chronicon* of Maximus, under the year 562; a third time in the sixth volume of John Tamaius de Salazar’s *Spanish Martyrology*, p. 3, on 12 November; and finally in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, collected and published through the efforts of Luc d’Achery and John Mabillon, volume or century I.

He also composed a hymn in praise of the same holy man in iambic senarii, as the author says at the end of the dedicatory letter to this Life. The hymn passed, as is believed, into the Isidorian Breviary and into the feast of this holy man Aemilianus, where it is still read. It begins:

> O great Christ, illustrious ruler of all things,  
> Father of Olympus, to whom the stars perpetually belong, etc.

It is published in Bivarius’s commentary on Maximus, after the aforementioned Life of Aemilianus.

### Life of the Holy Martyrs Vincent, Sabina, and Christetis

To Braulio is attributed this Life, which otherwise circulates without an author’s name in a certain Codex of the Church of Toledo called the *Smaragdinus*. Bartholomew Quevedo, its canon and a thoroughly learned man, once informed Andrea Resende about it. This is clear from Resende’s reply to him, a letter worthy of so distinguished a man, whom we mentioned shortly before.

Resende writes:

> “Come now, holy Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, as you say, committed the history of these three martyrs to posterity, and the book of the Church of Toledo called the *Smaragdinus* displays Braulio’s name. I had no certain information about the author, nor does the Lectionary of our Church of Évora—which was certainly written three hundred and twenty years ago—bear the author’s name. Nevertheless, I believe that the *Smaragdinus* book is not displeasing to him.”

In the library of the monastery of Saint Aemilianus Cucullatus there is preserved a huge manuscript Codex entitled *Lives of the Fathers*. At its end the following note is attached:

> “This book was completed by Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, in the year 674 of the Spanish era.”

This is the year 636. It contains very many Lives of ancient Fathers, both Greek and Latin, most of which had already been published in Rosweyde’s collection on this subject.

Among other works is a short book *On the Arrival of the Holy Apostles James, Peter, and Paul in Spain*. There is also a work *On the Life or Miracles of the Holy and Most Blessed Aemilianus, Priest and Confessor*, who died at Vergegium on the day before the Ides of November.

There follows another little work, or poem, *On the Vanity of the Wisdom of the World*, perhaps by the same author.

> **Note [Col. 0643D].** This is a prose work, not a poem, entitled *On the Vanity of the Wisdom of the World*. Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi aevi*, book II, identifies Valerius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Mounts among the Asturians, as its author; it should not be attributed to Braulio.

Indeed, the eyewitness who once brought this Aemilianian Codex to our attention, Don Antonio Zapata y Aragón, a man trained in ancient letters, thought that everything contained in it belonged to Braulio, with only a few exceptions explicitly assigned to their respective authors. He would have been more deserving of esteem if he had kept in his own hand certain chronicles found among his papers instead of releasing them, since learned men regard their authenticity as entirely worthless.

A few years ago Juan Luis López, a Caesaraugustan jurist of refined judgment and learning, which he had received from our friend Don Juan Lucas Cortés, published at Caesaraugusta the Passion of the innumerable martyrs of Caesaraugusta, who suffered under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian on the third day before the Kalends of November, together with a commentary on law 12 of the Code, *On Religious Persons and Funeral Expenses*, from Cortés’s parchment Codex, apparently more than five hundred years old and written in Gothic letters.

The distinguished Don Juan Lucas believes, on the basis of conjecture, that its style breathes the spirit of the seventh century and seems to be that of our Braulio. Juan Luis López, the editor of the Passion, agrees with him in his second preface and in the notes with which he learnedly illuminated this little work, a genuine gem of antiquity. The judgment of such eminent men has persuaded us.

John Tamaius, however, extracted these Acts of the innumerable martyrs for 3 November, though his version is entirely different.

> **Note [Col. 0643D].** The Acts, or Passion, of the innumerable martyrs of Caesaraugusta, which some learned men regard as Braulio’s, were recently published from a very ancient Codex of the Church of León by the distinguished continuator of *Hispania Sacra*, the Augustinian Friar Manuel Risco, vol. XXX, p. 305 onward, with a lengthy and learned commentary. He does not, however, dare to determine that Braulio was the author of the Passion; indeed, he inclines toward another author.
>
> The Leonese Codex was copied by the exceptionally learned and incorruptibly honest Don Carlos Espinós, canon of that Church, who died not long ago. He generously distributed a copy to several learned men throughout Spain. It contained many letters by Braulio to various persons that had until then remained unpublished: two to the priest Jactatus; one to the priest Taius; one to the archdeacon Floridius; two to Frunimianus, priest and abbot; one to his sister Bassila; one to Apicella; one to Bishop Wiligildus; one to his kinswoman Pomponia, abbess; two to Hoio and Eutrocia; one to Pope Honorius I in the name of the Sixth Council of Toledo; one to Bishop Eutropius; two to Unianimus, bishop of Valencia; two to the priest and abbot Aemilianus; one to Ataulfus; one to Gundesinda and Agivarius; one to Wistremirus; two to King Chindaswinth; one to Nebridius; one to Eugenius, primate of Toledo; another to King Chindaswinth in the name of Braulio, Bishop Eutropius, and others; two to King Recceswinth; one to the priest and abbot Taius; and finally one to the priest Fructuosus.
>
> The distinguished continuator of *Hispania Sacra* wisely included all of them in volume XXX of his work, beginning on p. 328.

> **Note [Col. 0645C].** They contain much that is extremely useful for understanding both the ecclesiastical history of that age and, above all, the discipline then prevailing in Spain concerning the customs and rites of the Church—matters not easily learned from elsewhere.

> In the Escorial Codex, recently copied from an older manuscript, shelfmark digramm. and pluteus IV, no. 23, there is a “Continuation by Braulio of Caesaraugusta to Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*.”
>
> Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi aevi*, book I, p. 273, attributes to Braulio the *Life of Saint Leocadia, Virgin of Toledo*.

Concerning Braulio’s letters to Isidore and Isidore’s to Braulio, we have said something when treating Isidore. Among the Isidorian materials there is one or another letter written by Braulio to him, containing various matters. Chief among them is an extremely urgent complaint, though expressed in courteous language, that he should send him the book of the *Etymologies*, which rumor had already reported completed, and should cease frustrating him after the six years during which he had awaited the work whose promoter he had been.

Among the letters is also one that deserves praise, said to have been written to the supreme pontiff of that age, according to the testimony of Isidore of Pax and Rodrigo of Toledo. In the words of those writers, Rome, mother and mistress of cities, greatly admired it.

> **Note [Col. 0645D].** This is certainly the letter that Braulio sent in the name of the entire Sixth Council of Toledo to Pope Honorius I. The council met in the Spanish era 676, or A.D. 638, on 9 January. In the letter he defends himself and the Spanish and Narbonensian Gallic Fathers against certain slanders maliciously spread about them and charges brought against them by Honorius. It is found in the distinguished continuator of *Hispania Sacra*, vol. XXX, p. 348 onward.

That pontiff must necessarily have been Honorius, who governed the Roman Church from 626 to 638, if the letter concerned matters dealt with at the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in 633, as the bishop of Pax seems to suggest. Alternatively, it may have been one of Honorius’s three successors—Severinus, John, or Theodore—who lived contemporaneously with Braulio thereafter.

Pseudo-Julian, in his usual manner, pretended that he had seen another letter by Braulio to Fructuosus of Braga in the archive of Saint Justa at Toledo.

> *Adversus* 488.

We have already spoken in our treatment of Isidore about the labor of this great prelate on the work of his master, Saint Isidore, the *Etymologies*. Braulio says:

> “I divided into twenty books the Codex of the *Etymologies*, distinguished by excessive size and divided by headings rather than by books. Since he produced it at my request, although he himself left it unfinished…”

This occurs in the preface to the works of the holy bishop.

Braulio left other little works besides these, as reported not only by Ildephonsus but also by Isidore of Pax and, following him, Rodrigo of Toledo.

> **Note [Col. 0645D].** Our author does not seem to remember here the *Preliminary Notice to the Works of Isidore*, which bibliographers unanimously attribute to Braulio. Yet it should least of all be omitted now, since an eminent man, my fellow citizen and, during his lifetime, my singular friend and patron of my studies, Gregorio Mayans y Siscar, has raised a dispute about it.
>
> In the *Life of Nicolás Antonio*, prefixed to his immortal *Censure of Fictitious Histories*, §125, he asserts that this *Preliminary Notice* was falsely attributed to Braulio, and promises that he will prove the point at greater length wherever the place or occasion permits.
>
> If these words refer to that older and fuller *Preliminary Notice* of Braulio which we mentioned elsewhere, which Grial says Cyprian Suárez discovered in the Prologue to his edition, while John Mariana testifies in his notes to Isidore’s book I, *Against the Jews*, chapter 2, that he saw it in two very old Codices, we need not be greatly concerned. For we are now discussing the *Preliminary Notice* that is handled by everyone and commonly prefixed to collections of Isidore’s works.
>
> And concerning this notice, to speak frankly, nothing could ever have pleased me more than to be instructed by so great a man in the reasons that led him to this opinion. For we should not suppose that the statements we have reported from him were made gratuitously or arbitrarily. Perhaps something in our scanty store of knowledge might have been available to weaken or otherwise qualify them.
>
> In the meantime, until time brings those reasons to light, I consider the agreement of all the ancient Codices I have seen, and of nearly all bibliographers—for whom the *Preliminary Notice* of Braulio under discussion has always served as a torch and guiding star for distinguishing Isidore’s genuine works—more than sufficient to prevent us from removing it in any way from the position it has hitherto held among critics.

There also circulates under Braulio’s name, among the fig-tree wares of the Toledan author of pseudonymous chronicles, an appendix at the end of the work that bears the title of Marcus Maximus. It is more an addition than a continuation of history, mingled with other similar additions that present Helecanus, or Heleca, bishop of the same city of Caesaraugusta in the ninth century, as their author.

The materials are so confused that Bivarius himself admits that, in his edition of Maximus, it was extremely difficult for him to determine the author of each item. The editors of the Caesaraugustan and Sevillian editions, however, were not troubled by this difficulty: apart from the six earlier sections, or *Adversaria*, which they attribute to Braulio, they assign everything else through the end to Helecanus.

The Madrid Bivarian edition differs remarkably from those two earlier editions in the arrangement of the *Adversaria*, so that the examples clearly do not all seem to have been derived from one source. Rather, they appear to have proceeded from the same author or inventor, distributed among different recipients in whatever order he pleased.

All these works were fabricated by a man who, lest he should offer his usually rash—or rather insane—thoughts for sale in vain, attached to them the name of some ancient person whose authority might give them value and attract the curious to obscure matters.

He falsely and absurdly presents the genealogies, relationships, journeys, orders, dates of death, and physical appearances of men of the Gospel as though they had been reported by others, although he himself dreamed them up. He invents the histories of other holy men at his own pleasure. In order to claim the glory of cutting off questions that had arisen from various documents pressing upon him, he makes two people out of one. In short, this twin brother of Dexter and Maximus industriously exercises all their arts of deception and lying.

I should like to leave here one example of the matter, until an opportunity arises to crush these enemies of truth with the club of style. The section of Helecanus truly concerns what we now intend to attack; but we direct our pressure against Braulio, who has been joined and mixed with Helecanus—or who is one and the same person with him.

For a long time a controversy has been debated among us and the Gauls concerning the present tomb of Saint Vincent, a Spanish deacon and martyr, who was first buried at Valencia. The Portuguese claim to possess it at Lisbon; the Gauls boast that they possess it at Castres in Aquitaine.

On this subject, so as not to be prolix, consult Andrea Resende in his learned letter to Quevedo, which we mentioned not long ago. Since sacred relics are venerated in both places and attributed to the famous martyr Vincent, Pseudo-Braulio, the author under discussion, thought it would bring him credit if he could reconcile the two parties, long opposed without compromise, by composing a story resembling history about one and the other Vincent—one formerly buried and preserved at Valencia, from which the first was transferred to the Sacred Promontory of Portugal and the second to Gaul.

This is the purpose of what is reported in no. 7 of the Bivarian edition concerning two Vincents: one from Huesca in Spain, the other from Agen in Gaul, both archdeacons under Valerius, bishop of Caesaraugusta, and both buried after their martyrdom at Valencia in our Spain.

He adds:

> “The Spaniard was brought first to the Sacred Promontory; this one”—the Gaul—“was brought to Gaul, to the monastery of Castres, about the year 850; the Spaniard in 757, when Valencia was being besieged by Abd al-Rahman.”

You hear the year in which Vincent of Agen was carried from the city of Valencia to Castres. Yet shortly afterward he attributes mention of this translation to Julian, archbishop of Toledo, who had lived nearly two hundred years earlier:

> “A temple was built at Toledo by Gundemar in honor of Saint Vincent, the Spanish deacon; and another was built by Julian, archbishop of Toledo, in honor of Saint Vincent of Agen, in the upper part of the royal city. Julian was exceedingly devoted to him and composed this poem for him:
>
> Vincent, who at Agen endured as a steadfast martyr,  
> Holy deacon, flying through blood to the stars,  
> The fatal sword took your head from you; but by that sword  
> You received a sacred, undying crown.  
> Gaul gave you birth, and Augusta Caesarea taught you as a minister;  
> you flourish under Valerius’s piety.  
> Gaul again receives you, teaching sacred words;  
> Maximianus, demented, kills you with the sword.  
> After your ashes, the loving bishop Murila carries you away;  
> Valentinus himself keeps watch over you in his own house.  
> At last, as the years revolve, Audaldus rejoicing  
> Brings you back to your ancestral home, himself so commanded.  
> Pray for us, Vincent, etc.”

This is the translation to Castres from Valencia—or from Caesaraugusta—made by Audaldus, a Gallic monk of the monastery called Conkittas, otherwise Okatas, after the year 855, during the reign of Charles the Bald in Gaul.

The history of this translation was written by Aimo, a monk.

> **Note [Col. 0647D].** He is different from Aimo of Fleury, who lived later and is discussed by Labbe in the second volume of *Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Aimo lived at this very time and said that he had received the account from Audaldus’s own mouth. James Breulius, a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, first published it; it was later published again in the great work on the Acts of the Saints, under 22 January.

The same Aimo composed the same history in verse. At its beginning he expressed the year in this way:

> When twice four hundred and ten times five had rolled away,  
> With four further cycles, since Christ the high priest,  
> Ever born of virginal and sacred stock,  
> Audaldus, known by such a name,  
> Was a monk at Castres.

> **Note [Col. 0647D].** An account of the revelation to Audaldus and Illebert, and of the translation of the relics of the most holy deacon and martyr Vincent from our Valencia to the monastery of Castres in Aquitaine, survives in an old Escorial Breviary apparently from the beginning of the thirteenth century, shelfmark L, pluteus III, no. 4. It is more abbreviated than the account in the *Acts of the Saints* under 22 January.
>
> There the entire story of his journey and the miracles performed everywhere by the relics of the holy martyr are carefully described. On that occasion his parents Euticius and Enola are named, as though these facts too had been revealed to Audaldus and Illebert. Such details depart considerably from the character and simplicity of history and are therefore relegated by Andrea Resende, in his letter to Bartholomew Quevedo, together with other stories of this sort that commonly circulate on the subject, to the category of old women’s tales.
>
> In another, older Codex of the same library, from the twelfth century, shelfmark L, pluteus III, no. 3, in the fourth reading of the Matins office of the holy deacon, the following further details are found concerning his lineage and the homeland of one of his parents: “For Vincent was born of a father, Euticius, who was the son of the most noble consul Agressus. His mother Enola is said to have been born in the city of Oscha.”

Do you still hesitate, reader, to hold up to ridicule by the nose this impostor, so disastrously careless in fabrication and exposing himself to laughter through an anachronism of two centuries?

Julian, bishop of Toledo and successor of Quiricus, who wrote the *Prognostic of the Future Age*, the book *On the Demonstration of the Sixth Age*, and other works, died in the third year of Egica, king of the Goths, while their rule still flourished in Spain, in the year 728 of the Spanish era—that is, A.D. 690. Felix, his successor in the same Church of Toledo, reported this.

> **Note [Col. 0648D].** It is found together with Saint Ildephonsus’s little book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

And yet, if we lend our ears to the fig-tree fabrications of Braulio or Helecanus, this Julian composed a poem about the translation of Saint Vincent’s relics by Audaldus—a translation known to have occurred in 855, according to Aimo, or about 850, as this absurd and careless narrator himself admits.

You should measure the remaining additions of this appendix, whether they bear the name of Braulio or of Helecanus, by this standard and in this measure, reader, and acknowledge that the author of the already mentioned *Historical Synopsis of the Acts of the Saints* rightly said:

> “We dare assert with still greater certainty that those ten years of additions—from the Spanish era 342 to 352—inserted into the fictitious Chronicle published under the name of Maximus of Caesaraugusta came from the same workshop from which Pseudo-Dexter and the other monstrosities of similar invention emerged.”

But let us turn to other matters.

The feast day of Saint Braulio is celebrated on 18 March in the Church of Caesaraugusta, as the Aragonese themselves inform us, not on 26 March, as Thomas Truxillus mistakenly first recorded it. He caused Baronius to err, Baronius caused Pseudo-Luitprandus to err, and Pseudo-Luitprandus finally caused John Tamaius to err, as noted in the aforementioned *Historical Synopsis*, no. 20.

> **Note [Col. 0648D].** Carrillo, *History of Saint Valerius and Catalogue of the Prelates of Zaragoza*, p. 231.

Our historians add more about Braulio’s royal blood and about miracles at his election and death, but these accounts lack the foundation of antiquity.

---

## Letters of Saint Braulio, Bishop of Caesaraugusta

*(Flores, *España Sagrada*, vol. XXX.) (C)*

### Letter I. Isidore, Bishop of Hispalis, to Braulio the Archdeacon (C)

In the name of the Lord. To Braulio the archdeacon, my most beloved and dearest brother in Christ, Isidore.

Since I cannot enjoy you with the eyes of the flesh, let me at least enjoy your words, so that it may itself be a consolation to me to learn through your letters that you are safe and well, since I desire to see you. Both would be good if it were permitted; but since it is not now permitted, let me at least refresh my mind with you, if I cannot do so by bodily sight.

When we were together, I asked you to send me the sixth decade of Saint Augustine.

> **Note [Col. 0649C].** The Bollandist Fathers say that it is now neither easy nor worthwhile to guess which of Augustine’s little works were contained in this decade, since the memory of such an arrangement has disappeared, *Acts of the Saints*, vol. II for March, p. 636.
>
> I, however, have no doubt that Augustine’s sixth decade was a definite portion of his exposition of the Psalms, namely that which extends from Psalm 51 through Psalm 60. Both Cassiodorus, in his preface to the Psalms, testifies that Augustine’s entire commentary was once divided into decades, and several manuscript Codices demonstrate the same. See the preface by the monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur in vol. IV of Augustine’s works.

I ask you, somehow, to make me known to him.

> **Note [Col. 0649D].** These words are foreign to Isidore’s intention and completely absurd. For how could Braulio make Isidore known to Augustine, who had died almost two centuries earlier? The sense has therefore been disturbed by the carelessness of copyists. I think it should be restored by changing a few letters: “I ask you, somehow, to make it known to me”—namely, the sixth decade of Augustine’s commentary on the Psalms.

We are sending you the little book of the *Synonyms*, not because it is of any use, but because you wanted it. I commend this boy to you, and I commend myself as well, so that you may pray for me, a wretched man, since I am gravely weakened both by bodily infirmities and by the guilt of my mind. In both matters I ask your protection, because I deserve nothing through my own merits.

For the rest, I ask that, whenever the opportunity arises for the bearer of this letter to return to us while life permits, you order us to be gladdened by your words.

### Letter II. The Same Isidore to Braulio the Archdeacon (C)

To Braulio the archdeacon, my most beloved and dearest son in Christ, Isidore.

When you receive a friend’s letters, dearest son, do not delay to embrace them as you would a friend. For this is the second consolation among those who are absent: when the person who is loved is not present, letters embrace him in his place.

We have sent you a ring as a token of our affection, and a cloak as the covering of our friendship; from this antiquity derived the term.

Pray for me, therefore. May the Lord inspire you so that I may yet deserve to see you in this life; and may you, whom your departure made sorrowful, one day gladden me again by presenting yourself to me.

We have sent the *Quaternio of Rules* by Maurentius, the chief clerk.

> **Note [Col. 0650C].** This is how it is found in the editions I have seen. I nevertheless read *primiclerus* or *primicerius*. The dignity of the chief clerk is mentioned in the Council of Mérida, chapters 10 and 14; in the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, in the subscriptions; and in the Council of Compostela, chapter 1.
>
> It was his office to distribute offerings to the clergy according to each person’s dignity and virtue. On the office of the *primicerius*, see Isidore’s letter to Ludifredus, bishop of Córdoba.

For the rest, I desire always to know that you are well, my most beloved lord and dearest son.

### Letter III. Braulio, Bishop of Caesaraugusta, to Isidore

To my lord, and truly my lord, Isidore, chosen by Christ, chief among bishops, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God.

O pious lord and most eminent of men, my inquiry is late, and the opportunity to write has come to me slowly. For, as my sins pressed upon me, I was hindered from making inquiry not only by the evil of barrenness and lack, but also by the horrifying onslaught of plague and hostility.

Now, although worn down by a thousand necessities and a thousand cares, after a long period of misery, and, so to speak, awakened from the heaviness of an evil sleep, I venture through the words of this petition to render the service of salvation. Prostrate in humility of heart and body, I implore the most excellent authority of your blessedness: command that the particular servant whom, with that pious gaze of sacred favor, you have always received into your care may remain commended to you to the end.

For I too—Christ knows it—am tortured by severe sorrow because, after so long a time has passed, I still do not deserve to behold your presence. But I hope in him who does not forget to show mercy and does not reject forever, because he will hear the prayer of the poor and will bring me, wretched as I am, before your sight.

I also earnestly suggest and beg with every kind of supplication that, remembering your promise, you order the book of the *Etymologies*, which we have heard has now, by the Lord’s favor, been completed, to be sent to your servant. For, as I am conscious, you labored there in large part at the petition of your servant.

Therefore be generous to me first, so that among the assemblies of the saints you may be regarded as both blessed and foremost.

I also ask that, through your prompting, the acts of the synod in which Sintharius was subjected to the fire of your examination—although not purified, he is nevertheless found to have been boiled—be sent to us quickly by your son, our lord the king. For our own petition likewise sought his glory, since much depends upon the council for the investigation of the truth.

For the rest, I earnestly implore the mercy of the Most High Creator: may he command that the crown of your blessedness be preserved for a long time, for the integrity of the faith and the condition of his Church; may he render me secure through the grace of your intercession amid the varied and innumerable dangers of the barking present world; and may the most holy Trinity, through your prayers, make me, hidden in the bosom of your remembrance, safe from every storm of sin.

And in his own hand:

> I, Braulio, servant of the Lord, to Isidore:  
> May I enjoy you in the Lord,  
> O burning and unfading lamp.

### Letter IV. Isidore to Braulio, Bishop (C)

To my lord and servant of God, Braulio, bishop, Isidore.

When I learned that you were safe and well, I gave thanks to Christ. Would that, while in this body, I might look upon the well-being and the face of him whose safety I have learned of!

But I shall reveal what happened to me because of my sins. I was not worthy to read through your words, because as soon as I received your brief note, a royal boy came to me. I gave the note to my chamberlain and immediately went to the prince, intending to read it afterward and reply.

When I returned from the royal palace, I found not only that your writing was gone, but that everything else that had been on the papers had also perished. And therefore, the Lord knows, I bewailed what I deserved, because I had not read through your message.

I ask you, then, whenever an opportunity arises, to write back to me. Do not withhold the grace of your word, so that what I lost through my fault I may receive again through your favor.

And in his own hand:

> Pray for us, most blessed lord.

### Letter V. Braulio to Isidore

To my lord, and truly my lord, Isidore, chosen by Christ, chief among bishops, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God.

The inner and spiritual man is usually filled with joy when he engages in the inquiry of one who loves. Therefore, my most reverend lord, it is my desire—unless the wall of my sins stands in the way—that you kindly embrace my inquiry and patiently receive the reproach of my complaints. I am doing both: I am fulfilling the duty of inquiry, and I am directing against you the claims arising from my needs. As I prostrate myself at the entrance and harbor of this dictation, I ask this of the summit of your apostolate: although the charge of reproach falters where there is the intervention of tears, since tears are not signs of reproach, nevertheless I wish there to be both tearful reproaches and reproachful tears. Yet I do this through the boldness permitted by love, not through the rashness of arrogance. [Col. 0651D]
