But now I shall begin my case. If I am not mistaken, seven years have revolved since I remember asking you for the books of the *Etymologies* that you had composed. In various and differing ways you have frustrated me when present, and, when absent, written me nothing about them; but by subtle delay—sometimes alleging that they were not yet finished, sometimes not yet written, sometimes that my letters had been lost, and raising many other objections—we have reached this day and remain without the result of my request. [Col. 0652A]

For this reason I too shall turn my prayers into a complaint, so that what I could not obtain by supplication I may perhaps gain by pressing you with reproach. A beggar’s shouting often proves useful.

Why, then, I ask you, my lord, do you not grant what is asked of you? Know this one thing: I shall not give up, pretending that I do not want what has been denied. I shall seek, and I shall seek insistently, until I either receive it or draw it forth, at the command of the most merciful Redeemer: “Seek, and you will find”; and with the addition: “Knock, and it will be opened to you.” I have sought, and I am seeking; I am even knocking. Thus I cry out that you open. For I am consoled by the discovery contained in this argument: you who have disregarded the petitioner may perhaps hear the complainant. [Col. 0652B]

Thus I press what you already know upon you—not boastfully. I, a fool, presume to suggest something; yet I am not ashamed, though inexperienced, to speak to the most eloquent, remembering the apostolic command by which you are instructed willingly to bear with a fool. Therefore receive the cries of my complaint.

Why do you continue to withhold the distribution of the talents and the dispensation of the provisions entrusted to you? Now open your hand; share them with the households, lest they perish from want and hunger. You know what the Creditor, when he comes, will demand back from you. Whatever you give us will not be diminished for you. Remember the multitude that was fed with a few loaves, and the abundance of the fragments that remained after the loaves. [Col. 0652C]

Do you think that the gift bestowed upon you was given for you alone? It belongs both to you and to us; it is common, not private. Who, unless insane, would presume to say that you should rejoice in what is private, when you know that you may rejoice blamelessly only in what is common?

Since God has granted you stewardship over his treasure and over the riches of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge, why do you not pour out with a generous hand what is not diminished by being given? Or, since each member of the heavenly Head possesses in another what it has not received itself, so that it knows that what it has must be possessed by another, are you perhaps sparing toward us because you find nothing that you can receive back from us in exchange? But if you give to one who has, you carry away the fruit of so small a reward. If, however, you give to one who has nothing, you fulfill the evangelical commands, so that it may be returned to you in the reward of the righteous. [Col. 0652D]

For this reason my conscience also reproaches me, because I perceive that there is nothing good in me that can be shared, since we are commanded through charity to serve one another, and each person is to administer to others the grace he has received, “as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.” Each person, according to the measure of faith that God has apportioned and joined into one body of members, ought to share it with the other parts, because “all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills.”

But I return to the one particular aid I mentioned earlier—to friendly persistence on behalf of those deprived of friendship and adorned by no grace of honorable members. [Col. 0653A] Therefore hear my voice across all the lands that lie between us. Give back, give back what you owe. For you are the servant of Christ and of Christians, so that there you may be greater than all of us; and since you perceive that the grace bestowed upon you was given for our sake, do not disdain to distribute it to minds thirsting and tormented by hunger for knowledge.

Am I not at least a foot, able to run to the tasks assigned to me and, by the movement of obedience, serve the belly of the Church—that is, the judge of the members—and, by obeying the command of the Head who rules, please him? Indeed, even if I know that I am one of the less honorable members, let it suffice that I am worthy to bring forth through me what you clearly received from the Head, and that you not refuse to bring forth through me, though I am the least, one redeemed nevertheless by the blood of Christ.

For the Head does not say to the feet, “You are not necessary to me,” since “those members of the body that seem to be weaker are more necessary,” and “upon those that we think less honorable we bestow greater honor,” while “our less honorable members have greater respectability.” [Col. 0653B] Thus our Creator and steward orders all things: when the divine gifts that one person does not perceive in himself are granted to another to possess, charity is increased.

In short, manifold grace is well administered when the gift received is entrusted even to those who do not possess it, when it is understood to have been given for the sake of the one to whom it is supplied. Your charity’s prudence knows very well that the whole of the apostolic passage that I cited in part above applies to this matter, and whatever I have touched upon briefly you undoubtedly know better than anyone. [Col. 0653C]

Therefore only this remains, and this I earnestly ask: grant what is requested, if not for me, at least for charity itself, which has been bestowed by God. For we are commanded through it both to know and to perform all things, and without it all things are nothing.

But if I have poured out anything superfluous, negligent, less humbly, or rather uselessly than I should have spoken, I ask you kindly to receive everything, forgive everything, and pray that God may forgive everything.

I also make this known: I ask my lord for the books of the *Etymologies*, although I know that many people already possess mutilated and damaged copies. Therefore I ask you to be graciously willing to send them to me transcribed, complete, corrected, and properly arranged, lest, carried away by eagerness, I be forced to take defects from others in place of virtues. [Col. 0653D]

For my part, although you need nothing, and voluntary gifts are said to stink, and although your gracious esteem commands us to do what we can and are able, I desire only that you make use of our service—or rather, enjoy charity, which is God.

When these matters have been completed, I shall have questions concerning the sacred and divine books, whose explanation the light of your heart would disclose to me, provided that you also command it to shine upon us and to unlock the obscurities of divine law. Nor, if I receive what I ask, shall I remain silent about those matters; rather, you will open the way to the confidence of asking, provided that on this first occasion you do not pierce me with the goads of shame, but grant forgiveness to my sluggishness, since you have not ordered the rejection of one whom you loved, however unworthy he may be. For it seems exceedingly shameful and base if someone not yet satisfied with charity is found to withdraw from the one he loved. [Col. 0654A]

In obedience to my servitude I render the duties of greeting, and I ask the goodness of your most holy authority that you deign to pray for me, so that through your intercession you may daily win for God my soul, tossed about amid evils, and lead it, rescued from miseries and scandals, to the harbor of eternal tranquility.

It was sweet for me to speak to you at length, as though you were present before me and I were seeing the face of your countenance. Therefore I did not avoid verbosity and perhaps incurred rashness. Yet I had to do either this or something else, provided that what you did not wish to grant through humility you might at least grant through my tumultuous insistence.

Behold how much boldness your gracious favor has given me. Therefore, if anything in this displeases you, let your favor blame itself, since it loves so greatly that it removes fear. “Perfect love casts out fear.” [Col. 0654B]

Relying also upon this special favor, and upon a special lord in whom the strength of the holy Church rests, I suggest that, since our metropolitan Eusebius has died, you take care for mercy. Suggest this also to your son and our lord, so that he may appoint to that place a useful man whose doctrine and holiness may be a pattern of life to the others.

I commend this man, who is present, in every respect to your most blessed authority, so that through him I may deserve to be enlightened by your words both concerning what we have suggested here and concerning what we complained of above.

## LETTER VI. ISIDORE TO BRAULIO (C)

To my lord and servant of God, Braulio, bishop: Isidore.

The letter of your holiness found me in the city of Toledo. I had been summoned on account of the council. But although the ruler’s command, while I was on the road, had instructed me to turn back, I nevertheless preferred not to interrupt the course of my journey, since I was nearer to his presence than to returning. [Col. 0654C]

I came into the ruler’s presence and found your deacon there. Receiving your words through him, I embraced and read them, and gave thanks to God for your good health, longing with every desire—although weak and exhausted, yet having confidence through Christ in this life to see you—for “hope does not disappoint” through the charity “that has been poured into our hearts.”

I sent the *Codex of the Etymologies* along with the other books from the journey. Although, because of ill health, it was uncorrected, I had nevertheless decided to offer it to you for correction once I reached the council’s appointed place.

Concerning the appointment of the bishop of Tarragona, I did not perceive the king’s decision to be what you requested. Nevertheless, even he remains uncertain about where he will more definitely turn his mind. [Col. 0654D]

I ask you to deign to stand as an intercessor for me before the Lord because of my sins, so that through your petition my offenses may be erased and my crimes forgiven.

Written in his own hand. Pray for us, most blessed lord and excellent brother.

## LETTER VII. THE SAME ISIDORE TO BRAULIO (C)

To my lord and servant of God, Braulio, bishop: Isidore.

Here, as I promised, I have sent you a work on the origin of certain things, collected from the recollection of ancient reading and annotated in certain places in the manner in which it stands written in the style of our forefathers.

## LETTER VIII. THE SAME ISIDORE TO BRAULIO (C)

[Col. 0655A]

To my lord and servant of God, Braulio, bishop: Isidore.

With every desire I have longed to see your face, and would that God might at some time fulfill my wish before I die. For the present, I beg you to commend me to God in your prayers, so that he may fulfill my hope in this life and grant me a share in your blessedness in the life to come.

Written in his own hand. Pray for us, most blessed lord and brother.

[Note: Floresius places this title before this and the following letters: “Previously unpublished letters of Braulio, [Col. 0656D] and most recently discovered in a very ancient Gothic manuscript of the holy church of León.” EDITOR.]

## LETTER IX. OF BRAULIO, BISHOP, TO THE PRIEST JACTATUS

To my lord Jactatus, priest: Braulio.

I perceive, most blessed brother, that you wish to demand from me nourishment of the divine word, although I understand that this is beyond my powers. I approve your devotion all the more because you do not restrain your persistence even in the exercise of holy study, where you know that you are likely to find little knowledge in what you seek. [Col. 0655B]

Since you meditate daily upon the law of the Lord and turn over the pages of the most blessed and most learned Fathers, what is there in us, or how little is it, that you might wish either to learn yourself or from which you might nourish your sacred desire? It is enough—more than enough—for you to read your friend Saint Augustine, Jerome, Hilary, and the other most learned men. It would take me too long to name them, and there is no doubt that you will find them useful. Let their speech feed you and their judgments instruct you; indeed, let these men teach you everything you seek. Content with them, do not drag our little poverty into the open, nor expose it naked and visible to the eyes of the envious. [Col. 0655C]

There is one thing suitable for me which, although I do not feel capable of accomplishing it effectively, I nevertheless desire to accomplish: to ask the singular and inexhaustible mercy of our common Lord and Redeemer to grant you and us life in shared happiness and to deign to give us the opportunity to see one another, so that, speaking face to face, we may feed one another with conversation and enjoy the tranquility desired in the Lord.

I ask you in turn to pray that this may happen as quickly as I wish. But, as I think, this would easily come about if your holiness, when passing through Tirasona, were pleased to come to us.

Concerning the relics of the revered apostles, which you demanded and said ought to be sent to you, I faithfully report that I do not possess any of the martyrs in such a way that I can know which relics belong to whom. It was the decision of my predecessors and lords that, since through the affection of many they were compelled, everywhere or secretly, even unwillingly and under compulsion, either to give away or to go without portions of what they possessed, the identifying labels of all should be removed, lest any indication of their title be known to anyone, and they should be placed together in one chamber. [Col. 0655D]

Nevertheless, about seventy have been retained for use; among these, those you seek are by no means found.

In short, it is clear that I greet you warmly and earnestly, again and again, asking you to order prayers to be offered for us. [Col. 0656A] I dictated this quickly, as it occurred to me; excuse my negligence if I have omitted anything.

## LETTER X. OF THE SAME BRAULIO TO THE PRIEST JACTATUS

To the most holy and venerable brother in Christ, Jactatus, priest.

Your letter, while the hands of cares held me completely hidden away and withdrawn, brought me back to myself. For, overwhelmed in feeling by the anxieties and storms of the world—which daily threaten shipwreck in the place over which we preside—we are not permitted to be what we either are said to be or ought to be.

But when your letter moved me, I set everything else behind me. Looking upon you and myself, I saw nothing between us except love itself, which is the Creator of both of us. [Col. 0656B] Turning to him, and eager to offer thanks, I could do nothing worthy; I merely remember that I wished to do so, for so small a person cannot render so great a gift. He himself stirred your conscience to show concern for me. Therefore, since immeasurable thanks are owed to him, I ask you, turning them toward yourself, to fulfill the duties both of repayment and of devotion.

I confess that I am constricted by the very hardships with which you complained that you were being pressed, as though they had been extended to me immediately after you. I ask myself why those joined by one love should be separated by so great a distance, should have those from whom they wish to be free, and lack those whom they wish to have.

Yet again I see that this is not the homeland of the devout. For this reason they are separated in the land of mortals, so that they may be joined together in the land of the living. Let it suffice for pilgrims to possess an unbroken bond of charity, to be consoled in it, and in mind to serve the law of him who truly is charity, while in the flesh they are separated from those they love. Thus, for those deprived of their loved ones, charity itself is sweet, through which the memory of the absent becomes sweet. [Col. 0656C]

But if you loved intensely, you would break through delays, undertake the journey, and come to me; neither distance nor any occasion of necessity would stand in your way. Therefore drive yourself forward as with spurs, pierce your mind with goads, and awaken within it the force of love and the fire of affection, so that it may burn and cannot be extinguished by many waters.

Why have I said this? Clearly, because you came to Tirasona, often lingered there almost indefinitely, and disdain to see us. Acknowledge your fault if you want me to forgive you, and with diligent inquiry provide the opportunity by which you ought to present yourself to us immediately after Easter. [Col. 0656D]

For my part, I greet you in the Lord Jesus Christ with manifold affection and varied reverence, earnestly and repeatedly asking you to commend me to my Creator with your most ready prayer. May the omnipotence of Christ our God increase his grace in you, perfect it once increased, and preserve it once perfected.

You sent us what is offered in the sacrament of the body of Christ. We have sent you what prefigures the blood in the mystery of the same Lord—namely, two measures of wine. We have also sent a measure of oil and a bushel of olives, signifying the twofold commandment of charity: one referring to the love of God, the other to the love of one’s neighbor.

One bushel of Damascene plums, about which I find nothing to say, except perhaps that at the Lord’s birth the power of that city, from which this kind of fruit originated, is promised as an offering. [Col. 0657A] This is the gold that the holy Gospel reports as having been offered by the Magi.

## LETTER XI. OF THE SAME BRAULIO TO THE PRIEST TAJO

To my lord Tajo, priest: Braulio.

You are shaken by the turbulence of your mind and tossed about by stormy tempests of impatience, so that it is fitting to say: “You have little patience; why are you disturbed?” Would that you were moved in such a way that you fled to humility rather than turning to abuse and insults.

For believe this with certainty—for I speak before God—that I wrote in my letter, as a joke and not to disparage you, about that donkey upon which I urged you to mount. It is easy to see this from the very playfulness of the passage. [Col. 0657B]

In return, like an Aesopian jackdaw swollen with pride, you ordered me to mount a camel and to beware lest I strike my head against the church doors. You poured out these remarks less prudently and not sufficiently elegantly, unaware that our Head, who is Christ, does not strike against the doors of the Church—though perhaps against the synagogue of Satan.

Therefore we do not perceive the insult in the wording but in the meaning. Nor do we altogether blame your ignorance; rather, we want your mind to be more humble. For patience under injury reveals a humble man, and on this occasion I have learned how much of it there is in you.

What shall I say about the rest of what you wrote, when, while trying to cleanse the accusations brought against you, you do not cease to soil what has already been cleansed? If I wished to refute them as they deserve, neither difficulty nor labor would have hindered me, since destroying the accusations would have required nothing more than opposing those same accusations with antitheses. But lest our story cause long delays, I take Lord Leo as witness to the spirit in which I wrote to you. I also take you yourself as witness, although you are ungrateful and unwilling: you say that our speech injured you, yet you confess that this very thing contributes to your improvement. [Col. 0657C]

But lest we offend our friend through excessive speech, keep this firmly in mind: if I wished, I could bite back; if injured, I could drive in my tooth. For, following Horace, we too have learned our letters, and we have often withdrawn our hand from the schoolmaster’s rod. It may be said of us: [Col. 0657D]

“He has hay on his horn; flee far away.”

Or rather, in Virgil’s words [Note: This Virgilian verse, taken from *Aeneid* XII, is read very corruptly in the manuscript, which has: “And we likewise, the weapon and iron, or the right hand weak.” EDITOR.]:

> And we too, father, scatter weapons and iron  
> Not weak in our right hand; and blood follows from our wound.

Your paradigm, arranged in military armor, would have been easy for me to trample underfoot, as they say, except for that which, with Gregory’s permission, I saw had been stolen—or rather corrupted. But while we strive both to serve charity and not to lose you, we leave everything aside and insert nothing worthy of laughter, lest our story have ungrateful jokes, as Ovid would put it, and lest, according to Appius, we seem to exercise canine eloquence. [Col. 0658A]

But, as I said, setting these things aside, fulfilling the duty of our office, and holding fast to the humility of the Master and Lord Christ, we prefer to follow him who said: “I gave my back to the whips and my cheeks to the hands.” When he was cursed, he did not curse in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten. Therefore, dearest friend, let us reject those things and follow these sweet examples.

Let us cast away resentments, which arise through various suspicions. The Lord knows that I neither suspected some of the things you wrote to me in your letter nor dictated them with the meaning in which I see that you understood them. As for some other points, granting pardon, I do not see that they were sufficiently clear to you, since you answered me with other things, not those matters.

But since either error or suspicion is introduced among us by the enemy, let us reject him together in Christ and remain in the unity of love. This is what I desire more and more. [Col. 0658B]

For the rest, if it pleases my God, I shall go there, and I think that, for whatever I have said not otherwise than I intended, I shall quickly obtain forgiveness from you. Meanwhile, you have despised charity so greatly that, moved by indignation, you yourself gave effect to your request.

I, however, am not moved by your insults. I receive what you wrote with gentleness, ask your forgiveness if I have offended you, and desire that you love me more and more, remembering that we are Christians and that we must fear the loss of our souls, not love it.

Behold: if there was agitation before, let there now be moderation. And whoever prefers wine to words should beware of wine, lest words offend him.

Behold, while I wish to fashion a small pitcher, as Terence says, my hand has fashioned an amphora. I had intended to write a brief note, but the letter has almost become lengthy. You, however, sent a testament in place of a letter—perhaps one that will not be confirmed until after your death, since it has not yet been legally opened. [Col. 0658C]

Farewell, dearest one, whom I must love through charity; and forgive me, because, presuming upon your love, I have written to you even more than necessary.

## LETTER XII. OF THE SAME BRAULIO TO FLORIDIUS, ARCHDEACON

To my lord Floridius, archdeacon: Braulio, unworthy servant of the saints of God.

I faithfully confess, beloved son, that while held amid anxious cares and various occupations I received your letter in such a way that I was certainly pleased to learn of your good health, but was unable to answer quickly concerning what you requested. [Col. 0658D]

I feared either to pour out what you asked in a hurried speech—not with the maturity of writing but with the rashness of dictation—or at least to fail to complete everything necessary to explain these matters. If such things are said less fittingly than they should be, they turn not into instruction but into ruin.

A most difficult time has come, when it was better for me to be silent than to speak [Note: From Jerome’s letter to Augustine, numbered 172 among the Augustinian letters; Braulio has inserted these words here.]. Thus the studies of the diligent have ceased, all the more those of the lazy, while it is more necessary for us to consider the necessities of life and the means of salvation than, in Appius’s phrase, to exercise canine eloquence.

[Col. 0659A]

Therefore, although you asked me to send you matters suited to your understanding, the time of various affairs found me impeded. As I said above, it was better to ask your forgiveness than to fail fully to satisfy your wish.

Accordingly, while asking forgiveness, I beg you to pour out a prayer for us before the Lord, so that through your intercession there may be forgiveness for my sin. Moreover, if God allows me to see you, I shall explain in person, face to face, what you ask more effectively than I could write it in your absence.

In short, unless someone has first learned those numbers in Greek, he will not easily be able to understand this, especially since they are one way in Greek and another in Latin. The length of such a work demands almost the size of a book rather than a letter, so that it may be expressed more clearly and nothing may be omitted. [Col. 0659B]

But, as I said, what is present can more easily be conveyed to one who is present. The living voice possesses some hidden force, and when poured into the ear it sounds more powerfully: the listener opens up what he does not perceive clearly, and the one who explains knows where to linger in greater detail.

Indeed, given the shortness of time, I would prefer, following the Apostle who says, “The time is short,” to devote myself rather to charity, which builds up, than to knowledge, which can scarcely avoid either puffing up or provoking envy.

Nevertheless, since I perceive that you ardently wish to exercise your intellect, I shall accommodate you and shape this letter so that I do not leave it unfinished. It will now be your task, with the sharpness you possess and the intelligence in which you excel, either to approach these matters knowingly or to await my explanation.

For the rest, I offer you my most fervent greetings and beg you most abundantly, whenever you find the opportunity, to refresh me with your words. [Col. 0659C]

## LETTER XIII. OF THE SAME BRAULIO TO FRUNIMIAN, PRIEST AND ABBOT

To my lord Frunimian, priest and abbot: Braulio, unworthy servant of the saints of God.

I too am affected by no lesser distress when I learn that your sadness is exposed to impending trials. But your prudence knows better than our speech can suggest what ought to be done in such circumstances.

You know very well, my lord, that monastic life does not need penitence, since it is so suited to humility and daily sorrows that penitence is not regarded as foreign throughout the whole course of that life. You also see more clearly that you must not lose, for the sake of your own repose, the reward you have sought for so long, lest, while wishing to increase your merit, you seem to squander and destroy what has already been won. [Col. 0659D]

For it is a serious matter to disdain care for the brothers, or rather to undervalue your presiding over those who delight in it. Concerning what has arisen, I advise and suggest that, during your lifetime, you do those things by which you will not incur scandal, and do not allow the tranquility acquired over so long a time to be disturbed.

Therefore it is fitting that during your life, when you will have to give an account before God, you should not abandon care for the brothers, nor place over them one whom they do not want. Thus you will avoid scandal, and in your days there will be peace and the fruit of doctrine and work. Do not think about what will happen afterward, since the Ruler of all will govern that congregation as he has ordained. [Col. 0660A]

For I confess, my lord, that I am greatly astonished that you are so disturbed by the adversity of scandals arising on every occasion that you wish to withdraw from the exercise of your office as elder and prefer to spend your life in silence rather than remain in what has been entrusted to you.

And where will blessed perseverance be if patience is absent? You remember the Apostle’s saying: “Tribulation produces patience.” And also: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution.”

Persecution does not consist only in what is carried out during the confession of the Christian name by sword, fire, or various kinds of punishment. Differences of character, the obstinacy of the disobedient, the arrows of malicious tongues, and various temptations are also included in this kind of persecution, for no undertaking exists without dangers. [Col. 0660B]

But who will steer a ship through the waves if the pilot withdraws? Who will guard the sheep from wolves if the shepherd does not keep watch? Or who will drive away the robber if rest removes the lookout from his watch?

One must remain in the work entrusted and in the labor undertaken. Justice must be maintained and mercy shown. Sins must be hated, not people. The weak must be tolerated and the proud corrected. Even if tribulation presses upon us beyond our strength, let us not be afraid as though we were resisting by our own powers; rather, let us pray with the Apostle that God may provide a way through the temptation, so that we may endure it. Our strength and counsel are Christ, without whom we can do nothing and with whom we can do all things.

Behold, I am verbose while wishing to answer your questions. But, to say something also about what I mentioned above, you yourself know best, my lord, that no one ought to be placed over unwilling people, lest he be either despised or hated, and lest the subjects become less religious while striving to engage in conflict. [Col. 0660C]

Those who receive one whom they do not want do not obey him as they ought. Through disobedience scandal arises and the intended purpose is lost. But it is your prudence that must moderate all these things: you must bring them the sweetness of charity, place future matters in the hope of God, and yourself arrange matters properly as seems best (the manuscript reads *debeat*, “as ought”), so that you may lead a quiet life during your own time and they may serve God with the greatest devotion during yours.

For they cannot possess obedience if they have been provoked to defiance. It would be a detestable calamity if, while wishing to provide for the future, we disturbed in the present the order of submission.

I have received everything you sent me; I have given thanks for everything and have not yet ceased to do so. But I beseech Christ our God, by his mercy, to preserve and richly adorn your life and the summit of your blessedness, for my healing and intercession with the Lord. [Col. 0660D]

I feel myself unequal to responding in proportion to such great benefits. Meanwhile, I ask you to pray for me, your servant, for temptations do not spare us either, and we are afflicted by various evils. Therefore I ask you to support me by the help of your prayer, lest you grieve over me when I have been shattered by shipwreck.

## LETTER XIV. OF THE SAME BRAULIO TO FRUNIMIAN, PRIEST AND ABBOT

[Col. 0661A]

To my lord Frunimian, priest and abbot: Braulio.

We do not have enough parchment either, and therefore we lack what is needed to send you. But we have sent money with which, if you order it, you can purchase some.

First read carefully the commentary on the Apostle that we sent, arrange it in order, and, since it also contains the opinions of various writers written even in the margin, join each passage into the body of the work wherever you see that it agrees with the Catholic faith and where the order requires it. Write it out carefully, so that the commentaries follow each individual chapter and the work itself is not divided among the pages as this one is, lest we again have to write back to you about it. [Col. 0661B]

But you, my lord, according to your custom, ask us to tell you what you know perfectly well; and while you display your humility, you prove our ignorance.

I ask you, however, that if I say anything carelessly here, the responsibility may fall upon you, since you command us to inquire beyond what you have supplied and prefer to demand more than you have taught.

You ask whether, on Good Friday, after each reading, “Amen” ought to be answered, or whether “Gloria” should be sung in the customary manner. This is done neither among us nor anywhere else where we have seen it done, nor in the case of my lord Isidore, of most distinguished memory—not even at Toledo or Gerunda.

At Rome, as they say, no service is celebrated on that day. [Col. 0661C] I believe that the reason is nothing other than that the memory of the Lord’s Passion may always be renewed and the true sadness of the soul displayed in the body through the observance proper to that time. Or perhaps it is so that the Apostles’ distress may be shown by the abandonment of the service on that same day. Rather, perhaps the Church, taking its beginning from Peter on that day, began from sorrow so that it might reap joy in the resurrection.

Or is it because every Christian, living devoutly in this life in imitation of Christ, reaches the kingdom of God through tribulations, and therefore this recurring annual reminder of sorrow is signified to us in Christ, so that we may unquestionably imitate Christ?

For this reason also it seems to me that the sorrow of that night was instituted, so that the things accomplished bodily in Christ may be visibly fulfilled by the Church, which is still visible in this world. [Col. 0661D] Just as the Lord’s resurrection is signified once in joy, so ours is signified doubly at Easter: in the present age and in the age to come. Therefore it is necessary that sorrow precede on that day, as though it were the form of the present life, and that joy be taken in the glorious resurrection of our Redeemer.

Behold what I have thought; I have offered it quickly, as it occurred to me, and with as much brevity as I could. It is for you to choose whatever you judge better and, if anything is objectionable, to correct or remove it according to your judgment.

Concerning the vesting of the altar, or the hanging of veils, this is the custom of the Churches: as the day begins to decline toward evening, the church is adorned and the true Light, rising from the underworld, is received with ceremony. [Col. 0662A] For those virgins who prepared their lamps also awaited the bridegroom’s arrival in the glory of the resurrection.

Therefore the festivals are celebrated throughout that night until the night has passed its midpoint. At that hour we too believe that we shall rise, and that the Lord will judge the living and the dead; for what preceded in the Head will follow in the members.

For the rest, I devoutly render the duties of my service and entrust myself, tossed about in the storm of this life, to be saved by your prayers, if perhaps the Lord will look down from heaven, forgive me, and grant mercy to those over whom we preside unworthily.

## LETTER XV. OF THE SAME BRAULIO TO BASILLA, HIS SISTER

[Col. 0662B]

To my lady and most beloved daughter in Christ, Basilla: Braulio, unworthy servant of the saints of God.

Harassed amid the storms of a dreadful message, I am compelled to answer your letter, since you have inquired of me; and my mind is greatly concerned about what I ought to take up first: whether to disclose my own sorrows or to offer you consolation; or, if it is suitable, to report my present state, if indeed a life afflicted by sorrows may be called a state of well-being. For behold, every day the good depart from the Church, and every day the wicked increase; their loss grieves us no less than the success of these others. Indeed, the Apostle forbids us to mourn our dead, but who does not mourn when he is presently deprived of a good person? [Col. 0662C] For the very Vessel of Election rejoices that Epaphras had been restored to him from the neighborhood of death; and in this case, just as he certainly had joy at his restoration, so without doubt he ought to have had sorrow at his departure. We are raised up by hope, since we do not doubt that the faithful are changed into a better life, and we have before God as stronger intercessors those whose desolation here and now leaves us bereft. Yet somehow, amid the commands to console and the hope of resurrection, however believing the mind may be, the emotion of longing breaks it. But when no other harbor is found by which we may escape, we must embrace this very one with all our strength. Since in him who justifies the ungodly and raises the dead hope does not disappoint, we believe that we shall be with those who have already fallen asleep [Col. 0662D] in the blessed region [Note: [Col. 0661D] Manuscript: “the blessed region” (accusative).].

Indeed, he is not an excellent comforter whom his own groans overcome, and whom tears or sobs exclude from speech. For behold, while I myself, mourning, desire to console one who is mourning, tears roll down my face, and with my mind hardened I cannot conceal what I suffer. But what are we to do, since after sin this is the single decree imposed upon our mortal condition? The pious and the impious, the just and the criminal, the upright and the wicked are all swept away; but hereafter the holy and the condemned will not be held together under one decree or in one dwelling. Therefore let us endure the bitterness of the present life, patiently awaiting what we shall one day become; and let us rejoice in the Lord over the hope of a blessed life, praying and entreating together [Col. 0663A] that he may meet both those dear ones who have gone before us and us who follow, appeased everywhere, and that he may not examine us everywhere according to the severity of his judgment; but may mercy exalt itself above judgment, and, in his customary compassion, deign to gather us, when it pleases him, into the refreshment of his storehouse.

Let us be encouraged by this hope, let us serve him with this devotion, and in him let us have toward one another both the affection of love and the remedy of consolation. But you, most especially, lady daughter and sister, I exhort and beseech to offer consolation so wisely not only to yourself but to all those to whom the departure of so great a man has brought sorrow, that you may seem to be awaiting him rather than to have lost him; and that you may not grieve because you have been deprived of such a protector, but rejoice because you have had such a one.

[Col. 0663B] For the rest, I greet everyone with equal affection; with equal entreaty I ask you all both to pray for me and to temper with equanimity the sadness that has occurred. I am not unaware how much lamentation this evil news has brought you.

## LETTER XVI. THE SAME BRAULIO TO APICELLA

To my lady and daughter in Christ, Apicella, Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s saints.

Although this book had been written for someone else, since we could not disregard your request, we have sent it to you. For I believe that this happened by heavenly providence, so that what had been prepared for another might be given to you. In it you have the holy Tobit, whose loss of sight may console your spirit over the loss of your husband; [Col. 0663C] you also have Judith, who, adorned in widowhood, may teach you that your widowhood is made honorable by virtues, and that the one who was mortified in your body has been represented beforehand in the figure of Holofernes, so that you may obtain the blessing of your people and of your faith, and in future generations be regarded as blessed, to perpetual remembrance and renown.

Farewell in the Lord, and, mindful of me, deign to pray for us.

## LETTER XVII. THE SAME BRAULIO TO WILIGILD, BISHOP

To my lord in Christ, the most blessed, venerable among the members of Christ, and to be embraced with every affection, Wiligild, bishop, Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s saints.

[Col. 0663D] I am not unaware that I have acted against the decrees of the Fathers and the canons, since I know that I ordained your monk, who had come from the asylum of the monastery, first as subdeacon and then as deacon. For although the Church of Christ, spread throughout the whole world, is held to be one in the catholic community, nevertheless it relies upon its rulers and is governed by its bishops; and although divided in its privileges, it is held to be one in the structure of its faith. Therefore I recognize that I have exceeded the proper order. For this reason I have taken care to place this at the very beginning of my letter, so that, by confessing my error, I might receive forgiveness more readily.

For when I reflect upon this very matter—that although the organization of the churches is divided in many respects by its different rulers, nevertheless we unquestionably remember it to be one—I am encouraged by the hope of charity, which compelled me both to presume so much upon you [Col. 0664A] and almost to set aside proper order. For charity, as one of the Fathers says, knows no order; and the Apostle says: “Charity does not seek what is its own.” Thus, when I presumed upon what belonged to you, I did not seek what was mine. I believed that you too would act in this way, if I should learn that you had spared this man; and therefore I granted ordination to this servant of yours, though not without examining and bearing witness to his life.

Therefore I ask you to forgive both me and him, so that, if my position far from your jurisdiction makes me immune from the judgment of your severity, you may at least show your kindness here, when, out of consideration for piety and goodness toward this man present before you, you remit punishment on my behalf. If I obtain this, I ask you to permit him to retain the grades he received from me—or rather, which he received through the hands of my weakness—and to pray continually to Christ the Lord for the unhappiness of my insignificance [Col. 0664B], so that I may feel not only that I have received forgiveness from you, but also that, supported by the aid of your prayer, I am helped by the Lord in this mortal life, with clear signs of his favor.

Offering respectful greeting with religious humility and the most devoted service to your blessedness, I ask that, whenever opportunities arise, I may be worthy to be enlightened by your letters. These same greetings also to the priest and abbot Ayulfus.

## LETTER XVIII. THE SAME BRAULIO TO HIS KINWOMAN POMPONIA, ABBESS

To my lady and daughter in Christ, Pomponia, abbess, Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s saints.

Struck through by one wound and tortured by great pain, [Col. 0664C] when the office of my tongue did not allow me to give expression to the bond of bitterness, and it was easier for me to weep than to speak, behold, another affliction came upon affliction, and crushing upon crushing fell, as when someone flees from the face of a lion and encounters a bear, or when a serpent’s bite is added to one already howling from the blow of a scorpion. So I feel myself everywhere cast down and afflicted by the misery of crushing.

For I confess, my lady, that whenever I wished to write something to you about the passing of your sister, the lady Bassilla, whose memory is holy, I was each time so affected by bitterness that I fell into bewilderment of soul, dullness of sense, and torpor of tongue, because, occupied with mourning, I was mentally present at the funeral. But while, as time passed, I wished to speak with some relief from my pain, struck again by a doubled misfortune [Col. 0664D], I waste away in tears; that is, the departure of my lord Nunnitus, bishop, whose revered memory remains, has proved fatal to me. Thus, overcome, I utter whatever few words and groans I can.

O how much goodness we have lost in these two of our times! What a light of truth! What an example of good action! How much intercession for our sins! Where now is our protection, which they had with God? Where is the refuge of the wretched? Where is the welcoming of strangers? Or where is the refreshment of monks and nuns? You undoubtedly see what I touch upon and what I cannot express. I show only my affection; for I do not even begin to recount their goodness, knowing that, even if I had a wealth of speech, eloquence of tongue, and a memory equal to my intellect [Col. 0665A], I would have considered it impossible for me to revive in words their most holy deeds. But, as I have said, I merely show what I mourn and how much mourning I suffer within me.

Woe, woe to the present life, which ought rather to be wept over than embraced, hated rather than loved. Good things pass away, evil things succeed them, and we ourselves pass on in an unceasing course; yet, by I know not what drunkenness of mind, we suppose that we shall remain. For the times flee imperceptibly, and death approaches, while hope for the present imagines for us the joys of temporal things. Blessed are those whose joy is God, and whose gladness is in the blessedness of what is to come; whose suffering and reproach are with Christ under the banner of his cross, so that they may be stored up in eternal triumph. Therefore let all our affection be directed toward him, let all our service be extended there [Col. 0665B], so that our inner person may be consoled by him who suffered for us, and that he may never and nowhere leave us alone.

Therefore provide consolation for your soul through meditation on the holy Scriptures, and let the other sisters be consoled through you. At the same time, deign to pray that, amid the shipwrecks of the present life and its various dangers, divine omnipotence may direct toward me the supports of its compassion through the protection of your prayers, so that through your intercession I may be worthy, together with you, to enjoy the presence of the Almighty in eternal life.

I greet all who are dedicated with you to the service of Christ the Lord. Greeting you above all with singular affection, I ask that, just as you had perceived the love of her good devotion toward me, so you may bestow upon me your holy love [Col. 0665C]. For you do nothing foreign if you love me, since you know the character of my mind and share my blood.

Here ends.

## LETTER XIX. THE SAME BRAULIO TO HOJO AND EUTROCIA

To my lords and children, Hojo and Eutrocia, Braulio.

I know, I know that he is not an excellent comforter who needs a comforter, nor one who can relieve another’s grief when his own groans overcome him. Yet because this law was given to the world when humanity sinned, and this is God’s decree—that as many as human birth brings into the light, bitter death should destroy—it is necessary that this should come to consolation both for me and for you: namely, that at the funeral of our Hugnanus we are neither the first nor the last to endure this [Col. 0665D].

But, to recall something of higher and better things, Christ, the hope of all believers, calls those who depart from the world “asleep,” not “dead,” saying: “Lazarus, our friend, sleeps.” The holy Apostle also does not want us to grieve over those who sleep. Therefore, if our faith holds that all who believe in Christ, according to the evangelical word, will not die forever, then by faith we know that neither has he died, nor shall we die. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in him will rise. Let the hope of resurrection therefore encourage us, since those whom we lose here we shall see again there. It is enough that we believe rightly in him, obeying his commands—he for whom it is a supreme power to raise the dead more easily than it is for us to rouse those given over to sleep.

[Col. 0666A] Behold, we say these things, and yet, by I know not what emotion, we are drawn back into tears, and the feeling of longing breaks the believing mind. Alas, the pitiable human condition—and without Christ, all that we live is vain! O death, which divides those joined together, and harshly and cruelly separates those united in friendship! Your strength is already broken; your impious yoke has already been crushed by him who threatened you sternly through Hosea: “O death, I shall be your death.” Therefore through the Apostle we taunt you: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” He who conquered you redeemed us, he who handed over his beloved soul into the hands of the wicked in order to make the wicked his beloved.

Long indeed, and very much so, would be the material from the divine Scriptures that ought to be repeated for our common consolation. But let the hope of resurrection and the lifting of our eyes toward the glory of our Redeemer suffice for us; in him we believe that we have already risen through faith, as the Apostle says: “For if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him.” Therefore I ask you, as Christian women, as wise and strong women, to console yourselves and not allow those orphans of yours to perish through lamentation. For to a wise person mourning is sufficient for seven days, corresponding, so to speak, to the present world, which runs its daily course in that number.

Therefore take comfort in the Lord and in the omnipotence of his power, who receives orphans and widows, governs all by his grace, administers justice for the orphan [Col. 0666C] and widow, and justifies the humble and poor, lest you appear to have placed your hope in a human being rather than in the Lord.

For I know that the recollection of the dignity you have lost torments you: one of you has lost a child, the other a husband, and we ourselves a friend. But what can we do, or what should we do, since all flesh is grass, and all the glory of the world is like the flower of grass? If the will of our Creator—or rather, since this is his will—is thus expressed, as the Apostle says: “The sun rose with its scorching heat and dried up the grass, and its flower fell,” then his will ought to be dear to us. To reject it is impious, and not to embrace it is wicked, since without doubt what endures immutable and firm is not what pleases us but what pleases him. For we are not our own [Col. 0666D], but belong to him who redeemed us; our will must always depend upon his will. Therefore in prayer also we say: “Your will be done.”

For this reason, at a funeral we must say with Job: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.” Let us say this with Job here, so that there we may not be found unlike him in the present matter.

Now I shall bring my speech to an end, lest I burden the reader with weariness. For what remains, I ask the Almighty Lord to grant you both the healing of consolation and protection in life, and to show me, through your letters, relief from your sorrow. Send Hermenfredus back to me now, so that, after seeing me, he may return to you.

Here ends.

## LETTER XX. THE SAME BRAULIO TO THE SAME

[Col. 0667A]

To my lords and children, Hojo and Eutrocia, Braulio.

As far as I hear, you have no consolation after the seventh day. You ought already to have laid aside your mourning, because excessive sorrow, however great its piety, is impiety toward the Lord.

You act against the will of the Creator if you mourn beyond measure. For we shall hasten to Hugnanus; he, however, will not return to us. Therefore he must be endured by us as one absent, not as one dead. He must be released, so that we may seem to await him rather than to have lost him. Therefore I beseech you: do not perhaps stir up God’s anger against yourselves. Lay aside your mourning; take up consolation, lest you fall into despair. For it is an unjust thing to bewail with singular obstinacy what happens commonly to everyone.

[Col. 0667B] Conquer, as much as you can—or rather, more than you can—the softness of your souls, and restrain your abundantly flowing tears; for what does not please Christ ought not to please Christians. We too have already placed the memory of his name upon the offering at the Lord’s altar and commended his soul to Christ the Almighty.

As I have learned, you acted in the same way. We commended him to Christ the Lord, the Creator, who created him and received him. He has dealt with his own work as he wished. For who can say to him, “What have you done?” Or who can stand against his judgment? Can the clay say to its potter, “Why have you made me thus?” since it is in his power to shape when he wills and to break when he wills.

The Lord created you rational beings: give an account to yourselves [Col. 0667C], since you can contribute nothing to him by your affliction; and take care lest, while he rightly becomes angry with those who act against the will of God, he should also become angry with you. One thing remains: that you should receive consolation and pour out a daily prayer before the Lord for his rest, for this is what we also do. This alone is permitted; it is not permitted to mourn further. Therefore I beseech you by the Lord to console yourselves, and to take care rather for those who remain than for him whom you cannot help.

May the Almighty Lord grant you this: that you neither offend him nor spend your life in this world without peace.

## LETTER XXI. THE SAME BRAULIO, IN THE NAME OF THE SIXTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO, TO HONORIUS I

[Col. 0667D]

To the most reverend lord, Pope Honorius, worthy of honor for the merits of apostolic glory, all the bishops established throughout Spain.

You discharge excellently, fully, and most appropriately the duty of the chair entrusted to you by God, when, with holy concern for all the Churches, with the light of doctrine shining before you, and stationed as one upon the watchtower, you provide worthy defenses for the Church of Christ; when with the divine sword of the word and the heavenly weapon of zeal you pierce those who mock the Lord’s tunic; and when, after the likeness of Nehemiah, by your zeal and vigilance you cleanse the holy house of God, our mother, from wicked transgressors and accursed deserters.

[Col. 0668A] This intention had already long ago taken root in the minds of our most glorious son, our prince, King Chintila, through the highest inspiration and sacred meditation. But while he hastened to fulfill his vows, your exhortations, by God’s favor, were brought to him. For we had already been gathered together in one college, all the bishops of Spain and of Narbonese Gaul, when, through the deacon Turninus as bearer, your decree was delivered to us; by it we were made both stronger in the faith and more eager to cut away the destruction of the faithless.

Therefore we confess, most excellent of bishops and most blessed lord, that it was not human or mortal counsel that labored here, but that the provident and never-faltering judgment of the Almighty Creator was present everywhere. For when, despite so many intervening lands and such vast stretches of sea [Col. 0668B], the one who gives life to all and rules souls moved the heart of the prince and your heart simultaneously and in conformity toward religion, what else is this to be understood as meaning except that he whose care is for all divinely inspired both sides with what, in the wisdom of his eternity, he foresaw would benefit the catholic Church?

Therefore with indescribable affection we return thanks to the Lord, the King of heaven, and exalt his blessed name beyond every proclamation of praise. For what is greater, or what can be more beneficial to human beings, than to obey divine commands and, through the emulation of discerning knowledge, bring the minds of the despairing back to the way of salvation through vigilant zeal? Nor do we believe that this labor will be fruitless for your crown, by which you strive both to make those already aroused more eager for the faith and to kindle those who burn less fervently with the warmth of the Holy Spirit.

Indeed, we were not so overcome by torpor that, forgetful of our duty, we could be moved by no prompting or prospect of heavenly grace. Rather, the administration of preaching was adapted to the conditions of the times; and what until now has not been settled by us, let your blessedness know was accomplished prudently rather than negligently or through fear, as the Apostle urges, saying: “Correcting those who think differently with gentleness, lest perhaps God grant them repentance for the recognition of the truth, and they recover from the snares of the devil.”

Therefore we wished to act with skillful moderation, so that those whom we saw could scarcely be bent by strict discipline might be moved by Christian kindnesses, and that we might subdue their native hardness by the constant and prolonged encouragement of preaching.

For we do not believe that it causes harm when victory is extended through delay, since nothing is slow where a matter is weighed with greater discernment. And although your holiness has improperly brought up against us, in this particular action, the matters of which you accuse us, and we have no regard for that charge, still, although all the prophets speak with one Spirit, we especially address the testimony not of Ezekiel but of Isaiah: “Mute dogs, unable to bark.” If your blessedness deigns to consider what we have said, this does not apply to us in any way. For, carrying out the guardianship of the Lord’s flock in continual vigilance, by his inspiration, we frighten away wolves with our bite and thieves with our barking [Col. 0669A], while he does not sleep or slumber within us who guards Israel.

For we are his workmanship, created for good works, which he prepared so that we might walk in them. Indeed, at suitable places we have issued disciplinary judgments because of transgressors, and we have not kept silent about the duty of preaching. Lest the summit of your apostolate suppose that we offer this in excuse rather than for the sake of truth, we have considered it necessary to send you both the events of past times and the records of the present.

Therefore, most blessed and honorable lord Pope, in that charity which is for us the chief gift from God, and with the reverence which we owe to the apostolic see, to your holiness, and to your honor, we confidently make known, with a good conscience and unfeigned faith, what we think in this matter.

[Col. 0669B] We believe that false speakers have thought that the ears of your gentleness would readily lie open to a sinister opinion, since false speech often wanders without an author and, through its own fickleness, penetrates unstable minds, so that those who are ignorant of truth and nourished in the bosom of deceit may be cherished; and since no open truth brings them comfort, at least a disguised iniquity may protect them.

But because God destroys the mouth of those who speak wickedness, we do not believe that the serpent’s fabrication has left a trace upon Peter’s rock, which we know to be founded upon the stability of the Lord Jesus Christ. And although you, most holy father, mindful of your office, exhort us with the most sacred admonition to be zealous for divine worship, we nevertheless do not believe that the poison of so deadly a lie has found an open place in the peace of your heart. [Col. 0669C] For we know that it is a sign of the best mind to believe evil things with difficulty.

It has also been reported to us—though this seemed incredible to us and was not believed at all—that the Jews who had been baptized were permitted by the oracles of the venerable Roman prince to return to the superstition of their religion. How false this is, your holiness knows better. For the crafty and everywhere treacherous enemy of the human race, when he perceives that the expense of his labor produces no result, tries to console the hearts of the condemned through a lie about their reputation.

But you, most reverend among men and most holy among the Fathers, press on—press on with the strength by which you are powerful in the Lord, with the preaching in which you excel, and with the industry in which you burn—and as swiftly as possible, through this opportunity, lead the enemies of Christ’s cross and the devil-worshipers of Antichrist into the bosom of Mother Church [Col. 0669D]. Let each side, East and West, warned by your voice and aided by your divine protection, feel that assistance is present among them, and strive to demolish the faithlessness of the wicked. Thus, while you show yourself another Elijah, punish the ill-fated prophets of Baal, and, tormented by greater zeal, complain that you alone remain, may you hear the heavenly voice that many remain who have not bent the knee before Baal.

We suggest these things to your blessedness neither inflated by a spirit of boasting nor of pride, but as worshipers of truth. We considered it right to make the truth known about us, with humility preceding it, so that truth may stand between us when falsehood deceives the faithless.

And although reason would require us to respond to you point by point, still, lest a prolonged speech bring weariness to your ears [Col. 0670A], we have responded briefly but, as we think, sufficiently. For a few words suffice for a wise man.

But this above all, and most earnestly, we ask of the honor of your holiness: when, before the Lord, you direct prayers for the state of the whole Church to the memorials of the blessed Apostles and of all the saints, deign also to pour them out more abundantly in kindly compassion for the humility of our insignificance. Thus, by the smoke of your supplication, arising from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, may the foul sewer of our sins be dissolved, lest in the present or future age we pay penalties worthy of our deeds; for we know no mortal who crosses this great sea without danger.

[Col. 0670B] Therefore, especially and most excellent of bishops, extend to God the help of your intercession both for the serenity of your son, our prince, and for us and the peoples entrusted to us; may it advance your holiness toward eternal glory. For this too is our labor: to ask the Almighty Lord to grant his Church a tranquil and peaceful temporal course within the dignity of a most religious way of life, so that the ship of faith—which is continually tossed among the rocks of temptations, the Charybdis of pleasures, the waves of persecutions, and the barking and fury of the Gentiles—may, through his governance and moderation, be led most peacefully into the harbor of salvation, and so that, once the sea and winds have been rebuked, all things may come to it with a prosperous outcome according to the desire of its happiness.

At the end of this letter we have judged it appropriate to offer something in a special manner, as it were to the head of our administration, so that the excellence of your apostolate may weigh with the gravest balance of examination whether those implicated in any crime ought to be struck by us with so severe a sentence that your blessedness judged these men, stained by the blemish of transgression, worthy of condemnation. For we have never found this either performed anywhere or at any time in the deeds of our predecessors, or inserted in the divine words of the pages of the New Testament.

## LETTER XXII. THE SAME BRAULIO TO EUTROPIUS, BISHOP

To my lord the bishop, Braulio.

[Col. 0670D] Since I cannot offer worthy thanks for the concern of your blessedness, by which you deign to inquire after one unworthy, how much less can I reply adequately? But may he who alone made himself a debtor on behalf of the poor, and who takes care to answer for the impossible, answer my lord for me, and may he himself repay the kindness you show me.

Regarding the feast of Easter, about which you ordered our humility to inquire, let your holiness know that it is correct for Easter to be celebrated this year on the sixth day before the Ides of April, on the twenty-first day of the moon. Thus our ancient predecessors prescribed: Theophilus to the Emperor Theodosius; so also his successor Cyril; so Dionysius; so Proterius to Pope Leo; likewise Paschasinus and the others, whose names it would take too long to mention; [Col. 0671A] and also the distinguished man of our own time, Isidore of Seville. Nor do I believe that, in so great and necessary a matter, they could have gone wrong through neglect of diligence and labor.

In the little calendar [Note: [Col. 0671D] Manuscript: “into the little calendar.” “Laterculus” was a term especially common among ecclesiastical writers, particularly in Braulio’s time, for a tablet on which movable feasts were recorded.], which you, my lord, examined, as your holiness writes, there is perhaps an error in a faulty codex or by a copyist, and therefore it contains the date not as it ought to, but as it happened to be written. For on the Kalends of April this year it is not the Christians’ Easter but that of the Jews that occurs, according to the Old, not the New Testament.

But since it is necessary that theirs come first and ours follow, because the Old Testament existed first and the New afterward, the Lord ate the old Passover with his disciples on Thursday; and after that he consecrated for us the Sabbath, which dawns into the Lord’s Day, by his passion and resurrection. Therefore [Col. 0671B] we cannot celebrate with them at the same time, as the Council of Nicaea also forbids; this is reported in the seventh book of ecclesiastical history.

Therefore Easter must be celebrated by us on the following Sunday, which will be, as I stated, the sixth day before the Ides of April, on the twenty-first day of the moon, while theirs is celebrated on the preceding Sunday, on the Kalends of April, on the fourteenth day of the moon.

Moreover, what in our practice runs its course with the third part omitted [reading uncertain], among them is left unfulfilled, because they do not celebrate Easter unless the fourteenth day has been completed.

But to give a brief answer: our Lord Jesus Christ, who came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it—for Christ is the end of the law—completed [Col. 0671C] the Passover first established by the law with these words: “I shall not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on.” Then, to inaugurate the New, to distinguish it from the Old, and not to confuse the Old and the New into one, he began in this way: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood.” And to separate it from the Old in this manner, he distinguished it by saying: “Do this in remembrance of me.”

Behold, my lord, I have offered this to you as it occurred to me in brief; but I ask that I not be considered either wordy or superfluous. For what I have said is not mine alone; truth is common to all. Therefore, if I have said anything worthy, it is God’s gift; and in this you rightly claim more than I do, since we all share in it. If truth speaks through me, it belongs to you more [Col. 0671D] than to me, because you love truth more than I do. And because every good gift is from above, it belongs more to you, since you belong to him who is above.

But if there is anything in these words that displeases reason, that is mine, not God’s. Thus, when we speak what is true, it belongs to God, not to us; and it belongs more to the one who is more his than his own. When you find in me what belongs to him, you find what is yours, and in me you possess him whose are the things you possess.

For the rest, I offer respectful and loving greetings, and I entrust myself to your prayers, that I may be saved.

## LETTER XXIII. THE SAME BRAULIO TO UNIANIMUS VALENTINUS, BISHOP

[Col. 0672A]

To my lord Unianimus Valentinus, bishop, Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s saints.

The letters of your holiness were brought to us with great pleasure and delight, especially because they were tokens of your affection and indications of your goodwill, providing in turn an opportunity—which we trust is dear to you—for us to return mutual love. But since we believe that nothing happens without the ordering and governance of our Creator, we returned thanks to him—as much as our heart can do, though our tongue cannot speak them. For what better thing can we hold in our mind, speak with our mouth, or set forth with our pen than thanksgiving to him? I think nothing can be said more worthily, [Col. 0672B] heard more briefly, thought of more joyfully, or understood and practiced more profitably.

I read your letter, and, persuaded by your flattering speech, I perceived that I was burdened rather than relieved by the services with which you count me as having obeyed you. For we feel that we possess little or nothing of those things that your benevolence attributes to us. But if anything true has been said there on my behalf, it must be referred to him from whom every perfect gift comes; from him also proceeds your merit, such that no one can answer you except kindly.

And you, my lord, write in this way to show your affection toward us. But I ask you not to be deceived by love, although you appear to place that love not [Col. 0672C] merely in your writing but also in your heart. Therefore, since I do not fail to recognize that I am your debtor, if I repeat your praises I shall not indeed be a liar, but I fear that I shall be superfluous, since I could say truly of you what no one is unaware of. I have also spared your modesty, lest, amid my praises, I make you blush, as your most chaste nature would overcome your consciousness of your merits.

But what am I to do? It is written: “Repay what is owed, and owe nothing to anyone.” Yet in this matter I prefer to remain a debtor rather than a repayer, lest, while you again strive to balance the debt owed to me, you should think that I want to hear such things about myself. Therefore I ask you that, whenever I enjoy your words, I may feel rather the benefits of your prayer than my own benefits, undeservedly [Col. 0672D] enumerated.

Behold, I have replied to what occurred to me at this moment, inflamed by the love of charity. When I answer you with much, though in small words, for your few words, may the very lingering length of my speech be the satisfaction of my longing; for whatever I pour out in writing rather than speak, I seem to converse with you as though I were present before your face.

Since you are another soul of mine—or rather, since your soul and mine are one in Christ—I ask and beseech you to make your prayer to God for me most earnest. Do not think me to possess any merit, lest your intercession [Col. 0673A] for me grow sluggish because you suppose that I have what I lack, and pray less that I may become what you perhaps believe me to be. For if you should penetrate the hidden matters of my conduct, you would find more in me that needs to be wiped away than anything over which you could rejoice by ceasing to pray.

May I be worthy, whenever the occasion offers, to be enlightened by your communications; this I earnestly seek in my petitions, and I offer the duties of the fullest greeting, as though I were present before your eyes.

## LETTER XXIV. THE SAME BRAULIO TO VALENTINUS, BISHOP

To my lord Valentinus, bishop, Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s saints.

Whether you complain that your peace is disturbed by such storms and tempests, know that I suffer from the same most grievous affliction. For what can be safe for those amid whom the ends of the ages have already arrived, so that, with the world, so to speak, tottering and growing old, and shaken by the most acute illnesses, we experience rather the effects of its diseases and collapses than are restored by the tranquility of maturity and gravity? But we must have recourse to God, with whom rests the supreme government and power of all things, so that He may not repay us according to our merits with what is just, but may, in His accustomed mercy, come to the aid of our pressures and necessities. From His clemency we confidently hope, while we are still established in this body, to be granted the opportunity of seeing you, and, having received your blessing, of enjoying your presence, so that one day we may behold with our own eyes what we greatly desire.

And although bodily absence does not divide those whom a like unity in the Lord binds together, because wherever we may be, we are one in Him who is everywhere, since we love Him as one and, in Him, our neighbor; nevertheless, since we consist of body and soul, for the support of this fleeting life it seems somewhat better to see the person whom one longs for than to long for the person whom one sees. Burning with this love, we both desire one another and greet one another.

But while expressing the most abundant thanks for your graciousness, which loves in such a way that it seeks, I ask pardon for my negligence, which does not seek as it ought, since the people of our region are afraid to travel there on account of robbers. [Note: In the manuscript: “a man would go there.”] Indeed, I ask that no return service be rendered to me, but that whenever access is open, a message informing me of your safety be sent.

## LETTER XXV. THE SAME BRAULIO TO AEMILIANUS, PRESBYTER AND ABBOT

To my lord Aemilianus, presbyter and abbot, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God.

Although you are continually shaken on every side by the turmoil of worldly affairs, since by divine providence you have been appointed to the administration of things for the abundant gain of souls, nevertheless I have learned that the anchor of your mind is founded above upon the most solid heavenly rock [Note: the manuscript omits “above”], so that, however the world may rage, the sea swell, and this great sea raise its whirling neck, it cannot be wholly dissolved, nor be swallowed up by Charybdis, nor devoured by the barking dogs of Scylla, nor undone by the melody of the Sirens. Therefore Truth rightly spoke of such a wise man: “Because you built your house upon the rock, the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck against that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon the rock.”

Why do I say this? Clearly because the sweat of your unceasing activity has reached me, as has the labor of your peaceful mind on behalf of all, and because you proceed, in a manner, along a twofold path: you endure the disturbances of the present age for the multiplication of good works, and you obtain the fruits of holy devotion through holy conduct. Thus I do not bring these things forward merely in flattery or with deceitful compliments—for the flatterer is considered pleasant indeed, but an enemy—but to strengthen your spirits [Ms.: vos, “you”] and to offer consolation amid temptations and endurance amid storms, without which this life cannot be lived. I have said these things so that adversity may be endured courageously, prosperity may be guarded against, and we may walk between the two in such a way that the labors of the present life become for us an exercise, not a destruction.

Since you have deigned to be my patron, and I do not doubt that you are a part of my soul, concern for you presses upon me as it does for myself—God knows this. Therefore I commend your present servant to your kindness, so that he may be presented by you to our glorious lord and may be instructed by your care how he ought to proceed.

Nevertheless, I ask that, since I seek the treatise on the Apocalypse by Aprincius, bishop of Beja, and do not find it, you have it sent to me by you for copying. It will easily be possible for you, because of your very great authority and the prominence of the city, even if you do not possess it, to inquire who does possess it, so that it may be presented to us through you. I know that some time ago it was in the possession of Count Laurentius. It will now be for my lords to search for it wherever it may be and to fulfill my request; for it will quickly be copied and sent back.

For the rest, I offer all the services of my service to you with complete devotion [Ms.: offenda], and I greatly desire to be continually enlightened by the most learned style of your speech, sent without interruption. [Manuscript: “Per in rem directum.” The passage is corrupt in the manuscript. It is conjectured that Braulio wrote: “sent continually,” as though asking Aemilianus for an uninterrupted exchange of letters.]

## LETTER XXVI. AEMILIANUS, PRESBYTER AND ABBOT, TO BRAULIO (C)

To my lord Braulio, bishop, Aemilianus, a sinner.

With what service or affection of heart can I thank my lord for the benefit of your kindness and grace, by which you deign both willingly to admonish my lowliness and to instruct me with salutary counsel? Since I cannot express this adequately in words, I ask God, with every prayer and supplication, to be your recompense. I ask your lordship to deign to obtain through your merits and prayers before God that what you specially admonish me of in your words may be accomplished in me, so that I may deserve, through your blessings, to attain what may be pleasing both to our God and to your souls.

As for the book which you ordered to be sent to your blessedness once it had been found through my search, God is my witness that I sought it with every effort I could. When I was unable to find it elsewhere, I mentioned it to your son, our lord, and he ordered that it be sought among his books; but this codex could not be found at all. We were also concerned about Laurentius’s books, but because at that time his property, as you know, was dispersed, we could investigate nothing further.

In reverently rendering the service of my service, I likewise entrust myself to the secret care and protection of your mind, and I humbly ask that, whenever the opportunity presents itself, I may deserve to be informed by your words of your own prosperity.

## LETTER XXVII. BRAULIO TO AEMILIANUS, PRESBYTER AND ABBOT

To my lord Aemilianus, presbyter and abbot, Braulio, a humble servant of the saints of God.

If I had deserved to know of your arrival, the road, the time, and finally the appointed place where I could see your presence, I would not have incurred blame. For, ignorant of all these matters, God knows that I both desire to be brought into your presence and do not know how this could happen. But if both things are possible, I ask that you not despise the sight of our littleness, for the redemption of which the Redeemer of the human race made himself visible by assuming our weakness.

If this is not pleasing, I ask you to pray for me, miserable as I am, and to regard me as though you had seen me received with the utmost attentiveness. For since I am both your guest and your servant in body and soul—this I say without pretense before God—I could have reached you wherever you might be. But spiritual elevation is one thing, whereas I am carnal, sold under the correction of weakness. [Note: I would prefer to read “corruption,” which seems to suggest the corruption that follows.] Therefore our desire is spiritual, while the means of elevation, by contrast, are corruptible. Thus there is concordant discord [Ms.: consors] and discordant concord; and so, with misery prevailing, we do not do what we wish, but do what we do not wish.

But it is already enough, for prudent ears, to have disclosed the result and acknowledged the impossibility.

For the rest, commending myself and what has been entrusted to me, I ask you to be favorable toward us and to deign to protect us not only with your prayers but also under the height of your protection.

## LETTER XXVIII. THE SAME BRAULIO TO ATAULF
