To my lord Ataulf, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God.

As I have heard, your mother-in-law, my lady Mello, has departed this life. I think that, since your soul is Christian, you grieve. But apply your grief in such a way that you can console both your wife and your relative. It is the mark of a prudent man both to endure present evils with strength of spirit and to conceal adversity.

Therefore, dearest lord, it is fitting that you apply to your own people the consolation with which you possess strength, so that you do not show yourself broken by grief—not that you should not grieve at all, since the Apostle rejoiced at the restoration of Epaphroditus; and for the restoration of one over whom he rejoiced, he ought to have grieved had he died. For one who is overcome by his own lamentations is not the best consoler.

Nevertheless, on this uncertain road, guide the little vessel of your spirit in such a way that you offer solace to those who mourn and do not give your enemies an opportunity to boast.

For the rest, I greet you with all humility and reverence, and I ask divine mercy to deign to preserve you in all its grace.

## LETTER XXIX. THE SAME BRAULIO TO GUNDESVINDA AND AGIVARIUS

To the illustrious lords, and most beloved in Christ, Gundesvinda and Agivarius, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God.

He more rightly laments the miseries of human life who expects each day that he will die; and therefore it is not so much that she has passed from the world as that she lived with the world that is grievous.

Moreover, if one lives in such a way as to serve Christ, that is to conquer the world, not to live with the world. We believe that your mother, of holy memory, did this; therefore she should be congratulated, because she has been freed from temptations, even though she left us amid various afflictions.

For the departure of Christians is undoubtedly a cause of joy, concerning which the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be saddened, as the others are who have no hope.” And again: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” If our Redeemer is our hope, in whom we are granted both victory over death and the glory of resurrection, there is no reason for us to lament the fate of those whom we know to have passed well.

Therefore take consolation in the Lord and in the omnipotence of his power, who can both be our refuge and the refreshment of those who depart. Do not mourn that you have lost her, but rejoice that you have sent your mother ahead to eternal life. For there those who precede us await our arrival. Would that, by God’s gift, it might be such a place that not only they but also the angels of peace rejoice.

Why do I prolong this? The river of mortality cannot stand still: it runs and carries us along with it. Thus we must endure what our condition, subject to sin, entails. The Savior too came to this world, and when he called Lazarus and likewise the young girl from sleep, he nevertheless said of himself, as he drank the bitterest turbulence of this torrent: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” He said this for us, not for himself.

But since there is no way to evade the unavoidable torment of this evil, it is necessary to endure patiently what no human being can escape. It has happened neither to us first nor to us last. If it had happened first, we would say that it ought to have begun with someone else; if last, we would seek that it ought to have ended with someone else, so that in some manner it might be removed from us. But since, as we have said, no one’s foot is free from the snare of this trap, let us do what Christians ought to do: endure evil and hope for good; let us be restored by charity, glory in the Lord, take consolation in Christ, and, insofar as he himself helps us, follow his teaching.

He is powerful enough to grant rest to her and help to us, a kingdom to her and guidance to us.

## LETTER XXX. THE SAME BRAULIO TO WISTREMIRUS

To my lord Wistremirus, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God.

Although the one who is overcome by his own lamentations is not the best consoler, I nevertheless wished to take upon myself the whole of our common grief, provided only that I might hear your consolation. For that fatal messenger had already exhausted me when, renewed and restored to life through your letter, you came to me.

Alas, the bitter condition of death, and how vain is everything we live without Christ! Tears escape, dullness of spirit intervenes, the very dictation is trembling [Ms.: dicatio], and the continual shaking caused by grief does not proceed in its proper order. Speech departs: she whom we loved has departed, she in whom you had both the bond of the flesh and every consolation, and in whom we had a cause of honor and an example of affection.

She was your glory and our praise; your adornment and our rejoicing. Who would have believed that she would depart at so young an age, she whom divine providence seemed to have given to your old age to revive you when weary and comfort you amid the anxieties of worldly cares? But what we did not expect has occurred, and what we did not anticipate has come. Woe to mortal life, which fades even as people live each day!

But what can we do, since this is the condition of mortals? Let us take consolation in the Lord, in whom there is the consolation of a far better life. Let us not cease, as true faith teaches, to hope for her, since she has been led to better things and freed from the misery of the present life. For who would wish to live amid such great evils as arise? I do not know whether I could find such a person; if one were found, he would be either foolish or senseless.

Therefore, because our Creator and Redeemer, who foresees the future and holds the present, saw what was fitting for that soul, I think she was taken away because he loved her, lest the wickedness of the world change her understanding; for “sufficient for the day is its own evil.” Therefore we ought to rejoice with her, not mourn—not because we have lost her, but because we had such a woman: you as a wife, and we as a sister.

But because it is the mark of your prudence to live according to an order that does not give your enemies cause for reproach, take consolation and disdain grief with greatness of spirit. To speak more briefly, show within yourself both love for the absent woman and rational consolation. I believe this can more easily be achieved with the passage of time. But begin now; for everything long meditated upon and frequently considered, however terrible, becomes gentle. Therefore apply yourself to this endeavor, most illustrious of men, so that you may console both yourself and your people, and so that you do not forget through her death those whom you loved with her, lest you appear to have lost the affection you had for them through her while she lived.

## LETTER XXXI. THE SAME BRAULIO TO KING CHINDASVINTH

To be brought before our glorious lord King Chindasvinth, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God and of you.

The almighty Lord, in whose likeness the good powers of this world reign, is moved by the prayers of those who supplicate him; he has pity in view of their miseries and again consoles those afflicted by desolation. For he forgave the Ninevites, looked upon the miseries of Zedekiah, and, although Ahab was wicked, was moved by his afflictions and spared him.

I mention this, most sacred prince, so that at last you may look upon me, afflicted, miserable, and asking for a remedy: stripped of consolation, deprived of counsel, oppressed by the frailty of weakness, and whose life, placed in bitterness, longs rather to enter death than to breathe the air of the present life.

I had, in however slight a measure, a consolation in this life, though I was established amid many necessities: the sight of your servant, my archdeacon Eugenius. Although the Church to which we had been unworthily assigned was shaken by various losses and our heart was embittered, nevertheless, returning to the word of God—for “man does not live by bread alone,” which is rightly understood as the support of this life—we were refreshed by every word of God, since it is written: “A brother helping a brother will be exalted”; and: “Iron is sharpened by iron, and a man sharpens the face of his friend.”

But now, by the command of your glory, a part of my soul is taken away, and I do not know what I can do at this age. I am dim-sighted in bodily vision, I waver in strength, I am deprived of knowledge; therefore I send my prayers that you not separate him from me, so that you may not be separated from the kingdom of God, and that your offspring may possess your kingdom.

For, to speak faithfully, I truly do not know how much he could accomplish there. Yet his absence from this city of yours causes much obstruction, because, as I have said, I am now capable of nothing, whereas he was suited to everything: to receiving ambassadors, to carrying out your command, and to providing assistance in every kind of circumstance.

To you, most devout prince, we confess everything. May he who searches out hidden and secret things and weighs our necessities inspire your minds as to how you may order one Church without abandoning another.

## LETTER XXXII. KING CHINDASVINTH TO BRAULIO (C)

The Lord to the holy and venerable Father Braulio, bishop.

We have received the petition of your eloquence, adorned with the most flourishing language and compressed into every verbal harmony, which your holiness took care to send to our clemency. In it, through the diligent labor of your words, we are given to understand that no necessity of understanding has compelled you, nor any lack of wisdom reduced you, to retain among yourselves Eugenius the archdeacon.

What you seek from our glory with poured-out prayers is that, our purpose having been changed, he should rather be released to you. Indeed, your holiness may not unreasonably believe that this has come about because the mind of our serenity ardently strives to summon him to this honor. For almighty God, at whose nod all things serve, inspires wherever he wills until he fulfills his good will, so that a person may approach to offer a sacrifice pleasing to his Creator. For the surpassing mercy of the Lord has foreknown those whom it also desires to predestine to better things.

Therefore, if these matters persist in the will of God, as we trust they do, we ought not to do anything other than what pleases him. Nor, under this request of yours, should we neglect justice: he himself arose from the place where we now desire to appoint him as a consecrated watchman.

Since justice is undoubtedly evident on our side, what has been promised to our devotion will not be withheld, for it will be pleasing to Christ. Your blessedness ought not to receive this with displeasure; for thereby you will be able to obtain a great reward before the Lord, when you release him to God as a watchman to be offered. Your praise before God can also become more exalted if, through your teachings, the holy Catholic Church shines forth.

Therefore, most blessed man, since you cannot believe that I can do anything other than what is pleasing to God, it is necessary that, in accordance with our exhortation, you yield this Eugenius the archdeacon to our Church as its priest.

## LETTER XXXIII. BRAULIO TO KING CHINDASVINTH

To be brought before our glorious lord King Chindasvinth, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God and of you.

Although the bond of fellowship by which I was joined in the Lord to your servant Eugenius the archdeacon was broken rather than cut, nevertheless, as your glory’s command required, we sent him into your presence—not without hope in your piety, by which you are accustomed both to look upon the miserable and to aid the afflicted—namely, so that you may restore him to your patron, Saint Vincent, in the office in which he has hitherto served.

But if the providence of heavenly disposition has turned the heart of your clemency away from our request, what mortal will desires must necessarily yield. And while the ordinance of your glory has been fulfilled, we commend to you, with as much entreaty as we can, his lamentable exile.

## LETTER XXXIV. THE SAME BRAULIO TO NEBRIDIUS

To my lord Nebridius, especially my son in Christ, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the servants of God.

This fugitive and smoky life, persuading and deceiving, and deceiving before it fulfills what it has persuaded us to do, is understood by the wise and prudent to be nothing; you are one of them. Its emptiness is foreseen each day by our eyes and by events themselves as they slip away.

It has reached me that my daughter, your wife, beloved by both of us—alas!—has departed this life. I grieve not so much over her as over the lot of human life, and I sigh uncertain about what may happen to us. [Note: The manuscript reads, “The lot of human life—not, however, in her, than …”]

Meanwhile, let there be consolation for us in the Lord and our Redeemer, who conquered death by his own death. May he, in whose power and at whose command our death and life consist, himself be our defense against the power of the second death. He alone was able to penetrate the underworld, condemn the punishments of death, and return to the heights on the third day. Hoping in him, we do not fail in faith, because his mercy will surround those whose hope remains in him.

You yourself know that your wife held this faith, and we too are undoubtedly not ignorant of it. For this reason she was a Christian, and so are we. Upon the stability of this anchor the Apostle urges us to take consolation when he says: “I do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not be saddened like the others who have no hope.” For among Christians life is not taken away by the Lord, but exchanged for a better one. Hence the dead are called sleepers, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel about Lazarus: “Our friend Lazarus is sleeping.”

This sleep will be the fullness of life for the faithful in the resurrection. Therefore, because we are Christians, we ought to take consolation not in ourselves but in him who raises the dead and gives life.

I believe that this giving of life is already your consolation. But present desolation afflicts the heart amid the commands of virtue and the hope of resurrection. Yet if we were the first to encounter this, or were thought to be the last, we might say: “Why did this not happen before us, or why will it not happen after us?” Let it therefore be a consolation that this occasion of death comes to those who are neither the first nor the last.

Nevertheless, since the whole world passes away in this manner, and this fate is feared for us every day, let us possess our souls in patience, and let there be in us the endurance that ought to exist in a Christian soul. Let grief cease where no remedy comes to our aid, as we pour out our souls before him who is rest for the dead and mercy that brings relief to the living.

But why is it necessary for me to say anything at length to you, when one whom personal grief overcomes in this matter cannot be an impartial consoler? Yet may patience and hope in the Lord console both you and me, so that we may hope for better things and endure what comes upon us. I ask him who holds both the present and the future life in his power to grant her rest and to deign to bestow salvation in himself upon us.

Many things occurred to me to write to your affection.

## LETTER XXXV. OF SAINT EUGENIUS III, PRIMATE OF TOLEDO, TO BRAULIO (C)

To my lord, and truly my own lord, Bishop Braulio, Eugenius, your little servant.

Two matters have arisen in my Church, and because of them my soul is wasting away; unless you provide counsel, our knowledge has no idea what remedy to apply. We have discovered that a certain brother, without having received the rank of presbyter, is performing the office of a presbyter. So that you may recognize the matter more precisely, I shall set everything out individually.

This same brother was extremely troublesome to my lord Eugenius. When he was asked by the king to ordain him a presbyter, and could not resist the command of the prince, he devised the following kind of action. He led him to the altar, did not lay his hand upon him, and, while the clergy were singing on high, poured out a curse instead of a blessing. He later made this known himself to suitable persons who were especially dear to him, binding them by oath to keep silent about it as long as he lived.

What does your prudence command should be done about this? Inform me by your command as quickly as possible, for I do not know whether this man should be regarded as a presbyter, or whether those who have been baptized and marked with chrism by him should rightly be called worshipers of Christ.

Resolve for me this question, concerning which I greatly doubt, just as Christ may loose the bond of your sin, if indeed there is any.

Likewise, in certain places we have observed deacons administering chrism, and I do not know what we ought to do with those who have been chrismated by them. Should the anointing with holy chrism be repeated? Or, if it is not to be repeated, should what was perhaps done under compulsion of presumption or through ignorance be regarded as chrism? I ask what I ought to observe in this matter, so that your piety may make it known to me.

After these two matters comes a third. Certain presbyters, contrary to the law and prohibition of the canons, presume to mark the baptized with chrism that they themselves prepare—if this is indeed to be called chrism. I confess that I do not know what remedy can be provided for those marked in this way, or what correction can be given to the presbyters. But I ask you to enlighten me concerning these matters, since, endowed with the greater light of divine wisdom and devoting yourself daily to meditation on the holy law, you both vigorously pursue the hidden factions of dark hearts, and wisely discover and acutely resolve them.

Although there was once in us a small vein of a tiny bit of learning, with illnesses pressing upon us and the many storms of cares, it has so completely dried up and failed that it does not drip even with the slightest exertion. Therefore, through him by whose gift you are blessed and by whose instruction you are proven learned and taught, I ask you to inform me as quickly as possible, by the sacred command of your mouth, concerning these matters.

## LETTER XXXVI. BRAULIO TO EUGENIUS, PRIMATE OF TOLEDO

To my singular lord Eugenius, primate of the bishops, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God.

If immense kinds of care did not surround me, if the wickedness of the world did not envelop me in its storms, if, finally, the clamor of envious people barking against me were silent; if the solitude in which I have deservedly arrived abandoned did not frighten me, even so I would readily, as you command, give an answer to your questions, unfamiliar and untried though they are to me. For an unknown matter disturbs the mind, and matters not previously foreseen or long considered do not easily admit of an answer.

Nevertheless, I perceive that your prudent sharpness wishes to test in me something that cannot hinder me, and to display the expertise that is lacking in others. I sense your good will, but I do not fail to recognize my own limitations. For what is there in us, or how much, that you raise so high with the proclamation of your learned voice that you force a sluggish and almost aged man, forgetful of himself, to reach lofty things, and introduce one already a veteran—and would that I had not grown old!—into questions in which ignorance is destructive and knowledge presumptuous?

Nevertheless, since the one heavenly Master and Teacher who teaches human beings knowledge says, “Without me you can do nothing, but with me you will be able to do all things”; and again the prophet says, “The Lord will give the word”; and again, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it,”—for the sake of your command, for the sake of my service, for the hope of the divine promise, and because nothing is impossible for one who believes, I shall attempt to speak as I am able and as he sees fit to supply me, he who governs his Church; if I can find any answers, I shall set them before you, my lord, as accords with reason.

It will now be your task, with the discernment in which you excel, the diligence in which you are strong, and the instruction in which you are especially capable, both to approve what is right and correct what is mistaken, to conceal what is unworthy and disclose what is worthy.

Let us therefore now come to the matters themselves. In your letters, you say that two matters have arisen in your Church, because of which your soul is wasting away, and that you have no knowledge at all of what remedy to apply. You write, namely, about a certain brother who, without having received the rank of presbyter, performs the office of a presbyter. To set out the whole matter, you relate that he had been extremely troublesome to your predecessor, who, when asked by the king to ordain him a presbyter, could not resist the command of the prince—to use your own words—and devised this kind of action.

He led him to the altar, did not lay his hand upon him, and, while the clergy were singing on high, poured out a curse instead of a blessing. Your predecessor himself later made this known to suitable persons who were especially dear to him, binding them by oath to keep silent about it as long as he lived.

You command me to seek what should be done about this, since you say that you do not know whether he should be regarded as a presbyter, or whether those who have been marked with chrism by him should rightly be called worshipers of Christ.

After this, you adjure my ignorance to resolve the question. This is your first inquiry. Although, as I have said, many matters hinder me from answering, the upshot is that one shrouded in darkness cannot provide guidance to one who sees.

Since you command me to say what I think, let the person who is said to have been subjected to a curse be investigated. At the time of the cursing, if he was present and performed the office of a presbyter, and yet was not prohibited by the very man who cursed him; if he baptized, if he administered chrism, if he offered the sacrifice, and the other man allowed him to do these things even though he knew that he had cursed him, then the one who seems to me guilty is not this man but rather the other, who acted one way through evil deceit and pretended another.

Accordingly, the man whose action proceeded to such great wickedness will, as it seems to me, bear his own burden. Your holiness, however, will be free from this offense, since you permit each person to remain in the vocation in which you found him. Nor do I see why he should not be regarded as a presbyter, if the man who did not want him to be a presbyter publicly declared him to be one. Nor do I see why those marked with this sacred ointment should not be called worshipers of Christ, since, although he was unworthy to administer chrism, they were nevertheless truly anointed.

Your prudence knows very well that the ancient institutions of the canons prescribe that a presbyter must not dare to administer chrism; we know that both the East and all Italy have observed this until now. Later, however, it was decreed that presbyters might administer chrism, but from chrism blessed by bishops, so that this privilege might not appear to belong to presbyters, since they sanctify the people of God with that holy anointing, but rather to bishops, by whose blessing and permission they perform these offices as though from the hand of a bishop.

If this is so, why should those whom this man chrismated not be regarded as Catholics, since, as I have said, they were anointed with true and holy chrism consecrated by a bishop and with his permission? It is evident that baptism given in the name of the Trinity must not be repeated. We are not prohibited from chrismating heretics whom we find to be strangers to true chrism. But this man administered true chrism, as I have already said; therefore what he did does not seem to me to be invalid.

Added to this is the fact that the man who permitted him never objected and did not hesitate to hand over to him chrism blessed by himself. Therefore, what this man did, the other also did. For what difference does it make whether it was done by pretext or in truth? Since it was done within the Catholic Church, it need not be repeated.

Those who report that, after the death of your predecessor, he told such things will do better to reserve this matter for another life. For once he has departed, who will now be able either to contradict them or to clear him of the accusations? Nevertheless, it is not fitting for you to destroy what he did not destroy, remembering that saying: “Do not judge anything before the time.” And again: “What is open is for you; what is hidden is for God.”

This is what seemed appropriate to my ignorance and to the smallness of my capacity. I have offered it neither with complete affirmation nor with total rejection.

Let us proceed to the other questions, if this does not displease you. You also write that in certain places you have found deacons administering chrism. I find nothing more in this question than in the first, except that the sacred chrism should continue by your authority and episcopal indulgence; and that those who perpetrated these acts, whether through ignorance or presumption, should experience upon themselves both the fitting punishment of discipline and the rule of ecclesiastical order under penalty and penance. They should be punished in such a way that, given as an example to others, they will by no means presume to do such things again.

After these two questions have been briefly set out, your prudence brings a third before my ignorance, writing that certain presbyters presume to mark the baptized with chrism that they themselves prepare—if it is indeed to be called chrism.

I openly and emphatically acknowledge that there is good reason to doubt that this is chrism, since it appears to have been consecrated not only without bishops but by presbyters presuming to act contrary to the law and prohibition of the canons. For if the heavenly Master and Lord left his vicariate to bishops, what has been established by them has been established by the Spirit of Christ, according to the Apostle; and if anyone despises their commands, he despises the commands of Christ.

Therefore it seems to me that those who have been anointed by such men through deceit ought to be marked again with holy and true chrism. The discipline of the presumptuous, however, is placed within your judgment: the error is to be corrected in one way, and the presumptuous offender condemned in another. It now belongs to your wisdom both to deal more gently with the ignorant and to punish the presumptuous severely.

Because of the impediment of my unlearned tongue, I wanted this letter’s course to be brief; but, as you know, while I was trying to make a small jug, my hands fashioned a large vessel.

I now offer my greetings and commend my daily troubles and continual afflictions to be nurtured by your prayers. By Christ I adjure you: whatever you find poured out in this little page uselessly or contrary to reason, do not reveal it to others before informing me of it in your letter. For there was neither time to think about it nor leisure to dictate; what my tongue brought forth I wrote down with another’s hand, and I had no opportunity to revise it.

## LETTER XXXVII. THE SAME BRAULIO TO KING CHINDASVINTH

To be brought before our most glorious lord King Chindasvinth, Braulio and Eutropius, your little servant bishops, together with the presbyters, deacons, and all those entrusted by God to them, and also Celsus, your servant, together with the territories entrusted to him by your clemency.

He who holds the hearts of kings in his hand, as our faith teaches, governs all things as well. Therefore it is not without his inspiration that we desire to make this suggestion to your Clemency. Thus, pious lord, willingly receive the petitions of your servants, which you see straining toward you with the intention of faith. For, reflecting with hope and frequent thoughtful concern—by which each person desires the tranquillity of his life and avoids dangerous circumstances—and conferring together in turn, while remembering the dangers of the past, we have realized how many dangers, how many necessities, and how many attacks by adversaries we have endured. When we see that, by heavenly mercy, you have been aroused and that we have been rescued by your rule; when we consider your labors and provide for our country’s future; wavering between hope and fear, yet with confidence overcoming fear, we have resolved to have recourse to your piety.

Since we can foresee nothing more advantageous either for your peace or for our circumstances, during your lifetime and while you remain in good health we ask for your servant, our lord Recesvintus, as our lord and king. Since he is of an age both to wage war and to endure the sweat of wars, with the assistance of heavenly grace may he be our lord and defender, and the refreshment of your serenity, so that the plots and uproar of enemies may subside and the life of your faithful may remain secure and free from fear. For it cannot be to your glory to reject such a son, or to deny the son of so great a father the advancement due to him.

Therefore, with a humble prayer we ask the King of heaven and ruler of all thrones, who appointed Joshua (Jesus) as Moses’ successor and established Solomon, his son, upon David’s throne, mercifully to disclose to your minds what we suggest and, by the aid of his omnipotence, to bring about what we desire to be done at your hands in his name. For although we have incurred the rashness of petitioning, it is not through the insolence [Note: [Col. 0685D] Manuscript: *non per insolentiam*, “not through insolence.”] of presumption, but through the necessity of the reflection we have already set forth.

## EPISTLE XXXVIII. THE SAME BRAULIO TO KING RECESVINTUS

To our glorious lord Recesvintus, king: Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s servants and your servant.

Although delaying what has been promised is a form of falsehood, I nevertheless wish to explain the reason for my delay. The faulty condition of the Codex which I received for correction armed all its forces against my obscurities; and while I wished to conquer them, the very sight that was failing seemed to turn its hand against me and multiply the darkness to its own detriment.

Yet how great the labor there has been, how great the urgency of the work, how often I have despaired of correcting it, how often I have stopped because of various illnesses, and how often I have returned to the interrupted work, urged by my determination to fulfill your command, will be evident to your Glory from the additions to its verses and the erasures of its letters. For it is so burdened with the scribes’ negligences that scarcely any sentence is found which does not require correction; indeed, it would have been more expedient to write it anew than to correct it after it had been written.

By the command of your serenity, we desire with all our wishes to acknowledge the prosperity of your kingdom, and we ask almighty God to strengthen the happiness of your Clemency.

## EPISTLE XXXIX. KING RECESVINTUS TO BRAULIO (C)

To the holy and venerable father Braulio, bishop.

Our rejoicing Clemency received and opened your most graceful words, depicted in the elements of writing. Through them, the effort of your labor in correcting the Codex long ago presented to you by our Glory becomes known to us, not without sighs. You indicate that, amid the frequent faults of this work which obstruct your efforts, the sharpness of your sight is being blunted [Note: [Col. 0685D] The manuscript lacks *inter*, “amid.”]. We certainly sympathize with your holy, trickling sweat; yet we are partly refreshed when, as you write, we learn that your Holiness has raised the sails of its vigilance and, with favorable winds, is flying by divine grace to uproot or correct the incompetence of the copyists.

The strength of your powers will therefore be granted to your wish by the Lord, together with abundant foresight of your inner lights, when your understanding has steadfastly begun to cut away and remove the rottenness and faults of the scribes. Then our Glory will immediately rejoice more happily, when your fatherhood, as we hope, has fulfilled its promises by its deeds.

For the rest, we are pleased often to learn that your blessedness is safe and sound, as we ourselves remain safe and sound by God’s gift.

## EPISTLE XL. BRAULIO TO KING RECESVINTUS

[Col. 0686A]

To our glorious lord Recesvintus, king: Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s servants and your servant.

While I desire to satisfy the command of your Glory, I have exposed the hidden laziness of my own inadequacy. As you commanded, I have sent the text of this Codex under headings; would that I had done so as effectively as obediently. If it displeases you, the fault lies in the brevity of my understanding; but if it pleases you—which I hope more strongly—it will be the gift of him who disciplined asinine sluggishness through the forms of human speech.

Nevertheless, most serene prince, I beg your piety not to consider my uselessness in this matter. Even if I could not do what I wished, I nevertheless offered my patience as I was able. Thus, wherever what I have gathered may seem less complete to any of your servants [Manuscript: *aliqui*, “someone”], let him not disdain to turn to the places from which these things were published [Manuscript: *aderas*, uncertain reading].

What remains, however [Note: [Col. 0685D] The end of the epistle is lacking.]

## EPISTLE XLI. KING RECESVINTUS TO BRAULIO (C)

Our lord to the holy and venerable father Braulio, bishop.

We received the suggestion of your blessedness, in which you reveal the laziness that was hidden in this book which our serenity had given to your Holiness for correction. It is customary for the wise to judge themselves ignorant, lest through the spur of arrogance they seem to incur elation.

But because the inspiration of divine power inspires each person according to its will, we rightly praise the work you have undertaken. In this Codex you have both offered diligent obedience and, as I wished, wisely gathered its effectiveness while it was in preparation. For these things we offer insufficient thanks to your fatherhood, and, returning the service of greeting for them, we ask that you deign to pray for us.

[Note: [Col. 0685D] This fragment must be assigned to the epistle which Taio sent to Braulio, as we said above, p. 189, both because its subject is the same as that treated in what follows and because Braulio himself praises the opening words of this fragment, writing: “Pious, as you yourself say, is the religion, but uncertain it will waver.” The most learned Dom. Franciscus Cerda, most deserving assistant custodian of the Royal Library, correctly observed that much is missing here from what Taio had asked. He copied these letters from the Leonese Codex with the greatest diligence and communicated them to us; this itself also shows that Braulio’s reply must be regarded as entirely authentic.]

## FRAGMENT OF THE EPISTLE WHICH THE PRESBYTER AND ABBOT TAJUS WROTE TO BRAULIO (C)

[The beginning is lacunose.]

“Indeed, such religion is pious, but I confess that to me it is doubtful.

“Therefore, holiest of men, I bring such a little question to your hearing. If it must be believed with the utmost certainty, as I have stated, that the Lord’s blood remained with certain people after his resurrection, I desire you to enlighten me with the most certain testimonies and truest proofs. Would that I might receive from your generosity a little book on this matter. The Lord Jesus Christ will provide me with a great demonstration, without ambiguity, if my prayer is able to obtain this.

“For the rest, with such humility as I possess, I presume to greet the holiness of my lord, beseeching that I may deserve to be commended to your prayers and that, through your letters, I may as soon as possible be refreshed concerning the matter about which I have made my suggestion.”

## EPISTLE XLII. BRAULIO TO TAJUS, PRESBYTER AND ABBOT

To the venerable and most reverend brother in Christ, Taio, presbyter and abbot: Braulio, an unworthy servant of servants.

I confess that I did not answer your letters immediately because I was constrained by various necessities, but above all by an illness of the eyes and the distress of various infirmities. Now, however, because I have been able somehow to breathe amid my difficulties, I have returned to reread your letters. In them I found that your kindness expects many things from me which I feel entirely unable to fulfill.

For what, or how little, is there in me that you should expect from us an image of such great and distinguished men? Their reading is regarded by you as examined for [lacuna], their meaning has been diligently investigated, and their words, so to speak, have nested in your heart. You possess holy leisure, whereas we are distressed by the waves of the present life, like some inexperienced sailor, or one battered by the bilge, or lying wounded in a sea-going boat.

Yet even if the things you ask had been brought to me, undeservedly, by the keenness of nature, I would not have presumed to offer them. You know that our doctrine holds aloft the standard of humility and that it prefers to rest upon level and firm ground rather than to climb dangerously toward the heights with straining steps.

Therefore, dearest friend, I ask you to complain less about the tepidity or greed of those living around you, since you ought patiently to endure everything. For how does the bad conduct of others harm the good? It is not very praiseworthy to be good among the good, but to be good among the wicked.

Hence it is written of the Church: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.” Those whom we believe to be such may perhaps be content, according to the Apostle, to know Christ, and him crucified; for he himself teaches us: “Not aspiring to high things, but consenting to the humble.” And: “Do not be wise in your own estimation.” For “knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up,” and the rest, which cannot be unknown to you.

By such an understanding Catholic humility is held, and the statement, “Let each person abound in his own understanding,” is undoubtedly fulfilled. Therefore the same Apostle commanded us to please not ourselves but our neighbors. And he writes to the Philippians that in humility we should consider one another superior to ourselves, seeking not each his own interests but those of others.

It is the virtue of the humble not to boast of knowledge, because it is common to all. This is very useful for restraining the boldness of the mind: we should neither regard others as contemptible nor claim for ourselves singular knowledge or holiness, lest we hear from the heavenly oracle: “I have left for myself seven thousand men,” and so forth.

I ask your charity to regard these words as having been spoken because of my love for you. As for the question on which you decided to consult me, know that I believe and expect nothing concerning the resurrection of the dead other than what Saint Augustine has discussed, in his various works that have come into my hands, with prudent intelligence and elegant language. I have not repeated his arguments in order to spare myself the labor, and because through your letter I have learned that you hold them without hesitation.

Since, then, I do not doubt that our blood too must be restored in the resurrection, I do doubt whether all that is removed throughout life will be restored in its entirety according to its quality. Some of it is found to be superfluous—not ours, according to the physicians, but harmful to us. If the beauty which the saints will possess permits this, I believe that it will happen. If that beauty does not permit it, then one must believe here also what you have understood from Saint Augustine’s teaching concerning the superfluous portions of fingernails and hair, which will be restored in the joining of nature to the other parts of the limbs.

It belongs to the omnipotent artistry of our Maker to shape great things and enlarge small things as he wishes. Yet we must not believe that anything indecorous will be restored in the limbs of the saints at the resurrection.

For this reason I think that the Lord mentioned and circumscribed the smallest and outermost parts of our limbs when he spoke of hairs. If hairs do not perish, how much less will the greater limbs perish. Nevertheless, he did not intend to include superfluous humors, from which corruptions arise or defects are generated—things which certainly will not exist in the restored body.

I said “nature” strictly speaking, according to which the human body is understood to be whole and healthy. Thus, since we cannot exist without blood, in which the power of the soul in the body is asserted by divine authority, what must be restored is not the superfluous but the natural—that is, not something foreign but our own.

But why say more? This seems credible to me, and not difficult to affirm: it is clear that each person will receive at the resurrection, except for corruptions and defects, as I have already said, whatever his body could reasonably have possessed in that age when the Lord suffered, when his body was constituted in complete integrity. The Apostle says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.” And elsewhere: “Until we all meet in a perfect man, in the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.”

Yet we must be cautious in this inquiry. The Vessel of Election forbids us to think beyond what we ought to think, but to think with sobriety. Otherwise we may advance so far that we are judged superstitious, like those who inquire about aborted fetuses—things which certainly consist of the bodies of both sexes—and ask what may be thought concerning menstrual blood and impure male fluid, which throughout nearly the whole of life must also naturally be expelled. In such matters they will be superstitiously concerned about what is superfluous.

But why should it not be believed that human blood, when removed, also perishes, since it too is a generative humor and blood, just as the abortive fetus is not restored to either parent at the resurrection?—if indeed one should call the person a parent whose foul fluid or lifeless fetus is poured out.

Nevertheless, those who assert that the Lord’s blood truly exists and is held by certain people, as you say, among relics, do not thereby assert that this blood was not assumed in the resurrection of the Lord’s body, as though it had not been assumed at all. Hence that column in Jerusalem, stained with blood, is reported to have been seen and recorded many centuries later by the distinguished holy presbyter Jerome and by others. We ought rather to regard this as testimony to the divine Passion than to invalidate it as a testimony of piety, since it has already been set down in the writing of our forefathers.

Moreover, people of that time knew that many things occurred which were not recorded. Thus, concerning the linen cloths and the napkin in which the Lord’s body was wrapped, it is read that they were found, but it is not read that they were preserved. For I do not think that the apostles neglected to reserve relics from them for future times, along with other such things.

Nevertheless, on this occasion we must not give the enemies of the Catholic faith an opportunity, lest they wish to corrupt Christ’s chaste virgin either with the poison of falsehood or for the sake of reviling. Or perhaps the blood erased from that same column by the faithful, in honor of relics, was scattered throughout the whole world. I could easily believe this, so that it might have been preserved among the leaders of the Churches, handed down through successive generations; for I do not see how the fame of so great a matter could be doubtful to Christians.

But let me say something further. Perhaps that sweat of the Lord which the Gospel reading reports to have flowed like blood was gathered by the disciples with such care. Or certainly, when the Lord’s body was struck by the lance and blood and water flowed, it may have been preserved as a relic through someone’s solicitude. But I am amazed that this can be approved by anyone, since the disciples’ doubt could later be found even during the Passion, and only John, together with the women, stood beside the Lord’s cross.

Yet when writing his Gospel, he did not relate that either he or anyone else had done anything of this kind. He bore witness and wrote a true testimony: that the Lord’s body had been struck by a lance and that blood and water had flowed. Nevertheless, he does not mention that anyone collected it.

If, in the place where he says, “Jesus did many other signs which are not written in this book,” someone asserts that he was also speaking about this blood, let him prove it if he can. It seems altogether difficult to me to make this a sign. If he does not establish it by the authority of Scripture, then the pious belief, as you yourself say, will waver uncertainly. For the bride of truth receives not only what is pious with truth, but also what is true with piety; and what is pious is firm only when it does not waver in truth. Let whoever can affirm this do so; I confess that I do not know it.

Therefore, leaving these matters aside and entrusting them to the reader’s judgment—for they do not entirely prejudice faith in the resurrection, and we ought not to prescribe the understanding of a better inquiry, nor oppose the authority of the multitude which asserts that such relics are found in cathedral churches, although no such relic has ever been found in my own church during the time of any bishop—it is better to doubt concerning hidden things than to quarrel over uncertainties.

Let us turn to what is true and firm, which cannot at all become a matter of confusion or dispute for any Christian who is rightly Catholic: namely, that for us, through the sacrament, the bread and wine offered to God are the true body and blood of Christ, according to the Lord’s own words and the sacred Scriptures arranged by the Holy Spirit. Every day, upon his altar, the Catholic Church offers this to Christ Jesus according to the order of Melchizedek, in mystical understanding and with the ineffable poverty of human speech, because transcendent grace surpasses everything.

Let this suffice, dearest friend: as the matter occurred to me and as the time required, I have written these few things back to you. Although I have not answered your great ardor as it deserved, I have nevertheless tried, as my occupations allowed, to comply with your wishes. For the rest, I most earnestly ask that the prayers of your blessedness assist me.

There is one matter which was necessary above all others to me and which I had omitted here. I ask that Christ make the course of your purpose glorious, so that you may quickly send me the unexpounded books of Saint Pope Gregory. They were not yet in Spain and have been brought here from Rome through your zeal and labor for copying. I am not the only petitioner for such a thing; my lord and brother, who loves you, is also a petitioner. Therefore you will satisfy both if you provide for one, and you will slight both if you reject one.

Let your charity believe me: I will return these books at the time you determine. I thought this letter would be short, but as scruples whispered to me from every side, I could neither maintain brevity nor say everything that still troubled me.

Farewell in the Lord, dearest brother, and venerable one whom I embrace among the members of Christ.

## EPISTLE XLIII. THE PRESBYTER FRUCTUOSUS TO BRAULIO (C)

To my own lord Braulio, bishop: Fructuosus, insignificant and always yours.

From the narrative of sacred Scripture we have learned how welcome to a person is good news from a distant land. What other or better news can we expect than the love of Christ; the undefiled profession and propagation of the Catholic Church; the sincere life, blessed conduct, and faithful teaching of God’s friends and Christ’s priests? We confess, most blessed father, that we ardently desire these things and long to know them.

This alone is the news which often nourishes the parched inner parts of our mind. Amid the hoarse-sounding straits of the foaming sea, the whirlpools of the Ocean, and the restless waters, the happiness of your deeds sweetens the hearing of our humility. Your ever-majestic teaching ennobles your Zaragoza, and the life of your eminence, flourishing day by day, overflows with devotion to divine law in proportion as it is continually and diligently fortified by the proclamation of good works.

For this we unceasingly offer praises to our King and Creator, the Lord: as the world now approaches its end, you are such a great bishop, endowed both with the merit of life and with the gift of teaching, that in all things you follow the apostolic footsteps. With them you will receive the ineffable glory of the heavenly homeland, whose incorrupt life you yourself pursue amid this worldly storm.

Perhaps rashly undertaking this task, I presume to greet your most pious crown, and I pray that we may be refreshed by the news of your well-being, which we desire, and by the indications contained in your sacred writings. Begging, I ask for the leftover crumbs of your tables; and from a spiritual father overflowing with the treasures of heavenly riches, I request the gift of some small talent. In order to receive it, I, an importunate petitioner, keep vigil through the hours of the night. Though negligent, I nevertheless seek, ask, and knock; supported by the aid of God’s saints, by whose consolations we are strengthened, I ask you, unworthy and most insignificant as I am, to open what I do not know and to grant what I do not possess.

First, therefore, I beg you to explain briefly and clearly on a little page certain things which the father of holiness and sharer in your glory, the most blessed and learned man Jerome, omitted to unravel. Drawing from the reading of the ancient fathers and filled with the teaching of the Holy Spirit, may my lord deign to do this for me, your leprous and novice Eleazar—so may the heavenly Lord open to you the entrance to the kingdom just as the aforementioned man testifies that Methuselah lived fourteen years after the Flood.

And if all flesh that did not enter the ark was destroyed by the cataclysm, where was this man, about whom the question is raised, so that he might escape? We do not read that he entered the ark with the others.

I also wish to know how that other statement which he added is to be explained: that Hagar, fleeing from her mistress, carried the already fully grown young Ishmael upon her shoulders.

He also raised a similar question about Solomon in its proper place, because, when the total sequence of times and years is reckoned, he is found, according to the text of Scripture, to have begotten Rehoboam as a son in the eleventh year, which could scarcely have happened.

I ask that this be disclosed to me and to my fellow captives, not through the trick of facility which some employ, but through the pure and sincere affection of your love and through the impulse of the knowledge of truth.

In particular, my lord, since what follows is not found in this region where we live, I humbly suggest that, as a reward for your labor, you enlighten these monasteries from Cassian’s *Collations*, and through your generosity provide our insignificance with the lives of the holy men Honoratus and Germanus, and of your most blessed new Aemilianus. You who continually fill others with the honey of your eloquence, do not despise us, who are far away and oppressed by the darkness of the western region.

Act, most pious lord, so that your reward for this may shine before the Lord. We already possess the seven *Collations* which the aforementioned Cassian wrote to Jovinianus, Minervius, Leontius, and Theodorus, thanks to Christians who have supplied them here. We do not possess the remaining ten, which he says he published for the bishops Helladius and Leontius, nor the other seven which he says he published for Saint Honoratus and Eucherius. We beseech you, through your generosity, to make us worthy to receive these.

Farewell in the Lord, and remember us, blessed father.

Our fellow poor servants, the insignificant servants of yours, greet your holy crown with the greatest reverence and ask that you not reject the prayer of your outcast, but support the wishes of one who supplicates. May the saints of God remember your graciousness.

## EPISTLE XLIV. BRAULIO TO THE PRESBYTER FRUCTUOSUS

To the most excellent lord and most beloved son among the members of Christ, Fructuosus the presbyter: Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s servants.

Amid the praises of me which you proclaim and the merits of my actions, I ought to preside as a fair judge by the judgment of reason and assess myself by the truth of the evaluation as I feel myself inwardly, not as I hear others, who think differently, judging me outwardly.

For it often happens, from benevolence alone, that a good person brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart; certainly, a sweet fountain cannot produce bitter waters. Yet human judgment often proves mistaken: a bad person is judged good, and a good person bad. Woe to those who call good evil and evil good—whether they are deceived by love, or certainly judge a bad person good because of their own goodness [lacuna].

Rather, those people must beware whose vices please them as virtues, or whose virtues displease them as vices. By the rule of this perversity they judge either a bad person good or a good person bad. But whoever calls a person good whom he thinks just, while not knowing that he is unjust, is deceived not in the doctrine of good and evil things but in the hidden aspects of human conduct.

I nevertheless know that I am not such as you praise me, and you should know that I truthfully profess this.

I say these things properly to you, whom I receive among the members of Christ and in Christ for the grace of Christ. But our conduct must by no means be open to those of whom it is said: “Let the oil of the sinner not anoint my head.” For such people this very flattery of oil will finally fail among the foolish and senseless virgins.

What good is it to reveal one’s conscience to someone from whom one cannot receive remedies for one’s faults? Therefore, we ought to confess our sins to those through whose prayers we receive assistance or to whom we give examples of conversion. “The just man,” he says, “will correct and rebuke me in mercy.” And of such people it is said: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another.”

But since it would be burdensome and lengthy to disclose my shameful habits to you and recount them to you in order, let it suffice me to reveal this to your most sacred soul: I am not as you judge me to be. Rather, I ask you to pray that God may make me such as you judge me to be.

Now if I, who forbid you, myself proceed to praise you, you may perhaps say: “Why do you do what you forbid?” But I necessarily favor my own side while rendering to you what is due, because we are instructed by the Apostle to render to all what is due and to owe nothing to anyone.

For perhaps, so far as I am concerned, I am not deceived; but I refrain from saying how great you seem to me out of regard for your modesty. Would that you had preserved it more by saying less in my praise.

I do indeed praise your soul, but in the Lord, in whom we ought to praise the upright. Hence the Psalmist said: “Praise befits the upright,” and, “In the Lord my soul shall be praised”—the one to whom and from whom every good comes. To him also we give thanks for the progress you are striving toward.

Therefore, the more I know that you speak about me with a faithful heart, the more I seem burdened by what I owe you. So accept what I wish to say.

Blessed are you who, despising the affairs of this world, have preferred holy leisure. I understand, delight in, love, and embrace your ardor, the vigor of your spirit, and the brightness of your light shining through the Holy Spirit. With a thirsting dryness I long that these may prevail before the Lord on behalf of my sins and crimes.

Blessed is that desert and vast solitude, once acquainted only with wild beasts, now filled through you with the dwellings of monks gathered together to sing God’s praises: strangers to the world, citizens of God, captives of Babylon, and those predestined for Jerusalem.

I exalt you and your people in Christ with praise. Their devotion adorns the desert, which the most learned and outstanding men Jerome and Eucherius once made beautiful with marvelous flowers of words and thoughts. To gather much into a little, and as though I wished to paint the world on a small tablet—for I have neither a long period of time nor the industry of genius nor eloquence of tongue—I shall turn an ancient proclamation of a Gentile poet toward you, saying only this: “O sacred glory of Spain.”

Please do not think that I am performing either the vice of an obsequious person or the office of a flatterer. Since the duty of one who proclaims truth is not to conceal what he thinks about you, I must speak. There is only this qualification: may your perseverance be brought through patience all the way to the end. For we are commanded to possess our souls through patience, and “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.” The end of the commandment is charity; according to John, charity is God, and God is Christ, for whose sake all things exist and for whose sake alone we ought to act.

In him the Psalmist saw the end of all consummation; hence certain psalm titles are inscribed “for the end.” When we reach this end, there will be no further destination toward which the course of the faithful should be directed, since he himself says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.”

Let your zeal burn as it has begun, and let it send forth greater flames in the Lord. For if it does not advance, it will fail; and like a boat in the swiftest current of a river, if it does not progress upstream, it will drift downward.

Beware also of the poisonous doctrine of Priscillian, formerly found in that region, by which we find that Dictinus and many others, and even the holy Orosius himself, were infected, although afterward corrected by Saint Augustine. For in his zeal for his perversity he so corrupted the sacred Scriptures that we still find many passages distorted by the blemish of that corrupter.

Nor let the vanity of empty glory or popular applause turn you aside, because this is the final contest among God’s athletes, in which lies the last danger.

Now, lest I extend this discourse beyond the proper length of a letter, I shall turn to the questions you proposed and draw out, as you expected, the opinions of our forefathers from what I have read, as it comes to mind. For the sake of brevity I shall compose some matters in my own words.

This is how you begin your request:

“First, I beg you to explain briefly and clearly on a little page certain things which the father of holiness and sharer in your glory, the most blessed and learned man Jerome, omitted to unravel, drawing from the reading of the ancient fathers.”

Why you said this I do not know, since that most holy man gave me a clear exposition and a sufficiently suitable explanation. In his book *Hebrew Questions* he opened the following solution.

It is a famous question, discussed throughout all the Churches, that according to careful calculation Methuselah is reported to have lived fourteen years after the Flood. For when Methuselah was 167 years old, he begot Lamech; then, when Lamech was 188, he begot Noah. Together, up to the day of Noah’s birth, Methuselah’s years of life amount to 355.

The Flood occurred in Noah’s six-hundredth year. Therefore, when the calculation is made in parts, it is proved that the Flood occurred in Methuselah’s 955th year. Yet since he is said to have lived more than 969 years, there is no doubt that he lived fourteen years after the Flood. How then is it true that only eight persons were saved in the ark?

Thus far is the proposition; from here begins the solution.

It remains, therefore, that in this matter, as in many others, there is an error in the number. For I find it written in the Hebrew and Samaritan books as follows:

“And Methuselah lived 187 years, and begot Lamech; and Methuselah lived, after he begot Lamech, 782 years, and begot sons and daughters; and all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died. And Lamech lived 182 years, and begot Noah.”

Therefore, from the day of Methuselah’s birth to the day of Noah’s birth there are 369 years [Note: [Col. 0693D] The manuscript reads “death,” but this is extremely erroneous, since it is clear that more than 1,300 years elapsed from Methuselah’s birth to Noah’s death. Therefore “birth” must be read. For when Methuselah had lived 187 years, he begot Lamech; and Lamech, aged 182 years, begot Noah. These numbers, collected into one sum, make 369. Therefore, the same number of years must be reckoned from Methuselah’s birth to Noah’s birth.].

Add to these Noah’s six hundred years, because the Flood occurred in the six-hundredth year of his life. Thus it comes about that Methuselah died in the 969th year of his life, in the very year in which the Flood began.

To believe the truth of this more certainly, turn to the translation of that most holy man himself, and you will have no doubt. Saint Augustine too, in the fifteenth book of *The City of God*, while discussing the disagreement in years between the Hebrew Codices and the translation of the Septuagint, affirming that the translation was made from Hebrew, says among other things at the end of his discussion of this matter:

“All the years of Methuselah’s life are reckoned as 969”; and shortly afterward: “When 955 is subtracted from the birth of Methuselah up to the Flood, fourteen remain, during which he is believed to have lived after the Flood. For this reason some think that he was for a time, if not on earth—for it is established that every creature which nature does not permit to live in the waters was destroyed there with his father, who had been translated—somewhere else, and lived there until the Flood had passed. They do not wish to detract from the authority of the Codices, that is, from the translation of the Septuagint, which the Church received as more renowned in authority; and believing that the Jewish [codices], rather than these, do not possess what is true.”

“For they do not admit that it could more likely have been an error of the translators here than that there should be something false in the language from which it was translated into ours through the Greek Scriptures.” And after some further remarks:

“Let each person accept this opinion, or this reception of it, as he thinks fit. It is nevertheless certain that Methuselah did not live after the Flood, but died in that same year.”

Then, after inserting certain discussions and duly deleting them, he says: “It would be more credible to say that, when they first ordered these things to be copied from the library of Ptolemy, something of this kind could have occurred in a single manuscript, but in the one first copied from it, whence it would then spread more widely. There, indeed, a copyist’s error could also have intervened; but in that question concerning Methuselah’s life, it is not absurd to suspect this.” A little later: “Thus that difference in the numbers, which are presented one way in the Greek and Latin manuscripts and another way in the Hebrew ones”; and he adds: “It should be attributed to the error of the copyist who first received for copying the manuscript from the library of the aforesaid king.”

Then, after some further discussion: “However this may be understood—whether one believes that it happened in this way or not, whether, finally, it is so or is not so—I should by no means doubt that it is right, whenever something different is found in the two manuscripts, since both cannot accord with the facts recorded, that language should rather be trusted from which the translation into the other was made by interpreters. For Methuselah has also been found in three Greek manuscripts, one Latin manuscript, and one Syriac manuscript agreeing among themselves, to have died six years before the Flood.” Thus Saint Augustine wrote, at intervals, in the manner we have presented it, as blessed Jerome likewise relates.

Nor are we permitted to think otherwise than these most learned men thought. Moreover, Eucherius, a man of outstanding knowledge and exceptional understanding, abundantly rich in judgments and copiously eloquent, describes this question among his other questions as follows:

“What is the reason that, according to a careful calculation, fourteen years are found (*reperiuntur*; Ms.: *reprehenduntur*, ‘are criticized’) to extend beyond the Flood, when it is reported that only eight persons were in the ark?”

**Answer.** “There is an error in the number, since the Hebrew books read in such a way that this number of fourteen years is completed before the time of the Flood.”

These three seemed sufficient to us for confirming this solution, since it is written: “At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand.” Many have written much on this subject; but in our own times Isidore, a man of incomparable learning and bishop of Seville, while explaining the origin of this name in his book *Etymologies*, admitted the following:

“Methuselah is interpreted, ‘he died.’ The etymology of the name is evident. For some thought that he had been translated with his father and had survived the Flood; therefore the name is expressly translated ‘he died,’ to show that he did not live after the Flood but died in the same catastrophe. For only eight human beings escaped the Flood in the ark.”

As for Ishmael, concerning whom you ask—whether his mother carried the boy upon her shoulders—Saint Jerome, in the aforementioned book of *Questions*, presents the matter as follows:

“And she saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, playing.” The words that follow, “with Isaac his son,” are not found in the Hebrew.

The Hebrews therefore explain this in two ways: either that he made idols in play (*ludo*; Ms.: *luto*, ‘in mud’), in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play”; or that, in opposition to Isaac, he was claiming the birthright for himself in jest (*joco*; Ms.: *loco*, ‘in place’) and play, as though he were older. When Sarah heard this, she could not endure it. This is confirmed by her own words: “Cast out this slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.”

“And he took bread and a skin of water, and gave them to Hagar, placing them upon her shoulder, together with the child, and sent her away.” When Isaac was born, Ishmael was thirteen years old; after Isaac’s weaning, Ishmael played (*ludit*; Ms.: *lit*), and he was expelled from the house with his mother.

Among the Hebrews, however, there is disagreement: some assert that the time of weaning was fixed at the fifth year, while others claim the twelfth year. Let us therefore choose the shorter age. We shall reckon that Ishmael was expelled with his mother after eighteen years, and that it is not fitting that an adolescent should already have sat upon his mother’s shoulders. The Hebrew idiom is therefore correct: every son, in comparison with his parents, is called an infant and a little child.

Nor should we be surprised that the Hebrew language (*Hebraeam*; Ms.: *barbaram*, ‘barbarian’) has its own usages, since even today at Rome all sons are called *infantes* (“infants”). Abraham therefore placed the bread and the skin upon Hagar’s shoulder; after doing this, he gave the boy to his mother—that is, he entrusted and commended him to her hands—and so sent her away from the house.

As for what follows: “And she cast the boy under a fir tree, and, going away, sat opposite him at a distance, as far as an arrow’s shot; for she said, ‘I shall not see the death of my child,’ and she sat opposite him”; and immediately afterward: “And the boy cried and wept, and God heard the voice of the boy from the place where he was, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven,” and the rest—let no one be troubled by this. For in the Hebrew, after the words “I shall not see the death of my child,” it is read that Hagar herself sat opposite the boy, raised her voice, and wept, and that God heard the voice of the child. While the mother was weeping and miserably awaiting her son’s death, God heard the boy, concerning whom He had promised Abraham, saying: “Moreover, I will make the son of your slave woman into a great nation.” Otherwise, the mother too would have been lamenting not her own death but that of her son.

God therefore spared the one for whom she had poured out her tears as well. Finally, what follows says: “Arise, take the boy, and hold his hand.” From this it is clear that the one who is held was not a burden to his mother but her companion. The fact that he is held by his parent’s hand shows the attentive affection involved.

[Col. 0697B] I confess that I have read other ecclesiastical writers on this question as well; but, since my memory is more suited to forgetting, I cannot recall in which work each of them treated it, except for those who wished to allegorize it according to the Apostle. To state the matter briefly: whereas the Hebrews reckon, according to their differing opinions, either five or twelve years at weaning, we find in the books of the Maccabees that three years alone are assigned to weaning. Thus a Maccabean mother exhorts her son, among other things, saying: “My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, nursed you for three years, and brought you to this age.” Therefore, if this authority is accepted, after subtracting two years, sixteen remain.

But when we return to the sequence of divine Scripture, it is not found in the Hebrew text that Ishmael was carried upon his mother’s neck. Why, then, should we undertake labor where we have no difficulty?

It remains for us to inform you concerning Solomon of what we have understood you to know from your writings. Insofar as we were able to understand it when reading your letters, you are not unaware of what the letter of the aforesaid blessed man Jerome, written to the presbyter Vitalis, contains concerning Solomon and King Ahaz, nor of what Jerome himself writes that he heard in his own time under the testimony of an oath. At the end of that letter he also defined a firm and certain judgment concerning the omnipotence of God.

Certainly, I too can think nothing contrary to the authority of so great a man, except to follow in his footsteps and, with Christian humility, not depart from the paths of our predecessors, as David says: “I have not walked among great things, nor among things too wonderful for me.” For a person exalts himself when, departing from the lines laid down by his predecessors, he tries to appear learned in matters beyond his powers. Hence it also follows: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul, as a child weaned from his mother, so may you requite my soul.”

Accordingly, it is beneficial for us to think humbly, as the Apostle says: “Not being wise in high things, but consenting to the humble”; and to receive weaning with Isaac, so that we may partake of stronger food, rather than carry with Ishmael, the son of the slave woman, a skin with water and no wine, and be excluded from the eternal inheritance.

[Col. 0698A] Having thus arranged these matters according to your wishes, I did not find duplicate copies of the manuscripts which you ordered us to send you; indeed, I found none, not even single copies. I noticed that they had been removed from our bookcase, and the press of other business prevented further searching. But, if God wills and life accompanies me, I hope both to find them and to send them to you.

Behold, I have replied in plain and personal language, because we ought to devote ourselves not so much to clinging to words as to attending to meanings, so that our speech may retain evangelical simplicity and avoid the froth of pagan eloquence. The excessive length of the letter now compels me to be silent, but your desire forces me to speak. I wished to receive your embrace with outstretched hands, so that by mutual discussion we might either learn something or teach something—for this is not impossible for the almighty Lord, before whom no word is difficult.

Nevertheless, I daily hope for an end to the sickness of my mortality. Yet I would prefer that, if God grants what I mentioned above, our exercise might concern the allegorization and mystical understanding of questions and the affirmation of the Old Testament in the New, rather than that our inquiry should remain on the surface of history, so that truly “the deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts.” The former precedes in time; the latter in dignity. This is the nourishment of the Christian soul, for the soul feeds on what delights it. I hold your talent in admiration and contemplate with great wonder the infinite resources of your speech.

Courage in virtue, from which such shoots spring forth as produce fruitful grain in abundance! When the study of the divine Scriptures is added to so great a gift, especially in mutual discussion, it will soon send forth branches and bear the sweetest clusters, both yielding the fruits of its own nature and supplying others with the joy of delight. I have observed nothing mediocre in you. Believe the love that speaks the truth: if it were possible, I should desire whatever has been granted to others in part and reserved in part for knowledge to be perfected entirely in you and to reach its highest degree, since this accords with the end of the ages, when Christ’s chosen vessels are being prepared for the struggle against Antichrist.

Do not, I beg you, wish to be considered contemptible because you complain that you have been weighed down by the dark western region. You are all the more radiant because you see yourselves to be in darkness. The Lord said to the Pharisees: “If you were blind, you would not have sin.” And certainly we all know that bodily stains are seen more clearly the nearer we come to the light. The true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world, did not immediately shine upon the world from its setting [Ms.: vanity]. Hence the prophet also says: “The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light; upon those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, light has arisen.”

The province in which you dwell also claims a Greek origin for itself, and Greece is the teacher of letters and intellect. You remember that outstanding and highly learned men arose from it—among others, the presbyter Oresius, Bishop Turibius, Idatius, and Carterius, a bishop of celebrated old age and holy learning. Thus the grace of Christ should be proclaimed all the more abundantly, rather than the region blamed for its sluggishness.

Behold, since love does not know order, I have burdened my letter more with words than with usefulness; and, as someone has said, while I tried to make a jug, my hand fashioned an amphora. Finally, this remains: deign to pray for me with your fellow pilgrims or those poor in spirit, for I am a sinner beyond all other people, so that perhaps the inexhaustible mercy of the Redeemer of humankind may drain away the foulness and gulfs of my wickedness and crime—

Farewell in the Lord, my brother in affection, my lord by merit, my son in age, my colleague in dignity, and my father by kinship. Pray for me—you and yours—and whenever you have the opportunity, take care to send me some of your discourse.

## [On Saint Aemilianus]

[Col. 0699]

## Preliminary Observations on the Life That Follows

1. Besides the martyr Aemilianus, whom the city of Caraca venerates on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, just as Córdoba venerates its own on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, Spain recognizes two saints who are equally popular and nearly contemporary, bearing the same name: Aemilianus, bishop of Vercelli, on the third day before the Ides of September, and another Aemilianus, surnamed Cucullatus (“Milan of the Cowl”). Concerning the latter, Usuard writes in his *Martyrology*: “On the day before the Ides of November, in Tarraconese Spain, in the city of Tirassona, Blessed Aemilianus, presbyter and confessor, whose admirable life Bishop Braulio of Zaragoza described in simple language.” Ado uses the same words for that day.

2. This later Aemilianus, whose acts we present, is called an abbot by most more recent writers. They also suppose that he first introduced the Rule of Saint Benedict into Spain, or at least was among the first to profess it. Both claims are supported by the commonly circulated *Chronicle of Maximus of Zaragoza*; but it is certainly painful to conduct our inquiry on the authority of such a writer, whether fictitious or corrupted as it stands.

It is clear from chapter 2 of the *Life* that Aemilianus first lived as a hermit, and from chapter 5 that he later served as a parish priest; yet nowhere will you find Braulio explicitly calling him an abbot. Nevertheless, chapter 27 sufficiently suggests that he held this office, where Braulio writes that he had a community with the presbyter Asellus, evidently of monks, as the following words prove: “His body was carried with the great attendance of religious men and deposited where it remains, in his own oratory.”

Moreover, that Saint Aemilianus adhered to the Benedictine Rule is affirmed by his ancient epitaph, written long ago in Gothic letters, which we shall report in the notes, as well as by the monastic breviary restored at the command of Pope Paul V. We shall discuss this matter more fully in our preface.

3. Michael Martinez de Villars, in his book on the antiquities of the city of Calatayud, attempts to claim the homeland and body of Aemilianus Cucullatus for the Aragonese. But Usuard and Ado, together with Saint Braulio, claim Aemilianus for the Spaniards of Tarragona; Braulio says that the holy man’s body remained in his own oratory.

The Aragonese do indeed possess relics of a Saint Aemilianus, but of the bishop of Vercelli. John Tamayus, following Philip Ferrarius, noted in the *Hispanic Martyrology* on the third day before the Ides of September that these relics are preserved in Castro Libyco, or Torre de las Peñas.

4. Finally, that Saint Braulio is the author of this *Life* is testified by Saint Ildefonsus in his book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 12, in these words:
