“Braulio, the brother of John, who died at Zaragoza, succeeded to his place; a man who, though joined to him by brotherhood, was not at all inferior in intellect … He wrote the life of a certain monk named Aemilianus, who by his own account both commends and illuminates the memory and virtue of this holy man. He held the priesthood for nearly twenty years; when these were completed, he ended the life of the present age,” evidently around the year 646.

The same author also wrote a hymn concerning Saint Aemilianus, mentioned in his dedicatory letter. Out of reverence for the author, we have considered it wrong to omit that hymn.

[Col. 0699]

# Life of Saint Aemilianus the Confessor, Surnamed Cucullatus, by Saint Braulio, Bishop of Zaragoza

*(Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order, from the Hispanic Martyrology)* (C)

## To the Presbyter Fronimianus

[Col. 0699D] To the man of God, my lord and brother, the presbyter Fronimianus: Braulio, unworthy bishop of Zaragoza, sends greetings.

During the time of my lord and elder brother, the bishop John, of blessed memory, our common instructor in holy life and doctrine [Note: Concerning John, bishop of Zaragoza, Saint Braulio’s brother and predecessor, Saint Ildefonsus speaks honorably in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 6], I had undertaken—obedient both to his commands and to your instructions—to touch upon in writing, as far as the strength and health of my ignorance permitted, the trustworthy life of our unique father and patron, singularly chosen for Christ in our own times, Blessed Aemilianus the presbyter. This account had been gathered under the testimony of the venerable abbot Citonatus [Note: Saint Citonatus, or Zitonatus, succeeded Saint Aemilianus in the governance of his monastery, as Antonius Yepez writes in the lists of the abbots of that monastery, *Benedictine Chronicle*, year 574, chapter 3], the presbyters Sophronius and Gerontius, and Potamia, a religious woman of holy memory.

But because, while I was working at the very beginning to determine what I should say, a full page had been lost through the negligence of those responsible for it, and because I was then occupied with recording his virtues and with the various events and unsettled times that followed, it had almost slipped from my intention that I should devote any attention to the matter, even though you yourself urged me to do so.

Now, however, by divine prompting, as I believe, when I wished to inspect a certain manuscript concerning what had occurred to my mind and had ordered a search to be made, and the pile of books was being turned over, that long-lost record was suddenly found without being sought. For the searchers’ efforts had already ceased, when all hope of finding it anywhere had disappeared.

But because, as the prophet says, “I was found by those who did not seek me,” my heart rejoiced—not indeed with the enthusiasm of a lamp set alight, but with the joy of a drachma that had been found—and my inmost being exulted. Finally, believing that this itself had not occurred without heavenly providence, I strengthened my mind so that I might both receive the fruit of obedience and comply with your frequent request.

2. Therefore I dictated as best I could and, in plain and open language, composed a short little book on the life of that saint, as such a work ought to be written, so that it might be read without delay at the celebration of his Mass. I sent it addressed to you, my lord, and took care to place this very letter of mine at its beginning, entrusting it to your judgment for approval, so that, if anything in it displeased you, you might either correct or reject it once you had recognized it as yours.

If it pleases you, keep it for yourself and grant permission for it to be given to whomever you wish; and return thanks for me to our Creator, to whom all good things belong. I wish, however, that since the most holy presbyter Citonatus and Gerontius are still living in the body, they should first review everything I have written about him. After their examination has tested it, let it be regarded as confirmed, provided that I have not been mistaken either in the names or in the facts.

I have also added at the end of this little book, as I received them from you, those things which I learned had been divinely accomplished there during the past year. I have likewise sent the hymn concerning the feast of that saint which, as you ordered, I composed in iambic senarii meter.

I thought it superfluous to dictate a sermon for the same day, since no exhortation seems greater to me than the narration of his virtues, and since such a sermon would occupy so much time that, if it were added, it might burden the minds of the hearers.

[Col. 0702B] 3. I therefore beg that what I have done may be acceptable both to you, whose commands I obeyed, and to the saint himself, whose virtues inspired the aforesaid men to give this testimony and whose similar deeds you yourselves experience daily, so that you asked me to touch upon them. I, for my part, undertook what you had ordered, moved by the desire to receive my reward.

I also directed my beloved son, the deacon Eugenius, to recite the Mass for the same solemnity, thinking that it would not be foreign to my duty if his tongue—whose mind I keep as a participant in all my counsels and thoughts—should perform this service in honor of this most blessed man. At the same time, I considered that, just as I use him as a partner in other matters, I might also enjoy him as a sharer in the reward of this work.

May the grace of Christ deign to keep Your Blessedness safe and mindful of me.

## Preface

[Col. 0701C] 4. The remarkable miracles of the apostolic and most pure presbyter Aemilianus, performed almost in our own times, are as compelling to narrate because of the novelty of the events as they are frightening because of the immensity of the narrative. What human pen devoted to earthly affairs could worthily bring forth the deeds of a heavenly man who, compared with those of past ages, appears radiant like the greatest star, and who in the present age shines with an incomparable virtue?

Even if the fountains of Cicero were to recount them, overflowing most abundantly through streams of eloquence, and even if a multiplicity of expressions thickened the wealth of his judgments, they could not explain everything that Christ, who alone works wonders, has worked and continues to work through him in the form of spiritual gifts—from his contempt for the world not only to the transcendence of his own body but even beyond the age itself.

When I consider this, fear is added to my mind, since I possess not an abundance but a poverty of knowledge, and not a richness but a sterility of words. Nor am I unaware of my own incompetence. Yet the truth of Christ’s promise drives away my fear—He promises and confirms us with such an address: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it”; and elsewhere: “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize, with great power.” And also: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

This assurance is entirely suited to the present matter, and thus the mind is lifted up once the weapon of fear has been repelled. Behold, what was already afraid ventures to proceed with steady step, taking comfort in your great power, O Christ: for you who enabled an animal to speak in human words can grant a human being the ability to speak in fitting utterances.

To this is added what appears to hold the citadel of my mind, and the anchor of my hope, most securely: I believe that I shall not otherwise obtain the reward of this work and labor, by which I might wash away my utterly defiled and polluted life as though with some kind of lye. In accordance with this, one of the ancient poets most elegantly says:

> “This work—yes, this perhaps will rescue me from the fire.”

5. One matter remains, and it is the last: since I preferred to commit these things to cheap sheets rather than conceal them in prolonged silence, lest the distant silence of those who came before deprive posterity of confidence in the truth. But I also wish to respond briefly to those who strive to display their eloquence. Let them know that the mockery of detractors is considered worthless when ecclesiastical law does not impose upon humble and simple Christians an empty verbosity to be followed, nor the frivolity of human restlessness, nor finally the windy display of ostentation, but rather the sober, modest, measured gravity of truth.

It is better for true things to be narrated with less learning than for false things to be narrated eloquently. This is very easily understood from the Gospels of the Savior, which are preached to the people in simple language. I therefore do not disparage the eloquence of prudent men on account of my own incompetence; rather, I strongly reject the fleeting frivolity of malicious critics.

Nor do I think that honest, prudent, mature men—by no means ignorant that offerings should be made in the house of the Lord by everyone according to his strength, even to the hairs of goats—could be angry with me because I undertook this work. If they themselves wished to speak here, as I said above, not only would they not lack material, but they would certainly be unable to explain everything.

For this reason, although I have touched to some extent upon the study of secular disciplines, I have entirely chosen not to employ them here, lest I make understanding difficult for the less learned and disturb the Israelite camp with the language of Jericho.

6. Since I am therefore about to speak of the matters I have undertaken to discuss, I wish to warn the reader and hearer not to offer an ear hungry for words but one filled with religious devotion. If that is not what he seeks, let him depart now, lest he spend his time uselessly. But if he desires to know what follows, let him approach with devotion in order to receive it.

Let him first know that some of the deeds related here are matters which we, or anyone else, ought to imitate; while others were bestowed upon that most approved man in such a singular way that no one can attempt to imitate them without harm to himself. Nevertheless, they ought to affect us with admiration and keep us intent upon praising God.

For general rules belong to the general class of people, while special gifts ought to be possessed only by those to whom almighty God has commanded that they be granted. The jurists also hold this principle concerning benefits bestowed by decree of their rulers.

7. I shall not go back any further, nor, following the rhetoricians, pursue the praises of his grandfathers and great-grandfathers. According to those same rhetoricians, if he was born of an obscure family, he is to be praised all the more because he adorned the obscurity of his lineage with the dignity of his character.

Therefore, with Christ favoring us and the prayer of this blessed man assisting our efforts, let us begin our account with his conversion, describing what he was like from his twentieth year.

The venerable priests of the Churches of Christ, Citonatus, a man of holy and most pure life, and the presbyters Sophronius and Gerontius, in whom the Church has no small confidence, faithfully related to us what they themselves had seen. To these most trustworthy witnesses is added the testimony of Potamia, a religious woman of blessed memory, whose noble birth was made nobler by the course of a nobler life.

I have chosen these four as witnesses to the miracles performed in the body, apart from the testimonies concerning these matters given by the peoples and provinces—testimonies to which nearly all Spain bears witness. We have necessarily omitted those deeds which, because they have become almost daily through frequent repetition, cannot be fully encompassed, as stated above; and if anyone desires to know them, he would do better simply to believe what he has seen.

# The Life Begins

[Col. 0703]

## I. The Beginning of the Holy Man’s Conversion

[Col. 0703C] 8. Therefore, as I had begun to say, the witnesses mentioned above related that this was how he was converted and how he lived thereafter.

The future shepherd of human beings was then a shepherd of sheep, and he drove the sheep into the inner regions of the mountains. As is customary among shepherds, he carried a lyre with him, lest lethargy impede his mind while it was idle and less occupied with exercise in guarding the flock.

When he reached the place appointed by heaven, sleep divinely fell upon him. For that Craftsman of hearts and worlds, in his accustomed manner, applies the work of his art: he transforms the material of the lyre into an instrument of letters, and the shepherd’s mind into the compunction of heavenly contemplation.

Awakened, he meditated upon the heavenly life; and, leaving the countryside, he made his way to the regions of the desert.

## II. He Goes to a Certain Monk in the Fortress of Bilibium

[Col. 0703D] 9. He had learned by reputation that there was a certain hermit named Felix, a most holy man, to whom he might appropriately offer himself as a disciple. Felix was then living in the fortress of Bilibium [Note: Michael Martinez de Villars interprets Bilibium here as Bilbilis, once a famous town of Aragon. But one should read Bilibium, a fortress near the city of Nájera, belonging to Tarraconese Spain, as does the body of Saint Aemilianus, which we stated above is preserved in the monastery of Saint Aemilianus Cucullatus. This monastery, most famous throughout Spain and founded by Saint Aemilianus, occupies the Rioja, part of old Cantabria, about three leagues from Nájera and six from Logroño. It is bounded by an extension of the Jubera Mountains, to which the lofty ridges of Saint Lawrence adhere. The part of the rocks that confronts those traveling toward Valvanera bears the name of the Distercian Mountains. See Yepez, *Benedictine Chronicle*, year 574, chapter 2].

He set out and reached him. Once he had submitted himself as ready for his service, Felix instructed him how he might direct his steps toward the heavenly kingdom. By this act, I believe, he teaches us that no one can rightly strive toward the blessed life without the instruction of teachers.

Neither did this man do so, nor did Christ instruct Paul, nor did divine power permit Samuel to do so, when it commanded this man to return to the hermit, Paul to Ananias, and Samuel to Eli—although it had already encouraged all of them by signs and by its own address.

## III. He Comes to the Place Where His Oratory Is Situated

10. After being thoroughly instructed by Felix in the ways of life and richly endowed with the treasures and wealth of discipline and salvation, he returned to his own region, abundant in teaching. Thus he came to a place not far from the village of Vergegio [Note: A smaller funerary inscription, reported by Yepez under the year 569, reads as follows: “Aemilianus was born to devout parents in the town of Vergegio. When he reached his twentieth year, he left his father’s sheep, and, with the Holy Spirit inspiring and guiding him, went to the fortress of Bilibium, fifteen miles from the aforementioned town and twelve from Tritium, in order to place himself under the instruction of Felix the confessor.” This distance clearly suits Verceo, a quarter of a league from Saint Aemilianus and lying at the foot of Mount Distercium; nor can these facts in any way be transferred, as Michael Martinez attempts, to the city of Calatayud, which lies more than fifty miles from these places], where his glorious little body is now kept.

After remaining there for only a short time, he saw that the crowd of people flocking to him was becoming an impediment.

## IV. From There He Seeks the Wilderness and Remains There for Forty Years

[Col. 0705A] 11. He sought higher places, and his eager spirit moved lightly along difficult paths, so that, advancing not only in heart but also in body through the valley of weeping from virtue to virtue, he seemed in a certain way to be climbing Jacob’s ladder.

When he reached the more remote recesses of Mount Distercium, approaching its summit as far as the nature of the sky and forest permitted, and becoming a guest of the hills, deprived of human companionship, he relied only upon the consolations of angels. There he lived through forty cycles of years.

What invisible and visible struggles he experienced there, what temptations by varied and crafty means, what deceptions of the most ancient deceiver—only those know best who strive to experience such things in themselves. There he directed every affection, every desire, every impulse, and finally his entire course toward the goal of the holy devotion he had once undertaken irrevocably.

O immense gift! O singular man! O most excellent soul! He was so devoted to divine contemplation that this world seemed to claim nothing for itself in him. How often, as I suppose, inspired by divine ardor amid the densest and loftiest forests, the high peaks of the hills, and the headlands reaching toward heaven, he cried out in a loud voice to Christ: “Alas for me, that my sojourning is prolonged!” (Psalm 119:5).

How often, groaning with sighs, he cried: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). How often, in the greatest anguish and with his inmost being stirred, he lamented, saying: “As long as I am in this body, I am absent from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6).

Meanwhile, he was shaken by the cold, deprived by solitude, drenched by harsh rain, and tormented by the force of the winds. Yet through love of God, contemplation of Christ, and the grace of the Holy Spirit, he received the violence of the cold, the squalor of solitude, the onset of rain, and the harshness of the wind not merely with endurance but willingly and eagerly.

But since a city set upon a mountain could not remain hidden for long, the fame of his holiness spread so far that it came to the knowledge of almost everyone.

## V. Bishop Didymus Assigns Him a Church

12. When this too had been reported to Didymus, who at that time held the episcopal office in Tirassona [Note: The place where Saint Aemilianus’s monastery was founded, formerly subject to the diocese of Turiassona, or Tarazona, now belongs to Calahorra, Catgnora], he pursued the man, wishing to incorporate him into the ecclesiastical order, since he was in Didymus’s diocese.

At first this seemed harsh and burdensome to Aemilianus. He shrank from it, resisted it, and seemed to be dragged down from heaven into the world, transferred from the rest he had almost attained to laborious duties and from the contemplative life to the active.

At last he was compelled to obey unwillingly; consequently, he served as a presbyter in the church of Vergegio. Then, having abandoned the pursuits to which men of this order—at least the men of our own time—are usually devoted, he bestowed holy care upon the church. In this life, to which he had been recalled, he nevertheless persisted in uninterrupted prayer, weekly fasting, perpetual vigil, true discretion, certain hope, great frugality, gentle justice, solid patience, and, to put it briefly, the greatest and tireless restraint from every evil thing.

He had also plucked flowers of wisdom from the meadows of ineffable Divinity so abundantly that he who had scarcely committed the eighth psalm to memory far surpassed, by incomparable and distant superiority, the ancient philosophers of the world in knowledge, prudence, and insight.

And not without reason, certainly, since what secular diligence had granted to them, heavenly grace had divinely granted to him. In vocation, education, and miracles, he was, as I infer, entirely like the heavenly Anthony and Martin.

But, to pass over much, among his other ecclesiastical concerns, this was his greatest diligence: that he might vigorously and carefully, as soon as possible, drive mammon from the temple of the Lord. Therefore he bestowed Christ’s resources upon Christ’s needy members, making the Church of Christ rich not in wealth but in virtues, not in revenues but in religion, and in Christians rather than possessions. He knew that he could be held accountable to Christ not for the loss of temporal goods but for the sake of human beings.

## VI. The Clerics Accuse the Holy Man before the Bishop
Source/review notes: The source’s true opening and closing fragments and all textual apparatus are retained.

13. For this reason, as is customary with the worst sort of clerics, certain members of his clergy stood before the aforesaid bishop, plainly to provoke him on account of the loss of church property. Quarreling, they declared that the Church was suffering losses and that the goods entrusted to it had been diminished on every side. The bishop already mentioned was inflamed by the torches of anger and pierced by envy because of the man’s virtues. Looking upon the man of God, he assailed him vehemently; and when, as happens with a mind drunk on fury, he had belched forth the surfeit of his wrath, the eminent man of God, fortified by holiness and protected by patience, remained unmoved in his accustomed tranquility.

Then, released from the ministry he had undertaken earlier, he spent the rest of his life harmlessly in what was thereafter called his oratory. Thus far concerning his conversion and manner of life. And although those spiritual gifts that remained hidden—the gifts which the Lord appoints for battle and which we find established by Paul, the teacher of the nations, in faith and truth—were more excellent than those that displayed themselves openly through various gifts of virtue, these latter deeds themselves are more numerous than could be written down. Nevertheless, let us go on to describe, in a humble style, by what signs he thereafter shone gloriously.

## VII. He wrestles with a demon

[Col. 0706D]

14. One day it happened that the enemy of the human race encountered the athlete of the eternal King on the road and addressed him in these words: “If you wish, let us engage in combat and test by our strength what each of us can do.” He had not yet finished speaking when he approached him with visible bodily contact and tormented him, wrestling with him for a long time. But as soon as the holy man earnestly implored Jesus in prayer, divine assistance strengthened his faltering step, and immediately turned the fleeing and retreating spirit, dissolved, into the air. If this perhaps seems incredible to anyone—that an invisible spirit could indeed be touched—let him understand, without prejudice to the mystical meaning, how the divine Scripture tells us that Jacob wrestled with an angel, although a good one. I would nevertheless say this: Satan attempted the servant with less boldness than the Lord, Aemilian than Christ, a human being than God, a creature than the Creator.

## VIII. He cures a monk

15. But, as I had begun to relate, a certain monk named Armentarius, afflicted with constipation and a swelling of the belly, came devoutly to him for a remedy. When the saint laid his hand upon the swelling and traced the sign of the cross, the illness immediately withdrew from him; and, restored to health, he blessed the Lord.

## IX. A paralytic woman is healed

16. A certain woman named Barbara, brought from the borders of Amaya, was afflicted and severely tormented by a contracted paralytic illness. By the prayer of the saint she was restored to the health she had long since lost.

## X. A lame woman walks

17. Another woman from the same territory was brought and carried in a cart. Since she had long been lame and unable to use her feet, during the days of Lent she begged him to cure her. Out of reverence, he refused to visit her during those days—for it was his custom at that time to be content with his cell alone and not to see anyone except one of his own people, who, for the support of this life, supplied him with only the smallest amount of cheap food. And so, as I have said, although he disdained to see her, she earnestly persisted in asking that she at least be permitted to kiss his staff.

When the man of God heard this graciously, he immediately sent it to her. As soon as she saw the staff extended toward her, she kissed it; her soles became firm and steady, and she stood unharmed. Rejoicing in the divine gift, she immediately went about joyfully.

## XI. He gives sight to a senator’s maidservant

18. A maidservant of the senator Sicorius, deprived of sight for a long period, asked him to restore the use of her eyes. Then the man of God, by word and touch, with Christ as his guide, obtained her healing. She immediately obeyed the command, and, recovering her sight, surveyed the forms of things in the clearest light.

## XII. He cures a possessed deacon

[Col. 0707D]

19. A certain man chosen for the ministry of the diaconate, violently possessed by a most insolent demon, was brought before him by others who had bound him tightly, to be cleansed by the saint. While the possessed man, driven by madness in the manner of one deranged, raged about, the most blessed man commanded the unclean spirit to depart from him. There was no delay: the disobedient spirit learned to obey, and, afflicted by invisible punishments, was made a stranger to the dwelling it had occupied. After the spirit left the man, the man loudly proclaimed God’s praises.

## XIII. Another servant

20. A servant of a certain Tuentius, named Sibila, had been seized by unclean spirits and was dragged by his people to the blessed man. When the saint saw him, he asked how many spirits possessed him. They indicated that there were five; each one disclosed itself by its own name. When he commanded them by the power of Jesus Christ, they all immediately departed with great terror and noise, and the healed man returned safely to his own people.

## XIV. Another servant of a count

21. He also restored to health and safety a servant of Count Eugenius who had been infected and afflicted by a demon. The demon had already held him in its power through a prolonged invasion, but the incomparable power of divine omnipotence gave him back whole and unharmed.

## XV. Two married people likewise

22. What shall I say about the senators Nepotianus and Proseria? They were so closely joined in marriage that they were likewise joined in demonic possession: their bodies, joined as the bond between husband and wife, were each believed to be inhabited by a single spirit. The perverse spirit, having carried out a twofold possession, seemed to claim a right over them. How manifest this was may be understood from the fact that the story was so widely published that, unless it should fade from people’s minds as the generations passed, it would seem superfluous to insert it here, since there is no Cantabrian who could not have seen or heard of it.

But when they were brought to our Aemilian, he commanded the unclean enemy to leave the bodies of the aforementioned people. Unable in any way to endure his command, the demon carried out the order. Both, set free, resounded with praise of the King of heaven.

## XVI. Another woman likewise

23. A demon had attacked Columba, the daughter of the curial Maximus, by a dreadful assault and had caused the uncontrolled movement of her limbs. She was brought before the servant of God with great expectation of healing. When he impressed the sign of the cross upon the threshold of her forehead, the demon was immediately driven away and expelled, and she obtained the remedy of health.

## XVII. He drives a demon from a senator’s house

24. The house of the senator Honorius was afflicted by a most criminal and seditious demon. It haunted that household so monstrously that every day it inflicted the foulest and most shameful outrages, and no one could endure the demon’s activity. Indeed, whenever the master of the house reclined at a banquet, the unclean spirit often brought animal bones and, for the most part, dung and placed them among his dishes. Frequently at night, when it had given the people to sleep, it would steal the clothing of men and women and hang it from the roofs as though it were some sort of covering for filth.

Honorius, nevertheless, anxious and not knowing what to do, kept his mind under control amid his anguish, confident in the virtues of this man and encouraged by hope. He sent to summon him and dispatched vehicles for his assistance. The messengers came and pleaded with him to approach and drive out the demon by whatever means he could.

At last, worn down by their pleas, he set out on foot, not by vehicle, to display the power of our God. When he came to Parpalines [Al.: Pampilona]—for that was where the matter took place—he found everything as it had been reported to him in order. He himself also suffered certain seditious disturbances there. He proclaimed a fast and gathered to himself the company of priests living in that place.

On the third day, after completing the prescribed fast, he exorcised salt and mixed it with water according to ecclesiastical custom, and began to sprinkle the house itself. Then the envious spirit burst forth from the inner part of the house. Seeing that it was being expelled and driven from its own dwelling, it hurled stones at him; but he remained safe, protected by an unconquerable shield. Finally, put to flight and vomiting flames with a most dreadful stench, it withdrew into the wilderness. Thus the inhabitants of that house rejoiced that they had been saved through the saint’s prayer.

## XVIII. Divine protection guards him

25. Why say more? Such was the abundance of holiness in that man, such the protection of divine power, and such the authority of heavenly command, that when a crowd of possessed persons gathered, he was not merely shown to be fearful at the slightest sign; rather, he would shut himself in alone with all of them, where by divine grace he was going to cure them.

Often, too, when he had laid his limbs upon his little bed, they were eager to burn him with fire. They would carry a burning bundle of straw as far as his bed, but when they brought it up to the bed, the force of its heat failed. Repeatedly attempting the same thing, they spent the night laboring in vain. Thus, whenever he perceived this, at his command the madmen bound one another with chains, and their hands became an aid to healing, although their hearts were full of madness.

For I must not conceal what I now see lying openly before the world.

## XIX. A piece of wood grows through his prayer

26. I speak of a piece of wood, fashioned by craftsmen, which he had carried for the construction of a granary. Once measured against the other pieces of wood fitted to that work, it proved to be shorter. When he perceived this, he ordered the craftsmen to take their meals with calmer minds, while he withdrew to implore the Creator’s regard.

When he had completed the synaxis at the sixth hour in his customary and particular manner, he understood that what he had wished had been obtained. Returning to the laborers, he said: “Do not suppose that you have been cheated of the payment for your work; place the wood in its proper position.” When they lifted it and set it down as he had ordered, they found it longer than the others and grown by more than a palm.

At that spot he made a sign which remains clearly visible to this day. Thus, through his prayer, those hired for the work neither exhaust their labor in vain nor lose the payment for their work. The piece of wood itself has continued to be a remedy for the sick who approach it devoutly, and it is celebrated for such great virtues that it has almost acquired a daily use in providing health to the infirm. It would take an immense amount of speech if I wished to recount all the signs of healing that are visibly bestowed through it.

But now I think it worthwhile to touch briefly upon his generosity and chastity.

## XX. He gives the poor the sleeves of his tunic

27. At one time, when crowds of needy people had gathered to him and were asking for their customary alms of assistance, he either because what ought to have been distributed was lacking or because it was not at hand, did not fail in his innate compassion. He cut off the sleeves of his tunic and kindly offered them, together with the cloak he was wearing.

Then one of them, more importunate than the rest—as is the custom of beggars—getting ahead of the others, took them and put them on. O another Martin, who clothed Christ in a poor man! And rightly they received the same reward, since they possessed one spirit of generosity.

Yet, so that this man’s importunity should not go unpunished, the other beggars, seeing it and indignant at his presumption, rose armed with their staffs, rushed upon him in a crowd, and, as anger drove each of them, seized him indiscriminately, so that he plainly deserved the punishment of his own heedlessness.

28. I shall mention another incident, which I would prefer the grasping to hear, so that they might cease thinking about tomorrow. It happened that a great crowd of people gathered when the blessed man had very little wine. But because those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing, the enormous multitude was, as they say, abundantly satisfied with scarcely a sextarius. They admit that an even greater thing happened on another occasion.

## XXII. He supplies food for those who come to him

29. As the fame of his holiness spread, crowds of visitors came to him every day. By their right as guests, he compelled them to remain in the town and, out of charity, to refresh themselves. When his servant had learned this from clear evidence, he reported that nothing remained for them to eat at midday.

The saint rebuked his servant with mild displeasure, called him a man of little faith, and implored Christ to provide what was necessary for food. He had not yet finished speaking when suddenly wagons abundantly loaded, sent by the senator Honorius, entered through the door.

The beloved of God received what had been sent and, having been heard, gave thanks to the Creator of all things. He set sufficient food before the guests and ordered the remainder to be preserved for those who would arrive later.

Thus he lived between the duties of hospitality and his own self-restraint, so that, whenever food was placed on the table, there was never even for an hour less than enough for the guests’ meal. Yet he was so tightly bound by frugality that he was never seen except sober in mind and exhausted in body.

He refreshed the bodies of those who came with food and their souls with his word. He was so elegant in comparisons and so subtle in urging the spiritual life that whoever came to him for any reason departed improved and delighted, since neither his life nor his speech was ever without instruction.

And, not to prolong the account, he so gained the palm of victory by subduing the flesh that his Aquilo, never conquered, did not kindle the pot, nor did he provide fuel for the fires of Nebuchadnezzar.

## XXIII. A demon reproaches him for living with women

[Col. 0710D]

30. The spirits who had deserted God also wished, through possessed persons, to provoke him with insults by the cunning of their malice. Since they had nothing that they could bring against the servant of Christ, they attempted only to reproach him for living with Christ’s virgins. The enemy was employing his ancient art: when he cannot overthrow a person by deeds, he at least strives to pollute him by reputation; and when he cannot prevail against a person’s conscience, he defames his life.

By entangling people in his own allurements, he offered examples of consolation, since they think that no one is good; they despair of finding anyone whom they ought to imitate in good works; and therefore they consider it a remedy for themselves if no innocent person is found, consoling their own condemnation by the multitude of those who perish.

What can the infamy of Christ’s servants profit you, inventor of evil, when their Lord and Redeemer promises them the kingdoms of heaven through glory and dishonor, through infamy and good reputation?

This holy man, devoted to abstinence and kindness even in old age, did indeed live with sacred virgins. From the eightieth year of his life onward, when he was constrained by holy labor and suffering, he accepted all their services with gentleness, as a father could, through the ministry of the servants of God.

But, as I have already indicated, he was so removed from wicked incitements that at that age he experienced not even the trace of an unchaste impulse. Since he had reached such an advanced age, he arrived at the necessity that, when he was suffering from dropsy, he allowed those same holy women to wash his body, while he himself remained entirely alien to every illicit thought.

This certainly is that special gift which we find granted to only a few, and which no one ought to attempt, lest rashness bring danger. Let each person remain before God in the vocation in which he was called. For David says: “I have not walked among great things, nor among marvelous things beyond me” (Psalm 130). He walks among things beyond him who attempts to do what has not been divinely granted to him.

## XXIV. A horse stolen by thieves is restored

31. But I shall relate something that should make even robbers afraid and make thieves cautious. Two men named Sempronius and Thuribius, instigated by the devil and prompted to robbery, came to the dwelling of the man of God. Since it is written concerning the just man, “No evil shall come near you, and no scourge shall approach your tent” (Psalm 90), these men were nevertheless permitted to approach as their own scourge or example, but were forbidden to inflict a scourge; indeed, they experienced the scourge of divine correction upon themselves.

When these thieves reached the dwelling of the holy man, they secretly led away outside the animal on which he customarily rode to the church. They did not long rejoice in their deception. Not long afterward they came back, each having lost one eye, asking pardon and bringing back the animal.

The holy man of God received the horse, reproved himself for having possessed it, and immediately sold it, distributing its price to the poor. He did not restore their sight to them, being, as I think, instructed by the spirit of discernment, lest they should cease from such crimes only if deprived of their eyes; and, if they wished to commit a similar act, the bodily mark and the reputation of their name would quickly betray them from their hiding places.

For who would think that he could not obtain this from the Lord, when he knows that, both during his life and after his death, he often restored sight to the blind? Yet it was lighter for them to suffer this punishment in life than after life, in accordance with the saying: “It is better to enter the kingdom of heaven with one eye than to be assigned to Gehenna with two” (Matthew 18).

## XXV. He foreknows the day of his passing

32. Nearly a year before his departure, and in the hundredth year of his life, when it had been revealed to him that he would bring his human labors to an end and receive the most holy promises of the Almighty, he turned to a stricter way of life. He had already dried out his limbs with vigils and fasts, yet, like a veteran soldier, he once more took up a new campaign, so that his end might be more excellent—for what is more praiseworthy and better before Christ is always the end that perseveres, as he says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24).

## XXVI. He foretells the destruction of Cantabria

[Col. 0712B]

33. In that same year, during the days of Lent, the destruction of Cantabria was revealed to him.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] John of Biclaro, in his Chronicle, assigns this event to the eighth year of the emperor Justin and the sixth year of Leovigild, that is, to A.D. 574. “In those days,” he says, “King Leovigild entered Cantabria, killed the invaders of the province, seized Amaya, took possession of their wealth, and brought the province under his own rule.” The year of Saint Aemilian’s death is recorded in an epitaph written in Gothic letters, which Yepez reports under A.D. 569 as follows: [Col. 0712D] “Here lies buried the body of the most pure and apostolic man Aemilian, who, after leading the eremitical life for many years and then the clerical life, finally professed the monastic life under the rule of the admirable Benedict. He died in the Lord while exercising the care of an abbot, illustrious for miracles and the spirit of prophecy. Era 612,” which corresponds to A.D. 574 in the Christian era.]

Therefore, after sending a messenger, he ordered the senate of that place to be present on the feast day of Easter. They assembled at the appointed time. He related what he had seen and rebuked their crimes, murders, thefts, incest, violence, and other vices. He preached that they should do penance for all these things.

When everyone listened respectfully—for he was revered by all as though he were one of the disciples of our Lord Jesus Christ—a certain man named Abundantius said that, because of his old age, he was losing his mind. The saint declared that Abundantius would experience the matter for himself. The outcome afterward proved it, for he was killed by the avenging sword of Leovigild.

Since the others likewise did not repent of their former deeds, divine anger hanging over them, Leovigild attacked them in the same way through perjury and deceit and stained himself with their blood.

## XXVIII. His death and burial

34. When the time of his death was approaching, he summoned the most holy priest Asellus, with whom he had shared a community. In the priest’s presence, that most blessed soul was released from the body and returned to heaven.

Then, through the devoted care of that most blessed man, his body was carried with the attendance of many religious people and placed—and there it remains—in his own oratory.

Farewell, farewell, blessed Aemilian. Free from the labor of mortals, enjoy your good in the company of the pious; and, mindful of your useless biographer Braulion, come to my aid as an intercessor, so that through you I may find pardon, since I cannot escape my own evils. May I deserve this reciprocal reward: that, although I have recorded your virtues with my pen, my prayers may, through your favor, be heard for the forgiveness of my sins, and that at the final judgment I may be found worthy to stand among those over whom I preside, unworthy though I am, in pastoral care.

I feel that the end of this little book presses upon me. But since we have spoken of the miracles of the living, why should we be silent about the spiritual gifts of the dead? I shall bring forward two or three miracles, so that those things which have been related to us by the testimony of others and confirmed under written annotation may become more credible.

## XXVIII. The blind receive sight at his tomb

35. From the time of this saint’s death to our own memory, how many blind people have received sight at his tomb, how many possessed people have been cleansed, and how many suffering from various illnesses have been healed—it would be appropriate to add all this to the account announced in this little book. But I have thought it worthy to commit only this to writing: immediately after his passing, two people deprived of their eyes were restored to the light.

## XXIX. A candle is lit by divine power

36. A year having passed after this, when the feast of Saint Julian the martyr was approaching and there was no oil with which to prepare the lamps, a candle was not lit. Yet when they rose for the vigils, they found it so full of oil and burning that it not only provided light for the service until morning, but, through the abundance of its remains, one virtue produced another.

## XXX. A blind and lame woman is healed

37. A certain woman named Eufrasia was brought there from a place called Banonicus. She was lame and blind, yet upright and enlightened by the faith, as is shown by what happened to her. When her eyes and feet had been anointed, by the favor of God she immediately obtained light and the power to walk.

Let those who see these things performed in our own times believe what has been reported by witnesses. Indeed, both the place where she lives and the woman herself, formerly infirm and now healed, are still known.

## XXXI. A lifeless girl is raised

[Col. 0713C]

38. Another girl, about four years old, from a place called Prato, not far from his oratory, was seized by illness and brought to the point of death. Her parents, moved by devotion and fearing that they would lose her, decided that she ought to be carried to the memorial of the blessed man of God.

They picked her up, but on the way she appeared to have breathed her last. Nevertheless, their faith did not fail. They carried her lifeless and laid her at the altar. As evening was already falling, they withdrew, leaving no one there.

After an interval of three hours, they returned to investigate carefully. Worn out with grief, they wished to learn what the Creator had determined to do with her. They found alive the one whom they had left dead—and not merely alive, but playing with the altar cloth.

They magnified Christ, the Creator of all, who had looked upon their devoted contrition. Behold another Elisha in these last times and in our own age, whose dead bones give life to lifeless limbs—except that those men fled in fear, whereas these, full of confidence, carried and laid down the girl.

Here we must consider that the one and the same God of the Old and New Testament, our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone performs wonders, then, under the Law, concealed the hope of sweetness from those who feared him, because they were trembling with fear and not yet strengthened by charity, which casts out fear—for fear has punishment. Here, however, under the grace of faith, he perfects with confidence those who hope in him.

The power that raises the dead is one and the same; but the circumstances differ according to the time, and so too do the motives of those who carried the dead. The former carried the dead in order to bury them; these carried the girl in order to receive her back alive.

From this it may be understood how great is the blessed rest enjoyed there by holy men, through whose memorials the Almighty Lord performs such wonders.

We have fulfilled our promise. It remains for us to close the course of our discourse and open our thanksgiving to Christ, the King of heaven. Through his help and inspiration we see this little work begun and completed, and he grants us, for the consolation of our present miseries, the contemplation of the lives of holy men. He lives with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0713]

# HYMN ON SAINT AEMILIAN (C)

[Col. 0713C]

O great Christ, illustrious ruler of all things,

eternal Father of heaven, to whom the stars belong [the text is elliptical];

grant us vows favorable to the annual feasts,

and provide what is chaste and sober,

that they may appease your clemency.

Behold, the whole people, bowed in heart and body,

fulfills the duty owed at the recurring cycle of days.

Trusting in mind, they implore your aid,

so that indulgence, weighing the burdens of each person’s pleas,

may lift up our blessed hearts.

It offers a joyful song in harmonious melodies,

and forms a chant with resonant mouth and throat,

so that, by your powerful right hand,

removing our shameful deeds, you may correct us,

and be the helper of those who inwardly weep over their evils.

We can always obtain what we ask:

healing for our morals once they have been purified,

if you look upon us with kindness and mercy—

you who have bestowed so much upon such little servants,

so that this patron may lack no grace.

We, most wretched, disclose our sins in groaning;

we do not believe that we shall lose our service to you.

For while the abundant power of the King is nourished,

the best intercessor stands beside us,

who can bend a harmful anger.

May the enemy not perceive that the misfortunes of warfare are springing up among the blessed companies;

may neither what is transient [reading uncertain] nor hatreds germinate,

nor fraud or deceit be stirred up by schemes,

nor flame consume chaste children.

While we turn these things over in our minds,

we delight to proclaim the devoted servant,

your minister, Christ Jesus, your little household servant.

And as we compose feasts mingled with joys,

may all praise of you follow from them.

You, Father, have sacred temples;

you, God, have celestial shrines consecrated through the ages.

You possess the kingdom, and in the presence of your rule

you are seen as wondrous among the holy ones,

while reigning alone and displaying wonders by your deeds.

For this reason we beseech you that our offerings may be purified,

that those who are lost may return fully through the synaxis,

and that you may receive and place them in heaven’s royal palace.

You who grant that bodies struck down may rise again,

grant also that hearts may grow strong through grace.

We come forward confessing our guilt.

May the restrained blow cease;

may the sentence that renders the conscience dark and dreadful

be brought to an end.

When the will is favorable, grant us to ask

and reveal to the exposed the open door.

No moment flies away into time

that is not stained by our crimes.

We ask that purification may precede the contagion,

such purification as is worthy of our worst deeds,

and that the avenger may assign the punishment owed to those deeds.

We see the blind restored to light

and the lame leaping upon swollen feet;

limbs consumed by disease grow strong,

and those pressed down by the sleep of death finally rise,

then come together, joyful and sound.

We see grim demons driven away and put to flight,

howling amid the punishments and torments of Tartarus.

We see the crafty angel approach heaven,

secretly pierced by his own wound,

and crushed, wounded by his own weapons.

As these miracles of the Creator are openly displayed,

so may the most wicked serpent, driven away,

depart from those who limp with sickness of mind;

so may black hearts, clouded by dullness,

shine brilliantly with his radiance.

This most sure power is Christ himself:

the power that carried Aemilian through the arduous triumphs of life,

and was his crown and reward,

so that he might be imitated in our age;

and he flourishes as a strong advocate for the lowly.

Join me in harmonious songs;

tell all things, proclaim them, and sing psalms

to the everlasting King, to whom all these things belong.

May the songs of our cry resound,

and may the temples of heaven echo with hymns.

Offer glory to the Most High and Exalted One;

offer the greatest honor to the Trinity;

offer thanks to the Prince of the ages;

offer a psalm with voices and deeds;

offer praise throughout everlasting ages. Amen.

[Col. 0715]

# ACTS OF SAINT BRAULIO, BISHOP OF CAESARAUGUSTA, CONCERNING THE MARTYRS OF CAESARAUGUSTA, OR THE PASSION OF THE NUMBERLESS HOLY MARTYRS OF CAESARAUGUSTA, WHO SUFFERED UNDER THE EMPERORS DIOCLETIAN AND MAXIMIAN ON THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER (303). (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0715C]

1. The deeds of the men of ancient times, whose obstinacy consisted in breaking through the battle lines of warriors and shedding the innocent blood of those who faithfully guarded the laws of their own lands, the roofs and enclosures of their homes—not only did the gymnasia of the Greek philosophers resound with these deeds, but the learned pursuits of the Latin pagans also echoed with them.

Their renown is sung both by the monuments of historians and by the books of poets. Therefore, lest the substance of these various books should perhaps perish through the long passage of time, they engraved and impressed the letters of their words upon tablets of metal, whether marble or bronze, and [lacuna] so that, raising up the triumphs of their fellow citizens with the proclamation of many praises, they might transmit their deeds and achievements in writing to be read by generations yet to come, lest the memory of those whom they had loved in the passing age should utterly fade away.

2. Therefore, if gentile and sacrilegious men—despite being doomed to perish, and although those whom they celebrated were likewise destined to perish or perhaps had died a horrible death after the shedding of human blood—wrote down such great and extraordinary oracles as though they were miracles, so that after their death these might serve as certain beginnings of consolation, what ought we Christians, born of Christian parents, to do concerning Christians, except that the services of our tongue should be devoted to the victories of Christ’s soldiers and to the praises of our Emperor, who armed his martyrs with the triumphal standard so that they might fight most fiercely against the enemy and conquer?

3. Let the organs of our hearts resound with measured voices, so that, while we share in and join ourselves to their sufferings, we may deserve, with the assistance of Christ the Lord, to be associated with them in the eternal dwelling places through their prayers.

4. Now, therefore, following the order of the account I have received, I shall hasten through those matters which the report of ancient times, transmitted to us through the testimony of pagans, has carried down to our own day.

5. In the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, throughout the world they issued commands under sacrilegious institutions that the gatherings of all Christians should not only be expelled from the cities, but that everyone should be granted permission to pursue and kill them.

Their first aim was, through many flatteries and persuasions, to incline the intention of those minds toward the worship of demons; then, if they refused to fulfill the imperial commands and to sacrifice ceremonies to the gods, they were to eradicate completely the religion of the Christian name together with its adherents.

Immediately bands of attendants fulfilled the savage commands of the rulers. Taken up for these diabolical duties, companies of raging officials traversed the regions of the whole world, like lion cubs driven by the necessity of hunger, tearing apart and mangling the bodies of the holy martyrs.

But the more savagely their impiety raged, the more ardently the religion of Christ’s soldiers increased. Among them, their standard-bearer, Datianus, whose profane and sacrilegious mind was especially pestilential to all, received from those most impious emperors the title of governor so that he might proceed to Spain and rage with greater ferocity against the members of Christ.

6. When, hastening toward the province of Spain, he had arrived there, the savagery of his brutality could not remain hidden. Like a rabid lion, by the bitterness of his disastrous cruelty he began to seek out every Christian and tear their bodies with bloody teeth.

But by the providence of the almighty Lord it was brought about that, for the illumination or protection of certain cities, he should, under the prompting of a sacrilegious spirit, dedicate holy victims to Christ the Lord upon the sacred altar, so that through their intercession the Lord’s grace might frequently come to the citizens.

While he was carrying out these sacrilegious duties, he entered the city of Caesaraugusta.

[Note: The manuscripts of Barcelona read: “He attacked the city of Caesaraugusta.”]

Armed with a diabolical spirit, he dedicated to us the distinguished holy triumphant martyr Vincent, who, at the height of his most blessed illumination, adorned not only the city of Caesaraugusta but also Valencia with the distinction of his body.

[Note: The manuscripts of Barcelona read: “He consecrated him illustrious by his body.”]

Then, under the inspiration of his savage cruelty, he shed the innocent blood of eighteen illustrious men: Quintilianus, Matutinus, Urbanus, Faustus, Felix, Primitivus, Caecilianus, Fronto, Apodemus, Cassianus, Publius, Martialis, Successus, Januarius, Euolus, Optatus, Lupercus, and Julius.

He also added to them the most glorious holy virgin of God, Engratia, drenched in the dew of her purple blood.

### 7

Since Datianus could not overcome the intention of the minds devoted to holy worship and dedicated to Christ the Lord [Note: [Col. 0717D] Barcinonian manuscript: “the intention of minds dedicated to Christ the Lord.”], but since the holy soldiers, out of love for the eternal King, were more willing to pour out their sacred blood, the devil armed him, advising him to seek the aid of other devices [Note: [Col. 0717D] Barcinonian manuscript: “his counsellor.”]. Accordingly, after summoning his satellites, as the unquestionable tradition of ancient times relates, the crafty serpent disclosed the madness of his heart in these turbulent words [Col. 0717D]:

“Nothing, soldiers of our rulers, do we accomplish by laboring in this line of battle, nor can we bend the courage of Christian minds toward the worship of our gods; and while we desire to overcome them by raging against them more savagely, we are serving their victories to the full. Let the plan of our strategy therefore remain secret: let none of you be a betrayer or revealer, and let none of them hear, whether beforehand or later, the arrangement of our plan [Col. 0718A]. This innumerable multitude of Christians, enclosed within the circuit of this city, must be destroyed by secret counsel rather than by the violence of our strength. If we have decided to inflict upon them individually various kinds of torture for the worship of our gods, while we cannot conquer the intention of their hearts, we shall procure a perilous death for ourselves rather than for them.

“But let the duties of the heralds precede us around the whole circuit of the city, so that the multitude of them who are concealed behind the walls of the buildings may be driven out of this city as quickly as possible, as though generous permission had been granted them to remain there and tend their household shrine wherever each person should wish. Thus no one belonging to their religion, from masters down to slaves, will be found in the little dwellings of this city to be associated with our fellowship [Col. 0718B].

“Finally, our fellow soldiers, bring out weapons from the public arsenals [Note: [Col. 0717D] Barcinonian manuscript: “from the armaments.”]; bind the joints of your loins with double-edged swords; procure the gallows of hidden places as quickly as possible; and, when you are about to wage war against an unarmed enemy, suddenly spring forth from concealed places and hasten, in rivalry with one another, to overwhelm the battle line of their multitude. Cut down with sharp swords everyone whom you find.

“We therefore order the entrances of every gate to be closed, so that if anyone, perhaps escaping the line of the sword, should wish to return to the city, he may find everything shut. Nevertheless, he will perish by the sword—he who has become a fugitive before the sword’s edge. Of those whom we cannot bend to the worship of our gods, let none survive who preferred to worship Christ, so that no one who remains may escape punishment.”

### 8

Then bands of satellites run ahead through the quarters of the whole city [Note: [Col. 0717D] Barcinonian manuscript: “the lodgings.”]; the duties of the heralds resound with the hoarse clamor of their voices: the barriers of the western gates are opened, and crowds of the devout rejoice, of both sexes; companies of people go forth in throngs.

The old hasten to support their tottering limbs with trembling hands and staffs, lest they be deprived of the comfort of their fellow Catholics [Note: [Col. 0717D] The manuscript copy read as follows: “lest they be left to the comfort of the sinews of Catholics” [Col. 0718D]. The Bollandist Fathers rejected this reading as corrupt and judged that it should read: “lest they be deprived of the comfort of their fellow Catholics.” We have adopted this reading with the greater confidence because it is found in the Barcinonian manuscript.].

The multitude of young men and adolescents spontaneously leave open the barriers of their houses. The weaker sex of women, stronger in spirit than in the weakness of their sex, hastens along with troops of crying infants and clamorous little servants. You might have thought that the entire population of the city was migrating completely to witness the world in turmoil, as the distinguished Preacher says: “We have become a spectacle to this world, to angels and to human beings.”

What more need be said? The whole crowd of Christians went out, rejoicing and singing:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

Then the gates of the whole city were closed by the authorities, so that none of them might find an entrance back to safety. Suddenly wedges of armed men sprang forth from hidden places; with deadly swords they attacked the bands of Christians [Note: [Col. 0718D] Barcinonian manuscript: “they attack.”] [Col. 0719A], and, like a great supply of lambs, they cast down the bodies of the Catholics, who offered no resistance. The spear-bearers of the demons are drenched with the blood of the innocent; they grow thick with the corpses of the dead, and even then are not sated with their manifold cruelty toward the dead.

### 9

Then that deadly and most twisted dragon, the governor Datianus, ordered the pagan multitude to consign the piled-up bodies of the slain to the flames before the sight of the whole city. And lest perhaps anyone, lying far away or nearby in the hiding places of the Christians, should seize for himself the ashes of the holy martyrs, he ordered all those guilty of various crimes, whom the city’s hidden prisons held, to be quickly brought out of their cells. After their heads had been cut off, he ordered their accursed bodies to be joined to the bodies of the saints [Col. 0719B], and thus burned in the flames.

The beautiful bodies of the martyrs are burned together with the bodies of murderous robbers, following the example of our head—namely, the true God and man—who is known to have been crucified for our salvation between two robbers, granting the just the everlasting joys of the heavenly paradise, but to the others the punishments of their merits, which will never end.

### 10

Woe to you, Datianus, servant of the devil! Is it not enough for the increase of your crimes that you envy the merits of the living and extinguish the life of innocent citizens contrary to the commands of the laws [Note: [Col. 0719C] Barcinonian manuscript: “the care of the laws.”], unless you also contrive to add the cause of this wicked crime? What did the savagery of so many monstrous acts profit you? What did the deranged frenzy of these cruelties accomplish?

You destroyed the innocent populace of the earthly city [Col. 0719C], and you dedicated the people of our City—Jerusalem, rejoicing forever with Christ. Now, therefore, the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death will not touch them. But you are held bound by the torments of infernal fires that will never end.

They eagerly await the reception of their slain bodies [Note: [Col. 0719C] I judge that this should be read from the Barcinonian manuscript in place of “deception,” which was previously read.], so that, among the other companies of martyrs, they may be crowned with a double reward. You, too, are in no way willing to receive the sheath [Note: [Col. 0720C] The Barcinonian manuscript has “the case,” or rather perhaps “the casket.”] of your criminal body with you, lest, with the double destruction of soul and body, you be handed over to eternal fires together with the devil and his angels.

Behold, with our eyes we see the ashes of countless holy martyrs [Col. 0720A] and venerate them with the greatest joy; rejoicing in their triumphs, we are united with them in sympathy. Finally, we have consecrated a hall to almighty God in honor of the saints, so that the Christian people, celebrating, may not permit those whose name your savagery preferred utterly to extirpate to be joined to their festive joys.

O exceedingly happy, and more than happy, Caesaraugusta, sprinkled all around with the blood of the blessed, which dedicated so many thousands of martyrs as offerings to the Lord! Let the cities of the whole world, adorned with the precious blood of martyrs, rejoice with you.

Finally, let golden Rome itself rejoice, the head of the noblest nations and cities, which, together with the two great consuls of Christ, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, bears the sweet-smelling increase of countless martyrs [Col. 0720B], like a growth of roses.

Let the multitude of the people of the entire region of Spain also rejoice with us, bearing with you the dignity of the Christian name. Although the inhabitants of certain cities enjoy the support of a few martyrs—one, two, or three, perhaps even four—you overflow more abundantly with the increase of innumerable martyrs.

But while those who enjoy the patronage of a few martyrs join in the festivals of our saints, and rightly [Note: [Col. 0720C] Barcinonian manuscript: “and not undeservedly.”] share with us in their fellowship, let us, whom the unity of holy Catholic faith has joined to the merits of these present holy martyrs, rejoice each year in their festivals and triumphs, and celebrate vigils with the utmost devotion, so that we may deserve to share in the merits of their lives [Note: [Col. 0720C] Barcinonian manuscript: “properly.”].

Let us exult in the Lord; let us rejoice to God our Savior; let us come before his face with thanksgiving, and rejoice to him with psalms, because we are his people and the sheep of his flock. May he who granted his holy martyrs the triumph of victory deign to grant us the grace to imitate their example; and may he who prepared heavenly dwelling places in the power of his kingdom grant us the swift indulgence of his mercy, so that we may deserve to receive everlasting refreshment in the heavenly dwelling places. This may the Lord Jesus Christ himself grant, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 646. Taio, Bishop of Caesaraugusta

[Col. 0719]

## Historical Notice Concerning Taio

*(Nic. Antonio, Bibliotheca veterum Hispaniae, vol. I, p. 424.)*

[Col. 0719D] Taio, bishop of Caesaraugusta and successor of Saint Braulio, is better known than to require a full account here. It is commonly reported that he was sent by King Chindaswinth, or by the Fathers of the Seventh Council of Toledo, to Rome, where the pontiff Theodore then presided, to seek the books of Saint Gregory’s *Moralia on Job*, which had once been sent by their author to Leander, bishop of Seville, but could no longer be found. It is said that a revelation was made to him in Rome in the church of Saint Peter, and that the same Saint Gregory pointed out with his finger the place where a copy deposited in the Roman library lay hidden.

The history of this event is commonly published at the beginning of the *Moralia* among the works of the most holy Doctor; it is also celebrated among historians of Spain [Note: [Col. 0721D] Roderic of Toledo, book II, chapter 20; Mariana, book VI, chapter 8; Morales, book XI, chapter 25; Padilla, century VII, chapter 36.]. We shall discuss it below.

We read in the additions to Maximus’s *Chronicle* a poem by this Taio, intended to be placed upon the tomb of Honoratus, whom Taio calls his brother, a citizen of Caesaraugusta, and moreover archbishop of Seville. Certainly a certain epitaph, preserved mutilated on a half-worn and scattered stone at Seville, was copied by Benedict Arias Montanus and afterward by Juan de Torres, as Rodrigo Caro reports in his notes on this poem. But [Col. 0721B] neither the name of Honoratus nor any mention of the city of Seville appears on that stone.

Moreover, the epitaph carved on this stone, insofar as it can be read, does not entirely agree with the epitaph attributed to Taio. Yet such agreement would necessarily be required if it were to be thought that Taio’s poem was one and the same poem intended for the tomb of Honoratus. We therefore rather believe that this sepulchral poem was fabricated under Taio’s name by someone who had seen at Seville, or possessed a copy of, that mutilated inscription discovered by Arias Montanus, and who supplied the erased and fading letters by conjecture so that the inscription would be adapted to the tomb of Honoratus, bishop of Seville.

We leave the judgment of this hypothesis to learned men for examination. Certainly Rodrigo Caro, in his note on this epitaph, clearly charges it with fabrication [Col. 0721C] and imposture.

I know that John Mabillon, the Benedictine, attributed to this same Taio, in his notes on his *Old Analecta* (vol. I, p. 317), the five books of *Sentences* drawn from the works of Saint Gregory. It is clear that these books were otherwise called *Collectanea*. For Peter Gussanvillaeus, a priest of Chartres, informed us in the preface to the third volume of the works of the great Doctor in the latest Paris edition of 1675 that a *Collectaneum* drawn from the works of Saint Gregory by Taio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, and composed in the year 650, exists in the Paris library, written in a very ancient and excellent manuscript.

Afterward, the aforementioned Mabillon, in another volume of his *Analecta* published for the public, published the preface of Taio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, to Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona, concerning the five books of *Sentences* which Taio had collected from the works of Pope Saint Gregory, together with the beginning of the work itself. This fragment of that ancient age must be regarded as extremely precious [Col. 0722A], since the preface mentions a certain rebellion of Froia against King Recceswinth, as well as an incursion into Spain—especially into nearby Tarraconensis—by the Basques, driven from the Pyrenean mountains by a tyrant, and the victory won over them by one of the king’s commanders. Roderic of Toledo briefly discusses these events in book XI, at the very end.

At that time, Taio says, he was shut up in the city of Caesaraugusta because of fear of the enemy. During the leisure of the night, he collected and excerpted the chapters of the *Sentences* of Saint Pope Gregory of Rome, divided into five books and gathered into a single text of a codex. In this way he set forth, in an ordered arrangement of reason, the citizens of Jerusalem and Babylon—that is, the elect and the reprobate, devoted respectively to virtues and vices—from the very formation of the first man. He also notes that when he could not find material in Gregory’s little works with which to complete the chapter titles, he took care to gather a few passages from the books of Saint Augustine.

These are nearly the author’s own words. Mabillon also published the following poem, attached to the preface:

> Whoever loves to learn the sacred law, reader,  
> Read through this book of our study.  
> You will easily find whatever you may wish to know.  
> It bears all things that flower [then], and carries green meadows.  
> It feeds the loving sheep, the guileless creatures of Christ;  
> It displays the lofty homeland and the mighty kingdom,  
> The Tartarean fires and the grievous things that never end.  
> Behold, Christ is present to confer the kingdom upon the blessed;  
> To the impious, on the contrary, he grants dreadful punishments.  
> Lofty soul, climb up to the royal halls of heaven;  
> Hasten eagerly, lest you lack such great rewards,  
> And look down upon the dreadful flames of the pitch-black spring.

From this it is clear that Taio was not merely a learned man but also a competent poet [Col. 0722C].

There follows the beginning and the first title of the first book of the *Sentences*: “That God exists immutable, supreme, and eternal.” A few words from the text follow, as well as Quiricus’s answering letter, concerning which we shall speak under Quiricus.

It should seem strange, however, that when praising Gregory and making use of him, Taio makes no mention of the books of the *Moralia* of the holy Doctor which he claims to have discovered miraculously at Rome, since this is said to have happened under the auspices of Chindaswinth, whereas he wrote these things when King Recceswinth was already reigning.

Mabillon appends a note to all this, stating that he saw this work in that manuscript of the Thuanean library. He also says that Taio seems to him to have been the first, after whose example others—including Peter Lombard—formed similar collections. He recommends the preface as useful for illuminating Spanish history [Note: [Col. 0721D] The five books of Taio’s *Sentences*, collected for the most part from the work of Gregory the Great’s *Moralia*, have now been published for the first time by the learned continuator of Flórez’s *España Sagrada*, from an old manuscript of San Millán de la Cogolla, in vol. XXXI of the *Hispania Sacra*, beginning at p. 171. They are preceded by Taio’s letter to Eugenius of Toledo and by the preface of the work to Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona, in which there is also mention of Froia, or Froianus, who rebelled against Recceswinth, as well as Quiricus’s reply to Taio. The fifth book, however, lacks the end of chapter 33, “On the eternal punishments of the reprobate,” and the whole of chapter 34, “On the everlasting rewards of the elect”; these two chapters are indicated in the list prefixed to that book. A letter of Taio to Eugenius is also found in the distinguished Gothic manuscript of Gregory’s *Moralia* at Toledo, written in the year 983, on the third day before the Ides of April. In the same learned continuator of the *Hispania Sacra*, vol. XXX, p. 377, there is a “Fragment of a letter which Taio, priest and abbot, wrote to Braulio.” I believe that both were the same Taio and Taion. It seems, however, that our author failed to include in this number the promised mention of Quiricus of Barcelona, which, so far as I know, appears nowhere else in his work. Yet, besides the letter in which Quiricus replies to Taio’s letter or preface concerning the five books of Gregory’s *Sentences* addressed to him—beginning, “Behold, most blessed of men,” and mentioned above—there are two further letters, first published by d’Achery and Mabillon and reprinted by the learned Matthaeus Aymerichus, addressed to Ildefonsus of Toledo. The first is a letter of thanksgiving for the copy of the little book *On the Perpetual Virginity of Holy Mary* sent to him. It begins: “When, returning from you to the places of the flock entrusted to me …,” and is found in Aymerichus, p. 449. The second is a letter of supplication, in which he asks Ildefonsus, for the benefit of his mother, who is still alive, to disclose certain matters from the mysteries of Sacred Scripture. It begins: “Since, as you know, everything new …,” p. 452. Aymerichus discusses Quiricus more fully from p. 261 onward.].

The volume of Taio’s *Sentences*, which Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, is known from d’Achery’s *Chronicle of Fontenelle* to have donated to the monastery of Fontenelle around the year 823, must be understood as referring to this same work.

The fragments which Pseudo-Julian praises in his *Chronicle*, no. 414, as belonging to this same Taio, together with those of Braulio and Heleca, are nothing of the kind. He is alluding to the epitaph of Honoratus of Seville, which we discussed above [Note: [Col. 0724A] I believe that Bracarius, bishop of Seville, may conveniently be mentioned here. He is said to have occupied that see after Isidore, Honoratus, Antonius, and Fugitivus, according to the Aemilianian catalogue of the bishops of Seville; this occurred at the end of the seventh century, as the learned Flórez has inferred from the strongest conjectures, vol. IX, p. 221, n. 25. That he wrote “On the souls of human beings: that they were not created at the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor created only once, against Origen, nor sown together with bodies through sexual intercourse, against the Luciferians,” is inferred from the writings of John of Seville, a ninth-century author, to Alvarus of Córdoba, first published by Flórez in vol. XI, and especially from the sixth letter among Alvarus’s works, p. 144, n. 5. The same Flórez should be consulted for his extensive treatment of Bracarius of Seville, vol. IX, beginning at p. 220.].

[Col. 0723]

## Letter of Taio, Bishop of Caesaraugusta, to Eugenius, Bishop of Toledo

*(In Flórez, Spain Sacred, from Baluze, vol. IV of the *Miscellanea*.) (C,S)*

[Col. 0723B] To my most holy and venerable lord Eugenius, bishop of the city of Toledo: Taio, the least of the servants of God, bishop of Caesaraugusta.

He who lacks the use of his own strength rightly and most necessarily seeks the assistance of one stronger; and he advances his bodily steps all the more easily when he is drawn by the right hand of one more powerful, so that, with the stronger's help, he may at least complete the course he desires rather than remain sluggish in the middle of his journey.

So I, my venerable lord, although weak, yet aided by your prayers, have preferred to approach the beginnings of a difficult work, as though of some very great mountain. Its surface displays, as it were, the height of a great paradise: groves rising high, whitening with flowers, sweetened with fruits, green with leaves, shining with the beauty of lilies, glowing with the red of roses, resplendent with the purple flowers of violets, and for the most part gleaming with saffron colors. They never wither at any time but flourish in perpetual greenness, arranged with marvelous skill and fitted together in straight rows of lines. They provide such grace to those who love them that, through their sweetness, they refresh not only the outward senses of the body but also the inner secrets of the heart.

As I gazed upon such things with attentive eyes and saw many people being satisfied with these manifold banquets [Col. 0723D], I was kindled by an immeasurable desire. Like one of a company of hungry children, driven onward by the compulsion of starvation, I approached the gate of that same paradise step by step. Like a rash explorer entering within, while I was held in extreme wonder as I surveyed the most beautiful and varied spaces, I gathered some little flowers of the branches as children gather them in play, and plucked them with eager hand.

I quickly prefaced these principal matters, with a certain curiosity, by comparisons in simple words, as though I were opening the entrance of a stopped-up mouth, only so that at the very beginning of my speech I might set forth by certain parables the incomparable excellence of that man—namely, the holy Pope Gregory—and might to some extent reveal to those who do not know, or rather are ignorant, the greatness of his wisdom, by which he illumined the holy Church with such clear light [Note: [Col. 0723D] Everyone will notice that an error has crept in here. If there is room for conjecture, I think it should be punctuated and read as follows: “I plucked them. Why these things … except that I might set before the mind, by certain parables, the incomparable excellence of that man … and might to some extent reveal to those who do not know, or who are ignorant, the greatness of his wisdom?”].
