Indeed, I had wished to be present now in your company, so that, as it is written, “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you,” I might take the pattern of my work from the wisdom of your mouth. At the beginning of this work I could then set forth, as it were, the texture of a web of words; or certainly, from the skillful hand of your heart, I might carry upon my own shoulders, as though building some great structure, the polished and squared stones of words. For “brother helping brother will be exalted, like a fortified city” [Col. 0724D].

The order of reason demands that what follows be joined to what precedes by a certain bond of continuity, so that the justice expressed in both may reveal its rectitude and, guided along the path of truth, proceed joyfully to its appointed end.

Therefore, let us now disclose in clearer words what shortly before we set forth by comparisons. For the following discourse, with a brief account, introduces the works of that same most holy man. I considered it fitting first to unfold a few things about his works.

We saw, we saw our Gregory, stationed at Rome—not with the eyes of the body, but with the gaze of the mind. For we saw him not only in his scribes but also in his attendants, who faithfully rendered bodily service to him; and having learned much about his virtues from their report, I shall briefly unfold a few things.

In the end, by the grace of Christ he was formed in every uprightness of conduct: serene in spirit and countenance, kind in heart, pure in conscience, discerning in behavior, radiant in virginity, filled with charity, outstanding in compassion, distinguished in patience, incomparable in modesty, singular in self-restraint, devoted to hospitality, attentive to strangers, generous in almsgiving, an excellent steward of ecclesiastical possessions, bound to his friends, a supporter of the oppressed, a comforter of the afflicted, sharp in intellect, prudent in counsel, polished in speech, eloquent in expression, articulate in wisdom, endowed with knowledge, manifold in learning, manifold in interpreting the divine Scriptures, an acute investigator of hidden mysteries, a magnificent defender of the Catholic faith, a strong champion against heretics [Col. 0725C], upright in authority toward the proud, and submissive with ready devotion toward the humble.

He was so adorned with the four virtues of the soul—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—that he seemed not a human being but an angel among human beings.

Who in our time, eloquent in speech, endowed with prudence, and profound in wisdom, could praise Gregory with worthy praises? Even the foremost philosophers of Greek and Roman eloquence—I mean Socrates, Plato, Cicero, and Varro—if they had been present in our time, would not, I think, have produced words worthy of him.

But lest I appear to speak in panegyrical language, I shall pass over the many things about his virtues which I learned by hearing and turn the offices of my tongue toward his writings, which are expressions of beauty.

Therefore, while I was stationed at Rome and diligently searching for the volumes of his works that were lacking in Spain, and while I copied them with my own hand after finding them, the great sweetness of his words caressed my mind with immeasurable delight. I perceived in them something special and supremely excellent, without comparison to anything else.

While he labored to examine the history of blessed Job through a threefold investigation—that is, historical, typological, and moral—and to traverse the first and final portions of the prophet Ezekiel with an equal exposition, revealing with serene disclosure the depths of so many mysteries after driving away the cloud of ignorance, he laid open almost all the secrets of the New and Old Testament [Col. 0726A]. It came about that, through this opportunity, that bread which descended from heaven satisfied us with the altogether fitting sweetness of this most faithful servant.

But since, amid the great length of these volumes, whenever the exposition of each testimony is required, the right order of almost the entire work was left uncertain, there was no small need for investigation, and the intention of the ardent mind often grew cold. I preferred to undertake the greatest labor once rather than endure a suspect difficulty continually.

Accordingly, I went through all the monuments of his books, and, with the help of Christ Jesus, who perfects praise from the mouths of infants and sucklings and releases the tongues of the mute from the bond of silence, I diligently copied and brought together in their proper order almost all the testimonies of Sacred Scripture which were contained in his writings, in various places, for the proof or exposition of each matter [Col. 0726B].

Whoever seeks in these volumes the explanation of any sacred testimony, lest he be wearied by repeated reading and fail to find quickly what he desires, will, by turning to these excerpts, suddenly find what he sought with the freedom of a satisfying discernment.

The reader of this work must be warned to take careful note that many chapters of testimonies in these same volumes, situated in different places, as we mentioned above, are known to have been collected by me in order, just as they were found expounded.

Other material, which he seemed already to have explained in earlier or later sections and then unfolded again and again in different places with different words but the same meaning, I have taken care to insert in some places with the preceding testimonies, as the order of the matters to be explained required, and to leave other passages aside. Thus what follows might depend upon what precedes, and what follows might be more usefully fitted to what preceded.

For if everything were placed in the sequence of this work in a carefully differentiated order, the size of the volumes would undoubtedly exceed the limits of brevity; and, offending the reader’s mind by its own repetitions, it would nevertheless create weariness through the repeated material.

I took care to complete this work in six codices—four, namely, of the Old Testament, and two of the New Testament—joined together in their proper order, while omitting the Scriptures which that most holy man treated in order in those same books [Leg. [Col. 0726D] “the same”].

I also excerpted the prefaces corresponding to those codices and placed them at the heads of the books, so that the one who, by the grace of Christ, has abounded toward us in manifold services might himself be placed before his own words.

I preferred also to entrust these codices, collected with exceedingly laborious concentration, to your prudence for examination. If your most discerning investigation should find anything disorderly in them, let it attribute this not so much to negligence as to necessity [Perhaps: “to the necessities”]. For, while I, a solitary sailor, was preparing to cross an immense sea in a tiny boat [Note: [Col. 0727A] It seems that “little boat” should be read.], I traversed the expanses of this broad ocean amid the greatest difficulties and at last, with Christ as my pilot, reached the desired rest of the shore.

Behold, most prudent of men, in attempting to touch upon the order of the matters one by one, I have exceeded the limits of brevity. As a certain very learned man says, while the potter’s wheel was running and his hand attempted to make a jug, he fashioned an amphora [Col. 0728A].

But while I preferred to write a brief little page, an unskilled hand has composed a little book.

I therefore beseech you, most holy of men, and all those who will not dislike reading this work, to deign to place these little books, like the two small coins, in the treasuries of the Lord’s temple, and not to disdain to implore his mercy with vigilant attention for the cleansing of my sins, so that, freed from everlasting fires, I may deserve to be comforted by eternal refreshment.

Farewell, my venerable and most holy lord.

[Col. 0727]

## The Five Books of the Sentences of Taio, Bishop of Caesaraugusta

*(From Flórez’s *España Sagrada*, where they were first published from the Gothic manuscript of the monastery of San Millán de la Cogolla.) (C,S)*

### Preface

## To Quiricus, Bishop of Barcelona

[Col. 0727B] To my venerable and most holy lord Quiricus, bishop, Taio, the unworthy bishop of the city of Caesaraugusta, also called Samuel.

Remembering your most gracious request and my most devoted promise, I have preferred to send to your holiness the text of this little book, marked beforehand with elegant titles of its sentences, so that, just as we are joined by the bond of one holy charity, so also we may rightly share in the grace of labor and reading.

The order of reason demands that I first disclose to your ears, as briefly as I can, the causes of its origin—or rather of its calamities—how it was produced, and amid what anxieties it was brought to completion and written; and that only then the discourse proceed to the remaining matters.

### 2

Your Blessedness knows very well that time when the twisting serpent, with its poisonous mouth, had scattered the tares of its venomous seeds in the minds of certain people, and by fraudulent deception had removed the steps of ruined minds from the path of the right way.

At that time, a pestilential man of deranged mind, Froia, assuming tyrannical power and taking to himself the perverse supporters of his crime, approached the task of waging war against the Christian fatherland with arrogant determination, while deceitfully pretending schemes against Recceswinth, the orthodox and great worshiper of God.

Because of this crime, the savage nation of the Basques, driven from the Pyrenean mountains, ravages the land of Iberia by laying it waste with various devastations.

Alas, the magnitude of the calamity interrupts the effort of speech! Yet at last the discourse must come to what it fears.

The innocent blood of many Christians is poured out: some are wounded in the throat, others by missiles, and many by various spears. An innumerable multitude of captives is led away [Col. 0728B], and immeasurable spoils are taken. Unholy war is brought against the temples of God; sacred altars are destroyed. Many members of the clergy are cut down by swords, and the unburied corpses of many of the slain are exposed to dogs and birds.

Thus, not without reason, the inscription of the seventy-eighth Psalm seems appropriate to that calamity.

### 3

When the circuit of the walls enclosed us in the city of Caesaraugusta on this account, and we awaited the arrival of the aforesaid prince, we most earnestly besought the mercy of almighty God that he would by no means allow the yoke of tyrannical domination to be laid upon our necks, and that he would speedily grant the aid of his right hand to the most pious prince against the most impious enemy [Col. 0728C].

But the Lord immediately heard the prayers of the poor and the entreaty of the most merciful prince. Having therefore sent from heaven a most valiant champion, he supported the former by the help of his omnipotence, but condemned the latter, the author of tyrannical impiety, by a sudden downfall: granting the one an abundant palm of victory, but inflicting upon the other the ignominy of a most dreadful death. God destroyed him with his right hand, and plucked him out of his tabernacle and his root from the land of the living, so that we might rightly sing to the Lord: “Your right hand, O Lord, struck down the enemy, and in the multitude of your power you crushed our adversaries” (Exod. XV, 6, 7).

## 4

In the turbulence, then, of the storm mentioned above, although, with dangers raging everywhere on successive days, we were scarcely able to do anything, and there was no freedom to go anywhere or to cultivate any rural land, nevertheless we accumulated, during the leisure of the nights, an increase of spiritual labors. From the sacred volumes—namely, those of the holy Pope Gregory of Rome—we extracted, with the Lord’s help, chapters of sentences divided into five books and contained in a single textual codex [Col. 0728D–0729A]. Thus, amid bitter days, we gathered sweet courses with tears, remembering the testimony of the Psalmist:

> Those who sow in tears  
> reap in joy.  
> Going forth, they went and wept,  
> casting their seeds;  
> but coming, they shall come with rejoicing,  
> carrying their sheaves.  
> (Ps. CXXV, 6–8)

Beginning, therefore, with the Trinity of the immutable essence of the omnipotent Lord, and proceeding from the origin of the world and the psalmody of humankind to the consummation of this age, we carefully twisted, as it were, the strands of a very long cord. With the assistance of Christ’s grace, and with such ingenuity as we possessed, we drew together and marked out, by noting the titles of the sentences according to their ordered divisions, the lines of their arrangement, as we have said [Col. 0729B].

But because we were entirely unable to find, in the works of the same holy pope, the chapters of certain titles needed to complete the subject, we took care to gather a few passages from the books of Saint Augustine the bishop. And, as though sprinkling over the whole a few very beautiful flowers of aromatic, sweet-smelling spices, we added them as delicate adornments, so that the mind of the diligent reader, while being nourished by the accumulation of both kinds of material, might be made more eager in both directions.

From the very fashioning of the first human being, therefore, this book sets forth, in an ordered arrangement of reason, the citizens of Jerusalem and Babylon—that is, the elect and the reprobate, devoted respectively to virtues and vices. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” whereas Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” The prudent reader will be able, by very easy investigation, to foresee which people pass through the roads of this world toward the vision of peace and which toward the shame of confusion [Col. 0730A].

No prudent Christian, surely, doubts that the terrifying heavenly Judge, when he comes, will say to the saints:

> Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.

And, conversely, to the reprobate:

> Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

> And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.  
> (Matt. XXV, 34, 41, 46)

Behold the ends toward which the peoples of these two cities arrive: the one, so that they may enjoy the rewards of eternal recompense with the holy angels; the other, so that they may be consigned with the devil and his angels to the fires of everlasting punishments.

## 5

Let the person who is fastidious and reluctant to read much—or indeed any diligent reader who perhaps prefers to read but is quite unable to possess an abundance of many volumes—not deign to regard the labor of this little work of ours as insignificant, and not delay to run through the text of this manual book by reading it [Col. 0730B]. For here such a reader will discover where he ought to cling more firmly and from what he should strive to withdraw as quickly as possible, so that, by Christ the Lord’s generosity, he may reach the company of the heavenly citizens and obtain the everlasting rewards of those realities.

You also, my venerable lord, I beseech—and all those touched by the water of the most sacred font, whom the reading of this little book pleases, I entreat, for the unity of the holy Catholic Church, which is joined to Christ the Lord, her bridegroom, in the holiness of faith—not to consider it burdensome to ask God’s mercy for the cleansing of the heaps of my sins. May I thereby be spared the punishments of the infernal fires and, even if only in the smallest dwellings, deserve to be consoled by eternal refreshment.

# RESPONSE OF QUIRICUS THE BISHOP TO TAIO THE BISHOP

[Col. 0729]

### 1

To the truly most holy, like-minded, and specially beloved lord Taio, bishop: Quiricus, your little servant.

Behold, most blessed of men, the intention of the Holy Spirit, with which you labored in the fruitful work of this composition, has made evident and clear to all who can recognize it the fruit of your labor: namely, how the inducements of every vice may either be guarded against, so that one does not fall into them, or, after a fall, how one may rise from them; and likewise how the gifts of the virtues may be desired without becoming proud because of them.

For through you the grace of the Holy Spirit has recalled many from wantonness, restrained many from anger, and removed others from the arrogance of pride. It has taken some away from the vice of gluttony, and removed others from the desires of avarice. To speak more particularly, it has freely instructed everyone to despise things that are fleeting and perishable and to seek, with every subtlety of understanding, what is certain and eternal [Col. 0729C–D].

For the fruit of this work, first of all our common mother, the Catholic Church, gives immense thanks. After her, I and those who resemble me—sleeping in the darkness of night through the provocations of vices, and yet also breaking forth after the darkness into the light—offer our many and boundless thanks, first to the Lord, by whose inspiration you committed this work to completion, and then to you.

O salt of the earth, by which our innermost hearts are seasoned, lest they be made vain by the error of the world! O lamp placed upon the Church’s lampstand, which, shining with the light of truth, dispels the cloud of error from many by your splendid speech [Col. 0730C]! For that testimony which a certain wise man spoke is rightly fitted to you:

> Behold, you have instructed many,  
> and you have strengthened the weak hands.  
> (Job IV, 3–4)

May the Lord, therefore, in return for the zeal devoted to this work, grant your holy soul forgiveness of all sins and, after the course of this present life, fellowship with all the saints.

In the end, I was slow to send you this same Codex because, when I wished to offer it through my own hand and at the same time to give thanks with voice and tears as far as I was able, I proved less useful than I should have been. For this reason, I ask you, who recognize the fault, kindly to forgive it. I had also intended to send the same Codex to you through my little boy; but because you bound me by an adjuration in God’s name to transmit it without any delay, I have therefore sent it by the present bearer [Col. 0730D].

For the rest, I offer my lord greetings as humble as they are sincere and filled with abundant charity. I beg you to pray to the Lord for your servant with pious concern, for the adornment of your Church. Whatever God commands to be provided, I hope, aided by your prayers, to furnish to you as he enables me.

**Here ends the work.**

# EPIGRAM OF THE FOLLOWING WORK

[Col. 0731]

Whoever, reader, loves to learn the sacred law,  
read through this book of our study.  
You will easily find whatever you may wish to know.

It bears every flower [then?],  
and carries green meadows;  
it feeds the sheep of Christ the lover—  
innocent creatures.

It shows the lofty homeland  
and the powerful kingdom,  
the Tartarean fires  
and sorrows that shall not end.

Behold, Christ is present for you,  
to grant the kingdom to the blessed;  
but to the impious, in contrast,  
he grants dreadful punishments.

Lofty soul, ascend to the royal courts of heaven;  
hasten eagerly, lest you be deprived of such great rewards,  
and look down upon the dreadful flames of the pitch-black spring.

# BOOK ONE OF SENTENCES

## CHAPTER ONE  
### That God exists immutable, supreme, and eternal

[Col. 0731A]

*(Saint Gregory, Moralia, Book XII, chapter 33, no. 38.)* God alone is immutable in himself, because he alone possesses immortality. Concerning him James says:

> With whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning.  
> (James I, 17)

Accordingly, because mutability does not arise in God, no alternation of shadow interrupts his light.

**[Note: [Col. 0731C] The latest edition reads: “No shadow of change interrupts his light.”]**

For what is the mutability of things except a kind of death? When it changes anything into something else, it kills, as it were, what had been, so that what had not been may begin to be. For it is written of the immutable God:

> Who alone possesses immortality  
> and dwells in inaccessible light.  
> (1 Tim. VI, 6)

**[Edit.: immutability.]**

[Col. 0731B]

All the saints by nature do not possess their own stability in themselves. But because they always earnestly desire to cling to immutable truth, by clinging they act so as to become immutable. And when they hold fast to it with their whole affection, they eventually receive the power, being lifted above themselves, to overcome what they have been in themselves—namely, mutable.

*(Moralia XI, 29, no. 41.)* Although God is immutable by nature, he is not disturbed in the anger of judgment. Yet the severity of his righteousness, by which human wickedness is struck, is often called God’s movement in human speech, just as blessed Job says:

> As soon as he moves, you will be troubled  
> [Edit.: “he will trouble you”],  
> and his terror will fall upon you.  
> (Job XIII, 11)

Almighty God, although he himself is eternity, nevertheless how he is eternity itself remains unknown.

*(Moralia XVI, 43, no. 54.)* In what we hear concerning the power of the divine nature, we are sometimes accustomed to think of things that we know by experience. Everything that begins and ends is enclosed by a beginning and an end. If its completion is delayed for a little while, it is called long. When someone turns the eyes of the mind backward through memory and stretches them forward through expectation within this length of time, he expands it, as it were, across a span in the mind.

When the human mind, attending in its human manner, hears of God’s eternity, it proposes to itself long stretches of life in which it may always measure: what has gone behind that could be retained in memory, or what remains ahead that could be awaited through expectation [Col. 0731C–0732A]? The mind, in its human frailty, is utterly unable to comprehend this.

**[Note: [Col. 0731C] The following words are absent from the Gregorian codices, both in the edition [Col. 0732C] and in the manuscripts.]**

*(No. 55.)* Whenever we think of past or future times in eternity, we have not yet understood eternity. For there is that which neither begins with a beginning nor ends with an end; there is neither anything expected to come nor anything that passes and ought to be remembered. It is one reality that always is.

**[Note: [Col. 0732C] The edition reads: “always to be is.”]**

Even if we and the angels begin to see God with a beginning, nevertheless we see that he exists without a beginning. There, “to be always without end” means that the mind never stretches toward what follows, as though everything that exists were multiplied and made long [Col. 0732B].

Through the Spirit of prophecy it is said:

> Lord, you who reign forever  
> and unto the age of the age, and beyond.

*(Perhaps Exodus XV, 18; see the latest edition.)* In the manner of sacred speech, the Spirit spoke to human beings in a human way, saying “and beyond” where there could be no expectation—saying “and beyond” where there could be no expectation. For eternity does not have a “beyond”: it always has being. No part of its length passes away so that another part may follow. Rather, it is wholly present at once, so that nothing appears to be lacking which it does not behold. In eternity the mind sees everything that is as not slow and yet long.

It is written:

> The Lord said to Moses: “I am who I am,”  
> and you shall say to the children of Israel:  
> “He who is has sent me to you.”  
> (Exod. III, 14)

*[In Ezechiel, Book I, homily 2, no. 20.]* To be God means to remain eternal and immutable. For everything that changes ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. The being of almighty God is never to be unlike himself. He alone truly is, because he alone remains immutably.

*(Moralia XVIII, 50, no. 82.)* Everything that is now one way and now another is close to not-being. It cannot remain in its own state. In some manner it moves toward not-being when, through the moments of time, it is led from what it had been to something else. Therefore, if we are to be something through participation in that essence, let us recognize ourselves, because we are close to nothingness.

*(Moralia IV, 32, nos. 65, 67.)* The greatest virtue is to breathe after the joy of eternity belonging to him to whom nothing comes and from whom nothing passes. Truth, in order to pour its own perpetual being into us in some measure, intimates this through Moses, as was said above, declaring:

> I am who I am,  
> and you shall say to the children of Israel:  
> “He who is has sent me to you.”  
> (Exod. III, 14)

When the Psalmist contemplated the immutable state of God’s eternity [Note: [Col. 0733D] The edition reads: “the immutability of eternity.”], he said:

> You are the same,  
> and your years shall not fail.  
> (Ps. X, 28)

He declares this to be the dwelling of the elect, saying:

> The children of your servants shall dwell there.  
> (Ibid., 29)

The supreme, eternal, and immutable God, who contains all things without location, remains for us, when we come to him, a non-local place. When we reach that place, we see how great the disturbance of our mind has been even in this life. For although the righteous are already at rest in comparison with the wicked, nevertheless, when the innermost rest is considered, they are not entirely at rest.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### On the immensity and omnipotence of God

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 5, nos. 10–11.)* Almighty God possesses within himself the power to arrange mutable things without mutation, to accomplish diverse things without any diversity in himself, and to form unlike things without any succession of thoughts. God, who is everywhere and wholly everywhere, therefore works unlike things in a manner utterly unlike them, without ever being unlike himself.

It is written:

> Heaven is my throne,  
> but the earth is the footstool of my feet.  
> (Isa. LXVI, 1)

And again it is written:

> He measures heaven with a span  
> and encloses the earth in a handful.  
> (Isa. XL, 12)

From this it is necessary to consider that he who presides over heaven as over a throne is both above it and within it. And he who measures heaven with a span and encloses the earth in a handful is outside, above, and below it. To indicate that almighty God is within and above all things, he declared heaven to be his throne. To show that he surrounds everything, he says that he measures heaven with a span and encloses the earth in a handful [Col. 0733C].

*(Augustine, in the *Speculum*, chapter 23.)* Almighty God is himself within and outside, himself below and above: above by governing, below by carrying; within by filling, outside by surrounding. Thus he is within so that he is also outside; he surrounds in such a way that he penetrates; he presides in such a way that he carries; he carries in such a way that he presides.

Let us understand almighty God to be within all things, but not enclosed; outside all things, but not excluded [Col. 0733D]. He is within so that he may contain all things; he is outside so that by his immensity he may enclose all things. By being outside, he is shown to be the creator; by being within, he is demonstrated to govern all things. And lest created things exist without God, God is within all things; but lest anything exist outside God, God is outside, so that all things may be enclosed by him.

God does not fill heaven and earth so that they may contain him, but rather so that they themselves may be contained by him. Nor does God fill all things piecemeal; although he is one, he is wholly everywhere.

*(In Isidore, Book I of the Sentences, chapter 2.)* Almighty God encloses all things within the immensity of his power, and no one will be able to find a way of escaping his power, because he constrains everything on every side.

All things are confined within the omnipotence of the divine **rule** [Edit.: **judgment**]: both those that must be preserved so that they may be safe and those that must be cut off so that they may perish. Therefore, we absolutely cannot say that anyone can escape God. Whoever does not have him appeased will certainly not escape him when he is angry.

The completion of some deed is called perfection. But God, who was not made, how is he perfect? Human poverty takes this expression, as it does other expressions, from our ordinary usage, so that what is ineffable may nevertheless be spoken in some fashion, since human speech says nothing worthily about God.

God must not be thought to be in all things in such a way that each thing receives him according to the size of its portion—that the greatest receives more and the smallest less. Rather, he himself is wholly in the whole and wholly in all things, or all things are in him.

Although God is not local, he nevertheless moves locally in his saints, since they preach him from place to place. God, who is moved neither by place nor by time, is nevertheless moved in his servants both by time and by place whenever he is preached by them.

## CHAPTER THREE  
### That God is invisible and uncircumscribed

*(Book XVII of the Moralia, chapter 27, no. 32.)* Almighty God is by no means seen in his brightness by those below, because he rules in the heights. For it is written:

> Darkness is beneath his feet.  
> He mounted upon the cherubim and flew.  
> (Ps. XVII, 10–11)

“Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore he is said to have mounted above the fullness of knowledge and to have flown, because no knowledge comprehends the height of his majesty. Almighty God flew because he carried himself far upward beyond our understanding. He flew above the wings of the winds because he transcends the knowledge of souls.

While we are darkened by the gloom of our weakness, God is hidden from us through our ignorance, so that he may not now be seen by us in his eternal, innermost, and uncircumscribed brightness, just as it is written:

> He made darkness his hiding place.  
> (Ibid., 12)

*(Moralia XXIII, chapter 19, no. 36.)* How can we see the uncircumscribed omnipotence that we are utterly unable to comprehend?

There is, however, something that we ought to transfer from the experience of the flesh to the understanding of the spirit. If someone lies in darkness with his eyes closed and the sudden light of a lamp breaks forth before him, his closed eyes are struck by the arrival of the light itself, so that they open. Why, then, were they disturbed if, while closed, they saw nothing? Yet what they were able to see with closed eyes was not something complete. For if they had seen the whole thing perfectly, why, once opened, would they seek what they might see?

When we try to behold something of the incomprehensible Godhead, the mind is struck by the splendor of wonder itself and, as though it sees what cannot be seen, being placed in darkness it sees the power of the light through closed eyes.

*(Moralia V, 7, no. 12; XXVI, 12, no. 17.)* Our almighty Creator has withdrawn from us the light of his vision and hidden himself from our eyes as if in a hiding place of darkness. We cannot yet see God, but we are already moving toward his vision if we marvel at him in the things he has made.

We therefore call creation his footprints, because by following the things that come from him we proceed toward him. Hence Paul says:

> His invisible attributes are understood and seen through the things that have been made;  
> his eternal power also and divinity.  
> (Rom. I, 20)

God’s inner nature is not yet known to the human mind, which has been scattered outward by its own sin. But while he displays the beauty of his work outside, he gives us signs, as it were, by which he hints at himself and shows us what we should pursue within.

## CHAPTER FOUR  
### On God the almighty Father

[Col. 0735B]

The incomprehensible mysteries of the Godhead are separated from the knowledge available to our weakness, and his power transcends the nature of creation. For the height of the Godhead neither began to be nor ceases, neither arises through a beginning nor is narrowed by an end.

God the almighty Father begot his Son without time.

*(Moralia XXIII, chapter 19, no. 36.)* Who could speak worthily of that ineffable birth: that he who was born from the eternal is coeternal; that the one existing before the ages begot an equal; that the one born is not later than the one who begets?

*(Book II on the Gospels, homily 25, no. 6.)* We can marvel at these things, but we are by no means able to behold them. To be able already to marvel, in some measure, at the power of that birth is itself a kind of seeing.

Whoever thinks the Son lesser than the Father specifically detracts from the Father, since he confesses the Son’s wisdom to be unequal to the Father’s. What powerful man could bear calmly if someone said to him: “You are indeed great, but your wisdom is less than you”?

The almighty Lord himself says:

> I and the Father are one.  
> (John X, 30)

And again he says:

> The Father is greater than I.  
> (John II, 51)

It is also written of him:

> He was subject to his parents.  
> (Luke II, 51)

What wonder, then, if in his humanity he asserts himself to be lesser than the Father in heaven, since in his humanity he was also subject to his parents on earth?

Everything we say passes away; what we write remains. The tongue of the Father is called the pen of a scribe (Ps. XLIV), because from him comes his Word, generated coeternally and without passing away.

The prophet David, speaking in the person of God the Father, says:

> From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.  
> (Ps. CIX)

*[From Augustine’s Dialogue with Orosius, question 1.]* This does not mean that God the Father has a womb as we do or is to be thought corporeal; rather, by “womb” he wished substance to be understood, from which the Son was born.

What the Father is, that he begot: God from God, light from light, God equal to himself from God, the Word with God, the Word of God through whom all things were made; light from light, coeternal with the one who begot him and one with the one who begot him.

Thus God the Father begot the coeternal Son neither from nothing nor from some other substance, but from himself.

*(Augustine, Dialogue on the Unity of the Holy Trinity.)* “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are appellative names. Although “Father” is spoken in relation to the Son and “Son” in relation to the Father, these names are called relative. “God,” however, is the proper name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as it is written in the Psalm:

> According to your name, O God,  
> so is your praise to the ends of the earth.  
> (Ps. XLVII, 11)

Therefore, “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are appellative names, while “God, God, and God” are proper names.

It is written:

> Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God.  
> (Deut. VI, 4)

In this testimony he united a threefold designation of God. “The Lord,” he says, “God, and God.” Thus you have what the Father, what the Son, and what the Holy Spirit is. And immediately he added, “is one”: the one who is one God in a trinity of persons.

## CHAPTER FIVE  
### On the Son of God the Father

*(Moralia, Book XXIX, chapter 1, no. 1; Book XXX, chapter 23, no. 68.)* The Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is the power and wisdom of God, was born from the Father before time—or rather, because he neither began to be born nor ceased to be born, let us speak more truly and say: he was always born.

We cannot say “he is always being born,” lest he appear to be imperfect. But so that he may be designated both eternal and perfect, let us say both “always” and “born”: “born” pertains to perfection, and “always” to eternity. Thus, in whatever way possible, that essence without time may be designated by temporal speech.

Our Redeemer could not be known by the human race in that divine birth. Therefore he came into humanity so that he might be seen, and he wished to be seen so that he might be imitated.

The Son of God the almighty Father, insofar as he is God, gives all things with the Father; but insofar as he is human, he received all things from the Father, as it is written:

> He gave him authority to execute judgment,  
> because he is the Son of man.  
> (John V, 27)

And again it is written:

> Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands.  
> (John XIII, 1)

Or, as he himself says:

> Everything that the Father gives me will come to me.  
> (John VI, 37)

*(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 3.)* In Sacred Scripture God is sometimes named by designation, and sometimes spoken of according to essence.

He is named by designation, as it is written:

> Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh.  
> (Exod. VII, 1)

And as the Psalmist says:

> God stands in the assembly of gods;  
> in the midst he judges among the gods.  
> (Ps. LXXXI, 1)

God is spoken of according to essence, as he himself says to Moses:

> I am the God of Abraham,  
> and the God of Isaac,  
> and the God of Jacob.  
> (Exod. III, 6)

Therefore the apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the designated name of God from the essential one, says:

> To them belong the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever.  
> (Rom. IV, 5)

The designated god is among all things, whereas the essential God is over all things. The apostle Paul, in order to show that Christ is God by nature, called him not merely “god” but “God over all,” because any righteous person may be called a god, but is not over all. Christ, however, is God over all because he is God by nature.

*(Moralia, Book XXIX, chapter 1, no. 1.)* The Son, born from the Father without time, consented to be born from his mother in time, so that by enclosing his birth between a beginning and an end he might open to the eyes of the human mind a birth that is neither taken up in a beginning nor confined by an end.

*(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 7.)* The Son is called the arm of the Lord because through him all things were made. Of him the Psalmist also says:

> Let your hand be with me to save me.  
> (Ps. CXVIII, 173)

The hand of God, which through divinity was not made but begotten, was made through humanity so that it might heal the wounds of the human race.

*(Ibid., no. 37.)* Almighty God, the Son of the Father, presiding over angels, archangels, and all the powers, is like the appearance of electrum: one from both natures and in both natures. He remained God with the Father and became mortal with humanity for our redemption.

*(Book XXX of the Moralia, chapter 4, no. 17.)* Almighty God, the Son of the Father, declares openly to his disciples that he announces the Father, because at that time, through the unveiled appearance of his majesty, he showed both how he arises equal from the one who begets him and how the Spirit of both proceeds, coeternal with both.

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 20.)* The invisible God, the Only-Begotten of the Father, is a hidden fountain. The same God incarnate is an open fountain. This open fountain is rightly called the house of David, because our Redeemer came to us from the lineage of David.

*(Book XXXI of the Moralia, chapter 26, no. 51.)* The spirit of our Redeemer is said to be in his nostrils, so that his knowledge may be understood to exist in foreknowledge: whatever he made known that he knew in the nature of his humanity, he certainly foreknew before the ages by his divinity.

Isaiah the prophet immediately adds why he had the spirit in his nostrils, saying:

> For he himself was regarded as exalted.  
> (Isa. II, 22)

It is as though he said: “He foreknew what was to come in the lower regions because he came down to the depths from the heavenly places.”

*(Book XIII of the Moralia, chapter 24, no. 27.)* God the Father is the witness of the Son, concerning whom he himself says in the Gospel:

> The Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me.  
> (John V, 37)

He is also rightly called his associate in knowledge, because the Father always works with the Son in one will and one counsel. He is also his witness because no one knows the Son except the Father.

## CHAPTER SIX  
### On the Holy Spirit

*(Book V of the Moralia, chapter 36, no. 65.)* The Holy Spirit, proceeding coeternally from the Father and the Son, is poured gently into the weakness of our understanding.

Yet when he comes upon the apostles, he is manifested **[through an outward sound, as through a mighty wind]**, when it is said:

> Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like the arrival of a mighty wind.  
> (Acts II, 2)

**[Note: [Col. 0737D] Our manuscript reads: “over the immensity of a most vehement spirit.”]**

Every creature is narrow in relation to the Creator, through that same Spirit who possesses nothing in himself or beside himself except himself always. And what is it for us always to seek the present except to breathe after the joy of eternity, to which nothing comes and from which nothing passes?

When the Holy Spirit insinuates himself into the weakness of human understanding, he is expressed both by the sound of a mighty Spirit and by the voice of a gentle breeze, because when he comes he is both mighty and gentle. He is gentle because he tempers his knowledge to our senses, so that it may somehow be known. He is mighty because, however much he tempers himself, by his coming he nevertheless disturbs the blindness of our weakness by illuminating it.

*(Book II on the Gospels, homily 30, no. 7.)* It is written concerning the Holy Spirit:

> His Spirit adorned the heavens.  
> (Job XXVI, 13)

The ornaments of heaven are the virtues of those who preach. Paul enumerates these ornaments, saying:

> To one is given through the Holy Spirit a word of wisdom;  
> to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit;  
> to another faith in the same Spirit;  
> to another gifts of healings in one Spirit;  
> to another the working of miracles;  
> to another prophecy;  
> to another the discernment of spirits;  
> to another kinds of tongues;  
> to another the interpretation of speeches.  
> All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes,  
> distributing to each as he wills.  
> (1 Cor. XII, 8–11)

**[Note: [Col. 0738D] The words preceding this are absent from our manuscript.]**

Therefore, as many as are the good qualities of those who preach, so many are the ornaments of heaven.

> By the word of the Lord the heavens were established,  
> and by the breath of his mouth all their power.  
> (Ps. XXXII, 6)

The Word of the Lord is the Son of the Father. But in order that these same heavens—that is, the holy apostles—might be shown to have been wrought by the whole Trinity together, the divinity of the Holy Spirit is immediately added:

> And by the breath of his mouth all their power.  
> (Col. 0738A–B)

The strength of the holy apostles was received from the Holy Spirit, because they would not have dared to oppose the powers of this world unless the strength of the Holy Spirit had made them steadfast.

*(Ibid., no. 6.)* I delight in raising the eyes of faith toward the power of this craftsman and considering, as though scattered before me, the Fathers of the New and Old Testaments.

Behold, with open eyes I look upon David, Amos, Daniel, Peter, Paul, and Matthew, and I wish to consider what kind of craftsman the Holy Spirit is.

The Holy Spirit fills the young harpist and makes him a psalmist (1 Sam. XVI, 18). He fills the shepherd who tends cattle and pricks sycamores and makes him a prophet (Amos VII, 14). He fills the abstinent boy and makes him a judge of elders (Dan. XIII, 46). He fills the fisherman and makes him a preacher (Matt. IV, 19). He fills the persecutor and makes him a teacher of the nations (Acts IX, 1). He fills the tax collector and makes him an evangelist (Luke V, 27–28).

O what a craftsman the Holy Spirit is! No delay is involved in teaching **[Edit.: learning]**; he acts in whatever he wills. As soon as he touches the mind, he teaches. To touch it is itself to have taught it. For as soon as he illuminates the human mind, he changes it: suddenly he rejects what it was and presents what it was not.

*(Book XXX of the Moralia, chapter 4, no. 17.)* After this life we shall openly see how the Son arises equal to the Father who begets him; how the Spirit of both proceeds, coeternal with both; how that which, in being born, is subsequent to the one from whom it arises is not later than him; and how the one produced through procession is not preceded by those who produce him.

Then we shall openly see how one is three divisibly and three are one indivisibly.

## CHAPTER SEVEN  
### On the Trinity and the unity of the Godhead

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 47, no. 7.)* The spiritual Fathers of the Old Testament believed almighty God to be a Trinity, just as the Fathers of the New Testament spoke openly of the same Trinity.

David, likewise holding this belief, says:

> May God, our God, bless us;  
> may God bless us.  
> (Ps. LXVI, 8)

Although he had said “God” three times, in order to show that this was one, he added:

> And may all the ends of the earth fear him.  
> (Rom. XI, 16)

The apostle Paul says:

> For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.

“From him,” namely from the Father; “through him,” through the Son; “in him,” in the Holy Spirit. When he had thus spoken of him three times, he added:

> To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

For by not saying “to them” but “to him,” while saying “him” three times, he distinguished the persons; and by adding “to him be glory,” he did not divide the substance.

*(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 19.)* Whether we seek to contemplate the Trinity of almighty God in its own nature or consider investigating its hidden judgments, because its heights are impenetrable to us, whatever good we thought might exist in us becomes contemptible in our eyes.

And we who believed ourselves to fly into even a small measure of knowledge stand humbly with our wings lowered, weighing the invisible nature above us and its impenetrable judgments [Col. 0739A–B].

Moses said:

> In the beginning God made heaven and earth.  
> (Gen. I, 1)

And shortly afterward he continued:

> And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.

The Spirit is the third person in the Trinity.

*(Saint Augustine, Dialogue with Orosius, question 1, and Dialogue on the Unity of the Holy Trinity.)* Without doubt, under the name “God” the Father is to be understood; under the name “beginning,” the Son; and under the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit himself.

God is a Trinity in the one who begets, the one begotten, and the one proceeding—that is, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—in appellative or relative names. In proper names, however, there are “God, God, and God.” This triple designation is not admitted, because God is one.

If the Trinity did not exist in relative names, Jesus would never have said:

> Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father,  
> and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.  
> (Matt. XVIII, 19)

He thereby taught the Trinity in the relative names of the persons, while showing the name “God,” which is not tripled, in its singularity.

## CHAPTER EIGHT  
### That no succession of times is to be ascribed to God
In almighty God, the times that are to come always exist as present; for neither do future things arrive for him, nor do past things depart, but all things stand together before his eyes. Eternity has no “having been” or “being destined to be”; for it neither does the past pass away nor does the future supervene, because it sees all things as present. (Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 8.)

Divine eternity precedes all times, and in God nothing is believed to be past, present, or future; rather, all things are said to be present in him, because by his eternity he embraces everything. Otherwise God would have to be considered changeable if successions of time were attributed to him. If certain times always existed with God, it would not be time but eternity; nor would times change, but they would subsist in eternal stability. Having a present, past, and future belongs to us, not to God.

Nor is the departure or arrival of the angels themselves a succession of times. There are, indeed, two things among created beings to which the alternation of times does not apply: the angels, because they cleave to the unchangeable Creator; and that formless matter which existed before all those things that now revolve temporally were formed from it—for even then time did not apply to it. It is understood that time pertains not to those creatures that are above the heavens, but to those that are beneath the heavens. For times neither approach nor succeed except for us, who dwell beneath the heavens in this lowest world.

## CHAPTER IX. That the invisible God is recognized through the beauty of creation.

(From Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 4.) The bodily greatness of created things is often compared with the incorporeal greatness of the Creator, so that great things may be considered from small ones, invisible things judged from visible ones, and the maker of the work recognized from the beauty of what has been made—not, however, through an equal likeness, but through a certain subordinate and created form of goodness.

Just as art turns praise back upon the artist, so the Creator of things is praised through his creature. How much more excellent he is is shown by the very condition of his work. God causes his beauty, which cannot be circumscribed, to be understood from the beauty of circumscribed creation, so that by the very footprints through which man turned away, he may return to God. Since, through love of the beauty of creation, he withdrew from the form of the Creator, let him return once more through the splendor of creation to the beauty of the Creator.

By certain stages of understanding, man advances through creation toward understanding God the Creator: that is, rising from insensible things to sensible things, from sensible things to rational things, and from rational things to the Creator. Intelligible beings praise God in themselves; irrational and insensible things do not praise him in themselves, but through us, when, by contemplating them, we praise God. Yet they are said to praise him because the cause of their existence produces that same praise.

The ancients said that nothing is so dull that it does not possess some sense directed toward God. Hence the spark that is struck from hard flint. And if there is fire in the stone, then surely a kind of sense is perceived there where life itself does not perceive itself.

## CHAPTER X. That certain forms derived from human affections are referred to God.

The power of the divine majesty, which created all things without necessity, presides over all without disdain, sustains everything without labor, governs without occupation, and corrects without agitation. Thus it readily shapes human minds toward whatever it wills, without passing into the shadow of diversity from the light of its own unchangeableness.

Divine words accommodate themselves to human limbs, so that the work of the omnipotent Lord may in some measure be grasped by man. (Book XVII of the *Moralia*, chapter 2, no. 2.)

It must be understood that God is never properly said to remember. For one who cannot forget, how can he remember? But because we embrace those whom we remember and distance those whom we hate, God is said, in accordance with human usage, to remember when he grants gifts, and to forget when he abandons someone in guilt.

Almighty God weighs all things and considers everything without interruption or alternation. He remembers the good, though he never forgets them; and he does not remember the wicked, though he always beholds them in judgment. It is as though God returns to the memory of the good, which he nevertheless never abandoned; and as though he does not look upon the wicked, whose deeds he considers, while reserving the judgment of condemnation against them at the end. (Book V of the *Moralia*, chapter 18, no. 37.)

When we become angry, we are inflamed by the breath of fury. Therefore, when the Lord is shown as contemplating vengeance, he is said to blow in anger. This does not mean that his nature undergoes a change of state, but that, after long patience, when he executes vengeance upon the sinner, he who is tranquil in himself appears turbulent to those who perish.

The reprobate mind, because it sees the judge opposed to its deeds, is as though he were shown to be agitated; for it is itself disturbed by its guilt in his sight. In our usage God is said to be jealous or to grieve. But there is no disturbance from these motions in God, with whom there is eternal tranquility.

God provides so mercifully for human weakness that, since we cannot recognize him as he is, he makes himself known to us according to the manner of our speech. Hence he is also written to possess the qualities of our limbs, and he wished what is unworthy of him—namely, the passions—to be called worthy of him, so that through what belongs to us he might draw us toward what belongs to him, and, by accommodating himself to us, enable us to rise toward him.

In many ways God draws forms from lower things to himself in order to signify himself to human beings. Yet it is certain that, according to his proper substance, he is invisible and incorporeal.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the wonders of God.

[Col. 0741C] (*Moralia* VI, 15, no. 18.) What human being is sufficient to investigate the wonders of almighty God: that he created all things from nothing; that the very structure of the world was ordered by the wondrous power of his might; that the heavens are suspended above the air and the earth balanced above the abyss; that this whole universe consists of invisible and visible things; that the eternal God made man, gathering together, so to speak, in a small compass another world, but a rational one; and that, forming man from soul and flesh, he mingled spirit and clay by an arrangement of power that cannot be investigated?

From God’s wondrous creation we know one thing and are another; yet we neglect to wonder, because those things that are wondrous through incomprehensible investigation have become cheap in human eyes. Thus, if a dead man were raised, everyone would leap up in amazement; yet daily a man who did not exist is born, and no one wonders—although it is undoubtedly clear to all that creating what did not exist is greater than restoring what did exist.

Because Aaron’s dry staff blossomed, everyone wondered. Daily a tree is produced from dry earth, and the power of dust is turned into wood, yet no one wonders. Because five thousand men were satisfied with five loaves, everyone wondered that food increased in their mouths. Daily scattered grains multiply into the fullness of ears of grain, yet no one wonders. When they saw water once changed into wine, everyone wondered. Daily the moisture of the earth, drawn into the root of the vine, is changed through the cluster into wine, yet no one wonders.

Blessed Job, when he said, “He does great things,” immediately added, “and unsearchable things” (Job 5:9). For it would have been less to do great things if what had been done could nevertheless have been investigated. He rightly added also, “and wondrous things without number,” because his greatness would have been less if he had made few things that are unsearchable. (No. 19.)

It must undoubtedly be understood that divine miracles should always be considered through diligent study, but never dissected by human understanding. Often the human mind, seeking the explanation of certain things and failing to find it, plunges itself into an abyss of doubt.

Thus some people observe the bodies of the dead reduced to dust; and, because they cannot gather from reason how the power of resurrection works, they despair that those bodies will return to their former state. The miracles of God, which must be believed through faith, are not to be investigated by reason. If reason could unfold them to our eyes, they would not be wondrous.

When the mind perhaps falters before the wonders of God, it must bring back to memory those things that it knows by experience but cannot comprehend by reason, so that an example of a similar matter may strengthen the faith which it discovers to be weakened by its own cleverness.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the condition [the printed reading *conaitione* is uncertain] or perpetuity of the angels, and the ruin of the proud.

The angels were created in such a way that, if they willed, they could remain in the light of blessedness; but, if they did not will it, they could also fall. Hence Satan fell with the legions that followed him. But after his fall, the angels who remained were so strengthened that they could not fall at all. (Book XXVII of the *Moralia*, chapter 39, no. 65.)

The angelic powers that remained fixed in divine love received this as a reward when the proud angels fell: that they would no longer be gnawed by the rust of creeping sin, that they would remain in contemplation of the Creator without end to their happiness, and that they would persist in eternal stability in the condition in which they had been created.

In Moses, the words concerning the historical origin of the world bear witness to this, when heaven is first said to have been made and afterward called the firmament (Gen. 1:6). For the angelic nature was first created subtle in the higher regions, and afterward, lest it should ever be able to fall, was more wondrously confirmed.

When the holy angels see the losses of their own nature in those who are falling, they now stand more cautiously and more firmly in themselves. (*Moralia* XXXIV, 7, no. 13.)

Thus, with the Lord of all things wondrously arranging everything, it comes about that even the heavenly homeland of the elect spirits benefits from the loss caused by its own ruin, since it has been more firmly built up from the place where it had been partly destroyed. [Note: Col. 0741D, edition: “even the losses caused by its own ruin benefit.”]

When the first angel fell from the citadel of blessedness, it is certain that the elect angels also trembled at his fall. When the fall of pride expelled him from their number, that very fear made them stand more firmly. It is written concerning the apostate angel: “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified” (Job 41:16).

They were purified, because when he departed with his reprobate legions, only those who would live blessedly remained in the heavenly dwellings. (No. 13.) Satan’s fall both terrified and purified the good angels: it terrified them lest they should proudly despise their Creator; it purified them because, when the reprobate departed, the elect alone remained.

God, the maker of all things, who knows how to use even the evil action of the reprobate for the protection of the good, turned the fall of the angels who fell into the advancement of those who remained. From the place where the guilt of the proud was punished, an increase of merits was found and strengthened in the humble angels; for when the former fell, it was granted to the latter that they could not fall at all. (*Moralia* XXXII, chapter 23, nos. 47–48.)

That first apostate angel is capable of so much strength because the Creator made him first in the substance of created things, as it is written in the Book of Job: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40:14). For when God made all things, he created him first and made him more eminent than the other angels.

He is said to have been made beautiful in many ways and with dense foliage, because he was set over the other legions of angels, and such beauty made him more splendid in proportion as the multitude of angels placed beneath him adorned him. The apostate angel had in the paradise of God as many dense branches, so to speak, as he saw legions of heavenly spirits placed beneath him.

He was condemned without pardon when he sinned because he had been created great beyond comparison. Through the prophet Ezekiel it is said to the apostate angel: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:12–13).

Since he was about to speak of his greatness at length, the prophet embraced everything in his first phrase. What good did the first angel not possess, if he was the seal of the likeness of God? From the seal of a ring a likeness is impressively expressed such as is substantially present in the seal itself.

Although man was created in the likeness of God, the prophet, as though attributing something greater to the apostate angel, does not say that he was created in the likeness of God, but that he was himself the seal of God’s likeness. Thus, the subtler the nature, the more fully the likeness of God is believed to have been expressed in him.

The prophet Ezekiel, still considering the height of the apostate angel’s authority, adds: “You were an outstretched cherub, protecting on the holy mountain of God; you walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones” (Ezek. 28:14).

“Cherub” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” He is therefore called a cherub because he is undoubtedly believed to have surpassed all the angels in knowledge. He walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones because, among the ranks of angels, he shone with the glory of his creation, like one burning with the fire of charity. (No. 49.)

The prophet indicates such wondrous things about the apostate angel—what he possessed and what he lost—in order to show terrified humanity what it will suffer from the guilt of pride if it becomes arrogant, since God did not spare him by striking him down even though, by creating him, he had raised him to the glory of such great splendor. (*Moralia* IV, chapter 1, no. 5.)

An angelic spirit, or a human soul, is immortal in such a way that it can die, and mortal in such a way that it cannot die. For it ceases to live blessedly if it destroys itself through vice or punishment. But it does not lose essential life either through vice or through punishment. It falls away from the quality of living, but it does not experience annihilation in its manner of subsisting, even when it dies.

To put it briefly: it is both immortally mortal and mortally immortal. The elect spirits of the angels, when they saw others fall through pride, themselves stood more firmly and more humbly; for those inhabitants of the heavenly region gained even from their losses, and that region was more solidly prepared for the state of eternity through the destruction suffered in part by its own members.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the nine orders of angels.

[Col. 0744B] (*Moralia* XVII, chapter 13, no. 18.) Human reason cannot know the number of the heavenly spirits, because it does not know how great is that multitude of the invisible army of which it is rightly said: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10).

The number of the heavenly citizens is expressed as both infinite and definite, so that what is countable to God may be shown to be uncountable for us. To stand before God is one thing; to minister is another. Those angelic powers undoubtedly stand before God that do not go out to announce certain things to human beings. Those minister who come to carry out the duties of messengers; nevertheless, through contemplation they do not depart from the innermost presence.

And because there are more who minister than those who principally stand before God, the number of those who stand is shown as though definite, while that of those who minister is shown as indefinite. (Book II on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 14.)

The prophet Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (Isa. 6:1). The throne of God is the angelic or human creature over which he presides through the understanding he has given it. Isaiah calls this throne high and lifted up because human nature, raised to heavenly glory, advances, and the angelic creature, having already been strengthened in heaven through the fall of many spirits so that it will not fall, has been lifted up from the place where it was confirmed.

His temple is the same as his throne, because the eternal King dwells where he sits. (Book II on the Gospels, homily 34, nos. 6–7.)

The Lord created the nature of angels and human beings so that they might know him. Since he willed that this nature should endure unto eternity, he undoubtedly created it in his own likeness.

There are nine orders of angels. But, in order to complete the number of the elect, man was created as the tenth. He did not perish from his Creator even after his sin, because eternal Wisdom, shining with miracles through the flesh, restored him from the light of the vessel of clay.

We have said that there are nine orders of angels because, as sacred speech testifies, we know that there are angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim.

Nearly all the pages of sacred eloquence testify to the existence of angels and archangels; and, as is well known, the books of the prophets often speak of cherubim and seraphim. The apostle Paul also enumerates the names of four orders to the Ephesians, saying: “Above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion” (Eph. 1:21). Likewise, to the Colossians he says: “Whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers” (Col. 1:16).

He had already described dominions, principalities, and powers when speaking to the Ephesians. But, when he was also going to mention them to the Colossians, he prefaced them with thrones, of which he had not yet said anything to the Ephesians.

When, therefore, thrones are joined to the four that he had previously named to the Ephesians—principalities, powers, virtues, and dominions—five orders are specifically expressed. When angels and archangels, cherubim and seraphim are added to these, it is undoubtedly found that there are nine orders of angels.

Through the prophet it is said to the angel who was created first: “You were a cherub, the seal of likeness, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:12).

Here it must be noted that he is said not to have been made in the likeness of God, but to have been the seal of likeness, so that the subtler the nature in him, the more closely the image of God might be understood to have been expressed in him.

Immediately afterward the passage continues: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (ibid., 13).

Behold, nine names of stones are mentioned, because there are plainly nine orders of angels. The first angel was adorned and covered with these orders because, having been placed over all the angelic ranks, he was more splendid by comparison with them.

In Greek, angels are called *angeloi*, “messengers,” while archangels are called *archangeloi*, “chief messengers.” (No. 8.)

It must also be understood that “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. Those holy spirits of the heavenly homeland are always spirits, but they cannot always be called angels, because they are angels only when something is announced through them.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Who makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4), as though he plainly said: “He makes those whom he always possesses as spirits into angels also, whenever he wills.”

It must be understood with particular care that those who announce lesser things are called angels, while those who announce greater things are called archangels. This is why Gabriel the archangel, not just any angel, was sent to the Virgin Mary. It was fitting that one who announced the greatest of all things should come for this greatest ministry.

The holy angels are designated by personal names, so that their names may also indicate what they are capable of accomplishing in their work. And when they come to minister something to us, among us they also derive names from their ministries. (No. 9.)

Whenever something of wondrous power is done, Michael is said to be sent, so that from both the deed and the name it may be understood that no one can do what God is able to do. “Michael” is interpreted as “Who is like God?”

Gabriel is called “the strength of God.” Gabriel, who is called the strength of God, was also sent to Mary. He came to announce the one who, in order to conquer the powers of the air, deigned to appear in humility.

Raphael is interpreted as “the medicine of God,” because, when he touched Tobias’s eyes as though performing the office of healing, he wiped away the darkness of his blindness. Since he was sent to heal, it was fitting that he should be called the medicine of God.

But since we have briefly touched upon the names of the holy angels by interpreting them, what remains is to explain briefly the names of their offices. (No. 10.)

Those spirits through whom signs and miracles are more frequently performed are called virtues. Those are called powers who have received this more powerfully than the others in their order, so that hostile virtues are subjected to their authority and restrained by their power from being able to tempt human hearts as much as they wish.

Those are called principalities who preside even over the good spirits of the angels. While arranging whatever good things must be done among those subject to them, they exercise principality over them in fulfilling the divine ministries.

Those are called dominions who transcend even the powers of the principalities by a lofty superiority. Thus those ranks of angels that excel through wondrous power are called dominions because the others are subjected to them for obedience.

Those ranks are called thrones over which almighty God always presides in order to exercise judgment. Since in Latin we call thrones *seats*, those are called thrones who are so filled with the grace of divinity that the Lord sits in them and decrees his judgments through them. Hence the Psalmist says: “You sit upon the throne, judging righteousness” (Ps. 9:5).

“Cherubim” means “fullness of knowledge.” Those higher ranks are therefore called cherubim because they are filled with more perfect knowledge in proportion as they contemplate the brightness of God more closely. In accordance with the measure of a creature, they know all things more fully insofar as, by the merit of their dignity, they draw nearer to the vision of their Creator.

Those ranks of holy spirits that burn with incomparable love because of their singular nearness to their Creator are called seraphim. Seraphim means “burning” or “kindling.” Because they are so joined to God that no other spirits stand between them and God, they burn more intensely insofar as they see him more closely.

Their flame is certainly the ardor of charity, because the more subtly they behold the brightness of his divinity, the more powerfully they burn with love for him. (No. 11.)

That heavenly city consists of angels and human beings. We believe that as many human beings will ascend to it as elect angels happened to remain there, as it is written: “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. 32:8).

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the holy angels who preside over the nations.

(*Moralia* XVII, chapter 12, no. 17.) Since supreme peace is maintained among the lofty orders of angels, what is the meaning of the words spoken by the angel to Daniel: “I came because of your words; but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Dan. 10:13)?

A little later the angel says: “Now I will return to fight against the prince of Persia. When I was going out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming” (ibid., 20).

Whom else does he call the princes of the nations except angels, who could have resisted him as he went out? How, then, can there be peace in the heights if even among the angelic spirits themselves there is a struggle of battle, when they always stand before the sight of Truth?

Certain angelic ministries have been placed over the governance of the individual nations. When the conduct of those subject to them deserves the assistance of the spirits appointed over them against one another, the spirits who preside are said to come against each other.

The angel who spoke to Daniel is recognized as having been placed over the Israelite captives who were settled in Persia. Michael is found to have been appointed over those of the same people who remained in the land of Judea.

Hence this same angel says to Daniel a little later: “I have no helper against all these except Michael your prince” (ibid., 21). He also says what we cited above: “Behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (ibid., 13). Since Michael is said not to have been present with him but to have come to his aid, it is openly recognized that he was placed over the people who were being held captive in another region.

What does it mean for the angel to say, “I came because of your words; but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me” (ibid., 13), except that he is announcing to his subjects the actions assigned to him? It is as though he plainly said:

“The merits of your prayers demand that the Israelite people be released from the yoke of their captivity. But there is still something in that people that must be purified under Persian rule. Therefore the prince of Persia rightly opposes me in securing their release, although the tears of those who were left in Judea assist your prayers.”

The angel who spoke to Daniel said: “Michael your prince came to help me.” When he went out to fight against the prince of Persia, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming toward him.

From this it is indicated that Judea had committed something against the Greeks, whose cause was resisting its release. The angel hears the prophet’s prayers, but the prince of Persia resists, because, although the life of the righteous man praying already demands the release of the people, the life of that same people still contradicts it. Since those who had been led into captivity had not yet been fully purified, the Persians still rightly ruled over them.

Michael helps, but the prince of the Greeks comes to battle, because the long captivity of the oppressed could indeed have merited pardon; yet what they had also committed against the Greeks stood in the way of their release.

It is rightly said that the angels come against one another, because the merits of the nations entrusted to them contradict one another in turn. For the lofty spirits who preside over those nations do not fight on behalf of those acting unjustly; rather, they examine their deeds by judging them justly.

When the guilt or righteousness of any nation is brought before the council of the heavenly court, the spirit appointed over that nation is said either to have prevailed in the contest or not to have prevailed. Yet the victory of all of them is one: the supreme will of their Maker over them; because they always behold it, they never will what they are unable to obtain.

## CHAPTER XV. That evil has no substance, but was first discovered by the devil.

[Col. 0748A]

(Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XVIII, chapter 14; likewise, *Enchiridion*, chapters 12–15.) Evil is not a nature, but this name has been given to the privation of good. Every nature is good: great if it cannot be corrupted, small if it can. Therefore what is called evil would not exist if there were no good. But good that lacks every evil is complete good. Whatever contains evil is a good that has been damaged or made defective.

Nor can any evil exist where there is no good at all. Evil would not exist in any way unless what is good existed, since every nature is good; nor would anything be evil if the thing itself that is evil were not a nature.

Every nature, even if it is defective, is good insofar as it is a nature; insofar as it is defective, it is evil. Evils arise from good things and exist only in certain good things. There was no source from which any nature of evil could arise. For if it existed, then, insofar as it was a nature, it would certainly be good.

There was absolutely no source from which evil could first arise except the good nature of an angel and of a human being. From the good nature of a human being there can arise either a good will or an evil will. Accordingly, we speak of a good angel and an evil angel, a good person and an evil person. The good is what belongs to the angel; the evil is what belongs to the defective one. The good is what belongs to the human being; the evil is what belongs to the defective one.

When we say “good,” we praise the nature. When we say “evil,” we detect not the nature but the defect that exists in the good nature. (The same, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 11.)

Therefore evil did not exist anywhere or at any time from which the devil could become evil. Rather, because evil is a defect, while he was a good angel he became evil through pride. Hence evil is rightly said to have been discovered by him. Evil was therefore not created by the devil but discovered; and for this reason evil is nothing, because it has no substance. For without God nothing was made, but God did not make evil.

Heretics believe that the mind was created by God and defects by the devil, and from this they suppose that there are two natures, a good one and an evil one. But defects are not a nature; and although they truly come from the devil, they were not created.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the beginning of the world and the creation of heaven and earth.

[Col. 0748D] (*Moralia* XXXII, chapter 12, no. 16.) The substance of things was created all at once, but their visible form was not formed all at once. What existed simultaneously in the substance of matter did not appear simultaneously in the form of its visible shape.

When heaven and earth are described as having been made together, it is indicated that spiritual and bodily things were made together, that everything arising from heaven was made together, and that everything produced from the earth was made together. Moses had said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1).

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 1, no. 2.) But who would believe that he was speaking truthfully about the past if he had not also said something about the future? At the end of the very book whose beginning contained those statements about the past, he mingled a prophecy concerning future things through the voice of Jacob, saying: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10).

(*Moralia* XXXII, chapter 12, no. 26.)
