The one who had narrated that heaven and earth, shrubs, and grasses were created on different days now reveals that they were made in a single day, so that he might clearly show that all creation came into existence simultaneously in substance, although it did not come forth simultaneously in visible form.

(From Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 10.) The order of the world must be considered from the single example of a human being. For just as man moves toward his end through the stages of his ages, so the world, by being extended through time, declines. For by the same process through which man and the world appear to grow, both are diminished.

(Augustine, *Confessions*, book XII, chapter 29.) The matter from which the world was formed preceded the things made from it in origin, though not in time, as sound precedes song. Sound is prior to song because the sweetness of the melody belongs to the sound of the voice, not the sound to the sweetness. Thus both exist together, but the one to which the song belongs—that is, the sound—is prior.

The matter from which heaven and earth were formed was called formless because those things that remained to be formed had not yet been formed from it. Yet the matter itself had been made from nothing.

It is one thing for something to be able to come into being and another for it to be necessary that it come into being. What God has implanted in natures must come into being; what can come into being is what the Creator, outside the appointed course of natures, wished to reserve so that he might at some time bring it about.

(Augustine, *Confessions*, book XIII, chapters 6–7.) After the creation of heaven and earth had been recounted, the Spirit is named in Genesis (1:3), so that, since it was necessary to say that he was borne above the waters, those things should first be named over which the Holy Spirit, their Creator, was said to be borne. The Apostle also indicates this (Rom. 5:5), when he demonstrates the way of charity that surpasses all things.

The Spirit is therefore said to be borne above the waters because he is the gift of God, in whom we who subsist find rest, and because, by protecting us, he is borne above us.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the essence of heaven and earth will subsist forever.

(*Moralia* XVII, chapter 9, no. 11.) Heaven and earth pass away with respect to the appearance they now possess, but in essence they subsist without end. Hence Paul says: “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:31). Hence Truth itself says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). Hence it is said to John by an angelic voice: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21:1).

These will not be created as different things; rather, these same things will be renewed. Heaven and earth both pass away and will remain, because they are cleansed by fire from the form they now possess, yet are preserved forever in their own nature.

Hence the Psalmist says: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Ps. 102:27). At the end of this age, heaven and earth announce to us their final transformation through the very alternations by which they unceasingly change for our use.

The earth declines from its winter appearance through dryness and becomes green again through the moisture of spring. From this, then, let every believer understand both that the form of heaven and earth perishes and that it is restored through renewal—although now it is continually repaired, as it were, from decline through the successive alternation of its forms.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the distinction of creatures.

(Moral., Book IV, chapter 20, no. 55.) From insensible things we learn what we should think about sensible and intelligible things. For the earth is made fruitful by the air, while the air is ordered according to the quality of the sky. Human beings rule over animals, angels over human beings, and archangels over angels. That human beings rule over animals we both see from experience and learn from the words of the Psalmist, who says: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet, all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field” (Ps. VIII, 8).

That angels rule over human beings is attested by the angel speaking through the prophet: “The prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me” (Dan. X, 13). That angels are administered by the powers of higher angels is affirmed by the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Behold, the angel who was speaking in me went out, and another angel went out to meet him; and he said to him: Run, speak to that boy, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall” (Zech. II, 3). For if the highest powers did not arrange the lowest in the offices of the holy spirits, the angel would in no way have learned from another angel what he should say to the human being.

Because the Creator of all things holds everything in himself, yet governs all things by assigning some to administer others, in order to distinguish the beautiful order of the universe, we rightly understand the angelic spirits to be rulers: the more familiarly they serve the Author of all things, the more they govern those subject to them. Human beings would have rested with the angels if they had not wished to follow the tongue of the tempter. Hence the angels are not improperly called “consuls,” because they care for the spiritual commonwealth while joining us to themselves as companions in the kingdom. When, through the announcements of the holy angels, we recognize the will of the Creator, we undoubtedly find in them counsel amid the distress of our tribulation.

## CHAPTER XIX. That rational creation, angels and human beings, was created simultaneously

(Moral. XXXII, chapter 12, no. 17.) It cannot be doubted that every creature was created simultaneously by God the Creator, who in his action is in no way stretched out by the prolongation of time. And if we examine the causes of things with subtle inquiry, we understand that the angel and the human being were made simultaneously—not, to be sure, by unity of time, but by the understanding of reason; simultaneously through the image of wisdom they received, but not simultaneously through the joined substance of their form.

It is written concerning the human being: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). And through Ezekiel it is said to Satan: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of paradise” (Ezek. XXVIII, 12). Thus, in the whole of creation, the human being and the angel came into existence simultaneously, because they proceeded distinct from every irrational nature. In the entire order of created things, no rational animal exists except the angel and the human being. Whatever cannot use reason was not made together with the human being.

(Moral. Book IX, chapter 49, no. 75.) Although all things were created through the coeternal Word of the Father, nevertheless the very manner of creation shows how greatly the human being is preferred to all animals and to the heavenly, though insensible, things. “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. CXLVIII, 5). But when God resolves to make the human being, he first says what must be considered with reverence: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). For it is not written of him, as of the other things, “Let it be,” and it was made (ibid. 3); nor, as the water produced the flying creatures, did the earth produce the human being. Rather, before he was made, it is said, “Let us make,” so that, because a rational creature was being created, he might appear to have been made, as it were, with deliberation.

The human being was fashioned from the earth, as it were, through deliberate workmanship, and was raised up by the Creator’s inspiration in the power of the living spirit, so that he who was made in the Creator’s image might exist not through the voice of command but through the dignity of the work. It is written: “God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he made them” (Gen. I, 27).

(Moral. Book XXXII, chapter 12, no. 16.) Eve has not yet been described as made, and already the human being is declared to be male and female. But because the woman was undoubtedly to proceed from Adam’s side, she is already counted in him according to the substance from which she was to be produced according to form.

We can consider this even in the smallest things, so that from the smallest we may reflect upon the greater. When a plant is created, neither fruit nor seed is yet visible in it. Nevertheless, even when it is not apparent, fruit and seed are present in it, because they are surely together in the substance of the root, though they do not emerge together through the stages of time.

(Moral. Book IV, chapter 3, no. 8.) God had made two creatures capable of understanding him, namely the angelic and the human. Pride struck both and broke them from the state of their innate uprightness. But one possessed the covering of flesh, whereas the other bore nothing weak from flesh. The angel is spirit alone, while the human being is both spirit and flesh.

Therefore, the Creator, in order to redeem the human being, had to bring back to himself the flesh which, in the perpetration of sin, plainly possessed some element of weakness. And he had to thrust the apostate angel down more deeply because, when he fell from the strength of perseverance, he bore nothing weak from flesh.

The Psalmist rightly, when saying that the Redeemer had mercy on human beings, also expressed the very reason for the mercy, saying: “And he remembered that they were flesh” (Ps. LXXVII, 39). It is as though he said: “Because he saw their weakness, he did not wish to punish their sins with strict severity.”

There is still another reason why fallen humanity had to be restored, whereas the proud spirit could not be restored: namely, that the angel fell through his own malice, while the human being was cast down through another’s.

## CHAPTER XX. On the perfection of the number seven

The whole course of time unfolds in seven days. For the eternal day that follows when the succession of seven days has been completed is the eighth day.

(Gregory, Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 4, no. 2.) Hence, when the Psalmist considered the day of the resurrection and was about to speak of the severity of the final judgment, he prefaced it with the title: “For the end: a psalm of David, for the eighth” (Ps. VI, 1). To show which eighth day he meant, he followed it at the beginning of the psalm with that day of terrifying dread, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (ibid. 2).

(Moral., Book XXXV, chapter 8, no. 16.) The number seven indicates the perfection of eternity, since the seventh day is called sanctified for the Lord’s rest. It is not said that evening is present in it, because the rest of eternal blessedness is confined by no boundary. Hence also, when the law was given, the seventh day was commanded to be a day of rest (Lev. XXV, 8–9), so that eternal rest might be signified through it.

(No. 17.) That the totality of the present life is signified by the number seven is shown more clearly when an eight is also added after it. When another number follows seven, the ending of time is expressed by the very addition, namely, that completed times are enclosed by eternity. It is written: “Give a portion to seven, and indeed also to eight” (Eccl. XI, 2).

Through the number seven, the present time, which is accomplished in seven days, is expressed; through the number eight, perpetual life is signified, which the Lord nevertheless revealed to us through his resurrection. He rose on the Lord’s Day, which, following the seventh day—that is, the Sabbath—is found to be the eighth from the creation.

(No. 16.) In the course of years, the number seven, multiplied seven times, with one unit added, reaches fifty, so that the most sacred rest of the jubilee, signifying perpetual blessedness, may be observed.

(No. 15.) The number seven is regarded by the wise men of this age as perfect according to a certain principle of its own, because it is completed from the first even number and the first odd number. The first odd number is three, and the first even number is four. Seven consists of these two numbers, and when it is multiplied by its own parts it rises to twelve. For whether we multiply three by four or four by three, we arrive at twelve.

But because we have received the categories of truth as a gift from above, we trample these notions underfoot, looking down upon them from the height of fixed knowledge. We retain this without doubt through unshaken faith: that those whom the sevenfold Spirit of grace fills, he perfects, granting them not only knowledge of the Trinity but also the operation of the four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the soul and its senses

[Col. 0752D]

(Moral., Book XI, chapter 33, no. 45.) In sacred Scripture, teeth are sometimes understood as the inner senses, as Jeremiah testifies when he says: “He broke my teeth according to the number” (Lam. III, 16). Food is broken by the teeth so that it may be swallowed. Hence we rightly understand the inner senses by the teeth, since they, as it were, chew and break up each individual thing that they think about and send it to the stomach of memory.

The prophet calls the inner senses of the soul teeth broken according to number, because blindness of understanding is generated in the senses according to the measure of each person’s sin. In proportion to what each person has done outwardly, he becomes dull in that which he could have understood concerning inner and invisible things.

“Every person who eats a sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge” (Ezek. XVIII, 2; Jer. XXXI, 30). What is a sour grape except sin? A sour grape is fruit before its time. Whoever desires to be satisfied with the pleasures of the present life hastens, as it were, to eat fruit before its time.

Whoever eats a sour grape has his teeth set on edge, because the person who feeds on the pleasure of the present world has his inner senses bound, so that he can no longer chew—that is, understand—spiritual things. For by what they have delighted in outwardly, by that they become dull within. And while the soul feeds on sin, it cannot eat the bread of righteousness, because teeth bound by the habit of sin can in no way eat what tastes righteous within.

We must consider carefully what the righteous customarily do. Whenever they detect in themselves anything carnal, however slight, they reconsider it in their inner senses and pursue it fiercely within themselves; they wear themselves down through affliction and, by great torments, judge and condemn even the least sinful things in themselves through repentance.

The elect act daily so that, as far as possible, they may themselves be found irreproachable in the sight of the eternal Judge; and those who see them judging themselves in this way are stirred to correct themselves from more serious faults.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the condition of the first human being

(Moral., Book XXV, chapter 3, no. 4; Book XI, chapter 50, no. 68; Book XXV, chapter 3, no. 4; Book IV, chapter 28, no. 54.) The first human being was created in such a way that, while he remained, time would pass, but he himself would not pass away with time. He stood while the moments flowed onward, because he was in no way advancing toward the end of life through the increase of days.

Before sin, the first human being could possess a fixed state, because time passed while he stood. He stood more firmly the more closely he clung to the One who always stands. But after he sinned, he placed himself, as it were, on a kind of slippery ground of temporality. And because he ate the forbidden food, he immediately discovered the failure of his state. As soon as he had offended the Creator, he began to proceed along with time.

For this purpose the human being had been created in paradise: if he bound himself to obedience to his Creator by the bonds of love, he would eventually pass without the death of the flesh to the heavenly homeland of the angels. Thus the first human being was created immortal, yet in such a way that, if he sinned, he could die; and he was created mortal in such a way that, if he did not sin, he could not die [Note: [Col. 0753D] The edition reads more correctly, “could also not die.”]—and through the merit of free choice he could attain the blessedness of that region in which he could neither sin nor die.

In the happiness of eternal blessedness, to which the elect pass after the time of redemption, with death intervening, the first parents could undoubtedly also have been transferred without the death of their bodies if they had remained in the state of their creation.

The first human being possessed a kind of silence when he received free choice against his enemy. But because he willingly succumbed to him, he immediately found within himself something that clamored against him. Although the human being had been created in silence by the Author, once he had willingly subjected himself to the enemy, he endured the cries of battle. For the very suggestion of the flesh is, as it were, a kind of cry against the quiet of the mind.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the trees of paradise and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil

(Moral., Book XXXV, chapter 14, no. 29.) There was certainly no evil tree in paradise, the touching of which God forbade the human being. But so that the well-created human being might grow more fully through the merit of obedience, it was fitting that he should be prohibited even from something good. In this way, the virtue he practiced would be all the more genuine: by refraining even from something good, he would show himself all the more humbly subject to his Author.

“Eat from every tree of paradise,” God said, “but do not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. II, 16). For when he forbids those subject to him from some one good, it is necessary that he grant many others, lest the mind of the obedient perish utterly if it fasts, completely rejected, from all good things.

The Lord permitted all the trees of paradise when he prohibited one, so that his creature, whom he did not wish to destroy but to advance, might be restrained from one thing all the more easily the more broadly he gave him access to all the others.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the transgression of the first human being

(Moral., Book XXIV, chapter 7, no. 14.) The cunning enemy and foe of the human race does not cease to do daily what he did in paradise. He strives to tear the words of God from human hearts and to plant in them the deceptive charms of his promises. Every day the ancient enemy softens what God threatens and invites people to believe what he falsely promises.

For he falsely promises temporal things in order to lessen in human minds those punishments that God threatens as eternal. When the adversary of the human race promises the glory of the present life, what else does he say than: “Taste, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. III, 5)? It is as though he openly said: “Touch temporal desire, and appear exalted in this world.”

When the ancient enemy attempts to remove from human hearts fear of the divine sentence, what else does he say than what he said to the first human beings: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” (ibid. 1).

But because, through the divine gift, the redeemed human being has received the righteousness that he lost when he was first created, he now exercises himself more vigorously against the blandishments of cunning persuasion, because experience has taught him how greatly he ought to obey the commandment. The guilt that once led him to punishment now restrains him from guilt through his punishment: he fears to sin all the more because, compelled by punishment, he himself now condemns what he has committed.

(Book I on the Gospels, Homily 16, nos. 2–3.) The cunning adversary rose up against the first human being, our ancestor, with three temptations: he tempted him with gluttony, vainglory, and avarice. By tempting him, he overcame him, because he subjected him to himself through his consent.

He tempted him through gluttony when he showed him the forbidden fruit of the tree and persuaded him to eat. He tempted him through vainglory when he said: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. III, 5). He tempted him through avarice when he said: “Knowing good and evil” (ibid.). Thus he drew him into pride by stirring in him the avarice of exaltation.

By the same methods through which the devil struck down the first human being, he himself was overcome when he tempted the second human being. He tempted him through gluttony when he said: “Command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matt. IV, 3). He tempted him through vainglory when he said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (ibid. 6). He tempted him through the avarice of exaltation when he showed him all the kingdoms of the world, saying: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me” (ibid. 9).

(Moral. XXVIII, chapter 1, no. 6.) [Note: [Col. 0755D] These words are absent from our manuscript through the carelessness of the scribe; nevertheless, I thought it appropriate to supply them from Gregory so that the sense might be complete.]

What does it mean that the Lord walks about in the afternoon breeze, except that the more fervent light of charity had departed and that the coldness of sin was constricting the sinful soul? He therefore rebuked Adam while walking about, so that he might reveal his wickedness to blind minds not only through words but also through actions.

Thus the sinful human being heard through words what he had done; through the walking about, he saw the instability of his mutability after losing the state of eternity; through the breeze, with the heat of charity driven away, he recognized his torpor; and through the declining sun, he understood that he was drawing near to darkness.

(Moral., Book II, chapter 5, no. 6.) It is written: “God called Adam and said to him: Where are you?” (Gen. III, 9). Why does the Lord seek Adam after his fall, saying, “Where are you?” Did divine power not know into what hiding places the servant had fled after his sin? But because he saw him fallen into sin, already hidden under sin, as it were, from the eyes of Truth, and because he does not approve the darkness of his error, he acts as though he does not know where the sinner is.

The almighty Lord both calls Adam and seeks him, saying: “Where are you?” By calling him, he gives a sign that he is recalling him to repentance. By seeking him, he openly indicates that he does not fail to know those who are justly condemned as sinners.

(Moral., Book XI, chapter 43, no. 59.) The human race possessed in paradise the contemplation of the innermost light. But, pleasing itself, it withdrew into itself, lost the light of the Creator and his face, and fled among the trees of paradise because, after sin, it feared to see the One whom it had been accustomed to love.

But behold: after sin it came into punishment; from punishment it returned to love, because it discovered what had been the fruit of sin. And the face that it had feared in sin it sought, awakened by punishment, so that it might now flee the darkness of its blindness and dread deeply the very fact that it did not see its Author.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the change and mutability of time

(Moral., Book XI, chapter 50, no. 68.) We cannot possess a fixed state of time in the present age, since we came into it in order to pass away, and our very living each day is a passing from life. The first human being could not have possessed this passing of time before sin, because time passed while he stood. But after he sinned, he placed himself, as it were, on a kind of slippery ground of temporality. And because he ate the forbidden food, he immediately discovered the failure of his state.

The human being suffers the mutability of time not only outwardly but also inwardly, when he strives to rise toward better works. For the mind is continually driven by the weight of its mutability toward something other than what it is. Unless it is held firmly in its state by strict discipline of vigilance, it continually slips into lower things [Note: [Col. 0756D] The edition reads, “into worse things.”].

Because she abandoned the One who always stands, she lost the state that she had [Note: [Col. 0756D] The edition reads, “that she could have had.”].

(Moral. IV, chapter 1, no. 4.) For as long as every period of time in our mortality holds us in the corruption of our mutability, the unchangeableness of eternity does not appear to us. Therefore, whoever already sees the day of eternity endures with difficulty the day of his mortality.

It is written in the Book of blessed Job: “Let the day perish in which I was born” (Job III, 3). The human being was created in the day of righteousness, but he was already born in the time of sin. Adam was created, but Cain was the first to be born.

What does it mean to curse the day of one’s birth except openly to say: “Let the day of mutability perish, and let the light of eternity break forth” (No. 5)?

This time of our mutability will at some point perish—that is, pass away—not in such a way that it will be evil, but so that it will no longer exist at all, as the angel testifies in the sacred word: “By him who lives forever, time shall be no more” (Rev. X, 6).

For although the Prophet says: “Their time shall be forever” (Ps. LXXX, 16), because time fails moment by moment, he called their downfall by the name of their time, showing that those who are separated from the consolation of the innermost vision fail without any remainder whatsoever.

(Moral. Book XXV, chapter 3, no. 4.) Since we are born from the stock of the first human being, we retain the bitterness of the root as though in a young shoot. Because we derive our origin from him, by being born we receive his course, so that in the very daily moment in which we live we continually pass away from life, and the span of living that seems to grow for us diminishes from the same source.

As infancy passes into childhood, childhood into adolescence, adolescence into youth, and old age passes toward death in the course of the present life, the wretched human being is driven toward loss by his very increases. He always declines from the place where he believes he is progressing toward a longer span of life.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the discord between the holy angels and human beings placed under transgression

[Col. 0756D]

(Book I on the Gospels, Homily 8, no. 2.) Before our Redeemer was born in the flesh, we were at odds with the angels, from whose brightness and purity we were far removed because of the merit of our first sin and our daily transgressions.

Because, by sinning, we were estranged from God, the angels, citizens of God, counted us as strangers to their fellowship. But because we came to know our King, the angels recognized us as their fellow citizens. Since the King of heaven assumed the earth of our flesh, the angelic majesty does not despise our weakness.

The angels return to our peace and set aside their former intention of discord; those whom they once despised as weak and rejected, they now honor as companions. In the Old Testament, Lot and Joshua worship angels, yet they are not forbidden to worship. John wished to worship an angel in the Apocalypse, but that same angel restrained him from worshiping him, saying: “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers.”

Why is it that before the Redeemer’s coming angels are worshiped by human beings and remain silent, but afterward they refuse to be worshiped? Is it not because, after they saw our nature—which they had previously despised—assumed above them, they feared to see it subjected to themselves? They no longer dared to scorn as weak beneath them the nature that they venerated above them in the King of heaven. Nor do they disdain to have as a companion the human being whom they worship above themselves as God.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the heavenly Jerusalem and its citizens

(Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 1, no. 5.) Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” Those who fix their minds upon the vision of inner peace dwell in Jerusalem. It is written: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. CXXI, 3). Since that vision of inner peace is constructed from the gathering of holy citizens, heavenly Jerusalem is built as a city.

While that heavenly Jerusalem is struck by scourges and beaten by tribulations in this land of pilgrimage, its stones are squared every day. It is the city—namely, the holy Church—which will reign in heaven but still labors on earth. To its citizens Peter says: “You also, as living stones, are being built up” (I Pet. II, 5). And Paul says: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (I Cor. III, 9).

The city of Jerusalem already possesses here a great building in the conduct of the saints. In a building, one stone is placed upon another, and the one who carries another is himself carried by another.

(Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 9, no. 10.) The prophet Isaiah says: “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI, 9). For it is more to be a furnace than to be fire, because there can be a small fire, whereas in a furnace a larger flame is kindled.

Zion is called “watchtower,” while Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.” For the present we watch for our peace here, so that afterward we may see it fully there. From love of the almighty Lord, there is fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem, because here we burn to some extent with the flames of his love when we contemplate something of him. But there we shall burn fully, where we shall fully see the One whom we love.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Babylon and its citizens

(Moral., Book XIV, chapter 53, no. 65; Book VI, chapter 16, no. 25.) It should be known that Shinar is a very broad valley in which the tower of Babylon had begun to be built by the proud. Shinar is interpreted as “their stench.” That tower, which was destroyed by the diversity of languages, was also called Babylon, because of the very confusion of minds and tongues. Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.”

Rightly, therefore, the barren mind is called the daughter of Babylon. Since it produces no good works and is not ordered according to a rule of upright life, it is born, as it were, from confusion as its mother.

It is written: “Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground; there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans” (Isa. XLVII, 1). Thus, after the human mind has lost the state of salvation, it is called “virgin,” or “uncorrupted,” because that is what it once was, for the increase of its confusion. Appropriately, therefore, the divine voice says to it by way of rebuke: “Come down.”

The human mind stands on high when it longs for heavenly rewards. But it descends from this state when, shamefully overcome, it subjects itself to the flowing desires of the world.

(Moral. XIV, chapter 17, no. 21.) The daughter of Babylon is most certainly told: “Sit in the dust.” Since the earth is always dust, what should we understand by dust except thoughts? When they fly about importunately and silently in the mind, they blind its eyes. And what is signified by the earth except earthly action?

The mind of the reprobate is first cast down into the consideration of evil things and afterward into their performance. Rightly, therefore, the daughter of Babylon, who has descended from the judgment of inner uprightness, is told by the striking sentence that she should first sit in dust and afterward on the earth, because unless she had prostrated herself in thought, she would not have become fixed in evil work.

(Moral. VI, chapter 16, no. 25.) For when she descends, she sits in the dust, because, abandoning heavenly things and covered with earthly thoughts, she becomes degraded in the lowest places.

(Moral. III, chapter 31, no. 60.) There are some who, when they do small things, think great things about themselves. They lift their minds on high and suppose that they surpass others in the merits of virtue. These people abandon within themselves the dung-heap of humility and climb the heights of self-exaltation.

They imitate the one who first exalted himself in his own estimation but brought himself low by exalting himself. They imitate the one who was not content with the dignity of his created condition, saying: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne” (Isa. XIV, 13).

Babylon, the confused multitude of sinners, joined to the apostate angel, says: “I sit as queen, and I am not a widow” (Isa. XLVII, 8, according to the Septuagint). Whoever therefore swells up inwardly has set himself on high in his own estimation, but he sinks himself more grievously into the depths because he refuses to think truthfully of himself as lowly.

(Moral. V, chapter 21, no. 41.) By the name of a lioness, the city of this world—that is, Babylon—is sometimes signified. It rages against the life of the innocent with the savagery of cruelty. Joined to the ancient enemy as to a most savage lion, it conceives the seeds of his perverse persuasion and gives birth from itself to reprobate sons in his likeness, like cruel cubs.

The lion’s cubs are all the reprobate who are generated for an evil life through the error of wicked spirits. Together they make up the entire city of the world that we have called Babylon; yet these same individuals are each called sons of Babylon, as though they were not a lioness but cubs of a lioness.

Just as Zion as a whole is called the Church, while the sons of Zion are mentioned individually as the particular saints, so the sons of Babylon are each the individual reprobate, while Babylon itself collectively is all the reprobate.

(No. 42.) As long as holy men are in this life, they guard themselves with careful vigilance, lest the prowling lion steal upon them through ambush—that is, lest the ancient enemy kill them under some appearance of virtue—and lest the voice of the lioness ring in their ears, that is, lest the glory of Babylon turn their understanding away from love of the heavenly homeland.

## CHAPTER XXIX. What the ark of the Flood signifies

(Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 4, no. 16.) The ark of the Flood, which is described as broad below but narrow above, represents the holy Church. It is drawn together from three hundred and sixty and thirty cubits to one cubit (Gen. VI, 15), because, gradually narrowed from the breadth that the holy Church still possesses in its weaker members and advancing upward, it tends toward one.

Reason requires us to believe that in the breadth of that ark all the beasts, quadrupeds, and reptiles were in the lower parts, while human beings and birds were in the upper parts. Near the upper part there was a window in the side, from which the human being sent out a raven and a dove so that he might learn whether the waters of the Flood had already passed away. And because the same ark was completed in one cubit, human beings and birds were near that cubit.

The ark rightly signifies the whole Church, which is still broad in its many carnal members and narrow in its few spiritual ones. And because it is gathered toward the one human being who is without sin, it is completed, as it were, in one cubit.

(Book II on the Gospels, Homily 38, no. 8.) The ark on the waters of the Flood bore the type of the Church, since it was broad below and narrow above; at its summit it grew to the measure of one cubit. It should be believed that below it had quadrupeds and reptiles, while above it had birds and human beings.

The ark was broad where it held the beasts and narrow where it preserved human beings, because the holy Church is broad among the carnal and narrow among the spiritual. Where it tolerates people with beastlike ways, there it spreads its bosom more widely. But where it possesses those supported by spiritual understanding, there it is indeed led to the summit; yet, because they are few, it is narrowed.

“For broad is the way that leads to destruction, and there are many who go by it; and narrow is the gate that leads to life, and there are few who find it” (Matt. VII, 13). The ark is narrowed at its heights until it is brought to the measure of one cubit, because in the holy Church the holier people are, the fewer they are.

At the summit it is brought to him who alone is human among human beings and was born holy without comparison with anyone. In the words of the Psalmist, “He became like a solitary sparrow on the building” (Ps. CI, 8).

## CHAPTER XXX. On the elect who arose before the Law or under the Law
(Moral. IV, 32, no. 65.) Many of the elect arose from the very beginning of the world, before the time of redemption, and yet they took care to mortify themselves to this world. Although they did not possess the tablets of the written law, [Col. 0760A] they were, as it were, dead from the womb, because they feared their Creator by the natural law; and, believing that the Mediator would come, they strove with the utmost diligence to observe, by mortifying their pleasures, even commandments which they had not received in writing. That period which, near the beginning of the world, brought forth our fathers dead to this age was like an abortive womb. There were Abel, of whom it is not written that he resisted his brother when the latter killed him (Gen. IV, 8, 24); Enoch, who displayed such a life that he was transferred while walking with the Lord (Gen. V, 22); Noah, who, because he pleased the divine judgment, survived when the world perished (Gen. VII, 23); the patriarch Abraham, who, while he lived as a stranger to the age, became God’s friend (Gen. XII, 1); Isaac, whose bodily eyes had grown dim and who, because of his age, did not see present things, but who, [Col. 0760B] through the power of the prophetic spirit, shone with the great light of vision even into future ages (Gen. XXVII, 1); Jacob, who humbly fled from his brother’s anger and mercifully subdued it (Gen. XXXIII, 4). He was indeed fruitful in offspring, but still more fruitful in the abundance of his spirit, and he bound that same offspring within the bonds of his prophecy.

From the beginnings of the world, while we learn of a few elect men through Moses’ writing, the greater part of the human race remains hidden from our knowledge. For it is not to be believed that there existed only as many righteous men before the law was received as Moses briefly mentioned. Since, therefore, a multitude of good people brought forth from the beginning of the world is for the most part withdrawn from our knowledge, it is called, as it were, a hidden abortive birth (Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 1, no. 4).

There were holy men—patriarchs [Col. 0760C] and prophets—in the Israelite people who might rightly be called mountains, because through the merit of their life they drew near to heavenly things. But the Only-Begotten, once incarnate, was not equal to these mountains, because through his divinity he surpassed the nature, life, and merits of them all. The Lord Jesus Christ is called a mountain above the summit of the mountains, because, lofty in his divinity, he was found even above the peaks of the saints (Isa. II, 2), so that those who had made great progress in God could scarcely touch his footprints from the summit of their thought.

The elect who were born into this world after the law had been received were conceived for their Creator through the admonition of that same law.

(Moral. IV, chap. 32, no. 64.) Yet, although conceived, they did not see the light at all, because they could not reach the advent of the Lord’s incarnation, even though [Col. 0760D] they believed it faithfully. The incarnate Lord says: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII, 12). And the Light itself says: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matt. XIII, 17). Though they were roused by the open voices of the prophets to hope for the coming Mediator, they were by no means able to behold his incarnation. Before the advent of our Redeemer, the multitude of the elect possessed the form of faith, but did not carry it through to the open vision of the divine presence, because intervening death snatched them from the world before manifest Truth enlightened the world.

(Moral. IV, chap. 33, no. 66.) The Gentile peoples found, for the repose of their life, the advent of the Mediator for which the fathers placed under the law had long waited. Paul bears witness to this when he says: [Col. 0761A] “What Israel sought, it did not obtain, but the elect obtained it” (Rom. XI, 7).

## CHAPTER XXXI. On elect men who arose before Christ’s advent

(Preface to the Book of Job, chap. 6, no. 13.) It is a pleasure to contemplate the wondrous works of the divine dispensation: how, to illuminate the night of the present life, the various stars come in their appointed turns into the face of heaven, until, at the end of the night, the Redeemer of the human race rises like the true Lucifer. For the nocturnal span, while it is illuminated by the courses of stars that set and succeed one another, is brought to completion with great adornment of the heavens.

Thus, so that the ray of stars, brought forth in turn and exchanged in due season, might touch the darkness of our night, Abel came to display innocence; Enoch came to teach purity of [Col. 0761B] action; Noah came to suggest steadfastness in hope and work; Abraham came to make obedience manifest; Isaac came to demonstrate chastity in married life; Jacob came to suggest endurance of toil; Joseph came to return the grace of a good recompense for evil; Moses came to display gentleness; Joshua came to form confidence against adversity; Job came to display patience amid afflictions.

Behold how many shining stars we figuratively see fixed in heaven, so that with an unhindered step we may walk the path of our night’s work. The divine dispensation presented to human knowledge as many righteous men as though it had sent stars into the heaven above the darkness of sinners, until the true Lucifer should rise, who, announcing eternal morning to us, would, [Col. 0761C] shine from his divinity more brightly than the other stars.

(No. 14.) All the elect, by going before the Mediator of God and humanity through a good life, prophetically promised him both in deeds and in words. For there was no righteous person who did not become, through a figure, his herald. It was fitting that all should display in themselves the good from whom all good people would come and which they knew would benefit everyone. Hence what was to be received without measure and retained without end had to be promised without ceasing, so that all the ages together might declare what the end of the ages would reveal in the common redemption.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On love of God and neighbor

The first virtue of obedience is charity; and this [Col. 0761D] charity is distinguished in two commandments, so that God and one’s neighbor may be loved. Right action is completed through the fulfillment of the Decalogue, so that, once good deeds have begun to be done, no evil may thereafter be committed.

(Moral. VII, chap. 14, no. 28.) There are two commandments of charity: namely, love of God and love of neighbor. Through both of these, the sayings of Sacred Scripture give us life, because in the divine utterances we grasp love of God and neighbor. Love of neighbor is begotten through love of God, and love of God is nourished through love of neighbor. For whoever neglects to love God plainly does not know how to love his neighbor.

We make fuller progress in the love of God if, within the embrace of that same love, we are first nourished by love of our neighbor as by milk. Because the love of God generates love of neighbor, the Lord, when he was about to say through the law, “You shall love your neighbor,” first said: [Col. 0762A] “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. VI, 5; X, 12; Matt. XXII, 37, 39), so that he might first fix the root of his love in the soil of our hearts, in order that brotherly love might afterward sprout through its branches.

The love of God grows strong through love of neighbor, as John testifies when he reproves certain people, saying: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (I John IV, 20). Yet this divine love is born through fear, but as it grows it is transformed into affection.

(No. 29.) Often almighty God, dispensing all things in wondrous order so that it may become known how far each person is from his love and that of his neighbor, or how far he has advanced in it, presses some down with afflictions and supports others with successes. And when he temporarily abandons some, he reveals what [Col. 0762B] evil lies hidden in the hearts of others. For often those who relentlessly pursue us are the very people whom we have esteemed as happy beyond comparison.

(Book II on the Gospels, Homily 30, no. 10.) Our journey on earth proceeds with an unhindered step if God and neighbor are loved with an undivided mind. For neither is God truly loved without one’s neighbor, nor is one’s neighbor truly loved without God.

The Holy Spirit is read to have been given to the disciples a second time: first by the Lord while he dwelt on earth, and afterward by the Lord while he presided from heaven. On earth, so that one’s neighbor might be loved; from heaven, so that God might be loved. But why first on earth and afterward from heaven, unless it is plainly shown that, in accordance with John’s words, “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (I John IV, 20)?

Let us love and embrace our neighbor, who is [Col. 0762C] beside us, so that we may be able to reach the love of him who is above us. Let the mind consider in its neighbor what it may offer to God, so that we may deserve perfectly to rejoice in him together with our neighbor. Then we shall reach that joy of the heavenly assembly of which we have now received the pledge of the Holy Spirit.

Let us direct all our love toward this end, namely, love of God and neighbor. Every commandment concerns love alone, and all the commandments are one commandment. For whatever is commanded is established in charity alone. The Lord’s commandments are both many and one: many in the diversity of their works, one in the root of love. He himself indicates how love of God and neighbor is to be maintained: in many passages of his Scripture he commands that friends be loved in him and enemies be loved for his sake.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the old law

[Col. 0762D]

(Moral. XI, 17, no. 26.) The severity of the law decreed that every sinner should be punished by bodily death. But after our Redeemer tempered the harshness of the legal sanction through gentleness, he no longer established that death of the flesh should be inflicted for sin, but showed how greatly the death of the spirit ought to be feared.

(Book II on the Gospels, Homily 33, no. 8.) It is written in Exodus: “Moses’ hands were heavy. So they took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat upon it; while Aaron and Hur supported his hands” (Exod. XVII, 12). Moses therefore sat upon the stone when the Law rested in the Church. Yet this same Law had heavy hands, [Col. 0763A] because it did not bear with sinners mercifully but struck them with severe discipline.

Aaron, the priest, means “mountain of strength,” while Hur means “fire.” Whom, then, does this mountain of strength signify if not our Redeemer, of whom the prophet says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isa. II, 2)? Or whom does fire signify if not the Holy Spirit, of whom the same Redeemer says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII, 49)?

Aaron and Hur support Moses’ heavy hands and, by supporting them, make them lighter, because the Mediator of God and humanity, coming with the fire of the Holy Spirit, showed us through spiritual understanding that the commandments of the Law—when they were held carnally, they could not be carried—were more [Col. 0763B] bearable. He made Moses’ hands light, as it were, because he turned the burden of the Law’s commandments toward the strength of confession.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On history and allegory

(Moral. XXI, 1, no. 1.) The understanding of sacred speech must be weighed between text and mystery with such balance that, with the scales of both sides moderated, neither is it depressed by the weight of excessive investigation nor, on the other hand, left empty by the torpor of negligence.

Many passages of sacred speech are so pregnant with allegorical meanings that anyone who attempts to hold them only as history is deprived of their knowledge through his own negligence. Others, however, serve external commandments in such a way that if someone desires to penetrate them more subtly, he finds nothing within but also conceals from himself what they say [Col. 0763C] outwardly.

(No. 2.) The sayings of the fathers who preceded us are placed before the eyes of our consideration like variegated rods. In them, whenever we flee the literal meaning, we withdraw the bark, as it were. And whenever we follow the literal meaning, we preserve the bark, as it were. When the bark of the letter is removed from them, the inner brightness of allegory is revealed; and when the bark is left, the verdant examples of outward understanding are displayed.

Jacob placed variegated rods in the channels of water (Gen. XXX, 38), because our Redeemer fixed in the books of sacred knowledge those sayings by which we are inwardly infused. When the rams and sheep look upon these, they mate, because our rational spirits, while fixed upon [Col. 0763D] their meaning, mingle with them in each of their actions, so that they produce offspring of works corresponding to the examples of those who preceded them, as seen in the words of the commandments—that is, so that the offspring of good work may have a different color.

Sometimes, when the bark of the letter has been removed, our mind considers inner matters more sharply; and sometimes, when the covering of history has been preserved, it forms itself well in outward matters. In sacred speech there is great discernment of understanding.

(According to Paterius, Book II, chap. 29, on Exodus.) Often, in certain passages, both history and allegory must be preserved; often, in certain passages, allegory alone must be sought; and sometimes it is necessary that history alone be retained.

In certain passages, as we have said, history and allegory must be held together, so that the slower may be nourished through history and those quicker [Col. 0764A] in understanding through allegory. Thus, when God was speaking and the people saw lamps, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain, they were terrified and asked that the Lord speak to them through Moses, as it is written: “The people stood far off, but Moses approached the darkness in which God was” (Exod. XX, 21).

The crowd of the people cannot penetrate the darkness of allegories, because it belongs to very few to search out spiritual understanding. Since the minds of the carnal are often nourished by history alone, when God was speaking the people stood far away. But because spiritual people penetrate the cloud of allegories in order to know God’s words spiritually, Moses approached the darkness in which God was.

(According to Paterius, Book V, chap. 9, on Deuteronomy.) The Law of the Old Testament placed eggs in a nest when it said: “An eye for an eye, a tooth [Col. 0764B] for a tooth” (Exod. XXI, 24); but afterward it produced chicks when it said: “You shall not seek vengeance, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens” (Lev. XIX, 18).

It should be noted that concerning the mother of the chicks it is said: “You shall not keep her with her young, but shall let her go, retaining the young for yourself” (Deut. XXII, 6). In certain passages, therefore, history must be passed over, so that the chicks of the mother alone—that is, the meaning of spiritual understanding—may come to us as food, and we may be nourished not by the mother but by the chicks. For we ought not to be satisfied by the example of history, but by the meanings of spiritual understanding.

When we read that the gold and silver of the Egyptians were taken away by the Israelite people through a deceptive request (Exod. XII), and again when we read that carnal sacrifices were offered to almighty God, what is to be understood in this nest of words except that the mother is to be let go [Col. 0764C] and the chicks retained?

When we draw from secular people the vigilance of their intellect for the defense of truth and turn their eloquence to the service of righteousness, what else are we doing than taking gold and silver from the Egyptians, so that we may become rich from it and they may be shown to be poor? As it is written: “Bringing every understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ” (II Cor. X, 6).

We let the mother go and eat the chicks when we leave aside the examples of history but retain in our minds the meanings of allegories. To this is rightly added: “That it may be well with you and you may live for a long time” (Deut. XXII, 8). For the one who apprehends the years of eternity through spiritual understanding lives for a long time.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On predestination

[Col. 0764D]

(Gregory, Book I of the Dialogues, 8.) The things that holy men accomplish through prayer are so predestined that they are obtained through prayers. For even the predestination of the eternal kingdom has been arranged by almighty God in such a way that the elect reach it through labor, so that by asking they may deserve to receive what almighty God determined before the ages to give them.

We know most certainly that the Lord said to Abraham: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI, 13). He had also said to him: “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (Gen. XVII, 4). Again he promised him, saying: “I will bless you, and I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea” (Gen. XXII, 17).

From this it is plainly [Col. 0765A] established that almighty God had predestined Abraham’s offspring to be multiplied through Isaac; and yet it is written: “Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren; and he heard him and granted Rebecca conception” (Gen. XXV, 21). If the multiplication of Abraham’s descendants through Isaac was predestined, why did he receive a barren wife? It is clearly evident that predestination is fulfilled through prayers, since the one in whom God had predestined Abraham’s offspring to be multiplied obtained through prayer the ability to have children.

(Book VI of the Hypognosticon, chaps. 2, 5–8, in the appendix to vol. X of Augustine’s works.) Predestination is so called from foreseeing or preordaining something future. Therefore God, for whom foreknowledge was not accidental but was always and is [Col. 0765B] his essence, predestines whatever he foreknows before it exists, and he predestines it because it will be such as he foreknows it will be. Hence the Apostle also says: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined” (Rom. VIII, 29).

God does not predestine everything he foreknows. He merely foreknows evils, but he both foreknows and predestines good things. Whatever is good, foreknowledge predestines—that is, it preordains it before it exists in reality. Once it has begun to exist with its creator, he calls, orders, and arranges it. Hence it follows: “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.”

The just and merciful God, who knows the future, from the condemnable mass [of humanity], not by accepting persons but through the irreproachable—indeed incomprehensible—judgment of his equity, prepares by free mercy those whom he foreknows for eternal life; that is, he predestines them. But the rest [Col. 0765C] he punishes with the punishment they deserve. He punishes them because he foreknew what they would be, yet he himself did not make or predestine them to be punished; he merely foreknew them within the condemnable mass.

[We have said] that, from the condemnable mass of the human race, God foreknew by mercy, not by merits, those whom he predestined to life through the election of grace. But the rest, who by the judgment of his justice are deprived of this grace, he merely foreknew as destined to perish through their own fault; he did not predestine them to perish.

We rightly confess that almighty God, just and merciful, did not preordain or compel those whom he foreknew in works of ungodliness and death. Among these are those who provoke God to anger and either refuse to accept the faith of salvation preached to them, or, under God’s judgment, cannot accept it, or misuse what they have accepted; and for this reason they are handed [Col. 0765D] over to a depraved mind, so that they do not do what is fitting. We confess that punishment has been predestined for these.

When God had foreknown that Judas would be utterly wicked through the vices of his own will—that is, that he would misuse the discipleship graciously conferred upon him by Christ, and, inflamed by avarice, would hand the Lord over to the Jews for money—he predestined punishment for him according to his merit. The Holy Spirit says through David: “O God, do not be silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the deceiver has been opened against me” (Ps. CVIII, 2), that is, the mouth of Judas or of the Jews against Christ.

Judas said: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matt. XXVI, 15). And after the promise of money, giving the sign of betrayal, he said: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him.” Therefore he says, “It has been opened against me.” For when he gave the sign, he opened with a deceitful mouth the identity of the one they were to seize.

The same is true of the Jews, who, wishing to destroy him by deceit, as the Gospel reveals, cried out, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him!” (John XIX, 6).

[This rule must be held without wavering:] all sinners, before they existed [Col. 0766A] in the world, were merely foreknown in their evils, not predestined; but punishment was predestined for them according to what was foreknown about them. Infants also who have not been reborn through water and the Holy Spirit are subject to predestined punishment. They were foreknown not in their own wills, in which there is neither good nor evil, but only in Adam’s sin, which they drew in their birth and in which they remained until they completed the time of their present life.

It must be said without doubt that the elect who live according to God’s purpose were foreknown and predestined through the election of his free grace, and that the kingdom [Col. 0766B] of heaven was predestined for them. The Apostle Paul proves this when he testifies that they were predestined and elected before the world was established. Writing to the Ephesians, he says: “As he chose us in him, that is, in Christ, before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love, having predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself” (Eph. I, 4).

Let the human tongue be silent, lest it boast of merits in predestination. Consider the Apostle’s words: “God chose us before the foundation of the world.” This gift belongs to the divine will, not to the merit of human weakness.

Finally, consider what follows: “In whom,” he says, “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness [Col. 0766C] of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which has abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, for the administration of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him. In him we have also been predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we may be to the praise of his glory, we who first hoped in Christ.”

To the predestined apostles, or generally to all the elect, it is said: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI, 41). And again: “Watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand [Col. 0766D] before the Son of Man” (Luke XXI, 36).

Those who are without the grace of predestination—that is, who are alien to God’s purpose—and persist in evil works, if they also depart from this life, we do not say that they were so ordered by God that they should perish, as though he himself had created their evil character or had driven them unwillingly into every work of death. Far be this from the divine purpose. For “God is not a God who wills iniquity” (Ps. V, 5); nor did he command anyone to act wickedly, nor give anyone license to sin (Eccl. XV, 21). For he made all things to exist, and “the nations of the world are health-giving” (Wisdom I, 14). But “through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wisdom II, 24). Therefore those who belong to his party imitate him.

To deny predestination is a monstrous blasphemy. We must understand it not only of the apostles, [Col. 0767A] but also of patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, confessors, and all the saints and those who serve God worthily. Let no one glory in himself except in God. Let no one despair. For the Lord alone knows who are his (II Tim. II, 19). As far as we can, let us exhort all people to good works; let us give no one cause for despair. Let us pray for one another and humble ourselves before God, saying: “Your will be done” (Matt. VI, 10). It belongs to his power to change the judgment of condemnation deserved by us and to bestow the undeserved grace of predestination.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On wisdom

(Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 6, no. 2.) Wisdom and knowledge [Col. 0767B] of spiritual teaching are true riches, in comparison with which things that pass away are called false. Apart from the fact that spiritual riches lead to the eternal homeland, they differ greatly from earthly riches, because spiritual riches increase when distributed, whereas earthly riches either diminish when distributed or, when retained, are of no use. Those, therefore, who contain these true riches within themselves are rightly called treasuries of the spiritual building.

(Moral. V, chap. 5, no. 8.) Wisdom does not lie upon the surface of things; it shines because it lies hidden in invisible realities. We grasp wisdom by our mortification when, abandoning visible things, we are hidden within invisible ones. As though digging out the heart [Note: [Col. 0767D] In the editions: “si sic hanc, cor effodientes.”], we seek wisdom, so that the mind may cast away from itself by the hand of holy discernment [Col. 0767C] everything earthly that it thinks about, and recognize the treasure of virtue that had been hidden from it.

Anyone easily finds the treasure of wisdom if he drives away from himself the mass of earthly thought that had pressed upon it wrongly.

(Moral. XXV, 12, no. 29.) It is written: “Wisdom cries out at the head of the ways; she stands in the midst of the paths” (Prov. VIII, 1). Perhaps we could have passed through the way of temporal life in ignorance of her if this same wisdom had stood at the corners of the path.

(No. 30.) She would have needed to be investigated if she had wished to remain hidden. The exceedingly wise Solomon says: “Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn out her seven pillars; she has sacrificed victims; she has mixed wine; she has set her table; she has sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and the walls of the city” (Prov. IX, 1–3), and so forth.

(Moral. XXXIII, 16, no. 32.) Wisdom built a house for herself when the only-begotten Son of God created for himself, within the Virgin’s womb and through the mediation of a soul, a human body. The body of the Only-Begotten is called the house of God, just as it is also called a temple—yet in such a way that the one and same Son of God and of humanity is himself the one who dwells in it and himself the one who is indwelt.

The house of Wisdom is called the Church. She hewed out for herself seven pillars because she raised up minds of preachers, separated from love of the present age, to bear the structure of that same Church. Because they are supported by the virtue of perfection, they are designated by the number seven.

Wisdom sacrificed victims because she permitted the lives of preachers to be slaughtered in persecution. She mixed wine because she proclaimed to us alike the mysteries of her divinity and her [Col. 0768A] humanity. She also set a table because, by opening it, she prepared for us the nourishment of Sacred Scripture.

(Moral. XVII, 32, no. 43.) The Wisdom of God set a table—that is, Sacred Scripture—which refreshes the weary and those coming to it from the burdens of the age with the bread of the word, and strengthens us by its nourishment against adversaries. Hence elsewhere the Church says: “You have set a table before me in the presence of those who trouble me” (Ps. XXII, 5).

She sent her maidservants, namely, the souls of the apostles, weak at the very beginning, to call to the citadel and the walls of the city, because, while they proclaim the inner life, they raise us to the lofty walls of the heavenly city; and surely only the humble ascend those walls.

(Moral. XXXIII, 16, no. 32.) This Wisdom of God sent her maidservants to call us [Col. 0768B] to the citadel and the walls of the city, because she chose to have preachers who were weak and despised, so that they might gather faithful peoples to the heavenly buildings of the spiritual homeland.

(Moral. XVII, 29, no. 43.) From this same Wisdom it is added: “If anyone is little, let him come to me” (Prov. IX, 4). It is as though she openly said: Whoever considers himself great in his own estimation narrows the way of access to me; for the higher one reaches me, the more truly each person’s mind is humbled in his own sight.

(Moral. XI, 6, no. 8.) It must be observed very carefully that, although wisdom is one, it dwells in one person less and in another more; it grants one person this and another something else; and, as though in the manner of the brain, it uses us as though we were various senses, so that, although it is never unlike itself, it may nevertheless always perform diverse and unlike works through us, so that one may receive the gift of wisdom, [Col. 0768C] another of knowledge, one the varieties of tongues, another the grace of healings.

(No. 7.) The words of wisdom that the reprobate hear, the elect not only hear but also taste, so that what sounds only in the ears of the reprobate may be savory to the elect in their hearts. It is one thing merely to hear the name of food, and another to taste it as well. The elect therefore hear the food of wisdom in such a way that they taste it, because what they hear becomes deeply savory to them through love.

The knowledge of the reprobate extends only to recognizing the sound, so that they indeed hear of virtues but, with cold hearts, do not know how they taste.

(Chap. 7, no. 10.) Those sayings are established in the root of wisdom which, through the practice of living, also grow strong through the experience [Col. 0768D] of actions. For longer life is granted to many, while the grace of wisdom is not bestowed. Rightly it is said through blessed Job: “With him is wisdom and strength; he has counsel and understanding” (Job XII, 13).

(Chap. 8, no. 11.) We appropriately understand these words of the Only-Begotten of the supreme Father, so that we may recognize him as the Wisdom and Strength of God. Paul also bears witness to our understanding when he says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 24), who is always with him, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I, 1). God has counsel and understanding: counsel, namely, because he orders his own affairs; understanding, because he knows ours.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. How God is seen by holy men in this age

[Col. 0769A]

(Moral. XVIII, 54, no. 88.) Blessed Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend, said to him in the very course of his speech: “If I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself openly, so that I may see you” (Exod. XXXIII, 13). Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” and not, “Show me yourself.” But if the one with whom he spoke face to face was God, why did he ask to see the one whom he was seeing? His request makes clear that he thirsted to behold, through the splendor of God’s unbounded nature, the one whom he had already begun to see through certain images, so that the heavenly essence might be present to the eyes of his mind, and no created image might temporally intervene between him and the vision of eternity.

The fathers of the Old Testament saw God, and yet, according to John’s statement, “No one has ever seen God” (John IV, 12); and, according to blessed Job’s saying, Wisdom, which is God, “is hidden from the eyes of all living things” (Job XXVIII, 21). For those abiding in this mortal flesh could both see him through certain bounded images and could not see him through the unbounded light of eternity.

(No. 89.) If the eternal splendor of God can be seen by some who still live in this corruptible flesh but nevertheless grow through immeasurable virtue, by a certain sharpness of contemplation, this too does not conflict with the judgment of the same Truth, which says: “For no man shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 21). For whoever sees Wisdom, which is God, dies completely to this life, so that he may no longer be held by love of it. No one who still lives carnally has seen God, because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. Whoever sees God dies precisely insofar as, either in the intention of his heart or in the effect of his works, he wholly separates himself from the pleasures of this life.

(Moral. XXXV, 8, no. 13.) Truth is perceived from the Catholic Church alone, when the Lord declares that there is a place with him from which Moses may see him. Hence Moses is also placed upon the rock so that he may contemplate the appearance of God, because unless someone holds firmly to the solidity of faith, he does not recognize the divine presence. Concerning this solidity the Lord says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18).

While Truth itself says, “No one has ever seen my face,” how does Jacob testify: “I saw the Lord face to face” (Gen. XXXII, 30)?

(Moral. XXIV, 6, no. 11.) When the inner eye of the human mind has been purified, and the rust of all vices has been burned away by the fire of tribulation, then, once the eyes of the heart have been cleansed, the joy of the heavenly homeland is opened to them. First we must cleanse ourselves by mourning what we have done; afterward, through joy, we contemplate more clearly what we seek. First, with burning sorrow interposed before the mind’s gaze, the darkness of evils is wiped away; then it is illumined by the bright, sudden flashing of unbounded light.

When it has seen this, however faintly, it is absorbed into the joy of a certain security; and, as though carried beyond itself after the death of the present life, it is in some way renewed in a certain newness. There the mind is sprinkled from an immense fountain by an outpouring of heavenly dew; there it contemplates that it is not sufficient for what it has been carried away to behold; and, by sensing the truth, it sees that it does not see how great the truth itself is. Each person considers himself so much farther from the highest and unbounded truth the more he approaches it, because unless he saw it in some way, he would not perceive that he could not see it.

(No. 12.) When the effort of the soul is directed toward the vision of God, it is thrown back by the flashing presence of his immensity. For that presence, filling all things, surrounds all things; and therefore our mind cannot enlarge itself sufficiently to grasp the unbounded presence, because the narrowness of its own bounded nature constricts it. Thus the soul quickly slips back to itself and, having perceived what are, as it were, certain traces of the truth, is recalled to itself.

[Note: In the edition of the Maurist Fathers: *ad sua ima*, “to its lowest depths.”]

The vision of the highest truth produced by contemplation is not solid and enduring but, so to speak, a kind of imitation of vision; it is called the face of God. Since we recognize anyone by the face, we rightly call the knowledge of God his face. Blessed Jacob, after wrestling with the angel, said: “I saw the Lord face to face” (Gen. XXXII, 30), as though he were saying: “I came to know God, because he himself deigned to know me.” Paul testifies that this knowledge will be made fully complete at the end, saying: “Then I shall know even as I am known” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

Paul wrote to Timothy, saying: “Whom no man has seen, nor can see” (I Tim. VI, 16).

(Moral. XVIII, 54, no. 92.) In his customary manner, he calls all people “human” who have human concerns, because those who have divine concerns are, as it were, above human beings. We shall therefore see God if, through a heavenly manner of life, we deserve to be above human beings. Yet we shall not see him as he sees himself. For the Creator sees himself in a manner vastly different from that in which the creature sees the Creator. So far as God’s immensity is concerned, a certain measure of contemplation is imposed upon us, because we are bounded by the very weight of being creatures.

(No. 93.) Certainly, we do not contemplate God as he contemplates himself, just as we do not rest in God as he rests in himself. Our vision or rest will in some measure resemble his vision or rest, but it will not be equal to it. So that we may not lie inert in the torpor of negligence, the wing of contemplation lifts us up, and we are raised from ourselves to gaze upon God. Carried away by the intention of the heart and by the sweetness of contemplation, we in some manner go from ourselves into him; and this very going of ours is no less than resting, because to go in this way is to rest perfectly.

Perfect rest is that in which God is seen; yet our rest cannot be made equal to his rest, because he does not pass from himself into something else in order to rest. His rest is therefore, so to speak, both similar and dissimilar, because what resting is for him, our rest imitates.

The vision of God is begun now through faith, but then it is brought to completion in manifestation, when we drink at its very source the Wisdom coeternal with God, which we now receive from the mouths of preachers as though through flowing streams.

# CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Ways in Which God Speaks to Human Beings

(Moral. XXVIII, 1, no. 2.) We must understand above all that divine speech is distinguished in two ways: either the Lord speaks through himself, or his words are formed for us through an angelic creature. When the Lord speaks through himself, only the inward power of inspiration is disclosed to us. When he speaks through himself, the heart is taught by his word without words or syllables; for his power is recognized in a certain inward elevation, by which the mind, when full, is lifted up, and, when empty, is weighed down.

The power of divine speech is a kind of weight that lifts every soul which it fills. It is incorporeal light, which both fills the inner regions and encompasses externally what it has filled. It is speech without noise, which opens the hearing and yet knows nothing of sound.

Concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit it is written: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one rested upon each of them” (Acts II, 2). The Lord appeared through fire, but through himself he spoke inwardly. Neither was God the fire, nor was that sound God; rather, by what he displayed outwardly, he expressed what he accomplished inwardly. The Holy Spirit, who made the disciples inwardly both burning with zeal and instructed in speech, displayed fiery tongues outwardly.

The elements were therefore brought forward symbolically, so that bodies might experience fire and sound, while hearts were instructed by invisible fire and a voice without sound. The fire that appeared was therefore outward, but the fire that gave knowledge was inward. God’s speech made inwardly to us is perceived more than heard, because, while it presents itself without delay, it illumines the darkness of our ignorance with sudden light.

(No. 5.) When the Lord makes his will known through an angel, he sometimes demonstrates it by words, sometimes by things, sometimes by words and things together, sometimes by images displayed to the eyes of the heart, sometimes by images temporarily assumed from the air before the eyes of the body, sometimes through heavenly substances, sometimes through earthly substances, and sometimes through earthly and heavenly substances together. Sometimes God speaks to human hearts through an angel in such a way that the angel himself is also presented to the mind’s gaze.

(No. 4.) God most often speaks through an angel by words when nothing is displayed in an image, but the words of heavenly speech are heard, as when the Lord says, “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you,” and the immediate reply is given: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XVII, 1). Almighty God, who timelessly cries out by the force of an inward impulse, did not at a particular time utter through his substance that voice which he divided into words bounded by time through human speech. Rather, speaking of heavenly things, he formed the words he wished human beings to hear through the agency of a rational creature.

(No. 5.) Sometimes God speaks through angels by things, when nothing is said in words but future events are announced through an image taken from the elements. Thus Ezekiel, hearing the riddling expressions of words, saw the appearance of electrum in the midst of fire (Ezek. I, 4), so that, by looking only at the appearance, he might understand what was to come in the last days.

(No. 6.) Sometimes God speaks through angels by words and things together, when he indicates through certain movements what he describes in words.

(No. 7.) Sometimes God speaks through angels by images displayed to the eyes of the heart, as Jacob, while sleeping, saw a ladder supported by heaven (Gen. XXVIII, 12), and as Peter, carried away in ecstasy, saw a sheet full of reptiles and four-footed animals (Acts X, 11). Unless he had seen these things with incorporeal eyes, he would not have been in ecstasy.
