Sometimes God speaks through angels by images temporarily assumed from the air before the eyes of the body, as Abraham was able not only to see three men but also to receive them into an earthly dwelling and not merely to receive them but even to provide food for their use (Gen. XVIII, 2). Unless the holy angels assumed bodies from the air for a time, announcing certain inward things to us, they would certainly not appear to our outward gaze; nor would they eat food with Abraham unless, for our sake, they bore something solid from the heavenly element.

(No. 8.) Sometimes God speaks through angels through heavenly substances, as it is written that, when the Lord had been baptized, a voice sounded from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17).

Sometimes God speaks through angels through earthly substances, as when he reproved Balaam and formed human words in the mouth of a she-ass (Num. XXII, 28).

Sometimes God speaks through angels through earthly and heavenly substances together, as when, on the mountain, he spoke the words of his command to Moses, joining fire and a bush together (Exod. III, 2), uniting what was above with what was below.

(No. 9.) Sometimes God also pours the power of his inspiration into human hearts through angels, by their secret presence. Hence Zechariah says: “The angel who spoke in me said to me” (Zech. I, 14). By saying that the angel spoke to him and yet within him, he clearly shows that the one who spoke words to him was not outside in bodily form. Hence a little later he adds: “And behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out” (Zech. II, 3).

Often the holy angels do not appear outwardly but, as angelic spirits, make God’s will known to the minds of the prophets. In this way they raise them to sublime things, showing as present in their original causes whatever is to come in events.

The human heart, weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh and sustaining its very corporeality as though it were an obstacle, cannot penetrate inward things. [Note: In the Maurist Fathers’ edition: *hanc*, “this.”] It lies heavily outward because it does not possess within itself the hand that lifts it.

Sometimes the subtlety of angelic power itself appears to the minds of the prophets as it truly is, and their minds are raised by the subtle spirit with which they are touched. No longer sluggish and inert, lying below, they ascend to higher things, filled with inward breathings; and from there, as though from a certain summit of reality, they see what is to come below them.

# CHAPTER XXXIX. The Ways in Which God Questions Human Beings

(Moral. XXVIII, 4, no. 15.) Almighty God customarily questions the human race in three ways: either he strikes us with the severity of a scourge and shows how much patience we possess or lack; or he commands certain things that we do not wish to do and reveals to us our obedience or disobedience; or he discloses some hidden things to us and conceals others, making known to us the measure of our humility.

God questions a person with a scourge when he strikes with afflictions a mind that has been peacefully subjected to him, as happened to blessed Job. He is praised by the Judge’s testimony (Job II, 3, 7), yet he is handed over to the blows of the one who strikes him, so that his patience might shine forth all the more truly the more harshly it had been tested.

Sometimes God questions us by commanding difficult things. Abraham is ordered to leave his land (Gen. XII, 1; cf. XXII, 2) and go where he did not know; to lead his only son up the mountain and sacrifice the son whom, as an old man, he had received for his consolation (Gen. XXII, 2). To Abraham, who answered this questioning well—that is, who obeyed the command—it is said: “Now I know that you fear God” (ibid., 12). Or, as it is written: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. XIII, 3). For God’s testing consists in questioning us through his great commands; and his knowing consists in making us know our obedience.

God questions us by opening certain things to us and closing others, as it is said through the Psalmist: “His eyelids question the children of men” (Ps. X, 6). With open eyelids we see; when they are closed, we see nothing. What then are God’s eyelids except his judgments, which in one respect are closed to human beings and in another opened? People who do not know themselves become known to themselves, so that, while they understand some things, yet cannot know others at all, their hearts may secretly inquire into themselves—whether God’s closed judgments fail to stir them or his opened judgments inflate them.

The apostle Paul was tested by this questioning. After receiving inward wisdom, after the gates of paradise had been opened, after ascending to the third heaven, and after the mysteries of heavenly speech, he still says: “I do not consider that I have grasped it” (Phil. III, 13). Again: “I am the least of the apostles, and am not worthy to be called an apostle” (I Cor. XV, 9). And again: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III, 5).

Having been questioned by God’s opened eyelids, he answered rightly: he touched the secrets above and yet stood sublimely in humility of heart.

Again, when Paul examined the hidden judgments of God concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, and could not reach them, he was questioned as though by God’s closed eyelids. Yet he gave a thoroughly correct answer, wisely submitting himself to God in that very ignorance, saying: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. XI, 33).

Behold: with the mysteries hidden, Paul was questioned as though by closed eyelids, and he gave a pleasing and correct answer. Knocking at the entrance to the secret place, he could not be admitted within through knowledge; therefore, through confession, he stood humbly before the doors and praised in fear what he could not comprehend within.

# CHAPTER XL. Concerning the Synagogue, or the Israelite People Established under the Law

(Moral. XI, 16, nos. 24–25.) Before the Lord’s incarnation, the Jews were truthful, because they believed and announced that he was to come. But after he appeared in the flesh, they denied that he was the one they had foretold would come; they denied him as present whom they had proclaimed as future. Hence blessed Job rightly says: “Changing the speech of the truthful and taking away the teaching of the elders” (Job XII, 20), because the Jews did not follow in faith what they remembered their fathers had foretold.

While the Jewish people remained within the commandment of the Law and the entire Gentile world knew none of God’s precepts, the former seemed to hold primacy through faith, while the latter lay pressed down in the depths through unbelief. But when Judea denied the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, the Gentiles believed; the leaders fell into contempt, and those who had been oppressed under the guilt of unbelief were raised into the freedom of true faith.

Jeremiah, perceiving the fall of the Israelites long beforehand, says: “The Lord has become like an enemy; he has cast down Israel; he has overthrown its walls and destroyed its defenses” (Lam. II, 5). For that ancient people, which seemed faithful to God, was rejected and repulsed in heart, so that, deceived by its own unbelief, it might afterward rise up against the very one whom it had previously proclaimed.

(Moral. XIX, 23, no. 40.) If the Israelite people had not faltered at all in good works, the Psalmist would never have said in the Lord’s voice: “Foreign sons have lied to me; foreign sons have grown old and have limped from their paths” (Ps. XVII, 46). The Israelite people is called lame because it did not have a sound step in its actions; it refused to use both feet, accepting one Testament and rejecting the other. When the holy Church receives this people as it comes to her, adding the New Testament to the Old Testament it already holds, she joins, as it were, a second foot in order to straighten its steps.

(Moral. XXXI, 15, no. 29.) The Jewish people may be understood as the one-horned beast, because, having received the Law, it took from it not works but only exaltation among all human beings, and thus carried a single horn among the other beasts. In place of the Synagogue, from which he was born according to the flesh, the Lord joined the holy Church to himself in love and contemplation, so that she who had previously been near through kinship—that is, known through predestination—might afterward, once joined in enduring love, become his wife.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 3, no. 1.) The Synagogue is not recognized by its author because, holding to observance of the Law, it lost spiritual understanding and fixed itself outwardly upon guarding the letter.

# BOOK II

## CHAPTER I. On the Incarnation of Christ, or His Nativity

(Moral. XXX, 25, no. 73.) Our almighty Lord Jesus Christ encompasses all things through the power of his majesty, and yet, through the grace of his dispensation, entered the Virgin’s womb, redeeming us by his dispensation, embracing all things in his divinity and assuming humanity within the womb. In the womb in which he was incarnate he was enclosed, yet he was not confined; for he was within the womb through the substance of weakness, and outside the world through the power of majesty.

(Book II on the Gospels, homily 29, nos. 10–11.) In coming for our redemption, Christ made certain, so to speak, leaps, and we must recognize these leaps of his. From heaven he came into the womb; from the womb he came to the manger; from the manger he came to the cross; from the cross he came to the tomb; from the tomb he returned to heaven. Behold, so that he might make us run after him, the Truth manifested in the flesh made certain leaps for us: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVIII, 6), so that we might say to him from the heart: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song I, 3). Therefore we ought to follow in our hearts where we believe that he ascended in his body.

(Moral. XXXIII, 1, no. 2.) Christ is called the Lord’s mountain, who deigned to become incarnate in the Israelite people; the Lord became a mountain on the summit of mountains, surpassing the height of the prophets.

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 1, no. 4.) The incarnate Only-Begotten of the Father was not equal to these mountains—that is, the patriarchs, prophets, and all the saints—for by his divinity he surpassed the nature, life, and merits of them all.

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 23.) The incarnate Only-Begotten of the Father, through having become human, was below the angels, as it is written of him: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII, 6). But rising again and ascending into heaven, he presides over all angelic powers; as it is written of him there again: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (ibid., 7); and as he himself says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

When the Divinity assumed the weakness of our flesh, the human race received again the light it had lost. For by the fact that God suffers human things, the human being is raised to divine things. The Mediator of God and human beings had, through the incarnation of his humanity, to be born, grow, die, rise again, and pass from place to place. Since there is no mutability in divinity, and to be changed is to pass from one place to another, this passing is from the flesh, not from the divinity. Through divinity, however, his state is always to stand, because, being present everywhere, he neither comes through movement nor departs through movement.

(Book II on the Gospels, homily 26, no. 2.) Almighty God the Father sent his Son into this world because he determined that he should become incarnate for the redemption of the human race. He willed that the Son should come into the world for suffering; yet he loved the Son whom he sent to suffer. The Lord likewise sends the chosen apostles into the world not for the world’s joys but, as he himself was sent, for sufferings. Since the Son is loved by the Father and yet is sent to suffer, so the disciples are loved by the Lord and yet are sent into the world to suffer.

Almighty Lord, just as he was able to make good things from nothing, so, when he willed, through the mystery of his incarnation he also restored lost good things.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 2, no. 8.) Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and human beings, although he is Lord and Creator of the angels, came into the Virgin’s womb to assume the nature that he had created. Yet he did not wish to be born into this world through the wealthy; he chose poor parents. Hence no lamb was available to be offered for him, and his mother found young pigeons and a pair of turtledoves for the sacrifice (Luke II, 24). Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and human beings, is not one in his humanity and another in his divinity.

(Moral. XVIII, 52, no. 85.) He was not conceived and born as a mere human being and afterward granted the status of God on account of merit; but when the angel announced and the Spirit came, at once the Word was in the womb, at once within the womb the Word was flesh. While the unchangeable essence remained—the essence that Christ shares coeternally with the Father and the Holy Spirit—he assumed flesh within the Virgin’s womb, where the impassible could suffer, the immortal die, and the eternal before the ages become temporal at the end of the ages. Thus, through an ineffable mystery of holy conception and inviolate birth, according to the truth of both natures, the same Virgin was both the Lord’s servant and his mother.

Thus Elizabeth says to Mary: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke I, 43). And the Virgin herself, conceiving, says: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid., 38). Although Christ is one thing from the Father and another from the Virgin, he is not one person from the Father and another from the Virgin; rather, he is himself eternal from the Father and himself temporal from his mother. He is himself the one who made, and himself the one who was made. He is himself beautiful in form beyond the sons of men through his divinity, and himself the one of whom it was said: “We saw him, and he had no appearance, nor beauty or comeliness” (Isa. LIII, 2), through his humanity. He is himself before the ages from the Father without a mother; himself at the end of the ages from his mother without a father. He is himself the temple of the Creator and himself the Creator of the temple. He is himself the author of the work and himself the work of the author. Remaining one from both natures, he is neither confused by the union of the natures nor doubled by their distinction.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 10, no. 1.) When the King of heaven was born, the king of earth was troubled, because earthly height is utterly confounded when heavenly loftiness is revealed. We must ask why, when the Redeemer was born, an angel appeared to the shepherds in Judea, whereas a star, not an angel, led the Magi from the East to adore him. For, since the Jews were as though rational beings, an intelligent creature—that is, an angel—ought to preach to them; but the Gentiles, because they did not know how to use reason, are led to know the Lord not by a voice but by signs. Thus prophecy was given to the Jews as to believers [the source has *non infidelibus*, “not to unbelievers”], and signs to the Gentiles as to unbelievers [the source has *non fidelibus*, “not to believers”] (I Cor. XIV, 22).

(No. 6.) We who are contained within the bosom of the holy Church should offer gold to the newborn Lord, acknowledging that he reigns everywhere; we should offer frankincense, believing that the one who appeared in time existed as God before time; we should offer myrrh, believing that the one whom we believe impassible in his divinity was also mortal in our flesh.

We offer gold to the newborn King of heaven if we shine before him with the splendor of heavenly wisdom; we offer frankincense if we kindle the thoughts of the flesh upon the altar of the heart through the holy practice of prayer, so that we may be able to give off a sweet fragrance to God through heavenly desire; we offer myrrh if we mortify the vices of the flesh through abstinence.

## CHAPTER II. On Christ’s Preaching

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 19.) If almighty God were silent about his virtues, no one would recognize him and no one would love him. He therefore announces his virtues, not so that he himself may gain anything from praise, but so that those who have come to know him through his praise may attain the eternal inheritance.

(Moral. XVIII, 7, no. 14.) God makes his praises known so that, by hearing him, we may be able to know him; by knowing him, love him; by loving him, follow him; by following him, attain him; and, having attained him, enjoy his vision. “The Lord,” says the Prophet, “has declared the power of his works to his people, in order to give them the inheritance of the nations” (Ps. CX, 6). It is as though he plainly said: He makes known the strength of his work so that whoever hears it may be enriched with gifts.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 19, no. 5.) The prophet David says: “I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX, 6). When the Lord announces, the faithful are multiplied beyond number, because sometimes even those who do not attain the number of the elect come to the faith. They are mingled with the faithful here through confession, but because of their rejected life they do not deserve to be numbered there in the lot of the faithful.

(Moral. XXV, 8, no. 21.) The Prophet, seeing so many apparently believing when the Lord calls and announces—so many, indeed, as certainly surpass the fixed number and total of the elect—says: “They were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX, 6). It is as though he said: When many enter the Church, even those who are excluded from the number of the heavenly kingdom come outwardly to the faith, because by their multiplicity they surpass the total of the elect.

## CHAPTER III. On the Calling of the Apostles

(Moral. XXXV, 8, no. 15.) The holy apostles, who were to be filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, were chosen as twelve when Christ called them. For they were sent to make known the Trinity, which is God, in the four parts of the world. They were therefore chosen as twelve so that the reason for the number itself might make clear that they would preach the three highest things through the four lowest.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 5, no. 1.) At the voice of a single command, Peter and Andrew, leaving their nets, followed the Redeemer. They had not yet seen him perform any miracles; they had heard nothing from him about the reward of eternal recompense; yet at one command of the Lord they forgot what they seemed to possess.

(No. 21.) Our holy apostles purchased the perpetual life of the angels by giving up their nets and boat. The kingdom of God has no price corresponding to its value, yet it is worth as much as you possess.

(No. 4.) The holy apostles, called by the Mediator of God and human beings, took care in this world to love nothing and desire nothing. Isaiah, rightly observing them, says: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. LX, 8). He saw them despise earthly things, draw near to heavenly things in mind, rain down words, and flash with miracles. Since both holy preaching and sublime life had lifted them above earthly contagion, he calls them flying doves and clouds alike.

The elect are therefore like doves at their windows: they desire nothing in this world, look upon everything simply, and are not drawn by a predatory impulse toward the things they see. For it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

(Book II on the Gospels, homily 30, no. 7.) The Word of the Lord is the Son of the Father. The strength of the heavens, therefore, was taken from the Spirit, because the apostles would not have dared to oppose the powers of this world unless the strength of the Holy Spirit had made them steadfast.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Unbelief or Cruelty of the Jews toward Christ.

(Morals XXXV, chapter 14, no. 26.) Isaac, with his dimming eyes, signifies the Jews blinded by the unbelief of their hearts. Their former knowledge and subsequent ignorance are well and briefly represented (Genesis 27). For when he blessed Jacob, he both saw what would happen to him in the future and did not know who was presently standing before him. The people of Israel received the mysteries of prophecy, yet kept blind eyes in contemplation, because they did not see him present of whom they had foreseen so much in the future. They were utterly unable to recognize him placed before them, whose coming they had announced long beforehand.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 10, no. 2.) In all the signs that were manifested at the Lord’s birth and death, we must consider how great was the hardness in the hearts of certain Jews, which recognized him neither through the gift of prophecy nor through miracles. All the elements testified that their Creator had come. To speak of them in ordinary human terms: the heavens recognized that this was God, because they immediately sent a star. [Col. 0779A] The sea recognized him, because it offered itself to be trodden beneath his feet. The earth recognized him, because it trembled when he died. The sun recognized him, because it hid the rays of its light. The rocks and walls recognized him, because they were split at the time of his death. Hell recognized him, because it restored to life those dead whom it held. And yet the hearts of the unbelieving Jews still do not recognize as God him whom all the insensible elements perceived as Lord; harder than rocks, they do not wish to be split open for repentance, and they deny confessing him whom the elements, as we have said, proclaimed to be God either by their signs or by their rending.

Some Jews, to increase the measure of their condemnation, knew long beforehand that he whom they despised when born would be born. They knew not only that he would be born, but also where he would be born. For when questioned by Herod, they specify the place of his birth, which they had learned from the authority of Scripture. And they produce the testimony showing that Bethlehem would be honored by the birth of a new Ruler, so that their very knowledge might become for them a testimony of condemnation and for us an aid to faith.

Isaac aptly represented the Jewish people when he blessed his son Jacob, because, with dimming eyes and while prophesying, he did not see in the present the son concerning whom he foresaw so much in the future. For the Jewish people, filled with the spirit of prophecy yet blind, did not recognize in the present the one about whom they had foretold many things in the future.

(Morals XXIX, chapter 26, no. 52.) The Jews feared that, if the Lord were not killed, they would lose both their place and their nation. But why did these things happen to wretched men? Because their hearts lacked knowledge of eternity, and no teaching nourished them with the food of inward verdure. [Col. 0779C]

(Morals, book XVIII, chapter 32, no. 51.) The Synagogue, which brought forth the commandments of God through the Law, persecuting the Church at her birth, consumed itself in the fire of envy. Was it not burning in the flames of its jealousy when, seeing the signs of our Redeemer, it said through some of its own people: “What are we to do? For this man is performing many signs” (John 11:47)? Or certainly: “You see that we are accomplishing nothing. Behold, the whole world has gone after him.” The Jews saw the reason for which they ought to have been converted, and because of it became more perverse. They sought to extinguish the one whom they saw giving life to the dead. They held the Law in their mouths, but persecuted the author of the Law.

(Morals, book XVII, chapter 33, no. 54.) Before our Redeemer allowed himself to be seized by the Jews, he questioned his persecutors, saying: “Whom do you seek?” Immediately they answered him: “Jesus the Nazarene” (John 18:4). When he suddenly said to them, “I am he,” he uttered only the voice of a most gentle reply, and immediately struck his armed persecutors to the ground. What, then, will he do when he comes to judge, who by a single voice overcame his enemies even when he came to be judged? What will be the judgment that the immortal one brings forth, whose single voice could not be endured when he came to die? Or who could endure his anger, whose very gentleness could not be endured?

(Morals, book II, chapter 2, no. 2.) Concerning Peter, who was about to deny him, it is said beforehand: “Because it was cold, and he was standing by the charcoal fire and warming himself” (John 18:18). Peter had already grown cold within, deprived of the warmth of charity, and, with desire burning for the love of the present age, he warmed himself as though at the persecutors’ fire. [Note: [Col. 0779D] The edition reads, “with weakness burning, he grew warm again.”]

(Preface to Morals, book IV, chapter 4.) The mountains of Gilboa signify the proud hearts of the Jews, who, while flowing downward into the desires of this world, mingled themselves with the death of Christ, that is, of the Anointed One. And because the Anointed King dies bodily among them, they themselves are dried up from every dew of grace. The proud minds of the Hebrews bear no first fruits, because, for the most part remaining in unbelief at the Redeemer’s coming, they refused to follow the beginnings of faith.

(Morals, book XXVII, chapter 26, no. 49.) Were not the hearts of the persecuting Jews the devil’s cavern? He lay hidden for a long time in their counsels, but suddenly burst forth in the voices of those crying: “Crucify, crucify” (John 19:6). And because, by tempting, he could not reach the tearing apart of the mind, he thirsted in our Redeemer for the death of the flesh. [Col. 0780B]

## CHAPTER V. On the Passion and Death of Jesus Christ

(Morals XII, chapter 12, no. 16.) As the Lord drew near to his Passion, he took upon himself the voice of the weak and assumed their fear in order to draw it away from them, saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). And again, displaying the force of courage through obedience, he said: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” Thus, when what we do not wish to happen is imminent, we should ask in weakness that it not happen, so that through courage we may be ready for the will of our Creator to be done even against our will.

(Morals II, chapter 38, no. 62.) Our Redeemer, questioned during the time of his Passion, testified that he was the Son of God. Hence his accusers also say: “What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, we ourselves have heard the blasphemies” (Matthew 26:65). Yet he said nothing foolish against God, because, speaking the truth, he declared this about himself to the unbelievers even by dying, which shortly afterward the Redeemer demonstrated to all by rising again. [Note: [Col. 0779D] The edition reads, “to all the redeemed.”]

(Morals XXXIII, chapter 15, no. 31.) The devil had confessed that he was the Son of God (Matthew 8:29), yet believed that he was merely a man who would die, and for whose death he stirred up the souls of the persecuting Jews. But at the very time of the betrayal, he is understood to have recognized too late that he would be punished by that death. [Note: [Col. 0780D] The edition reads, “that he himself would be punished by it.”] Therefore he terrified Pilate’s wife through dreams, so that her husband would cease persecuting the Just One. But, once the matter had been arranged by an inward dispensation, no scheme could oppose it. It was greatly fitting that the death of the Just One, dying unjustly, should undo the death of sinners who die justly. Because the devil remained ignorant of this until the time of his Passion, he was deceived like a bird: while he bit the bait of Christ’s humanity, he was caught in the snare of his divinity.

(Book II on the Gospels, homily 21, no. 7.) If Christ had descended from the cross at the time of his Passion, yielding to those who insulted him, he certainly would not have shown us the virtue of patience. But he waited a little, endured insults, bore mockery, preserved patience, and deferred the wonder;  and he who did not wish to descend from the cross (Matthew 27:42) rose from the tomb. It is therefore greater to rise from the tomb than to descend from the cross. It was greater to destroy death by rising again than to preserve life by descending.

When the Jews did not see Christ descend from the cross in response to their insults, they believed that they had conquered him. They rejoiced as though they had extinguished his name. But behold, his name grew throughout the world out of the death by which the unbelieving crowd believed it had extinguished him; and those who rejoiced that he had been killed grieve at his death, because they recognize that through suffering he has reached his glory.

(Morals XIV, chapter 49, no. 57.) When the hour of the cross had come, a great fear arising from the persecution of the Jews seized the Lord’s disciples: they fled one by one, while the women stood by. Of these blessed Job rightly says figuratively: “When my flesh has been consumed, only the lips around my teeth remain” (Job 19:20). Thus, when the flesh had been consumed, the Lord’s mouth clung to his skin, because, at the time of his Passion, while the disciples fled, his strength found the women standing beside him.

Peter indeed stood for some time during the Lord’s Passion, but afterward, terrified, he denied him (Matthew 26:70). John also stood; to him, at the very time of the cross, it was said: “Behold, your mother” (John 19:27). Yet he could not persevere, because it is also written concerning him: “A certain young man was following him, clothed in a linen garment over his naked body, and they seized him; but he, abandoning the linen garment, fled from them naked” (Mark 14:51). [Col. 0781C]

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 24.) Although afterward he returned to the cross for the hour in order to hear the words of his Redeemer, he had first fled in terror. The women, however, are remembered not only as having neither feared nor fled, but also as having remained there all the way to the tomb.

Concerning the Lord Jesus Christ it is written before his Passion: “Behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matthew 4:11). Yet, as he drew near to his Passion, so that the weakness of his humanity might be revealed, it is again written concerning him: “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke 22:43). Thus, as evidence of both natures, he is described as one to whom angels minister and as one whom an angel strengthens. He is one in both natures, because he who existed as God before the ages became man at the end of the ages. Before his Passion angels ministered to him, and an angel strengthened him. After his Passion and resurrection, angels can minister to him, but they can no longer strengthen him.

(Morals XVIII, chapter 40, no. 64.) In the midst of these events, I would gladly direct the eyes of the mind toward that thief who climbed from the devil’s jaws to the cross, and from the cross to paradise. Let us consider what sort of man he came to the gibbet as, and what sort he departed from the gibbet as. He came guilty of a brother’s blood; he came bloodstained, but on the cross he was changed by inward grace. And the man who had inflicted death on his brother proclaimed the life of the dying Lord, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

Nails fastened this thief’s hands and feet to the cross, and nothing in him remained free from punishment except his heart and tongue. Under God’s inspiration, he offered him everything that he found free within himself, so that, according to what is written, he might “believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation” (Romans 10:10). The thief confessed as God the one whom he saw dying with him in human weakness, while the apostles denied the one whom they had seen performing miracles by divine power.

(No. 65.) But those who maintain that a human being is saved by his own powers suppose that this same human confession proceeds from the human being’s own strength. If that were so, the Psalmist would not say in praise of God: “Confession and magnificence are his work” (Psalm 110:3). Therefore, we receive the ability to confess rightly from the one from whom we also receive the ability to do great things.

(Morals XXIX, chapter 14, no. 26.) When Jesus approached the distress of death, he extended his faith among the nations and stretched the holy Church toward countless hearts of believers. To her the prophet says: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and extend the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare; lengthen your cords and strengthen your pegs. For you shall penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring shall inherit the nations” (Isaiah 54:2). This breadth across the earth certainly would not have come about unless he had first despised by dying the life that we know and displayed by rising again the life that we do not know.

Our Redeemer opened the eyes of our mind through his death and showed what the life to come would be. Therefore, maintaining this order in the Gospel, he says to his disciples: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations” (Luke 24:46).

Our Redeemer came to death in order to redeem us from death, and endured in his body the weakness and punishments of our flesh. Before he reached the gibbet of the cross, he allowed himself to be seized, spat upon, mocked, and struck with blows. Behold to what great disgrace he consented to come for our sake!

(Morals III, chapter 16, no. 29.) When the Lord handed himself over for our redemption into the hands of Satan’s members, what else did he do than permit Satan’s own hands to rage against him, so that by the means through which he outwardly succumbed, he might free us outwardly and inwardly?

If Satan’s hands are understood as his power, our Redeemer endured his hands according to the flesh, whose power over his body he tolerated even to spitting, blows, scourges, the cross, and the spear. Hence, coming to his bodily judge, Pilate, for his Passion, he says: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). Yet he compelled this power, which had been given to Pilate outwardly against him, to serve his own gains inwardly.

Pilate—or Satan, who had become the head of that Pilate—was held under the power of the one over whom he had received power. For our Redeemer himself, who is above, had arranged this: what happened below he endured at the hands of the persecutor, so that, although it arose from the evil mind of unbelievers, their very cruelty might nevertheless serve the benefit of all the elect. Thus, inwardly he piously arranged what outwardly he wickedly permitted to be inflicted upon himself. [Edition: accedens (“approaching”) for accidens (“happening”).]

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 2, no. 1.) Our Redeemer, foreseeing that the minds of the disciples would be disturbed by his Passion, foretold to them long beforehand both the suffering of that Passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that, when they saw him dying as had been foretold, they would not doubt that he would also rise again.

## CHAPTER VI. On Christ’s Single Death and Our Double Death

(Morals, book IV, chapter 16, no. 31.) To erase human sins before the eyes of God, the Mediator of God and human beings came, taking upon himself for us only the death of the flesh and wiping away the true death of sinners through the shadow of his own death. Our Redeemer descended to us in merciful compassion. We were held in the death of spirit and flesh; he brought to us his one death and dissolved the two deaths that he found in us. If our Redeemer had assumed both deaths, he would have freed us from neither. But he mercifully accepted one and justly condemned both. He joined his single death to our double death, and by dying subdued our double death.

The Mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, appropriately lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. Therefore, since he accepted for us only the death of the flesh, he endured the shadow of death and concealed from the eyes of God the guilt that we had committed.

## CHAPTER VII. On Christ’s Resurrection

(Morals, book XXXI, chapter 49, no. 99.) The Mediator of God and human beings, Christ Jesus, came to restore all things, so that, after redeeming the human race, he might repair the losses among the angels and perhaps enrich still more fully the number of the heavenly homeland. [Note: [Col. 0783D] In the edition of the Maurist Fathers: praeruptionem (“a breaking-off”).] For this restoration it is said of the Father: “He set forth in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, both those in the heavens and those on earth, in him” (Ephesians 1:9–10).

In him, those things that are on earth are restored when sinners are converted to righteousness. In him, those things that are in heaven are restored when humbled human beings return there from which the proud apostate angels fell.

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 23.) The Father’s Only-Begotten Son, by becoming human, was made lower than the angels, as it is written concerning him: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:6). But, rising again and ascending into heaven, he presides over all angelic powers, as it is again written there concerning him: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (ibid. 7). And as he himself says: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18).

(Morals, book XIV, chapter 53, no. 68.) Our Redeemer accepted death so that we would not fear dying. He showed the resurrection so that we might trust that we can rise again. Therefore, he willed that this same death should last no more than three days, lest, if resurrection were delayed in him, all hope of it should utterly be lost in us.

The prophet David says of our Redeemer: “He drank from the torrent on the way; therefore he lifted up his head” (Psalm 109:7). He graciously drank, as it were, from a certain river of our Passion not in a dwelling but on the way, because he encountered death only in passing, that is, for three days; and in that death which he encountered he did not remain, as we do, until the end of the age.

When Christ rose on the third day, he showed what would follow in his body, that is, the Church. He demonstrated by example what he promised as a reward, so that, just as the faithful recognized that he had risen, they might likewise hope for the rewards of resurrection in themselves at the end of the world.

Behold, through the death of the flesh we remain in the dust until the end of the world, but he flourished on the third day from the dryness of death and showed us the power of his divinity in the renewal of his flesh: “He drank,” he says, “from the torrent on the way; therefore he lifted up his head.” [Note: [Col. 0783D] The edition reads: “so that he might show ….”]

(Book II on the Gospels, homily 25, no. 7.) In the human race, from the very beginning of the world, a torrent of death had flowed. But the Lord drank from this torrent on the way, because he tasted death in passing. Therefore he lifted up his head, because what he had placed in the tomb by dying, he raised above the angels by rising again. From the place where he temporarily permitted the hands of persecutors to rage against him, he struck down the ancient enemy forever.

(Book II on the Gospels, homily 21, no. 7.) That most powerful Samson signified our Redeemer. When he had entered the city of the Philistines, Gaza, the Philistines immediately recognized his arrival, suddenly surrounded the city with besieging forces, appointed guards, and rejoiced that they had already captured Samson, so mighty in strength (Judges 16:1–3).

But we know what Samson did. At midnight he removed the city gates and climbed to the summit of a mountain. Whom does that Samson signify in this deed, if not our Redeemer? What does the city Gaza signify, if not hell? What is demonstrated by the Philistines, if not the unbelief of the Jews?

When they saw the Lord dead and his body placed in the tomb, they immediately appointed guards. [Edition: viderent (“when they were seeing”) for viderunt (“when they saw”).] They rejoiced that they had captured, as it were, like Samson in Gaza, the one who had shone forth as the author of life, holding him imprisoned in the confines of hell.

Samson not only went out at midnight, but also carried away the gates. Thus our Redeemer, rising before dawn, not only went forth free from hell, but also destroyed hell’s very confines. He carried away the gates and climbed to the summit of the mountain, because by rising again he removed the confines of hell, and by ascending he entered the kingdoms of heaven.

(As cited by Paterius, book VI, chapter 7.) That Samson, strong in the power of his might, killed a few while he lived; but when he overturned the temple, even while dying he struck down a very great multitude of his enemies. Thus, while Christ our Lord was preaching, few believed; but when he died, countless peoples of the nations followed the way of life.

(Morals 29, chapter 14, no. 26.) While our Redeemer was still living in a condition capable of suffering, he endured the proud; but when dead, he struck down those capable of suffering in life. [Note: [Col. 0784D] The edition reads, “but from the life capable of suffering.” Other manuscripts read: “but from the life capable of suffering he struck down many while he was dying.”] For the Lord destroyed a few who were puffed up with pride while he lived, but many more when the temple of his body was destroyed; and all at once, by dying, he cast down the elect from the nations whom he had endured while living.

(Morals 29, chapter 12, no. 23.) It is written: “You made the depth of the sea a way for the redeemed to cross over” (Isaiah 51:10). If, according to the manner of divine speech, the sea should be understood as the world, there is nothing to prevent us from understanding the deep places of the sea as the confines of hell.

The Lord entered this depth of the sea when, intending to rescue the souls of his elect, he entered the lowest regions of hell. Before the Redeemer’s coming, this depth of the sea was not a way but a prison, because it confined within itself even the souls of the good, although not in places of punishment.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Saints Who Were Held in the Prisons of Hell before Christ’s Incarnation

(Morals XII, chapter 9, nos. 13–15.) Before the incarnation of our Redeemer, the souls of the righteous are believed to have descended into hell, but not to have been held in places of punishment. We must believe that there are higher places of hell and other lower ones, so that the righteous might rest in the higher and the unrighteous be tormented in the lower.

It is beyond doubt that every human being, however pure and proven his life might have been, descended before the coming of the Mediator of God and humanity into the confines of hell. For the human being who fell by himself could not return by himself to the rest of paradise, unless he came who, through the mystery of his incarnation, would open for us the way to that same paradise.

Hence blessed Job rightly asks the Lord, saying: “Who will grant that you protect me in hell?” (Job 14:13). The Psalmist likewise says: “You have rescued my soul from the lower hell” (Psalm 85:13).

Blessed Job, knowing that before Christ’s coming he would descend into hell, asks there for the protection of his Creator, so that he may remain apart from the places of punishment, where, while he is led to rest, he may be hidden from torments. Hence he adds: “That you may hide me until your anger passes away” (ibid.).

For the anger of almighty God daily exercises the force of his strict judgment in this: that he consigns those who live unworthily to punishments they deserve. God’s anger now passes, but at the end it will pass completely, because it is now being carried out but will be completed at the end of the world.

Yet, as regards the souls of the elect, this anger passed away at the coming of our Redeemer, because the Mediator of God and humanity, when he mercifully descended there himself, brought them from the confines of hell to the joys of paradise.

The souls of the righteous were at some time to be freed by the Mediator’s coming from the places of hell, although not from places of punishment. Blessed Job also foresees this and adds in his petition: “And appoint for me a time when you will remember me” (ibid.).

But when the fullness of time had come, “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Galatians 4:4–5). Awaiting the coming of our Redeemer, the man of the Lord Job, among whom many also from the Gentiles were to be freed, says: “Although you hide these things in your heart, yet I know that you remember all” (Job 10:13).

He asks almighty God that a time of his remembrance be appointed for him, saying: “Behold, I wait for you to restore to me the time when you will remember me.”

In the Gospel the Lord says: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32)—that is, all the elect. For when returning from hell, the Lord did not draw both the elect and the reprobate together, but raised from there all those whom he had foreknown would cling to him.

Through the prophet Hosea the Lord says: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hosea 13:14). What we kill, we act so that it may no longer exist at all. From what we bite, we remove one part and leave another. Therefore, because the Lord utterly killed death in his elect, he became the death of death; but because he removed one part from hell and left another, he did not kill hell completely but bit it: “I shall be your death, O death”—that is, “In my elect I utterly destroy you”; “I shall be your bite, O hell”—because, after removing them, I pierce you in part.

(Morals XIII, chapter 43, no. 48.) All the elect who came into this world before the coming of our Redeemer, no matter how great the virtue of their righteousness, could in no way be immediately received into the bosom of the heavenly homeland when taken from their bodies, because he had not yet come who would, by his descent, unlock the confines of hell and establish the souls of the righteous in their eternal dwelling.

Hence blessed Job, feeling affliction and knowing that the reward of the righteous was still being delayed, aptly added: “If I wait, hell is my house, and in darkness I have made my bed” (Job 17:13).

(Chapter 44, no. 49.) The earlier saints, taken from their bodies, could not yet be freed from the places of hell, because he had not yet come who would descend there without guilt in order to free from guilt those who were held there: so that they would still descend there on account of original sin, yet would not suffer punishment for their own actions.

It was a grievous weariness for the elect, after the dissolution of the flesh, still not to see the appearance of the Creator. Blessed Job not unworthily calls this weariness “darkness.” But because this came from the punishment of weakness, he rightly immediately added the same weakness, saying: “I said to corruption: You are my father; to my mother and my sister: the worms” (Job 17:14).

(Chapter 43, no. 48.) We all who have been redeemed by the grace of our Creator now have this through the gift of heaven [Note: [Col. 0785D] In the edition of the Maurist Fathers: coelestis muneris (“of the heavenly gift”).]: that, when we are withdrawn from the dwelling of our flesh, we are immediately led to heavenly rewards. For when our Creator and Redeemer penetrated the confines of hell and led out from there the souls of the elect, he does not permit us to go there from which he has already freed others by descending.

(Morals IV, chapter 29, no. 56.) Before our Redeemer paid the penalty of the human race by his death, even those who followed the ways of the heavenly homeland were held after the departure from the flesh in the confines of hell—not so that punishment might chastise them as sinners, but so that, while they rested in more remote places, the guilt of original sin might prevent them from entering the kingdom, since the Mediator’s intercession had not yet arrived.

According to the testimony of our Redeemer, the rich man who is tormented in hell sees Eleazar resting in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:19). If the elect were not still in the lower regions, he, who was placed in torments, would certainly not see them. Therefore, the same Redeemer, dying because of the debt of our sin, enters the lower regions in order to lead to heaven his own who had clung to him.

But to the place where the redeemed human being now ascends, he would certainly have reached even without redemption, if he had not wished to sin.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Holy Apostles and Their Preaching

(Morals, book IX, chapter 9, no. 10.) By the name “heavens,” the heavenly life of the apostles as preachers is signified. In sacred Scripture they themselves are said to be the heavens, and they themselves the sun: the heavens, because they protect by interceding; the sun, because by preaching they display the power of light.

When raging Judea roared with the force of persecution, the Lord spread the life of the apostles throughout the knowledge of all nations. While that people was scattered captive throughout the world by judgment, these men were extended everywhere in honor through grace.

The heavens were narrow when one people contained so many outstanding preachers. For who among the Gentiles would have known Peter if he had remained in the preaching of the Israelite people alone? Who would have recognized Paul’s virtues if Judea, by persecuting him, had not sent him into our knowledge?

The holy apostles, rejected by the Israelite people through scourges and insults, are honored throughout the ends of the world, because, by a hidden and wondrous dispensation of counsel, the Lord caused his preachers to be oppressed in one nation, from there to be spread to the corners of the world.

(Morals XX, chapter 20, no. 38.) The eminent Psalmist David says: “Before his brightness the clouds passed away; hail and coals of fire” (Psalm 17:13). Before his brightness the clouds passed away, because the holy preachers traversed all the expanses of the world in the splendor of miracles.

They were also called hail and coals of fire, because they strike through correction and kindle through the flame of charity. The free rebuke of the saints is fittingly expressed by the nature of hail: hail, when it comes, strikes; when melted, it waters. Holy men strike the hearts of their hearers by filling them with fear, and pour themselves into them by offering consolation.

The prophet testifies to how they strike, saying: “They shall speak of the power of your terrible acts, and they shall tell of your greatness” (Psalm 144:6). He added how they water by offering consolation: “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they shall rejoice in your righteousness” (ibid. 7).

(Morals XXVII, chapter 11, no. 20.) It is written: “You shall multiply lightning, and you shall trouble them” (Psalm 143:6, according to the Septuagint). Therefore, through these clouds the Lord flashes with his light, because through the holy preachers he also illuminates the darkness of our insensibility by miracles.

(No. 21.) When these clouds—that is, the holy apostles—rain with their words and reveal by miracles the power of flashing light, they convert even the farthest ends of the world to divine love. “You shall multiply lightning,” he says, “and you shall trouble them.”

(Morals XXX, chapter 2, no. 6.) Lightning comes forth from clouds, just as wondrous works are displayed through holy preachers. As has often been said, they are accustomed to be called clouds because they flash with miracles and rain with words. When human hearts have not been moved by the preaching of the saints, they are troubled by these flashes of miracles. “You shall multiply lightning,” he says, “and you shall trouble them.” It is as though he said: “When they do not hear the words of preaching, they are troubled by the miracles of the preachers.”

Through the prophet Habakkuk it is said: “Your arrows will go forth in light, in the brightness of the flashing of your weapons” (Habakkuk 3:11). For God’s arrows going forth in light means that his words resound with open truth: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6).

(As cited by Paterius, XI, 68.) What are signified by the name “heavens” if not the holy apostles, who rain with words and flash with miracles, whose strength is strengthened by the gift of the Spirit?

(Book II on the Gospels, homily 30, no. 7.) Therefore, as many as are the good works of the preachers, so many are, as it were, the ornaments of heaven. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.” The Word of the Lord is the Son of the Father. But, so that the same heavens—namely, the holy apostles—might show that the whole Trinity was at work together, the text suddenly adds concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit: “And by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6). The strength of the heavens was taken from the Spirit, because the holy apostles would not have dared to oppose the powers of this world unless the strength of the Holy Spirit had made them steadfast.

(Morals XIX, chapter 30, no. 55.) Hence it is finally written: “They enter there with arrows and bow” (Isaiah 7:24), because the holy apostles came to strike the hardness of pagan life with the sharp shafts of their words.

(Book II on the Gospels, homily 29, no. 2.) When Truth sends the holy apostles to preach, what else does he do in the world than scatter grains of seed, sowing a few grains so as to receive the harvest of many crops from our faith? For such a harvest of believers would not arise throughout the whole world if those chosen grains of the preachers had not been scattered from the Lord’s hand upon rational soil. [Note: [Col. 0787D] The edition reads, “had not come.”]

Truth himself says to the disciples: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). The name “every creature” may also designate every nation of the Gentiles. For earlier it had been said to the apostles: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matthew 10:5). But now it is said: “Preach the Gospel to every creature.” Thus the preaching of the apostles, first rejected by Judea, would afterward become an aid to us when that proud people rejected it as a testimony to its own condemnation.

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 13.) While persecution was taking place in Judea, the holy preaching of the apostles was scattered throughout the whole world. [Col. 0788D]

## CHAPTER X. On the Holy Evangelists
(Lib. I on Ezekiel, homily 4, no. 1.) The four living creatures that Scripture often numbers signify the four evangelists, as the beginnings of each individual Gospel book themselves testify. Since Matthew began with human generation, he is rightly represented by a man; since Mark began with a cry in the wilderness, appropriately by a lion; since Luke began with a sacrifice, fittingly by a calf; but since John began with the divinity of the Word, he is worthily signified by an eagle. When he says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1), he directed his gaze toward the very substance of divinity, fixing the eyes of his mind upon the sun, as an eagle does.

All the elect are members of our Redeemer, while our Redeemer himself is the head of all the elect. Since his members have been represented by these figures, there is no objection if he himself is also signified in all of them. The only-begotten Son of God truly became man; in the sacrifice of our redemption he graciously died as a calf; through the power of his strength he rose as a lion. The lion is also said to sleep with its eyes open, because in that death in which our Redeemer could sleep according to his humanity, he remained immortal and watchful according to his divinity. After his resurrection, ascending into heaven, he was raised on high as an eagle. Thus he is all these things together for us: by being born he became man, by dying a calf, by rising a lion, and by ascending into heaven an eagle.

But since we have said above that the four evangelists, and simultaneously all the perfect under their appearance, are signified through these living creatures, it remains for us to show how each of the elect is expressed by these visions of the creatures.

(No. 2.) Every elect person who is perfect in the way of the Lord is simultaneously man, calf, lion, and eagle. Man is a rational animal; the calf is customarily slaughtered in sacrifice; the lion is a strong beast, as it is written: “The lion is strongest among beasts and retreats before no one” (Prov. XXX, 30). The eagle flies up to lofty places and fixes its unblinking eyes upon the rays of the sun.

Therefore everyone who is perfect in reason is a man. Since he mortifies himself with respect to the pleasures of this world, he is a calf. Because through that voluntary mortification he possesses a secure strength against every adversity—whence it is written, “The righteous is confident as a lion and will be without fear” (Prov. XXVIII, 1)—he is a lion. Because he contemplates sublimely those things that are heavenly and eternal, he is an eagle. Since each righteous person becomes a man through reason, a calf through the sacrifice of his mortification, a lion through the strength of his confidence, and an eagle through contemplation, every perfect person may rightly be signified by these holy creatures.

We say this in order to demonstrate that what has been said about the four creatures also pertains to each of the perfect individually.

In the later time, which is the present, the holy Church has evangelists and teachers.

(Lib. II on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 6.) Since “Gospel” means good news, we call evangelists those who announce the good things of the heavenly homeland to uneducated peoples. Such evangelists and teachers existed indeed in the earlier time, but by the Lord’s bounty they remain even to the present; for we know that even now unbelieving peoples are daily being drawn to the faith, and that the faithful are instructed by teachers in good conduct.

(Lib. I on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 15.) Concerning the holy evangelists the prophet Ezekiel says: “And in the midst of it was the likeness of four living creatures” (Ezek. I, 5). Whether “in its midst” is understood of electrum or of fire, there is no obstacle to understanding it; for these four creatures—that is, the holy evangelists—were both strengthened in the power of faith through the incarnation of the same Lord and afflicted with many tribulations in the fire of persecution.

(Ibid., homily 3, no. 1.) If you ask what Matthew thinks about the Lord’s incarnation, he thinks precisely what Mark, Luke, and John do. If you ask what John thinks, unquestionably it is what Luke, Mark, and Matthew do. If you ask what Mark thinks, it is what Matthew, John, and Luke do. If you ask what Luke thinks, it is what John, Matthew, and Mark think.

The faces of the four evangelists are one, because the knowledge of faith by which they are known to God is the same in one as it is simultaneously in all four. Whatever you find in one, you recognize in all four together [Ed., “you rightly recognize”]. The four evangelists unanimously preach the Son of almighty God, the Lord Jesus Christ; raising the eyes of their minds toward his divinity, they fly on the wing of contemplation.

The faces of the evangelists pertain to the Lord’s humanity, and the wings to his divinity, because in him whom they see as bodily they direct their gaze toward a face. But while they announce that, according to his divinity, he is uncircumscribed and incorporeal, they are lifted through the wing of contemplation, as it were, into the air [Ed., “are raised”].

Because there is one faith in Christ’s incarnation among all the evangelists, and an equal contemplation of his divinity in each, Ezekiel rightly says: “Four faces belonged to one, and four wings belonged to one, and their feet were straight” (Ezek. I, 6–7). What is signified by the feet of the evangelists except the steps of their actions? The feet of the four creatures are therefore described as straight, because the works of the holy evangelists and of all perfect people have not been turned aside to follow iniquity. Those do not have straight feet who turn back toward the evils of the world that they had abandoned. Of them it is written: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (Prov. XXVI, 11).

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the Scripture of the Old and New Testaments

(Moral. XX, ch. 1, no. 1.) Holy Scripture surpasses all knowledge and teaching without comparison: it proclaims what is true; it calls us to our heavenly homeland; it changes the heart of the reader from earthly desires to the embrace of heavenly things; by more obscure sayings it exercises the strong, while with humble speech it caresses the little ones.

Holy Scripture is not so closed that it ought to be feared, nor so open that it becomes cheap. Through use it removes distaste, and it is loved all the more the more it is meditated upon. It assists the reader’s mind with humble words and lifts it with sublime meanings. In a certain way it grows together with its readers: it is as if recognized by uneducated readers, yet it is always found to be new by the learned.

To say nothing of the weight of its subject matter, sacred Scripture surpasses all sciences and teachings even in the manner of its speech. In one and the same discourse it narrates the text and reveals the mystery; it knows how to speak of past events in such a way that, by that very fact, it proclaims the future. Without changing the order of its speech, in the very same words it knows both to describe what has happened and to announce what must happen.

(Lib. I on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 16.) Holy Scripture goes to the hearts of human beings through the law of the Old Testament, marking out the mystery. Through the prophets it goes somewhat more openly, prophesying the Lord. Through the Gospel it goes by presenting the one whom it prophesied. Through the apostles it goes by preaching him whom the Father presented for our redemption.

The sacred utterances contain knowledge of the commandments together with the presentation of works. They go, as it were, through four parts, because they speak in distinct periods, or certainly because they preach the Lord incarnate in every region of the world.

(Lib. I on Ezekiel, homily 10, nos. 1–2.) Some people, when reading the writings of the same sacred utterance and penetrating its more sublime judgments, despise with an inflated mind the lesser commandments given to the weaker, and wish to alter them into another meaning. If they rightly understood the lofty things in it, they would not despise even the smallest commandments, because the divine precepts speak in some passages to the great in such a way that in others they suit the little ones, who grow through stages of understanding, as though by certain steps of the mind, and arrive at the comprehension of greater things.

The Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: “Son of man, whatever you find, eat” (Ezek. III, 1). Everything found in sacred Scripture must be eaten, because its lesser things shape a simple life, while its greater things build a subtle understanding.

(Lib. I on Ezekiel, homily 7, no. 16.) We must recognize very clearly that Scripture has two Testaments, both of which the Spirit of God wished to be written in order to free us from the death of the soul. Or certainly, because there are two commandments of charity—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—the sayings of sacred Scripture give life to us through both. When we grasp love of God and neighbor in the divine utterances, we come back to life through the commandments of Scripture, we who had lain dead in guilt.

Hence the Psalmist says to almighty God: “I will not forget your justifications forever, because by them you have given me life” (Ps. CXVIII, 93). The Lord’s commandments are called justifications, because by correcting us in them he justifies us. Concerning them the same Psalmist says more plainly: “I will meditate on your justifications; I will not forget your words” (ibid., 16). In them, therefore, he gives us life, because through them he shows us spiritual life and, through the breath of the Spirit, pours it into our minds.

(No. 8.) Holy men understand in sacred Scripture how they should live morally and raise themselves into contemplation. The more each of the saints has progressed in this same Scripture, the more sacred Scripture progresses for him, because the divine utterances grow together with the reader. For each person understands it more deeply in proportion as he applies himself to it more deeply; unless the minds of readers progress toward lofty things, the divine words lie below, as it were, uncomprehended.

When the speech of sacred Scripture seems tepid to a reader, the meaning of the divine utterance does not stir his mind [Note: [Col. 0791] Edition: “If the meaning of the divine utterance seems tepid”], and no illumination of understanding shines forth in his thought. But if he seeks the order of living well and, by the step of the heart, discovers how to set down the foot of good action [Ed., “the step”], he finds as much progress in the sacred utterance as that utterance itself has progressed in him. The wondrous and ineffable power of the sacred utterance is recognized when the reader’s soul is penetrated by heavenly love.

(Moral. XIX, ch. 30, no. 55.) Often in sacred Scripture the name “bow” signifies holy Scripture, as it is said through Isaiah: “They will enter there with arrows and bow” (Isa. VII, 24). In the bowstring the New Testament is understood, and in the horn the Old Testament. In a bow, when the string is drawn, the horn is bent; so in this same sacred utterance, when the New Testament is read, the hardness of the Old Testament is softened.

The rigor of the letter bends toward the spiritual and gentle commandments of sacred Scripture, because, when the New Testament is drawn as if by the arm of good action, the laws of severity in the Old Testament are bent. It is not inappropriate to say that the bowstring corresponds to the New Testament, which is known to have come into existence through the Lord’s incarnation. The string is therefore drawn and the horn bent, because when the incarnation of the Mediator is recognized in the New Testament, the rigor of the Old Testament is inclined toward spiritual understanding.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the Beginning of the Nascent Church

(Moral. XXVI, ch. 41, no. 75.) Almighty God does not abandon his Church without a worthy administration. When he calls the strong to their reward, he strengthens the weak for battles in their place. When he receives and rewards the former, he supplies the latter with the powers of labor for which he will reward them [Ed. “strength”]. Those who are later appointed are substituted in the strength of the ancient fathers. For when aged trees are cut down, tender shoots grow up in their strength.

Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. XLIV, 17). “God will be known in her steps, when he receives her” (Ps. XLVII, 4).

(Lib. II on Ezekiel, homily 3, no. 3.) When the Lord receives the holy Church, he is known in her steps, because her glory is revealed through her growth. For the more the holy Church progresses by ascending, the more God becomes known to human beings through her virtues.

Blessed Job also speaks of these steps, saying: “I will declare him through my every step” (Job XXXI, 37).

[Note: [Col. 0791] Paterius assigns this to homily 15 on Ezekiel, which nevertheless is not extant among Gregory’s works.]

Almighty God is recognized in the steps of the Church, because through each of her virtues and miracles he is shown to all as one who ought to be feared and loved—namely, when he receives her as she returns to him from her sins through repentance.

(Moral. VIII, ch. 48, no. 82.) “The daughter of kings” is the holy Church, generated in good works through the preaching of spiritual princes. She has glory within, as it is written: “All the glory of the daughter of the king is within” (Ps. XLIV, 14), because what she does daily she does not possess as a boast of outward display.

(Mor. XXXV, ch. 18.) For if she sought glory outside, she would not have within her the beauty that the king would desire.

(Mor. XIX, ch. 12, no. 20.) Because the holy Church has preserved her outward things irreproachably from her beginnings until now, the Psalmist rightly says of her: “Clothed round about in golden fringes, adorned with variety” (Ps. XLIV, 14), so that she may be beautiful both within herself and outwardly to others, advancing herself through inward glory and instructing others through the outward examples of her works.

(Apud Pater., ch. 53, on Genesis; Moral. lib. XIV, ch. 43, no. 51.) The Church of the elect alone was to be joined to the only-begotten Son of God the Father; yet the Only-begotten himself, by predestination and by his presence, did not already regard her as a stranger. As often as the holy Church learned commandments from the preaching of our Redeemer, she received as many kisses from his mouth, as it is written: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (Song I, 1). As though she were saying in clear words:

(Moral. XXVII, ch. 17, no. 34.) “Previously he extended a kiss to me through the proclamations of the prophets, as though through certain lips; but now let the very sweetness of the presence of the only-begotten Son, my Redeemer, touch me.”

(Moral. XIX, ch. 12, no. 19.) All the Churches that together make up the one catholic Church are called young women—not old through guilt, but new through grace; not sterile through age, but suited by the age of their minds to spiritual fruitfulness.

(Apud Pater., cited above.) From the earlier people the holy Church showed that she had known the law of nature, and she received the words of preaching in the broad bosom of charity. Hearing the words of life and coming to the conduct of true faith, the holy Church took care not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly.

(Lib. I on the Gospels, homily 17, no. 7.) Yet she supplied earthly wages to the preachers; when the apostle Paul received them as though they were nothing, he said: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap carnal things from you?” (I Cor. IX, 11).

(Apud Pater., cited above.) The holy Church, which previously received through faith, obedience, and action, later grew and became strong even for spiritual gifts, so that, filled with the spirit of prophecy and the grace of virtues, she might grow rich through her gifts, now increased.

The only-begotten Lord and our Redeemer, when the Church came to him, remained in the minds of those whom, though born from Judaea, not the chill of sluggishness but the fervor of charity possessed. From that people came the prophetess Anna; from it came Simeon, who received the Lord into his arms.

The holy Church satisfied the desire of her preachers through the strength of her faith. Because she confessed the God whom she had heard, she offered her preacher, as it were, water for refreshment and cooled his mind. Rebecca signified this in particular when she placed the water jar from her shoulder into her arms and offered water to Abraham’s servant for drinking.

Because the holy Church did not remain empty in what she believed, she immediately strove to preach what she had heard, and by teaching she produced many preachers from herself.

(Moral. lib. I, ch. 15, no. 21; apud Pater., lib. I on Genesis, ch. 53.) What does it mean that Rebecca is brought to Isaac on the back of a camel, except that Rebecca signifies the Church, while the camel on which she rides signifies the people of the Gentiles, crooked in morals and burdened with the worship of idols? For those who found gods for themselves to worship had, as it were, grown upon themselves a burden on their back to carry.

The more subtly the holy Church recognizes her Redeemer, the more diligently she abandons the enticement of a carnal life through humility, and contradicts within herself crookedness of vice. Rebecca signifies this when, after seeing Isaac, she descended from the camel; for once the Lord was known, the Gentiles abandoned their vices and, from the exaltation of pride, sought the depths of humility.

(Moral. lib. XXX, ch. 25, no. 71.) Following Christ, the holy Church covers the vices of earthly desire through repentance. Rachel rightly signified this when she covered the idols of her father Laban by sitting upon them. Of this covering of vices the prophet says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1). Rachel therefore represented us, who press down idols by sitting upon them if, through repentance, we condemn the faults of greed.

(Lib. II on the Gospels, homily 29, no. 4; Reg. Past., part II, ch. 4.) At the beginning of the nascent Church, signs and miracles were necessary. For in order to grow toward faith, she had to be nourished by miracles.

In the priest’s vestment, according to the divine word, bells are joined to pomegranates. What is signified by pomegranates except the unity of faith? For just as many seeds are protected within one pomegranate by its outer rind, so the unity of faith covers the countless peoples of the holy Church, while diversity of merits holds them within.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the Grace of Baptism

(Preface to Moral. IV, 3.) Whoever is not released by the water of regeneration remains bound by the guilt of the first bond. What baptismal water accomplishes among us was accomplished among the ancients either by faith alone in the case of little ones, by the power of sacrifice in the case of adults, or by the mystery of circumcision in the case of those who came forth from Abraham’s stock.

Everyone is conceived with the guilt of the first parent, as the prophet testifies, saying: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities” (Ps. L, 7). And because the one whom the water of salvation does not wash away does not lose the punishment of original guilt, Truth itself openly declares, saying: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not have eternal life” (John III, 5).

(Lib. II on the Gospels, homily 29, no. 3.) We are truly faithful if we fulfill in works what we promise in words. On the day of baptism we promise to renounce all the works and all the pomps of the ancient enemy. Therefore let each of you turn the eyes of his mind back upon himself; and if, after baptism, he preserves what he vowed before baptism, let him rejoice, certain now that he is faithful.

(Moral. lib. XV, ch. 51, no. 57.) We derive original sin from our parents, and unless we are released through the grace of baptism, we also bear the sins of our parents, because we are still, so to speak, one with them. It is written in the book of Exodus: “You repay the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons” (Exod. XXXIV, 7). The Lord therefore repays the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons when, because of the parent’s guilt, the soul of the offspring is stained by original sin. And again he does not repay the iniquity of the parents upon the sons, because when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we no longer possess the sins of our parents, but those that we ourselves have committed.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Communion

(Moral. lib. XIII, ch. 23, no. 26.) Every sinner, taking the price of his redemption, confesses and praises God and, in whatever words he can, makes this very thing known to his neighbors [Note: [Col. 0795D] In the edition, “in words, this very thing” is omitted.]. Thus blessed Job says under the figure of our Redeemer: “Earth, do not cover my blood” (Job XVI, 19).

For the earth did not cover Christ’s blood, because the holy Church has now proclaimed the mystery of her redemption throughout all the parts of the world. The very blood of redemption that is received is the cry of our Redeemer. The apostle Paul says: “And the sprinkling of Christ’s blood, speaking better than Abel” (Heb. XII, 24).

It had been said of Abel’s blood: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. IV, 10). But Jesus’ blood speaks better than Abel’s, because Abel’s blood sought the death of the fratricidal brother, whereas the Lord’s blood obtained life for his persecutors.

So that the sacrament of the Lord’s passion may not be fruitless in us, we must imitate what we receive and preach to others what we venerate. Hence blessed Job again says: “Let my cry find no place to hide in you.” His cry finds a place to hide in us if the tongue is silent about what the mind believes. But so that his cry may not be hidden in us, each person must, according to the measure of his vivification, make the mystery known to his neighbors.

(Lib. II on the Gospels, homily 22, no. 7.) We have learned what the blood of Christ is, not now by hearing but by drinking. His blood is placed upon both doorposts (Exod. XII, 7) when it is imbibed not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart. The blood of the lamb is placed upon both doorposts when the sacrament of Christ’s passion is received by the mouth for redemption and contemplated with an attentive mind for imitation.

We eat the flesh of the lamb at night, as it were, when we now receive the Lord’s body in the sacrament, while we do not yet see one another’s consciences.

(No. 8.) For it profits nothing to receive the body and blood of Jesus Christ with the mouth and to oppose him by perverse conduct. Those who live wickedly in the Church and do not cease to receive Communion, thinking that they are cleansed by such communion, should learn that they gain nothing from cleansing.
