The Prophet says to them: “What is it that my beloved has done many crimes in my house? Will holy flesh remove your wickedness from you?” (Jerem. XI, 15). And the Apostle says: “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup; for whoever receives this unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI, 28).

## CHAPTER XV. What the Breadth and Length of God Signify [Note: [Col. 0795D] Our manuscript has “of the cross,” but incorrectly, since when Gregory and Augustine speak of God and of his charity toward us, they make no mention of the cross], as well as Height and Depth

(Moral. lib. X, ch. 9, no. 15.) He has breadth because almighty God extends his love even to the gathering in of persecutors. He has length because, bearing with us patiently, he leads us to our homeland of life. He has height because he surpasses even the understanding of those who will be received into the heavenly assembly. He has depth because, below, he incomprehensibly exercises the judgment of his strictness upon the condemned.

God exercises these four things upon us who are placed in this life individually: he displays his breadth by loving, his length by bearing with us, his height by surpassing not only our understanding but also our desires, and his depth by strictly judging the hidden and unlawful movements of our thoughts.

No one recognizes how unfathomable the height and depth of almighty God are except one who has either begun to be raised to the highest things through contemplation or, resisting hidden movements, begun to be troubled by the importunity of temptations.

(Augustine, in Spec., ch. 14; also Isidore, book I of the Sentences, ch. 2.) Although nothing worthy can be said of almighty God according to position, quality, condition, or movement, breadth, length, height, and depth are nevertheless present in him in some manner.

In almighty God there is the breadth of charity, by which he both corrects us from error and keeps us in truth. There is also length in him, by which he patiently bears with us who are evil until, once corrected, he restores us to our future homeland. There is height in him, by which, through the immensity of his knowledge, he surpasses every understanding. There is depth in him, by which, arranging those who are to be condemned below according to equity, he foreordains them.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the Calling of the Gentiles Who Come Together into the Church

(Lib. II on the Gospels, homily 33, no. 6.) The Gentiles, called to faith and desiring to kiss the footsteps of their Redeemer, do not cease their commitment to good works, because they sigh with continual love for him. Hence, in the voice of the bride, she begins in the Song of Songs concerning that same Redeemer: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (Song I, 1). She rightly desires the kiss of her Creator who prepares herself to serve him through love.

(Moral. lib. XXX, ch. 25, no. 72.) When the Lord rescued the Gentiles, he overcame the yoke of their burden, freeing them by his coming from the servitude of demonic tyranny. He overcame “the rod of their shoulder” (Isa. IX, 4) when, having redeemed the human race, he restrained the blows of that tyranny, which had grievously oppressed it through perverse action. He overcame the scepter of their exactor when he destroyed in the hearts of the faithful the kingdom of that devil who, on account of the pestilence of committed vices, had been accustomed to demand due tribute of punishments.

(Moral. lib. I, ch. 16, no. 23.) It is written: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isa. I, 3). By the ox the workers of Judaea are signified; by the donkey, the Gentile peoples.

For who was the ox except the Jewish people, whose neck the yoke of the Law wore down? And who was the donkey except the Gentile world, which every deceiver found like a brutish animal resisting by no reason, and drove beneath whatever error he wished?

The ox therefore recognized its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger, because the Hebrew people found the God whom it worshiped but did not know, while the Gentile world received the nourishment of the Law, which it had not possessed.

After the Mediator’s coming, the catholic Church has simple donkeys, because the called peoples of the Gentiles, desiring to reach rest, willingly carry all the burdens of the commandments.

(No. 24.) Hence Jacob, addressing his sons, prophetically took care to signify well that the Gentile people would desire this rest, saying: “Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good and the land excellent, and he placed his shoulder beneath the burden” (Gen. XLIX, 14–15).

(Moral. lib. II, ch. 35, no. 37.) The prophet Isaiah cries out, saying: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel” (Isa. IX, 8). Jacob is called “Supplanter,” while Israel is called “Seeing God.” What is signified by Jacob except the Jewish people, and by Israel except the Gentile people? For the Gentiles saw through the eyes of faith the one whom Jacob strove to supplant through the death of the flesh.

The word sent to Jacob therefore fell upon Israel, because the Gentile people, suddenly confessing, found the one whom the Jewish people rejected when he came to them.

(Lib. II on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 5.) When the prophet knew that the Jewish people were perishing from faith and foresaw the holy apostles rising in the Church, through whom many from the Gentiles were established in strength of faith and life, he spoke in great consolation, saying: “The bricks have fallen, but we will build with squared stones” (Isa. IX, 10).

Seeing the apostles, martyrs, and teachers arise in the holy Church, he grieved less over the fall of the bricks—that is, over the destruction of the Jews—because he saw the building of almighty God, namely the holy Church, being constructed from squared stones.

(Lib. II on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 21.) Hence the same prophet says: “And the bridle of error that was on the jaws of the peoples will be a song for you” (Isa. XXX, 28–29).

The bridle of error had bound the jaws of the peoples when the Gentiles, fettered by the error of idols, did not know how to give the true God the praise of confession. But this very bridle of error has now been turned into a song for us when, rejoicing, we sing and chant: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. XCV, 5). And again: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands. They have mouths and will not speak; they have eyes and will not see” (Ps. CXIII, 4).

When we say these things to almighty God while singing psalms, we make the bridle of our error, which had bound our mouths so that they could not praise God, into a song for the true Lord. Well is it added: “Like the night of a sanctified solemnity” (Isa. XXX, 29), because when we render the praise of confession to God, we rejoice in a sanctified solemnity.

(Moral. lib. XXIX, ch. 26, no. 52.) It is written: “In the dens where dragons formerly dwelt, the green growth of reed and rush will arise” (Isa. XXXV, 7). The green growth of reed and rush arises in the dens of dragons because among those peoples whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed there accumulate both the knowledge of teachers and the obedience of hearers.

(Lib. II on Ezekiel, homily 1, no. 11.) “The green growth of reed and rush will arise in it”—that is, in the holy Church writers and hearers arise. The writers should be understood by the reed, and the hearers by the rush.

Rush and reed generally grow through the moisture of water. Both flourish from one and the same water. The reed is taken for writing, whereas writing cannot be done with the rush. What should we understand by the rush and the reed except that there is one doctrine of truth that waters many hearers?

Some, once watered, progress so far in the word of God that they even become writers, like reeds. Others hear the word of life and retain the greenness of good hope and upright works, but cannot progress to writing. Who are these in the water of faith [Note: [Col. 0797] Edition: “What are these in the water of God”] except certain people who, so to speak, are rushes? They make progress by becoming green, but they cannot express letters.

(Lib. I on the Gospels, homily 20, no. 3.) In faith in the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, the Gentile world received the fullness of grace, while Judaea, through the error of unbelief, lost what had made it swell with pride.

The Lord made the desert into pools of water (Isa. XLI, 18), because he gave the streams of holy preaching to the Gentiles, which previously, through the aridity of their minds, had produced no fruits of good works. The very land to which, because of the harshness of its dryness, the way had previously not been open to preachers afterward poured forth streams of doctrine.

(Moral. lib. XXVII, ch. 43, no. 71.) It is written: “I will say to the North, ‘Give,’ and to the South, ‘Do not hinder’” (Isa. XLIII, 6).

Just as the Gentiles are signified by the North, so Judaea is signified by the South. It grew warm as though beneath the midday sun, because when the Redeemer came in the flesh, it first received the fervor of faith.

“Give” is said to the North when the Gentiles are commanded to offer the gifts of their faith to God. The South is ordered not to hinder, because the Hebrews who stand in the faith are commanded not to reject or despise the life of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0797] Edition: “Condemn.” But Taius reads as it is found in the Vindocian manuscript.]

(Moral. lib. XX, ch. 25, no. 58.) Just as the whole Church in general is called the garment of Christ, so the souls of individuals are garments of the Church. Having been converted from error, they surround that same Church by believing in her and faithfully clinging to her.

(Moral. lib. XXIX, ch. 6, no. 13.) The holy Church is now clothed, as though in so many garments, as she is adorned by the veneration of the faithful. To the holy Church, displayed by the Lord to the nations through the prophet, it is said: “As I live, you will be clothed with all these things as with an ornament” (Isa. XLV, 18).

(Moran. lib. XX, ch. 29, no. 58.) For if the holy Church were not the garment of Christ, the apostle Paul certainly would not say: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V, 27)—that is, neither a spot through sin nor a wrinkle through duplicity. For she is clean through righteousness and stretched taut through single-minded intention. She has therefore been washed so that she may have no spot, and stretched so that she may have no wrinkle; she is indeed a garment.

(Moral., lib. XXV, ch. 8, no. 21.) The holy Church extends to the right among so great a multitude of Gentiles when she receives some who are to be justified. She also spreads to the left when she admits to herself some who will remain in iniquity.

Because of this multitude, which lies outside the number of the elect, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16).

(Lib. I on Ezekiel, homily 10, no. 39.) When the Jews fell away from the faith, the hearts of the Gentiles ran toward knowledge of the faith. These peoples open the mouth of their hearts to the nourishment of sacred reading and eat in secret like a poor person, because they receive the words of life by reading them with haste and silence.

(Moral. XXIX, ch. 14, no. 26.) When our Redeemer sought the straits of death, he expanded his faith among the Gentiles and stretched the holy Church into countless hearts of believers. Through the prophet it is said to her: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and extend the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. For you will penetrate to the right and to the left, and your seed will inherit the nations” (Isa. LIV, 2).

This breadth across the earth certainly would not have come about unless he himself had first despised, by dying, the life that we know and had shown, by rising again, the life that we do not know.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the Holy Preachers
(Apud Paterium, chapter 53 on Genesis.) Holy men, when they deliver the word of preaching to good minds, become, as it were, stewards appointed to join each soul to the only-begotten Son. In what they say about the Lord, they display within themselves the riches of virtue, so that they may draw their hearers to follow God all the more quickly because they show in themselves what they proclaim. Each preacher of the holy faith, bearing within himself the adornments of virtue, both composes the ear of Holy Church through obedient discernment and adorns the hands through the merit of good works [Note: Alulfus also cites these words in his commentary on the Second Epistle of blessed Paul to the Corinthians, chapter 18.]. For every preacher, the heart of his hearer is, as it were, a spacious place in which to remain—the breadth of goodness. Hence it is said to certain people: “Receive us; we have wronged no one, corrupted no one. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections” (2 Cor. 6:12). It is as though they were plainly told: “Make a spacious place in your minds for receiving instruction; but remain narrow-minded with regard to thinking about carnal things.”

There are many who are prepared to support their teachers with temporal provisions, but holy preachers do not wish to receive temporal things unless they first obtain eternal ones. For if they find no fruit in souls, they disdain to accept bodily remuneration. When holy preachers obtain the life of their hearers through preaching, they immediately give thanks to the one from whose gift they received this, so that they attribute nothing of that work to themselves, but return thanks to the Author of all things together with the gain of souls.

Although holy preachers already excel both in understanding and in expressing the things above, they nevertheless still feel within themselves the opposition of the flesh. For they see “another law in their members warring against the law of their mind and bringing them captive” [Note: The edition reads, “bringing himself captive”; but our reading in Taius is better.] “under the law of sin” (Rom. 7:23). Thus, lest the greatness of revelations exalt them, “a thorn of the flesh” has been given them (2 Cor. 12). Holy preachers have treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness may belong to the power of God and not to them. Those who speak heavenly things through the flesh, yet still feel within the flesh the opposition arising from vice—what else are they than men carrying riches over the crooked backs of camels?

Holy preachers desire God to be loved more than feared; but if they do not instill fear, they do not lead people to the love of intimate devotion. Therefore they customarily speak first of terrible things and afterward of sweet ones. As it is said through the Psalmist: “They shall speak of the might of your terrors, and they shall proclaim your greatness” (Ps. 144:6).

(Moral. book VII, chapter 4, no. 4.) The words of holy preaching are sometimes represented by arrows, because, in striking vices, they pierce the hearts of those who live wickedly. Concerning these arrows it is said to the coming Redeemer: “Your arrows are sharp, most powerful; peoples shall fall beneath you into the heart” (Ps. 44:6). Isaiah says of him: “I will send some of those who have been saved to the nations across the sea, to Africa, Lydia, Italy, and Greece, bearing the arrow” (Isa. 66:19).

It is written: “Lord, incline your heavens and descend” (Ps. 144:5). [Moral. book XXX, chapter 13, no. 48.] Who, then, are signified by the name “heavens” if not the order of preachers? Unless holy preachers descended from that summit of inner contemplation which they grasp to the lowliness of our weakness through the humblest preaching—as though by a kind of inclination—they would never beget children in the faith. They could not benefit us if they persisted in maintaining themselves erect in the height of their own greatness.

If holy men wished to preach everything they grasp while they are intoxicated by heavenly contemplation, and did not moderate their knowledge with a certain restraint and sobriety, who could contain those streams of the heavenly fountain within the narrow basin of understanding? When holy teachers draw themselves down in their preaching, they pour the knowledge of divinity into our hearts. God would in no way descend to us if his preachers remained inflexible in the rigor of contemplation. The heavens incline so that the Lord may descend, because holy preachers bend down so that we may be born into the new light of faith. For if they did not condescend to our weakness, they would never raise us to their exalted height.

A law has been laid upon preachers: by living, they must fulfill what they hasten to persuade others to do by speaking. For the authority of speech is lost when the voice is not supported by works.

(Moral. book XXIII, chapter 1, no. 8.) Each spiritual preacher of the holy universal Church carefully examines himself in everything he says, lest, while preaching what is right, he exalt himself through the vice of pride; lest his life disagree with his tongue; and lest he lose within himself the peace that he announces in the Church by teaching well but living badly. The holy preacher strives with the utmost care, against the malicious rumors of his opponents, both to defend by speaking what he lives and to adorn by living what he says. In all these things he seeks not his own glory but that of the Author; and he does not consider that he received the whole grace of wisdom by which he was enabled to speak through his own merits, but through the intercession of those for whom he speaks.

Each chosen preacher, when he casts himself down through humility, rises above others, because what he is able to accomplish in goodness contributes more to his own reward when he attributes it to the merits of others. He judges himself unworthy of everyone, even while he lives worthily for all. The preacher knows very well that the good things made known to people can scarcely be without danger. Although he feels himself to be wise, he would nevertheless prefer to be wise without appearing so; and he fears in every way that which is revealed by speaking. If permitted, he desires to remain silent, since he sees that silence is safer for many and considers those happier whom a lower place within Holy Church conceals through silence.

When the preacher is driven to speak by the force of charity, he undertakes the duty of speaking out of necessity; but out of great desire he seeks the leisure of silence. He preserves the latter by his vow and practices the former as a ministry. The arrogant do not understand this manner of speaking. They do not speak because circumstances arise, but desire circumstances to arise so that they may speak.

(Ibid., chapter 10, no. 17.) Holy preachers regard this as their proper portion: that inwardly they themselves rejoice in wisdom, while outwardly they restrain others from error. By speaking they do not go forth from themselves in such a way as to place the joy of their mind in the display of eloquent speech. Rather, they meditate upon the good of knowledge in the secrecy of the heart, and rejoice where they receive it, not where they are compelled to make it known amid so many snares of temptation. When preachers make known the good they have received, they rejoice through the intervention of charity in the progress of their hearers, not in their own display.

(Ibid., chapter 11, no. 28.) It often happens that wise men, when they see that they are not being heard, command their mouths to be silent. But frequently, when they see that the crimes of the wicked increase while they themselves remain silent and do not correct them, they endure a kind of force within their spirit, so that they burst forth into open speech of correction.

When the prophet Jeremiah had imposed silence upon himself in preaching, saying, “I will not remember him, nor speak any more in his name,” he immediately added: “And there arose in my heart, as it were, a burning fire, shut up in my bones; and I grew weary, unable to bear it, for I heard the insults of many” (Jer. 20:9). The hearts of the righteous are inflamed when they see the deeds of the wicked increasing without correction, and they believe themselves participants in the guilt of those whom, by remaining silent, they permit to grow in iniquity.

After the prophet David had imposed silence upon himself, saying, “I set a guard over my mouth, when the sinner stood against me; I was silent and humbled, and kept silence from good things” (Ps. 38:2), he burned with this zeal of charity in that very silence, and immediately added: “My sorrow was renewed; my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire burned” (ibid., 4). The heart grew hot within because the ardor of love refused to flow outward through the speech of admonition.

(Moral. book XXX, chapter 2, no. 6.) The fire burned in the meditation of the heart because the rebuke of offenders grew cold through the restraint of the mouth. Holy preachers strike their adversaries with their words as with darts, but defend themselves with weapons—that is, with miracles—so that the force of their darts may proclaim how much they should be heard, while their miraculous weapons reveal how much they should be revered.

(Book I on the Gospel, homily 11, no. 4.) That man is a learned preacher in Holy Church who knows how to speak both new things concerning the sweetness of the kingdom and old things concerning the terror of punishment, so that punishments may frighten those whom rewards do not attract. Let each person hear about the kingdom what he may love, and about punishment what he may fear, so that, if love does not draw the sluggish soul, clinging forcefully to the earth, toward the kingdom, fear may threaten it with eternal punishment.

(Pastoral Rule, part I, chapter 7.) Some rightly desire the office of preaching, while others are rightly compelled and drawn into it. We recognize this clearly if we consider the deeds of two prophets: one willingly offered himself to be sent to preach, whereas the other refused to go with fear. When the Lord asked whom he should send, Isaiah freely offered himself, saying, “Here am I; send me” (Isa. 6:8). Jeremiah, however, is sent, yet humbly resists lest he be sent, saying, “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a boy” (Jer. 1:6).

Behold: from both there came forth externally different voices, but they did not flow from different sources of love. In both prophets we must carefully observe that the one who refused did not resist completely, while the one who wished to be sent first saw himself purified by the coal from the altar, lest anyone either dare approach the sacred mysteries while unpurified or, under the guise of humility, proudly contradict the one whom heavenly grace has chosen.

(Moral. book XXIX, chapter 26.) It is written: “He produces hay on the mountains and grass for the service of men” (Ps. 147:8, no. 52). What is signified by “grass” if not the support of preachers? Hay is produced on the mountains, and grass for the service of men, when the powerful of this world, called to the knowledge of the faith, bestow transient sustenance upon the holy preachers who spiritually serve them on the journey of this life.

(Moral. book XXIX, chapter 23, no. 47.) Very often preaching reaches the ears, but, when inward grace is absent, it does not pass into the hearts of the hearers. Concerning the words of such preaching it is said for the sake of the elect: “Indeed, your arrows have passed through” (Ps. 77:19). The arrows of God pass through when his words of preaching descend from the ears into the hearts.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Divine Mysteries and Miracles

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 10.) The mysteries of divine power, which cannot be comprehended, are not to be examined by understanding but revered by faith. We must know that whatever can be comprehended by human reason can no longer be called wonderful. In miracles, the only explanation is the power of the one who performs them.

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 5, no. 11.) However intently the soul may apply itself, it is not sufficient to penetrate itself perfectly; how much less, then, the greatness of him who was able to create the soul? When the prophet David struggled to understand the knowledge of God, he grew weary and, failing, said: “Your knowledge has become wonderful beyond me; it is strengthened, and I cannot attain it” (Ps. 139:6).

(Book I on the Gospel, homily 2, no. 1.) The miracles of our Lord and Savior must be understood in such a way that they are believed to have truly occurred and yet, through their signification, communicate something to us. The works of our Redeemer reveal something through power and speak something through mystery. This is well signified by that blind man who sat begging beside the road (Luke 18:35). When our Creator therefore approaches Jericho, the blind man returns to the light: because, when the Divinity assumed the weakness of our flesh, the human race received again the light it had lost. For from the very fact that God suffers human things, man is raised up to divine things.

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 5, no. 12.) Perfect men, through contemplation of the mind, are able somehow to touch beforehand the mystery of inward sweetness, as though from a flash of light; they therefore strive continually to pour forth its memory by recollecting and speaking of it. Hence the Psalmist aptly admonishes us, saying: “Light has risen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart. Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous, and give thanks to the memory of his holiness” (Ps. 97:11).

(Book II on the Gospel, homily 22, no. 8.) What we cannot understand and penetrate concerning the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, we humbly reserve for the power of the Holy Spirit, so that no one may presumptuously dare either to despise or to denounce what he does not understand, but may consign to the fire what he reserves for the Holy Spirit [Note: The edition reads “he consigns,” while reserving it for the Holy Spirit].

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Holy Martyrs

(Moral. book III, chapter 17, no. 32.) No one comes into this life among the elect who has not endured the adversities of the ancient enemy. Even those who suffered cruel things while living devoutly from the very beginning of the world were members of our Redeemer. Abel declared himself to be a member of our Redeemer: he signified the death of the one of whom it is written, “As a lamb before its shearer he will be silent and will not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7), not only by pleasing God in sacrifice but also by dying in silence. From the very beginning of the world the ancient enemy has attempted to overpower the body of our Redeemer; beginning with the first human beings, he raged onward until he reached the very head of the Church [Edition: “the pure”; the better reading is “the first.”].

(Moral. book III, chapter 21, no. 50.) When the holy martyrs are caught up in the battle of tribulations, and at one and the same time endure some who strike and others who persuade, they oppose to the former the shield of patience and hurl at the latter the darts of instruction. By suffering, the martyrs despise the enemies who rise against them; by compassion, they lead weakened fellow citizens back to salvation. They resist the former lest they carry others away; they fear for the latter lest they utterly lose the life of uprightness.

(No. 40.) Let us see the apostle Paul, a soldier of God’s army, fighting on both fronts. “Outside,” he says, “fights; inside, fears” (2 Cor. 7:5). Holy martyrs extend themselves carefully toward both sides. When they are perhaps struck by tribulations, they undertake external battles in such a way that they anxiously consider how the inner lives of their neighbors might not be torn apart. Thus holy men stand firm as strong fighters in battle: on one side striking hostile breasts with darts, on the other defending the weak who have fallen behind with a shield. In both directions they remain watchful with swift vigilance, so that they may pierce the bold before them and protect the fearful behind them from injury.

(Moral. book XXX, chapter 25, no. 74.) With these elect our Lord destroys the adversaries of the faith; with them he descends into the battles of preaching—men who are able to know divine things and who know how to hold a perfect understanding of the Trinity, which is God. Christ advances with them into battle against the enemies of the faith: those who, while drawing in the streams of instruction, do not bend the uprightness of their deeds. They go forth to war with Christ as their leader who show by their works what they proclaim with their mouths, who spiritually draw in the streams of instruction and yet are not carnally bent toward wicked deeds.

(No. 75.) Our leader brought such men with him to the battle of preaching: men who, despising the safety of their bodies, would overthrow their enemies by dying and overcome their swords not with weapons and swords but with patience. Our martyrs came armed to battle under their leader, but with trumpets, jars, and lamps. They sounded the trumpets when they preached; they broke the jars when they exposed their bodies, destined to be released through suffering, to the swords of their enemies. They shone with lamps when, after the dissolution of their bodies, they flashed forth through miracles.

Then the enemies were put to flight, because, when they saw the bodies of the dead martyrs shining with miracles, they were broken by the light of truth and believed what they had attacked. Our soldiers sounded the trumpets so that the jars might be broken. The jars were broken so that the lamps might appear. The lamps appeared so that the enemies might be put to flight. That is: the martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved in death; their bodies were dissolved in death so that they might shine through miracles; they shone through miracles so that they might overthrow their enemies by the divine light, so that those enemies would no longer stand upright against God but, subjected, would fear him.

(No. 77.) The martyrs of Christ consider the grace of preaching a great thing, but the usefulness of their bodies a small thing. Whoever values bodily usefulness more than the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in his left hand and the jar in his right. If the grace of preaching is attended to first and the usefulness of the body afterward, it is certain that the trumpet is held in the right hand and the jar in the left.

When a righteous person is made so through the death of suffering for the truth, he is restored in the greenness of eternal life; and he who flourished here through faith flourishes there through vision. Often, through the suffering of a righteous person, the faithful are multiplied in their love of the heavenly homeland, and they receive the greenness of spiritual life when they rejoice that he acted bravely for God. When the righteous person has been bodily extinguished, it is most certain that, by the example of his suffering itself, he raises the hearts of many and displays the greenness of faith’s uprightness.

(Moral. book XIII, chapter 13, no. 16.) When the holy people of the Church begin to suffer adversities severely and see their weak members falling into worse things, they recall in their minds the times of their peace, when they fed their faithful with the abundance of their preaching. Hence it is aptly said figuratively through blessed Job: “I, once prosperous, was suddenly crushed” (Job 16:13).

(Moral. book XIII, chapter 44, no. 17.) By asserting that he was suddenly crushed, he portrayed the heedless mind of the weak. Since they do not know how to foresee the evils that are to come, those evils become all the more grievous for them because they endure them unexpectedly.

Each elect person loves martyrdom through the strength of the spirit, though he does not desire it because of the weakness of the flesh. One person trembles at punishments according to the flesh but exults in glory according to the spirit. Each person unwillingly wills the torment of martyrdom, and loves it while hating it, just as, when we seek the joy of salvation, we take the bitter cup of purification. The bitterness displeases us in the cup, but the salvation restored through bitterness pleases us.

(Moral. book IV, chapter 16, no. 30.) Through the voice of the holy martyrs the Psalmist says: “You humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us” (Ps. 44:20). The shadow of death is therefore understood as the death of the flesh, because just as the true death is that by which the soul is separated from God, so the shadow of death is that by which the flesh is separated from the soul. Those who plainly die not in spirit but only in flesh say that they are covered not by true death but by the shadow of death.

(Moral. book XXXIII, chapter 3, no. 6.) The shadow of death oppresses God’s elect [Note: The older editions and two German manuscripts have this same reading; the Benedictine Fathers, however, think that *covers* should be read, both from other manuscripts and from the testimony of Scripture, which Gregory explains in these words], when the death of the flesh—which is an image of eternal death—separates them from this life; because just as eternal death separates the soul from God, so this death separates the body from the soul.

(Moral. book XX, chapter 27, no. 56.) The present life is the place of affliction. Therefore the holy martyrs were humbled in this place of affliction, because in eternal life—that is, in the place of joy—they are exalted.

(Moral. book XXVI, chapter 28, no. 54.) Those who strive toward the eternal homeland now despise themselves temporarily in the place of affliction, so that then they may truly be exalted in the place of joy.

(Book I on the Gospel, homily 3, no. 4.) Although the opportunity for persecution is absent in this time of peace, our peace nevertheless has its own martyrdom. For even if we do not submit the neck of the flesh to the sword, we nevertheless slaughter carnal desires in the mind through spiritual joy.

(Book II on the Gospel, homily 27, no. 9.) Therefore, if we do not offer our bodies in suffering for Christ, let us at least conquer our mind in a time of peace. God is appeased by this sacrifice. In the judgment of his mercy he approves the victory of our peace; he sees the contest of our heart; and he who rewards those who have conquered helps those who are now fighting.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Persecutors of the Martyrs

(Moral. book XIII, chapter 10, nos. 12–13.) The ancient enemy of the Church gnashes his teeth against her as though with teeth [Edition: “rages”] and gazes upon her with terrifying eyes, because through some he carries out cruel deeds and through others he devises what he is to carry out. The teeth of this enemy are the persecutors and executioners of the good, who tear apart the members of the Church when they afflict her elect through their persecutions. The eyes of the ancient enemy are those who devise the evils they will inflict upon her and inflame the cruelties of her persecutors by their counsels.

The ancient adversary of the Church gnashes against the Church with his teeth when through cruel reprobates he persecutes the life of the good within her. He gazes upon her with terrifying eyes because, through the counsels of the wicked, he does not cease seeking evils by which he may continually afflict her more severely.

(Ibid., chapter 11, no. 14; chapter 12, no. 15; chapter 13, no. 16.) We must know that the reprobate chiefly persecute in Holy Church those whom they see will be useful to many—those who crush the life of carnal people by the word of correction and turn them spiritually within the body of the Church. Blessed Job rightly says figuratively: “They struck my cheek; they were satisfied with my sufferings” (Job 16:11).

The wicked strike the cheek of the Church when they persecute good preachers. And because the reprobate then think they have accomplished something great when they kill the life of preachers, it is aptly added after the striking of the cheek: “They were satisfied with my sufferings.” The suffering that chiefly chastises the mind of the Church satisfies them.

Again it is written: “God has shut me up with the wicked and delivered me into the hands of the impious” (ibid., 12). The people of the elect are shut up with the wicked when their flesh is temporarily handed over to the persecutions of the ancient enemy. They are delivered not to the spirit but to the hands of the impious, because, insofar as the wicked cannot contain them in their minds, they burn all the more cruelly against their flesh.

(Moral. book III, chapter 25, no. 76.) The persecutors resisted the holy faith while the martyrs were still in the body. But after the bodies had been released, when miracles appeared, the persecutors were put to flight, because, overcome by fear, they ceased persecuting the faithful.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Elect Who Leave Everything and Come with Christ the Judge

(Moral. book X, chapter 31, no. 52.) At the end of the world those who are now unjustly judged for God will come as judges with God. Their light will then shine all the more widely because the hand of their persecutors now constricts them so harshly. Then it will be evident to the eyes of the reprobate that those who willingly left all earthly things were supported by heavenly power.

Truth says to his elect: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). The court of that inner assembly will not have more than twelve judges; rather, by the number twelve the totality of the whole is expressed. Whoever, stirred here by the goad of divine love, leaves what he possesses will undoubtedly obtain there the summit of judicial power, so that he who now chastises himself through voluntary poverty in consideration of the judgment may then come as judge together with the Judge.

Of the Bridegroom of Holy Church it is said through Solomon: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31:23). Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3:14). Hence Truth declares that these same elders are no longer servants but friends, saying: “I no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15) [Note: The edition reads “elders.” But *Gemet* agrees with our reading, “senators.”].

(Moral. book XX, chapter 16, no. 41.) Behold: by leaving temporal things behind, they have purchased the glory of eternal power. What, then, is more foolish in this world than to abandon one’s possessions? And what is nobler in eternity than to come as judges with God?

(Moral. book VI, chapter 7, no. 9.) Our Redeemer renders judgment with the holy preachers of the Church, as he himself says in the Gospel: “You who have left everything and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” All who are now perfect in the Church learned the uprightness of their perfection through the Gospel.

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 18.) Therefore those who have been united to our Redeemer and joined to his majesty will appear with him as judges—those who now follow perfect works according to the precepts of the Gospel. Whoever in this world obeyed the Lord’s commandments will afterward come with him as judge to judge the peoples, as it is said to those who leave everything: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

(Moral. book XI, chapter 22, no. 33.) It is right that those who completely abandon the present world in obedience to the words of God should dispute with God concerning the peoples in judgment; and that those who have now been close to him in voluntary poverty or in prayer should afterward come as judges with God.

(Moral. book XV, chapter 31, no. 37.) It is written: “He summoned the heavens above and the earth, to judge his people” (Ps. 50:4). He summons the heavens above when those who, leaving all they possess, have maintained a heavenly way of life are called to sit with him in judgment and come as judges with him. The earth, too, is summoned above when those who were bound to earthly activities nevertheless sought heavenly gains more than earthly ones. To them at the end it is said: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. 25:35).

(Moral. book XXVI, chapter 27, no. 51.) Elect men who leave everything are not judged but reign; they transcend even the precepts of the law by the virtue of perfection [Note: The edition reads “by the perfection of virtues.”]. For they are not content merely to fulfill what the divine law commands everyone; with a more excellent desire they seek to offer more than they could have heard in the general commandments.

The elect are not judged at the final judgment but reign, because they come as judges even with their Author. By leaving everything, they have carried out with readier devotion more than they heard commanded in general. By a special command addressed to a few more perfect persons, not generally to all, the rich young man heard: “Go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

For if a general command bound everyone under this precept, it would certainly be sinful for us to possess anything of this world. But one thing is what sacred Scripture commands everyone generally, and another is what it orders the more perfect in particular. The righteous who leave everything are rightly not held under the general judgment, since by living they have surpassed the general commandments. For just as those who, persuaded by unbelief, disdain to be bound by the law are not judged but perish, so those who, persuaded by devotion, advance even beyond the general commandments of the divine law are not judged but reign.

The apostle Paul, a vessel of election, surpassed the special commandments and exhibited more by his work than he had received by the institution of permission. For although he had received permission to live from the Gospel while preaching the Gospel, and although he brought the Gospel to his hearers, he nevertheless refused to be supported by the proceeds of the Gospel. Why, then, should the one who received less to observe but found something greater to live be judged so that he might reign?

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Interpreters of the Divine Scriptures

(Epistle addressed to Leander, chapter 2.) Whoever speaks about God must take care to examine whatever instructs the morals of his hearers, and he should regard this as the proper order of speaking: when the opportunity for edification requires it, he should usefully turn aside from what he had begun to say. For the interpreter of sacred eloquence ought to imitate the nature of a river. When a river flows through its channel, if it encounters hollow valleys to the side, it immediately diverts the course of its rushing waters into them; and when it has sufficiently filled them, it suddenly pours itself back into its channel.

Thus, indeed, the interpreter of the divine word ought to be: when discussing any subject, if he happens to find, beside the matter at hand, an opportunity for suitable edification, he should turn the waves of his speech toward the neighboring valley, as it were. When he has sufficiently flooded the field of the instruction that follows, he should return to the channel of the discourse he had begun.

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 7, no. 8.) Holy men understand from sacred Scripture how they should live morally and elevate themselves in contemplation. The more each interpreter progresses in sacred Scripture, the more that same Scripture progresses in him, because divine words grow together with the reader. Each person understands them more deeply in proportion as he applies himself to them more deeply. For unless the minds of readers advance toward higher things, the divine sayings lie below, like things not understood.

“If someone opens a cistern, digs it, and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall repay the price of the animals” (Exod. 21:33–34).

(Moral. book XVII, chapter 26, no. 38.) What does it mean to open a cistern if not to penetrate the hidden things of sacred Scripture with a strong understanding? What is signified by the ox and the donkey—that is, a clean and unclean animal—if not respectively a believer and an unbeliever?

Therefore, whoever digs a cistern should cover it, lest an ox or a donkey fall into it. That is: whoever already understands lofty things in sacred eloquence should conceal sublime meanings through silence from those who cannot grasp them, lest, through the scandal of their minds, he destroy either a weak believer or an unbeliever who might have been able to believe.

The price of the animals must be paid, because he is convicted of having lost that for which he is held guilty and bound to perform penance [Edition: “committed”]. Whoever reaches the lofty streams of knowledge but does not conceal these things from the dull hearts of his hearers is liable to punishment if, through his words, either a clean or an unclean mind is caught in scandal.

Lofty knowledge must be covered before weak and childish minds, lest the very thing by which the heart of the teachers is raised to the heights cause the weakness of the hearers to fall into the depths.

(Epistle addressed to Leander, chapter 3.) What should the sayings of truth be regarded as, if not nourishment for the restoration of the mind? By discussing them in many ways and with alternating forms, we offer a meal through our mouth, so that we may drive away the distaste of our invited reader, as of a guest of ours; when he sees many things set before him, he may choose what he judges more elegant.

Sometimes we neglect to explain the clear words of the historical sense, lest we reach obscure matters too slowly. At other times, however, the words cannot be understood according to the literal sense, because, if accepted superficially, they produce not instruction but error in the readers. When the words of the letter cannot be made to agree with one another, they point within themselves to something else that should be sought, as though they were saying through certain expressions: “When you see that we are destroyed on the surface, seek within us what can be found ordered and harmonious.”

(Ibid., chapter 4.) At other times, however, the person who neglects to accept the words of the historical sense according to the letter conceals from himself the light of truth offered to him. While he laboriously seeks to discover something else within them, he loses what he could have grasped without difficulty on the surface.

For the divine discourse wisely exercises the mind through mysteries, while very often it refreshes the simple by its surface meaning. In public it has what may nourish the little ones; in secret it preserves what may suspend the minds of the exalted in wonder. It is, so to speak, like a river—flat and deep—in which a lamb may walk and an elephant swim.

Therefore, as the suitability of each passage requires, so the order of exposition changes through careful study, so that it may discover the meaning of divine speech all the more truly as it varies according to the kinds of circumstances, in whatever way each matter demands.

Through sacred eloquence, the frivolity of fruitless loquacity is carefully restrained by its interpreters, since one is forbidden to plant a grove in the temple of God. We all unquestionably know that whenever the stalks of a luxuriant but badly bearing crop grow abundant in leaves, the grains swell with a smaller fullness of ears.

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 1.) It is written: “It is the glory of kings to conceal a word, and the glory of God to investigate a matter” (Prov. 25:2), because it is an honor for human beings to conceal their secrets, while it is the glory of God to open the mysteries of his word. Truth itself says to the disciples: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light” (Matt. 10:27), that is, explain openly what you hear amid the obscurities of allegories. The very obscurity of God’s words is of great usefulness, because it exercises the understanding, so that through weariness it may be enlarged, and, once exercised, may grasp what the idle cannot grasp.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the Sacred Scriptures Should Not Be Searched Too Excessively
*(Morals XXI, chapter 1, no. 3.)* Divine statements must sometimes be searched out inwardly, and sometimes observed outwardly. For it is written: “He who presses the breasts forcefully to draw out milk presses out butter; and he who milks too vigorously draws out blood” (Prov. 30:33). We press the breasts forcefully when we weigh the words of sacred Scripture with subtle understanding; and while by that pressure we seek milk, we find butter, because while we seek nourishment even through a modest understanding, we are anointed with the richness of inward fatness. Yet this must be done neither excessively nor always, lest, while milk is sought from the breasts, blood should follow.

Many interpreters, while examining the words of sacred Scripture more than they ought, fall into a carnal understanding. He draws out blood who milks too vigorously, because what is perceived through an excessive scrutiny of the spirit becomes carnal. Often it is necessary for us to examine certain words of sacred law according to the weight of their historical meaning, lest, if the mind investigates them spiritually more than necessary, blood should answer us from the breasts of its words instead of milk.

When sacred Scripture mingles certain mysteries into the narration of its works, it is necessary for the mind, once stirred, to return to those matters to which the discourse of the speaker itself, as can be understood, calls it.

It is written in Proverbs: “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you, lest, having been filled, you vomit it up” (Prov. 25).

*(Morals XVI, chapter 5, no. 8.)* To find honey is to taste the sweetness of holy understanding. It is eaten sufficiently when our understanding is kept under restraint according to the measure of the meaning. For he vomits up honey when filled who desires to penetrate farther than he comprehends, and loses that by which he could have been nourished.

*(Morals XX, chapter 8, no. 18.)* Whoever desires to eat the sweetness of spiritual understanding beyond what he can contain vomits even what he had eaten; for while he seeks to understand the highest things beyond his strength, he loses even what he had understood well. The glory of the invisible Creator, when sought in moderation, raises us up; when investigated beyond our strength, it weighs us down. Hence Solomon rightly says: “As it is not good for one who eats much honey, so he who is an investigator [Editor: “searcher”] of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:27).

Whatever we do not understand in sacred Scripture, we ought not arrogantly to criticize, but humbly to venerate.

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 5, no. 6.)* Hence it is also written of the Lord: “His eyelids question the children of men” (Ps. 10:5). His eyelids are his judgments, which close something to us and open something else. The eyelids of God—namely, his judgments—question us by opening, asking whether we are not lifted up when we understand; and they question us by closing, asking whether we do not despise what we are unable to understand.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the continual growth of holy Church

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 10, no. 22.)* When the holy Church of the elect raises itself from this world in ardent love through holy prayers, it ascends through the wilderness that it leaves behind “like a column of smoke from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense” (Song 3:6). Smoke is produced from incense; and through the Psalmist it is said: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140:2). Smoke usually draws forth tears. Thus smoke from perfumes is the compunction of prayer conceived from the virtues of love.

*(Morals I, chapter 36, no. 54.)* The holy Church ascends like a column of smoke from perfumes, because from the virtues of its life it advances daily toward the uprightness of inward incense. It does not dissipate, scattered among thoughts, but gathers itself within the secrets of the heart into a rigid column. The holy Church, which acts daily while never ceasing to reconsider and review itself, possesses myrrh and frankincense in its works, but dust in its thoughts. It is rightly said: “of myrrh and frankincense.”

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 10, no. 23.)* Frankincense is burned for the Lord in sacrifice according to the law. By myrrh, dead bodies are embalmed so that they will not be corrupted by worms. Therefore they offer a sacrifice of myrrh and frankincense who afflict the flesh so that the vices of corruption may not dominate them, and who burn before the Lord a fragrant offering of their love.

It is especially noteworthy that in the Church the virtues of those who act well are called not perfumes but powders. When we do any good, we offer perfumes; but when we also review the good things we do and, through the judgment of reconsideration, attend lest anything in them be wrong, we make, as it were, powder from perfumes, so that through discernment and love we may kindle our prayer to the Lord more finely.

*(Morals XVIII, chapter 48, no. 78.)* The holy Church desires to see the appearance of her Bridegroom in his divinity, yet cannot do so, because the form of his eternity, which it desired to behold, was hidden from its eyes by the humanity he had assumed. In mourning it says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall” (Song 2:9); as though it plainly said: “I desire now to see him in the appearance of his divinity, but I am still excluded from his vision by the wall of the flesh he assumed.”

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 1, no. 15.)* He displayed to human eyes what our Redeemer assumed from mortal nature, while remaining invisible in himself. To the Church seeking to see him openly, he stood as though behind a wall, because he did not present himself to be seen in manifest majesty. For he stood, as it were, behind a wall because he displayed the nature of humanity that he had assumed and concealed the nature of divinity from human eyes.

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 4, no. 15.)* The holy Church, or each elect soul, is a friend of the heavenly Bridegroom through love, a dove through the Spirit, and beautiful through the loveliness of its conduct. When it is already led out from the corruption of the flesh, winter certainly passes away for it, because the torpor of the present life departs. The rain also goes away and recedes, because when it is led forth to contemplate almighty God in his own substance, drops of words will no longer be necessary for the rain of preaching to be poured upon it. For what it was able to hear only imperfectly, it will then see more fully.

Flowers appear on the earth when the Church begins to taste in advance something of the sweetness of the life of eternal blessedness; and, as though already among flowers, it perceives by their fragrance what, once it has gone forth, it will possess more abundantly in fruit.

*(Ibid., homily 3, no. 14.)* “The litter of our king” (Song 3:9) is the holy Church, which has been constructed from strong Fathers—that is, from minds incorruptible. It is rightly called a litter because each day it carries souls to the eternal banquet of its Creator.

Of the holy Church it is written: “The wings of the dove are covered with silver, and the back parts of its body are like the appearance of gold” (Ps. 67:14). For here, filled with the spirit of gentleness like a dove, it has silver-covered wings; in the back parts of its body it contains the appearance of gold, because here it clothes its preachers with the light of the word, while in the age to come it displays in itself the splendor of glory.

At the beginning of the Church’s birth, a very great multitude of the faithful reached the kingdom through the blood of martyrdom. “Our king made a purple ascent in the litter” (Song 3:10), because one reaches the brightness seen within through the tribulation of blood.

*(Morals IX, chapter 11, no. 18.)* The Church has one beauty of conduct, in which it is now seen, and another beauty of rewards, in which it will then be raised up through the appearance of its Creator. All the elect are its members; because they proceed simply toward all things, they are called its dove-like eyes. They shine with great light, because they also flash with the miracles of signs.

“Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, O bride” (Song 4:3). A ribbon binds the hair of the head. The bride’s lips are like a ribbon because, through the exhortation of holy Church, all the thoughts scattered in the minds of its hearers are bound, lest they flow loosely, lest they spread themselves among unlawful things, and lest, once scattered, they lower the eyes of the heart. Instead, they gather themselves toward a single intention, while the ribbon of holy preaching binds them.

*(Morals XXIV, chapter 8, no. 17.)* It rightly declares it to be scarlet, because the preaching of the saints blazes with the heat of love alone. Again it is written: “Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies” (Song 4:5). What are the two breasts except the two peoples coming from Judea and the Gentiles, who are fixed in the body of holy Church by the purpose of wisdom in the secret place of the heart?

Those who have been chosen from the Jewish or Gentile people in holy Church are compared to fawns of gazelles because, through humility, they understand themselves to be small and sinful; but when they run through love, they cross whatever obstacles arising from temporality meet them, and by leaps of contemplation they climb to heavenly things. To accomplish this, they look upon the examples of the saints who preceded them. Hence they are also said to feed among lilies. For what is signified by lilies except the life of those who truly say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15)?

“Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within you” (Song 6:6).

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 4, no. 8.)* The cheeks of the holy Church are its spiritual Fathers, who now shine within it through miracles and appear venerable, as though on its face. When we see many performing wonders, foretelling what is to come, abandoning the world completely, and burning with heavenly desires, the cheeks of the holy Church grow red like the rind of a pomegranate.

When the Bridegroom admired the cheeks of the Church, he rightly added: “apart from what is hidden within you”; as though it were plainly said: “The things in you that are not hidden are indeed great, but those that are hidden are altogether ineffable.”

*(Morals IV, chapter 11, no. 19.)* Often the Church is described as resembling the dawn, because through knowledge of faith it is changed from the darkness of its sins into the clear light of righteousness. Hence the Bridegroom also admires it, saying: “Who is this that rises like the dawn?” (Song 6:9). The Church of the elect rises like the dawn because it abandons the darkness of its former wickedness and transforms itself in the splendor of new light.

*(Morals XIX, chapter 12, no. 9.)* The age of the holy Church is described in the same way as the age of each human being. It was then small, when, newly born, it was unable to preach the word of life. Hence it is now said of it: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts” (Song 8:8). Before the holy Church advanced through growth in virtue, it could not provide the breasts of preaching to its weaker hearers.

The Church is called mature when, joined to the word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, it conceives children through the ministry of preaching—giving them birth by exhorting and bringing them forth by conversion.

*(Morals XVII, chapter 27, no. 39.)* After the holy Church had described the Lord’s death and resurrection and his ascension, filled with the prophetic Spirit it cries to him: “Flee, my beloved, flee” (Song 8:14). As though it said: “You who became comprehensible through the flesh, exceed our understanding through your divinity, and remain incomprehensible to us in yourself.”

## CHAPTER XXV. On the prosperity and adversity of this world

*(Morals V, chapter 1, no. 1.)* When holy men see that the prosperity of this world is available to them, they are troubled by fearful suspicion. For they fear that they may be receiving here the fruit of their labors. They fear that divine justice may see a hidden wound within them and, heaping external gifts upon them, drive them away from inward things.

When elect men silently consider that they do good only to please God alone and do not rejoice even in the abundance of their prosperity, they fear less that hidden judgments concerning them may lie concealed in prosperity. Nevertheless, they endure that same prosperity reluctantly, because it hinders them from their inmost intention; and they bear the allurements of the present life with displeasure, because they know that through these they are in some measure delayed in their inward desire.

In this world, honor occupies more than contempt, and the height of prosperity weighs more heavily than the adversity of need. Through adversity, when a person is pressed outwardly, he is sometimes released more freely to desire the things within. Through prosperity, however, the mind, while compelled to obey many demands, is held back from the course of its desire.

Holy men fear prosperity in this world more than adversity. They know that when the mind is pressed by flattering occupation, it sometimes willingly turns toward outward things. They know that often a hidden thought deceives it so that it does not realize how it has been changed.

Elect men consider the eternal goods they desire and recognize how insignificant everything is that temporally smiles upon them with charm. Their minds endure all the prosperity of this world so reluctantly because they have been wounded by love of heavenly happiness. They are raised up all the more in their rejection of present sweetness because they see that it secretly flatters them in contempt of eternal glory.

*(Ibid., chapter 2, no. 2.)* Holy men trample upon the prosperity of the world with the same disdain with which they endure its adversity by trampling upon it. Finally, through the great elevation of their minds, laying both the adversities and the prosperities of the world beneath them, they say: “As is its darkness, so also is its light” (Ps. 138:12). As though they said more plainly: “Just as its sorrows do not oppress the strength of our intention, so its flatteries do not corrupt it.”

Holy men, who recognize themselves as wretched in the misery of this exile, refuse to shine in its prosperity. Hence blessed Job rightly says: “Why is light given to the miserable?” (Job 3:20). Light is given to the miserable when those who, contemplating sublime things, recognize themselves as wretched in this pilgrimage receive the brightness of transitory prosperity.

When the righteous deeply lament that they are returning to their homeland late, they are compelled to bear the burdens of honor as well. Love for eternal things crushes them, while glory from temporal things smiles upon them.

Elect men consider what they hold below and what they do not see above, what supports them on earth and what they have lost from heaven. They are gnawed by sorrow over their prosperity because, although they see that they are not utterly overwhelmed by it, they carefully weigh how to divide their thoughts between love of the Lord and the administration of his affairs.

*(Morals III, chapter 31, no. 61.)* It must be understood that often, amid prosperity, the mind is touched by an unwelcome temptation; yet sometimes we also suffer adversity outwardly and are wearied inwardly by the impulse of temptation, so that lashes may torment the flesh while carnal suggestion nevertheless floods the mind.

*(Morals IV, chapter 12, nos. 23–24.)* Blessed Job, considering how greatly the human race is lifted up by confidence in prosperous circumstances, or how greatly it is broken by agitation from adversity, returns in his mind to the state of unchangeability that the human race could have possessed in paradise. He declared by cursing how contemptible he saw the fall of mortality, which varies through prosperity and adversity, saying: “May the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived’” (Job 3:3).

It is like a certain day when the prosperity of this world smiles upon us. But this day ends in night, because temporal prosperity often leads into the darkness of tribulation. The prophet had despised the day of prosperity when he said: “I have not desired the day of man; you know” (Jer. 17:16). The Lord announced that he would suffer the night of tribulation at the end of his incarnation when, through the Psalmist, he said as though in the past: “Until night my kidneys reproached me” (Ps. 15:7).

*(Morals XII, chapter 2, no. 2.)* It has been determined for a person how far the prosperity of this world may follow him and how far adversity may strike him, lest either immoderate prosperity exalt the elect of God or excessive adversity weigh them down.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On heretics

*(Morals XIX, chapter 18, no. 27.)* When the authors of every heretical perversity do not fear to interpret God’s dispensation perversely, they drag the peoples subject to them not onto the way that is Christ, but into a pathless place. It is rightly said that contention is poured out over them, because they contradict one another through their mutual arguments.

Arius, accepting three persons in the Godhead, also believed in three gods. In opposition to him, Sabellius, accepting one God, believed there was one person. Between them holy Church, holding unwaveringly to the straight path of its preaching, confesses one God and asserts three persons against Sabellius; and while asserting three persons, it confesses one God against Arius.

When Manichaeus discovered that virginity was praised in sacred Scripture, he condemned marriage. Jovinianus, on the other hand, because he recognized that marriage was permitted, despised the purity of virginity. Thus it happens that, while heretics are always confused by perverse understanding, their wickedness agrees with itself in guilt but differs in doctrine.

Holy Church proceeds in ordered peace through the disputes of heretics on both sides. It knows how to accept higher goods while also venerating lower ones, so that it neither equates the highest with the lowest nor despises the lowest when it venerates the highest.

*(Morals XI, chapter 28, no. 39.)* Heretics defraud God because they assert things that do not please the very one on whose behalf they speak; and while they attempt to defend him, they offend him. They collapse while running in opposition to the one whom they seem, through their preaching, to serve. He is both enemy and defender who attacks the God whom he preaches.

*(Preface to Job, chapter 6, no. 15; Morals XI, chapter 28, no. 39.)* Every heretic is both an enemy and a defender of almighty God, because by what he attempts, as it were, to defend him, he opposes his truth. But since nothing can be hidden from God, he judges in them what they feel inwardly, not what they appear outwardly to serve.

*(Morals XVIII, chapter 30, no. 49.)* When all heretics mockingly scorn the preaching of holy Church and its fruitfulness, what else do they despise except the offspring of the mother? We rightly call her their mother as well, because those who speak against her come forth from her, as John testifies when he says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

*(In the Preface to Blessed Job, chapter 7, no. 16.)* All heretics, in what they say about the Lord, are called nothing but oldness, because they seek to appear preachers not with right intention but from desire for temporal glory. The minds of the faithful raise themselves to contemplate heavenly things; but while heretics seek to pervert the words of those who contemplate rightly, they attempt, as it were, to destroy a watchtower.

If heretics did not despise the Lord, they would never think perversely about him; and if they did not drag along the heart of oldness, they would not err in understanding the new life. And if they did not destroy the contemplation of good things, heavenly judgments would never reject them with such strict examination because of the fault of their words.

By despising the Lord, then, heretics hold themselves in the oldness of their iniquity; but by holding themselves in oldness, they harm the contemplation of the upright through their perverse words.

*(Morals V, chapter 11, no. 28.)* Heretics have this characteristic: they mix good things with evil so that they may easily deceive the understanding of their hearer. If heretics always spoke perversely, they would be recognized more quickly in their perversity and would persuade no one of what they wished. Again, if they always thought rightly, they would plainly not be heretics. But while they serve both sides by the art of deception, they infect good things with evil and conceal evil things beneath good things so that they may be accepted.

Just as one who offers a cup of poison touches the rim of the cup with the sweetness of honey, and while what is sweet is sampled at the first taste, what is deadly is also unquestionably swallowed, so heretics mix right things with perverse ones: by displaying good things they attract hearers to themselves, and by presenting evil things they corrupt them with a hidden pestilence.

*(Morals XVI, chapter 47, no. 60.)* The prophet Jeremiah designates any heretic under the figure of a wild ass, saying: “A wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of its soul, draws in the wind of its passion” (Jer. 2:24). The wild ass is a savage animal; and heretics are rightly compared here to wild asses because, abandoned to their pleasures, they are alienated from the bonds of faith and reason.

Every heretic is like a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness because, while he does not cultivate the soil of his heart through the virtue of discipline, he dwells where there is no fruit. He draws in the wind of his passion in the desire of his soul because what he has conceived in his mind from a desire for knowledge he can inflate, but not build up. Against such people it is said: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1).

## CHAPTER XXVII. On faith

*(Book II on the Gospels, homily 26, no. 8.)* Faith is the proof of things that cannot appear. Things that are apparent do not have faith, but recognition, as the Apostle Paul says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). Isaiah says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9).

*(Morals, book II, chapter 46, no. 71.)* We truly become wise for understanding when we offer the faith of our belief to everything that the Creator says. If this faith is not first generated in our heart, none of the other things can be good, even if they appear good. For it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

*(Book II on the Gospels, homily 29, no. 3.)* In the Gospel the Truth says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). Perhaps each person may say to himself: “I have already believed; I will be saved.” He speaks truly if he holds faith through works. For true faith is that which does not contradict in conduct what it says in words.

Of certain false believers the Apostle Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). Hence John says: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4). Since this is so, we ought to recognize the truth of our faith by examining our life. We are truly faithful when we fulfill in works what we promise in words.

On the day of baptism we promised to renounce all the works and all the pomps of the ancient enemy. Therefore let each of you turn the eyes of the mind back upon himself; and if, after baptism, he keeps what he vowed before baptism, let him rejoice, certain now that he is faithful.

But suppose that a person has in no way kept what he promised in baptism, and that he who ought to have been faithful has fallen away into practicing wicked works and desiring the pomps of the world. Let us see whether he now knows how to mourn that he has gone astray. For before the merciful Judge, even the one who returns to the truth after lying will not be considered deceitful, because almighty God, while gladly receiving our repentance, hides from his own judgment what we did wrong and gathers us into the bosom of faith.

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 3, no. 1.)* Through belief in holy faith we are known by almighty God, as he himself says of his sheep: “I am the good Shepherd, and I know my own, and my own know me” (John 10:14).

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 10.)* All who stand in faith are like the many members contained in one body. They are diverse in function, but because they mutually fit together, they become one. Thus the foot sees through the eye, and the eyes walk through the feet; the hearing of the ears serves the mouth, and the tongue hastens to the hearing of the mouth; the stomach is supported by the hands, and the hands work for the stomach.

In the very arrangement of the body we learn what we should preserve in our conduct. It is therefore exceedingly shameful not to imitate what we are.

*(Morals, book XXXIII, chapter 10, no. 18.)* Faith is sometimes expressed by the name “cord,” as it is written: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. 4:12). Faith, woven from knowledge of the Trinity by the mouths of preachers, remains strong among the elect but is torn apart in the heart of the reprobate alone.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On hope

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 22.)* One does not reach the single hope of the calling unless one runs toward it with a mind united to one’s neighbors, as the Apostle says: “One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. 4:4).

*(Morals, book XVIII, chapter 40, no. 64.)* The Apostle testifies that three virtues above all remain in the hearts of the faithful, saying: “But now faith, hope, and love remain” (1 Cor. 13:13). Filled with sudden grace, the thief both received and preserved all three on the cross.

The thief had faith, for he believed that the Lord whom he saw dying alongside him would reign. He had hope, for he asked entrance into his kingdom, saying: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). He also held love vigorously in his death, for he both reproved his fellow criminal, who was dying for a similar crime, for his iniquity and preached to him the life he had come to know, saying: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong” (Luke 23:40–41).

The man who came to the cross such as this from guilt—behold, how he departed from the cross by grace. The same thief confessed the Lord whom he saw dying alongside him in human weakness, at the very time when the apostles were denying the one whom they had seen performing miracles by divine power.

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 4.)* Each soul that is already filled with the freshness of hope and the love of good works dwells, as it were, in gardens. The hope of this world is dry, because everything loved here withers quickly.

*(Morals, book XIII, chapter 5, no. 5.)* He knows well how to remain amid outward miseries who knows always how to rejoice in inward hope. In everything they do, the virtues of the saints bring forth hope, faith, and love, so that faith, hope, and love may joyfully lead whatever each virtue administers into a good work.

*(Morals, book V, chapter 32, no. 56.)* Whenever heavenly things are shown to us, the spirit is shaken by fear, but hope nevertheless presumes. Hope rises from there toward greater things to be dared—from the very place where the spirit is troubled; and it sees heavenly things first.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On love

*(Morals, book XXVIII, chapter 22, no. 46.)* Love is called the bond of perfection because every good that is done is bound by it so that it may not perish. Any work is quickly torn away by the tempter if it is found loosened from the bond of love.

If a person’s mind is bound by love of God and neighbor, then whenever the movements of temptations suggest anything unjust to it, love itself opposes them as a barrier and breaks the wave of wicked persuasion through the sacrifices of the virtues and the bar of inward love.

*(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 10, no. 31.)* To perform God’s commandments because of an order is the action of a servant and an obedient person; to perform them out of love is the action of one who is obedient and loving. For through knowledge the love of mercy is learned, and through the love of mercy knowledge is multiplied. It is as though one wing strikes another within us, because virtue arouses virtue.

*(Book II on the Gospels, homily 27, no. 1.)* Every commandment proceeds from love alone, and all commandments are one commandment, because whatever is commanded is established in love alone. The Lord’s commandments are both many and one: many in the diversity of their works, one in the root of love.

He himself indicates how this love is to be maintained: in many statements of his Scripture he commands that friends be loved in him and enemies be loved for his sake. A person truly has love who loves a friend in God and loves an enemy for God’s sake.

There are some who love their neighbors through affection for kinship and the flesh. Sacred Scripture does not contradict them in this love. But one thing is what nature freely bestows, and another is what, through love, is owed in obedience to the Lord’s commands.

Those who love their neighbors carnally do not attain the sublime rewards of love, because they bestow their love not spiritually but carnally. Therefore, when the Lord said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:12), he immediately added: “As I have loved you.” As though he plainly said: “Love for the purpose for which I loved you.”

*(No. 4.)* The one and supreme proof of love is whether one loves even the person who opposes him.
