Hence the Truth himself both endured the cross and nevertheless offered the affection of love to his very persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). What wonder, then, if disciples love their enemies while they live, when the Master also loved his enemies while he was being killed?

*(No. 3.)* For the virtue of love to remain unconquered in disturbance, it must be nourished through mercy in tranquility, so that it may first learn to offer its possessions to almighty God and afterward itself.

In the Gospel the Truth says: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father” (John 15:15).

*(No. 4.)* What are all the things that he heard from his Father and wished to make known to his servants in order to make them his friends, except the joys of inward love and the festivities of the heavenly homeland, which he daily impresses upon our minds through the inspiration of his love? When we love the heavenly things we have heard, we already know the things we love, because love itself is knowledge.

Let no one think that he immediately possesses love when he loves someone, unless he first examines the power of his own love.

*(Book II on the Gospels, homily 38, no. 11.)* If someone loves another person but does not love that person for God’s sake, he does not have love, although he thinks he does. True love exists when a friend is loved in God and an enemy is loved for God’s sake. He loves those whom he loves for God’s sake who already knows how to love even those by whom he is not loved.

*(Book II on the Gospels, homily 9, no. 6.)* Whoever has love also receives the other gifts; whoever does not have love loses even the gifts that he seemed to have received. We must therefore watch over the preservation of love in everything we do. True love is to love a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake. Whoever does not have it loses every good that he possesses.

*(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 6.)* When we set the battle line of spiritual warfare against wicked spirits, it is supremely necessary that we always be found united and bound together through love, never broken apart by discord. Whatever good works there may be in us, if love is absent, discord opens a place in the battle line through which the enemy can enter to strike us.

*(Book I on the Gospels, homily 17, no. 1.)* There are two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor; and love cannot exist with fewer than two. No one is properly said to have love toward himself, but love extends toward another in order that it may be love.

Our Redeemer sends his disciples to preach in pairs, quietly suggesting to us by this that whoever does not have love toward another must in no way undertake the office of preaching.

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 1, no. 5.)* In a building, one stone carries another because one stone is placed upon another; and the one who carries another is carried by another. Thus, in holy Church, each person both carries another and is carried by another. For neighbors mutually bear with one another so that through them the building of love may rise.

Hence Paul admonishes us, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2).

## CHAPTER XXX. On the grace that precedes and follows us

[Col. 0820B]

Textual and editorial notes: At the opening, the editors read *premit* (“presses”) for *exprimit* (“presses out”); Laudunensis, Germanensis, and Vallicellensis have the same reading. At the phrase “the discourse of the speaker,” the editors read *ordo* (“order”) for *sermo* (“discourse”). At Proverbs 25:27, the text has *scrutator* (“investigator”), while the editors read *perscrutator* (“searcher”). At “hidden … by the humanity he had assumed,” the edition reads *assumpta humanitas* (“assumed humanity”) rather than *assumpta humanitate* (“by assumed humanity”).

The bracketed phrase in the source, “[and offer a sacrifice of myrrh and frankincense],” is retained in the translation above as “they offer a sacrifice of myrrh and frankincense.” In the discussion of worldly prosperity, the edition reads *liberius* (“more freely”) for *liberior*; it also reads *de* for *in*, and omits *se* (“themselves”) in “what supports them on earth.”

In the heretics section, the edition reads *corruunt* (“fall”) for *currunt* (“run”), *quo* for *quem* in “the God whom he preaches,” and *fuissent* (“would have been”) for *essent* (“were”); it also reads *quia* (“because”) for *qui* (“who”) in the wild-ass passage. In the baptism passage, the printed editions omit “and he who ought to have been faithful” and “and gathers [us] into the bosom of faith.” In the bodily-members comparison, the edition instead reads, “and the tongue hastens to the ears for its own use, etc.” In the hope passage, the edition reads *ad eam* (“toward it”) for *eadem* (“the same”). Finally, at the opening of the charity passage, the edition reads *per scientiam charitatis misericordia discitur* (“through knowledge of love mercy is learned”) for *per scientiam charitas misericordiae discitur* (“through knowledge, the love of mercy is learned”); the text also notes that Taio’s reading is supported by the Longipontine, Vallicellensis, and Norman manuscripts.

(Lib. I on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 2.) By the grace of almighty God we can indeed strive toward good works, but we cannot bring them to completion unless he himself, who gives the command, helps us. The apostle Paul admonishes the disciples, saying: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12). Immediately he added who works these very good things in them, saying: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (ibid., 13). Hence the Truth himself says to the disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

We must consider this: [Note: [Col. 0819] The edition reads, “sic bona nostra si,” etc.; but the reading of our Taio is better.] if our good works are so wholly gifts of almighty God that nothing of our own is present in them, why do we seek eternal recompense as though it were owed to our merits? But if they are ours in such a way that they are not gifts of almighty God, why do we give thanks to almighty God for them? We must know that our evil deeds are ours alone, whereas our good deeds belong both to almighty God and to us: for he anticipates us by inspiring us to will, and then follows after us by helping us, so that our willing is not fruitless but that we are able to accomplish what we will.

When grace precedes and good will follows, what is the gift of almighty God becomes our merit. Paul explains this well in a brief statement, saying: “I labored more than all of them” (1 Cor. 15:10). But lest he seem to attribute what he had done to his own strength, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.” Because Paul was preceded by a heavenly gift, he acknowledged himself as alien to his good work, saying: “Yet not I.” But because preceding grace had made his free will good, and in his work he followed that same grace by his free will, he added: “But the grace of God with me”—as though he were saying: “In the good work I labored—not I, but also I. Insofar as I was preceded by the Lord’s gift alone: not I. But insofar as I followed the gift by my will: also I.” (Moral. XIX, chap. 4, no. 7.)

For God to look upon is to restore to his grace those things that had been lost and ruined. By looking upon us, he restrained the evils of our fickleness and granted us the great merits of maturity. (Moral. XVII, chap. 16, no. 22.)

Blessed Job says: “The moon does not shine, and the stars are not pure in his sight” (Job 25:5). For neither does holy Church shine with so many miracles by her own virtue unless the gifts of preceding grace pour over her. Nor are the minds of individual people who live well free from the stains of sins if they are judged apart from mercy. In the eyes of the strict Judge, each person’s corruptibility defiles him unless the grace of the merciful one wipes it away daily.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the four orders of those who govern

(Lib. II on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 6.) Holy Church has received four orders of rulers for the instruction of the faithful peoples. The apostle Paul enumerates them as gifts of the almighty Lord, saying: “He gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers” (Eph. 4:11). He names pastors and teachers as one order of rulers, because the one who teaches is truly the one who feeds the flock of God.

At her beginnings holy Church had apostles and prophets. By prophets we mean not those who existed among the ancient people, but those who arose in holy Church after the apostles. In the later age, which is the present one, she has evangelists and teachers. Since “gospel” means good news, we call those evangelists who announce the good things of the heavenly homeland to peoples who are still unformed. Evangelists and teachers also existed in the earlier period, but by the Lord’s generosity they remain even to this day, since we still see daily both unbelieving peoples being led toward the end and the faithful being instructed by teachers in good conduct.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On pastors of souls, and what sort ought to be chosen in the Church

(Preface to Part I of the *Pastoral Rule*.) When necessity demands it, one must carefully consider how a person comes to the summit of governance, how he lives after rightly attaining it, how he teaches after living well, and with what degree of consideration he recognizes his own weakness each day after teaching correctly—lest either humility avoid the approach to office, or one’s life contradict one’s attainment, [Note: [Col. 0821D] That these words, absent from other codices, are Gregory’s is plainly inferred from this passage.] or doctrine abandon one’s life, or presumption exalt one’s doctrine. Therefore fear should first temper ambition; afterward, life should commend the ministry of teaching, which is received by one who did not seek it. Then it is necessary that the good of the pastor, which is displayed in living, should also be propagated through speech. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 4.)

Finally, every perfect work must be weighed down by consideration of one’s own weakness, lest the swelling of pride extinguish it before the eyes of the hidden Judge. [Note: [Col. 0822D] The same reading is found in the Laon and Troyes codices.]

The prophet Isaiah says: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). Whoever approaches the priesthood assumes the office of a herald, so that before the Judge’s arrival—who follows in terror—he himself may go ahead by crying out. If a priest is ignorant of preaching, what voice of shouting will the mute herald give? (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 11.)

Strong and persevering teachers should be sought like imperishable wood. Always adhering to instruction from the sacred books, they proclaim the unity of holy Church and, as though inserted into rings, carry the ark of the Lord. To carry the ark of the Covenant on its poles is for good teachers, by preaching, to lead holy Church toward the untutored minds of unbelievers. They are commanded also to be overlaid with gold, so that when they resound to others in speech, they may themselves shine with the splendor of their lives.

It is therefore necessary that those who keep watch over the office of preaching not withdraw from study of sacred reading. For this reason the poles are always commanded to remain in the rings of the ark: whenever the opportunity to carry the ark requires it, there should be no delay in inserting the poles for carrying it. For when the pastor is questioned by his subjects about something spiritual, it is exceedingly disgraceful if he then seeks to learn what he ought to explain. Let the poles of the ark of the covenant cling to its rings, so that teachers, always meditating on the sacred words in their hearts, may raise the ark of the Testament without delay and immediately teach whatever is necessary.

Hence the first pastor of the Church rightly admonishes the other pastors, saying: “Always ready to give an answer concerning the hope that is in us” (1 Pet. 3:15). It is as though he plainly said: “So that no delay may hinder the carrying of the ark, let the poles never leave the rings.” (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 6; and *Moralia*, Book XXI, chap. 15, nos. 22 and 25.)

When holy men preside, they should attend not to the power of their rank in themselves, but to the equality of their condition. They should not rejoice in ruling people, but in benefiting them. We must know that our ancient Fathers are remembered as pastors of flocks rather than as kings of men. When the Lord said to Noah and his sons after the flood, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” he added: “And let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth” (Gen. 9:1, 7). Human beings were by nature set above irrational animals, but not above other human beings. Therefore it is said that he should be feared by animals and not by human beings, because it is contrary to nature to be proud and wish to be feared by an equal.

All who preside should consider not the power of their rank in themselves, but the equality of their condition. For, as we have said, our ancient Fathers are remembered as pastors of flocks, not as kings of men. It is necessary that rulers be feared by their subjects when they discover that those subjects scarcely fear God, so that at least through human fear those who do not fear divine judgments may fear to sin. Superiors should in no way grow proud because of the fear of their subjects [Edition: “ex hoc quaesito,” “from this sought fear,”], since in that fear they seek not their own glory but the justice of their subjects. But in requiring fear from those who live perversely, they rule not, as it were, over human beings but over animals; for in the measure that their subjects are beastlike, in that measure also they ought to lie subdued by fear. [Edition: “formidini” rather than “formidine.”] (*Moralia*, Book XIII, chap. 20, no. 23.)

The faces of holy Church are those who, placed in positions of governance, appear first, so that the honor of the faithful people may derive from their appearance, even if something deformed lies hidden in the body. These leaders, set over the peoples, mourn the faults of the weak and afflict themselves over others’ falls as though they were their own. Often good rulers, when they see some people return to pardon after their sins while others persist in wickedness, marvel at the hidden judgments of almighty God but cannot penetrate them. They are astonished at what they do not understand. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chap. 10.)

The person who is already spiritually alive by dying to all the passions of the flesh, who has put the world’s prosperity behind him, who fears no adversity, and who desires only inward things, should by every means be drawn forward as an example of living. In harmony with this intention, his body should resist neither altogether through weakness nor excessively through affliction. [Note: [Col. 0823] The edition reads: “nor does the spirit resist excessively through contumacy.”]

Likewise, the person should be advanced to the dignity of pastoral office who is not led to covet what belongs to others but distributes what is his own; who is quickly moved to forgive by the compassion of mercy, yet nowhere, by forgiving more than is fitting, is bent away from the stronghold of righteousness; who commits no unlawful acts, but mourns those committed by others as his own; who compassionates another’s weakness from the affection of his heart and thus rejoices in his neighbor’s good as in his own progress.

The person rightly attains the dignity of pontifical excellence who presents himself to others as worthy of imitation in everything he does, so that among them he has nothing for which he would blush, at least concerning the past; who strives to live in such a way that he can water the parched hearts of his neighbors with the flowing waters of doctrine [Edition: “fluentis” rather than “fluentibus.”]; who by the practice and experience of prayer has already learned that he can obtain from the Lord what he asks; to whom, through the effectiveness of his deeds, it is said almost personally: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isa. 58:9).

If someone were to come and lead us to intercede on his behalf with some powerful man who is angry with him but unknown to us, we would immediately reply: “We cannot come to intercede, because we do not know him through familiarity.” If, then, a person is ashamed to become an intercessor with another person whom he scarcely presumes upon, with what frame of mind does one assume a place of intercession with God on behalf of the people when he does not know himself to be familiar with God’s grace through the merit of his life? Or how will he ask him to pardon others when he does not know whether God is favorable toward himself?

In this matter there is something else to be feared even more anxiously: lest the person who is believed able to appease wrath should himself deserve that wrath through his own guilt. We all clearly know that when someone who displeases is sent to intercede, the angered person’s mind is provoked to worse things. Let the person who is still bound by earthly desires beware, lest, while more gravely kindling the anger of the strict Judge, he become—because he delights in the place of glory—the author of ruin to his subjects. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chap. 11.)

Let each person carefully measure himself, lest he dare assume a position of governance while a condemnable vice still reigns in him, lest one whom his own crime deforms desire to become an intercessor for the sins of others.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How rulers should conduct their lives

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 2.) A ruler should always be pure in thought, so that no impurity may stain one who has undertaken this office in order to wipe away the stains of pollution from the hearts of others as well. The hand that undertakes to wash away the filth of others must strive to be clean, lest, if it holds the mud while pursuing what is dirty, it soil whatever it touches even more. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11). Those who receive into the trustworthiness of their conduct the souls of their neighbors, to be led to the eternal sanctuaries, carry the Lord’s vessels. Let them observe how much they themselves must be cleansed, since they carry living vessels in the bosom of their own commitment toward the temple of eternity.

Hence the divine voice commands that the breastplate of judgment be fastened with binding ribbons upon Aaron’s breast (Exod. 28:15ff.), so that fleeting thoughts may not possess the priestly heart, but reason alone may hold it fast. Whoever is set up as an example for others and ought always to display, by the gravity of his life, how much reason he carries in his breast must think of nothing indiscriminate or useless.

On the breastplate of judgment placed upon Aaron’s breast, the names of the twelve patriarchs are commanded to be inscribed. To carry the inscribed Fathers always upon one’s breast is to think without interruption about the lives of the ancients. A priest walks irreproachably when he continually looks upon the examples of the Fathers who went before; when he unceasingly considers the footsteps of the saints and suppresses unlawful thoughts, lest he extend the foot of his conduct beyond the boundary of his order.

A ruler must always distinguish good from evil by subtle examination and carefully consider what is suitable, for whom, when, and how; and he must seek nothing as his own, but assign his own advantages to those near him. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 3.)

Let a ruler be preeminent in action, so that by living well he may announce the way of life to his subjects, and the flock, which follows the pastor’s voice and conduct, may walk better by examples than by words. Through the divine law the priest is commanded to take and set apart the right shoulder for sacrifice (Exod. 29:22), so that it may be shown that his action must be not only useful but also distinctive: he must not do what is right merely among the wicked, but must surpass his subjects who act well in moral virtue just as he surpasses them in the honor of his rank.

The breast is given to the priest for food together with the shoulder, so that he may learn from the sacrifice to offer to the Creator from himself what he is commanded to take from the sacrifice; and so that he may not only think in his breast about what is right, but also invite those who observe him to lofty things by the shoulder of his deeds.

Let no ruler desire anything in the present life, and let him fear nothing. In view of the inward fear, let him despise the world’s flatteries; in view of the sweetness within, let him scorn its terrors. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 5.)

Let a ruler be near to each person through compassion, yet lifted above all through contemplation, so that through the compassion of mercy he may take the weakness of others upon himself, and through the height of contemplation he may also transcend himself by desiring invisible things. Let him not, while seeking lofty things, despise the lowly concerns of his neighbors; nor, while accommodating himself to the lowly concerns of his weaker neighbors, abandon the pursuit of lofty things. [The text reads “infima” (“lowly things”), where the edition has “infirma” (“weak things”); later it reads “infimis,” where the edition has “infirmis.”]

Pastors not only seek upward, by contemplation, the holy Head of the Church, namely the Lord; they also descend downward in mercy toward his members. Hence Moses frequently enters and leaves the tabernacle: within, he is carried away into contemplation; outside, he is pressed by the affairs of the weak. Within, he considers the mysteries of God; outside, he carries the burdens of those subject to the flesh.

Saint Moses always returned to the tabernacle concerning doubtful matters, and consulted God before the ark of the Testament. He thereby undoubtedly offered rulers an example: when they are uncertain outside about what they should decide, they should always return to the mind as though to the tabernacle; and, as though before the ark of the Testament, consult the Lord by searching inwardly through the pages of sacred speech for answers concerning the matters about which they are uncertain.

The Truth himself, shown to us through the assumption of our humanity, remains devoted to prayer on the mountain and performs miracles in the cities (Luke 6:12), thus laying before good rulers a path of imitation: even if they seek the highest things through contemplation, they must nevertheless mingle with the needs of the weak through compassion.

Charity then rises wondrously to lofty things when it mercifully draws itself down to the lowly concerns of neighbors; and the more kindly it descends to what is lowest, the more vigorously it should return to what is highest.

Those who have been placed over others in pastoral governance should show themselves to be such that their subjects do not blush to reveal their secrets to them. Thus, when the little ones endure the waves of temptations, they may return to the pastor’s mind as though to a mother’s breast. What they foresee will defile them with the filth of an assaulting fault, they may wash away through the comfort of his exhortation and the tears of prayer. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 7.)

Let a ruler not diminish care for inward things amid outward occupations, nor abandon concern for outward things amid anxiety over inward matters. He must not collapse inwardly through devotion to external affairs, nor, occupied solely with interior matters, fail to provide to his neighbors what he owes them outwardly. Inferior matters should be handled by subjects, while rulers should think about higher things, so that concern over dust does not obstruct the eye that stands above to watch over the steps. [Edition: “so that concern over dust does not obscure the eye.”]

All who preside are the head of their subjects. In order that the feet may be able to take the right paths, the head must undoubtedly oversee them from above; otherwise the feet will grow sluggish along the path of their advancement when the head, because the body’s posture has been bent, inclines itself toward the ground.

All who preside ought indeed to have external concerns, but they must not devote themselves to them excessively. Priests are rightly forbidden both to shave the head and to grow the hair long, so that they neither cut off the thoughts of the flesh concerning the life of their subjects completely nor again allow them to grow without restraint. By the law priests are commanded to cut their heads by cutting their hair (Ezek. 44:20), so that they may provide for the concerns of temporal care as much as necessary, yet cut them back quickly lest they grow beyond measure. [Note: [Col. 0825] The edition reads: “The concerns of temporal care, and as much as is necessary, may come forth.”]

Thus, while the life of the body is protected through the administration of external care, and while it is not obstructed by a measured attention of the heart, the hair on the priest’s head is both preserved, so that it may cover the skin, and cut back, so that it may not cover the eyes. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 8.)

A ruler must watch carefully lest the desire to please people assail him; lest, while diligently penetrating inward matters and prudently administering outward matters, he seek to be loved by his subjects more than he seeks the truth; lest, when supported by good deeds he appears alien to the world, his own love make him alien to the Creator.

The enemy of the Redeemer is the person who desires to be loved by the Church in the Redeemer’s place because of the righteous works he performs. He is guilty of adulterous thought if the servant desires to please the eyes of the bride through whom the Bridegroom has sent his gifts.

Good rulers, because they do not know how to love themselves with a private love, regard the free and pure word of their subjects as an act of humble obedience. It is exceedingly necessary for rulers to temper the care of governance with such an art of moderation that, when the minds of their subjects are able to perceive certain things rightly, they may come forth into freedom of speech, yet freedom may not burst into pride. Otherwise, if they grant their subjects’ tongues an excessive freedom, the subjects may lose humility of life.

Good rulers should therefore desire to please people in such a way that, through the sweetness of their reputation, they draw their neighbors toward love of the truth—not by desiring to be loved themselves, but by making their own affection a kind of path through which they may lead the hearts of their hearers into love of the Creator. For however rightly he may proclaim, a preacher who is not loved is scarcely heard willingly.

He who presides should therefore strive to be loved, yet should not seek love for his own sake, lest he be found to resist by a hidden tyranny of thought the one whom he is seen to serve through his office. The apostle Paul makes this clear when he reveals to us the hidden character of his own zeal, saying: “As I also please all people in all things” (1 Cor. 10:33). Yet again he says: “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10). Paul therefore both pleases and does not please: in seeking to please, he seeks to please not himself, but the truth through himself, for people. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 9.)

A ruler of souls must distinguish virtues and vices with vigilant care, lest his heart be occupied by stinginess and he rejoice in being considered parsimonious in his distributions; or, when something is squandered lavishly, he boast of being generous as though out of compassion; or, by remitting what he ought to have punished, he lead his subjects toward eternal punishments; or, by punishing excessively what has been done wrong, he himself sin more gravely; or, by prematurely anticipating what could have been done rightly and seriously, he weaken it; or, by delaying the merit of a good action, he exchange it for worse things. (Ibid., chap. 11.)

Everything we have set forth above is rightly done by a ruler if, inspired by the spirit of heavenly fear and love, he diligently meditates each day on the precepts of sacred speech. Thus the words of divine admonition may restore in him the force of concern and the prudent watchfulness directed toward heavenly life, which the practice of human society continually destroys; and the one who is led toward old age through association with worldly people may always be renewed toward love of the spiritual homeland by the breath of compunction, though association with worldly people leads him into oldness.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the humility of superiors

A ruler should be discerning in silence and useful in speech, so that he neither says what should be left unsaid nor keeps silent about what should be said. For just as careless speech leads into error, indiscreet silence leaves in error those who could have been instructed. (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapters 4 and 6.)

Let a ruler, through humility, be a companion to those who act well, but through zeal for justice stand upright against the vices of wrongdoers. Thus he should in no way place himself above the good, yet when the fault of the wicked demands it, he should immediately recognize the authority of his prior office. In this way, while suppressing the honor of his rank, he may consider himself equal to subjects who live well, and yet not fear to exercise the rights of righteousness against the perverse.

Nature gave birth to all human beings as equals, but by the changing order of merits, guilt placed some beneath others. This very difference, which arose from vice, is administered according to divine judgment, so that, because not everyone can stand equally, one may be governed by another.

All who preside should consider not the power of their rank in themselves, but the equality of their condition; nor should they rejoice in ruling people, but in benefiting them. The person governs this power well who knows both how to hold it and how to oppose it. He governs it well who knows how through it to rise above faults, and knows how with it to join himself to others in equality. He rightly administers this power who carefully knows both how to take from it what benefits others and how to overcome what tempts him; how to see himself as equal with others while possessing it, and yet how to place himself above sinners through zeal for punishment. (*Moralia* X, chap. 6, no. 8.)

Every preacher should strive to mitigate the threats of the powerful by reasoning; to relieve, as far as he can, the distress of the oppressed; to oppose patience to those who resist outwardly, and to display discipline together with patience toward those who are proud inwardly. Toward the errors of his subjects, gentleness should temper zeal in such a way that it does not weaken devotion to justice; zeal should burn for punishment in such a way that, while burning, it does not cross the boundary of mercy.

It should be the office of a ruler to provoke the ungrateful to love through benefits, and to preserve the grateful in love through acts of service; when he cannot correct the evils of his neighbors, to remain silent; and to fear that silence may be consent concerning whatever can be corrected by speaking. [Note: [Col. 0827D] The edition reads: “and when they can be corrected by speaking.” But the Corbie and German codices agree with our reading.]

## CHAPTER XXXV. How superiors should teach their subjects and prudently watch over themselves

(Prologue to Part III of the *Pastoral Rule*.) Since we have shown above what sort of person a pastor ought to be, let us now demonstrate how he ought to teach. The same exhortation does not suit everyone, because the same quality of character does not bind everyone equally. Often what benefits some harms others: herbs that nourish certain animals frequently kill others; a gentle whistle calms horses but excites puppies; medicine that diminishes one person’s illness adds strength to another; and bread that strengthens the life of the strong destroys that of little children.

The speech of teachers must therefore be shaped according to the character of their hearers, so that it may suit each individual’s circumstances while never departing from the art of common edification. For what are the attentive minds of hearers, if I may put it this way, except certain stretched rows of strings on a harp, which the player strikes in different ways so as not to produce a melody unlike himself? The strings return a harmonious modulation because they are struck by one plectrum, though not with one and the same stroke.

Thus every teacher, in order to build everyone up with the one virtue of charity, should touch the hearts of his hearers from one doctrine, but not with one and the same exhortation. (Epistle 25, formerly 24, Book I.)

A teacher who is compelled by the necessity of his position to speak of lofty things is compelled by that same necessity to display lofty things. That voice penetrates the hearts of hearers more willingly which the speaker’s life commends, because what he commands by speaking, he helps bring about by demonstrating.

Through the prophet the Lord says: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. 40:9). Thus the person who makes use of heavenly preaching should already have abandoned the lowliness of earthly works and appear to stand at the summit of things, drawing his subjects more easily toward better things insofar as he cries from above by the merit of his life.

The priest is also rightly commanded to have an ephod made of gold, violet, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and twisted linen, so that it may be shown with what diversity of virtues he ought to shine. [Note: [Col. 0828D] “To be made” or “to have” is redundant.]

In the priest’s clothing, gold shines first of all, so that the understanding of wisdom may principally gleam in him. Violet, which shines with an airy color, is added to it, so that through everything he penetrates by understanding, he may rise not toward lowly praise but toward love of heavenly things. Otherwise, if he is carelessly captivated by his own praises, he will be emptied even of his understanding of the truth.

To gold, violet, and purple, scarlet twice dyed is added, so that before the eyes of the inward Judge all the good things of the virtues may be adorned by charity; and so that all that shines before human beings may be kindled before the sight of the hidden Judge by the flame of inward love. Charity, because it loves God and neighbor simultaneously, shines as though from a double dye. Whoever pants after the likeness of the Creator in such a way that he neglects the care of his neighbors, or carries out the care of his neighbors in such a way that he grows sluggish in divine love, does not know how to have scarlet twice dyed in the ornament of the ephod, because he neglects one or the other of these things. (Part II of the *Pastoral Rule*, chap. 4.)

When a ruler prepares to speak, he should consider with how much caution he must speak. Otherwise, if he is carried away disorderly into speech, the hearts of his hearers may be struck by the wound of error; and while he perhaps wishes to appear wise, he may foolishly sever the bond of unity.

In the Gospel the Truth says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). Salt signifies the wisdom of speech. Whoever strives to speak wisely must greatly fear that the unity of his hearers may be thrown into confusion by his eloquence. Hence Paul says: “Do not be wiser than you ought to be, but be wise with sobriety” (Rom. 12:3).

Therefore, lest a careless ruler rush into speaking, the Truth himself cries out to the disciples in the words already cited: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). Figuratively, it is as though he were saying through the priest’s clothing: “Join pomegranates to bells, so that in everything you say you may preserve the unity of faith with careful observance.”

A priest must always have the voice of preaching, lest through silence he offend the judgment of the heavenly Inspector. A priest entering or leaving the tabernacle dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes the anger of the hidden Judge if he proceeds without the sound of preaching.

Bells are fittingly described as inserted into the pontiff’s garments. For what else should we understand the priest’s garments to be than righteous works, as the prophet testifies when he says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 132:9)? Thus bells cling to his garments, so that the priest’s works themselves may proclaim the way of life together with the sound of his tongue. (*Moralia*, Book XXIII, chap. 13, no. 25.)

Because we are weak human beings, when we speak to human beings about God, we must first remember what we are, so that from our own weakness we may consider by what method of teaching we should care for our weak brothers. Let us therefore consider whether we are such as some whom we correct, or whether we were once such, even if through the working of divine grace we are no longer so. Then we shall correct them with all the greater moderation of heart, insofar as we recognize ourselves more truly in those whom we amend.

But if we priests were never and are not such as those whom we undertake to correct, let us beware lest our heart grow proud and fall more disastrously because of that very innocence. In correcting their faults, let us call other good qualities of theirs before our eyes. If they possess none at all, let us return to the hidden judgments of God. For just as we received the good that we possess without any merits of our own, so grace may also pour the power of heaven into them, so that, awakened later, they may even surpass the good things that we received earlier.

Who would have believed that Saul would one day surpass Stephen, who was stoned, in the merit of apostleship, when at Stephen’s death he guarded the garments of those who were stoning him (Acts 7:58)? Therefore the heart must first be humbled by these reflections, and only then should the wickedness of wrongdoers be reproved.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the zeal of pastoral office toward subjects
*(Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 12, §§29–30.)* Every spiritual zeal fries the teacher’s soul, because he is deeply distressed when he sees the weak abandoning eternal things and taking delight in temporal ones. For no sacrifice is so acceptable to almighty God as zeal for souls, as the Psalmist says: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68:10). The apostle Paul, tormented by zeal for souls, said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11:29). What else had he made his own heart—which he had kindled with zeal for souls—than a frying pan, in which he burned with love of the virtues against vices? That which was burning was a frying pan. For it was set aflame and cooked, because it was ignited by bitterness; yet from his afflicted reflection he prepared nourishment for the virtues.

(§30.) What does the prophet Ezekiel mean by placing the frying pan as an iron wall between himself and the city (Ezek. 4:3), unless it is that this same strong zeal, which now operates in the teacher’s mind, will on the day of the final judgment stand as a witness between him and the soul against whose vices he is zealous?

[Note: [Col. 829D] The edition reads *zelat* (“is zealous”). Gemeticus and most Norman witnesses, however, read *zelatur* (“is zealously concerned for”).]

Thus, even if the one being taught refuses to listen, the teacher will nevertheless not be held guilty of the hearer’s negligence because of the zeal he displays. The prophet places an iron wall between himself and the city because, at the time of vengeance, the teacher is protected from the danger of condemnation by that very thing through which he now suffers the burning of watchful zeal.

[Col. 830B] How much the burning of the heart produced by spiritual zeal appeases almighty God is clearly shown when the Law commands fine flour to be offered in sacrifice. For it is written: “It shall be fried in a pan sprinkled with oil, and the priest who succeeds his father by right shall offer it hot, as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, and the whole of it shall be burned on the altar” (Lev. 6:21–22). The fine flour is fried in the pan when the pure mind of the just person is consumed by the holy ardor of zeal. It is commanded to be sprinkled with oil—that is, to be mixed with the charity of mercy—

[Note: [Col. 830D] The edition reads *charitatis misericordiae* (“the charity of mercy”).]

which burns and shines in the sight of almighty God. Let the mind that is fried in the pan therefore be sprinkled with oil, because the strictness of holy zeal must both burn and shine through the virtue of mercy. For it loves the very one whom it appears to pursue.

Hence it is commanded to be offered hot to the Lord as a most pleasing fragrance, because if zeal does not possess love, the fine flour offered from the pan has lost its warmth. It is very important to observe who is commanded to offer the fine flour: namely, the priest who succeeds his father by right. For that person succeeds his father by right as priest who demonstrates by his conduct that he is a son of almighty God and whose inner nobility is not contradicted by the ignobility of his works.

It is commanded to be wholly burned on the altar, so that it may become a whole burnt offering. The fine flour in the pan, therefore, is the pure mind of the just person in the affliction of spiritual zeal, fried through concern for souls; and it is reckoned before the Lord not only as a sacrifice but also as a whole burnt offering.

[Col. 830D] Let us therefore take an iron frying pan and place it as an iron wall between ourselves and the city—that is, let us assume strong zeal, so that afterward we may find this strong protection between ourselves and the soul of our hearer. We shall find this iron wall then if we now hold it firmly: by teaching, guarding, persuading, reproving, soothing, frightening—acting sometimes gently, but sometimes also more severely.

Concerning this severity it is rightly added through Ezekiel: “And you shall set your face firmly against it” (Ezek. 4:3), “and it shall be for a siege.”

(§31.) What does it mean to set one’s face firmly against Jerusalem depicted on the brick, unless it means that when the teacher announces to the soul the vision of heavenly peace, and sees that it is still weakened in its actions, he should by no means show himself more lenient or more merciful toward it?

It is written: “Do you have daughters? Preserve their bodies, and do not show a cheerful face toward them” (Sir. 7:26). Weak souls, devoted to desire for the world, are sometimes better preserved through severity: so that a firm face—that is, a face closed by the guardianship of severity against every expectation of frivolous indulgence—may terrify the unstable soul and constrain it from the pleasure of vices by the force of strictness.

When this is done by the teacher, it is always necessary that sweetness and humility be retained in the heart, so that he may love greatly and never grow proud through arrogance against the person for whose benefit he nevertheless refuses to display his love and humility.

(§32.) The teacher surrounds the hearer’s soul when he declares that traps of temptation can be laid in everything done in this life, so that, while the mind becomes fearful everywhere, it may also be watchful everywhere; and the more timid it is, the more vigilant it may live.

*(Morals V, 45, §82.)* The zeal for righteousness itself, while it agitates the mind with unrest, immediately darkens its vision, so that in its agitation it does not see higher things which it had previously perceived well in tranquillity. Yet from the very place where it is temporarily struck so as not to see, it is more subtly led back to higher things. For the very emulation of righteousness, after a little while, opens more abundantly in tranquillity what it temporarily closes through agitation; and from the point at which the mind is troubled so that it cannot see, it makes progress toward seeing more truly and clearly.

[Col. 831C] It is like an ailing eye when eye-salve is applied: light is entirely denied it, but afterward it receives the light truly from the very source through which it healthfully loses it for a time. Contemplation is never joined to agitation, nor can a disturbed mind perceive what even a tranquil mind can scarcely desire to behold. The sun’s ray is not seen when troubled clouds cover the face of heaven; nor does a disturbed spring return the image of the person looking into it, which it shows clearly when tranquil, because the more its water trembles, the more it obscures within itself the appearance of the reflected likeness.

(§83.) When the spirit is moved by zeal, the greatest care must be taken that anger itself—which is taken up as an instrument of virtue—does not dominate the mind; it must not go before as a mistress, but, like a servant ready for obedience, must never withdraw from behind reason.

[Col. 831D] For anger is raised more vigorously against vices when it serves reason as a subordinate. However much anger may arise from zeal for righteousness, it tears apart the undisciplined mind. It immediately refuses to serve reason, and expands itself with greater shamelessness in proportion as it considers the vice of impatience a virtue.

Above all, the person moved by zeal for righteousness must attend to this: anger must not pass beyond the mind’s control. Rather, considering the time and measure appropriate for punishing sin, he should restrain the disturbance arising in his spirit by carefully reconsidering it, suppress his resentment, and regulate his heated movements according to equity. Thus he will be a more just avenger of another person’s fault in proportion as he has first proved victorious over his own.

The person moved by zeal for righteousness should correct the faults of wrongdoers in such a way that he himself, the one correcting, first grows through patience and judges his own fervor by rising above it, lest, excited without restraint by that very zeal for righteousness, he stray far from righteousness.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That the Unworthy and Inexperienced Should Not Presume to Approach Pastoral Teaching

*(Pastoral Rule, Part I, introduction.)* There are many pastors who, because they do not know how to measure themselves, desire to teach what they have not learned. They judge the burden of teaching to be so much lighter because they are ignorant of its greatness, and, since they are unlearned and rashly aspire to hold the citadel of teaching, they are driven back from the audacity of their rashness at the very gate of speech.

*(Ibid., chapter 1.)* No art is presumed to be taught unless it has first been learned through attentive study. With what rashness, then, is pastoral teaching undertaken by the inexperienced, when the governance of souls is the art of arts? Who does not know that the wounds of the mind are more hidden than wounds of the flesh? Yet often those who have in no way learned spiritual precepts are not afraid to profess themselves physicians of the heart, while those who do not know the power of medicines are ashamed to appear physicians of the body.

There are some who, within holy Church, seek the glory of honor under the appearance of governance. They desire to be seen as teachers, long to rise above others, and, as Truth bears witness, seek the first places at banquets and the chief seats in assemblies (Matt. 23:6–7). The more they have reached the teaching of humility through sheer arrogance, the less able they are to administer worthily the pastoral office they have undertaken.

[Col. 832C] The tongue itself is put to shame in teaching when one thing is learned and another taught. Against unworthy pastors the Lord complains through the prophet, saying: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8:4). They reign from themselves and not by the decision of the supreme ruler when, supported by no virtues and not called by God, but inflamed by their own desire, they seize the height of governance rather than attain it.

The inner Judge both promotes useless priests and does not acknowledge them, because those whom he tolerates by permitting them he certainly rejects by judgment. Hence, even after miracles, he says to some who come to him: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know who you are” (Luke 13:27).

The inexperience of pastors is rebuked by the voice of Truth when it is said through the prophet: “The shepherds themselves had no understanding” (Isa. 56:11). Again the Lord detests them, saying: “Those who held the law did not know me” (Jer. 2:8). Thus Truth complains that it is not known by them, and declares that it does not know the leadership of the ignorant; for those who do not know the things of the Lord are certainly not known by the Lord, as Paul testifies: “But if anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38).

Often the inexperience of pastors corresponds to the merits of their subjects. Although they may lack the light of knowledge because their own fault demands it, nevertheless, by a strict judgment, it is arranged that through their ignorance even those who follow them may stumble. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14).

Hence the Psalmist, not with the spirit of one who wishes this, but in the mystery of prophecy,

[Note: [Col. 833D] The edition reads *ministerio* (“by ministry”). The first two Gemeticus manuscripts, the second Audomarus manuscript, and the Lyre and Rouen witnesses have the same reading as our text.]

declares: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and bend their backs continually” (Ps. 68:24). The eyes are those who, placed at the very forefront of supreme honor, have undertaken the duty of providing the way; those who cling to them afterward are rightly called backs. When the eyes are darkened, the back is bent, because when those who lead lose the light of knowledge, those who follow are bent beneath the burden of carrying sins.

*(Pastoral Rule, Part I, chapter 2.)* Every unworthy person would flee from the burden of so great a guilt if he considered with an attentive heart the sentence of Truth, which says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matt. 18:6).

*(Chapter 3.)* Let no one who is unequal to these sacred offices dare to profane them and, through desire for the summit, undertake leadership that leads to destruction. Hence James piously forbids this, saying: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers” (James 3:1).

Here also the Mediator of God and humanity himself avoided receiving an earthly kingdom, although he reigns in heaven before the ages, surpassing even the knowledge and understanding of the heavenly spirits.

Often the heart is pressed under the discipline of adversity; but if it bursts forth to the summit of governance, that discipline is immediately changed into arrogance by the habitual exercise of power. Thus Saul, who had earlier fled while considering himself unworthy, swelled with pride as soon as he received the reins of the kingdom. Desiring to be honored before the people, and unwilling to be publicly reproved, he tore apart the very man who had anointed him as king (1 Sam. 10:22; 15:17, 30; Acts 13:22; 2 Sam. 11:3).

Thus the prophet David, pleasing in nearly all his actions according to the judgment of his Creator, as soon as he was freed from the weight of oppression, broke out into the swelling of a wound. He became cruelly harsh in the death of a man who had been weakly yielding in his desire for a woman; and he who had previously known how to spare the wicked piously afterward learned to rush without hesitation even toward the death of the good (2 Sam. 11:15). Earlier he had refused to strike the discovered persecutor; afterward, even at the cost of exhausting his army, he destroyed a devoted soldier. His fault would have dragged him far from the number of the elect had scourges not recalled him to forgiveness.

Often those who desire to undertake pastoral teaching also propose certain good works to themselves. Although they seek it with an intention of arrogance, they nevertheless consider that they will accomplish great things. Thus it happens that the hidden intention suppresses one thing, while the surface of thought displays another to the mind that is considering it. For the mind often lies to itself about itself: it pretends to love a good work which it does not love, and not to love the glory of the world which it does love.

Often a mind desiring to rule becomes fearful while seeking, but bold once it has attained its goal. While striving toward it, it trembles lest it fail to arrive; but when it suddenly arrives, it considers the position to which it has come to be its rightful due. Once it begins to enjoy the office of authority in a worldly manner, it willingly forgets whatever it had thought in a religious spirit.

When thought is carried beyond actual practice, it is necessary that the eye of the mind immediately be recalled to past deeds. Let everyone consider what he did while subordinate, and he will suddenly recognize whether, as a superior, he can do the good things he had proposed. No one can learn humility at the summit who did not cease to be proud while in a lowly position. Anyone who learned to pant after praise when it was absent does not know how to flee from it when it is available. Nor can a person overcome greed when he reaches out to support many people, if his own resources were not sufficient even for himself alone.

Let each person therefore discover himself from his past life, lest the image of his thoughts deceive him in his desire for the summit.

[Col. 834B] Often, in the occupation of governance, even the practice of good works that had been maintained in tranquillity is lost, because an inexperienced person can steer a ship correctly on a calm sea, whereas in a storm even a skilled sailor becomes confused amid the waves of the tempest.

What is the power of the summit except a storm of the mind? In it, the ship of the heart is continually shaken by the tempests of thought and incessantly driven this way and that, so that through sudden excesses of speech and action it is shattered as though against opposing rocks.

Among the matters we have set forth, what must be followed and held except this: the person rich in virtues should come to governance only under compulsion, while the person devoid of virtues should not approach it even under compulsion? If the virtuous person resists completely, let him beware lest, tying up the money received in a napkin, he be judged for having hidden it (Matt. 25:18). To tie money in a napkin is to conceal received gifts in the idleness of sluggish torpor.

Let every unworthy person, when he desires governance, take care lest, by the example of an evil work, he become an obstacle to those seeking entry into the kingdom in the manner of the Pharisees (Matt. 23:13), who, in the words of the Teacher, neither enter themselves nor allow others to enter.

It must also be considered that when an elected bishop undertakes the case of the people, he approaches them like a physician approaching a sick person. If the passions are still alive in his own conduct, with what presumption does he hurry to heal one who has been struck, when he himself carries a wound on his face?

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Authority Given to Bishops to Bind and to Loose

*(Book II on the Gospels, Homily 26, §§4–5.)* The holy preachers who fear God’s strict judgment become judges of souls and condemn or free others, although they feared being condemned themselves. In the Church today the bishops occupy their place. Those who receive the rank of governance take up the authority to loose and to bind.

The honor of the episcopate is great, but the burden of that honor is heavy. It is difficult for one who does not know how to govern his own life to become the judge of another’s life. It often happens that the person who holds the place of judgment is one whose life does not at all correspond to that position. It often happens that he either condemns the innocent or, himself bound, looses others.

Often, in loosing and binding subjects, he follows the movements of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Thus the very power of binding and loosing is forfeited by the person who exercises it according to his own desires and not according to the merits of his subjects.

It often happens that a pastor is moved toward a particular neighbor by hatred or favor. But those who follow either their own hatred or their own favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects rightly. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “They put to death souls that do not die, and they gave life to souls that do not live” (Ezek. 13:19). He puts to death one who does not die when he condemns a righteous person; and he tries to give life to one who will not live when he attempts to release the guilty from punishment.

*(Morals, Book XIX, chapter 25, §46.)* Almighty God, in order to restrain us from delivering a hasty sentence, although all things are naked and open to his eyes, nevertheless did not wish to judge the sins of Sodom merely on hearsay. He says: “I will go down and see whether they have completed in action the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18:20).

Why does the almighty Lord, who knows everything, appear to doubt before investigation, unless it is to set before us an example of seriousness, so that we do not presume to believe people’s sins before examining them? What else does this example admonish us than that we should never be hasty in delivering a sentence, should not judge matters rashly without investigation, should not be moved by every report of evil, and should not believe statements indiscriminately without proof?

The cases must be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing must be exercised.

*(Book II on the Gospels, Homily 26, §6.)* It must be seen what fault has been committed and what repentance has followed the fault, so that those whom almighty God visits through the grace of remorse may be absolved by the pastor’s sentence. The presiding minister’s absolution is true when it follows the judgment of the inner Judge.

This is well signified by the raising of the four-day-dead man. It demonstrates that the Lord first called and restored the dead man to life, saying: “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43). Then the man who had come out alive was loosed by the disciples, as it is written: “When the one who had been bound with bandages had come out, Jesus then said to his disciples: ‘Loose him and let him go’” (John 11:45).

That is, the pastors of the Church ought to remove the punishment deserved by the person who was not ashamed to confess what he had done.

Under great restraint the pastors of the Church should strive either to loose or to bind. But whether the pastor binds justly or unjustly, the pastor’s sentence must nevertheless be feared by the flock, lest the subordinate who is perhaps unjustly bound merit the sentence of his binding through another fault.

Let every pastor fear absolving indiscriminately or binding indiscriminately. Let the person who is under the pastor’s hand fear being bound, whether justly

[Note: [Col. 835D] The edition omits *juste* (“justly”).]

or unjustly. Nor should he rashly criticize his pastor’s judgment, lest, even if he has been bound unjustly, the fault that did not previously exist be created by the pride of his swollen criticism.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Pastors Who Do Not Walk Uprightly

*(Pastoral Rule, Part I, chapter 2.)* There are some who investigate spiritual precepts with diligent care, but trample in their lives upon what they penetrate by understanding. They suddenly teach what they have learned not through practice but through study, and by their conduct oppose what they preach in words. Thus it happens that when the pastor walks over precipitous places, the flock follows him to destruction.

Through the prophet the Lord complains against the contemptible knowledge of pastors, saying: “You drank the clearest water, but troubled the remainder with your feet; and my sheep ate what had been trampled by your feet, and drank what your feet had troubled” (Ezek. 34:18–19).

Pastors drink the clearest water when they rightly draw in the streams of truth. But to trouble that same water with their feet is to corrupt the disciplines of holy meditation by living badly. The sheep drink the water troubled by the pastors’ feet when those who are subject do not follow the words they hear, but imitate only the depraved examples they see.

When they thirst for the words but are perverted through the deeds, they take in mud as though from polluted springs. No one does greater harm in the Church than one who acts perversely while possessing the name or rank of holiness. No one dares to rebuke such a delinquent, and the fault is greatly extended as an example when the sinner is honored out of reverence for his rank.

He who, elevated to the appearance of holiness, destroys others either by word or by example would certainly have been better off if earthly acts had confined him to death under an exterior appearance, rather than if sacred offices had displayed him to others as an example to imitate in guilt. For if he alone had fallen, the punishment of hell would at least have tormented him more tolerably.

*(Pastoral Rule, Part I, chapter 4.)* Often the burden of governance strikes the heart in different directions, and a person unequal to individual tasks is found incapable of each one, being divided among many matters with a confused mind. Hence a certain wise man rightly forbids this, saying: “My son, do not let your activities be many” (Sir. 11:10), because the mind is not gathered fully into the reasoning of any single task when it is divided among different things.

When it is drawn outward by an intrusive concern, it is emptied of the solidity of inner fear. While the mind is anxious in arranging external matters, it is ignorant of itself alone, and knows how to think about many things without knowing itself. When it entangles itself in external matters more than necessary, it forgets, as though occupied on a journey, where it was heading.

Thus, estranged from the study of self-examination, it does not even consider the losses it suffers, and does not know how greatly it sins.

King Hezekiah did not at all believe that he had sinned when he showed his storehouses of spices to foreigners who came to him (2 Kings 20:13); yet, to the condemnation of his descendants who would follow, he endured the Judge’s anger for what he had considered himself free to do (Isa. 39:4).

Often, when many opportunities are available and subjects can admire the things that can be done because they have been done, the spirit is lifted up in thought and fully provokes the Judge’s anger, even though it does not break out into wicked deeds outwardly. The one who judges is within, and what is judged is within. When, therefore, we sin in the heart, human beings do not know what we are doing within ourselves; nevertheless, with the Judge himself as witness, we sin.

In saying these things, we do not condemn the power of governance; we protect the weakness of the heart against desiring it, lest imperfect people dare to seize the summit of governance and those who stagger while standing on level ground place their foot on a precipice.

A pastor is blind if he is ignorant of the light of heavenly contemplation (Lev. 21:18). Burdened by the darkness of the present life, he does not see the light to come because he does not love it

*(Pastoral Rule, Part I, chapter 11),*

and therefore does not know where to direct the step of his action.

A ruler is lame if he sees where he ought to go but, through weakness of mind, cannot perfectly keep to the way of life that he sees. Since unstable habit is not raised to the state of virtue, his feet do not effectively follow where his desire strives to go.

A person has a small nose if he is not capable of maintaining the measure of discernment. We distinguish smells and stinks by the nose. Thus discernment is rightly expressed through the nose, because through it we choose virtues and reject sins.

There are some who, unwilling to be considered dull, often exercise themselves in certain investigations more than necessary and are deceived through excessive subtlety. Hence it is rightly said: “Or one with a large and crooked nose” (ibid.). A large and crooked nose is an excessively subtle discernment which, when it grows beyond what is proper, itself confounds the rectitude of its action.

A person has a broken foot or hand if he is entirely unable to proceed along the Lord’s way and is wholly deprived of good actions. He does not even retain them with weakness, like a lame person; rather, he is altogether alien to them.

A person is hunchbacked when the weight of earthly concern depresses him so that he never looks toward higher things, but attends only to what is trampled underfoot below. Even if he sometimes hears something about the good of the heavenly homeland, he does not lift the face of his heart toward it, weighed down by the burden of perverse habit. He cannot raise the posture of his thought, because earthly habits of concern keep it bent.

A person is bleary-eyed whose natural intelligence shines toward knowledge of the truth, but whose carnal deeds nevertheless obscure it. In bleary eyes the pupils are healthy, but because fluid continually runs down, the weakened eyelids become thickened.

[Note: [Col. 837D] The edition reads *infirmatae palpebrae* (“the weakened eyelids”). The Benedictine editors and the Maurist congregation note that the manuscripts show remarkable variation at this passage. The reading of our Tatius manuscript is also found in the Carnot and first Audomarus manuscripts, and the following *quorum* indicates that this is the genuine reading.]

Because the pupils are repeatedly irritated by the discharge, their vision too is impaired. There are some whose understanding is wounded by the activity of carnal life. By their intelligence they could see what is right with subtlety, but through the practice of wicked deeds they become dim-sighted.

A bleary-eyed person, therefore, is one whose understanding nature sharpens, but whose depravity of conduct confuses. To him the angel rightly says: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see” (Rev. 3:18). We anoint our eyes with eye-salve so that we may see when we assist the vision of our understanding with the medicine of good works, in order to recognize the brightness of the true light.

A priest has a white film over his eye when he is prevented from seeing the light of truth because he is blinded by arrogance concerning wisdom or righteousness. The black pupil of the eye sees; one suffering from a white film sees nothing. Thus, if the understanding of human thought recognizes itself as foolish and sinful, it apprehends the thought of inner brightness. But if it attributes to itself the whiteness of righteousness or wisdom, it excludes itself from the light of heavenly understanding

*(The edition reads “knowledge,” *cognitionis*,)*

and penetrates the brightness of the true light not at all, to the degree that it exalts itself before itself through arrogance.

As it is said of certain people: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1:22).

A person has continual mange on his body when the wantonness of the flesh ceaselessly dominates his mind.

[Note: [Col. 838D] The edition omits *in mente* (“in the mind”).]

In mange, the heat of the internal organs is drawn toward the skin. Lust is rightly signified by this, because if the temptation of the heart leaps forth into action, the inner heat bursts out as far as the itching of the skin. Mange wounds the body outwardly because, when pleasure is not restrained in thought, it also dominates in action.

Paul was trying to wipe away the itching of the skin, as it were, when he said: “No temptation has overtaken you except a human one” (1 Cor. 10:13). It is as though he were saying openly: It is human to endure temptation in the heart; but it is demonic to be overcome in the struggle with temptation and in action.

Anyone whose mind is ravaged by greed has a skin disease on his body. If it is not restrained in small matters, it expands without measure. A skin disease occupies the body without pain, and, growing without troubling the person whom it has occupied, disfigures the beauty of the limbs. So greed ulcerates the mind it has captured while seeming to delight it. By presenting to thought the things to be acquired, it kindles hostility, yet causes no pain in the wound because it promises abundance to the heated mind through guilt.

The beauty of the limbs is lost through the skin disease because greed corrupts the beauty of other virtues as well; and it irritates the entire body, as it were, because it undermines the mind through every vice, as Paul testifies: “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10).

A person is heavy when he does not practice disgraceful behavior in action but is nevertheless burdened in his mind by continual, unrestrained thoughts of it. He is not dragged all the way to the detestable deed, but his mind takes pleasure in the delight of lust without any impulse of resistance.

There is a disease of heaviness when the moisture of the internal organs descends toward the genitals, which swell with the burden of disgrace. A person is heavy when, flowing toward wantonness with all his thoughts, he carries the weight of disgrace in his heart. Although he does not practice wickedness, he is nevertheless not torn away from it in his mind.

Nor can he rise openly to the practice of good works, because a heavy burden hidden within disgraces him.

[Note: [Col. 838D] The edition reads: “A shameful burden weighs him down in hidden places.”]

Whoever, therefore, is overcome by any one of these vices is forbidden to offer loaves to the Lord, lest the person who is still ravaged by his own sins prove unable to cleanse the sins of others.

*(Morals XI, chapter 15, §23.)* When a priest does not do the good things he speaks, even speech is withdrawn from him, so that he does not dare to speak what he does not practice, as it is said through the prophet: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16).

Hence the Psalmist also prays, saying: “Do not take the word of truth from my mouth forever” (Ps. 118:43). He understood that almighty God gives the word of truth to those who do it and takes it away from those who do not do it. Therefore, when he asked that it not be taken from his mouth, what else did he seek except the grace of good action? It was as though he were saying openly: Do not permit me to stray from good works, lest, when I lose the order of right living, I also lose the rectitude of speaking.

Often a teacher who dares to teach what he neglects to do, once he has ceased to speak the good things he refused to practice, begins to teach his subjects the wicked things he himself does. Thus, by the just judgment of almighty God, he no longer has even a tongue for goodness, since he refused to have a good life. When his mind is inflamed by love of earthly things, he always speaks about earthly things.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matt. 12:34). “The good person brings good things out of the good treasure, and the evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure” (Luke 6:45). John likewise says: “They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world” (1 John 4:5).

## CHAPTER XL. On Bishops Who Gladly Accept Gifts for Ordinations

[Col. 839C]

*(Book I on the Gospels, Homily 4, §4.)* Some bishops are accustomed to turn the gift of the received Spirit toward commercial use and to bend the signs of miracles toward the service of greed.

*(Acts 8:18.)* Hence Simon, desiring to receive the miracles produced through the laying on of hands

[Note: [Col. 839] The edition reads *conspiciens* (“seeing”). Several manuscripts cited here by the Benedictine editors agree with the reading of our Tatius manuscript.]

wanted to obtain the gift of the Holy Spirit with money, evidently so that he might sell more wickedly what he had bought wickedly.

Our Redeemer made a whip of cords and drove the crowds from the temple; he overturned the seats of those selling doves (John 2:15). To sell doves is to confer the laying on of hands, through which the Spirit is received, not for the merit of life but for a reward.

There are some who do not accept monetary rewards for ordination, yet bestow sacred orders for human favor and seek from that generosity nothing but the return of praise. They certainly do not give freely what was received freely, because for the sacred office they have bestowed they seek a coin of approval.

When the prophet Isaiah described the righteous man, he said: “Who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. 33:15). He does not say, “Who shakes his hands free from a gift,” but adds “from every” gift, because one kind of gift comes from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue.

A gift from service is an improperly rendered submission; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore, the person who confers sacred orders shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favor.

*(Morals XII, 54, §62.)* It often happens that someone refuses to accept gold or bodily goods from human beings, but, because he does not accept these things, seeks greater praise from them. Perhaps he does not consider himself to have received a gift because he refuses to accept bodily goods.

As was said above, sometimes a gift is offered by the hand, and sometimes by the mouth. The person who gives a coin gives a gift from the hand; the person who offers a word of praise brings forth a gift from the mouth.

Often a priest refuses to accept external gifts for the laying on of hands, gifts that perhaps correspond to earthly necessity, but he seeks something greater in return for himself when, desiring to be praised beyond his merit, he seeks a gift from the mouth.

## CHAPTER XLI. On Those Who Could Be Useful in Governance but Avoid the Same Office for the Sake of Their Own Quiet

[Col. 840B]

(Reg. Past., part I, ch. 5.) There are some who receive exceptional gifts of virtue and are exalted with great gifts for the training of others: purified by zeal for chastity, strong through the power of abstinence, filled with the nourishment of doctrine, humble through the long endurance of patience, upright through the strength of authority, [kind through the grace of piety, strict through the severity of justice]. If such men, when called, refuse to accept the summit of governance, they often deprive themselves of the very gifts that they received not for themselves alone, but also for others. And when they consider their own gains rather than those of others, they deprive themselves of the very goods that they desire to possess privately.

To the disciples Truth says in the Gospel: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden, nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matt. V, 15). Hence he says to Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John XV, 16–17). When Peter immediately answered that he did love him, he heard: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” If, therefore, the care of feeding is the proof of love, whoever, though endowed with virtues, refuses to feed God’s flock is shown not to love the chief Shepherd.

When we care for our neighbor as we do for ourselves, it is as though we protect both feet with footwear. But whoever, thinking of his own advantage, neglects his neighbors loses, as if with disgrace, the shoe of one foot. There are some who, enriched with great responsibilities, burn with zeal for the pursuits of contemplation alone and, in preaching, refuse to serve the advantage of their neighbors; they love the secrecy of quiet and seek the solitude of contemplation. If they are strictly judged, they are undoubtedly guilty in proportion to the benefit they could have provided by coming into public life. With what reason does one who would have shone for the benefit of his neighbors prefer his own seclusion to the advantage of others, when the Only-Begotten of the supreme Father himself, in order to benefit many, came forth from the Father’s bosom into our public life?

(Reg. Past., part I, ch. 6.) There are some who refuse out of humility alone, lest they be preferred to those whom they consider themselves unequal to. Their humility is truly before God when, being accompanied by the other virtues, it is not obstinate in rejecting what it is usefully commanded to undertake. For one is not truly humble who understands the will of the heavenly command that he ought to preside, yet scorns to preside. Subject to divine arrangements and free from the vice of obstinacy, when the summit of governance is imposed upon him—if he has already been endowed with gifts by which he may benefit others—he ought both to flee from it wholeheartedly and to obey unwillingly.

## CHAPTER XLII. On good subjects placed under pastoral governance

(Reg. Past., part III, ch. 4.) Subjects must be admonished not rashly to judge the life of their superiors if they perhaps see them doing something blameworthy, lest, while rightly reproving evil, they are driven by pride into deeper evils. Subjects must be admonished that, when they consider the faults of their superiors, they should not become bolder against them; rather, even if they judge some of their actions to be very wrong, they should judge them privately in such a way that, constrained nevertheless by fear of God, they do not refuse to bear the yoke of reverence under them.

We can show this more clearly if we bring forward David’s deed. Saul the persecutor had entered a cave to relieve himself, and David was there with his men. David had already endured the evils of Saul’s persecution for a very long time. When his men urged him to strike Saul, he restrained them by his answer, because he ought not to lay a hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Yet he rose secretly and cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak (1 Sam. XXIV, 4).
