What is signified by Saul except wicked rulers, and by David except good subjects? Saul’s relieving his bowels signifies wicked superiors extending the evil conceived in their hearts into deeds of foul odor, and showing by the execution of harmful thoughts what they had conceived within themselves. David feared to strike Saul because pious minds among subjects, abstaining from every plague of slander, do not strike the lives of their superiors with the sword of the tongue, even when they reproach their imperfections.

Good subjects, when through weakness they can scarcely restrain themselves from speaking, though humbly, of certain extreme and external faults of their superiors, cut silently, as it were, the edge of the cloak. For when they detract, at least harmlessly and secretly, from the dignity placed over them, they stain, as it were, the garment of the king set above them. Yet they return to themselves and rebuke themselves most severely, even for the slightest tearing of a word. Hence it is rightly written there: “After this David’s heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak” (ibid., 6).

The deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are rightly judged deserving of reproach. If the tongue at any time slips against them even in the smallest matter, the heart must be weighed down by the affliction of repentance, so that it may return to itself and, having sinned against the authority placed over it, fear the judgment against itself of the one by whom that authority was placed over it. For when we sin against our superiors, we oppose the arrangement of the one who placed them over us. [Ed., *praelata* in place of *praelatus* (“placed over”).] Hence Moses too, when he learned that the people were complaining against him and Aaron, said: “What are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord” (Exod. XVI, 8).

[Reg. Past., part III, ch. 10.] Well-disposed subjects must be admonished to rejoice in the goods of others in such a way that they also desire to possess goods of their own. They should praise the deeds of their neighbors with love, so that they may also multiply them by imitation; otherwise, if in the contest of this present life they stand as devoted supporters but idle spectators of another’s struggle, they will remain without a prize after the contest because they do not labor now in the contest, and then, afflicted, they will look upon the crowns of those whose labors they now continue to observe in idleness.

We sin greatly if we do not love the good deeds of others. But we gain no reward if, insofar as we can, we do not imitate the things we love. Well-disposed subjects must be told that, if they do not hasten to imitate the good things that they approve by praising them, the holiness of virtue pleases them just as the vanity of theatrical arts pleases foolish spectators. Those spectators exalt the deeds of charioteers and actors with their applause, yet do not desire to be like those whom they see to be what they praise. They admire that the performers have done what pleases them, yet avoid pleasing in the same way.

Well-disposed subjects must be told that, when they observe the deeds of their neighbors, they should return to their own hearts and not presume upon the actions of others, lest they praise good things while refusing to do them. For those will be struck with a more severe final punishment who were pleased by what they were unwilling to imitate.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On envious or insolent subjects

[Col. 0842C]

(Reg. Past., part III, ch. 8.) Often subjects placed under pastoral governance, while presumptuously exalting themselves, disdain others with reproaches and consider everything they do to be uniquely great. The deeds of insolent people should therefore be subtly examined by the one who reproves them, so that they may be shown that the very things in which they take pleasure displease God. We correct the insolent more effectively when we show that the things they believe they have done well were badly done, so that useful shame may follow from the very source from which glory was thought to have been gained.

Sometimes subjects, when they recognize that they have not committed the vice of insolence, come more quickly to correction if they are shamed by another more obvious fault, sought out from the side and found in their own [fault]. [Note: [Col. 0841] The edition reads “in their own reproach”; but the Codex Rothomagensis and the Codex Longipontanus read “in their own vice.”] Thus, from what they cannot defend, they may recognize that they wickedly cling to what they are defending.

When Paul saw the Corinthians insolently puffed up against one another, so that one said he belonged to Apollo, another to Paul, another to Cephas, and another to Christ (1 Cor. I, 12; III, 4), he brought forward among them the sin of incest, which had both been committed among them and remained uncorrected, saying: “It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not occur even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst” (1 Cor. V, 1–2). It is as though he plainly said: “Why do you speak insolently of this one or that one, when through the laxity of your negligence you show that you belong to no one?”

[Reg. Past., part III, ch. 10.] Envious subjects must be admonished to consider the blindness of those who fail because of another’s progress and waste away because of another’s exaltation. [Note: [Col. 0843D] The edition reads *exsultatione* (“exultation”); but Gilot and later editors, as does our Taio, read *exaltatione* (“exaltation”).] How miserable are those who become worse through the improvement of their neighbor and, while looking upon the growth of another’s prosperity, suffer anxiety within themselves and die from the plague of their heart. What is more miserable than the envious, whom the happiness they behold afflicts and whom punishment makes worse?

If they loved the good things of others, which they cannot possess, they would have made them their own. [Ed., *facerent* (“would make”) in place of *fecissent* (“would have made”).] The good things of others are truly ours when, even if we cannot imitate them, we love them in others; and whatever we love becomes ours through that love. Let the envious therefore consider how great a virtue charity is: it makes the works of another’s labor ours without labor.

While the envious fail to guard themselves from jealousy, they sink into the ancient wickedness of the crafty enemy. Of him it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. II, 24). Because he himself had lost heaven, he envied the human being whom God had created, and, though already lost, he increased his own condemnation by causing others to be lost.

Let the envious recognize how many stages of growing ruin lie before them, because, while they do not cast jealousy from their hearts, they descend into the open wickedness of their deeds. If Cain had not envied his brother’s accepted sacrifice, he would never have proceeded to destroy his life. Hence it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, but upon Cain and his offerings he did not look. Cain was exceedingly angry, and his face fell” (Gen. IV, 4–5). Thus jealousy of the sacrifice became the seedbed of fratricide. He grieved that the other was better than he, and therefore cut him off so that he might not be so in any respect.

Envious people must be told that, while they consume themselves inwardly with this plague, they also destroy whatever other good they seem to possess. Hence it is written: “A sound heart is the life of the flesh, but envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Prov. XIV, 30). Through the vice of jealousy, even what appears strong to human eyes perishes before the eyes of God. For the bones rotting through envy signify the destruction of even certain strong things (Moral. XXVI, ch. 1, no. 1).

The subject who is truly humble in good things is not a defender of evil things. For when a subject is reproved for his evils and becomes inflamed against the words of the one reproving him, then, when he hesitates as though humbly concerning his good qualities, he desires to adorn himself by the voice of humility, not to be instructed.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On what clerics ought to be like

(Lib. II on the Gospels, homily 17, no. 18.) A cleric must be admonished to live in such a way that he provides secular people with a good example through his life. If anything is rightly reproved in a cleric, the reputation of our religion itself is burdened by his fault.

(Reg. Past., part III, ch. 4.) Clerics must learn to fulfill what their elders command them and to submit humbly to their orders, so that neither submission crushes them nor a higher position exalts them. Clerics must learn how to order their inner lives in humility and obedience before the eyes of the hidden Judge, so that they may not be punished as reprobates but share eternal rewards with the elect.

Clerics must be admonished to live with all the greater vigilance concerning themselves because they are not entangled in the care of others. Clerics must be told not rashly to judge the lives of their superiors if they perhaps see them doing something blameworthy, lest, while rightly reproving evil, they are driven by pride into deeper evils. Clerics must be admonished that, when they consider the faults of their superiors, they should judge their wrongs privately in such a way that, constrained nevertheless by fear of God, they do not refuse to bear the yoke of reverence under them; for the deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are rightly judged deserving of reproach.

(Ibid., chs. 6–7.) For most clerics, only harsh rebuke restrains the vice of shamelessness, because, being unaware that they are doing wrong, they must be rebuked by many. Modest exhortation generally reforms modest clerics for the better, because it is enough for their conversion that the teacher gently recalls their evils to their memory. Modest clerics make greater progress when what is reproved in them is touched obliquely, as it were, by the hand of a flattering tongue.

(Ibid., ch. 8.) We more appropriately bring fainthearted clerics back to the path of good conduct if we look for certain good qualities in them indirectly, so that, while correcting some things in them by reproof, we praise others by embracing them. Thus the praise they hear may nourish their tenderness, while the fault for which they are rebuked chastises them. Often we make better progress with clerics if we also recall their good deeds.

(Reg. Past., part III, ch. 11.) If they have done anything disorderly, we should no longer reprove them as though it had already been committed, but prohibit it as though it must not yet be committed. Many clerics, while fearing to be discovered in their fault, are always seeking wicked defenses and are always tormented by fearful suspicions. Nothing is safer for defense than purity, and nothing is easier to say than the truth. For when someone is forced to protect his deception, his heart is exhausted by harsh labor.

Often clerics caught in fault, while refusing to be recognized for what they are, hide themselves beneath the veil of deception [Ed., *velamine*, “veil,”] and attempt to excuse what they are doing and what is already plainly visible. Often it happens that the one who strives to rebuke the faults of wicked clerics, misled by clouds of scattered falsehood, sees himself almost deprived of what he had already held as certain concerning them.

Through the prophet it is said: “There the hedgehog had its lair” (Isa. XXXIV, 15). By the name “hedgehog” the duplicity of an impure mind that cleverly defends itself is signified. When a hedgehog is caught, its head is seen, its feet are visible, and its whole body is apparent; but as soon as it has been seized, it gathers itself into a sphere, draws its feet inward, hides its head, and within the hands of the person holding it everything that had previously been seen all at once is suddenly lost.

When impure minds are caught in their transgressions, the hedgehog’s head is seen, because the beginning by which the sinner approached his fault is apparent. The hedgehog’s feet are visible, because the tracks by which the wickedness was committed are recognized. Yet when excuses are suddenly produced, the impure mind draws its feet inward, as it were, because it hides all the traces of its iniquity. It withdraws its head because, through marvelous defenses, it does not even show that it began some evil.

The hedgehog remains like a sphere in the hand of the one holding it, because the person who reproves suddenly loses everything he had already understood. He holds the sinner wrapped up within his own conscience, and the one who had seen everything by discovering it is deceived by the wicked evasiveness of the defense and knows nothing at all. [Note: [Col. 0845D] The edition reads *amittens, involutum intra conscientiam* (“losing [him], wrapped within the conscience”).] The hedgehog has its lair among the reprobate, because the duplicity of a malicious mind, gathering itself inward, hides within the darkness of its defense.

Through the prophet Habakkuk it is said: [Note: [Col. 0845D] This passage is sought in vain in Habakkuk; it is found, somewhat altered, in Zephaniah I, 14–16.] “Behold, the day of the Lord comes, great and terrible, against all the fortified cities and against all the lofty corners.” What is signified by fortified cities except suspicious minds, surrounded always by deceptive defenses, which, whenever their fault is reproved, do not admit the darts of truth? What is signified by lofty corners—for a corner always has two walls—except impure hearts? When they flee the simplicity of truth, they fold back upon themselves, as it were, through the perversity of duplicity.

The anger of the final judgment destroys human hearts both when they are closed against the truth by their defenses and when they are entangled in duplicity. Then the fortified cities fall, because minds impenetrable to God will be condemned. Then the lofty corners collapse, because hearts that exalt themselves through the prudence of impurity are cast down by the sentence of justice.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the life or conduct of monks

(Moral., book V, ch. 3, no. 3.) All monks who leave the world do not cease to punish by weeping the offenses they have committed. They afflict themselves with deep sorrow because, having been cast far from the face of the Creator, they are not yet in the joys of their eternal homeland. Concerning their heart Solomon rightly says: “The heart knows the bitterness of its own soul, and no stranger shares in its joy” (Prov. XIV, 10). The hearts of good monks know their own bitterness because they understand the misery of exile by which they, having been cast out, are torn apart; and they feel how peaceful were the things they lost and how miserable the things into which they fell.

(No. 4.) Monks who are in the bitterness of soul desire to die utterly to the world, so that, just as in the world they desire nothing, so now they may no longer be held by the world through any obligation. Often it happens that a monk no longer holds the world in his mind, yet nevertheless binds the monk to itself through certain occupations: he himself is already dead to the world, but the world still lives in him. The world still desires him [Ed., “sees him”], while striving to snatch him, intent upon something else, into its activities.

When the apostle Paul completely despised the world and saw himself become such that the world could no longer desire him at all, he said that, having broken the bonds of this life, he was free: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14). The world had been crucified to him because he did not love it, since it was already dead to his heart. But he had also crucified himself to the world because he strove to present himself to it as one whom, like a dead man, it could not desire.

If a dead and a living person are in one place, the dead person does not see the living, but the living person still sees the dead. If both are dead, neither sees the other. So one who no longer loves the world but is still loved by it, though he himself, as one dead, does not see the world, is nevertheless still seen by the world, which is not yet dead. But if he neither retains the world in his love nor is retained by the love of the world, both are mutually dead to one another; since neither desires the other, the dead does not attend to the dead.

Paul, the vessel of election, because he neither sought the glory of the world nor was himself sought by the world’s glory, declares that both he was crucified to the world and the world to him. Because many monks desire this but do not rise completely to the summit of extinction, they rightly say with groaning: “Why was light given to the miserable, and life to those who are in bitterness of soul?” (Job III, 20). When the glory of this world is given to those who are sorrowful and groaning, they feel themselves afflicted by the punishment of the greatest fear. For even if they themselves do not hold the world, they still fear that they are such as may be held by the world; for unless they lived for it to some small degree, it would certainly not love them for its own use.

The sea retains living bodies within itself, but immediately casts dead bodies out of itself.

(Ibid., ch. 4, no. 6.) Sometimes monks do not reach the desires they have conceived so that, through the delay itself, the opening of their mind may be widened toward those desires; and what, once fulfilled, might perhaps have been diminished is arranged by a great providence to grow more abundantly when refused. Many monks desire to die to the present world in such a way that, if permitted, they might already contemplate fully the face of their Creator. But their desire is delayed so that it may advance, and it is nourished in the bosom of delay so that it may grow.

In the Song of Songs, the bride, longing for the face of her bridegroom, cries out: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, and I did not find him” (Song III, 1). The bridegroom hides himself when he is sought so that, when not found, he may be sought more ardently; and the seeking bride is delayed from finding him so that, made more capable through her delay, she may at last find more abundantly what she sought.

(No. 7.) When spiritual monks fully desire their mortification, the closer they come to the end, the more ardent they show themselves in their work. Therefore they do not grow weary through labor but grow more capable of labor; and the nearer they consider the rewards to be, the more joyfully they sweat in their work.

The apostle Paul, speaking as though to certain monks seeking the hidden treasure of their eternal homeland, says: “Not abandoning our assembly, as is the custom of some, but comforting one another, and so much more as you see the day approaching” (Heb. X, 25). To comfort one who is laboring is to persist together in the labor, because the sight of a fellow laborer is a lifting of the burden of labor.

(Moral. V, 31, no. 55.) Many monks, because they are lulled to sleep from the works of the world not by sluggishness but by virtue, sleep more laboriously than they could have kept watch. For, in overcoming the activities of this age by abandoning them, they fight daily against themselves in a vigorous struggle: lest the mind grow sluggish through negligence; lest, subdued by idleness, it grow cold toward impure desires; lest it burn more than is proper even in good desires; and lest, sparing itself under the appearance of discretion, it grow weak in the pursuit of perfection.

A good monk completely withdraws from the restless desire of this world and abandons the clamor of earthly activities; and through the pursuit of quiet, his mind, intent upon the virtues, sleeps as though awake. No monk is brought to contemplate inward things unless he deliberately withdraws from those things that entangle him outwardly. [Ed., *subtrahatur* (“may be withdrawn”) in place of *subtrahitur* (“is withdrawn”).]

Hence Truth itself says: “No one can serve two masters” (II Tim. II, 4). Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (Matt. VI, 24). Through the prophet the Lord admonishes us, saying: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV, 11). For inward knowledge is by no means perceived unless one ceases from outward entanglement.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On their humility and work

[Col. 0847C]

A monk must be admonished always to observe the reverence appropriate to his habit in his actions, speech, and thoughts, and to abandon completely the things of the world; what he displays to human eyes by his habit, he should present before the eyes of God by his conduct.

(Moral., book V, ch. 11, no. 20.) When the administration of external concerns is absent, pious minds among monks do not seek to become entangled in external matters. Yet even when such concerns are present, they bear them heavily, because they fear leaving themselves through the care of external things. All monks who refuse to be scattered among external concerns remain simple in thought and dwell within the habitation of their conscience.

Hence it is written of Jacob: “Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents” (Gen. XXV, 27). To dwell in tents is to confine oneself within the secrets of the mind and not to scatter oneself outwardly through desires. When prosperity in passing things smiles upon elect monks, they pretend, as though unaware, not to notice the world’s favor; and with a firm step they trample inwardly upon the very thing by which they are raised outwardly.

Elect monks do not resound with the clamor of any wicked action, nor are they swept away by the turbulent desire for temporal ambitions; indeed, they refuse to be occupied immoderately even with the necessary concerns of the present life. [Note: [Col. 0847D] The edition reads “are swept away, but also with concerns”; the reading of our Taio is “are swept away, but indeed they refuse to be occupied with concerns.”]

(No. 21.) Often monks who are doing good still feel the scourges of the Father, so that they may come to the inheritance all the more perfect, the more the discipline that strikes them lovingly purifies them daily even from the smallest faults.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On their lax conduct

(Moral. book XII, ch. 52, no. 59.) There are some who return to themselves after a wasted life and, with conscience accusing them, abandon perverse paths, change their actions, oppose their former wickedness, flee earthly activities, and pursue heavenly desires. But before they become firmly established in these holy desires, through mental sluggishness they return to the things they had begun to judge and run back to the evils they had resolved to flee.

It often happens that, for the benefit of many, even holy men serve in external activities and are occupied in governing peoples. The weak see this and, still seeking to imitate them through their old pride, insert themselves into external activities; but because they come to them without being instructed by spiritual disciplines, they carry them out in a carnal way. Unless the heart first grows strong through long discipline and prolonged conduct in heavenly desires, when it is poured back into external affairs it is uprooted from every state of good work.

(Ch. 53, no. 60.) There are some who, after perverse paths, desire to follow holy ways; but before good desires are strengthened in them, as we have said, some prosperity of the present age seizes them. It entangles them in external matters and, while drawing their minds away from the warmth of inward love, extinguishes them as though through cold. Whatever flower of virtue seemed to appear in them, it kills.

If a weak and lukewarm monk perhaps begins to do something good, before he grows strong in it through the passage of time he slips into external things and perversely abandons what he had seemed to begin rightly. The mind grows very cold in earthly activities if it has not yet been strengthened through inward gifts.

It is very necessary that greater positions or external works, which will benefit human needs, be undertaken there by those who know how to judge them and hold them down beneath themselves through inward strength. When anyone weak is drawn either to a position of governance or to external activities, and is thereby led, as it were, outside himself, he is uprooted. A tree that has not first sent its roots high upward is quickly thrown to the ground by the force of the winds if it raises itself to a lofty summit; [Note: [Col. 0848D] The edition reads *ad altum vertice* (“with its top high”); the present text reads *ad altam verticem* (“to a lofty summit”).] and the higher it has grown in the air without roots, the more quickly it falls to the depths.

Sometimes heat, not cold, dries up a flourishing vine. When it is touched by excessive warmth, its flower is shaken off and the cluster withers. It often happens that those who do not approach good works with a right intention, when they see that they please people, are inflamed more intensely to perform those same works. They anxiously strive to do what will please human eyes and seem to burn with holy zeal.

What, then, happens to these people except that heat strikes them in the flower [Ed., *contigit* in place of *contingit*], since the desire for human praise has made them barren of fruit? In the Song of Songs Solomon says: “Let us rise early and go to the vineyards; let us see whether the vineyard has flowered, whether the flowers are bringing forth fruit” (Song VII, 12). Vineyards flower when the minds of the faithful resolve upon good works. But they do not produce fruit if, overcome by some errors, they weaken in the very thing they had resolved upon.

(No. 61.) We must not therefore look merely to see whether the vineyards are flowering, but whether the flowers grow strong enough to bring forth fruit. It is no great wonder if someone begins good things; but it is very wonderful if he perseveres in good work with a right intention. Hence it often happens that, if a right intention is not maintained in good work [Ed., *non tenetur*, “is not maintained,”], the very work that is considered good is lost.

(No. 60.) When an olive tree is in flower, if it is touched by an excessive mist, it is emptied of the fullness of its fruit. Whenever those beginning good works start to be praised by those who observe them and take pleasure in their praises, a fog of understanding arises in their thoughts, so that they can no longer discern with what intention they do what they do; and they lose the fruit of their work, as though through the mist of favor.

(No. 61.) We have often seen certain monks abandon the earthly possessions they had owned and no longer seek anything transitory, nor involve themselves in quarrels for the sake of this life. When each of them displays this in himself, he has, as it were, produced the flower of an olive tree. But when some of these people begin again to seek the glory of the world that they had despised, to cling insatiably to earthly things that they seemed to have rejected, to devote themselves to quarrels, and to seek opportunities to injure their neighbors, the olive tree has certainly cast off the flower it produced. For it did not bring the beginnings of good zeal to perfected works.

We must know above all that this often happens to monks who do not follow God with pure and simple zeal, as is written in the book of blessed Job: “The congregation of the hypocrite is barren” (Job XV, 34). They would not lose the good things they had begun if they had not been hypocrites. Hypocrites too gather good works, but their gathering is barren, because through what they do they do not desire to receive fruit in eternal recompense. They appear fruitful and green in their works to human eyes, but in the sight of the hidden Judge they appear barren and dry.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On monks who entangle themselves in worldly concerns

(Moral. V, ch. 11, no. 19.) The monk’s mind is not lifted to heavenly things if it is continually occupied below amid the tumult of cares. What can an occupied mind obtain concerning God when even in leisure it struggles to grasp something of him? The Psalmist rightly says: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV, 11), because whoever neglects to be still for God hides from himself, by his own judgment, the light of God’s vision.

Monks who are occupied with temporal matters arrange external things well when they carefully flee inward; when they do not love the noise of disturbances outside, but rest within themselves in the bosom of tranquility.

(No. 20.) The wicked minds of monks do not cease to turn over within themselves the tumult of temporal affairs, even when they are at leisure. For in their thoughts they preserve images of the things they love; and although they do nothing outwardly, they nevertheless labor within themselves under the burden of restless quiet. If the administration of those same things is given to them, they utterly abandon themselves and pursue these fugitive temporal matters through the steps of their thoughts. [Note: [Col. 0849D] The edition reads “they pursue them through the continuous steps of their thoughts in the course of their intention.”]

In the book of Genesis it is written: “Esau became skilled in hunting, a man of the countryside” (Gen. XXV, 27). What is signified by Esau’s hunting except the life of those monks who, spread out among external pleasures, pursue carnal activities? He is also described as a man of the countryside because lovers of this age inhabit external things all the more the more they leave their inner selves uncultivated. [Note: [Col. 0850D] The edition reads “cultivate”; but our Taio reads “inhabit,” as do the manuscripts.]

(No. 21.) Monks must disregard the things that flatter them outwardly, restrain [the things that clamor within], and avoid [the things that entangle them as though necessary]; yet even in all these matters they must still fear the scourges of a strict examination. Often our very perfection is not free from fault unless the severe Judge weighs it mercifully in the subtle balance of his examination.

(Lib. I on the Gospels, homily 17, no. 14.) For the more intent we are upon secular cares, the more insensitive we become inwardly, even as we appear more diligent concerning outward things. Through habitual concern for earthly matters the mind grows hardened away from heavenly desire; and, while it becomes hard through the very practice of worldly action, it cannot be softened toward those things that belong to the love of God.

The holy Church speaks of its weakened members: “They appointed me as a keeper of the vineyards, but I did not keep my own vineyard” (Song I, 5). Our vineyards are our actions, which we cultivate through the practice of daily labor. But, appointed as keepers in the vineyards, we do not guard our own vineyard, because, while we are entangled in foreign thoughts [Ed., “activities”], we neglect the ministry of our own work.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the lukewarmness of monks
(Moral. Book V, chapter 31, no. 55.) Some monks flee the activities of the world, but do not exercise themselves in any virtues. These men, plainly, sleep through sluggishness, not through devotion; and for that reason they do not perceive the things within, because they have placed their head not upon a stone but upon the earth. It often happens to monks that, the more securely they abstain from external activities, the more broadly, through idleness, they heap up within themselves the turmoil of unclean thought. Hence, under the figure of Judaea, the soul languishing in idleness is lamented by the prophet when it is said: “Her enemies saw her, and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. 1:7). By the commandment of the law, one abstains from external work on the Sabbath. Therefore her enemies see and mock her Sabbaths when evil spirits drag the very leisure of withdrawal into illicit thoughts, so that each soul, the more it believes that it is serving God by being removed from external activities, serves their tyranny all the more by thinking illicitly. (Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 34.)

Through the most wise Solomon it is said: “He who is lax and negligent in his work is the brother of one who destroys his own work” (Prov. 18:9). The strong hand of one who works does not raise beginnings of good deeds to perfection if the very slackness of working fights against what has been accomplished. A monk who does not strictly carry out the good things he has begun imitates, through the dissolution of negligence, the hand of one who destroys.

To the Church of Sardis the angel says: “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest, which were about to die; for I have not found your works complete before my God” (Rev. 3:2). Since her works had not been found complete before God, he foretold that even the remaining things that had been done were about to die. If whatever in us is subject to death is not kindled into life, then what is held as though still alive is also extinguished. In this world the human soul is like a ship struggling against the force of a river: it is not permitted to remain in one place, because it slips back to the depths unless it strives toward the heights.

BOOK THREE.

[Col. 0851]

CHAPTER I. On the will and permission of God.

[Col. 0851A]

[Col. 0851B] (Moral. VI, 18, no. 33.) As the just and merciful God orders the deeds of mortals, he favorably grants some things and, in anger, permits others; and what he permits he tolerates in such a way that he turns them to the use of his plan. In a wondrous manner, what is done without God’s will is not contrary to God’s will, because, when evil deeds are turned to good use, even what resists his plan serves his plan. It is written: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. 110:2). His works are great in this way: through everything that human beings do, his will is sought. For often it is accomplished precisely through what seemed to be rejected. Again it is written: “Everything whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 134:6). Hence Solomon says: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21:30 [printed citation: 21:39]). It remains, therefore, that in everything we do we should seek the force of the heavenly will. Once it is known, our action ought devoutly to serve it and follow it as the guide of its journey, lest, even unwillingly, it serve that will if it proudly turns away from it. For the force of the heavenly plan can in no way be avoided; but a person restrains it with great virtue by holding himself in check beneath its commands, and lightens its burdens for himself by willingly carrying them upon the shoulder of a submissive heart.

CHAPTER II. On divine governance.

(Dialogues III, chapter 14.) Great is the governance of almighty God, and it often happens that, to those to whom he grants greater gifts [Ed., “goods”], he does not grant certain lesser ones, so that their mind may always have something by which it may reprove itself [Col. 0851D] [Note: [Col. 0851D] The edition orders and reads the following words differently, as follows: “reprove itself: so that, while they desire to be perfect but cannot, and labor at what they have not received but nevertheless do not prevail by laboring, they may not exalt themselves at all in the things they have received; but may learn that those who cannot overcome small and ultimate vices in themselves do not possess greater goods from themselves.”] . The elect often desire to be perfect, but cannot; they labor at what they have received from the Lord, but nevertheless do not prevail by laboring. Yet they do not exalt themselves at all in the things they possess, and they learn that those who cannot overcome small vices in themselves do not possess greater goods from themselves.

When the Lord had led the people into the promised land, destroying all its strong and exceedingly powerful adversaries, he preserved the Philistines and Canaanites for a longer time, so that, as it is written, “Israel might be tested” by them (Judg. 3:4). Sometimes, as has been said, the Lord leaves even those to whom he grants great gifts with certain small reprehensible faults, so that they may always have something against which to wage war; and, once their great enemies have been defeated, they may not lift up their minds when even their lesser adversaries still weary them. In a wondrous manner it comes about that one and the same mind is strong in virtue and grows weary through weakness, so that it is built up in one respect and sees itself destroyed in another. Thus, through the good it seeks but cannot possess, it may humbly preserve what it does possess.

What wonder, then, that we say this about human beings, when that heavenly realm itself suffered partial losses among its citizens and stood firm in part, so that the elect angelic spirits, seeing others fall through pride, stood all the more firmly the more humbly they stood? Thus it also happens in every soul that, in the guardianship of humility [Ed., “into the guardianship of humility”], it is sometimes preserved for the greatest gains through the smallest loss.

(Moral. IV, 24, no. 44.) Those who already shine with great virtues often still endure something resistant from the darkness of sin, so that they may shine with the great brightness of their life and yet unwillingly drag along the remnants of night. By the great governance of almighty God it is brought about that the mind advancing toward the virtue of justice [Note: [Col. 0852D] Ed., “toward the virtue of its justice”] is strengthened more effectively through weakness, and shines more truly in good things precisely where small reprehensible faults, even against its will, humbly darken it.

When the promised land was being apportioned to the Israelite people, the gentile Canaanite population in the territory of the tribe of Ephraim is said not to have been killed but made tributary, as it is written: “The Canaanite dwelt in the midst of Ephraim as a tributary” (Josh. 16:10). What does the Canaanite—namely, the gentile people—signify except vice? Often we enter the promised land through great virtues, because we are strengthened by an inward hope of eternity. But while we retain certain small vices amid lofty deeds, we allow the Canaanite, as it were, to live in our land. The Canaanite, therefore, is made tributary because we humbly turn to our own advantage the very vice that we cannot subdue, so that the mind may regard itself as vile in the highest matters precisely because, by its own strength, it cannot conquer even the small things it desires.

CHAPTER III. How Holy Scripture expresses the sentence of a curse.

[Col. 0853A]

(Moral. IV, 1, no. 1.) Since we know with certainty that Holy Scripture forbids cursing, why do we say that cursing is sometimes rightly done, when we know that the same sacred utterance commands it to be avoided? We must understand that Holy Scripture mentions cursing in two ways: one kind it approves, the other it condemns. A curse is pronounced in one way by the judgment of justice, and in another by the spite of vengeance.

A curse by the judgment of justice was pronounced when the first human being sinned, upon his hearing: “Cursed is the earth in your works” (Gen. 3:17) [Note: [Col. 0853D] Ed., “to the first human being when he sinned.” But our reading is also found in some manuscripts]. A curse by the judgment of justice is pronounced when it is said to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse you” (Gen. 12:3). Again, because a curse is pronounced not by the judgment of justice [Col. 0853B] but by the spite of vengeance, we are admonished by the voice of the preaching Paul, who says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14). And again: “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10).

Almighty God is said to curse, and yet human beings are forbidden to curse, because what a human being does through the malice of vengeance, God does only through the scrutiny and power of justice. When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, it does not burst forth from a desire for vengeance but from the judgment of justice [Note: [Col. 0853D] Ed., “from the judgment of justice”; the old edition and other editions have our reading]. Within, they perceive the subtle judgment of God, and they recognize that the evils rising outwardly ought to be struck by a curse. They therefore do not sin in cursing, because they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

The apostle Peter hurled a sentence of cursing against Simon, who offered him money, saying: “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts 8:20). For by not saying “is” but “may it be,” he indicated that he had spoken these words not in the indicative but in the optative mood. Finally, Elijah said to the two captains of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire descend from heaven and consume you” (2 Kings 1:10). The outcome of the matter showed with what truthfulness the sentences of both men had prevailed. Simon perished in eternal destruction, and a flame descending from above consumed the two captains of fifty.

The power that follows testifies with what intention a sentence of cursing is pronounced. For when the innocence of the one who curses remains intact, while the curse nevertheless consumes the one who is cursed even unto destruction, it is inferred from the outcome on both sides that the sentence against the guilty person was hurled by one inward judge [Col. 0853D] .

(Num. 3.) If we carefully weigh how the words of each blessed person express a sentence of cursing in Holy Scripture, his curse does not proceed from the malice of one who transgresses but from the righteousness of a judge; it is not the anger of one who is agitated but the instruction of one who is tranquil. For the one who brought forward such a righteous curse did not succumb to the fault of disturbance but provided the teaching of instruction.

CHAPTER IV. On the five ages of the world and of human beings.

(Moral. XI, chapter 46, no. 62.) We must understand very carefully that, just as there are bodily stages of growth, so there are also stages of age in the mind. The first age of a human being is infancy: although the infant lives innocently, it does not know how to express the innocence it possesses. Childhood follows, in which the child is already able to say what it wishes. Adolescence succeeds it, which is the first age suited to activity. Youth follows, suited to strength; and afterward old age, already appropriate, in due course, to maturity.

We recognize adolescence as the first age suited to good deeds. When righteous men advance to great maturity of mind, they sometimes recall the beginning of their actions and reproach themselves for their beginnings in proportion to how far they have advanced through the gravity of mind. For they discover that they were as undiscerning as they later attain the heights of discernment more fully. The morning, then, is the childhood of our understanding.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 19, no. 2.) The third hour can be understood as adolescence, because the sun already rises toward its height, as the warmth of age increases. The sixth hour is youth, because the sun is fixed, as it were, at the center, while the fullness of strength is consolidated in that age. The ninth hour is understood as old age, in which the sun descends, as it were, from its high axis, because that age declines from the warmth of youth [Note: [Col. 0854D] Ed., “in which the sun descends as it were from its high axis, because that age…”]. The eleventh hour is the age called decrepit or very old. Hence the Greeks call those who are very advanced in years not *gerontes* but *presbyteroi*, indicating that those whom they call more advanced are more than merely old.

(Moral. XI, chapter 50, no. 68.) As infancy passes into childhood, childhood into adolescence, adolescence into youth, youth into old age, and old age into death, in the course of the present life a human being is driven toward loss by the very increases of life; and he continually declines precisely where he believes himself to be advancing through the extension of life. We cannot possess a fixed state in this world, since we have come here only to pass away; and this very living of ours is daily a passing away from life. For the mind, under the weight of its mutability, is always driven toward something other than what it is; and unless it is held firmly in its proper state by the discipline of vigilant custody, it continually slips into worse things.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 19, no. 2.) Since it has always abandoned the one who stood firm, it has lost the state it could have possessed. One is led to the good life in childhood, another in adolescence, another in youth, another in old age, and another in decrepitude; thus workers are called to the vineyard at different hours.

[Col. 0854D] (Ibid., no. 1.) From righteous Abel to the last elect person who will be born at the end of the world, Holy Church has produced as many saints as though she had sent forth branches. The master of the household in the Gospel hires workers to cultivate his vineyard in the morning, at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, because from the beginning of this world to its end he does not cease to gather preachers for the instruction of the faithful people [Note: [Col. 0854D] Ed., “did not cease”]. The morning of the world was from Adam until Noah, with the following hour [Note: [Col. 0854D] The edition omits “with the following hour”]. The third hour was from Noah until Abraham. The sixth was from Abraham until Moses. The ninth was from Moses until the Lord’s coming. The eleventh was from the Lord’s coming until the end of the world. At that hour the holy apostles were sent as preachers, and, though they came late, they received the full reward.

Therefore, in order to instruct his people, the Lord never ceased sending workers to cultivate his vineyard. First, through the Fathers; afterward, through teachers of the law and prophets; and finally, through the apostles, he cultivated the conduct of his people and labored with the greatest care, as it were, through workers in the cultivation of the vineyard.

CHAPTER V. On the brevity and misery of the present life.

(Moral. Book XI, chapter 50, nos. 67–68.) What are the nations [Note: [Col. 0855D] Ed., “people born”] in the world except certain flowers in a field? Let us direct the eyes of our heart across the breadth [Note: [Col. 0855D] Ed., “into this breadth”] of the present world, and behold: it is as full of flowers as of human beings. Thus life in the flesh is a flower in hay. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “Man’s days are like hay; like a flower of the field, so he will bloom” (Ps. 102:15). Isaiah also says: “All flesh is hay, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. 40:6).

A human being emerges secretly like a flower and suddenly appears in public; then he is immediately withdrawn from public view through death into secrecy. The freshness of the flesh displays us, but the dryness of dust removes us from sight. We appeared like a flower who did not previously exist; we wither like a flower who appeared for a time. And because at every moment a human being is daily driven toward death, it is rightly said in the book of blessed Job: “He flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job 14:2).

(Moral. XII, chapter 19, no. 24.) Here a human being received the strength to live for a short time, so that he might pass into eternity, where the end would not terminate his life; but in this brief span, in which he has been strengthened, he gathers what he may find in eternity, either so that he may rejoice forever or so that he may not escape the punishments he has incurred.

(Moral. XIII, 27, no. 31.) Everything that passes is brief, even if it seems to come to an end more slowly. We walk on the path of death, from which we do not return—not because we are not restored to the life of the flesh by rising again, but because we do not return again to the labors of this mortal life or to acquiring the rewards of labor [Ed., “to the labors”].

(Ibid., chapter 29, no. 33.) Whoever considers what he will be in death always becomes fearful in his activity; and by the very fact that he already seems, in his own eyes, not to live, he truly lives in the eyes of his Creator. He desires nothing that passes and contradicts all the desires of the present life. He considers himself almost dead, because he does not fail to recognize that he will die.

The perfect life is an imitation of death. While the righteous carefully practice it, they escape the snares of sins. Hence it is written: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Sir. 7:40). However long the time of the present life may be, it is brief precisely because it does not endure. Nor is it fitting that anything enclosed by an end should be judged lasting.

[Col. 0856A] Blessed Job, considering the misery of the human condition, says: “A man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14:1).

(Moral. XI, chapter 49, no. 66.) Behold, in the words of holy men, punishment has been briefly expressed for human beings [Note: [Col. 0855D] Ed., “for the human being”; Taio’s Vindobonensis, Uticensis, Bigotianus, and Lyre edition read as ours], because life is narrowed for them while misery is expanded. If everything done here is carefully considered, it is punishment and misery. To serve the corruption of the flesh even in necessary and permitted things is misery: clothing is sought against the cold, food against hunger, and coolness against heat. The body’s health is guarded with great care, yet often it is lost even after being guarded; when lost, it is restored with great labor; and even once restored, it always remains uncertain. What else is this than the misery of mortal life?

We love friends who can be offended by suspicion [Note: [Col. 0856D] Ed., “friends lest they be offended through suspicion”; but Vindobonensis has our reading]; we fear enemies, and yet we are not secure about those whom we fear. Often we speak to enemies as confidently as to friends; and sometimes we receive the sincere words of our neighbors, and perhaps of those who love us greatly, as though they were the words of enemies. Although we never wish either to be deceived or to deceive, through our caution we make the more serious mistake.

It is a misery of human life that, having been expelled from our heavenly homeland, a human being delights in exile, is burdened by cares, and yet pretends not to consider how grievous it is that many things are being considered; that he has been deprived of inward light, and yet wishes to endure his blindness in this life for a long time. What else is this than a misery born from our punishment? But although he desires to remain here for a long time, the very course of mortal life nevertheless drives him out.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 9, no. 2.) All the good things of the present life are few, however many they may seem; but the faithful servant is set over many things when, having conquered every burden of corruption, he rejoices in eternal joys in that heavenly dwelling. Then the servant is perfectly admitted to the joy of his Lord, when, received into that eternal homeland and joined to the companies of angels, he rejoices inwardly in the gift in such a way that he has nothing outwardly remaining to grieve him because of corruption.

(Moral. XVII, chapter 7, no. 10.) The glory of the wicked, because it is often extended over a great number of years, is judged by weak minds to be long and almost stable. But when a sudden end interrupts it, it proves without doubt that it was brief, since the ending that determines it reveals that what could pass away was slight [Note: [Col. 0856D] Ed., “since the determining end reveals…”].

CHAPTER VI. On youth and old age.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 1, no. 5.) In human youth the body is vigorous, the chest remains strong and sound, the neck is muscular, and the arms are full [Edition, “the bronchi”]; but in old age the empty frame bends, the dried-up neck droops, the chest is oppressed by frequent sighs, strength fails, and breath cuts short the words of the speaker. For if illness is absent, old age itself is often a sickness for the elderly.

In its earlier years the world flourished as though in youth. It was strong for propagating the human race, green with bodily health, and rich with an abundance of possessions. But now it is weighed down by its own old age and, as though approaching death, is pressed by increasing troubles. Do not love the aging world, which you see cannot remain standing for long. Place in your hearts the apostolic commands, by which he admonishes us, saying: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; for if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15).

CHAPTER VII. On married people.

(Moral. XXVI, chapter 26, no. 44.) In the usage of mortal life, some things are harmful in themselves, while others harm us because of what surrounds them. Some things are harmful in themselves, such as sins and crimes; others sometimes harm us through what surrounds them, such as temporal power or marital intercourse. Marriage is good, but the things that grow up around it from the cares of this world are evil. Hence the apostle Paul says: “He who is with a wife considers the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (1 Cor. 7:33).

Persuading some toward better things, the same apostle Paul recalls them from marriage, saying: “I say this for your benefit, not to lay a snare upon you, but for what is honorable and for what makes it possible to serve the Lord without impediment” (ibid., 35). Therefore, while what does not harm is retained, what harms is often committed through things placed beside it. We often travel along a straight and clean road, yet we are caught by our garments on the thorns that grow beside the way. We do not stumble on the clean road itself, but something grows at its side by which we are pierced.

(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 27.) Those who cling to carnal intercourse but, outside the proper purpose of begetting children, are not released into any carnal pleasure are established, as it were, on a mountain. To stand on a mountain is not to seek the fruit of procreation in the flesh. To stand on a mountain is not to cling carnally to the flesh.

There are many who indeed abandon the crimes of the flesh, yet, placed in marriage, preserve only the rights of the proper use. Lot went out of Sodom, but he did not immediately reach the mountains, because a condemnable life has already been abandoned, but the height of marital continence is not yet carefully maintained.

In the midst there is the city of Zoar, which saves the fleeing weak person. For when married couples unite through incontinence, they flee the fall into crimes and yet are saved through pardon. They find, as it were, a small city in which they are defended from the fires, because this married life is not remarkable in virtues but is nevertheless secure from punishments.

Prefiguring the continence of married life, Lot, while fleeing from Sodom, said to the angel: “There is the city of Zoar, to which I can flee; it is small, and I shall be saved in it. Is it not little, and my soul shall live in it?” (Gen. 19:20). It is therefore described as nearby and nevertheless declared safe for salvation, because married life is neither far removed from the world nor alien to the joy of salvation.

Then married couples guard their life in the activity of carnal intercourse as though in the small city of Zoar, when they intercede for themselves with continual prayers. Rightly the angel says to that same Lot: “Behold, I have also accepted your prayers in this matter, so that I will not overthrow the city for which you have spoken” (ibid., 21), because when supplication is poured out before God, such a married life is by no means condemned.

Concerning this prayer Paul admonishes us, saying: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5). When the apostle Paul learned that some were living incontinent lives, he admonished them, saying: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (ibid., 2). Since a wife ought to be taken only for the sake of procreating children, he granted married couples something by which they could still rise toward better things, so that no one might fall into the guilt of fornication.

The same outstanding preacher Paul says of married people: “Such people will have tribulation in the flesh” (1 Cor. 7:28).

(Moral. XII, chapter 22, no. 27.) But even those who live spiritually can suffer tribulation in the flesh. Why, then, is tribulation of the flesh said to belong especially to married people, when it is not far removed even from the life of spiritual persons? It is because those who delight in the pleasures of the flesh frequently receive greater tribulations from the flesh.

We who undertake the care of pastoral office, when we see someone wandering and slippery, ought to admonish him to strive to restrain his iniquity through marriage, so that through what is permitted he may learn to overcome what is not permitted. But when we see a married person, we ought to admonish him to exercise care for the world without postponing the love of God, and to please his spouse without displeasing his Creator.

CHAPTER VIII. On virgins and those who practice continence.

(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 28.) Those who do not know the sins of the flesh must fear precipitous ruin all the more anxiously because they stand at a higher level. Let them therefore know that the more prominently they stand, the more frequently they are assailed by the arrows of the ambusher. He usually rises up all the more fiercely the more strongly he sees himself defeated, and he resents defeat all the more unbearably when he sees the camps of weak flesh arrayed against him in integrity.

Those who preserve chastity should be admonished to look continually toward their rewards and, without doubt, willingly to trample underfoot the labors of the temptations they endure [Ed., “will trample”]. For if the happiness that is attained without passing away is kept in view, what is endured in passing becomes light.

Let those who do not know the sins of the flesh hear what is said through the prophet: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Those who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I will, and hold fast my covenant—I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isa. 56:4–5). Eunuchs are those who, restraining the movements of the flesh, cut off from themselves the inclination toward evil action. It is shown what place they hold with the Father, since in the Father’s house—that is, in the eternal dwelling—they are even preferred to sons.

In the Apocalypse it is said through John: “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4), and they sing a song that no one can sing except those 144,000. To sing the Lamb’s song uniquely is to rejoice with him forever, before all the faithful, even in the incorruption of the flesh. The other elect, however, can hear that song, although they cannot sing it, because through love they rejoice in the exalted state of those others, even though they do not rise to their rewards.

Let those who do not know the sins of the flesh hear what Truth itself says about this integrity: “Not all receive this word” (Matt. 19:11). He made it known to be supreme by denying it to all; and, while declaring that it is difficult to receive, he indicated to his hearers with what care it must be held [Note: [Col. 0859D] Ed., “has been received.” Corb., like ours, agrees with this reading].

Those who do not know the sins of the flesh must be admonished to know that virginity is superior to marriage, yet not to exalt themselves over married people. Thus, while they prefer virginity and place themselves second, they neither abandon what they judge to be better nor fail to guard themselves from the empty exaltation of self.

They must be admonished to consider that the life of those who practice continence is often put to shame by the conduct of worldly people, when the latter undertake works beyond their condition while the former do not rouse their hearts in accordance with their own order. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. 23:4). For Sidon is brought to shame, as it were, by the voice of the sea when, by comparison with the life of worldly people and those who fluctuate in this world, the life of one who appears fortified and almost stable is condemned.

Often some who return to the Lord after sins of the flesh display themselves more ardently in good works because they see themselves as more blameworthy for their evils. Often, however, some who persevere in bodily integrity, when they pay less attention to what they have to mourn, think that the innocence of their life is fully sufficient for them and kindle themselves with no goads of ardor toward spiritual fervor.

It often happens that a life burning with love after sin is more pleasing to God than an innocence growing sluggish through security. Hence it is said by the voice of the Judge: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47), and: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:10).

We gather this more readily from the matter itself if we weigh the judgments of our own mind. We love more the earth that, after being plowed among thorns, produces abundant fruit than the earth that had no thorns but, once cultivated, produces a sterile crop.

Those who do not know the sins of the flesh must be admonished not to prefer themselves to others because of the eminence of their higher order, since they do not know how much better those of lower rank may act. In the judgment of the just Judge, the quality of actions changes the merits of ranks.

Who, considering the very images of things, does not know that in the nature of gems the carbuncle is preferred to the hyacinth? Yet the blue-colored hyacinth is preferred to the pale carbuncle, because the beauty of its appearance adds what the order of nature takes away from it, while the quality of its color disfigures the one whom the natural order had preferred.

So, in the human race, some are worse in a better order, and some are better in a worse order, because the latter surpass the condition of their inferior rank by living well, while the former diminish the merit of their higher place by failing to carry it out in their conduct.

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 4.) A white life of the flesh is like a lily, sweetly fragrant with the incorruption of virginity, like the flower of a lily arising from the fruit of true honor.

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 12, no. 1.) There are many who practice continence, guarding themselves from outward desire and being carried inwardly by hope. They mortify the flesh and, with their whole desire, long for the heavenly homeland; they seek eternal rewards and do not wish to receive human praise for their labors. These plainly do not place their glory in the mouth [Ed., “in the honor”] of human beings but conceal it within their conscience.

The purity of chastity must be preserved through the guardianship of humility. For if the spirit is devoutly pressed beneath God, the flesh is not illicitly lifted above the spirit. The spirit has been entrusted with dominion over the flesh, provided that, beneath the Lord, it recognizes the lawful rights of servitude.

CHAPTER IX. On those recently converted from the world.

(Moral. Book V, chapter 31, no. 55.) There are some who flee the activities of the world but exercise themselves in no virtues. These, plainly, sleep in sluggishness rather than in zeal, and therefore do not behold inward things, because they have laid their head not upon a stone but upon the earth. It often happens to them that, the more securely they abstain from external activities, the more widely they accumulate within themselves, through leisure, the din of unclean thought.

In Deuteronomy it is written: “You shall not plow with the firstborn of an ox, nor shear the firstborn of your sheep” (Deut. XV, 19). (Moral. Book VIII, chapter 47, nos. 78–79.) What else did Moses prohibit by this example of prohibition than that those beginning a good life should not be exercised in worldly occupations? To plow with the firstborn of an ox is to display the beginnings of a good way of life in the practice of public activity. To shear the firstborn of sheep is to strip our nascent good deeds from the covering of their concealment before human eyes. We are forbidden to work with the firstborn of an ox and restrained from shearing the firstborn of sheep, because, even if we begin something vigorous, we ought not immediately to exercise it openly. And when our life begins something simple and innocent, it is fitting that it should not abandon the veils of its secrecy, lest, with its fleece removed, it display itself naked to human eyes.

Let the firstborn of oxen and sheep be used only for divine sacrifices, so that whatever innocent thing we begin, we may sacrifice on the altar of the heart in honor of the inward Judge. Without doubt, that offering is accepted by him all the more willingly insofar as, being hidden from human beings, it is not stained by any desire for praise. [Note: [Col. 0860D] Edition: “so that whatever we begin, however innocent it may be.”]

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 3.) Often the beginnings of a new way of life are still mingled with carnal life, and therefore they ought not to be disclosed too quickly, lest, when the good things that please are praised, the soul, deceived by its own praise, be unable to detect in them the evils that lie hidden. We also understand the firstborn of an ox as the good works of our first period, in the weakness of youth. Yet one must not plow with it, because while the first years of our adolescence or youth are still upon us, we must continue to refrain from preaching, so that the plowshare of our tongue does not dare to cut into the soil of another’s heart.

As long as we are weak, we must contain ourselves within ourselves, lest, by displaying our tender good works too soon, we lose them. For planted shrubs, if they have not first been rooted in the earth, quickly wither when touched by hand; but once they have firmly taken root, a hand touches them and yet does no harm. Winds drive them, yet the driving winds do not injure them. Walls that have been built, if pushed, collapse unless they have first been dried by their own moisture. Each person’s mind, until it has been thoroughly dried of the moisture of its perversity, ought not to be touched by another’s tongue, lest, before it fully takes hold, it lose its firmness and fall when shaken; lest, like a shrub without roots, it wither in the blasts while being disturbed beyond what it can endure.

Only what is firm should be displayed for imitation by others. The mind must first grow strong and afterward be shown for the benefit of one’s neighbors, when it can no longer fall because it has been lifted up by praise, nor waste away because it has been struck by blame. For the Apostle Paul also says to Timothy: “Command and teach these things; let no one despise your youth” (I Tim. IV, 11–12). Yet it must be understood that his youth was in years, not in conduct, although in sacred Scripture youth is sometimes called adolescence. Hence it is written: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccl. XI, 6).

## CHAPTER X. On Fasting or Abstinence

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, 19.) Those who abstain must always watch carefully lest, while fleeing the vice of gluttony, they generate sharper vices from their virtue; lest, while mortifying the flesh, the spirit burst forth into impatience [Edition: “burst forth,” plural]; and lest what the flesh conquers be any virtue at all if the spirit is overcome by anger.

Those who abstain must be admonished always to preserve abstinence in their discipline [Note: [Col. 0861D] Edition: “always, without diminution.”], and never to regard it before the hidden Judge as an exceptional virtue, lest, if it is perhaps believed to be a great merit, the heart be lifted up in pride. Through the prophet Isaiah the Lord says: “Is this the fast that I have chosen? Rather, break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house” (Isa. LVIII, 5). Here we must consider how little the virtue of abstinence is valued in itself, since it is commended only through other virtues.

The prophet Joel, teaching what kind of fasting is acceptable to the Lord, says to the Israelite people: “Sanctify a fast” (Joel II, 15). To sanctify a fast is to display an abstinence from the flesh that is worthy of God by joining it to other good works. Those who abstain must know that they offer an abstinence pleasing to God when they give to the needy what they take away from themselves in food.

We must listen carefully to what the Lord rebukes through the prophet, saying: “When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month during these seventy years, did you fast for me? And when you eat and drink, do you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” (Zech. VII, 5 ff.) [Note: [Col. 0862D] Edition: “you ate, and you drank”; but Laudunensis, Valcellianus, Gemeticensis, and Taio’s witnesses have the reading given here.] A person does not fast for God but for himself if he does not give to the poor what he temporarily takes away from his stomach, but preserves it to be offered later to his stomach.

Abstainers are often accompanied by the fault of impatience, and frequently by that of pride. For unless impatience often shook the minds of those who abstain from the bosom of tranquility, Peter would certainly not have added watchfully, after saying, “Supply virtue in your faith, knowledge in virtue, and abstinence in knowledge” (II Pet. I, 5): “And in abstinence, patience” (ibid., 6). He foresaw that abstainers would lack patience and admonished them so that it might be present in them.

Unless the thoughts of those who abstain were sometimes pierced by the fault of pride, Paul would never have said: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. XIV, 3). Thus, while the flesh is worn down through abstinence more than is necessary, humility is displayed outwardly; but inwardly there is grave pride concerning that very humility. Unless the mind sometimes swelled with the virtue of abstinence, the arrogant Pharisee would never have made a point of counting it among his great merits, saying: “I fast twice a week” (Luke XVIII, 12).

(Book I on the Gospels, homily 12, no. 1.) There are many who afflict the body through abstinence but seek human favor because of that very abstinence. They serve doctrine and give much to the needy; but they are, as it were, foolish virgins, because they seek only the reward of passing praise.

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 8.) Great is the virtue of abstinence; but if someone abstains from food in such a way that he judges others concerning food and even condemns the foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful, what has the virtue of abstinence become for him except a snare of guilt?

When we subdue our bodies through abstinence, what else do we offer to almighty God than fleshly sacrifices, as it is said through Paul: “That you may present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Rom. XII)? The outstanding Psalmist David, indicating that there is no abstinence without harmony, says: “Praise him with the timbrel and choir” (Ps. CL, 4). In the timbrel, dry hide resounds; in the choir, voices sing in harmony. What, then, is signified by the timbrel if not abstinence, and what by the choir if not the harmony of charity? Whoever therefore maintains abstinence while abandoning harmony praises God with the timbrel, but does not praise him with the choir.

## CHAPTER XI. On Voluntary Poverty

(Moral. Book X, chapter 31, no. 52.) Whoever, stirred by the goad of divine love, leaves possessions here will undoubtedly obtain there the summit of judicial power, so that he may then come as a judge with the Judge—he who now chastises himself through voluntary poverty in consideration of the judgment. Those who leave temporal things and attain voluntary poverty have purchased the glory of eternal power.

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 16.) What, then, is more foolish in this world than to abandon one’s possessions? And what is nobler in eternity than to come as judges with God? The holy person does not abandon earthly things so that he may possess them more abundantly in this world, according to what the Truth says: “Everyone who has left all things for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX, 29).

Whoever abandons the earth for earthly ambition does not abandon the earth but desires it. Nor will the person who abandons one wife receive a hundred wives; rather, perfection is signified by the number one hundred, after which eternal life is also promised. Whoever, for God’s name, despises temporal and earthly things receives perfection of mind even here, so that he no longer desires what he despises, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life.

He receives a hundredfold what he gave who, receiving the spirit of perfection, has no need of earthly things even when he does not possess them. The person who lacks what he does not have is poor. But the person who does not possess something and does not desire to possess it is rich. Poverty lies in the neediness of the mind, not in the amount of one’s possessions. For one to whom poverty is entirely agreeable is not poor. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3).

(Moral. XXVI, 27, no. 49.) Sacred Scripture commonly calls the humble “poor,” because, although riches visibly display people as powerful, those who are not proud in their consciences are poor in spirit before themselves.

## CHAPTER XII. On Providing Supports for the Needs of the Body

(Moral. XX, 14, no. 28.) When we generally serve the needs of our nature more than is fitting and neglect the care of the mind, we add the squalor of guilt to the weakness of our misery. The needs of the present age commonly have this very dangerous feature: it is often impossible to distinguish what is done concerning them out of a concern for usefulness and what is done through the vice of pleasure.

Frequently, when an opportunity for indulgence has been found, while we render what is owed to necessity, we serve the vice of pleasure; and our excuse cloaks itself before the eyes of discernment under the veil of weakness [Edition: “For, when an opportunity for seduction has been found”] and hides itself under the protection of a pretext, as though the useful thing had to be fulfilled [Edition: “and, as though under the protection of a pretext, hides the thing to be fulfilled”].

To relax the weakness of our nature through negligence is nothing other than to add misery to calamity and to multiply the squalor of vices from that same misery. Holy men carefully discern in everything they do lest the weakness of their nature demand more from them than is owed to it, lest the vice of pleasure grow within them under the cover of necessity.

The elect endure one thing from weakness and another from the suggestion of temptation. Stationed, as it were, as most upright judges between necessity and pleasure, they support the former through prudent care and relief, and restrain the latter by suppressing it [Note: [Col. 0863D] Edition: “consoling and relieving the former.”]. Thus, even if they endure the calamity of their weakness, they do not descend through negligence into the squalor of misery.

To be in calamity itself means to endure the needs of nature because of the weakness of still-corruptible flesh. The Psalmist wished to escape the needs of this present life when he said: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. XXIV, 17). He knew that the faults of pleasure frequently burst forth from the occasion of necessities; and, lest he willingly admit anything unlawful, he sought to have uprooted the very thing he unwillingly endured from its root.

(No. 29.) The wicked, therefore, rejoice in these necessities of their corruption, because they turn necessity back toward the use of pleasure. When they serve nature by restoring their bodies with food, they descend through the delight of gluttony into an excess of pleasure [Edition: “they are distended in an excess of pleasure”].

Many, when they seek clothing to cover their limbs, desire not merely garments that cover but also those that exalt them; and, against the torpor of cold, not merely those that protect through their thickness but also those that delight through their softness—not merely those that soothe through softness alone but also those that seduce the eyes through color.

Desiring to be freed from such necessities, the Psalmist says: “Deliver me from my necessities.” For to turn the cause of necessity into the use of pleasure—what else is it than to join the squalor of one’s calamity to the misery of one’s wretchedness? [Edition: “to join squalor to calamity”; Gemeticensis and other Norman witnesses, together with one Laudunensis witness, read as our text does.]

(Moral. IV, 34, no. 68.) Often we fill the body with nourishment lest it fail from being weakened. We weaken it through abstinence lest, when filled, it oppress us. We keep it vigorous through movement lest it perish through the stagnation of immobility; but we quickly bring it to rest by settling it, lest it succumb through that very vigor. We cover it with the aid of clothing lest cold destroy it; and we cast away the aids we have sought lest heat consume it.

Encountering so many different circumstances, what are we doing except serving our corruptibility, so that at least the multiplicity of our attentive service may sustain the body burdened by the anxiety of frail mutability?

## CHAPTER XIII. On Holy Men Who Cherish a Quiet Life

(Moral. IV, 30, nos. 58–60.) Holy men, because they desire nothing of this world, are undoubtedly oppressed by no tumults of heart. With the hand of holy reflection they drive every disordered movement of desire from the chamber of the heart; and because they despise all transitory things, they do not suffer the insolence of thoughts arising from them.
