They desire only the eternal homeland, and because they love nothing of this world, they enjoy great tranquility of mind. Great is the mind’s repose: to drive the tumult of earthly desires from the heart’s secret place and, with one intention, to yearn for the love of inward quiet and the eternal homeland.

The prophet David had sought, amid the tumult of temporal affairs, a great retreat—a quiet mind in which he might see God more purely, insofar as he found him alone while he himself was alone. Hence he rightly says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord” (Ps. XXVI, 4).

Let us therefore examine somewhat more closely this consul whom we have just mentioned, and consider how he scatters the tokens of virtue before the ranks of subject peoples, providing examples of a more exalted life. Behold, to commend the repayment of good for evil, he confesses concerning himself, saying: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. VII, 5).

To stir love for the Creator, he says: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28). To impress upon us the pattern of holy humility, he reveals the secrets of his heart, saying: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Ps. CXXX, 1).

To rouse us by his example to imitate the uprightness of zeal, he says: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and do I not waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 22).

To kindle in us desire for the eternal homeland, he laments the length of the present life, saying: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX, 8) [Note: [Col. 0865D] Edition: “Alas for me”; Vindocensis, Compendiensis, Saint-Albini, and others read as our text does.]

He who shone forth, plainly consoled by generosity [Note: [Col. 0865D] Edition: “by the consulship”; but older editions, together with the ancient Remensis and German witnesses, have our reading], scatters before us so many tokens of virtue by the example of his own way of life.

The outstanding prophet David says: “Behold, I have gone far away, fleeing, and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV, 8). He goes far away by fleeing because he lifts himself from the crowd of temporal desires into the heights of the contemplation of God. He remains in solitude because he perseveres in the mind’s withdrawn intention.

Concerning this solitude the prophet Jeremiah says to the Lord: “I sat alone because of your hand, for you filled me with threats” (Jer. XV, 17).

(Moral. IV, 34, no. 68.) Although no tumult of carnal desires possesses just men, the burden of their corruption nevertheless binds them, placed as they are in this life, with harsh bonds of distress. For it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15).

The elect are weighed down by the burden of their corruption precisely because they are still mortal, and they are bound by the burden of distress because they have not yet risen into the freedom of incorruptible life. Holy men endure one thing in the mind and another in the body, and every day they labor in inward struggle against themselves.

Are not those bound by a harsh bond of distress whose mind, without effort, slips into ignorance and is instructed only through laborious exertion? It is forced upright, lies down willingly, is scarcely lifted from lowly things, and yet, once lifted, immediately slips. By laboriously conquering itself, it gazes upon heavenly things; but, struck back, it flees the light that had illumined it.

The just are bound by a harsh bond of distress when the spirit’s ascent draws them with full desire into the bosom of inward peace; but the flesh disturbs them through frequent struggle. Although it no longer confronts them as an opposing battle line before their face, it still mutters behind the mind’s back, as though held captive; and although fearful, it nevertheless stains the appearance of beautiful quiet with shameful noise in the heart.

Although all the elect bravely overcome everything, when they desire the security of inward peace they are nevertheless afflicted by grave distress [Note: [Col. 0865D] Edition: “it is a grave distress for them still to have”] because they still have something to conquer [Note: [Col. 0866D] Our codex has “they hinder,” in place of which we have printed “they are afflicted,” since the former is plainly erroneous and the latter is closer to Taio’s period style].

Apart from these struggles, they also endure the bonds imposed externally by grave necessity. Hunger, thirst, and weariness are bonds of corruption. These cannot be loosed until our mortality is exchanged for the glory of immortality [Note: [Col. 0866D] Edition: “until our mortality is exchanged into that glory of immortality”].

The outstanding preacher, the Apostle Paul, says: “For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly but because of him who subjected it, in hope; because creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII, 20).

Creation is subjected unwillingly to vanity because the human being, who willingly abandoned the state of innate steadfastness, serves unwillingly the corruptions of mutability, oppressed by the weight of just mortality. But creation is then rescued from the slavery of corruption when, rising incorruptible, it is lifted into the glory of the children of God.

The elect are bound by distress because they are still weighed down by the punishment of corruption. But when we are stripped of corruptible flesh, we are loosened, as it were, from the bonds of distress by which we are now held. We already desire to be presented to God, but we are still hindered by the constraint of the mortal body.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Holy Men Devoted to the Active and Contemplative Life

The more just men desire to cling to heavenly things through the ray of contemplation, the more they refuse to establish themselves on earth, where they know themselves to be pilgrims and strangers, as Paul testifies when he says: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). And again: “But you are being built into a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V, 1).

When holy men desire to rejoice in what is their own, they refuse to be happy in what is another’s. But the farther the unjust are separated from the inheritance of the eternal homeland, the more deeply they lay the foundations of their thoughts in the earth.

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 5.) The people of the elect rise to contemplation through some, while through others they flourish only in the works of the active life. Hence Isaac rightly says: “May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth” (Gen. XXVII, 28).

Dew falls subtly from above; and we receive dew from heaven whenever, through the infusion of inward contemplation, we see something of heavenly things dimly. But when we perform good works through the body as well, we are enriched by the fatness of the earth.

(Moral. Book V, chapter 31, no. 54.) The patriarch Jacob, sleeping on a journey, saw a ladder extending from earth to heaven, angels ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder (Gen. XXVIII, 11).

To sleep on a journey is, during the passage of this present life, to rest from love of temporal things and, amid the course of passing days, to close the eyes of the mind to the desire for visible things. To see angels ascending and descending is to contemplate the citizens of the heavenly homeland: either how greatly they cling to their Creator above themselves in love, or with how great compassion of charity they stoop to our weaknesses.

(No. 55.) It must be carefully noted that the one who places his head upon a stone is the one who sees angels while sleeping. For the person who withdraws from external works and penetrates inwardly is the one who, with an attentive mind—the mind being the human being’s ruling part—keeps before him the example of his Redeemer. To place one’s head upon a stone is to cling to Christ in the mind.

Those who are removed from the activity of the present life but are drawn toward heavenly things by no love may sleep, but they cannot see angels, because they disdain to keep their head upon the stone.

(Moral. Book V, chapter 6, no. 9.) Holy men do not cease to mortify themselves with the sword of the sacred word, freeing themselves from the importunity of temporal desires, the tumult of useless cares, and the clamor of disturbing upheavals; and inwardly they hide themselves before the face of God in the heart’s bosom.

Hence it is rightly said through the Psalmist: “You will hide them in the secret place of your face from the disturbance of men” (Ps. XXX, 21) [Note: [Col. 0867D] Edition: “in the hidden place of your face, from the tumult.”]

Although this is accomplished perfectly only afterward, it is even now carried out in large part, when they are drawn inward with delight from the tumults of temporal desires, so that, while their mind is wholly stretched toward the love of God, no useless disturbance tears it apart.

The Apostle Paul saw disciples dead through contemplation of the mind and hidden, as it were, in a tomb; to them he said: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3–4). Whoever desires to mortify himself rejoices greatly in the rest found through contemplation, so that, dead to the world, he may lie hidden and conceal himself from all disturbances of external things within the bosom of inward love.

(Moral. Book XXIII, chapter 21, no. 41.) The holy David, contemplating the eternal homeland, weighing the evils in which he was and considering the good things in which he was not yet, said: “I said in my fear: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” (Ps. XXX, 23).

Lifted up in ecstasy—something our translators did not properly call “fear” [Note: [Col. 0867D] Edition: “properly called ‘fear.’ But other printed editions follow our reading”]—he saw that he had been cast away from the sight of God’s eyes. For every elect person returns to himself after the vision of the inward light, which has shone forth in his soul through the grace of contemplation as a ray of splendor; and, having gained knowledge, he discovers either what good things he lacks there or what evils are present here.

(Nos. 42–43.) This compunction commonly affects the perfect soul more intimately, because it shakes off all bodily imaginings that insolently confront it [Edition: “because it examines all bodily imaginings”; Vindocensis and Norman witnesses read as our text does] and directs the eye of the heart to fix itself upon the ray of unbounded light.

It drew these forms of bodily images inward to itself from the weakness of the body; but, once perfectly pierced with compunction, it watches most carefully [Edition: “here it watches most carefully”] lest, while it seeks the truth, imagination deceive it with a circumscribed vision.

Sometimes the mind of the just person is admitted to an unusual sweetness of inward savor and, suddenly breathed upon in some way by an ardent spirit, is renewed. It loves all the more as it tastes more deeply that which it loves [Edition: “it yearns all the more”]. It desires within itself what it has sensed to taste sweet inwardly, because, through love of that sweetness, the heart became contemptible to itself before itself; and, after it was able to perceive this sweetness in some fashion, it discovered what it had previously been without it.

Every holy person already strives to cling to unbounded truth, but is still driven back from its strength by his own weakness. Because he cannot be brought into harmony with its purity [Edition: “cannot despise its purity”], he finds sweetness in weeping and spreads before himself, as he falls back upon himself, the tears of his weakness.

For he cannot fix the eye of the mind upon what he had suddenly glimpsed within himself, because the habit of his former state compels him to descend. Amid these things he pants, burns, and strives to rise above himself; but, overcome by exhaustion, he slips back into his familiar darkness.

The Psalmist rightly says: “I said in my fear: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” (Ps. XXX, 23).

(Moral. XVIII, 41, no. 66.) Having contemplated the inward joys of the vision of God and the fellowship of the angels who remain, he brought his eyes back to lowly things. He saw where he lay, because he had been created for this purpose: that he might have been able to stand in heavenly places. He considered where he was [Edition: “what he lacked”; Paterius supports our reading] and what he was, and he groaned. He grieved that he had been cast away from the sight of God’s eyes, because, by comparison with the inward light, he felt more heavily the darkness of his exile that he endured below.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Elect Living Well amid the Tumults of the Reprobate

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 22.) Many of us complain about why not all those who live with us are good. We do not wish to bear the evils of our neighbors; we decide that everyone ought already to be holy, while we do not wish to be what we must bear from our neighbors. But in this matter it is clearer than daylight how much we ourselves still lack of goodness. For no one is perfectly good unless he is good even among the wicked.

Blessed Job asserts this concerning himself, saying: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches” (Job XXX, 29). Hence the Apostle Paul says to his disciples: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. II, 15).

Hence Peter, shepherd of the Lord’s flock, says: “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the conduct of the wicked.” For he was righteous in sight and hearing while living among those who day after day tortured the righteous man’s soul with wicked deeds (II Pet. II, 7).

When we often complain about the lives of our neighbors, we want to change our place and strive to choose a more secluded way of life [Note: [Col. 0868D] The edition omits “we want”], not realizing that if the spirit is absent, place does not help. Lot was holy in Sodom but sinned on the mountain (Gen. XIX, 2 ff.).

Since places do not fortify the mind, the first parent of the human race himself bears witness to this: he fell gravely even in paradise (Gen. III, 7). But all the things we say are still matters of earth. For if place could save, Satan would not have fallen from heaven.

The Psalmist David, seeing that temptations exist everywhere in this world, sought a place to which he might flee, but could not find a fortified place without God. Therefore he asked that God himself become his place, for whose sake he had sought a place, saying: “Be for me a God who protects and a fortified place, so that he may save me” [Edition: “so that you may save me”] (Ps. XXX, 3).

In the Song of Songs it is written: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song II, 2). It is as though he plainly said: Those are truly good who can persist in goodness even among the wicked.

(Moral. I, chapter 1, no. 1.) It is not especially praiseworthy to be good among the good, but to be good among the wicked. Just as it is a more serious fault not to be good among the good, so it is a matter of immense praise to have been good even among the wicked.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Afflictions of the Elect

(Moral. XXVII, chapter 37, no. 61.) For one who lives well, the strict rule is not a broad road but a narrow path, on which each of the elect is carefully confined, because he is anxiously restricted under the guardianship of the commandments.

It is, as it were, a narrowness of the journey to live in this world but possess nothing of this world’s desire; not to covet what belongs to others; not to retain what belongs to oneself; to despise the praises of the world; to love reproaches for God’s sake; to flee glory and seek contempt [Note: [Col. 0869D] Edition: “to follow contempt”]; to despise flatterers and honor those who despise; to dismiss the evils of those who harm us from the heart; and to retain an unwavering grace of love toward them in the heart.

All these are paths, but great ones, because the narrower they are in the present life for the preservation of right living, the more widely they open out in eternal reward.

(Moral. XXVI, chapter 13, no. 21.) The wickedness of the reprobate, in the manner of threshing, presses and purifies the life of the elect, separating the grain from the chaff [Edition: “presses it in order to purify it”; the Ebroicensis and other witnesses read as our text does]. The wicked, while afflicting the good, free them more from the desires of this world; for, by inflicting many violent things upon them here, they compel them to hasten toward heavenly things.

This was well signified in the Israelite people when Moses called and King Pharaoh raged (Exod. III, 7). Moses was sent to call that people precisely when Pharaoh had already been aroused to oppress them with harsh works, so that one, by calling, might draw along the minds of the Israelites shamefully attached to Egypt, while the other, by raging, might drive them forward; and the people, fixed shamefully in servitude, might be moved either by the attraction of good things or by the pressure of evil.

[The same.] This happens daily in the present age [Edition: “This happens daily”], when the reprobate are permitted to rage against the elect while heavenly rewards are preached: so that, if we neglect to depart when called to the promised land, we may at least be driven out by raging afflictions.

Thus this Egypt—that is, the present life—which oppressed us while flattering us, may help us by pressing upon us; and, while it cherishes us, crushes us under the yoke of servitude; while it torments us, it displays the way of freedom [Note: [Col. 0870D] Edition: “which cherished us and crushed us under the yoke of servitude”].

Nor is it without cause that the just are allowed to be afflicted by the unjust [Note: [Col. 0870D] Edition: “so that it may show”; this is certainly the reason. Many Norman witnesses read “so that it may show. This, therefore, is the reason”]: namely, so that, while they hear of future good things that they desire, they may also suffer present evils that they dread; and, while love calls them toward an easier departure, torment may drive them onward.

(Moral. XXVI, chapter 16, no. 26.) The Psalmist David says: “You are my refuge from the affliction that surrounds me; my joy, redeem me from those who surround me” (Ps. XXXI, 7). Behold, he names affliction as though it were night [Edition: “Behold, he names night”; Vindocensis: “Behold, from the night”], and yet calls his deliverer his joy amid afflictions. Outside there was night in the surrounding affliction, but within, songs resounded from the consolation of joy.

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 32.) Each of the elect, while declaring that he is surrounded by afflictions and nevertheless naming God as his joy, undoubtedly sings, as it were, a song in the night, so that he may arrive happily at the day of the life to come.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Miracles of the Elect
*(Book II on the Gospel, Homily 29, no. 4.)* The holy Church performs spiritual miracles every day, just as in former times it performed bodily miracles through the holy apostles. Thus it is written: “These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well” (Mark 16:17).

When the priests of the Church, through the grace of exorcism, lay a hand upon believers and deny that evil spirits dwell in their minds, what else do they do but cast out demons? Whenever the faithful abandon the worldly words of their former life and sound forth the holy mysteries, the praises of their Creator, and, as far as they can, proclaim his power, what else do they do but speak in new tongues? Thus, when the elect remove wickedness from the hearts of others through their good exhortations, they pick up serpents. Whenever many of the faithful hear poisonous suggestions but are nevertheless not drawn into wicked action, what they drink is deadly, but it does not harm them. Whenever the faithful of the holy Church see their neighbors weakened in good works and strengthen their lives by the example of their own conduct—those neighbors whose conduct had been faltering—what else do they do but lay hands upon the sick, so that they may be well?

[Note: The edition reads, “who falter in their own conduct.”]

The miracles, therefore, that the elect perform are greater in proportion as they are spiritual, and more wondrous in proportion as through them not bodies but souls are raised up. By God’s authority we frequently see signs occurring in the Church; yet the person who performs them cannot attain holy life from those outward signs.

[Note: The text reads *operanti* (“by the person performing these things”); the edition reads *operantibus* (“by those performing them”).]

For bodily miracles sometimes reveal holiness, but do not produce it; spiritual miracles, which take place in the mind, do not reveal the virtue of life but produce it. The wicked too may possess the former, but no one except the good can enjoy the latter.

The outward miracles performed through the apostles were necessary at the beginning of the Church. For, in order that faith might grow, it had to be nourished by miracles: just as when we plant saplings, we pour water upon them until we see that they have already become strong in the soil.

[Note: The edition reads, “For faith to grow.” The Mechlin edition reads, “As our manuscripts read.”]

But once they have put down roots, irrigation ceases.

[Note: The edition reads, “We cease watering.” The Vulgate readings support our text.]

This is why Paul says: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14:22).

*(Moral Commentary, Book XXXI, chapter 1, no. 1.)* When unbelievers saw new virtues in the apostles, they later marveled at the miracles of those whose lives they had previously despised. When the unbelievers saw the apostles’ miracles, they immediately returned fearfully to their own hearts and came to dread in the miracles the holiness they had despised in the apostles’ instructions. Thus the strong were confounded by the weak, because when the life of the humble rose in honor, the arrogance of the proud fell.

[Note: The edition reads, “into honor” (*in venerationem*).]

*(Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 5, no. 16.)* In everything the elect do, they always return to the praise of the Creator, so that they may remain firmly established in the virtue they have received. For if they attributed anything to themselves, they could not stand in what they had received.

A certain wise man rightly says: “The rivers return to the place from which they flow, so that they may flow again” (Ecclesiastes 1:7). For whether in virtues or in teaching, what are holy men except rivers that water the dry soil of carnal hearts? Yet whether in the work they perform or in the words of their teaching, they would quickly dry up unless, through the intention of their hearts, they always carefully returned to the place from which they flow.

Many of the elect who shine with miracles, if they do not return inwardly to their hearts and bind themselves by the bonds of desire to the love of their Creator, find that their hand grows weak in what it was doing and their tongue dries up in what it was saying. The elect always return to the inmost recesses of their hearts through love of their Creator; and what they pour forth publicly in their actions and speech, they draw privately from the fountain of love. For by loving they learn what they express in teaching.

Thus they return like rivers to the place from which they flow, so that they may flow again, because they continually draw the water of wisdom from its source, lest, after it has run its course, it should dry up.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the miracles of the reprobate

[Col. 0871D]

*(Book II on the Gospel, Homily 29, no. 4.)* Outward signs, or miracles, can be performed not only by the elect but also by the reprobate. Hence the Truth says to some: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity’” (Matthew 7:22–23).

*(Moral Commentary, Book XVII, chapter 5, no. 7.)* Every perverse person, even if he appears to hold the right faith within the bosom of the universal Church and to shine with miracles, indeed understands rightly through faith what concerns the Creator; yet because he refuses to preserve the works of faith, he is rightly convicted of unbelief, since by his manner of life he is condemned by the very thing he professes to believe.

*(Moral Commentary, Book VIII, chapter 42, no. 66.)* Heretics often perform wondrous works of signs, drive spirits from possessed bodies, and, through the gift of prophecy, anticipate future events by knowing them beforehand. Yet they are separated from the giver of so many gifts by the intention of their knowledge, because through his gifts they seek not his glory but their own favor. When the reprobate exalt themselves in their own praise through the good things they have received, they fight against the giver with the very gifts themselves. For they grow proud against the one who gives precisely in those matters by which they ought to have been more humble before him. But afterward a stricter judgment strikes them, because now the heavenly goodness pours itself more generously even upon the ungrateful.

Often the abundance of a gift becomes for the reprobate an increase of condemnation, because, though watered, they produced no fruit; rather, under the appearance of greenness, they grow empty toward the heights.

[Note: The edition reads, “They do not bear fruit.”]

*(Moral Commentary, Book XX, chapter 7, no. 17.)* Sometimes heretics perform signs and miracles so that here they may receive the rewards of their affliction and abstinence—that is, so that they may seek human praise.

[Note: The edition reads, “the praises that they seek.”]

But because they are rejected by the Lord’s voice, which says, “Depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7:23), this sentence clearly teaches that what ought to be honored in human beings is the humility of charity, not signs of virtues. Even if miracles are performed by heretics, the holy Church despises them, because she recognizes that they are not evidence of holiness.

[Note: The edition reads, “a specimen.” The reading “appearance” is found in the German, Bec, Utrecht, Corbie German, and many other manuscripts.]

The proof of holiness is not to perform signs, but for each person to love another as himself, and to think truly about God and better things about his neighbor than about himself.

*(Book II on the Gospel, Homily 29, no. 4.)* Signs or miracles are not to be loved when they can be shared with the reprobate. Rather, the miracles of charity and piety are to be loved—miracles that are safer in proportion as they are hidden, and for which there is a greater reward with God in proportion as there is less glory among human beings.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the divine charisms

*(Moral Commentary, Book XXVIII, chapter 10, nos. 21–22.)* Almighty God, by the secret governance of his inward judgment, grants to one the word of wisdom, to another full faith, to another the grace of healings, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of speech (1 Corinthians 12:8–10). Thus, in the one and same Spirit, one person may be powerful in the word of wisdom and yet not be supported by the word of knowledge—that is, by teaching—because it is enough for him to perceive and discover even what he has not grasped through diligent study.

Another, having been preceded by the gift of grace, shines in the word of knowledge but does not grow strong in the word of wisdom, because he is capable of carrying out as much as he has learned, yet does not rise by himself to perceive something subtle. One of the elect, through faith, commands the elements, but does not heal bodily illnesses through the grace of healings. Another removes diseases through the power of prayer, yet cannot bring rain to parched earth by his word.

Often a holy man recalls even the dead to the present life through the working of miracles, yet, lacking the grace of prophecy, remains ignorant of what is to come. Another regards future events as though they were present, yet does not display himself in any working of signs. Sometimes an elect person, through discernment of spirits, subtly perceives minds in their actions, yet does not know languages of different kinds. Another examines languages of different kinds, yet does not discern unlike hearts in similar matters. Still another prudently weighs and interprets the force of speech in the one language he knows, yet patiently lacks the other good gifts he has not received.

Our Creator and governor so orders all things that the person who might have become proud because of the gift he possesses is humbled by the virtue he lacks. Thus, when he raises each person up through an abundant grace, he also subjects one person to another through a differing gift, so that each may regard as superior in another gift the person who is subject to him. Although he may feel that he surpasses another in certain respects, he nevertheless considers himself inferior to that same person in other respects.

[Note: The edition reads, “and in other respects.” The Vindobonensis agrees with our text.]

Almighty God so orders all things that, while each gift belongs to all through a certain bond of charity, all become the possession of each individual. Each person possesses in another what he himself has not received, while humbly offering to the other for possession what he has received.

*(Moral Commentary, Book XI, chapter 16, no. 25.)* Some gifts strengthen us; others adorn us. Prophecy, teaching, kinds of tongues, and the power of healing are like certain walls of the mind. Even if someone does not possess them, he can stand fortified through faith and justice.

*(Moral Commentary, Book XXVIII, chapter 10, no. 23.)* The holy Church is the body of its heavenly Head. In it one person is an eye, seeing lofty things; another is a hand, acting rightly; another is a foot, running to assigned tasks; another is an ear, understanding the voice of commandments; another is a nose, discerning the stench of evil and the fragrance of good.

For just as the bodily members, by mutually supplying one another with the functions they have received, make one body out of themselves, so, while they perform different tasks in charity, they prevent the place in which they are contained from becoming divided. If everyone performed one and the same task, they would not be a body composed of many members, because something joined and gathered together in many ways could not exist if the harmonious diversity of the members did not hold it together.

[Note: The editions omit “gathered together.”]

When the Lord distributes the gifts of virtues among the holy members of the Church, he sets out measures as though for the earth, just as the apostle Paul says: “To each one according to the measure of faith that God has assigned” (Romans 12:5). And again: “From him the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, makes the body grow for its building up in charity” (Ephesians 4:16).

[Col. 0874A] By a wondrous plan our Creator and governor grants to one what he denies to another, and denies to one what he grants to another. Therefore, whoever tries to exceed the measures assigned to him, attempting to do more than he has received, is striving to go beyond his limits.

If one of the faithful has perhaps been given only the ability to explain the hidden meanings of the commandments but attempts also to shine with miracles, or if one whom the gift of heavenly power strengthens for miracles alone also strives to disclose the hidden meanings of divine law, he is stretching out his foot toward a precipice because he does not observe the limits of his measures. Often he loses what he was capable of doing because, boldly and hastily, he seizes what he cannot attain.

We use the ministries of our members properly when we preserve their distinct functions. We see light with our eyes, but hear a voice with our ears. If someone, changing the proper order, were to apply his eyes to a voice and his ears to light, both would be open to him in vain. If someone wished to distinguish odors with his mouth or taste flavors with his nose, he would destroy the service of both senses by perverting them. For when these organs are not adapted to their proper uses, they abandon their own functions without rising to those of others.

The distinguished preacher says: “You are the body of Christ, and members of a member” (1 Corinthians 12:27).

*(Moral Commentary, Book XXXIV, chapter 4, no. 8.)* One thing is a member of the body, another is a member of a member. A member of the body is a part in relation to the whole; a member of a member is a small part in relation to a part. A finger is a member of a member in relation to the hand, and the hand in relation to the arm; but all these together, in relation to the whole body, are a member of the body. Likewise, in the spiritual body of the Lord, we call those “members of a member” who in his Church are governed by others.

## CHAPTER XX. On the four virtues, namely prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice

*(Moral Commentary, Book II, chapter 49, no. 76.)* The solid structure of our mind is supported by prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice, because the entire framework of good works rises upon these four virtues. Hence the four rivers of paradise water the earth, because, when the heart is infused with these four virtues, it is restrained from the heat of all carnal desires.

[Sometimes, when…]

Sometimes indolence steals upon the mind and prudence grows cold, for when the mind is weary and sluggish, it does not foresee what is to come. Sometimes a certain pleasure steals upon the mind and our temperance withers; for in proportion as we are drawn toward present pleasures, we restrain ourselves less from unlawful things. At times fear insinuates itself into the heart and disturbs the strength of our fortitude; and we are weaker against adversity in proportion as we fear more excessively to lose things we have loved beyond measure.

Sometimes, however, self-love intrudes upon the mind and, by a hidden movement, turns it aside from the rectitude of justice. In proportion as the mind neglects to surrender itself wholly to its Creator, it resists within itself the rule of justice.

*(Moral Commentary, Book XXXV, chapter 8, no. 15.)* Those whom the Spirit of the sevenfold grace fills, he perfects. He grants them not only knowledge of the Trinity but also the practice of the four virtues, namely prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. Through knowledge of the Trinity the activity of the four virtues is received, and through the activity of the virtues one reaches the manifest vision of the Trinity.

*(Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 3, no. 8.)* We may understand the four principal regions of the world as signifying the four virtues from which the other virtues arise: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. We truly receive these virtues when we preserve their order. Of the four virtues, prudence is first, fortitude second, justice third, and temperance fourth.

For what benefit can prudence provide if fortitude is absent? To know what one cannot do is more a punishment than a virtue. But whoever prudently understands what he should do and courageously does what he has understood is already, without doubt, just. Yet temperance must follow his justice, because justice often falls into cruelty if it has no measure. Justice itself is truly justice when it is moderated by the bridle of temperance, so that the person who burns with zeal is also temperate.

[Note: The edition reads, “self-restrained.”]

He must not burn too fiercely and thereby lose justice, because he does not know how to preserve its proper limits.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the active and contemplative life

*(Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 3, no. 9.)* There are two lives of holy men, namely the active and the contemplative. The active precedes the contemplative in time, because one advances from good works to contemplation. The contemplative, however, is greater in merit than the active, because the former labors in the practice of present works, while the latter already tastes inwardly the rest that is to come.

The prophet Ezekiel says: “The hands of a man were under their wings on their four sides” (Ezekiel 1:8). What is signified by hands except the active life, and by wings except the contemplative life? Thus the hand of a man is under the wings: that is, the virtue of work is under the flight of contemplation.

The two women in the Gospel—Martha and Mary—represent the active and contemplative lives. Martha was busy with much serving, while Mary sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his words. One, therefore, was devoted to work, the other to contemplation. One served the active life through outward service; the other served the contemplative life through the suspension of her heart in the word.

Although the active life is good, the contemplative is better, because when the former comes to an end with mortal life, the latter grows more fully in immortal life. Hence it is said: “Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

If through the active life we do something good, nevertheless through the contemplative life we fly toward heavenly desire. Hence among Moses’ people the active life is called servitude, while the contemplative is called freedom (Numbers 10). Although both lives are gifts of grace,

[Note: The edition reads, “Each life is a gift of grace.” The German, Norman, Val-Dieu, and our manuscripts have our reading.]

as long as we live among our neighbors, one is necessary for us and the other voluntary. No mortal who knows God enters his kingdom without first acting well. Therefore, those who do not neglect to perform the good they are able to perform can enter the heavenly homeland without the contemplative life. But they cannot enter without the active life if they neglect to do the good they are able to do.

*(Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 6, no. 5.)* The active life, therefore, is necessary, while the contemplative is voluntary; the former is servitude, the latter freedom.

The people of the elect rise to contemplation through some of their members, while through others they grow rich only in the works of the active life, as it is written: “May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth” (Genesis 27:28). Dew falls gently from above, and we receive the dew of heaven whenever, through the infusion of inward contemplation, we see something of heavenly things dimly. But whenever we perform good works through the body as well, we are enriched with the richness of the earth.

*(Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 2, no. 10.)* Jacob’s two wives, Leah and Rachel, signify the active and contemplative lives. Leah is interpreted as “laboring,” while Rachel means “sheep” or “the beginning of vision.” The active life is laborious, because it sweats in work; the contemplative life, however, is simple and longs only to see the beginning—that is, the one who says: “I am the beginning, and therefore I speak to you” (John 8:25).

Blessed Jacob desired Rachel, but received Leah at night (Genesis 29:16), because everyone who turns to God desires the contemplative life and longs for the rest of the eternal homeland. Yet first it is necessary for him to work during the night of the present life, to do the good he can, and to sweat in labor—that is, to receive Leah—so that afterward he may rest in Rachel’s embrace in order to see the beginning.

Rachel was seeing but barren; Leah had weak eyes but was fertile. Rachel was beautiful and unfruitful because the mind that desires the leisure of contemplation sees more but bears fewer children for God. When it directs itself to the labor of preaching, it sees less but gives birth to more.

The contemplative life is very beautiful in the soul, but when it desires to rest in silence, it does not give birth to children through preaching. It sees but does not bear, because, intent upon the pursuit of its rest,

[Note: The edition reads, “because it loves the pursuit of its rest.” Laon and Suessa agree with our text.]

it is less inflamed for gathering others. And the more it sees inwardly, the less it is able to disclose to others by preaching.

Leah, Jacob’s wife, had weak eyes and was fertile, because the active life, while occupied in work, sees less. Yet by sometimes speaking and sometimes setting an example, it kindles its neighbors to imitation and gives birth to many children in good works. Even if it cannot direct its mind toward contemplation, nevertheless, from what it does outwardly, it can beget followers.

*(Moral Commentary, Book VI, chapter 37, no. 61.)* After embracing Leah, Jacob came to Rachel as his wife, because every perfect person is first joined to the active life for fruitfulness and afterward joined to the contemplative life for rest.

It is written: “If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years” (Exodus 21:2).

*(Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 3, no. 11.)* “Hebrew” is interpreted as “passing over.” A Hebrew servant is bought and commanded to serve for six years whenever someone who has already passed over mentally from this world is subjected to the service of the omnipotent Lord. The person who has learned to pass over mentally from this world truly desires to serve God.

A Hebrew servant is bought and commanded to serve for six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free without payment. What is signified by the number six except the perfection of the active life? What is signified by seven except the contemplative life? He serves for six years and goes out free in the seventh who, through the active life he has perfectly displayed, passes over to the freedom of the contemplative life.

The Hebrew servant who was bought goes out free without payment after six years, because those who, after doing everything, say that they are useless servants will undoubtedly receive the contemplative life by grace, just as the active life itself was a gift.

The same servant must go out wearing the clothing in which he entered, because it is altogether necessary that each of us persevere in what he begins and remain until the end of his work in the intention with which he began. He passes well to the contemplative life who does not change the garment of his intention for something worse during the active life.

It is written in the Apocalypse: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Revelation 8:1).

*(Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 2, no. 14.)* Heaven is the soul of the righteous, just as the Lord says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne” (Isaiah 66:1). And: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:1). Therefore, when the rest of the contemplative life takes place in the mind, silence occurs in heaven, because the clamor of earthly actions ceases in thought, so that the mind may apply its ear to the innermost secret.

Since perfect rest of mind cannot exist in this life, the silence in heaven is not said to last a whole hour but “about half an hour.” Even that half-hour is not fully experienced, since “about” is added: as soon as the mind begins to raise itself up and be suffused with the light of inward rest, the clamor of thoughts quickly returns, and the mind is confounded by itself; in its confusion it becomes blind.

*(Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 2, no. 12.)* Great is the effort of the mind in the contemplative life when it raises itself toward heavenly things, when it stretches its spirit toward spiritual realities, when it strives to pass beyond everything visible bodily, and when it contracts itself in order to be enlarged. Sometimes it prevails and overcomes the resisting darkness of its blindness; it secretly and subtly touches something of the unbounded light.

[Note: The edition reads, “secretly and faintly touches.”]

But immediately it is struck back upon itself,

[Note: The edition reads, “it returns, struck back.”]

and from that light toward which it passes in aspiration, it returns with a sigh to the darkness of its own blindness.

*(Moral Commentary, Book VI, chapter 37, no. 56.)* In the Book of Genesis it is written: “Abraham buried his wife in a double tomb” (Genesis 23:19). The active life is like a tomb because it covers the dead from wicked works; but the contemplative life buries more perfectly, because it completely separates one from all the actions of the world.

## CHAPTER XXII. On prayer

*(Moral Commentary, Book XV, chapter 47, no. 53.)* When God is not sought in prayer, the mind soon grows weary in prayer. For when someone asks for things that God perhaps refuses to grant according to his hidden judgment, the one who does not wish to give what is requested becomes wearisome to him.

[Note: The edition reads, “what is loved.”]

The Lord, Creator of the universe, desires to be loved more than the things he has created, and desires that eternal things be requested rather than earthly ones, since the Truth himself says: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). For he did not say “they will be given,” but “they will be added,” clearly indicating that one thing is given as the principal gift and another is added afterward.

Because eternity should be our object of intention, while temporal things should serve our use, the former is given and the latter is added in abundance. Often, when people ask in prayer for temporal goods but do not seek eternal rewards, they ask for what is added and do not desire the place where it is to be added. They do not consider their petition successful if they are temporarily poor here but live eternally rich in blessedness there. Intent only upon visible things, as has been said, they refuse to purchase invisible things through the labor of petition. If they sought heavenly things, they would already be laboring with profit.

When the mind of each of the elect, inflamed by divine desires, longs in prayer for the vision of its Creator, it is joined to heavenly things and separated from lower ones. Through the heat of its love it opens itself in order to receive, and, receiving, it is set aflame. To love higher things is already to ascend. And while it gazes toward heavenly things with great desire, in a wondrous way it tastes precisely what it seeks to receive.

*(Moral Commentary, Book XXXV, chapter 11, no. 21.)* The sacrifice of an offering is more willingly accepted when it is prepared in the sight of the merciful Judge through love of one’s neighbor. A person truly accumulates such an offering when he offers it even for his enemies.

The prophet Isaiah says: “Enter into your chamber and shut your door” (Isaiah 26:20). And the Truth says: “Pray to your Father in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you” (Matthew 6:6).

[Note: The edition reads, “in secret.” The Laon manuscript has “in concealment,” as our text does.]

*(Moral Commentary, Book XXII, chapter 17, no. 43.)* A person asks in his chamber with the door shut when, with his mouth silent, he pours out the affection of his mind before the heavenly mercy. The voice is heard in secret when one cries out silently through holy desires. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the desire of their heart” (Psalm 19:17).

[Note: The edition reads, “the preparation.” Two Saint-Germain manuscripts, Laon, Val-Dieu, Norman, and the old Paris edition have our reading.]

Again, the Truth says: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:8).

*(Book I on the Gospel, Homily 2, no. 7.)* He wishes us to ask for what he already knows we will ask and that he will grant. Thus he urges us to pray persistently and inspires us to ask, while seeking by this means to awaken the hearts of his hearers to prayer.

When the Truth was instructing his disciples in devotion to prayer, he said to the Father: “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth” (Matthew 6:10).

*(Moral Commentary, Book XXVII, chapter 39, no. 65.)* By heaven may be signified the angelic spirits who were created in heavenly places, so that the will of God may be carried out by the higher creation and likewise be observed in all things by human weakness.

“Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11).

*(Moral Commentary, Book XXIV, chapter 7, no. 13.)* Behold, we call it “our” bread, and yet we beg the Lord to give it to us. It becomes ours when it is received, yet it remains God’s because it is given by him. It is therefore God’s by gift, and truly becomes ours through reception.

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

*(Moral Commentary, Book X, chapter 15, no. 30.)* Thus, the good that we ask from God when moved to compunction, we should first do in our dealings with our neighbor. We raise our face without stain in prayer when we neither commit forbidden evils ourselves nor retain, through personal resentment, the evils committed against us.

[Note: The edition reads, “the evils committed against us are retained through personal resentment.”]

Our mind is weighed down by grievous shame at the time of its prayer if either its own conduct still defiles it or the pain it has preserved over another’s wickedness accuses it. Once a person has cleansed these two things, he immediately rises willingly to what follows.

“And do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13).

*(Moral Commentary, Book III, chapter 5, no. 6.)* The Truth does not lead us into temptation,

[Note: The edition reads, “the Lord.”]

for he always mercifully protects his subjects from temptation. Yet to lead us, as it were, into temptation means not to fortify us against the allure of temptation. Almighty God does not lead us into the snare of temptation when he does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear.

*(Book I on the Gospel, Homily 2, no. 5.)* When we suffer crowds of phantasms during prayer, we sense Jesus passing by in some measure. But when we persist vigorously in prayer, Jesus stands still to restore the light, because God is fixed in the heart and the lost light is restored.

*(Moral Commentary, Book XVIII, chapter 5, no. 10.)* For with the Lord these two things necessarily fit together: action must be supported by prayer, and prayer by action. The prophet Jeremiah says: “Let us examine our ways and search them out, and let us return to the Lord. Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God in heaven” (Lamentations 3:40).

To examine our ways is to scrutinize the inner things of our thoughts. A person lifts his heart together with his hands when he strengthens his prayer with works. Whoever prays but refuses to act lifts his heart but does not lift his hands; whoever acts but does not pray lifts his hands but does not lift his heart.

The apostle John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God” (1 John 3:21). The heart receives confidence in prayer when no wickedness of life contradicts it.

*(Moral Commentary, Book X, chapter 15, no. 27.)* The heart condemns us in our petition when it remembers that we resist the commandments of the one whom we are asking. Prayer becomes detestable when it turns away from the judgment of the law. It is entirely fitting that a person be excluded from the benefits of one whose commands he does not wish to obey.

*(No. 28.)* In prayer there is a salutary remedy: when the mind condemns itself because of the memory of sin, it should first mourn that it has gone astray. Thus, while the stains of error are cleansed by tears, the face of the heart appears pure before its Creator in its petition.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the distribution of the sevenfold Spirit
(Lib. II on Ezekiel, homily 7, no. 7.) In the minds of the faithful, the first step of ascent is fear of the Lord; the second, piety; the third, knowledge; the fourth, fortitude; the fifth, counsel; the sixth, understanding; the seventh, wisdom. The prophet Isaiah, enumerating in Christ the sevenfold stages of grace, says:

> The spirit of the Lord rests upon him [Note: [Col. 0880D] Edition: “shall rest . . . and shall fill.” But Laudunensis reads as Taius does]: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him (Isa. XI, 2–3).

Speaking, that is, of heavenly things, he counted these stages in descending rather than ascending order [Col. 0880B]: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear. And since it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. IX, 10), there is no doubt that one ascends from fear to wisdom, not that one returns from wisdom to fear; for wisdom certainly possesses perfect charity, as it is written: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (I John IV, 18).

Isaiah, therefore, because he was speaking from heavenly things down to lower ones, began with wisdom and descended to fear. But we, because we are striving from earthly things toward heavenly ones, should count the same stages in ascending order, so that we may be able to arrive from fear at wisdom.

There is fear of the Lord in the minds of the faithful; but what kind of fear is it if piety is not joined to it? For whoever does not know how to have mercy on his neighbor, whoever pretends not to share in his neighbor’s tribulation, has no fear at all before the eyes of almighty God. Such a person is not raised up to piety [Note: [Col. 0880D] Edition: “because he is not raised up to piety.” But often, etc.]. Yet piety often errs through disordered mercy, if it should perhaps spare what ought not to be spared. Sins that can be struck by the fires of Gehenna must be corrected by the scourge of discipline. But disordered piety, when it spares someone temporarily, drags him toward eternal punishment.

For piety to be true and rightly ordered, it must be raised to another stage, namely, to knowledge, so that one may know either what to punish out of mercy [Note: [Col. 0880D] Edition: “out of judgment.”] or what to forgive out of mercy. But what if someone knows what ought to be done yet lacks the strength to do it? Our knowledge, therefore, must grow into fortitude, so that when it sees what ought to be done, it may be able to do it through strength of mind [Col. 0880D], lest it tremble with fear and, collapsing through dread, be unable to defend the good it recognizes.

Often fortitude, if it is imprudent and insufficiently watchful against vices, falls through its own presumption. It must therefore ascend to counsel, so that by foresight it may fortify in advance everything it is able to accomplish courageously.

Counsel cannot exist if understanding is absent. For one who does not understand the evil that weighs down the person committing it, how can he solidify the good that helps him? Let us therefore ascend from counsel to understanding.

But what if understanding remains alert with great acumen [Col. 0881A] yet does not know how to govern itself through maturity? Let us then ascend from understanding to wisdom, so that wisdom’s maturity may order what acute understanding has discovered [Note: [Col. 0881D] Edition: “wisdom maturely.”]

Since, therefore, through fear we rise to piety, through piety we are led to knowledge, through knowledge we are strengthened for fortitude, through fortitude we advance to counsel, through counsel we progress to understanding, and through understanding we come to the maturity of wisdom, we ascend by seven steps to the gate through which the entrance to the spiritual life is opened for us.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Not Returning Evil for Evil

(Moral. book X, chapter 6, no. 8.) It is written in both Testaments: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV, 16; Matt. VII, 12). By the commandments of both Testaments, malice is restrained through one, while kindness is extended through the other: each person, by not doing the evil he does not wish to suffer, should cease from the work of harming; and again, by offering the good he desires to have done to himself, he should exercise himself in kindness toward his neighbor’s welfare.

When these two principles are considered with careful attention, the heart is directed toward innumerable services of virtue: the restless mind must neither burn with desires to inflict what it ought not to inflict, nor grow slack in idleness when it should provide what it ought to provide.

When a person takes care not to do to another what he himself in no way wishes to endure from another, he must carefully examine himself lest pride exalt him and, lowering his spirit to the point of despising his neighbor, raise him up in his own estimation; lest ambition tear his thoughts apart and, when it broadens them toward desiring what belongs to others, constrict them. One must be exceedingly careful lest lust pollute anyone’s heart and, subjecting it to desires, corrupt it through unlawful things. Let not anger embitter it and inflame it to the point of uttering insults. Let not envy bite it and, emulating the happiness of others, consume it with its own fire.

Each person should guard himself with vigilant watchfulness lest excessive talkativeness drag his tongue along and extend it into the wantonness of detraction. Let not hatred be stirred up by malice and provoke the mouth into the weapon of a curse.

When a person considers that he should do to another what he expects another to do to him, he rightly weighs that he should answer evil with good and good with better: toward the aggressive he should display the gentleness of patience, and to those weakened by the plague of malice he should show the grace of kindness [Col. 0881D] [Edition: “offer.”]

It is fitting for every faithful person to unite the divided in peace and to bind those already united to the desire for true peace; to give what is necessary to those in need and show the way of righteousness to those who have gone astray; to soothe the afflicted by word and compassion; and to restrain by admonition those inflamed by the desires of this world [Note: [Col. 0881D] Edition: “extinguish.” Most manuscripts of Normandy and Corbie Gem., “restrain.”]

Let each of the faithful endure silently whatever he keeps quiet about, but not conceal within his heart the poison of grief. Let him offer the gift of kindness to the malicious, but not, through kindness, depart from the rule of righteousness. Let him provide his neighbors with everything he is able to provide, but not become swollen with pride in providing it. Thus, in the good things he offers, let him fear the precipice of arrogance, yet not grow numb toward the practice of goodness.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Peace and Concord

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 22.)* Those who are peaceful must be admonished lest, while they love the peace they possess more than is necessary, they fail to desire to attain eternal peace. For the tranquillity of circumstances often tests the minds of people more severely, so that, because the things they possess are not troublesome, the things they are called toward become less lovable; and, because present things delight them, eternal things are not sought.

Truth itself, speaking and distinguishing earthly peace from heavenly peace, and urging the disciples from the present toward what was to come, says: “My peace I leave you; my peace I give you” (John XIV, 27). He leaves, that is, a passing peace; he gives an abiding one. If, therefore, the heart is fixed upon the peace that has been left, it never reaches the peace that is to be given.

The peace of the present must be held in such a way that it is both loved and despised, lest, if it is loved immoderately, the soul of the one who loves it be caught in guilt.

Those who are peaceful must be admonished lest, while they desire human peace too greatly, they fail entirely to rebuke the wicked conduct of human beings and, by consenting to the perverse, separate themselves from the peace of their Creator; lest, while they fear outward quarrels among human beings, they be struck by the rupture of the inward covenant [Note: [Col. 0882D] Edition: “severing”; Belv. and the two earlier manuscripts of Chartres, “discussion.”]

What is passing peace except a kind of footprint of eternal peace? What, then, could be more foolish than to love footprints impressed in dust but not love the one by whom they were impressed?

It must be known with absolute certainty that, however many virtues people may possess, they can in no way become spiritual if they neglect to be united with their neighbors through concord. For it is written: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace” (Gal. V, 22). Therefore, whoever does not care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the Spirit.

Hence Paul likewise says: “When there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” (I Cor. III, 3). Again he says: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. XII, 11). The apostle Paul, exhorting them, says: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. IV, 3–4).

One does not, therefore, reach the one hope of the calling if one does not hasten toward it with a mind united to one’s neighbors.

Often some people, when they receive certain special gifts, lose through pride the gift of concord, which is greater. Thus, if someone perhaps subdues his flesh more than others through restraint of appetite, he may, because of his abstinence, disdain to live in harmony with those whom he surpasses.

In the Gospel Truth says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX, 49). Salt without peace is not a gift of virtue but a proof of condemnation.

Often birds of one and the same kind do not abandon one another as they fly together, and brute animals feed in groups. If we observe this carefully, irrational nature, by living in concord, shows how great an evil rational nature commits through discord, since the latter has lost through the exercise of reason what the former preserves by natural impulse.

The prophet David, binding his whole self to the bonds of inward peace, testifies that he did not maintain concord with the wicked, saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become my enemies” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 21–22).

To hate God’s enemies with perfect hatred means to love what they were made to be and rebuke what they do.

Those who are peaceful must be admonished not to fear disturbing their temporal peace if they spring forward with words of correction. They must again be admonished to preserve inwardly, with undivided love, the same peace that they outwardly disturb for themselves through reproach.

The prophet David plainly shows that he preserved both, when he says: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. CXIX, 7). Behold, even while speaking and being attacked, he was peaceful, because he neither ceased to rebuke those who raged nor neglected to love those whom he had rebuked [Note: [Col. 0883D] Edition: “while speaking he was attacked, and yet was peaceful.”]

Commending the concord of peace, Paul says: “If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, be at peace with all people” (Rom. XII, 18). For when he was about to exhort the disciples to have peace with people, he prefaced it by saying, “If it is possible,” and then added, “as far as it depends on you.” It was difficult, after all, for them to rebuke evil deeds and still be able to have peace with everyone.

When temporal peace in the hearts of the wicked is disturbed by our rebuke, it is nevertheless necessary that it be preserved inviolate in our own heart. The Apostle therefore rightly says, “As far as it depends on you,” as if he were saying: “Because peace subsists through the agreement of two parties, if it is expelled by those who are being corrected, it must nevertheless be preserved whole in the mind of you who correct” [Note: [Col. 0883D] In the edition, “as far as it depends on you” is lacking.]

Again Paul admonishes the disciples, saying: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame” (II Thess. III, 14). And immediately he adds: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother” (ibid., 15). As if he were saying: “Break outward peace with him, but preserve inwardly and profoundly the peace you have toward him, so that your discord may strike the mind of the sinner in such a way that peace does not depart, denied, from your hearts.”

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 23.)* In the Gospel the Lord says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V, 9). From the opposite, people may infer that if those who make peace are called sons of God, without doubt those who place their trust in discord are sons of Satan. Therefore those who devote themselves to making peace must be admonished that they should first pour the love of inward peace into the minds of the wicked, so that outward peace may afterward be of benefit to them.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Patience

*(Book II on the Gospel, homily 35, no. 5; and Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 9.)* Solomon indicates the lofty excellence of the virtue of patience when he says: “The patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities” (Prov. XVI, 32). Victory over cities is the lesser victory, because the things conquered are outside oneself. But what is conquered through patience is greater, because the soul itself is overcome and subjects itself to itself when patience lays it low in humble endurance.

“The patient man,” he says, “is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities.”

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 7.)* The patient man is rightly preferred to the conqueror of cities, because in the former action a human being is victor over other human beings, whereas in the gentleness of patient endurance the soul is victor over itself.

The good soil produces fruit through patience, because none of the good things we do are truly good if we do not also endure the evils of our neighbors with equanimity. It is written: “Charity is patient” (I Cor. XIII, 4). Therefore, when it is not patient, it is not charity.

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 9.)* Through impatience, moreover, the teaching that is itself the nurse of the virtues is destroyed. Solomon says: “The teaching of a person is known through patience” (Prov. XIX, 11). Thus, the less patient someone is shown to be, the less learned he is proved to be. For he cannot truthfully offer good things by teaching if, in his life, he does not know how to endure the evils of others with equanimity.

In Ecclesiastes it is written: “The patient man is better than the arrogant” (Eccl. VII, 9), because the patient person chooses to endure any evils rather than allow his good deeds to be exposed through the vice of ostentation.

When patience is abandoned, the other good things already accomplished are also destroyed. Hence Ezekiel rightly states that there is a trench on God’s altar (Ezek. XLIII, 13), so that the holocausts placed upon it may be preserved there. For if there were no trench on the altar, a sudden breeze would scatter whatever sacrifice it found upon it.

The Lord showed that patience is the guardian of our condition, for he taught us through it to possess ourselves, saying: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19).

Those who are patient must be admonished not to grieve inwardly over what they bear outwardly through patience, lest they corrupt within by the plague of malice the sacrifice of so great a virtue, which they offer whole outside.

Those who are patient must be told to strive to love what they must endure. Otherwise, if love does not follow patience, the virtue displayed may be transformed into the worse guilt of hatred.

When the apostle Paul said, “Charity is patient” (I Cor. XIII, 4), he immediately added, “It is kind,” showing that those whom charity tolerates through patience it also does not cease to love through kindness.

The same outstanding teacher, when urging patience upon the disciples, said: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be removed from you” (Eph. IV, 31). As though everything outward had already been put in order, he returns to the inward when he adds, “with all malice.” For indignation, clamor, and blasphemy are removed from outward behavior in vain if malice, the mother of vices, rules within. Wickedness is cut off from the branches outside to no purpose if it is preserved within at the root, where it will rise again in greater abundance.

It often happens to those who are patient that, at the very time when they are suffering adversity or hearing insults, they are struck by no pain at all [Col. 0885A], and so display patience that they do not fail to preserve the innocence of their hearts. But after a little while, when they recall to memory the very things they endured, they inflame themselves with the fire of grief, seek means of revenge, and, turning over in their minds the gentleness they had shown while enduring, transform it into malice.

Those who are patient must be admonished to fortify their hearts after victory; to watch for the enemy, defeated in open warfare, as he lies in ambush around the walls of the mind; and to fear the sickness that creeps farther within, lest the cunning enemy afterward rejoice with greater exultation in deception because he tramples the stiff necks of those who once stood rigidly against him [Edition: “because he tramples,” rather than “that he tramples”].

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 2.)* In our love of neighbor, patience and kindness must be preserved, because of this same love it is now said: “Charity is patient, it is kind” (I Cor. XV, 4). It is patient so that it may bear with equanimity the evils inflicted by neighbors; it is kind so that it may generously offer its own good things to neighbors.

*(Book II on the Gospel, homily 35, no. 4.)* Patience is to endure the evils of others with equanimity and not to be gnawed by any pain against the person who inflicts those evils. For whoever bears the evils of his neighbor while nevertheless grieving silently and awaiting the time of a fitting repayment does not exhibit patience but merely displays it.

Every soldier of God, caught in the war of adversity, must hold the shield of patience before him lest he perish; and, ready for preaching, he must hurl the darts of love in order to conquer.

It is written: “Will the poor be forgotten forever? Will the patience of the poor perish forever?” (Ps. IX, 19) [Note: [Col. 0885D] These words are found verbatim in Paterius, book II on the Psalms, chapter 21.]

However patient we may be in adversity or humble in prosperity, let us in no way seek present good things as our recompense in this life. The good things to be hoped for in return for the labor of patience belong to the life to come, so that the reward for our labor may begin when all labor has already entirely ceased.

The patience of the poor seems to have perished when the humble receive no recompense for it in this life. But the patience of the poor will not perish forever, because its glory is received when all things involving labor come to an end together.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Humility

*(Moral. book XXXIV, chapter 23, no. 54; Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 17.)* For this reason the only-begotten Son of God assumed the form of our weakness; for this reason the invisible one appeared, even as one despised [Note: [Col. 0885D] Edition: “For this reason the invisible one appeared not only visible but also despised”]; for this reason he endured the mockery of insults, the disgrace of derision [Note: [Col. 0885D] Edition: “the disgrace of derision.” Several manuscripts read “the disgrace of deception” [Col. 0886D]], and the torments of suffering: so that God, humble, might teach human beings not to be proud.

How great is the virtue of humility, and how lofty its sublimity, for the sake of teaching which alone, in truth, he who is great beyond estimation became small even unto suffering?

Because the devil made himself the source of our destruction [Note: [Col. 0886D] Edition: “to our destruction.” Laud., Pratel., Gemet., two German manuscripts, the old Paris edition, and Bartholomew read as we do], the humility of God was found to be the instrument of our redemption.

Our enemy, created among all things [Note: [Col. 0886D] Edition: “great among all things”], wished in his exaltation to appear above all things. But our Redeemer, remaining great above all things, deigned to become small among all [Edition: “all things”].

Humility is the teacher and mother of all virtues, as Truth says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI, 29). For when humble people abase themselves, they rise to the likeness of God. What, then, is more exalted than humility, which, while lowering itself to the depths, unites itself to its Creator, who remains above the highest things?

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 17.)* The signs of true humility are for each person to recognize his own iniquity and, once recognized, to disclose it by verbal confession.

It must be impressed upon the humble how true is the excellence they hold by hope, how eternal are the things they desire, and how transient are the things they despise.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Simplicity

[Col. 0886B]

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 11.)* The simple must be admonished to strive never to speak falsely, but also to know never to suppress the truth [Note: [Col. 0886D] Edition: “But they must be admonished to…”]. For just as falsehood has often harmed the one who speaks it, so truths heard have sometimes harmed certain people.

The simple must be admonished that, just as they always usefully avoid deceit, so they should always usefully speak the truth.

They must be admonished to join prudence to the good of simplicity, so that they may possess the security of simplicity without losing the vigilance of prudence. Hence the teacher of the nations says: “I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil” (Rom. XVI, 19).

Truth itself admonishes his elect, saying: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X, 16). For in the hearts of the elect, the serpent’s craft should sharpen the dove’s simplicity, and the dove’s simplicity should temper the serpent’s craft, so that they may neither become clever through prudence and be deceived, nor grow sluggish through simplicity and withdraw from the pursuit of understanding.

*(Moral. book XII, chapter 39, no. 44.)* Nothing is happier than a simple heart, because, when it displays innocence toward others, it has nothing to fear suffering from others. Its simplicity is, as it were, a fortress of strength; it is not suspected of suffering what it does not remember having done.

Solomon rightly says: “In the fear of the Lord is confidence of strength” (Prov. XIV, 26). Again he says: “A secure mind is like a continual banquet” (Prov. XV, 15). For the tranquillity of security is itself, as it were, a continual banquet.

“He who walks simply walks confidently” (Prov. X, 9).

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 11.)* Simplicity of conduct is the assurance of great security, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. I, 5).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Intention of the Heart and Body

*(Moral. book XXVIII, chapter 11, no. 30.)* “The lamp of the body is the eye,” because the merits of action are illuminated by the ray of good intention, as Truth says: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be luminous” (Matt. VI, 22).

By the eye is expressed the intention of the heart that precedes its work. Before it exercises itself in action, it already contemplates what it desires.

What, finally, is designated by the term “body” except each action, which follows its intention as a seeing eye? If the intention is rightly directed through simplicity of thought, a good work is produced, even if it appears to be less good.

For “if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark,” because when something right is done with a perverse intention, even if it is seen to shine before human beings, it is nevertheless darkened in the judgment of the inward Judge.

“If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?” (ibid., 23). If we darken through a bad intention what we believe we are doing well, how great are those evils which we do not fail to recognize as evil even while committing them? If, therefore, we discern nothing there where we hold what is seemingly the light of discernment, with what blindness do we stumble over those things we commit without discernment?

With vigilant care, our intention must be weighed in all our works, so that it may desire nothing temporal in what it does and may fix itself wholly upon the solidity of eternity. Otherwise, if the structure of our action is placed outside its foundation, it will collapse when the earth opens beneath it.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Gentleness

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 16.)* The gentle often suffer from the torpor of laziness, which is close to them and, as it were, placed beside them; through an excessive relaxation of gentleness, they soften the force of strictness beyond what is necessary. Often the gentle grow sluggish through weariness with dissolution, because a vice is secretly joined to their virtue.

They must therefore be admonished to flee what lies close beside them and to embrace diligence, which sharpens the negligence that accompanies great kindness.

For this reason the Holy Spirit has been shown to us both in a dove and in fire: he makes all whom he fills gentle with the simplicity of a dove and burning with the fire of zeal. No one is truly filled with the Holy Spirit who either abandons the fervor of zeal in the tranquillity of gentleness or, conversely, loses the virtue of gentleness in the ardor of zeal.
