Paul the apostle, the vessel of election, gave two disciples different forms of assistance in preaching, though not different in charity [Note: [Col. 0887D] Edition: “to two disciples endowed not with different charity, but with different forms of assistance.”]

Admonishing Timothy, he says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (II Tim. IV, 2). He also admonishes Titus, saying: “Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority” (Titus II, 15).

What does it mean that the outstanding teacher distributes his instruction with such discernment that, in one case, he prescribes authority, and in the other, patience, except that he saw Titus to possess the gentler spirit and Timothy to be somewhat more fervent? He inflames the one through zeal and tempers the other through the gentleness of patience. He adds to the one what is lacking and removes from the other what is excessive. He seeks to urge the one on with a goad and governs the other with a bridle.

Every great cultivator of the Church entrusted to him waters some branches so that they may grow, while, when he sees others growing beyond what is proper, he cuts them back, lest either they bear no fruit by failing to grow or lose what they have produced through growing excessively.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Obedience

*(Moral. book XXXV, chapter 14, no. 30.)* It must be understood with the greatest care that obedience is sometimes nothing if it possesses something of its own, and is minimal if it possesses nothing of its own.

When success in this world is commanded, when a higher position is ordered, the person who obeys in order to obtain these things empties obedience of its virtue if he also longs for them from his own desire. For a person does not place himself under obedience when he serves the lust of his own ambition in order to obtain the prosperity of this life.

When contempt for this world is commanded, when insults and humiliations are ordered, unless the mind itself also desires these things, it diminishes the merit of its obedience, because it descends unwillingly and reluctantly to what is despised in this life.

Sometimes obedience leads to harm when, in receiving the insults of this world, the mind is not accompanied in any degree by its own wishes. Obedience must have something of its own in adversity; and, conversely, in prosperity it must by no means possess anything of its own, so that in adversity it may be all the more glorious insofar as it joins itself to the divine order even through desire, and in prosperity it may be all the truer insofar as it entirely separates from the mind the present glory it receives divinely [Note: [Col. 0888D] We have restored these words from the edition; in our manuscript they had been omitted, making the sense entirely defective.]

*(No. 28.)* Obedience must be preserved toward almighty God even unto death, as Truth says: “I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge” (John V, 30). If he judges as he hears, then he also obeys the Father when he comes as Judge of this world.

Lest obedience seem burdensome to us until the end of our present life, our Redeemer shows that he preserves it even when he comes as Judge. What wonder, then, if sinful human beings subject themselves to obedience during the brief span of the present life, when the Mediator of God and human beings does not abandon it even when he rewards those who obey?

*(No. 29.)* It must be understood that evil is never done through obedience, although sometimes the good that is being done ought to be interrupted through obedience. For the tree in paradise that God forbade the human being to touch was not evil. But so that the well-created human being might grow better through the merit of obedience, it was fitting that God should also prohibit him from something good, so that the virtue of his action might be all the truer insofar as, abstaining from something good, he more humbly showed himself subject to his Creator.

We must note with the greatest care what the Lord said to the first human beings: “Eat from every tree of paradise” [Edition: “eat” rather than “feed”], “but you shall not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. II, 16). For whoever forbids those under him some one good must necessarily grant many others, lest the mind of the obedient perish utterly if it is completely deprived and starved of all good things.

*(No. 28.)* It is written in the book of Solomon [Note: [Col. 0889D] “Samuel” seems to need to be substituted for “Solomon”; for in Ecclesiastes, chapter IV, verse 17, the sentence reads: “For obedience is much better than the sacrifices of fools.”]: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (I Sam. XV, 22). Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because through sacrifices another person’s flesh is slaughtered, but through obedience one’s own will is put to death.

Each person therefore appeases God more quickly in proportion as, suppressing the pride of his own will before God’s eyes, he sacrifices himself with the sword of the commandment.

The sin of divination is called disobedience, so that the greatness of the virtue of obedience [Edition: “obedience”] may be demonstrated. What is thought of obedience’s praise is therefore better shown by its opposite. If resistance is like the sin of divination and refusal to yield like the crime of idolatry, obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it, anyone is proved to be an unbeliever, even if he appears to be faithful.

In praise of obedience Solomon says: “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Prov. XXI, 28). An obedient man speaks of victories because, when we humbly submit to another’s voice, we overcome ourselves in our hearts.

Commending the virtue of obedience, Truth says: “Whoever comes to me I will not cast out, because I have come down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John VI, 37).

What does this mean? If he did his own will, would he have cast out those who came to him? Who does not know that the will of the Son does not differ from the will of the Father?

But because the first human being, wishing to do his own will, departed from the joy of paradise (Gen. III, 24), the second, coming for the redemption of humanity, showed that he did the Father’s will and not his own, and taught us to remain within through the merit of obedience.

When Christ the Lord does not do his own will but the Father’s, because through his example he subjects us to obedience, he does not cast out those who come to him, and he closes against us the path of departure [Note: [Col. 0889D] The edition has this sentence differently and better: “Since, therefore, he does not do his own will but the Father’s, he does not cast out those who come to him, because through his example he subjects us to obedience and closes against us the path of departure.”]

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Modesty

Modest minds are sometimes shaped toward a better life by gentle and restrained exhortation, because often it is enough for their conversion that a teacher recall their evils to their memory, at least gently *(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 7)*.

Often greater progress is added to the modest if what is reproved in them is touched, as it were, indirectly [Note: [Col. 0890D] Edition: “if it is brought forward.”]

The Lord refreshes a people who feel shame through the prophet, saying: “You will forget the shame of your youth, and you will not remember the reproach of your widowhood, because he who made you will rule over you” (Isa. LIV, 4).

The apostle Paul, an outstanding preacher, rebuked the faults of those who felt shame as though he were sympathizing with them, saying: “I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that now at last you have revived your concern for me, as you did indeed concern yourselves; but you lacked opportunity” (Phil. IV, 10).

Thus the outstanding teacher healed the faults of those who felt shame with medicinal kindness, while moderating and veiling their negligence with gentler speech.

As modesty is praiseworthy in evil, so it is blameworthy in good *(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 10, no. 17).* To blush at evil is wisdom; to blush at doing good is foolishness.

Hence it is written: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty” (Luke IX, 26).

A certain wise man says: “There is a shame that brings glory” (Eccl. IV, 25). Whoever blushes with shame and repents of the evils he has done reaches the freedom of life. But whoever is ashamed to do good falls from the state of righteousness and moves toward condemnation.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Mercy and Piety
He acts well in matters of piety who knows first to preserve what is just, so that the stream of mercy bestowed upon his neighbors may be drawn from the fountain of justice (Moral. book XIX, chapter 23, no. 38). Many extend what seem to be works of mercy to their neighbors, but do not abandon deeds of injustice; if they truly wished to show mercy to their neighbors, they ought first to show mercy to themselves by living justly. Hence it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sirach 30:24). Whoever wishes to show mercy to his neighbor must necessarily draw the beginning of his mercy from himself [Col. 0890C]. For it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 19:19). How, then, is he pious toward another by showing mercy, when by living unjustly he is still impious toward himself?

For mercy to be shown fully and outwardly to those in need, two things are necessarily required: a person who gives, and something that is given. But a person is incomparably better than a possession. Hence a certain wise man says: “Who will be good to one who is bad to himself?” (Sirach 14:5). In the work of mercy itself, the inner Judge usually weighs the disposition more than the deed.

It should also be noted that blessed Job declares himself to have been an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame [Note: [Col. 0890D] The edition reads *caeco oculum . . . pedem claudo*, “an eye to the blind . . . a foot to the lame”; the German, Beauvais, and Norman manuscripts agree with our reading.] (Job 29:15); by saying this, he clearly indicates that he had extended his hand to the one and supported the other by carrying him. From this we understand how greatly the compassion of his heart was poured out over the needy and the weak. The same blessed Job says: “I was a father to the poor” (Job 29:16; Moral. book XIX, chapter 24, no. 41). He therefore does not testify that he was the patron, neighbor, or helper of the poor, but their father. For through the great service of charity he turned his devotion to mercy into an effect of nature, so that through love he regarded as sons those over whom he presided as a father through protection.

[Col. 0891A] Because the force of blessed Job’s mercy had imitated nature, he recalls that he had been a father to the poor; and there he adds: “And the case that I did not know I investigated most carefully” (Job 29:16; Moral. book XIX, chapter 25, no. 42). In these words everything deserves consideration: how distinctly all matters are narrated [Note: [Col. 0891D] The edition reads *narrentur*, “are narrated,” rather than *narrantur*, “are being narrated.”], and how no work of mercy is omitted by him. He is just in his actions, compassionate toward the weaknesses of his neighbors, and diligent in the affairs of the poor. Whoever thinks about the good of eternal recompense must necessarily extend himself mercifully to every matter that will lead to reward. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever fears God neglects nothing” (Ecclesiastes 7:19). Hence Paul says: “Ready for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:21).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Almsgiving

[Col. 0891B]

Whoever gives external possessions to a needy neighbor but does not guard his own life from wickedness gives his property to God, but himself to sin. He offers the Creator what is lesser, and preserves for iniquity what is greater (Moral. book XIX, chapter 25, no. 38). Sometimes the proud wealthy oppress those beneath them and seize what belongs to others, yet they distribute certain gifts to others as though generously; and although they crush many, they sometimes bring the aid of defense to some, and seem to pay a price for iniquities that they never abandon (Moral. book XII, chapter 51, no. 57).

Whenever we give alms after sin, we seem to pay a price for our evil deeds. Hence the Prophet says of one who does not act in this way: “He will not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul” (Psalm 48:8–9). The price of almsgiving frees us from guilt when we lament and renounce the sins committed. For whoever wishes both always to sin and, as though always, to give alms offers the price in vain, because he does not redeem the soul that he does not restrain from vices.

The expenditure of alms cannot redeem a proud rich man, since the robbery he has committed at the same time does not permit his gift to rise before God’s eyes. Hence Eliphaz says: “Let him not believe, deceived by error, that he will be redeemed at some price” (Job 15:31).

Often proud rich people, when they give alms, distribute them not out of desire for eternal life but to prolong their temporal life. They believe that they can delay death by their gifts, but by what they spend they can in no way obtain escape from the end appointed to them. In the Gospel, Truth says: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6:3; Pastoral Rule, part 3, chapter 20); that is, the glory of the present life must in no way mingle with the pious administration of goods; rather, the desire for praise must be unaware of the work of righteousness.

People often give much to the poor, not because they love those poor, but because, if they gave nothing, they fear the anger of the heavenly Judge. If they did not fear God, they would be unwilling to give what they possess.

Those who mercifully distribute their possessions must be admonished not to exalt themselves in proud thought above those to whom they give earthly goods [Col. 0892A], and not to consider themselves better merely because they see that others are restrained from possessing those things by their own means. Those who mercifully distribute what they possess should recognize that they have been appointed by the heavenly Lord as stewards of temporal resources, and should give with humility in proportion as they understand that what they distribute belongs to another.

So that those who give good things may not rejoice excessively, let them hear what is written: “When you have done everything that was commanded you, say: ‘We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17:10). And so that sadness may not corrupt generosity, let them hear what is written: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

So that those who give alms may not seek a return for the grace bestowed, let them hear what is written: “When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends” [Note: [Col. 0891D] The edition adds: “nor your brothers, nor your relatives.”], [Col. 0892B] “nor your relatives, nor your wealthy neighbors, lest they too invite you” [Note: [Col. 0892D] The edition reads “invite you in return.”], “and repayment be made to you. But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind; and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you” (Luke 14:22 ff.).

So that those who give may not delay in giving what ought to be given, let them hear what is written: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I will give,’ when you can give immediately” (Proverbs 3:28).

So that distributors may not scatter uselessly what they possess under the pretext of generosity, let them hear what is written: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand.” And so that, when much is necessary, they may not give little, let them hear what is written: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Corinthians 9:6).

So that, when little is appropriate, those who give may not offer too much and afterward, unable to endure poverty, break out into impatience, let them hear what is written: “Not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you, but that from your abundance their need may be supplied, and that their abundance may be a supplement to your need” (2 Corinthians 8:13–14). Therefore, when the mind of the giver does not know how to endure poverty, if he takes much away from himself, he seeks an occasion for impatience against himself. The mind must first be prepared for patience; then, whether much or everything is to be given, it should be given, lest, when the poverty that falls upon him is endured with insufficient equanimity, both the reward of the generosity already offered perish and the murmuring that follows afterward destroy the mind even more seriously.

So that distributors may not give nothing at all to those to whom they ought to contribute at least a little, let them hear what is written: “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30) [Col. 0892D]. And so that they may not give even something to those to whom they ought to give nothing at all, let them hear what is written: “Give to the good, and do not receive the sinner; do good to the humble, and do not give to the impious” (Sirach 12:4).

A certain wise man says: “Place your bread and wine upon the burial of the just, and do not eat and drink from it with sinners” (Tobit 4:17). He gives his bread and wine to sinners who bestows support upon the wicked because they are wicked. But whoever gives his bread even to a needy sinner—not because he is a sinner, but because he is a human being—clearly nourishes not the sinner but the just person, because in him he loves not guilt but nature.

Those who mercifully distribute what they possess should carefully strive to guard against this: while redeeming sins already committed by alms, they may not continue to commit sins that will still require redemption; nor should they regard God’s justice as for sale, supposing that, when they take care to give money for their sins, they can sin with impunity. “The soul is more than food, and the body, that is, more than clothing” (Matthew 6:25). Therefore, whoever gives food and clothing to the poor but is nevertheless polluted by iniquity of soul or body offers what is lesser to justice and gives what is greater to guilt. He gives his possessions to God but offers himself to the devil.

Let us carefully consider that those whom we now see in poverty we shall one day see in abundance; and that we who are seen to abound, if we neglect to give, shall one day be poor (Moral. book XXI, chapter 19, no. 30). Whoever now gives temporal support to the poor, later to receive from him what is everlasting, cultivates, so to speak, the earth for harvest: what it has received, it returns more abundantly.

It remains, therefore, that pride should never arise from almsgiving, since the rich person, by what he gives to the poor, acts so that the poor person may not remain poor forever. Honor those whom you see as poor, and regard those whom you see outwardly despised by the world as inwardly friends of God (Book II on the Gospels, homily 40, no. 12). Share with them what you have, so that one day they may deign to share with you what they have [Note: [Col. 0893D] The edition reads: “so that they may share this.”] (Moral. book X, chapter 6, no. 8).

Let every chosen person give what he possesses in such a way that he considers how great is the generosity of the one who rewards. When he gives earthly things, let him not think more than necessary about his own poverty, and let not sadness obscure the light of joy in the offering of his gift.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Suffering of the Elect and Compassion for Their Neighbors

Holy men, caught amid the warfare of tribulations, at one and the same time strike some and strike others by persuasion [Note: [Col. 0893D] The edition reads “they carry on.”] (Moral. book III, chapter 21, no. 39). Against the former they raise the shield of patience; against the latter they hurl the arrows of instruction. Through the remarkable art of virtue, the elect raise themselves to both modes of warfare, so that they teach wisely within and bravely despise adversity without; by teaching they correct the latter, and by enduring they restrain the former.

The elect despise hostile attackers by enduring them, but restore their weakened fellow citizens to salvation by showing compassion. They resist the former, lest they carry others away as well; they fear for the latter, lest they utterly lose the life of righteousness.

Let us see the Apostle Paul, the soldier of God’s camp, fighting against both. For he says: “Battles without, fears within” (2 Corinthians 7:5). He enumerates the wars that he endures externally, saying: “In dangers from rivers, in dangers from robbers, in dangers from my own people, in dangers from the Gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers at sea, in dangers from false brothers” (2 Corinthians 11:26). In this spiritual warfare, let him add what darts Paul hurls against the adversary [Col. 0894A]: “In labor and hardship, in many watchings, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness” (ibid.).

Caught amid so many kinds of conflict, let the Chosen Vessel say with what rampart of watchfulness he also guards the camp. For he says: “Besides those things that are external, my daily pressing concern is the care of all the churches.” Behold: he bravely undertakes battles, and mercifully devotes himself, through compassion, to protecting his neighbors. He recounts the evils he suffers and adds the good things he bestows. Let it be considered what labor it was for the Apostle Paul, at one and the same time, to endure adversity without and protect the weak within.

He suffers battles outwardly because he is torn by blows and bound in chains; inwardly he endures fear because he fears that his suffering may harm not himself but his disciples. The Apostle feared for the downfall of others in his own suffering, lest, when the disciples saw him himself afflicted and beaten for the faith, they should refuse to profess themselves believers. Hence he writes to them: “Let no one be moved by these tribulations. For you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this” (1 Thessalonians 3:3).

O immense compassion of the Apostle Paul! He despises the sufferings that he himself endures and takes care that his disciples suffer nothing of corrupt persuasion in their hearts. In himself he disregards wounds [of the body, and in others] he heals wounds of the heart. The righteous have this distinctive quality: when placed in the pain of their own tribulation, they do not abandon concern for another’s welfare; while suffering adversity and grieving over themselves, they foresee what is necessary for others by teaching them, and, like certain great physicians, they are themselves sick though they have been struck. They endure the lacerations of their own wounds and offer medicines of healing to others.

It is a much lesser labor either to teach when one endures nothing, or to endure when one teaches nothing. Holy men diligently extend themselves to both kinds of battle, of suffering and of compassion; and when they are perhaps struck by tribulations, they undertake outward wars in such a way that they carefully consider how the inward parts of their neighbors might not be torn.

While brave men stand in the battle line, there they strike hostile breasts with arrows; here, placing the shield behind them, they protect the weak. Thus on both sides they remain vigilant with watchful speed, so that they may pierce the bold before them and defend the fearful behind them from wounds.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. What Jubilation Is

Jubilation is said to occur when ineffable joy is conceived in the mind—joy that can neither be concealed nor disclosed in words, yet is revealed through certain movements, although it cannot be expressed in any precise terms (Moral. book XXIV, chapter 6, no. 10). The prophet David, observing that the souls of the elect conceive such great joy in their minds that they cannot disclose it in speech, says: “Blessed is the people who know jubilation” (Psalm 88:16). For he does not say, “who speaks,” but “who knows,” because jubilation can indeed be known by understanding, but cannot be expressed in speech [Note: [Col. 0894D] The edition reads *sed dicto*, “but by a saying.” Our reading is found in the manuscript of Vendôme.]. Through jubilation one perceives what is beyond perception; and when the consciousness of the one who feels scarcely suffices for contemplation, how can the tongue of the one who speaks suffice for expression?

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Desire for the Heavenly Kingdom

[Col. 0895A]

The great cry of the saints is great desire: each person cries out less in proportion as he desires less, and expresses a greater voice in the ears of the unbounded Spirit in proportion as he pours himself more fully into his desire [Note: [Col. 0895D] The edition reads *desiderium*, “desire,” rather than *desiderio*, “in his desire.”] (Moral. book II, chapter 7, no. 11).

Since the mind that asks is accustomed to be moved in one way and the mind that is asked in another, and since the souls of the saints cling to God in the bosom of the inner secret in such a way that they rest through clinging, how are they said to ask when it is clear that they in no way differ from the inner movement [Note: [Col. 0895D] The edition reads “from the inner will.”]? How are they said to ask when it is certain that they know both the will of God and the things that are to come? Yet, because they are placed in him, they are said to ask something from him—not because they desire anything that differs from the will of the one whom they behold, but because, the more ardently they cling to him in mind, the more they receive from him the ability to ask for what they know he wills to do.

Let no one who is heard more slowly believe that he is neglected by heavenly care (Moral. book XXVI, chapter 19, no. 34). Often our desires are heard precisely because they are not fulfilled quickly; and what we eagerly ask to be accomplished prospers better through the very delay. Often our voice is perfected by being postponed; and when our petition seems to be neglected on the surface, our vows are fulfilled more deeply in the root of our thoughts—just as the seeds of crops, pressed down by frost, are strengthened, and the slower they emerge to the surface, the more abundantly they rise toward harvest.

Our desires are extended by delay so that they may advance; they advance so that they may grow strong for what they are to receive; and they are exercised in struggle so that they may be increased by greater rewards in recompense. The labor of the battle is prolonged so that the crown of victory may grow.

Therefore, when the Lord does not hear his own quickly [Note: [Col. 0895D] The edition reads “does not hear.”], when he is thought to repel them, he continually draws them onward [Note: [Col. 0896D] The edition omits *assidue*, “continually.”]. The inner physician cuts and removes from us the contagions of sins that he rejects as deeply present in us, cutting out the poison of corruption with the iron of tribulation; and he pretends not to hear the sick person’s cries precisely as he works to bring about the end of his illness.

The prophet David says: “I will cry by day, and you will not hear; by night also, and it will not be folly for me” (Psalm 21:5) [Note: [Col. 0896D] The edition reads “and by night.”]. As though he were saying: “It does not profit me toward folly that you continually fail to hear me when I cry day and night, because by the very fact that in temporal tribulation you seem to abandon me and do not hear me [Note: [Col. 0896D] The edition omits “and do not hear me.”], you instruct me more deeply in eternal wisdom.”

Again the Psalmist says: “A helper in times of opportunity, in tribulation” (Psalm 9:10). In speaking of tribulation, he first mentioned opportunities, because often we are crushed by tribulation, yet it is not yet opportune that we should be helped toward the desire for deliverance.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Harmony of the Good

Charity makes us free from the yoke of guilt when, through love, it subjects us mutually to one another’s service; when we believe that the goods of others are our own, and offer and present our own goods to others as though they were theirs (Pastoral Rule, part 3, chapter 22). Let people know with complete certainty that, however greatly they may possess the power of virtues, they can in no way become spiritual if they neglect to be united with their neighbors in harmony. It is written: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace” (Galatians 5:22) [Note: [Col. 0896D] The edition reads “but the fruit.”]. Whoever therefore does not care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the Spirit. Hence Paul also says: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” Again he says: “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Preserving Friendship

[Col. 0896B]

A friend is so called as the guardian of the soul (Moral. book XXVII, chapter 15, no. 28). Hence, not without reason, whoever strives to guard God’s will in his commandments is called his friend, as Truth says to the disciples: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends.” And again: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14–15; Moral. book VII, chapter 24, no. 29).

When someone is loved as a friend while placed in prosperity, it is very uncertain whether prosperity or the person is being loved. The loss of happiness tests the strength of love. Hence a certain wise man rightly says: “A friend is not recognized in good fortune, and an enemy is not concealed in adversity” (Sirach 12:8). Prosperity does not reveal a friend, nor does adversity conceal an enemy. The former is often covered by respect for our prosperity, while the latter is exposed by the confidence of adversity.

Our Redeemer indicates how friendship is to be maintained: in many statements of his Scripture he commands that friends be loved in him and enemies be loved for his sake (Book II on the Gospels, homily 27, no. 1). He truly possesses charity who loves his friend in God and loves his enemy for God’s sake.

## CHAPTER XL. On Constant Reading

Sacred Scripture calls the mind of its reader to the heavenly homeland and turns the reader’s heart from earthly desires toward embracing what is above; through more obscure sayings it exercises the strong, and through humble language it caresses the little ones (Moral. book XX, chapter 1, no. 1). The more sacred Scripture is meditated upon, the more it is loved, and the practice of reading removes weariness; it assists the reader’s mind with humble words and raises it with sublime ones.

Sacred Scripture in some way grows along with its readers: it is almost recognized anew by unlearned readers, yet it is always found new by the learned (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 10, no. 2). To the prophet Ezekiel it is said: “Son of man, whatever you find, eat” (Ezekiel 3:1). Whatever is found in sacred Scripture is to be eaten, because its small matters establish a simple life, while its great matters build subtle understanding.

By reading the precepts of sacred Scripture we come back to life, though we had lain dead in guilt (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 7, no. 16). Hence through the Psalmist it is said to the almighty Lord: “I will never forget your words” [Note: [Col. 0897D] The edition reads “your ordinances.”], “because through them you have given me life” (Psalm 118:93).

Sacred Scripture has become for us, amid the darkness of the present life, a light for the journey (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 7, no. 17). Hence Peter says: “To which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Peter 1:19).

When the language of sacred Scripture seems tepid to any reader, the meaning of the divine utterance does not stir his mind, and in his thought it emits no light of understanding [Note: [Col. 0897D] The edition reads “it shines with no light of understanding.”] (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 7, no. 8). But if he seeks a pattern for living well and discovers through the movement of his heart how to place the foot of good work, he finds as much progress in sacred speech as he himself has made in relation to it.

It often happens that someone perceives the words of sacred Scripture to be mystical if, kindled by the grace of contemplation, he raises himself toward heavenly things. For the marvelous and ineffable power of sacred speech is recognized when the reader’s mind is penetrated by heavenly love.

When we attend to sacred utterances, we often endure the ambushes of evil spirits more severely, because they scatter the dust of earthly thoughts over our minds in order to obscure the eyes of our attention from the light of inward vision (Moral. book XVI, chapter 18, no. 23). The patriarch Isaac aptly represents this when the Philistines filled with heaps of earth the wells that he had dug for drawing water (Genesis 26:15). We dig wells, so to speak, when we penetrate deeply into the hidden meanings of Scripture. Yet the Philistines secretly fill them when unclean spirits pour earthly thoughts into us as we strive toward higher things and, as it were, take away the water of divine knowledge that we have found.

The Psalmist had endured the ambushes of evil spirits while examining God’s commandments, when he said: “Depart from me, evildoers, and I will examine the commandments of my God” (Psalm 118:115) [Note: [Col. 0897D] The edition reads *scrutabor*, “I will examine,” rather than *praescrutabor*, “I will examine beforehand.”]. He clearly indicates that he could not examine God’s commandments while enduring the ambushes of evil spirits in his mind.

Readers of sacred speech, while they are uncertain outwardly about what they should determine in their minds, always return, as it were, to the tabernacle; and, like those before the ark of the covenant, they consult the Lord when, concerning matters about which they doubt, they seek within themselves the pages of sacred speech (Moral. book XXIII, chapter 20, no. 38).

## CHAPTER XLI. On Spiritual Delights

Spiritual delights increase desire in the mind even while they satisfy it, because the more their flavor is perceived, the more one recognizes what is to be loved with greater avidity (Book II on the Gospels, homily 36, no. 1). For this reason what has not been possessed cannot be loved, since its flavor is unknown. Who can love what he does not know?

The Psalmist admonishes us, saying: “Taste and see how [Note: [Col. 0898D] The edition reads “that.”] sweet the Lord is” (Psalm 33:9); as though he were openly saying: “You do not know his sweetness if you do not taste it at all. Touch the food of life with the palate of your heart, so that by testing its sweetness you may be able to love it.”

A human being lost spiritual delights when he sinned in paradise. For when he was driven out [Note: [Col. 0898D] The edition reads “he went outside, when he closed his mouth to the food of eternal sweetness.”], he closed his mouth to the food of eternal sweetness. Hence we, too, born amid the hardship of this pilgrimage and already arriving with an aversion to food, do not know what we ought to desire. The more the illness of our aversion grows, the more the mind withdraws from eating that sweetness. It no longer desires inward delights because it has long and extensively grown unaccustomed to eating them.

We waste away from the weariness of our misery and are exhausted by the prolonged disease of hunger. And because we do not wish inwardly to taste the sweetness prepared for us, miserable as we are, we love our hunger outwardly. Yet heavenly mercy does not abandon us even when we abandon it. For it recalls those despised delights before the eyes of our memory, sets them before us, shakes off our sluggishness through the promise, and invites us to repel our aversion, saying: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Book II on the Gospels, homily 36, no. 2).

## CHAPTER XLII. On Discernment

The subtlety of discernment is a great mastery of discipline, so that every ruler may know how to spare the faults of offenders with discernment and cut them away with compassion (Book II on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 20). Those who forgive sins in such a way that they do not correct them, or who strike as though correcting in such a way that they do not forgive, do not possess the spirit of discernment.

It is written in the book of Genesis: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Genesis 4:7, according to the Septuagint). An offering is made rightly when something is done with right intention. But it is not rightly divided if what is done piously is not also examined with subtle discernment. To divide offerings rightly means to weigh and distinguish each of our good efforts. Whoever neglects to do this sins even while offering rightly.

Often, when we do something with good zeal but carefully neglect to discern it, we do not know by what outcome it will be judged; and sometimes what is thought to be the cause of virtue becomes the guilt of a crime (Moral. book III, chapter 13, nos. 23–24). We therefore offer rightly when we perform a good work with good zeal; but we do not divide rightly if we postpone exercising discernment in a good work (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 11, no. 12).

For the person who enters the narrow way is carefully constrained in everything he does by the subtlety of discernment. Whoever expands himself with a secure mind according to his own desires closes the entrance of the narrow gate against himself (Moral. book XXVIII, chapter 11, no. 26). Holy Church observes through discernment what causes produce temptations, and detects from afar the wars of vices that are to come.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Silence

[Col. 0899A]

The tongue must be restrained with discernment, not bound in an unbreakable bond. For it is written: “The wise person will remain silent until the proper time” (Sirach 20:7; Moral. book VII, chapter 37, no. 61). Thus, when he considers the time appropriate, he sets aside the judgment of silence and devotes himself to the service of usefulness by speaking what is fitting.

Concerning the discernment of silence and speech, Solomon says: “A time to speak, and a time to be silent” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). The times of alternation must be weighed with discernment, lest either, when the tongue ought to be restrained, it flow uselessly through words [Note: [Col. 0899D] The edition reads “unrestrainedly release itself,” rather than “flow uselessly.”], or, when it can speak usefully, it restrain itself sluggishly.

Considering the great usefulness of silent restraint, the Psalmist says: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth [Col. 0899B], and a door of enclosure around my lips” (Psalm 149:3). He does not ask that a wall be placed before his mouth, but a door, which can be opened and closed. Hence we too must speak cautiously, so that a discerning mouth may open its voice at the appropriate time [and silence may close it again at the appropriate time].

Those who are excessively silent should carefully strive to consider not only what sort of people they show themselves to be outwardly, but also what sort of people they ought to present themselves inwardly, so that they may fear judgment concealed in their thoughts more than reproach from their neighbors in their words (Pastoral Rule, part 3, chapter 14).

It must be pointed out to those who are excessively silent that, while they carelessly flee certain vices, they become secretly entangled in worse ones. Often, because they restrain their tongue too immoderately, they endure heavier loquacity in their heart, so that their thoughts boil all the more because the violent custody of indiscreet silence constricts them.

Often those who are excessively silent range more widely in their thoughts because they consider themselves more secure, since outwardly they are not seen by their critics. Sometimes the mind of the silent person is lifted up in pride, and he despises those whom he hears speaking as though they were weak. While he closes the mouth of the body, he does not recognize how widely he opens himself to vices through pride.

Often it happens that the mind of the excessively silent person presses down the tongue but elevates the mind. Since he gives no consideration to his own wickedness, he accuses everyone else all the more freely, both more privately and more secretly.

Often those who are excessively silent, when they suffer some injustice, move into sharper pain because they do not speak about what they endure. For if the tongue were calmly to express the troubles inflicted, the pain would flow out of the conscience. Closed wounds cause more torment. When the corruption that seethes within is expelled, the pain is opened toward healing.

Those who are silent beyond what is appropriate should know that, amid the troubles they endure, they intensify the force of pain by holding back their tongue. They must be admonished that, if they love their neighbors as themselves, they should not remain silent about matters for which they rightly reprehend them. Through the medicine of speech the well-being of both parties is served: the wrongful action is restrained in the one who inflicts it, and in the one who suffers it the heat of pain is moderated by opening the wound.

Those who see the evils of their neighbors and nevertheless restrain their tongue in silence are like people who, after seeing wounds, withhold the use of medicine [Col. 0900A]. They become the authors of death precisely because they refused to heal the poison that they could have cured.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On Avoiding Detraction

Those who feed themselves on detraction from another’s life are undoubtedly filled with the flesh of others, as it is written: “Do not eat with those who provide flesh for eating” (Proverbs 23:20; Moral. book XIV, chapter 52, no. 61). To provide flesh for eating means, in conversation marked by disparagement, mutually to speak disparagingly of the faults of one’s neighbors [Note: [Col. 0899D] The edition reads “to speak of,” rather than “to speak disparagingly of.”].

Solomon rightly says of detractors: “For those who are devoted to drink and contribute their share will be consumed, and drowsiness will be clothed in rags” [Note: [Col. 0899D] The edition reads *dormitatio*, “drowsiness,” rather than *dormitio*, “sleep.” The manuscripts of Vendôme, Beauvais, and Utica agree with our reading.] (ibid.). Those are devoted to drink who intoxicate themselves on the disgrace of another’s life. To contribute one’s share means that, just as each person customarily contributes food for eating from his own portion, so in a conversation of detraction he contributes words [Note: [Col. 0900D] The edition reads “for his share.”] [Col. 0900B].

“Those devoted to drink and contributing their share,” he says, “will be consumed,” because, as it is written: “Every detractor will be uprooted” [Note: [Col. 0900D] Perhaps Proverbs 15:5.]. “Drowsiness will be clothed in rags,” because death finds the person whom the languor of his detraction has occupied here in the investigation of crimes in another’s life despised and destitute of all good works.

## CHAPTER XLV. On Compunction
External discipline washes away sins, and compunction pierces the mind stretched out in repentance’s punishment (Morals, Book XXIII, chapter 21, no. 40). Yet these two differ in this respect: the wounds inflicted by blows cause pain, whereas the laments of compunction have a sweet savor. The former torture by afflicting; the latter restore while afflicting. In the former there is sorrow amid affliction; in the latter, joy amid sorrow.

Every sin is a thorn, because, while it drags the mind toward pleasure, it tears it as though by pricking (Morals, Book XX, chapter 10, no. 21). Hence, in the voice of the righteous and penitent, it is said: “I was turned into misery [my misery] when the thorn was broken” (Psalm 31:4). For the mind is turned toward lamentation so that, through repentance, the prick of sin may be broken.

“You have broken my bonds,” he says; “to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Psalm 115:16). The Lord then breaks our bonds when he both shows us the evils we have committed and helps us mourn over those same evils once we recognize them (Morals, Book IX, chapter 62, no. 94). The almighty Lord sets before us the sins of our deeds and, with the gracious hand of his grace, loosens the bonds of the heart, so that our mind may rise toward the leisure of repentance and, freed from the fetters of the flesh, may direct its free step of love toward its creator.

When the vehement spirit of repentance occupies the mind, it disturbs every examination of reprehensible joy within it, so that it now desires nothing except to weep and gives attention to nothing that could terrify it (Morals, Book IV, chapter 19, no. 35). The mind of each of the elect places before its eyes, on one side, the strictness of justice and, on the other, the merit of its sin. It sees what punishment it would deserve if the compassion of the one who spares did not, through present lamentation, customarily rescue it from eternal punishment.

When the powerful force of compunction healthfully overwhelms our minds, devoted to this world as to the sea, with dew, God, as in a violent spirit, shatters the ships of Tarshish (in Paterius, Book XI on the Psalms, chapter 108).

[Note: The following passages are not found among the works of Saint Gregory.]

The almighty Lord afflicts the minds of the carnal, which previously wandered amid the waves of this world, through the coming of the Holy Spirit and in the sorrow of repentance, so that, crushed by pride, they may healthfully lie in humility—those whom previously, in this sea of the world, the wave of their prosperity had lifted to the heights of vanity [Note: [Col. 0901D] The editor reads, “was lifting.”].

Often the minds of the carnal, converted to Christ through repentance, come to regard as burdensome being honored by people, whereas previously they had considered being despised by people a punishment. Those who formerly were accustomed to perpetrating evil and rejoicing in it later do not fear even to be afflicted for the sake of good.

There are four conditions by which the soul of a righteous person is profoundly affected in compunction: when it remembers its evils and, considering where it was, reflects; when, fearing the sentence of God’s judgments and asking itself, it considers where it will be; when, carefully attending to the evils of the present life, it sorrowfully considers where it is; and when, contemplating the good things of the heavenly homeland, which it has not yet attained, it mournfully sees where it is not (Morals, Book XXIII, chapter 21, no. 41).

Paul remembered his former evils and afflicted himself because of what he had been, when he said: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 15:9). Carefully weighing divine judgment, the apostle Paul feared that he would fare badly in the future, saying: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

The same Paul considered the evils of the present life when he said: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6). And: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:22).

Again, that vessel of election contemplated the good things of the eternal homeland, saying: “Now we see through a mirror in an obscure manner; but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12). And again: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, an eternal house not made by human hands in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1) [Note: [Col. 0901D] The editor omits “not.”].

Considering the evils of the present life, blessed Job says: “Human life upon earth is a trial” (Job 7:1). Hence David also says: “Every living human being is wholly vanity” (Psalm 38:6). And although a human being walks in the image of God, nevertheless he will be troubled in vain.

Contemplating the eternal homeland, weighing these evils in which he was and considering those good things in which he was not yet, the Psalmist says: “Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged!” (Psalm 119:5) [Note: [Col. 0902D] The editor reads, “because.”]. And: “I said in my fear: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” (Psalm 30:23).

There are some who have already received, as a gift, the freedom to speak in defense of justice, to protect the oppressed, to give what they possess to the needy, and to possess the fervor of faith; but they still do not have the grace of tears. They have, so to speak, southern and arid land, but still need irrigation. Since they are established in good works, in which they are great and fervent, they must lament intensely either the evils they previously committed, out of fear of punishment, or because of love for the heavenly kingdom.

Although compunction is divided into many forms, since each individual sin is mourned by penitents—for this reason Jeremiah too says in the voice of penitents: “My eye has brought down divisions of waters” (Lamentations 3:48)—nevertheless there are principally two kinds of compunction. For the soul thirsting for God is first pierced by fear, and afterward by love [Note: [Col. 0902D] The editor omits “toward.”].

First it afflicts itself with tears, because, recalling its evils, it fears that it will suffer eternal punishments for them. When the dread has been consumed by prolonged anguish of sorrow, a certain security concerning the presumption of pardon is born, and the spirit is inflamed with love for heavenly joys. The one who first wept lest he be led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom.

Often the mind contemplates what the choirs of angels are, what the fellowship of the holy spirits is, and what the majesty of God’s inner [Note: [Col. 0902D] The editor reads, “eternal.”] vision is; and it laments more because it is absent from everlasting goods than it had wept earlier when it feared eternal evils. Thus perfect compunction of fear hands [Note: [Col. 0902D] The editor reads, “draws”; Longipontanus and the editions agree with our reading.] the soul over to compunction of love.

In the sacred and truthful history, this is represented through a figurative narrative: Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, sitting on a donkey, sighed (Joshua 15:18 and following). Her father said to her: “What do you have?” She replied: “Give me a blessing. You have given me southern and arid land; join to it irrigated land.” Then her father gave her upper and lower irrigation.

Achsah sits upon a donkey when the soul presides over the irrational movements of its flesh. Sighing, she asks her father for irrigated land, because tears of compunction must be sought from our Creator with great groaning. Since, as I said, there are two kinds of compunction, her father gave her upper and lower irrigation. The soul receives upper irrigation when, through tears, it afflicts itself from desire for the heavenly kingdom; it receives lower irrigation when, weeping, it fears the punishments of hell (Dialogues, Book III, chapter 34).

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the Hope and Fear of the Elect

Often the mind of the righteous both laments what it remembers having done perversely and abandons its evil deeds, punishing them with the bitterest laments; yet, while it remembers what it has done, it is terrified by grave fear of the judgment (Morals, Book IV, chapter 36, no. 71). Each of the elect has already converted perfectly, but still does not raise himself to perfect security. As he weighs the strictness of the final examination, he trembles anxiously between hope and fear, because he does not know what the righteous Judge, when he comes, will count among the deeds committed and what he will forgive.

Often the mind of a penitent remembers the wrongs it has committed; but it does not know whether it has wept over these deeds worthily, and it fears lest the enormity of its guilt exceed the measure of its repentance [Note: [Col. 0903D] The editor reads: “whether he has worthily wept over the deeds committed.”]. Often truth has already forgiven the guilt, but the afflicted mind, while deeply anxious for itself, still trembles concerning forgiveness.

Every holy person receives mercy even here, but does not know that he has received it, because a human being abandons his sin by correction and repentance, yet still fears the strict Judge concerning its retribution. There every righteous person sings the Lord’s mercies freely in eternity, without any fear (Psalm 88:1), where there will no longer be uncertainty about forgiveness of sin, where the memory of guilt will no longer enslave the secure mind, where the spirit will not tremble under accusation but will rejoice freely in its pardon (Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 29).

When the prophet David asked, saying, “Turn your eyes away from my sins” (Psalm 50:11), he had said shortly before: “My sin is always before me” (Psalm 50:5). It is as though he were saying: “I ask you not to look upon my sin, because I myself never cease to look upon it.” Hence through another prophet the Lord says: “I will not remember your sins; but you, remember” (Isaiah 43:25).

Those who lament their sins must take care to consider each individual offense, and, while they lament the defilement of their error in each one, cleanse themselves wholly with tears. Through Jeremiah it is said, when the individual sins of Judah were being weighed: “My eye has brought down divisions of waters” (Lamentations 3:48). We bring down divided waters from our eyes when we give separate tears to individual sins. For the mind does not grieve equally over everything at one and the same time; but when it is more sharply touched now by the memory of one fault and now by that of another, it is moved concerning all of them together through each individual one and is cleansed.

Those oppressed by fear and dread must be admonished to trust in the mercy they ask for, lest they perish through excessive affliction. The Lord would not mercifully place sins to be mourned before the eyes of sinners if he intended to strike them strictly by himself. It is clear that he wished to hide from his judgment those whom, by mercifully anticipating them, he made judges of themselves. Hence it is written: “Let us come before his face in confession” (Psalm XCXIV, 2). Hence Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31).

Since holy persons remember that they have sinned, and fear and lament it, what else do they do but cover the body (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 4, no. 5)? They hide their carnal deeds beneath the good works laid over them, through strict examination [Note: [Col. 0903D] The editor reads, “from strict examination.”]. It is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31:1). We cover sins when we place good deeds over evil acts. Everything that is covered is placed underneath, and that with which it is covered is drawn over it from above. Therefore, when we reject the evils we have committed and choose the good things we do [Note: [Col. 0903D] The editor reads, “may do.”], we place a covering over that which we are ashamed to have seen.

Holy persons, while still established in this life, have something that they ought to cover before the eyes of God, because it is wholly impossible for them never to sin either in deed, speech, or thought (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 4, no. 6).

Through blessed Moses the Lord says: “You shall not take as a pledge the upper or lower millstone” (Deuteronomy 24:6). The upper or lower millstone is hope and fear: hope carries one upward, while fear presses the heart downward. The upper and lower millstone are necessarily joined to each other, so that one is useless without the other (Morals, Book XXXIII, chapter 12, no. 24).

Therefore hope and fear must continually be joined in the breast of the sinner, because he hopes in vain for mercy if he does not also trust in mercy [Note: [Col. 0904D] The editor reads: “because he hopes in vain for mercy if he does not also fear justice; he fears justice in vain if he does not also trust in mercy.”]. The upper or lower millstone is forbidden to be removed as a pledge, because the preacher must arrange his preaching with such balance that he neither removes fear while leaving hope behind nor, after removing hope, abandons the sinner to fear alone. The upper or lower millstone is removed if, through the preacher’s tongue, either fear is separated from hope in the sinner’s heart or hope from fear.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Repentance

Every sinner ought to have a double sigh in repentance (Morals, Book XXXII, chapter 3, no. 4). For he both failed to do the good he ought to have done and did the evil he ought not to have done. When we do not rise to good works, we must mourn ourselves doubly, because we have not done what is right and have carried out what is wrong.

Through blessed Moses one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin, and another as a burnt offering (Leviticus 15:29–30). A holocaust is so called because it is wholly burned. We therefore offer one turtledove for sin when we give a sigh for our guilt; we make a holocaust of the other when, for what we neglected to do [Note: [Col. 0904D] The editor reads, “neglected to do in the past.”], we burn completely with the fire of sorrow and, setting ourselves ablaze, burn.

Blessed Job, advancing through scourges and dissenting from himself in severe reproach, says: “Therefore I reproach myself and do penance” (Job 42:6). To do penance is, after contemplating the supreme essence, to recognize oneself as nothing other than dust and ashes (Morals, Book XXXV, chapter 5, nos. 6–7).

In sackcloth there is the roughness and pricking of sins; in ashes the dust of the dead is displayed. For this reason both are customarily applied to repentance, so that in the prickling of sackcloth we may recognize what we have done through guilt, and in the ashes’ dust discern what we have become through judgment. Let the piercing vices therefore be considered in sackcloth, and in ashes let the just punishment of the vices that follows through the sentence of death be considered.

For after sin the shame of the flesh arose. Let a person see in the roughness of sackcloth what he did through pride; let him see in the ashes how far he reached by sinning. The sinner is pricked by a kind of sackcloth when, in his mind, he is rubbed by the sharp goads of reproaches. He does penance in ashes because he carefully considers what he became through just judgment as a result of the first sin (Morals, Book IV, chapter 14, no. 26; Job 3:4).

We turn day into darkness when, strictly punishing ourselves, we torment through the severe laments of repentance the very blandishments of sinful pleasure, and pursue with tears whatever we silently sin in our hearts through pleasure. Every faithful person, knowing that thoughts will be examined subtly in judgment, searches himself inwardly and subjects himself to intense examination before judgment, so that the strict Judge may come peacefully because he sees the guilty person whom he wishes to examine already punished for his guilt.

Almighty God carefully considers our deeds, yet mercifully forgives them to penitents (Morals, Book XII, chapter 16, no. 20). He sees hardness in sinners, yet, with grace preceding, softens it for repentance. God counts our sins when he turns us toward mourning each thing we have done. He mercifully forgives them because, while we punish ourselves, he does not judge them at the final examination; as Paul testifies when he says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31; Morals, Book XII, chapter 17, no. 21).

What we do outwardly, unless we wash it away through repentance, is kept hidden in the secrecy of God’s judgments, so that eventually it may emerge from the seal [Note: [Col. 0905D] The editor reads, “from the sack of secrecy.” The reading in our text is supported by old and recent examinations.] of secrecy into the public forum of judgment.

But when we are worn down by the scourge of discipline for the evils we have committed and lament them through repentance, he both marks and heals our iniquity, because he neither leaves it unpunished here nor reserves it for punishment in judgment. God therefore marks our sins because he carefully attends to them here in order to strike; but he heals them because through the scourge he entirely forgives them.

Blessed Job, assuming the person of the human race, says: “You have sealed up my sins as in a sack” (Job 14:17). Our sins are sealed in a sack when we always weigh the evils we have committed with a troubled heart. For what is the human heart other than God’s sack? We carry our sins sealed in God’s sack because our merciful creator forgives the faults that we recognize by looking upon them and repenting.

Rightly, after the sins sealed in the sack, it is said: “But you have healed my iniquity” (Job, same passage), as though he openly said: “What you now seal, so that I may see it through repentance, you undoubtedly act upon so that it may not be seen in retribution.”

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On Confession

It is a testimony of humility both for each person to recognize his own iniquity and, once recognized, to disclose it by the voice of confession (Morals, Book XXII, chapter 15, no. 30). It is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling [Note: [Col. 0905D] The editor reads, “by concealing.” Laudensis, Corbeiensis, Germanus, the second hand, and Vallicellianus agree with our reading.] and not to reveal the sin committed by confessing it, but to defend it by denying it and, by defending what has been exposed, to multiply it [Note: [Col. 0906D] The editor reads: “and to hide what was committed by denying it, and to multiply it when exposed,” etc.].

From that fall of the first human being we derive these increases of wickedness, since from it we drew the very root of guilt. The first human being had been summoned for this purpose: to erase through confession the sin he had committed by transgression. He was asked where he was so that he might look upon the guilt he had committed and, by confessing, recognize how far he was from the presence of his creator (Genesis 3:10).

The signs of true confession are present if, when someone calls himself a sinner, he does not contradict another person who says the same thing about him (Morals, Book XXII, chapter 15, no. 33). It is written: “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning” (Proverbs 18:17). Anyone who confesses himself a sinner without being accused does not wish to appear more a sinner than righteous.

The truth of confession is proved when another person rebukes the evil we have done. If we defend ourselves proudly, it is clear that we were falsely calling ourselves sinners. We must take the greatest care both to confess willingly the evils we have done and not to deny them when others accuse us. For it is a vice of pride that what someone deigns to confess as though voluntarily, he disdains to have said about him by others. The confession of the sinner is the debtor’s pledge; a pledge is taken from a debtor when the confession of sin is held from the sinner.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the Gravity of Counsel

It is one thing to be serious through counsel and another through sin; one thing to be serious through steadfastness and another through guilt. The former seriousness has the weight of virtue; the latter, the weight of a burden (Morals, Book XIX, chapter 5, no. 8).

In view of heavenly reward, souls often receive this benefit: they no longer fall away from their intention toward God through a light movement, but remain fixed in him with the grave steadfastness of constancy. The Jewish people were lightly moved; concerning them the prophet says: “He went wandering in the way of his heart. I saw his way and dismissed him” (Isaiah 57:17).

Serious counsel drives out all instability of wandering. There are souls that, through a light movement, desire now this thing and now that [Note: [Col. 0906D] The editor reads, “desire.”]. Almighty God, therefore, because he does not lightly weigh the light fluctuations of minds, judges the wandering of the heart by abandoning it. But when by grace he looks upon the wandering mind, he fixes it in the stability of counsel.

When almighty God mercifully deigns to look upon the light movements of a human being, he immediately forms that person toward the maturity of steadfastness and, through the regard of heavenly grace, suddenly brings his heart to the gravity of counsel.

## CHAPTER L. On Hospitality

It is very necessary for us to love the hospitality of brotherhood and to cherish works of charity (Book II on the Gospel, homily 23, no. 2). Hence the distinguished preacher, commending both to us, says: “Let brotherly charity remain among you, and do not forget hospitality” (Hebrews 13:1).

Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, commends to us the grace of this hospitality, which must be shown kindly to our brothers, saying: “Be hospitable to one another without murmuring” (1 Peter 4:9). Hence Truth itself says: “I was a guest, and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35). With wondrous compassion, our Redeemer speaks from the compassion of his members, saying: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40). He therefore helps us because he is our head, and he is helped in his members through our good works (Morals, Book XVI, chapter 2, no. 2).

We must consider how much the hospitality of brotherly compassion is worth, and how greatly the bowels of mercy join us to almighty God (Book II on the Gospel, homily 39, no. 10). We draw near to him who is above all things precisely by lowering ourselves beneath ourselves through compassion for our neighbor. In bodily matters no one touches high places unless he is stretched upward; in spiritual matters, however, it is certain that the more we are drawn downward through compassion, the more truly we approach what is above.

For the building up of the human race, the Redeemer did not consider it sufficient merely to declare that at the final judgment he would say: “As long as you did it for one of these least of my brothers, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:42), unless he also showed before the judgment that this was true in himself, demonstrating that whoever now performs good works for the needy renders them especially to the one for whose love he performs them. And each person receives a greater reward in himself to the extent that he does not despise the one who appears more worthy of contempt.

## CHAPTER LI. On the Corruption of the Present Life

For the righteous who are placed in this life, the very burden of their corruption is heavy: vigils weary them, and sleep is sought so that the labor and anxiety of vigils may be moderated (Morals, Book XII, chapter 13, no. 17). Sometimes even sound kills, hunger wears down the body, and food is required to drive away its necessity. Yet often food itself weighs down those who had sought it to repel the burden of weakness.

Very heavy is the burden of corruption. If it were not exceedingly burdensome, Paul would never say: “The creature was subjected to vanity, not willingly but because of him who subjected it in hope, because the creature itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that every creature groans [Note: [Col. 0907D] The editor reads, “sighs.”] and is in labor until now” (Romans 8:20).

As long as we are subject to corruption, we do not at all respond to our Creator, because, since corruption is far removed from incorruption, there is no suitable likeness for our response (Morals, Book XII, chapter 14, no. 18). Blessed Job, desiring the state of eternal incorruption, says: “You will extend your right hand to the work of your hands” (Job 14:15; Morals, Book XII, chapter 15, no. 19) [Note: [Col. 0907D] The editor reads, “you will extend your right hand.”].

It is as though he plainly said: A corruptible creature can persist toward incorruption because it is raised up by the hand of almighty God and held in persistence by the grace of his regard. The human creature, precisely because it is a creature, possesses within itself the tendency to flow downward; but from its creator the human being receives the ability both to be carried above itself in contemplation and to be held within itself in incorruption [Note: [Col. 0907D] The editor reads, “in corruption.”]. The human creature, subject to corruption, is raised by the right hand of its Creator to the state of immutability, so that it may not flow downward beneath itself but persist in incorruption.

## CHAPTER LII. On Bodily Health

Those who are healthy must be admonished to use bodily health for the health of the mind, lest, if they turn the grace of the health they have received toward the use of wickedness, they become worse through the gift and subsequently deserve heavier punishments, because they now do not fear to misuse God’s more abundant benefits (Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 12).

Those who are healthy must be admonished not to despise the opportunity of earning health forever. For it is written: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2) [Note: [Col. 0908D] The editor reads, “now is the acceptable time.”]. They must be told not to refuse to please God when they can, lest, when they wish to do so, they later be unable.

When bodily health, received for doing good works, is neglected, its value as a gift is understood only after it has been lost; and health that was granted at a suitable time but not beneficially used is sought at the end, but without profit.

Through the wisest Solomon it is said: “Do not give your labor to strangers, nor your years to the cruel one, lest strangers be filled with your strength, your labors be in another’s house, and you groan at the end, when you have consumed your flesh and your body” (Proverbs 5:9 and following) [Note: [Col. 0908D] The editor reads, “your honor.”].

Who are strangers to us except the evil spirits, who have been separated from the lot of the heavenly homeland? And what is our honor except that, although we have been formed in earthly bodies, we have nevertheless been created in the image and likeness of our creator? Or who is the cruel one except that apostate angel who, by his pride, struck himself with the punishment of death and, though ruined, did not spare the human race from inflicting death upon it?

He gives his honor to strangers who, created in the image and likeness of God, administers the times of his life to the pleasures of evil spirits. He gives his years to the cruel one who spends the span of life granted to him according to the will of a wickedly dominating adversary.

Whoever, through the bodily health he has received and the wisdom of mind bestowed upon him, labors not to exercise virtues but to perpetrate vices, does not multiply his own household through his own strength but multiplies the dwellings of strangers—that is, those made for unclean spirits—acting either in lust or in pride, so that the number of the lost may increase by his addition.

Often the health received by the flesh is spent on vices. But when it is suddenly withdrawn, when the flesh is worn down by afflictions, and when the soul is already compelled to depart, health, long possessed badly, is sought as though for living well. Then people rightly groan that they did not wish to serve God, when they are utterly unable, by serving him, to recover the losses caused by their negligence. Hence elsewhere it is said: “When he slew them, then they sought him” (Psalm 77:34).

## CHAPTER LIII. On Bodily Illness

The sick must be admonished to recognize that they are God’s children precisely because the scourges of discipline chastise them. For if he had not intended to give an inheritance to corrected children, he would not have cared to educate them through afflictions (Pastoral Rule, as above).

The sick must be told that, if they believe the heavenly homeland is theirs, it is necessary for them to suffer hardships in this life as in a foreign land. The stones of the Lord’s sanctuary were hewn outside so that they might be placed in the construction of the temple without the sound of a hammer. For now we are hewn outside through scourges, so that afterward we may be arranged within God’s temple without the blows of discipline. Thus whatever is superfluous in us may now be cut away by the blows, and then only the harmony of charity may bind us together in the building.

The sick must be admonished to consider how severely the scourges of discipline chastise the sons of the flesh for the sake of receiving earthly inheritances [Note: [Col. 0909D] The editor reads, “carnal sons.”]. Why, then, is the punishment of divine correction burdensome to us, through which we both receive an inheritance that can never be lost and avoid punishments that will always endure [Note: [Col. 0910D] The editor reads, “what then?”]?

The sick must consider how great a health of heart bodily affliction is. It recalls the mind to knowledge of itself, and the memory of infirmity reforms the mind that health often casts down, so that the spirit, which is led outside itself in exaltation, may remember to what condition it is subject from the flesh that has been struck and that it endures.

Often the sluggish flesh, through its affliction, reveals God to the mind by its scourge—God whom the mind itself, presiding over the flesh, did not see—so that it obstructs the anxiety of the spirit that desires to advance in this world, as though journeying along a road, until the invisible one who confronts it becomes known.

The sick must be admonished to consider how great a gift bodily affliction is: it both washes away sins already committed and restrains those that might be committed; taken from outward wounds, it inflicts the wounds of repentance upon the shaken mind.

In Solomon’s Proverbs it is written: “The bruise of a wound wipes away evils, and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly” (Proverbs 20:20). The bruise of a wound wipes away evils because the pain of scourges washes away either contemplated or perpetrated wickedness. When we are struck outwardly, we are silently and sorrowfully recalled to the memory of our sins. We bring before our eyes everything we have done wrongly, and through what we suffer outwardly we grieve more deeply over what we have done inwardly.

Thus, amid the open wounds of the body, the secret wound of the belly cleanses us more fully, because the hidden wound of sorrow heals the wickedness of evil deeds.

The sick must be admonished to preserve the virtue of patience, continually considering how many evils the Redeemer endured from those he had created. Why, then, is it thought harsh for a human being to endure scourges from God for his evils, if God endured so many evils from human beings for the sake of their good? Or who, possessing sound understanding, could remain ungrateful for his own affliction, if the one who lived here without sin did not depart from here without scourging?

## CHAPTER LIV. On Bodily Death
The days appointed for each person by God’s foreknowledge cannot be increased or diminished, unless it happens that they are foreknown in such a way that they are longer with the best works, or shorter with the worst, just as Hezekiah earned an extension of his days by the outpouring of his tears, and as it is written concerning the perverse: “Death confronts the undisciplined” (Moral. XII, ch. 52, no. 58). Everything that we labor for according to the present age scarcely lasts until death (Book II on the Gospel, homily 27, no. 5). For intervening death cuts off the fruit of our labor; but what is done for eternal life is preserved even after death, and it begins to appear when the fruit of bodily labors has ceased to be seen. That recompense therefore begins where this life ends.

Our Lord wished the final hour to be unknown to us for this reason: so that it might always be feared; so that, while we cannot foresee it, we may prepare for it without interruption (Book I on the Gospel, homily 13, no. 6). Since we do not know the time of the death that is to come, and cannot work after death, it remains for us to seize the time granted before death. Thus death itself will be conquered when it comes, if it is always feared before it comes (Moral. XIV, ch. 55, no. 68).

Our Redeemer accepted death so that we would not fear dying. He displayed the resurrection so that we might trust that we can rise again. For this reason he wished that same death to last no more than three days, lest, if resurrection were delayed in him, hope of it should be entirely lost in us. Through the death of the flesh we remain in the dust until the end of the world; but on the third day Christ blossomed again from death’s barrenness, and in the renewal of his flesh he showed us the power of his divinity.

Once the soul has been stripped of the flesh, the sight of man no longer perceives it, because after death he does not free the one whom grace did not restore to pardon before death (Moral. VIII, ch. 15, no. 30). Blessed David says: “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth” (Psalm CXLV, 4). Then the spirit is cast down to earth through knowledge of its guilt, when the flesh—which it regards as its life—is compelled to return to dust.

Man is strengthened for a little while in the present life, because here he receives the strength to live for a short time, so that he may pass into eternity, where no end will confine his life (Moral. Book XII, ch. 19, no. 24). But in this brief span, in which he has been strengthened, he gathers what he will find in eternity—either so that he may rejoice forever, or so that he may not escape the punishments he has incurred.

In the Book of blessed Job it is written: “You will change his face and send him away” (Job XIV, 20; Moral. Book XII, ch. 20, no. 25). A person’s face is changed when his appearance is worn away by death. He is sent away because he is compelled, unwillingly, to pass into eternity from those things that he willingly held. And when he is brought to those things, he does not know what has become of the things he long pondered and held after they have been left behind.
