Just as those who are still alive do not know where the souls of the dead are kept, so the dead do not know how the life of those living in the flesh after them is ordered, because the life of the spirit is far removed from the life of the flesh; and just as corporeal and incorporeal things differ in kind, so they are also distinct in knowledge (ibid., ch. 21, no. 26). This, however, must not be understood of holy souls, because those who see within the splendor of almighty God cannot in any way be thought to be ignorant of anything that exists outside.

Almighty God wished our end to remain hidden from us so that, while we are uncertain when we will die, we might always be found ready for death [Note: [Col. 0911C] The edition reads, “that we may be found.”] (Moral. Book I, ch. 38, no. 43). Why, then, does one exalt himself as though secure, whose life is held under the penalty of uncertainty [Col. 0911B]?

The outstanding preacher Paul says: “We who are in this dwelling groan, being weighed down, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Corinthians V, 4; Moral. Book XXXI, ch. 33, no. 70). Behold, he desires to die, and yet fears to be stripped of the flesh. Why is this? Because although victory rejoices forever, the punishment of death nevertheless disturbs him in the present [Note: [Col. 0911C] The edition lacks “of death.”]. And although love of the reward that follows prevails, the stroke of pain still touches the soul, not without sorrow.

For just as a brave man, when he girds himself with weapons for the battle that is already near, both trembles and hastens, both quakes and rages—he appears to fear through his pallor, yet is driven forward vehemently by anger—so a holy man, when he sees himself drawing near to the ordeal of death, is shaken by the weakness of his nature and strengthened by the firmness of his hope [Col. 0911C]. He trembles at the death that is near, and yet rejoices that through dying he will live more truly.

No holy man can pass to the kingdom except by death intervening. Therefore he is, as it were, doubtful while trusting, and trusting while doubtful; he fears while rejoicing, and rejoices while fearing, because he knows that he will not reach the prize of rest unless he crosses with labor what lies between.

When we wish to drive illnesses from our body, we indeed take the bitter cup of purgation sadly, but rejoice with certainty in the health that follows. Since the body cannot otherwise attain health, we willingly drink even what is distasteful. And when the soul sees that life is contained in bitterness, it grows cheerful even while troubled by sorrow.

In the Book of Solomon it is written: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, wherever it falls, there it will remain” (Ecclesiastes XI, 3; Moral. Book XII, ch. 4, no. 5). By the name of the tree the just or even the unjust man is signified, as the Lord says through the prophet: “I, the Lord, have humbled the lofty tree” (Ezekiel XVII, 24).

On the day of his death the just man falls toward the south, while the sinner falls toward the north, because the just man is led through the fervor of the spirit to joys, whereas the sinner is rejected in the coldness of his heart together with the apostate angel who said: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isaiah XIV, 13).

Wherever the tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, there it will remain, because when, at the time of human death, either a holy or a wicked spirit receives the soul departing from the enclosure of the flesh, it will retain it with itself forever, without any change. Thus neither will the one raised up fall into punishment at the judgment [Note: [Col. 0912C] The edition reads, “into punishment.”], nor will the one sunk in eternal punishments rise again to the remedy of deliverance (Moral. Book VIII, ch. 15, no. 30).

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0911]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the fourfold character of speech

Everything that is said can be distinguished according to a fourfold character: whether evil things are said evilly, good things well, evil things well, or good things evilly (Moral. Book XXII, ch. 1, [Col. 0911D] no. 15).

An evil thing is said evilly when a wicked course is urged, as it is written: “Bless God, and die” (Job II, 9). A good thing is said well when what is right is proclaimed rightly, as John says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew III, 2).

An evil thing is said well when a vice is expressed through the speaker’s mouth for the purpose of condemning it, as Paul says: “Their women exchanged natural use for that which is against nature” (Romans I, 26). In that passage he also added the detestable crimes of men, but narrated dishonorable things honorably, so that by narrating dishonorable things he might recall many to the pattern of honor.

A good thing is said evilly when something right is not brought forth with a right intention, as the Pharisees are reported to have said to the man whose sight had been restored: “You be his disciple” (John IX, 28). They said this as a curse, certainly, not as a prayerful wish. Or as Caiaphas said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, so that the whole nation may not perish” (John XI, 50). He spoke something good, but not well, because while he sought the cruelty of death, he prophesied the grace of redemption.

## CHAPTER TWO. On divine judgments

Since the divine judgments by which, in this life, good people are sometimes treated badly and bad people well are exceedingly hidden, they are even more hidden when good people are treated well here and bad people badly (Moral. Book V, ch. 1, no. 1).

For when good people fare badly and bad people well, this may perhaps be discerned: good people receive here whatever they have done wrong, so that they may be more fully freed from eternal damnation; and bad people find here the good things they do for this life, so that they may be led afterward to punishments alone. Hence the rich man burning in hell is told: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke XVI, 25).

When good people fare well in the present age and bad people badly, it is very uncertain whether the good receive good things for this reason: that, being encouraged by them, they may grow toward something better; or whether, by a just and hidden judgment, they receive here the reward of their works so that they may be emptied of the rewards of the life to come. Likewise, it is uncertain whether adversities strike the wicked in order to correct them and protect them from eternal punishments, or whether their punishment begins here, so that when it is completed it may lead them to the final torments of Gehenna.

Because the human mind is weighed down by the grave darkness of its uncertainty amid the divine judgments, holy men, when they see worldly prosperity available to them, are troubled by fearful suspicion. They fear that they are receiving here the fruit of their labors; they fear that divine justice sees a hidden wound in them and, piling up external gifts upon them, rejects them from within.

Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “His eyelids question the children of men” (Psalm X, 5; Book II on Ezekiel, homily 5, no. 6). For the eyelids of God are his judgments, which close something to us and open something to us. By opening, they question us whether we are not lifted up through understanding. By closing, they question us whether we do not despise what we are unable to understand. With open eyelids we see; with closed ones we see nothing (Moral. Book XXVIII, ch. 4, no. 13).

What, then, do we understand by the eyelids of God except, as was said a little earlier, his judgments? These are closed to human beings in one respect and opened to them in another. With the veil of our ignorance cast over us, the incomprehensibility of divine judgment cannot in any way be penetrated by the eye of the human mind, as it is written: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” [Note: [Col. 0913D] The edition reads, “Your judgments are a great abyss.”] (Psalm XXXV, 7; Moral. Book XXIX, ch. 30, no. 57).

Let no one desire to scrutinize the divine judgments—why one person is rejected and another chosen, or why one is chosen and another rejected—for, as Paul testifies, we have learned: “His judgments are inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable” (Romans XI, 33; Moral. Book IX, ch. 15, no. 22).

The deeds of divine judgment must always be venerated without questioning, because they can never be unjust. To seek a reason for his hidden counsel is nothing other than to act arrogantly against his counsel. When the reason for God’s judgments cannot be discerned, it remains for us to be silent with humility beneath his deeds, because the understanding of the flesh is never sufficient to penetrate the secrets of his majesty.

Let the human mind return to itself, and let it not seek what it cannot grasp concerning the divine judgments, lest, if the cause of divine anger is investigated [lacuna: “examined further”], it be provoked, and pride ignite ineradicably what humility could have appeased. Through the apostle Paul it is said: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans IX, 20; Moral. IX, ch. 14, no. 21).

Considering himself, man falls silent and fears to scrutinize the divine judgments, recognizing that he is dust. He is shown to be unable to answer God because he is called man. For, since he was taken from the earth, he is not worthy to scrutinize the judgments above.

The same outstanding preacher, considering the hidden judgments of God, says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!” (Romans XI, 35; Moral. Book XXVIII, ch. 4, no. 13). When he was examining the hidden judgments of God concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, and could not reach them, he gave a thoroughly proper answer: in that very ignorance, he knowingly bowed before God. However greatly anyone may advance in virtue, however much he may grow in knowledge, he is not sufficient to penetrate the manner by which the Creator governs us through his judgments.

## CHAPTER THREE. On those who fall into sins, and how they can rise after their fall

Those who have experienced the sins of the flesh should at least fear the sea after shipwreck and dread, now that they know them, the dangers of their destruction, lest those who were mercifully preserved after committing evil should die by wickedly repeating it (Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 28).

To the sinful soul that never ceases from sin it is said: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed” (Jeremiah III, 3). Those who have fallen must therefore be admonished to strive that, if they were unwilling to preserve intact the good things of nature, they may at least repair what has been torn.

What will those who have experienced the sins of the flesh have to say if, while others remain whole, they do not recover even after their losses? What will they say if, while many carry others with them to the kingdom, they do not bring even themselves back to the Lord who awaits them?

Those who have fallen must be told to consider their past offenses and avoid those that threaten. Let them recall their former faults to memory and be ashamed to be defiled in the future.

Through the prophet Ezekiel it is said concerning the daughters of Judah: “They committed fornication in Egypt in their youth” [Note: [Col. 0914D] The edition reads, “In Egypt, in their youth they committed fornication.”]; “there their breasts were pressed down, and the breasts of their puberty were broken” (Ezekiel XXIII, 3).

In Egypt the breasts are pressed down when the will of the human mind is subjected to the shameful desire of this world. In Egypt the breasts of virginity are broken when natural faculties, still intact in themselves, are corrupted by the defilement of concupiscence that assails them.

Those who have experienced the sins of the flesh must be admonished to observe with vigilant care how great a benevolence God displays toward us when, after our offenses, we return to him and he opens the lap of his mercy.

Through the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says: “If a man dismisses his wife, and she, departing, marries another man, will he return to her again? Will that woman not be polluted and defiled? Yet you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jeremiah III, 1).

Behold, an argument from justice is proposed concerning a woman who has fornicated and been abandoned [Note: [Col. 0914D] The edition reads, “is proposed.”]; yet when we return after our fall, not justice but mercy is shown to us. From this let us gather how wickedly we sin if, when we offend, such mercy is shown to us, and yet we do not return.

Or what pardon will there be from him for the wicked person who does not cease calling him after his sin?

The prophet Isaiah says: “Your eyes will see your teacher, and your ears will hear the word of one admonishing from behind” (Isaiah XXX, 20). Anyone perceives God’s words of admonition as though God were placed before him when, before committing sins, he recognizes the commands of God’s will. He still stands before his face, since he has not yet despised him by sinning.

But when, abandoning the good of innocence and choosing iniquity, he pursues it, he now turns his back upon God’s face. Almighty God, as though following us from behind, admonishes us because even after sin he persuades us to return to him. He recalls the one who has turned away, does not look upon the offenses committed, and opens the lap of his mercy to the returning person.

We hear the voice of the one admonishing from behind if, after our sins, we return with a humble and contrite heart. We ought therefore to be ashamed of the mercy of the one who calls us if we do not wish to fear his justice, because he is despised with a more serious wickedness when, despite being despised, he still does not disdain to call us.

Through the prophet Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0915D] The edition reads, “through another prophet.” And indeed the testimony cited by Gregory is not from Jeremiah but from Micah.] the Lord says: “You will go as far as Babylon; there you will be delivered” (Micah IV, 10; Book I on Ezekiel, homily 10, no. 22).

Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” Often, after someone has fallen into the confusion of vices, he returns to repentance, ashamed of the evils he has committed, and raises himself from his falls by living well. What, then, has such a person done except come as far as Babylon and there be delivered?

Sometimes, ashamed of the evils he has done, a person rises against himself and returns to a state of uprightness by doing good. He is therefore delivered in Babylon who, through divine grace, is shown to have been saved even from confusion.

The prophet is therefore speaking of transmigration when he rebukes those who, through transmigration, have fallen from a state of uprightness into the vices of error [Note: [Col. 0916D] The edition reads, “by migrating.”].

## CHAPTER FOUR. On gifts or offerings to be offered to God

Almighty God does not accept a gift from the hand when it is offered by a heart bound to wickedness. The mind of the person who wishes to offer a gift to God must first be cleansed, because everything given to God is weighed according to the mind of the giver. Every stain of wickedness must be wiped away from our inner person through a change of thought, because an offering does not know how to appease the judge’s anger unless the purity of the offerer makes it pleasing (Moral. Book XXII, ch. 14, nos. 27–28).

In the Book of Genesis it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts; but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look” (Genesis IV, 4–5). Sacred Scripture does not say: “He looked upon Abel’s gifts, but did not look upon Cain’s gifts.” Rather, it first says that he looked upon Abel, and then adds, “and upon his gifts.” Again, it says that he did not look upon Cain, and then adds, “nor upon his gifts.”

For what is given is received from the heart of the giver. Thus it was not Abel because of the gifts, but the gifts offered because of Abel, that were pleasing. The Lord is first read to have looked upon the one who gave, before looking upon what he gave. By attending to the order of this narrative, we learn that external gifts are seasoned by the inner purity of the heart.

The virtue of discernment should teach each of us what our disposition ought to be when we supply external goods not only to God through the vow of offering but also to our neighbors. The Lord does not wish to receive a sacrifice from those who are at odds with one another; he refuses to accept a burnt offering. From this we should judge how great the evil of discord is, since it causes even that to be rejected through which guilt is loosened (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 9).

In the Book of Ecclesiasticus it is written: “Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV, 24; Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 21). What could be more intolerable than the death of a son before his father’s eyes? This sacrifice is therefore shown to be regarded with such anger that it is compared to the grief of a bereaved father.

It is one thing to show mercy on account of sins; it is another to sin in order to show mercy. The latter can no longer even be called mercy, because what grows bitter through the poison of a pestilential root does not produce sweet fruit.

Through the prophet the Lord condemns the sacrifices of wicked people, saying: “I am the Lord, loving justice and hating robbery in a burnt offering” (Isaiah LXI, 8). Many people take things away from the needy and give them to God. But how severely the Lord rejects them he demonstrates by saying: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, being offered from crime” (Proverbs XXI, 27).

Very often the worst people consider how much they give to God through their offering, but refuse to consider how much they steal; as though they count the wages of their works while refusing to weigh the guilt of their crimes.

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the five bodily senses

Almost no one is unaware that the five senses of our body—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—draw from the brain the power of discernment and sensation for everything they sense and distinguish (Moral. Book XI, ch. 6, no. 8).

Although the brain’s sensory faculty is one judge, presiding within, it nevertheless distinguishes the five senses through their own channels. Almighty God has worked in the human race with marvelous arrangement so that the eye does not hear, the ear does not see, the mouth does not smell, the nose does not taste, and the hands do not smell. Although everything is directed by the one sense of the brain, none of these senses can do anything other than what, by the Creator’s arrangement, it has received the capacity to do.

From these bodily and external senses we must gather interior and spiritual realities, so that through what is public in us we may pass to what is secret within us and hidden from us. Thus in the Gospel the five talents express knowledge of the five senses, that is, the external senses (Matthew XXV, 15; Book I on the Gospel, homily 9, no. 1). The two talents signify understanding and action; the one talent signifies understanding alone.

Each person subsists in the five bodily senses. But when the five is doubled, it completes the number ten (Book I on the Gospel, homily 12, no. 1). And because a multitude of the faithful is gathered from both sexes, holy Church is declared to resemble ten virgins.

To preserve purity of heart, we must maintain discipline over our external senses (Moral. Book XXI, ch. 2, no. 4). For however greatly the mind may excel in virtue, however strong it may be in gravity, the carnal senses nevertheless prescribe something childish externally. Unless they are restrained by the weight of inner seriousness and by a kind of youthful vigor, they drag the weakened mind toward every fleeting and trivial thing.

We often fall into guilt through sight if we carelessly look upon what is forbidden. Although the soul is invisible, it is not touched by the delight of bodily things except insofar as, being joined to the body, it has in the body’s senses certain openings through which it may go forth.

The prophet Jeremiah, speaking of the bodily senses, says: “Death has climbed through our windows; it has entered our houses” (Jeremiah IX, 21). Death climbs through windows and enters houses when, coming through the bodily senses, desire bursts into the dwelling of the mind.

Through the prophet Isaiah it is said of the just: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isaiah LX, 8). The just are said to fly like clouds because they are lifted above earthly contaminations; and they are like doves at their windows because through the bodily senses they do not look upon external things with predatory intent, and carnal desire does not carry them outward.

Holy Job, who presides as a most just judge over the bodily senses he has received as subordinate ministers, sees faults before they come and closes the windows of his body against death lying in wait [Note: [Col. 0917] The edition reads, “against the enemy lying in wait.” The German and Corbie manuscripts nevertheless also have “against death lying in wait.”], saying: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin” (Job XXXI, 1).

Although the soul is invisible, it is not touched by the delight of bodily things except insofar as, being joined to the body, it has in the body’s senses certain openings through which it may go forth. The five bodily senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—are like certain roads of the mind, through which it comes outward and desires what lies outside its substance.

Through these bodily senses, as through certain windows, the soul looks upon external things; looking upon them, it desires them. Whoever looks carelessly outward through these windows of the body often falls into the delight of sin even against his will; and, bound by desires, begins to will what he did not will.

The reckless soul, because it did not take precautions beforehand against seeing carelessly what it might desire, afterward, once blinded, begins to desire what it saw. Hence the prophet’s mind, which had often been raised up and occupied with inner mysteries, because it carelessly saw another man’s wife, was later darkened and joined itself unlawfully to her (II Samuel XI, 2).

## CHAPTER SIX. On Satan’s temptations and the deceptions of demons

The ancient enemy circles around the paths of the good with such an art of ambush that, through the good deeds he has observed them perform, he seeks an entrance to evil (Moral. Book XXXIII, [Col. 0918A] ch. 8, no. 15).

For when he sees one person giving generously, he uses this to kindle another with the flame of discord. When he sees one showing mercy, he persuades another to become angry, so that, by insinuating that the good was not done in common, he may sever harmonious minds from the good of shared grace.

Very often, when the ancient enemy cannot break the minds of the just by persuading them to evil, he strives to sow evil among them through their good actions. But holy men overcome these ambushes all the more swiftly because they detect them more subtly.

When a certain Corinthian had committed the crime of incest, the outstanding teacher handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, for the satisfaction of repentance, and preserved his spirit safe for the day of the Lord (I Corinthians V, 5). Through a great art of instruction, he was handed over under compulsion to the one to whom he had voluntarily submitted in guilt, so that the one who had been the author of wickedness leading to vice might himself become the scourge of discipline.

The ancient enemy, inflamed by the torch of his own malice, is at odds with the sincerity of divine innocence, but even in being at odds with it he does not deviate from its judgment (Moral. Book XXXIII, ch. 14, II, 28). The enemy of the human race always desires to test the just by his malevolent art, but the Lord permits this to happen for their testing, either mercifully or justly.

The permission granted to the devil as tempter is called God’s covenant: in it the tempter’s desire is carried out, yet through it, in a marvelous manner, the will of the just dispenser is fulfilled. The Lord often subjects his chosen ones to the tempter in order to instruct them. Thus, after the gates of paradise and after the secrets of the third heaven, lest Paul be exalted by the greatness of his revelations, an angel of Satan was given to him (II Corinthians XII, 7).

But through this very temptation it is arranged that those who might have perished through being exalted are saved from destruction through being humbled. By the secret order of divine dispensation, from the very point where the devil’s iniquity is permitted to rage, God’s kindness is piously brought to completion.

Hence Paul says: “For this I pleaded with the Lord three times, that he might depart from me; and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (ibid.; Book II on the Gospel, homily 27, no. 6).

The name of the Son is Jesus; Jesus is said to mean “Savior,” or also “salutary.” Therefore the person who asks in the name of the Savior is the one who asks for what pertains to true salvation.

This is why the apostle Paul is not heard: if he were freed from temptation, it would not benefit him for salvation. O Paul, you already see Jesus in heaven, you are carried into paradise, you know the secret words of God, and yet you are still tempted by an angel of Satan? How are you so strong that you are carried up to heavenly things? How are you so weak that, while you flee from man on earth, you still endure adversity from an angel of Satan?

Because the one who lifts you up also regulates you again with the most subtle measure, so that in your miracles you may proclaim to us the power of God, and again, in your fear, make us remember our own weakness (Moral. Book XIX, ch. 6, no. 11).

Yet lest this weakness, when it assails us, lead us into despair, when you asked the Lord concerning your weakness and were not heard, you also told us what you heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (ibid., no. 12).

By God’s clear voice, therefore, it is shown that bodily weakness is the guardian of virtue. We are guarded inwardly when, by God’s dispensation, we are tolerably tempted outwardly—sometimes by vices, sometimes by hardships. For even those whom we know to have been men of virtue were not without temptations and struggles against vice.

There are two kinds of temptation. One occurs even in the mind of a just person through a sudden event: he is tempted so suddenly that an unexpected occurrence shakes and overthrows him, and he sees his fall only after he has fallen. The other comes gradually into the mind and infects the resisting soul with gentle suggestions; it consumes all the soul’s powers of justice not through its intensity but through its persistence (Moral. Book XII, ch. 18, no. 24).

There is a temptation that generally overthrows the just by a sudden assault, as it is written: “A mountain falling collapses, and a rock is moved from its place” (Job XIV, 18). That is, the holy mind, whose place had been justice, is suddenly moved by an impulse toward guilt.

There is another temptation that gently pours itself into the human heart and corrupts and consumes every firmness of strength, as it is written in the Book of Job: “The waters hollow out stones” (ibid., 9). For constant and gentle caresses of lust absorb the mind’s firmness, and a slow and subtle vice corrupts the mind’s hard and strong resolve.

When the Lord, by a just judgment, permits temptation suddenly to dominate the mind of one who appears to stand on high, he makes the mountain fall and collapse, as it were; and when the will is changed toward vice, the rock is moved, as it were, to another place.

When almighty God permits a slow and subtle yet persistent temptation to prevail over the minds of those believed to be strong, it is as though waters hollow out stones and the earth is gradually consumed by the alluvial flow, because the mind’s hardness, subdued by gentle suggestion, is softened.

The demons cast down from higher places flee the minds of those who cling humbly to God and delight in the wicked works of the proud. Like beasts playing in the grass, evil spirits play when they draw human hearts toward unlawful thoughts (Moral. Book XXXII, ch. 2, no. 4).

Is it not the play of unclean spirits to deceive minds created in the image of God sometimes by a feigned promise, sometimes to mock them with empty terrors, sometimes to impress upon them transient joys as though they would last, and sometimes to make lasting punishments seem transient?

This man had undoubtedly feared the deception of such beasts when he said: “My God, in you I trust; I shall not be ashamed, nor let my enemies mock me” (Psalm XXIV, 2).

Through the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lamentations I, 7; Book I on Ezekiel, homily 12, no. 19). The enemies mocked the Sabbaths when evil spirits inject wicked thoughts into an idle mind, so that, even if it rests from work, it does not rest from delight in evil works.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. How many dream temptations there are
It should be understood that images in dreams affect the soul in six ways (Moral. book VIII, 4, no. 44). For dreams are sometimes produced by fullness or emptiness of the stomach, sometimes by deception, sometimes by thought together with deception, sometimes by revelation, and sometimes by thought together with revelation. The first two that we have mentioned are known to all by experience; the four that follow, however, we find in the pages of Sacred Scripture.

For unless dreams were usually produced through deception by the hidden enemy, the wise man would never have said: “Dreams have led many astray, and empty illusions” (Ecclus. 34:7). Or certainly: “You shall not practice divination, nor observe dreams” (Lev. 19:26). These words plainly show what detestation is attached to things associated with divinations.

Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with deception, Solomon would certainly not have said: “Dreams follow upon many cares” (Eccles. 5:2). Unless dreams sometimes arose from the mystery of revelation, Joseph would not have seen in a dream that he was to be preferred to his brothers (Gen. 37:7); nor would the Truth have warned Mary’s husband in a dream to flee to Egypt after taking the child away (Matt. 2:13–14).

Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with revelation, the prophet Daniel, explaining Nebuchadnezzar’s vision, would never have begun from the root of thought, saying: “You, O king, began to think upon your bed what would happen after these things, and he who reveals mysteries has shown you what is to come” (Dan. 2:29). And shortly afterward: “You were looking, and behold, there stood before you something like a great statue; that statue was great, and its stature lofty” (ibid., 31), and so forth.

Thus, while Daniel reverently indicates that the dream was to be fulfilled and makes clear from what thought it arose, it is plainly shown that a dream is often generated from thought together with revelation. Since dreams vary according to so many kinds of causes, one ought to believe them with all the greater difficulty, since it is also less easy to discern from what impulse they come (Dial. book IV, ch. 48).

Holy men distinguish, by a certain inward perception, between illusions and revelations, and between the very voices or images of visions, so that they know either what they receive from a good spirit or what they suffer from a deceiver. If the mind is not cautious concerning dreams, it plunges itself into many vanities through the deceiving spirit, which sometimes customarily foretells many true things so that at the end it may be able to ensnare the soul through some single falsehood.

Often the evil spirit promises prosperity in sleep to those whom he sees awake through love of the present life; and to those whom he observes fearing adversity, he attacks them more harshly with images of such things in dreams, so that he may affect the undiscerning mind in different ways and confuse it, either raising it up by hope or depressing it through fear (Moral. VIII, ch. 24, no. 43). [Note: [Col. 0919D] Edition: “intercepts,” instead of “sees.”]

Often the ancient enemy also strives to trouble the hearts of the saints with dreams, so that at least for a moment they may be diverted from the purpose of firm thought, although they immediately shake their minds free from the imagination of the illusion. But the enemy lying in ambush attacks them more severely in sleep precisely because he cannot overcome them while they are awake. The dispensation from above mercifully permits the enemy of the human race to act wickedly even through dreams, lest sleep itself should be entirely deprived of the reward of suffering in the hearts of the elect.

## CHAPTER VIII. On nocturnal illusions

A nocturnal dream is a hidden temptation by which something shameful is conceived in the heart through darkened thought, although it is not completed in the body (Moral. book IX, ch. 55, no. 84). The law commands one polluted by a nocturnal dream to go outside the camp (Deut. 23:10), because it is plainly fitting that one who has been polluted by an unclean thought should consider himself unworthy of the fellowship of all the faithful, set the desert of his guilt before his eyes, and regard himself as despised in the estimation of the good.

To go outside the camp after being polluted by a nocturnal illusion is for one afflicted by a shameful assault to despise himself in comparison with the continent. He who washes himself with water toward evening does so when, recognizing his failing, he turns to the lamentation of repentance, so that by his tears he may wash away everything that hidden defilement accuses the soul of.

The one polluted by a nocturnal dream is commanded by the law to wash with water after sunset and return to the camp, because it is necessary that, when the heat of temptation has cooled, each person should again take confidence in relation to the fellowship of the good. He returns to the camp after washing with water at sunset who, after the lamentation of repentance and as the flame of illicit thought grows cold, is restored to presume upon the merits of the faithful, so that he no longer considers himself far removed from the others, rejoicing that he has been cleansed through the death of his inward and illicit ardor.

## CHAPTER IX. On Satan’s manifold stratagems

By destructive stratagems the ancient enemy raises up the forces of his cunning and corrupts the unstable hearts of mortals (Moral. XXXII, ch. 20, no. 35). Hence the divine voice says to blessed Job: “The sinews of his testicles are intertwined” (Job 40:12).

His testicles are evil suggestions, by which he burns amid the corruption of the mind, and the defiled soul gives birth to the offspring of an evil deed. The sinews of Behemoth’s testicles are intertwined because the arguments of his suggestions are bound together with great force, so that they make most people sin in such a way that, if they perhaps desire to flee from one sin, they cannot escape it without another snare of sin; they incur guilt while avoiding it, and can never free themselves from one bond unless they consent to be bound by another.

It often happens that someone, while seeking the friendships of this world, binds himself by oath to another person living a similar life, promising to conceal that person’s secrets in complete silence. But the person to whom the oath was given is discovered to be committing adultery, even attempting to kill the adulteress’s husband (Moral. XXXII, ch. 10, no. 36). [Note: Edition: “but he.”]

If the person who gave the oath returns to his senses and is assailed by conflicting thoughts from every side, he fears to remain silent, lest by keeping silent he become a participant in both adultery and murder; yet he hesitates to disclose the matter, lest he bind himself by the guilt of perjury. [Note: [Col. 0921D] Edition: “and disclose it.”] He is therefore bound by the intertwined sinews of the testicles who, whichever way he turns, fears that he will not be free from the contagion of transgression. [Note: [Col. 0922D] Edition: “because.”]

Sometimes a person abandons everything belonging to the world and seeks in every way to break his own wills, wishing to submit himself to another’s rule; but through insufficiently careful inquiry he fails to discern the person who ought to preside over him before God (ibid., no. 37). Perhaps, once this man—chosen without judgment—has begun to preside, he forbids his subordinate to do what belongs to God and commands him to do what belongs to the world. The subordinate therefore weighs either the guilt of disobedience or the contagion of secular life: he fears to obey and fears not to obey, lest by obeying he abandon God in the superior’s commands, or, by not obeying, despise God in the one chosen as his prior.

Thus this man is plainly bound, through the fault of his lack of discernment, by the intertwined sinews of Behemoth’s testicles, since whether he obeys or does not obey, he is bound by the guilt of transgression. He was striving to break his own wills, yet he takes care to strengthen them even while disregarding his superior. He had resolved to abandon the world completely, yet by another’s will he is compelled to return to the world’s cares. The sinews of Behemoth’s testicles are intertwined when the enemy’s arguments bind us in such a way that the knots of guilt tighten more harshly at the very point where one seeks to loosen them.

For the arguments of the devil’s machinations become more entangled in order to hold us precisely as they seem to be loosened so that they may release us (ibid., no. 38). There is, however, a stratagem that is usefully employed to destroy Satan’s cunning: when the mind is constrained between lesser and greater sins, if no means of escaping without sin is open at all, the lesser sins should always be chosen. For even one who is enclosed on every side by the circuit of walls so that he cannot escape throws himself into flight where the shorter wall is found.

## CHAPTER X. On manifold vices

The ancient enemy attacks us on every side with the wound of his temptation. Often, while the appetite is restrained in order to subdue lust, the goad of vainglory strikes the mind (Moral. book XIII, ch. 16, no. 19). But if the body is not worn down by the hardship of abstinence, the flame of lust rises up against the mind.

Often, while we strive to preserve frugality, we slip into stinginess. And often, while we give away what we possess extravagantly, we are led into avarice, because we again seek to gather what we may give away. The cunning enemy indeed persuades us to every sin, but by consenting to his persuasions and continually committing sins, we heap them up.

Many people, while stirring up within themselves crowds of vices or carnal desires, trample with the foot of wretched repetition upon the mind lying prostrate (Moral. IV, ch. 30, no. 57). One has submitted himself to the dominion of lust and fashions before the eyes of his mind images of shameful acts. When the deed itself is not performed, it is enacted all the more frequently in the intention of thought. He seeks the perfection of pleasure, and his weakened mind, agitated and blinded in every direction, searches out an opportunity for the most wicked consummation.

Such a mind therefore suffers something like a people, devastated by the insolent tumult of vices. Another has thrown himself beneath the rule of anger; and what does he enact in his heart except quarrels, even those that are absent? He often does not see those present, contradicts those absent, utters insults within himself and receives them, and responds more harshly to those he has received. When no opponent is present, he arranges quarrels in his heart with loud cries. He therefore bears a crowd within, pressed down by the heavy burden of inflamed thought.

Another has surrendered himself to avarice and, disdaining his own possessions, covets what belongs to others. Often unable to obtain what he desires, he turns the day into idleness and the night into thought. He is sluggish in useful work because he is wearied by illicit thought. He multiplies plans and expands the bosom of his mind more widely through the inventions of his thoughts.

Often a person strives to reach what he covets and seeks the most secret passages of circumstances by which to obtain it. As soon as he thinks that he has discovered something subtle in the matter, he rejoices as though he had already obtained what he desired; he then considers what he might add to the thing acquired and reflects on how it ought to be cultivated into a better condition.

Sometimes the human mind, overcome by desire for another’s property, already possesses as though in reality what it has conceived, and by the impulse of thought brings it, as it were, to a more attractive appearance. But soon it considers the snares of the envious and weighs what quarrel may be stirred up against it. It searches out what answer it should give, and, although it possesses nothing, it already struggles in defense of the property. Thus, although it has received nothing of what it coveted, it nevertheless already has in its heart the fruit of covetousness: the labor of quarrelsomeness. It is therefore pressed by something like a large population, devastated by the tumult of urging avarice.

Another subjects himself to the tyranny of pride, and, while raising the wretched heart against human beings, places it beneath the vice. He longs for the insignia of high honors, seeks to be exalted by success, and paints in his thoughts before himself everything he desires to be. Already he presides as though from a tribunal; already he sees himself preparing the services of his subjects; already he rises above others; already he inflicts injuries upon some and repays others because they have inflicted injuries; already, surrounded in his imagination by battalions, he proceeds into public and observes by what services he is supported.

A person subject to vices, while being tossed here and there in empty thought amid many phantasms, tramples some and raises up others. Already he satisfies his hatreds concerning those he has trampled; already he receives favors from those he has raised up. What else, then, does one who impresses so many phantasms upon his heart see except something like a waking dream? While he endures all the causes of the things he imagines, he plainly carries within himself crowds born from his desires.

Another now avoids illicit things, but nevertheless fears to lack the goods of the world. He desires to retain what is permitted, is ashamed to appear inferior among human beings, and takes the greatest care not to be poor at home or despised in public. He seeks what is sufficient for himself and what the needs of his dependents require; and, in order to fulfill adequately the rights of patronage toward his subordinates, he seeks patrons whom he himself may serve.

Often, while a person familiarly joins himself to vices, he is certainly entangled in the causes of those vices: he often consents with them to illicit things and commits, for the sake of other things that he has not abandoned, evils that he would not seek for their own sake.

Sometimes the wretched man, moved by empty thought, fears that his honor in this world may be diminished and approves before persons of higher standing what he already condemns by his own judgment. While he anxiously considers what he owes to his patrons, what to his subordinates, what increases his standing, and what benefits him in his affections, he is pressed by a crowd of disturbances as great as the importunity of his cares by which he is torn. [Note: [Col. 0923D] The word “in” is absent in the edition.]

## CHAPTER XI. On certain vices that pretend to be virtues

Vices often pretend to be virtues. For stinginess frequently disguises itself under the name of frugality, while extravagance hides itself under the title of generosity (Pastoral Rule, part II, ch. 9). Often disordered leniency is considered piety, and unrestrained anger is judged a virtue of spiritual zeal. Often rash action is regarded as the effectiveness of speed, while slowness in acting is thought the counsel of gravity.

It is necessary that every elect person distinguish virtues from vices with watchful care, lest either stinginess occupy the heart and he rejoice in appearing frugal in his distributions; or, when something has been squandered extravagantly, he glory in being generous as though out of compassion; or, by sparing what he ought to have struck, he lead his subjects to eternal punishments; or, by striking savagely what has been done wrong, he himself commit a graver wrong; or, by prematurely anticipating what could have been done rightly and seriously, he make it trivial; or, by delaying the merit of a good action, he exchange it for worse things.

Sometimes the ancient enemy insinuates something apparently pious into the human mind [Note: [Col. 0923D] Edition: “pretends”], in order to lead it to the limit of cruelty—as when he forbids a fault to be punished through discipline, so that what is not restrained here may be struck by the fire of Gehenna (Moral. book III, ch. 36, no. 68).

Sometimes the unclean spirit presents to human eyes the appearance of discernment and leads them into the snares of lack of discernment. This occurs when, at his prompting, we grant ourselves more food than our weakness requires, supposedly with discernment, but without discernment stir up against ourselves the battles of the flesh.

Sometimes the devil pretends to produce the effect of good works, but through this he inflicts the burdens of unrest—as when someone is unable to rest and fears being judged for idleness.

Sometimes the adversary of the human race displays the appearance of humility in order to remove the effect [Note: [Col. 0923D] Edition: “affection,” though in this place the Benedictine Fathers note that the older edition and many manuscripts read “effect,” not without good sense.] of humility [Note: [Col. 0924D] Edition: “usefulness”]. This occurs when he declares certain people to be weaker and more useless than they are, so that, considering themselves excessively unworthy, they fear to offer the services by which they could benefit their neighbors.

The hand of compunction examines with great subtlety all the vices that the ancient enemy conceals under the appearance of virtues (ibid., no. 69). For one who truly grieves inwardly carefully foresees what should be done outwardly and what should not. When the force of compunction afflicts us in our inmost being, every tumult of evil suggestion is silenced, because if the heart truly grieves, vices have no tongue with which to accuse us (ibid., ch. 37, no. 70).

For when the fullness of a life of uprightness is sought, superfluous suggestion of wickedness is hardened [Note: [Col. 0925D] Edition: “stopped”; nevertheless, the reading “hardened” is supported by our Taius, the first Remigius, one Vindoc., Corb. Germ.]. If we restrain ourselves with vigorous effort against the incentives of vices, we even transform the vices themselves into the service of virtue.

Anger possesses some people, but when they subject it to reason, they turn it into the service of holy zeal. Pride raises some people up; but when they incline their minds before divine strength [Note: [Col. 0925D] Edition: “fear”], they transform it into a voice of free authority for the defense of justice. The strength of the flesh entices some people; but when they subject their bodies to the performance of pious works, they reap gains of piety from the very source from which they suffered the sting of iniquity.

Hence blessed Job rightly offered a sacrifice for his friends after many struggles. Those whom he had long endured as enemies through contention, he eventually made fellow citizens through sacrifice.

Often, while a person exalts himself over the purity of chastity, he is defiled by the filth of avarice. While he appears attractive through the virtue of generosity, he is stained by the spots of lust. While he is clothed in the beauty of chastity and generosity, he is darkened, as though by zeal for justice, through the savagery of cruelty (Moral. book V, ch. 20, no. 39).

Often a person is clothed in a beautiful appearance through generosity, chastity, and piety, but is marked by the darkness of infused pride [Note: [Col. 0926D] Edition: “intermingled”]. Thus it happens that, when vices are mixed in, the hypocrite does not display a pure appearance in himself, just as a tiger can never have only one color.

Often certain vices pretend to be virtues: extravagance sometimes wishes to appear mercy, stinginess sometimes frugality, and cruelty sometimes justice (Moral. book XXIII, ch. 11, no. 19). Frequently the anxiety of vainglory, unable to contain itself within silence, inflames the mind toward an impulse to speak as though it were zeal for charity; and the force of the desired display drives it toward unrestrained speech, while the desire to appear breaks out under the pretext of a concern to advise.

Every arrogant person does not care, in speaking, what may be useful, but what may be seen; nor does he strive to correct the evil that he perceives, but to display the good that he feels.

## CHAPTER XII. That virtues arise from virtues and vices from vices

All virtues raise one another up through reciprocal assistance in the sight of the Creator, so that, since one virtue without another is either entirely nonexistent or very small, they may support one another through their mutual union (Moral. book XXI, ch. 3, no. 6).

All other good qualities are worthless if they are not approved by the eyes of the hidden Judge through the testimony of chastity. If humility abandons chastity, or chastity leaves humility, neither proud chastity nor defiled humility can accomplish anything in the sight of the author of humility and purity.

Thus sins are born from sin: when lesser sins are not avoided, one falls into the greatest; and when sins already committed are defended rather than lamented, one proceeds from wickedness to pride (Isidore, Sentences, book II, ch. 33). Hence the person who both admits crimes by his will and defends them through the swelling of obstinacy is guilty of a doubled crime.

Thus vice is begotten by vice, just as virtue is conceived by virtue. Vice is born from vice, as with David, who, by not avoiding adultery, also committed murder. Likewise virtue is conceived by virtue, as the apostles, through the virtue of evangelical preaching, earned the virtue of martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 0926D] Edition: “truth.”]

In the hearts of those living according to the world, vices succeed one another, so that when one has departed another may take its place, according to the testimony of the prophet Joel, who says: “What the locust left, the young locust ate; what the young locust left, the caterpillar ate; and what the caterpillar left, the rust consumed” (Joel 1:4–5).

These things are therefore gathered under the allegory of vices, because what follows is: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep.” Sometimes it is useful to fall into lesser vices so that greater ones may be avoided more usefully. Read the apostle Paul permitting lesser sins so that greater ones may not be committed. Vices are truly healed when they are excluded by virtues, not by vices. In some people, hidden vices become apparent only when they cease from other vices.

## CHAPTER XIII. On harmful and harmless thoughts

Often we learn from good works how much purity of life we should construct in thought (Moral. book X, ch. 15, no. 26). Nearly all good things proceed from thought, but some subtle insights of thought arise from action. For just as action is taken from the soul, so the mind is again instructed by action.

It is very necessary that, when thought is led beyond ordinary use, the eye of the mind should immediately be recalled to actions already completed, and that each person should weigh what he has done while subject to others; then he suddenly recognizes it. Often merciful God washes away the sins of the heart all the more quickly because he does not permit them to pass into action; and the more quickly conceived wickedness is dissolved because it is not bound so tightly by the effect of the deed (Pastoral Rule, part III, ch. 29). [Note: Edition: “And conceived wickedness is dissolved all the more quickly because…”]

Through the excellent Psalmist it is said: “I said: I will declare my injustices to the Lord against myself, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Ps. 31:5). By submitting the wickedness of his heart, he indicated that he wished to declare the injustices of his thoughts. When he says, “I said: I will declare,” and immediately adds, “And you forgave,” he shows how readily forgiveness is granted for thoughts. While he was still promising to ask, he obtained what he was promising.

Sometimes the offense occurs only in thought, and because the guilt does not reach action, repentance does not reach torment. Yet affliction over what was thought cleanses the mind more quickly, while merely thought-out iniquity defiles it.

The same Psalmist says: “My scars became foul and putrid because of my foolishness” (Ps. 38:6; Moral. book IX, ch. 55, no. 83). Often what has already been wiped away from the sight of the Judge through intervening tears returns to the mind through thought; and, although the guilt has been conquered, it strives again to creep into delight and is revived by a renewed assault in the old struggle, so that what it first did in the body it afterward turns over in the mind through persistent thought.

When nothing is done outwardly in action, but sin is committed only inwardly in thought, the mind binds itself under a strict charge unless it cleanses this through diligent lamentation.

Often the ear of the heart is closed by the throng of earthly thoughts when they resound loudly; and in the inner chamber of the mind, the less the sound of clamorous cares is restrained, the less the voice of the presiding Judge is heard (Moral. book XXIII, ch. 20, no. 37). For a person divided between the two is not fully sufficient for either; while he seeks to be instructed inwardly, he is nevertheless entangled outwardly, and from the very point at which he opens his hearing outwardly, he becomes deaf inwardly.

Holy men who, because of the necessity of their office, are compelled to serve in external ministries always diligently retreat to the secrets of the heart. There they ascend to the summit of inward thought and receive the law, as it were, upon a mountain, while, setting aside the tumult of temporal actions, they search out the judgment of the heavenly will at the summit of their contemplation (ibid., no. 38).

Holy Moses frequently returns from matters of uncertainty to the tabernacle; there he consults the Lord in secret and learns what he should decide with greater certainty. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Edition: “certain”; nevertheless, Norm. and Colb. support the reading “with greater certainty.”]

To return to the tabernacle after leaving the crowds is, after setting aside the tumult of external things, to enter the secret of the mind through the practice of good thought. There the Lord is consulted, and what must be done outwardly is silently heard within.

When the elect recognize that they cannot discern uncertain matters, they return to the secret thought of the mind as to a certain tabernacle. Having considered the divine law, they consult the Lord as though the ark had been placed before them; and what they first hear inwardly in silence they afterward make known by acting outwardly.

So that the elect may serve external duties without offense, they continually take care to return to the secrets of the heart. Thus they hear the voice of God as if in a dream, while in the thought of the mind they are withdrawn from carnal senses [Note: [Col. 0927D] Edition: “from carnal movements”; nevertheless, Vindoc., Norm., and others seen by Gussanville read “senses.”]

Often emerging thoughts pollute the hearts of the righteous and touch them with the delights of earthly things. But when they are quickly driven away by the hand of holy discernment, care is taken at once that the darkness of temptation not cover the face of the heart, which had already been touched by illicit delight (Moral. book XVI, ch. 42, no. 53).

Sometimes, during the very sacrifice of our prayer, thoughts intrude themselves importunately and are able to snatch away or defile what we offer to God with tears. When the patriarch Abraham was offering a sacrifice at sunset, he endured the birds that hovered around it and diligently drove them away so that they would not snatch the sacrifice he had offered (Gen. 15:11).

So, while we offer a holocaust to God upon the altar of the heart, let us guard it from unclean birds, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts snatch away what our mind wisely considers offering to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0928D] Edition: “hopes to offer.”]

Burdened by the weight of corruptible nature, certain superfluities of thought erupt from the womb of our mind, like burdens from the belly (Moral. book XXXI, ch. 27, no. 54). But we ought to carry a peg beneath our belt, so that, always girded for reproving ourselves, we may have around us a sharp goad of compunction. This should continually pierce the earth of our mind with the pain of repentance and conceal what bursts forth from the womb of our thoughts as something foul-smelling (Moral. book III, ch. 30, no. 59).

Jerubbaal killed a kid, placed its flesh upon a rock, and poured out the broth of the meat over it (Judg. 6:11–12, 19). We therefore place flesh upon a rock when, in imitation of Christ, we afflict our body. He pours the broth of the meat over it who, through a vow of good conduct, also drives carnal thoughts away from himself. For the broth flows from the flesh onto the rock when the mind is emptied of the fluidity of carnal thoughts.

When the power of divine assistance does not abandon our intention, the angel touches the sacrifice placed upon the rock with his staff. Fire comes out from the rock and consumes the broth and the flesh, because the Spirit breathed upon us by the Redeemer burns our heart with such a flame of compunction that it consumes everything illicit in it, both in action and in thought.

All who either desire illicit things or wish to appear as something in this world are compressed in their hearts by dense tumults of thought (Moral. book IV, ch. 30, no. 57). The sea signifies the human mind, and the thoughts of the mind are like the waves of the sea: sometimes they swell through anger, become tranquil through grace, and flow away with bitterness through hatred (Moral. book XII, ch. 7, no. 10). The human mind, enduring so many temptations, is moved as though by so many winds (Moral. book XI, ch. 44, no. 60).

Often tumults of empty thoughts depress the human mind; anger disturbs it, and when anger withdraws, foolish joy succeeds it. It is driven on by the goads of lust, while the heat of avarice stretches it far and wide toward the pursuit of earthly things. Sometimes pride raises it up, while at other times disordered fear casts it down into the lowest places.

## CHAPTER XIV. On pride and vainglory

[Col. 0928D]

The devil’s pride became the occasion of our destruction, while the humility of God was found to be the means of our redemption (Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 17). What is more contemptible than arrogance, which, while it stretches above itself, is distanced from the height of true sublimity? The beginning of every sin is pride (Ecclus. 10:15; Morals XXXIV, 21, no. 40). But what is pride except the desire for a perverse height? For that height is perverse when, abandoning the one to whom the mind ought to cling as its beginning, it somehow makes itself its own beginning and principle (Morals [Col. 0929A] XXVI, 17, no. 28).

Pride has often been the seedbed of lust, because while the spirit raised them, as it were, on high, the flesh plunged them into the depths. Those who are first secretly exalted through pride afterward fall publicly, because while they swell inwardly through hidden movements of the heart, they fall outwardly through open bodily lapses. Thus, in a just retribution, the arrogant were to be struck down, so that because they prefer themselves to human beings through pride, they might through lust be brought down to the likeness of beasts.

We must take care, and guard the mind with every vigilance against the swelling of pride. For our thoughts do not flit emptily before the eyes of God, and no moments of time pass through the mind without a corresponding state of retribution. God sees within what exalts the mind, and therefore permits that which brings it down to grow strong outwardly. What is first exalted within is afterward struck outwardly by the corruption of lust. An open blow follows the hidden guilt of pride, so that the interior is punished by exterior evils, and the heart publicly falls that was secretly swelling.

Through the prophet Hosea it is said against the Israelites: “A spirit of fornication is among them, and they have not known the Lord” (Hos. 5:4). To show that the cause of lust had burst forth from the fault of elation, he immediately added: “And the arrogance of Israel shall answer to his face” (ibid., 5). If a human being, through pride, despises his Creator, it is just that he should also receive battle from the flesh subject to him. Thus the first disobedient man, as soon as he sinned through pride, covered his nakedness (Gen. 3:7); because he had inflicted an insult upon God in his spirit, he immediately encountered an insult in his flesh. And because he did not wish to be subject to his Creator, he lost authority over the subject flesh that he ruled, so that the shame of his disobedience might rebound upon him personally, and, having been overcome, he might learn what he had lost through exaltation.

When a good work is undertaken, its elation must first be conquered in the heart, lest, if it proceeds from the root of a wretched intention, it produce the bitter fruits of wickedness (Morals XXIII, ch. 11, no. 20). When the pride of the heart extends outward as far as the body, it is first revealed through the eyes. Inflated by the arrogance of their swelling, they look down, as it were, from a height; and the more they abase themselves, the higher they raise themselves (Morals XXXIV, ch. 22, no. 46).

Unless pride displayed itself through the eyes as through certain windows, the Psalmist would never have said to God: “You will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud” (Ps. 17:28). Unless pride poured itself forth through the eyes, Solomon likewise would not have said of the arrogance of Judaea: “A generation whose eyes are lofty, and whose eyelids are raised on high” [Note: Ed., “raised on high” (altum).] (Prov. 30:13; Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 17).

The assertion of an unrestrained voice commonly accompanies the arrogant. They speak indeed through the arrogance of pride, yet believe that they speak through the freedom of uprightness. Sometimes the uncontrolled swelling of pride drives the arrogant to rebuke what they ought not to rebuke, or to rebuke more severely than they ought, under the appearance of freedom.

We must consider that we often correct the arrogant more effectively if we mingle certain incentives of praise with their correction. We must bring before them either other good qualities that they possess, or certainly those that they could possess if they do not yet have them; and only then should the evils displeasing to us be cut away, once the good things pleasing to them have first made their minds receptive to hearing what is agreeable. We first touch untamed horses with a gentle hand, so that afterward, even by means of lashes, we may bring them more fully under our control. Honey is added to a bitter medicinal drink, lest the bitterness that will bring health be felt as harshness in the very act of tasting; while the taste is deceived by sweetness, the deadly humor is expelled through bitterness.

In dealing with some arrogant people, the beginnings of an admonition should be tempered by interwoven praise, so that, while they accept the approval they love, they may also receive the corrections they hate. We can often persuade the arrogant of what is useful more effectively if we say that their improvement will benefit us rather than them, and if we ask that their betterment be pursued more for our sake than for theirs.

Every proud person, precisely because he desires to appear exalted, becomes through elation far removed from the true being of God (Morals XVII, ch. 8, no. 10). They cannot stand, because they are separated from the solidity of eternal being; and they suffer this first ruin because, through private glory, they fall within themselves, as the Psalmist says: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72:18). They fall inwardly in the very measure that they wrongly rise outwardly.

Thus a straw is carried aloft by the breath of the winds, but is quickly brought back down by its fall. Thus smoke rises to the clouds, but suddenly, swelling upward, is dispersed into nothing. Thus a mist rises from the depths as it thickens, but the ray of the sun, once it has arisen, wipes it away as though it had never existed. Thus moisture is sprinkled over the surface of plants during the hours of night [Note: Ed., more correctly, “of the nightly dew.”], but it is dried by the sudden heat of daylight. Thus the foaming bubbles of water, raised by the first rains, emerge eagerly from the depths; but the more quickly they burst and perish, the more they extend themselves upward through swelling. And as they grow so as to be seen, by growing they accomplish their own inability to remain.

For it is written: “All his days the wicked man is proud” (Job 15:20; Morals XII, ch. 37, no. 42). The elect, too, often become proud in some of their thoughts and actions; but because they are elect, they cannot be proud all their days, since before they end their life they change their hearts from elation to the fear of humility. Every wicked person is proud throughout all his days, because he ends his life without withdrawing from elation. He looks around at what flourishes for a time, and neglects to consider what is judged for eternity. He places his confidence in the life of the flesh and supposes that what he presently possesses will endure for a long time.

The mind is made firm in elation, every neighbor is brought into contempt; he never considers how suddenly death may creep upon him, nor ever weighs how uncertain his happiness is. No one ought to have been proud even if he could have known the exact number of his years, so that, knowing how long he would live, he might foresee when he would withdraw from elation (ibid., ch. 38, no. 43).

It must be understood that every proud person exercises tyranny according to his own circumstances. What one person sometimes exercises in the commonwealth—that is, through the power received with office and rank—another exercises in a province, another in a city, another in his own household, and another, through hidden wickedness, exercises over himself in his own thoughts.

The proud often perceive the anger of the heavenly Judge as already present, but are not turned away from evil, so that they may thereby be turned away from their own destruction (ibid., ch. 41, no. 46). Their conscience accuses them, and they fear being struck; yet they continually increase the very thing for which they will be struck. The proud person despises returning, despairs of pardon, and glories in his guilt; yet inwardly he has fear as a witness to his wickedness. Although he seems outwardly to act boldly in evil, he is nevertheless compelled to tremble inwardly about it.

Through the prophet Isaiah it is said: “My sword is intoxicated in heaven” [Col. 0931B] (Isa. 34:5; Morals XXXII, ch. 23, no. 49). It is as though he said openly: “Consider with what anger I shall strike the proud of the earth, if I did not spare to strike even those whom I created beside me in heaven for the fault of elation.”

## CHAPTER XV. On Greed

Greed, which is the service of idols (Eph. 5:5), like an amphora keeps the mouth of the heart open all around (Morals XIV, ch. 53, no. 63). Many are dull in understanding, but in the things they desire they are aroused by the goads of greed; and those who are blind to the sight of good things become vigilant for the performance of evil when rewards stir them up.

Through the prophet Zechariah the nature of greed is described: “This is their eye in all the earth. And behold, a talent of lead was being carried” (Zech. 5:6). What is the talent of lead except the weight of sin arising from that same greed? Through lead, a metal whose nature is heavy in weight, the sin of greed is specially signified, because it makes the mind it infects so heavy that it cannot in any way be raised to desire sublime things.

“The desire for money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10; Morals XIV, ch. 53, no. 65); and because every kind of evil is begotten through greed, it is fitting that the house of greed should be built in foulness. The same prophet Zechariah said to the angel: “Where are these women carrying the jar?” And he said to me: “To build a house for it in the land of Shinar” (Zech. 5:11).

Shinar is called their foulness, because just as good odor comes from virtue, so, conversely, foulness comes from the vice of desire. It must be understood that Shinar is a very broad valley in which a tower had begun to be built by proud people, but was destroyed through the diversity of languages. That tower was called Babylon, on account of the confusion of minds and languages itself. Nor is it without reason that the jar of greed is placed there, where Babylon—that is, confusion—is built, because since it is certain that all evils arise through greed and impiety, greed and impiety themselves are rightly said to dwell in confusion.

People inflamed by the heat of greed display greater works before human eyes in proportion as they desire greater gifts to be offered to them by human beings. In the Book of blessed Job it is written: “Fire shall devour the tents of those who gladly receive gifts” (Job 15:34; Morals XII, ch. 54, no. 62). For just as the body dwells in a tent, so the mind dwells in thought; but fire devours the tents when the heat of greed ravages the thoughts.

When greedy people burn with desire to be filled all at once with riches, let them hear what is written: “The one who hastens to become rich will not be innocent” (Prov. 28:20; Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 20). Whoever strives to increase his wealth neglects to avoid sin; and, like a bird caught, when he greedily desires the bait of earthly things, he does not recognize the snare of sin by which he will be strangled.

When they generally desire the profits of the present world and do not know what losses they will suffer in the future, let them hear what is written: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. 20:21). Those who hasten to inherit at the beginning cut themselves off from a share in blessing at the end, because while they desire to multiply their possessions here through the wickedness of greed, there they become disinherited from the eternal patrimony.

Desire often arises secretly in the mind, but openly produces in action the stings of every sin (Morals XX, ch. 10, no. 21). The distinguished preacher immediately indicates these stings arising from this root when he says: “Some, desiring it, have gone astray from the faith and pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (1 Tim. 6:10; Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 20).

The prophet Isaiah, rebuking the human race for the immensity of its greed, says: “Woe to you who join house to house and unite field to field, even to the boundary of the place. Will you dwell alone in the midst of the earth?” (Isa. 5:8). It is as though he said openly: “How far will you extend yourselves, since in the common world you cannot possibly lack fellow-sharers?” You oppress those who are joined to you, and you always find someone against whom you can extend yourselves.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Anger

When anger often cuts through the tranquility of the mind, it disturbs it as though torn apart and split, so that it is not in harmony with itself and loses the force of its inner likeness [to God] (Morals V, ch. 45, no. 78). Let us consider how great is the guilt of anger, through which, when gentleness is lost, the likeness of the heavenly image is damaged.

Through anger wisdom is lost, so that one is altogether unaware of what should be done or in what order, as it is written: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccl. 7:10), because it removes the light of understanding when it confuses the mind by agitating it. Through anger life is lost, and even if wisdom seems to be retained, as it is written: “Anger destroys even the prudent” (Prov. 15:1), because a confused mind does not carry out what it is capable of understanding prudently.

Through anger justice is abandoned, as it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (Jas. 1:20), because when a disturbed mind sharpens the judgment of its reason, it considers everything that fury suggests to be right. Through anger the grace of social life is lost, as it is written: “Do not be a constant companion of an angry man, lest you learn his ways and take a stumbling-block for your soul” (Prov. 22:24–25), because one who does not restrain himself by human reason must live alone like a beast. [Note: Ed., “he perceives.” The reading is uncertain in this context.]

Through anger harmony is broken, as it is written: “An angry man produces quarrels, and an irascible man digs up sins” (Prov. 15:18). The angry person digs up sins because he makes even wicked people worse when he carelessly provokes them to discord.

Through anger the light of truth is lost, as it is written: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26), because when anger casts the darkness of confusion upon the mind, God hides from it the ray of his knowledge.

Through anger the splendor of the Holy Spirit is excluded. On the contrary, according to the ancient translation, it is written: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). For when he said “humble,” he immediately added “quiet.” If anger therefore takes tranquility away from the mind, it closes the dwelling of the Holy Spirit.

When the mind has been emptied through anger by the departure of the Holy Spirit, it is immediately led into open madness and is scattered from its innermost foundation of thought all the way to the surface. For the heart kindled by the goads of anger throbs, the body trembles, the tongue becomes entangled, the face burns, the eyes grow harsh, and familiar people are no longer recognized (Morals V, ch. 45, no. 79). With the mouth it forms a cry, but does not know what its sense is saying. Thus this person is no different from those possessed, since he is not conscious of his own actions.

Often anger leaps as far as the hands, and the farther reason withdraws, the more boldly it rises. The mind cannot restrain itself, because it has become subject to another’s power; and fury exercises the limbs outwardly in blows precisely because inwardly it holds captive the mind, the mistress of the limbs.

Sometimes a person does not extend his hands through anger, but turns his tongue into a dart of cursing. He asks in prayer for his brother’s destruction and desires God to carry out what that perverse person himself either fears or is ashamed to do. Thus he commits murder by wish and word, even while refraining with his hands from injuring his neighbor.

Sometimes anger, disturbing the mind, imposes silence as though by judgment; and in proportion as it does not express itself outwardly through the tongue, it burns more fiercely within, so that an angry person withholds his conversation from his neighbor and, by saying nothing, says how completely he is estranged.

At times this severity of silence is practiced as a dispensation of discipline, provided that the pattern of discretion is carefully preserved in the depths of the heart. Sometimes, while the inflamed mind is restrained from its customary speech, with the passage of time it becomes entirely separated from love of its neighbor. More violent goads come to the mind when causes that irritate more severely arise, and the speck in the angry person’s eye becomes a beam, when anger is changed into hatred.

Anger often shut up in silence within the mind burns more fiercely, forming loud silent voices. It presents to itself words by which it may be provoked and, as though placed in a judicial examination of the case, answers itself with greater harshness.

Sometimes the mind, disturbed by anger, experiences a greater uproar in its silence, and the flame of closed-up anger consumes it more severely. [Note: Ed., “the flame of closed-up anger.” In the Colbertine, Corbie, German, and other manuscripts the reading is: “The flame of closed-up anger.”]

It must be understood that anger kindles some people more quickly and leaves them more easily, while it moves others slowly but holds them more harshly. Some, when inflamed by anger, resemble reeds set alight: while they resound with their voices, they give off something like the noises of their own ignition. They quickly make a flame, but immediately grow cold into ash (Morals V, ch. 45, no. 80).

Angry people often take a long time to become inflamed, but once inflamed they are extinguished with greater difficulty; and because they rouse themselves more slowly to harshness, they preserve the fire of their fury more stubbornly. Often, and what is worse, people both take up the flames of anger quickly and lay them down slowly; others, however, take them up slowly and lose them quickly. In these four modes the reader clearly recognizes that, in regard to the good of tranquility, the last approaches it more closely than the first, while in evil the third surpasses the second.

## CHAPTER XVII. How Anger Should Be Restrained

Anger becomes unaccustomed to possessing the mind once it has been broken in two ways (Morals V, ch. 45, no. 81).

The first is for the vigilant mind, before beginning any action, to set before itself all the insults it may suffer, so that, while considering the reproaches endured by its Redeemer, it may prepare itself for adversity.
