It receives what comes with proportionately greater strength because it has armed itself more carefully through foreknowledge. The person whom adversity finds unprepared is found, as it were, sleeping before the enemy; and the enemy kills him more quickly because he pierces one who offers no resistance.

The person who marks beforehand, through vigilance, the evils that threaten awaits hostile attacks like one awake in ambush. He is therefore bravely equipped for victory precisely where he was thought to be caught unaware. The mind should carefully meditate upon all adversities before the beginning of its action, so that, always thinking of them and always protected against them by the breastplate of patience, it may [with foresight overcome whatever comes and regard whatever does not come as] gain.

The second way of preserving gentleness is that, when we observe the excesses of others, we should think of our own sins by which we have exceeded in relation to others. Consideration of our own weakness excuses the evils of others to us. The person who patiently endures an injury inflicted upon him remembers piously that perhaps he still has something in which he himself ought to be endured.

Fire is extinguished by water when, as fury rises in the mind, each person’s own fault is recalled to him, because he is ashamed not to spare sins when he remembers that he himself has often sinned in ways requiring pardon from God or from his neighbor.

We must carefully understand that one anger is aroused by impatience, while another is formed by zeal. The former arises from vice, the latter from virtue. If no anger arose from virtue, Phinehas would not have appeased the assault of divine judgment with the sword (Morals V, ch. 45, no. 82). Because Eli did not possess this anger, he aroused against himself the movement of heavenly vengeance without mitigation. For in proportion as he was lukewarm toward the vices of his subjects, the anger of the eternal ruler burned more strictly against him. [Note: Ed., “the judgment of the eternal ruler burned against him.”]

The Psalmist says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). Those who think that this means we should be angry only with ourselves [and not also with neighbors who sin] do not understand it correctly. For if we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, it remains that we should be angry at their errors just as at our own vices.

Hence Solomon says: “Anger is better than laughter, because through the sadness of the face the mind of the delinquent is corrected” (Eccl. 7:4). The same Psalmist says: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6:8). Anger arising from vice blinds the eye of the mind; anger arising from zeal, however, troubles it, because when people are shaken by an emulation of righteousness, contemplation—which can be perceived only by a tranquil heart—is disrupted.

Often zeal for righteousness agitates the mind with restlessness and immediately obscures its vision, so that in its agitation it does not see higher things that it had previously discerned well while tranquil. Yet from the very point at which it is temporarily struck so that it cannot see, it is more subtly led back to higher things. The upright emulation of zeal, through gentleness, eventually opens the eye of the mind more fully in eternal tranquility, although for a time it closes that eye through agitation. From the point at which the mind is disturbed so that it cannot see, it makes progress so that it may become clearer for seeing truly.

When medicine is put into an ailing eye, light is wholly denied it; yet afterward it receives the light truly from the very point at which it temporarily lost it for its healing.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Envy

We can envy only those whom we think better than ourselves in some respect (Morals V, ch. 46, no. 84). The person who is killed by envy is therefore small, because he himself bears witness that he is lesser than the one whose envy torments him.

The cunning enemy, by envying the first human being, stole from him because, after losing blessedness, he recognized himself as lesser than that man’s immortality. Cain fell into the commission of fratricide (Gen. 4:5–7), because when his own sacrifice was rejected, he roared against the one preferred to him, whose offering God had accepted; and the one he dreaded as better than himself he cut off, lest he should be better in any respect.

Esau burned with persecution against his brother for this reason: having lost the blessing of the firstborn—which he himself had sold for a meal of lentils—he grieved that he was lesser than the one whom he preceded by birth (Gen. 25:34; 27:41).

Joseph’s holy brothers sold him to passing Ishmaelites because, after learning the mystery of his revelation, they tried to obstruct his advancement lest he become better than they (Gen. 37:27–28). King Saul pursued David, his subject, by hurling a spear at him, because he feared that the man whom he perceived growing daily through the success of his virtues might increase beyond him. [Note: Ed., “through great success”; nevertheless, the reading of Tai is found in the manuscript of Beauvais.]

The person who is killed by envy is small, because unless he were himself inferior, he would not grieve over another’s good.

It must be understood with the greatest care that, although through every vice committed the ancient enemy pours his poison into the human heart, in this wickedness the serpent shakes all his inward parts and vomits forth the pestilence of the malice he seeks to imprint (Morals V, ch. 46, no. 85). Of him it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. 2:24).

When the corruption of envy has ruined the conquered heart, external signs also reveal how severely madness drives the mind. Through envy the complexion is affected by pallor, the eyes are cast down, the mind is inflamed, and the limbs grow cold. Madness arises in thought and gnashing in the teeth; and when the hatred growing in the hiding places of the heart is concealed, the wound enclosed within pierces the conscience in blind grief. [Note: Ed., “bores through.” The reading of Tai is nevertheless supported by the Coc. edition and those following it.]

Nothing joyful in one’s own possessions is pleasing, because its own punishment wounds the withering mind, while another’s happiness torments it. The higher the structure of another’s work is raised, the more deeply the foundation of the envious mind is dug out, so that in proportion as others hurry toward better things, it itself falls more disastrously. Through that fall even what was thought to have risen through perfect achievement in other actions is destroyed. For when envy has withered the mind, it consumes everything good it finds.

Through the wisest Solomon it is said: “The life of the flesh is health of heart, but envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Prov. 14:30). What is signified by flesh except certain weak and tender things? And what by bones except strong deeds? It often happens that some, with true innocence of heart, appear weak in certain actions, while others already perform deeds that appear strong before human eyes, yet inwardly waste away through the pestilence of envy toward the good of others.

It is therefore rightly said: “The life of the flesh is health of heart,” because if innocence of mind is guarded, even those things that are weak outwardly are eventually strengthened. And it is rightly added: “Envy is the rottenness of the bones,” because through the vice of envy even strong deeds of virtue perish before the eyes of God. For the rotting of bones means that even certain strong things are destroyed through envy.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Suppressing Envy

It is difficult for one person not to envy what another desires to obtain, because whatever temporal thing is possessed becomes less for each individual in proportion as it is divided among many. Hence envy torments the mind of the one who desires, because what he seeks is either taken away entirely when another receives it, or is reduced in quantity (Morals V, ch. 46, no. 86).

Whoever desires to be completely free from the plague of envy should love that inheritance which the number of co-heirs does not restrict; an inheritance that is one for all and whole for each, and that appears more generous in proportion as the multitude of those who receive it expands.

The diminution of envy is the affection arising from inward sweetness; its complete death is the perfect love of eternity. When a person is perfectly carried away in love of the heavenly homeland, he is also firmly established in love of his neighbor without any envy, because when he desires nothing earthly, there is nothing to oppose his charity toward his neighbor. What is true charity other than the eye of the mind free from envy? If that eye is touched by the dust of earthly love, it is immediately struck and recoils from the contemplation of the inner light.

Because the person who loves earthly things is small, while the person who desires eternal things is great, the saying may also appropriately be understood in this way: “Envy kills the little one” (Job 5:2), because no one dies from the sickness of this pestilence unless he is still weak in his desires.

## CHAPTER XX. On Malice

In the Gospel the Truth says: “What you wish people to do for you, you also do for them” (Matt. 7:12; Morals X, ch. 6, no. 8). By these two commandments of both Testaments, malice is restrained by the one and kindness is put forward by the other, so that each person, by not doing what he does not wish to suffer, may cease from the work of harming.

We must take the greatest care that each person show the gentleness of patience toward the insolent, display the grace of kindness to those languishing under the plague of malice [Note: Ed., “bestow”], unite the discordant in peace, and equip those already in harmony for the desire of true peace.

The Lord Jesus Christ, rebuking the malicious, says: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye and do not see the beam in your own eye?” (Matt. 7:3; Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 9). The disturbance of impatience is a speck, but malice in the heart is a beam in the eye. The former is shaken by the breath of temptation, while the latter, the completion of wickedness, bears its burden almost immovably.

For the text rightly continues: “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will see to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” It is as though it were said to the wicked mind, grieving inwardly and displaying itself outwardly as holy through patience: “First shake the mass of malice from yourself, and then rebuke others for the lightness of their impatience, lest, while you do not strive to conquer malice, it become worse for you to tolerate the perversity of another.” [Note: Ed., “pretense” rather than “malice.”]

The very wicked heart wastes away from its own malice, not from another’s (Book X on Ezekiel, Homily 2, no. 12), as it is written: “Zeal has seized the unlearned people, and does not consume the adversaries by signs” [Note: Ed., “will consume.”] (Isa. 16:11, according to the ancient version; Morals II, ch. 31, no. 51).

[Note: The Benedictine Fathers observe that in Book II of the Morals, chapter 31, no. 51, it is not sufficiently clear what prophecy this is. They suspect that the text cited by Gregory is found literally in none of the prophets and therefore take refuge in saying that by “prophecy” the whole of Holy Scripture may be understood. They further note that the Apostle, in Romans 10:2, writes of the Jewish people that they “have a zeal, but not according to knowledge,” which is almost equivalent to saying that an unlearned people have seized zeal—that is, zeal without knowledge. But lest there be any further doubt about the passage from which the prophecy “Zeal has seized the unlearned people” was taken, it is worth observing that it is found in Isaiah, in the chapter cited by us, not according to the newer Vulgate but according to the ancient version; it is also cited by Ambrose in his commentary on Psalm 118 and by Augustine in Book XX of The City of God, chapter 12.]

Just as the fire of love raises the mind, so the fire of malice envelops it, because the Holy Spirit elevates the heart that he fills, whereas the heat of malice always bends it toward lower things. The wicked are not only tormented afterward by fire in retribution; even now they burn through envy, because those who will later be punished with the penalty of retribution now inflict upon themselves the torment of malice.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Discord

Those who are in discord must be admonished to know with certainty that, however many virtues they may possess, they can in no way become spiritual if they neglect to be united in harmony with their neighbors (Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 22). One cannot reach the single hope of the calling unless one runs toward it with a mind united to one’s neighbors.

Often some people, in proportion as they receive certain special gifts, become proud and lose the gift of harmony, which is greater. Thus, if someone perhaps subdues the flesh more than others through restraint of appetite, he may despise in abstinence those whom he surpasses rather than live in harmony with them.

Whoever separates abstinence from harmony should consider what the Psalmist commands when he says: “Praise him with tambourine and choir” (Ps. 50:4). In a tambourine, dry skin resounds when struck; in a choir, voices agree through fellowship. Therefore whoever afflicts his body but abandons harmony praises God with the tambourine, but does not praise him in the choir.

Often, while greater knowledge raises certain people up, it separates them from the society of others; and the more they know, the more foolishly they depart from the virtue of harmony. The better someone knows, the worse he sins when he abandons harmony; and for that reason he will deservedly receive punishment without excuse, because, had he wished, he could prudently have avoided sin. [Note: The phrase “abandoning harmony” is absent from the Ed. edition but is also found in Laud.]

To some who withdraw from harmony James rightly says: “If you have bitter zeal and contentions in your hearts [Note: Ed., “and there are contentions in your heart.”], do not boast and lie against the truth. This is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic; whereas the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable” (Jas. 3:14–15, 17). It is pure because it understands chastely; it is peaceable because through elation it does not become alienated from the charity of its neighbors.

It is written: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24). From this command we must consider what kind of rejection is shown by the refusal of the offering and how intolerable the guilt is. Since all evils are washed away by the good things that follow, let us consider how great are the evils of discord, which, unless they are utterly extinguished, do not permit good to follow.

Those in discord must be admonished that, if they turn their ears away from heavenly commandments, they should open the eyes of their minds to consider the things that occur below.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Hatred

If we remain silent about rebuking people because we fear that hatred will rise against us, then we are certainly seeking not God’s gain but our own (Morals XX, 21, ch. 21, no. 47).

We must carefully understand that sometimes the wicked, when rebuked, become worse and pursue us with great hatred. Therefore, if we refrain from rebuking them out of love for them, we spare not them but ourselves. At times we must patiently endure the hateful as they are by remaining silent, so that through living they may learn in us what they are not.

The just person must not fear that, while someone is being corrected, he will inflict insults; rather, he must fear that, being drawn into hatred, he may become worse (Morals VIII, ch. 42, no. 67). We must be extremely careful lest loquacity drag the tongue beyond measure and extend it as far as the wantonness of detraction, lest it arouse hatred through malice and bend the mouth toward the dart of cursing [Note: Ed., “lest it provoke the mouth as far as the dart of cursing.”] (Morals X, ch. 6, no. 8).

In the Gospel the Truth says: “What you wish people to do for you, do also for them” (Matt. 7:12). It is as though he said openly: “What you hate to have done to you by another, take care not to do to another through hatred” (Tob. 4:16).

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Lust of the Eyes
Whoever carelessly looks outward through the windows of the body often falls, even unwillingly, into the pleasure of sin, and, once bound by desires, begins to want what he did not want before (Moral. Book XXI, chapter 2, no. 4). The headlong soul, because it does not beforehand take care not to see incautiously what it may desire, afterward, blinded, begins to desire what it has seen. Thus the prophet’s mind, which, often lifted up, participated in inward mysteries, incautiously saw another man’s wife and afterward, darkened, unlawfully joined himself to her (2 Samuel 11:2).

The holy man, because he presides over the received bodily senses as over subordinate ministers, like a most equitable judge, perceives faults before they arise and, as though against an ambushing [Note: [Col. 0939D] The edition reads “enemy.” But the Fathers Benedictine argue that Taius’s reading is better.] death, closes the windows of the body, saying: “I have made a covenant with my eyes, so that I would not even think about a virgin” (Job 31:1)—namely, so that they might not first look incautiously upon what he would afterward love unwillingly.

[Col. 0939D] Once the appearance of a form has been fastened to the heart through the eyes, it is scarcely released by the hand of great struggle. Therefore, so that we may not turn slippery things over in our thoughts, we must take care, because one ought not to look upon what it is not permitted to desire. So that the mind may be kept pure in thought, the eyes must be restrained from the wantonness of their pleasure, as though they were robbers leading us into guilt. For Eve would not have touched the forbidden tree unless she had first looked upon it incautiously. It is written: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food, and beautiful to the eyes, and pleasing to look upon; and she took of its fruit and ate” (Genesis 3:6).

We must consider with the greatest care how greatly we ought to restrain our sight from unlawful things, we who live as mortals, if even Eve, the mother of the living, came to death through her eyes. In the voice of Judea, which, desiring what was external because she saw it, had lost the good things within, the prophet says: “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lamentations 3:51). By desiring visible things, she lost invisible virtues. Thus she who lost the inner fruit through outward sight suffered the plundering of her heart through the eye of the body.

It is written in the Gospel: “Everyone who looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:27; Moral. XXI, chapter 2, no. 5). For through Moses [lust committed in deed is condemned, but by the author of purity lust conceived in thought is condemned].

### CHAPTER XXIV. On the Concupiscence of Gluttony

We must know that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways (Moral. Book XXX, chapter 18, no. 60). Sometimes it anticipates the time of need; sometimes it does not anticipate the time, but seeks more lavish foods; sometimes it demands that whatever is to be eaten be prepared with excessive care [Note: [Col. 0940D] The edition reads “whatever things are to be eaten.”]; sometimes it agrees both with the quality of the food and with the time, but exceeds the measure of nourishment in the very quantity consumed [Note: [Col. 0940D] The edition reads “of moderate nourishment.”]. Sometimes, however, what it desires is more humble, yet by the very act of eating it sins more grievously through the heat of its immense desire [Col. 0940C] [Note: [Col. 0940D] The edition reads “in the fever.”].

We shall show these modes of vice more clearly if we establish them by more evident examples. Jonathan incurred the sentence of death from his father’s mouth because, in tasting honey, he anticipated the appointed time for eating (1 Samuel 14:27). The people led out of Egypt perished in the wilderness because, despising manna, they asked for meat, which they considered more luxurious (Numbers 21:5). The first sin of the sons of Eli arose because, at their request, the priest’s servant wanted to receive sacrificial meat not cooked according to the ancient custom, but raw, so that he might present it with greater care (1 Samuel 2:12ff.).

When it is said to Jerusalem, “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance” (Ezekiel 16:49), it is openly shown that she lost salvation because, together with the vice of pride, she exceeded the measure of moderate nourishment [Col. 0940D] (Genesis 25:33).

Esau lost the glory of the firstborn because, with the great heat of desire, he craved a cheap food, namely lentils. By preferring it even to the sale of his birthright [Note: [Col. 0940D] The edition reads “to the selling of his birthright.”], he showed how passionately he panted after it. For it is not the food but the appetite that is at fault. Hence we often consume more luxurious foods without guilt, while we taste humbler ones not without a guilty conscience.

Esau lost his primacy by eating lentils, whereas Elijah preserved his bodily strength [Note: [Col. 0941D] Several old and recent editions read “strength of spirit,” a reading that seems preferable; see the observation of the Benedictine Fathers on this passage.] by eating meat (1 Kings 17:6). The ancient enemy, knowing that the cause of condemnation is not food but desire for food, subjected the first man to himself not through meat but through an apple, and tempted the second not through meat but through bread (Genesis 3:6; Matthew 4:3).

The guilt of our first parent is often committed even when humble and worthless things are consumed. For Adam alone did not receive the command of prohibition so that he might refrain from the forbidden apple; rather, when God indicates that certain foods are harmful to our salvation, he recalls us from them, as though by a sentence [Note: [Col. 0941D] The edition reads “forbids us.”]. And when we touch harmful things out of desire, what else are we doing but tasting what is forbidden? We should consume in food what the necessity of nature requires, not what the appetite for eating suggests, lest, if this moderate discernment does not look carefully enough to the matter, someone plunge himself into the abyss of unlawful desire (Moral. XXX, chapter 18, no. 61).

Superfluity of speech, frivolity in action, and lust accompany those devoted to gluttony (Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 19). If immoderate talkativeness did not carry away those devoted to gluttony, the rich man, who is said to have feasted splendidly every day, would not burn more grievously in his tongue. For he says: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24). These words clearly show that he had sinned repeatedly with his tongue by feasting every day, since, burning all over, he especially sought refreshment for his tongue.

Because frivolity of action immediately follows those devoted to gluttony, sacred authority testifies, saying: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exodus 32:6). Often excessive eating leads as far as lust, because, when the belly is distended with satiety, the goads of desire are aroused.

To the crafty enemy, who opened the first man’s mind to desire for the apple but tightened it in the snare of sin, the divine voice says: “You shall crawl upon your breast and belly” (Genesis 3:14). As though it were openly said to him: “You shall rule over human hearts by thought and gluttony.”

Because lust follows those devoted to gluttony, the prophet bears witness. While recounting outward things, he announces hidden ones, saying: “The prince of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 39, according to the Hebrew text and according to the Septuagint). For the prince of the cooks is the belly, to which the cooks devote great care so that it may be filled delectably with food. The walls of Jerusalem, however, are the virtues of the soul, raised toward the desire for heavenly peace. Thus the prince of the cooks casts down the walls of Jerusalem, because, when the belly is stretched by gluttony, the virtues of the soul are destroyed by lust.

### CHAPTER XXV. On the Struggle of the Virtues against the Vices

When we oppose the lord of vices; when we resist iniquity, which separates us from God [Note: [Col. 0942D] The edition reads “which had seized us.”]; when we resist custom firmly [and] violently, and, trampling perverse desires underfoot, claim against it the right of our inborn freedom [Note: [Col. 0942D] In our manuscript we find the words “law, Scripture, equity, or power” inserted here.], we resist the armies of the vices in the fiercest conflict (Moral. IV, chapter 36, no. 71).

When we strike down our faults through repentance and wash away the stains of filth with tears, we struggle bravely against the vices. Holy men then cleanse themselves more truly from the filth of the vices, when individual virtues are set against individual vices (Isidore, Sentences, book II, chapter 37).

Sometimes the vices contend with the virtues for our benefit, so that through the struggle itself either the mind may be exercised or the mind, shaken by pride [Note: [Col. 0942D] In Loaysa’s edition: “by the clash of pride”; in the Regal and Paris manuscripts: “turned back.”], may be restrained. The assaults of the vices must be fought with opposing virtues. Purity must be brought against lust; love must be prepared against hatred; patience must be set against anger; courage must be applied against fear; and zeal must fight against sluggishness. Joy must also be set against sadness, fortitude against acedia, generosity against greed, and humility against pride.

Thus each virtue restrains the vice arising against it and extinguishes the movements of temptation through the power of divine love. Abstinence tames lust. For to the extent that the body is weakened by fasting, the mind is recalled from unlawful desire. Endurance fights against anger. Anger kills itself, whereas patience bears away the victory by enduring. The hope of eternal joy overcomes the sorrow of sadness; and the sweetness of inward tranquility soothes the distress that the troubled mind suffers from external things. Charity must be prepared against envy, and tranquility of gentleness applied against the fires of anger.

### CHAPTER XXVI. On Excessive Speech

Those who devote themselves to excessive speech must be admonished to look attentively at how far they fall from the state of uprightness while they dissipate themselves through their many words (Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 14). The human mind, enclosed like water, gathers itself upward because it seeks again the place from which it descended; but, when released, it perishes because it uselessly scatters itself downward. Whoever is dispersed by superfluous words from the discipline of silence is led outside himself through many channels. Thus the mind is not able to return inward to knowledge of itself, because, scattered through excessive speech, it excludes itself from the secrecy of inward contemplation. It exposes itself entirely to the wounds of the ambushing enemy because it encloses itself with no defensive guard.

It is written in Proverbs: “Like an open city, without the surrounding of walls, is the man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Proverbs 25:28). Because it has no wall of silence, the city of the mind lies open to the enemy’s arrows. And when it casts itself outside itself through words, it shows itself open to its adversary. The enemy overcomes it all the more easily, the more the mind itself, which is being conquered, fights against itself through excessive speech (Gregory, as cited above, and Moral. Book VII, chapter 37, no. 57).

Often the sluggish mind is driven by certain stages into a pit. When we neglect to avoid idle words, we arrive at harmful ones: first we take pleasure in speaking about the affairs of others; afterward we wound by detraction the life of those about whom we speak; finally, the tongue bursts forth into open insults. Through the unbridled tongue, goads are sown, quarrels arise, the torches of hatred are kindled, and peace is extinguished in hearts.

Hence Solomon says appropriately: “He who releases water is the beginning of quarrels” (Proverbs 17:14). To release water is to relax the tongue into a flood of speech. But the one who releases water becomes the beginning of quarrels, because through the incontinent tongue the origin of discord is supplied (Moral. Book V, chapter 13, no. 30).

Because no one who serves excessive speech can in any way preserve the rectitude of justice, the prophet testifies, saying: “The talkative man shall not be directed upon the earth” (Psalm 139:12; Moral. Book VII, chapter 37, no. 58). Solomon again says: “In much speaking sin will not be absent” (Proverbs 10:19). The prophet Isaiah says: “The work of justice is silence” (Isaiah 32:17), indicating that the justice of the mind is laid waste when it does not spare itself from immoderate speech.

James says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious, not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1:26). Wicked people, just as they are shallow in understanding, are precipitous in speech, and neglect, when considering what they say, to keep silent (Moral. [Col. 0943C] Book V, chapter 13, no. 30). What a shallow conscience conceives, a still lighter tongue immediately produces.

Truth itself admonishes us, saying: “People will give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word that they have spoken” (Matthew 12:36; Moral. Book VII, chapter 37, no. 58). An idle word is one that lacks either the reason of just necessity or the intention of pious usefulness. If an account is therefore demanded for idle speech, let us consider what punishment awaits excessive speech, in which one also sins through harmful words.

### CHAPTER XXVII. On Perverse Speech

Just as perfect men ought not to flee from their perverse neighbors, because they often draw them toward uprightness and are themselves never drawn toward perversity, so all who are weak ought to avoid the company of the wicked, lest they take pleasure in imitating the evils that they frequently see but are unable to correct (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 23).

By hearing the words of our neighbors every day, we take them into our minds just as, by blowing and breathing, we draw air into our bodies. As bad air, drawn in through continual breathing, infects the body, so perverse speech, heard continually, infects the mind of the weak, so that it wastes away in delight in evil conduct and in the iniquity of continual speech. Hence Paul says: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33).

### CHAPTER XXVIII. On Those Who Live Joyful or Sorrowful in This World

[Col. 0944A]

The joyful must be admonished in one way and the sorrowful in another (Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 3). To the joyful must be brought the sorrows that follow from punishment; to the sorrowful must be brought the joys that are promised from the kingdom. Let the joyful learn from the severity of the threats what they should fear; let the sorrowful hear of the joys of the rewards in which they may place their hope.

To the former it is said: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn” (Luke 6:25). The latter hear from the same Teacher: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

It often happens that some are not joyful or sorrowful because of circumstances, but are such by temperament. They must certainly be instructed that certain vices accompany certain temperaments [Note: [Col. 0943D] The edition reads “are close to certain temperaments.”]. The joyful have lust close at hand, while the sorrowful have anger. Therefore each person must consider not only what he suffers from his temperament, but also what is more dangerously urged upon him by what lies near it, lest, while he does not fight at all against what he endures, he also succumb to the vice from which he thinks himself free.

### CHAPTER XXIX. On Folly

Foolish people observe with the whole attention of their hearts only that by which they may be brought to the end of an earthly desire (Moral. XVII, chapter 7, no. 9). It is written: “The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth” (Proverbs 17:24). A fool would never fix the gaze of his contemplation upon earth if he lifted the eyes of his mind toward the paths of his holy Redeemer.

It is written: “The fool shall serve the wise” (Proverbs 11:29; Moral. XX, chapter 24, no. 52). Often we see the wise placed beneath others, while fools hold the citadel of power; the wise obey in servile fashion, while fools rule with tyrannical pride. How, then, according to the definition of the divine judgment, does the fool serve the wise, when he so often oppresses him by the right of temporal power?

But we must know that, when a prominent fool exercises the terror of power against the life of a wise man, when he exhausts him with labors and tears him with insults, he purifies him by burning away every rust of vice. Often the fool serves the wise even while ruling him, because by pressing him down he raises him to a better condition.

Sometimes slaves preside over young masters as instructors, frighten them, oppress them, and beat them; yet they do not in any way cease to be slaves, because they have been appointed for this very purpose: to serve their advancing masters even by beating them. Since the evils of foolish reprobates purify the good by afflicting them, the power of the wicked also serves the benefit of the righteous.

Just as, when a door is closed, one does not know what members of the household are hidden inside, so often, if a fool remains silent, it is hidden whether he is wise or foolish—provided no other deeds emerge that reveal the understanding even of one who is silent (Moral. XI, chapter 24, no. 35). Solomon says: “If a fool keeps silent, he will be considered wise” (Proverbs 17:28).

But because, when a fool speaks, he cannot sufficiently weigh the words of the wise against what he himself brings forward, blessed Job rightly says: “Hear, then, my corrections, and attend to the judgment of my lips” (Job 13:6). He appropriately introduced correction first and judgment afterward, because unless the fool’s swelling is first brought low through correction, the judgment of the just is not understood through intelligence (Moral. XI, chapter 25, no. 36).

Sometimes fools, when they observe the deeds of prudent people, regard all of them as blameworthy. Forgetting their own ignorance and weakness, they judge others more intently the more deeply they remain unaware of themselves (Gregory, as cited above, chapter 27, no. 38).

### CHAPTER XXX. On Lust

The evil of lust is committed either in thought or in deed. For when our crafty adversary is driven away from the completion of the act, he attempts to defile the secrets of thought [Note: [Col. 0945D] The edition reads “through thought.” But Taius’s reading is supported not only by recent editions but also by the Corbie manuscript.] (Moral. XXI, chapter 2, no. 5).

The Lord says to the serpent: “You shall crawl upon your breast and belly” (Genesis 3:14). The serpent crawls upon its belly when the slippery enemy exercises lust through human members subjected to him, all the way to the completion of the act. The serpent crawls upon its breast when it defiles in thought those whom it cannot overcome in the act. Whoever commits lust in action has the serpent crawling from its belly; whoever turns over in his mind the act that is to be committed has the serpent crawling from its breast.

To flee burning Sodom is to avoid the unlawful fires of the flesh (Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 27). Whoever, raised up by the successes of this world, feels himself tempted by the goads of lust through the seductive joy of his heart should recall what happened to Joseph and preserve himself in the stronghold of chastity (Moral. Book XXX, chapter 10, no. 38).

When slippery pleasure tempts amid prosperity, prosperity itself must be opposed to it as the goad of temptation, so that we may be ashamed to commit evil precisely because we remember that we have received our good things from God as gifts [Note: [Col. 0945D] The edition reads “freely.”]. Sometimes the pleasure that arises from prosperity must be struck by consideration of that same prosperity, so that our enemy may die from the source from which he arises.

The prophet David suddenly fell through lust when, walking upon the roof, he desired and took another man’s wife; he killed her husband, with the loss of his army, and fell by a sudden collapse, when that mind, accustomed to heavenly mysteries, was overcome by an unexpected temptation and subjected to the most monstrous disgrace [Col. 0945D] (2 Samuel 11:4; Moral. Book XII, chapter 18, no. 23).

It was as though a stone had been moved from its place when the prophet’s mind, excluded from the mysteries of prophecy, came to think upon disgraceful things. That once most wise Solomon was overcome by an excess of lust and, through the immoderate use and constant presence of women, was brought to the point of building a temple for idols. He who had previously built a temple for God did not fear, through continual lust, to build temples for idols, having also been subjected to faithlessness (1 Kings 11:7).

Thus it came about that from continual wantonness of the flesh he reached faithlessness of mind, because, as the infusion of sin gradually stole upon him, the soil of his heart slipped away toward [Note: [Col. 0946D] Editions read “consumption.”] ruin.

Not without reason those who desire the low things of this carnal life are called “beasts of the earth” (Moral. XXVI, 17, no. 27) [Note: [Col. 0946D] The edition reads “by the use”]; seductive pleasure casts them down into the lowest places. To them sacred Scripture says: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding” (Psalm 32:9).

To lovers of carnal pleasures it is said: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed” (Colossians 3:5). The apostle Paul rebukes those devoted to the wantonness of the flesh in a public denunciation, saying: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Romans 1:21; Gregory, cited above, no. 28).

He then added how they fell into the pleasure of beasts—or rather, of things worse than beasts—saying: “He handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness” (Romans 1:24). Through lust, the flesh plunged some into the lowest places, although proud knowledge had lifted them on high; and they fell from the flight of birds beyond the appetite of beasts. They were cast down beneath themselves from the very place from which they seemed to rise above themselves.

Often the poison of lust arises from the root of pride. The flesh then conquers when the spirit secretly swells, because the soul falls into the wantonness of beasts through the origin of its fault precisely when, by exalting itself, it flies like a bird farther than it ought (Gregory, cited above, no. 29).

Sometimes, through the vice of pride, long continence is suddenly undone, and virginity preserved even into old age is often violated. Because humility of heart is neglected, the just Judge also despises bodily integrity, and at times publicly reveals as reprobate those whom he had long tolerated as reprobate in secret.

Whoever suddenly loses a good long preserved had another evil within himself, from which he suddenly burst forth into another evil [Note: [Col. 0946D] The edition reads “another.” Taius’s reading is reported in the Vindobonensis manuscript.]. Through that evil he had already been alienated from almighty God even when, by bodily purity, he appeared to cling to him.

Often elevation of mind leads to pollution of the flesh, and the heart of the reprobate sinks from the flight of birds into the wantonness of beasts (Moral. XXI, chapter 3, no. 7).

We must know with the greatest care that one thing is what the mind suffers from the temptation of the flesh, and another is what happens when it is bound by consent to pleasures. Often it is struck by an evil thought but resists. Often, however, when it conceives something perverse, it also turns it over within itself through desire. An unclean thought does not pollute the mind when it strikes it, but when it subjugates it to itself through pleasure.

The outstanding preacher Paul says: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (1 Corinthians 10:13). Human temptation is that by which we are often touched in thought even unwillingly, because the fact that unlawful things sometimes come into the mind is something we possess within ourselves from the burden of corruptible humanity.

The temptation is demonic, not human, when the mind binds itself through consent to what the corruptibility of the flesh suggests. The same apostle Paul says: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6:12). He forbade sin not to be in the mortal body, but to reign, because in corruptible flesh it cannot fail to exist, though it can be prevented from reigning.

It belongs to the human race to be tempted by sin. Since we cannot wholly escape it as long as we live, holy preaching, because it could not expel it, removed its reign from the dwelling of our heart, so that although unlawful desire often secretly inserts itself into our good thoughts like a thief, at least, if it enters, it may not rule.

It is written in Genesis: “The Lord rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah” (Genesis 19:24; Moral. Book XIV, chapter 19, no. 23). What is expressed by sulfur if not the stench of the flesh, and by fire if not the burning of carnal desire? When the Lord therefore determined to punish the sins of the flesh of those dwelling in Sodom and Gomorrah, he marked the stain of the crime in the very character of the punishment. Sulfur has a stench, and fire has heat. Thus those who had burned toward perverse desires from the stench of the flesh deserved to perish together by sulfur and fire, so that from the just punishment they might learn what they had done through unjust desire.

### CHAPTER XXXI. On Sluggishness of Spirit

Often the human mind is struck while asleep to the care of its own vigilance, yet does not feel the blows, because, just as it does not foresee the evils that threaten, so it does not recognize what it has done (Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 32). It is dragged along without perceiving it, because it is led through the enticements of the vices, yet is not awakened to guard itself.

Although a person is oppressed by the sleep of sluggishness and so prevented from guarding himself, he nevertheless strives to remain awake for the concerns of the world, so that he may always be intoxicated with pleasures. While he sleeps with regard to what he ought diligently to watch over, he desires to remain awake for something else, with regard to which he could commendably have slept.

Solomon says in Proverbs: “You shall be like one sleeping in the middle of the sea, and like a drowsy helmsman who has lost the rudder” (Proverbs 23:34). He sleeps in the middle of the sea who, placed amid the temptations of this world, neglects to foresee the movements of the attacking vices, like heaps of waves threatening him. He loses the rudder like a helmsman when the mind loses the diligent care required to steer the ship of the body.

To lose the rudder at sea is not to maintain a watchful purpose amid the storms of this age. If the helmsman holds the rudder carefully, at one moment he directs the ship against the waves, and at another cuts diagonally through the force of the winds.

It is written: “The lizard grasps with its hands and dwells in the palaces of kings” (Proverbs 30:23; Moral. VI, chapter 10, no. 12). Often birds, which the feather of their wings lifts into flight, sit among thorns; but the lizard, which has no wings for flight, holds fast to the royal building by grasping with its hands.

Often, indeed, people of great intelligence, while they grow sluggish through negligence, remain in wicked actions; while simple people, whom the feather of intelligence does not assist, are lifted by the virtue of their deeds to obtain the walls of the eternal kingdom. The lizard dwells in the king’s palaces by grasping with its hands, because the simple person reaches by the intention of upright action the place to which the intelligent person scarcely ascends.

A question arises: why is the gift of understanding sometimes given to the negligent, while a diligent person is hindered by the slowness of his understanding? The answer is given more quickly when it is immediately added [Note: [Col. 0947D] The words “through Solomon” have been inserted here. The testimony cited, however, is from the Book of Job.] through Solomon: “Nothing upon the earth is without cause” (Job 5:6; Moral. VI, chapter 11, no. 13).

The sluggish person often receives intelligence so that the negligent may be punished more justly [Note: [Col. 0948D] The edition reads “so that he may be punished for negligence.”], because he scorns to know what he could have attained without labor. And sometimes the diligent person is weighed down by slowness of understanding so that he may find greater rewards in his recompense, in proportion as he labors more in the effort of discovery.

Nothing, therefore, is without cause upon the earth, since slowness benefits the diligent person for reward, while swiftness increases the punishment of the one who desires it. The sloth of the mind, when it is not kindled by appropriate fervor, is utterly cut off from the desire for good things as sluggishness secretly grows stronger (Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 15).

Solomon says: “Slothfulness brings on sleep” (Proverbs 19:15). The lazy person is awake in thinking rightly, although he grows sluggish by doing nothing; but slothfulness is said to bring on sleep because, when the practice of good works ceases, even the vigilance of right thinking is gradually lost.

Concerning sluggishness of spirit, it is rightly written in Proverbs: “The unrestrained soul shall hunger” (ibid.). Whoever does not direct himself upward by applying himself to higher things spreads himself downward through neglected desires. When he is not restrained by the strength of elevated pursuits, he is wounded by the hunger of low desires, so that, to the extent that he refuses to bind himself through discipline, he scatters himself hungrily through desires for pleasure.

Again Solomon writes: “Every idle person is in his desires” (Proverbs 21:26). Hence Truth himself, preaching, says that when one spirit has gone out, the house is called clean, but when it returns in greater numbers, it occupies it because it lies vacant (Matthew 12:44–45).

### CHAPTER XXXII. On Laziness

The lazy must be persuaded not to lose the good things that ought to be done by postponing them; for, although they are unwilling to do at the proper time what they can do, shortly afterward, when they wish to do it, they may no longer be able (Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 15).

Often the lazy person, while neglecting to do what is necessary, puts certain difficulties in his own way and carelessly fears others. By seeming to find something that he may supposedly fear justly, he shows that he grows sluggish in idleness as though not unjustly.

Solomon says to the lazy person: “Because of the cold the lazy man would not plow; therefore he shall beg in summer and nothing shall be given him” (Proverbs 20:4). Because of the cold the lazy person does not plow when, constrained by the sluggishness of indolence, he refuses to do the good things he ought to do. While he fears small evils that confront him, he neglects to perform great works.

It is rightly added: “He shall beg in summer, and nothing shall be given him.” Whoever does not sweat now in good works, when the sun of judgment appears more fiercely, will beg in summer, asking vainly for entrance to the kingdom and receiving nothing.

Again it is written: “The lazy man hides his hand beneath his armpit and does not bring it to his mouth” (Proverbs 19:24). No one is so lazy that he would consider it a labor to bring his hand to his mouth even for the sake of eating. But the lazy man does not extend his hand to his mouth because he does not wish to do even what he says (Book II on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 15).

The hand signifies action, while the mouth signifies speech (Moral. XXII, chapter 9, no. 20). For the lazy person it is a labor to bring his hand to his mouth, because the slothful preacher does not wish to do even what he says. To bring the hand to the mouth is to make one’s action agree with one’s speech.

The same Solomon says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, it was all overgrown with nettles; thorns covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Proverbs 24:30–31). To pass by the field of a lazy man and the vineyard of a foolish man is to examine the life of anyone who is negligent and consider his works (Moral. XX, chapter 25, no. 54).

Nettles or thorns fill it because, in the hearts of the negligent, earthly desires that cause itching and the stings of vices spring up. “Its stone wall had been destroyed,” that is, the discipline of the fathers had been dissolved in his heart. Since he saw that the destroyed stone wall signified a dissolved discipline [Note: [Col. 0949D] The edition reads “the wall having been destroyed.” Earlier editions, however, read as Taius does.], he immediately added: “When I saw this, I applied it to my heart and learned discipline from the example” (Proverbs 24:32).

When the vigor of discipline is dissolved in the hearts of the reprobate because laziness rules, all good works are despised before their eyes. They consider worthless whatever they see in the virtues of the elect.

### CHAPTER XXXIII. On Murmuring

If vinegar is poured into natron, the natron foams, as it is written: “As vinegar upon natron, so is one who sings songs to a most wicked heart” (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 33). When a perverse mind is corrected by rebuke or persuaded toward good by the sweetness of preaching [Note: [Col. 0949D] The edition reads “or good is persuaded by the sweetness of preaching.” Taius’s reading seems better, and other manuscripts agree with it.], it becomes worse through correction. It is thereby inflamed into the iniquity of murmuring precisely where it ought to have been restrained from iniquity.

Whoever is struck because of sin, unless he resists by murmuring, already begins to be just by that very fact: he does not accuse the justice of the one who strikes him.

### CHAPTER XXXIV. On Lying
The way of truth is altogether smooth, whereas the path of falsehood is arduous, as it is written: “They have taught their tongue to speak falsehood; they have labored to act unjustly” (Jer. 9:5; *Moralium* XII.42.47). Whoever, having abandoned the truth, deliberately decides to lie in order to deceive the minds of his hearers—how great an effort it is for him carefully to guard against having his very deception detected! He places before his eyes what those who know the truth might answer him, and with great deliberation considers how, by arguments of falsehood, he might surpass the proofs of truth. Laboring under deception, falsehood shields itself on every side and seeks, against whatever point might expose it, a reply resembling the truth; yet if he wished to speak the truth, he could certainly do so without effort.

Every lie is iniquity, and every iniquity is a lie, because whatever disagrees with the truth plainly departs from righteousness (*Moralium* XVIII.3.5). Sometimes it is worse to devise a lie than to speak one. For speaking is often the result of rashness, whereas devising one is the product of deliberate perversity; and who does not understand how greatly guilt differs according as someone lies rashly or deliberately?

Every lie must be avoided with the greatest care, although sometimes a particular kind of lie may involve lesser guilt—if someone lies in order to save another. It is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). And: “You will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7). Perfect men also diligently avoid this kind of lie, so that neither anyone’s life may be preserved through their deception nor may they harm their own souls while striving to save another’s flesh [Note: [Col. 0950D] The edition reads, “to preserve life”; Tajo is supported by the Norman manuscripts], although we readily believe that this very kind of sin is easily forgiven. For if any fault is usually cleansed by a subsequent good deed, how much more easily is this one wiped away, when piety itself—the mother of a good deed—accompanies it?  

Some try to assert, on the basis of the deception of the midwives, that this kind of lie is not a sin, especially since, after they had lied, it is written: “Because the Lord built houses for them” (Exod. 1:21; *Moralium* XVIII.3.6). In the recompense given to the Egyptian midwives, however, it can be understood what reward the guilt of lying deserves. The reward for their kindness, which could have been repaid to them in eternal life, was, because of the guilt mingled with it, diverted into an earthly recompense: in the life that they had sought to preserve by lying, they received the good things they had done, but they did not obtain thereafter the reward of their merits that they might have expected. If the matter is weighed carefully, the Egyptian midwives lied out of love for the present life, not with the intention of obtaining a reward. By sparing, they tried to conceal the infants’ lives; by lying, their own (*Moralium*, ibid. 7).

[Note: In our manuscript *necare* (“to kill”) has been added here; I judge the word to be an intrusion contrary to Gregory’s intention.]

And although some such examples may be found in the Old Testament, a diligent reader will find that almost never did perfect men admit this or a similar kind of lie. For just as a building is constructed with stones, so a lie is constructed with words (*Moralium* XI.23.34). Where there is not deceitful speech but the meaning of truth, something like a fortified mass rises, not from workmanship but from nature.

Blessed Job says to his friends, who were thinking incorrectly: “Does God need your lie, that you may speak deceitfully for him?” (Job 13:7; ibid., 26.37). God does not need a lie, because truth does not seek to be supported by the aid of falsehood.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The Ways in Which Sin Is Committed

Sin is committed in the heart in four ways, and brought to completion in action in four ways. In the heart it is committed through suggestion, delight, consent, and the boldness of self-defense (*Moralium* IV.27.49). Suggestion comes from the adversary, delight through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the boldness of self-defense through pride. Often guilt, which ought to have terrified the mind, raises it up; and by casting it down it elevates it, but by elevating it overturns it more grievously.

Thus the ancient enemy shattered the uprightness of the first human being by these four blows: the serpent suggested, Eve delighted, Adam consented; and when asked, he refused in his boldness to confess his guilt. What took place in the first parent of our race is enacted daily in the human race. The serpent suggested, because the hidden enemy secretly suggests evil to human hearts. Eve delighted, because the carnal sense immediately submits itself to delight at the serpent’s words. Adam, who had been placed over the woman, gave his assent, because when the flesh is carried away into delight, the spirit too, weakened from its uprightness, is bent down. When questioned, Adam refused to confess his guilt, because the spirit, separated from the truth by sinning, is hardened more wickedly in the boldness of its fall.

Adam had fled in order to hide himself through fear; yet, when questioned, he revealed how much he was swollen even while afraid (*Moralium*, ibid. 50). For when the present punishment resulting from sin is feared, but the lost face of God is not loved, fear arises from pride, not from humility. The person who would not abandon sin if permitted to go unpunished is proud.

Just as sin is committed in the heart in four ways—through suggestion, delight, consent, and the boldness of self-defense—so sin is brought to completion in action in four ways (*Moralium*, ibid. 49). At first the hidden guilt is enacted; afterward the offense is openly revealed before human eyes without shame; then it is made habitual; and finally it is nourished either by the deceits of false hope or by the wretched obstinacy of despair.

We learned from our first parent that every wickedness of sin is committed in three ways: through suggestion, delight, and consent (*Pastoral Rule* III.29). The first is committed through the enemy, the second through the flesh, and the third through the spirit. The ambusher suggests what is evil; the flesh submits itself to delight; and finally the spirit, overcome by delight, consents. In paradise the ancient serpent suggested what was evil; Eve, like the flesh, submitted herself to delight; and Adam, like the spirit, overcome by suggestion and delight, assented.

Through the devil’s suggestion we sometimes recognize sin; through delight we are overcome; and through consent we are also bound. Therefore, with the Apostle, we must cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24), so that we may hear the consolation that follows: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid., 25).

Very often one and the same sin is both the punishment and the cause of sin. We demonstrate this more clearly if we bring the matters themselves before us (*Moralium* XXV.9.24). For the unrestrained gluttony of the belly drives the fullness of the flesh toward the heat of lust; and once lust has been committed, it is often concealed by perjury or murder, lest it be punished by the vengeance of human laws.

Let us place before our eyes someone who loosened the reins of his appetite and, overcome by gluttony, committed adultery. When discovered in adultery, he secretly killed the adulteress’s husband so that he would not be brought to trial. This adultery, situated between gluttony and murder—arising from the former and generating the latter—is both sin and the punishment and cause of sin. It is sin in itself; it is the punishment of sin because it increased the guilt of gluttony; and it is the cause of sin because it generated the subsequent murder.

The prophet Jeremiah says: “I will visit upon you according to the fruit of your practices” (Jer. 21:14; *Pastoral Rule* III.32). Sins committed deliberately differ from other sins. The Lord does not pursue deeds as much as he pursues the deliberate purposes of wickedness. In deeds, sin often arises from weakness and often from negligence; in deliberate purposes, however, it always arises from a malicious intention.

Blessed Job, designating the type of sinners within the Church, says: “He has struck me with wound upon wound” (Job 16:14; *Moralium* XII.17.20). The holy Church is struck in her weak members with wound upon wound when sin is added to sin, so that guilt is greatly increased. When avarice drags someone to robbery, robbery leads him to deceit, so that the guilt already committed may also be defended by falsehood, what is he but one struck down by wound upon wound?

The prophet rightly says: “Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2). Blood touches blood when guilt is heaped upon guilt. Therefore, when wound is added to wound, the strength of the ancient enemy is stirred up more violently against us.

Although we sin in every place by thinking, speaking, and acting, the mind is carried away in these three ways with greater abandon when it is lifted up by the prosperity of this world (*Moralium* V.11.17).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Manifest and Hidden Sins

The hidden guilt of each person is, as it were, the womb of sin, which secretly conceives the sinner and conceals his offense in darkness (*Moralium* IV.27.51).

From the womb one emerges from the uterus when the sinner is no longer ashamed to commit openly what he had committed in secret. For it is written: “Why did I not perish immediately upon coming forth from the womb?” (Job 3:11)—that is: After I went out into open iniquity, why did I not at least then recognize that I was lost? He would have perished in his own judgment if he had recognized that he was lost.

Those of whom the prophet said, “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and did not hide it” (Isa. 3:9), had, as it were, emerged from the womb of their concealment.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Those Who Return to Sin After Tears

There are some who, when they return to their senses, contemplate God’s justice and uprightness and tremble in prayer and weeping. But when the hour of contemplation has passed, they return so boldly to iniquity as though, placed behind its back, they were not at all seen by the light of justice (*Moralium* XI.29.40).

Whoever relapses into sin after tears inwardly beholds, as it were, God’s bodily-seeing face [Note: The edition reads, “they receive him as one who sees bodily.”]. When they come into his presence, they flatter him with their tears; and when they withdraw, as it were, from his sight, they disparage him by their conduct. They deserve to be struck for their evils all the more severely because, even in the secrecy of their thoughts, they recognize God’s righteous judgments.

There are some who, after losing their life, return to themselves. Their conscience accusing them, they abandon their perverse paths, change their actions, oppose their former wickedness, flee earthly activities, and pursue heavenly desires. But before they become firmly established in these holy desires, through the sluggishness of their minds they return to what they had begun to condemn and go back to the evils they had resolved to flee (*Moralium* XII.52.59).

If a person perhaps begins to do something good, before he grows strong in it through the passage of time he falls back into exterior things and perversely abandons what he seemed rightly to have begun. There are some who, after following perverse paths, desire to pursue holy ways; but before their good desires are strengthened, some prosperity of the present age overtakes them, entangles them in exterior things, and, by drawing their minds away from the warmth of inward love, extinguishes them as though through cold. It destroys whatever seemed to appear in them of the flower of virtue (*Moralium* XII.53.60).

We must take the greatest care lest anyone rush back into what he rejoices to have cleansed with tears, lest, when the fault that was lamented is committed again, those very laments be made lighter in the sight of the just Judge (*Moralium* X.15.28).

It is written in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “Whoever is baptized from the dead and again touches him, what benefit is there in his washing?” (Sir. 34:30; *Pastoral Rule* III.30). Whoever does not preserve the innocence of life after tears neglects to remain clean after washing. Thus those who do not cease to weep over what they have committed, but commit again what must be wept over, are washed but by no means clean. Someone is baptized from the dead when he is cleansed from sin by tears; but after baptism he touches the dead when he repeats his fault after tears.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Habit of Sinning

When a sinner is no longer ashamed of his iniquity, he is strengthened in that same iniquity by the support of a most evil habit (*Moralium* IV.27.51). The sinner is cherished by various pleasures so that he may grow, while guilt is strengthened by habits so that it may flourish. When guilt begins to emerge into practice, it feeds itself either on a false hope of divine mercy or on the manifest misery of despair, so that a person does not return to correction precisely because he either falsely imagines his Maker to be merciful toward him or irrationally fears what he has done.

Blessed Job, contemplating the fall of the human race and considering into what precipices it had plunged itself in the pit of iniquity, says: “Why did I not die in the womb?” (Job 3:11)—that is: In the very secret commission of sin, why did I not choose to be put to death away from the life of the flesh? “Why,” he says, “was I received upon the knees?”—that is, even after open guilt, why did habit still receive me into it, making me stronger for wickedness and supporting and fostering me in depraved practices?

Often, when guilt has become habitual, the mind resists it more weakly even if it desires to do so, because as often as it is bound by repeated wrongdoing, it is tied to the mind, as it were, by that many bonds. Sometimes it happens that a weakened mind, unable to free itself from the habit of sin, turns toward certain consolations of false comfort, promising itself that the Judge who is to come will show it such great mercy that he will not utterly destroy even those whom he finds deserving of reproach.

This becomes even worse because the speech of many like-minded people agrees with it, when many magnify the evil deeds of human beings with praise. Thus guilt often grows without ceasing, nourished by approval. A wound that appears worthy of the reward of praise is neglected instead of being cured.

Solomon says in Proverbs: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent” (Prov. 1:10; *Moralium* XXXIII.10.18). Sinners entice when they either introduce evils to be committed with flattering words or exalt evils already committed with approval.

The prophet Isaiah says: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isa. 5:18). Iniquity is drawn with cords of vanity when guilt is prolonged through the growth of habit. Blessed David speaks of the habit of sinning: “The cords of sinners have entangled me” (Ps. 118:61). Because a cord is twisted by adding to it so that it grows, the habit of sin is rightly represented by a cord: when it is repeatedly practiced by a perverse heart, it grows increasingly through the enlargement of habit.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Lesser Sins

Sin is frequently committed either through ignorance or through weakness, so that a person either does not know what he ought to will or is unable to do everything he wills (*Moralium* XIX.23.39). When the mind dies in sin, it is brought back to life more quickly if vigilant thoughts remain alive concerning it.

## CHAPTER XL. Graver Sins

Every sin that is not quickly cleansed is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin (*Moralium* XXV.9.22). For a sin that repentance does not wash away immediately draws a person toward another sin by its own weight. Thus it becomes not only sin but also the cause of sin. From that vice arises the subsequent guilt by which the blinded mind is led, so that it may be bound more grievously by another sin.

The sin that arises from sin is no longer merely sin, but sin and the punishment of sin, because by a just judgment almighty God darkens the heart of the sinner, so that by the merit of his preceding sin he may also fall into other sins. He struck by abandoning the one whom he did not wish to free. It is rightly called the punishment of sin when, through a just blindness inflicted from above, something is committed as vengeance for a preceding sin. This takes place by an arrangement ordered above but confused below by iniquity, so that the preceding guilt is the cause of what follows, and in turn the subsequent guilt is the punishment of what preceded it.

The Apostle Paul had perceived, in the unbelieving and licentious, something like a seed of error when he said: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Rom. 1:21; *Book I on Ezekiel*, homily 11.24). Here is sin and the cause of sin. He adds what follows from that cause: “And their senseless heart was darkened; for, claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (Rom. 1:22–23). Here is sin and the punishment of sin.

But it would be merely sin and the punishment of sin if no further sin followed from this sin. For after their unbelief he adds: “Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves” (ibid., 24). Those who knew God but did not glorify him as God were led from that sin, which was both sin and the cause of sin, to fall also into the worship of serpents and birds. But because through this blindness they fell as far as impurity and the dishonoring of the flesh, their very blindness in unbelief is both sin and the punishment of sin with respect to the preceding understanding. With respect to the impurity that followed, it became sin and the cause of sin.

Those who, by understanding, committed the sin of pride because they knew God are also blinded, so that they do not understand what they are committing (*Moralium* XXV.9.22). Those who refuse to follow their understanding in sin and as the cause of sin lose the very light of understanding in sin and as the punishment of sin. By the deserved consequence of their earlier sin, the pit of subsequent sins is covered over, so that the one who knowingly commits evil may thereafter justly fall into other evils without knowing it. This takes place so that sins may strike sinners, and so that the very increase of vices may become the punishment of those who sin (*Moralium*, ibid. 23).

There are many sins that we commit, and for that reason they do not seem serious to us: because, loving ourselves with a private affection, we flatter ourselves in our own deception with our eyes closed (*Book I on the Gospels*, homily 4.9). It often happens that we judge our own grave sins lightly and the light sins of our neighbors gravely.

It is written: “People will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3:2). And we know that private love powerfully closes the eye of the heart. Hence what we do is often not thought serious by us, while the same thing done by our neighbor appears exceedingly detestable to us. But why does what seemed insignificant to us in ourselves appear serious in our neighbor, unless it is because we do not see ourselves as we see our neighbor, nor our neighbor as we see ourselves? If we looked at ourselves as at our neighbor, we would see our blameworthy acts with strictness. And again, if we looked at our neighbor as at ourselves, his action would never appear intolerable to us, since we have often perhaps done similar things and thought that we had done nothing intolerable to our neighbor.

Moses tried to correct the wrongly divided judgment of our mind through the precept of the Law when he said that the measure should be just and the sextarius equal (Lev. 19:36). Solomon says: “A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure—both are abominable before God” (Prov. 20:10). We know that in the double weight of merchants one is greater and the other smaller. They have one weight by which they weigh for themselves and another by which they weigh for their neighbor. They prepare lighter weights for giving and heavier ones for receiving.

Everyone who weighs what belongs to his neighbor one way and what belongs to himself another way has a weight and a weight. Both are therefore abominable before God, because if he loved his neighbor as himself, he would love him in himself as himself; and if he looked at himself as at his neighbor, he would judge himself in evils as he judges his neighbor.

## CHAPTER XLI. The Despair of Sinners

False hope does not always seize the mind; sometimes a worse dispensation pierces it. While it completely destroys all hope of pardon, it nourishes the soul more abundantly with the milk of error (*Moralium* IV.27.52).

Blessed Job, taking upon himself in his speech the person of every despairing individual, says: “Why was I suckled at the breasts?” (Job 3:12; *Moralium* IV.27.53). As if he were saying: Would that, after committing evil, I had at least not wished to flatter myself, so that I would not bind myself to guilt all the more wickedly by fostering myself in it too gently.

Whoever succumbs to ungodliness abandons the life of righteousness by dying (*Moralium* VIII.18.34). But whoever is also overwhelmed after sin by the weight of despair—what else does he do but bury himself after death in the punishment of hell?

It is written in Solomon’s books: “When the wicked comes to the depth of sins, he despises” (Prov. 18:3; *Moralium* XXVI.37.69). He delays returning because he despairs that mercy can be shown to him. But by sinning more through despair, he is like someone removing the bottom from his own well, so that he may find nowhere to be held.

Everyone who abandons the way of life and casts himself into the darkness of sins plunges himself, as it were, into a well or pit. But if he is also oppressed by the habit of iniquity through long practice, so that he can no longer rise to higher things, he is constricted as though by the narrow mouth of a well (*Moralium*, ibid. 65).

The prophet David, praying in the person of sinners, says: “Let not the storm of waters overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor let the well close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16). Whoever has been shaken from the stability of the good by the iniquity of an evil deed has been carried away like a storm of water. But if habit has not yet prevailed, it has not overwhelmed him. He has already fallen into the well who has committed what the divine Law prohibits. But if long habit has not yet depressed him, the well has not completely narrowed its mouth over him. Therefore, he escapes all the more easily the less he is constricted by habit.

The narrowness of a closed mouth is something like the condition of wishing to rise from an oppressive evil habit but being unable to do so: already to reach toward heavenly things in desire, but still to remain in the lowest things in action; to go ahead in the heart but not follow in deed, and to suffer contradiction within oneself by oneself (*Gregory, as cited above*, 66).

# BOOK FIVE

## CHAPTER I. Lovers of the World

All the wicked, because they neglect to pass in their hearts to eternal things and do not consider all present things because they are passing away, fix their minds in love of the present life and build for themselves in it, as though it were a long dwelling, a foundation, because they become established through desire in earthly things (*Moralium* XVI.10.15).

Cain is described as the first to have built a city (Gen. 4), so that it might plainly be shown that the one who was alienated from the stability of the eternal homeland set his foundation upon earth. A wanderer from the heights, he laid his foundation in the depths: he placed the intention of his heart in earthly delight.

In Cain’s line Enoch, whose name means “dedication,” is born first. In the lineage of the elect, however, Enoch is remembered as having been seventh, because the reprobate dedicate themselves by building themselves up in this life, which comes first. The elect, however, await the dedication of their building at the end of time, that is, in the seventh generation.

Often we see many people thinking only about temporal things, seeking honors, panting after things to be acquired, and seeking nothing after this life. What do such people do but dedicate themselves in the first generation? Conversely, we see the elect seeking none of the glory of the present, willingly enduring poverty, and patiently suffering the evils of the world so that they may be crowned at the end. Thus Enoch is born for the elect in the seventh generation, because they seek the dedication of their joy in the glory of the final recompense.

All the wicked dedicate themselves at the beginning, because they plant the root of their hearts in this life, which comes first, so that they may flourish here according to their desire and wither completely from the delights of the homeland that follows (*Moralium* VIII.54.92).

The lovers of this age inhabit exterior things all the more because they leave their interior lives uncultivated. A certain Wise Man says: “You shall not appear empty before the Lord” (Exod. 23:15; *Moralium* VII.29.38). Whoever loves the present world and carries away none of the fruit of his labor appears empty before the Lord.

All who love earthly rather than heavenly things toil: one sweats in the pursuit of honors, another burns with the multiplication of wealth, and another pants after winning praise. But because each person abandons all these things here when he dies, he appears empty before the Lord, because he has brought nothing with him before the Judge.

Every tree stands broad near the ground in its strength, but becomes narrower as it grows upward. The higher it rises, the thinner it becomes (*Moralium* XIX.27.49). To what, then, are such trees similar except to earthly minds, broad below and narrow above? All lovers of this age are strong in earthly things but weak in heavenly ones. They desire to toil even unto death for temporal glory, but for the hope of eternity they do not remain in labor even briefly.

Lovers of the world endure every kind of injury for earthly profits, but for heavenly reward they refuse to bear even the insults of a very slight word. The more intent they are upon worldly cares, the more insensitive they become inwardly, because they are more devoted to exterior things.

All who are conformed to this age by earthly thought attempt, in everything they do, to leave behind a memorial of themselves in this world (*Moralium* XI.30.42). Some labor earnestly through the distinctions of wars, others through the lofty walls of buildings, and others through the eloquent books of secular learning, building for themselves a name in memory.

But since life itself hastens more swiftly toward its end, what can stand fixed in it when it too passes quickly in its own swift movement? However much someone labors to create glory for his name, he has placed his memory like ashes, because the wind of mortality quickly carries it away. And everything he eagerly loves from this world he immediately loses.
