The Psalmist says: “Who has not received his soul in vain?” (Ps. 23:4; *Moralium* VII.20.38). He receives his soul in vain who, neglecting its life, puts care of the flesh before it, thinking only about present things and failing to consider what will follow him forever.

## CHAPTER II. The Adornment of Clothing

Let no one suppose that there is no sin in the flow and care of clothing, because if this were not a fault, the Lord would in no way have praised John for the roughness of his clothing (*Book I on the Gospels*, homily 6.3). If the adornment of clothing were not a fault, the Apostle Peter would certainly not have restrained women in his Epistle from the desire for expensive clothing, saying: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Pet. 3:3).

We must carefully consider what fault it is for men also to desire the adornment of clothing from which the pastor of the Church took care to prohibit women. Concerning John the Baptist, Truth says: “What did you go out into the desert to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings” (Matt. 11:8). John is described as having been clothed in garments woven from camel hair. What does it mean to say, “Behold, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings,” except to demonstrate plainly that those who refuse to endure hardships for God serve not a heavenly but an earthly kingdom, devoting themselves solely to exterior things and seeking the softness and pleasure of the present life?

[Note: The edition reads *Regi* (“king”) instead of *regno* (“kingdom”). Tajo’s reading, however, is also found in the Beauvais manuscript, the first manuscript of Carnot, the manuscript of Val-Dieu, and that of Longipont.]

## CHAPTER III. Those Bound by Earthly Desires

Those who are conquered by love of earthly things take no delight at all in God, because they are entangled in the pleasures of this world (*Moralium* XVIII.9.16). The soul can never be without delight: it delights either in lowly things or in lofty ones. The more ardently it burns with concern for what is lowly, the longer and more damnably it grows cold toward what is lofty. For the two cannot be loved simultaneously and equally.

The Apostle John, knowing that the thorns of worldly loves cannot bring forth the harvest of heavenly charity [Note: The edition reads “among the thorns.”], removes the harvest of worldly loves from the hearts of his hearers with the holy hand of the word before bringing forth the seeds of eternal love, saying: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15).

The same Apostle continues concerning the vain love of this world, saying: “If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him.” As if he were saying plainly: These two loves cannot fit together in one heart; nor does the crop of heavenly charity sprout in one whose lower thorns of delight kill it.

The same Apostle John enumerates the pricks that arise from the lowly delight of this world, saying: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from this world; and the world passes away, and its desire” (ibid., 16–17).

A person subjected to love of this world cannot delight in God, because heavenly desires do not emerge in the mind that is pressed down by the thorns of earthly love. When someone in this age finds the fulfillment of the happiness he sought, he does not seek the author who granted that very happiness, because, through private love, he is not ashamed to attain this world (*Gregory, as cited above*, chapter 10.17).

## CHAPTER IV. The Wise of This Age

The wise of this age must be admonished to cease knowing what they know and to desire to know what they do not know (*Pastoral Rule* III.6). The first thing that must be destroyed in them is their belief that they are wise. For it is written: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19).

The wise of this world must be told to become foolish more wisely, to abandon foolish wisdom, and to learn the wise foolishness of God, as it is written: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise” (ibid., 18).

Often the wise of this age turn the arguments of reasoning more effectively than examples, so that those who stood rigid in their obstinacy lie defeated in their own arguments. The outstanding teacher, the Apostle Paul, debtor to the wise and the foolish, was admonishing some of the Hebrews who were wise and others who were more sluggish. Speaking about the completion of the Old Testament, he overcame their wisdom by an argument, saying: “What is becoming obsolete and growing old is near to disappearance” (Heb. 8:13). Thus victorious reasoning might break them and persuade them through the argument of gentle speech to turn toward better things.

## CHAPTER V. Those Hardened by God’s Judgment

Just as no one resists the generosity of God who calls, so no one opposes the justice of God who abandons (*Moralium* XI.9.13). The Lord does not harden the heart of the sinner, but is said to harden it when he does not free it from hardness (*Book I on Ezekiel*, homily 11.25). He is said to harden it by justice when he does not soften the heart of the reprobate by grace.

It belongs to God to close by not opening what is shut, but to leave sinners in the darkness of their own works (*Moralium*, as cited above). In his mercy, God grants us time for repentance; but when we turn the patience of his grace into an increase of guilt, he turns that very time, which he mercifully ordained for sparing us, more strictly toward striking us (*On Ezekiel*, as cited above).

When someone refuses to return from the dark paths of his error even after being granted an interval of time, he increases his guilt through the very means by which he could have cleansed it, had he wished to turn back.

## CHAPTER VI. Those Who, Because of Love of the World or Desire for Present Things, Voluntarily Undertake the Hardships of Tribulation
Those who, through love of the present age, are alienated from the judgment of reason, consider whatever they endure for the sake of the world light; they do not perceive the bitterness of the labor they bear, because they are led pleasurably toward everything in which they are wearied painfully (Moral. VII, ch. 21, no. 25). The prophet Jeremiah, seeing the human race intoxicated by its own pleasures, says: “He intoxicated me with wormwood; [Col. 0960C] he filled me with bitterness” (Lam. III, 16; Moral. XX, ch. 15, no. 39). For the intoxicated person does not know what he suffers. But whoever is intoxicated with wormwood both finds what he has consumed bitter and yet does not understand the very bitterness with which he is filled. So indeed are lovers of this age: they become embittered by the manifold distresses of labors and tribulations, yet, like drunkards, are rendered insensible through the madness of their desire. The human race, abandoned by the just judgment of God to its pleasures and through those same pleasures handed over to voluntary tribulations, is drunk with wormwood, because what it endures for love of this age is bitter, yet it does not recognize that same bitterness through the blindness of desire, as though through the insensibility of drunkenness. Whoever thirsts for worldly glory, when he encounters many tribulations [Col. 0960D] on its account, drinks something bitter; but because he has swallowed it with excessive eagerness, he is unable, through that very drunkenness, to discern the evil of the same bitterness. Perverse people love even tribulations for the glory of this world; they willingly serve it through all their toil and most devotedly submit their necks to the yoke of heavy labors.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Prosperity of the Reprobate

Whoever is turned away from God and prospers becomes as much closer to perdition as he is found to be farther from the zeal of discipline (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 12, no. 18). Some commit iniquities and do not cease rejoicing: “They are glad when they have done evil, and [Col. 0961A] exult in the worst things” (Prov. II, 14; Moral. VI, ch. 16, no. 26). Some of the reprobate, when they act wickedly and prosper, are not uplifted by well-being but by the madness by which they ought to have been afflicted; and thus, miserable, they sink into exultation precisely where they are mourned by the good. Many of the reprobate, while they are bound by the chains of their sins, do not return at all to the path of justice. They are like the minds of the frenzied, who regard the madness that possesses them as strength; they do not know that what they can do beyond the healthy results from illness, and they imagine that they have grown stronger while they are approaching the end of life through the progression of their sickness. Sometimes the reprobate, like the frenzied, because they lack the perception of reason, are mourned and laugh. They expand themselves in great exultation all the more because, being insensible, they do not recognize the evil that they [Col. 0961B] suffer (Moral. XXXI, 24, no. 43).

It is written in the book of Ecclesiastes: “I saw servants on horses, and princes walking like servants upon the earth” (Eccles. X, 7). Everyone who sins is a servant of sin. Servants are on horses when sinners are exalted by the dignities of the present life. Princes walk like servants when no honor raises up many who are filled with the dignity of virtues. But the highest adversity presses them down as though they were unworthy. Through the Psalmist it is said: “Those who mounted horses slumbered” (Ps. LXXV), that is, those who trusted in the honor of the present life closed the eyes of their minds to the light of truth in the death of the soul.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Concord of the Wicked

When the wickedness of perverse people is joined in peace, their evil deeds are certainly strengthened [Col. 0961C] (Pastoral Rule, part III, ch. 23). For the more they agree with one another in wickedness, the more powerfully they strike against the afflictions of the good. By the divine voice, concerning Leviathan, it is said to blessed Job: “The members of his flesh cleave to one another” (Job XLI, 14). “His body is cast shields, compacted with scales pressing upon one another; one is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them” (ibid. VI, 7). The followers of Satan, in that they are not divided among themselves by any adversity of discord, are thereby gathered together more heavily for the destruction of the good. Whoever unites the wicked in peace supplies strength to iniquity, because they oppress the good more grievously when they persecute them with one accord. Those whom a similar guilt unites, perverse defense also binds together in obstinate concord, so that they protect one another from their crimes by mutual defense [Col. 0961D] (Moral. XXXIII, ch. 30, no. 54). Each person fears for himself when he sees another being admonished or corrected. Therefore he rises up with one accord against the words of those who rebuke, because he protects himself in the other. While the wicked protect one another by proud defense, they permit the openings of holy exhortation to enter them in no way.

Blessed Job indicates the destructive concord of the wicked under the scales of Leviathan, saying: “One will cleave to another, and, holding fast to one another, they will not be separated” (Job XLI, 8). Those who could have been corrected when divided persist united in the obstinacy of their iniquities (Moral. XXXIII, ch. 30, no. 55). And they become daily more separated from knowledge of justice in proportion as they are not separated from one another by any rebuke. Just as it is usually harmful when unity [Col. 0962A] is lacking among the good, so it is destructive when it is not lacking among the wicked. Unity sometimes strengthens the perverse when they agree, and makes them all the more incorrigible by making them unanimous.

Concerning the unity of the concordant reprobate, Solomon says: “A bundle of straw is the assembly of sinners” (Sir. XXI, 10). Of this the prophet Nahum says: “As thorns embrace one another, so is the banquet of those who drink together” (Nahum I, 10). The banquet of the reprobate is the enjoyment of temporal pleasures. At this banquet they drink together because they mutually intoxicate one another in concord with the allurements of their pleasure.

The members of Satan—that is, all the wicked—whom the word of God compares to scales joined together, are brought into agreement by equal guilt for their defense, as it is said concerning Leviathan’s scales to blessed Job: “One will cleave to another, and, holding fast to one another, they will not be separated” [Col. 0962B] (Moral. XXXIV, ch. 4, no. 8). Those who hold fast to one another cannot be separated, because they are bound together for their mutual defense in proportion as they remember that they are in every respect alike.

It is written in Exodus: “The water was divided, and the children of Israel entered through the midst of the sea on dry ground” (Exod. XIV, 22). The just are rescued when the wicked are divided through discord; and the desires of the elect reach fulfillment when the armies of the reprobate are thrown into confusion by the bond of discord. When the wave of the Red Sea is divided into two parts, the chosen people proceed toward the promised land, because when the unity of the wicked is split apart, good minds are brought to what they seek. If the unity of the wicked [Col. 0962C] had not been harmful, divine providence would never have scattered the tongues of the proud in such diversity. If the unity of the wicked had not been harmful, the Prophet would not have said concerning the enemies of holy Church: “Hurl them down, Lord, and divide their tongues” (Ps. LIV, 10).

## CHAPTER IX. On the Princes of the World

The princes of this world, the more they recognize that they have been placed over many hosts of peoples, should humble themselves under the discipline of the holy faith, so that they may strive not merely to rule but rejoice to benefit many. For whoever is exalted by the multitude of peoples subject to him is rightly punished by the ruin of his own fall through the very pride of his elevation, by which he seeks to climb to the heights, as it is written: “You cast them down when they were being exalted” [Col. 0962D] (Ps. LXXII, 18; Moral. XXXII, ch. 9, no. 11). The Psalmist did not say, “You cast them down after they had been exalted,” but “when they were being exalted.” Therefore princes should fear this first fall: they who do not fear loving private glory for themselves, because they commonly fall inwardly in proportion as they rise wrongly outwardly.

All who rule in this world are weighed down in their hearts by dense tumultuous thoughts. While they stir up within themselves the crowds of their desires, they trample their prostrate minds under the foot of wretched preoccupation (Moral. XVII, ch. 8, no. 10). Sometimes a prince swells with the pride of his thoughts simply because he stands above others. While everything is subject to his use, while commands are swiftly fulfilled according to his will, while all subjects exalt in praise whatever has been done well but oppose nothing done badly with any authority [Col. 0963A]—while they often praise even what they ought to have rebuked—his mind, seduced by what is subjected beneath him, is lifted above itself; and while he is surrounded outwardly by immense favor, he is emptied inwardly of truth (Pastoral Rule, part II, ch. 6, and Moral. book XXVI, ch. 26, no. 44). Forgetful of himself, he pours himself out into the voices of others and believes himself to be as he hears himself described outwardly, not as he ought to discern himself inwardly.

Princes often despise their subjects and do not recognize them as equal to themselves by the order of nature; and those whom they have surpassed by the lot of power, they believe they have also surpassed in the merits of life. They judge themselves wiser than all those whom they see themselves able to command more. They establish themselves, so to speak, upon a summit in their own eyes. And because they are bound to others by an equal condition of nature, they disdain to look upon others as equals [Col. 0963B]. Thus they are led to resemble him of whom it is written: “He sees every lofty thing, and he himself is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI, 25).

Whoever, endowed with the power of honor, is lifted above his subjects by the arrogance of pride is led to resemble him who, desiring a solitary summit and despising the fellowship of the angels, said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14). Thus, by a marvelous judgment, he finds inwardly a pit of abasement while outwardly exalting himself at the summit of power. He is made like the apostate angel when a human being disdains to be like another human being.

King Saul, by the merit of humility, grew through the summit of power into a swelling of pride; through humility he had been raised up, through pride he was rejected [Col. 0963C], as the Lord bears witness, saying: “When you were little in your own eyes, did I not make you head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Sam. XV, 17). Saul had seen himself as little before receiving power, but, supported by temporal authority, he no longer saw himself as little. Preferring himself to others in comparison with them, he judged himself great in his own eyes. Yet, in a marvelous way, when he was little in his own eyes he was great before the Lord; when he was great in his own eyes, he was little before the Lord.

Often, when the mind of a prince is inflated by the abundance of his subjects, it is corrupted into the luxury [Note: [Col. 0963D] Edition: “flux.” Taio agrees with Gilot and the recent edition.] of pride, with the very height of power serving as its enticement. But it is one thing not to possess any good things, and another not to know how to possess good things well (Moral. XXVI, ch. 26, no. 45).

In everything that a prince does, he is surrounded by tribulation and [Col. 0963D] distress (ibid. XII, ch. 42, no. 47). For his heart is confused by anxiety and suspicion, as it is said through blessed Job: “Tribulation will terrify him, and distress will surround him, like a king prepared for battle” (Job XV, 24; Moral. book V, ch. 11, no. 17).

Although a prince may sin in thought, speech, or deed wherever he is placed, his mind is nevertheless carried more recklessly into these three things when it is more frequently lifted up by the prosperity of this world. When a prince sees that he surpasses others in power, he thinks and feels lofty things about himself with pride. When no one resists the authority of his voice, his tongue is more freely unrestrained along precipitous paths. When a prince is often permitted to do whatever he wishes, he judges that [Col. 0964A] everything he wishes is rightly permitted to him.

King [Col. 0964A] Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, while turning over in his proud mind the words, “Is this not Babylon, which I built?” (Dan. IV, 27), was immediately changed into an irrational animal. He lost what he had been made, because he did not humbly conceal what he had done. And because he exalted himself above human beings through the pride of his thoughts, he lost the very human understanding that he had in common with human beings.

Princes who are in power often break out into indiscriminate insults against their subjects, and through the loquacity of their tongues they lose what they gain by devoting themselves to government. Solomon says: “Woe to you, land, whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccles. X, 16). A king is not improperly called a child when the person who rules delights in childish [Col. 0964B] acts under the care of government and does not withdraw from the perpetration of sin.

Therefore Isaiah rightly says: “The child of a hundred years shall die, and the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed” (Isa. LXV, 20; Moral. XVII, ch. 6, no. 8)—that is, the child’s life is prolonged so that he may be corrected from childish deeds. But if he is not restrained from the perpetration of sin even by the passage of a long time, that very length of life, which he received through mercy, increases for him as an accumulation of condemnation.

Who, possessing sound judgment, would not know that the kings of the earth are as far from solitude as they are surrounded by countless throngs of attendants (Preface to the fourth book of the Moralia, ch. 3)? It is difficult for those to move toward rest who are bound by such hard chains of numerous concerns. Scripture bears witness, saying: “The severest judgment will be upon those who rule” [Col. 0964C] (Wis. VI, 6). Hence Truth also says in the Gospel: “From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required” (Luke XII, 48).

Blessed Job, having exercised the honor of princely authority, indicates how great was his elevation and how great his kindness (Preface to the Moralia, ch. 3, no. 7), saying: “Princes ceased speaking and placed a finger upon their mouth” (Job XXIX, 9). And again: “When I sat like a king with an army standing around me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the mourners” (ibid., 25).

Often those who rule by power lose the good things they rightly do because they think proudly; and while they judge themselves useful for everything, they even condemn the merit of the usefulness they have shown (Moral. book V, ch. 11, no. 17). For the more worthy a prince’s deeds are, the more necessary it is that they always appear unworthy to him in his own eyes, lest the good action lift up the heart of the one who performs it and, by lifting it up, cast down its author through pride more than it may perhaps benefit those to whom it is rendered [Col. 0964D] (Note: Edition: “those whom it perhaps benefits.”).

Power, when it is held, must often both be directed toward the usefulness of many and concealed on account of swelling pride. Thus the person who uses it may know that he possesses the ability to benefit others, as he ought, and may not know that he possesses it, as he ought not to be exalted (ibid., no. 18).

## CHAPTER X. On Good Princes

Great is princely power, because before God it has its own merit from the good administration of government (Moral. book XXVI, ch. 26, nos. 44–45). Princely power is good [Col. 0965A] in its proper order, but it requires a ruler’s careful life. He exercises it well who knows through it to rise above faults and knows, together with it, how to maintain equality with others.

The human mind is often lifted up even when supported by no power; how much more does it raise itself on high when power is also joined to it? Nevertheless, it is prepared by suitable execution for the correction of the faults of others. Hence Paul says: “For he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath” (Rom. XIII, 4).

When the summit of princely power is assumed, one must watch with the greatest care, so that each person may know both how to take from it what helps and how to conquer what makes trial of him. When princes are supported by the power of this world, they bring themselves under a stricter discipline of mind in proportion as they know that the impatience of power persuades them to regard illicit things as though they were more freely permitted [Col. 0965B] (Moral. book V, ch. 11, no. 17). For they restrain the heart from considering glory, hold the tongue back from immoderate speech, and guard their actions from restless wandering.

It must be known above all that a king prepared for battle is so suspicious of the enemy that he also fears the army he leads, lest it be weakened and, through the abandonment of his soldiers, expose him to the arrows of his enemies [Note: [Col. 0965D] Edition: “the same [army].” But Taio’s reading is the best; it is also found in the ancient edition and was formerly read at Utica.] (Moral. XII, ch. 42, no. 47). Often a king prepared for battle is surrounded by excessive distress, because he fears that he may suddenly lose his soldiers and be caught through some negligence in the ambushes of attacking enemies.

A prince governing an earthly republic punishes a citizen who sins within in one way, and an enemy who rebels without in another (Moral. XXVI, ch. 27, no. 50). In the case of the citizen, he has regard for his own laws and subjects him [Col. 0965C] to punishment with words of appropriate denunciation. Against the enemy, however, he takes up war, employs instruments of destruction, and repays his wickedness with punishments appropriate to it. As for the enemy’s evil, he does not ask what the law provides; for one who could never be held by the law need not be put to death by the law.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Proud Rich

Those who in the present age pant after multiplying riches—what joys of the other life do they hope for? (Moral. book XVII, ch. 22, no. 32.) The very occupation with secular dignities is weighed down by vices all the more readily in proportion as it is burdened by greater cares. Would that the human mind, even when at rest, were able to see and avoid sins! [Col. 0965D]

Let us consider what kind of corpses of the rich lie in the tomb, what image of death there is in that extinguished flesh, and what [Note: Edition: “what corruption’s decay.” Perhaps in Taio it should be read: “what decay of corruption there is.”] decay with corruption (Moral. book XI, ch. 31, no. 43). They were certainly the very people who were exalted by honors, swollen with possessions, despised others, and rejoiced as though they alone existed. And because they did not consider where they were heading, they did not know what they were, as blessed Job says: “And their necks shall be reduced to clay” (Job XIII, 12). The neck is reduced to clay because those who swelled with vanity lie despised in putrefaction. The neck is reduced to clay because the decay of corruption proves how much the power of flesh is worth.

Like one with a fattened neck, [Col. 0966A] the person who turns temporal abundance into pride raises himself against God (Moral. book XII, ch. 43, no. 49). The powerful and wicked have this characteristic: occupied with deceptive riches, they neglect the true riches of God; and the less they seek what is true, the more they are lifted up by false riches. The more the manifold care of earthly things occupies a person, the more it blinds him. Hence it is written: “Fatness covered his face” (Job XV, 27; Moral. XII, ch. 44, no. 50). Fatness covered his face because the desired abundance of earthly things weighs down the eyes of the mind and, by burdening it with manifold cares, defiles before God’s eyes what ought to have been honorable in those things.

Some become proud because they are attached to greater patrons [Note: Edition: “assisted by.” All the Norman witnesses support Taio’s reading.] and, through the exalted [Col. 0966B] power of those patrons, are lifted up in the madness of pride against the poor. Whoever clings to a powerful and wicked person also swells through his exalted power, as though through the fatness of possessions (Gregory, cited above, ch. 45, no. 51). Following the iniquity of a perverse patron, such a person does not fear God; he afflicts the poor as much as he can, and raises his heart through temporal glory. When someone who clings to a powerful wicked person is such, he plainly hangs from that person’s side like a piece of fat.

The throngs of attendants of the perverse are established in great wickedness. Their cries praise the perverse patron when he is driven by wickedness toward evil deeds (ch. 46, no. 52). Hence it is written: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who acts wickedly is blessed” (Ps. IX, 24).

Those who cling to a perverse patron in temporal service [Col. 0966C] imitate his example: they pant after earthly advancement, are kindled by the torches of avarice, and are burned by the fires of carnal desires (Gregory, cited above, ch. 48, no. 54). If someone rich in possessions were to attach to himself certain people who sought the eternal homeland, he would certainly have green branches within himself (ch. 49, no. 55). But because those who are joined to him also burn with earthly desires, and the flame of desire kindles the minds of his dependents, the fire evidently dries up his branches, as it were, so that they do not bear the fruit of good works, because they pant through wickedness after the pursuit of lowly things (ch. 50, no. 56).

The proud rich man, the more powerful he is in this life, the more boldly loosens the reins of his tongue, so that he may speak every kind of perverse thing. He fears no one because of his words; he strikes some with insults and hurls curses [Col. 0966D] at others. Sometimes the perverse rich man is swept into blasphemy against the Creator. Hence it is written: “They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue traversed the earth” (Ps. LXXII, 9).

That rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen, when placed in the fire, asked that water be dripped from Lazarus’s finger onto his tongue. From this it is understood that where he had sinned more greatly, there he burned more severely (Luke XVI, 24). The proud rich man received the sentence of punishment precisely where he had not restrained the breath of his mouth under fear of God, as it is written: “And he shall be taken away by the breath of his mouth” (Job XV, 29).

Just as there are dishonorable members in the body, so there are [Col. 0967A] certain powerful and insolent people within holy Church. Since they cannot be struck by open denunciation, they are covered, as it were, by the honor of a garment (Moral. XIII, ch. 5, no. 7). Truth says in the Gospel that “cares, pleasures, and riches suffocate” (Matt. XIII, 22; Luke VIII, 7–8). They suffocate because they strangle the throat of the mind with their burdensome thoughts. And since they do not allow a good desire to enter the heart, they kill, as it were, the passage of the vital breath (Book I on the Gospel, homily 15, no. 3).

It should be noted that two things are joined to riches: cares and pleasures. For cares oppress the mind, while abundance relaxes it. In fact, contrary forces make their possessors both afflicted and pleasure-seeking. Pleasure cannot coexist with affliction: at one time they afflict their possessors through the anxious care of guarding them, and at another [Col. 0967B] soften them toward pleasures through abundance.

We speak here of the hidden sins of the powerful. But when they sin while others know it, they must also be rebuked while others know it, lest, if the preacher remains silent, he appear to have approved the fault, and lest this growing evil come to serve as an example that the shepherd’s tongue does not cut away.

It is written: “The rich became needy and hungry” (Ps. XXXIII, 11; Moral. book XV, ch. 8, no. 9). If their need and hunger referred to outward hunger, the rich would certainly not be rich, since they would lack bodily bread. But because, while they multiply outwardly, they become empty inwardly, they are said to be both rich and needy, since they are by no means worthy to be satisfied with the bread of wisdom.

## CHAPTER XII. On Judges

[Col. 0967C]

The judges of this age endure many insults for earthly profits, yet for a heavenly reward they refuse to bear even the insults of the slightest word (Moral. book XIX, ch. 25, no. 49). Judges are strong enough to stand before an earthly tribunal for the entire day, but in prayer before the Lord they grow weary after a moment of a single hour.

Often some judges endure nakedness, abasement, and hunger in order to acquire riches and honors; they torment themselves through abstinence from food and hurry to obtain earthly things. But they are all the more reluctant to seek heavenly things laboriously in proportion as they think those things are rewarded only after a longer delay.

Judges who pursue earthly things and do not seek heavenly ones are, like trees, broad below [Col. 0967D] and narrow above, because they stand firmly in lower matters but fail in higher ones. Often some judges seek earthly rewards, defend justice, consider themselves innocent, and rejoice that they are defenders of righteousness (Moral. IX, ch. 25, no. 38). If the hope of money is taken away from them, they immediately cease defending justice; yet they think themselves defenders of justice and assert that they are upright, although they seek not righteousness but money.

Against the wickedness of delinquent judges, Moses says: “You shall execute what is just, and only what is just” (Deut. XVI, 20). He executes what is just unjustly who is stirred to defend justice not by zeal for virtue [Col. 0968A] but by love of temporal reward; he executes what is just unjustly who does not hesitate to sell the very justice he pretends to uphold. To execute what is just justly, therefore, is to seek justice itself in the assertion of justice.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Desire for Human Praise and the Favor of Flatterers

Everyone who desires human praise because of what he does seeks a witness on earth; but whoever hastens to please the almighty Lord through his deeds hastens to have a witness in heaven [Note: Edition: “considers.”] (Moral. book XIII, ch. 24, no. 28). When many magnify evil deeds with praise, the result is that guilt, nourished by favor, continually increases (Moral. book IV, ch. 28, no. 51). The wound is neglected when it appears worthy of the reward of praise.

Solomon rightly [Col. 0968B] says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent” (Prov. I, 10). Sinners entice when they introduce evils to be committed through blandishments or exalt evils already committed through favor. Everyone is caressed by the tongue of flatterers when he is the one of whom the Psalmist says: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who acts wickedly is blessed” (Ps. IX, 24).

It is very difficult for one whom, after the practice of an evil habit, the tongues of flatterers also receive to be recalled from the death of his mind (Moral. IV, ch. 28, no. 52). Truth says in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke IX, 60). The dead bury the dead when sinners crush a sinner with their favors. For what else is sinning than falling dead? But those who pursue a sinner with praises hide him, as though dead, beneath the mound of their [Col. 0968C] words.

As soon as the wind touches a reed, it bends it to the other side. And what is signified by the reed except the carnal mind, which, as soon as it is touched by favor or detraction, inclines in any direction (Book I on the Gospel, homily 6, no. 2)? If the breeze of favor has blown from someone’s mouth, the seeker of human praise grows cheerful, is lifted up, and bends himself entirely, as though toward approval. But if the wind of detraction bursts forth from the place where the breeze of praise had come, it immediately inclines him, as though to the opposite side, toward the force of anger.

The tongues of flatterers must not be tolerated with equanimity, nor should they be postponed to a later time (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 11, no. 14). If the tongue of a flatterer is received patiently even for a time, it grows stronger and gradually caresses the mind, so that it softens from the firmness of its rectitude [Col. 0968D] into delight in speech. Lest flattery gradually and uncheckedly increase, it must immediately and without delay be struck down by the sword of the mouth and utterly extinguished through the justice of zeal.

In the Gospel the foolish virgins are rebuked with the words: “Go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves” (Matt. XXV, 9; Book I on the Gospel, homily 12, no. 3). The sellers of oil are flatterers. For those who offer the splendor of glory through their empty praises for any favor they have received sell oil, as it were.

The head is the principal part of our body. By the designation “head,” the mind that rules the soul [Note: Edition: “the body.”] is meant. Therefore the oil of the sinner fattens the head when the favor of the flatterer caresses the mind.

Solomon [Col. 0969A] says: “As silver is tested in the crucible and gold in the furnace, so a person is tested by the mouth of one who praises” (Prov. XXVII, 21; Moral. XXII, ch. 8, no. 19). If silver or gold is worthless, it is consumed by fire; but if it is genuine, it is revealed by fire. So it is with the understanding of every person who acts: what sort of person he is is shown in the very thing for which he is praised. Whoever exalts himself when he hears his praises—what else was he than worthless gold or silver, whom the furnace of the tongue consumed?

If someone who hears his favors returns to consideration of the heavenly judgment and fears being burdened by them before the hidden Judge, he grows, as though through the fire of purification, toward the greatness of brightness; and from the source of the fire of fear that he endures, he shines more brightly [Note: Edition: “before the Judge.”].

For flatterers to lick our [Col. 0969B] wounds is to praise, through the wicked favor of their tongues, even the very evils that we ourselves commonly condemn in ourselves (Book II on the Gospel, homily 40, no. 2).

## CHAPTER XIV. On Hypocrites and the Cunning
A hypocrite is called *simulator* in Latin, because he does not desire to be righteous, but to appear so; and therefore he is a greedy robber, because, while acting unjustly, he desires to be honored for holiness and robs another’s praise of life (Moral. XVIII, 7, no. 13). It is usually the hypocrites’ practice both to conceal what they are and to make known to people that they are what they are not. Thus they surpass their proper measure in estimation and display themselves as surpassing others in the name of their conduct. Hypocrites shrink from being seen as they are [Col. 0969C], and before human eyes they clothe themselves with a kind of superimposed respectability of innocence.

They are rightly rebuked through the Gospel by the voice of our Redeemer as pretenders, when he says to them: “Woe to you, hypocrites, because you have become like whitened tombs, which outwardly indeed appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity. So you also outwardly indeed appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of greed and iniquity” (Matt. XXIII, 27). It is written: “Pretenders and the crafty provoke the wrath of God” (Job XXXVI, 13; Moral. XXVI, c. 32, no. 58).

When he said “pretenders,” he aptly added “and the crafty,” because unless they are skilled in ingenuity, they cannot suitably pretend to be what they desire to appear. There are certain vices that even people of sluggish understanding easily commit. Anyone, however dull his senses, can swell with pride, yearn amid the fires of greed, or succumb to lust when it presses upon him. But no one who lacks a subtler intelligence can carry out the falsehood of pretense.

Whoever is skilled in hypocrisy is divided, as it were, by constant vigilance for the protection of these two things: he must cleverly know both how to conceal what he is and display what he is not; how to suppress true evils and exhibit false goods; and he must not openly exalt himself in that which he appears to be. Rather, in order to secure greater glory, he often pretends [Note: [Col. 0970D] Ed., *simulare*. Other editions, *simulat*.] to decline glory. Often the hypocrite, because he cannot seize glory by pursuing it before human eyes, strives to retain it by fleeing from it.

Hypocrisy and craftiness are wholly incompatible with simplicity [Col. 0970A], because if they were compatible, people would no longer be simple. To deserve the wrath of God is also to sin unknowingly (no. 59). To provoke him, however, is knowingly to oppose his commands: to know the good but despise it; to be able to do it but not to wish to do so.

Pretenders grow dark inwardly through the perpetration of wickedness, while outwardly they are whitened on the surface through the display of righteousness. By displaying themselves outwardly, pretenders preserve what they inwardly oppose by their way of life. Inwardly, they intensify the evils they contemplate, which outwardly they conceal by superimposing something else upon them.

Before the strict Judge, hypocrites can no longer claim ignorance as an excuse, because, while they display every appearance of holiness before human eyes, they themselves bear witness that they do not fail to know how to live well. Every pretender, in desiring to appear righteous, does not show himself wholly pure, because, while he assumes certain virtues and secretly subjects himself to vices, certain hidden vices suddenly burst forth upon his face and reveal the skin, as it were, of the superimposed pretense to be variegated by their mixture [Col. 0970B] (Moral. V, c. 20, no. 39). Hence it is often astonishing that a person who is seen to possess such great virtues should also be stained by such reprehensible acts.

Every hypocrite is like the beast called a tiger, because, while a pure color is derived from pretense, it is made variegated by the interruptions of black vice. Often the pretender, while he is exalted for the purity of chastity, is defiled by the filth of greed. And while he is displayed as beautiful through the virtue of generosity, he is stained by the spots of lust. Often, while the hypocrite is clothed in the beauty of chastity and generosity, he is darkened, as though by zeal for justice, through the savagery of cruelty [Col. 0970C]. Often, indeed, he is clothed in the beautiful appearance of generosity, chastity, and piety, but is marked by the darkness interposed by pride. Thus, when vices are mingled in, he does not display a pure appearance in himself, just as a tiger can by no means possess a single color.

We must know that we come into the sight of the Lord in two ways (Moral. XI, 36, no. 49). In one way, when here we weigh our sins carefully, punish ourselves in his sight, and judge ourselves with tears; for whenever we recall the power of our Creator to our understanding, we stand in his sight. Hence it is rightly said through Elijah, the man of God: “The Lord God of Israel lives, in whose sight I stand” (III Kings XVII, 1).

In the other way, we come into the sight of the Lord when, at the final judgment, we stand before his tribunal. The hypocrite therefore comes before the Judge’s sight through the final examination; but because he now pretends to consider and bewail his faults, he refuses to come into the Lord’s sight.

Just as righteous men, when they contemplate the severity of the Judge who is to come, recall their sins, mourn what they have committed, and judge themselves strictly so that they may not be judged, so hypocrites, the more they please people outwardly, the more they neglect to examine themselves inwardly. Hypocrites pour themselves out entirely into the words of their neighbors and consider themselves holy because they reckon that everyone regards them in this way. When they have scattered their minds through words of their own praise, they never bring them back to knowledge of their guilt and never consider where they offend the inward Judge [Col. 0971A]. They fear nothing of his severity, because they believe that they have pleased him as they have pleased human beings.

If all hypocrites brought the fear of God back to their minds, they would fear more the very fact that, while established in an evil intention, they please people; as it is written: “No hypocrite shall come into his sight” (Job XIII, 16), because he does not set God’s severity before his eyes while he desires to please human eyes. If, examining his mind, he were to punish himself in God’s sight [Note: [Col. 0971D] Ed., *poneret* (“were to place”). Taio agrees with Vindoc.], he would certainly not be a hypocrite.

When the scourges of affliction strike pretenders, they do not lead them to a simple confession (Moral. XXVI, 33, no. 60). For they shrink from being recognized as sinners, since they were generally regarded by all as holy. Every hypocrite, though he is wicked, does not fear being called holy by people [Col. 0971B] (no. 61). Even if he silently reproves himself in thought as wicked, nevertheless, when he repeatedly begins to hear himself called holy, he loses what he inwardly held about himself.

Every hypocrite, while pouring out his heart outwardly, because he gladly accepts false testimony about himself from outside, does not inquire what sort of person he is inwardly. Consequently, he seeks the fuel of empty praise even when it is lacking. He forgets what he is and desires to appear what he is not.

All hypocrites, while pretending to be righteous before human judgments and displaying their actions as worthy of praise to the eyes of those who observe them, are subjected to a hidden judgment, so that, in the very measure by which they strive outwardly to deceive others, they are also inwardly deceived about themselves. To them the prophet rightly says: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isa. XLVI, 8). For if they returned to their heart, they would not pour themselves out through words that testify to them outwardly [Col. 0971C].

The praise of the present age torments the righteous and exalts pretenders. While tormenting the righteous, it purifies them; while gladdening pretenders, it reveals them as reprobate (Gregory, cited above, c. 34, no. 62).

## CHAPTER XV. On Apostates

Just as there are two ways of departing from God, so in two ways people become apostates from God (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 6). For each person departs from his Creator either in faith or in conduct. Just as one who departs from the faith is an apostate, so one who returns to the perverse conduct he had abandoned is, without any doubt, reckoned an apostate from almighty God, even if he appears to retain the faith.

Solomon says in Proverbs: “An apostate man, a worthless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, scrapes with his foot, and speaks with his finger. With a crooked heart he devises evil, and at all times sows quarrels” (Prov. VI, 12; Pastoral Rule, part III, c. 23).

Behold: the one whom he wished to describe as sowing quarrels he first called an apostate, because unless, in the manner of the proud angel, he had first fallen inwardly from the sight of his Creator through the turning away of his mind, he would not afterward have come outwardly as far as sowing quarrels.

It is said of every apostate that he winks with his eyes, speaks with his finger, and scrapes with his foot. For there is an inward guardianship that keeps the limbs outwardly ordered. Therefore, whoever has lost the stability of mind subsequently flows outward into inconstancy of movement and, through outward restlessness, reveals that he has no inward root by which he stands [Col. 0972A].

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Devil and His Members

The devil and all the wicked are one body, so that often the body is designated by the name of the head, and the head is called by the name of the body (Moral. XIII, 34, no. 38). The body is designated by the name of the head when it is said of a wicked man: “One of you is a devil” (John VI, 71). Again, the head is called by the name of the body when it is said of that apostate angel himself: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. XIII, 28).

This prince of all the wicked has some as sons and others as companions. Who are his companions except those apostate angels who fell with him from the seat of the heavenly homeland? Or whom does he have as other sons except wicked people, who are generated in the work of evil through his perverse persuasion? Hence, by the voice of Truth, it is said to the unbelieving: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII, 44).

This perverse author of error promises spoil to his companions, because he promises evil spirits the souls of the wicked, to be seized at their end. While the ancient enemy arouses human desires to hope for earthly things alone, he makes them love what they cannot possess for long (Moral. XIII, 34, no. 39).

The devil is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are members of this head, just as Pilate was a member of the devil, and the persecuting Jews and the soldiers who crucified him were members of the devil (Book I on the Gospels, homily [Col. 0972C] 16, no. 1).

## CHAPTER XVII. What Difference There Is between Sinners and the Ungodly

There are two divisions: the elect and the reprobate; but within each of these divisions there are two orders (Moral., book XXVI, c. 27, no. 50). Some are judged and perish; others are not judged and perish. Some are judged and reign; others are not judged and reign.

Those who are judged and perish are addressed by the Lord’s proclamation: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” [Note: [Col. 0971D] According to the second version of the antiphon.]; “I was a stranger, and you did not receive me” [Note: [Col. 0971D] So Clarom. and Arnob.]; “I was naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me” [Note: [Col. 0972D] Corb. 1, Ms. Gat., the Coptic version, and Ambrose, *On Joseph*, chapter V.] (Matt. XXV, 42–43). “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

Others, at the final judgment, are not judged and perish; concerning them the Prophet says: “The ungodly do not rise in the judgment” (Ps. I, 5). And the Lord says concerning them: “But those who do not believe in me have already been judged” (John III, 18). And Paul says: “Those who are without the law will perish” (Rom. II, 12; Moral. XXV, c. 10, no. 25).

Sinners are distinguished from the ungodly by this difference: although every ungodly person is a sinner, not every sinner is ungodly. Even one who is devout in faith can be called a sinner. Hence John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (I John I, 8). But properly speaking, one is called ungodly who is separated from the piety of religion. Of such people it is said: “The ungodly do not rise in the judgment” (Ps. I, 5; Moral. XXVI, c. 27, no. 50).

At the final judgment all unbelievers do rise, but for torment, not for judgment. Their case is not then examined; they [Note: [Col. 0973D] The editions read *quia* (“because”); others read with Taio *qui* (“who”).] come into the presence of the strict Judge already bearing the condemnation of their unbelief. Those who retain the profession of faith but do not possess the works of that profession are rebuked so that they may perish. But those who retained not even the sacraments of faith do not hear the Judge’s rebuke in the final examination, because, already condemned by the darkness of their unbelief, they do not merit to be rebuked by the denunciation of the one they despised.

Those who have the profession of faith hear the Judge’s words at the final judgment, because they retained at least verbally the faith they professed [Col. 0973B] [Note: [Col. 0973D] Ed., “they retained the words.”]. These others, in their condemnation by the eternal Judge, do not even receive his words, because they did not wish to preserve reverence for him even in words [Note: [Col. 0973D] Ed., *voluerunt* (“wished”); Vindoc., Pratel., and other Norman witnesses support our reading, *maluerunt* (“preferred”).].

The former perish according to the law, because, placed under the law, they sinned. To the latter, in their destruction, nothing is said from the law, because they made no effort to possess anything belonging to the law.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What Difference There Is between Iniquity and Sin, Crimes and Offenses

Although the Apostle John declares that there is no difference between iniquity and sin when he says, “Iniquity is sin” (John III, 4; Moral. XI, c. 42, no. 57), nevertheless, in ordinary usage the word “iniquity” conveys more than “sin.” Every person freely confesses that he is a sinner; but he is sometimes ashamed to say that he is wicked.

There is this difference between crimes and offenses: a crime exceeds even the weight of sin, whereas an offense does not exceed the weight of sin. When the law commands a sacrifice to be offered, it plainly prescribes one for an offense as well as for sin. Sometimes a crime exists in an act [Note: [Col. 0973D] Ed., “and a crime exists only in an act.” The older and more recent editions read as Talus does; hence their reading, rejected by the Benedictine Fathers as corrupt, has the authority of Taio in its favor.], whereas an offense is often found only in thought. Hence the Psalmist says: “Who understands offenses?” (Ps. XVIII, 13). For sins of action are recognized all the more quickly because they are seen outwardly. But sins of thought are more difficult to understand because they are committed invisibly.

Whoever, anxious for eternity, desires to appear clean before the Judge who is to come examines himself now all the more subtly, because he reflects that he must then stand free from that Judge’s terror; and he begs that what displeases the Judge be shown to him, so that he may punish it in himself through repentance and, judging himself here, become beyond judgment.

We must consider how great a punishment of our exile has struck us, since we have come into such blindness that we do not know ourselves (Moral. XI, c. 42, no. 58). Hence blessed Job says: “Show me how many iniquities and sins, crimes and offenses I have” (Job XIII, 23; Moral. XI, c. 41, no. 56; c. 42, no. 58).

Our Redeemer appeared to human eyes through the flesh he assumed and disclosed to human beings the sins they both committed and did not know. We commit evil, yet we do not quickly perceive even what we have committed. For when the soul has been shut out from the light of truth, it finds nothing in itself but darkness. Often it extends its foot into the pit of sin and does not know it. This is what a person suffers from the blindness of his exile alone: because he has been rejected from the illumination of the Lord, he has lost the ability to see himself, because he has not loved the face of his Creator.

## CHAPTER XIX. On What Is Written: “I Am the Lord, Making Good and Creating Evils” (Isa. XLV, 7)

The evils that do not subsist by any nature of their own are not created by the Lord. Rather, the Lord indicates that he creates evils when he forms things that were well created into a scourge for us who act badly, so that those same things are evil for sinners through the pain by which they strike, but good through the nature by which they exist (Moral. III, c. 9, no. 15).

Poison, for example, is death to a human being, but nevertheless life to a serpent. For through love of present things we have departed from love of our Creator. And when the perverse mind subjected itself to the pleasure of the creature [Note: [Col. 0974D] The editions read *dilectioni* (“love”); very many manuscripts support Taio’s reading, *delectationi* (“pleasure”).], it separated itself from the fellowship of the Creator.

Therefore, the mind had to be struck by those things which, in its error, it had placed before its Creator, so that from the very things through which a person, in pride, did not fear to admit guilt, he might find punishment by which he could be corrected, and might return all the more quickly to what he had lost when he perceived that the things he had sought were full of pain.

The prophet rightly says: “Forming light and creating darkness” (Isa. XLV, 7). For when the darkness of pain is created outwardly through scourges, the light of the mind is kindled inwardly through instruction [Col. 0974C]. “Making peace and creating evils” (ibid.). For peace with God is restored to us when those things that were well created but not rightly desired are turned into scourges that are evil for us. Through our guilt we became estranged from God; it is therefore fitting that through scourges we should return to his peace, so that, when each well-created thing is turned into pain for us, the corrected mind may be humbly restored to peace with its Creator.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Upper and Lower Hell

Some have thought that hell is in a certain region of the earth; others believe that it is beneath the earth (Dialogues IV, 42). Yet this question presses upon the mind: if we call hell “hell” because it lies below, then, as the earth is below heaven, so hell ought to be below the earth. Hence perhaps it is said: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell” (Ps. LXXXV, 13), so that the upper hell may be understood to be on the earth [Note: [Col. 0974D] Ed., “in the earth.” The German and Norman witnesses preserve Taio’s reading.], while the lower hell is beneath the earth.

John’s statement agrees with this understanding. When he said that he had seen a book sealed with seven seals, and that no one was found worthy to open the book and break its seals, neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor beneath the earth, he added: “And I wept greatly” [Col. 0975A] (Rev. V, 4). Yet afterward he says that the book was opened by the Lion of the tribe of Judah.

What else is signified by that book than Holy Scripture? Our Redeemer alone opened it: by becoming human, dying, rising again, and ascending, he disclosed all the mysteries that had been closed within it [Note: [Col. 0975] Ed., “within him.” The Gemetian and other Norman witnesses approve our reading.].

No one in heaven was found worthy to open the book, because there was no angel; no one on earth, because there was no living human being in the body; no one beneath the earth, because no souls separated from the body could open for us the secrets of the sacred utterance apart from the Lord. When no one beneath the earth is said to have been found worthy to open the book, I do not see what prevents us from believing that hell is beneath the earth.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Purgatorial Fire, through Which It Is Believed That Sins Are Loosed after Death

Every weight of a structure is borne by its foundation, because our Redeemer alone sustains the character of all together (Book II on Ezekiel, homily 1, no. 5). For it is written: “No one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (I Cor. III, 11).

The foundation bears the stones, and is not borne by the stones, because our Redeemer bears all that is ours, while there was no evil in him that ought to have been borne. For he himself is the foundation of foundations, because he is both the beginning of those who are beginning and the steadfastness of the strong (Moral. XXVIII, c. 5, no. 14; Dialogues IV, 39).

The outstanding preacher says: “But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become manifest. For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire; and the fire will test what sort of work each one’s is. If anyone’s work which he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work burns, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (I Cor. III, 12).

Although what we have set forth above can be understood of the fire of tribulation applied to us in this life, nevertheless, if anyone understands it of the fire of future purification, he must carefully consider that the Apostle said that a person can be saved through fire—not one who builds iron, bronze, or lead upon this foundation, that is, greater and therefore more difficult sins, already insoluble at that time, but wood, hay, and straw, that is, lesser and very light sins, which the fire can easily consume.

This must nevertheless be known: there, no one will obtain purification even from lesser sins unless, while still placed in this life, he has earned through good works what he is to obtain there.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Wrath or Indignation of God

The wrath of almighty God exercises the force of its severity daily in this: that it consigns those who live unworthily to punishments they deserve (Moral. XII, c. 10, no. 14). This wrath now passes by, but at the end it passes through completely, because it is active now but is brought to completion at the end of the world.

With respect to the souls of the elect, this fury passed over at the coming of our Redeemer, because the Mediator between God and human beings, when he mercifully descended there, led them from the confinement of hell to the joys of paradise.

We must know that the word “fury” is not properly applied to the Divinity, because no disturbance confounds the simple nature of God. Hence it is said to him: “But you, sovereign of strength, judge with tranquillity and govern us with great reverence” (Wis. XII, 18; Moral. XXXII, c. 7, no. 9). The Creator of all is supremely immortal precisely because he is not changeable in the manner of creatures.

It is written: “But you, Lord, judge with tranquillity” (ibid.). And again: “The land has been made desolate because of the face of the wrath of the dove, because of the face of the fury of the Lord” (Jer. XXV, 38). What the prophet had called the wrath of the dove, he subsequently called the fury of the Lord.

The dove is a very simple animal, and because no inequality of fury creeps into God, he called the Lord’s fury the wrath of the dove. To show that the force of divine severity is undisturbed, the prophet spoke both of wrath and of the dove, as though he were saying more openly: “He who remains gentle punishes by exercising an unshaken judgment.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Various Divine Scourges Inflicted upon the Elect and the Reprobate

There are different kinds of blows (Preface to Blessed Job, c. 5, no. 12). One blow strikes a sinner so that he may be punished without reprieve; another strikes a sinner so that he may be corrected; another sometimes strikes a person not so that he may correct past faults, but so that he may not commit future ones; another often strikes a person through which neither past guilt is corrected nor future guilt prevented, but so that, when unexpected salvation follows the blow, the power of the one who saves may be recognized and loved more ardently; and, when an innocent person is worn down by the scourge, the full measure of his merits may be increased through patience.

Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be punished without reprieve, as is said to doomed Judea: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel correction” (Jer. XXX, 14). And again: “Why do you cry to me over your crushing? Your pain is incurable” (ibid., 15).

Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be corrected, as it is said to a certain man in the Gospel: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John V, 14). The Savior’s words indicate that the preceding sins had demanded the force of the pain he suffered [Col. 0976D].

Sometimes a person is struck not to wash away a past fault but to prevent a future one. Paul openly testifies to this concerning himself when he says: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (II Cor. XII, 7). For by saying not “Because it exalted me,” but “Lest it exalt me,” he plainly indicates that he is restrained by that blow so that the fault may not occur, not that a fault that has occurred may be cleansed.

Sometimes a person is struck neither for a past nor for a future iniquity, but so that the power of divine strength alone may be revealed through the removal of the blow. Hence, when the disciples asked the Lord in the Gospel concerning the man born blind, “Did this man sin, or his parents, that he should be born blind?” (John IX, 2), the Lord replied: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but so that the works of God might be manifested” (ibid., 3).

What is accomplished in this manifestation except that, through the scourge, the power of merit is increased, and, when no past iniquity is wiped away, great strength is generated through patience (Moral. XII, 38, no. 43)?

Almighty God reserves not only future punishments for those who act perversely, but also entangles their hearts here, where they transgress, in punishments, so that by the very act through which they sin they may strike themselves. Thus, always fearful and always suspicious, they dread suffering evils from others which they remember having inflicted upon others.

When someone is struck in such a way that his strength is overcome by the blow, the Lord no longer strikes him like a son through discipline, but like an enemy through wrath [Col. 0977B] (Moral. XIV, 37, no. 45). When scourges surpass the strength of our patience, we must greatly fear that, because our sins demand it, we are being struck by the Lord not as sons by a father but as enemies.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Various Strikings of the World

Those who love God are commanded to rejoice and be glad at the end or striking of the world, because they will soon find the one whom they love, when the one whom they did not love passes away (Book I on the Gospels, homily 1, no. 3). Far be it [Note: [Col. 0977] Ed., “far be it, then, that.” Belvac. and the third Gemetian witness agree with our reading and with Taio.] from any believer not to desire to see God and to mourn over the world’s strikings, when he knows that the world is brought to an end through those very strikings.

It is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James IV, 4). Therefore, whoever does not rejoice as the end of the world approaches demonstrates that he is its friend and is thereby proved to be an enemy of God.

Far be this from the hearts of the faithful: that they should not rejoice at the end of the world. Far be it from those who both believe through faith that another life exists and love it through their works. To mourn the destruction of the world belongs to those who have planted the roots of their hearts in love of it, who do not seek the life to come, who do not even suspect that it exists.

We, who have come to know the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland, ought to hasten toward them as quickly as possible. We should desire to depart sooner and reach that life in perpetual happiness.

What evils does the world not suffer? What sadness, what adversity does not afflict us? What is mortal life except a road? Let us first consider what it is like to grow weary on a road through labor and yet not wish that same road to end.

Our Redeemer makes clear, by a careful comparison, that the world ought to be trodden underfoot and despised, when he says in the Gospel: “Observe the fig tree and all the trees. When they already produce fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.”

It is as though he were saying openly: “Just as summer is recognized as near from the fruit of the trees, so the kingdom of God is known to be near from the ruin of the world.”

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Conversion of the Jewish People near the End of the World

In her beginnings, the holy Church was made fruitful by the multitude of the nations; only scarcely, at the end of the world, will she receive the Jews whom she finds (Preface to book IV of the *Moralia*, c. 4) [Col. 0978A]. Gathering the last, she will set them in place like the gleanings of the harvest.

Concerning these remnants of the Jewish people Isaiah says: “Even if the number of the children of Israel were like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. X, 22).

When Elijah comes, it is promised that he will turn the hearts of the children to their fathers, so that the teaching now removed from the heart of the Jews may then, by the Lord’s mercy, return, when the children begin to understand concerning the Lord what their fathers proclaimed (Mal. IV, 6; Moral. XI, c. 15, no. 24).

Esau, who returns late to his father, signifies that the Jewish people returns late in order to please God (Book I on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 6). To him this is said in the blessing: “And there will be a time when the yoke will be removed from your neck” (Gen. XXVII, 40).

At the end of the world the Jewish people will be freed from slavery to sin, as it is written: “Until the fullness of the nations should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI, 25). And as the Prophet says: “If the number of the children of Israel were like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. X, 22).

While still placed in this life, the holy Church receives double gifts for the labors it endures (Preface to Blessed Job, c. X, no. 20), when, after fully receiving the nations, as we have said, it also turns the hearts of the Jews to itself at the end of the world, as it is written: “Until the fullness of the nations should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI, 25).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Times of Antichrist
The ancient enemy, about to tempt more cruelly at the end of the world, undertakes his assault; for he becomes all the more ardent in cruelty the nearer he feels himself to punishment (Morals, book XXXIV, chapter 1, no. 1). For he considers that the time is near when he will lose the license of his most wicked freedom; and, the more he is confined by the brevity of time, the more widely he expands in manifold cruelty. In the Apocalypse it is said: “Woe to the earth and to the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has only a short time” (Apoc. XII, 12). Thus he expands himself in the heat of great wrath, lest he who could not stand in blessedness should fall with the few into the pit of his damnation. Whatever the devil is able to do wickedly, he seeks more craftily at the end of the world; then he raises the neck of his pride higher and, through that condemned man whom he carries, wickedly displays whatever he prevails over in temporal affairs.

John likewise says: “The dragon’s tail was dragging a third of the stars of heaven and cast them onto the earth” (ibid., XII, 4). Heaven is the Church, which, during this night of the present life, while it contains within itself the innumerable virtues of the saints, shines with the stars radiating from above (Morals, book XXXII, chapter 15, no. 25). The dragon’s tail casts the stars onto the earth because that extremity of Satan, raised up through the audacity of the man whom he has assumed, reveals as reprobate certain people whom it finds in the Church as though they were God’s chosen, by bringing them under its power. For stars to fall from heaven onto the earth is for some, having abandoned hope of heavenly things, to aspire under his leadership to the pursuit of secular glory. Thus this dragon sent out his tail and dragged away a third of the stars (Morals, book IV, chapter 10, no. 17). For part of the stars is dragged away by the dragon’s tail because, by the final persuasion of Antichrist, certain people who seem to shine will be carried off.

Some maintain that Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, as it is said through the patriarch Jacob: “Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider may fall backward” (Gen. XLIX, 17; Morals, book XXXI, chapter 24, no. 43). In this passage Dan is declared both to be a serpent and to be biting. Hence, not without reason, when the Israelite people were receiving their territories in the division of the camps, Dan was the first to encamp toward the north: he signified the one who had said in his heart: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13). Concerning him the prophet also says: “From Dan the snorting of his horses has been heard” (Jer. VIII, 16).

Antichrist is called not only a serpent but also a horned serpent. For *kerata* (κέρατα) is Greek for “horns”; and this serpent is said to be horned. Through it the coming of that same Antichrist is fittingly indicated, because he arms himself against the life of the faithful not only with the poisonous bite of his preaching but also with the horns of power. Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Thus Dan becomes a serpent on the road because he urges those to walk in the broadness of the present life whom he flatters as though sparing them; but he bites on the road because he consumes with the poison of his error those to whom he grants freedom. He becomes a horned serpent on the path because those whom he finds faithful and restricting themselves to the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment he attacks not only with the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also presses with the terror of power; and, during the weakness of persecution, [Note: [Col. 0979D] The edition reads “anguish” (*angore*). See, however, the annotation of the Benedictine Fathers on this passage.] after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of power.

This horse whose hooves the horned serpent is said to bite signifies the present world, which, through its arrogance, foams under the assault of passing times. And because Antichrist strives to seize the final period of the world, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s hooves. To bite the horse’s hooves is to strike at and reach the extremities of the age: “So that its rider may fall backward” (Gen. XLIX, 17).

The unbelieving Jewish people, caught in the snares of their error, await Antichrist instead of Christ. In the same passage Jacob is rightly and suddenly changed into the voice of the elect when he says: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (ibid., 18)—that is, “I do not believe faithfully in Antichrist, as the unbelievers do, but in the true Christ, who is to come for our redemption.”

Solomon says in Proverbs: “And the one who appeared foolish, after he had been raised on high. For if he had understood, he would have put his hand over his mouth” (Prov. XXX, 32; Morals, book XXX, chapter 3, no. 10). Antichrist will indeed be raised on high when he pretends that he is God. But, raised on high, he will appear foolish, because in that very exaltation he will fail at the coming of the true Judge. If he had understood, he would have put his hand over his mouth: that is, if he had foreseen his punishment when he began to grow proud, he—who had once been well created—would not have been lifted up in such a display of arrogance. [Note: [Col. 0979D] The edition reads “in such a display of arrogance” (*in tantae jactationem superbiae*). The Norman and Vallicellian manuscripts read *ut Taius* (“as Taius does”).]

Antichrist will walk in deceit, but, in proportion to the brief duration of the present life, his deceit itself will prosper for him. Hence it is said through the prophet Daniel: “Power was given him against the perpetual sacrifice, because of sins; and truth will be cast down upon the earth, and he will act and prosper” (Dan. VIII, 12). What Solomon says—“He proceeds successfully” (Prov. XXX, 29; Morals, book XIV, chapter 23, no. 27)—Daniel expresses by saying: “He will act; he will prosper.”

It is written concerning the times of Antichrist: “In his day the last will be astonished, and horror will seize the first” (Job XVIII, 20). For then iniquity will rage so unrestrainedly against the just that even the hearts of the elect will be struck by no small fear: “So that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led astray” (Matt. XXIV, 24). This is said not because the elect will fall, but because they will tremble amid great terrors. Then the last and the first elect are said to have a struggle of justice against Antichrist, because those who will be found elect at the end of the world are to be struck down in the death of the flesh, while those who came forth from the earliest ages of the world—namely Enoch and Elijah—will also be recalled to this age and will suffer his cruelty while still in their mortal flesh.

The ancient enemy, handed over to his own strength, is released for a short time, but with great power against us (Morals, book XXXII, chapter 15, nos. 22–23). Although the force of his cruelty stretches him out toward cruelty, heavenly mercy nevertheless confines him by shortening the days. For Truth itself says: “Then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be” (Matt. XXIV, 21). Again he says: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (ibid., 22). Since the Lord sees that we are both proud and weak, he says mercifully that the days he has introduced as exceptionally evil have been shortened (Morals, book XXXII, chapter 15, no. 27), so that he may terrify pride through the adversity of the time and sustain weakness through its brevity. [Note: [Col. 0980D] The edition adds *dierum* (“of the days”), which is absent not only from Taius but also from the two German manuscripts, Pratellus, and Utica.]

The prophet Daniel, speaking of the times of Antichrist, says: “I was considering the ten horns, and behold, another small horn arose from the midst of them, and three of the first horns were torn out before its face; and behold, eyes like human eyes were in this horn, and a mouth speaking great things” (Dan. VII, 8). Since transgression is expressed by the number eleven, the eleventh horn of this beast indicates the author of transgression himself. It arises small because a mere human being is born; but it grows monstrously because it advances to the point of being joined to the power of angelic strength.

That condemned man at the end of the world tears out three horns that are before him because he subjects to his dominion three kingdoms that are near him. His eyes are like human eyes, but his mouth speaks great things, because in him a human form is seen, while by his words he raises himself above human beings. What the Apostle Paul says—“exalting himself above everything called God or worshiped” (II Thess. II, 4)—the prophet Daniel confirms by saying: “A mouth speaking great things.” That Daniel says he speaks great things, and Paul says he is exalted above the worship of deity, is the same as what blessed Job compares to a cedar in divine speech (Job XL, 12). For, like a cedar, he strives toward lofty things, prospering in every arrogance of deceit, in strength of power, and in exaltation of eminence.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Antichrist or His Members

The strength of Antichrist is not fortified by his own powers, because he is raised by Satan’s power into the glory of perdition, as it is written: “A king of shameless face and understanding riddles will arise, and his strength will be strengthened, but not by his own powers” (Dan. VIII, 23; Morals, book XXXII, chapter 15, no. 26).

The prophet Daniel says of this same Antichrist: “He cast down from the strength, and from the stars, and trampled them; and he was magnified even to the Prince of strength, and from him he took away the perpetual sacrifice and cast down the place of his sanctuary. Power was given him against the perpetual sacrifice because of sins; and truth will be cast down upon the earth” (ibid., 10–12).

That principally condemned man is called the cymbal of wings (Isa. XVIII, 1; Morals, book XIII, chapter 10, no. 13), because those who fly upward through pride into the heights of thought resound by proclaiming that same perverse man.
