This land is rightly said to lie beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. Ethiopia indeed produces a black people; and since this world produces every human being as a sinner, it is, as it were, the parent of a black people. But the land to which woe is pronounced is said to lie beyond the rivers of Ethiopia because that condemned man is so immense in wickedness that he surpasses the sins of all sinners. [Editorial insertion: “Ethiopia produces a people. But the land to which woe is pronounced is said to lie beyond the rivers of Ethiopia.”]

That perverse man sends messengers across the sea because he scatters his preachers throughout the world. Concerning them it is rightly added how they are sent, when it is said: “In vessels of papyrus upon the waters” (Isa. XVIII, 1). For paper is made from papyrus. What, then, is signified by papyrus if not secular knowledge? The vessels of papyrus are therefore the hearts of secular teachers.

In the Apocalypse, through John, it is said: “I saw another beast rising from the earth” (Apoc. XIII, 11; Morals, book XXXIII, chapter 35, no. 59). He had described the earlier beast—that is, Antichrist—in the preceding account. This other beast is said to have risen after him because after him a multitude of his preachers grows fat on earthly power. To rise from the earth is to grow proud from earthly glory. [Note: [Col. 0981D] The edition reads “glories” (*gloriatur*).]

This beast has two horns like those of a lamb because, through hypocrisy of holiness, it falsely claims that the unique wisdom and life which the Lord truly possessed in himself are present in it. But because, under the appearance of a lamb, serpentine venom is poured into reprobate hearers, [Note: [Col. 0981] The edition reads “pours in” (*infundit*). The Turonensis, the two German manuscripts, and many others have Taius’s reading.] it is rightly added there: “And it spoke like a dragon” (Apoc. XIII, 11). This beast—that is, the multitude of preachers—if it spoke openly like a dragon, would not appear like a lamb; but it assumes the appearance of a lamb in order to carry out the work of a dragon.

The bitterness of perverse minds does not at this time break out externally in the voice of depraved freedom; but surely a time will come when the perverse and carnal will openly preach what they now devise in secret thought (Morals, book XIX, chapter 9, no. 15). A time will come when they will oppress the Catholic Church not only with unjust words but also with cruel blows.

In the Gospel Truth says: “False Christs and false prophets will arise and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error” (Matt. XXIV, 24). Now our faithful perform wonders when they endure perverse things; but then the satellites of Antichrist will perform wonders even while inflicting perverse things (Morals, book XXXII, chapter 15, no. 24).

Let us consider what the temptation of the human mind will be in the times of Antichrist, when the devout martyr both subjects his body to torments and, before his eyes, the torturer nevertheless performs miracles. Whose strength will not then be shaken from the very depths of his thoughts, when the one who tortures him with scourges flashes with signs? For then he will be exalted by the reverence inspired by miracles and hardened by the cruelty of torment. He will not then be raised up by power alone, but will also be supported by the display of signs (no. 25).

“They will arise,” he says, “false Christs and false prophets, and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect will be led into error.” In this matter it must be carefully asked how those who are elect can be led into error, or why, as though from uncertainty, it is added, “if it were possible,” when the Lord, who foreknows all things, awaits what is to happen (Morals, book XXXIII, chapter 36, no. 61). The heart of the elect in the times of Antichrist will be shaken by anxious thought, yet their steadfastness will not be moved. In this one statement the Lord has embraced both things, saying: “So that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error.” For to waver in thought is, as it were, already to err; but immediately “if it were possible” is added, because assuredly it is impossible for the elect to be completely seized by error.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Second Coming of Our Lord Jesus Christ

Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and human beings, just as he came humbly to the Passion, so will he appear terrible at the final judgment in the vengeance of the reprobate. The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The powers of heaven will be shaken, and then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty” (Luke XXI, 26–27; Book I on the Gospel, homily 1, no. 2).

For whom does the Lord call the powers of heaven, if not the angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers? This multitude of angels will visibly appear before our eyes at the coming of the strict Judge, so that then they may rigorously demand from us what the invisible Creator now bears with patience. They will see Christ in power and majesty, whom they refused to hear when he was placed in humility, so that they may then feel his power all the more strictly because now they do not incline the neck of their hearts to his patience.

The prophet Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and their princes” (Isa. III, 14; Morals, book XXVI, chapter 27, no. 51). Christ will come to judgment with those of whom he himself says in the Gospel: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28). When Solomon saw this judgment drawing near for the recompense of the holy Church, he said: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. XXXI, 23). It is as though he openly said: “He determines the sentence of the final judgment together with the holy preachers of that same Church.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Resurrection of the Dead

There are some who are uncertain about the resurrection of the flesh. When they see flesh reduced to corruption and bones to dust in the tombs, they doubt that flesh and bones can be restored from dust; and so, reasoning within themselves, they say: “When is a human being brought back from dust? When does ash become alive?” (Book II on the Gospel, homily 26, no. 12.)

For God it is far less to restore what has existed than to create what has not existed. Or what is remarkable if he raises a human being from dust, when he created all things together from nothing? It is more remarkable for God to establish heaven and earth from things that did not exist than to restore the human being from earth. The ash of a dead person is observed in a tomb, and it is despaired of that it can return to flesh; and the power of divine operation is sought to be grasped, as though by reasoning.

What is remarkable if God restores bones, sinews, flesh, and hair from dust, when every day he restores wood, fruit, and leaves in the great mass of a tree from a small seed? When, therefore, a doubting mind seeks an explanation of the power of resurrection, questions must be placed before it concerning those same things that continually occur and yet can by no means be comprehended by reason. Thus, when it cannot penetrate through the sight of a thing to what it sees, it may believe from the promise of divine power what it hears.

The psalmist David says: “Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification” (Ps. CXXXI, 8; Book II on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 6). The Lord arose into his rest when he raised his flesh from the tomb. After him the ark also rises, because the Church rises.

Through the prophet Ezekiel it is said: “Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I will bring spirit into you, and you will live” (Ezek. XVII, 4 ff.). Hence another prophet saw the human race raised up at the end through resurrection and said: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we will live in his sight” (Hos. VI, 3).

When the Lord was speaking of himself, he said: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice. And those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28–29). Hence Paul says: “From there also we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. III, 20). Again he says: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep” (I Thess. IV, 14). Again he says: “Christ, the first fruits of those who sleep” (I Cor. XV, 20). For if we do not rise from the sleep of death, how do we have the Lord’s resurrection as first fruits?

Behold, the ancient and the new Fathers agree with one another in one spirit concerning the resurrection of the flesh (Book II on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 7). Behold, Truth itself first taught by its voice what it later demonstrated by its work concerning the resurrection of the flesh; and yet the weakness of some still lacks faith, standing within the house of faith.

The elements themselves and the forms of things themselves proclaim to us an image of the resurrection. The sun dies every day before our eyes and rises every day. The stars set for us in the morning hours and rise again in the evening. We see trees full of leaves and fruits in the summer seasons; in winter they remain bare of leaves, flowers, and fruits, as though dry. But when the spring sun returns, once moisture has risen from the root, they are again clothed in their own beauty.

Why, then, is the resurrection of human beings doubted when what appears to happen in trees is believed? Often faithless people, when they look upon the dust of decaying flesh, say: “From where will flesh and hair be restored in the resurrection?” Let them therefore, when asking such questions, look at the small seeds of mighty trees and, if they can, say: “Where in them is hidden such a mass of strength, such a diversity of branches, such a multitude and greenness of leaves, such beauty of flowers, such abundance, taste, and fragrance of fruits?” Do the seeds of trees have the fragrance or taste that the trees themselves later produce in their fruits?

If, therefore, what cannot be seen can be produced from a tree’s seed, why is it doubted that from the dust of human flesh a form that cannot be seen can be restored? If you cannot comprehend the effect of the resurrection by reasoning, consider how many things there are whose manner of being you do not understand, yet whose existence you do not doubt (no. 7). Tell me, I ask, if you know the circuit of heaven, the hinges of the earth, and the depths of the waters: where do they end, and where are they suspended? We know, however, that what was made from nothing hangs upon nothing.

Why do you doubt the glory of the resurrection by debating and examining it, when you have believed without examination so many mysteries? (no. 10.) Yet if you do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh, you have believed everything in vain, because in this spectacle of the angels you appear indeed to run swiftly, but after completing the race you oppose yourself lest you receive the prize. Through the Apostle Paul it is said: “Run so that you may obtain” (I Cor. IX, 24). Again he says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (I Cor. XV, 19).

The mysteries of divine power, which cannot be comprehended, are not to be examined by understanding but revered by faith. We must know that whatever can be comprehended by human reason can no longer be wonderful; in miracles, the only explanation is the power of the one who performs them. Just as a sleeping person, quickly awakened from sleep, is awake, so the body rises swiftly from death at the Creator’s command.

The outstanding preacher calls the Lord’s death “death”; but the death of the Lord’s servants he calls not death but sleep, because, considering the weak hearts of his hearers, he composes the medicine of his preaching with marvelous skill. He does not hesitate to present as dead the one whom they already knew to have risen (Morals, book XII, chapter 8, no. 12). But those who had not yet risen, in order to suggest the hope of resurrection, he calls not dead but sleeping. The Apostle did not fear to call Christ dead, whom his hearers knew already to have risen, but he feared to call dead those whom they scarcely believed would rise.

In the glory of that resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but palpable through the reality of its nature. Speaking of the true resurrection of the body, blessed Job says: “Again I will be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I will see God; whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another” (Job XIX, 26; Morals, book XIV, chapter 56, nos. 72, 76). Behold the true resurrection; behold the skin; behold the flesh—he confesses them in unmistakable words. What, then, remains from which our mind could doubt?

Following the faith of blessed Job, and truly believing that the body of our Redeemer was palpable after the resurrection, we confess that our flesh after the resurrection will be both the same and different: the same in nature, different in power (chapter 57, no. 77). After the resurrection our flesh will be subtle, yet palpable, because it will not lose the substance of its true nature.

The dead descend into the earth, not in spirit but in body (Book II on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 6). Therefore those who descend into the earth proceed in the sight of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0985D] The edition reads “fall prostrate” (*procidunt*). See the note of the Benedictine Fathers.], because by rising they come to judgment—those who now decay in dust—as it is written: “In his sight all who descend into the earth proceed” (Ps. XXI, 29). The same psalmist says again: “My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly also my flesh” (Ps. LXII, 2). The soul thirsts to see God. What does the flesh thirst for, if not to rise?

Again he says: “Take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust” (Ps. CIII, 29). Immediately he adds concerning the resurrection of the flesh: “Send forth your spirit, O God, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (ibid., 30).

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Terrible Judgment of the Eternal King

When the almighty God the Son comes as Judge of the dead and the living, he will appear both gentle to the just and terrible to the unjust (Book II on the Gospel, homily 21, no. 3). Coming to judgment, he soothes the former through the gentleness of his mildness; but he terrifies the latter through the strictness of justice.

When a storm arises, gentle waves come first, and afterward larger billows are stirred; finally the waves raise themselves high and, by their very height, overturn all who are sailing (Morals, book XXI, chapter 22, no. 35). Thus, indeed, the storm of souls hastens toward that final event which will overthrow the whole world. The storm of the future judgment now shows us its beginnings through wars and disasters, as though through certain waves; and the nearer we become each day to the end, the more grievous billows of tribulations we see rushing upon us.

Finally, when all the elements have been shaken, the heavenly Judge comes and brings the end of all things, because then the storm also lifts its waves into heaven. Hence it is said: “Yet a little while, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Hag. II, 7). Because holy men watchfully observe this storm, they fear the waves swelling over them each day and foresee from the tribulations that strike the world what will follow.

What will the terrible Judge do when he comes in person and his wrath blazes forth for the vengeance of sinners, if he cannot now be endured when he strikes us through the thinnest cloud (Book I on the Gospel, homily 1, no. 6)? What flesh will stand in the presence of his wrath if, when he stirs the wind, he overturns the earth, agitates the air, and lays so many buildings low?

Considering this strictness of the coming Judge, Paul says: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. X, 3). The psalmist expresses this strictness when he says: “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him” (Ps. XLIX, 3). A storm and fire accompany the strictness of such justice, because the storm examines those whom the fire will consume.

Through the prophet Zephaniah it is said: “The great day of the Lord is near, very near and swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be troubled there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast against all fortified cities and against all lofty corners” (Zeph. I, 14 ff.).

The day of the Lord, full of vengeance and punishment, comes against fortified cities and lofty corners because the wrath of the final judgment destroys human hearts closed against the truth by defenses and dissolves those wrapped in duplicity (Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 12). Then the fortified cities fall because minds impenetrable to God will be condemned. Then the lofty corners collapse because hearts that raise themselves through the prudence of impurity are cast down by the sentence of justice.

Concerning this day of judgment the Lord again says through the prophet: “Once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Hag. II, 22; Book I on the Gospel, homily 1, no. 9). If, when he shook the air, the earth could not remain standing, who could endure it when he shakes heaven? The terrors that we now see are heralds of the wrath that follows. Therefore it must be considered that these tribulations differ from that final tribulation only as the person of a herald differs from the power of a judge.

Let us therefore think with complete attention upon that terrible day, correct our life and conduct, overcome tempting evils by resisting them, and punish the evils we have committed with tears. For we shall one day see the coming of the eternal Judge with all the greater security in proportion as we now anticipate his strictness by fearing it.

At the examination of the terrible Judge, all the elect, separated from the reprobate, will rejoice, because when the final vengeance strikes all the wicked, they themselves will be joyful over the glory of a worthy recompense (Morals, book VI, chapter 30, no. 48). Once established in eternal life, the just will no longer pity the condemned out of human feeling, because, cleaving to divine justice through its manifestation, they will be made firm by the unshaken strength of inward strictness.

For the Redeemer of the human race, to build us up, it was not enough to declare what he would say at the final judgment: “As long as you did it for one of these least of my brothers, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV, 40; Book II on the Gospel, homily 39, no. 10), unless before the judgment he also showed this in himself which he had said, so that he might demonstrate that whoever now presents good works to the needy renders them specifically to the one for whose love he has presented them.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Fruitless Repentance of the Reprobate

When the eternal Judge comes, each of the reprobate is brought back to himself, so that, since he can no longer perform holy deeds, he may feel what is holy and learn what is right, which he ought to have followed, from the punishment of his crookedness (Morals, book XXVII, chapter 24, no. 45).

Through the prophet Jeremiah it is said: “Gather them like a flock for sacrifice, and sanctify them on the day of slaughter” (Jer. XII, 3). On the day of slaughter the reprobate are sanctified because then they recognize the holy things they ought to have done, when they can no longer escape the punishments deserved by their wickedness.

All the reprobate then fear being struck, when they are struck by the Judge’s sentence with the final vengeance; and his terror then awakens them from the sleep of their torpor, when punishment disturbs them (Morals, book XI, chapter 29, no. 41). Through the prophet it is said: “Only vexation will give understanding to hearing” (Isa. XXVIII, 19). When the wicked begin to be beaten by vengeance for the commandments of God that they despised and rejected, then they understand what they heard.

The psalmist also says: “When he slew them, then they sought him” (Ps. LXXVII, 34). At the final judgment, all the impious, recognizing their condemnation, will say: “We have erred from the way of truth; the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. V, 6; Morals, book XXXIV, chapter 14, no. 25). It is as though they openly said: “The ray of inward light did not shine upon us.”

The impious person does not know the evils he has done until he has begun to be punished for those very evils (Morals, book XV, chapter 51, no. 58). Then he understands what he heard, when he grieves that he is already being tormented for his contempt, as it is written: “Only vexation will give understanding to hearing” (Isa. XXVIII, 19; Morals, book VII, chapter 27, no. 33).

The reprobate do not understand eternal things until they are punished in temporal things, with no possibility of correction. Then the mind burns, and inflames itself with the fires of fruitless repentance; it fears being led to punishment and clings to the present life out of desire. But it is released from its place, because, abandoning the delights of the flesh, its hardness is melted through punishment.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Damnation of the Devil and the Demons

When the eternal Judge appears in terror, with legions of angels standing by, the entire ministry of the heavenly powers assisting, and all the elect brought to this spectacle, the devil—a cruel and powerful beast—is brought captive into the midst. Together with his body, that is, with all the reprobate, he is consigned to the eternal fires of Gehenna, when it is said: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41; Morals, book XXXIII, chapter 20, no. 37).

What a spectacle that will be, when this most monstrous beast is displayed before the eyes of the elect—the beast that in this time of battle could have terrified them exceedingly if it had been seen! But by the hidden and wondrous counsel of God it is arranged that now, by his grace, it may be conquered by those who fight without seeing it, and then may be seen captive by the rejoicing victors.

Then the just will recognize more fully how much they are debtors to divine help, when they see so powerful a beast as the one they, though weak, have now conquered. In the monstrosity of their enemy they will perceive how much they owe to the grace of their defender (Morals, book IV, chapter 5, no. 10).

The ancient enemy, bound by the chains of his wickedness, suffers one thing now and another at the end. Since he fell from the order of the innermost light, he now confounds himself inwardly in the darkness of error. At the time of his damnation the ancient enemy is enveloped in bitterness, because, by the desert of his voluntary darkness, he is tormented by the eternal punishment of Gehenna.

Blessed Job rightly says concerning Antichrist: “Let darkness seize him; let him be wrapped in bitterness” (Job III, 5). Everything that is wrapped up does not clearly disclose its end, as it does not show where it begins and does not reveal where it ends. Thus the ancient enemy is said to be wrapped in bitterness because punishments for his pride are prepared for him, not only in every respect but also without end.

The punishment of Antichrist begins when the strict Judge comes for the final judgment. Hence it is rightly added: “Let a dark whirlwind possess that night” (Job III, 6; Morals, book IV, chapter 6, no. 11). A dark whirlwind possesses that night because that storm snatches the apostate spirit away from the sight of the strict Judge toward the eternal punishments it must fear. The night is therefore possessed by a whirlwind because its proud blindness is struck by a strict punishment.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Eternal Punishments of the Reprobate

The justice of almighty God, foreknowing future things, created the fire of Gehenna from the very origin of the world, so that it would begin to exist once as the punishment of the reprobate, yet would never bring its burning to an end even without wood (Morals, book XV, chapter 29, no. 35).

It must be known that all the reprobate who sinned with soul and flesh together will there be tormented in eternal punishment both in soul and in flesh. Through the prophet David it is said: “You will place them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence” (Ps. XX, 10). A furnace burns inwardly. But one who is devoured by fire begins to be burned from the outer part. [Note: [Col. 0989] Here the Gothic Codex of San Millán ends; nevertheless, we have supplied this passage from Gregory. The remainder of this chapter and the whole of chapter 34 are missing.] Thus, in order that the sacred Scriptures might demonstrate that the reprobate burn both externally and internally, they testify that they are both devoured by fire [Col. 0990A] and placed like a furnace, so that they may be tormented by fire in the body and burn through pain in the mind.

## APPENDIX

### ON THE VISION OF BISHOP TAIO

(From Baronius, *Annals*, under the year 646.) (C, S)

[Col. 0989B] … It is said to have happened in the final year reckoned for King Chindaswind of Spain, when that same holy man Martin, Roman pontiff, had begun to occupy the papal seat, that a revelation was divinely made concerning the books of the Moralia of Pope Gregory. We shall describe it in precisely the words in which it is found written. If, because of its great age, you find it covered with rags, do not recoil; rather, once these have been removed, contemplate the naked meaning, shining with the brightness and simplicity of truth, since all the writers of Spain who have treated this matter rightly subscribe to it without any controversy. It runs as follows:

Chindaswind, king of the Goths, magnificently summoned a synodal assembly of thirty bishops, together with the entire clergy, to be held in the city of Toledo in the fifth year of his reign. He sent Taio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, a man sufficiently instructed in literary learning and a friend of the Scriptures, to Rome, at his own request, to obtain the remaining [Col. 0989C] books of the Moralia. While he was being put off day after day by the Roman pope—as though the little book, sought amid the multitude of books in the archive of the Roman Church, could by no means readily be found—Taio, keeping vigil through the night and imploring the Lord’s mercy at the footsteps of blessed Peter the apostle and prince, was shown by an angel the chest in which the book was kept. As soon as the pope perceived that he had been reproved, he provided him with assistants, with the greatest reverence, for copying it, and sent it to the Spaniards for rereading. For they had retained only what had been expounded from the books of blessed Job and had been brought over by blessed Leander, bishop of Seville, and long ago honorably carried away. When Taio was questioned and adjured by Martin, the first Roman pope, how the location of those books had been shown to him so truthfully, after much entreaty he confessed to him with great eagerness that one night he had requested permission from the doorkeepers of the church of blessed Peter the apostle to keep watch. When he had obtained this, and in the middle of the night had prostrated himself before the tomb of blessed Peter the apostle amid very great lamentations, light sent from heaven shone throughout the whole church with such an indescribable radiance that not even the church’s lamps seemed to shine at all. Together with that light, and with the voices of those singing psalms and the lamps shining back, a host of saints entered. Finally, when he had been terrified by an overwhelming dread, after their prayer had been completed, two white-haired old men gradually came out from that assembly of saints and began to approach the place [Col. 0990B] where the bishop was engaged in prayer. When they found him almost dead, they greeted him gently and restored him to his senses. When they asked him why he had endured so great a hardship, or who, hastening from the West, had undertaken such a long journey by sea, they listened as he related this and that to them, as though they were ignorant of it, and considered it worthwhile. Then, after comforting him with many words, they showed him the chest in which the books were hidden.

Accordingly, when those holy men were asked who that company of saints was that accompanied them with such brilliant light, they answered that it was Peter, the apostle of Christ, together with Paul, holding one another by the hand, and all the successors of the Church who rested in that place. When they themselves were then asked who the lords were who had held such a marvelous conversation with him, one of them replied that he was Gregory, whose book Taio himself desired to see; and that he had therefore come to reward him for so great a hardship and to make his long-standing desire still greater.

Then Taio asked whether the learned Augustine was finally present in that holy multitude, since from his earliest childhood he had always loved to read the books of Augustine as well as those of blessed Gregory, with great eagerness. He is reported to have received only this answer: “That illustrious man, Augustine, most welcome to the expectation of all, whom you seek, is held by a place higher than ours.”

Since it is said that only those who had been buried in that basilica of the saints appeared to him, this seems to be the answer concerning Augustine: that he was held in another place; and thus what is written, “he was held in a higher place,” should be corrected to “he was held in another place.” Otherwise, how could it truthfully be said that Augustine was placed in a more exalted location in heaven, when the princes of the apostles and many other martyrs and bishops, who had been buried in that same church, appeared in the vision at that time? But the author continues:

Certainly, when he began to fall at their feet, that most holy man alone vanished from his eyes, together with the light, while the doorkeepers themselves were terrified. From that day onward, therefore, Taio became glorious and venerable to everyone in that apostolic see, whereas previously he had been despised as cowardly.

Thus far the account, which you have in revised form in the appendix to the Seventh Council of Toledo.

But who were those books whose absence in Spain the bishop of Caesaraugusta so deeply lamented? We can understand this from the letter of that same blessed Gregory to Leander, where the following is read:

“Because I cannot see you, separated as you are from me by so great a distance of land, the charity which your affection inspired in me has led me to send to your Holiness, through our common son, the priest Probinus, the book of the Pastoral Rule, which I wrote at the beginning of my episcopate, and the books which you knew long ago that I had composed as an exposition of blessed Job. I have not sent your charity the codices of the third and fourth parts of that work, because I find only those codices from those same parts which I have already given to monasteries. Let your Holiness therefore read through these diligently,” etc.

Thus you see that the Spaniards lacked the first and second parts of the Moralia. It is therefore not surprising that Martin the pontiff could not easily find those books: they were not even so readily available to Gregory himself that he could send them to Leander, to whom he had addressed the complete work, nor could he find other parts of the same work except those which, as he says, he had handed over to monasteries.

Roderick of Toledo should be corrected when he says that, through the negligence of the Spaniards, that part of the books of the Moralia was lost for the recovery of which Taio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, undertook his journey to Rome. Nor do we approve his statement that such a Roman embassy had been decreed by the Seventh Council of Toledo, since that council took place two years earlier, namely in the year of the Lord 646. At that time, I think, Taio had not yet been made bishop of Caesaraugusta; he is found subscribed near the very end of the Eighth Council of Toledo, as a junior member. I was also astonished that the historian Ambrosius says that this occurred under Theodore, the Roman pontiff, when that account, faithfully reproduced by García, a most careful man, testifies that it occurred under Pope Martin. (Thus far Baronius, in the place cited above.)

## ADDENDA

[Col. 0991]

# CRITICAL DISSERTATION: WHETHER POPE HONORIUS I WAS CONDEMNED IN THE YEAR 680 BY THE SIXTH GENERAL COUNCIL

Dedicated to all professors and candidates of Sacred Theology and Ecclesiastical History by Fr. Marcellinus Molkenbuhr, emeritus lecturer of the stricter observance of the Order of St. Francis, former minister of the Province of Saxony of the Holy Cross, and Doctor of Sacred Theology at the most ancient University of Heidelberg (Münster in Westphalia, 1798).

“Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything other than what we preached to you, let him be anathema.” (St. Paul the Apostle, Galatians 1:8.)

# PREFACE

[Col. 0991C] I. The fact that I published no Latin dissertation in the previous year arose from various impediments and other occupations. Among the last of these was a little work recently published by me at Paderborn in the German language against Thomas Paine, who, in a book printed in Paris in 1796 and translated into German—entitled *The Age of Reason*, or *Das Zeitalter der Vernunft*, Part Two—had maintained that all the books of the New and Old Testaments were forgeries and that the Christian religion was the most false of all.

II. In Dissertation 19, published in 1796, I had promised that in this twentieth work I would publish my final dissertation on the year in which Christ was born, baptized, and crucified. But for reasons that I consider unnecessary to enumerate here, I changed my mind. That work on the years of Christ will remain the final one, or number 21; it has now merely been prepared for the press. I nevertheless place before it this extremely intricate dissertation on Pope Honorius I, which I may have said I would publish in Dissertation 18, section 25.

III. This question concerning Pope Honorius I is one of the most famous [Note: [Col. 0991D] Only two historical cases are commonly brought forward that cause difficulty and trouble if one wishes to excuse all the Roman pontiffs from error against the faith, namely the lapses of Liberius and Honorius. Thus Benignus Bossuet, bishop of Meaux (*Meditations on the Gospel*, day 27, in Laurent Veiht, in the dissertation on the Primacy of the Roman Pontiff, § 45, printed at Augsburg in 1797). That the lapse of Liberius was fictitious was proved with the greatest force by Stilting in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, published in 1757—therefore after Bossuet’s death. The most learned men followed Stilting’s opinion. I added certain material in defense of Liberius, Hosius of Corduba, and the Council of Ariminum in Dissertation 13, section 33, and Dissertation 18, sections 171 and 177.] among ecclesiastical historians and dogmatic theologians. Various opinions have arisen concerning it, which can be reduced to the following three: first, that Pope Honorius erred in the faith, either by teaching heresy [Note: [Col. 0992D] Benignus Bossuet explained that Honorius erred only as a private teacher (see Soardi, Book II, chapter 1, § 3). Others maintain that he answered *ex cathedra*.] or by showing it excessive favor; second, that the general council erred in condemning Honorius on account of letters that Honorius either did not write or understood in a Catholic sense; third, that neither party erred, since the bishops assembled in synod did not condemn the pope. I embrace this last position, persuaded by stronger arguments. Let critics read and judge.

IV. As for my preceding dissertations, the first fourteen of them were announced by the Roman censors in their public journals to the learned world in 1794 as learned and entirely Catholic, and as apparently supported by arguments of the greatest validity. At the same time, however, they warned the reader not to give me hasty assent, since solutions to my arguments might perhaps still be discovered. I was entirely satisfied with this judgment, and therefore publicly asked the aforesaid censors to publish any replies they might find (see Dissertation 16, Preface, section 5). I have now waited four years, but they have remained silent; from their silence I infer that they have not found a solution to my arguments.

V. Among those first fourteen dissertations is also my assertion that St. Peter was never bishop of Antioch. This too, although published as early as 1788, has so far been publicly challenged by no one. I considered it necessary to note this because, although some have approved my opinion very strongly, it has displeased certain learned men. For a clearer understanding, I shall briefly set out my system here.

VI. St. Luke, in the Acts of the Apostles, from chapter 1 through chapter 12, described the deeds of St. Peter and his journeys within Palestine from Christ’s Ascension until Peter’s imprisonment under Herod, which occurred at Easter in the year 42. That Peter, before he was imprisoned, ever went to Antioch in Syria or left Palestine is not indicated by the aforementioned St. Luke. Therefore, up to that point St. Peter had not been seated at Antioch [Note: [Col. 0993C] In addition, the ancients of the second century—such as Apollonius, cited by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 18), and Clement of Alexandria—asserted on the basis of tradition that the apostles, and therefore St. Peter also, remained in Palestine during the first twelve years. Consequently, those ancient writers did not know that St. Peter had been seated at Antioch before his imprisonment. Eusebius, in the fourth century, seems to have agreed with Apollonius. Moreover, those twelve years can be understood as incomplete at both ends, just as in Christ’s words: “The Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights,” and, “After three days I shall rise again” (Matthew 12:27. See 1 Kings 30:20; Esther 4:16).]

In the year 42, after his imprisonment, Peter, according to that same St. Luke (Acts 12:17), first went to another place; that is, he preached outside Palestine. As can be inferred from the First Epistle of St. Peter (chapter 1, verse 1), he preached in Cappadocia, Pontus, Galatia, Asia Minor, and Bithynia [Note: [Col. 0993D] It is most probable that St. Peter already intended at that time to journey to Rome and establish his see there. Thus, although he founded churches in those regions, he did not establish his see there.]. Then, around the year 43, according to Eusebius, Jerome, and others, he came to Rome [Note: [Col. 0993D] Thus there do not remain seven years, or even five, during which the defenders of the see of Antioch assert that Peter had previously been seated at Antioch.] as to a new Babylon, where he wrote his first epistle to the churches of the aforementioned regions [Note: [Col. 0993D] There is no mention here of Syria, whose metropolis was Antioch. Indeed, since Cephas, whom Paul rebuked at Antioch (Galatians 2), was not St. Peter, as I demonstrated with moral certainty in Dissertation 17, section 84, there remains from Sacred Scripture no sufficient reason for asserting that St. Peter was ever at Antioch.], while the evangelist St. Mark was still present there. According to Eusebius, Mark was sent from Rome by St. Peter to Egypt around the year 45.

The church founded by St. Peter at Rome from Jews and Gentiles grew so greatly that Paul, while still traveling through the East, repeatedly desired to see it and around the year 56 wrote to the Romans: “Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Romans 18).

In the year 49 all the Jews were ordered by the emperor Claudius to leave Rome, as is clear from St. Luke (Acts 18:2), and, as appears from Suetonius (*Life of Claudius*, chapter 25), because the faith of Christ was being preached there. Therefore Peter, being Jewish by origin and the first apostle of Christ, also had to leave Rome. On this occasion he returned to Jerusalem, where he settled the dispute that had arisen against Paul at Antioch, taking Paul’s side while he was in Jerusalem.

After Claudius’s death, in the year 54, under Nero, the Jews were again permitted to return to Rome. St. Peter also returned there and was crucified there [Note: [Col. 0994C] I also accept the following three most ancient traditions: first, that the apostles remained within Palestine during the first twelve years while evangelizing; second, that St. Peter survived Christ’s Passion by thirty-seven years; and third, that he governed the Roman Church for twenty-five complete years. Christ was crucified in the year 31 of the common era, Peter in the year 68.

[Col. 0994D] Concerning the day of death of Saints Peter and Paul, it now seems more probable to me that the apostles suffered on 21 February and that their sacred relics were transferred on 29 June. Nevertheless, even if it is granted that Christ suffered in the year 29 or 33 of the common era and that the apostles were crowned with martyrdom in the year 68, on 29 June—and therefore after the death of Nero, who perished on 9 June—the defenders of the see of Antioch gain nothing from this. The day on which St. Peter came to Rome, for example whether 18 January, cannot be determined.]

(See the two dissertations on the sees of Peter.) The objections later successively raised against this system of mine I resolved in Dissertation 15, beginning at section 30; Dissertation 17, section 90; Dissertation 18, section 108; and Dissertation 19, section 225.

VII. In these works I finally discovered that all the arguments thus far cited in favor of Peter’s Antiochene see from the first four centuries—drawn from Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Origen, Eusebius, Jerome, and Chrysostom—are of doubtful authority. Indeed, the opinion that Cephas, whom Paul rebuked at Antioch, was St. Peter is older than the other opinion that Peter was bishop of Antioch. The first opinion was transmitted by pseudo-Cyprian in his letters against Pope St. Stephen, written at the end of the fourth century, and was truly accepted by Saints Augustine and Chrysostom. The second opinion, concerning Peter’s Antiochene episcopate, is not of such ancient origin.

I am prepared, in this important matter, to answer publicly or privately anyone regarding whatever further objections may be communicated to me. Therefore:

VIII. Since the authority of the Roman Breviary has recently again been brought against me, although I believe that I already answered it sufficiently in the Dissertation on the Sees, section 127, I shall nevertheless now present that argument again and at greater length.

The Feast of the Chair of Peter—without specifying whether it was at Rome or Antioch—has from time immemorial been celebrated once a year, on 22 February [Note: [Col. 0994D] In ancient documents, and even in common usage, by the Feast of the Chair of Peter—German *Petri Stuhl-Feyer*—the day of 22 February is understood.] at Rome and everywhere. In 1558 Pope Paul IV instituted another feast of the Chair, which was already being celebrated in certain particular churches on 18 January, for the city and the world. In the bull that he issued on the matter, he stated that Peter had remained for some time at Antioch before reaching Rome. He added that the Roman Chair of Peter, according to the testimonies of our most ancient holy Fathers, fell on 18 January and was celebrated on that day in various parts of the world, especially in Gaul and Spain. He therefore wished the Roman Chair of Peter also to be celebrated on the 18th, or rather restored to its ancient celebration. But:

**Response 1.** That bull is not dogmatic with respect to its historical portions [Note: [Col. 0994D] Bellarmine (*On the Roman Pontiff*, Book IV, chapter 14) says: “It is clear that many things are found in decretal letters which do not make a matter one of faith, but merely declare to us the opinions of the pontiffs concerning that matter.”]. In it Paul IV also asserts that St. Peter governed the Roman see for twenty-five years. I have proved this elsewhere to be entirely true, but many more recent Catholic writers do not accept it, such as Valesius (on Book II of Eusebius, chapter 16), Pagius (on the year 43), Mansi (in his notes to Natalis), and Calmet.

When Paul IV declared that St. Peter had been seated at Rome for twenty-five years, he followed the tradition of his Roman Church, transmitted from the earliest centuries. But when he introduced the new feast of the Chair on 18 January, he imitated, as he himself added, certain lesser churches, particularly those of Gaul and Spain. In the meantime, the most ancient writers who can be named in connection with a January celebration of the Chair are Venerable Bede, from the eighth century, and the Gauls Usuard, a monk, and Ado, a bishop, from the ninth century, in their martyrologies.

It is clear, however, from the Second Synod of Tours, assembled in the year 567 (Canon 22), that even in the sixth century the Gauls, though already Christian, knew only one feast of the Chair: the one celebrated on the day when pagans offered food to the dead, namely 22 February.

Moreover, many things are narrated in the Roman Breviary that are not matters of divine faith—for example, that St. Dionysius the Areopagite was bishop of Paris; that Martha, Magdalene, Lazarus, and Maximinus, one of the seventy-two disciples, came to Gaul; and that Lazarus and Maximinus were the first bishops of Marseille and Aix respectively. These histories seem to have originated in Gaul.

**Response 2.** The Feast of the Chair of Peter is now indeed celebrated twice a year. Nevertheless, nothing false is contained either in the office or in the readings; in the heading for 22 February, the word “Antioch” could simply be omitted again. To me the arguments that St. Cletus, commemorated on 26 April, and Anacletus, commemorated on 13 July in the Breviary [Col. 0995B], were truly distinct persons seem stronger than the arguments that St. Peter ever occupied the see of Antioch. But human judgments vary! Many recent writers maintain that Cletus and Anacletus were one person—which I too accept—yet they regard the alternative opinion, that St. Peter held only one episcopate, namely at Rome, as almost reckless.

IX. The authority of Pope St. Innocent I has also again been brought against me. In a letter written in the year 416, and therefore in the fifth century, to Alexander, bishop of Antioch, he asserted that St. Peter had been seated at Antioch before Rome.

**Response 1.** As before: this letter is not dogmatic with respect to its historical portions. It is preserved in its entirety by Labbe and Hardouin, taken from the collection of Isidore and Dionysius, authors who are not irrefragable authorities.

**Response 2.** For many internal reasons considered together, that letter seems suspect to me, as I briefly indicated in Dissertation 18, section 108, and must now explain at greater length. In it the supreme pontiff, writing back to the bishop of Antioch, asserts:

1. That he considers it an honor to have been consulted by the bishop of Antioch;

2. That the Church of Antioch had been established by the First Council of Nicaea over several provinces because it was shown to be the place of the first see of the first apostle;

3. That the most celebrated assembly of the apostles had taken place there;

4. That the Church of Antioch would not yield to the Roman Church except because Peter, passing through Antioch but remaining at Rome, had occupied the see in both places;

5. That Arians and other heretics cannot validly confer the sacrament of orders, because they have lost the Holy Spirit through heresy and therefore cannot give him to those whom they ordain.

[Note: [Col. 0995C] The pope relates that, exhausted by the power of the Arians, the Cypriots had failed to observe the Nicene canons in the consecration of bishops. I doubt whether this is true; shortly before, St. Epiphanius had been metropolitan in Cyprus, a man who did not fear the Arians. He concludes to the Antiochene: “Let your Gravity bring this to the knowledge of your fellow bishops.” Yet there is no mention of St. John Chrysostom, recently deceased, whose enrollment in the sacred diptychs Innocent I and the aforementioned Alexander had at that time been vigorously urging against others.]

The last, or fifth, assertion [Note: [Col. 0995D] This is reported in Gratian’s *Decree* (Question 1, chapter “Arians”), where several spurious items are also found.] plainly smells of heresy; nevertheless Bellarmine attempted to remove this difficulty (*On the Roman Pontiff*, Book IV, chapter 10). The first assertion seems less appropriate: the pope is the universal teacher, so why would he consider it an honor to be consulted by the bishop of Antioch?

The second smacks of fable if it is understood to mean that in the fourth or fifth century the material seat on which St. Peter had physically sat was shown at Antioch [Col. 0996A]. The Council of Nicaea had made no mention of Peter’s Antiochene see [Note: [Col. 0995D] It is indeed read in the *Recognitions* of Pope Clement I (Book X, section 71) that a chair for St. Peter had been established at Antioch by the entire people in the great basilica of Theophilus, previously consecrated as a church. But learned men now agree that those books were either falsely attributed to Clement or seriously corrupted by another author.].

The third assertion is supported by no testimony. The fourth—that Peter, assuming he was not Cephas, passed through Antioch—cannot be sufficiently proved from any more ancient record. At the end of the fourth century, Pope Damasus and the Greek bishops still seem to have been unaware that St. Peter had ever been seated at Antioch (see the Dissertation on the Sees, sections 117 and 118; Theodoret, Book V, chapter 9) [Note: [Col. 0995D] Indeed, in the year 451, at the Council of Chalcedon (Act 7), the bishop of Antioch did call his see the “see of Peter,” but he did so alone. Only with the consent of the bishop of Jerusalem did he obtain that both Phoenicias and Arabia should then be subject to him; there was complete silence concerning the aforementioned letter of St. Innocent I.].

X. Pope St. Leo I remains. Around the year 450, in Sermon 80, certainly a genuine work, he mentioned that St. Peter founded the Church of Antioch—obviously by preaching there—before reaching Rome under Claudius [Note: [Col. 0996D] Therefore, even according to St. Leo, St. Peter went to Rome under Claudius. But in which year of Claudius? Certainly the second, as the earlier writers, whom St. Leo did not contradict, transmitted: namely, the year 42 of the common era, or approximately then.].

**Response.** It does not follow from this that St. Leo I also thought that St. Peter had occupied the see of Antioch as bishop of that church. In any case, I assert only that no solid argument in favor of Peter’s Antiochene see can be produced from the first four centuries. I now think that I have answered sufficiently the objections communicated to me thus far; at least I have knowingly and willingly concealed none of importance.

XI. My dissertations have attracted the attention not only of the Romans, as stated in section 4, but also of several learned men in Germany. Although I do not dare to claim that each one obtained their full assent, taken as a whole they have nevertheless been valued by many—whose letters I could produce—more highly than I expected.

Permit me to present one public testimony. On account of these dissertations, the Catholic theological faculty at the most ancient University of Heidelberg, considering them truly learned, promoted me in my absence to the doctorate in 1796 without charge. On this occasion I cannot fail to mention this with a most grateful spirit. Yet far be it from me to infer from this that the famous faculty approved each of my individual assertions. I have exposed all of them, once printed, to the public judgment of everyone.

XII. They have also pleased certain French theologians. Nevertheless, to conceal nothing, some others, and especially Mr. Jary [Note: [Col. 0996D] I repeatedly urged him, both personally and through others, to communicate his reasons either to me or to the public, so that the truth might become more widely known. But I could not obtain this, and therefore I am unable to answer his reasons.], a theological canon of the cathedral church of Arras, have strongly disapproved them.

This does not surprise me greatly, since my new assertions—as I already noted in Dissertation 18, section 25—withdraw a large part of the arguments from those who have until now defended their “Gallican Liberties” against the Roman curia, as they call it.

For the sake of advancing the truth, I thought it appropriate to warn on this occasion that the famous and extensive work entitled *Defense of the Declaration of the Gallican Clergy of 1682 Concerning Ecclesiastical Power*, by D. Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, bishop of Meaux, was falsely attributed after his death [Note: [Col. 0996D] Bossuet died in 1704. The *Defense* is said to have been composed in 1688, but it was first published in 1730, and then by an anonymous author. It was later printed several times, especially at Mainz in 1788, in quarto, filling 1,019 pages. In addition to Liberius and Honorius, the author of the *Defense* cites fourteen other Roman pontiffs, including St. Gregory VII, all of whom, he says, erred in matters of faith or morals by teaching or answering openly. He cites Bossuet repeatedly and also honorifically calls him “Lord Bossuet,” “most reverend,” “most illustrious,” “most learned prelate,” “one of the more eminent theologians and doctors,” and so forth. Would the most modest Bossuet have spoken of himself in this way? Further indications of its spurious attribution may be found in the authors cited.].

This was amply demonstrated by the most learned Italian Soardi and by the author of the book *Who Is Peter?*, a German work; the former was printed at Heidelberg in 1793, the latter at Cologne in 1790. In that spurious work, in the preliminary dissertation, *Gallican Orthodoxy* (§§ 54–58 and Book VII, chapters 21–29), it is stated in elegant and penetrating style that Pope Honorius was truly condemned as a heretic at the Sixth Council, indeed as one who had taught heresy *ex cathedra*. The Fourteenth Council of Toledo is also exalted as having been celebrated by the most learned and courageous Spanish bishops; this single council is portrayed as blowing apart the entire machinery of all those who have attempted to clear Honorius. I shall faithfully present that council in section 100.

XIII. Since sad reports concerning the Church now resound from every direction, I may also preface a few words about these matters. A month ago, in February, Rome was captured by the French without resistance and converted into a republic; our most holy and excellent Father, Pius VI, was taken away from Rome, and all temporal sovereignty was removed from the pontiffs. Let us pray, but let us not be disturbed: nothing is new under the sun.

From this dissertation alone it will become clear that earlier ages too were not without their own tribulations. In the seventh century Rome was still subject in temporal matters to the Greek emperors [Note: [Col. 0998B] At the end of the eighth century Rome was withdrawn from the power of the Lombards by Pippin, king of the Franks, and first given to St. Peter. This donation was confirmed by Charlemagne, Pippin’s son and emperor, and by other successors (see Natalis, on the fourth century).]. Under them the papal episcopal residence was plundered, the cardinals were driven into exile, and the see remained vacant for a year and a half (section 12). Pope St. Martin I was taken from Rome to Constantinople and from there deported to Chersonesus beyond the Black Sea (section 22). The churches in the West were stripped of their temporal possessions (section 39). The Saracens defeated the Christians in Asia and Africa; the Persians carried away the Holy Cross (sections 8 and 110). These things occurred in the seventh century.

During the first three centuries almost all the pontiffs, beginning with St. Peter, were killed at Rome by pagans. Later Rome was captured by enemies several times: by the Goths in 409, under St. Innocent I; by the Vandals in 455, under St. Leo I; again by the Goths in 546, under Vigilius I [Note: [Col. 0998B] From this one may infer how much weight should be assigned to the well-known verse:

“Always under the sixths, ruined Rome has been.”], and by the imperial troops in 1526, under Clement VII.

Thus far there has always followed:

“… after clouds, Phoebus.”

# THE DISSERTATION BEGINS

[Col. 0997]

[Col. 0997B] 1. Arguments that Pope Honorius Was Condemned as a Heretic.—That Pope Honorius, who died in the year 638, was a heretic, or at least was condemned by the Church as a heretic, is supported by extremely weighty arguments. In the seventh century, in the year 680, the Sixth General Council, or Third Council of Constantinople, was celebrated. In its proceedings one repeatedly reads: “Anathema to Honorius, the heretical pope.” The acts of the synod were subscribed by the legates of St. Agatho, who at that time governed the Church.

After Agatho’s death in 682, Pope St. Leo II confirmed the Sixth Council and expressly declared in his confirmatory letter: “We anathematize Sergius, Pyrrhus … and also Honorius.” St. Leo II repeated the same in letters to the Spaniards. Likewise, Honorius was condemned in the Council of Trullo, or the Quinisext Council.

In the eighth century, at the Seventh General Council, or Second Council of Nicaea, celebrated in 787, Pope Honorius was repeatedly condemned as a heretic—not only in the synodal letters of the patriarchs Tarasius of Constantinople and Theodore of Jerusalem, which were read there, but also in the definition [Col. 0997D] of faith issued there synodally.

In the ninth century, at the Eighth General Council, or Fourth Council of Constantinople, held in 869, the letter of Pope Hadrian II is read and approved; in it he confirms that Pope Honorius had been synodally condemned for heresy.

That Honorius was a heretic and was condemned was also attested by the most ancient historians: Venerable Bede, who flourished at the end of the seventh and beginning of the eighth century; Hincmar, archbishop of Reims in the ninth century, who, speaking of the authority of councils, says: “They also anathematized after his death Pope Honorius, who was found and most clearly proved to have thought contrary to the faith and to have consented to those thinking perversely, as is found in the Sixth Council.”

Similar testimony was handed down from the ninth century by Anastasius the Roman Librarian, Ado of Vienne, St. Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople, and later by many other ancient writers. They were followed by Melchior Canus, a Spaniard and bishop of the Canaries; Natalis, Graveson, Pagius, Fleury, the Frenchmen; and several other more recent writers.

The defenders of the Gallican liberties, and all who adhere to the principles of the pseudo-Bossuet in the defense of the declaration of the Gallican clergy, embrace this opinion with open arms. The Febronians drew it from them.

Melchior Canus was so convinced of this matter that he wrote in Book VI, chapter 11:

“Let Pighius defend Liberius—he had maintained that no pontiff had ever fallen into heresy—whom Jerome testifies in his *Chronicle* to have subscribed, wearied by the tedium of exile, to an heretical perversity” [Note: [Col. 0997D] It was not St. Jerome but pseudo-Jerome who taught that Pope Liberius had subscribed to a formula smacking of Arianism. See Dissertation 15, sections 38 and 154.].

“Let him excuse Marcellinus, who is recorded to have offered sacrifice to idols, broken by fear” [Note: [Col. 0997D] Almost all critics now acknowledge, together with St. Augustine, that the alleged lapse of Pope St. Marcellinus was a fable invented by the Donatists in the fourth century.].

“Let him defend Victor, whom the Paulianists falsely claimed as their own” [Note: [Col. 0998D] Since, as Canus admits, the Paulianists lied, Pope St. Victor needs no further defense; Canus could have omitted St. Victor.].

“Let him free Anastasius, whom Gratian accused of heresy without certain and probable testimony” [Note: [Col. 0999D] Therefore, according to Canus, it is not Pope Anastasius but Gratian, who condemned a pope for heresy without probable testimony, who needs a defender.].

“But how will he vindicate Honorius from error?” [Note: [Col. 0999D] Thus, according to Canus, Honorius alone remains who cannot be defended. We shall see.]

For Psellus, in his work *On the Seven Councils*, Tarasius, and others report that he was a heretic.

## 2. Authorities for Honorius

Latins who wrote in defense of Honorius before the Sixth Council were Pope John IV [Note: [Col. 0999D] I omit Saints Martin I and Agatho I, who, together with two Roman synods, maintained that none of their pontifical predecessors had ever erred in the faith, as may be gathered from what follows. I also omit Jonah, abbot and disciple of Saint Columbanus, to be cited in no. 4, [Col. 1000D] because it is not clear to me whether he wrote before or after the Sixth Council.]; and after the aforesaid council, John de Turrecremata, Hosius in book II Against Brentius, Cardinals Baronius, Bellarmine, and Sfrondratus; Albert Pighius of Kampen, John of Leuven, Binius, Desirantius, Onuphrius in his annotations to Platina’s Life of Honorius, Cornelius Hazart, Frassen, and more recently Bartholus, bishop of Feltre, and Widmannus, professor at Eystätt. Among the Greeks, before the Sixth Council, Saint Maximus the monk; after the Sixth Council, toward the end of the thirteenth century, Emmanuel Calecas, who, according to Onuphrius, published a notable work in defense of the Latins against all the heresies of the Greeks; and in the seventeenth century, Matthew Cariophilus, archbishop of Iconium.

According to these authors, Honorius did not err even in the slightest in matters of faith; rather, either the acts of the Sixth Council were corrupted, or, if they are genuine, the Greek Fathers at that Sixth Council erred concerning the question of fact about Pope Honorius. If the Sixth Council was deceived, or its acts were corrupted, then the testimony of the Fathers who followed it proves little against Honorius, since they all drew their material from the Sixth Council. Indeed, the testimonies of those Fathers too—especially the earlier ones, of Pope Saint Leo II and Bede—appear to be spurious. Anastasius the Librarian is cited by Widmannus in support of Honorius because he called the bishops who condemned Honorius [Col. 0999C] “slanderers.” Psellus is a Greek author from the eleventh century. Tarasius and the others will be discussed later. Moreover, Origen Adamantius, a presbyter of Alexandria, is said to have been condemned in more councils than Pope Honorius; nevertheless, there are very serious arguments that the errors on account of which Origen was wrongly counted among the heretics were attributed to him falsely.

## 3. The Heresy of the Monothelites

The heresy which Honorius is said to have held was that of the Monothelites, or of those who admitted only one will in Christ. In common with the preceding councils, they professed that Christ was true and perfect God and man; in Christ’s soul they acknowledged a rational and intellectual soul, but they denied a human will. [Col. 0999D] This error is very palpable; for nothing is more proper to the human mind than willing. I say nothing of the most evident passages of Holy Scripture asserting in Christ a created will, by which alone he could merit for us [Note: [Col. 1000D] According to his human will, Christ was sorrowful and prayed: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”].

Nevertheless, Honorius is alleged to have been guilty of this error. Let us examine, in chronological and historical order, how that supreme pontiff was accused, convicted, and condemned. [Col. 1000A]

For greater clarity, I shall distribute the present subject into three periods: 1. what should be judged concerning Honorius in view of the events preceding the Sixth Council; 2. what should be judged in view of the acts of the Sixth Council; 3. what should be judged after weighing the testimonies subsequent to the Sixth Council.

### § 1. What should be thought of Honorius in view of his life and of what followed during the first forty years after his death

### 4. Who and what was Pope Honorius?

Pope Honorius was a Campanian by nationality, born of a consular father, and was the sixth in succession from Saint Gregory the Great. He held the pontificate from 625 to 638. He labored greatly to complete the conversion of the English; for the Scots, who had already been enrolled in the Christian army, he consecrated two new bishops, namely Saints Wiron and Plechelmus. He attempted, by letters, to bring those same Scots, who celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, back to the common discipline. He severely rebuked the bishops of Cisalpine Italy who had agreed to the deposition of Adawald, the legitimate and Catholic king of the Lombards, and he intervened with the exarch of Ravenna on behalf of the king’s restoration, although without success.

He drove Fortunatus, the heretical patriarch of Grado, from his see and substituted Primogenius, a subdeacon of the Roman Church, with the pallium. In this way he reconciled to the universal Church the Church of Aquileia and all of Istria, which had been separated in schism for seventy years on account of the famous Three Chapters and which Saint Gregory the Great had been unable to bring back. He built several basilicas in Rome, which at that time was still subject to the emperor in temporal affairs; he restored them and adorned them with gifts and verses. “A most praiseworthy pontiff,” says Natalis, “unless he had stained his glory by showing excessive favor to Sergius, the leader of the Monothelites.”

Meanwhile, as long as Honorius lived, he was regarded by everyone as truly Catholic, and no one accused him of excessive leniency toward heretics. He died in Rome and was buried in the church of Saint Peter among the other pontiffs, and was honored with a distinctive epitaph in which he was compared with Saint Gregory I, who is now rightly called the Great. In one inscription, among other things, the following is read concerning Christ:

> Full man among us, and the same one is born  
> wholly God everywhere from the Virgin’s womb.

[Note: [Col. 1000D] These four syllables overturn the whole of Monothelitism; for if Christ assumed the whole human nature, he cannot have been without a human will.]

After a brief account of Peter’s primacy, the praise of Honorius follows [Col. 1000D]:

> Istria bears witness, possessed through hostile years  
> seventeen years by the plague of schism.  
> But the good bishop, Honorius, leader of the people, by holy arms  
> restored to the Church her members torn away.

In another inscription Honorius is celebrated in the following verses:

[Col. 1001A]

> The sacred rewards of praise illumine the great shepherd,  
> who, having discharged this supreme office in Peter’s place, holds it.  
> For Bishop Honorius shines forth in these tombs,  
> whose magnanimous name and honor endure.  
> Governing the rights of the apostolic see through his merits,  
> he recalls the scattered and brings back excellent gains;  
> and, wise in mind and strong in divine song,  
> as a shepherd he knew how to lead the sheep to life.

Then, after mention of Istria and the Jews who had been overcome, there follows:

> Thus his diligent care for his homeland stirred him,  
> so that the desired peace might everywhere belong to the peoples.  
> Him whom powerful teaching, whom the rule of sacred life,  
> likewise sanctioned as possessing the dignity of pontiffs.  
> The sayings of your holy-speaking teachers  
> always shone forth in you, as though exceedingly fruitful.  
> For while you eagerly follow the footsteps  
> and bear the merit of so great a righteous Gregory,  
> by Christ’s gracious will, possess now with the holy Fathers  
> the everlasting day of eternal light.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] See more in Baronius under the years 638 and 683. If Honorius was later condemned as a heretic, even during that same century, it is exceedingly strange that these public epitaphs of a condemned man were not destroyed. Anastasius the Librarian reports that, once the council had ended, the images of all the condemned patriarchs were removed from the churches.]

[Col. 1001B] To these epitaphs is added the testimony of Jonah, an abbot in Ireland in the seventh century. He lived until 692 and celebrated Honorius in these words:

> The venerable bishop Honorius was most holy in life and character, shrewd in mind, vigorous in counsel, distinguished in learning, outstanding in faith, rich in sweetness and humanity, reformer of the clergy, propagator of the Gospel, a most devoted cultivator and founder of the Churches within and outside the City, worthy that posterity should praise him, bishops imitate him, the faithful look up to him, and all honor him.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] See Georgius Josephus ab Eggs, canon of Rheinfeld, in the book entitled *The Learned Pontiff*, printed at Cologne in 1718.]

From these facts it is clear that, if the Monothelites had craftily wished to fabricate the claim that one of the Roman pontiffs had favored their sect, they would not have acted unwisely in attempting to draw the truly great Pope Honorius over to their side. I shall soon explain in what order and manner this was accomplished; but so that certainties may be more clearly distinguished from uncertainties, the following assertions must first be set forth.

### 5. He was not accused of heresy while alive, nor condemned during the first forty years after his death

First. Pope Honorius was condemned by no one for heresy, or even accused of it, during his lifetime. As far as I know, no one denies this proposition; and it will be true even if everything brought forward against Pope Honorius down to the present day were genuine. This will become clear from what follows.

Second. Pope Honorius was not condemned for heresy during the first forty years after his death; indeed, he was not even legitimately accused, although during that interval two large councils were held, one at Rome, in the place where the alleged offense had occurred, and against the Monothelites—namely, in 649 under Saint Martin I, with 105 bishops [Col. 1002A]—and another in 680 under Saint Agatho, with 125 other bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] I omit the African councils held in 646 against Paul of Constantinople and others whose acts are not extant.]

[Note: [Col. 1001D] Natalis, proposition 1 in reply to objection 3, says: “Honorius was tacitly condemned at this council; for in the fourth session the letter of Paul of Constantinople was read aloud, in which he asserted: ‘Sergius and Honorius became concordant and harmonious.’ No one uttered even a word in defense of Honorius.” But the answer is: Then Saints Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria were also tacitly condemned at that council; for Paul of Constantinople asserted in the aforesaid letter: “Saints Athanasius, Cyril, and all the teachers of piety taught one will in Christ . . . and Sergius and Honorius became concordant and harmonious with them.” No one said even a word for Saints Athanasius and Cyril. Moreover, there is no reason for surprise. The sole reason why Pope Saint Martin ordered that Paul’s letter be read aloud was to establish that Paul had in fact taught two wills in Christ and could therefore justly be condemned.]

The truth of this assertion will likewise become clear from what follows; for Honorius was first legitimately accused and condemned in 681 at the Constantinopolitan Council on account of a letter to Sergius, brought forth at that time from the Constantinopolitan library. The judges immediately committed to the flames the original letter for which they condemned a dead man, because it was pernicious; nevertheless, they inserted a copy of the burned letter into the acts.

These two assertions cannot be denied—if the acts of the Sixth Council are genuine, as all who count Pope Honorius among the condemned heretics maintain. [Col. 1002B] It is absolutely certain that Honorius was not even named in the preceding councils, in which Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, the patriarchs of Constantinople, and others were anathematized. Let us now proceed to the history.

### 6. A letter of Pope Honorius to Sergius, not produced during Honorius’s lifetime

While Pope Honorius was alive, Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, wrote him a letter seeking advice about one or two wills in Christ. Honorius replied through the abbot John Symponus in a Latin letter that there are not in Christ’s humanity two contrary wills, as there are in us. After Adam’s sin there exists a rebellion of the flesh against the spirit; Christ assumed the whole man, but without sin.

That Honorius wrote some such letter to Sergius is certain from no. 15; it is said to have been issued in 633. Meanwhile, it is not recorded that Sergius, who lived until 639, ever produced it publicly, or communicated it to his followers, Cyrus the patriarch of Alexandria and others, or brought it forward against Sophronius of Jerusalem and the other adversaries. This deserves consideration.

### 7. Cyrus of Alexandria promotes Monothelitism

At approximately the same time [Note: [Col. 1002D] If Sergius’s letter to Honorius, which I shall report from no. 66 onward, is genuine, Saint Sophronius would first have been raised to the patriarchal see in 632. But if the Chronicle of Nicephorus is to be trusted, Saint Modestus, Sophronius’s predecessor, died in 631; hence it might be suspected that Saint Sophronius had attained the episcopate before 632.] Saint Sophronius the monk was elected patriarch of Jerusalem. Cyrus, transferred there from Phasis, was archbishop of Alexandria. Under the pretext of bringing the heretical Theodosians back to the Catholic Church, he had published nine chapters, in the seventh of which only one operation [Col. 1003A]—equivalently, only one will, and that a divine one—was attributed to Christ.

### 8. Saint Sophronius opposes the Monothelites

Saint Sophronius was deeply grieved by this innovation of the Alexandrian. To avert the evils that threatened, he published two books filled with six hundred testimonies of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 1003D] Thus Stephen, Saint Sophronius’s legate, later testified in 649 in the public session of the Roman council under Saint Martin I, session 2, when he had come to Rome for the third time. These works of Sophronius have since been lost.] in favor of two wills in Christ.

He judged that Pope Honorius should be warned. Therefore, since he himself could not travel to Rome, he first sent Stephen, bishop of Dor, one of his suffragans, to Rome. Beforehand he led him to Mount Calvary and addressed him as follows:

> Remember that one day you will have to give an account to him who was crucified in this holy place and who will come to judge the living and the dead, if you now abandon the faith that is in danger. Therefore do what I cannot do because of the incursions of the Saracens [Col. 1003B]. Go to the apostolic see, the Roman see of Saint Peter, where the foundations of orthodox doctrines are laid. Make known to the holy men who live there all that is taking place here, and do not cease entreating them until, through apostolic prudence, they bring about the complete destruction, according to the canons, of the doctrines newly introduced.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] These were most wretched times. The idolatrous Persians had ravaged the East; Muhammad, the false prophet, had subjected Arabia to himself. He had indeed died in 630, but the Muslims were making daily progress, slaughtering the Persians and subjecting the greatest provinces of the Roman Empire—Syria, Palestine, and Egypt—with the speediest victories. Antioch was captured by them in 638 and Alexandria in 640; afterward they occupied Africa and finally, in 713, almost all Spain. While Sophronius was undertaking these actions, the Muslims were already threatening Jerusalem. After enduring a two-year siege, it surrendered to the Saracens in 636, with the eventual consent of Saint Sophronius, who negotiated and secured safety for the Palestinian Christians and died shortly thereafter.]

### 9. Stephen is sent by Sophronius to Rome; the Monothelites attempt to prevent him

Because of these urgent appeals from Sophronius and others—especially the bishops in Cyprus—Stephen set out for Rome. When the Monothelites learned of this, they made every effort to hinder him as he traveled, sending orders to various places that Bishop Stephen should be captured and dragged back in chains.

Stephen escaped all the plots successfully [Col. 1003C] and reached Rome without being disappointed in his hope. As Stephen himself later told Saint Martin I at the place cited, God did not despise the tearful prayers offered by his supplicants; rather, he stirred up, to no small degree, “your predecessors and apostolic bishops to admonish and likewise to bear witness against the aforesaid men” (perhaps Cyrus and Sergius, who had attempted to obstruct Stephen’s journey), “although your predecessors were in no way able to move them” [Note: [Col. 1004D] Saint Maximus agrees, writing to Peter the Illustrious: “What did the Church not ask of these men [the Monothelites]? What pious and orthodox bishop did not entreat them? And what of the divine Honorius? What of the aged Severinus after him? What of the holy John? Moreover, did the most blessed Theodore, who now presides, omit anything appropriate to supplication? Behold, the divine Honorius will be counted, around the year 645, as the first among those who opposed the Monothelites.”].

When Saint Sophronius sent Stephen to Rome, Honorius was still alive. If Stephen found Honorius alive, then Honorius wished to move the Monothelites, though he was entirely unable to do so.
