But let us suppose that Stephen arrived in Rome after Honorius’s death. Why, nevertheless, did the Monothelites attempt to prevent him by such great machinations from informing the Roman bishop of their heresy, if they already possessed a letter from Honorius teaching one will or prohibiting two wills in Christ? Honorius’s first letter approving the Monothelite doctrine is said to have been written in 633.

### 10. Whether Honorius imposed silence on the patriarchs Cyrus and Sophronius by letter

If Honorius’s second letter—which first became known after 680—is genuine, then: first, Pope Honorius wrote to the patriarchs Sophronius and Cyrus that each should abstain from preaching one or two operations in Christ; second, the legates sent by Sophronius to Honorius promised that Sophronius would certainly cease asserting two operations, provided that Cyrus too abstained from asserting one operation.

But this second letter of Honorius seems to me fictitious. Here are my reasons:

1. It is incredible that Saint Sophronius—whatever may meanwhile be said about Honorius’s character—would have agreed to the suppression of the two wills, or that his legates would have promised this.

2. The first legate of Saint Sophronius was Stephen of Dor, whom we heard about in the preceding section; he certainly did not make such a promise to Honorius, even on the supposition that he found him alive.

3. No letters of Honorius to the patriarchs Sophronius and Cyrus are extant.

4. Sophronius does not appear to have received any letter from Honorius.

### 11. Whether Sophronius gave occasion for the heresy

The Monothelites brought another calumny against this Saint Sophronius: namely, that because he began to preach two wills at an inopportune time [Col. 1004C], he was the reason others asserted only one. Saint Maximus refuted this calumny [Note: [Col. 1004D] See Saint Maximus’s Disputation with Pyrrhus, reported by Baronius and others. Pyrrhus had succeeded Sergius in the see of Constantinople and in his heresy. Pyrrhus had brought up against Maximus the aforementioned story about Sophronius, who at that time was already dead. Pyrrhus was converted through that disputation. See no. 18.] by testifying, first, that Sergius had already attempted to establish one will by circulating a pamphlet of Menas, another of Theodore of Pharan, and a letter addressed to Cyrus, then still bishop of Phasis, while John the Almsgiver, Cyrus’s predecessor in the Alexandrian see, was still alive; and, second, that Sophronius—perhaps still a monk—afterward went to Sergius, humbly prostrated himself at Sergius’s feet, and implored him, by the passion of Christ, not to revive the voice of the heretics, which had formerly been thoroughly extinguished by the holy Fathers above.

Who, then, was the author of the scandal? Was it Sophronius? This is what Saint Maximus says about Saint Sophronius. [Col. 1004D] Let us now return to the Roman pontiffs.

[Col. 1005A]

### 12. Severinus succeeds Honorius

Honorius died in October 638. After a year and a half [Note: [Col. 1005C] Perhaps Severinus was elected by the clergy but confirmed late by the emperor, and therefore was not consecrated earlier.] Severinus of Rome succeeded him. He occupied the see for only two months [Note: [Col. 1005D] The ancient writers were silent about Severinus’s condemnation of the *Ecthesis*; hence Baronius and Combefisius denied it. Pagius affirms it because the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs contains the following profession of faith, formerly recited by the Roman pontiff: “We profess all the decrees of the pontiffs Severinus, John, Theodore, and Martin, who professed two natural operations.” But the *Liber Diurnus* does not possess public authority.], and died in 640.

At that time the emperor was Heraclius, the patron of the Monothelites. His minister, Isaac the patrician and exarch of Italy, came to Rome after Honorius’s death, drove the leading men of the Church individually into various exiles, and plundered the property left by Honorius and the Lateran episcopate, which was filled with immense wealth. The emperor received part of the spoils.

### 13. The *Ecthesis* of Heraclius is published

In 639, the final year of his life, Sergius of Constantinople published a new exposition of the faith called the *Ecthesis of Heraclius*, because it was published under Heraclius’s name. In every other respect it was said to be Catholic [Col. 1005B]: “We confess one will in Christ.”

Cyrus of Alexandria approved the *Ecthesis*, but warned Sergius: “Our common brother Severinus, who is being ordained, must profess this as well.” Saint Martin I testified at the Lateran Council that the *Ecthesis* had never been received or accepted, but rather had been condemned and anathematized by apostolic authority. Meanwhile, that *Ecthesis* had been publicly posted at Constantinople.

### 14. The *Ecthesis* is condemned by John IV; it had been composed by Sergius of Constantinople

In 640 John IV the Dalmatian succeeded to the chair of Peter. After convening a council at Rome, he condemned the *Ecthesis* and anathematized the heresy of the Monothelites. The bishops of Africa immediately followed the pope’s example. Thus Theophanes reports in Baronius [Col. 1005C].

Heraclius wrote back to Pope John IV:

> Sergius composed the *Ecthesis* five years ago, requested that it be issued in my name, and asked that it be signed by my hand. I granted this at his request. But now, since I see that disputes have arisen from it, I make known to all that I am not the author of this writing.

Up to this point, no mention had been made of Pope Honorius’s having issued anything against two wills in Christ in favor of the Monothelites.

### 15. The Monothelites produce a letter of Honorius; Pope John explains it

Heraclius died on 11 February 641. The *Ecthesis* remained posted. Moreover, the Monothelites spread the report that Sergius had once received from Honorius a letter [Note: [Col. 1005D] This is said to have been written in 632; in its dogmatic content, as we shall see below, it agrees with the *Ecthesis*. Why was it not produced by Sergius or Heraclius, if it truly favored them? If Sergius was conscious of Honorius’s agreement, why did he conceal his *Ecthesis* for several years? Why did he not publish it while Honorius was alive? Pagius says: “Sergius did not wish to irritate Honorius while he was alive.” But how could Honorius have been irritated if this letter is genuine? In it Honorius writes to Sergius [Col. 1006C]: “Preach these things with us; we unanimously preach them with you.” See nos. 23–25.] favoring one will in Christ.

Therefore Pope John IV, through the same abbot whom Honorius had used as his secretary in no. 6, wrote a letter to the emperor Constantine III, son of Heraclius, or rather an apology for Honorius, whom he calls “the Catholic father, the pope of holy memory.” He says:

> I shall recount with the most subtle precision what happened a short time ago. Sergius informed Honorius that some people said there were two contrary wills in Christ. When the aforesaid pope learned this, he replied that, just as our Savior was perfect God, so also he was perfect man, without sin, and therefore had one human will, as Adam had before sin—not two contrary wills, as we have, who are born from Adam’s sin. Thus my aforesaid predecessor taught that in Christ there were not, as in us sinners, contrary wills of mind and flesh. Certain people, twisting this to suit their own interpretation, suspected that he had taught Christ to have one will of his divinity and humanity [Note: [Col. 1006D] For this reason Honorius cannot be said to have been accused.], which is entirely contrary to the truth [Note: [Col. 1006D] The pope alluded to the *Ecthesis* in these words: “We earnestly desire that you order the booklet publicly posted—which has been a scandal to all the faithful in the West, and even to the people of Constantinople—to be torn down. Come, as you begin your reign, grant this request to the prayers of your mother, the Church!”].

Thus Honorius was absolved by Pope John’s letter to the emperor from every suspicion of heresy [Note: [Col. 1006D] Thomassinus, dissertation 20 on the Sixth Council, argues that Honorius was later, namely at the Sixth Council, rightly condemned because, although he did not teach heresy from the Roman chair—since he had convened no council—he nevertheless offended against the Catholic faith in his private letter to Sergius. But John V, speaking of that very private letter which Thomassinus considers heretical, stands against Thomassinus. Saint Maximus the Greek, likewise to be cited in no. 18 and a contemporary witness, also stands against Thomassinus, asserting against the Monothelite Pyrrhus that nothing heretical had been taught in that letter.].

On this occasion the people of Constantinople could and indeed should have produced Honorius’s letter, if it favored the *Ecthesis*, and convicted Pope John of falsehood. Constantine reigned for only three months before being poisoned by his stepmother. The *Ecthesis* remained posted. No one contradicted Pope John.

[Col. 1006C]

### 16. Pope Theodore; Pyrrhus flees; Paul the heretic is substituted

In 641 Theodore of Jerusalem succeeded Pope John. Pyrrhus, who had succeeded Sergius in 639, was suspected of complicity in Constantine’s death. Under Constans, Constantine’s son, he suffered a revolt by the populace and fled from Constantinople to Africa in 642, since Africa had defected from the emperor.

Paul was substituted for Pyrrhus by the emperor Constans. As was customary, he announced his promotion to the pope and at that time feigned the Catholic faith. The pope, because Pyrrhus was still alive and had not yet been legitimately deposed, refused for the time being to recognize Paul. He ordered his apocrisarius Martin and the others first to investigate Pyrrhus’s case judicially, since Pyrrhus’s writings were publicly extant and his crimes notorious. [Col. 1007A]

Paul paid no attention to this; indeed, he later wrote to the pope: “We believe that there is one will in Christ.”

### 17. The bishops of Cyprus write to Pope Theodore

In 643 the bishops of Cyprus, in their synodical letter to Pope Theodore, confessed that God had established the Roman see as the immovable foundation of the faith. They insisted that the *Ecthesis* be removed at Constantinople or that its supporters be anathematized.

“You are Peter,” they said to Theodore; “you are the remover of profane heresies; you are the prince and teacher of orthodox and undefiled faith.”

These bishops, who declared themselves ready for martyrdom, seem to have been unaware that Honorius, Theodore’s predecessor, had agreed with the Monothelites or had stained the Catholic faith.

### 18. The Monothelites sinisterly interpret Honorius’s letter

In 645 Pyrrhus held a public disputation in Africa with Saint Maximus the most learned monk, who had emigrated from Constantinople some time earlier. The disputation is still extant in Baronius and others.

In it Pyrrhus, arguing for one will, appealed to the authority of the Roman pontiffs and said:

> How, then, did Pope Vigilius of Rome accept a booklet presented by Menas of Constantinople that contained one will?

[Note: [Col. 1007D] Pope Vigilius was present at Constantinople in 547. It is said that the patriarch Menas of Constantinople then handed him a booklet, but this is false. If the pope accepted it, he could then be said to have tacitly approved it.]

**Maximus:** I am astonished that, although you are patriarchs, you dare to lie [Note: [Col. 1007D] No one should think that these words were spoken merely in the heat of disputation or out of hatred; Saint Maximus published these acts after Pyrrhus had already been converted and before he relapsed.]. Your predecessor wrote to Honorius that he had been informed about that booklet, but that it had not been presented or shown to him. You wrote to Pope John [Col. 1007C] that it had been presented [Note: [Col. 1007D] That the booklet was not presented by Menas to Pope Vigilius was later established at the Sixth Council. See no. 37.] and shown, and that it had also been read by Constantine the quaestor. Whom, then, shall we believe—you or your predecessor? For both cannot have spoken the truth.

**Pyrrhus:** Did my predecessor write that?

**Maximus:** He did.

**Pyrrhus:** Let it be so concerning Vigilius. What of Honorius, who openly taught my predecessor one will of Christ?

**Maximus:** Who was a worthy interpreter of that letter in faith and authority—the man who wrote it in the person of Honorius, who was still alive, and who illuminated the entire West both by his other virtues and by the doctrines of the Christian faith—or those who, at Constantinople, spoke what was in their hearts?

**Pyrrhus:** The man who composed it.

**Maximus:** That very man, then, when he wrote to the emperor Constantine in the person of Saint Pope John, said: “We have spoken of one will in the Lord, not of his divinity and humanity, but of his humanity alone. For when Sergius had written that certain people said there were two contrary wills in Christ, we asserted that Christ did not have two contrary wills—namely, of flesh and spirit—as we have after sin. That this is so is demonstrated by the obvious fact that he mentioned members and flesh, which certainly do not permit the statement to be understood of that divinity.”

**Pyrrhus:** My predecessor accepted this simply.

**Maximus:** I am speaking of the matter itself. Nothing alienated me so greatly from your predecessor as his changeability and inconsistency—that is, his passing at one time into one opinion and at another time into another, and remaining firm in no position. And why was it necessary to produce documents, namely the *Ecthesis*, and so forth?

At last Pyrrhus surrendered, having been defeated, as will be related in the following section.

### 19. The Monothelites corrupted Honorius’s letter in translating it into Greek

Moreover, the Monothelites not only interpreted Honorius’s letter sinisterly; by the time of Saint Maximus they had already corrupted it to some extent.

Saint Maximus, in his letter to Martin as quoted by Natalis, cited the testimony of the abbot John, who had written Honorius’s letter. John asserted that Honorius had in no way made mention, by a numerical expression, of one all-embracing will, although this has now been fabricated by those who translated it into the Greek expression [Note: [Col. 1007D] It is evident from this that Honorius dictated the letter in Latin, and that neither he himself nor his secretary translated it into the Greek language. The Greeks who condemned Honorius at the Sixth Council—if the acts of that council are genuine—boasted that they had found his original letter in Latin together with its Greek translation, and on account of these documents, then discovered, anathematized Pope Honorius. But it is not plausible that Pope Honorius added a Greek translation; at least, Saint Maximus knew nothing of it.].

Rather, John said that Honorius had taught the absence of that will which exists in us, a will that is blameworthy and struggles against the spirit. Meanwhile, the letter that is now extant appears to be genuine in large part, because it contains assertions explicitly indicated by Saint Maximus himself. But whether it is wholly genuine will be examined later, in no. 23.

Pyrrhus, converted by Saint Maximus, went to Rome and voluntarily abjured his errors. He was restored by Pope Theodore to his former patriarchal dignity, but when he reached Ravenna he soon relapsed and returned to the East. He died in 652. It is not sufficiently clear whether he recovered his see after Paul’s death in 651, although he attempted this by various methods.

### 20. Pyrrhus and Paul are excommunicated

Meanwhile, Paul had been admonished by the pope and other bishops to state his faith more clearly. He replied that Christ had one will, but not two contrary wills. He added that this had been the teaching of Sergius, Honorius, Saints Cyril and Athanasius, Gregory the Theologian, the entire Council of Chalcedon, and therefore also Pope Saint Leo I.

At last he decided to remove the *Ecthesis*, but he persuaded the emperor Constans to publish an edict imposing silence on both parties, so that neither one will nor two wills might be mentioned. [Col. 1008D] This was called the *Type of Constans*, or of Constantius.

Around the year 648 Pyrrhus [Note: [Col. 1008D] The Greek Theophanes and the author of the synodical booklet report that when Pope Theodore wished to excommunicate Pyrrhus, he requested the divine chalice, and that some of the life-giving blood dripped into ink; he then wrote with his own hand the deposition of Pyrrhus, who had been excommunicated. But Bede, an author nearly contemporary, Anastasius the Librarian, and other Latins were unaware of this detail concerning the use of Christ’s blood. [Col. 1009D] See Baronius under the year 648, no. 15. Pagius judged that this method of excommunication was customary among the Greeks, because Nicetas, in the Life of Saint Ignatius of Constantinople, asserts that at the Constantinopolitan Council of 869 the Fathers excommunicated Photius by dipping a pen in the Savior’s own blood. But that detail is not found in the Acts, which are extant in full. Nicetas, nevertheless, who flourished in 880, added: “I received that detail from those who know.” See Baronius under the year 869, no. 39.] and Paul were excommunicated by Pope Theodore.

### 21. Saint Martin I condemns the Type of Constans, Sergius, [Col. 1009A] etc.

Theodore was succeeded in 649 by Saint Martin I, who had formerly resided in Constantinople as the apocrisiary of Pope Theodore. In that same year he convened a synod of 105 bishops. The occasion for this synod seems to have been that the emperor had demanded from the newly elected pope approval of his Type. The case of the Monothelites was then discussed more fully. The Type of Constans was condemned [Note: [Col. 1009D] In his Type the emperor had prohibited, under the gravest penalties—excommunication, deposition, confiscation of goods, and exile—that anyone should preach either two or one wills in Christ. The heretics mocked this by saying that Catholics were now at last ashamed to confess the truth, namely, either one or two wills.], as were the Ecthesis of Heraclius, Sergius and Pyrrhus of Constantinople, Cyrus of Alexandria, and Theodore of Pharan [Note: [Col. 1009D] At this synod the letters of Cyrus of Alexandria to Sergius of Constantinople, his replies, and other Monothelite arguments were also read. In his seventh chapter Cyrus had adduced the words of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, attributing to Christ one theandric, or God-human, operation. The Catholics assumed that the books of Dionysius—which modern critics judge to be spurious—were genuine, and observed that Saint Dionysius did indeed preach a new operation of Christ, but not one theandric operation, as Cyrus had claimed. Since there is one divine person in Christ, any human operation of his can be called theandric.]. Saint Maximus attended the council, although, because he was only an abbot, he did not subscribe.

### 22. Saint Martin and Saint Maximus suffer persecution; one of them speaks against the Type

The emperor, greatly enraged, ordered Martin to be taken from Rome to Constantinople. After suffering imprisonment and the most severe hardships [Col. 1009B], the pope died in exile in 654, on 12 November. He is venerated as a martyr and was renowned for miracles both before and after his death.

Saint Maximus likewise was dragged to Constantinople, cruelly mutilated in tongue and hand, and worn down by prisons, hardships, exile, and other punishments. He died in 658, nearly eighty years old. He had been subjected to the strongest pressure to communicate with the Church of Constantinople, but he steadfastly refused. He declared his accusers, the Monothelites, guilty of various falsehoods, and fearlessly repeated in Constantinople at his trial what he had formerly proclaimed at Rome against the Type:

“The Type destroys the Creed … The Arians in the time of Constantine the Great proposed the same remedy in letters which they sent: ‘Let us suppress the words “consubstantial” and “different in substance,” so that the Churches may be united.’ [Col. 1009C] But our Fathers did not agree; rather, they preferred persecution and death to this peace, although Constantine had favored this remedy. No emperor has ever been able to bring the Fathers to connive at the heretics of their own age by employing ambiguous expressions. Instead, they have always used clear expressions proper and appropriate to the question.

“Here there would have been an excellent opportunity to object that Honorius also—if his letters, as they now exist and as they were produced in the council at Constantinople in 680, had already been known—had ordered the expression ‘one or two wills’ to be suppressed. Here are the clauses concerning this matter from the said letters.”

### 23. The first letter of Pope Honorius, whose opening appears inauthentic

Honorius is said to have begun his first letter as follows:

“We have received the letter of your fraternity, through which we have learned that certain disputes and new questions concerning terminology were introduced by a certain Sophronius, then a monk but now, as we hear, bishop of Jerusalem, against our brother Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, who was preaching, after turning from heresy, one operation of Christ. When Sophronius finally came to your fraternity and submitted a complaint of this kind, he was instructed in many ways and requested that what he had received from you orally should be set forth in writing. Having received and examined a copy of the letter directed to the same Sophronius, we praise your fraternity for having written with sufficient foresight and prudence, removing the novelty of the term, which could cause scandal to the simple. For we, etc.”

This is the opening of the first letter, which seems to me inauthentic [Note: [Col. 1010D] The most illustrious Bartholi, formerly professor of canon law at the University of Padua and later bishop of Feltre, and Joseph Widmann, professor of theology at Eichstätt, already observed in their *Dogmatic Theology*, printed at Augsburg in 1776, that this first letter of Honorius had been corrupted by the Monothelites, while the second, discussed below in no. 26, had been entirely fabricated by those same heretics.], and to have been unknown to Saint Maximus and to Stephen, later the legate of Sophronius. Moreover, the letter of Sergius to Sophronius, which Honorius supposedly approved, is nowhere else found to have been produced.

### 24. A sufficiently Catholic confirmation

After many other matters, which I omit, the letter continues:

“Therefore we confess one [Note: [Col. 1010D] The word ‘one’ was not present in the original Latin letter; see no. 19. The letters of Honorius that we now possess are taken from the Greek Acts of the Sixth Synod cited below; the year and day on which Honorius wrote them are absent.] will of Christ, because our nature was plainly assumed by the divinity, not sin. That is, it is the nature which was created, not the nature which was corrupted [Col. 1010C] after the transgression … For there was not in Christ another law in his members, nor a different and contrary will … Although it is written, ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father,’ and, ‘Not as I will, but as you will, Father,’ and other statements of this kind, these do not refer to different wills, but to the dispensation of the assumed humanity. These things were said for our sake, to whom he gave an example, so that we might follow his footsteps: the pious teacher instructing his disciples so that each of us might prefer, in all things, not his own will but rather the will of God the Lord.”

These final statements are certainly Catholic, and they most clearly assert a human will in Christ, which the Monothelites denied. Accordingly, this section appears to be a genuine fragment of a letter written by Honorius, to which the following conclusion was attached.

### 25. A suspect conclusion favoring the Type of Constans

“It is not appropriate, with certain stammerers, to preach one or two operations in Christ … Whether one or two operations ought to be said or understood should not be transferred to dogma; we leave that to grammarians … Those things must be overthrown which, through the novelty of the expression, are known to cause offense to the holy Churches of God, lest perhaps those who are infants, taking offense at the expression ‘two operations,’ should think that we hold what Nestorian madness holds; or, if we confess one operation of Christ, lest they should think that we confess, to their astonished ears, the foolishness of the Eutychians … We consider it preferable that philosophers who weigh the natures, conduct affairs at leisure, and puffed up against us resound with the voices of frogs, rather than that simple and humble Christians should remain unfed [Note: [Col. 1011D] This is not the language of one teaching the Church, but of one fearing the light of truth. If confessing two operations favors the Nestorians, it should not for that reason be suppressed; and if the Eutychians hold the truth by asserting one will in Christ, they should not be contradicted. For truth, even when spoken by the mouths of heretics, ought to be welcome to Catholics. Simple Christians would remain unfed if, when they asked whether there are one or two wills in Christ, or whether Christ, as man, possessed a will, an arrogant teacher of the Church treated these questions with contempt as ‘the voices of frogs’ and refused to give a categorical answer. Catholics ought to have been offended by such silence, and heretics could have gloried in it greatly. Did Pope Honorius fail to perceive this?] …

“Let your fraternity preach these things with us, just as we unanimously preach them with you. We exhort you, therefore, while avoiding the term ‘operation,’ introduced by the novel expression ‘one’ or ‘double,’ to preach with us, in orthodox faith and Catholic unity, one Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, operating in two natures.”

How splendidly the emperor Constans and Paul of Constantinople, who defended the Type, could have invoked this exhortion of Honorius on their own behalf, had they known it. Yet the opening and the conclusion do not agree with the confirmation, as will be evident to anyone who considers the matter. The argument of the letter would be as follows: Christ did not have two contrary wills; therefore, we ought not to preach of Christ either two wills or one.

### 26. The second letter of Honorius, which appears spurious

The second letter of Honorius to Sergius had never previously been cited by anyone. It was first produced in 681 at the council of Constantinople. It was not read in full or inserted into the Acts; instead, the librarian recited to the Fathers, at his own discretion [Note: [Col. 1011D] No one admonished the librarian to read the letter in full rather than only a portion.], two fragments of the following tenor:

“We also wrote to our brother Cyrus, bishop of the city of Alexandria [Col. 1012A], that the expression of the novel invention of one or two operations should be abolished, because … the newly introduced expression of one or two operations must be expelled from the preaching of the true faith [Note: [Col. 1011D] The emperor Constans, by issuing the Type, would have been carrying out the apostolic letters of Pope Honorius. Hence Pseudo-Bossuet, in his defense of the Declaration of the Gallican Clergy, book VII, chapter 23, argued that Saint Martin I, by condemning the Type of Constans, also condemned Honorius, although without naming him. I admit this, if this letter of Honorius is genuine. But was Pope Martin, the most courageous martyr for the dogma of two wills, entirely fair when he condemned the emperor’s edict and remained completely silent about this letter of Honorius, if he knew it? I think he did not know it.]. Those who say these things suspect nothing other than this: just as there are one or two natures of Christ our God, so also there are one or two operations [Note: [Col. 1012D] Certainly so: because we confess two natures in Christ, we also admit two operative wills and two operations.]. Concerning this divine Scripture says admirably: to understand or proclaim that Christ has or had one operation or two is plainly vain [Note: [Col. 1012D] If divine Scripture contains this statement, then both the Catholics at the Roman and Constantinopolitan synods and the Monothelites—indeed Sergius, Cyrus, and the others as well—sinned against it.].”

The Acts then continue:

“And indeed we judge that these matters should be declared by the present letter, so that those who have doubted may be instructed. But as regards dogma, we ought to define neither one nor two [Col. 1012B] operations, but to confess that both natures, united in one Christ, operate and act in association with one another [Note: [Col. 1012D] If each nature operates and acts, then there is a duality of will and a duality of operation.]. We ought not to define or preach one or two operations. We agree with your holiness … Moreover, we write to our brothers Cyrus and Sophronius, the bishops, so that in the future they may not be seen to insist upon or persist in a new expression, namely, the designation of one or two operations … Although we dealt with those whom Sophronius sent, so that they would not continue thereafter to preach the expression ‘two operations,’ they promised altogether that the aforesaid man would do this, if Cyrus ceased to say ‘one operation.’”

This letter seems to me unworthy of Saint Honorius dictating it and of the abbot John, who was a very learned man, composing or writing it. See no. 10. According to the first letter, Sophronius had already assented to Sergius. See no. 23. Why, then, would Honorius now write again to Sophronius and Cyrus? Who were those legates sent by Sophronius who came to Honorius, promised Honorius that Sophronius would cease preaching two wills, and did so on the condition that Cyrus cease proclaiming one?

### 27. Successors in the Roman and Constantinopolitan sees

In the Roman see, Saint Martin was succeeded by Eugenius, then Vitalian, then Adeodatus, then Donus, and finally Saint Agatho, under whom the Sixth Synod was convened in 680, as stated in no. 1.

After Paul, the occupants of the Constantinopolitan see were Peter, Thomas, [Col. 1013A] John, Constantine, Theodore, and George. Peter wrote a synodical letter to Pope Eugenius, exceedingly difficult to understand, in which he asserted neither one nor two wills in Christ. This letter was rejected by the Romans, even under pressure from all the clergy and people.

Thomas is said to have written a Catholic synodical letter to Vitalian, which the librarian produced at the council of Constantinople under the pretext that Thomas had been unable to send it to Vitalian because of the continually imminent incursions of the Saracens, as you know, and because of the siege which lasted for the two years during which he held the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1013C] That Constantinople was exhausted by a two-year siege beginning in 656, when Thomas assumed the patriarchate, is not mentioned even slightly either by Theophanes, who records the events of the emperors year by year, or by any other Greek writer. Thus Baronius, under the year 656, no. 40, thinks that the Acts of the Constantinopolitan council were filled with many falsehoods. From the Acts of Saint Maximus it is clear that, while present in Constantinople, he steadfastly refused to communicate with Thomas as a heretic.].

It is not recorded that John and Constantine openly disagreed with the Roman Church. Yet that Thomas of Constantinople—whose orthodoxy Baronius himself doubted—was not hostile in spirit to the Roman see is evident from the fact that the name of Pope Vitalian was received into the Constantinopolitan diptychs, probably not by Peter, and therefore by Thomas; at least, not by Theodore, who attempted to erase the name of Pope Vitalian from the diptychs and leave only the name of Honorius [Note: [Col. 1013D] In my opinion, the name of Honorius was entered by the Constantinopolitans into the diptychs as soon as he assumed the governance of the Church. For that reason Theodore did not erase it, since at the time of Honorius no public schism had yet erupted. Moreover, Honorius was held in such high esteem that the Constantinopolitans could hardly have despised him or refused to receive him in the diptychs.].

### 28. The emperor’s letter to the pope convening a general synod

In the year 678 of the Christian era, the emperor Constantine IV Pogonatus, or “the Bearded,” after making peace with the Saracens, considered restoring peace to the Churches that had been divided since the time of his great-grandfather Heraclius. He had wished to convene a universal synod of Latins and Greeks; but because such an assembly would have been more difficult, he decided to summon only the Easterners to Constantinople, while arranging that the Roman pope should graciously participate through his own legates and those of the Roman synod. The emperor offered them the expenses necessary for so great a journey. Here is an extract from his letter to Pope Donus:

“Constantine, emperor, to Donus, archbishop of our ancient Rome and universal pope … When Theodore had been ordained for this royal city of ours, he suggested to our serenity that he was reluctant to send the customary synodical letter to your paternal blessedness, lest it perhaps not be received, as had happened under his predecessors, the patriarchs. But since he thought it better to write an exhortatory letter to your paternal blessedness, he sent one, as will be known. Afterwards, however, we questioned Theodore himself and Macarius, patriarch of Antioch [Note: [Col. 1013D] Theodore was deposed shortly afterward, for a reason that is not entirely clear. George succeeded him, as appears from the Acts of the Sixth Synod; in 682 he again became patriarch of Constantinople. Macarius was a most obstinate Monothelite and was therefore deposed and anathematized at the Sixth Synod.], about what difficulty existed between your apostolic see and them. They replied that certain novel expressions had been introduced, some introducing them through ignorance, others improperly investigating the incomprehensible works of God.

“Therefore we exhort your blessedness to send here useful, modest, and learned men, clothed with the authority of your apostolic see and its council, bringing also the books that ought to be produced, so that, meeting with Theodore and Macarius, they may investigate the matter with all gentleness and modesty … Let three or more persons be sent from your Church, if that seems appropriate, as many as you please; and from the Roman council, twelve bishops.

“Both Theodore and Macarius, the patriarchs, have pressed us greatly to remove Vitalian from the diptychs, asserting that Honorius is commemorated in the diptychs out of respect for the apostolic dignity of our ancient Rome. For they did not agree that the patriarchs who succeeded Honorius [Note: [Col. 1013D] That the Monothelites gloried in the claim that Honorius had denied two wills is evident everywhere. See no. 6. Those who succeeded Honorius condemned the Monothelites too openly [Col. 1014C].] should be commemorated in the aforesaid Holy Roman Church. But we did not permit Vitalian to be removed from the diptychs …”

Subscription: “May the Divinity preserve you for many years, most holy and blessed Father.”

This letter was given at Constantinople on the day before the Ides of August, in the sixth indiction, that is, on 21 August 678.

### 29. The emperor’s letter to the patriarchs of Constantinople and Antioch

In the same year, 678, Donus died, and the emperor’s letter was delivered to Saint Agatho, his successor. He offered himself ready to send legates. Accordingly, the emperor also sent a letter to George of Constantinople, in the following terms:

“Emperor Constantine … to George, archbishop of Constantinople and universal patriarch [Note: [Col. 1014C] By right and by the force of the Council of Chalcedon, the title ‘universal patriarch’ belongs only to the Roman pontiffs. Out of modesty they themselves did not use it, but Sergius and Pyrrhus of Constantinople arrogantly usurped it. When in the eighth century the patriarch of Constantinople, Tarasius, was called ‘universal patriarch’ by the emperors, Pope Hadrian I immediately wrote to the emperors that this title was contrary to the canons and tradition. See the Bollandists’ preliminary dissertation to volume I for August, on the Patriarchs of Constantinople, nos. 309 and 323.].

“We decree, exhorting you, that your paternal blessedness assemble [Note: [Col. 1014D] I do not wish to challenge the authenticity of this letter. Nevertheless, I thought it should be noted that there is a great difference in writing style if we consider the Latin edition. The first letter, reported in the preceding section and addressed to the pope, has this superscription: ‘The emperor Constantine, faithful and great emperor, to the most holy archbishop of Rome and universal pope; given at Constantinople on the day before the Ides of August, in the sixth indiction.’ The second has this: ‘The pious and peaceful emperor Constantine, faithful in Jesus Christ, to the most holy and blessed archbishop of Constantinople and universal patriarch; given at Constantinople on the fourth day before the Ides of September, while the most pious and perpetual Augustus Constantine was reigning, in the twenty-eighth year of the emperor Constantine and the twelfth after his consulship.’ See no. 32, where the thirteenth year after his consulship is combined with the twenty-seventh year of Constantine. Moreover, it seems superfluous that the emperor, being in Constantinople, should have written this letter to the patriarch of Constantinople. Finally, Anastasius the Librarian, in the *Life of Agatho*, states that the Roman legates entered Constantinople on 10 November 680.] all the bishops belonging to your most holy see in this royal city of ours, so that the most diligent investigation may be made of the doctrine concerning the will and operation of Christ, our true God. Let this also be made known to Macarius, archbishop of the great city of Antioch, so that he too may prepare bishops from his own synod to assemble here for this same purpose [Note: [Col. 1015D] Why were the patriarchs of Alexandria and Jerusalem not summoned? Perhaps because those cities had already been occupied by the Muslims at that time. Meanwhile, legates of those patriarchs appear in the Acts of the council.].

“For we have already exhorted Donus, the bishop of the apostolic see of our ancient Rome, by our letters concerning this matter. After his death, Agatho, recently ordained pope in the aforesaid apostolic see, received our letters and has now sent Theodore and George, presbyters, and John, deacon, clothed with his authority. In the name of his entire council he has sent John, Abundantius, and John, bishops, together with the other clergy and monks. They presented us with two petitions, one from the same most holy Pope Agatho and the other from his council. Therefore let your paternal blessedness hasten to have the aforesaid bishops arrive quickly in this royal city of ours.”

This letter was given on 10 September [Note: [Col. 1015D] Thus the Roman legates must already have reached Constantinople by 10 September and delivered their letters to the emperor before the Eastern bishops were summoned. The latter, as will be said in no. 32, began the synod on 7 November. Thus, within two months, the ecumenical synod would have been convened and assembled. It is also remarkable that the emperor wrote that Agatho had been recently ordained, since, according to Pagi, he was ordained on 27 June 678.] in the year 680.

### 30. The Roman synod under Pope Saint Agatho and the legates sent to Constantinople

In the year 679 [Note: [Col. 1015D] Pagi proves this decisively from the fact that Saint Wilfrid from England was present; in 678 he had gone to Rome to appeal against his archbishop. Baronius and others had thought that the synod was celebrated in 680 [Col. 1016D].] Pope Saint Agatho celebrated a synod at Rome of 125 bishops. They unanimously defined that there are two wills and two operations in Christ, and condemned Sergius, Pyrrhus, and the others. No mention was made of Honorius.

In the name of the aforesaid synod, the three bishops indicated in the preceding section were sent to Constantinople: John of Portus, Abundantius of Paternum, and John of Reggio. The pope expressly instructed his legates not to consent to any innovation that the Greeks might attempt.

### 31. Honorius was judged Catholic until the year 680

Up to this point, nothing has appeared from which it could be inferred that Honorius had been condemned by any pope or particular council, or even legitimately accused as a heretic or supporter of heresy. Much, however, has occurred which proves that Honorius was judged by everyone to be truly Catholic and that he remained in possession of a good reputation for more than forty years after his death.

The two letters which I presented beginning with no. 23 were brought to light, at least, only in the following council, in the year 680. But now let us examine the Acts of the council.

## § II. Whether, in view of the Acts of the Sixth Synod, Honorius ought to be considered a heretic or condemned by the Church

### 32. The first session of the Third Council of Constantinople, or Sixth Synod: order of assembly and seating

The first session of the Council of Constantinople is said to have been held on 7 November [Note: [Col. 1016D] Anastasius reported that the legates were received by the emperor in a solemn procession on 17 November and that the first session was held in the basilica on 22 November. Thus the author of the Acts and Anastasius do not agree well.] in the year 680, the twenty-seventh year of Constantine, the thirteenth after his consulship, the twenty-second year of Heraclius and Tiberius, his brothers, and the ninth indiction, in the *trullus*, or palace, of the emperor, who also presided, attended by thirteen former consuls.

The ecclesiastics are said to have assembled in the following order:

1. The legates of Agatho;
2. The patriarch of Constantinople, the patriarch of Alexandria through a legate, and the patriarchs of Antioch and Jerusalem likewise through legates;
3. The legates of the Roman synod;
4. The legate of the archbishop of Ravenna;
5. Thirty-three Greek bishops;
6. Six Latin and Greek abbots.

[Note: [Col. 1016D] The following order of seating is reported. The patricians and consuls were beside the emperor. To the emperor’s left were the legates of Agatho and of the Roman synod, the legate of Ravenna, the bishop of Gortyna from Crete, the legate of Jerusalem, and the remaining bishops from Agatho’s Roman council. To the right were the patriarch of Constantinople, the patriarch of Antioch, the bishop of Ephesus, and the other bishops from both the Constantinopolitan and Antiochene patriarchates. It is not added whether any suffragan bishops from the patriarchates of Alexandria and Jerusalem were present.]

The Latins, representing the apostolic see of Agatho and the Roman synod, began to speak first:

“Because for approximately forty-six years the bishops who at various times governed this royal city—namely Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, as well as Cyrus, formerly bishop of the city of Alexandria, and also Theodore, who was bishop of the city of Pharan, together with certain others who followed them—introduced certain novel expressions contrary to the orthodox faith and asserted one will and one operation in Christ; and because the apostolic see has repeatedly pressed them on this matter, then pleaded with them, yet has so far been unable to draw them away from such an opinion, we ask those who are from the Church of Constantinople to say where this novelty of terminology originated.”

### 33. Pope Honorius is accused of heresy but not proved guilty. Macarius fails for the first time in proving one will

The emperor said: “Let George and Macarius, the patriarchs, answer what has been said by the representatives of the apostolic see.”

Macarius, archbishop of Antioch, together with his disciple Peter, a presbyter and monk, and the bishops Peter of Nicomedia and Solomon of Claneas [Note: [Col. 1016D] George of Constantinople remained silent; at least, the Acts do not record that he spoke.], answered on behalf of the sees of Constantinople and Antioch:

“We did not introduce novel expressions, but whatever we have received both from the universal councils and holy Fathers and from the bishops of this city—namely Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, as well as Honorius, who was pope of ancient Rome, and Cyrus, who was pope of Alexandria—we have believed, believe, and preach concerning the will and operation; and we are prepared to produce the statements concerning them.”

Macarius would have given greater force and dignity to his response if he had called Honorius “pope of the apostolic see,” the title which the emperor had granted to the Roman bishop.

Meanwhile Macarius requested that the books of the holy synods be brought forth from the patriarchate of Constantinople. The books were brought, and Stephen, a disciple of Macarius, read from the Acts of the Third Synod, that is, the Council of Ephesus, an oration in which Saint Cyril of Alexandria asserted: “Through Christ kings reign … for his will is almighty.”

Macarius said: “Behold, emperor, I have produced a passage that speaks of one will in Christ.”

But those representing the apostolic see, together with certain bishops from the Constantinopolitan synod and the judges, rose up and exclaimed:

“Saint Cyril has been wrongly cited by Macarius. He was speaking of the divine nature of the Word, which possesses an almighty will shared with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Besides, Saint Cyril did not even set forth such a will as one numerically.”

Thus in the first session Macarius failed with respect to Saint Cyril and the Council of Ephesus. He offered no proof concerning Honorius. Therefore, since he found no acceptance concerning Saint Cyril, he deserves none concerning Honorius either.

### 34. Whether the accusation against Honorius was interpolated. The legates of Agatho are said to have remained silent regarding Honorius’s condemnation

It may also be questioned whether the passage concerning Pope Honorius was not interpolated at this point.

First, Macarius could have boasted that one will had been asserted by Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, Peter, and Cyrus, and he was not obliged to prove it, since Sergius, Paul, and the others had been condemned at Rome in councils under the pontificates of Saints Martin I and Agatho precisely on account of that doctrine. But that Honorius too had asserted one will would have required proof, because this had formerly been solemnly denied by Pope John IV and by Saint Maximus, the most learned of the Greeks, and had not been decided even in any Greek tribunal.

Second, if Macarius had been so shameless as to count Honorius openly among the Monothelites, it is not likely that all the others would have remained silent in the face of this accusation, and especially that the legates of Pope Agatho or of the Roman synod would have produced nothing in defense of Honorius. They had been ordered, as we shall hear in no. 38, to consent to no innovation, and they could easily have defended Honorius by the arguments advanced earlier by Pope John and Saint Maximus.

Some people, following Pagius (*Ad annum* 681, no. 9), say: “The legates of Saint Agatho were excessively timid.” But if this were so, the legates would have been especially culpable, since they ought to have spoken by virtue of their office yet remained silent in a matter of such gravity concerning the Catholic faith. The fact that the legates were upright and fearless men is spoken to by all the circumstances [Col. 1018A].

Natalis (*Proposition* 1, objection 2) says: “The legates were ignorant men.”

Reply: As regards secular sciences, I concede it; in matters of faith and ecclesiastical history, I deny it. One of them was later raised to the chair of Peter.

Others assert: “By permitting one Honorius, although supreme pontiff and whether innocent or not convicted, to be counted among the heretics, the legates acted prudently, since in this way they could more easily obtain from Macarius and the other Greeks that Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople be counted among the Monothelites.”

But in my theology this prudence would have been gravely illicit on the part of the Latins. It also presupposes that all the Greeks were unfair men, who would not have agreed that the condemnation already pronounced against Sergius, Pyrrhus, and the other Constantinopolitans in the Roman councils should be repeated at Constantinople unless Pope Honorius too were included among those condemned.

We shall see in no. 36 that the Roman legates prevented Mennas of Constantinople and Pope Vigilius of Rome from being counted among the Monothelites. Why, then, would they have silently left Pope Honorius—whom Pope John and the Greek Saint Maximus had long before defended—in the hands of the heretics?

Moreover, if the Roman legates had denied that Honorius asserted one will, Macarius would not for that reason have said that one will was not asserted by Sergius, Pyrrhus, and the others. Indeed, if Macarius had said this, he would have harmed himself, not the Catholics, who maintained that the doctrine of one will was new and had been transmitted only by Sergius, Pyrrhus, and the others.

In any case, let us admit that the passage concerning Honorius is genuine. Even then, it proves just as little against Honorius as against Saints Cyril, Dionysius the Areopagite, and the other Fathers whom Macarius claimed as his own.

### 35. Session 2. Macarius fails for the second time: Saint Leo did not favor the Monothelites

The second session was held on 10 November. The Acts of the Fourth Synod, that is, the Council of Chalcedon, were read, including the following words of Pope Saint Leo I:

“Each form acts in communion with the other in what properly belongs to it: the Word performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh; one of these shines with miracles, while the other submits to injuries.”

Those who represented the apostolic see of Rome rose and said:

“Behold! Saint Leo plainly preaches two operations. The holy synod inscribed this very discourse as a foundation of the orthodox faith.”

Macarius passed on to the theandric operation asserted by Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, but the emperor ordered the remainder of the Acts to be read. Thus Macarius achieved nothing from the two synods to which he had appealed. Meanwhile he adduced certain passages from the synods; but he cited no text from Honorius.

## 36. Session 3. Macarius fails for the third time; for the Acts of the Fifth Council are discovered to have been corrupted with respect to the sermon of Mennas

Session 3 was held on 13 November. From Book I containing the Acts of the Fifth Council there was read aloud: “The sermon of Mennas, archbishop of Constantinople, to Vigilius, pope of Rome, concerning the fact that Christ has one will.” The representatives of the Apostolic See rose and exclaimed: “This present book of the Fifth Council has been falsified; let the sermon said to be Mennas’s to Vigilius by no means be read, because it is fabricated [lacuna].”

[Note: [Col. 1019C] Behold, the representatives kept watch in order to vindicate Mennas, patriarch of Constantinople; yet would they never have said anything on behalf of Honorius if he had been among the heretics and, indeed, repeatedly rejected by the Greeks? Likewise they vindicated Pope Vigilius, as will be seen in the following section.]

The representatives then pointed out, first, that when the Acts had been written at the Fifth Council, the aforesaid sermon had in no way been prefixed to them, since Mennas had already been dead for six years before that council. Second, the emperor, the former consuls, and certain bishops examined the book and discovered that the first three quires, which contained the aforesaid sermon, had been written in a different hand from the remaining quires. Moreover, in those first three quires no number had been written at the bottom, as was customary; indeed, the fourth quire bore the number one, the fifth the number two, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] St. Gregory the Great had earlier complained that the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon had been corrupted by the Greeks. He says: “The Council of Chalcedon was falsified in one place by the Church of Constantinople” (*Epistle* 14, Book IV). Later, several other falsifications were either made or detected by others. Some critics assert that certain canons of the First Council of Nicaea have been lost; others maintain that Canon 20, concerning not kneeling on Sundays and during the paschal season, was appended later. See Father John Chrysostom of St. Joseph, *Dissertation 2, On the Number of the Nicene Canons*, chapter 8, no. 4. In Theodoret, Book V, chapter 9, the Greeks, in their synodal letter to Pope Damasus, cite from the Nicene Council a canon stating that a bishop should be elected by the provincials. This canon is not found among the Nicene canons, although it does exist as Canon 5 among the canons of Sardica.]

Thus the fraud was plainly detected. The emperor therefore ordered that the aforesaid three quires be omitted and that the remaining Acts be read.

It should be noted that this book had been produced from the patriarchal archives of Constantinople. Who, I ask, first corrupted that book, or concealed it there after it had been corrupted? But let us hear of the remaining corruptions.

## 37. The letters of Pope Vigilius are fictitious

When, from this book, Session 7 of the Fifth Council was reread, two letters of Pope Vigilius appeared: one to the emperor Justinian and the other to the empress Theodora. In them the pope was said to have written: “We anathematize Theodore of Mopsuestia, who does not confess in Christ one hypostasis [essence], one person, and one [lacuna] operation.”

The Roman representatives exclaimed: “Vigilius did not say ‘one operation.’ These are not letters of Vigilius. This book has been falsified, just as the opening sections of the present Fifth Council have been falsified. For if Vigilius had taught one operation and had been accepted by the council, then the definition would likewise contain a mention of one operation.”

The book was reread, and nothing concerning one operation was found. The conclusion was reached that Macarius had not proved from the councils either one will or one operation, as he had promised. Macarius therefore requested a postponement and promised that he would prove his assertion from other Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 1020C] The question had been sufficiently discussed for several years, and Macarius had been able to prepare himself long before this council; indeed, he had prepared himself. Nevertheless, he now requests and receives a new postponement.]

## 38. Session 4. Pope Agatho asserts that none of his predecessors had ever erred in the faith

In Session 4, on 15 November, the letter of Pope St. Agatho to the emperor Constantine and his brothers was read aloud.

[Note: [Col. 1020D] The Acts add that Diogenes, the imperial secretary, translated the letters of Agatho and of the Roman council from Latin into Greek, and that these translations were read aloud. Thus the pope and the Roman council had written in Latin to the emperor and his brothers, as men not unacquainted with the Roman language.]

The pope expressed his sorrow over the new doctrine and listed all the representatives sent in his own name, in the name of the Roman council, and in the name of the archbishop of Ravenna:

“Let them strive only to set forth what this Apostolic Church believes and proclaims—not through secular eloquence, which is not available to uneducated men,

[Note: [Col. 1020D] They were simple as doves, but at the same time prudent as serpents and extremely well versed in the books of the holy Fathers, as the Acts clearly demonstrate. Their simplicity will be discussed again in section 39.]

but through the sincerity of the apostolic faith [lacuna]. They have been charged only with presuming to add, diminish, or change nothing, but sincerely to recount the tradition of this Apostolic See, as it was instituted by its apostolic pontiffs who preceded us [lacuna].

“This is the tradition of the apostolic faith: that we proclaim two natures in Christ [lacuna], two natural wills and two operations, not contrary to one another; nor do we call them mutually opposed, as those who stray from the way of truth accuse the apostolic tradition [lacuna].

“Most Christian lordly sons! With flowing tears I beg you: deign to extend your right hand to the apostolic dogma, so that Peter’s doctrine may not be hidden under a bushel, but may be proclaimed throughout the whole world more clearly than a trumpet [lacuna].

“This Apostolic Church of Peter has never deviated from the way of truth in any matter of error. Its authority, since it belongs to the chief of all the apostles, has always been embraced by the entire Catholic Church of Christ and by universal councils [lacuna].

“By the grace of almighty God, this Apostolic Church of Christ will be shown never to have erred from the path of apostolic tradition, nor to have succumbed, corrupted by heretical novelties; rather, it remains undefiled to the end, in accordance with the Savior’s promise: ‘Peter, Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers’ [lacuna]. He who promised that Peter’s faith would not fail admonished him to strengthen his brothers. This the apostolic pontiffs, my predecessors in my lowliness, have always freely done [lacuna].”

[Note: [Col. 1020D] How would St. Agatho have dared to write thus to Constantinople if, at that time, even the slightest suspicion still remained that Honorius, in his letter—and even in his second letter—had favored the Monothelites? St. Agatho is not speaking of the clergy but of the Roman pontiffs, saying that they had always strengthened their brothers in the faith and proclaimed the faith sincerely.

Some say: “Honorius erred not as a public teacher but as a private individual.” But the pseudo-Bossuet, Book VII, chapter 22, replies: “Honorius had been questioned and, in his official capacity, answered the three patriarchs of Constantinople, Alexandria, and Jerusalem. He accepted Cyrus, who was preaching one operation of Christ to converts from heresy, and he wrote back to Sergius: ‘Your fraternity teaches this together with us.’ Therefore he erred as a public teacher.” I admit this—if the letters of Honorius that now exist are genuine.]

“It is known to all. My littleness desires to follow them. Woe to me if I neglect to proclaim the truth of my Lord, which they themselves proclaimed sincerely. Woe to me if I conceal the truth in silence [lacuna]. Therefore those bishops of apostolic memory who preceded my mediocrity, instructed by the Lord’s teaching, against which the prelates of the Church of Constantinople set about introducing a heretical novelty, never failed to exhort and admonish them, entreating them to abandon, even in silence, the evil doctrine of heretical error.”

After this, St. Agatho proved the article of faith concerning the two wills in Christ by adducing very many texts from Holy Scripture, from the general councils, and from the holy Fathers, both Greek and Latin—especially Augustine, Ambrose, Leo, Hilary, Dionysius the Areopagite,

[Note: [Col. 1021C] Or the author of the book *On the Divine Names*, whose authority, as though he were Dionysius the Areopagite, the Monothelites had abused. See section 35.]

Gregory Nazianzen and Gregory of Nyssa, Chrysostom, Anastasius, Cyril of Alexandria, and Cyril of Jerusalem.

He then enumerated earlier heretics who had proclaimed one will in Christ, namely Apollinaris, Severus, and Theodosius. He added the more recent bishops Cyrus of Alexandria and Theodore of Pharan, as well as four patriarchs of Constantinople: Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Caranza erred egregiously in his *Summary of the Councils* when he included Honorius among those just mentioned, for Honorius was pope of ancient Rome.]

He reported the letters and books in which these unstable men at one time proclaimed one will or operation and at another time two wills or operations. He cited the letters of Pyrrhus to John, of Paul to Theodore, and of Peter to Vitalian, Roman pontiff, as well as the letter of Sergius to Cyrus of Alexandria and other works of Sergius. Agatho says not a word about Honorius.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Melchior Cano, Book VI, question 11, wrongly says that Agatho placed Honorius among the heretics. Pagius, Thomassinus, and others likewise wrongly asserted that Agatho implicitly and obscurely condemned Honorius. If Honorius was liable to condemnation, St. Agatho did not act sincerely in passing over him.]

Indeed, he does not even reveal that Sergius had written any letter to Honorius either for or against the two wills in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] One cannot help wondering why Agatho made no mention of either Sergius’s letters to Honorius or Honorius’s letters to Sergius. There are three possible answers. First, by that time every suspicion that the bishops of Constantinople had raised against Honorius had already been removed by the apology of Pope John IV and the disputation between St. Maximus and Pyrrhus; therefore it did not occur to St. Agatho that he ought to make a special mention of Honorius. Second, Sergius’s letter to Honorius was an inquiry, not a heretical letter; indeed, the letter of Sergius to Honorius that now exists does not reveal a heretical mind. See section 66. Third, Agatho may in fact have mentioned Honorius, but the mention was later omitted.

On this last hypothesis, one must further ask whether Agatho had mentioned Honorius as an accomplice in heresy or as innocent. The first possibility is incompatible with the context, in which Agatho repeatedly and in various ways asserted that Peter’s successors had never failed in teaching. Moreover, if Agatho had identified Honorius as a heretic, it is not likely that this would have been suppressed by the same writer who now carefully notes, in Session 14, that Honorius was condemned by the Sixth Council. If, however, Agatho had excused or defended Honorius, it is easier to understand why the person who inserted in Session 4 that Honorius had been condemned by this council omitted, in that same Session 4, what St. Agatho had written to the council on behalf of Honorius. Furthermore, the day and year on which this letter was issued are also missing.]

Against this letter—in which St. Agatho repeatedly stated that none of his predecessors had failed in the faith or in the duty of strengthening their brothers—none of the Greeks is reported even to have murmured, not even Macarius. What testimony for the innocence of Pope Honorius!

## 39. The letter of the 125 Latin bishops to the Sixth Council contains nothing against Honorius

In the same session, the letter of 125 bishops from the Roman council to the emperor Constantine and the Sixth Council was also read aloud. They wrote:

[Note: [Col. 1022D] From England there were present Wilfrid, bishop of York and representative of the council constituted for greater Britain; three representatives of the council constituted for the provinces of Gaul; nine bishops from Istria; and others.]

“Our whole life is filled with anxieties. The hand of the nations surrounds us, and the nourishment of our bodies is obtained through labor, since the ancient possession of the Churches is gradually collapsing, weakened by various calamities. Our only substance is our faith, with which to live is the highest glory and for which to die is eternal gain [lacuna].

“This is our perfect knowledge: that with our whole mind we preserve the boundaries of the Catholic and apostolic faith, which the Apostolic See has until now both held together with us and handed down [lacuna].

“We have all acknowledged that this rule of pure, Catholic, and apostolic confession was proclaimed by the council that met in this city of Rome under Pope Martin [lacuna].

“The authors of the new error are Theodore of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople [lacuna].

“We judged it proper to select these persons so that the city in which the see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, was founded—and whose authority all Christian peoples together with us truly adore and venerate—might be shown to be superior to all nations. They were to bring our report, that is, the report of all the bishops in the northern and western regions, but in such a way that they would not argue about uncertain matters; rather, in a brief definition they would present them as firm, stable, and unimpaired [lacuna].”

[Note: [Col. 1022D] Therefore the Roman representatives could not lawfully have consented to the condemnation of Honorius, pope of Rome, by the Greeks.]

“We utterly reject worldly wisdom and empty deceit, as blessed Paul says; nevertheless, we teach and defend the rule of true proclamation with the utmost simplicity of truth.”

Then followed the subscriptions, which were likewise read aloud and inserted into the Acts. They included:

“Agatho, bishop of the Apostolic Church of the city of Rome, have consented and subscribed to this submission [lacuna], as stated above.

“Andrew, bishop of the Church of Ostia, have subscribed to this submission, which we unanimously composed on behalf of our apostolic faith.”

In exactly the same manner, each of the remaining bishops subscribed, testifying that they had unanimously composed the aforesaid submission.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] No Latin is ever reported—if we set aside Pope Honorius—to have consented to the utterly foolish Monothelite heresy of one will in two natures.]

## 40. No reply was made by the Greeks to those letters

I would have expected that the emperor, together with the few Greeks who had gathered at Constantinople, would at once have agreed with this unanimous definition of the Latin bishops, as a matter sufficiently discussed—especially since it is evident that Christ possessed a human will and Macarius had so clearly failed in proving the contrary.

But, to my considerable astonishment, in this Session 4 and those immediately following, it is nowhere mentioned whether the Greeks accepted or rejected these Latin submissions concerning the two wills in Christ. Indeed, the emperor, as though he had judged these submissions insufficiently decisive, is reported to have said:

“What has been read today is sufficient. Let Macarius and those who are with him produce on another day the statements of the holy Fathers that they promised.”

## 41. Session 5. Macarius is said to have produced new texts

The Acts of Session 5,

[Note: [Col. 1023D] Authors have differed in their transcription of the Acts of the Sixth Council. Hardouin contains two editions. In the second, almost the entire third session is omitted; what is called Session 4 according to the first edition is called Session 3 according to the second, and so forth.]

which is said to have been held on 7 December, are in no way satisfactory to the inquisitive reader. Macarius is said, at the emperor’s request, to have produced the statements he had promised long before—indeed, two books. The heading of the first book was:

“Testimonies of the holy Fathers teaching one will of Christ, which is also the will of the Father and of the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 1023D] The Monothelites held a correct view concerning the Holy Trinity, but denied a will to Christ’s humanity.]

Both books are said to have been read aloud. In the earlier sessions, whatever was read aloud was also inserted in writing into the Acts. But in this Session 5, apart from the title of the first book, not even a syllable is recorded. Meanwhile, Macarius is said to have been informed that, if he wished, he could produce more statements for his opinion in the following session. I am astonished at the excessive indulgence shown to Macarius.

## 42. Session 6. Macarius is said to have added new texts, which were sealed

Session 6 is said to have been held in the twenty-seventh year of Constantine, after his thirteenth consulship, in the ninth indiction, on 11 February.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] Indictions and the years of the Greeks were reckoned from autumn; nevertheless, the consulship seems to have been calculated from the Kalends of January. Therefore this was the year after Constantine’s fourteenth consulship. But see Pagius.

Natalis pointed out that at that time a threefold indiction was in use: first, the Constantinopolitan, beginning on the Kalends of September; second, the Caesarean, beginning on the eighth day before the Kalends of October; third, the Roman, or papal, beginning on 1 January. Yet Venerable Bede (*On the Nature of Things*, chapter 47) seems to have been unaware of this division. He says: “When an emperor dies in the middle of the year, it can happen that one historian assigns that year to his predecessor and another to his successor. Therefore, so that error may not arise from this, the year of the indiction was added; it begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.”]

Thus it was the year 681 of the common era.

[Col. 1023D] Macarius and those who were with him presented a third book entitled “The Following Testimonies Concerning the Will.” This third book is said to have been read aloud, but nothing from it was inserted into the Acts.

The emperor is said to have ordered that the three books presented by Macarius now be sealed by the judges, the Roman representatives, and the bishops of this council. I am astonished at this apparatus, since such great care was not observed regarding the letters of Agatho and of the Roman council presented by the Roman representatives. Those letters were read and immediately inserted into the Acts; they were not sealed and set aside for future sessions. Concerning the book presented by the Romans, see section 44.

## 43. The Roman representatives offer new texts in support of the two wills

After the sealing had taken place, the Roman representatives informed the emperor that Macarius had truncated the texts written by him in the aforesaid books. At the same time, they offered testimonies of the holy Fathers in support of the two wills, as well as testimonies of heretics in support of one will. The emperor ordered that the reading be postponed until the next session.

There was still no mention of Honorius. Nevertheless, the Acts are reported in such a way as though the question of one or two operations in Christ had not yet been sufficiently decided.

## 44. Session 7. The texts offered by the Roman representatives are read aloud

Session 7 is said to have been held on 27 February, and so forth, as before. The emperor ordered that the testimonies offered the previous day by the Roman representatives be read aloud. He asked the representatives whether they wished to produce further testimonies. They replied that these were sufficient and insisted that the council declare what it thought concerning the letters sent by Agatho and by the Roman council and read aloud in Session 4.

The patriarchs George of Constantinople and Macarius of Antioch are said to have replied that they wished first to compare the texts cited in the aforesaid letters with the books preserved in the patriarchal archives of Constantinople and afterward to give their response. The emperor agreed and ordered that the book offered by the representatives be sealed.

I do not understand the reason why these books, offered by the representatives and by Macarius, were sealed with such extraordinary care. Was there perhaps a suspicion that Agatho’s secretary—whom I shall cite in section 104—or someone else might falsify the books that had been offered and already read aloud?

## 45. Session 8. The letter of St. Agatho is received by the bishops subject to Constantinople

Session 8 was held on 7 March, and so forth, as before. The emperor asked the patriarchs George of Constantinople and Macarius of Antioch whether they agreed with the letters sent by Agatho and by the Roman council.

George replied:

“I have compared the texts cited by Agatho and by the Roman council and found them to agree with the books preserved in the patriarchal archives of Constantinople, and I agree with them; thus I profess and believe.”

[Note: [Col. 1024D] As though there had been a suspicion that the pope and the Roman council had brought forward false texts! And if a discrepancy had been discovered, would the Constantinopolitan books have been preferred? See section 56.]

Then the individual replies of fourteen Greek bishops were reported. Every one of them subscribed to the opinion of Pope Agatho, without adding that they had examined the texts cited by the pope. Among them, Domitius, bishop of Prusias, said:

“I receive and embrace the letters of our father Agatho, most holy archbishop of the Apostolic and principal see of ancient Rome [lacuna], as dictated by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of St. Peter and written by the finger of the aforesaid thrice-blessed Pope Agatho.”

Afterward all the remaining bishops subject to the see of Constantinople rose and exclaimed:

“We agree with the submissions of Pope Agatho and of the council subject to him; we believe in two wills in Christ; we anathematize those who say there is one will.”

It should be noted, first, that in the Roman submissions Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter of Constantinople, and Cyrus of Alexandria were condemned, but Honorius was not even named; second, that none of these Greeks objected to the omission of Honorius—not even George of Constantinople or Macarius of Antioch.

## 46. Bishop Theodore is openly said to have lied

The following episode was also inserted:

“Bishop Theodore of Meletina entered and, standing in the midst, said: ‘I am an unlearned man, and I ask that this document be read.’ It contained the following:

‘None of the five general councils has defined that there are two wills in Christ. The testimonies of the Fathers differ. Therefore we ask the emperor that nothing be defined concerning one or two wills, and that none of the deceased be condemned on account of one or two wills.’”

When the emperor asked Theodore from whom he had received that document, he replied: “From the bishops of Nicomedia, Claene, and Hypaepa, and from Stephen, the presbyter of Macarius.”

But these three bishops—not Stephen the abbot, who was also a presbyter—came forward and said:

“Bishop Theodore of Melitene has lied. That document was prepared and handed over without our knowledge. We are ready to profess the orthodox faith.”

They were ordered to submit this statement in writing.

Afterward Theodore was asked from whom he had received the document. He replied: “From that Stephen the abbot who belongs to the patriarchal household of Antioch.”

[Note: [Col. 1025D] The Acts add: “Theodore pointed him out standing behind the seat in which the venerable archbishop of Antioch, Macarius, was sitting.” I am astonished that this circumstance was entered in the synodal Acts. Was it also approved?]

## 47. The name of Pope Vitalian is restored to the diptychs

George of Constantinople is then said to have asked the emperor “that the name of Pope Vitalian, which had been removed from the diptychs at the insistence of Macarius of Antioch, be restored.”

[Note: [Col. 1025D] The sentence reporting this episode is obscure. Moreover, it seems contrary to the emperor’s testimony, since he wrote that he had prevented the name of Vitalian from being erased from the diptychs. See section 28. Nor is it likely that Macarius later prevailed against the emperor.]

The emperor said: “Let it be done.”

Then the holy council exclaimed:

“Many years to the emperor Constantine, guardian of the orthodox faith; many years to Agatho, pope of Rome; many years to George, the patriarch; and many years to the sacred senate.”

Meanwhile, the entire council had not yet expressed its judgment, as will be clear from the following section.

## 48. Macarius, patriarch of Antioch, refuses to agree with the Romans

After the acclamation, Macarius, patriarch of Antioch, was asked whether he followed the submissions sent by Pope Agatho. He replied:

“I do not affirm two wills or two operations in Christ, but one will and one divine-human operation.”

Then the four bishops from the patriarchate of Antioch who were present each gave his judgment, subscribing to the Roman submissions.

But what the representatives of the patriarchs of Alexandria and Jerusalem did is completely omitted. Is it possible that they remained entirely silent, or that the emperor and the other bishops failed to notice or concealed that silence? If some falsifier composed or corrupted these Acts, it would have been easy for him to forget the aforesaid patriarchal representatives.

## 49. Macarius, together with his Stephen, refuses to confess two wills

In the same Session 8, the three books formerly presented by Macarius, bearing three seals, were produced and returned to Macarius so that he might identify whether they were the ones he had handed over. Macarius took them in his hands, examined them, and confessed:

“They are indeed the same.”

[Note: [Col. 1026D] This excessive solicitude increases my suspicion.]

Then the most holy Macarius confessed only one will in Christ, and that a divine one. His profession of faith was read aloud in the following form:

“Exposition or confession of faith of Macarius, the heresiarch.”

[Note: [Col. 1026D] At the very least, the word “arch-heresiarch” was appended by some corruptor; for at that time Macarius had not yet been judged or condemned as a heretic. Moreover, what sort of designation is this: “heresiarch ... beloved of God”?]

“I believe in one God [lacuna]. We accept the five holy and universal councils [lacuna]. We anathematize every heresy from Simon to the present, especially Arius [lacuna], and also Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius. In addition, we anathematize the Three Chapters and Maximus,

[Note: [Col. 1026D] I have been unable to discover who this Maximus was or why he was condemned by Honorius. Is St. Maximus, cited in section 18, perhaps intended? He was certainly never condemned by Honorius.]

whose impious doctrine our Fathers formerly rejected—that is, Honorius, Sergius, Cyrus [lacuna], and your great-grandfather Heraclius, and so forth.”

[Note: [Col. 1026D] This profession of faith is extremely long, and it was exceedingly tedious for me to read.]

Macarius, beloved of God, added:

“I will not say that there are two wills in Christ, even if I should be cut limb from limb or thrown into the sea.”

## 50. Part of the texts cited by Macarius is read aloud
