Then, from the three books indicated in the preceding section, the first was read aloud. From it, to prove one will in Christ, very extensive fragments were read from St. Athanasius of Alexandria; Augustine (*Book V Against the Pelagianist Julian*); Ambrose (*Book to the Emperor Gratian*);

[Col. 1027A]

[Note: [Col. 1027C] The author of the Acts behaved, as we shall later see, as though the Greek Fathers had not understood Latin, while the Romans nevertheless understood Greek. On this occasion he reports that testimonies from the Latin Fathers Augustine and Ambrose were read and examined, but he forgot to add by whom or through what medium they had been translated into Greek. See section 56. It should be noted that these testimonies from the Latin Fathers were cited by Macarius, a Greek.]

Dionysius the Areopagite, and Chrysostom.

The Roman representatives immediately added the context to each text cited by Macarius. From this it became evident that the aforesaid holy Fathers had believed in two wills. Macarius was then anathematized by the council as a heretic and falsifier and was deposed from the episcopate. Nevertheless, he is still reported to have disputed for a long time afterward.

At last the emperor said:

“What has been reread today is sufficient.

[Note: [Col. 1027D] In reality, very much is said in this session to have been read aloud and written down. If it was also discussed and examined, an entire day could easily have been spent.]

Let the remainder of this book be left for the next session.”

## 51. Session 9. The number of resident bishops

Session 9 is reported to have been held in the twenty-eighth year of the emperor Constantine,

[Note: [Col. 1027D] This is how it is read in the Latin edition; in the Greek edition, however, it says “in the twenty-seventh year.”]

after his thirteenth consulship, in the twenty-second year of Heraclius and Tiberius, his brothers, on 8 March, in the ninth indiction.

In addition to the thirty-two Greek bishops assembled, four bishops are mentioned: Peter of Nicomedia, Theodore of Melitene, Antonius of Hypaepa, and Solomon of Claene.

[Note: [Col. 1027D] They are present in the Latin edition, although they are omitted at this point in the Greek edition. But why should those bishops not have been allowed to sit in the customary place, as in the preceding sessions?]

These four latter bishops were either not present on this occasion, or what follows is false.

## 52. Four bishops and Stephen, the presbyter of Macarius, enter and are received

“While the bishops were seated, Constantine, chief secretary of the notaries of this most holy Catholic and Apostolic great Church of God,

[Note: [Col. 1027D] Until this point, only the Roman Church had been called Apostolic. This title is now attributed for the first time by the person who wrote the Acts to the Church of Constantinople.]

said: ‘The bishops Peter of Nicomedia, Solomon of Claene, Antonius of Hypaepa, Theodore of Melitene, and Stephen the monk, disciple of Macarius, are standing before the veil [lacuna].’

[Note: [Col. 1028C] Macarius no longer appears either among these men or among the resident bishops, among whom he had until then always been listed. Nevertheless, three bishops now appear among the residents who had not previously been present: Marinus of Sardis, John of Seda, and John of Erizorum.]

The emperor and the holy council said: ‘Let them enter.’ And they entered.

The emperor and the holy council said: ‘Let what was formerly enacted be reread.’ And it was reread.

[Note: [Col. 1028D] It is not likely that all the preceding sessions could have been read aloud.]

## 53. Macarius and Stephen are condemned as falsifiers

“The emperor said: ‘From the first book, which was presented by Macarius and Stephen, let the remainder be reread and compared with the books of the venerable patriarchal archives.’

Two fragments were read aloud: one again from St. Athanasius,

[Note: [Col. 1028D] Macarius—or whoever enlarged or composed these Acts—maintained no fixed order in the texts he transcribed. Thus, for example, he recited fragments from St. Athanasius, then from St. Augustine, St. Ambrose, and others, and soon afterward again from St. Athanasius, and so forth.]

and the other from St. Cyril.

The Greek bishops observed that Macarius and Stephen had truncated these texts, and that nevertheless the texts were contrary to the system of one will. Therefore the council said:

“You, Stephen, and your teacher Macarius have corrupted the doctrines of the holy Fathers. We therefore define that you are excluded from every priestly dignity and ministry.”

## 54. Four other bishops are restored because they offered a profession of faith, whose reading is postponed

“As for the bishops who are now standing in the midst and rightly confess with us,

[Note: [Col. 1028D] This had not yet been sufficiently established, because their profession of faith had not yet been read aloud.]

we have determined that they should sit in their proper places. Let them present to us, in the following session, the documents concerning their own faith that they promised [lacuna].

“Many years to the orthodox emperor; evil years to the new Eutyches; cast the heretic out.”

Stephen, the disciple of Macarius, was pushed out and expelled.

The four bishops—Peter of Nicomedia, Theodore of Melitene, Solomon of Claene, and Antonius of Hypaepa—said:

“We are ready to present our documents.”

The council said:

“Let it be done. Let the book previously offered by the Romans also be presented in the following session and compared with the books preserved in this patriarchal archive. But let the two remaining books presented by Macarius and Stephen and now read aloud not be compared, because they do not pertain to this dogma.”

[Note: [Col. 1028D] No one can pass judgment on these two books, because nothing from them was inserted into the Acts.]

## 55. Session 10. The reading is postponed again

Session 10 was held on 19 March, with the rest as before. Ten new bishops now appear among the resident bishops.

Peter of Nicomedia and the other three now wished to present their documents. But the emperor and the council said:

“Let what was formerly enacted be reread.”

And it was reread.

The emperor and the council said:

“The bishops Peter of Nicomedia and the others promised to present their books. It follows, however, that the book offered by the Romans, which remains under seal, should be brought forward, reread, and compared with the books of this patriarchal archive.”

## 56. The texts cited by the Romans are read and examined to determine whether they are genuine

“And a document of this kind, bearing a seal, was brought forward. After it had been unsealed, Peter the notary took the authentic book extracted from the treasury—that is, from the place of the sacred vessels—a parchment volume covered with silver.

And Solomon the notary reread the aforesaid book of testimonies, bearing the following heading:

‘Testimonies of the holy and approved Fathers demonstrating two wills [lacuna] in Christ.’

1. “Pope Leo of Rome, from his second letter to the emperor Leo: ‘Whatever Christ received in time [lacuna].’”

[Note: [Col. 1029D] This and the following testimonies are extremely long passages from the Fathers, all of which were inserted into the Acts. To avoid causing excessive tedium for readers, I omit them. Many other texts from St. Leo, Ambrose, and Augustine among the Latins, and from Dionysius the Areopagite, Gregory Nazianzen, and others among the Greeks, are cited in the letter of St. Agatho mentioned in section 38; I have likewise omitted them.]

[lacuna]

This testimony was compared with the aforesaid book from the treasury and was found to agree.

2. “Saint Ambrose (Letter 2 to the Emperor Gratian) . . . . . This testimony was likewise compared with the very ancient paper book of the Constantinopolitan library, and it agrees.

3. “The same Saint Ambrose (On Luke) . . . . . This testimony was compared with a codex written in Latin letters, with Constantine, a Constantinopolitan presbyter and Latin grammarian, interpreting, and it agrees.

[Note: [Col. 1029D] What are we to say? Was the booklet which the Romans are said to have presented at this synod written in Greek or in Latin? Saint Ambrose’s text (from the letter to Gratian) was compared by the Greeks without any Latin interpreter; the same text in his work on Luke was compared with a Latin codex, with a Latin grammarian interpreting. Saint Augustine’s text, to be cited below, is likewise said to have been compared through an interpreter. The remaining Fathers who are cited were all Greeks, except Saint Leo I, pope.]

4. “Saint John of Constantinople (Sermon: ‘Again, the Circus’) . . . . . This testimony was likewise compared with a parchment book from the Constantinopolitan library, and it agrees.

5. “The same John of Constantinople (On Matthew) . . . . . [Col. 1029B] This testimony was likewise compared with a paper codex from the Constantinopolitan library, and it agrees.

6. “Saint Athanasius of Alexandria (Book on the Trinity) . . . . This testimony was likewise compared with a saffron-coloured parchment book from the Constantinopolitan library, and it agrees.

7. “Saint Gregory of Nyssa (Against Apollinaris) . . . . . This testimony was likewise compared with a paper book of the Constantinopolitan library, and it agrees.

8. “The same Saint Gregory (From the Book on the Contemplation of Man, chapter 4) . . . . . Also from the Book Against Eunomius, chapter 35 . . . . This was compared . . . . and it agrees.

9. “Saint John of Constantinople (Sermon: ‘Father, if it is possible’) . . . . This testimony was compared with a paper book . . . . and it agrees.

[Col. 1029C] 10. “The same Saint John Chrysostom (Sermon 66: ‘The Present Life Is Sweet’) . . . . It was compared with a parchment book . . . and it agrees.

11. “Saint Cyril of Alexandria (Book On the Treasures, chapter 24) . . . . It was compared with a paper book . . . and it agrees.

12. “The same Saint Cyril (From the same book) . . . It was compared with the same book . . . and it agrees.

13. “The same Saint Cyril (Book III Against Julian) . . . . It was compared with a parchment book . . . and it agrees.

14. “The same Saint Cyril (On Matthew, tome XI) . . . . Also another passage (From tome XII) . . . . These two testimonies were compared with a paper book, and they agreed.

15. “The same Saint Cyril (Book on John) . . . . . . Also another passage (From the same sermon) . . . . . These two [Col. 1030A] were compared with a paper book . . . . . and they agreed.

16. “Three testimonies of the same Saint Cyril (From Books VIII, X, and XII on John) . . . . These three were compared with a paper book, and they agreed.

17. “Saint Epiphanius . . . It was compared with a paper book . . . and it agrees.

18. “Saint Gregory of Nazianzus . . . . It was compared with a book of saffron-coloured parchment . . . and it agrees.

19. “Saint Cyril of Alexandria (On the Treasures, Book XXIV) . . . It was compared with a paper book . . . and it agrees.

20. “The same Saint Cyril (On John, Book IV) . . . . It was compared with a paper book, and it agrees.

21. “Saint Athanasius of Alexandria . . . It was compared with a book made of saffron-coloured parchment . . . and it agrees.

22. “Saint Augustine (Book V Against the Pelagian Julian) . . . [Col. 1030B] It was compared with a book written in Latin letters, with Constantine, the Constantinopolitan presbyter and Latin grammarian, interpreting, and it agrees.

[Note: [Col. 1030D] The Greek bishops seem to have trusted this grammarian presbyter more than the Roman legates.]

23. “Saint Leo, pope (Letter to Flavian) . . . . It was compared with a parchment book covered in silver and taken from the repository of sacred vessels, and it agrees.

24. “The same Saint Leo (Letter 2 to the Emperor Leo) . . . . It was compared with a parchment book covered in silver and taken from the repository of sacred vessels, and it agrees.

25. “Saint Justin . . . It was compared with a paper book of this library, and it agrees.

26. “Saint John of Constantinople (Sermon on the Apostle Thomas and Against the Arians) . . . . It was compared with a parchment book brought by the Roman legates [Note: [Col. 1030D] It would follow from this that Saint Chrysostom’s book did not exist at Constantinople—whether in the patriarchate, in a church, or in a library—from which places, respectively, the Greeks produced the books for comparison. The same applies to the testimonies of Ephraem and Anastasius, patriarchs of Antioch, which are soon to be cited.] and it agrees.

[Col. 1030C] 27. “Saint Gregory of Nyssa (Against Eunomius, from tome V and from tome XII) . . . These two testimonies were compared with a book made of saffron-coloured parchment from the patriarchal library, and they agreed.

28. “The same author (From the letter to Eustathius on the Holy Trinity), containing the following: ‘Let them therefore show,’ etc. [Note: [Col. 1030D] Among other things, the following are added: ‘Therefore, if we observe operations differing from one another, performed by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we perceive from the diversity of the operations that the natures are diverse and operative.’ These statements suggest tritheism, and they are now read in Letter 80 of Saint Basil the Great to Eustathius the Physician, which I long ago noted as suspect in my dissertation On Saint Basil the Great, no. 226.] . . . Also another passage by the same author from the same book . . . These two testimonies were compared with a book made of saffron-coloured parchment, and they agreed.

29. “Saint Cyril of Alexandria (Sermon to the Emperor Theodosius) . . . It was compared with the parchment book of the Third, or Ephesian, Synod . . . and it agrees.

30. “The same author (Sermon 32 of the Treasures) . . . It was compared with a paper book . . . and it agrees.

[Col. 1031A] 31. “The most pious Emperor Justinian (Book Against the Nestorians) [Note: [Col. 1031B]

Thus, Justinian I would have been counted among the holy Fathers by the pope and the Roman synod, and received by the ecumenical council, while Pope Honorius was meanwhile denounced by them among the heretics. It will be useful to add a few remarks about that emperor.

Justinian obtained the empire in the year 537. He is best known for the body of civil law published by him. He was little educated in letters, fierce and avaricious, though generous toward the Churches. He built the famous church of Holy Wisdom at Constantinople and several others; he summoned the Fifth Synod and accomplished many things successfully and auspiciously. Yet he involved himself in ecclesiastical controversies more than was fitting for an emperor. Finally, in the year 563, he fell into heresy and publicly taught by edict that Christ’s body had been incorruptible and incapable of suffering even before the resurrection. He drove Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople, who resisted his impiety, from the episcopate and into exile. While he was issuing a sentence of deportation against Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, and that patriarch’s priests, he was struck by an invisible blow and died in the year 565. See the Greek and contemporary author Evagrius, Book IV, chapters 6 and 40, where he observes that Antioch began to be called Theopolis in the year 528, by which name it is called in the aforementioned body of civil law. See Baronius and Fleury. Indeed, Evagrius, Book V, chapter 1, added: ‘When Justinian had filled everything with turmoil and disturbances, and at the end of his life had received a fitting recompense for these deeds, he passed over to the punishments prepared in the underworld.’

In the lengthy letter of Pope Agatho indicated at no. 38, after testimonies from Saints Leo the pope, Augustine, and others had been produced, the following is added: ‘There are also testimonies of other venerable Fathers who clearly declare two operations in Christ . . . Ephraem and Anastasius, most worthy bishops of the great Church of Theopolis; and above all Justinian Augustus . . . whose religious memory is judged worthy of veneration among all nations, and whose rectitude of faith is praised as having been spread throughout the world by his most august edicts.’ This praise of Justinian seems to me excessive and interpolated into Agatho’s letter. I do not know whether Antioch was elsewhere called Theopolis by the Romans—that is, ‘city of God.’

In the letter of the Roman synod indicated at no. 39, the Latin bishops are said to have addressed the emperor and his brothers as follows: ‘Deign to receive the bishops sent by our humility, so that through their testimony your praise among all nations may grow, as did that of the great Constantine, whose fame . . .; and that of the great Theodosius, whose piety . . .; and that of the distinguished Emperor Marcian, who . . .; and that of the last indeed, but most excellent and greatest of all, that great Justinian, whose piety, no less than his valour, restored everything to a better order . . . For we too, although unworthy, beseech God’s mercy, that we may be preserved without falling . . . We teach in simple truth . . . We do not wish to possess rhetorical displays of words.’ At least this digression in praise of Justinian, exalted above all others, seems to me suspect.]

. . . It was compared with a parchment book . . . and it agrees.

32. “The same Justinian, of holy memory (From his dogmatic letter to Zoilus) . . . and Saint Cyril (Book XXXII of the Treasures) . . . and in the passages addressed to Theodosius . . . These two testimonies were likewise compared with a parchment book . . . and they agreed.

33. “Saint Ephraem, archbishop of Antioch . . . two testimonies (From the Defense on behalf of the Council of Chalcedon and from Pope Leo’s Tome) . . . Compared with a paper book brought by the Roman legates, and they agreed.

34. “Saint Athanasius, archbishop of Antioch [Note: [Col. 1032C] Concerning these patriarchs of Antioch, the following is inserted: ‘We know that Ephraem is listed in the sacred diptychs . . . The whole East calls Anastasius a saint; may God anathematize anyone who does not accept him.’ But which Anastasius is this? From the year 559 to 610 three Anastasii occupied the see of Antioch. I have no doubt that Anastasius I is intended, the one who was driven into exile by the Emperor Justin II, the successor of Justinian I, and who is commemorated on April 21. Meanwhile, his Defense on behalf of Pope Leo survives nowhere. See the Bollandists.] (From the Defense on behalf of Pope Leo’s Tome) . . . Compared with a paper book brought by the Roman legates

[Col. 1031B] 35. “Saint John of Scythopolis . . . . . Compared with a paper book of the patriarchal library, and it agrees.”

After this, another sixteen testimonies from various Greek heretics who asserted one will in Christ were read out and inserted in full into the Acts. Each of them is likewise said to have been compared with parchment and paper books, some brought from Rome and some preserved at Constantinople, and to have agreed.

[Note: [Col. 1032D] I began to wonder whether such enormous efforts were necessary—or appropriate—for confirming the doctrine of Pope Agatho and the Roman synod concerning two wills in Christ. Did each of the Fathers inspect the paper, parchment, yellowed, and silver-covered books? At least Pope Leo II, who later confirmed the synod, could not testify that everything agreed. Moreover, it follows from what has been said that the Latins were extremely well versed in reading Greek authors.]

37. The profession of the four bishops, mentioned repeatedly, is read. —When these matters had been completed, the bishops Peter of Nicomedia, and the others indicated at no. 54, presented their substantial profession of faith, in which they confessed two wills and subscribed to the Roman proposals. Then George, the apocrisarius of Theodore of Jerusalem, who is listed among the presiding officials, is said to have approached and asked: “Let the synodical letter of Sophronius, archbishop of Jerusalem, be read. It was sent by him to Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, but was not received by Sergius; I have it in my hands, so that it may be determined whether it is Catholic or not.” The emperor and the synod said: “Let it be read on another day.”

58. Session 11. The number of bishops increased. —Session 11 is said to have been held on March 20, in the ninth indiction, as before. No one was present in the name of the see of Antioch; but the number of the remaining bishops had greatly increased. [Col. 1032B] Namely, eighty-one resident bishops now appear. Likewise, in the preceding session the bishop of Selymbria was called Sergius, whereas now he is called George, and so forth. Constantinople, which up to this point had been called “the great,” is now called “great-sounding” (*magnisona*).

59. Sophronius’s synodical letter is read first. —First the emperor and the synod said: “Let the proceedings formerly held be reread.” And they were reread.

[Note: [Col. 1032D] If even one session, the tenth, had been read carefully, this reading must have greatly wearied both the reader and the hearers.]

Then they said: “Let the synodical letter of Sophronius of Jerusalem be read.”

[Note: [Col. 1032D] If it were all printed here, it would easily occupy twenty-five pages.]

And the book containing it was brought out, which Agatho, the lector-notary,

[Note: [Col. 1032D] The notaries who performed the readings are variously and carefully named in the different sessions. This Agatho is said to have been the lector and to have written the original Acts. See no. 104.]

reread in these words:

[Col. 1033A] “To the most holy and most blessed lord of all, my brother and fellow minister, Sergius, archbishop and patriarch of Constantinople, Sophronius, unworthy servant of the holy city of Christ our God. Pope, pope! Most blessed one, how great is the grace, repose, and length of life that I now enjoy—how much more pleasing to me than before, since I . . . rose from dung and dust . . . to the pontifical see . . . Clerics, monks, laymen, and all the citizens violently compelled and tyrannically forced me.”

After a lengthy prologue there follows a very long profession of faith, containing extended explanations of the mysteries of the most holy Trinity, the Incarnation, and creation, as well as a catalogue of all the heretics from Simon Magus to John, Sergius, Thomas, and Severus; the last four are said still to be living and to be Syrians by nationality.

[Note: [Col. 1033C] I have been unable to discover who those John, Sergius, and Thomas were who lived in Sophronius’s time and were declared heretics; nor did Sophronius add what heresy they taught.]

He says:

[Col. 1033B] “I accept the Fifth Synod, which first cast out the madman Origen.”

[Note: [Col. 1033D] In the genuine Acts of the Fifth Synod, Origen’s condemnation is not found. Thus Halloixius replied in his book *Origen Defended*. Natalis, *On the Third Century*, dissertation 16, section 2, answered that those Acts were mutilated and appealed to the testimony of Sophronius mentioned above. But this testimony itself is suspect: Sophronius anathematizes two Origens—Origen and another Origen, who is also called Adamantius. Which Origen was condemned by the Fifth Synod? Origen? Or the other Origen, who is also called Adamantius? Natalis likewise appeals to this Sixth Synod and to the confirmatory letter of Leo II. But concerning this, see no. 93.]

“. . . I name the persons themselves whom I anathematize and condemn, not merely with tongue and mouth, but with heart and spirit . . . Let Simon Magus always be anathema and catathema . . . and Origen, the other Origen who is also Adamantius . . . Didymus and Evagrius, the most wicked leaders of the follies of Origen . . . I anathematize and catathematize all these in soul, heart, mouth, and mind, in prayer and words . . . Receive kindly, spiritually, and joyfully the bearers of this letter, Leontius the deacon . . . the chancellor and chief notary of our secretariat, and the brother Polyeuctus . . . and send them back to us quickly, rejoicing and exulting that they have been deemed worthy to see such a bishop of the Byzantines . . . Pray for me, most holy brother!”

[Col. 1033C] 60. Whether it is genuine. —Three things would now have to be examined: first, whether that letter is orthodox; second, whether all those whom Sophronius anathematized really taught some heresy; third, whether that letter is genuinely the work of Saint Sophronius. On this occasion the synod said absolutely nothing about the letter. Although it will elsewhere call it Catholic, it never asserted that it was genuine. Therefore, it will be permissible to fear that it may perhaps be spurious. There are reasons for apprehension.

1. That letter is said to have been written to Sergius in the year 632, but it was first produced publicly in the year 681, so that it might be examined to determine whether it was Catholic.

2. The letter bears no indication from which it might appear that it was composed at some council.

[Col. 1033D] [Note: The Greek Theophanes, who died at the beginning of the ninth century, reports: “Sophronius of Jerusalem, having gathered the bishops over whom he presided, condemned the doctrine of the Monothelites and sent the synodical proceedings to Sergius, bishop of Constantinople, and to the bishop of Rome.” But throughout the entire period in which Sophronius was patriarch of Jerusalem, Honorius governed the Roman Church. See no. 9 and the Bollandists, in the Life of Saint Sophronius, under March 11. Theophanes is said not to have been an exact writer.]

The author indicates that he had only recently been raised to the see and was communicating his faith to Sergius as his senior, expecting to be instructed by him. But it is not credible that Sophronius would have written so humbly to Sergius, who at that time was merely suspected concerning the faith.

3. Stephen, bishop of Dor, was indeed sent by Sophronius to Rome, and explained the Monothelites’ efforts orally and in writing; nevertheless, he seems neither to have brought nor to have known of any synodical letter of Sophronius.

[Note: [Col. 1034D] Sophronius had personally gone to Sergius, perhaps before he became a bishop; afterward, when he was already patriarch, he sent Stephen to Rome. Theophanes may perhaps have had these efforts of Sophronius in mind.]

4. Sophronius’s letter is addressed to Sergius alone. It contains no indication that it was sent to Rome, although a synodical letter ought above all to have been sent there.

61. Three other books published by Macarius are read out. —After the aforementioned synodical letter had been read, “the emperor [Col. 1034B] and the synod said: We have now been informed of what was read from the synodical documents. Let the Roman legates say whether they still have other texts of the holy Fathers.” The Romans replied: “We still have others, but those brought are sufficient.”

Then the legates informed the emperor and the synod that other writings by Macarius and Stephen in favor of one will were still stored in the patriarchate of Constantinople, and earnestly requested that they be brought and read. “George the deacon and chartophylax was asked by the emperor and the synod whether this was true; he affirmed it. Accordingly, he was ordered to produce those writings. He immediately went out and quickly returned, bringing two codices and a paper quire, and said: ‘These codices, my lord, and the paper quire that is with them, were found in the imperial house called Philippicus,

[Col. 1034C] in a lodging belonging to the monastery of Christopolis, together with various other codices.’”

[Note: [Col. 1034D] I am surprised that the legates of Saint Agatho knew that the manuscripts of Macarius and Stephen were hidden there. Who, I ask, had concealed them there? Who had disclosed this to the Romans? Indeed, why had Macarius not openly produced them, since they were so strongly favorable to him?]

“These two books, together with the paper quire, are recognized as the little works of Macarius and Stephen both from the handwriting of the monk Stephen and from their superscription.”

[Note: [Col. 1034D] If what is to be said about the letters of Honorius was interpolated into the Acts, suspicion may consequently arise that the intricate account we are now considering was inserted by the interpolator so that the fraud concerning the letters of Pope Honorius, soon to be produced and condemned, would be noticed less readily.]

“. . . Antiochus the notary read the paper quire . . . afterward the first codex, entitled: ‘Sermon Acclaimed by Macarius to the Emperor Constantine.’”

The abbot Theophanes of Sicily—and therefore a Latin—related that this sermon had been sent by Macarius both to Sardinia and to Rome and to other places.

[Note: [Col. 1034D] From this sermon the following assertion of Macarius has been inserted into the Acts: “They absolutely condemned and anathematized all who asserted one will of the Lord; one of these was Honorius the Roman, who most explicitly preached one will.” But this bare assertion of Macarius proves nothing; otherwise it would follow that Pope Honorius had already been condemned and anathematized before this synod—certainly not by another ecumenical council, nor by any pope. By whom, then? Meanwhile, if it is genuine, it is very surprising that the Romans made no reply to it.]

The emperor said: “We do not know that we received that sermon from Macarius. But he presented us with certain papers, which until now we have neither reread.”

[Note: [Col. 1035D] Among those papers the letters of Pope Honorius are to be found. In the meantime, patience is necessary until the bundle is unrolled.]

“But in the next session we shall produce them . . . Now let the other codex of Macarius be read, entitled: ‘Sermon Sent by Macarius to Luke the Presbyter and Monk in Africa . . .’”

The reading continued for a long time. Then six passages extracted from these codices of the heretic Macarius were produced, each asserting one will. In addition, propositions likewise asserting one will were gathered from the books of the heretics Themistius, Apollinarius, and Anthimus. All these passages are inserted in the Acts.

62. The emperor withdraws from future sessions. —At the end of this eleventh session the emperor announced that he would no longer attend the council and appointed two patricians and two former consuls in his place as future presidents of the synod. Meanwhile, the following sessions, which contain the condemnation of Honorius, took place in the same round-domed hall, or imperial palace, in which the earlier sessions had been held.

63. Session 12. Papers and three codices sent by the emperor. —Session 12 is said to have been held on March 20

[Note: [Col. 1035D] The Greek reads “22.”]

in the ninth indiction, and so forth. Eighty-six Greek bishops are named as present; the Church of Constantinople is called “great-sounding” and “apostolic.”

“The chief notary said . . . Before the curtain stands the most glorious patrician and quaestor John, sent by the emperor, carrying certain papers, and we submit the matter for consideration.”

The most glorious judges (*ἄρχοντες*, “rulers”) and the holy synod said: “Let the proceedings formerly held be read.” And they were read. They said: “Let John the quaestor enter.” And he entered.

John [Col. 1035C] the quaestor said: “When the emperor had inquired into the papers which, as he recalled, had been handed to him by Macarius on the previous day, he gave me the papers and booklets which I am presenting, ordering me to deliver them to your holy synod, which must examine them. The emperor also informs you that until this time he has not read them, nor even their superscription.

[Note: [Col. 1035D] The emperor, who had eagerly attended the preceding sessions, seems on this occasion to have been rather incurious. Moreover, since he neither inspected the papers received from Macarius nor read their superscription, he could be less certain that these were the very papers which Macarius had formerly handed over.]

But he found them among the booklets now present. He has sent all these booklets, together with the papers, sealed, as you see.”

The judges and synod said: “Let the papers and booklets brought by John the Quaestor be received.”

The papers were handed over. They bore a wax seal displaying the emperor’s monogram; likewise, the aforementioned codices also bore the same seal.

[Note: [Col. 1036D] What painstaking care, whether to avoid fraud or to commit it! See no. 46 and no. 49, note.]

. . .

[Col. 1036A] 64. The first codex is read out. —“The judges and synod said: Let John the Quaestor return to his duties, and let the aforementioned papers be read.”

The notary read the first codex, entitled: “Sermon Acclaimed by Macarius to the Emperor Constantine.” When the reading had proceeded a little, they said: “That sermon was already read in the preceding session.”

[Note: [Col. 1036D] That is, the sermon mentioned at no. 61 as having been sent to Rome, Sardinia, and elsewhere; yet it now exists nowhere in its entirety, so that it can be examined.]

“Let the paper found with that codex be read . . .”

The paper was read in part and judged not to pertain to the present matter. Accordingly,

65. (The second codex, or Sergius’s letter to Cyrus, where repeated mention is made of Mena’s letters to Vigilius and likewise of Vigilius’s letters to the emperors.) —The second codex was read. In it was a letter of Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, to Cyrus, bishop of Phasis, of the following tenor:

[Col. 1036B] “It has indeed become clear to us, etc.”

In this letter Sergius is said to have been asked by Cyrus whether there are one or two wills and operations in Christ, and to have replied: “Nothing concerning this has been defined in the councils. Saint Cyril of Alexandria said in some of his writings that there is one operation of Christ. Moreover, Mena, archbishop of this imperial city, likewise asserted in an address delivered to Pope Vigilius that there is one will and one operation of Christ . . . We took care to have that address transcribed, and ordered it to be sent to you with this letter of ours, etc., etc.”

[Note: [Col. 1036D] If this letter is genuine, Sergius of Constantinople appears to have been the first to publish the false letter of Mena. See no. 18.]

“When the reading of this letter was finished, Mena of Constantinople’s address to Pope Vigilius was read. After it had been read, the judges and synod said: ‘The reading of this address was superfluous, since it is fabricated and false, nor is it found in the registers of the letters written by Mena at Constantinople.’

[Note: [Col. 1036D] The Greeks rejected the address of Mena, who died in 552, as spurious because it was not extant in the Constantinopolitan registers in the year 681. Would it not likewise have been fair to investigate whether both letters of Honorius, on account of which that pope was to be condemned as a heretic, existed in the Roman archives?]

But it was also found in the third session that three false quires had been sewn into the first book of the Acts of the Fifth Synod, containing this address.”

From the same codex two letters of Vigilius to Justinian and the empress were read.

“The judges and synod said: ‘In session 3 we already declared these to be fabricated.’” See nos. 36 and 37. Then,

66. (The third codex, containing Sergius’s letter to Honorius on the first origin of the Monothelites.) —The third codex was read. It began as follows:

“Copy of the letter

[Note: [Col. 1036D] It is certain that Sergius wrote some letter to Honorius, but it is disputed whether this copy is genuine. According to Berti, Book XXVI, chapter 11, no. 21, Desirant denied it. The first reason for doubt may be that this copy was taken from the codex of the forger Macarius, although it is said to have been compared with another copy taken from the patriarchate. The second is that it relates various suspicious circumstances, as will become clear in the course of the account. Meanwhile, all who have hitherto written about the origin of the Monothelites have drawn from this copy.]

of Sergius, archbishop of Constantinople, to Honorius, pope of Rome.”

[Col. 1037A] “Some time ago, when the Emperor Heraclius was conducting the expedition

[Note: [Col. 1037C] Pagi assigned this to the year 622 of the Christian era.]

against the Persians, he came into Armenia,

[Note: [Col. 1037C] For greater clarity and brevity, here and elsewhere I have altered certain words, but not the meaning, as will be clear to anyone making the comparison.]

where Paul the One-Eyed, a follower of Severus’s heresy, presented him with an apology on its behalf. That emperor, being exceedingly learned in divine doctrines, completely defeated the aforementioned Paul in debate; on that occasion he said that there is one operation in Christ.

After some time the same Heraclius came into the region of the Laz people, and there, in the presence of Cyrus—then bishop of Phasis, now bishop of Alexandria—he mentioned his dispute with Paul.

[Note: [Col. 1037C] Thus the Emperor Heraclius would have been the first author of the Monothelites; yet he shifted the blame onto Sergius, no. 14.]

Cyrus replied to Heraclius that he did not know correctly whether one or two operations should be preached concerning Christ. Accordingly, at the emperor’s command, Cyrus questioned us, Sergius.

[Note: [Col. 1037C] According to Saint Maximus, to be cited shortly, neither Heraclius, nor Paul the One-Eyed, nor Theodore, but Sergius appears to have been the first and principal author of the Monothelites.]

For this reason we informed him by letter of what lay within our knowledge

[Col. 1037B] (see the preceding note). We also added an address which Mena, patriarch of this city, had delivered to Pope Vigilius while he was present here.

[Note: [Col. 1037D] The synod declared that this address was fabricated, no. 65. But this letter of Sergius also appears suspect, no. 67.]

We, however, defined nothing, as may be recognized from our letter to Cyrus, which we enclose.”

[Note: [Col. 1037D] When Saints Maximus and Pyrrhus debated, as in nos. 11 and 18, they seem to have been unaware of this letter of Sergius. Pyrrhus asserted that Sophronius, because he had raised the question of the operations at an inopportune time, was the first occasion of the scandal. Maximus replied:

“When Sergius wrote to Theodore of Pharan, also sending him the booklet which he says belonged to Mena, urging him to disclose what he thought about one will and one operation—and Theodore replied, approving it—where then was Sophronius? Or when he wrote to Paul the One-Eyed, a follower of Severus, also sending him Mena’s booklet and that of Theodore of Pharan, with his approval? Or where was he when he wrote to George Arsas, the Paulianist, asking him to send authorities concerning one operation? Or when he replied to Cyrus, bishop of Phasis, concerning one operation, after Cyrus had asked him, also sending him the aforementioned booklet of Mena? What, then? After Sergius had corrupted the greater part of the Church, if blessed Sophronius humbly admonished him, throwing himself at his feet and, by the Passion of Christ, entreating Sergius not to renew the voice of the heretics—was he himself the author of this scandal?”

Behold, Saint Maximus and Pyrrhus say nothing about Heraclius; and Sergius—or whoever the author is—mentions Heraclius but is silent about Theodore of Pharan. Heraclius, however, shifted all the blame onto Sergius, as though he had been entirely unaware of the fateful letter of Sergius in which Heraclius himself is said to be the author.]

“And from that time this controversy was wrapped in silence.”

“After a short time—though the author nowhere determines the interval [Note: [Col. 1038C] The author nowhere specifies the length of time.]—Cyrus, patriarch of Alexandria, piously and moderately exhorted those who in Alexandria were divided by the various heresies of Eutyches, Dioscorus, Severus, and Julian, to join the Catholic Church. After many discussions and labors, which he undertook with the greatest prudence and most useful administrative skill in this matter, he achieved what he was striving for . . . The entire people of Alexandria, almost the whole of Egypt and the Thebaid and Libya and the remaining Egyptian provinces, have now all become one; they have come together under one head concerning one operation of Christ [Note: [Col. 1038C] It is not plausible that all the Catholics peacefully consented to such a union. Moreover, Libya and Egypt and Alexandria were nearer to Rome [Col. 1038D] than to Constantinople; if so great a change had occurred throughout Egypt and Libya, it would immediately have been reported to Rome and to Pope Honorius.].

“When these matters had proceeded in this way, the monk Sophronius—who, as we have learned merely by report, has now been elected bishop of the Jerusalemites [Note: [Col. 1038D] This letter, then, would have been written at the very beginning of the time when Sophronius was elevated to the episcopate of Jerusalem, and therefore no later than the year 632. Since this matter concerned Sophronius personally, it is strange that it was nowhere mentioned either by him or by his legate Stephen (see notes 8 and 9).]—for we have not yet received his synodical letter in the customary manner [Note: [Col. 1038D] The synodical letter of Sophronius that now survives appears to be fictitious, although sufficiently Catholic; see note 59—was then staying in Alexandria with the most holy Pope Cyrus. He opposed the doctrine of one operation. When Cyrus produced for him the holy Fathers confessing one operation and added that the holy Fathers had often concealed some article of faith in order to win more souls [Note: [Col. 1038D] Saint Maximus, cited in note 22, proved this false. The example of Saint Basil the Great is commonly brought forward; but it is spurious (see the Dissertation on Saint Basil the Great, nos. 61 and 173–175).], Sophronius in no way accepted this accommodation.

“Accordingly, he came to us with Cyrus’s letter [Col. 1038B] and also delivered a speech before us, earnestly pressing us to suppress the expression ‘one operation’ from the aforementioned chapters, which we regarded as harsh . . . We exhorted him to produce for us testimonies of the holy Fathers affirming two operations, but he was completely unable to do so [Note: [Col. 1038D] If Sergius truly wrote this, he lied egregiously (see note 8).].

“To suppress all contention, we wrote to Cyrus that, after he had made peace with the heretics and received them into the Church, he should henceforth allow no one to put forward either one or two operations. The reason was that, although the expression ‘one operation’ had been used by some of the holy Fathers, it was nevertheless new and disturbed certain people who thought that it was being advanced in order to abolish Christ’s natures. Likewise, the expression ‘two operations’ offended many, since none of the holy Fathers had used it; [Col. 1039A] moreover, it implied that in Christ there were two wills opposed to each other [Note: [Col. 1039C] Christ’s human will perfectly obeyed the divine will and subjected to it the appetite of his flesh, which was indeed innocent but naturally avoided suffering.], two agents with contrary purposes . . .

“Finally, Sophronius promised us that henceforth he would raise no question concerning one or two operations [Note: [Col. 1039D] It is not plausible that Saint Sophronius made this promise to Sergius; consequently, it is also not plausible that Sergius, while Sophronius was alive, reported these matters to Rome, where their falsity could easily have been demonstrated.]. But he asked us for a written letter which he could also show to others. We willingly gave it to him [Note: [Col. 1039D] As far as I know, this letter was never produced, not even by Stephen, Sophronius’s legate, who traveled to Rome three times in this matter (see note 8).], and Sophronius departed with it.

“Recently, however, the emperor wrote to us from the city of the Edessenes [Note: [Col. 1039D] Heraclius stayed at Edessa in 628; Sergius would have reported these matters to the pope in 632. How, then, could he have written, ‘Recently, when . . .’?], asking us to send him the passages of the Fathers cited by Mena in his address to Vigilius in support of one operation. We did so. At the same time, we warned the emperor that it was not necessary to investigate one and two operations. For this reason we received from the emperor a reply containing matters appropriate to his serenity, which is directed by God [Col. 1039B] [Note: [Col. 1039D] If it is said that the whole story concerning these codices was interpolated into the Acts, then Sergius’s letter becomes even more suspect.].

“I considered it necessary to report all these matters individually to your Blessedness in this letter, which we ask you to read and to supplement if you discover that anything is missing [Note: [Col. 1039D] That Sergius was a Monothelite is established elsewhere, especially by the Roman synod held under Saint Martin I, at which, in the third secretariat, Sergius’s letter to Cyrus was read. Otherwise he should not have been condemned as a heretic on account of the aforementioned letter, in which Sergius submits himself to the judgment of the Roman Church.] and to inform us of whatever seems appropriate.”

The day and year in which the letter was written are not added.

### 67. Sergius’s Letter to Honorius Appears Suspect

This letter of Sergius is sufficiently submissive in its epilogue; nevertheless, at least in its earlier part, it seems to me suspect on account of various indications already suggested here and there. The fact that a copy of this letter was read in some codex sent by the emperor to the Sixth Synod in 681 is not sufficient. For that codex also contained the letters of Mena to Vigilius, of Vigilius to Justinian, and of Vigilius to Theodora; nevertheless, the synod twice declared those three letters fictitious. Therefore that codex does not possess sufficient authority. Indeed, because the aforementioned letter of Sergius to Honorius was taken from that suspect codex and inserted into the Acts of the Sixth Synod, it may for that reason alone be regarded as suspect unless its authenticity is proved from another source.

### 68. The Reply-Letter of Honorius to Sergius

“Likewise, a copy of the letter of Pope Honorius to Sergius was reread from the same codex.”

If a copy of Honorius’s letter was read from the codex, then this copy was nothing other than a transcript of a letter whose original had not yet been produced. Furthermore, if Sergius’s letter to Honorius is suspect, the same will apply to Honorius’s reply to Sergius, which was likewise produced from the aforementioned suspect codex. We shall see in due course that the synod itself did not yet place complete confidence in those codices.

### 69. The Original Letters of Sergius and Honorius Are Produced

“The judges and the synod said: ‘The registers and dogmatic writings of Sergius—whether addressed to Honorius, to Cyrus, or to Sophronius—and of Honorius to Sergius must be brought before us. They are stored in the library of this patriarchate, so that they may be compared with the booklets delivered to the emperor by Macarius and now read.’

“George the librarian said: ‘I shall go immediately, and whatever I can find I shall bring with me.’ Three bishops, together with secretaries, were also sent to ask Macarius whether the two booklets and the paper quires really were Macarius’s writings, and whether the three codices just read had in fact formerly been delivered by Macarius to the emperor.

“The bishops found Macarius in a small cell of the patriarchate. Macarius replied: ‘The two booklets and the paper quire are my writings, and the three remaining codices [Note: [Col. 1040C] It was from these codices that the synod first learned of the copy of Honorius’s letter to Sergius; where Macarius obtained it is not stated. Soon another letter of Honorius to Sergius will be disclosed. Meanwhile, these excessive evasions [Col. 1040D] increase my suspicion.] I delivered to the emperor last year.’

“The bishops reported Macarius’s aforesaid reply to the synod. Likewise, George the deacon and chartophylax brought from the library of the patriarchate whatever codices or registers he could find, containing the letters of Sergius, Honorius, and Sophronius [Note: [Col. 1040D] I am surprised that Sophronius’s very long letter was still found in the Constantinopolitan patriarchate, since note 57 stated that it had not been accepted by Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople.].”

Accordingly—

### 70. Sergius’s Letters and Honorius’s Authentic Letter Are Compared

“1. From a codex, or register, of various letters of Sergius, the letter of Sergius to Cyrus was reread. It was compared with Macarius’s appendix, which had been brought by John the quaestor, and it agreed.

“2. From another codex [Note: [Col. 1040D] The title of this codex is not recorded.] the letter of Sergius to Pope Honorius was read. It was compared with Macarius’s codex, and it agreed.

“3. Likewise, George the deacon and chartophylax produced the authentic Latin letter of Honorius . . . to Sergius, together with its interpretation [Note: [Col. 1040D] This interpretation would have been in the Greek language, although neither Honorius nor his secretary would have produced it (see note 19). The original letter would have been Latin, a language which the Fathers are said not to have understood; nevertheless, on the testimony of one John of Porto that the Greek copy agreed with the Latin text, they condemned their superior, Honorius, while the legates of Pope Agatho remained silent about everything? Let Apella the Jew believe it. Moreover, the letter itself, as it is read inserted in the Acts, bears signs of adulterine origin (notes 23–25).] and it was compared [Note: [Col. 1040D] It is not clearly stated whether the comparison was made with the Greek interpretation or with Macarius’s codex. Moreover, the Latin letter itself, together with the Greek interpretation and Macarius’s codex, was later burned by order of this council (nos. 74 and 76).]. The same Latin letter was compared by John, bishop of Porto, legate of the Roman synod, and it agreed.”

Nothing is reported concerning Sophronius’s letter.

### 71. Judgment on Them Is Deferred

“The judges said: ‘When the synod has learned what has now been read and compared—the letters of Sergius, Honorius, and Sophronius [Note: [Col. 1041D] The writer of these Acts does not remember that Sophronius’s letter was compared; nevertheless, it will be judged Catholic in note 73—let it state what it thinks.’

“The synod replied: ‘Concerning the registers of the letters written by Sergius, the authentic letter of Honorius, and also the synodical letters of Sophronius that have now been read, we shall speak on another day’ [Note: [Col. 1041D] The following is then added: ‘The judges, having been ordered by the emperor, asked the synod whether Macarius, if he should repent, could be restored to his former rank; the synod replied in the negative. Likewise, the bishops subject to the see of Antioch requested that a new bishop of Antioch be elected; this election was similarly deferred to the following session.’].”

### 72. Session 13. Honorius’s First Letter Is Condemned as Heretical

Session 13, in which Pope Honorius is said to have been condemned for the first time, was held on 28 March. Eighty-three Greek bishops are named as present; the Constantinopolitan Church is called “great-sounding” and apostolic.

“The judges and the synod said: ‘Let the previous Acts be reread.’ And they were read. The judges admonished the synod to deliver the sentence promised earlier.

“The synod said: ‘We have examined the letters of Sergius to Cyrus and to Honorius, and likewise the reply of Honorius to Sergius . . . We reject them as heretical. We decree that the names also of those whose impious doctrines we abhor must be expelled from the holy Church of God: namely, Sergius of Constantinople, Cyrus of Alexandria, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople, then also Theodore of Pharan, all of whose persons Agatho mentions in his petition and expels as those who thought contrary to our orthodox faith; we likewise decree that they be subjected to anathema. In addition to these, Honorius also, etc.’”

Thus it is plainly implied that Saint Agatho did not subject Honorius to anathema, nor notify the Greeks that he was to be investigated or condemned.

### 73. Pope Honorius Is Condemned as a Heretic. Was There Sufficient Cause for Condemning Honorius?

“In addition to these, we judge that Pope Honorius also must be expelled from the Church and struck with anathema, because we have found from writings made by him to Sergius [Note: [Col. 1041D] Up to this point, only Honorius’s first letter to Sergius had become known; therefore it was on account of this letter, and not the second, that Honorius was condemned.] that he followed Sergius’s opinion in everything . . . We have judged Sophronius’s synodical letters to be orthodox.”

From this it is again clear:

1. Until that time Honorius had been condemned by no one, either as a heretic or as a supporter of heresy.

2. The letter of Honorius on account of which he was anathematized had now been discovered for the first time, apparently by chance [Col. 1041D]; consequently, it had remained hidden for more than forty years. When, more than forty years earlier, murmuring by certain Greeks against Honorius began to arise, Pope John IV, in letters sent to the emperor, defended the position that nothing heretical had been asserted in Honorius’s letter. Why, I ask, did none of the succeeding patriarchs ever produce Honorius’s letter or appeal to it?

When the writings of Macarius, patriarch of Constantinople, were produced, he was first asked whether those writings were his. How much more ought Pope Honorius to have been questioned, or sufficiently proved, to be the true author of the aforesaid letter produced at this synod?

But someone will say: “The pope was already dead, and therefore could not be questioned.”

I reply: Then he should not have been condemned either, especially since he had already been acquitted long before.

Another will reply: “John, bishop of Porto, compared the authentic Latin letter of Honorius,” as stated in note 70.

I answer: How is it established that the Latin letter which, as is said, was taken from the Constantinopolitan patriarchate and shown to John was authentic? But let it have been authentic. The judges nevertheless, as is supposed, did not understand it. One John testified that the Latin letter agreed with the copy translated into Greek; and let us grant that this Greek copy was heretical. But is one witness sufficient to condemn a pope—one who was dead and had previously been acquitted?

What, I ask, did the bishop of Porto testify? That the Latin letter agreed with the Greek interpretation, or with the codex of Macarius the forger?

Since numerous other fictitious documents had already been produced from the Constantinopolitan patriarchate, how could Honorius, already dead, be condemned merely because a letter had been found in that patriarchate under his name, written forty years earlier and containing an opinion favorable to heresy [Note: [Col. 1042D] Many authors defend the position that neither of Honorius’s letters contains a definitely heretical meaning; therefore Pope Honorius was innocently condemned as a heretic by a general council. I prefer to say that the Acts, or history, of this council were largely interpolated, although it is difficult to distinguish each spurious portion from what is genuine.]?

How did it happen that the legates of Pope Agatho consented to such a condemnation, when they had been instructed to permit no innovation?

### 74. The Case of Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter Is Examined Again

After Honorius had been condemned, the judges asked the synod that an investigation be made in the patriarchate to determine whether, besides the letters of Sergius, Honorius, and Sophronius, there remained writings of Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople, Cyrus of Alexandria, and Theodore of Pharan, which likewise ought to be examined [Note: [Col. 1042D] The same men reported the emperor’s response: that the suffragan bishops and clergy of the see of Antioch should, according to customary practice, elect a new patriarch to be presented to the emperor.].

The synod considered this unnecessary, since the heretical teaching of these men was manifest to everyone, and Pope Agatho had clearly shown that they held the same views as Sergius, who began [Note: [Col. 1042D] This agrees with the statements of Saint Maximus, who asserted that Sergius was the principal promoter of the error.] to introduce a new expression into the Church.

The judges insisted on a new and more exact examination. George the librarian went, searched, returned, and said:

“I found a letter of Cyrus, written by the bishops of Phasis to Sergius of Constantinople fifty-six years earlier, in the fourteenth indiction; another letter of Cyrus, patriarch of Alexandria, to the same Sergius, together with copies of the agreement made between the Theodosians and Cyrus; a letter of Theodore of Pharan to Sergius of Arsenoë and various other books of the same Theodore; likewise interpretations of various patristic testimonies.

“I also removed from this library six other books containing the writings of Pyrrhus of Constantinople, most of them written in Pyrrhus’s own hand. Likewise, I produced a register of various letters of Paul of Constantinople to Theodore the pope, and three prosphonetic writings of Paul—that is, acclamatory volumes addressed to the emperor Constans.

“Also [I found writings] of Peter, who after Paul was raised to the patriarchate of this city; likewise a register of various letters containing his dogmatic letter to Pope Vitalian.

“The synod said: ‘Let all these be reread in order.’”

Antiochus the notary read first the two letters of Cyrus to Sergius and the copy of the agreement [Note: [Col. 1043D] These were inserted in full into the Acts; I omit them for the sake of brevity, so as not to increase the readers’ tedium excessively. Great patience was surely required of those who translated the complete Acts from Greek into Latin. Two different Latin editions exist; perhaps because of Honorius?].

Then he read the codex of Theodore of Pharan to Sergius of Arsenoë, along with five different fragments from one discourse asserting one operation, and six other fragments from another discourse by the same author.

He also read a fragment from the dogmatic volume of Pyrrhus and another fragment from Paul of Constantinople’s letter to Theodore the pope [Note: [Col. 1043D] These fragments too were inserted into the Acts.]. The letter of Peter of Constantinople to Pope Vitalian was likewise read.

While the same letter, containing various statements of the Fathers, was being read, the legates of Saint Agatho said:

“The patristic statements produced in this letter of Peter that is now being reread have been truncated by Peter himself in order to prove one operation.”

The judges and the synod said:

“The patristic statements have been truncated; the reading of the rest of the letter shall not continue.”

The synod added:

“Pope Agatho rightly and justly expelled from his petition Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, the patriarchs of this city [Note: [Col. 1043D] Sergius is omitted both in the Greek and in the Latin editions, evidently because he had already been condemned together with Honorius (note 72)], as well as Theodore of Pharan and Cyrus of Alexandria . . . We too decree that they be expelled from the sacred diptychs and subjected to anathema, and we abhor and declare that their writings, as full of impieties, ought to be abolished [Note: [Col. 1043D] Meanwhile, they had already been inserted into the Acts, which were to be published throughout the world.].”

### 75. Their Successors Are Judged Catholic and Placed in the Diptychs

“The judges continued to insist that the letters of the later patriarchs of Constantinople—namely, Thomas, John, and Constantine—also be produced [Note: [Col. 1043D] Theodore succeeded Constantine, the man mentioned in note 28. He had been deposed shortly before this synod but was restored in 682. In the Acts he is mentioned only once, and then as a forger (note 77). The letter of this Theodore to Pope Donus was not produced.].

“George the chartophylax said: ‘The codex, or register, containing the copies of the synodical letters composed by Thomas, John, and Constantine is here with me. With it there is also an authentic sealed synodical letter composed by Thomas of Constantinople to Pope Vitalian. He had wished to send it to him, but because of the continually imminent incursions of the Saracens, as you know, and the siege that lasted two years [Note: [Col. 1044D] No other historian knows of this siege, or two-year incursion (see note 27). Nevertheless, if these Acts were not otherwise suspect, we ought certainly to believe in that siege on account of George’s testimony given before the full synod.], during which he held the episcopate, he was unable to send it.

“I also searched for booklets composed by various bishops concerning one will, and I set them aside in the library so that they might be presented to you.’

“The judges and the synod said: ‘Let the synodical letters of Thomas, John, and Constantine be read aloud in the hearing of us all.’

“Agatho, lector and notary of the most holy patriarch of Constantinople, received the authentic sealed synodical document of Thomas. The seal attached to it was removed in the presence of everyone, and he read as follows:

“‘To the most holy brother Vitalian, Thomas, unworthy . . .’

“This synodical letter was compared with the register brought by George the librarian, and it agreed without any defect from beginning to end.

“Moreover, the synodical letters of John and Constantine were read. After these had been read from beginning to end, the synod said:

“‘We find that Thomas, John, and Constantine neither thought nor wrote anything contrary to the true faith [Note: [Col. 1044D] The synod had required the librarian to swear an oath over the book of the Gospels that he had concealed no heretical letters of the aforementioned patriarchs. George swore as follows: ‘By these holy Scriptures and by God, who spoke through them, after searching most diligently I did not find any booklets composed and delivered by those three patriarchs—Thomas, John, and Constantine—concerning one will and operation.’ For another oath, see note 77.]. . . Let them therefore be entered in the sacred diptychs . . . But let George the librarian immediately bring us the booklets written by various persons during the time of Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter.’”

### 76. A Second Letter of Honorius Is Found and Burned

“When George had gone out briefly and returned shortly afterward, bringing various papers, he said:

“‘I bring all the booklets . . . and papers relating to the present dogmatic controversy, among which another Latin letter of Pope Honorius was also found, together with its interpretation. I also bring various other dogmatic writings, particularly those of Pyrrhus of Constantinople to Pope John.’

“Only two fragments of this letter of Honorius were read, as indicated in note 26. Finally, the entire letter [Note: [Col. 1044D] It is not stated that this second letter of Honorius was compared or examined by any Latin.] and everything else were handed over to the fire as harmful and burned, as in note 5.

“Until this point it had been unknown that Pope Honorius had written two letters to Sergius concerning the same matter. While this synod was in session, the Greeks first discovered the originals. On account of the first letter, they condemned the recently deceased Pope Honorius as a heretic and expelled him from the Church; after doing so, they burned the original letters and inserted copies into the Acts.

“Who would not be astonished at this procedure [Col. 1045A]? Why would the original letters—if they had been stored in the patriarchate, as previously stated—have been more harmful than their transcripts inserted into the Acts and now published everywhere? Furthermore, in this highly extraordinary and wholly singular case, in which a deceased pope was condemned as a heretic by the Greeks, the original letters ought to have been preserved with the utmost care, so that they might be shown to Pope Agatho or even to the emperor, who was then absent, if they later refused to subscribe to the condemnation.”

### 77. Session 14. The Fictitious Nature of the Letters of Mena and Pope Vigilius Is Confirmed Again. The Patriarchs Paul, Theodore of Constantinople, and Macarius Are Said to Have Falsified the Fifth Synod

Session 14 is said to have been held on 5 April [Col. 1045B], in the ninth indiction. Theophanes [Note: [Col. 1045C] He is called Theophanius by Bede (note 110).], the new patriarch of Antioch, and eighty-seven other Greek bishops are named.

“The judges and the synod said: ‘Let what has already been done be read.’ And it was read. Then they ordered George the librarian to bring again from the patriarchate the two parchment books and the other paper book from which, in sessions 3 and 12, the letters of Mena to Pope Vigilius and of Vigilius to the emperors had been read.

“George was ordered to swear that nothing had meanwhile been changed in those books. He swore and further reported that he had now found another paper codex in which the Acts of the Fifth Synod had been written.

“Then the books first mentioned were again carefully inspected, examined, and compared with the newly discovered paper book and with other ancient codices containing the Acts of the Fifth Synod [Col. 1045C]. It was again discovered that the letters of Mena to Vigilius and of Vigilius to the emperors were fictitious, inserted into the aforementioned books by another hand; and finally those letters were subjected to anathema [Note: [Col. 1045C] They did not exercise such caution in the case of Honorius (see notes 76 and 63, note).].”

After a further examination, it was discovered that several other copies of the Fifth Synod existing outside the patriarchate had been falsified in the same manner. The Greek copies had indeed been corrupted through the agency of the patriarchs Theodore [Note: [Col. 1045D] Theodore, patriarch of Constantinople, appears only here, and as a forger. If he was such, it is surprising that he was restored to the patriarchal chair in 682. Indeed, this Theodore is venerated as a saint by the orthodox Greeks (see Bollandist, preliminary dissertation to volume I of the month of August).] of Constantinople and Macarius of Antioch, while the Latin copies had been promoted by Paul [Col. 1046A], patriarch of Constantinople and a Monothelite [Note: [Col. 1045D] If we admit that the Acts of the Sixth Synod as we now possess them were not corrupted, and therefore that Honorius was truly condemned on account of the letters produced in it, then suspicion arises as to whether one of the aforementioned patriarchs may have composed or falsified the letters of Honorius and deposited those fictitious documents in the Constantinopolitan library.].

The synod exclaimed:

“Anathema to Mena’s booklet to Vigilius; anathema to the two letters of Vigilius to Justinian and Theodora; anathema to those who falsified the Acts of the Fifth Synod [Note: [Col. 1045D] If the Greek and Latin Acts of the Fifth Synod were falsified, as the Sixth Synod asserts, I do no injustice to the Fathers assembled at the Sixth Synod if I fear that even its own Acts may later have been corrupted by others acting with ill will.].”

### 78. Session 15. The Monothelite Polychronius Attempts to Raise a Dead Man and Is Excommunicated

Session 15 is said, both in the Greek and in the Latin text, to have been held in the twenty-eighth year of Constantine, the twenty-second of Heraclius and Tiberius, on 26 April [Note: [Col. 1045D] According to Anastasius, cited in note 81, the Sixth Synod was completed before Easter in the year 681 [Col. 1046C]; therefore it did not continue until 26 April. Nevertheless, Bede too reported that a certain Polychronius was condemned at that synod; see note 110.].

Polychronius, a monk and an aged Monothelite, was admitted to the council. He promised [Note: [Col. 1046D] He also said: ‘If I had been heard this year, we would not have suffered what we suffered in the war with Bulgaria.’ No writer mentions a war in the Roman Empire in the year 680.] that by the power of his faith he would raise a dead man. He placed a document written by himself upon a corpse displayed in a public place in a silver coffin, and for several hours whispered to the dead man, but he did not revive.

Then the people exclaimed:

“Anathema to the new Simon.”

Afterward, when the synod admonished Polychronius to repent and he remained obstinate, he was deposed and anathematized.

### 79. Session 16. The Monothelite Constantine Is Condemned and Excommunicated

Session 16 was held in the twenty-eighth year of Constantine, after his thirteenth consulship, in the twenty-third year of Heraclius and Tiberius, on 9 August [Note: [Col. 1046D] This session was therefore separated from the preceding one by three months. Pagi (in the year 668 and in his Hypatic Dissertation on the Consuls) deduced from these chronological indications that Constantine had been declared Caesar by his father Constans in 654, and Heraclius and Tiberius before 9 August 659; but the venerable Bede, Nicephorus, Theophanes, and others state that Constantine Pogonatus, who died in 685, ruled for seventeen years. Therefore they counted Constantine’s years from the death of Constans. There is also some difficulty concerning the consulship, which by itself began on 1 January.], in the ninth indiction.

The vicar of the bishop of Ravenna and the bishop of Thessalonica, who until then had always sat after the bishops who were legates of the Roman synod, now precede them immediately and are named in addition to the Roman legates and the patriarchs. There are 141 Greek bishops.

No mention is made of the preceding Acts being read.

A certain presbyter of Apamea in Syria, named Constantine, presented himself to the synod and urged that peace be made with the Monothelites. He denied that there were two wills in Christ. When he did not repent after being admonished, he was excommunicated.

### 80. Honorius Is Condemned Again

“Then George, patriarch of Constantinople, proposed:

“‘I and a few bishops under my authority ask that, if possible, the persons not be anathematized by name in the acclamations—namely, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter [Note: [Col. 1046D] No one intervened on behalf of Honorius to prevent his condemnation.].’

“The synod said:

“‘Those who have once been condemned and long ago expelled from the sacred diptychs . . . must also be anathematized by name in the acclamations . . .’

“All exclaimed:

“‘Anathema to the heretics Theodore of Pharan, Sergius, Cyrus, HONORIUS [Note: [Col. 1047D] If the condemnation of Honorius was interpolated elsewhere, his name could easily have been inserted here.], Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter, Macarius, Stephen, Polychronius, and Apargius [Note: [Col. 1047D] I cannot find who this Apargius was.] of Parga.’

“The synod said:

“‘These things are sufficient [Note: [Col. 1047D] This session contains no extensive proceedings worthy of particular notice.]. In the next session we shall establish the definition of faith synodically.’”

### 81. The Report of Anastasius the Librarian Concerning the Sixth Synod

Here I consider it necessary to make a point from Baronius (under the year 681).

Anastasius the Librarian, in his account of Agatho, omitted many matters concerning this Fifth Synod, reporting only six sessions. He stated that the synod was completed before Easter in the year 681, and said nothing about the sessions in which the condemnation of Honorius is now read.

After reporting the condemnation of the heretics carried out there, he added the following:

“Then they removed from the diptychs of the churches the names of the patriarchs, or removed their images from the church, from its doors, or from wherever they could be found—that is, those of Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and also Peter.”

Nothing is added concerning Honorius, whose epitaphs remained, as stated in note 4.

Anastasius added that John, bishop of Porto, on Low Sunday, celebrated a public Mass in Latin before the emperor and patriarch in the church of Hagia Sophia, for the joy of the people or council, and that all, united in one voice, proclaimed in Latin the praises and victories of the most pious emperors [Note: [Col. 1047D] Bede also testified concerning this Mass; see note 110.].

Anastasius likewise did not report the story that the synod had made an agreement with Polychronius concerning the raising of a dead man, as indicated in note 78.

When, according to Anastasius, this synod began is discussed in note 32.

### 82. Session 17. A Decree of Faith Is Issued

Session 17 [Col. 1047C] is entitled:

“Definition of the Orthodox Faith Made in the Royal City during the Reign of the Emperor Constantine.”

It is said to have been held in the twenty-eighth year of Constantine, after his thirteenth consulship, in the twenty-third year of Heraclius and Tiberius, on 11 September, in the tenth indiction. Eighty-six Greek bishops are named [Note: [Col. 1047D] In the preceding session, in which Honorius was condemned, 141 bishops are listed.].

The definition of faith is said to have been read, although it is itself reported word for word in the following session.

### 83. Session 18. A Different Order of Seating. The Decree of Faith, in Which Pope Honorius Is Condemned and the Successors of Peter Are Exalted

Session 18 is said to have been held on 16 September, in the twenty-eighth year of the emperor Constantine, who is again said to have been personally present, and in the twenty-third year of Heraclius and Tiberius [Note: [Col. 1047D] In this year the emperor Constantine removed his brothers Heraclius and Tiberius from imperial authority [Col. 1048D]. Baronius and Pagius think that this occurred after 16 September, because on that date the brothers are still mentioned in the Acts of the Sixth Synod. However, these Acts are not of indisputable reliability (see note 78).], in the tenth indiction.

The order of seating and signing is considerably confused. The following are listed:

1. The legates of Agatho;

2. The patriarchs of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem;

3. The bishop of Thessalonica, the legate from Cyprus, and the legate of Ravenna;

4. John, bishop of Porto, legate of the Roman synod;

5. Two bishops, one from Corinth and the other from Crete;

6. Two Latin bishops who were legates of the Roman synod;

7. The remaining bishops.

The Constantinopolitan Church is called “great-sounding” and apostolic.

The decree of the synod was read aloud, in which the Fathers profess that they follow the five ecumenical synods. They recite the Nicene and Constantinopolitan creeds, and then add:

> “These things would indeed have been sufficient . . . but the devil, having now found instruments suited to his will . . . Theodore of Pharan, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, who were bishops of this imperial city, and moreover Honorius, who was pope of Old Rome [Note: [Col. 1048D] If this passage is omitted, the context is not disturbed at all. Meanwhile, the same could be said of Cyrus.], Cyrus, who was bishop of Alexandria, and Macarius, who was formerly bishop of Antioch, and Stephen [Col. 1048B], his disciple—through these men he did not cease to stir up in the Church the scandals of the heresy of one will and one operation in the two natures of Christ our God . . . sowing the heresy of Apollinaris . . . This holy and ecumenical synod faithfully receives and with uplifted hands embraces the suggestion of the most holy and most blessed pope Agatho, who by name expels those [Note: [Col. 1048D] Among those whom Saint Agatho expelled by name are Cyrus, Sergius, and others, but not Pope Honorius (see no. 48).] who, as was shown earlier, proclaimed and taught one will of Christ . . . Likewise, it also accepts the other synodal suggestion of the 125 bishops assembled under the same most holy and most blessed pope, etc., etc.”

The Fathers subscribed, 174 in number [Note: [Col. 1048D] According to Bede, 150 were present; but at the first session scarcely 50 bishops were present (see nos. 32 and 110).]. First came the three legates of Pope Agatho: “I have subscribed”; then the others in the order given above: “As defining, I have subscribed.” The Jerusalemite legate calls his Church apostolic [Col. 1048C]. The abbots did not subscribe.

### 84. The clause concerning Honorius appears to have been interpolated

I believe that the profession of faith mentioned above is genuine, except for the passage concerning Honorius, which I judge to have been interpolated. For if the holy synod embraced Agatho’s suggestion with uplifted hands; if Pope Agatho expressly forbade anything to be added to his suggestion; how, I ask, would this most obedient synod toward the pope have dared to include among those anathematized in the decree of faith Honorius, the Roman pope, whom Agatho had not named, indeed had positively excluded by teaching that none of his predecessors had erred in the faith? Honorius, whom Pope John IV and Saint Maximus had invincibly demonstrated always to have been Catholic [Col. 1048D]?

Moreover, if the passage concerning Honorius was interpolated here [Col. 1049A], then whatever was scattered above concerning the heresy of Honorius must be considered spurious. Conversely, if the letters produced above under the name of Honorius are either forged or corrupted, the condemnation of the pope must be judged to have been interpolated here, since it would then rest upon no solid foundation. But—

You will object: Agatho’s letter also does not contain Macarius, Stephen, Polychronius, or Constantine, and nevertheless these men were anathematized by name. I reply: these men too had first confessed their heresy with their own mouths in this sixth synod; therefore they could not have been condemned by Agatho. The controversial case of Honorius had already long before been decided in favor of Honorius by Pope John IV.

### 85. Honorius is condemned again after the subscriptions

After the subscriptions mentioned above [Col. 1049B], the emperor is said to have asked whether the decree had been issued with the consent of all; and the synod is said to have exclaimed:

> “We all believe thus . . . This is the faith of the apostles . . . Anathema to Theodore of Pharan; anathema to Sergius and Honorius; anathema to Pyrrhus and Paul; anathema to Cyrus and Peter; anathema to Macarius and Stephen and Polychronius [Note: [Col. 1049C] Polychronius is not named in the decree of faith, no. 83; Constantine, who is read as having been anathematized together with Polychronius in the Acts, no. 79, is omitted here and in the acclamation in the following section.].”
