This entire passage—that after the subscriptions mentioned above the emperor asked again, and that all again exclaimed, “Anathema to Honorius,” and so forth—appears to me not to have been included in the original Acts, but rather to have been attached by another hand. What follows is:

### 86. An acclamatory sermon in which Honorius is condemned again

The synod’s acclamatory sermon, called *prosphoneticus* [Col. 1049C], addressed to the emperor. It contains many praises and expressions of gratitude to the emperor, who was present, for having convened this universal synod in imitation of Constantine the Great, Theodosius, Marcian, and Justinian. Finally it adds:

> “We agree with the dogmatic letters of our most holy father and supreme pope Agatho . . . Christ is perfect man . . . We glorify two wills in Christ . . . We subject to anathema Theodore of Pharan, Sergius and Paul, Pyrrhus together with Peter, who were bishops [Col. 1050A] of Constantinople, and furthermore Cyrus, who was a priest of Alexandria; and with them Honorius, who was bishop of Rome, since he followed them in these matters [Note: [Col. 1049D] It is false that Honorius followed Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter; for he died while Sergius was still alive, and therefore before Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter had become known. Meanwhile, it may be said that the entire passage was interpolated.]. Above all, Macarius, and . . . Stephen . . . and likewise Polychronius, a man childish in understanding and a delirious old man, who professed that he would raise the dead, have been anathematized. Nor should anyone perhaps accuse the most holy pope’s divine zeal, or this synod [Note: [Col. 1049D] If Honorius was condemned, the synod—but not Pope Agatho—could be accused.]. For we have followed the apostolic and paternal traditions both of him [Agatho] and of those before us, and he with us . . . The prince of the apostles was giving us the greatest assistance; for we had him as an imitator and successor of his chair, exhorting and confirming us [Note: [Col. 1049D] If they condemned Pope Honorius, why do they boast so greatly that they had the imitator and successor of Peter’s chair exhorting and confirming them? They should have condemned this man in Honorius.]. Rome of old has offered you the confession prescribed by God [Note: [Col. 1049D] And would Old Rome have offered a heresy suggested by the devil under Pope Honorius? At least Pseudo-Bossuet maintains that Honorius spoke *ex cathedra* of Saint Peter in his letter to Sergius (no. 38).]: [Col. 1050B] the light of doctrine has arisen from the West; paper and ink were seen, and Peter spoke through Agatho. Grant a seal, imperial confirmation, and firmness to what we have defined . . . Know that we have falsified nothing [Note: [Col. 1049D] An unsolicited excuse! If someone maintains that this passage was inserted by the person who introduced the condemnation of Honorius, I will not contradict him.]. . . Rejoice, New Rome, Constantinople! Rejoice, city of Zion, summit of the world! The gates of hell will not prevail against your orthodox empire [Note: [Col. 1049D] The author of the letter does not appear to have been a good prophet. [Col. 1050C] At Constantinople, orthodoxy was formerly suppressed by the Arian patriarchs Eusebius and Eudoxius; by the heresiarchs Macedonius and Nestorius; and recently by the emperors Heraclius and Constantine under the patriarchs Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and others. [Col. 1050D] In 1453 the Turks occupied the temporal dominion.].”

One hundred fifty-three Fathers subscribed. Among them, the legates of Pope Agatho appear first, under these words: “I have subscribed to this *prosphoneticus* petition.”

I judge this acclamation unworthy of the Romans, either entirely spurious or grossly interpolated. Meanwhile, Pope Saint Leo II is said to have sent it to Spain (see nos. 94, 96, and 97).

### 87. Was the entire body of the Acts sent to the five patriarchal Churches?

The Acts add [Note: [Col. 1050D] It is also inserted that, after the acclamation had been made, at the emperor’s recommendation Citonatus, bishop of the Church of Caralis in Sardinia, was admitted to the synod. This Citonatus is read as having subscribed with the others before the acclamation: “As defining, I have subscribed.”]:

> “The synod said: We ask the emperor that copies of the decree that was read [Note: [Col. 1050D] Thus it would have been only the decree of faith reported in no. 83 that was sent to Rome and to the three other patriarchal Churches, and therefore only this decree was confirmed by the pope and received by the others—not the entire body of the Acts, as they now exist.] be delivered to the five patriarchal sees with the imperial signature. The emperor said: We shall piously accomplish this [Note: [Col. 1050D] Yet I am surprised that the Fathers, among whom were the Roman legates, should have entrusted so important a matter to the emperor, a layman.].”

> “It should be known that, as the emperor had promised, he provided copies of the decree signed by him to the five patriarchal sees: to the apostolic see of Saint Peter, that is, to Agatho [Note: [Col. 1050D] On the basis of letters 91 and 92, to be cited below, Pagius and others maintain that the Roman legates were detained by the emperor for a long time before returning to Rome.]; to the apostolic see of the great Church of Constantinople [Col. 1051A] [Note: [Col. 1051C] The Church of Constantinople can in no way be called apostolic.]; to the apostolic see of Saint Mark the Evangelist at Alexandria, through the presbyter Peter; . . . to the see of Antioch, or of the Theopolitans, the great city, through Patriarch Theophanes; to the see of Jerusalem through George, a Sebastean monk, who later became patriarch of Antioch [Note: [Col. 1051C] In the synod of Trullo, said to have been held in 706, George is read as having subscribed as patriarch [Col. 1051D] of Antioch. Yet the Church of Antioch lacked a pastor from 702 to 713 because the Saracens ruled there (see Bollandists, vol. III, July).].”

These final expressions—“it should be known that the emperor, as he had promised, provided . . . through George, who later . . .”—plainly betray an author who wrote the history of the aforesaid council only afterward, or who later enlarged it.

### 88. Honorius is not proved to have been condemned from the Acts alone

Because of this and other critical observations scattered throughout, I judge that the Acts of the council, as they now exist, do not possess irrefragable authority, particularly with respect to the account in those Acts of Pope Honorius as condemned [Col. 1051B]. Thus, if only these Acts of the sixth synod are considered, it is not sufficiently established that Pope Honorius wrote heretical letters, or even that he was in fact anathematized on account of them.

Since, however, it is certain that he died in communion with the holy Church, and that for forty years after his death he continued to possess an unimpaired reputation as an orthodox prelate, he ought not to be deprived of that possession on the strength of Acts so suspect—without even mentioning the incompetence of the judges. Indeed, the honor of the sixth synod is also served if the Acts are regarded as interpolated. But this must now be examined.

## § III. Whether it can be proved from what followed the sixth synod that Pope Honorius was truly condemned

### 89. A letter of the sixth synod sent to the pope condemning Honorius

First, it must be noted that there is a copy of the letter sent by the holy and ecumenical sixth synod to Pope Agatho.

> “The holy council sends greetings in the Lord to the most blessed pope [Note: [Col. 1051D] Throughout the letter Agatho is never called ‘Father.’ The Church of Jerusalem is called apostolic.]. The greatest illnesses, as you know, most blessed one, require the greatest remedies; therefore Christ revealed your revered holiness as a wise physician . . . With the Emperor Constantine leading us [Note: [Col. 1051D] In the decree of faith the bishops subscribed, ‘I define’; the emperor, following last, added, ‘We have consented and subscribed.’], we overthrew the error of impiety . . . As for those who sinned against the faith, we slew them with anathemas in the morning outside the camp of the courts of God [Col. 1052A], as I may say with David [Note: [Col. 1051D] The author of the letter alludes to Psalm 100:8, where it says: ‘In the morning I destroyed all the sinners of the earth.’], according to the sentence previously pronounced against them in your sacred letters [Note: [Col. 1051D] Saint Agatho had certainly pronounced nothing against Honorius.]: Theodore of Pharan, I say, Sergius, Honorius [Note: [Col. 1051D] The Greeks ought to have written to Agatho the Roman at the same time, explaining what sort of Honorius this was.], Cyrus, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter . . . Besides these, Macarius, who was bishop of Antioch, and Stephen his disciple, and Polychronius . . . We did not mock their fall, nor did we rejoice and exult over their madness, nor did we become excessively elated on that account [Note: [Col. 1051D] The author—who corrupted the Acts of the sixth synod and added the name of Pope Honorius to those condemned, or inserted other material out of hatred or favor—could hardly fail to rejoice at his fraud.]. We did not learn to act thus concerning these matters, O venerable head! We did nothing out of favor or hatred, as you may learn from the Acts that were sent to your blessedness [Note: [Col. 1052C] Since, at the end of the synod, no. 87, careful provision was made that the emperor should send the decree of faith to Rome, it is not likely that the synod sent the entire body of the Acts to Saint Agatho and nevertheless added this synodal letter.]. Furthermore, through the legates sent by your holiness and by the Roman synod, who contended in accordance with your instruction [Note: [Col. 1052D] The legates had been ordered to add nothing to the suggestions supplied by the pope and the Roman synod. How, then, did they contend in accordance with their instructions if they consented to the condemnation of Pope Honorius? The case of Macarius, Stephen, and Polychronius is different (see no. 84). Natalis says: The legates were not openly granted the authority to condemn Honorius in the synodal letter, but perhaps this was entrusted to them in private instructions, as is customary in disagreeable affairs. Did Saint Agatho and the Roman synod not dare openly to defend Honorius, for whom Pope John IV and Saint Maximus openly contended?] . . . we greet most warmly the whole fraternity that is with your blessedness. George, bishop of Constantinople: I have subscribed . . . George, of the apostolic see of Jerusalem: I likewise have subscribed . . . Citonatus of the island of Sardinia: I likewise have subscribed for myself and for the synod subject to me.”

Fifty-six bishops are read as having subscribed; among them the three legates of Saint Agatho do not appear. The day and year on which this letter was issued are lacking. It seems to me entirely spurious.

### 90. A public edict by which the emperor confirms the sixth synod and twice condemns Honorius

The second item is the edict of the Emperor Constantine, posted in the third court [Note: [Col. 1052D] The author carefully added the place where the edict was posted, but forgot to add the day and year in which it was issued or displayed.] of the most holy and great church near the palace called Dicymbala.

It is very lengthy and dogmatic. The author [Col. 1052C] calls himself “the most pious emperor,” faithful in Jesus Christ God. Among other things he says:

> “Sacrilegious priests [Note: [Col. 1052D] In this edict he was silent about his father, who had subjected Pope Saint Martin, Maximus, and others to martyrdom.] governed the Churches perversely. They are these: Theodore . . . Sergius . . . and in addition Honorius, who was pope of ancient Rome, a confirmer of this kind of heresy, and who was also his own opponent. Likewise Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, patriarchs of this city; Macarius . . . and Stephen . . . and Polychronius . . . But because we desire to be made equal to those who piously reigned before us from the beginning, and because we burn with zeal for the right faith . . . we convened a holy universal council [Col. 1053A] [Note: [Col. 1053C] The emperor convened bishops from only two patriarchates (see nos. 28 and 29).] . . . We anathematize . . . the heresiarchs and defenders of new doctrines: Theodore, I say . . . Sergius . . . and, in addition, Honorius, pope of Old Rome, who was in every respect their fellow-heretic, associate, and confirmer of heresy; and Cyrus . . . Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter; and besides them Macarius . . . Stephen . . . and Polychronius . . . But if anyone should tamper with this our pious edict, whether bishop, cleric, or monk, he shall be deposed, etc.”

I judge this edict as I did the document in no. 89. In addition:

### 91. A letter of the Emperor Constantine to Pope Leo II

The third item is a letter of the most pious Emperor Constantine to Leo, the Roman pope, sent through those who had been dispatched from there by the surviving Agatho [Note: [Col. 1053C] The men sent by Agatho had returned to Rome either while Agatho was still alive or at least before the emperor had recognized the new pope; for John, bishop of Porto, was one of the three bishops who consecrated Leo II, as Pagius admits [Col. 1053D] (on the year 683, no. 4).]. It was sent on 13 December, in the tenth indiction [Note: [Col. 1053D]

In December of the tenth indiction, that is, in the year 681, Saint Agatho the pope was still alive, as everyone admits, including Pagius (on the year 683, no. 5), who maintains that “December” entered through a scribal error and that the letter was written in the year 682, in a month other than December. But why would the emperor have delayed until 682 sending to Rome the Acts of the synod, which had been completed in 681 around Easter—or at least in September?

If you say, “The entire superscription appears to have been attached by another hand,” I reply: then the place, day, and year in which the aforesaid letter was given are missing, as is even the name of the author who compiled it, since nothing about these matters is added at the end of the letter.]

The place where this letter was written is not specified [Col. 1053B]. In it the author tells Pope Leo how he convened the synod and discovered Pope Agatho’s suggestion to be Catholic. He adds:

> “We admired Agatho’s letter as though it were the voice of the divine Peter himself . . . Only Macarius, together with those whom he drew to himself, defected . . . What need is there for a more extensive account, when these matters are narrated in detail in the Acts, which have been sent to you, so that you will have even the smallest detail of everything that was discussed . . . We have confirmed the decree of faith issued by the synod with our pious edict [Note: [Col. 1053D] I judged this edict spurious (see no. 90).] . . . Be a strong and vigorous man, and gird yourself with the sword of the word . . . stand firm . . . and be ready and eager in spirit to cut off every heretical teaching, just as Peter earlier removed the sense of Jewish hearing, struck with a sword [Col. 1053C] . . . We ask your most sacred Eminence to send without delay an *apocrisiarius*, so that, residing in this city [Note: [Col. 1054C] From this passage Hincmar of Rheims traced the origin of *apocrisiarii* at Constantinople to the fourth century: ‘The office of *apocrisiarius*,’ he says (vol. II, p. 206), ‘began at the time when Constantine the Great built his seat in his own city, which had previously been called Byzantium.’], he may represent your holiness in all ecclesiastical affairs. Farewell, most blessed one! And rise to pray more earnestly for our power. The subscription of the pious emperor: May God preserve you for many years, most holy and most blessed Father.”

This letter does not mention Honorius, but Baronio nevertheless rejected it among the spurious letters, since its style differs greatly from that of the letter indicated in no. 28. I agree with Baronio. The following is next.

### 92. A letter of the same emperor to the Roman synod

The fourth item is a letter of the same pious Emperor Constantine to the synod of the apostolic see at Rome, sent through the same synodal envoys [Note: [Col. 1054D] This title—that it is a letter of the same emperor sent through the same men—suggests an author other than the emperor.]. Its inscription is: “To all the holy synods existing everywhere that belong to the synod of the apostolic see.”

The author of this letter praises the suggestion of the Roman synod composed under Agatho, whom he calls the universal prince of pastors. He adds:

> “We admired Agatho’s letter as though it were the voice of the divine Peter himself. For no one defected except Macarius with his own disciples . . . How you have fallen from heaven, from the priestly height, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning [Note: [Col. 1054D] This letter, like the preceding one, also inserts the claim that the emperor, at the request of the entire synod, sent Macarius and his associates to Rome to be punished by the pope. I do not deny that this occurred, but I did not notice this account in the Acts of the synod.]. . . Our empire has confirmed the definition of this council by pious edicts [Note: [Col. 1054D] I discussed the confirmation of an ecumenical synod by imperial edicts in no. 91. Moreover, this confirmation, said to have been made by the emperor, would again be confirmed by Pope Leo II in no. 93; and Pope Leo’s confirmation, at his request, would be confirmed by a certain particular synod in Spain in nos. 94 and 100, and again by another emperor, Justinian II, in no. 101—if all these documents were genuine.]. . . Farewell, most sacred bishops of piety, and pray for our power.”

In the Greek edition, the year, day, and place in which this letter was issued are not given. Nevertheless, one of the Latin editions adds:

> “Given on 23 December, at Constantinople, in the imperial palace, under the most pious and perpetual Augustus, the Emperor Constantine, in the twenty-ninth year, and in the thirteenth year after his consulship, in the tenth indiction.”

Thus this letter, which likewise does not mention Honorius, would have been issued on 23 December 681. It seems to me spurious, like the preceding letter. The following is next.

### 93. The first confirmatory letter of Pope Leo concerning the preceding documents

The fifth item is a letter sent by the most holy Roman pope to Emperor Constantine, confirming and approving what had been done and defined in the holy and universal sixth council [Note: [Col. 1054D] Whoever has the right to confirm and approve a definition issued by a general council, and strengthened by the emperor—if that is appropriate—does he not also have the right to examine [Col. 1055B] and reject it? Would he not therefore be superior? Thus the definition of the sixth synod would not have possessed irrefragable force unless it had been confirmed by the Roman pontiff [Col. 1055C].]

The pontiff praises the emperor’s zeal and humility, by which the most exalted prince desired to number himself as one of the college of priests. He relates that the legates sent by Agatho in the eighth indiction, during the recently elapsed [Note: [Col. 1055C] It would therefore have to be inferred that this letter was written in the eleventh indiction, that is, in the year 683 after July, indeed after the summer, no. 42. Yet, as we shall soon hear, it is said to have been written in May; therefore it would have been issued in the year 684. But Pope Leo did not sit for more than ten months and seventeen days: he was consecrated on 17 August 682 and died on 3 July 683 (see Pagius, on the year 684, no. 2).] tenth indiction, in the month of July [Note: [Col. 1055C] If they returned during July of the year 682, they therefore returned while the see was vacant—a circumstance the letter nevertheless conceals—and would have been traveling from December 681 until July 682. Constantinople is not so far from Rome. Moreover, it is more probable that the legates, after successfully completing their mission, no. 81, hurried to return to Rome.], returned to Rome with the synodal Acts and the emperor’s letters.

The pope adds:

> “When reviewing the sequence of the synodal proceedings, and demanding with painstaking diligence that each event be set forth, we found that they agree with what the legates of the apostolic see had reported, the written records being in harmony [Note: [Col. 1055C] Anastasius of Nicaea—who lived after the Council of Trullo—reported that the legates, while returning to Rome, were robbed on the road and lost the authentic codex of the Acts of the synod (see Pagius, on the year 686, no. 3). Yet the author of this letter was unaware of that robbery, and no pontiff is recorded as having complained of it.]. We have truly approved this holy sixth synod . . . adding or subtracting nothing from the statutes of orthodox faith . . . But it is also truly worthy and most pleasing to God that the truth of apostolic preaching has resounded throughout the whole world through the edict of Your Most August Piety [Note: [Col. 1055D] Pope Leo could not have written this in the first days after the legates had returned to Constantinople. Moreover, the edict is spurious (no. 92).]. We anathematize and execrate all heresies . . . Arius, Sabellius . . . Origen, also called Adamantius [Note: [Col. 1055D] Here only one Origen is condemned (see no. 59).], Didymus and Evagrius . . . Likewise we anathematize the inventors of the new error: Theodore, bishop of Pharan; Cyrus of Alexandria; Sergius; Pyrrhus; Paul; Peter, more usurpers than bishops of the Church of Constantinople; and also Honorius, who did not enlighten this apostolic Church with the doctrine of apostolic tradition, but attempted to subvert the undefiled faith by profane tradition . . . Likewise we anathematize Macarius, Stephen, and with them Polychronius, a new Simon, as he was rightly called, who promised to raise the dead . . . O holy Mother Church, arise! . . . Behold, your most steadfast son, your defender, the prince . . . The new David, the most steadfast of the Augusti, lives . . . The Churches [Col. 1056A] are now fortified by the chief protection, whereby Your August Benevolence promises, in the Lord’s words and in imitation of Christ: ‘Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.’ May Your royal magnanimity graciously receive Constantine the subdeacon, the bearer of this letter, who recently attended the synod held there as a legate of Agatho [Note: [Col. 1055D] Among the legates of Agatho who subscribed to the council or were present at it, no Constantine the subdeacon is recorded. Nevertheless, in Agatho’s letter mentioned in no. 38, Constantine the subdeacon appears listed among the other papal legates. He must therefore be said not to have reached the synod, prevented by death, illness, or some other cause.].”

“Given on 9 May, in the tenth indiction [Note: [Col. 1055D] At the beginning of the letter it was said that the tenth indiction had recently elapsed.].”

Thus this letter would have been written in the year 682, on 17 May, when Leo II, as even Pagius admits, was not yet pope. Furthermore, the legates are said to have returned to Rome in July [Note: [Col. 1056B] This could be admitted if the synod is said to have been completed at Easter, as in no. 81.], and the pope would not have replied to the emperor until the following May—a delay that appears excessive.

After carefully weighing all these matters, I say with Baronio: the purported letter of Pope Leo to Constantine is forged [Note: [Col. 1056C]

Baronio (on the year 682) includes the following letter, produced from the Floriacensian records:

> “Agatho, bishop, to Saint Edictus, archbishop of Vienne. Your priest Donatus brought us joy in the synod at which nearly one hundred bishops were sitting at Rome by reporting your good health. We have entrusted to him the task of conveying to Your Holiness the account of what happened at Constantinople, as our legates reported it, where you will find that the Antiochene bishop, Macarius, was condemned for his error. When you have read this, most blessed brother, send it to all the bishops of Gaul to be read, avoided, and observed. Know also that Theophanes was ordained in his place. Given on the day before the Kalends of March, under the most pious Constantine Augustus.”

If this simple letter is genuine, it was written in the year 682, on the last day of February. Therefore: first, by that time the legates had already returned; second, a new synod of one hundred bishops had already been held at Rome; third, no bishop was subjected to condemnation at the sixth synod except the Antiochene bishop—therefore not Pope Honorius. Sergius, Pyrrhus, and the others had already been condemned in the Roman synod reported in no. 39. Fourth, the pope makes no mention of the acclamatory sermon or of the emperor’s edict confirming the synod. Yet, to conceal nothing, according to Pagius, no Edictus who was bishop of Vienne at that time is found in the histories of the Gauls. Perhaps an error entered the superscription? The substance of the letter bears no trace of fraud. Anastasius the Librarian wrote that Pope Agatho died on 10 January 682, but Baronio thinks that “June” should be read instead of “January.” Moreover, Anastasius lived in the year 680. Whatever the case may be, this letter can be set against the letters of Leo II and others, which display more signs of forgery than this one.]

.

### 94. Leo II’s second letter to the bishops of Spain, in which Honorius is again condemned

**VI.** Four other letters of Leo II addressed to Spain are extant [Note: They survive complete in the collection of general councils published by Labbe; Binius and Harduinus, however, mark them as suspect.]. Each refers to the Sixth Synod and explicitly or tacitly confirms that Pope Honorius was condemned. So concerned was Leo II to publish the condemnation of Pope Honorius!

Baronius (followed by Frassenius, Widmannus, Binius, and others) long ago demonstrated that all four letters are likewise spurious [Note: It is true that these letters exist only in Latin; hence the pseudo-Bossuet, book II, chapter 26, exclaimed: “What Greek forged Leo’s letters written in Latin?” Answer: I do not determine whether a Greek or a Latin forged them; at that time there were men in Constantinople and elsewhere among the Greeks who were skilled in the Latin language.]. I agree with Baronius and provide a brief extract from each.

In the letter to the bishops of Spain, Pope Leo II invites them all to subscribe individually to the Sixth Synod, whose subscriptions he then wished to deposit in the Roman church of Saint Peter [Note: The article concerning the two wills in Christ had never been challenged among the Latins and had moreover already been unanimously declared in two Roman councils under the pontificates of Saints Martin and Agatho; therefore it had also been approved in Spain.]. He writes:

> “Let your sincerity know that, in the city of Constantinople, when the emperor Constantine had gathered bishops from every part of the world [Note: No bishop attended from Africa, Germany, Gaul, Spain, or England; from Egypt there was only one presbyter, in the name of the patriarch of Alexandria.], during the recently elapsed ninth indiction [Note: If the acts were genuine, the Sixth Synod was held during the ninth and tenth indictions (see nos. 82 and 83). For the present I agree that it was completed in the ninth indiction (see no. 81). But when the author of the letter says ‘during the recently elapsed ninth indiction,’ he implies that he is writing in the tenth indiction, when Leo was not yet pope (see no. 93, note).] he celebrated the universal Sixth Council. For its celebration, presbyters and deacons were sent in the person of our predecessor, the lord Pope Agatho of apostolic memory. From the various councils subject to this see, archbishops were also sent by us [Note: Pope Leo sent no one to the Sixth Synod, for it was completed under Agatho. No archbishops were sent to it by the Romans; rather, two presbyters and one deacon presided in Agatho’s name, while three bishops attended in the name of the Roman synod.]. . . . Those who had rebelled against the purity of apostolic tradition were punished with eternal condemnation: namely, Theodore of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter of Constantinople [Note: These men had long before been condemned in the Roman councils, a fact that could not have been unknown to the Spaniards.], together with HONORIUS [Note: How could the Spaniards fail to be deeply moved, when until then they had heard nothing about the condemnation of Pope Honorius? Leo ought to have explained to them the history of the pontiff’s fate, especially since he had not sent them the acts of the synod.], who did not extinguish the flame of heretical doctrine at its beginning, as apostolic authority required, but by neglecting it fostered it [Note: The text adds that Macarius, Stephen, and Polychronius were brought as exiles from Constantinople to Rome, so that they might acknowledge the disgrace of their guilt (see no. 92, note).]. . . . And because, on account of the diversity of language, the matters enacted in that council—since they were written in Greek and had not yet been translated into Latin—were not available, we have meanwhile sent to your charity, through the bearer of this letter, Peter the regionary and notary of our Church, the definition of that same council and the acclamation (which is called *prosphoneticus*) of the whole council to the most pious emperor [Note: Concerning this acclamation and the edict, see nos. 86 and 90.], together with the emperor’s edict translated from Greek into Latin. We shall also send the acts of the entire council when they have been carefully translated [Note: This letter would have been written in the autumn of 683 (see no. 100). Thus, until then, that famous Sixth Synod—in which the Roman pope was solemnly condemned in 680 or 681—would have remained unknown to the Spaniards; indeed, it was so little attended to by the Romans that it had not yet been translated into Latin. Moreover, in the autumn of 683 Pope Leo II had only just died.], if this also pleases your charity [Note: In the Roman Breviary, on 28 June, it is stated that Saint Leo II approved the Sixth Synod and translated it into Latin. If this latter statement is true, one might infer that the acts were then much shorter than they are now. The acts presently extant are twice as long as this entire dissertation of mine. There are, moreover, two Latin translations, as I indicated in no. 41; neither seems to me to be the genuine work of Saint Leo, who governed the Church for ten months and seventeen days.]. Let the subscriptions of all the bishops be appended to the same definition . . . and let them be brought here by the bearer of this letter, Peter.”

[Col. 1057C] In this and the following letters of Leo, the day and year in which they were issued are not apparent; indeed, it is not even reported that the pope confirmed the synod.

### 95. Leo’s third letter to Quiricius, confirming the preceding letter

**VII.** Leo II’s third letter is addressed: “To his most beloved brother Quiricius.” It states:

> “We announce that we have hastened to send there, with the bearer of this letter, Peter . . . with a circular letter to all the bishops and also to the most Christian king [of Spain], to the glorious count [Note: The names of the king and count are first expressed in the following letters. Concerning the recently elapsed ninth indiction, I have spoken in no. 93.] . . . together with the definition of the council celebrated in the city of Constantinople during the recently elapsed ninth indiction, as well as the acclamation of the bishops and the edict of the most pious and most merciful emperor.”

### 96. Leo’s fourth letter to Simplicius, confirming the preceding letters

**VIII.** In the letter to the count Simplicius [Note: In the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, celebrated in 683, twenty-two counts are recorded as having subscribed; Simplicius, however, does not appear among them.], the author states:

> “We have hastened to send there, through the bearer of this letter, Peter . . . so that the definition of the Sixth Council, celebrated in the city of Constantinople in the ninth indiction [Col. 1058B], together with the acclamation of all the bishops (which is also called *prosphoneticus*) and the edict sent here by our most pious Augustus, may also become known in your provinces.”

### 97. Leo’s fifth letter to the king of Spain, confirming the preceding letters and again condemning Pope Honorius

**IX.** In Leo’s letter to King Ervig of Spain [Note: This letter of Leo is attributed by others to Benedict II, the successor of Leo II; in my opinion it should be attributed to neither.], the author states:

> “During the recently elapsed ninth indiction . . . the most Christian emperor, sending an imperial letter to Pope Agatho, urged him [Note: This passage too argues that the letter is a forgery. For the convocation of the council, the emperor had written not to Agatho but to Donus, and in the sixth, not the ninth, indiction (see no. 28). In his reply, referred to in no. 38, Saint Agatho praises the emperor’s letter addressed to Donus; if he had received from the emperor a letter addressed to himself, he ought above all to have replied to that one.] to send legates to Constantinople. When they arrived, he convoked a council . . . where all the authors of the heretical assertion were condemned: namely Theodore of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, formerly bishops of Constantinople, and together with them HONORIUS the Roman, who consented to stain the immaculate rule of tradition that he had received from his predecessors . . . Therefore we have arranged to send there, through the bearer of this letter, Peter . . . the definition of the holy council and the acclamation of the bishops (which is called *prosphoneticus*) addressed to the emperor, as well as the edict of the most merciful emperor, composed for the confession of the true faith and promulgated everywhere [Note: The king of Spain was not subject to the emperor. Why, then, did Pope Leo introduce to the king of Spain, to the bishops, and to the counts the edict of the Greek emperor—and that in matters of faith? I suspect that someone who was Greek rather than Latin forged those Latin letters of Leo, together with the whole history of the condemnation of Honorius. The quality of the Latin is not so great that someone of Greek origin could not have achieved it, and I do not know whether a Latin would have been so concerned about the word *prosphoneticus*.] . . . so that all the bishops of your kingdom may append their subscriptions to the same definition.”

In chronological order, the following comes next.

### 98. (A letter of Pope Benedict II confirming the preceding letters)

**X.** A letter of Pope Benedict II to Peter, the regionary notary:

> “Benedict, presbyter-elect [Note: Benedict II was raised to the pontificate on 2 June 684. Since he calls himself merely ‘elect,’ it may appear that he had not yet been consecrated.] of the apostolic see. In accordance with what Pope Leo intended, when he arranged for your zeal to go to the province of Spain, to the king, the bishops, and the count, in order to make known the definition of the Sixth Synod, the acclamation (which is also called *prosphoneticus*) of the bishops, and the emperor’s edict [Note: There is no mention of bringing the complete acts to Spain. Perhaps they had not yet been translated into Latin.], carry out the commission entrusted to you [Note: If the letter is genuine, we must suppose that the acts of the Sixth Synod and the condemnation of Pope Honorius, carried out in 680 or 681, had still not become known to the Spaniards in 684]. Arrange for the bishops’ subscriptions to be appended after the same synodal definition, so that those bishops may be shown to be fellow participants with us in the faith.”

Baronius rejected this letter as spurious, and Binius, Harduinus, and others do not disagree. The author added neither the year nor the day on which it was issued. I consider it unquestionably fabricated; the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, said to have been celebrated in 684, likewise ignored it, as we shall shortly see.

### 99. The Thirteenth Council of Toledo: Leo’s letters still unknown in Spain in 683

We must now consider, in chronological order, two Spanish councils. The first, the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, was celebrated in November of the year 683 according to the Christian era; it lasted until 13 November. The heading in Labbe reads as follows:

> “The Thirteenth Council of Toledo, of forty-eight bishops, held in the fourth year of King Ervig, in the era 721, in the year of Christ 683, under Pope Leo II” [Note: This title was probably not prefixed by the Fathers themselves, for at that time the Spaniards—and others as well—did not yet reckon from the year of Christ. Harduinus shortened the title by omitting the final part concerning the year of Christ and Pope Leo II. The entire title seems to me to have been written by a foreign hand, since the Fathers themselves stated the year, day, and place in the very preface. [Col. 1060D] I consider the acts of this council genuine.].

> “Moved by the impulse of unblemished charity . . . gathered together in one in the church of Saints Peter and Paul, in the fourth year of Prince Ervig, on the day before the Nones of November, in the era 721. Since each one of us, etc.”

The council was completed on the Ides of November. Forty-eight bishops, Spanish and Gallic, subscribed; eight abbots; twenty-seven deputies of absent bishops; and, besides the king, twenty-two other counts and some nobles.

In this council, which—if we leave aside the title—displays no indication of falsity, thirteen different canons were enacted. No mention was made of the two wills in Christ; therefore, as I conjecture, because none of the Spaniards or neighboring Gauls had denied them. There was no mention of the Sixth Synod, because, as I think, it concerned the Greeks more than the Latins. There was no mention of the letters recently sent by Pope Leo to the Spaniards. I am therefore further confirmed in my opinion that all Leo II’s letters to the Spaniards [Col. 1060B] are fabrications.

### 100. The Fourteenth Council of Toledo, referring to Leo’s letters

**XI.** The Fourteenth Council of Toledo is said to have been celebrated in November 684. Seventeen Spanish bishops attended, together with the deputy of the bishop of Narbonne in Gaul [Note: A large part of Gaul was at that time subject to the king of Spain.] and nine other deputies of absent bishops [Note: The names of the bishops and of Peter the regionary seem to have been taken from the Thirteenth and Fifteenth Councils of Toledo, as becomes clear to anyone who reads them again. Three bishops who had attended the Thirteenth through representatives—namely those of Beatia, Acci, and Valeria—are said to have subscribed to this Fourteenth Council in person. At the time of the Thirteenth Council the bishop of Dianium was Felix; at the time of the Fifteenth he was Marcian, who is also reported to have subscribed personally to the Fourteenth.].

The heading in Labbe reads:

> “The Fourteenth Council of Toledo, of seventeen bishops, in the era 722, in the fifth year of Ervig, in the year of Christ . . . 684, celebrated under Benedict II” [Note: This title also appears not to have been issued by the Spanish bishops assembled together.].

> “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit begin the synodal acts enacted by the bishops of the province of Carthage.”

The bishops offer lengthy explanations for why, in the preceding council, they had made no mention of the Sixth Synod, the two wills in Christ, or the letters of Pope Leo. They imply that these materials had arrived in Spain during the preceding winter, when the council mentioned above had just been completed, and that, because of the severity of the winter, all the bishops could not meet again. For this reason King Ervig ordered that the bishops of the province of Carthage [Note: At the same time, representatives attended from other provinces, namely Tarraconensis, Narbonensis, Emeritensis, Bracarensis, and Hispaliensis; all of these had been metropolitan provinces, as is clear from the division of the provinces made under King Wamba and approved at the Eleventh Council of Toledo on 7 November 675.] should now hold a provincial synod in the royal city of Toledo, whose decrees would then be approved by the remaining provincial synods. Thus, they say, “there would be one indivisible synodal edict of all the Spanish bishops throughout Spain and Gaul.”

> “Accordingly, we, the bishops of the province of Carthage, in the year mentioned above [Note: If the title is excluded, nowhere in the entire acts does the year in which this council was celebrated appear. Thus the person who composed the title concerning the year of Christ and Benedict II also seems to have compiled the acts of the council itself.], on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, confidently following the proper procedures in the aforesaid church [Note: Nowhere in the acts does it appear which church this ‘aforesaid church’ was. The author of this Fourteenth Council of Toledo seems to have referred to the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, which was celebrated in the church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul (no. 99).], thus began with open and common voice:

> “A clear understanding possesses all peoples: that the synodal acts have been brought to our fellowship by the bearer of the Roman bishop, in which the doctrine of Apollinaris was destroyed at Constantinople [Note: Apollinaris denied Christ a human soul; the Monothelites denied him only a will. Paul of Constantinople anathematized Apollinaris in the dogmatic statement cited in no. 5. The Spaniards, therefore, had not distinguished the two sufficiently.]. Together with these acts, we also received the letters of Pope Leo [Note: They speak of Leo as though he were still living, although he had died more than a year earlier. Nothing is revealed concerning the letter of Benedict II mentioned in no. 98.], through which the entire order of events and the acts of the proceedings were made clear to our understanding, as they had occurred [Note: How could the Spaniards assert this?] . . . since we received those letters at a hostile time, when the whole land had been stiffened by winter frost and the enormous frozen mass of snow [Note: Spanish Carthage lies between the thirty-seventh and thirty-eighth degrees of northern latitude, where I suppose the winter to be extremely mild. The author who fabricated the synod was perhaps Greek, or even Latin, and imagined that Spain lay in the north. In the same seventh century several councils of Toledo—which lies between the thirty-ninth and fortieth degrees of latitude—were held in winter: the Fourth on the Nones of December, the Sixth on 8 January, and the Eighth on 27 December.]—and also at a time when it was already evident that we had already been dismissed from the general council. We were then unable to assemble again, since the recent conclusion of the council had sent us back, reduced in number, to our own sees [Note: From this it would follow that this Fourteenth Council of Toledo was celebrated by the bishops still remaining at Toledo, and therefore in 683. But the Thirteenth Council of Toledo began on 4 November and was confirmed by King Ervig—who was present at Toledo—on 13 November. The Fourteenth Council of Toledo is said to have begun on 14 November. How can these facts be reconciled?], and the adversity of stormy weather did not permit the dispersed to gather together again.

> “Although at that time the fellowship of all the Spaniards could not be gathered generally into one place . . . nevertheless, while scattered in our separate sees, we undertook to examine the aforesaid rules of the acts, read them through, and approve the confession of the two wills and operations in Christ, just as we then made known through representatives of Spain to the Roman pontiff [Note: Nothing concerning this survives.]. Now, however, let our replies, after renewed synodal examination in each of the provinces of Spain, also pass into the knowledge of the people through salutary publication.

> “Accordingly, by the common judgment of all, it is now pleasing that, since we could not gather all the bishops of Spain together generally in one place, we should at least celebrate councils in the separate provinces . . . Therefore we, first, all the bishops of the province of Carthage [Note: It is not established that any other province imitated the bishops of Carthage in this matter.] compared the acts of the aforesaid Constantinopolitan council with the ancient councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon [Note: The Second Council of Constantinople, preserved by the Greeks in the year 553 and called the Fifth Council, was entirely omitted. We should not be surprised at this, since it was omitted not only by the Spaniards at the Third Council of Toledo in 589 and the Thirteenth Council of Toledo in 683, but later also by Pope Saint Gregory the Great and others, because it dealt only with persons to be condemned, Origen and others, and not with doctrines to be believed, which are expressed in the four preceding councils.], and approved and received them as harmonious [Note: From this it could be inferred that a particular council had the right to examine and approve the decrees of a general council, even one approved by the pope. The pseudo-Bossuet boasts of this Fourteenth Council of Toledo (In Defense of the Declaration of the Gallican Clergy, book VII, chapter 29).], insofar as they do not depart from the councils mentioned above, indeed insofar as they appear to agree with them [Note: This clause would favor Honorius, who certainly had not been condemned in the councils mentioned above.].”

These acts should therefore be placed after the Council of Chalcedon. “Accordingly, we also confirm, with a similar force of honor and reverence, our replies once sent to the pope in this matter [Note: Apart from this passage, they are nowhere reported, nor are they received among the decretal letters.], and we decree that they shall remain in the place of decretal letters. Completed . . . in the year mentioned above.”

Although this council makes no explicit mention of Pope Honorius, it nevertheless seems to me spurious for the reasons just given in various places. It is not mentioned even at the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, where in 688 sixty-one bishops nevertheless discussed at length the will of the Word [Col. 1062B]; and three substances were asserted for Christ, namely divinity, human flesh, and a soul. There would therefore have been a highly suitable occasion to mention the Council of Toledo said to have been the Fourteenth, if it had truly been celebrated in 684.

In the case of Honorius, we must now pass once more from Spain to Constantinople.

### 101. A letter of the emperor Justinian confirming the Sixth Synod and reviewing its acts

In February 687, the emperor Justinian II, or the Younger, is said to have written a letter to Pope John V [Note: Pope John V was Syrian by birth and had been one of the legates sent by Pope Saint Agatho to the Sixth Synod; at that time he was a deacon of the Holy Roman Church.], in which he again confirmed the Sixth Synod.

When this emperor succeeded his father Constantine Pogonatus, who died in September 685, he was only sixteen years old, according to Nicephorus; and, having obtained the empire, he overturned everything that his father had established concerning peace and the other arrangements of the commonwealth [Note: This emperor was also suspect in matters of faith. Hated by everyone, he was driven from the throne in 695, mutilated by having his nose cut off, and exiled to Cherson. But in 705 he recovered the empire. Later he summoned the pope to Constantinople, publicly kissed his feet, and received the Eucharist from his hands as an orthodox Christian. Finally, toward the end of 711 or the beginning of 712, he was murdered by Philippicus, his successor and a Monothelite.].

In the letter he reports that he had reexamined the documents of the Sixth Synod, discovered them to be genuine, and locked them away so that they could never be corrupted or altered by anyone. He writes:

> “Immediately we summoned the patriarchs [Note: Apart from the patriarch of Constantinople, no patriarch personally attended the Sixth Synod except the patriarch of Antioch, who is said to have taken the acts to Antioch after the synod was completed (no. 85). Which patriarchs were now present at the examination in question?] together with the apocrisarius of your blessedness, the most holy senate, the metropolitans and bishops residing in this city, the soldiers dwelling in the palace, men from the popular guilds, the palace guards, and certain men from the armies, both those serving the imperial court and those from the Eastern, Thracian, Armenian, and Italian forces, and then from the Cabarisian and Septensian forces, that is, from the Sardinian and African army . . . And we ordered the aforesaid documents of the synodal acts to be brought into the midst and read before all those mentioned above [Note: Of all these people, not even one can be named as a witness, unless it may be argued that Paul, the patriarch of Constantinople, was present. Theodore succeeded George, who had attended the council; Theodore had formerly been deposed and died in 684. Paul, a layman promoted to that dignity, succeeded him.]. We had all of them listen carefully and caused them to sign the documents. The entire body of those who had listened [Note: Popular soldiers may have been auditors, but they could not have been judges, nor indeed witnesses, since it is not established that any of them attended the Sixth Synod, and the emperor himself had not attended the synod in 681.] delivered those documents into our hands, so that we might preserve and keep them inviolate, lest those who do not fear God should ever be able to corrupt or alter them [Note: Therefore, according to the emperor’s view, and that of the patriarchs and all the auditors—including Paul of Constantinople, if he was candid—only this single copy of the acts of the Sixth Synod existed.]. . . . We shall always preserve these documents intact and unaltered [Note: We shall hear in no. 103 that these acts were burned by the emperor’s successor.]. . . . Given at Constantinople on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, under the most pious emperor Justinian, in the second year of his reign, in the fifteenth indiction.”

Accordingly, this letter would have been written to John V on 17 February 687, at which time Pope John had already been dead for more than six months, and Pope Saint Conon had already governed the universal Church for four months. For, according to all the ancient writers, John died on 2 August 686, and Conon, originally a Thracian, succeeded him on 21 October. See Pagius, under the year 686, no. 2.

Pagius says that John’s death [Col. 1064A] remained unknown to the people of Constantinople throughout that period. But it is morally impossible that the emperor, who at that time was still ruler of Old Rome, had not been informed before 17 February 687 of John’s death and the election of Conon as Roman pontiff. What event could have been more worthy of an emperor’s attention than the death of the pontiff and the election of his successor?

### 102. Papebrochius’s objection rejected

Papebrochius asserts that John’s death and Conon’s election occurred in the year 687. But all the ancient historians oppose this, assigning them to the year 686. I believe that the aforesaid letter of Justinian II is spurious, although it says nothing about the condemnation of Honorius. If, however, it must be admitted as genuine, it gives rise to considerable suspicion that under the pretext of reviewing the acts, the first corruption of the synodal acts was arranged by this emperor [Note: Baronius thought that, under Justinian’s father, the emperor Constantine, around the year 683, the patriarch Theodore first corrupted the acts, erased his own name—although it had been written among the condemned—and substituted the name of Pope Honorius. But Theodore still appears in the extant acts as a forger (no. 77); therefore the fraud seems to have been committed after Theodore’s death.] and Paul, patriarch of Constantinople.

### 103. The acts of the Sixth Synod burned

In the meantime, whatever the truth may be, the acts of the Sixth Council—which Justinian II is said to have reviewed in the manner described—did not reach posterity intact. For the emperor Philippicus, Justinian II’s successor, burned with fire the acts of that council, which had been deposited in the imperial palace [Note: The letters of Honorius and the emperor’s original acts of the Sixth Synod are said to have been burned. Concerning the copy of the acts sent to Rome, see no. 93, note.].

At least this is what the notary Agatho and John of Constantinople, whom I shall cite shortly, asserted [Note: What happened at Constantinople concerning the Sixth Synod at the beginning of the eighth century is very obscure and complicated.

Theophanes reports that in 712 the emperor Philippicus held a conciliabulum against the Sixth Synod, deposed Cyrus, patriarch of Constantinople, and substituted John for him; and that the archbishops Germanus of Cyzicus and Andrew of Crete, together with all their colleagues, condemned the Sixth Synod by an anathema and openly subscribed to its condemnation. Nicephorus agrees concerning Saint Germanus and John, but says nothing about Andrew. The synodal booklet merely reports that Philippicus, after killing Justinian II, assembled an impious synod at Constantinople, revived the impiety of the Monothelites, expelled Cyrus [Col. 1064D], and substituted John for him. The acts of that conciliabulum do not survive.

In 715 Saint Germanus was transferred from the see of Cyzicus to Constantinople. According to Zonaras, John had died; according to Theophanes and Nicephorus, he had been deposed on account of heresy. Henschenius (in the Life of Saint Germanus, under 12 May) denied that Saint Germanus ever subscribed to the condemnation of the Sixth Synod, supposing that what Theophanes and Nicephorus reported about Saint Germanus had been excerpted from the deceitful documents of heretics. John—or whoever is the author—in the letter to be cited in no. 105 named no bishops who had agreed with him. I think that Theophanes and Nicephorus were deceived concerning Saint Germanus and Andrew; but I have no time to dwell on this longer.].

Therefore the acts now extant once again become suspect, and from documents suspect on every side the lapse of Honorius and his condemnation are not sufficiently established.

### 104. Testimony of the Deacon Agatho, who wrote the Acts of the Sixth Synod in his own hand [Col. 1065A]

**XII.** In addition to the materials already reported, there exists a book appended to the Acts of the Sixth Synod under the name of the deacon Agatho, who claims that he attended the Sixth Synod as both reader and notary and that, by order of the emperor Constantine, he wrote the synodal Acts in his own hand—the Acts in which Honorius was condemned. The book is entitled:

> “Epilogue [Note: This epilogue was discovered in Paris at the end [Col. 1065C] of the Acts of the Sixth Synod. It was written in Greek with a Latin translation and was reported by Hardouin, Labbe, Combefis, and Pagius (*On the Year 711*, no. 4). Moreover, if the Acts themselves are corrupt, this epilogue too becomes suspect, and conversely.] of the man who wrote this book [Note: That is, the book containing the Acts of the Sixth Synod, copied anew by Agatho after thirty-three years.] in his own hand, in which are also contained the things which the tyrant Barda [Note: That is, Bardanes, as will become clear from what follows.] dared to do against the Sixth Synod.

> “I, the sinner and least of all, Agatho [Note: Pagius praises this Agatho as ‘a man of entirely blameless life.’ To me he seems genuinely a sinner, an unworthy man, and an incompetent notary; I doubt whether he really attended the Sixth Synod. See no. 59.], unworthy deacon and librarian of this most holy great Church—the Church of Constantinople—and protonotary and second chancellor of the venerable patriarchal secretariat, approximately thirty-two years ago [Note: A competent notary who had attended the Sixth Synod would have determined the interval more precisely. The interval cannot be less than thirty-two years: the Sixth Synod was completed in 681, and adding thirty-one years brings us to 712, when Philippicus had not yet been deposed. Yet our protonotary reports not only Philippicus’s deposition [Col. 1065D] but also events that occurred afterward.], when, while still young, I had been enrolled in the rank of reader and was an incompetent notary, I offered my services to this holy and universal Sixth Synod. I followed in order everything that was discussed and investigated there, together with the holy Paul, later patriarch of this city, who at that time was still a layman and secretary of the emperor [Note: This Paul was in office from 688 to 693; he is said to have subscribed the Council of Trullo, concerning which see no. 106.], and with certain others.

> “I wrote in my own hand, in pure and elegant ecclesiastical script, all the volumes of the Acts, which, together with the decree of faith, were safely deposited in the imperial palace under seals [Note: The author seems to be speaking of the first deposit, not of the second, said to have been made under Justinian II in 687. See the preceding note.]. Moreover, by order of the emperor Constantine, I wrote copies of this decree and delivered them to the five patriarchal Churches [Note: Thus, even according to this Agatho, not the entire body of the Acts but only the decree of faith was sent to Rome and to the other patriarchs; from this, however, the condemnation of Pope Honorius is not sufficiently established. See no. 84.].

> “But when . . . God had taken pity on me, humble and incompetent, and had permitted me to live until now, I rightly desired and resolved to write this book also in my own hand; especially because in the preceding years many grievous evils had befallen the Christian commonwealth and the empire . . . particularly since, after the death of his father Constantine, Justinian, his successor, had not merely once fallen from the empire because of his extremely wicked and bloodthirsty disposition from the beginning [Note: This Agatho does not report that Justinian II had revised the Acts of the Sixth Synod or celebrated the Council of Trullo; he therefore seems to have written before the Acts of the Council of Trullo were fabricated.], but had suffered the same fate a second time after Leontius and Tiberius, who held the empire in the interval, and had finally perished by the sword with his neck severed . . .

> “His successor Bardanes, who called himself Philippicus, a disciple of the abbot Stephen, who himself had been a disciple of Macarius . . . having exercised imperial power, ordered the image of the Sixth Synod, which had already for several years been displayed in the vestibule of the imperial palace, to be thrown down . . . Moreover, he decreed that the names of Sergius and Honorius [Note: Here a witness is produced who had written the Acts. What more do we want? asks the pseudo-Bossuet (*Defense of the Declaration of the Gallican Clergy*, book VII, chapter 26). But since the patriarchs of Constantinople were forgers, I am also afraid to place confidence in this Constantinopolitan—notwithstanding that he may really have attended the Synod thirty-three years earlier—in so grave a matter as the condemnation of Pope Honorius, especially because he asserted that the original Acts, written by himself and signed by the bishops and the emperor, had been burned by fire.]—condemned by the Sixth Synod—should be entered in the sacred diptychs and that their images should be erected [Note: I accept this and the other histories reported by Agatho as true, provided that the claim that the image of Pope Honorius was erected by Philippicus at Constantinople is omitted. The Venerable Bede reports that Philippicus deposed Saint Cyrus, patriarch of Constantinople, wrote a heretical letter to Pope Constantine, and that the pope, after holding a council, rejected that letter; from then on he caused pictures representing the Acts of the six synods to be displayed in the portico of Saint Peter’s (in whose church Honorius was honored; see no. 4). For Philippicus had ordered such pictures to be removed when they were in Constantinople. Bede does not mention whether the memory of Pope Honorius was restored at Constantinople or erased at Rome.].

> “Afterward, when he had found the volumes of the Acts of the Sixth Synod written by my hand and deposited in the imperial palace, he committed them to the fire and destroyed them. He persecuted the orthodox and sent some of them into exile, especially those who refused to subscribe the pamphlet which he himself had issued against the Sixth Synod. After he had violently perpetrated these things for two years [Note: Pagius (*On the Year 711*, no. 2) maintains that an incomplete two-year period must be understood, namely one year and six months, because Bede says that Philippicus reigned one year and six months. But Agatho wished to show that Philippicus was punished quickly; why, then, did he use ‘two years’ instead of a year and a half? It is true that in the Basel edition of 1563 the text says that Philippicus reigned one year and six months; but the margin says that he reigned into the third year. Indeed, in the Basel edition of 1529 the text says that Philippicus ruled for two years and six months, which the margin confirms. Pagius is inconsistent with himself: for *On the Year 714*, no. 3, he admits that Philippicus ruled for two years and nine months, following Theophanes.] and had undertaken other wicked and shameful acts against nuns and sacred persons, divine vengeance soon overtook and destroyed him. On the vigil of Pentecost, in the eleventh indiction [Note: Pentecost together with the eleventh indiction indicates the year 713; yet, if Philippicus reigned a full two years, he was not deposed before 714. According to Anastasius the Librarian, Pope Constantine, returning from Constantinople, entered Rome on 24 October 711; three months later the sad news was heard that Justinian II had been killed and Philippicus had succeeded him. Philippicus therefore began to reign at the end of 711 or the beginning of 712.], he was thrown from the empire and immediately deprived of his sight . . .

> “On the following day of Pentecost, the orthodox Philartomius, later called Anastasius, was crowned in the apostolic church by John, patriarch of Constantinople [Note: This John had been appointed by Philippicus in place of the deposed Saint Cyrus.], and the Sixth Synod was proclaimed by him, by all the bishops who were present, and by the clergy. Shortly afterward John, as was proper, informed Pope Constantine of Rome by synodal letter of all the foregoing events [Note: The emperor Anastasius himself informed Pope Constantine of these matters and declared himself a preacher of the Sixth Synod. After two years Anastasius was compelled to leave the throne and was permitted by his successor Theodosius to embrace the monastic life. Theodosius restored the image of the Sixth Synod that Philippicus had thrown down. Thus the Venerable Bede must be cited, no. 110.].

> “Since Bardanes had removed the image of the Sixth Synod and substituted his own image and that of Sergius, these two images were thrown down [Note: No mention is made here of the image of Honorius.] and the image of the Sixth Synod was restored . . .

> “For greater credibility of what I had previously written [Note: Is the meaning: ‘for greater credibility of the synodal Acts written by me’?] and for the security and confirmation of those who will diligently read this book [Note: The protonotary feared that he would not be believed; but, as will be clear to anyone who considers the matter, the means by which he attempted to secure belief in himself seems inappropriate], I resolved to append to this book, without any omission, a copy of the letter sent by John of Constantinople to Pope Constantine of Rome.” [Col. 1067B]

The letter follows, etc., as in the next section.

This epilogue, which was appended to the Acts of the Sixth Synod after thirty-three or more years by the hand of the protonotary Agatho, seems to me spurious [Note: Consequently, the confession of faith of Andrew of Crete, composed in iambic verse and cited by Pagius (*On the Year 712*, no. 7) from Combefis, is also spurious. It bears the following title: “Iambics written by Andrew, most holy archbishop of Crete, to Agatho, most holy archdeacon and keeper of the books of this most holy great Church of God, when, after receiving this book, he copied it and sent it back.” In these iambics Andrew the archbishop sings thanks to Agatho for the loan of the book of the Acts of the Sixth Synod and of Agatho’s epilogue. These iambics would have been written no earlier than 714, a year which Andrew probably did not survive. See Cave.]; for if Philippicus burned the volumes of the original Acts written by Agatho’s hand, how could Agatho afterward inscribe on another copy—for example, one written by Paul’s hand—the words: “Epilogue of the man who wrote this book in his own hand”? Did that notary, already an old man, restore the Acts from memory, or did he once more copy them neatly and purely, in ecclesiastical script, from another copy? The notary did not assert this, although it would have been especially important to note. Appended to the aforesaid epilogue of Agatho is the following.

### 105. The Letter of John of Constantinople to Pope Constantine concerning the Acts of the Sixth Synod, copied by the hand of the patriarch Paul, is suspect [Col. 1067C]

**XIII.** An apologetic letter of John, archbishop of Constantinople, to Pope Constantine of Rome, concerning the events raised against the Sixth Synod during the time of Bardanes [Note: This title certainly was not composed by John of Constantinople himself but by another, more probably by the aforesaid Agatho, who also inserted the entire letter into his own document.].

> “To the most holy brother and fellow minister, the lord Constantine [Note: Pope Constantine died, according to Baronius, in 714; according to Pagius, in 715, on 8 April. Saint Gregory II succeeded him after forty days.], John, unworthy bishop, sends greetings.

John confesses concerning himself—without naming any accomplice—that through fear of persecution he consented to the suppression of the Sixth Synod, that is, of the confession of two wills in Christ. He proves by the authority of Aaron and of Saints Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus that this method of concealment was permissible or at least not gravely punishable. Thus he writes to the pope:

> “O head of the Christian priesthood! Until now we have been forbidden to write to you, since we were being tyrannically detained . . . [the tyrant] threw down [Note: Who is the tyrant who threw down . . . and wished, etc.? John, patriarch of Constantinople, had supposedly never previously written to the Roman pontiff; therefore, in this first letter, he ought now to have explained that Bardanes, or the emperor Philippicus, who had recently been deposed, was the tyrant who had done these things. Yet throughout John’s letter the name of Bardanes, Bardas, or Philippicus does not appear. Hence I infer that the person who supplied the title also composed the entire letter—namely, the pseudo-Agatho.] the image of the Sixth Synod placed in the courts of the imperial residence. He wished to place a heretic on this pontifical throne, but, compelled by the local clergy, he elevated us—John—to the pontificate, though we were gravely unwilling. Philippicus insisted that the Sixth Synod and the Roman pontiffs be subjected to anathema . . .

> “I omit saying how many troubles he truly caused us in order that we might send letters to your fraternal blessedness in accordance with the purpose of his madness, and how, with what policy and by what plan, we acted so as to repel his tyrannical force while reducing his insolence to something somewhat more moderate. God and the apocrisiarius of your see who resides here will be witnesses. When the storm was pressing upon us most severely, we satisfied him by an oath, revealing to him our inward faith: it is not expedient to behave too harshly toward authority.

> “The prophet Nathan did not openly rebuke David concerning adultery and murder; rather, after clothing the matter in a parable, he pronounced judgment against him from the latter’s own verdict. Therefore we too, as Basil the Great says, think that one ought to yield somewhat to a man’s character, so that the confession of faith might remain unharmed in matters of greater importance [Note: This is not the voice of a fervently Catholic shepherd. See no. 22. Meanwhile Pagius, *On the Year 712*, no. 5, praises this accommodation, which Pope Constantine rejected by his example; see no. 110.].

> “For the truth is in deeds, not in words, cries Gregory of Nazianzus . . . Dionysius the Areopagite also declares . . . We say these things not as though we wished to overturn the expressions already defined synodally . . . but so that, through our careful ingenuity—by remaining silent about the two wills and the two operations—the tyrant might be bent and prevented from openly introducing foreign doctrines into the Church. Thus God, who catches the wise in their craftiness, openly arranged through us what Gregory of Nazianzus narrated in his funeral oration about Basil the Great: that Basil, by a deliberate silence, did not call the Holy Spirit God but used other equivalent expressions [Note: I have already pointed out in my *Dissertation on Saint Basil the Great*, nos. 171 and 175, that this passage in the oration has been interpolated. Saint Basil replied to the tyrant who urged him to remain silent about the word ‘consubstantial’ that he would rather undergo the most atrocious torments than consent to the suppression of even one syllable. See Theodoret, book IV, chapter 19.].

> “The emperor burned the volumes of the Acts of the Sixth Synod deposited in the palace, believing—as it seemed to him—that by this act he would also destroy the word of truth [Note: Thus the emperor and his advisers thought that only one copy existed at Constantinople; they did not know of the second, written by Paul’s hand, nor of the third, soon to be mentioned.].

> “But while allowing him to be deceived, we carefully guarded with us the deposited volumes of that synod, in which are contained the subscriptions of all the bishops who attended the synod, together with the imperial signature [Note: This copy would therefore have been the original, written neither by the notary Agatho nor by Paul—but by whom? This is not added.]. We also have preserved among us a book of the Acts written in Paul’s own hand. He was the bishop of this Church and served at the Sixth Synod as secretary, so that no one can adulterate the Acts [Note: This precaution arouses suspicion that adulteration had taken place and presupposes that the Acts did not exist in the other patriarchal Churches. Meanwhile, this Paul must not be confused with Paul, patriarch and successor of Pyrrhus, the forger discussed in no. 77.].

> “Christ has granted us a pious and orthodox emperor who, consistently with his name—namely Anastasius—has caused ecclesiastical peace and concord to arise. We trust that he is also beginning the restoration of the commonwealth [Note: The author therefore indicates, or pretends, that he wrote while Anastasius was beginning his reign.].

> “Therefore, O sacred head, extend your hand to us! Receive those who fell because of the assault of external circumstances, and do not expel from your charity us, against whom force was used . . .

> “When Aaron had assisted the Israelites in fashioning the idol, he was indeed rebuked by his brother Moses; but since he asserted that he had been compelled by force, he received no rebuke from God . . . God looks wholly to inward things, for he formed our hearts individually, and not to outward recklessness . . . Pray for us, most blessed brother!”

This letter of John of Constantinople to Pope Constantine, although it does not assert that Honorius was condemned [Col. 1069C] and says nothing about the Council of Trullo, which will shortly be discussed, nevertheless now seems to me suspect [Note: Anastasius the Librarian reports nothing about John of Constantinople except that he sent a synodal letter to Pope Gregory II and received a reply from him. It is regrettable that neither letter survives.], all the more because it was so carefully commended to us by Agatho in no. 104. The year and day on which this letter was issued are not supplied.

### 106. The condemnation of Honorius is allegedly proved from the Council of Trullo, which is rejected [Col. 1070A]

**XIV.** In the Quinisext, or Trullan, Council, canon 1, it is reported that the Sixth Synod counted Pope Honorius among the heretics and condemned him [Note: From this first canon alone the entire synod immediately becomes suspect to me, because it seems impossible that at that time a large synod already believed that Honorius had been condemned in 681. See no. 108.]. Natalis says that this council was held approximately five years after the Sixth Synod [Note: The Acts of the Council of Trullo contain an obvious chronological contradiction. In canon 3 the author indicates by the year of the world 6199 that the year of Christ is 706, while by the fourth indiction he indicates the year of Christ 692. Natalis, Pagius, Hardouin, Baronius, and others have tried in various ways to soften this contradiction. See no. 107.], by 227 bishops, among whom were forty-three bishops who had attended and subscribed the Sixth Synod—certainly witnesses beyond all exception.

Yet this very council—which was called ecumenical, or the Seventh, by the Greek Iconoclasts at the Seventh Synod, or Second Council of Nicaea, in 787—is entirely spurious, together with its innumerable laws, as I have already pointed out in five dissertations on Saint Basil the Great, beginning at no. 74 [Note: There I still supposed that the letter of John of Constantinople reported in the preceding section was genuine.].

I shall repeat a few points from there and append them here. In the eleventh century Humbertus replied to the Greek Nicetas concerning the Trullan canons:

> “It is no wonder if you attribute to Pope Agatho and the holy Fathers of the Sixth Synod the ravings and the chapters which you either corrupted or fabricated.”

[Note: Splendid subscriptions have been added. In the first place appears the emperor Justinian II; the second place was left vacant for the Roman pope; in the third place four patriarchs are said to have been personally present, namely Paul of Constantinople, the unworthy, Peter of Alexandria, Anastasius of Jerusalem, and George of Antioch; fourth, other bishops follow, among whom, in the fifteenth place, appears Basil under the title: “from the island of Crete, representative of the whole Synod of the Holy Roman Church.” Meanwhile this note is false, and it should be observed that no one attended in the pope’s name.]

In the ninth century Anastasius the Librarian wrote in the preface to the Seventh Synod:

> “The Trullan canons have until now remained wholly unknown among the Latins, because they have neither been translated nor found in the archives of the other patriarchal sees—even though they use the Greek language—apart from Constantinople. The reason is surely that, when they were issued, none of those sees was found either to have promulgated them, consented to them, or even been present, although the Greeks claim that they were promulgated by the same Fathers who were present at the Sixth Synod. But they cannot prove this by any reliable evidence.”

He repeated the same statement in the preface to the Eighth Synod:

> “It is clear that the Trullan canons were issued privately by the Greeks long after the Sixth Synod.” [Col. 1070C]

[Note: It seems that not only the pseudo-Agatho but also the contemporary Venerable Bede was unaware of those famous canons. Meanwhile, Bede testified that some assembly had been held under Justinian II in these words: “Because Pope Sergius did not wish to favor or subscribe the wandering synod which he had held at Constantinople, Justinian II ordered him to be brought to Constantinople, but he was prevented by the armies of the cities of Italy.” Saint Sergius I was pope from 687 to 701.]

### 107. The authority of the Council of Trullo is allegedly proved from the Seventh General Council, or Second Council of Nicaea, which appears to have been interpolated

A story commonly cited in support of the authenticity of the Trullan canons is the following:

> “In the year 787, at the Seventh General Synod, held at Nicaea, in session 4, the presbyter Elias read from a document containing the definitions of the Sixth Synod canon 82 of the Council of Trullo under this title: ‘Canon 82 of the holy and universal Sixth Synod.’ The monk Sabbas said: ‘Why is it being read from a document and not from a codex?’ Then Tharasius, patriarch of Constantinople, replied: ‘Because it is the original document in which the Fathers subscribed . . . Some who are weak through ignorance are scandalized by these canons because they were not enacted at the Sixth Synod. Let them know, however, that the same Fathers who constituted the Sixth Synod met again after four or five years [Note: The author of the Trullan canons, canon 1, says that the Sixth Synod had previously been assembled.] and enacted these canons, and no one doubts them. For those who subscribed under Constantine at the Sixth Synod also subscribed under Justinian at the Council of Trullo, as is evident from the unchanging similarity of their handwriting in the present document.” [Col. 1071B]

[Note: As though Tharasius had brought the original Acts of the Sixth Synod and these had been compared with the original Acts of the Council of Trullo.]

Natalis says in Dissertation 3 on the eighth century:

> “I would be reluctant to believe that Tharasius erred in this matter.”

But the Greek Theophanes, in his *Life of Constantine Pogonatus*, warned:

> “It must be understood that those who assert that the Trullan canons were made after four years are chattering very foolishly.”

Therefore, according to Theophanes, Tharasius would have been greatly mistaken. I, however, believe that this story about Tharasius—which Theophanes, Anastasius, and others seem to have known nothing about—was interpolated into the Acts of the Seventh Synod. More about the Seventh Synod appears in no. 109.
