### 108. When was the fable about Honorius fabricated?

You may ask when the fable of Honorius’s condemnation was fabricated. It is difficult to determine this, but it seems more probable to me that the aforementioned fable was forged in the eighth century [Col. 1071C], after Philippicus had been expelled from the empire, indeed after the year 715 [Note: See nos. 104 and 105.], probably by one or more Greeks [Note: It was not, however, adopted by all Greeks. Theophanes and Calleca testify that Honorius was always fervently Catholic. Photius of Constantinople, who wrote around the year 860, reports that Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter were condemned at the Sixth Synod but is silent about Honorius; Zonaras likewise records the names of those condemned at the Sixth Synod but omits Honorius. See Bellarmine, *On the Supreme Pontiff*, book IV, chapter 11, under the seventh argument. Meanwhile, in the ninth century the condemnation of Honorius was accepted even by some Latins, including Anastasius the Librarian, Hincmar, and others. See nos. 1, 112, and 115.] who perhaps composed together the letters of Popes Leo II and Benedict II, the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, the synodal letter of John of Constantinople, the epilogue of the notary Agatho, and the iambics of Andrew of Crete.

If the same persons also invented the Trullan canons, they are shown to have proceeded with insufficient care, since neither the synodal letter of John of Constantinople nor the epilogue of the notary Agatho mentions the Council of Trullo—although, because of the number of its bishops and canons and the character of those canons, it would above all have deserved mention.

Moreover, since all the arguments that have so far been brought directly or indirectly against Pope Honorius are of doubtful credibility [Col. 1071D], the remaining arguments usually drawn from later authors are more easily overturned. In substance, they are as follows, according to Natalis.

### 109. Honorius was condemned six times in a general synod

**XV.** In the Seventh General Synod, which was assembled at Nicaea in 787, Pope Honorius is repeatedly said to have been condemned as a heretic.

1. In the third session, the letter of Tharasius of Constantinople to the patriarchs of Antioch, Alexandria, and Jerusalem was read. In it Tharasius professed:

> “I anathematize Origen, Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and all their followers.”

2. The letter of Theodore, patriarch of Jerusalem, was read. He said:

> “The holy Sixth Synod, like a sun of 289 Fathers [Note: It shone like the moon, since it had received its light from Saint Agatho the pope and from the Roman synods held under Saints Agatho and Martin I. The light of doctrine arose from the West, the Sixth Synod proclaimed. See no. 86.], anathematized those who asserted one will—that is, Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Peter, Honorius . . .”

3. In the seventh session, the definition of faith says:

> “We anathematize the fables of Origen, Evagrius, and Didymus, just as the synod assembled at Constantinople is known to have done. We also proclaim two wills in Christ, just as the Sixth Synod at Constantinople cried out when it rejected Sergius, Honorius, Cyrus, Pyrrhus, and Macarius.”

4. In the letter of Tharasius and the entire Seventh Synod to the emperors, we read:

> “We anathematize the madness of Arius . . . the fables of Origen; the will of Sergius and Honorius . . . and also the similar vanity that babbled against the images.”

5. In the letter to the clergy of Constantinople it says:

> “He reduced them—the Iconoclasts—to nothing, together with Arius . . . Sergius, Honorius, and their entire most wicked sect.”

[Note: Two other letters of Tharasius to Pope Adrian are also inserted in the Acts; neither mentions Honorius. In the first, Tharasius announces to the pope: “At the Second Council of Nicaea we all proclaimed the confession sent to us by you . . . and all the heretics were condemned by an equal deposition.”]

6. In the sixth session, the deacon Epiphanius openly counted Honorius among the Monothelites.

**Response.** The Acts of the Seventh Synod are extremely extensive [Note: This council was held solely because certain Greeks had attempted to abolish the religious veneration of images, which had prevailed until then; they were therefore called Iconoclasts. Many passages cited in that council are fabricated.], and were little attended to by the Latins. In the year 880 Anastasius the Librarian translated them from Greek into Latin, introducing them with these words:

> “The Latins do not possess the Seventh Synod, which was celebrated at Nicaea—not because it had never previously been translated by anyone, but because it was translated so incompetently that it becomes tedious to readers and is almost universally despised for that reason and judged unworthy of being read. Therefore I have endeavored to translate it for the Latins, considering it improper that the Roman Church should be deprived of that synod.”

It is well known that not everything inserted even in the Acts of genuinely general synods is an article of faith, especially when it concerns a question of fact [Col. 1072D].

Bellarmino says in the cited work, in response to the second argument:

> “It was almost the ordinary custom of the Greeks to corrupt books. The Sixth Synod, in sessions 12 and 14, reproved many corruptions made concerning the Fifth Synod. Leo, in letter 83 to the Palestinians, complains that the Greeks corrupted his letter to Flavian while he was still alive. Gregory I, book V, letter 14 to Narses, asserts that the people of Constantinople corrupted the Council of Chalcedon and says that he suspects the same concerning the Council of Ephesus. Nicholas I, in his letter to the emperor Michael, refers him to the letter of Adrian I—‘if,’ he says, ‘it has not been falsified in the Greek manner and is still preserved by the Church of Constantinople as it was sent from the apostolic see.’ Nor did he say this without reason: for the things that he himself cites in his letter to Photius from Adrian I’s letter to Tharasius are not found in that letter as it exists in the Acts of the Seventh Synod. The Greeks removed that passage because it was damaging to the honor of Tharasius.”

Thus Bellarmine.

Meanwhile, there were also forgers among the Latins, as has been abundantly demonstrated by the letters that I have shown in preceding dissertations to have been falsely attributed to Saints Cyprian, Jerome, and others as early as the fifth century. Certainly the Council of Sinuessa, supposedly consisting of 300 bishops and reporting the fall of Saint Marcellinus, is entirely fabricated, probably by Latins.

As for the first point: Tharasius too is said to have asserted that the Trullan canons were enacted by the Fathers who had celebrated the Sixth Synod four or five years earlier; in this he was grossly deceived. If the aforesaid letters are genuine, it is necessary to suppose that at that time there existed only forged documents, into which Tharasius, Theodore, and others had fallen.

As for the second point: Theodore certainly erred when he counted 289 Fathers at the Sixth Synod.

As for points three, four, five, and six: this does not mean that there were none who pronounced Origen free from every heresy and maintained that his books had been falsified. Those who condemned Origen certainly intended to condemn the author of the heresies contained in the books attributed to Origen; I too condemn that author. But I believe that he was not that Origen Adamantius, the presbyter who publicly taught at Alexandria in the third century [Note: He died in 252. The first synod in which he is reported to have been condemned is the Synod of Diospolis, consisting of fourteen bishops, in the fifth century. I said that the Acts of this synod are suspect in Dissertation 19, beginning at no. 300. The second is the Second Council of Constantinople, or the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, of 553; concerning this, see no. 59 and Dissertation 16, no. 83.].

Likewise, if some people in the eighth century condemned Pope Honorius, they understood by the name Honorius the author of those letters that were then, and still are, inserted in the Acts of the Sixth Synod. I agree that this author ought rightly and justly to be condemned [Note: Against Bellarmine and others, I agree with the pseudo-Bossuet that those letters are truly condemnable. See no. 38.], but I do not believe that those letters were written by Honorius. Indeed, I do not even believe that authentic Acts of the Sixth Synod survive.

### 110. The testimony of the Venerable Bede against Honorius. The history of the Monothelites, or Acephali, from Bede

**XVI.** The most powerful witness in this matter is the Venerable Bede, born in 672 and deceased in 735. In his book *On the Reckoning of Time*, which he wrote around the year 726, he expressly teaches that Honorius was condemned at the Sixth Synod.

Baronius responds to this argument that Bede had encountered Acts of the Sixth Synod that had only recently been corrupted. Bellarmine, however, judged that the name Honorius had been interpolated into Bede’s book. I agree with Bellarmine. For Bede, when treating Honorius expressly, never added that he had fallen into heresy or that he had been condemned because of it; indeed, he praised him considerably. In book II, chapters 17–19, of the *History of the Angles*, he speaks of Honorius as an excellent shepherd. In the *Life of Abbot Bertulf* he says:

> “Honorius was a venerable prelate, shrewd in mind, vigorous in counsel, distinguished in doctrine . . . The holy pope granted Bertulf the offered gift, namely the privileges of the apostolic see, so that no bishop might attempt to dominate the aforesaid monastery by any right.”

As for the book *On the Reckoning of Time*, or *On the Six Ages of the World*, here is the extract:

> “Heraclius reigned for thirty years. Anastasius the Persian, a monk, suffered martyrdom . . . together with seventy others . . . Heraclius overcame the Persians [Note: The Persians had occupied Jerusalem. They had destroyed the churches in Palestine and carried away the holy cross, which Heraclius recovered.] . . . At that time Pope Honorius rebuked by letter the error of the Quartodecimans, which had arisen among the Scots concerning the observance of Easter.

> “Heraclonas reigned for two years. Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, and Pyrrhus, bishops of the imperial city, reviving the heresy of the Acephali, dogmatized that there was one operation in Christ . . . [Note: There is no indication that Pope Honorius, who above all should have been named, favored the Acephali. Why would Bede, who wrote this around 726, have been silent about Honorius here if he intended in the following passage to list Honorius publicly among the condemned heretics, or if Honorius had truly been condemned at the Sixth General Council, at the Council of Trullo, at Rome by Pope Saint Leo II, and in Spain by the Fourteenth Council of Toledo?]

> “Of these, Pyrrhus . . . came to Rome from Africa under Pope Theodore and, with repentance that later proved to have been feigned, offered that pope, in the presence of the entire clergy and people, a document bearing his subscription, in which everything that he or his predecessors had written or done against the Catholic faith was condemned. He was therefore kindly received as though he were the pontiff of the imperial city. But when he returned home and again embraced his native error, the aforesaid Pope Theodore summoned all the priests and clergy to the church of Saint Peter and condemned him under the bond of anathema. See no. 20.”

“Constantine, son of Heraclius, for six months [Col. 1074D] [Note: This Constantine III is said by others to have reigned jointly with his brother Heraclonas; he was a Catholic, but was removed shortly afterward. See notes 15 and 16.]. Paul, successor of Pyrrhus, afflicts [Col. 1074C] Catholics not only with deranged doctrine, as did his predecessors, but also with open persecution. He inflicted imprisonment, exile, and beatings upon the representatives of the holy Roman Church who had been sent to correct him; moreover, he overturned and plundered their altar, consecrated in the venerable oratory in the house of Placidia, forbidding them to celebrate Masses there. Therefore he too, like his predecessors, was condemned by the Apostolic See with the just punishment of deposition.

“Constantine [Note: He is called Constans, or even Constantius, by others; he is mentioned in notes 20 and 21.], son of Constantine, for twenty-eight years. Deceived by Paul, just as his grandfather Heraclius had been by [Col. 1075A] Sergius, bishop of that same imperial city, he published the Typos … Hence Pope Martin, having assembled a synod of 105 bishops at Rome, condemned Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul as heretics … Martin was taken from Rome to Constantinople and afterward exiled to Cherson, where he ended his life, still shining there to this day through many signs of virtue.

“Constantine, son of the preceding emperor, for seventeen years … At the request of the most pious rulers Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius [Note: [Col. 1075D] Constantine IV had his two brothers, Heraclius and Tiberius, as associates in the empire. See notes 29 and 32.], Pope Agatho sent his legates to the imperial city. The legates were received with the greatest kindness by Constantine, the most reverend defender of the Catholic faith. They were instructed, after philosophical disputations had been set aside, to investigate the true faith in peaceful discussion; all the books of the ancient Fathers that they requested were supplied from the library at Constantinople. [Col. 1075B] One hundred and fifty bishops were also present, with George, patriarch of the imperial city, and Macarius of Antioch presiding. Those who asserted one will and one operation in Christ were convicted of having falsified very many statements of the Catholic Fathers. When the contest had ended, George was corrected [Note: [Col. 1075D] Anastasius also relates, in his Life of Agatho, that George finally professed in writing, on 17 February of the ninth indiction, that there are two wills in Christ, and on the 25th took his place among the Catholics. See Baronius, under the year 681, no. 2; Cozza, *De schismate Graecorum*, part II, chapter 27, no. 881. That circumstance is not reported in the acts now extant.], while Macarius, together with his followers and his predecessors Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius [Note: [Col. 1075D] Honorius appears among the condemned in this one place only [Col. 1076D], and indeed between the Constantinopolitan patriarchs], Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, was anathematized; in his place Theophanius, an abbot from Sicily, was made bishop of Antioch … John, bishop of Portus and one of the Roman legates, publicly celebrated Mass on the Sunday within the Octave of Easter in the church of Saint Sophia before the emperor and the patriarch. This synod was written in the Greek language.

“Justinian, son of Constantine, for ten years. Because Sergius [Col. 1075C], the pope, refused to subscribe to his errant synod … he ordered him to be transported to Constantinople, but was prevented … Deprived of the glory of the kingdom because of his treachery, he withdrew as an exile to Pontus.

“Leo, for three years [lacuna]

“Tiberius, for seven years. Because of ignorance of the faith, the synod held at Aquileia hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of blessed Pope Sergius, it too agreed to assent to it together with the other Churches of Christ.

“Justinian, for the second time, for six years … He sent Callinicus, the patriarch, to Rome after having had his eyes torn out, and gave the episcopate to Cyrus … He honorably received Pope Constantine … and confirmed all the privileges of the Roman Church.

[Col. 1075D] “Philippicus, for two years and six months. He expelled Cyrus from the pontificate (he substituted John, mentioned under no. 105) … He likewise sent Pope Constantine a letter containing a perverse doctrine, which the pope … rejected.

[Col. 1076A] “Anastasius, for two years. He sent a letter to Pope Constantine at Rome … in which he declared himself … a preacher of the Sixth Council.

“Theodosius, for one year … As soon as he received the kingdom, although he was a Catholic, he restored to its former place in the imperial city that venerable image on which the six holy synods had been depicted and which Philippicus had removed.

“Leo, for nine years [Note: [Col. 1076D] This Leo was the Isaurian. He began to reign in 717 and died in 741; in the tenth year of his reign he declared war against the images, and the Seventh Council, mentioned under no. 107, was held to settle the matter. Leo’s ninth year, in which the Venerable Bede’s account ends, fell in the year 725 of the common era].” … Thus far Bede.

### 111. Bede’s testimony is explained in favor of Honorius

After carefully weighing everything, I conclude: 1. The name of Honorius has been inserted; indeed, the history of Honorius’s condemnation was still unknown to the Venerable Bede. For if that historian had heard anything about the heresy or condemnation of Pope Honorius, he ought first, and at greater length, to have related it where he expressly described the life, character, and merits of Honorius, rather than postponing it until he reached the condemnation of Macarius. [Col. 1076B] 2. I conclude that the letters of Pope Leo II to the Spaniards concerning the condemned Honorius were also unknown to the Venerable Bede, as were the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, the address of the notary Agatho, and the doctrinal letters of John of Constantinople to Pope Constantine. 3. From the Venerable Bede—on the basis of whom Canus, Natalis, and Bertius attempted to prove that Honorius was condemned—it seems to me rather to become clear that Honorius was a holy pope, distinguished for his doctrine, and never condemned or convicted of heresy.

### 112. Honorius is also said to have been condemned at the Eighth Ecumenical Council and by Pope Adrian II

XVII. In the Eighth Ecumenical Synod, the Fourth Council of Constantinople, assembled in 869, [Col. 1076C] its seventh session reads and approves a letter of Pope Adrian II rebuking Photius, who had pronounced a sentence of deposition against Pope Nicholas I, in these words:

“This presumption is intolerable … Who among you has ever heard of such a thing? We read that the Roman pontiff has judged the bishops of all the Churches; but we do not read that anyone has judged him. For although Honorius was anathematized after his death by the Easterners, it must nevertheless be understood that he had been accused of heresy [Note: In such a case, if it were possible, anathema would also have had to be pronounced against Paul or the heavenly angels: ‘Even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you anything other than what we preached to you, let him be accursed’ (Galatians 1:8)]. For that reason alone it is permitted to inferiors to resist the motions of their superiors or freely reject their perverse opinions, although neither there—in a case of heresy or in an ecumenical council—nor among patriarchs or any other prelates would it have been lawful for anyone to pronounce judgment concerning him, that is, concerning the person of the pontiff, [Col. 1076D] unless the authority and consent of that same first see, the Roman See, had preceded it.”

[Col. 1076D] Reply: Adrian II was elevated to the pontificate in 867, and therefore, almost two hundred years after the Sixth Synod, he seems to have been deceived by the acts of the Sixth or [Col. 1077A] Seventh Synod, which at that time had been corrupted. See no. 108. In the meantime, Adrian did not assert that Honorius was a heretic, but only that anathema had been pronounced against him by the Easterners; for he did not suffer anything of the kind from the Westerners. Moreover, the pope’s statement seems hypothetical, and not very different from the following: “Even if the Sixth Synod, as is asserted, condemned Pope Honorius, it could not have done so unless it had previously received from Pope Agatho permission to proceed against Honorius’s person” [Note: If only the entire letter of Adrian II existed elsewhere! Then its true meaning could be determined from the context with greater certainty. Furthermore, the story that Pope Saint Marcellinus offered incense to idols and confessed this fault at the Council of Sinuessa before many—three hundred—bishops was asserted by Pope Saint Nicholas I in his letter to the emperor Michael, and is also read in the Roman Breviary on 26 April; yet [Col. 1078D] it is entirely false, as Natalis, Gravesonius, Pagius, and Papebrochius have acknowledged, and was more probably fabricated by the Donatists, as I have just pointed out in my *Dissertation on Saint Firmilian*, no. 78.].

But the Sixth Synod, as is clear from the letters of Agatho and of the Roman synod, had not received authority to investigate Honorius’s person. Therefore it could not condemn him; and, in my opinion, it did not condemn him.

### 113. The superiority of the pope over a council

Moreover, the passage from the aforesaid [Col. 1077B] Eighth Synod deserves close attention. For according to it:

1. Even an ecumenical synod is not above the pontiff, whether he is living or dead.

2. The following history is related there. In the year 503, Theodoric, king of Italy, wished to prosecute Pope Saint Symmachus on account of several charges, even to the point of condemnation, and ordered bishops from various provinces of Italy and from the island of Sicily to assemble at Rome. But the bishops replied to the king that the pope himself ought to summon the synod. When the synod had been held, no bishop dared to pronounce judgment against the pope; instead, each subscribed: “We have committed the whole case to the judgment of God.”

3. The Third Ecumenical Council, that is, the Council of Ephesus, is cited. It condemned John, patriarch of Antioch, because he had not feared to condemn the patriarch Cyril, the prelate of the prior [Col. 1077C] see [that is, of Alexandria] [Note: The Alexandrian patriarch was formerly first among all the Greeks, first after the Roman patriarch, and always superior to the Antiochene. See Dissertation 15.]. The synod wrote to Pope Saint Celestine as follows:

“Let your holiness therefore be suitably indignant at what has been done. For if permission is granted to those who wish to inflict insults upon the greater sees, and to pronounce sentence against them contrary to the laws and canons in matters over which they have no authority, the affairs of the Church will proceed to utter ruin.”

4. The Eighth Synod applauded Adrian II, confirmed what he had stated, and added that Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria, had therefore been condemned without restoration by the Fourth Synod, or Council of Chalcedon: he had presumed to summon an ecumenical synod against the privilege of the Roman See and to pronounce a sentence of condemnation against Pope Leo I [Col. 1077D].

### 114. From the eighth century onward, all the pope’s successors condemned Honorius in the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman Pontiffs

XVIII. In the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman Pontiffs, formerly in use, there was a profession of faith in which Honorius was anathematized; that book seems to have been composed in the eighth century.

Reply: 1. Let it be so. Nevertheless, it does not in the least follow from this that Honorius was truly a heretic, or that he was truly condemned in the seventh [Col. 1078A] century. See notes 106 and 109. 2. Either that book is considerably later than the eighth century, or that formula of profession was enlarged by some later person. If Anastasius, who will be cited in the following section, had known that Honorius was condemned by the Roman pontiffs themselves, he would not have called the Eastern bishops slanderers. Indeed, according to Widmann, Ivo of Chartres, who flourished at the end of the ninth century, reported another formula of faith, later inserted into Gratian’s *Decree*, in which the name of Honorius does not appear.

### 115. Anastasius admitted in the ninth century that Honorius had been condemned at the Sixth Synod, but considered the condemnation unjust

XIX. Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church in the ninth century, believed in his preface to the deacon John in the collection that Honorius had truly been condemned at the Sixth Synod.

Reply: Anastasius had not suspected [Col. 1078B] that the acts had been falsified, and therefore judged that the bishops who had condemned Honorius had been unjust judges. Several arguments, however, persuade him that Honorius ought not to have been condemned: namely, that the aforementioned pontiff had been sufficiently defended by Pope John IV and by Saint Maximus the monk; that, while he lived, he had never been admonished by anyone concerning error and therefore had not been obstinate; and that it had not been sufficiently proved that Honorius was the author of the letter in question. He says:

“The apology of Pope John IV makes Honorius sufficiently excusable, although the Sixth Synod pronounced an anathema against him as though he were a heretic … But who can tell us whether Honorius certainly dictated the letter from which the slanderers derived the pretext for anathematizing him? That Honorius [Col. 1078C] was not the author of the letter produced at the Sixth Synod, I stated in no. 73.”

## COROLLARIES

### 116. My new position in the case of Honorius

I have now sufficiently discussed the principal arguments on account of which Pope Honorius is said in no. 1 to have been condemned as a heretic, and it seems more probable to me:

1. That Pope Honorius taught no heresy;

2. that he wrote no letter in any way favoring heretics;

3. that in these matters he was sufficiently vindicated by Pope John IV and by Saint Maximus the Greek monk;

4. that the first of the letters of Honorius now extant in the acts of the Sixth Council was corrupted, while the second is fabricated;

5. that the acts of the Sixth Council are, for the greater [Col. 1078D] part, interpolated;

6. that the Fathers at that council could neither justly condemn Honorius nor did they condemn him;

7. that the definition of faith is indeed genuine, but that the edict of the emperor Constantine IV and the answering letter of Pope Leo II to the emperor are suspect;

8. that the five letters of Pope Leo II and one of Benedict II to the Spaniards are likewise suspect;

9. that the Fourteenth Council of Toledo is also suspect;

10. that the epilogue [Col. 1079A] of the deacon Agatho is spurious;

11. that the story of Honorius’s condemnation first gained currency at the beginning of the eighth century, and not earlier;

12. that, although it was reported at the Seventh Ecumenical Council, it did not thereby become true;

13. and that it acquired no additional firmness from the authority [Col. 1080A] of Pope Adrian II and the Eighth Ecumenical Council.

For the rest, let all these matters be submitted to the judgment of the Roman Catholic Church and to the critical judgment of scholars.
